BFD.quote: this document defines Seamless Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (S-BFD), a simplified mechanism for using BFD with a large proportion of negotiation aspects eliminated

rejected.why: MPLS is only one possible data plane for S-BFD packets, and it is defined in a separate document (RFC 7881).
IS-IS is used only as an example for advertising S-BFD discriminators; the document does not specify it.
The document calls S-BFD an OAM mechanism, but BFD is the more specific tag.
OSPF is mentioned only as an example application that may advertise discriminators.

RFC7881.title: Seamless Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (S-BFD) for IPv4, IPv6, and MPLS
RFC7881.summary: Defines the UDP port (7784), echo port usage, demultiplexing, and IP/MPLS header procedures for initiators and reflectors for Seamless BFD in IPv4, IPv6 and MPLS environments.

BFD.why: The whole document specifies Seamless BFD procedures: ports, demultiplexing, and packet field settings for initiator and reflector. S-BFD is a BFD variant, so the BFD tag fits.
BFD.quote: This document defines necessary procedures for using S-BFD in IPv4, IPv6, and MPLS environments.

rejected.why: MPLS label stacks are only the encapsulation for explicitly label-switched S-BFD packets. The document does not specify MPLS itself.
UDP is only the transport. The document allocates a port for S-BFD but says nothing new about UDP.
IPv4 and IPv6 are the environments where the procedures apply. The document does not specify or analyse IPv6.
The port allocation is boilerplate-level IANA content and not the document's subject.

RFC7882.title: Seamless Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (S-BFD) Use Cases
RFC7882.summary: Informational RFC describing use cases and derived requirements for Seamless BFD (S-BFD), a simplified BFD mode that removes discriminator negotiation to speed session establishment and path validation.

BFD.why: The whole document is about S-BFD, a BFD variant. It gives use cases and requirements for BFD session establishment and path monitoring.
BFD.quote: This document describes various use cases for Seamless Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (S-BFD) and provides requirements such that protocol mechanisms allow for simplified detection of forwarding failures.

rejected.why: Segment Routing is one use case (3.4, REQ 4) but the document is about BFD, not SR architecture.
MPLS LSP monitoring is a use case, not the subject of the document.
Per-ECMP-path BFD sessions are one use case (3.9). The document does not address ECMP itself.
Anycast monitoring is one use case (3.6), not the document's subject.
Centralized controllers are mentioned as motivation in 3.3 only.
BFD is the specific tag and already covers this; OAM is only a general framing.

RFC7883.title: Advertising Seamless Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (S-BFD) Discriminators in IS-IS
RFC7883.summary: Defines a new IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV sub-TLV (type 20) for advertising one or more S-BFD discriminators within an area or domain.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS by defining a new sub-TLV for the Router CAPABILITY TLV, including its encoding and flooding scope.
IS-IS.quote: The IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV as defined in [RFC4971] will be used to advertise Seamless BFD (S-BFD) Discriminators.

BFD.why: The payload is Seamless BFD discriminators, so BFD readers would want to find how they are advertised. S-BFD has no separate tag, so BFD is the closest fit.
BFD.quote: A new sub-TLV is defined as described below.  S-BFD Discriminators sub-TLVs are formatted as specified in [RFC5305].

rejected.why: RFC 5305 (IS-IS TE) is cited only for the sub-TLV format, not as a subject of the document.
The Security Considerations section is boilerplate and the document defines no routing security mechanism.

gaps.name: Seamless BFD (S-BFD)
gaps.why: The document is about advertising S-BFD discriminators, but the taxonomy has no S-BFD tag. BFD is used as the nearest fit.

RFC7884.title: OSPF Extensions to Advertise Seamless Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (S-BFD) Target Discriminators
RFC7884.summary: Defines a new OSPF Router Information LSA TLV (S-BFD Discriminator TLV) for flooding S-BFD target discriminators in OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF with a new RI LSA TLV, including flooding scope rules and SPF behaviour.
OSPF.quote: this document defines a new TLV (named the S-BFD Discriminator TLV) to be carried within the OSPF Router Information (RI) Link State Advertisement (LSA)

BFD.why: It carries S-BFD discriminators so that S-BFD initiators can map targets to discriminators; BFD readers would want it.
BFD.quote: S-BFD Discriminators can be advertised by the IGPs, and this document concerns itself with OSPF.

rejected.why: The mechanism applies to both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 equally, so the parent OSPF tag fits better than the OSPFv3 child.
The document only says the IGPs can advertise discriminators; it specifies OSPF only.
The IANA section only registers a TLV codepoint, which is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC7885.title: Seamless Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (S-BFD) for Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification (VCCV)
RFC7885.summary: Defines Seamless BFD (S-BFD) for pseudowire VCCV by adding two new CV Types (IP/UDP and PW-ACH/L2SS encapsulation), reflector/initiator procedures, capability selection, and IANA registrations, updating RFC 5885.

BFD.why: The document specifies S-BFD operation, CV Types, initiator/reflector procedures and encapsulation for VCCV, extending BFD.
BFD.quote: This document defines Seamless BFD (S-BFD) for VCCV by extending the procedures and Connectivity Verification (CV) types already defined for Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD)

pseudowire.why: It extends VCCV, the pseudowire control channel for connectivity verification, over single-segment PWs. Pseudowire readers need the new CV Types and capability selection.
pseudowire.quote: The new S-BFD CV Types are Pseudowire (PW) demultiplexer agnostic and hence are applicable for both MPLS and Layer Two Tunneling Protocol version 3 (L2TPv3) PW demultiplexers.

rejected.why: L2TPv3 is only one of the two PW demultiplexers and signalling options. The document defines no L2TP mechanism itself and refers to RFC 7886 for the AVP.
Advertising discriminators in LDP is explicitly left for further study.
MPLS is the substrate for the PWs. The document only registers CV Types and a G-ACh channel type.
UDP port 7784 is used only as an encapsulation detail.
The OAM subject is covered by the more specific BFD and pseudowire tags.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here and the document is not about IANA stewardship.

RFC7886.title: Advertising Seamless Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (S-BFD) Discriminators in the Layer Two Tunneling Protocol Version 3 (L2TPv3)
RFC7886.summary: Defines a new L2TPv3 AVP (type 102, S-BFD Target Discriminator ID) that lets LCCEs advertise S-BFD reflector discriminators during session negotiation.

BFD.why: The AVP carries S-BFD discriminators so peers can monitor connectivity with S-BFD. S-BFD is a BFD variant and the taxonomy has no separate S-BFD tag, so BFD is the best fit.
BFD.quote: allows L2TP Control Connection Endpoints (LCCEs) to advertise one or more Seamless Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (S-BFD) Discriminator values

L2TP.why: The document extends L2TPv3 with a new control-message AVP exchanged in ICRQ/ICRP/OCRQ/OCRP and registers it with IANA. Readers of L2TP would want it.
L2TP.quote: The S-BFD Target Discriminator ID AVP, Attribute Type 102, is an identifier used to advertise the S-BFD target discriminator(s)

rejected.why: L2TPv3 sessions can carry pseudowires, but the document is about the discriminator AVP and says nothing about pseudowire emulation.
The IANA section only registers AVP type 102. It is boilerplate and the document is not about IANA registries.

gaps.name: S-BFD (Seamless BFD)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no S-BFD tag. The document is specifically about S-BFD discriminators, so BFD is only an approximate fit.

RFC7887.title: Hierarchical Join/Prune Attributes
RFC7887.summary: Defines a hierarchical encoding of PIM Join/Prune attributes (in the Upstream Neighbor and Group Address fields) so shared attributes need only be specified once, adds a Hello Option for support, and renames the PIM address encoding types registry.

PIM.why: The document extends PIM Join/Prune message encoding and defines a new PIM Hello Option. Readers of PIM would expect to find it.
PIM.quote: This document provides a hierarchical way of encoding attributes and their values in a Join/Prune message

rejected.why: RFC 7761 is only the base specification whose Join/Prune message format is extended. This document does not specify or extend sparse-mode behaviour itself, so the generic PIM tag fits better.
It is implied as the parent of PIM, so it is not listed separately.

RFC7888.title: IMAP4 Non-synchronizing Literals
RFC7888.summary: RFC 7888 specifies the IMAP LITERAL+ and LITERAL- extensions, which allow non-synchronizing literals sent from client to server without waiting for a continuation request, and obsoletes RFC 2088.

IMAP.why: The document defines extensions to IMAP, changing literal syntax and capability advertisement, so it belongs on the IMAP page.
IMAP.quote: This document specifies 2 IMAP extensions: LITERAL+ and LITERAL-.

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax; the document is not about it.
Not relevant; the document concerns mail access, not mail transfer.
IMAP is already the more specific tag, so the parent email tag is implied.
BINARY and MULTIAPPEND interactions are mentioned only briefly and do not make the document about MIME.

RFC7889.title: The IMAP APPENDLIMIT Extension
RFC7889.summary: Defines the IMAP APPENDLIMIT extension, which lets an IMAP server advertise maximum message upload sizes (globally via CAPABILITY or per mailbox via STATUS/LIST-STATUS) so clients avoid failing APPENDs.

IMAP.why: The document specifies a new IMAP capability, a new STATUS attribute, and APPEND TOOBIG behaviour, so it is an IMAP extension.
IMAP.quote: This document defines an extension to the IMAP service whereby a server can inform the client about maximum message upload sizes

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax section; the document is not about ABNF.
Implied as the parent of IMAP; the more specific IMAP tag is chosen.
Messages being appended are not specified in MIME terms; not a subject here.
The document does not address message headers or format, only size limits for uploads.

RFC7890.title: Concepts and Terminology for Peer-to-Peer SIP (P2PSIP)
RFC7890.summary: Informational overview defining concepts, terminology, reference model and conceptual operations for Peer-to-Peer SIP (P2PSIP), where SIP registrar/proxy location functions are replaced by a RELOAD-based distributed hash table overlay.

P2PSIP.why: The whole document defines P2PSIP concepts, terminology, reference model and relationship to RELOAD and SIP, so it belongs on the P2PSIP page.
P2PSIP.quote: This document defines concepts and terminology for using the Session Initiation Protocol in a peer-to-peer environment where the traditional proxy-registrar and message-routing functions are replaced by a distributed mechanism.

rejected.why: SIP is the application P2PSIP serves, but the document is about the peer-to-peer overlay, not SIP itself. P2PSIP is the more specific tag.
The document is about P2P overlays, but only as used for SIP. P2PSIP is the specific tag.
NAT issues and ICE get short mentions (Sections 2.6 and 5.3), but they are not a substantial part of the document.
ICE is mentioned only as the mechanism RELOAD uses to set up connections.
TURN appears only in passing, as RELOAD's service discovery example.
mDNS and DNS-SD are named only as alternatives that the working group did not pursue.
The document does define terms, but the glossary is specific to P2PSIP, so the technology tag covers it.

gaps.name: RELOAD / Distributed Hash Table
gaps.why: The document centres on the RELOAD protocol and DHT-based distributed storage. The taxonomy has no tag for RELOAD on its own; P2PSIP is the nearest fit.

RFC7891.title: Explicit Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) Vector
RFC7891.summary: Defines a new PIM Join Attribute type, the Explicit RPF Vector, which encodes a strict hop-by-hop list of PIM neighbors for building multicast trees without unicast route lookup, and specifies mixed-vector, conflict, assert and suppression handling.

PIM.why: The document extends PIM by defining a new Join Attribute TLV and its processing rules (conflicts, asserts, join suppression). PIM is the protocol being extended.
PIM.quote: This document defines a new RPF Vector Attribute type such that an explicit RPF neighbor list can be encoded in the PIM Join Attribute

rejected.why: The document extends PIM Join Attributes (RFC 5384/5496) and only references PIM-SM for security considerations; it does not specify the sparse-mode protocol itself.
SSM is mentioned only as motivation for the Live-Live video model; the document is not about SSM.
Multicast-only fast reroute (RFC 7431) is only an informative reference; the document explicitly avoids PIM repair of broken paths.
OSPF and IS-IS are mentioned only as possible ways to compute the vector list, which is out of scope.
mtrace is mentioned only as a debugging tool; the document is not about it.
A more specific child tag (PIM) applies, so the parent is implied.

RFC7892.title: IANA Allocation Procedures for the GMPLS OTN Signal Type Registry
RFC7892.summary: Updates the IANA registration policy of the GMPLS "OTN Signal Type" subregistry (from RFC 7139) to Standards Action for Standards Track documents and Specification Required for others.

GMPLS.why: The document changes the allocation policy of a GMPLS signaling parameters subregistry for OTN signal types, so GMPLS/OTN control readers would look for it.
GMPLS.quote: IANA maintains "OTN Signal Type" subregistry of the "Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Signaling Parameters" registry

IANA.why: The whole document is a registry policy change, which fits IANA registries and considerations guidance.
IANA.quote: IANA has updated the registration policies for the "OTN Signal Type" subregistry to be "Standards Action" for Standards Track documents

rejected.why: GMPLS signalling is RSVP-TE based, but the document only changes a registry policy and does not specify or extend the signalling.
Only a registry policy is changed; no traffic engineering content.
The Specification Required policy is just an IANA registry rule and does not alter IETF procedures.

gaps.name: OTN (Optical Transport Network, G.709)
gaps.why: The registry covers OTN signal types, but the taxonomy has no OTN tag. GMPLS is the closest fit.

RFC7893.title: Pseudowire Congestion Considerations
RFC7893.summary: Informational RFC analysing whether pseudowires (elastic Ethernet PWs and inelastic TDM PWs) over IP compete acceptably with TCP traffic, concluding no PW-specific congestion control is needed provided unacceptable TDM PWs are shut down.

pseudowire.why: The whole document analyses pseudowire behaviour under congestion, both Ethernet and TDM PWs, so pseudowire readers would want it.
pseudowire.quote: Pseudowires (PWs) have become a common mechanism for tunneling traffic and may be found in unmanaged scenarios competing for network resources

congestion control.why: The document derives TCP-friendliness bounds using the TFRC equation and discusses circuit breakers, which is congestion-control analysis.
congestion control.quote: it is worthwhile specifying under what conditions such competition is acceptable, i.e., the PW traffic does not significantly harm other traffic or contribute more than it should to congestion

rejected.why: TCP is only the comparison baseline for the congestion analysis. The document does not specify or extend it.
The TFRC throughput equation is used as a tool, but the document is not about TFRC itself.
L2TPv3 is mentioned only as one possible PW encapsulation over IP.
MPLS PSNs are explicitly out of scope.
DCCP is mentioned only in passing as a rejected proposal for carrying PWs.
The packet-loss and voice-quality analysis is supporting material, not a measurement methodology.

gaps.name: TDM pseudowires / circuit emulation (SAToP, CESoPSN, TDMoIP)
gaps.why: The document's inelastic-PW analysis is about TDM circuit emulation over packet networks. The taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC7894.title: Alternative Challenge Password Attributes for Enrollment over Secure Transport
RFC7894.summary: Defines three new CSR attributes (otpChallenge, revocationChallenge, estIdentityLinking) to disambiguate the overloaded PKCS #9 challengePassword attribute in EST enrollment requests, with an ASN.1 module.

EST.why: The document extends EST with new CSR attributes and specifies how EST servers and clients indicate and process them.
EST.quote: This document defines a set of new Certificate Signing Request attributes for use with the Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST) protocol.

rejected.why: The otpChallenge attribute only carries a one-time password; generating and verifying it is explicitly out of scope, and HOTP/TOTP are only referenced.
The ASN.1 module is just the formal definition of the attributes, not the subject of the document.
TLS is the secure transport EST runs over; the document defines nothing new about TLS itself, only linking to its identity.
CSR attributes are PKI-related, but the document is about EST and does not profile certificates; EST is the more specific tag.
The parent of EST, so it is implied by the EST tag.
The document uses the S/MIME attribute OID arc and CMC-derived modules, but defines nothing about CMS.

RFC7895.title: YANG Module Library
RFC7895.summary: Defines the ietf-yang-library YANG module, letting a NETCONF or other YANG-based server report which YANG modules, submodules, features and deviations it uses, with a module-set-id for client caching and a change notification.

YANG.why: The document specifies a YANG module describing the YANG modules, submodules, features and deviations a server implements. Readers of the YANG subject would want it.
YANG.quote: The "ietf-yang-library" module provides information about the YANG library used by a server.

NETCONF.why: The module is aimed at NETCONF servers. It ties module-set-id changes to the NETCONF capability and to netconf-capability-change notifications, and it was produced by the NETCONF WG.
NETCONF.quote: a change of the "module-set-id" value results in a new value for the :yang-library capability

rejected.why: The document defines a YANG module, not an SNMP MIB module.
SSH is only the mandatory NETCONF transport, mentioned in Security Considerations.
XML namespaces are used only for module identification and IANA registration. The document is not about XML.
The IANA section only registers the module and its URI, which is boilerplate.

RFC7896.title: Update to the Include Route Object (IRO) Specification in the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP)
RFC7896.summary: RFC 7896 updates RFC 5440 to specify that the PCEP Include Route Object (IRO) is an ordered list of subobjects and to define the meaning of the subobject L bit as loose/strict hop, following RSVP-TE semantics.

PCE.why: The document specifies a change to PCEP's IRO object (RFC 5440 Section 7.12), so it belongs under PCE architecture and PCEP.
PCE.quote: The content of an IRO is an ordered list of subobjects representing a series of abstract nodes

rejected.why: Only referenced for the definition of abstract nodes and L bit interpretation; the document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE.
PCEP merely runs over TCP; mentioned only in Security Considerations.
Parent of PCE; the PCE tag is more specific and implied.

RFC7897.title: Domain Subobjects for the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP)
RFC7897.summary: Experimental RFC defining PCEP IRO/XRO/EXRS/ERO subobjects (4-byte AS number, OSPF area ID, IS-IS area ID) to encode a domain sequence for inter-domain path computation by PCEs.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP with new domain subobjects in IRO, XRO, EXRS and ERO, and specifies PCC/PCE procedures for using them.
PCE.quote: This document specifies a representation and encoding of a domain sequence, which is defined as an ordered sequence of domains traversed to reach the destination domain

RSVP-TE.why: The subobject types are identical to those in RSVP-TE, and the document discusses its relationship to RSVP-TE abstract nodes. The main specification is PCEP, so this is secondary.
RSVP-TE.quote: This is a companion document to Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) extensions for the domain identifiers [RFC7898].

rejected.why: 4-byte AS numbers per RFC 6793 are only referenced for encoding; the document does not specify or extend BGP.
OSPF area IDs are only carried as identifiers in PCEP subobjects; OSPF itself is not specified or changed.
IS-IS area IDs are only carried as identifiers in PCEP subobjects; IS-IS itself is not specified or changed.
The document mentions (G)MPLS TE LSPs as context, but it does not extend GMPLS.
The subject is covered by the more specific PCE and RSVP-TE tags.

RFC7898.title: Domain Subobjects for Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE)
RFC7898.summary: Defines new RSVP-TE ERO, XRO and EXRS subobjects for 4-byte AS numbers and OSPF/IS-IS area IDs so inter-domain TE LSP paths can include or exclude domains; an experimental companion to the PCEP domain subobjects in RFC 7897.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE signalling by defining new ERO, XRO and EXRS subobjects for domains, including their encoding and processing rules.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document specifies new subobjects to include or exclude Autonomous Systems (ASes), which are identified by a 4-byte AS number, and Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) areas during path setup.

rejected.why: PCEP is only a companion. RFC 7897 covers the PCEP subobjects, and this document just notes that the subobjects are interchangeable (Section 4).
GMPLS RSVP-TE extensions (RFC 3473) are background. The document does not extend GMPLS in any GMPLS-specific way.
Four-byte AS numbers come from RFC 6793, but this document only reuses the AS number format. It says nothing about BGP.
OSPF and IS-IS area IDs are only carried as identifiers in the subobjects. The document does not specify the IGPs.
The RSVP-TE tag already sits under traffic engineering, so I did not add the parent topic.
The IS-IS area ID format is referenced for encoding only. The routing protocol itself is not the subject.

RFC7899.title: Multicast VPN State Damping
RFC7899.summary: Specifies exponential-decay damping procedures for multicast VPN C-multicast routing state, Leaf A-D routes and P-tunnel state so that multicast churn in customer sites does not overload the provider's BGP/PIM control plane; updates RFC 6514.

MVPN.why: The whole document defines damping of C-multicast routes, Leaf A-D routes and P-tunnel state in BGP/MPLS multicast VPNs, and updates RFC 6514.
MVPN.quote: This document describes procedures to damp Multicast VPN (MVPN) routing state changes and control the effect of the churn due to the multicast dynamicity in customer sites.

PIM-SM.why: Section 5.1 specifies damping behaviour modifications to the PIM-SM upstream state machine for (S,G) and (*,G) states, a substantial part of the document.
PIM-SM.quote: This section describes procedures for (S,G) states in the PIM-SM protocol [RFC7761]

rejected.why: BGP route damping principles are adapted and BGP carries C-multicast routes, but the document is about multicast state damping in MVPN, not BGP itself.
VPLS multicast (RFC 7117) is covered by one short subsection (6.2) applying the P-tunnel procedures; not a main subject.
IGMP and MLD are only the membership protocols that trigger state changes; the document does not specify them.
Route reflectors are mentioned as places where damping may be applied, but the document is not about route reflection.
Section 6.2 title says Ethernet VPNs but the content refers to VPLS multicast (RFC 7117), not EVPN.

RFC7900.title: Extranet Multicast in BGP/IP MPLS VPNs
RFC7900.summary: RFC 7900 specifies procedures, route-target provisioning, new BGP extended communities and P-tunnel selection rules for providing extranet multicast between BGP/MPLS IP VPNs, updating RFCs 6513, 6514 and 6625.

MVPN.why: The whole document defines extranet service for Multicast VPN, updating the MVPN RFCs 6513/6514/6625 with new A-D route, RT and expected P-tunnel procedures.
MVPN.quote: it is sometimes desirable to allow multicast traffic whose source is in one VPN to be received by systems that are in another VPN.

rejected.why: Defines two new opaque extended communities (Extranet Source and Extranet Separation), but they are a small part of an MVPN procedures document.
PIM-SM is the customer protocol and a PE-PE option, but the document does not specify or extend PIM itself.
BGP/MPLS VPN (RFC 4364) is the substrate. The document is about the multicast extension, which is covered by MVPN.
BGP A-D routes and extended communities are used, but the document is not about BGP protocol behaviour in general.
RSVP-TE P2MP tunnels are mentioned only as one possible P-tunnel type.
The parent topic is implied by the MVPN tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC7901.title: CHAIN Query Requests in DNS
RFC7901.summary: Defines an experimental EDNS0 option (CHAIN) letting a validating forwarding resolver request a full DNSSEC validation chain in one query to an upstream recursive resolver, over source-IP-verified transport to avoid amplification.

EDNS.why: The document defines a new EDNS0 option (code 13, CHAIN), its format, and its processing rules.
EDNS.quote: This document specifies an EDNS0 extension that allows a validating resolver running as a forwarding resolver to open a TCP connection to another resolver

DNSSEC.why: The option exists to return the DNSSEC validation chain (DS, DNSKEY, NSEC/NSEC3, RRSIGs). It also covers negative trust anchors and DO/CD bit handling.
DNSSEC.quote: request all intermediate DNS data it requires to resolve and validate a particular DNS answer in a single round trip

rejected.why: TCP is only the source-IP-verified transport and keepalive substrate; nothing new is defined about TCP.
Privacy is discussed only briefly in Security Considerations, with a pointer to DoT; the document is not about encrypted DNS transport.
RFC 7858 is only mentioned as an optional privacy transport.
A short section on anycast considerations does not make the document about anycast operation.
The amplification-attack mitigation is a design constraint of the option, not the document's subject.

RFC7902.title: Registry and Extensions for P-Multicast Service Interface Tunnel Attribute Flags
RFC7902.summary: Creates an IANA registry for the PMSI Tunnel attribute Flags bits from RFC 6514 and defines a new "Extension" flag plus an "Additional PMSI Tunnel Attribute Flags" BGP Extended Community to carry more flags for MVPN.

MVPN.why: The document extends the MVPN BGP PMSI Tunnel attribute, updating RFC 6514, with a new flag and Extended Community and the procedures for handling them.
MVPN.quote: The BGP-based control procedures for Multicast Virtual Private Networks (MVPNs) make use of a BGP attribute known as the "P-Multicast Service Interface (PMSI) Tunnel" attribute.

rejected.why: BGP is the substrate. The document is specifically about the MVPN PMSI Tunnel attribute, which sits under MVPN, not about BGP in general.
It creates registries, but that is boilerplate-like and subordinate to the MVPN attribute extension. The registry is about MVPN flags, not IANA guidance.
It defines a new Extended Community, but only as a carrier for flags. It does not address BGP communities as a subject in general.
MVPN is the more specific tag.

RFC7903.title: Windows Image Media Types
RFC7903.summary: Registers the media types image/wmf, image/x-wmf, image/emf, image/x-emf and image/bmp for Windows Metafile, Enhanced Metafile and Windows Bitmap image formats, with security and interoperability notes.

media types.why: The whole document consists of media type registration templates for image/wmf, image/emf and image/bmp, plus deprecated x- aliases.
media types.quote: This document registers media types for certain image formats promulgated in Microsoft Windows, namely image/wmf, image/x-wmf, image/emf, image/x-emf, and image/bmp

rejected.why: The wmf DEFAULT_CHARSET parameter refers to the IANA Character Sets registry, but this is a minor parameter detail, not a subject of the document.
The IANA Considerations section only records the registrations, which is boilerplate.
Media types is the more specific child tag and fits; the document does not address MIME body structure or encodings generally.
Browsers and favicon.ico are mentioned only as use cases for the formats, not as web subject matter.

gaps.name: Image file formats (WMF, EMF, BMP raster/vector graphics)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for image or graphics formats, so the formats themselves have no subject home beyond their media type registrations.

RFC7904.title: A SIP Usage for REsource LOcation And Discovery (RELOAD)
RFC7904.summary: Defines a SIP Usage for RELOAD that lets SIP user agents register AORs in a P2P overlay, look them up, use GRUUs, and form direct SIP connections via AppAttach, replacing proxy/registrar servers.

P2PSIP.why: The document is a RELOAD Usage for SIP, defining the SIP-REGISTRATION Kind, AOR lookup and direct connection setup in a P2PSIP overlay.
P2PSIP.quote: This document defines a SIP Usage of RELOAD that allows SIP [RFC3261] user agents (UAs) to establish peer-to-peer SIP (or SIPS) sessions

SIP.why: It specifies how SIP registration, rendezvous, GRUUs and contact preferences work in a distributed overlay, which is of interest to SIP readers.
SIP.quote: The SIP Usage provides the functionality of a SIP proxy or registrar in a fully distributed system

rejected.why: ICE is only used implicitly by AppAttach for connectivity checks; the document defines nothing new about it.
DNS lookup is mentioned only as a fallback for finding alternative overlays; not a subject.
Only mentioned as a possible future extension.
(D)TLS is just the secured transport used by RELOAD links.
Certificates are used for access control matching but the document does not profile them.
The overlay configuration extension uses XML but the document is not about XML itself.

gaps.name: RELOAD (REsource LOcation And Discovery)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has P2PSIP (which includes RELOAD) but the document is mainly about a RELOAD Usage; P2PSIP covers it adequately, though a dedicated RELOAD tag would be more precise.

RFC7905.title: ChaCha20-Poly1305 Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC7905.summary: Defines seven ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD cipher suites for TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2, including nonce construction from the record sequence number, as a replacement for RC4 and CBC suites.

ChaCha20.why: The document specifies how ChaCha20 and Poly1305 are used as an AEAD in TLS cipher suites, including the nonce construction. Readers of the ChaCha20 subject would want it.
ChaCha20.quote: This document describes the use of the ChaCha stream cipher and Poly1305 authenticator in version 1.2 or later of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol

TLS.why: It defines new TLS cipher suites and updates RFC 5246. It is a TLS extension of cipher-suite coverage.
TLS.quote: The following cipher suites are defined:

DTLS.why: The suites apply equally to DTLS 1.2. The document updates RFC 6347 and gives DTLS-specific nonce details.
DTLS.quote: In DTLS, the 64-bit seq_num is the 16-bit epoch concatenated with the 48-bit sequence_number.

rejected.why: RC4 is mentioned only as motivation for replacement. The document is not about RC4 or its deprecation.
AES-GCM is mentioned only for comparison of nonce construction and performance.
RSA appears only in the names of key exchange suites that are unchanged.
ECDSA appears only in a suite name and its use is unchanged.
SHA-256 is used only as the PRF hash and is not the subject.
The IANA section is boilerplate registering the cipher suites.

RFC7906.title: NSA's Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Key Management Attributes
RFC7906.summary: Defines NSA key management attributes (key purpose, use, validity, TSEC nomenclature, classification, etc.) carried in CMS content types and asymmetric/symmetric key packages, with an ASN.1 module.

CMS.why: The document defines new CMS attributes, specifies where they may appear in CMS content types, and updates CMS attribute information object sets.
CMS.quote: The attributes can appear in asymmetric and/or symmetric key packages as well as the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) content types that subsequently envelope the key packages.

key management.why: The attributes describe key packages: key purpose, use, distribution and validity periods, wrap algorithm, split keys, and receivers.
key management.quote: This document defines key management attributes used by the National Security Agency (NSA).

security labels.why: A substantial section defines the classification attribute and security label conventions: policy identifiers, the classification hierarchy, and security categories.
security labels.quote: The classification attribute makes use of the ESSSecurityLabel defined in Section 17.1

rejected.why: ASN.1 is the notation used to define the attributes, not the subject of the document.
The document carries X.509 certificates in attributes and uses certificate syntax, but does not define or profile X.509.
The certificate and PKI path attributes are minor parts. The document is not about PKI.

RFC7908.title: Problem Definition and Classification of BGP Route Leaks
RFC7908.summary: RFC 7908 gives a working definition of BGP route leaks and a six-type taxonomy of observed leak incidents, as a problem definition for developing detection and mitigation solutions.

BGP.why: The whole document defines and classifies route leaks, a BGP policy and operations problem, with examples of leaked BGP announcements between ASes.
BGP.quote: A route leak is the propagation of routing announcement(s) beyond their intended scope.

routing security.why: Route leaks are framed as a systemic vulnerability that disrupts routing and enables traffic eavesdropping, and the document is the problem definition for developing detection and mitigation solutions. It describes the problem but specifies no RPKI or BGPsec mechanism.
routing security.quote: A systemic vulnerability of the Border Gateway Protocol routing system, known as "route leaks", has received significant attention in recent years.

rejected.why: Route origin validation is not discussed. The document only mentions mis-origination as Type 5 and proposes no validation mechanism.
No path validation mechanism is described. The document is a problem definition only.
The document does not address routing design principles or scalability, only the classification of policy-violating announcements.
Route leaks are an operational problem, but the document gives no operator practices or guidance, only a taxonomy.

RFC7909.title: Securing Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL) Objects with Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Signatures
RFC7909.summary: Defines a "signature" attribute for RPSL objects, using RPKI resource certificates, with canonicalization, creation and validation rules and per-object-type signed attribute sets.

RPSL.why: The document extends RPSL and RPSLng by adding a signature attribute and defining which attributes of each RPSL object type must be signed.
RPSL.quote: This document updates RFCs 2622 and 4012 to add the signature attribute to supported RPSL objects.

RPKI.why: Signatures are made with RPKI resource certificates, and the signer must hold resources covered by RFC 3779 extensions. The document defines how the RPKI is used to authenticate registry objects.
RPKI.quote: A potential use for resource certificates [RFC6487] is to use them to secure such (both imported and downloaded) database objects

rejected.why: DKIM's canonicalization approach is only borrowed as a model. The document does not specify or use DKIM itself.
It relies on the RFC 6487 resource certificate profile and RFC 3779 extensions but defines no new certificate profile. The RPKI tag covers this.
CIDR notation is only a canonical prefix format in the canonicalization rules.
RFC 3339 timestamps are used as field formats, not defined or extended here.
Base64 is only the encoding of the signature value.
The RPKI tag is more specific and already covers this.

RFC7910.title: Interoperability between the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol and PIM
RFC7910.summary: Informational document describing VRRP-aware PIM, a Cisco IOS mechanism in which PIM tracks VRRP state to adjust DR priority, Assert and BiDir DF metrics so multicast forwarding follows the VRRP master across failover.

VRRP.why: The document specifies how PIM interoperates with VRRP, tracking VRRP master/passive state. Readers of VRRP would want it.
VRRP.quote: VRRP-aware PIM, a redundancy mechanism for the Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) to interoperate with the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP)

PIM.why: The mechanism modifies PIM behaviour: DR election priority, Hello with GenID, Assert metric and BiDir DF election metric. It is a PIM extension and not specific to PIM-SM, so the parent PIM tag fits.
PIM.quote: PIM is responsible for adjusting the DR priority based on the group state.

rejected.why: RFC 7761 is only referenced. The document covers PIM generally, including BiDir DF election, and does not extend the sparse-mode specification.
HSRP gets only a brief note in Section 6, saying the scheme could also apply to it. It is not a substantial part of the document.
The parent topic is implied by the PIM tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC7911.title: Advertisement of Multiple Paths in BGP
RFC7911.summary: Defines the BGP ADD-PATH extension: a four-octet Path Identifier prepended to NLRI and an ADD-PATH capability (code 69) so a speaker can advertise multiple paths per prefix without implicit replacement.

BGP.why: The RFC extends BGP with a Path Identifier, extended NLRI encoding, a new capability and revised update procedures. It is a BGP protocol extension, so it belongs under BGP.
BGP.quote: This document defines a BGP extension that allows the advertisement of multiple paths for the same address prefix without the new paths implicitly replacing any previous ones.

rejected.why: The ADD-PATH extension is commonly used with route reflectors, but this document never discusses route reflection or confederations. It only mentions iBGP deployment in passing.
The document defines a protocol extension. It does not address routing architecture or design principles, although it mentions route oscillation and convergence as motivation.
The only IANA content is the boilerplate registration of Capability Code 69, which is not evidence that the document is about IANA.
No communities are involved. The extension concerns Path Identifiers and NLRI encoding.

RFC7912.title: Message Authorizing Email Header Field and Its Use for the Draft and Release Procedure
RFC7912.summary: Informational RFC defining the MMHS-Authorizing-Users email header field and a draft-and-release procedure in which authorizing users review and countersign (S/MIME or DKIM) military messages before release, plus an updated MIXER mapping to X.400.

message format.why: The document defines a new Internet message header field with ABNF syntax based on RFC 5322 mailbox-list, and the procedure for its use.
message format.quote: The MMHS-Authorizing-Users header field specified in this document MUST NOT appear more than once in message headers.

S/MIME.why: A substantial part of the document specifies how authorizing users countersign messages with S/MIME review signatures, including multiple signatures and triple wrapping.
S/MIME.quote: the Authorizing User ... allowing the addition of the S/MIME review signature

X.400.why: The document updates the mapping between RFC 5322/MIME and X.400 (IPMS.Heading.authorizing-users) for military message handling.
X.400.quote: This section provides an updated version of the MIXER mapping specified in [RFC2156] for MMHS applications.

rejected.why: DKIM is only mentioned as an alternative way to protect the header field and verify origination, not specified or extended here.
Message submission over SMTP/MSA is the substrate; the document defines no SMTP extension.
Parent of the chosen message format and X.400 tags; the document is about a specific header field rather than email in general.
ABNF is used only as notation for the header syntax.
Multiple signatures in CMS is referenced only via S/MIME; the document is not about CMS itself.
The registration of the header field is boilerplate-level IANA considerations.

gaps.name: Military Message Handling System (MMHS)
gaps.why: The document is specifically about MMHS (STANAG 4406 / ACP 123) release authorization; the taxonomy has no tag for military messaging.

RFC7913.title: P-Access-Network-Info ABNF Update
RFC7913.summary: Updates RFC 7315 by changing the ABNF of the SIP P-Access-Network-Info header field so extension-access-info uses generic-param and by adding the operator-specific-GI and utran-sai-3gpp values to the access-info list.

SIP.why: The document corrects the syntax of a SIP header field (P-Access-Network-Info), so it is a SIP extension and its readers would look for it under SIP.
SIP.quote: [RFC7315] defines the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) [RFC3261] P-Access-Network-Info header field.

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used to express the syntax change. The document is not about the ABNF notation itself.
The header field is mainly used in 3GPP networks, but the document only fixes ABNF syntax. It does not address cellular networks.
The document makes no registry changes.

RFC7914.title: The scrypt Password-Based Key Derivation Function
RFC7914.summary: RFC 7914 specifies the scrypt memory-hard password-based key derivation function, its parameters, algorithm steps, an ASN.1 schema/OID for use in PKCS#5/PKCS#8, and test vectors.

scrypt.why: The entire document specifies scrypt, its parameters, algorithm (BlockMix, ROMix), and test vectors.
scrypt.quote: This document specifies the password-based key derivation function scrypt.

ASN.1.why: The document defines an ASN.1 module with id-scrypt OID and scrypt-params for use in AlgorithmIdentifier and PBES2-KDFs, which is a substantial part of the document.
ASN.1.quote: This section defines ASN.1 syntax for the scrypt key derivation function (KDF).

rejected.why: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 is used as a building block inside scrypt, and test vectors are given only to verify it; the document is not about PBKDF2 itself.
Parent of scrypt, so it is implied and not listed separately.
HMAC-SHA-256 is only the PRF used inside PBKDF2 here.
SHA-256 is used only via HMAC as a substrate.
PKCS#8 encrypted private key syntax is only an intended application and test vector, not the subject.
The document is about a password-based KDF, which falls under password hashing rather than key establishment or provisioning.

RFC7915.title: IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm
RFC7915.summary: Specifies SIIT, the stateless algorithm for translating IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers and ICMP/ICMPv6 messages, obsoleting RFC 6145.

SIIT.why: The document is the SIIT specification itself, defining header and ICMP translation rules in both directions.
SIIT.quote: This document describes the Stateless IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm (SIIT), which translates between IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers (including ICMP headers).

ICMP.why: A large share of the document defines translation of ICMPv4/ICMPv6 types, codes, pointers and error payloads, which ICMP readers would want.
ICMP.quote: All ICMPv4 messages that are to be translated require that the ICMPv6 checksum field be calculated as part of the translation

PMTUD.why: The document gives substantial treatment to how PMTUD and fragmentation work across the translator, including MTU adjustment rules and Section 7 on Packet Too Big.
PMTUD.quote: Path MTU discovery is mandatory in IPv6, but it is optional in IPv4. IPv6 routers never fragment a packet -- only the sender can do fragmentation.

rejected.why: Stateful NAT64 is only referenced (RFC 6146); this document specifies the stateless translation algorithm.
IPv6 is one side of the translation, but the document is about the translation algorithm, which SIIT covers more specifically.
IPv4 is the other side of the translation; SIIT is the more specific tag.
MAP-T is mentioned only as an example user of stateless translation.
Checksum updates are part of translation but are not the document's subject.
IPsec appears only in the Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.

RFC7916.title: Operational Management of Loop-Free Alternates
RFC7916.summary: RFC 7916 gives operational feedback on IP Fast Reroute Loop-Free Alternates (RFC 5286, and remote LFA), and specifies policy-based alternate selection, activation granularity, and management/monitoring requirements.

IP fast reroute.why: The whole document concerns LFA operations, limitations of tiebreakers, policy-based selection and manageability of LFA/remote-LFA fast reroute.
IP fast reroute.quote: Loop-Free Alternates (LFAs), as defined in RFC 5286, constitute an IP Fast Reroute (IP FRR) mechanism enabling traffic protection for IP traffic

rejected.why: OSPF and IS-IS are only the IGPs used to compute and signal LFAs (overload bit, R-bit, tags); the document does not extend them.
Referenced for the overload bit and link/node tags only; document is about LFA, not IS-IS.
LDP/MPLS traffic protection is mentioned as an extension; not the subject.
Segment Routing is mentioned as a possible tunnel type for remote alternates only.
Syslog/SNMP traps are suggested only in passing for alerts, explicitly out of scope.
Management requirements are for LFA specifically, already covered by the IP fast reroute tag.

RFC7917.title: Advertising Node Administrative Tags in IS-IS
RFC7917.summary: Defines a new Node-Admin-Tag sub-TLV in the IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV to advertise 32-bit administrative tags that group nodes for locally defined policy.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with a new sub-TLV (type 21) in the Router CAPABILITY TLV, specifying format, flooding scope and procedures.
IS-IS.quote: This document describes an extension to the IS-IS routing protocol to advertise node administrative tags.

rejected.why: LFA policy is only an example use case; the document does not specify fast reroute.
Mentioned only in Manageability Considerations as future model work.
Only referenced as an operational analogy.
TE is mentioned only as one possible application of the tags.

RFC7918.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) False Start
RFC7918.summary: RFC 7918 specifies TLS False Start, an optional client-side behavior letting a TLS 1.2 client send application data before receiving the server's Finished message, with security conditions on cipher, version and key exchange.

TLS.why: The document specifies a modification to TLS client handshake behavior and its security restrictions, so TLS readers need it.
TLS.quote: the client can start to send application data when the full handshake is only partially complete

rejected.why: HTTP is only an example of an application protocol where the client sends data first.
TCP and TCP Fast Open are mentioned only as a note about a separate latency source.
AES-GCM suites are cited as examples of strong ciphers in the whitelist guidance, but the document is not about AES.
The document covers only TLS 1.2 and earlier over stream transport, not DTLS.
ECDHE and named curves appear only in the whitelist recommendations for key exchange.

RFC7919.title: Negotiated Finite Field Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral Parameters for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC7919.summary: RFC 7919 defines named finite-field Diffie-Hellman groups (ffdhe2048 to ffdhe8192) for TLS, reuses the supported_groups extension to negotiate them, and specifies client and server behaviour.

TLS.why: The document extends and updates TLS 1.0-1.2 with a negotiation mechanism for DHE groups via the supported_groups extension, with client and server behaviour rules.
TLS.quote: This document offers a solution to these shortcomings for compatible peers by using a section of the TLS "Supported Groups Registry"

cryptography.why: Defines specific safe-prime DH group parameters, strengths, short-exponent guidance and public key validation, which is cryptographic parameter content. No narrower DH tag exists in the taxonomy.
cryptography.quote: They are all safe primes derived from the base of the natural logarithm ("e"), with the high and low 64 bits set to 1

rejected.why: ECDHE is explicitly out of scope; the document only reuses the elliptic curve registry and extension for finite field groups.
IKE groups are mentioned only as a reason not to reuse them (Section 8.5).
The registry rename and codepoint allocation are boilerplate-like IANA actions supporting the TLS mechanism.
DTLS appears only as a DTLS-OK column in the registry table.
Mentioned only as a comparison for short exponents.

gaps.name: Finite field Diffie-Hellman (FFDHE) groups
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for Diffie-Hellman key exchange or DH group parameters, which is the core subject here.

RFC7920.title: Problem Statement for the Interface to the Routing System
RFC7920.summary: Problem statement motivating the Interface to the Routing System (I2RS): a data-model-driven, programmatic interface for applications to read and write routing system state, with the key protocol aspects required.

I2RS.why: The whole document defines the problem area, model, and required protocol aspects of I2RS.
I2RS.quote: This document proposes meeting this need via an Interface to the Routing System (I2RS).

rejected.why: Discussed only in Appendix A as an existing interface that may need extensions; not the subject.
Appendix A explains why SNMP is not a candidate solution; background only.
Mentioned once as prior work on forwarding plane models.
Mentioned as a possible delivery mechanism for measurement data only.
BGP-LS is cited as an example of existing topology export; not about BGP.
Related in spirit (programmable routing control), but I2RS is the more specific tag and no SDN framing is made in the text.

RFC7921.title: An Architecture for the Interface to the Routing System
RFC7921.summary: RFC 7921 describes the IETF architecture for the Interface to the Routing System (I2RS): clients, agents, routing elements, ephemeral state, security model, and the client-agent interface for programmatic state transfer in and out of the routing system.

I2RS.why: The whole document specifies the I2RS architecture: agent, client, services, ephemeral state, multi-headed control and notifications.
I2RS.quote: This document describes the IETF architecture for a standard, programmatic interface for state transfer in and out of the Internet routing system.

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are protocols to be reused and extended for I2RS, but the document is not specifying them.
YANG is the assumed data modelling language, but the document does not define YANG models or the language.
BGP, OSPF and IS-IS are mentioned as routing components exposed by I2RS services, not the subject of the document.
The I2RS tag is more specific than a generic routing architecture topic.
I2RS is a programmatic control interface, but the document does not frame itself as SDN.
Authentication and authorization are discussed only in the I2RS security context, not as an AAA framework.

gaps.name: I2RS (Interface to the Routing System)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists I2RS under network management, but I could not confirm that placement. If it is a valid tag it fits exactly. Otherwise the document has no dedicated tag.

RFC7922.title: Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) Traceability: Framework and Information Model
RFC7922.summary: Informational RFC defining a traceability framework and information model of trace log fields for recording interactions between I2RS clients and agents, with operational guidance on log storage, rotation and retrieval.

I2RS.why: The whole document specifies an I2RS-specific trace log framework and information model for recording client-agent interactions.
I2RS.quote: This document describes a framework for traceability in the Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) and the information model for that framework.

syslog.why: One of the retrieval methods maps the trace log fields onto syslog structured data, so syslog readers would find this relevant.
syslog.quote: the various fields described in Section 5.2 SHOULD be modeled and encoded as Structured Data Elements (referred to as "SD-ELEMENT")

rejected.why: Subscription to YANG datastores is only referenced via RFC 7923 for pub/sub retrieval; the document defines no YANG model.
RFC 3339 timestamps are used for the log fields but the document does not define or extend the format.
NACM is mentioned only as an example source of client priority.
Auditing and forensics are use cases, but the document is about a trace logging model, not security practices.
The parent topic is implied by the I2RS tag, which already sits under it.

RFC7923.title: Requirements for Subscription to YANG Datastores
RFC7923.summary: Informational requirements document for a publish/subscribe service that lets clients subscribe to pushed updates of YANG datastores, covering negotiation, filtering, periodicity, QoS, security and monitoring.

YANG.why: The whole document defines requirements for subscribing to YANG datastore content: subtrees, operational and configuration datastores, and filters on YANG nodes.
YANG.quote: This document provides requirements for a service that allows client applications to subscribe to updates of a YANG datastore.

NETCONF.why: The service fills a gap in NETCONF/RESTCONF, and NETCONF is the initially supported transport. The NETCONF Authorization Control Model is also referenced. Readers of NETCONF would want this document.
NETCONF.quote: fills a functional gap in existing YANG transports (i.e., Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) and RESTCONF)

telemetry.why: It specifies streaming operational data from network elements as pushed updates instead of polling. This is the telemetry subject.
telemetry.quote: What is needed is a push mechanism that is able to deliver object changes as they happen.

rejected.why: I2RS requirements motivate the work, but the document covers general YANG datastore subscription and is not about the routing system interface.
RESTCONF is named only as one of the existing transports the service must work over. The document does not specify it.
SNMP is mentioned only as a polling-based comparison point.
XMPP pub/sub (XEP-0060) is only a precedent whose requirements were adapted.
TLS appears only through the RFC 7589 reference as one way to secure NETCONF.

gaps.name: publish/subscribe
gaps.why: The document is about a generic pub/sub service for datastore updates. The taxonomy has no pub/sub tag.

RFC7924.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Cached Information Extension
RFC7924.summary: Defines the TLS cached_info extension, letting a client tell a server it has cached the server Certificate or CertificateRequest message (by SHA-256 fingerprint) so the server can omit them from the handshake.

TLS.why: The document specifies a new TLS extension (cached_info), including its handshake message modifications and a new IANA registry, so it is squarely about TLS extensions.
TLS.quote: This document defines an extension that allows a TLS client to inform a server of cached information, thereby enabling the server to omit already available information.

rejected.why: The text says it applies equally to DTLS, but it is only a passing note. The document is written for TLS.
Certificates are the cached objects, but the document does not profile or define anything about X.509. The appendix only shows an example certificate.
SHA-256 is only used as the fingerprint hash. The document does not define or analyse it.
Constrained IoT networks are the motivation in the introduction, but the document is a general TLS extension and not IoT guidance.
The new registry and the ExtensionType entry are boilerplate-level IANA actions. They are not the subject of the document.

RFC7925.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) / Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) Profiles for the Internet of Things
RFC7925.summary: Defines a TLS 1.2/DTLS 1.2 profile for constrained IoT devices, specifying credential types, ciphersuites, extensions, timeouts and other configuration choices, plus an appendix on carrying DTLS over SMS.

TLS.why: The whole document profiles TLS 1.2 for IoT: ciphersuites, extensions, credentials, error handling, and resumption.
TLS.quote: This document defines a Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) 1.2 profile that offers communications security for this data exchange

DTLS.why: DTLS is a co-equal subject of the profile, with DTLS-specific guidance on timeouts, fragmentation, cookie exchange and record overhead.
DTLS.quote: the main goal for this document is to protect CoAP messages using DTLS 1.2 [RFC6347]

6LoWPAN.why: Not tagged as primary: only a brief mention for avoiding nonce duplication; considered but weak.
6LoWPAN.quote: RFC 7400 [RFC7400] provides help with the use of the generic header compression technique for IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LoWPANs)

SMS.why: A normative appendix specifies conveying DTLS over SMS, including PMTU, segmentation, multiplexing and timeouts.
SMS.quote: This section is normative for the use of DTLS over SMS.

IoT.why: The profile targets constrained IoT devices and their deployment models, so IoT guidance readers would look here.
IoT.quote: A common design pattern in Internet of Things (IoT) deployments is the use of a constrained device that collects data via sensors

rejected.why: CoAP is the main motivating application and used in examples, but the document specifies TLS/DTLS configuration, not CoAP.
EAP-TLS appears as an example use of the guidance, not something the document specifies.
AES-CCM ciphersuites are recommended, but the document does not define the cipher; it only selects ciphersuites.
Section 4.4 profiles certificate content, but as part of the TLS profile; X.509 itself is not the subject.
Only a passing mention of RFC 7400 header compression in an appendix; the document is not about 6LoWPAN.

RFC7926.title: Problem Statement and Architecture for Information Exchange between Interconnected Traffic-Engineered Networks
RFC7926.summary: BCP defining the problem statement and an abstraction-layer-network architecture for exchanging TE reachability information between interconnected MPLS-TE/GMPLS domains, with applications to optical networks, the UNI and multi-AS L3VPNs.

traffic engineering.why: The whole document concerns TE information, TE reachability and end-to-end TE path computation across domains; no more specific tech tag covers the architecture itself.
traffic engineering.quote: This document sets out the problem statement for the exchange of TE information between interconnected TE networks in support of end-to-end TE path establishment

GMPLS.why: GMPLS control planes, UNI, optical domains and switching capabilities are central to the use cases and applications (Sections 6, 7).
GMPLS.quote: Traffic-Engineered (TE) systems such as MPLS-TE [RFC2702] and GMPLS [RFC3945] offer a way to establish paths through a network

PCE.why: PCE, BRPC and hierarchical PCE are discussed as existing work and used in the architecture's path computation; a meaningful but not primary part.
PCE.quote: The Path Computation Element (PCE) is introduced in [RFC4655]. It is an abstract functional entity that computes paths.

L3VPN.why: A dedicated section applies the abstraction layer network to multi-AS L3VPNs.
L3VPN.quote: Serving Layer 3 VPNs (L3VPNs) across a multi-AS or multi-operator environment currently provides a significant planning challenge.
L3VPN.section: 8. Application of the Architecture to L3VPN Multi-AS Environments

rejected.why: BGP-LS is noted as a candidate mechanism for advertising abstract links, but the document does not specify or extend BGP.
RSVP-TE signalling is relied upon without extension; the document explicitly says the problem is not about signaling.
OSPF-TE and ASON OSPF levels are discussed as options, but OSPF is not specified or extended here.
MPLS-TE is the substrate; the more specific traffic engineering and GMPLS tags fit better.
Layer 1 VPN is only summarized as existing work in Appendix A.5.
Considered, but traffic engineering is the more specific fit for this inter-domain TE information exchange.

gaps.name: Inter-domain / multi-layer TE information abstraction (abstraction layer network, TE reachability)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for inter-domain TE architecture or abstraction/aggregation of TE topology; traffic engineering is the nearest parent.

RFC7927.title: Information-Centric Networking (ICN) Research Challenges
RFC7927.summary: An IRTF ICNRG informational RFC describing technical research challenges for Information-Centric Networking: naming, security, routing scalability, mobility, wireless, congestion control, in-network caching, management and applications.

ICN.why: The whole document is about ICN and its research challenges, so the ICN technology tag is the primary fit.
ICN.quote: Information-Centric Networking (ICN) is an approach to evolve the Internet infrastructure to directly support accessing Named Data Objects (NDOs) as a first-order network service.

HTTP caching.why: A substantial section covers cache placement, content placement, request-to-cache routing and staleness detection. This is related to web caching but is ICN-specific, so the fit is partial.
HTTP caching.quote: Explicitly named data objects allow for caching at virtually any network element, including routers, proxy caches, and end-user devices.

rejected.why: Section 4.4 discusses mobility management, but only in contrast with Mobile IP anchors. The document is about mobility in ICN, not IP mobility.
Section 4.6 covers receiver-driven rate and congestion control for ICN transport. It is one challenge among many and the tags above already cover it.
DTN is mentioned only as a comparison for opportunistic forwarding and data mules.
Hierarchical ICN names are compared to URIs, but the document is not about URIs.
TLS is cited only as a mechanism that cannot serve as a general solution for ICN data integrity.
Section 4.9.3 on ICN for IoT is a short application subsection, not a main subject.

gaps.name: Named Data Networking / Content-Centric Networking (NDN/CCN)
gaps.why: The document discusses CCN/NDN architectures extensively, but the taxonomy has only the generic ICN tag, which covers them adequately.

RFC7928.title: Characterization Guidelines for Active Queue Management (AQM)
RFC7928.summary: RFC 7928 gives guidelines for lab characterization of Active Queue Management (AQM) schemes, covering metrics, test topology, traffic scenarios, stability, and deployment and implementation considerations.

AQM.why: The whole document is about how to evaluate AQM algorithms such as RED, CoDel and PIE, so the AQM tag fits as the primary subject.
AQM.quote: This document describes various criteria for performing characterizations of AQM schemes that can be used in lab testing during development, prior to deployment.

performance measurement.why: A substantial part of the document defines performance metrics (flow completion time, loss, goodput, latency, jitter) and measurement methodology. It does not specify a measurement protocol, so the topic tag fits better than a technology tag.
performance measurement.quote: This section presents the metrics that could be used to better quantify (1) the reduction of latency, (2) maximization of goodput, and (3) the trade-off between these two.

rejected.why: It cites RFC 2544 and RFC 2647, but the document is about characterizing AQM algorithms, not benchmarking methodology for network devices. performance measurement is a closer fit.
ECN interaction is covered in Section 4.5, but only as one scenario among many. It is not a main subject.
TCP NewReno is the test traffic source, so TCP is the substrate for the evaluations and is not specified or extended here.
CUBIC is used only as an example aggressive sender in the tests.
LEDBAT is used only as the baseline less-than-best-effort sender in one scenario.
The AQM tag is the more specific fit under congestion control, and the congestion control algorithms appear only as test traffic.

RFC7929.title: DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) Bindings for OpenPGP
RFC7929.summary: Defines the OPENPGPKEY DNS resource record (type 61) for publishing and locating OpenPGP public keys by email address, secured by DNSSEC, as an experimental DANE method.

DANE.why: The document is a DANE binding: it defines a new DANE-style record to associate OpenPGP keys with email addresses via DNSSEC.
DANE.quote: This document specifies a DANE method for publishing and locating OpenPGP public keys in DNS for a specific email address using a new OPENPGPKEY DNS resource record.

OpenPGP.why: The document is about distributing and discovering OpenPGP public keys, including how to minimize Transferable Public Keys for the record and how MUAs/MTAs use them.
OpenPGP.quote: The OPENPGPKEY DNS resource record (RR) is used to associate an end entity OpenPGP Transferable Public Key (see Section 11.1 of [RFC4880]) with an email address

DNS.why: It defines a new DNS resource record type with its wire and presentation formats, owner-name mapping, and size and transport guidance.
DNS.quote: This document uses a new DNS RR type, OPENPGPKEY, whose value 61 has been allocated by IANA

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the security mechanism the record relies on. The document does not define anything new about signing or validation.
Email is the use case and the identifier source (the local-part and domain). The document does not specify email transport or formats.
S/MIME is only mentioned as an alternative approach in the experiment-goal text and in a reference to a separate document.
Internationalized local-parts are discussed in a short section on mapping addresses to names, but the document is not about EAI.
DoT and query-name minimisation appear only as brief mitigation suggestions in Security Considerations.
SHA2-256 is used only to hash the local-part in the owner name.

RFC7930.title: Larger Packets for RADIUS over TCP
RFC7930.summary: RFC 7930 extends RADIUS over TCP (RFC 6613) to allow packets up to 65535 octets, defining the Response-Length and Original-Packet-Code attributes, a new Protocol-Error code, and compatibility and discovery rules.

RADIUS.why: The document extends the RADIUS protocol: it defines a new packet code, new attributes, and Status-Server processing changes.
RADIUS.quote: The maximum length of a RADIUS message is increased from 4096 to 65535.

RFC7931.title: NFSv4.0 Migration: Specification Update
RFC7931.summary: Standards Track update to NFSv4.0 (RFC 7530) that revises file system migration and transparent state migration, client ID string construction and trunking determination, and the SETCLIENTID operation.

NFS.why: The whole document revises NFSv4.0: migration, state transfer, client identity, SETCLIENTID, and error definitions.
NFS.quote: This Standards Track document corrects the existing definitive specification of the NFSv4.0 protocol described in [RFC7530].

rejected.why: NFS runs over ONC RPC, but the document only uses it as a substrate and specifies nothing about RPC.
The parent topic is implied by NFS. The document is about NFS specifically.
A UUID is only mentioned as one possible ingredient of a client ID string. The document is not about UUIDs.
The document has no IANA actions.

gaps.name: NFS (NFSv4.0)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an NFS tag in the text but with the id 'NFS' not listed; it exists as 'NFS' under storage. Use of that tag is intended, but I could not verify the id format against the list given.

RFC7932.title: Brotli Compressed Data Format
RFC7932.summary: Specifies the Brotli lossless compressed data format, combining LZ77, Huffman prefix coding, context modeling and a static dictionary, and registers the "br" HTTP content coding.

Brotli.why: The whole document is the authoritative specification of the brotli compressed data format, including stream, meta-block, prefix code, context map and static dictionary definitions.
Brotli.quote: This specification defines a lossless compressed data format that compresses data using a combination of the LZ77 algorithm and Huffman coding

rejected.why: Brotli borrows notation and text from RFC 1951 but is a different format; DEFLATE is only a reference.
The only HTTP link is the IANA registration of the 'br' content coding, which is boilerplate and not the body's subject.
Mentioned only as a compression-ratio comparison, not specified or profiled.
The parent topic is implied by the Brotli tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC7933.title: Adaptive Video Streaming over Information-Centric Networking (ICN)
RFC7933.summary: IRTF ICNRG informational document examining how adaptive video streaming (DASH, layered coding, PPSP P2P, IPTV, DRM) can be adapted to Information-Centric Networking and listing research issues.

ICN.why: The whole document analyses video streaming over ICN/CCN: naming, caching, interest forwarding, and ICN-specific research issues.
ICN.quote: considers the consequences of moving the underlying network architecture from the current Internet to an Information-Centric Networking (ICN) architecture on video distribution

streaming.why: Adaptive video streaming (DASH, layered encoding, rate adaptation) is the core subject; DASH has no specific tag, so the streaming topic fits.
streaming.quote: Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP (DASH) to work over ICN

PPSP.why: Section 6 maps PPSP tracker/peer protocol messages onto ICN named data.
PPSP.quote: This document discusses some preliminary concepts about the deployment of PPSP on top of an ICN that exposes a pull-based API

rejected.why: Not in the taxonomy as given; the closest listed tag PPSP exists under streaming, but I used it above. (Retained as a tag.)
A full section covers IPTV challenges over ICN, but it is a single scenario section, not the main subject; considered secondary at most.
DASH runs over HTTP, but the document replaces HTTP with ICN rather than specifying HTTP.
P2P streaming is discussed only via PPSP, which is tagged more specifically.
Multicast is mentioned only as an implicit ICN benefit.
AAA-based DRM is a brief subsection rather than a substantial treatment of AAA frameworks.

gaps.name: Information-Centric Networking / CCN / NDN
gaps.why: The taxonomy's ICN tag sits under internet layer; no distinct tag exists for DASH or for digital rights management, which the document covers.

gaps.name: Digital Rights Management (DRM) in ICN
gaps.why: A whole section covers broadcast-encryption and AAA-based DRM, with no matching taxonomy tag.

RFC7934.title: Host Address Availability Recommendations
RFC7934.summary: BCP recommending that IPv6 networks give general-purpose hosts multiple global IPv6 addresses (via SLAAC or a dedicated /64, e.g. DHCPv6 PD) rather than restricting hosts to one address, covering benefits, NAT66 drawbacks, options and operational considerations.

addressing.why: The document's core is IPv6 host address allocation practice: how many addresses per host, and how prefixes and addresses are provided. This is addressing guidance, not a change to IPv6 itself, so the topic tag fits better than the IPv6 tech tag.
addressing.quote: it is RECOMMENDED that IPv6 network deployments provide multiple IPv6 addresses from each prefix to general-purpose hosts.

SLAAC.why: SLAAC is a main option compared and recommended for letting hosts form addresses without explicit network requests.
SLAAC.quote: SLAAC allows hosts to create global IPv6 addresses on demand by simply forming new addresses from the global prefix(es) assigned to the link.
SLAAC.section: 6. Options for Providing More Than One Address

DHCPv6.why: Stateful DHCPv6 address assignment (IA_NA/IA_TA) and DHCPv6 PD are analysed and compared as ways of providing multiple addresses, including the roughly 30-address limit.
DHCPv6.quote: DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (PD) [RFC3633].  DHCPv6 PD allows the client to request and be delegated a prefix, from which it can autonomously form other addresses.
DHCPv6.section: 6. Options for Providing More Than One Address

NAT.why: A whole section argues that restricting addresses drives NAT66 proliferation and why that is undesirable, citing IAB guidance against IPv6 NAT.
NAT.quote: Unfortunately, NAT has well-known drawbacks.  For example, it causes application complexity due to the need to implement NAT traversal.
NAT.section: 5. Overcoming Limits Using Network Address Translation

rejected.why: The document is guidance on address provisioning, not the IPv6 specification. It is covered by the more specific addressing tag.
Used as an example of a function that needs an extra address, not specified or analysed here.
Mentioned only as a way to do host tracking in operational considerations.
ND cache limits are discussed as a scaling concern, but the document is not about ND.
Translation-based transition appears only as an example use case for multiple addresses.

RFC7935.title: The Profile for Algorithms and Key Sizes for Use in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure
RFC7935.summary: RFC 7935 profiles the signature algorithm (RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 with SHA-256), hash, 2048-bit RSA key format and signature format for RPKI certificates, CRLs, CMS signed objects and certification requests, replacing RFC 6485.

RPKI.why: The whole document is an algorithm and key-size profile for the RPKI, used by subscribers and relying parties. It belongs on the RPKI subject page.
RPKI.quote: This document specifies the algorithms, algorithms' parameters, asymmetric key formats, asymmetric key size, and signature format for the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) subscribers

RSA.why: It mandates RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signatures, RSA key sizes, the exponent and the RSAPublicKey encoding. These are a substantial part of the content.
RSA.quote: The RSA key pairs used to compute the signatures MUST have a 2048-bit modulus and a public exponent (e) of 65,537.

SHA.why: SHA-256 is the required hash algorithm, with SHA-1 as an exception for key identifiers. Readers of SHA-family usage would want this profile.
SHA.quote: The hashing algorithm used in certificates, CRLs, CMS signed objects and certification requests is SHA-256 [SHS]

rejected.why: Certificates and CRLs are the objects being signed, but the document does not profile X.509 itself. That is done in RFC 6487.
CMS SignedData algorithm identifiers are specified, but only as one place where the algorithms are applied. The document is not about CMS.
The RPKI tag is more specific and already covers this topic.
The RPKI tag is more specific than PKI.

RFC7936.title: Clarifying Registry Procedures for the WebSocket Subprotocol Name Registry
RFC7936.summary: RFC 7936 clarifies IANA's registration procedures for the WebSocket Subprotocol Name Registry from RFC 6455, stating that tokens are matched case-sensitively but IANA must decline registrations differing only by case.

IANA.why: The document exists to clarify instructions to IANA for a registry; it is about registry procedures. The IANA topic covers registry considerations guidance.
IANA.quote: This document is, in its entirety, a clarification of the registry policy for the WebSocket Subprotocol Name Registry.

WebSocket.why: It updates RFC 6455 by clarifying how WebSocket subprotocol name tokens are registered and matched, so WebSocket readers need it.
WebSocket.quote: The tokens registered in the WebSocket Subprotocol Name Registry created by Section 11.5 of RFC 6455 are matched using case-sensitive string match.

rejected.why: WebSocket relies on an HTTP handshake, but this document does not discuss HTTP at all.
It is a registry policy clarification, not an IETF process or procedures document. IANA is the better fit.

RFC7937.title: Content Distribution Network Interconnection (CDNI) Logging Interface
RFC7937.summary: Specifies the CDNI Logging interface between downstream and upstream CDNs: a reference model, the CDNI Logging File format (directives and HTTP request records), and an Atom-feed plus HTTP-pull protocol for exchanging log files.

CDN.why: The whole document defines the CDNI Logging interface, including the reference model, file format and exchange protocol, so it belongs on the CDN interconnection page.
CDN.quote: This memo specifies the Logging interface between a downstream Content Distribution Network (dCDN) and an upstream CDN (uCDN)

Atom.why: The log-file advertisement protocol is specified as an Atom Archived feed (RFC 5005), with entry and content element requirements. This is a substantial part of the protocol.
Atom.quote: The server-side implementation of the CDNI Logging feed MUST produce an Atom feed [RFC4287].

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate for pulling log files and for the logged request records. The document defines no HTTP extension.
TLS is only required as transport security in the Security Considerations; the document defines nothing new about it.
The log format is inspired by the W3C Extended Log File Format and is not syslog.
It registers a payload type for the existing application/cdni type, but this is minor IANA apparatus.
c-groupid anonymization and privacy considerations are discussed, but they are a feature of the record format rather than the document's main subject.
KPIs are discussed as uses of the logs, but the document specifies log exchange, not measurement methods.

gaps.name: CDNI (CDN Interconnection) logging
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a CDN tag but no CDNI-specific tag. A dedicated CDNI tag would group the CDNI interface RFCs (metadata, control, logging, framework).

RFC7938.title: Use of BGP for Routing in Large-Scale Data Centers
RFC7938.summary: Informational RFC reporting operational experience of using EBGP as the sole routing protocol in Clos-topology large-scale data centers, covering ASN allocation, ECMP, convergence, and route summarization options.

data center networking.why: The whole document is a routing design for large-scale data centers with Clos topologies, tiers, and clusters.
data center networking.quote: This document summarizes operational experience in designing and operating large-scale data centers using BGP as the only routing protocol.

BGP.why: It argues for EBGP as the only DC routing protocol. It covers ASN schemes, private ASNs, multipath relax, convergence, third-party route injection and MRAI.
BGP.quote: Experimentation and extensive testing have shown that External BGP (EBGP) [RFC4271] is well suited as a stand-alone routing protocol

ECMP.why: A full section covers ECMP fan-out, multipath across multiple ASNs, weighted ECMP and consistent hashing as core design requirements.
ECMP.quote: ECMP is the fundamental load-sharing mechanism used by a Clos topology.
