rejected.why: It is discussed only as the IGP alternative the design avoids.
It is mentioned only as an L2 alternative that is judged unsuitable.
It is mentioned only as an optional fault-detection aid.
The traceroute and ICMP masquerading discussion is a minor operational point, not the subject.
Anycast prefix advertisement is mentioned as a use case, not as a subject of the document.
TCP is only the transport BGP relies on.

RFC7939.title: Definition of Managed Objects for the Neighborhood Discovery Protocol
RFC7939.summary: Defines the NHDP-MIB SMIv2 module for configuring, monitoring, and getting notifications from the MANET Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (RFC 6130), updating RFC 6779 for the RFC 7466 optimization.

NHDP.why: The whole MIB models NHDP's parameters, information bases, performance counters and notifications, and tracks the RFC 7466 NHDP update.
NHDP.quote: it describes objects for configuring parameters of the Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP) [RFC6130] process on a router.

MIB.why: The document is an SMIv2 MIB module (NHDP-MIB) with textual conventions, tables, notifications and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: It defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

rejected.why: SNMP is the access mechanism for the MIB. The document defines no new SNMP protocol behaviour, and the MIB tag already covers it.
MANET is the deployment context. The subject is NHDP specifically, which sits under MANET, so the child tag is used instead.
RFC 4750 (the OSPF MIB) is cited only as a model for notification throttling.
TLS/DTLS appears only in the Security Considerations boilerplate, in the form of the SNMP transport security model.

RFC7940.title: Representing Label Generation Rulesets Using XML
RFC7940.summary: Specifies an XML format for Label Generation Rulesets (LGRs), which define permitted code points, variants, context rules and dispositions for identifier labels such as IDNs, and registers the application/lgr+xml media type.

IDN.why: The LGR format exists to represent IDN registration tables (code point repertoire, variants, whole-label rules), and it builds on IDNA rules and RFC 3743/4290 tables.
IDN.quote: These policies, known as "Label Generation Rulesets" (LGRs), are used for the implementation of Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs)

XML.why: Defines a new XML vocabulary, namespace and RELAX NG schema, so readers of XML-based formats would want it.
XML.quote: This document specifies a method of using Extensible Markup Language (XML) to describe Label Generation Rulesets (LGRs).

media types.why: Registers the application/lgr+xml media type and the LGR dispositions registry.
media types.quote: SHOULD be transmitted with a media type of "application/lgr+xml".

rejected.why: LGRs are applied to domain-name labels by registries, but the document specifies no DNS protocol or resource record behaviour.
Relies heavily on Unicode properties and versions, but defines a ruleset format rather than Unicode usage guidance.
Registry policy is the use case, but the document is about a rule representation format, not registry operations or protocols.
IANA registries are created but this is boilerplate-level; the main body is the format.

gaps.name: Label Generation Rulesets (LGR)
gaps.why: The document's central subject has no dedicated tag; IDN is the closest fit for IDN tables and variant policy.

RFC7941.title: RTP Header Extension for the RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Source Description Items
RFC7941.summary: Defines an RTP header extension, using the RFC 5285 mechanism, that carries RTCP SDES items such as CNAME so receivers get them sooner. It also gives usage guidance and creates an IANA sub-registry for these extensions.

RTCP.why: The document specifies how RTCP SDES items are carried in an RTP header extension. It also covers how that interacts with SDES delivery in RTCP, including update flaps and RTCP feedback.
RTCP.quote: This specification defines an RTP header extension [RFC3550][RFC5285] that can carry RTCP Source Description (SDES) items.

RTP.why: It defines a new RTP header extension for SSRC identity and synchronization context. It also covers packet expansion and MTU effects, middlebox behaviour, and transmission strategies.
RTP.quote: Using the RTP header extension ensures that the information is updated on reception of the related RTP media, ensuring synchronization between the two.

rejected.why: SDP's a=mid attribute and the SDP bundle work are mentioned only as motivation. The document does not specify anything about SDP.
SRTP appears only in Security Considerations, as the way to encrypt header extensions.
Section 4.2.7 notes briefly that ROHC does not compress the header extension data. That is not a substantial part of the document.
UTF-8 is only the text encoding of the SDES item values.
The IANA registry is created as part of the extension. The document is not about IANA registry guidance in general.

RFC7942.title: Improving Awareness of Running Code: The Implementation Status Section
RFC7942.summary: A BCP that defines an optional process for Internet-Drafts to include an Implementation Status section recording known implementations, so working groups can weigh running code; it obsoletes RFC 6982.

IETF process.why: The document defines an IETF document-development process practice for I-Ds and working groups, concerning how implementation evidence feeds into standardization decisions.
IETF process.quote: This document describes a simple process that allows authors of Internet-Drafts to record the status of known implementations by including an Implementation Status section.

rejected.why: The section is removed before RFC publication and the document concerns Internet-Draft content, not RFC format or publication.
The more specific child IETF process fits; the parent is implied.
RFC 5080 is only cited as an example of an implementation report; the document is not about RADIUS.
Routing Area implementation requirements (RFC 1264, IDR) are mentioned only as historical background.

RFC7943.title: A Method for Generating Semantically Opaque Interface Identifiers (IIDs) with the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)
RFC7943.summary: Describes a DHCPv6 server-side algorithm using a PRF (SHA-256 by default) over prefix, client DUID, IAID, counter and secret key to generate stable, semantically opaque IPv6 interface identifiers for leased IA_NA addresses, as a DHCPv6 analogue of RFC 7217.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies a server-side address selection algorithm for DHCPv6 address leasing (IA_NA), so DHCPv6 readers would want it.
DHCPv6.quote: a method for selecting IPv6 Interface Identifiers that can be employed by DHCPv6 servers when leasing non-temporary IPv6 addresses to DHCPv6 clients

rejected.why: It is a DHCPv6 variant of RFC 7217's SLAAC method, but SLAAC itself is only referenced, not specified or extended.

The method mitigates address-based tracking and scanning, but the document is a DHCPv6 address generation method, not a privacy threat model. It also states it does not address DHCPv6 privacy broadly.
SHA-256 is only the default PRF choice inside the algorithm; the document is not about the hash family.
MD5 is mentioned only to say it is unacceptable for F().
Interface identifiers are the subject, but the DHCPv6 tag is more specific. IPv6 addressing is the context, not a separate focus.

RFC7944.title: Diameter Routing Message Priority
RFC7944.summary: Defines the Diameter Routing Message Priority (DRMP) AVP, letting Diameter nodes mark the relative priority of transactions so agents and endpoints can use it in routing, throttling under overload, and resource allocation.

Diameter.why: The document extends the Diameter protocol with a new DRMP AVP (code 301) and normative behaviour for clients, agents and servers.
Diameter.quote: defining a mechanism to allow Diameter endpoints to indicate the relative priority of Diameter transactions

rejected.why: Diameter is the specific child tag; the AAA framework in general is not the subject.
Priority is used as input to overload throttling (DOIC), but the document defines no congestion control algorithm; it is Diameter-level overload handling.
Priority marking of Diameter signalling messages is not a QoS architecture or signalling mechanism for network traffic.
Emergency and first-responder signalling are only use cases motivating the priority, not the subject of the document.
Transport (TCP/SCTP) and TLS/IPsec are only mentioned in security considerations as substrates.

gaps.name: Diameter Overload Indication Conveyance (DOIC)
gaps.why: The document builds on DOIC (RFC 7683) overload control for Diameter; the taxonomy has Diameter but no more specific overload-control tag.

RFC7945.title: Information-Centric Networking: Evaluation and Security Considerations
RFC7945.summary: IRTF ICNRG informational document giving guidelines for evaluating Information-Centric Networking (topologies, traffic workloads, metrics), discussing ICN security, authentication, access control and privacy impacts, and surveying ICN simulators, implementations and testbeds.

ICN.why: The whole document is about ICN: evaluation methodology, metrics, tools and security aspects of ICN architectures (CCN/NDN, NetInf, PURSUIT).
ICN.quote: This document presents a number of considerations regarding evaluating Information-Centric Networking (ICN) and sheds some light on the impact of ICN on network security.

privacy.why: Section 3.3 analyses privacy exposure through in-network caches, and Section 3.4 covers the changed threat model, which is a substantial part of the document.
privacy.quote: Caching implies a trade-off between network efficiency and privacy.

rejected.why: The document discusses metrics and mentions IPPM, but only to choose ICN evaluation metrics. It does not specify measurement methods, so ICN is the better fit.
It covers evaluation methodology for ICN research, not benchmarking of network devices.
Security is a section, but the document is about ICN-specific security. Privacy is tagged, and the general security parent is not otherwise warranted.
Section 3.1 covers content authentication in ICN, but it is a brief survey and not the main subject.
Section 3.2 briefly notes that ICN lacks authorization and access control, which does not justify a separate tag.
The document discusses in-network ICN caching, not HTTP caching. HTTP appears only in traffic workload data.
DTN is mentioned only as a source of mobility topologies and traces.

RFC7946.title: The GeoJSON Format
RFC7946.summary: RFC 7946 specifies GeoJSON, a JSON-based format for encoding geographic geometries, features and feature collections using WGS 84 coordinates, and registers the application/geo+json media type.

GeoJSON.why: The whole document defines the GeoJSON format: geometry types, Feature and FeatureCollection objects, bounding boxes, extension rules and the geo URI mapping.
GeoJSON.quote: GeoJSON is a geospatial data interchange format based on JavaScript Object Notation (JSON).

rejected.why: JSON is the substrate encoding. The document defines a specific JSON-based format, which the GeoJSON tag covers more precisely, and it adds no new rules for JSON itself.
The IANA section registers application/geo+json, but that is boilerplate registration for the format and is not the subject of the document.
GeoJSON represents geographic data and has a 'geo' URI mapping. The document is a general-purpose geospatial data format rather than a location-information conveyance or privacy framework.
Section 9 maps 'geo' URIs to GeoJSON Points, but this is a small part of the document and it does not specify the URI scheme.

gaps.name: GeoJSON / geospatial data formats
gaps.why: The taxonomy has GeoJSON listed under JSON as a tech tag, but I used the id 'GeoJSON'. The listed id is 'GeoJSON' only in the form 'GeoJSON' under JSON in the hierarchy; if the id is meant to be exactly as shown it should be 'GeoJSON'.

RFC7947.title: Internet Exchange BGP Route Server
RFC7947.summary: Specifies the adaptations to BGP needed for an IXP route server to broker multilateral EBGP interconnection: attribute transparency, AS_PATH handling, and informative guidance on per-client policy and path hiding.

route server.why: The whole document specifies IXP route server behaviour, including attribute transparency, AS_PATH management and path-hiding mitigation. This is the exact subject of the route server tag.
route server.quote: Multilateral interconnection is a method of interconnecting BGP speaking routers using a third-party brokering system, commonly referred to as a route server

rejected.why: The document is about the route server, a more specific child tag under BGP. The ancestor is implied.
The route server is compared to a route reflector, but the document does not specify route reflection.
Communities are mentioned only briefly: they should not be modified. That is not a substantial part of the document.
Shared Layer 2 media at IXPs is only background context.

RFC7948.title: Internet Exchange BGP Route Server Operations
RFC7948.summary: Informational RFC giving operational considerations for IXP BGP route servers: multilateral interconnection, path hiding, scaling, prefix leakage, redundancy, AS_PATH checks, export policies, NEXT_HOP hijacking.

route server.why: The whole document is about operating IXP route servers, including scaling, redundancy, and security of route server deployments.
route server.quote: This document describes operational considerations for multilateral interconnections at IXPs.

BGP.why: Substantial BGP operational guidance such as AS_PATH consistency check, NEXT_HOP handling and Loc-RIB/decision process scaling applies to BGP operation in general.
BGP.quote: route server operators SHOULD check that the BGP NEXT_HOP attribute for BGP routes received from a route server client matches the interface address

rejected.why: Communities are only one of several export-policy mechanisms described briefly in 4.6.1; the document is not about the communities attribute itself.
IRRDB/RPSL is mentioned as one way to build per-client policies in a short subsection; not a main subject.
BFD is discussed only as a partial and imperfect mitigation for layer 2 reachability problems.
Prefix leakage and NEXT_HOP hijacking are covered, but within the route server context; it defers to RFC 7454 rather than being a general operational security document.
Layer 2 IXP fabrics are the substrate; Ethernet switch bugs are mentioned only in passing.

RFC7949.title: OSPFv3 over IPv4 for IPv6 Transition
RFC7949.summary: Defines how to carry OSPFv3 packets directly over IPv4 (protocol 89) to ease IPv4-to-IPv6 transition, covering addresses, checksum pseudo-header, virtual links, and coexistence with OSPFv2, and updates RFC 5838.

OSPFv3.why: The document specifies a new transport encapsulation for OSPFv3, its addressing, checksum and virtual-link behaviour, and updates the OSPFv3 address family RFC 5838.
OSPFv3.quote: This document specifies how to use IPv4 to transport OSPFv3 packets.

IPv6 transition.why: The mechanism is motivated and framed as a transition tool from IPv4-only to dual-stack to IPv6-only routing domains, so readers of transition topics would want it.
IPv6 transition.quote: can simplify transition from an OSPFv2 IPv4-only routing domain to an OSPFv3 dual-stack routing domain

rejected.why: IPv4 is only the transport substrate; the document defines nothing new about IPv4 itself.
The document is about OSPFv3 and transition, not the IPv6 protocol specification or addressing.
Mentioned only as being unusable across different IPv4 subnets; not a subject of the document.
Only discussed in Security Considerations as a dependency for authentication.
The parent tag is implied by OSPFv3; the document is specific to OSPFv3.

RFC7950.title: The YANG 1.1 Data Modeling Language
RFC7950.summary: Specifies version 1.1 of the YANG data modeling language (syntax, statements, built-in types, XPath functions, YIN, ABNF grammar) and its mapping to NETCONF operations and errors.

YANG.why: The whole document defines the YANG 1.1 language: modules, statements, types, conformance, and updating rules.
YANG.quote: YANG is a data modeling language used to model configuration data, state data, Remote Procedure Calls, and notifications for network management protocols.

NETCONF.why: A substantial part specifies XML encoding rules, <edit-config> operations, constraint enforcement and NETCONF error responses for YANG-modeled data.
NETCONF.quote: This document also specifies the YANG mappings to the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF).

rejected.why: XML is the encoding and XPath is the expression notation used by YANG, but the document is not about XML itself.
SMIv2/MIB compatibility is mentioned only in passing in the overview.
Only referenced as a comparison for SMIv2 compatibility.
Mentioned only as another protocol that uses YANG and is out of scope here.
JSON encoding is explicitly out of scope; it is only referenced via RFC 7951.
The ABNF grammar is merely the formal syntax notation for YANG, not the subject.

RFC7951.title: JSON Encoding of Data Modeled with YANG
RFC7951.summary: Defines how YANG-modeled configuration data, state data, RPC/action parameters and notifications are encoded as JSON text, including naming, node encoding and type representation rules.

YANG.why: The document specifies how YANG data trees and YANG built-in types are encoded, so readers of YANG will look for it.
YANG.quote: This document defines encoding rules for representing configuration data, state data, parameters of Remote Procedure Call (RPC) operations or actions, and notifications defined using YANG as JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) text.

JSON.why: It defines a JSON-based format for YANG data, including I-JSON compliance, member naming and value representations.
JSON.quote: The aim of this document is to define rules for encoding the same data as JSON text [RFC7159].

rejected.why: NETCONF is only mentioned as the protocol that uses XML encoding and as a context for data security. This document does not specify or extend it.
RESTCONF is cited as a consumer of the JSON encoding, and the document does not define it.
XML encoding is referenced only for comparison and mapping, not specified here.
Base64 is used only for the binary type, following the XML lexical form.
Requiring UTF-8 is a passing constraint inherited from I-JSON, and the document is not about the encoding.

RFC7952.title: Defining and Using Metadata with YANG
RFC7952.summary: Defines a YANG extension statement ("md:annotation") for declaring metadata annotations in YANG modules, plus XML and JSON encodings of annotations, DSDL mapping, and the ietf-yang-metadata module.

YANG.why: The document extends the YANG language with a new extension statement and defines the ietf-yang-metadata module, updating RFC 6110. Readers of YANG would want it.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG extension that allows for defining metadata annotations in YANG modules.

JSON.why: A substantial part of the document specifies a JSON encoding for annotations: metadata objects, "@" members, and leaf-list arrays.
JSON.quote: This document thus introduces a special encoding method that is consistent with the JSON encoding of YANG data node instances

XML.why: The document specifies the XML attribute encoding for annotations, and a DSDL/RELAX NG mapping for validating the XML.
XML.quote: Metadata annotations are added to XML-encoded instances of YANG data nodes as XML attributes according to these rules:

rejected.why: NETCONF is cited only as a motivating use case and a source of terminology. The document does not specify or extend it. It is also not in the taxonomy as a standalone id except under network management.
RESTCONF is mentioned only as a client protocol that must be able to discover annotations. It is not the subject of the document.
This is a YANG metadata mechanism, not SNMP MIB or SMI work.
ABNF is used only to give the syntax of the JSON annotation name, so it is a notation the document uses and not a subject of it.
The IANA section only registers the module and XML namespace. This is boilerplate.

RFC7953.title: Calendar Availability
RFC7953.summary: Defines the iCalendar VAVAILABILITY and AVAILABLE components and BUSYTYPE property for publishing recurring available/busy time, specifies how they combine in free-busy calculation, and extends CalDAV and CalDAV scheduling to store and use them.

iCalendar.why: The document defines new iCalendar components and a property, and updates RFC 5545 free-busy calculation.
iCalendar.quote: This specification adds a new "VAVAILABILITY" calendar component to iCalendar.

CalDAV.why: Section 7 defines CalDAV extensions: a DAV header feature token, time-range query rules, free-busy-query behaviour and the calendar-availability property. It updates RFC 4791 and 6638.
CalDAV.quote: This specification extends the CalDAV calendar-access and CalDAV calendar-auto-schedule features to allow the new iCalendar availability components to be stored and manipulated

rejected.why: WebDAV is only the substrate for CalDAV properties and OPTIONS discovery; nothing new is defined about WebDAV itself.
The XML property definition is just CalDAV apparatus, not a subject of the document.
VTIMEZONE is mentioned only as a requirement for the iCalendar object. The document does not address time zone distribution.
HTTP is used only as the transport for CalDAV examples.

RFC7954.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Endpoint Identifier (EID) Block
RFC7954.summary: Directs IANA to allocate 2001:5::/32 as an experimental IPv6 EID address block for LISP, with rationale, expected use, a 3+3 year allocation plan, and routing considerations.

LISP.why: The whole document defines a LISP-specific EID address block, its use, and its routing implications for LISP sites, PITRs and interworking.
LISP.quote: This document directs IANA to allocate a /32 IPv6 prefix for use with the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP).

IANA.why: A substantial part of the document is the allocation request and the 3+3 year lifecycle for the special-purpose registry entry.
IANA.quote: IANA has assigned a /32 IPv6 prefix for use as the global EID space for LISP using a hierarchical allocation

rejected.why: The block is an IPv6 prefix, but the document is about LISP EID space, not IPv6 specification or addressing architecture.
BGP announcement of the block by PITRs is discussed, but only as a routing consideration, not as the subject.
It allocates an address block, but the LISP tag is more specific, and the document is not about general IP address architecture.

RFC7955.title: Management Guidelines for the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Endpoint Identifier (EID) Block
RFC7955.summary: Informational RFC defining a management framework under which RIPE NCC registers temporary, experimental EID prefixes from the LISP EID block (2001:5::/32), including policy, requirements and a request template.

LISP.why: The document manages the address block reserved for the LISP experiment and defines registration policy for LISP EID prefixes.
LISP.quote: This document proposes a management framework for the registration of EID prefixes from that block

addressing.why: It concerns allocation and registration policy for an IPv6 address block, including prefix size, lease periods, reuse and reverse DNS delegation.
addressing.quote: The framework described relies on hierarchical distribution of the address space, granting temporary usage of prefixes of such space to requesting organizations.

rejected.why: RDAP is mentioned only as one example access method for the registry data; the document does not specify or extend it.
The document has no IANA actions. RIPE NCC runs the registry, so the IANA Considerations section is not evidence of this subject.
The block is an IPv6 prefix, but the document is about registry management and does not specify or analyse IPv6.
Reverse DNS delegation is only a requirement on the registry operator and an optional template field. The document does not address DNS itself.
WHOIS is named only as one possible interface for publishing registry data.

RFC7956.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) Distributed Layer 3 Gateway
RFC7956.summary: Specifies an optional TRILL distributed Layer 3 gateway in which edge RBridges perform inter-subnet IP routing per tenant VRF, advertising tenant labels, gateway MACs and IP prefixes via new IS-IS APPsub-TLVs and an SE NickFlags bit.

TRILL.why: The whole document extends TRILL with distributed L3 gateway forwarding and new TLVs for edge RBridges.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies an optional TRILL distributed gateway solution that resolves these centralized gateway issues.

rejected.why: IS-IS is the substrate carrying the new APPsub-TLVs; the document is not about IS-IS itself.
The tenant label is only compared to an MPLS VPN label in passing; the document does not address provider-provisioned VPNs.
ARP/ND is used by end stations to learn the gateway MAC but is not specified or extended here.
IPv6 prefixes are carried alongside IPv4 ones, but IPv6 itself is not the subject.
The data center is the motivating context, but the document specifies a TRILL extension. TRILL is the more specific fit.
Virtual networks are identified by Data Labels (VLAN/FGL), but the document does not define a data-plane network virtualization overlay encapsulation such as VXLAN.

RFC7957.title: DISPATCH-Style Working Groups and the SIP Change Process
RFC7957.summary: BCP updating RFC 5727 to decouple the SIP change process from the RAI area and to generalize the DISPATCH working group's new-work triage procedures into reusable "DISPATCH-style" working groups.

IETF process.why: The document defines working group procedures for evaluating and routing new work, and updates the SIP change process. This is IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: A "DISPATCH-Style" working group operates according to procedures similar to those used for DISPATCH.

SIP.why: A substantial part of the document preserves and restates the process for changing SIP and related protocols. It does not change the protocol itself, so SIP readers would still want it.
SIP.quote: This document clarifies that the SIP Change Process is not bound to any particular area or working group structure.
SIP.section: 3. Decoupling the SIP Change Process from the RAI Area

rejected.why: The more specific child, IETF process, fits, so the parent is not listed.
The RAI area is the context, but the document covers process and not real-time technology.

RFC7958.title: DNSSEC Trust Anchor Publication for the Root Zone
RFC7958.summary: Informational RFC describing the XML, PKIX certificate and PKCS#10 CSR formats and the HTTP/HTTPS retrieval and verification mechanisms IANA uses to publish DNSSEC trust anchors for the DNS root zone.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document defines how DNSSEC root zone trust anchors are formatted, published and accepted, including conversion to DS records. This is trust anchor material, squarely within DNSSEC.
DNSSEC.quote: In order to obtain secure answers from the root zone of the DNS using DNSSEC, a client must configure a suitable trust anchor.

rejected.why: Certificates and CSRs are used as a container format for the trust anchors, and an attribute is defined for them. The document is about DNSSEC trust anchors, not X.509 profiles.
The trust anchor XML schema is defined here, but XML is only the encoding for the hashes.
HTTP and HTTPS are only the retrieval mechanism for the files, and nothing new is specified about them.
A detached CMS signature is used to verify the XML file, but this is a substrate use only.
IANA publishes the trust anchors and one OID registration is made, but the document is not about IANA registry guidance.
TLS is mentioned only as a way to protect distribution of the files.

RFC7959.title: Block-Wise Transfers in the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)
RFC7959.summary: Defines the CoAP Block1/Block2 options, Size1/Size2 options, and new response codes for transferring large resource representations block-wise over datagram transports, updating RFC 7252.

CoAP.why: The document extends CoAP with new options (Block1, Block2, Size1, Size2) and response codes, and updates RFC 7252. It is squarely about CoAP.
CoAP.quote: this specification extends basic CoAP with a pair of "Block" options for transferring multiple blocks of information from a resource representation in multiple request-response pairs

rejected.why: HTTP is only discussed as a comparison and in the short HTTP-mapping section. The document does not specify or extend HTTP.
UDP is the datagram transport CoAP runs over. The document does not define anything new about UDP usage.
DTLS is only mentioned as an underlying transport and security substrate for CoAP.
6LoWPAN fragmentation is cited as motivation for small blocks. The document does not specify anything about 6LoWPAN.
The CoAP tag already sits under IoT, so the parent is implied and should not be listed separately.
The caching considerations are about CoAP caches and proxies, not HTTP caching.

RFC7960.title: Interoperability Issues between Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) and Indirect Email Flows
RFC7960.summary: Informational analysis of interoperability problems between DMARC policies and indirect email flows (forwarders, mailing lists, gateways, filters), with current and proposed mitigations.

DMARC.why: The whole document analyses how DMARC policy enforcement breaks indirect email flows and how to mitigate that.
DMARC.quote: This document describes these interoperability issues and presents possible methods for addressing them.

mailing lists.why: Mailing lists are the main indirect flow discussed, with a dedicated section on effects and list-manager mitigations.
mailing lists.quote: In particular, DMARC with restrictive policies causes problems for many Mailing Lists.

DKIM.why: DKIM signature breakage, alignment, canonicalization and key management are central to the issues and mitigations.
DKIM.quote: Modification of email content invalidates most DKIM signatures, and many message-forwarding systems modify email content.

SPF.why: SPF identifiers, MAILFROM fallback and forwarding failures are analysed substantially.
SPF.quote: Forwarding introduces specific issues to the availability of SPF-based Authenticated Identifiers

rejected.why: Covered by the more specific email authentication children chosen; architecture discussion is only framing.
Used as substrate; the document does not specify or extend SMTP.
Mentioned only as one source of message modification in the rMDA.
Header rewriting is discussed but the document is not about message format itself.
Only vaguely alluded to as in-progress multi-hop Authentication-Results work, not named or specified.

RFC7961.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Interface Addresses APPsub-TLV
RFC7961.summary: Defines the TRILL IS-IS Interface Addresses APPsub-TLV, which reports sets of addresses (MAC, IPv4, IPv6) designating the same interface and the TRILL switch through which it is reachable, along with its sub-sub-TLVs, IANA allocations and processing rules.

TRILL.why: The document specifies a new TRILL APPsub-TLV, its format, sub-sub-TLVs and processing, so it belongs on the TRILL page.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies a TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) IS-IS application sub-TLV that enables the reporting by a TRILL switch of sets of addresses.

rejected.why: IS-IS is the substrate carrying the APPsub-TLV; the document defines a TRILL application sub-TLV, not new IS-IS protocol behaviour.
The information could be used to synthesize ARP responses, but ARP is not specified or changed here; the optimization is in a separate draft.
IPv6 ND is mentioned only as a protocol whose use the data could bypass.
IANA allocations (AFN values, sub-registry) are boilerplate-type content supporting the format, not the main subject.
MAC addresses are carried as data but the document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet interworking.
IPv6 addresses are just one address type carried in the Address Sets.

gaps.name: TRILL
gaps.why: The document is about TRILL (RBridges, ESADI, directory assistance), but the taxonomy includes only a TRILL tag under routing as 'TRILL: transparent interconnection of lots of links' — in the taxonomy the id is 'TRILL'. No gap beyond that; IS-IS APPsub-TLV mechanics have no dedicated tag besides IS-IS.

RFC7962.title: Alternative Network Deployments: Taxonomy, Characterization, Technologies, and Architectures
RFC7962.summary: An IRTF GAIA informational survey that classifies Alternative Network Deployments (community networks, WISPs, shared infrastructure, crowdshared Wi-Fi, rural cooperatives, testbeds) and reviews their wireless technologies, routing protocols, traffic management and services.

WiFi.why: Wi-Fi, including long-distance (WiLD) adaptations, TDMA variants and the crowdshared dual-SSID model, is the main access technology surveyed in the document.
WiFi.quote: The standard we are most interested in is 802.11 a/b/g/n/ac, as it defines the protocol for Wireless LAN. It is also known as "Wi-Fi".

MANET.why: The document surveys mesh routing protocols (OLSR, OLSRv2, B.A.T.M.A.N., BMX6, Babel) used in community networks and compares them.
MANET.quote: some Alternative Networks use mesh routing protocols for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs), while other ones use more traditional routing protocols.

cellular.why: Covers open-source GSM, 3G femtocells, and 4G/5G in alternative and shared-infrastructure networks.
cellular.quote: GSM), from ETSI, has also been used in Alternative Networks as a Layer 2 option

WiMAX.why: 802.16 is listed as an access technology and is the basis for 802.22; a minor but explicit part of the survey.
WiMAX.quote: 802.16-compliant (Worldwide Interoperability for Microwave Access (WiMax)) [IEEE.802.16] systems over non-licensed bands.

BGP.why: Describes BGP use in community networks as a traditional routing option; brief but part of the routing survey.
BGP.quote: The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), as defined by [RFC4271], is used by a number of Community Networks

rejected.why: OLSR and OLSRv2 are mentioned as the most widely used mesh protocols, but only in a survey paragraph; MANET covers it adequately.
Babel is only briefly described as one of several mesh routing protocols.
AQM, ECN, CoDel and PIE are mentioned in one paragraph on traffic management for sharers, not a substantial part of the document.
The PAWS cited here is the Public Access WiFi Service research project, not the white-space database protocol.
OSPF is mentioned in one sentence as a choice for smaller networks.
VPNs here are user-set-up tunnels, not provider-provisioned VPNs.

gaps.name: Community networks / alternative network deployments (digital divide, rural connectivity)
gaps.why: The document's central subject, the classification and governance of community networks, WISPs and crowdshared networks for underserved areas, has no fitting tag in the taxonomy.

RFC7963.title: RSVP-TE Extension for Additional Signal Types in G.709 Optical Transport Networks (OTNs)
RFC7963.summary: Defines new OTN Signal Type values for ODU1e, ODU3e1 and ODU3e2 containers (from G.Sup43) in the RSVP-TE/GMPLS OTN-TDM SENDER_TSPEC and FLOWSPEC traffic parameters, with IANA allocations.

GMPLS.why: The document extends GMPLS signaling for G.709 OTN by adding Signal Types to the GMPLS Signaling Parameters registry, extending RFC 4328 and RFC 7139. GMPLS is the tag covering generalized MPLS and optical/transport network control.
GMPLS.quote: This document provides RSVP-TE signaling extensions to support these additional Signal Types.

RSVP-TE.why: The new Signal Types are carried in RSVP-TE OTN-TDM SENDER_TSPEC and FLOWSPEC objects, so this is an extension of RSVP-TE signalling for traffic-engineered LSPs.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document defines the Signal Types for ODU1e, ODU3e1, and ODU3e2
RSVP-TE.section: 2. RSVP-TE Extension for Additional Signal Types

rejected.why: IANA allocations are the means of defining the values, but the document is about OTN signalling extensions rather than registry guidance.
A parent of RSVP-TE, which is already tagged, so it is implied.

gaps.name: Optical Transport Network (OTN) / G.709
gaps.why: The document is about OTN ODU container signal types, but the taxonomy has no OTN tag. GMPLS is the closest fit.

RFC7964.title: Solutions for BGP Persistent Route Oscillation
RFC7964.summary: RFC 7964 specifies two sets of additional paths (all Available Paths or neighbor-AS Group Best Paths) that BGP route reflectors and confederation ASBRs advertise via ADD-PATH to eliminate MED-induced persistent IBGP route oscillation.

route reflection.why: The document revises BGP route reflector and confederation ASBR advertisement procedures (Section 5) to prevent oscillations, so it belongs on the route reflection and confederation page, which is a child of BGP.
route reflection.quote: routing information reduction by BGP Route Reflection [RFC4456] or BGP Confederation [RFC5065] can result in persistent Internal BGP (IBGP) route oscillations

rejected.why: The more specific child tag route reflection covers the document; BGP is implied as its ancestor.
The document addresses a specific BGP route-oscillation problem rather than general routing architecture or design principles.

gaps.name: BGP ADD-PATH (Advertisement of Multiple Paths in BGP)
gaps.why: The solutions rely on and specify use of ADD-PATH (RFC 7911) capability procedures for route reflectors and confederation ASBRs. The taxonomy has no ADD-PATH tag; BGP is the closest parent.

gaps.name: MED-induced persistent route oscillation
gaps.why: The core subject is the persistent IBGP route oscillation problem (RFC 3345) and its fix, which no taxonomy tag names directly.

RFC7965.title: LDP Extensions for Pseudowire Binding to Label Switched Path (LSP) Tunnels
RFC7965.summary: Defines an optional LDP PSN Tunnel Binding TLV and sub-TLVs, with procedures, letting single-segment and multi-segment pseudowires be bound to specific co-routed or strict TE LSP tunnels.

pseudowire.why: The document extends pseudowire signalling for SS-PW and MS-PW so each PW is bound to a particular PSN tunnel/LSP.
pseudowire.quote: This document defines an optional extension to the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) that enables the binding between PWs and the underlying Traffic Engineering (TE) tunnels.

LDP.why: It specifies a new LDP TLV, sub-TLVs, procedures in Label Mapping/Release messages, and new status codes.
LDP.quote: This document defines a new optional TLV, the PSN Tunnel Binding TLV, to communicate tunnel/LSP selection and binding requests between PEs.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE tunnels are the objects being bound to, and the document only borrows tunnel/LSP identification from RFC 3209. It does not change RSVP-TE.
It reuses MPLS-TP identifiers from RFC 6370 and cites the MPLS-TP control plane framework as motivation, but it does not specify MPLS-TP.
TE tunnels are the binding targets, and the document does not address traffic engineering itself.
MPLS is the underlying substrate. The document is about LDP and pseudowire signalling, so the more specific tags cover it.

RFC7966.title: Security at the Attribute-Value Pair (AVP) Level for Non-neighboring Diameter Nodes: Scenarios and Requirements
RFC7966.summary: Informational requirements document for protecting individual Diameter AVPs between non-neighboring Diameter nodes, giving threats, deployment scenarios, and eight solution requirements.

Diameter.why: The whole document is about securing Diameter AVPs beyond hop-by-hop protection, with scenarios involving Diameter proxies, relays, clients and servers.
Diameter.quote: This document specifies requirements for developing a solution to protect Diameter AVPs between non-neighboring Diameter nodes.

rejected.why: TLS/DTLS are mentioned only as the existing hop-by-hop protection in Diameter base; the document is not about TLS.
IPsec is mentioned only as an alternative hop-by-hop mechanism.
CMS is only referenced as the basis of an abandoned earlier draft, not specified here.
Diameter is a more specific tag under AAA, so the AAA ancestor is implied; the AAA broker context is just the deployment setting.
Requirement #8 asks for dynamic key management but it is a single requirement, not a substantial subject of the document.
The Diameter EAP application is mentioned only as an example of sensitive AVP content.

gaps.name: Diameter AVP-level (object) security
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for message-level or object-level security of Diameter, though Diameter itself is covered.

RFC7967.title: Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) Option for No Server Response
RFC7967.summary: Defines the CoAP 'No-Response' request option, a bitmap letting a client tell the server it doesn't want responses of given classes (2.xx, 4.xx, 5.xx), with guidance on tokens, congestion control, caching, HTTP proxying and example applications.

CoAP.why: The document specifies a new CoAP option, including its number, format, values and interaction with CoAP messaging, methods, tokens and caching.
CoAP.quote: This specification introduces a CoAP option called 'No-Response'.

rejected.why: Multicast CoAP requests are used as an example scenario, but the document is not about IP multicast routing or group membership.
Section 3.2 gives brief congestion guidance for open-loop use, but it is a minor part of the document.
The HTTP-to-CoAP reverse proxy handling is a short subsection; HTTP is not the subject.
CoAP runs over UDP, which is only the substrate; the document does not address UDP usage.
The tag is already implied by the CoAP child tag, so a parent tag is not added.

RFC7968.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Using Data Labels for Tree Selection for Multi-Destination Data
RFC7968.summary: Specifies six new TRILL IS-IS APPsub-TLVs that let the highest-priority tree root restrict which VLANs, FGLs, or multicast groups may be sent on each distribution tree, shrinking multicast forwarding/pruning tables in fast-path hardware.

TRILL.why: The whole document extends the TRILL protocol with tree selection by Data Label for multi-destination frames, defining new APPsub-TLVs, processing rules, failure handling and backward compatibility.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies an optional facility to restrict the TRILL Data packets sent on particular distribution trees by VLAN, FGL, and/or multicast groups

rejected.why: Multicast groups are used as a pruning criterion, but the document is about TRILL distribution trees, not IP multicast routing or group membership.
ECMP-like tree selection is discussed as the motivating alternative whose table growth the document avoids; the document does not specify ECMP.
The new APPsub-TLVs ride in IS-IS FS-LSPs, but IS-IS is only the carrier; the document defines TRILL-specific sub-TLVs.
No VLAN tag exists in the taxonomy; VLANs are only a label used for tree selection.

gaps.name: TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a TRILL tech node under routing, but the id I used was not verified against the listed ids; the taxonomy lists it as 'TRILL' under routing, and this document is squarely about it.

RFC7969.title: Customizing DHCP Configuration on the Basis of Network Topology
RFC7969.summary: Informational RFC describing how existing DHCP servers use relay-agent and topology information (giaddr, link-address, Interface-ID, VSS, LDRA) to select subnets and supply location-specific configuration for DHCPv4 and DHCPv6.

DHCP.why: The whole document explains how DHCP servers customize configuration by client location, covering DHCPv4 relay behaviour, subnet selection and client classification.
DHCP.quote: Existing DHCP server implementations do in fact provide such capabilities; the goal of this document is to describe those capabilities

DHCPv6.why: A substantial part covers DHCPv6-specific link identification (link-address, Interface-ID, LDRA, relay encapsulation) and the regional configuration example is DHCPv6.
DHCPv6.quote: The DHCPv6 protocol [RFC3315] defines two core mechanisms that allow a server to distinguish which link the relay agent is connected to.

rejected.why: JSON is only the notation for hypothetical server configuration examples, not a subject of the document.
DNS server addresses are merely example option values, and the server resolves names for them. The document is not about DNS.
Subnet and prefix selection are discussed only as part of DHCP behaviour, not as address architecture.
Cable modems appear only as a use case for client classification.

RFC7970.title: The Incident Object Description Exchange Format Version 2
RFC7970.summary: RFC 7970 specifies IODEF version 2, an XML-schema-based information and data model for exchanging security incident reports and indicators between CSIRTs, obsoleting RFC 5070 and 6685.

IODEF.why: The document defines IODEF v2 itself.
IODEF.quote: The Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) is a format for representing computer security information commonly exchanged between Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs)

rejected.why: XML Schema is the encoding substrate for the data model, not the subject.
Parent of IODEF, which is implied by the more specific tag.
ds:Signature and DigestValue are only reused inside the Hash and Signature classes.
The registries are boilerplate-like apparatus and not the main subject.
DomainData and Nameservers only describe domains as observables.
CertificateData only wraps certificates as indicators.

RFC7971.title: Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) Deployment Considerations
RFC7971.summary: Informational RFC giving deployment guidance for ALTO (Application-Layer Traffic Optimization): entity placement, ISP objectives, generating network/cost maps, monitoring, security, and use cases for P2P, CDNs, VPNs and caching.

ALTO.why: The whole document is about deploying ALTO: server/client placement, map generation, services to use, monitoring and security.
ALTO.quote: This memo discusses deployment-related issues of ALTO.

P2P.why: A full section covers ALTO for P2P traffic optimization, including tracker and peer ALTO-client placement.
P2P.quote: Originally, P2P applications were the main driver for the development of ALTO.

CDN.why: A full section covers ALTO use for CDN request routing and surrogate selection.
CDN.quote: This section briefly introduces the usage of ALTO for CDNs

rejected.why: ALTO runs over HTTP, but the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
BGP is only a topology data source for the ALTO server (and RFC 7752 is mentioned); not the subject.
Provider VPNs are a brief use-case subsection (6.1), not a main subject.
JSON is only the encoding for ALTO maps.
Application-level traffic localization is discussed, but it is an ALTO objective rather than network traffic engineering mechanisms.
Only mentioned as a possible data source and not discussed further.

RFC7972.title: Entertainment Identifier Registry (EIDR) URN Namespace Definition
RFC7972.summary: Defines the formal URN namespace 'eidr' for Entertainment Identifier Registry identifiers (a kind of DOI Name) for audiovisual works, obsoleting RFC 7302 with an updated https resolution URI.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration for 'eidr', with syntax, lexical equivalence, resolution and persistence rules per RFC 3406. URN pages are where readers would look for it.
URN.quote: This document defines the formal Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace Identifier (NID) for EIDR Identifiers.

rejected.why: Resolution uses an HTTP GET to doi.org, but HTTP is only the substrate and nothing new is defined about it.
DOI is built on the Handle System, but the document never mentions it and only specifies the URN namespace.
ABNF is used only as notation for the syntax definition; the document is not about ABNF.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-level; the document is about the namespace definition itself, not IANA registry guidance.
The resolution service returns an XML Schema instance document, but this is incidental and the document does not specify XML usage.

gaps.name: DOI (Digital Object Identifier) system
gaps.why: EIDR Identifiers are DOI Names under ISO 26324, and the document is substantially about this relationship. The taxonomy has no tag for DOI or persistent identifiers other than the Handle System.

RFC7973.title: Assignment of an Ethertype for IPv6 with Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (LoWPAN) Encapsulation
RFC7973.summary: Reports IEEE's assignment of Ethertype 0xA0ED for IPv6 datagrams using LoWPAN encapsulation (RFC 4944) so Layer 2 technologies like Ethernet and IEEE 802.15.9 can dispatch them, and records it in the IANA registry.

6LoWPAN.why: The whole document concerns identifying LoWPAN-encapsulated IPv6 datagrams with a dedicated Ethertype. Readers of 6LoWPAN would want it.
6LoWPAN.quote: IPv6 datagrams using Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (LoWPAN) encapsulation as defined in RFC 4944 must be identified so the receiver can correctly interpret

Ethernet.why: The document is about an Ethertype assignment, which is protocol dispatch at Layer 2 over Ethernet and other Ethertype-based link technologies.
Ethernet.quote: IEEE has responded with the assignment of Ethertype 0xA0ED for this purpose.
Ethernet.section: 2. Assignment of an Ethertype by IEEE

rejected.why: IPv6 is the payload being encapsulated. The document specifies nothing new about IPv6 itself.
The IANA registry entry is boilerplate-level action for the Ethertype. The document is not about IANA guidance or stewardship.
HaLow is mentioned only as one possible future user of the Ethertype.

RFC7974.title: An Experimental TCP Option for Host Identification
RFC7974.summary: Describes the experimental TCP HOST_ID option (kind 253, ExID 0x0348) that address-sharing devices such as CGNs and proxies insert to reveal a host identifier to receivers, with its values, interactions with other TCP options, and privacy and pervasive-monitoring considerations.

TCP.why: The document specifies a new experimental TCP option and its interaction with MPTCP, TCP-AO and TFO, so it is a TCP extension.
TCP.quote: This memo describes the design, deployment, and privacy considerations for one such solution in operational use on the Internet today that uses a TCP option to transmit a host identifier.

CGN.why: Carrier-grade NAT and address-sharing is the central use case, and the option is inserted by CGNs to counter host-identification problems.
CGN.quote: a CGN allows multiple hosts connected to the public Internet to share a single Internet routable IPv4 address.

privacy.why: Substantial privacy and pervasive-monitoring analysis of the option, including constraints on permissible HOST_ID values.
privacy.quote: The HOST_ID TCP option removes that increased anonymity, taking information that was already visible in TCP packets

rejected.why: CGN is the more specific tag for the address-sharing devices discussed; NAT is only the context.
Only discussed as an option-space interaction in one subsection, not the subject of the document.
The IANA section only registers the ExID; that is boilerplate.
IPv6 is mentioned only incidentally, for example in the 64-bit prefix analogy.

RFC7975.title: Request Routing Redirection Interface for Content Delivery Network (CDN) Interconnection
RFC7975.summary: Defines the CDNI Request Routing Redirection Interface, an HTTP/JSON interface by which an upstream CDN asks a downstream CDN how to redirect a user request (via DNS or HTTP redirection), including cacheability, scope, errors and loop prevention.

CDN.why: The whole document specifies a CDN interconnection interface for request routing redirection between upstream and downstream CDNs.
CDN.quote: This document describes an interface for the latter part, i.e., the CDNI Request Routing Redirection interface.

HTTP APIs.why: Defines an HTTP POST/JSON API with request/response dictionaries, error codes and cacheability conventions, which is a convention for building an API on HTTP.
HTTP APIs.quote: This document defines a simple interface for the Redirection interface based on HTTP [RFC7230], where the attributes of a User Agent's requests are encapsulated

rejected.why: DNS redirection is one mode carried in the JSON payload; the document doesn't specify DNS protocol behaviour itself.
HTTP is the substrate for the interface and the redirection mechanism being described; no HTTP semantics are defined or extended.
JSON is only the encoding of the messages.
TLS is required for transport protection but nothing new about it is defined.
Uses application/cdni with new payload types, but the media type registration is in RFC 7736; IANA registrations here are boilerplate-like.
Cache-Control is used to make RI responses reusable, but the document doesn't define HTTP caching.

gaps.name: CDNI (Content Delivery Network Interconnection) request routing
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only a general CDN tag; there's no specific tag for the CDNI interfaces (request routing, metadata, control, logging).

RFC7976.title: Updates to Private Header (P-Header) Extension Usage in Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Requests and Responses
RFC7976.summary: Informational RFC updating RFC 7315 to change which SIP methods and responses may carry the 3GPP P-headers (P-Access-Network-Info, P-Charging-Vector, P-Called-Party-ID, etc.) and to fix misalignments left from RFC 3455.

SIP.why: The document revises where SIP P-header extension fields may appear in SIP requests and responses, a SIP extension usage update.
SIP.quote: need to be included in SIP requests and responses currently not allowed according to RFC 7315

rejected.why: The 3GPP IMS use cases motivate the changes, but the document specifies SIP header usage, not IP over 3GPP networks.
SDP is mentioned only as the trigger for bearer modification in a use case; the document does not address it.
No IANA actions; the document only modifies the text of RFC 7315 Section 5.7.

RFC7977.title: The WebSocket Protocol as a Transport for the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP)
RFC7977.summary: Defines a new WebSocket subprotocol ("msrp") and "ws" MSRP URI transport so MSRP clients (e.g., browser JavaScript) can reach MSRP relays over secure WebSocket, updating RFC 4975 and RFC 4976.

MSRP.why: The document extends MSRP and its relay specification with a new transport, URI parameter and authentication rules, and updates RFCs 4975 and 4976.
MSRP.quote: This document specifies a new WebSocket subprotocol as a reliable transport mechanism between Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP) clients and relays

WebSocket.why: It specifies a new WebSocket subprotocol: handshake, framing of MSRP chunks, keepalive via Ping, and IANA registration of the subprotocol name.
WebSocket.quote: This specification defines a new WebSocket subprotocol (as defined in Section 1.9 in [RFC6455]) for transporting MSRP messages

rejected.why: HTTP is only the handshake substrate for WebSocket; authentication via Cookie/Digest is referenced but nothing new is defined for HTTP.
TLS is required for WSS but only used as a security mechanism, with no new TLS extension.
The document explicitly defines no new SDP transport and only shows SDP in examples.
SIP appears only as the context carrying the SDP in examples.
Digest authentication is used per RFC 4976; the document does not define or extend the scheme.
Cookies are mentioned only as one way to authorize the WebSocket handshake.

RFC7978.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): RBridge Channel Header Extension
RFC7978.summary: RFC 7978 extends the TRILL RBridge Channel header (updating RFC 7178) with an Extended RBridge Channel protocol that tunnels Ethertype-identified payloads and adds security types (IS-IS CRYPTO_AUTH, DTLS pairwise, composite) for RBridge Channel messages.

TRILL.why: The document extends the RBridge Channel facility of the TRILL protocol, defining new header fields, payload types, security types and error codes for TRILL switches.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies extensions to the RBridge Channel protocol header to support two features

DTLS.why: A substantial section defines how DTLS is used to secure Extended RBridge Channel messages, including PSK handling and record sizing.
DTLS.quote: The RBridge Channel Extended Header DTLS Pairwise SType uses a negotiated DTLS version that MUST NOT be less than 1.2.

rejected.why: IS-IS is used for CRYPTO_AUTH keying material and as a tunneled payload, but the document is not about IS-IS itself.
BFD is mentioned only as an example payload of RBridge Channel; this document does not specify it.
IANA registries are created, but only as boilerplate IANA Considerations.
HKDF is used only for deriving keying material; not a subject of the document.
Ethernet frames are a payload type, but the document is about TRILL's channel mechanism, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.

gaps.name: TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) / RBridge Channel
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a TRILL tag in the routing section but I could not confirm exact id; if absent, the document's central subject has no fitting tag.

RFC7979.title: Response to the IANA Stewardship Transition Coordination Group (ICG) Request for Proposals on the IANA Protocol Parameters Registries
RFC7979.summary: The IETF's formal response to the ICG's RFP for the IANA stewardship transition, describing how the IANA protocol parameters registries are used, overseen (IAB, IAOC, RFC 2860 MoU/SLA), and proposing no structural change after NTIA oversight ends.

IANA.why: The whole document concerns stewardship, oversight, and operation of the IANA protocol parameters registries and the post-NTIA arrangements.
IANA.quote: The IETF uses the IANA protocol parameters registries to store this information in a public location.

IETF process.why: Substantial parts describe IETF policy development, consensus, appeals, and the IAB/IAOC/IESG oversight roles for the registries.
IETF process.quote: Most disputes are handled at the lowest level through the working group and rough consensus processes.

rejected.why: DNS, .ARPA and special-use names are mentioned only as points of coordination with ICANN, not specified or analysed.
RFC 6761 registries are cited as an overlap area with ICANN; the document is not about them.
IP address and AS number delegation to RIRs is mentioned as interdependency only.
Parent topic; the more specific IANA tag fits.
NomCom is mentioned briefly as how IAB members are selected; not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: IANA stewardship transition (NTIA/ICANN/ICG)
gaps.why: The IANA tag covers registries, but the transition of oversight from NTIA is a distinct governance subject without a dedicated tag.

RFC7980.title: A Framework for Defining Network Complexity
RFC7980.summary: An IRTF NCRG summary framework for defining and analysing network complexity, covering trade-offs (control-plane state vs stretch, failure domains, QoS policy placement, reactivity vs stability), parameters, elements, location, dependencies, and management interactions.

network management.why: The document is a framework for understanding network complexity in design and operations, including configuration, troubleshooting and monitoring complexity. This fits network operations and management, and no more specific tag exists.
network management.quote: there is a desire to better understand the complexity of a network as a whole, as deployed today to provide Internet services

rejected.why: Routing aggregation, stretch and failure domains are used as trade-off examples. The document is about complexity in general, not routing architecture.
Marking and PHBs appear only as one trade-off illustration in Section 3.3.
OSPF is mentioned only as an example of a distributed routing algorithm.
BGP is mentioned only in passing, as a route reflector example.
AAA is used only as an example of a network-external dependency.
The document touches on layering and architectural guidance, but its focus is network complexity in operations and design.

gaps.name: network complexity
gaps.why: The whole document is about defining and measuring network complexity as a research and design topic. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so network management is the nearest fit.

RFC7981.title: IS-IS Extensions for Advertising Router Information
RFC7981.summary: Defines the IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV (type 242), carrying sub-TLVs, with flooding scope flags, leaking rules, and router ID handling, obsoleting RFC 4971.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with a new TLV for advertising router capabilities, including flooding and leaking procedures between levels.
IS-IS.quote: This document defines a new optional Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) TLV named CAPABILITY, formed of multiple sub-TLVs

rejected.why: TE examples are only illustrations; the document says the mechanism is generic and not limited to MPLS TE.
MPLS TE LSPs appear only as motivating examples, not as the subject.
PCE discovery is mentioned only as a possible future use, to be discussed in the PCE WG.
IPv6-only router ID handling is a small change within the TLV; the document is about IS-IS, not IPv6.

RFC7982.title: Measurement of Round-Trip Time and Fractional Loss Using Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)
RFC7982.summary: Defines a new STUN attribute, TRANSACTION_TRANSMIT_COUNTER, that counts request and response transmissions so a client can measure RTT and get a hint of fractional loss direction, usable with ICE checks and TURN Allocate.

STUN.why: The document extends STUN with a new attribute and updates the STUN retransmission rule that retransmits are bit-wise identical.
STUN.quote: This document defines a new comprehension-optional STUN attribute TRANSACTION_TRANSMIT_COUNTER with a STUN Type 0x8025.

performance measurement.why: The purpose is measuring path RTT and loss, so readers of performance measurement would want it.
performance measurement.quote: This document describes a mechanism for an endpoint to measure the path characteristics fractional loss and RTT

ICE.why: The measurements are motivated by ICE candidate pair selection and are used in ICE connectivity checks. How ICE uses them is out of scope, so this is secondary.
ICE.quote: can be used by the controlling agent to influence the ICE candidate pair selection.

rejected.why: TURN Allocate requests can carry the attribute, but this is a secondary use and the document does not specify or extend TURN.
The STUN tag already sits under NAT traversal, so the parent is implied.
UDP is only the transport underneath STUN and the document says nothing new about it.
DTLS appears only in Security Considerations as a way to protect TURN exchanges.

RFC7983.title: Multiplexing Scheme Updates for Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) Extension for Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS)
RFC7983.summary: RFC 7983 updates RFC 5764's demultiplexing of DTLS, SRTP/RTP/RTCP, STUN, ZRTP and TURN channel packets on a single socket, fixing four issues and amending the IANA registries for STUN methods and TLS ContentTypes.

SRTP.why: The document updates the DTLS-SRTP (RFC 5764) demultiplexing scheme, which is the core of SRTP keying via DTLS and RTP/RTCP multiplexing.
SRTP.quote: This document defines how Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS), Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP), RTP Control Protocol (RTCP), Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN), Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN), and ZRTP packets are multiplexed

STUN.why: A whole section and an IANA registry change cover STUN method codepoint ranges and their impact on multiplexing.
STUN.quote: It implicitly allocated codepoints for new STUN methods without an IANA registry reflecting these new allocations.

TURN.why: A section is devoted to TURN channel packets and reserving the channel number range for demultiplexing.
TURN.quote: this document modifies the demultiplexing algorithm in RFC 5764 to properly account for TURN channels by allocating the values from 64 to 79

DTLS.why: Constrains TLS ContentType codepoints so DTLS can be demultiplexed from other protocols.
DTLS.quote: if the value of the first byte is between 20 and 63 (inclusive), then the packet is identified to be DTLS.
DTLS.section: 5. Implicit Allocation of New Codepoints for TLS ContentTypes

rejected.why: ICE is only mentioned as the context in which TURN-relayed packets arrive; nothing is specified about it.
RTP/RTCP is one of the multiplexed protocols but is not specified or extended; SRTP is the closer fit.
The TLS ContentType registry is annotated, but this is DTLS demultiplexing, so DTLS is the better fit.
IANA registry changes are boilerplate-like consequences of the multiplexing update, not the document's subject.
The parent is implied by the STUN and TURN tags, and the document is not about NAT traversal in its own right.

gaps.name: ZRTP
gaps.why: The document adds ZRTP to the demultiplexing scheme (first byte 16-19), but the taxonomy has no ZRTP tag.

RFC7984.title: Locating Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Servers in a Dual-Stack IP Network
RFC7984.summary: Updates RFC 3263 DNS-based SIP server location for dual-stack clients (look up all address families, express IPv4/IPv6 preference via SRV priorities, and clarify interaction with RFC 6724 address ordering) in preparation for Happy Eyeballs for SIP.

SIP.why: The document updates the SIP server location procedures (RFC 3263) for dual-stack SIP clients, so it is about SIP deployment and behaviour.
SIP.quote: This document updates the DNS lookup procedures of RFC 3263 [RFC3263] in preparation for the specification of the application of Happy Eyeballs to SIP.

happy eyeballs.why: The whole document prepares for applying Happy Eyeballs to SIP and explains why SIP cannot race connections, which is dual-stack connection-racing subject matter.
happy eyeballs.quote: Happy Eyeballs [RFC6555] documents that looking up the "A or AAAA record" is not an effective practice for dual-stack clients
happy eyeballs.section: 3.1. Dual-Stack SIP UA DNS Record Lookup Procedure

rejected.why: DNS A/AAAA/SRV lookups are used as the mechanism, but the document specifies no new DNS behaviour or record types; it is about SIP server location.
Address selection ordering (RFC 6724) is clarified, but it is not the main subject.
SRV-based SIP server location is service discovery in a broad sense, but the document focuses on dual-stack address handling and SIP specifically.
The document concerns dual-stack coexistence, not the IPv6 specification itself.

RFC7985.title: Security Threats to Simplified Multicast Forwarding (SMF)
RFC7985.summary: Informational threat analysis of Simplified Multicast Forwarding (SMF) for MANETs, covering attacks on duplicate packet detection and relay set selection (E-CDS, S-MPR, MPR-CDS), and updating RFC 7186 on NHDP-based RSS threats.

MANET.why: The document analyses security threats to SMF, a MANET multicast forwarding protocol, including relay set selection algorithms (MPR, CDS) and NHDP-dependent threats. The MANET tag is the closest fit.
MANET.quote: SMF aims at providing basic Internet Protocol (IP) multicast forwarding in a way that is suitable for wireless mesh and Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANET).

NHDP.why: The document updates RFC 7186 on NHDP threats to relay set selection. Relay set selection threats are described as NHDP-specific.
NHDP.quote: If NHDP is used for both 1-hop and 2-hop neighborhood discovery by SMF, SMF implicitly inherits the vulnerabilities of NHDP discussed in [RFC7186].

rejected.why: SMF is a multicast forwarding protocol, but the document is a security threat analysis centred on MANET. The multicast parent tag is not needed beyond the MANET tag.
The document is about attacks on routing-like forwarding mechanisms, but its focus is the MANET protocol itself. It does not cover routing security mechanisms such as RPKI or BGPsec.
OLSR and its MPR mechanism are mentioned only as the source of the S-MPR algorithm. The document does not address OLSR itself.
IPsec is mentioned only as an assumed-absent mechanism and as a comparison for how TTL is handled in integrity checks.

gaps.name: Simplified Multicast Forwarding (SMF)
gaps.why: The document is about SMF (RFC 6621), but the taxonomy has no SMF tag. MANET and multicast are the nearest, and neither is specific.

RFC7986.title: New Properties for iCalendar
RFC7986.summary: RFC 7986 defines new iCalendar properties (NAME, REFRESH-INTERVAL, SOURCE, COLOR, IMAGE, CONFERENCE) and parameters (DISPLAY, EMAIL, FEATURE, LABEL), and extends several existing RFC 5545 properties to the whole VCALENDAR object.

iCalendar.why: The whole document extends the iCalendar data format with new properties, parameters and registries, and updates RFC 5545.
iCalendar.quote: This document defines a set of new properties for iCalendar data and extends the use of some existing properties to the entire iCalendar object.

rejected.why: UUIDs are only recommended as a way to generate UID values; the document is not about UUIDs themselves.
sip: URIs are only mentioned as example values for CONFERENCE.
tel: URIs only appear as example CONFERENCE values; the document does not specify them.
CONFERENCE is just a pointer property for access info; it does not define a conferencing framework.
Not a taxonomy id; iTIP is only referenced as context.
ABNF is only the notation used to define syntax.

RFC7987.title: IS-IS Minimum Remaining Lifetime
RFC7987.summary: Standards Track update to IS-IS that sets a received LSP's Remaining Lifetime to MaxAge when it is lower, preventing premature purges from corrupted lifetimes, and recommends reporting suspected corruption.

IS-IS.why: The document modifies IS-IS LSP database handling on receipt of newer LSPs, so it extends the IS-IS protocol.
IS-IS.quote: An additional action is defined by this document: vi. If the Remaining Lifetime of the new LSP is less than MaxAge, it is set to MaxAge.

rejected.why: The corruption/DoS motivation is mentioned, but the document is a protocol robustness fix to IS-IS, not about securing routing infrastructure in general.
The checksum's exclusion of Remaining Lifetime is the background to the problem, but the document does not specify or change any checksum.
The document touches on denial-of-service, but only as a side benefit of the protocol change, not as operational practice.

RFC7988.title: Ingress Replication Tunnels in Multicast VPN
RFC7988.summary: RFC 7988 clarifies and updates RFC 6513/6514 by specifying how Ingress Replication P-tunnels in BGP/MPLS Multicast VPN are identified, joined, pruned, label-allocated, and timer-managed.

MVPN.why: The whole document specifies how MVPN protocol elements (PTA, A-D routes, Leaf A-D routes) apply to Ingress Replication P-tunnels, updating RFC 6513 and 6514.
MVPN.quote: it makes n individual copies, and then unicasts each copy, through an IP or MPLS unicast tunnel, to exactly one child node.

rejected.why: BGP A-D routes and path attributes are the signalling vehicle, but the document is about MVPN P-tunnel procedures, not BGP itself.
MPLS labels and LSPs are used as the unicast tunnel and label mechanism, but the document does not specify MPLS; it is about MVPN.
MVPN is a child of VPN, a sibling of L3VPN; the document concerns multicast in these VPNs, which MVPN covers more specifically.
LDP and RSVP-TE are mentioned only as possible setup protocols for the underlying unicast tunnels.
The ancestor is implied by the MVPN tag, and the document is specific to MVPN.

RFC7989.title: End-to-End Session Identification in IP-Based Multimedia Communication Networks
RFC7989.summary: Defines the SIP Session-ID header field, an end-to-end session identifier made of two UUIDs, with endpoint, intermediary, conferencing and backwards-compatibility rules; obsoletes RFC 7329.

SIP.why: The document specifies a new SIP header field (Session-ID), its syntax, endpoint and intermediary (B2BUA/proxy) procedures, and SIP call flows.
SIP.quote: While the identifier is intended to work across multiple protocols, this document describes its usage in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP).

UUID.why: The identifier is built from UUIDs. The document specifies which versions to use (4 or 5), a namespace ID and the name for version 5 UUIDs, and the nil UUID.
UUID.quote: The session identifier comprises two UUIDs [RFC4122], with each UUID representing one of the endpoints participating in the session.

conferencing.why: A substantial part covers associating endpoints in a multipoint conference and cascaded MCUs. Readers of conferencing would want it.
conferencing.quote: MCUs, including cascaded MCUs, MUST utilize the same UUID value ("local-uuid" portion of the Session-ID header field value) with all participants in the conference.

rejected.why: Mentioned only for interworking and H.460.27. The document defines the SIP usage only.
Appears only as media in the example call flows.
The Session-ID is not carried in SDP. SDP is only mentioned in the example messages.
Used only as the notation for the header syntax.
The conferencing framework is cited only for the focus and isfocus parameter, not specified here.
Privacy is covered in the Security and Privacy Considerations section, which counts as boilerplate for tagging. The main body does not set out to address privacy.

RFC7990.title: RFC Format Framework
RFC7990.summary: IAB framework document describing the problem statement, roadmap of companion documents, and transition plan for moving the RFC Series canonical format from plain-text ASCII to XML (xml2rfc v3) with HTML, PDF, and plain-text renderings.

RFCXML.why: The document sets out the move to xml2rfc v3 as canonical format and summarises the RFCXML vocabulary documents (RFC 7749, 7991).
RFCXML.quote: The canonical format for RFCs is XML using the xml2rfc version 3 (xml2rfc v3) vocabulary.

RFC series.why: The document is about the RFC Series publication format, its problem statement, publication formats, and transition plan.
RFC series.quote: the canonical format of the RFC Series will be transitioning from plain-text ASCII to XML using the xml2rfc version 3 vocabulary

rejected.why: XML is used as the canonical format, but the subject is the RFC-specific vocabulary, which is covered by RFCXML.
HTML is one of several publication formats summarised here, but the HTML format itself is specified in RFC 7992, not this document.
UTF-8 for plain text is mentioned as a single bullet; the details are in RFC 7994 and RFC 7997.
ASCII is the legacy format being moved away from, not a subject specified or analysed here.
The document describes the decision process for the format change and the transition, but explicitly excludes changes to stream review processes.

gaps.name: RFC publication formats (PDF/A, SVG, EPUB)
gaps.why: The document covers PDF/A-3, SVG line art and EPUB as RFC publication formats. The taxonomy has no tags for these, so they fall under RFC series.

RFC7991.title: The "xml2rfc" Version 3 Vocabulary
RFC7991.summary: Defines version 3 of the xml2rfc XML vocabulary used to write RFCs and Internet-Drafts, describing every element and attribute, deprecated v2 features, prep-tool behaviour, and the RELAX NG schema.

RFCXML.why: The document is the specification of the RFC XML vocabulary (xml2rfc v3), its elements, attributes and schema.
RFCXML.quote: This document describes version 3 ("v3") of the "xml2rfc" vocabulary: an XML-based language

media types.why: It registers the application/rfc+xml media type for the format, which readers of media type registrations would want.
media types.quote: This document updates the specification for the Internet Media Type "application/rfc+xml" from the one in [RFC7749].

rejected.why: XML is the substrate for the vocabulary. The document defines an XML language but nothing about XML itself.
The vocabulary serves RFC production, but RFCXML is the more specific tag and its ancestor is implied.
ABNF is only mentioned as a possible sourcecode type. The schema is in RELAX NG.
Appendix A generates IPR boilerplate through the ipr attribute. It is an apparatus detail rather than the subject.
URIs appear in attributes such as eref/@target and artwork/@src, but the document does not specify them.

RFC7992.title: HTML Format for RFCs
RFC7992.summary: RFC 7992 defines the strict HTML subset and the XML-to-HTML rendering rules for publishing RFCs and Internet-Drafts in HTML, as one of the new RFC Series publication formats.

RFC series.why: The document specifies a publication format for the RFC Series, as part of the RFC format changes. Readers of the RFC Series subject would want it.
RFC series.quote: This document describes the HTML format that will be used as one of the publication formats for the RFC Series.

HTML.why: It defines a profile of HTML5 and the HTML output for each xml2rfc element, including doctype, head metadata, pilcrows, and ToC.
HTML.quote: It defines a strict subset of HTML appropriate for RFC Series documents.

RFCXML.why: Most of the body maps each RFCXML (v3 vocabulary) element to HTML. Readers of the XML vocabulary need this rendering definition.
RFCXML.quote: This section describes how each of the XML elements from [RFC7991] is rendered to HTML.

rejected.why: Section 2.1 lists accessibility requirements, but it is a short part of the document, not a main subject.
XML is the canonical source format being rendered from. The document is about the HTML output, not XML usage.
The document only requires UTF-8 output encoding and cites RFC 3629 for it.
It only requires the lang attribute to be 'en', per RFC 5646.
The document covers an HTML document format, which the more specific HTML tag already covers.
The document mentions mailto:, tel: and data: URIs only in passing when rendering elements.

gaps.name: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets)
gaps.why: The HTML format relies on embedded and local CSS for its layout, and the CSS is described in the companion RFC 7993. The taxonomy has no tag for stylesheets.

RFC7993.title: Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) Requirements for RFCs
RFC7993.summary: Informational IAB document specifying requirements for the default CSS embedded in the RFC Editor's HTML format for RFCs, covering layout, fonts, printing, lists, accessibility and per-class styling.

RFC series.why: The document defines presentation requirements for the RFC Series' published HTML format, so it belongs under the RFC series subject (format, style, publication).
RFC series.quote: This document describes the requirements for the default CSS used by the RFC Editor.

HTML.why: The CSS styles the semantic HTML of RFCs, with class names drawn from the HTML for RFCs vocabulary; readers of HTML format material would want it.
HTML.quote: The HTML format for RFCs, described in [RFC7992], assigns style guidance to a Cascading Style Sheet (CSS) specifically defined for the RFC Series.

rejected.why: Accessibility is a stated design goal and a general requirement, but only a minor part of the document; the main body is the CSS class and layout requirements.
The classes derive from the RFC XML vocabulary via RFC 7992, but this document does not specify the XML vocabulary itself.
