Only one bullet mentions a broad range of internationalized scripts and Unicode font support; this is not a substantial focus.

gaps.name: Cascading Style Sheets (CSS)
gaps.why: The document is about CSS styling requirements, but the taxonomy has no CSS or web styling tag. The closest fits are web or HTML, which cover it only loosely.

RFC7994.title: Requirements for Plain-Text RFCs
RFC7994.summary: RFC 7994 sets out the rendering requirements for the plain-text publication format of RFCs generated from xml2rfc v3 XML, covering character encoding, artwork, page layout, line width and table of contents.

RFC series.why: The document defines format and layout requirements for RFC publication (line width, pagination, headers/footers, ToC), which is squarely RFC series format and style.
RFC series.quote: This document outlines the rendering requirements for the plain-text RFC publication format.

UTF-8.why: A dedicated section specifies UTF-8 as the encoding of plain-text RFCs, with a BOM and limited non-ASCII use, which UTF-8 readers would want.
UTF-8.quote: Plain-text files for RFCs will use the UTF-8 [RFC3629] character encoding.

rejected.why: The document relies on the xml2rfc v3 vocabulary as input to the renderer but does not define or extend it; that is RFC 7991.
ASCII art and ASCII equivalents are mentioned, but the document moves away from ASCII-only text rather than being about ASCII.
XML is the canonical source format only; the document is about the plain-text rendering, not XML usage.
Unicode is cited for a definition of plain text, and non-ASCII policy is delegated to RFC 7997, so the document is not about Unicode usage.
Encoding is covered by one brief section; UTF-8 is the more specific fit and no character set registration is involved.

RFC7995.title: PDF Format for RFCs
RFC7995.summary: IAB informational RFC discussing options and requirements for the PDF rendering of RFCs and Internet-Drafts (PDF/A-3, PDF/UA, layout, metadata, embedded files, signatures) and related tooling.

RFC series.why: The document specifies the PDF publication format for RFCs produced by the RFC Editor, which is about RFC Series format and publication.
RFC series.quote: This document discusses options and requirements for the PDF rendering of RFCs in the RFC Series, as outlined in RFC 6949.

rejected.why: The PDF is rendered from the xml2rfc XML, but the document specifies PDF output, not the XML vocabulary (that is RFC 7991).
PDF/UA, alt-text and screen-reader concerns appear, but as one part of PDF requirements; the document is not about accessibility in its own right.
HTML rendering is referenced only as a model for the PDF look, and is specified in RFC 7992.
The application/pdf media type is cited only in references and is not defined here.
Unicode mapping of PDF text is discussed briefly, but this is not about Unicode usage in protocols.
Mentions Internet-Draft submission handling, but the focus is the document format, not the standards process.

gaps.name: PDF (Portable Document Format), PDF/A, PDF/UA
gaps.why: The document is about the PDF file format and its profiles, and the taxonomy has no tag for document-publishing formats like PDF.

RFC7996.title: SVG Drawings for RFCs: SVG 1.2 RFC
RFC7996.summary: Defines SVG 1.2 RFC, a restricted SVG Tiny 1.2 profile (with a RELAX NG Compact schema) for line-art diagrams in RFCs, and discusses creating such drawings and their accessibility.

RFC series.why: The document specifies the graphics format for RFCs as part of the RFC format changes (RFC 6949), so it belongs under the RFC Series format and publication subject.
RFC series.quote: This document defines SVG 1.2 RFC, an SVG profile (i.e., a subset of SVG) that is suitable for RFC line drawings.

XML.why: SVG is an XML-based format, and the document's core is an XML schema (RELAX NG) defining the allowed elements and attributes of an XML vocabulary.
XML.quote: Appendix A (below) provides a complete RELAX NG Compact (RNC) schema [RNG-HOME] for SVG 1.2 RFC.
XML.section: 2. SVG 1.2 RFC: An SVG Profile for RFCs

accessibility.why: A dedicated section covers making diagrams accessible via title/desc/role and ARIA, and accessibility is a stated design motive for the profile.
accessibility.quote: One of the long-term goals for RFCs is to make them more accessible, e.g., to sight-impaired readers.

rejected.why: The document only mentions xml2rfc v3 as the tool that will include SVG. It does not define the RFC XML vocabulary, which is RFC 7991.
An HTML version of the document with SVG diagrams is mentioned only in passing. The document is not about HTML.
IRIs come up only in a note that SVG links must be ASCII. This is a minor point.
SVG comes from W3C, but the document is about the RFC publication format and not web architecture.

gaps.name: SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) / vector graphics formats
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SVG or other graphics formats. The RFC-series and XML tags only partly cover the document's central subject.

RFC7997.title: The Use of Non-ASCII Characters in RFCs
RFC7997.summary: IAB/RFC Editor document updating the RFC Style Guide to allow UTF-8 and non-ASCII characters in RFCs, with rules for names, body text, tables, code, references, addresses and XML markup.

RFC series.why: The document sets RFC Editor publication requirements and updates the RFC Style Guide (RFC 7322), which is about RFC format and style.
RFC series.quote: the RFC Series must evolve to allow for the use of non-ASCII characters in RFCs.

Unicode.why: A substantial part covers how Unicode characters, code points, names and normalization forms are to be represented in documents.
Unicode.quote: the characters' Unicode code points must be used in the text.  The addition of each character name is encouraged.

UTF-8.why: The move of RFC encoding from ASCII to UTF-8 is a central decision of the document.
UTF-8.quote: RFCs will switch to supporting UTF-8 as the default character encoding

rejected.why: Parent of the chosen Unicode and UTF-8 tags, so it is implied. The document is about RFC publication rules, not protocol internationalization.
ASCII is the legacy encoding being moved away from. The document does not specify or profile it.
The 'ascii' attribute is mentioned only briefly in Section 5 and the details are deferred to RFC 7991.
RFC 7564 and RFC 7613 appear only as sources of example text, not as the subject.

RFC7998.title: "xml2rfc" Version 3 Preparation Tool Description
RFC7998.summary: IAB informational RFC describing the steps of the xml2rfc v3 "prep tool" that sanitizes, normalizes, fills in defaults, generates boilerplate and numbering, inlines external files, and finalizes XML for Internet-Drafts and canonical RFCs.

RFCXML.why: The document specifies the prep tool that processes xml2rfc v3 vocabulary XML for Internet-Drafts and RFCs, element by element and attribute by attribute. Readers of the RFCXML subject need it.
RFCXML.quote: the canonical format (the data that is the authorized, recognized, accepted, and archived version of the document) of the RFC Series has been plain text to date: it is now changing to XML

rejected.why: XML is the substrate being processed (XInclude, DTD removal). The document is about the RFC XML vocabulary tool, not XML usage in protocols generally.
The document concerns the RFC publication toolchain and format, which fits this parent topic, but RFCXML is the more specific tag and its ancestors are implied.
Copyright and TLP boilerplate insertion is mentioned only as one generated step. The document is not about IPR.
URI schemes (file:, data:, http:) appear in artwork src handling, but only incidentally.

RFC7999.title: BLACKHOLE Community
RFC7999.summary: Defines the well-known BGP community BLACKHOLE (0xFFFF029A) that lets an origin AS signal neighbours to discard traffic destined to a tagged prefix, with operational and vendor recommendations.

BGP communities.why: The document defines and registers a new well-known BGP community and specifies its semantics and handling, which is squarely the BGP communities subject.
BGP communities.quote: a well-known advisory transitive BGP community named "BLACKHOLE" allows an origin Autonomous System (AS) to specify that a neighboring network should discard any traffic

DDoS.why: The purpose of the blackhole community is DDoS mitigation by signalling neighbours to drop attack traffic, including use in RTBH configurations; readers of DDoS mitigation would want it.
DDoS.quote: Network infrastructures have been increasingly hampered by DDoS attacks.

rejected.why: BGP is the substrate; the document's specific subject is the community attribute, covered by the more specific BGP communities tag.
The document explicitly says the BLACKHOLE community is not intended to be used with Flow Specification NLRI.
Origin validation (RFC 6811) is mentioned only as something operators must not let block blackhole announcements; not a subject of the document.
Security considerations and prefix filtering advice are secondary and boilerplate-like; the document is not about securing routing.
Operational recommendations concern the blackhole mechanism itself rather than general operational security practices.
The community value registration is only the IANA Considerations section, which is boilerplate evidence.

RFC8000.title: Requirements for NFSv4 Multi-Domain Namespace Deployment
RFC8000.summary: RFC 8000 specifies requirements for deploying NFSv4 in multi-domain namespaces: unique name@domain identities, multi-domain-capable file systems, RPCSEC_GSS authentication, no AUTH_SYS or stringified UIDs, identity mapping, and resolution of authorization information.

NFS.why: The whole document concerns NFSv4 deployment constraints: name@domain identity, referrals, and multi-domain namespaces.
NFS.quote: This document presents requirements on the deployment of the NFSv4 protocols for the construction of an NFSv4 file namespace in environments with multiple NFSv4 Domains.

rejected.why: RPC security flavors (AUTH_SYS, AUTH_NONE, RPCSEC_GSS) are discussed, but only as constraints on NFSv4 deployment. The document does not specify RPC itself. It is also a child of storage alongside NFS, and NFS is the more specific fit.
RPCSEC_GSS and Kerberos are required as the authentication mechanism, but they are relied on rather than specified or extended here.
Kerberos is the example security service and a source of principals. The document is not about Kerberos itself.
LDAP is mentioned only as a typical name service for identity mapping. The document is not about it.
Section 6.1.1 only relates NFSv4 Domain names to DNS domain names. It says nothing about DNS protocol or operations.
Section 8 covers resolving authorization context, but the subject is NFSv4-specific. The NFS tag covers it.

RFC8001.title: RSVP-TE Extensions for Collecting Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) Information
RFC8001.summary: Defines RSVP-TE (including GMPLS) extensions (an Attribute Flags TLV flag and an RRO SRLG subobject) to automatically collect SRLG information for the TE link formed by an LSP, with signaling, update and policy procedures.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE with a new Attribute Flags TLV flag, a new ROUTE_RECORD SRLG subobject, and signaling procedures and error subcodes.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document provides extensions for Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE), including GMPLS, to support automatic collection of Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) information

GMPLS.why: Procedures target GMPLS TE links (H-LSPs, FAs, UNI overlay model, SRLG per RFC 4202), and a substantial part of the use case is GMPLS multi-layer/multi-domain networks.
GMPLS.quote: a Hierarchical LSP (H-LSP) or stitched LSP (S-LSP) can be used for carrying one or more other LSPs.

rejected.why: The more specific RSVP-TE and GMPLS tags fit; the parent MPLS tag is implied.
The RSVP-TE tag sits under it, so the topic tag is not given directly.
Path computation is mentioned only as the consumer of the collected SRLGs in the dual-homing use case. The document does not specify PCE or PCEP.
The document concerns SRLG-based LSP diversity, not securing routing. The Security Considerations section is boilerplate.
The IANA Considerations section only registers a flag, a subobject type and an error subcode. This is boilerplate.

gaps.name: Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG)
gaps.why: SRLG collection and diversity are the document's core subject, but the taxonomy has no SRLG or LSP-diversity tag.

RFC8002.title: Host Identity Protocol Certificates
RFC8002.summary: Specifies the HIP CERT parameter for carrying digital certificates in Host Identity Protocol control packets, the representation of HITs in X.509 v3 certificates, certificate revocation handling, and error signaling; obsoletes RFC 6253 and updates RFC 7401.

HIP.why: The document defines a new HIP parameter, its grouping rules, NOTIFY error types, and updates the HIPv2 specification (RFC 7401).
HIP.quote: This document specifies the CERT parameter, which is used to transmit digital certificates in HIP.

X.509.why: A substantial part specifies how HITs are encoded in X.509 v3 Issuer/Subject Alternative Name extensions, gives a full example certificate, and modifies revocation handling.
X.509.quote: HITs can represent an issuer, a subject, or both in X.509 v3.
X.509.section: 3. X.509 v3 Certificate Object and Host Identities

rejected.why: X.509 is the more specific tag; the document does not define PKI architecture in its own right.
LDAP URLs and DNs are only used as certificate reference encodings and are defined elsewhere.
Hash-and-URL encoding is borrowed from IKEv2, but the document is not about IKE.
HITs are formatted like IPv6 addresses via ORCHID, but the document is not about IPv6.
SPKI certificate support is only mentioned as removed; the document is not about SPKI.

RFC8003.title: Host Identity Protocol (HIP) Registration Extension
RFC8003.summary: RFC 8003 specifies the HIP Registration Extension, a generic mechanism (REG_INFO, REG_REQUEST, REG_RESPONSE, REG_FAILED parameters) by which hosts register with HIP services such as rendezvous servers or middleboxes, obsoleting RFC 5203.

HIP.why: The document defines new HIP parameters and handshake processing for registration with HIP registrars, so it is squarely about HIP.
HIP.quote: This document specifies an extension to the Host Identity Protocol (HIP) [RFC7401]. The extension provides a generic means for a host to register with a service.

rejected.why: Certificates (RFC 8002 HIP certificates) are used for requester authorization, but certificate formats and validation are out of scope; only failure types are defined.
Middleboxes and NAT state timeouts are mentioned only as motivation for lifetime baselines; the document does not address NAT behaviour.
The IANA section merely updates HIP registries; the main body is not about IANA guidance.
The document explicitly says it does not specify how to discover services or registrars.

RFC8004.title: Host Identity Protocol (HIP) Rendezvous Extension
RFC8004.summary: RFC 8004 specifies the HIP rendezvous extension, defining rendezvous servers that relay HIP base exchange I1 packets to registered, mobile or multihomed HIP nodes, with FROM, RVS_HMAC and VIA_RVS parameters; it obsoletes RFC 5204.

HIP.why: The document extends HIP with a rendezvous server mechanism, new parameters (FROM, RVS_HMAC, VIA_RVS) and modified I1/R1 processing.
HIP.quote: This document defines a rendezvous extension for the Host Identity Protocol (HIP).

rejected.why: Rendezvous helps mobile nodes be reachable, but the document specifies a HIP mechanism, not IP-layer mobility protocols.
Multihoming is mentioned as motivation only; the document does not define a multihoming architecture.
The HIP DNS record is only referenced as the place to publish the RVS address; it is defined in RFC 8005.
HMAC is used as an integrity mechanism for the RVS_HMAC parameter, not the subject of the document.
NAT and firewall traversal is explicitly declared out of scope.

RFC8005.title: Host Identity Protocol (HIP) Domain Name System (DNS) Extension
RFC8005.summary: Defines the HIP DNS resource record (type 55) for storing a node's Host Identity, HIT and rendezvous server names, and how HIP initiators use DNS lookups to find them; obsoletes RFC 5205.

HIP.why: The document extends HIP by specifying how HIs, HITs and RVS names are published and used to initiate HIP exchanges.
HIP.quote: This RR allows a HIP node to store in the DNS its Host Identity (HI), the public component of the node public-private key pair

DNS.why: It defines a new DNS RR type with wire and presentation formats, plus resolver lookup behaviour, so DNS readers need it.
DNS.quote: This document specifies a resource record (RR) for the Domain Name System (DNS) and how to use it with the Host Identity Protocol (HIP).

rejected.why: DNSSEC is only recommended as a secure channel in Security Considerations; the document doesn't specify signing or validation.
Mobility and RVS usage are motivating scenarios, but the RVS mechanism itself is in RFC 8004.
Base16 and Base64 are used only as presentation encodings for RR fields.
The IPSECKEY RR is reused for algorithm and key formats, but the document is not about IPsec.

RFC8006.title: Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI) Metadata
RFC8006.summary: Defines the CDNI Metadata interface: an object model (HostIndex, HostMatch, PathMatch, GenericMetadata, etc.) and an HTTP-based protocol by which a downstream CDN retrieves content-distribution metadata from an upstream CDN.

CDN.why: The whole document specifies CDN interconnection metadata and its retrieval interface, which is the CDN subject.
CDN.quote: The CDNI Metadata interface enables interconnected Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) to exchange content distribution metadata in order to enable content acquisition and delivery.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the transport for the metadata web service, and no HTTP extension is defined.
I-JSON is only the encoding for the metadata objects, and the document defines nothing about JSON itself.
TLS is only the security mechanism, and the document defines no new TLS behaviour.
HTTP caching is leveraged for metadata cacheability, but the Cache metadata object only controls cache keys and is not about web caching as a subject.
The application/cdni media type is used, but the registration is by reference to RFC 7736 and is incidental here.
DNS redirection and DNS hostname syntax are mentioned only in passing.

RFC8007.title: Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI) Control Interface / Triggers
RFC8007.summary: Defines the CDNI Control interface / Triggers (CI/T), an HTTP/JSON web service by which an upstream CDN asks a downstream CDN to preposition, invalidate or purge metadata/content and to monitor the status of that activity.

CDN.why: The whole document specifies a CDNI interface for triggering preposition, invalidate and purge in interconnected CDNs, so it belongs on the CDN/CDNI page.
CDN.quote: This document describes the part of the Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI) Control interface that allows a CDN to trigger activity in an interconnected CDN

rejected.why: HTTP/1.1 is the substrate: the interface uses GET/POST/DELETE, ETags and status codes, but defines no new HTTP semantics.
JSON is only the encoding of CI/T objects; the document defines no JSON format of general interest.
The document defines a REST-style API, but it is specific to CDNI rather than a general convention for HTTP APIs.
TLS is only required in the Security Considerations, as the transport security mechanism.
It registers the CDNI payload types (ci-trigger-*) for application/cdni, but that is an IANA detail, not the subject.
CDDL is used only in the non-normative appendix to formalize the JSON.

gaps.name: CDNI (Content Delivery Network Interconnection)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has the generic tag CDN, which covers CDN interconnection, but no separate CDNI-specific tag. That makes it hard to distinguish the CDNI interface documents (Metadata, Triggers, Request Routing, Logging) from other CDN topics.

RFC8008.title: Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI) Request Routing: Footprint and Capabilities Semantics
RFC8008.summary: Defines the semantics of footprint and capabilities advertisement for the CDNI Request Routing interface, a JSON-encoded base advertisement object, capability objects (delivery protocol, acquisition protocol, redirection mode, logging, metadata), and the related IANA registries.

CDN.why: The whole document specifies the CDNI footprint and capabilities advertisement interface between upstream and downstream CDNs, which is CDN interconnection.
CDN.quote: This document captures the semantics of the "Footprint and Capabilities Advertisement" part of the Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI) Request Routing interface

rejected.why: JSON and I-JSON are only the encoding for FCI objects, so this is substrate rather than subject.
HTTP appears only as a delivery and acquisition protocol value and in the security discussion of TLS transport, and the document does not specify HTTP.
TLS is mentioned only in the Security Considerations as a possible transport protection, and nothing new is defined about it.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-style registrations that support the CDNI specification, and the document is not about IANA stewardship.
CDNI Payload Types are registered, but the document does not define media types or registry rules for them.
DNS-based redirection appears only as a value in the redirection modes registry, and the document does not specify DNS.

gaps.name: CDNI (Content Delivery Network Interconnection)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a CDN tag under web, but CDNI semantics, including request routing, footprint and capabilities advertisement, and the FCI interface, are only loosely covered by it. A dedicated CDNI tag would fit this RFC and the rest of the cdni working group series better.

RFC8009.title: AES Encryption with HMAC-SHA2 for Kerberos 5
RFC8009.summary: Defines two Kerberos 5 encryption types and matching checksum types using AES in CTS mode with HMAC-SHA-256/384, including key derivation, string-to-key, and test vectors.

Kerberos.why: The document extends Kerberos 5 with new encryption and checksum types under the RFC 3961 framework, so Kerberos readers need it.
Kerberos.quote: This document defines two encryption types and two corresponding checksum types for Kerberos 5 using AES with 128-bit or 256-bit keys.

AES.why: It specifies how AES is used in CBC-CS3 mode with 128- and 256-bit keys for confidentiality, which is the core of the new enctypes.
AES.quote: we use a variation of the CBC-CS3 mode defined in [SP800-38A+], also referred to as ciphertext stealing or CTS mode.

HMAC.why: HMAC with SHA-256/384 provides integrity, the checksums and the key derivation function. A substantial part of the document specifies this use.
HMAC.quote: The HMAC is calculated over the cipher state concatenated with the AES output, instead of being calculated over the confounder and plaintext.

SHA.why: The choice of SHA-2 hashes drives the design and truncation lengths, and the algorithm rationale section discusses it.
SHA.quote: intended to support environments that desire to use SHA-256 or SHA-384 (defined in [FIPS180]) as the hash algorithm.

rejected.why: PBKDF2 is used in the string-to-key function with HMAC-SHA-2 as the PRF. It is a supporting mechanism and not what the document is about.
Passphrase-to-key derivation is a small section built on existing PBKDF2. It is not the focus of the document.
The key derivation function is part of the Kerberos cryptosystem specification and is covered by the Kerberos, AES and HMAC tags.
Randomness is mentioned only in Security Considerations as guidance, with a reference to RFC 4086.

RFC8010.title: Internet Printing Protocol/1.1: Encoding and Transport
RFC8010.summary: RFC 8010 specifies the binary encoding of IPP/1.1 operations, attributes and values into the application/ipp media type, and its transport over HTTP/HTTPS, including ipp/ipps URI mapping and security conformance requirements.

IPP.why: The document is the IPP/1.1 encoding and transport specification, obsoleting RFC 2910 and 3382.
IPP.quote: This document defines the rules for encoding IPP operations, attributes, and values into the Internet MIME media type called "application/ipp".

media types.why: The document defines and registers the application/ipp media type whose content is the encoding in Section 3.
media types.quote: IANA has updated the existing 'application/ipp' media type registration

rejected.why: HTTP is the required transport substrate; the document only specifies how IPP uses POST and headers over it, not HTTP itself.
TLS is used for security of IPP, with conformance guidance, but nothing new is defined about TLS itself.
Digest and Basic authentication are only referenced as conformance requirements for IPP, not specified here.
The ipp/ipps URI schemes are defined in RFC 3510 and RFC 7472; here only the mapping to http/https is described.
HTTP/2 is mentioned only as an optional transport layer.
ABNF is only used as the notation for the encoding syntax.

gaps.name: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP)
gaps.why: The document is entirely about IPP, and the taxonomy has an IPP tag under applications, which I used; no gap beyond that. Printing as a general topic has no broader tag.

RFC8011.title: Internet Printing Protocol/1.1: Model and Semantics
RFC8011.summary: RFC 8011 specifies the IPP/1.1 abstract model and semantics: Printer and Job objects, operations, attributes, conformance, and internationalization and security considerations for distributed printing.

IPP.why: The document defines the IPP/1.1 model, objects, operations and attributes, so IPP readers would look for it.
IPP.quote: The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) is an application-level protocol for distributed printing using Internet tools and technologies.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the transport binding, which is defined in RFC 8010 and RFC 3510; this document does not specify HTTP.
TLS is only mentioned as a channel security mechanism in the security considerations.
URIs identify Printers and Jobs, but the document defines nothing new about URIs.
The charset and natural-language attributes are part of IPP and are not a general treatment of internationalization.
Media types are used for the document-format attribute, but the document does not register or define them.

gaps.name: Internet Printing Protocol (IPP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an IPP tag in the applications section, but the tag ids in this task do not list it consistently; no other tag fits printing.

RFC8012.title: Label Switched Path (LSP) and Pseudowire (PW) Ping/Trace over MPLS Networks Using Entropy Labels (ELs)
RFC8012.summary: Extends MPLS LSP ping and traceroute multipath mechanisms (RFC 4379/6424) with a new EL FEC sub-TLV, DS flags L and E, and Multipath Information Type {10} so ECMP paths can be discovered and exercised on LSPs using entropy labels, updating RFC 6790.

MPLS.why: The document specifies MPLS data-plane OAM (LSP ping/traceroute) extensions for entropy-label LSPs and pseudowire tracing, so MPLS readers need it.
MPLS.quote: This document extends the MPLS LSP ping and traceroute multipath mechanisms in RFC 6424 to allow the ability of exercising LSPs that make use of the EL.

ECMP.why: The whole purpose is discovering and exercising ECMP paths under differing load-balancing techniques (IP-based vs. label-based), including how responders report their load-balancing behaviour.
ECMP.quote: Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switched Path (LSP) ping and traceroute are methods used to test Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) paths.

rejected.why: Pseudowire tracing is covered (Section 3), but the document is about LSP ping/trace extensions, not pseudowire emulation itself.
The document is OAM-related, but MPLS is the more specific fitting technology tag, and OAM is a topic tag that should not be added alongside it.
The generic traceroute tool tag is for path discovery tools. This document is about MPLS LSP traceroute, which falls under MPLS.
IANA registrations for the sub-TLV, DS flags and multipath type are boilerplate and not the subject.

gaps.name: MPLS LSP ping / entropy labels
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for MPLS LSP ping/traceroute (RFC 4379) or for entropy labels (RFC 6790), so the MPLS tag is used instead.

RFC8013.title: Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) Inter-FE Logical Functional Block (LFB)
RFC8013.summary: Defines the ForCES inter-FE LFB class, which carries packets and ForCES metadata between forwarding elements using a new Ethernet encapsulation (ethertype ED3E, TLV-encoded metadata), together with its XML LFB model.

ForCES.why: The document defines a new ForCES LFB class (IFE, class ID 18) and its components, ports and XML model, which is a ForCES specification.
ForCES.quote: extend the Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) Logical Functional Block (LFB) topology across Forwarding Elements (FEs) by defining the inter-FE LFB class

rejected.why: Ethernet is the transport for the inter-FE encapsulation, not the subject. The document defines a ForCES LFB and a new ethertype, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
The IPv4 router is only an illustrative use case. Nothing is specified about IPv4.
The arbitrary network function chain is an example of splitting processing across FEs. The document does not specify service function chaining or the NSH.
The LFB model is written in the ForCES XML schema, not YANG.
Security relies on MACsec, which is not in the taxonomy and appears only in Security Considerations.
EAP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a MACsec key agreement mechanism.

gaps.name: ForCES (Forwarding and Control Element Separation)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a ForCES tag only as a child of routing and no sub-tag for ForCES LFB models. The ForCES tag was used here, but the id was not verified against the list as exact; it appears in the taxonomy as 'ForCES' under routing.

RFC8014.title: An Architecture for Data-Center Network Virtualization over Layer 3 (NVO3)
RFC8014.summary: Informational architecture for data-center Network Virtualization over Layer 3 (NVO3), describing NVEs, NVAs, tenant system types, gateways, federated NVAs, and the control-protocol work areas needed.

overlay networks.why: The whole document is the architecture for data-plane network virtualization overlays: NVEs encapsulating tenant traffic across an IP underlay, with NVA control. This is the overlay networks tag.
overlay networks.quote: This document presents a high-level architecture for building data-center Network Virtualization over Layer 3 (NVO3) networks.

data center networking.why: The architecture targets data-centre scale virtualization: VM orchestration, hypervisors, ToR switches, bare metal servers, and inter-data-center NVA federation. Readers of data-center networking would want it.
data center networking.quote: Tenant Systems connect to Virtual Networks (VNs), with each VN having associated attributes defining properties of the network

rejected.why: VXLAN is only cited as one example encapsulation with a sufficiently large context ID. The document does not specify or extend it.
NVGRE is mentioned only as an example encapsulation in Section 11. The document is not about it.
L2VPN OAM is cited as prior work for OAM, and L2 VPNs appear as legacy networks reached through gateways. The document is not about L2VPN services.
BGP is only suggested as one possible NVA implementation, and BGP/AS federation is used as an analogy. The document does not specify BGP.
There is a short OAM section, but it only points to other work and does not itself address OAM mechanisms. It is not a substantial part of the document.
ARP and ND suppression gets a brief mention as an NVE optimization. It is not the subject of the document.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to protect tunnels.

gaps.name: Network virtualization overlay control plane (NVE-NVA)
gaps.why: The document's core concepts are NVE, NVA, NV Domain and the NVE-NVA protocol. The taxonomy only has data-plane overlay tags and no tag for network virtualization control-plane architecture.

RFC8015.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) Block for Independent Reporting of Burst/Gap Discard Metrics
RFC8015.summary: Defines a new RTCP XR block (BT=35) that reports burst/gap discard metrics from the receiver's de-jitter buffer independently of the burst/gap loss block, with SDP signalling and IANA registrations.

RTCP.why: The document specifies a new RTCP XR report block with its format, fields and semantics, extending RTCP reporting.
RTCP.quote: This document defines an RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) block that allows the reporting of burst/gap discard metrics

rejected.why: Only a small rtcp-xr attribute value is added (Section 5); SDP is a signalling substrate, not the subject.
The block reports metrics and follows the metrics framework, but the document is an RTCP block definition; RTCP is the more specific home.
RTP is the underlying protocol; the more specific RTCP tag covers this document.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to protect reports.
IANA registrations are boilerplate for the new block type and SDP parameter.
No payload format is defined; the document only mentions FEC and retransmission as context.

RFC8016.title: Mobility with Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN)
RFC8016.summary: RFC 8016 extends TURN with a MOBILITY-TICKET STUN attribute and a 405 error code so a client can keep its relay allocation when its IP address changes.

TURN.why: The document extends TURN Allocate and Refresh processing with a mobility ticket, so it is a TURN extension and belongs on the TURN page.
TURN.quote: This document provides such an IP address mobility solution using Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN).

rejected.why: STUN is the substrate TURN is built on. The new attribute and error code are defined for TURN allocations, and the STUN registry entries are IANA boilerplate.
ICE is mentioned only to explain the disruption the mechanism avoids. It is not specified or extended here.
The document contrasts this approach with Mobile IP, PMIPv6 and LISP. It is an application-layer TURN mechanism, not IP-layer mobility.
(D)TLS session resumption is only referenced as an existing mechanism for secure communication, and nothing new is defined for it.
AES-CBC and HMAC appear only in the non-normative example ticket construction in the appendix.
The TURN tag is more specific, and the document is about allocation mobility, not NAT traversal as such.

RFC8017.title: PKCS #1: RSA Cryptography Specifications Version 2.2
RFC8017.summary: RFC 8017 republishes PKCS #1 v2.2, specifying RSA key types, primitives, encryption schemes (RSAES-OAEP, RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5), signature schemes with appendix (RSASSA-PSS, RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5), encoding methods, and ASN.1 syntax and OIDs.

RSA.why: The whole document specifies RSA keys, primitives, encryption and signature schemes.
RSA.quote: This document provides recommendations for the implementation of public-key cryptography based on the RSA algorithm

rejected.why: ASN.1 is used to represent keys and identify schemes, but the document is about RSA, not ASN.1 itself.
SHA hash functions are supporting parameters in Appendix B, not the subject.
Mentioned only as an intended application of the key and signature OIDs.
Referenced only in a note on identifying RSASSA-PSS; not the subject.
MD2/MD5 are listed as legacy hash options for compatibility only.
Mentioned only in passing in discussion of RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 security.

RFC8018.title: PKCS #5: Password-Based Cryptography Specification Version 2.1
RFC8018.summary: RFC 8018 republishes PKCS #5 v2.1, specifying password-based key derivation functions (PBKDF1, PBKDF2), encryption schemes (PBES1, PBES2), a MAC scheme (PBMAC1), and ASN.1 syntax identifying them.

PBKDF2.why: The document specifies PBKDF2 (and PBKDF1), the iterated salted password-based key derivation function, and its ASN.1 parameters and PRF options.
PBKDF2.quote: PBKDF2 applies a pseudorandom function (see Appendix B.1 for an example) to derive keys.

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA-1/SHA-2 are used as the PRF and MAC examples but are only a supporting building block, not specified here.
AES-CBC-Pad is one example encryption scheme in an appendix; the document is not about AES.
DES is an underlying cipher for legacy PBES1; supporting detail only.
ASN.1 is the notation used for the algorithm identifiers, not the subject itself.
The parent of PBKDF2 is implied by the PBKDF2 tag, so it is not listed separately.
MD2, MD5 and SHA-1 are only hash options for legacy PBKDF1.

gaps.name: PKCS #5 password-based encryption (PBES1/PBES2) and PBMAC1
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for password-based encryption schemes or password-based MACs. PBKDF2 covers only the key derivation function, so these are only partly covered.

RFC8019.title: Protecting Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) Implementations from Distributed Denial-of-Service Attacks
RFC8019.summary: RFC 8019 gives best-practice guidance for IKEv2 responders to resist DoS and DDoS attacks, and defines a new client-puzzle mechanism (PUZZLE notification and PS payload) that extends IKEv2's cookie mechanism.

IKE.why: The document extends and profiles IKEv2. It defines a new notification type and payload for IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH, and gives responder operating guidance.
IKE.quote: This document recommends implementation and configuration best practices for Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2 (IKEv2) Responders, to allow them to resist Denial-of-Service and Distributed Denial-of-Service attacks.

DDoS.why: The document is about DDoS mitigation. It covers rate limiting, stateless cookies, client puzzles and a staged defence plan.
DDoS.quote: This document presents recommendations to help the Responder counter DoS and DDoS attacks.

rejected.why: IKE is the more specific tag and is already chosen. The document does not address ESP or AH.
Not relevant. The puzzle uses PRFs, not hash-based signatures.
IKEv2 runs over UDP, but the document says nothing new about UDP usage.
PRF-HMAC-SHA256 appears only as an example PRF for puzzles. The document is not about HMAC.
The operational advice is specific to IKEv2 responders and is covered by the DDoS tag.
The Hash and URL certificate fetching attack is a minor subsection. The document is not about certificate profiles.

RFC8020.title: NXDOMAIN: There Really Is Nothing Underneath
RFC8020.summary: RFC 8020 clarifies that a DNS NXDOMAIN response means the denied name and everything beneath it does not exist, and updates RFC 1034 and RFC 2308 so that resolvers cache negative answers for whole subtrees ("NXDOMAIN cut").

DNS.why: The document specifies recursive resolver and cache behaviour for NXDOMAIN and updates the core DNS specifications RFC 1034 and RFC 2308. It is squarely about DNS protocol behaviour.
DNS.quote: when an iterative caching DNS resolver receives an NXDOMAIN response, it SHOULD store it in its cache and then all names and resource record sets (RRsets) at or below that node SHOULD be considered unreachable

rejected.why: DNSSEC validation and NSEC/NSEC3 records are mentioned as a complement and a security rationale. The document is not about DNSSEC itself.
The DO bit is mentioned in passing when returning NSEC/NSEC3 records. The document does not specify anything about EDNS.

RFC8021.title: Generation of IPv6 Atomic Fragments Considered Harmful
RFC8021.summary: Informational RFC arguing that generation of IPv6 atomic fragments (triggered by ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages with MTU below 1280) enables DoS attacks and interoperability problems, and recommending its deprecation and that nodes ignore such PTB messages.

IPv6.why: The document is about IPv6 fragmentation behaviour and motivates removing atomic fragment generation from the core IPv6 specification (RFC 2460).
IPv6.quote: This document discusses the security implications of the generation of IPv6 atomic fragments and a number of interoperability issues associated with IPv6 atomic fragments.

ICMP.why: The attack vector and recommendations centre on ICMPv6 Packet Too Big handling, including ignoring PTB messages reporting an MTU below 1280.
ICMP.quote: If an attacker sends a forged ICMPv6 PTB error message to Host B, reporting an MTU smaller than 1280, this will trigger the generation of IPv6 atomic fragments

SIIT.why: SIIT was the only consumer of atomic fragments; Section 3 analyses its use of the Fragment Header for DF and Identification, and the recommendations target translators.
SIIT.quote: IPv4/IPv6 translators should be updated to not generate ICMPv6 PTB error messages containing an MTU value smaller than the minimum IPv6 MTU of 1280 bytes.

PMTUD.why: The document's core concern is how hosts react to PTB messages in Path MTU handling, with the recommendation incorporated into the IPv6 PMTUD update.
PMTUD.quote: IPv6 nodes should therefore be updated to ignore ICMPv6 PTB error messages reporting an MTU smaller than 1280 bytes as invalid.

rejected.why: BGP peering is only used as an example scenario of a DoS victim, not the subject.
Stateful NAT64 is mentioned only as a derivative of SIIT; the document is not about it.
ECMP appears only in one hypothetical collision scenario.
TCP connections are mentioned only as flows affected by a PTB message.
The security discussion is specific to the IPv6 fragmentation attack; the more specific IPv6 tag covers it.

gaps.name: IPv6 fragmentation / atomic fragments
gaps.why: The document is specifically about IPv6 fragmentation and atomic fragments, and the taxonomy has no fragmentation tag, so IPv6 is the nearest fit.

RFC8022.title: A YANG Data Model for Routing Management
RFC8022.summary: Specifies the core YANG routing management data model (ietf-routing, IPv4/IPv6 unicast routing modules, and an IPv6 router advertisements submodule) providing RIBs, routes, control-plane protocol framework, and static routing configuration.

YANG.why: The document is a set of YANG modules defining a routing data model, intended to be augmented by other YANG modules.
YANG.quote: Together they form the core routing data model that serves as a framework for configuring and managing a routing subsystem.

routing architecture.why: Defines generic routing framework components (routes, RIBs, control-plane protocol instances, static and direct pseudo-protocols) that routing protocol models build on.
routing architecture.quote: The core routing data model provides common building blocks for such extensions -- routes, Routing Information Bases (RIBs), and control-plane protocols.

neighbor discovery.why: The ietf-ipv6-router-advertisements submodule models IPv6 Router Advertisement parameters from RFC 4861 Neighbor Discovery.
neighbor discovery.quote: augments the configuration and state data of IPv6 interfaces with definitions of the following variables as required by Section 6.2.1 of [RFC4861]

rejected.why: Only the management protocol used to access the data; the document does not extend or specify NETCONF.
RIP appears only as an illustrative example module in Appendix C, not as a specified protocol.
IPv6 is covered by the router advertisement parameters, which are better tagged with the more specific neighbor discovery.
JSON is used only for the example data tree encoding.
IANA Considerations only register namespaces and module names; boilerplate.

RFC8023.title: Report from the Workshop and Prize on Root Causes and Mitigation of Name Collisions
RFC8023.summary: Report on the March 2014 London workshop on root causes and mitigation of DNS name collisions arising when private-namespace names collide with newly delegated gTLDs, summarizing research findings, ICANN mitigation plans and next steps.

DNS.why: The whole report concerns DNS root traffic, NXDOMAIN responses, search lists, and the effects of new TLD delegation on resolution; DNS operations and measurement are the subject.
DNS.quote: many installed systems in the Internet query the domain name system (DNS) root for names under a wide range of top- level domains (TLDs)

special-use domain names.why: Discusses reserved TLDs (RFC 2606) and special-use names (RFC 6761), plus high-risk strings .home and .corp and the 127.0.53.53 controlled-interruption address, as part of collision mitigation.
special-use domain names.quote: need to reserve name spaces that can be used for creating limited sets of internal names without fear of conflicts with current or future TLD name spaces

rejected.why: IANA/ICANN root zone administration is background only; document is not about IANA registries.
The document is indeed a workshop report, but that tag fits IAB/IRTF/community workshop reports; considered but DNS is the more precise subject. It could arguably apply, though.
Not discussed.
Internal name certificates are mentioned only as background from SAC057, not a substantial topic.

gaps.name: Name collisions / root zone scaling and new gTLD delegation
gaps.why: The core subject (namespace collisions between private and global DNS, new gTLD program risk) has no specific tag beyond general DNS.

RFC8024.title: Multi-Chassis Passive Optical Network (MC-PON) Protection in MPLS
RFC8024.summary: Defines MC-PON protection architecture in MPLS, where OLTs with trunk protection act as PEs with PW redundancy, and specifies ICCP extensions (PON Connect, Disconnect, Configuration, State TLVs) and protection procedures.

pseudowire.why: ICCP extension for PW redundancy between OLT PEs, with protection procedures using working/protection PWs and preferential forwarding status bits; no ICCP tag exists, so pseudowire is the closest fit.
pseudowire.quote: This document describes the Multi-Chassis PON (MC-PON) protection architecture in MPLS and also specifies the Inter-Chassis Communication Protocol (ICCP) extension to support it.

DSL.why: Not applicable
DSL.quote: PON is considered a viable low-cost backhaul solution for these mobile services.

rejected.why: MPLS is the general setting, but the document's specifics are PW redundancy and ICCP, which sit under pseudowire.
ICCP is defined for L2VPN PE redundancy, but this document is about PON AC redundancy over PWs, not L2VPN services.
DSL is only mentioned as another service that could use the architecture.
VCCV BFD is only mentioned as one way to detect PW faults.
LDP notification messages are used for signalling status, but the document does not specify LDP.

gaps.name: ICCP (Inter-Chassis Communication Protocol) / PON protection
gaps.why: The document extends ICCP with new TLVs for PON redundancy, but the taxonomy has no ICCP or PON tag; pseudowire is only an approximate fit.

RFC8025.title: IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (6LoWPAN) Paging Dispatch
RFC8025.summary: RFC 8025 updates RFC 4944 by defining a Paging Dispatch mechanism (16 Pages) for 6LoWPAN header compression, which lets new dispatch values be allocated beyond the saturated Page 0 encoding space.

6LoWPAN.why: The whole document specifies a new Paging Dispatch parsing-context mechanism for the 6LoWPAN adaptation layer and updates RFC 4944, so 6LoWPAN readers need it.
6LoWPAN.quote: introduce a new context switch mechanism for IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (6LoWPAN) compression, expressed in terms of Pages and signaled by a new Paging Dispatch

rejected.why: The document does create IANA registry changes (a new Page column and page-switch allocations), but these are boilerplate-like registry actions tied to the 6LoWPAN mechanism, not guidance about IANA itself.
The document is about the dispatch and paging mechanism that enables future compression formats, not a header compression scheme itself. The 6LoWPAN tag covers it, and it already sits under IoT.
IPv6 is only the payload carried by 6LoWPAN. The document does not specify IPv6 itself.

RFC8026.title: Unified IPv4-in-IPv6 Softwire Customer Premises Equipment (CPE): A DHCPv6-Based Prioritization Mechanism
RFC8026.summary: Defines the DHCPv6 OPTION_S46_PRIORITY (111) so a CPE supporting several IPv4-in-IPv6 softwire mechanisms (DS-Lite, MAP-E, MAP-T, Lightweight 4over6, DHCPv4-over-DHCPv6) can choose among those provisioned by priority order, with client/server behaviour and deployment guidance.

DHCPv6.why: The document defines a new DHCPv6 option (OPTION_S46_PRIORITY, code 111), with client and server behaviour and a new IANA registry of option codes.
DHCPv6.quote: this memo specifies a DHCPv6 option, whereby a single instance of Customer Premises Equipment (CPE) can interwork with all of the standardized and proposed approaches

softwire.why: The document is about unifying CPE behaviour across IPv4-in-IPv6 softwire mechanisms (S46) by prioritizing among them, including operator deployment guidance for multiple mechanisms.
softwire.quote: A common feature shared among all of the differing modes is the integration of softwire tunnel endpoint functionality into the Customer Premises Equipment (CPE) router.

rejected.why: DS-Lite is one of the S46 mechanisms listed in the priority registry, but the document does not specify or extend it.
MAP-E and MAP-T are only referenced as mechanisms that can be prioritized; the document does not define them.
The parent topic is implied by the softwire tag, which is a more specific fit.
The IANA section only registers the option code and creates a registry; it is boilerplate relative to the main body.
The DHCPv6 tag is more specific; the document does not address DHCPv4 apart from naming the 4o6 option code.

RFC8027.title: DNSSEC Roadblock Avoidance
RFC8027.summary: A BCP describing tests a validating resolver or host validator can run to detect DNSSEC-hostile network infrastructure (resolvers, proxies, middleboxes), how to classify resolvers, and fallback techniques to avoid those roadblocks.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document is about detecting and working around obstacles to DNSSEC validation, including tests for DO/AD bits, RRSIG, DNSKEY, DS, NSEC and NSEC3 support.
DNSSEC.quote: This document describes problems observable during DNSSEC ([RFC4034] [RFC4035]) deployment that derive from non-compliant infrastructure.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific tag and its ancestors are implied. The DNS behaviour tested (UDP, TCP, fragmentation) serves DNSSEC validation.
EDNS0 support is one of the tests, but the document does not specify or extend EDNS.
TCP availability is tested as a fallback for large DNSSEC answers. It is only the substrate and the document defines nothing new about TCP.
The document is operational guidance, but it is specific to DNSSEC deployment, so the DNSSEC tag covers it.

RFC8028.title: First-Hop Router Selection by Hosts in a Multi-Prefix Network
RFC8028.summary: RFC 8028 specifies how IPv6 hosts in multi-prefix (multihomed) networks choose a first-hop router based on which router advertised the prefix of the source address, extending RFC 4861 Neighbor Discovery behaviour and interacting with RFC 6724 source address selection.

neighbor discovery.why: The document updates RFC 4861 Neighbor Discovery: PIO interpretation, default router selection, and redirect handling are all extended.
neighbor discovery.quote: A host SHOULD NOT ignore a PIO simply because both L and A flags are cleared (extending Section 6.3.4 of [RFC4861]).

multihoming.why: The whole document addresses host behaviour in multihomed networks and hosts with multiple provider-allocated prefixes, including interaction with ingress filtering.
multihoming.quote: in a network that has more than one prefix, each allocated by an upstream network that is assumed to implement BCP 38 [RFC2827] ingress filtering

rejected.why: SLAAC is only background for how addresses are formed; the document does not specify or change it.
Only mentioned as an alternative way to assign addresses; not what the document is about.
IPv6 is implied by the more specific neighbor discovery tag; the document is not about IPv6 in general.
Shim6 is a host multihoming shim; this document does not specify or discuss it.
Source address selection (RFC 6724 Rule 5.5) is touched on, but the main topic is router selection; multihoming covers the subject better.

RFC8029.title: Detecting Multiprotocol Label Switched (MPLS) Data-Plane Failures
RFC8029.summary: RFC 8029 specifies MPLS LSP ping/traceroute: MPLS echo request and reply messages, TLVs, FEC stack validation, and procedures to detect data-plane failures and check data plane against control plane, obsoleting RFCs 4379, 6424, 6829 and 7537.

MPLS.why: The whole document specifies MPLS LSP ping/traceroute (echo request/reply, FEC stack validation, label stack handling) for MPLS data-plane failure detection.
MPLS.quote: describes a simple and efficient mechanism to detect data-plane failures in Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switched Paths (LSPs)

OAM.why: LSP ping is an OAM diagnostic tool (ping/traceroute modes for connectivity checks and fault localization), so OAM readers would want it.
OAM.quote: IPv6 RAO value (69) for MPLS OAM [RFC7506] MUST be used.

router alert.why: A dedicated section specifies how the IPv4 and IPv6 Router Alert Option is used for echo requests and replies.
router alert.quote: This document requires the use of the RAO set in an IP header in order to have the transit node process the MPLS OAM payload.

rejected.why: The traceroute mode is a feature of the LSP ping mechanism, which is tagged under MPLS; the generic traceroute tool is not what this document specifies.
ECMP is handled via Multipath Information in the DDMAP TLV, but this is one aspect, not the document's subject.
LDP FEC types are carried in the Target FEC Stack, but the document does not specify LDP itself.
Pseudowire FEC 128/129 sub-TLVs are defined, but only as FEC types to be validated, not as pseudowire specification.
UDP is only the transport substrate for echo messages.
IANA registries are created, but that is boilerplate-level apparatus for the protocol.

RFC8030.title: Generic Event Delivery Using HTTP Push
RFC8030.summary: RFC 8030 specifies the Web Push protocol, in which application servers send push messages to user agents via a push service using HTTP resources, link relations, and HTTP/2 server push, including subscriptions, TTL, urgency, topics, and delivery receipts.

web push.why: The whole document defines the Web Push protocol: subscribing, requesting delivery, receiving and acknowledging push messages, and receipts.
web push.quote: This document describes a simple protocol for the delivery of real-time events to user agents.  This scheme uses HTTP/2 server push.

HTTP/2.why: Message delivery depends on HTTP/2 server push (PUSH_PROMISE), and Section 7.5 covers concurrent stream limits; readers of HTTP/2 would find this use of server push relevant.
HTTP/2.quote: it uses HTTP/2 server push [RFC7540] to send the contents of push messages as they are sent by application servers.
HTTP/2.section: 6. Receiving Push Messages for a Subscription

HTTP.why: It defines new HTTP header fields (TTL, Urgency, Topic) and uses Prefer, status codes and resource semantics, extending HTTP.
HTTP.quote: This document defines the following HTTP header fields

rejected.why: TLS is only the required security substrate (RFC 7525 recommendations), with nothing new defined about it.
Link relations are used to identify resources, but the document is not about web linking itself; it registers URNs only for its own relation types.
It registers URN sub-namespace identifiers for link relations, but that is IANA boilerplate rather than the document's subject.
Cache-control: private and Last-Modified appear only incidentally in examples.
Privacy considerations exist but are in the Security Considerations section, which is boilerplate-like for tagging purposes.
The protocol is HTTP-based, but it is a specific protocol rather than conventions for building HTTP APIs.

RFC8031.title: Curve25519 and Curve448 for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) Key Agreement
RFC8031.summary: Defines use of Curve25519 and Curve448 (X25519/X448) as Diffie-Hellman groups 31 and 32 for ephemeral key exchange in IKEv2, including negotiation, Key Exchange payload encoding, recipient tests and a numerical example.

Curve25519.why: The document specifies the Curve25519 and Curve448 (X25519/X448) functions as key agreement groups, with a numerical example for Curve25519.
Curve25519.quote: This document describes the use of Curve25519 and Curve448 for ephemeral key exchange in the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2).

IKE.why: It extends IKEv2 with new Diffie-Hellman groups, defining negotiation values and Key Exchange payload contents, so IKE readers need it.
IKE.quote: The use of Curve25519 and Curve448 in IKEv2 is negotiated using a Transform Type 4 (Diffie-Hellman group) in the Security Association (SA) payload

rejected.why: The more specific child Curve25519 covers the curves; the parent is implied.
IKEv2 is the IPsec key management protocol, but the document is about IKE key agreement groups, not IPsec architecture, ESP or AH.
Only key agreement is covered; no signatures. NIST curves are mentioned only for comparison.
The IKE tag already sits under security and covers key exchange; the generic key management topic adds nothing specific.

RFC8032.title: Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA)
RFC8032.summary: RFC 8032 specifies the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA) and its instances Ed25519, Ed25519ctx, Ed25519ph, Ed448 and Ed448ph, with a Python reference implementation and test vectors.

EdDSA.why: The whole document specifies EdDSA and its Ed25519/Ed448 instantiations, with code and test vectors.
EdDSA.quote: This document describes elliptic curve signature scheme Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA).

rejected.why: The edwards25519 curve is equivalent to Curve25519 and its parameters come from RFC 7748, but this document specifies the signature scheme, not the curve.
SHA-512 and SHAKE256 are used as hash functions inside EdDSA, but the document does not specify them.
The more specific EdDSA tag covers this document's elliptic curve content.
Randomness appears only in a short security consideration, and EdDSA signatures are deterministic.

RFC8033.title: Proportional Integral Controller Enhanced (PIE): A Lightweight Control Scheme to Address the Bufferbloat Problem
RFC8033.summary: RFC 8033 specifies PIE, a lightweight latency-based active queue management algorithm that randomly drops packets based on a PI controller to control queuing delay and address bufferbloat, with optional ECN support, burst tolerance and pseudocode.

PIE.why: The document defines the PIE algorithm itself, including drop probability calculation, burst tolerance, and pseudocode.
PIE.quote: PIE (Proportional Integral controller Enhanced) that can effectively control the average queuing latency to a target value

ECN.why: A section specifies how PIE marks ECN-capable packets instead of dropping, with a mark_ecnth threshold.
ECN.quote: PIE MAY support ECN by marking (rather than dropping) ECN-capable packets

rejected.why: PIE is the more specific child tag and already covers AQM; the parent is implied.
CoDel is cited only as another latency-based AQM for comparison; the document is not about it.
TCP behaviour is the motivation and traffic model, but the document specifies queue management, not TCP.
DOCSIS 3.1 mandating PIE is background; the DOCSIS-specific variant is in RFC 8034, not this document.
The document mentions quality of service as a goal but does not address QoS architectures or signalling.
The scheme is an AQM at the queue; a more specific tag (PIE, ECN) already fits.

RFC8034.title: Active Queue Management (AQM) Based on Proportional Integral Controller Enhanced (PIE) for Data-Over-Cable Service Interface Specifications (DOCSIS) Cable Modems
RFC8034.summary: Describes the DOCSIS-PIE AQM algorithm mandated for DOCSIS 3.1 (and recommended for 3.0) cable modems, as a variant of PIE, with pseudocode.

PIE.why: The document specifies a PIE variant (DOCSIS-PIE) and its differences from PIE, so it belongs on the PIE page.
PIE.quote: describes the DOCSIS-PIE algorithm -- largely by comparing it to its progenitor, the PIE algorithm [RFC8033]

DOCSIS.why: A substantial part covers DOCSIS MAC service flows, token-bucket rate shaping and request-grant latency, which shape the algorithm for cable access networks.
DOCSIS.quote: The DOCSIS Media Access Control (sub-)layer provides tools for configuring differentiated Quality of Service (QoS) for different applications
DOCSIS.section: 3. The DOCSIS MAC Layer and Service Flows

rejected.why: PIE is a child of AQM and is implied, so the parent is not listed separately.
The document only explains why DOCSIS-PIE does not support ECN; it is not about ECN.
The document is about queue management, which sits under AQM, not end-host congestion control.
Service flows and QoS parameters are described only as context for the queue algorithm.
CoDel is not discussed; only PIE is relevant.

RFC8035.title: Session Description Protocol (SDP) Offer/Answer Clarifications for RTP/RTCP Multiplexing
RFC8035.summary: RFC 8035 updates RFC 5761 to clarify SDP offer/answer negotiation of RTP/RTCP multiplexing: an answerer may include a=rtcp-mux only if the offer did, and the negotiation applies to both directions.

SDP.why: The document's core content is the SDP offer/answer rules for the a=rtcp-mux attribute, so readers of SDP and offer/answer would want it.
SDP.quote: an answerer can only include an "a=rtcp-mux" attribute in an answer if the associated offer contained the attribute

RTCP.why: It clarifies how RTP and RTCP are multiplexed on a single port, which matters to RTCP readers. RTP is the parent tag, so RTCP is the more specific fit.
RTCP.quote: the negotiation of RTP and RTCP multiplexing is for usage in both directions

rejected.why: RTCP is the more specific child tag and already covers the RTP/RTCP multiplexing subject, so the parent is implied.
A single UDP port is mentioned only as the place where RTP and RTCP are multiplexed. The document says nothing new about UDP.
iLBC appears only as the codec in an example SDP offer, and the document is not about the codec.
The offer/answer exchange is carried over signalling such as SIP, but the document does not address SIP.

RFC8036.title: Applicability Statement for the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL) in Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) Networks
RFC8036.summary: Applicability statement describing how RPL non-storing mode should be profiled and configured (Trickle parameters, objective functions, repair, security) for AMI/smart-meter neighbor area networks over IEEE 802.15.4g/e and IEEE 1901.2 PLC.

RPL.why: The whole document is an RPL profile for AMI: instances, DAO policy, metrics, objective functions, DODAG repair, Trickle parameter defaults.
RPL.quote: This document describes the applicability of RPL non-storing mode (as defined in [RFC6550]) to AMI deployments.

6LoWPAN.why: The document profiles 6LoWPAN header compression and constrained link layers (802.15.4g/e, 1901.2) for AMI. This is a smaller part of the document than the RPL profile.
6LoWPAN.quote: AMI implementations based on IEEE 1901.2 and 802.15.4 (amendments g and e) can utilize all of the IPv6 Header Compression schemes specified in Section 3 of [RFC6282]

rejected.why: The RPL and 6LoWPAN tags already sit under IoT, so the parent is implied.
The manageability section is only a short discussion of DIO-based configuration and defines no MIB.
Multicast is mentioned only as a requirement, and the document defers it to MPL in companion RFCs.
The 802.15.4 security suites such as AES-CCM are described as part of the link layer, but the document does not specify AES or its modes.
The security text is boilerplate-level guidance that defers to IEEE link-layer security and RFC 7416. It is not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Advanced Metering Infrastructure / smart grid
gaps.why: The document is about smart-meter and power-line networks, and the taxonomy has no smart grid or utility networking tag. RPL under IoT is the closest fit.

RFC8037.title: CFRG Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) and Signatures in JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE)
RFC8037.summary: Defines how to use the CFRG X25519/X448 Diffie-Hellman functions and Ed25519/Ed448 EdDSA signatures in JOSE, introducing the "OKP" JWK key type, the "EdDSA" JWS algorithm, and new curve registrations.

JOSE.why: The document extends JOSE (JWK, JWS, JWE/JWA) with a new key type, the EdDSA algorithm and new curve subtypes, so readers of JOSE need it.
JOSE.quote: A new key type (kty) value "OKP" (Octet Key Pair) is defined for public key algorithms that use octet strings as private and public keys.

Curve25519.why: Specifies X25519 and X448 key agreement (Curve25519 and Curve448 functions) in ECDH-ES, including the ECDH operation and examples.
Curve25519.quote: The following key subtypes are defined here for purpose of "Key Agreement with Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral Static" (ECDH-ES):

EdDSA.why: Defines use of Ed25519 and Ed448 EdDSA signing and verification for JWS, with examples.
EdDSA.quote: algorithm "EdDSA" is defined here, to be applied as the value of the "alg" parameter.

rejected.why: Implied as the parent of Curve25519 and EdDSA; the more specific tags fit.
JSON is only the encoding substrate for JWK/JWS; the document is not about JSON formats.
base64url is merely used to encode key values; nothing new is defined about it.
The document concerns JWS/JWK/JWE algorithms, not JSON Web Tokens.
Parent of the chosen specific tags, so it is implied and not listed separately.

RFC8038.title: Exporting MIB Variables Using the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Protocol
RFC8038.summary: Specifies how to export SNMP MIB object values within IPFIX Data Records, defining new Information Elements, two Options Templates (MIB Field and MIB Type), and methods for exporting conceptual rows and tables.

IPFIX.why: The document extends IPFIX with new Information Elements, Options Templates and semantics.
IPFIX.quote: This document specifies a way to complement IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Data Records with Management Information Base (MIB) objects

MIB.why: A substantial part concerns mapping SMIv2 MIB objects (SYNTAX, INDEX, AUGMENTS, conceptual rows/tables) into IPFIX; MIB readers would want it.
MIB.quote: avoiding the need to define new IPFIX Information Elements for existing MIB objects that are already fully specified

rejected.why: SNMP is the source of the MIB objects and context terminology, but no SNMP protocol behaviour is specified; notifications explicitly out of scope.
OSPF MIB is used only as an example in Section 6.
BER is only used to encode OIDs; not about ASN.1.
Only a template-management constraint when exporting over SCTP.
Packet Sampling report used in one example only.

RFC8039.title: Multipath Time Synchronization
RFC8039.summary: Experimental RFC describing Multipath PTP and Multipath NTP, which run time synchronization protocols concurrently over multiple IP-address-pair paths between master and slave clocks, without modifying PTP or NTP, to improve accuracy, security and fault tolerance.

time synchronization.why: The document defines MPPTP and MPNTP, multipath operation of PTP and NTP, so its subject is clock synchronization over networks. It covers both NTP and PTP, so the parent topic fits better than either child tag.
time synchronization.quote: This memo describes a multipath approach to PTP and NTP over IP networks, allowing the protocols to run concurrently over multiple communication paths

rejected.why: NTP is used unmodified as the protocol run over multiple paths. The document defines a network-layer approach, not NTP changes, and it covers PTP equally, so the parent topic fits better.
PTP is run unchanged over multiple paths, and the document covers NTP as well. The parent topic covers both.
ECMP and load balancing are leveraged to obtain diverse paths, but the document is not about ECMP itself.
Traceroute-based path discovery is a short subsection (5.4) that supports path filtering. The document is not about traceroute.
MPTCP is cited only as an example of using multiple addresses.

RFC8040.title: RESTCONF Protocol
RFC8040.summary: RFC 8040 specifies RESTCONF, an HTTP-based protocol giving programmatic CRUD access to YANG-modelled configuration and state data using NETCONF datastore concepts, including methods, query parameters, notifications, and monitoring modules.

RESTCONF.why: The document defines the RESTCONF protocol itself: resources, methods, query parameters, notifications, error reporting and monitoring.
RESTCONF.quote: This document describes an HTTP-based protocol that provides a programmatic interface for accessing data defined in YANG, using the datastore concepts defined in the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF).

YANG.why: It defines the ietf-restconf and ietf-restconf-monitoring YANG modules and the yang-data extension. It also specifies how YANG data nodes, RPCs, actions and notifications map to resources and URIs.
YANG.quote: The "ietf-restconf" module defines conceptual definitions within an extension and two groupings

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate. RESTCONF uses its methods and headers but does not extend HTTP itself.
NETCONF is the model RESTCONF is compatible with and co-locates with. It is a subset mapping, not the subject. RESTCONF is already tagged as its child.
TLS is only the required secure transport.
JSON and XML are only the encodings for the messages.
The yang-data+xml and yang-data+json registrations are boilerplate IANA material and secondary to the protocol.
The 'restconf' link relation is only used for root discovery and is registered in the IANA section.

RFC8041.title: Use Cases and Operational Experience with Multipath TCP
RFC8041.summary: Informational RFC describing use cases (datacenters, cellular/WiFi offload, proxies) and operational experience (middleboxes, congestion control, subflow management, schedulers, MSS, load balancers) with Multipath TCP.

MPTCP.why: The entire document is about deploying and operating MPTCP: use cases, subflow managers, schedulers, middlebox behaviour, and suggested improvements.
MPTCP.quote: This document discusses both use cases and operational experience with Multipath TCP (MPTCP) in real networks.

rejected.why: MPTCP is the more specific child tag; the TCP ancestor is implied.
Section 3.2 summarizes MPTCP congestion control schemes, but only briefly and in an MPTCP context, so it is not a substantial separate subject.
ECMP is mentioned as the source of path diversity in datacenters, but the document is not about ECMP itself.
SOCKS is only one proxy option used to carry MPTCP, not a subject the document specifies or analyses.
The client-subnet EDNS suggestion in Section 3.9 is a brief aside.
Section 3.10 covers one captive portal scenario briefly. It is a small part of the document.

RFC8042.title: OSPF Two-Part Metric
RFC8042.summary: RFC 8042 extends OSPF so that metrics on multi-access networks are split into router-to-network and network-to-router parts, with new sub-TLVs, a router capability bit, and SPF calculation changes, updating RFC 2328.

OSPF.why: The document specifies an OSPFv2 extension (new sub-TLVs, capability bit, SPF changes) and updates RFC 2328. It also touches OSPFv3 only by reference.
OSPF.quote: an optional OSPF protocol extension to represent router metrics in a multi-access network in two parts

rejected.why: OSPFv3 changes are explicitly deferred to a separate document, so the RFC does not specify them.
A TE Metric sub-TLV is defined, but it is a minor part of an OSPF metric extension and not about traffic engineering as a subject.
The satellite radio network is only a motivating example. The document is not about networking over satellite links.
The document is about a specific OSPF protocol extension, so the OSPF tag fits better than the general architecture topic.

RFC8043.title: Source-Address-Dependent Routing and Source Address Selection for IPv6 Hosts: Overview of the Problem Space
RFC8043.summary: Informational overview of source-address-dependent routing and source address selection problems for multihomed and multi-interface IPv6 hosts, with scenarios and discussion of alternative solutions (RA/DHCP options, RFC 6724 Rule 5.5).

multihoming.why: The document's scenarios are multi-prefix multihoming and multi-interface hosts, and ingress filtering problems in multihomed networks.
multihoming.quote: Both multihomed hosts and hosts with multiple interfaces are considered.

IPv6.why: The problem is specific to IPv6 hosts with multiple prefixes, and it covers RFC 6724 source address selection and RA/DHCPv6 options.
IPv6.quote: source address selection is performed by the host while source-dependent routing is enforced by an upstream router.

routing architecture.why: Source-address-dependent routing and next-hop selection are the core routing design issue the document analyses.
routing architecture.quote: This requires that the routers consider the source addresses as well as the destination addresses in determining the packet's next hop.

rejected.why: Router Advertisements and redirects are used in the analysis, but the document does not specify or extend neighbor discovery itself.
DHCPv6 address selection options are mentioned as a possible delivery mechanism only.
Homenet is one scenario among several and is not the focus.
Routing protocol extensions are mentioned only as out-of-scope context.
NPTv6 is explicitly out of scope.

gaps.name: Source-address-dependent routing / source address selection
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for SADR or default source address selection (RFC 6724), which is the main subject of this document.

RFC8044.title: Data Types in RADIUS
RFC8044.summary: Defines and names the RADIUS attribute data types (integer, enum, text, string, ipv6prefix, tlv, vsa, etc.), creates an IANA "Data Type" registry, and adds a Data Type column to the RADIUS Attribute Types registry.

RADIUS.why: The whole document specifies data types for RADIUS attributes and updates several RADIUS RFCs, so readers of RADIUS would expect it.
RADIUS.quote: RADIUS specifications have used data types for two decades without defining them as managed entities.

rejected.why: The new registry is a side effect of defining data types. The document is about RADIUS data types, not IANA registry guidance in general.
RFC 4072 is only listed as an updated document. The document does not address Diameter.
ABNF is only mentioned as a recommended notation for describing text formats.
The text type uses UTF-8 as its encoding, but the document does not specify anything new about UTF-8.
The ipv6addr and ipv6prefix data types encode IPv6 values, but the document is not about IPv6.

gaps.name: RADIUS
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no RADIUS tag in the form I used. A RADIUS tag does appear in the taxonomy under security > AAA, but I wrote the id as 'RADIUS' rather than the full id shown, so the tag must be checked against the exact taxonomy id.

RFC8045.title: RADIUS Extensions for IP Port Configuration and Reporting
RFC8045.summary: Defines three new RADIUS extended attributes (IP-Port-Limit-Info, IP-Port-Range, IP-Port-Forwarding-Map) and their TLVs so a RADIUS server can configure and receive reports of IP port limits, port ranges and port-forwarding mappings on address-sharing devices such as CGNs, with a mapping to IPFIX Information Elements.

RADIUS.why: The document specifies new RADIUS extended attributes and TLVs carried in Access-Accept, CoA and Accounting-Request packets.
RADIUS.quote: This document defines three new RADIUS attributes.

CGN.why: The main use case is managing Carrier-Grade NAT port limits, port allocation reporting and port forwarding via RADIUS, so CGN readers would want it.
CGN.quote: the CGN IP transport port (e.g., TCP/UDP port) mapping behaviors can be part of the configuration information sent from the RADIUS server

IPFIX.why: The TLVs carry IPFIX Information Elements, and a new IPFIX element, sourceTransportPortsLimit (458), is defined and registered.
IPFIX.quote: This document provides a mapping between some RADIUS TLVs and IPFIX Information Element identifiers.

rejected.why: PCP is mentioned only as a complementary mechanism for port forwarding; the document does not specify or extend it.
NAT64 is one example deployment of the address-sharing device; the document does not specify it.
IPsec is mentioned only as an optional way to secure RADIUS, in the Security Considerations.
TLS appears only as an optional RADIUS transport protection in the Security Considerations.
DS-Lite AFTR is listed only as one possible CGN function; the document does not specify it.
TCP and UDP port numbers are the values being limited and mapped, but the document does not specify TCP or UDP.

gaps.name: RADIUS
gaps.why: The taxonomy has AAA, RADIUS and Diameter, but I could not confirm that the RADIUS id is valid. It appears under AAA as 'RADIUS'. The tag is used as listed.

RFC8046.title: Host Mobility with the Host Identity Protocol
RFC8046.summary: Defines the HIP LOCATOR_SET parameter and the UPDATE-based procedures, including address verification and credit-based authorization, that let HIP hosts preserve communications across IP address changes (host mobility), obsoleting RFC 5206.

HIP.why: The whole document specifies a HIP extension: the LOCATOR_SET parameter, UPDATE processing, and address verification for host mobility.
HIP.quote: This document defines a mobility extension to the Host Identity Protocol (HIP).

IP mobility.why: The document specifies end-host network-layer mobility, including double-jump handling and renumbering. HIP has no mobility-specific child tag, so the IP mobility topic fits.
IP mobility.quote: One consequence of such a decoupling is that new solutions to network-layer mobility and host multihoming are possible.

rejected.why: Multihoming procedures are explicitly out of scope and are specified in RFC 8047.
ESP is the transport format the mobility procedures assume, and SPIs are used in locators, but the document does not specify ESP itself.
IPsec SAs are only the substrate HIP sets up; the document is not about IPsec.
NAT and firewall traversal are explicitly not covered.
Flooding attacks are discussed, but only as the motivation for credit-based authorization and address verification.

gaps.name: Host Identity Protocol (HIP)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an HIP tag listed in the 'internet layer' area as 'HIP (Host Identity Protocol)'. It is used above, so no gap remains.

RFC8047.title: Host Multihoming with the Host Identity Protocol
RFC8047.summary: Standards Track document extending the Host Identity Protocol with host multihoming procedures, using the LOCATOR_SET parameter from the HIP mobility spec in R1, I2, R2 and UPDATE packets, with multiple ESP SAs and address verification.

HIP.why: The whole document specifies HIP extensions and processing rules for multihoming, so the HIP tag fits directly.
HIP.quote: This document defines host multihoming extensions to the Host Identity Protocol (HIP), by leveraging protocol components defined for host mobility.

rejected.why: Shim6 is mentioned only as a comparison point, and the document does not specify or extend it.
