ESP is the transport the HIP SAs run over. The document only discusses how SAs and anti-replay windows interact with multihoming, and does not define anything about ESP itself.
Mobility is covered by RFC 8046, which this document builds on. This document addresses multihoming and mentions mobility only briefly as a combined scenario.
This is the closest topic tag, but the HIP tag I chose already sits above it and covers the document more specifically.
IPsec SAs, the SPD and the SAD are background for the SA discussion. The document is not about IPsec architecture.

RFC8048.title: Interworking between the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP): Presence
RFC8048.summary: Defines a bidirectional mapping of basic presence (authorization, notification, polling) between SIP/SIMPLE and XMPP, implemented by gateways, and obsoletes RFC 7248.

SIMPLE.why: The SIP side of the mapping is SIMPLE presence: SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY with the presence event package, PIDF bodies and watcher info. The document specifies how this maps to XMPP.
SIMPLE.quote: directly map semantics from one protocol to another (i.e., from SIP/SIMPLE (SIP for Instant Messaging and Presence Leveraging Extensions) to XMPP and vice versa)

XMPP.why: Half of the mapping is XMPP presence stanzas and subscription states, with gateway behaviour specified in detail. Readers of XMPP would want this interworking document.
XMPP.quote: XMPP presence authorizations are managed using XMPP <presence/> stanzas of type "subscribe", "subscribed", "unsubscribe", and "unsubscribed".

PIDF.why: The syntax mapping tables map XMPP presence to PIDF basic status, tuple id, priority and note. The document also recommends embedding XMPP <show/> as a PIDF extension.
PIDF.quote: the XMPP <show/> element (qualified by the 'jabber:client' namespace) can be included directly in the PIDF XML.

rejected.why: SIP is the protocol the gateway speaks on one side, but the document is specifically about SIMPLE presence, which is the more specific tag.
The parent tag is implied by the XMPP and PIDF tags. The instant messaging mapping itself is out of scope here and covered by RFC 7572.
XML is only the encoding for XMPP stanzas and PIDF, not a subject of the document.
Not used. The SIP flows are SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY with no media negotiation.

gaps.name: SIP-XMPP interworking
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for gateway or interworking mappings between SIP and XMPP. This RFC belongs to a series (RFC 7247, 7572, 7573, 7702) that such a tag would group.

RFC8049.title: YANG Data Model for L3VPN Service Delivery
RFC8049.summary: Defines the ietf-l3vpn-svc YANG service data model that customers and operators use to request and manage BGP/MPLS Layer 3 VPN services at the management-system level, not on network elements.

L3VPN.why: The whole document models the L3VPN service (sites, VPN topologies, route targets, NNIs, extranets, CsC) for BGP/MPLS VPNs per RFC 4364.
L3VPN.quote: This document defines a YANG data model that can be used for communication between customers and network operators and to deliver a Layer 3 provider-provisioned VPN service.

YANG.why: The deliverable is a YANG module with tree diagrams and augmentation guidance, so readers of YANG models would want it.
YANG.quote: This document defines a Layer 3 VPN service data model written in YANG.

rejected.why: BGP is one selectable PE-CE routing protocol and a substrate of L3VPN, not specified or extended here.
NETCONF/RESTCONF are only mentioned as ways to access the model, not specified here.
Multicast service parameters are a part of the model but not the main subject.
QoS classification and profiles are abstracted service parameters, a minor part of the document.
OSPF is only an optional PE-CE routing choice in the model.
The service-to-config orchestration is described, but the document is not about SDN as a subject.

RFC8050.title: Multi-Threaded Routing Toolkit (MRT) Routing Information Export Format with BGP Additional Path Extensions
RFC8050.summary: Extends the MRT routing information export format with new BGP4MP and TABLE_DUMP_V2 subtypes to represent BGP Additional Paths (RFC 7911) path identifiers.

BGP.why: The document defines how BGP messages and RIB entries with Additional Paths (Path Identifiers) are encoded in MRT, a BGP-specific export format. BGP has no narrower fitting tag for MRT or Add-Paths.
BGP.quote: introduces additional definitions of MRT subtype fields to permit representation of multiple path advertisements

rejected.why: MRT is a routing data archive format, not a generic packet capture or trace file format. BGP is the closer subject.
BMP is a different BGP monitoring protocol. This document only extends the MRT file format.
The IANA section only registers subtype codes. It is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
BGP is the more specific tag, and its ancestors are implied.

gaps.name: MRT (Multi-Threaded Routing Toolkit) export format
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the MRT routing data archive format. Readers looking for RFC 6396 and its extensions would want a dedicated page.

RFC8051.title: Applicability of a Stateful Path Computation Element (PCE)
RFC8051.summary: Informational document describing general deployment considerations and use cases (LSP placement optimization, auto-bandwidth, recovery, defragmentation, IA-RWA, etc.) showing the applicability and benefits of a stateful Path Computation Element in MPLS-TE and GMPLS networks.

PCE.why: The whole document analyses the applicability, benefits and deployment of stateful PCE and PCEP use cases, so the PCE tag fits directly.
PCE.quote: A stateful Path Computation Element (PCE) maintains information about Label Switched Path (LSP) characteristics and resource usage within a network

rejected.why: GMPLS networks are the deployment context and some use cases (WSON, flexi-grid) apply to it, but the document is about PCE, not GMPLS itself.
MPLS-TE LSPs are the thing being computed and placed, but the document does not specify or extend MPLS.
RSVP-TE is mentioned only as the signalling that sets up LSPs (e.g. bandwidth increase behaviour in the deadlock case); it is not the document's subject.
Traffic engineering is implied by the PCE parent tag; PCE is the more specific fit.

RFC8052.title: Group Domain of Interpretation (GDOI) Protocol Support for IEC 62351 Security Services
RFC8052.summary: Defines GDOI (RFC 6407) extensions (ID_OID ID type, GDOI_PROTO_IEC_61850 SA TEK payload, auth/confidentiality algorithm registries, SA attributes, KD key mappings) to distribute policy and keys for IEC 61850/62351 GOOSE and sampled-value multicast protection.

GDOI.why: The document extends GDOI with new ID, SA TEK payloads and registries for IEC 61850, so readers of GDOI need it.
GDOI.quote: This memo defines GDOI payloads to support those security protocols.

rejected.why: AES-CBC/GCM/GMAC are merely algorithm identifiers listed for the SA TEK; the document is not about AES.
HMAC-SHA256 is one authentication option listed; not the subject.
DER-encoded OIDs are used as an encoding for selectors; only a substrate.
Registry creation is part of IANA Considerations boilerplate, not the main subject.
Implied parent of GDOI; the more specific GDOI tag is used.
GDOI is ISAKMP-based but this document does not specify IPsec; it targets IEC 61850 protocols.

gaps.name: IEC 61850 / IEC 62351 power utility automation security
gaps.why: The document is about securing substation GOOSE and sampled values traffic, a smart-grid/industrial control domain with no taxonomy tag.

RFC8053.title: HTTP Authentication Extensions for Interactive Clients
RFC8053.summary: Experimental RFC defining HTTP authentication extensions (Optional-WWW-Authenticate and Authentication-Control headers with login/logout redirection, timeout, and username parameters) so HTTP-level authentication can replace form/cookie-based web authentication.

HTTP authentication.why: The whole document extends HTTP authentication with optional authentication, an Authentication-Control header, and logout and redirect controls.
HTTP authentication.quote: This document specifies extensions for the HTTP authentication framework for interactive clients.

rejected.why: Cookies are discussed as the form-based alternative and for when to use them (Section 5.3), but the document does not specify or extend cookie handling.
The new headers are HTTP extensions, but HTTP authentication is the more specific child tag, so the parent is implied.
The document covers authentication UX and states the headers are not for security enforcement. It is not about a web platform security mechanism such as HSTS.
The generic authentication topic is covered by the more specific HTTP authentication tag.
ABNF is used only as syntax notation for the new headers.
The IANA registry of control parameters is boilerplate-level; the document's main body is not about IANA.

RFC8054.title: Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP) Extension for Compression
RFC8054.summary: Defines the NNTP COMPRESS extension, a new command and capability that enables DEFLATE compression of an NNTP connection, with its interaction with TLS, SASL and AUTHINFO, and an IANA registry of compression algorithms.

NNTP.why: The document extends NNTP with a COMPRESS command, capability label and response code 206.
NNTP.quote: This document defines an extension to the Network News Transport Protocol (NNTP) that allows a connection to be effectively and efficiently compressed

DEFLATE.why: DEFLATE is the mandatory algorithm. Section 4 gives zlib-specific guidance (windowBits, flush modes, compression levels) and DEFLATE is registered in the new registry.
DEFLATE.quote: The DEFLATE algorithm (defined in [RFC1951]) MUST be implemented as part of this extension.

rejected.why: TLS is only a layer COMPRESS combines with. The document specifies layering order and CRIME risks but defines nothing new for TLS.
SASL security layers are mentioned only for layer ordering.
The more specific DEFLATE tag fits, and the parent compression topic is implied by it.
The registry creation is boilerplate-level IANA Considerations, not the subject of the document.
ABNF is only the notation used for the syntax section.
Base64 is mentioned only as an attachment encoding in the efficiency discussion.

RFC8055.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Via Header Field Parameter to Indicate Received Realm
RFC8055.summary: Defines a new SIP Via header field parameter, 'received-realm', which lets a transit network entry point indicate the adjacent upstream network a request came from, using an operator identifier plus a detached JWS signature.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new Via header field parameter and specifies the behaviour of SIP entities that insert and consume it.
SIP.quote: This specification defines a new Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Via header field parameter, 'received-realm'

rejected.why: JWS and JWT are used as the signing mechanism for the parameter, and new JWT claims are registered. The document is not about JOSE itself.
The JWS payload follows JWT claim conventions, but JWT is only a substrate here and no JWT specification is defined.
The document concerns transit and interconnect between SIP networks, but it does not define SPEERMINT peering or its provisioning.
JSON is only the encoding of the JWS payload, which is a substrate use.
The IANA section registers a Via parameter and JWT claims. This is boilerplate and does not make the document about IANA.

RFC8056.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) and Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) Status Mapping
RFC8056.summary: RFC 8056 maps EPP object statuses to RDAP statuses and registers new RDAP JSON Values status entries to fill the gaps so every EPP status is expressible in RDAP.

EPP.why: The document analyses EPP status values from the domain, host, contact and grace period mappings and maps each one to RDAP. Readers of EPP would want it.
EPP.quote: This document maps the statuses defined in the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) RFCs to the list of statuses registered for use in the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP)

RDAP.why: It extends RDAP by registering new status values in the RDAP JSON Values registry, so it is about RDAP status representation.
RDAP.quote: registers RDAP statuses to fill those gaps to ensure that all of the EPP statuses specified in RFCs are supported in RDAP

rejected.why: RDAP JSON Values is only the registry and encoding substrate. The document defines status strings, not anything about JSON.
The IANA registrations are the mechanism for adding the statuses. The document is not about IANA registry policy.
The parent topic is implied by the EPP and RDAP tags.
DNS delegation publication is mentioned only in the hold status descriptions. The document is not about DNS.

RFC8057.title: Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespaces for Broadband Forum
RFC8057.summary: Registers three URN Namespace Identifiers (bbf, broadband-forum-org, dslforum-org) for Broadband Forum to identify its published resources such as data models.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration, defining NIDs, syntax, uniqueness and assignment rules for Broadband Forum URNs.
URN.quote: the registration of three specific Uniform Resource Name (URN) [RFC2141] Namespace Identifiers (NIDs) for use by BBF are being specified in this document

rejected.why: The example urn:bbf:yang:fast mentions YANG, but the document does not specify YANG models or the language.
The IANA registry entry is boilerplate; the document is about the namespaces, not IANA registry guidance.
XML namespaces are mentioned only in passing as a use of the identifiers.
DSL Forum is only the former organization name; the document does not address DSL access networks.

RFC8058.title: Signaling One-Click Functionality for List Email Headers
RFC8058.summary: Defines the List-Unsubscribe-Post header field and a DKIM-protected HTTPS POST mechanism so mail receivers can perform one-click unsubscription from List-Unsubscribe URIs without manual confirmation.

mailing lists.why: The document extends the List-Unsubscribe mailing list header (RFC 2369) with a new List-Unsubscribe-Post header for one-click unsubscription, which is a mailing list header and management matter.
mailing lists.quote: This document describes a method for signaling a one-click function for the List-Unsubscribe email header field.

DKIM.why: A DKIM signature covering the unsubscribe headers is a mandatory requirement, and the document specifies how DKIM is used as the authentication identifier for one-click. Readers of DKIM would want this usage requirement.
DKIM.quote: The List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post headers MUST be covered by the signature and included in the "h=" tag of a valid DKIM-Signature header field.

rejected.why: HTTPS POST is only the mechanism the action runs over. The document defines nothing new about HTTP itself.
It adds one header field with ABNF, but the document is about mailing list unsubscription signalling, not the Internet message format.
Spam filter auto-fetching and junk reports motivate the work, but the document does not address spam filtering or reporting.
It is implied as the parent of mailing lists and DKIM, so listing it separately would be redundant.
multipart/form-data and application/x-www-form-urlencoded are used as POST encodings, with no media type registration or rules.

RFC8059.title: PIM Join Attributes for Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Environments
RFC8059.summary: Defines two PIM Join/Prune attributes (Transport and Receiver RLOC) so receiver-site ETRs can choose unicast or multicast underlay and convey their RLOC to the root ITR when building multicast trees across LISP sites.

LISP.why: The attributes are designed for LISP multicast environments, involving ITR/ETR behaviour, RLOCs, and EID mobility via SMR and Map-Notify.
LISP.quote: construction of multicast distribution trees where the root and receivers are located in different Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) sites

PIM.why: The document specifies new PIM Join/Prune attribute TLVs (Transport, type 5; Receiver RLOC, type 6) extending RFC 5384 and RFC 7887.
PIM.quote: This document defines two PIM Join/Prune attributes

rejected.why: Document extends Join/Prune attributes generally and only references PIM-SM for the address family encoding; it is not about the sparse mode specification itself.
Parent of PIM; implied by the PIM tag, so not listed separately.
LISP encapsulation is the context but the document is not about data-plane virtualization overlays like VXLAN or Geneve.
The IANA registry creation is boilerplate-level; the body is about the PIM attributes.

RFC8060.title: LISP Canonical Address Format (LCAF)
RFC8060.summary: Defines the LISP Canonical Address Format (LCAF), an AFI-16387-based encoding with typed payloads for LISP control messages and Mapping Database lookup keys (instance IDs, AS numbers, geo-coordinates, NAT traversal, multicast info, ELP, security keys, etc.).

LISP.why: The whole document specifies LCAF encodings for LISP control messages and mapping system keys, so it belongs on the LISP page.
LISP.quote: This document defines a canonical address format encoding used in Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) control messages and in the encoding of lookup keys for the LISP Mapping Database System.

rejected.why: VXLAN, Geneve and NVGRE appear only as flags in the Encapsulation Format LCAF type; the document is not about those overlays.
The NAT-Traversal LCAF type is one encoding among many and defers details to another draft; NAT behaviour is not the subject.
The Multicast Info and Replication List Entry types are address encodings for the mapping database, not multicast routing.
The Geo-Coordinates type is a single encoding, with privacy caveats noted, and is not the document's main subject.
JSON is only the payload of an unapproved experimental LCAF type.
The IANA section creates the LCAF Types registry, but that is boilerplate for this protocol document.

gaps.name: LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol) — LCAF
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a LISP tag only as a tech under routing, and I used it. But the LISP tag in the taxonomy is written as 'LISP' with no separate id, so the id I used must be exactly as listed: it is shown in the taxonomy as 'LISP'. Verify this matches; if not, no better tag exists.

RFC8061.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Data-Plane Confidentiality
RFC8061.summary: Experimental RFC defining encryption of LISP-encapsulated data-plane traffic, with Diffie-Hellman key exchange carried in LISP Map-Request/Map-Reply messages, cipher suites, KDF, key-id bits in the LISP header, and rekeying.

LISP.why: The document extends LISP's data plane and control plane (Security Key LCAF in Map-Request/Map-Reply, KK bits in the LISP header) to provide confidentiality.
LISP.quote: This document describes a mechanism for encrypting LISP-encapsulated traffic.

rejected.why: The design is a LISP-specific alternative; it does not specify or profile IPsec.
AES modes appear only as cipher suite components, not as the subject.
ChaCha20-Poly1305 is one of the listed cipher suites, not the subject.
Curve25519 is only a DH group choice in some cipher suites.
Key exchange is central, but it is specific to LISP and is covered by the LISP tag. The key-exchange parts do not warrant a separate broad tag.
The topic is covered by the LISP-specific mechanism; the document is not general security guidance.
The registry creation is boilerplate-level IANA considerations.

RFC8062.title: Anonymity Support for Kerberos
RFC8062.summary: Defines Kerberos extensions (anonymous ticket flag and KDC option, anonymous PKINIT, PA_PKINIT_KX) letting a client obtain anonymous tickets and talk to services without revealing its identity, obsoleting RFC 6112.

Kerberos.why: The document extends Kerberos AS and TGS exchanges with an anonymous ticket flag, KDC option, anonymous realm and principal, and updates RFC 4120 and 4121.
Kerberos.quote: This document defines extensions to the Kerberos protocol to allow a Kerberos client to securely communicate with a Kerberos application service without revealing its identity

GSS-API.why: A dedicated section explains how anonymous Kerberos principals map to GSS-API anonymity, the anon_req_flag, and what initiators must check.
GSS-API.quote: GSS-API defines the name_type GSS_C_NT_ANONYMOUS [RFC2743] to represent the anonymous identity.

rejected.why: Anonymity is a core theme, but the document is a Kerberos mechanism extension, not a general privacy threat model or considerations document.
A generic topic. The Kerberos tag already covers it, so it was not added.
Anonymous PKINIT uses PKINIT and X.509 only as a mechanism; the document does not define PKI matters.
Certificates are mentioned, but the anonymous case omits them and the document does not profile them.
SignedData is only the encoding used in PKINIT messages, so CMS is substrate.
The PA_PKINIT_KX session key combination serves anonymous PKINIT and is secondary to the Kerberos extensions. Kerberos already covers it.

gaps.name: PKINIT (Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication in Kerberos)
gaps.why: The document defines anonymous PKINIT and the PA_PKINIT_KX padata. The taxonomy has no PKINIT tag, so Kerberos is the closest fit.

RFC8063.title: Key Relay Mapping for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol
RFC8063.summary: Defines an EPP extension mapping for a key relay object that lets EPP clients relay DNSSEC key material via the poll queue, to support changing DNS operators while preserving the DNSSEC chain of trust.

EPP.why: The document specifies a new EPP object mapping, with create command and poll response semantics and an XML schema, so it is an EPP extension.
EPP.quote: This document describes an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) mapping for a key relay object that relays DNSSEC key material between EPP clients

DNSSEC.why: The purpose is relaying DNSKEY material when changing DNS operator for signed zones, which DNSSEC operations readers would want. The document does not change DNSSEC itself.
DNSSEC.quote: This allows DNS operators to automatically, reliably, and securely bootstrap the transfer of a domain name while keeping the DNSSEC chain of trust intact.

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are only the encoding used for the EPP mapping, not the subject.
The DNS operator change is the use case, but the document specifies registry provisioning, not DNS protocol behaviour.
Covered by the more specific EPP tag, which implies this parent.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate for the namespace and extension registry and are not the subject.

RFC8064.title: Recommendation on Stable IPv6 Interface Identifiers
RFC8064.summary: RFC 8064 changes the recommended default for generating stable IPv6 interface identifiers with SLAAC to the RFC 7217 opaque scheme. It advises against embedding stable link-layer addresses in IIDs and updates a set of IPv6-over-link-layer RFCs accordingly.

SLAAC.why: The document's core recommendation is the default IID generation scheme for SLAAC-configured stable addresses.
SLAAC.quote: Nodes SHOULD implement and employ [RFC7217] as the default scheme for generating stable IPv6 addresses with SLAAC.
SLAAC.section: 3. Generation of IPv6 Interface Identifiers with SLAAC

privacy.why: The motivation is privacy and security: correlation, location tracking, address scanning. Readers of privacy considerations would want this RFC.
privacy.quote: The security and privacy implications of embedding a stable link-layer address in an IPv6 IID have been known for some time now

rejected.why: SLAAC is a child of IPv6 and is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
6LoWPAN documents are mentioned only as future-work items that may need updates, not as the subject.
RFC 2464 and the other link-layer mappings are only listed as documents being updated. The document is not about those media.
The document is about IID generation under SLAAC, which is covered by the more specific SLAAC tag.
Neighbor discovery is not discussed beyond a reference in the future-work list.

RFC8065.title: Privacy Considerations for IPv6 Adaptation-Layer Mechanisms
RFC8065.summary: Informational guidance for designers of IPv6 adaptation-layer specifications (IPv6-over-foo for low-power links) on how many bits of interface-identifier entropy are needed to mitigate address scanning, correlation and location tracking, with recommendations for IID construction from IEEE identifiers and Short Addresses.

6LoWPAN.why: The document is about adaptation layers for IPv6 over constrained low-power links (802.15.4, BLE, DECT ULE, MS/TP, G.9959, NFC) and gives recommendations for those specifications, which is the 6lo/6LoWPAN subject.
6LoWPAN.quote: provides advice to protocol designers on how to address such threats in adaptation-layer specifications for IPv6 over such links

privacy.why: It applies privacy threats (correlation, location tracking, address scanning) to IPv6 interface identifiers and gives privacy mitigations.
privacy.quote: RFC 6973 [RFC6973] discusses privacy considerations for Internet protocols, and Section 5.2 of that document covers a number of privacy-specific threats.

IPv6.why: A substantial part concerns IPv6 interface identifier and address generation, including temporary addresses and stable IIDs.
IPv6.quote: Technologies should define a way to include sufficient bits of entropy in the IPv6 interface identifier, based on the maximum link lifetime.

rejected.why: It mentions RFC 7217 and RFC 4941 address generation, but the document is about adaptation-layer IID design, not SLAAC itself.
Considered for IPv6 address entropy, but the IPv6 tag already fits more specifically and covers it.
The links are IoT-type, but the 6LoWPAN tag is the more specific fit.
RFC 6775 and DAD are mentioned only in passing.

RFC8066.title: IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (6LoWPAN) ESC Dispatch Code Points and Guidelines
RFC8066.summary: RFC 8066 defines the ESC extension type octet for the 6LoWPAN dispatch header, creates the IANA "ESC Extension Types" registry, and records the ITU-T G.9903/G.9905 usage as the initial allocation.

6LoWPAN.why: The document extends the 6LoWPAN dispatch header by defining the ESC Extension Type octet, its processing rules, and its placement relative to the mesh, fragment and LOWPAN_IPHC headers.
6LoWPAN.quote: This document updates RFC 4944 and RFC 6282 by defining the ESC extension octet code points and listing registration entries for known use cases

rejected.why: The document creates a registry, but only for 6LoWPAN ESC extension types. It gives no general IANA guidance, and the registry is part of the 6LoWPAN specification.
6LoWPAN carries IPv6 packets, but the document is about the link-layer adaptation dispatch header, not IPv6 itself.
RFC 6282 header compression (LOWPAN_IPHC) is mentioned only for header ordering. The document does not specify compression.
The IPHC dispatch ordering rule is incidental. The document is about dispatch extension octets.

gaps.name: G3-PLC / ITU-T G.9903 power line communication
gaps.why: The document records G.9903 and G.9905 ESC command IDs as the initial registry allocation. The taxonomy has no tag for power-line communication.

RFC8067.title: Updating When Standards Track Documents May Refer Normatively to Documents at a Lower Level
RFC8067.summary: BCP updating RFC 3967 so that explicitly documenting downward normative references in the IETF Last Call is strongly recommended but not required, leaving the IESG discretion over repeating Last Call.

IETF process.why: The document changes IETF Last Call and IESG procedure for handling normative references to lower-maturity documents, which is IETF standards process.
IETF process.quote: explicitly documenting the downward references in the Last Call message is strongly recommended but not required
IETF process.section: 2. The IESG's Responsibility with Respect to Downrefs

rejected.why: It concerns normative references in Standards Track documents and the Last Call process, not RFC format, style or publication.
It mentions terminology definitions only as an example of foundational documents, not as its subject.

RFC8068.title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Recording Call Flows
RFC8068.summary: RFC 8068 gives example SIP recording call flows showing the metadata snapshots (XML) that a Session Recording Client sends to a Session Recording Server in INVITE, re-INVITE and BYE messages, for unmixed, mixed, persistent-session and turret scenarios.

SIPREC.why: The whole document is a set of SIPREC call-flow examples showing SRC-to-SRS recording sessions and metadata. It exists to illustrate SIPREC metadata use.
SIPREC.quote: This document lists call flows with metadata snapshots sent from a Session Recording Client (SRC) to a Session Recording Server (SRS).

rejected.why: SIP is the signalling substrate for the recording sessions. The document is about SIPREC specifically, which sits under SIP, so the more specific tag is used.
SDP snippets appear in the examples (labels, sendonly), but the document does not define or extend SDP.
The metadata is XML, but the XML is only the encoding of the recording metadata defined in RFC 7865. The document says nothing new about XML usage.
RTP carries the recorded media, but it is not specified or discussed beyond mentions in the flow diagrams.
Conference focus and mixing models appear as SRC architectures, but the document is about recording metadata, not conferencing frameworks.

RFC8069.title: URN Namespace for IEEE
RFC8069.summary: Registers the 'ieee' URN Namespace Identifier in the IANA Formal URN Namespaces registry, defining its syntax, management by the IEEE Registration Authority, and lexical equivalence rules.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration: it defines the ieee NID, its NSS syntax, uniqueness, persistence and equivalence rules, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: the Namespace Identifier (NID) 'ieee' for Uniform Resource Names (URNs) used to identify resources published by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)

rejected.why: YANG is only mentioned as the catalyst for creating the namespace and in the example URN; the document does not specify or discuss YANG.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-level; the document's body is about the namespace definition, not IANA registry guidance.

RFC8070.title: Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication in Kerberos (PKINIT) Freshness Extension
RFC8070.summary: Extends Kerberos PKINIT so the KDC supplies an opaque freshness token, echoed in the signed PKAuthenticator, proving the client currently holds its private key during an AS exchange.

Kerberos.why: The document extends Kerberos PKINIT: new pre-authentication data type, modified AS exchange message flow with KRB_ERROR, and an extended PKAuthenticator.
Kerberos.quote: The client indicates support of freshness tokens by adding a padata element with padata-type PA_AS_FRESHNESS and padata-value of an empty octet string.

rejected.why: PKINIT uses certificates and public keys, but the document only adds a freshness token to the Kerberos exchange; it does not address PKI itself.
Client certificates are mentioned only as background (validity period); nothing about certificate profiles.
The extended PKAuthenticator is given in ASN.1, but that is only the notation, not the subject.
The Kerberos tag is more specific and already covers this authentication subject.
The IANA section only registers one padata type; it is boilerplate here.

RFC8071.title: NETCONF Call Home and RESTCONF Call Home
RFC8071.summary: Defines NETCONF Call Home and RESTCONF Call Home, in which the NETCONF/RESTCONF server initiates the TCP connection to the client and then SSH/TLS and the application protocol run with their usual roles, with client and server procedures and IANA port assignments.

NETCONF.why: The document specifies call home operation for NETCONF, including its SSH and TLS bindings, and the matching client and server behaviour.
NETCONF.quote: enable a NETCONF or RESTCONF server to initiate a secure connection to a NETCONF or RESTCONF client, respectively.

RESTCONF.why: RESTCONF Call Home is half of the document's subject, with its own port (4336) and its own client and server procedures.
RESTCONF.quote: RESTCONF Call Home only supports TLS, the same as the RESTCONF protocol [RFC8040].

rejected.why: SSH is the secure transport that NETCONF Call Home runs over. The document only notes that the 'client initiates the connection' statement in RFC 4253 does not apply, and it does not define a new SSH mechanism.
TLS is the substrate. The document requires the Heartbeat extension but defines no new TLS extension.
TCP is only the transport. The role reversal at the TCP layer is the core mechanism, but the document does not specify or extend TCP itself.
The YANG configuration models are explicitly out of scope and live in other documents.
Firewall and NAT traversal are only motivation scenarios, not the subject of the document.
The port assignments are boilerplate IANA Considerations and do not make the document about IANA.

RFC8072.title: YANG Patch Media Type
RFC8072.summary: Defines the YANG Patch media types (application/yang-patch+xml and +json) and a YANG module for ordered edit lists applied via HTTP PATCH to RESTCONF datastores, including status responses and a RESTCONF capability.

YANG.why: The document defines a new YANG module (ietf-yang-patch) with yang-data templates for patch requests and status responses, and the edit semantics for YANG-modelled data.
YANG.quote: This document describes a method for applying patches to configuration datastores using data defined with the YANG data modeling language.

RESTCONF.why: It extends RESTCONF with a new PATCH media type, a ':yang-patch' capability, and edit/error handling specific to RESTCONF servers and clients.
RESTCONF.quote: YANG Patch is designed to support the RESTCONF protocol, defined in [RFC8040].

rejected.why: HTTP PATCH is the substrate used to carry YANG Patch; the document does not extend HTTP itself.
NETCONF datastores and edit operations are referenced for alignment, but the document specifies a RESTCONF mechanism.
It registers two media types, but that registration is IANA boilerplate for the main subject, not a document about media type rules.
JSON and XML are only encodings of the YANG Patch data, via RFC 7951.
XML is only one of the two encodings used, not a subject of the document.

RFC8073.title: Coordinating Attack Response at Internet Scale (CARIS) Workshop Report
RFC8073.summary: IAB workshop report on the CARIS workshop (Berlin, June 2015) documenting discussions on coordinating attack response among CSIRTs, DDoS/botnet responders, DNS/RIR operators, and on trust, privacy and data sharing, with next steps on transports for incident information exchange.

workshop reports.why: The document is an IAB workshop report, which is exactly what this subject page collects.
workshop reports.quote: This report documents the discussions and conclusions from the Coordinating Attack Response at Internet Scale (CARIS) workshop that took place in Berlin, Germany on 18 June 2015.

incident response.why: The workshop's central subject is coordination and information exchange among CSIRTs and incident-response groups, including trust, data markings and transports such as RID.
incident response.quote: Coordination between CSIRTs and attack-response mitigation efforts

DDoS.why: A full session covers DDoS and botnet response, including comparing DOTS and RID, so readers of DDoS mitigation would want it.
DDoS.quote: Scaling response to Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) and botnets effectively and safely

rejected.why: DOTS is discussed only as a related IETF effort compared to RID. The report does not specify or analyse it.
RID (RFC 6545) is cited as a prior transport option and compared with DOTS and TAXII, but the report is not about it in depth.
XMPP-Grid is mentioned as a promising transport option, but only briefly in next steps.
A panel covers DNS providers and RIRs as infrastructure for attack responders, but no DNS protocol or operations are addressed.
The trust and privacy panel is about sharing incident data, not protocol privacy considerations.
SACM is mentioned only as the origin of XMPP-Grid.

gaps.name: Cyber threat information sharing / trust groups (TLP, TAXII)
gaps.why: The report is largely about sharing threat intelligence, trust and data markings such as the Traffic Light Protocol. The taxonomy has only the incident response tags for this.

RFC8074.title: Source Address Validation Improvement (SAVI) for Mixed Address Assignment Methods Scenario
RFC8074.summary: Standards-track document describing how multiple SAVI methods (FCFS, DHCP, SEND) coexist in one SAVI device via a shared binding table (SAVI-MIX) and how binding collisions between methods are avoided and resolved.

SAVI.why: The whole document specifies SAVI-MIX, the arbitration of binding entries among SAVI methods, and collision-resolution policies.
SAVI.quote: This document reviews how multiple SAVI methods can coexist in a single SAVI device and how collisions are resolved when the same binding entry is discovered by two or more methods.

rejected.why: SEND SAVI is one of the methods being combined, and CGA preference is mentioned, but the document does not specify or extend SEND itself.
SAVI-DHCP is one input method; DHCP is only an address assignment technique referenced for prefix separation and lifetime priority.
SLAAC is an address assignment technique analysed by FCFS SAVI. The document only references it for prefix separation, so it is not the subject.
DAD and Router Advertisement bits are used in the defence mechanism and separation recommendations, but the document is not about Neighbor Discovery itself.

gaps.name: SAVI (Source Address Validation Improvement)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a SAVI tag in the internet layer group, but I verified it appears in the list as 'SAVI'. No gap in coverage.

RFC8075.title: Guidelines for Mapping Implementations: HTTP to the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)
RFC8075.summary: Provides implementation guidelines for an HTTP-to-CoAP cross-protocol proxy, covering URI mapping and discovery, media type to content-format mapping, response code mapping, and caching, block-wise, multicast and timeout behaviour.

CoAP.why: The document specifies how CoAP requests and responses are produced from and mapped back to HTTP, including block-wise transfer, observe, multicast and the core.hc resource type.
CoAP.quote: implementing a cross-protocol network proxy that performs translation from the HTTP protocol to the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)

HTTP.why: The proxy acts as an HTTP server. The document maps HTTP status codes, headers and media types, so HTTP readers would want it.
HTTP.quote: This document describes how an HTTP request is mapped to a CoAP request and how a CoAP response is mapped back to an HTTP response.

URI.why: A substantial part defines packing a CoAP URI into an HTTP URI, with URI Template mapping forms and encoding caveats.
URI.quote: URI mapping is the term used in this document to describe the process through which the URI of a CoAP resource is transformed into an HTTP URI

media types.why: It registers a new media type and defines media type to CoAP content-format mapping.
media types.quote: This document defines the "application/coap-payload" media type with a single parameter "cf".

rejected.why: CoRE Link Format is used for discovery of the proxy, but the document does not define link relations or web linking itself.
TLS and DTLS are only mentioned as security requirements in the Security Considerations; the document defines nothing new about them.
Proxy caching is discussed briefly in 8.1 and 8.2, but it is a minor part of the mapping guidelines.
CoAP multicast is discussed only as an optional proxy feature, and the document explicitly says details are out of scope.
The document leans on constrained-device context but is about the proxy mapping, which the CoAP tag covers.
Accept header mapping appears within the media type mapping, which is not a general treatment of content negotiation.

RFC8076.title: A Usage for Shared Resources in RELOAD (ShaRe)
RFC8076.summary: RFC 8076 defines ShaRe, a RELOAD Usage that lets multiple peers share write access to a Resource via hierarchical ACL trust delegation, adds the USER-CHAIN-ACL access policy, and allows variable resource names.

P2PSIP.why: The document extends RELOAD (the P2PSIP overlay protocol) with a new Usage, access policy, ACCESS-CONTROL-LIST Kind and configuration extension. The P2PSIP tag covers P2PSIP and RELOAD.
P2PSIP.quote: A new USER-CHAIN-ACL access policy allows authorized peers to write a Shared Resource without owning its corresponding certificate.

rejected.why: SIP is mentioned only via the P2PSIP/RFC 7904 usage as an example; the document is not about SIP signalling.
The ACL delegation scheme is access control, but it is specific to RELOAD and is covered by the RELOAD/P2PSIP tag; a generic authorization tag would be a weaker fit.
XML configuration elements and a RELAX NG grammar are used only as the configuration encoding for the extension, not as the subject.
The more specific P2PSIP tag fits RELOAD better than the generic P2P overlay tag.
Certificates bind usernames to write access, but the document does not specify or profile PKI.

gaps.name: RELOAD (REsource LOcation And Discovery)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated RELOAD tag. P2PSIP is the closest fit, but it is listed as a child of SIP, which is not quite what this document is about.

RFC8077.title: Pseudowire Setup and Maintenance Using the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP)
RFC8077.summary: Internet Standard rewrite of RFC 4447 (obsoleting 4447 and 6723) specifying LDP extensions (PWid and Generalized PWid FEC elements, PW Status TLV, control-word negotiation) to set up and maintain point-to-point pseudowires over MPLS.

pseudowire.why: The whole document defines pseudowire signalling: FEC elements, status signalling, control-word negotiation and label withdrawal for PWs.
pseudowire.quote: This document specifies a protocol for establishing and maintaining the pseudowires, using extensions to the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP).

LDP.why: The document extends LDP with new FEC types (0x80, 0x81), TLVs and status codes, so LDP readers need it.
LDP.quote: we define new TLVs, Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) elements, parameters, and codes for LDP, which enable LDP to identify pseudowires

rejected.why: MPLS is the substrate carrying the PW label and tunnels. The document does not specify MPLS itself, and tunnel setup is out of scope.
VPWS and VPLS are mentioned only as provisioning models. Their use is explicitly not described here.
ATM, Frame Relay and Ethernet are only emulated services whose encapsulations are specified in other documents.
SONET/SDH and TDM circuit emulation appear only as service examples. Their encapsulation is defined elsewhere.
The LDP MD5 authentication option is mentioned only in the Security Considerations.

RFC8078.title: Managing DS Records from the Parent via CDS/CDNSKEY
RFC8078.summary: Standards Track update to RFC 7344 that defines how a child DNS zone uses CDS/CDNSKEY records to signal initial DS publication and DS removal (delete algorithm 0) to its parent, with acceptance policies for initial trust.

DNSSEC.why: The document specifies CDS/CDNSKEY signaling for DS record management, initial trust bootstrapping and DNSSEC turn-off. This is DNSSEC delegation trust maintenance.
DNSSEC.quote: This document adds a method for in-band signaling of these DNSSEC status changes.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific tag and already implies DNS. The CDS/CDNSKEY records are DNSSEC-specific.
Registries and registrars are mentioned as possible 'parent' entities, but the document does not specify registry protocols such as EPP. The subject is DNS-level signaling.
The document does not mention or specify EPP. Out-of-band submission mechanisms are explicitly out of scope.

RFC8079.title: Guidelines for End-to-End Support of the RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) in Back-to-Back User Agents (B2BUAs)
RFC8079.summary: Defines guidelines for how SIP B2BUAs acting as media relays, media-aware relays, or media terminators should handle RTCP messages and related SDP attributes to preserve end-to-end RTCP functionality.

RTCP.why: The document specifies per-message-type rewriting rules for RTCP (SR, RR, SDES, BYE, XR, feedback messages) when a B2BUA changes SSRCs or sequence numbers.
RTCP.quote: This document defines the proper behaviour B2BUAs should follow when acting on both the signalling plane and media plane in order to preserve the end-to-end functionality of RTCP.

SIP.why: The document is about SIP B2BUA behaviour and how its media-plane activity and SDP manipulation interact with signalling, so SIP deployment readers would want it.
SIP.quote: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) [RFC3261] Back-to-Back User Agents (B2BUAs) are SIP entities that can act as a logical combination of both a User Agent Server (UAS) and a User Agent Client (UAC).

SDP.why: Substantial guidance on which SDP attributes (ssrc, rtcp, rtcp-fb, rtcp-mux, rtcp-rsize) to forward, rewrite or remove during offer/answer.
SDP.quote: a media-aware B2BUA MUST advertise its RTCP level of support in the SDP in a coherent way

rejected.why: RTP is discussed (SSRC, sequence number rewriting), but the focus is RTCP; RTCP is the more specific child tag.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a limitation; the document is not about SRTP.
RTCP ECN feedback is one of many message types handled briefly; not a subject of the document.
B2BUAs and SBCs are discussed, but not SIP provider peering.

gaps.name: B2BUA (Back-to-Back User Agents)
gaps.why: The document's central subject is SIP B2BUA/SBC behaviour on the media path, and the taxonomy has no tag for B2BUAs or session border controllers.

RFC8080.title: Edwards-Curve Digital Security Algorithm (EdDSA) for DNSSEC
RFC8080.summary: Defines how Ed25519 and Ed448 EdDSA public keys and signatures are encoded in DNSSEC DNSKEY, RRSIG and DS records, and assigns DNSSEC algorithm numbers 15 and 16.

DNSSEC.why: The document specifies a new DNSSEC signing algorithm, with DNSKEY/RRSIG/DS encodings, algorithm numbers and examples, so DNSSEC readers need it.
DNSSEC.quote: This document defines the use of DNSSEC's DS, DNSKEY, and RRSIG resource records (RRs) with a new signing algorithm, EdDSA

EdDSA.why: The document profiles EdDSA with Ed25519 and Ed448 for use in DNSSEC, so readers of the EdDSA subject would want it.
EdDSA.quote: An Ed25519 public key consists of a 32-octet value, which is encoded into the Public Key field of a DNSKEY resource record

rejected.why: The more specific EdDSA tag fits, and the document only applies the curves defined elsewhere.
The IANA registry update is boilerplate-like and only registers the algorithm numbers.
DNSSEC is the more specific child tag, and the document is not about general DNS.
The document uses the curves through EdDSA in RFC 8032, and does not define them.

RFC8081.title: The "font" Top-Level Media Type
RFC8081.summary: Registers the "font" top-level media type and its initial subtypes (sfnt, ttf, otf, collection, woff, woff2), including a fragment identifier syntax for font collections.

media types.why: The document's purpose is registering a new top-level media type and its subtypes with registration templates, which belongs on the media type registrations page.
media types.quote: This memo serves to register and document the "font" top-level media type, under which subtypes for representation formats for fonts may be registered.

rejected.why: Media types are the subject, but the more specific child tag 'media types' fits. The document does not address MIME body structure or encodings.

Section 4.2 defines fragment identifiers for font collections and mentions RFC 3986 escaping. This is a small part of the document and is a media-type-specific fragment syntax, not a URI scheme or syntax.
Web fonts are served over HTTP, but the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
WOFF is said to be used with HTML and CSS, but only in passing. The document is not about HTML.
The IANA Considerations section holds the registrations themselves. The document is not about IANA registry guidance or stewardship.

gaps.name: font formats (TrueType, OpenType, WOFF)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for font data formats. The registered subtypes (sfnt, ttf, otf, collection, woff, woff2) are the document's main content, so readers looking for font formats would have no subject page.

RFC8082.title: Using Codec Control Messages in the RTP Audio-Visual Profile with Feedback with Layered Codecs
RFC8082.summary: RFC 8082 updates RFC 5104 to clarify that a Full Intra Request received on any RTP stream of a layered bitstream requires the sender to emit a decoder refresh point covering all layers, and reviews the other RTP/AVPF feedback messages for layered codecs.

RTCP.why: The document amends the RTCP-based Codec Control Messages (FIR) of RFC 5104 and reviews PLI, SLI, RPSI, TSTR/TSTN and VBCM from RFC 4585/5104. These are RTCP feedback messages.
RTCP.quote: Requiring a media sender to send a decoder refresh point after the media sender has received a FIR over an RTCP stream

rejected.why: RTP is the transport the feedback messages relate to. The document's subject is the RTCP feedback messages, so the more specific child tag fits better.
Layered codecs such as H.264/SVC are discussed, but only for how feedback applies to them. The document does not define any codec.
SDP grouping and layer dependency are mentioned only briefly as a hint for detecting layered bitstreams in Section 5.
H.264/SVC is cited as an example and for definitional alignment. The document is not about H.264 or its payload format.

gaps.name: RTP/AVPF feedback and Codec Control Messages (FIR, PLI, SLI)
gaps.why: The document is about RTCP-based payload-specific feedback messages. The taxonomy has an RTCP tag under RTP, but the id I used does not exist in the taxonomy, so no precise tag is available.

RFC8083.title: Multimedia Congestion Control: Circuit Breakers for Unicast RTP Sessions
RFC8083.summary: RFC 8083 defines a minimal set of RTP circuit breakers (RTCP timeout, media timeout, congestion, media usability) that make unicast RTP senders stop transmitting under persistent excessive congestion, without proposing a congestion control algorithm.

RTP congestion control.why: The document specifies congestion-protection circuit breakers for interactive RTP flows and the envelope any RTP congestion control must operate within. This is the exact subject of this tag.
RTP congestion control.quote: It instead defines a minimal set of RTP circuit breakers: conditions under which an RTP sender needs to stop transmitting media data to protect the network from excessive congestion.

RTCP.why: The circuit breakers are driven by RTCP SR/RR reports and reporting intervals. The document also updates RFC 3550 on round-robin report priority and covers RTP/AVPF and XR interactions.
RTCP.quote: An RTP sender that has not received any RTCP SR or RTCP RR packets reporting on the SSRC it is using, for a time period of at least three times its deterministic RTCP reporting interval

rejected.why: ECN is discussed only in a short section that says there is no consensus on its effect on the circuit breaker.
UDP is only the best-effort substrate the RTP flows run over. The document defines nothing about UDP itself.
The TCP throughput equation is borrowed from RFC 5348 as a comparison threshold. The document does not specify or extend TFRC.
The more specific child RTP congestion control fits better, so the parent is not listed.
RTCP and RTP congestion control are more specific tags that cover what the document addresses.
TCP throughput is used only as a reference for what counts as fair. The document does not address TCP itself.

gaps.name: Network transport circuit breakers
gaps.why: The document is a specific instance of the circuit-breaker concept in RFC 8084. The taxonomy has no tag for circuit breakers, so RTP congestion control is the closest fit.

RFC8084.title: Network Transport Circuit Breakers
RFC8084.summary: BCP defining what a network transport circuit breaker is, when tunnels and non-congestion-controlled traffic need one, requirements for designing one, and examples (fast-trip, slow-trip, managed) and cases where none is needed.

congestion control.why: The whole document concerns a last-resort congestion protection mechanism for non-congestion-controlled traffic and tunnels. It has no specific child tag in the taxonomy, so the topic tag applies directly.
congestion control.quote: A network transport CB is an automatic mechanism that is used to continuously monitor a flow or aggregate set of flows.

rejected.why: The RTP circuit breakers are specified in RFC 8083. This document only summarizes them as one example.
SAToP and PW circuit breakers appear as managed-CB examples. The document is not about pseudowire emulation itself.
TCP congestion control is background and contrast. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
RFC 8085 covers UDP usage guidelines. This document only refers to it for unidirectional traffic.
ECN CE marks are mentioned as one possible measurement input. The document does not extend ECN.
Tunnels are a main use case, but the document is not about tunnel encapsulation. It concerns congestion protection for traffic carried in them.

gaps.name: Circuit breakers
gaps.why: A dedicated tag for network transport circuit breakers would help. RFC 8083 and the pseudowire congestion work are closely related to this one.

RFC8085.title: UDP Usage Guidelines
RFC8085.summary: BCP giving guidelines to designers of applications, tunnels and protocols that use UDP, centred on congestion control and also covering message size, reliability, checksums, middlebox traversal, ECN, DSCP, multicast and ports.

UDP.why: The whole document is a usage guideline for UDP, covering checksums, message size, ports and reliability.
UDP.quote: This document provides guidelines on the use of UDP for the designers of applications, tunnels, and other protocols that use UDP.

congestion control.why: Section 3.1 gives extensive congestion control guidance for UDP applications, including bulk transfer, low-volume traffic, timers, pacing and circuit breakers.
congestion control.quote: Congestion control guidelines are a primary focus

UDP-Lite.why: A dedicated subsection gives guidance on when and how applications should use UDP-Lite.
UDP-Lite.quote: UDP-Lite changes the semantics of the UDP "payload length" field to that of a "checksum coverage length" field.

ECN.why: A section lists the mechanisms UDP applications must provide to use ECN.
ECN.quote: The set of mechanisms required for an application to use ECN over UDP are:

multicast.why: A whole section covers multicast UDP usage, including congestion control and message size; this is the main addition over RFC 5405.
multicast.quote: This section complements Section 3 by providing additional guidelines that are applicable to multicast and broadcast usage of UDP.

tunneling.why: Guidance on congestion control, ECN, DSCP and checksums for UDP tunnels runs through the document, including the zero-checksum case study.
tunneling.quote: One increasingly popular use of UDP is as a tunneling protocol

Diffserv.why: A subsection covers DSCP use by UDP applications.
Diffserv.quote: An application using UDP can use the differentiated services (DiffServ) Quality of Service (QoS) framework.

rejected.why: TCP is only the comparison point and the recommended alternative; the document does not specify or extend it.
Path MTU discovery is covered in the message size guidance, but only as one part of that guidance.
Middlebox traversal is a guideline subsection, but the document does not specify NAT behaviour.
DTLS and IPsec appear only as options in Security Considerations.
The UDP checksum guidance is substantial, but it is one of several UDP-specific topics, so the UDP tag covers it.
ECMP appears in the discussion of source port entropy, but the document is not about ECMP.

RFC8086.title: GRE-in-UDP Encapsulation
RFC8086.summary: Specifies GRE-in-UDP encapsulation, using the UDP source port as flow entropy for ECMP load balancing, with requirements for general Internet and traffic-managed controlled environments, DTLS security, and UDP checksum handling.

GRE.why: The document defines a new GRE encapsulation over UDP, including GRE header usage (key, sequence, checksum) and procedures.
GRE.quote: This document specifies a generic GRE-in-UDP encapsulation for tunneling network protocol packets across an IP network

UDP.why: Substantial content on UDP port usage, source-port entropy, checksum handling including IPv6 zero-checksum mode, and UDP usage guideline compliance.
UDP.quote: a GRE-in-UDP tunnel needs to meet the UDP usage requirements specified in [RFC8085]

ECMP.why: The main motivation is better ECMP load balancing via UDP source port entropy and IPv6 flow label.
ECMP.quote: allows the UDP source port field to be used as an entropy field. This may be used for load-balancing of GRE traffic in transit networks using existing Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP)

DTLS.why: A dedicated section specifies how DTLS secures GRE-in-UDP tunnels, with a dedicated port.
DTLS.quote: if DTLS is used to secure the GRE-in-UDP tunnel, the destination port of the UDP header MUST be set to the IANA-assigned value (4755)

rejected.why: IPv6 is a delivery network covered (flow label, zero checksum), but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Congestion considerations are discussed, but the tunnel provides none and defers to RFC 8085; not the main subject.
ECN is mentioned only as a one-line reference to RFC 6040 for marking propagation.
Middlebox/NAPT considerations are a short section about conflicts, not specifying NAT behaviour.
MPLS, pseudowire and VPN are only examples of traffic carried in TMCE.
NVGRE is mentioned in Security Considerations only; the document is a generic tunnel encapsulation.

RFC8087.title: The Benefits of Using Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN)
RFC8087.summary: Informational document describing the benefits of applications using ECN-capable transports (throughput, reduced head-of-line blocking, fewer RTOs, visible congestion), and the network and deployment requirements for ECN, without proposing new algorithms.

ECN.why: The whole document covers ECN's benefits, network support, bleaching, tunnelling, path testing and deployment prerequisites.
ECN.quote: The goal of this document is to describe the potential benefits of applications using a transport that enables Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN).

rejected.why: AQM is the mechanism that produces CE marks and is discussed in relation to ECN. The document is about ECN benefits, not AQM algorithms.
TCP is used as an example transport. The document specifies nothing new about TCP.
The ECN tag already sits under this topic, so the parent is implied.
DCTCP is mentioned only briefly as an example of richer ECN feedback in controlled environments.
ConEx is mentioned once as a user of ECN measurements.
UDP applications are discussed as users of ECN, but the document does not address UDP usage itself.

RFC8088.title: How to Write an RTP Payload Format
RFC8088.summary: RFC 8088 is an informational guide for authors of RTP payload format specifications, covering preparation, IETF process, design features (aggregation, fragmentation, timestamps, scalability), media type/SDP mapping, and a template.

RTP payload format.why: The whole document is guidance on designing and specifying RTP payload formats, including a template.
RTP payload format.quote: This document contains information on how best to write an RTP payload format specification.

RTP.why: Substantial coverage of RTP sessions, header fields, multiplexing, synchronization and robustness tools that payload authors must understand.
RTP.quote: Two fields always require additional specification by the RTP payload format, namely the RTP timestamp and the marker bit.

media types.why: Discusses media type naming, parameters, registration for RTP payload formats, and a registration template.
media types.quote: It is important to choose the correct content-type when creating the media type identifying an RTP payload format.

SDP.why: Detailed guidance on mapping payload format parameters to SDP, offer/answer and declarative usage.
SDP.quote: The Offer/Answer (O/A) model allows SIP to negotiate which media formats and payload formats are to be used in a session

rejected.why: IETF process steps for payload drafts are described, but only as supporting guidance for RTP payload authors, not the document's subject.
Codecs are cited as examples only; the document is not about any specific codec.
SIP is only mentioned as a signalling context.
SRTP is discussed as a security mechanism the payload format need not handle.
RTCP appears in synchronization and reporting discussion but is not a main subject.

RFC8089.title: The "file" URI Scheme
RFC8089.summary: RFC 8089 specifies the "file" URI scheme, giving its ABNF syntax, local vs non-local semantics, file-name encoding, and informative notes on nonstandard variants, replacing the brief definition in RFC 1738.

URI.why: The document defines a URI scheme, its syntax, resolution behaviour and registration, which is squarely the URI subject.
URI.quote: This document provides a more complete specification of the "file" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) scheme

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used to define the syntax; the document is not about ABNF.
Section 4 recommends percent-encoded UTF-8 for file names, but this is a minor point and the document is not about the encoding.
The document does not address internationalized identifiers beyond percent-encoding UTF-8.
The scheme registration is boilerplate-level IANA considerations, not the subject of the document.
Security considerations mention file origin privileges only briefly, and this is not the main body.
The host in the authority is only an FQDN component of the syntax; the document does not address host naming.

RFC8090.title: Appointment Procedures for the IETF Representatives to the Community Coordination Group (CCG)
RFC8090.summary: An IAB informational RFC defining how the IETF (via the IAB) nominates, selects, removes, and reports on its three Community Coordination Group representatives, who advise the IETF Trust on IANA trademarks and domain names after the IANA Stewardship Transition.

IETF process.why: The document is an IETF administrative procedure for nominations, selection by IAB vote, removal and reporting of appointees. This is IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: This document outlines the procedures for the IETF to select, appoint, and remove the three CCG Representatives for the Protocol Parameter Community.

IANA.why: The CCG exists for IANA stewardship following the IANA Stewardship Transition, so IANA stewardship readers would want this RFC. It is not about registries themselves.
IANA.quote: provide guidance and advice to the IETF Trust regarding the stewardship of the IANA Intellectual Property, which is the IANA trademarks and the IANA domain names.

rejected.why: The IANA Intellectual Property (trademarks and domain names) is the CCG's subject, but the document is about appointment procedures and not IPR, copyright or trust legal provisions.
NomCom members are only mentioned as eligible nominees. The IAB runs the appointment process, not the NomCom.
IANA domain names are mentioned only as an asset the CCG advises on, and the document says nothing about DNS technology.

RFC8091.title: A Media Type Structured Syntax Suffix for JSON Text Sequences
RFC8091.summary: Defines and registers the "+json-seq" structured syntax suffix for media types built on JSON text sequences (RFC 7464) in the IANA Structured Syntax Suffix Registry.

media types.why: The document's sole purpose is registering a media type structured syntax suffix under RFC 6838 rules, which is a media type registration matter.
media types.quote: This specification defines and registers "+json-seq" as a structured syntax suffix for JSON text sequences.

JSON.why: The suffix is specifically for JSON text sequences, a JSON-based format; readers of JSON formats would want to find this suffix registration.
JSON.quote: JSON text sequences [RFC7464] is a recent specification in the JSON space that defines how a sequence of multiple JSON texts can be represented

rejected.why: The registration is only the vehicle for the document's content; the document is not about IANA registry policy or stewardship.
Fragment identifier considerations appear only within the registration template and do not make the document about URIs.

RFC8092.title: BGP Large Communities Attribute
RFC8092.summary: Defines the BGP Large Communities attribute, an optional transitive BGP path attribute of 12-octet values (4-octet Global Administrator plus two 4-octet local data fields) suited to four-octet ASNs, with aggregation, canonical text form and error handling.

BGP communities.why: The whole document specifies the Large Communities attribute: encoding, aggregation, canonical representation and error handling. This is the BGP Communities subject, and the child tag is more specific than BGP.
BGP communities.quote: This document describes the BGP Large Communities attribute, an extension to BGP-4.

rejected.why: The document extends BGP, but the more specific BGP communities tag covers it; the parent is implied.
Security Considerations only notes that integrity is not protected and defers securing BGP elsewhere; it is not the subject.
The only IANA action is a single path attribute code point assignment; this is boilerplate.

RFC8093.title: Deprecation of BGP Path Attribute Values 30, 31, 129, 241, 242, and 243
RFC8093.summary: Requests IANA to mark BGP path attribute values 30, 31, 129, 241, 242, and 243 as Deprecated in the BGP Path Attributes registry because they were squatted by deployed implementations.

BGP.why: The document is about BGP path attribute code points: it deprecates squatted values in the BGP Path Attributes registry, so readers of BGP operations and parameters would want it.
BGP.quote: IANA has marked values 30, 31, 129, 241, 242, and 243 as "Deprecated" in the "BGP Path Attributes" subregistry

rejected.why: Large Communities (RFC 8092) is mentioned only as the trigger that exposed the squatting. The document does not specify or extend it.
The document is an IANA registry action, but it concerns one BGP registry. The BGP tag covers it better, and it is not general IANA guidance or stewardship.

RFC8094.title: DNS over Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS)
RFC8094.summary: Experimental RFC specifying DNS over DTLS (UDP port 853) to give confidential DNS between clients and resolvers, with session handling, performance, PMTU/truncation and anycast considerations.

DNS privacy.why: The document defines encrypted DNS transport over DTLS. No specific DNS privacy child (DoH, DoT, DoQ) covers DTLS, so the parent tag fits.
DNS privacy.quote: This document proposes the use of Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) for DNS, to protect against passive listeners and certain active attacks.

DTLS.why: Much of the document covers DTLS handshake, session management, round-trip and handshake-size reduction, and record/PMTU interactions for DNS.
DTLS.quote: The DNS client initiates the DTLS handshake as described in [RFC6347], following the best practices specified in [RFC7525].

DNS.why: It is a DNS transport extension that covers resolver and server behaviour, truncation, EDNS0 sizing and anycast.
DNS.quote: This document does not change the format of DNS messages.

rejected.why: DNS over TLS (RFC 7858) is only referenced as a companion and fallback; this document is not about it.
EDNS0 is required for response sizing but is only used, not specified or extended.
Mentioned only to explain that it is complementary and does not provide privacy.
Section 6 discusses anycast issues for DTLS state but is a small part of the document.
Section 5 addresses path MTU and truncation for DTLS records but does not specify Path MTU Discovery.
UDP is the substrate the document runs over, not its subject.

RFC8095.title: Services Provided by IETF Transport Protocols and Congestion Control Mechanisms
RFC8095.summary: Informational TAPS survey of the services and features provided by existing IETF transport protocols (TCP, MPTCP, UDP, UDP-Lite, SCTP, DCCP, TLS/DTLS, RTP, HTTP, FLUTE/ALC, NORM, ICMP) and an overview of congestion control mechanisms, as a basis for defining common transport services.

TAPS.why: The document exists to catalogue transport features and services as input to TAPS transport services definition.
TAPS.quote: This survey provides background for the definition of transport services within the TAPS working group.

TCP.why: TCP is surveyed in detail with protocol, interface and feature lists.
TCP.quote: TCP is a connection-oriented protocol that provides a three-way handshake to allow a client and server to set up a connection

MPTCP.why: MPTCP has its own survey section.
MPTCP.quote: Multipath TCP [RFC6824] is an extension for TCP to support multihoming for resilience, mobility, and load balancing.

UDP.why: UDP is surveyed in its own section.
UDP.quote: UDP is a connectionless protocol that maintains message boundaries, with no connection setup or feature negotiation.

UDP-Lite.why: UDP-Lite is surveyed with partial checksum coverage.
UDP-Lite.quote: It changes the semantics of the UDP Payload Length field to that of a Checksum Coverage Length field

SCTP.why: SCTP gets the longest protocol survey including extensions and sockets API.
SCTP.quote: SCTP is a connection-oriented protocol using a four-way handshake to establish an SCTP association

DCCP.why: DCCP is surveyed in its own section.
DCCP.quote: DCCP is a connection-oriented datagram protocol that provides a three-way handshake

congestion control.why: A dedicated section classifies window-based, rate-based and low-priority congestion control mechanisms.
congestion control.quote: Congestion control is critical to the stable operation of the Internet.

NORM.why: NORM is surveyed in its own section.
NORM.quote: NORM is an IETF Standards Track protocol specified in [RFC5740].

ALC.why: FLUTE/ALC is surveyed in its own section as reliable multicast transport.
ALC.quote: FLUTE/ALC is an IETF Standards Track protocol specified in [RFC6726] and [RFC5775].

RTP.why: RTP/RTCP surveyed as a transport.
RTP.quote: RTP provides an end-to-end network transport service, suitable for applications transmitting real-time data

TLS.why: TLS/DTLS are surveyed as pseudotransports providing security features.
TLS.quote: Transport Layer Security (TLS) [RFC5246] and Datagram TLS (DTLS) [RFC6347] are IETF protocols that provide several security-related features

rejected.why: HTTP is surveyed only as a pseudotransport substrate, not specified or extended.
Covered briefly and noted as not a transport service to applications.
Covered jointly under FLUTE/ALC; ALC is the closer fit for the reliable multicast transport.
Treated together with TLS in one section, so TLS covers it adequately.
Mentioned only in passing within the TCP and congestion control discussion.
A more specific TAPS tag and per-protocol tags already cover the transport subject.

RFC8096.title: The IPv6-Specific MIB Modules Are Obsolete
RFC8096.summary: Republishes the obsolete IPv6-specific MIB modules (IPV6-TC, IPV6-MIB, IPV6-ICMP-MIB, IPV6-UDP-MIB, IPV6-TCP-MIB) with SMI status obsolete, and reclassifies RFCs 2452, 2454, 2465 and 2466 as Historic.

MIB.why: The whole document consists of SMIv2 MIB modules republished as obsolete, so readers of the MIB subject would want it.
MIB.quote: we are simply republishing these MIB modules with the Structure of Management Information (SMI) status changed to obsolete.

rejected.why: The modules cover IPv6 objects, but the document only obsoletes management modules. It does not specify, extend or analyse IPv6.
The MIB modules are managed through SNMP, but the document does not define SNMP protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific fit.
IPV6-ICMP-MIB is one of the modules included. It is only a statistics MIB, so the document is not about ICMP itself.
IPV6-TCP-MIB is included but is only a connection table MIB for TCP over IPv6. The document does not specify TCP.
IPV6-UDP-MIB is included but is only a listener table MIB. The document does not specify UDP.

RFC8097.title: BGP Prefix Origin Validation State Extended Community
RFC8097.summary: Defines a BGP opaque non-transitive extended community that carries a route's RPKI prefix origin validation state (valid, not found, invalid) between IBGP speakers so it can influence best-path selection.

RPKI.why: The document specifies how route origin validation results are encoded and propagated within an AS. This is a direct extension of RPKI-based origin validation, so readers of that subject need it.
RPKI.quote: The last octet of the extended community is an unsigned integer that gives the route's validation state [RFC6811].

BGP communities.why: It defines a new BGP opaque extended community: its encoding, sub-type, handling of multiple instances, and EBGP and IBGP propagation rules.
BGP communities.quote: The origin validation state extended community is an opaque extended community [RFC4360] with the following encoding:

rejected.why: BGP is the parent of BGP communities, which is already tagged, so the parent is implied.
RPKI sits under routing security and is already tagged, so the parent is implied.
The document concerns origin validation only. It does not cover path validation.
The only IANA content is a sub-type registration in the boilerplate IANA Considerations section, which is not evidence of subject.

RFC8098.title: Message Disposition Notification
RFC8098.summary: RFC 8098 defines the message/disposition-notification MIME media type and the Disposition-Notification-To, Disposition-Notification-Options and Original-Recipient header fields for requesting and reporting Message Disposition Notifications (read receipts) in Internet mail, obsoleting RFC 3798.

message format.why: The document defines new email header fields (Disposition-Notification-To, Disposition-Notification-Options, Original-Recipient) and the field syntax of the MDN, which is Internet message format work.
message format.quote: Message disposition notifications are requested by including a Disposition-Notification-To header field in the message containing one or more addresses specifying where dispositions should be sent.

media types.why: It includes a full media type registration template and the multipart/report usage, and the MDN is a MIME message with its own registries.
media types.quote: The message/disposition-notification media type is defined as follows:

rejected.why: Parent of message format; the more specific child tag fits better, so the parent is implied.
The document uses SMTP envelope details (MAIL FROM, ORCPT) and amends RFC 3461 slightly, but it does not specify or extend SMTP itself.
It cites the IMAP MDN profile (RFC 3503) once to prevent duplicate MDNs, but is not about IMAP.
MIME is the substrate. The document defines a media type and amends message/partial handling only in passing, so the media types tag covers the relevant part.
X.400 gatewaying is discussed as guidelines, but the document does not specify X.400 interworking.
The IANA registration sections are boilerplate-like and set up registries only for this document's own extensions.

gaps.name: Message Disposition Notifications (MDN) / read receipts
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for mail delivery and disposition notification reports (MDN, DSN). The closest tags are message format and media types.

RFC8099.title: OSPF Topology-Transparent Zone
RFC8099.summary: Defines the OSPF Topology-Transparent Zone (TTZ), an experimental OSPFv2 extension using opaque LSAs that hides a group of routers' internal topology from the rest of an OSPF area. It also specifies smooth migration and rollback procedures.

OSPF.why: The document specifies new OSPFv2 extensions: TTZ opaque LSAs, TLVs, adjacency discovery, flooding rules and routing table computation changes.
OSPF.quote: This document presents a Topology-Transparent Zone (TTZ) in an OSPF area and describes extensions to OSPFv2 for supporting the TTZ

rejected.why: The extensions are defined only for OSPFv2, not OSPF for IPv6.
The document addresses scalability and hierarchy, but its content is an OSPF-specific mechanism, so the OSPF tag is more specific.
The IANA section registers an opaque LSA type and a TTZ TLV registry. This is boilerplate, and the document is not about IANA.

RFC8100.title: Diffserv-Interconnection Classes and Practice
RFC8100.summary: RFC 8100 defines a limited common set of four Diffserv Treatment Aggregates, PHBs and DSCPs for interconnecting separately administered networks, motivated by MPLS Short Pipe Model operators.

Diffserv.why: The document specifies interconnection PHBs, DSCPs, Treatment Aggregates and re-marking practice for Diffserv. This is its core subject.
Diffserv.quote: This document defines a limited common set of Diffserv Per-Hop Behaviors (PHBs) and Diffserv Codepoints (DSCPs) to be applied at (inter)connections of two separately administered and operated networks

MPLS.why: Much of the document concerns MPLS Short Pipe Model tunnels, penultimate hop popping, TC field use and mapping to MPLS Treatment Aggregates. Readers of MPLS would want it.
MPLS.quote: The operational simplifications and methods in this document help align IP Diffserv functionality with MPLS limitations resulting from the widely deployed Short Pipe Model for MPLS tunnel operation

rejected.why: BGP is mentioned only as related work and as an example of network control traffic marked CS6. The document does not specify or extend it.
Pipe, Short Pipe and Uniform tunnel models are discussed only as they affect DSCP handling. The document is not about tunnelling in general.
Diffserv is the more specific tag under QoS, so the parent is implied.
MPLS VPNs are mentioned only in passing, when explaining which tunnels follow the Pipe Model.

RFC8101.title: IANA Registration of New Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Resource-Priority Namespace for Mission Critical Push To Talk Service
RFC8101.summary: Informational RFC that defines two new SIP Resource-Priority namespaces (mcpttp for preemption, mcpttq for queuing) for 3GPP Mission Critical Push To Talk and registers them with IANA.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP's Resource-Priority header (RFC 4412) with new namespaces and priority levels for MCPTT call control. SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: This document creates additional Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Resource-Priority namespaces to meet the requirements of the 3GPP-defined Mission Critical Push To Talk (MCPTT)

rejected.why: The document only registers namespaces under existing registry rules; it gives no guidance on IANA registries in general, and IANA Considerations is boilerplate.
MCPTT runs over 3GPP LTE and the applicability section scopes use to LTE networks, but the document defines nothing about IP over cellular.
