Resource priority relates to prioritising access to network resources, but the document only defines SIP header namespaces, not QoS architecture or signalling.
MCPTT targets public safety, but the document is about namespace registration, not emergency calling.

RFC8102.title: Remote-LFA Node Protection and Manageability
RFC8102.summary: RFC 8102 extends Remote-LFA IP fast reroute with procedures to determine whether a PQ-node gives node protection for a destination, and to collect full alternate-path characteristics for operator policy selection.

IP fast reroute.why: The whole document extends remote-LFA fast reroute with node-protection computation and path-characteristic collection for LFA manageability.
IP fast reroute.quote: specifies procedures for determining whether or not a given PQ-node provides node protection for a specific destination

rejected.why: Link-state SPF computations are used but the document is not about OSPF; it only mentions IS-IS system-id in passing.
IS-IS is mentioned only for router-id naming; the document is protocol-agnostic.
ECMP primary next hops are handled as a case, but the document is about fast reroute, not ECMP forwarding.
Parent-level topic; the more specific IP fast reroute tag fits.

RFC8103.title: Using ChaCha20-Poly1305 Authenticated Encryption in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC8103.summary: Specifies how to use the ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD algorithm as a content-authenticated-encryption algorithm in the CMS AuthEnvelopedData content type, defining its OID, nonce parameter, S/MIME capability, and ASN.1 module.

ChaCha20.why: The document defines how the ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD algorithm is used in CMS, including its algorithm identifier and nonce parameter.
ChaCha20.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using ChaCha20-Poly1305 Authenticated Encryption with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)

CMS.why: It profiles the CMS authenticated-enveloped-data content type for a new algorithm and discusses CMS key management techniques.
CMS.quote: The AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 algorithm identifier is located in the AuthEnvelopedData EncryptedContentInfo contentEncryptionAlgorithm field.
CMS.section: 3. Using the AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 Algorithm with AuthEnvelopedData

S/MIME.why: A section defines the SMIMECapabilities encoding for the algorithm, and the OID is registered in the S/MIME algorithms registry.
S/MIME.quote: compliant software MAY include the SMIMECapabilities signed attribute to announce support for the AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 algorithm.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation for the module in the appendix, not the subject.
Random key generation appears only in Security Considerations as a brief pointer to RFC 4086.
Section 2 only describes the existing CMS key management options as they relate to nonce uniqueness. The document does not define key management.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate for the OID and module identifier.

RFC8104.title: Pseudowire (PW) Endpoint Fast Failure Protection
RFC8104.summary: Specifies a local-repair fast protection mechanism for pseudowires against egress AC, egress PE and S-PE failures, using context identifiers, upstream-assigned labels, bypass tunnels to a protector, and new LDP TLVs.

pseudowire.why: The whole document defines PW egress endpoint protection, covering single-segment and multi-segment PWs and their LDP signalling.
pseudowire.quote: specifies a fast mechanism for protecting pseudowires (PWs) transported by IP/MPLS tunnels against egress endpoint failures

LDP.why: Section 6 defines new LDP TLVs (Egress Protection Capability, Protection FEC Element) and label distribution procedures over targeted LDP sessions.
LDP.quote: this document defines a new "Protection FEC Element" TLV.

IP fast reroute.why: The mechanism is a fast-reroute style local repair with a PLR and pre-installed bypass tunnels, comparable to RSVP and IP/LDP FRR.
IP fast reroute.quote: It specifies a fast protection mechanism based on local repair to protect PWs against the following endpoint failures

rejected.why: The parent tag is implied by the chosen child tags (pseudowire, LDP).
BFD is only mentioned as one possible failure detection mechanism for the PLR.
RSVP-TE is cited only as an alternative bypass or transport tunnel option and is not extended.
ECMP is discussed only as an applicability case, not as the subject of the document.
The document concerns PW protection mechanics, not L2VPN services.
The Interface_ID TLV is borrowed from the GMPLS RFCs, but GMPLS itself is not the subject.

gaps.name: Pseudowire (PWE3) emulation
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no pseudowire tag, and the document is chiefly about PW protection. The nearest tags are MPLS and its children, which is why pseudowire is used above.

RFC8105.title: Transmission of IPv6 Packets over Digital Enhanced Cordless Telecommunications (DECT) Ultra Low Energy (ULE)
RFC8105.summary: Specifies how IPv6 is transported over DECT Ultra Low Energy links using 6LoWPAN techniques (header compression, optimized ND, IID derivation from DECT identities) in a star topology with the FP as 6LBR and PPs as 6LNs.

6LoWPAN.why: The document is an IPv6-over-link-layer adaptation for DECT ULE using 6LoWPAN (RFC 6282 compression, RFC 6775 ND, no mesh header, no fragmentation), the same kind of document as IPv6 over 802.15.4 and BLE.
6LoWPAN.quote: This document describes how IPv6 is transported over DECT ULE using IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (6LoWPAN) techniques.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the carried protocol, but the document is about its adaptation to a constrained link, which 6LoWPAN covers more specifically.
It profiles RFC 6775 ND for star topology, but this is part of the 6LoWPAN adaptation and not the main subject.
IID derivation and link-local address configuration are specified, but as a part of the 6LoWPAN mapping.
RFC 6282 compression is mandated, but it is not a new compression mechanism; it is covered under 6LoWPAN.
AES128/CCM is only the DECT link-layer security mechanism described in Security Considerations.
DECT is a cordless telephony air interface, not a 3GPP cellular system.

gaps.name: DECT ULE (Digital Enhanced Cordless Telecommunications Ultra Low Energy)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for DECT or this link technology, which is what the document is about, so 6LoWPAN is the closest fit.

RFC8106.title: IPv6 Router Advertisement Options for DNS Configuration
RFC8106.summary: RFC 8106 specifies IPv6 Router Advertisement options (RDNSS and DNSSL) that let routers advertise DNS recursive server addresses and a DNS search list to hosts, and obsoletes RFC 6106 with a higher default lifetime.

neighbor discovery.why: The document defines two new IPv6 Neighbor Discovery options carried in RAs, with their formats, lifetimes and host processing procedures.
neighbor discovery.quote: This document specifies IPv6 Router Advertisement (RA) options (called "DNS RA options") to allow IPv6 routers to advertise a list of DNS Recursive Server Addresses

SLAAC.why: The mechanism lets SLAAC-only hosts obtain DNS configuration from the same RA as prefix information, and the document discusses its applicability to SLAAC networks without DHCPv6.
SLAAC.quote: IPv6 SLAAC cannot stand on its own as an alternative deployment model in any practical network without any support for DNS configuration.

DNS.why: The document is about configuring DNS resolver information (recursive server addresses, search list) in hosts, including resolver repository handling, so DNS readers would want it.
DNS.quote: allow IPv6 hosts to perform automatic DNS configuration.

rejected.why: DHCPv6 DNS options are discussed as an alternative and for coexistence/precedence, but the document does not specify or extend DHCPv6.
SEND is recommended as a security mechanism for the RA options, but only in a supporting role; the document does not specify or extend it.
Parent of the chosen neighbor discovery and SLAAC tags, so it is implied.
RA messages are ICMPv6, but the document defines ND options, not ICMP itself.
No DNSSEC content; the security section concerns rogue RAs and DNS server spoofing, not signing or validation.

RFC8107.title: Advertising Digital Identifier (Ad-ID) URN Namespace Definition
RFC8107.summary: Defines the formal URN namespace identifier "adid" for Advertising Digital Identifiers (Ad-IDs), which identify advertising assets across media platforms, using the RFC 3406 registration template.

URN.why: The document's sole purpose is registering a new URN namespace (adid), with its syntax, equivalence, persistence and resolution rules. URN covers URN namespaces.
URN.quote: This document defines the formal Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace Identifier (NID) for Ad-IDs.

rejected.why: ABNF is only used as notation to express the URN syntax; the document is not about ABNF.
The IANA Considerations section only registers the namespace in the Formal URN Namespaces registry; this is boilerplate and the document is not about IANA registries in general.
URN is the more specific tag and already implies URI as an ancestor.
Ad-IDs are ASCII strings, but this is incidental to the identifier format and not what the document is about.

RFC8108.title: Sending Multiple RTP Streams in a Single RTP Session
RFC8108.summary: Updates RFC 3550 and RFC 4585 to specify how RTP endpoints with multiple SSRCs in one RTP session behave, focusing on RTCP reporting, aggregation, scheduling, feedback, SSRC add/remove and timeout rules.

RTCP.why: The core of the document is RTCP behaviour for multi-SSRC endpoints: reporting intervals, aggregation of compound packets, avg_rtcp_size, scheduling, feedback and SSRC timeout, updating RFC 3550 and RFC 4585.
RTCP.quote: implementations MUST treat each SSRC as a separate participant in the RTP session, so that an endpoint that has multiple SSRCs counts as multiple participants.
RTCP.section: 5. Use of RTCP by Endpoints That Send Multiple Media Streams

RTP.why: It clarifies RTP session semantics for multiple streams and SSRCs, including adding and removing SSRCs, bandwidth sharing and use cases such as mixers and multiple capture devices.
RTP.quote: This memo expands and clarifies the behavior of Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) endpoints that use multiple synchronization sources (SSRCs).

rejected.why: SRTP and RTP/SAVPF are mentioned only as secure profile variants and in one Security Considerations remark about the crypto context; the document is not about them.
SDP appears only for bandwidth lines (b=RR/RS/AS) and for signalling SSRCs; it is incidental.
CLUE telepresence is cited only as a motivating use case for multiple capture devices.
MIKEY appears only in a security aside about per-SSRC keying.
RFC 4588 retransmission and SVC payload formats are mentioned only as examples of why multiple SSRCs are used.
Congestion control is only mentioned in passing for bandwidth share; the document does not address it.

RFC8109.title: Initializing a DNS Resolver with Priming Queries
RFC8109.summary: BCP describing the priming queries (QNAME ".", QTYPE NS) a recursive DNS resolver should send to initialize its cache with the root NS RRset and root server addresses, including retry, target selection, DNSSEC and response-handling guidance.

DNS.why: The document specifies recommended resolver behaviour for priming queries and responses, which is core DNS resolver operation.
DNS.quote: A priming query is a DNS query used to get the root server information in a resolver. It has a QNAME of "." and a QTYPE of NS

rejected.why: DNSSEC is discussed in Section 3.3 only to explain that validation of priming responses is of little use currently; the document is not about DNSSEC.
EDNS(0) is recommended for priming queries but is only a mechanism used, not something the document specifies or extends.

RFC8110.title: Opportunistic Wireless Encryption
RFC8110.summary: RFC 8110 specifies Opportunistic Wireless Encryption (OWE), an IEEE 802.11 extension that performs an unauthenticated Diffie-Hellman exchange during association to derive a PMK for the 4-way handshake, giving encryption on open Wi-Fi networks.

WiFi.why: The whole document defines a new AKM, association elements and key derivation for IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs, so Wi-Fi readers would want it.
WiFi.quote: an extension to IEEE Std 802.11 to provide for opportunistic (unauthenticated) encryption to the wireless media

key management.why: A substantial part of the document specifies the DH exchange, HKDF-based PMK and PMKID derivation, and PMK caching, which is key establishment.
key management.quote: the client and AP perform a Diffie-Hellman key exchange during the access procedure and use the resulting pairwise secret with the 4-way handshake

rejected.why: The document provides link encryption against passive sniffing. It is not a privacy threat model or a protocol privacy-considerations document.
OWE explicitly provides no authentication, so the document is not about authenticating users or hosts.
Elliptic curve groups are used for the Diffie-Hellman exchange, but the document specifies no new ECC. It only references existing groups and encodings.
HKDF and HMAC are used as building blocks for key derivation. They are not what the document is about.
SHA hash selection by group size is an implementation detail, not the subject of the document.
The document uses only the IKE IANA registry of Diffie-Hellman groups. It does not specify or extend IKE.

gaps.name: Opportunistic security / opportunistic encryption
gaps.why: The document is a mode of opportunistic security (RFC 7435). The taxonomy has no tag for opportunistic encryption, and the security parent is too generic.

RFC8111.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol Delegated Database Tree (LISP-DDT)
RFC8111.summary: Specifies LISP-DDT, a hierarchical, statically delegated database of DDT nodes that lets LISP Map-Resolvers iteratively follow Map-Referral messages to find the Map-Servers and ETRs holding EID-to-RLOC mappings, including a signature-based security architecture.

LISP.why: The document defines a mapping-database architecture, new message type (Map-Referral) and node behaviour for LISP.
LISP.quote: LISP-DDT defines a new device type, the DDT node, that is configured as authoritative for one or more XEID-prefixes.

rejected.why: DNS referral-following is only mentioned as a conceptual analogy; DDT is not DNS and defines no DNS records or behaviour.
RFC 5011 is cited only for revocation precedent; DDT has its own signature scheme.
SIDR/RPKI is mentioned in Security Considerations as possible future work for prefix authorization only.
Messages go to UDP port 4342 but UDP is only the substrate.
RSA-SHA256 is a mandatory signature algorithm but only used as a building block.

gaps.name: LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a LISP tech entry under routing, but I used 'LISP' as the tag id. Checking: the taxonomy lists 'LISP' under routing, so it is valid; no gap beyond that.

RFC8112.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol Delegated Database Tree (LISP-DDT) Referral Internet Groper (RIG)
RFC8112.summary: Describes the "rig" diagnostic tool, which queries the LISP-DDT mapping database hierarchy by sending Map-Requests and displaying Map-Referral results, with syntax and sample output.

LISP.why: The whole document specifies a LISP-DDT diagnostic tool: Map-Requests, Map-Referrals, EIDs and RLOCs. Readers of the LISP subject would want it.
LISP.quote: The "rig" tool is a manual management tool to query the LISP-DDT mapping database hierarchy.

rejected.why: DNS appears only as a way a host obtains an EID, and as an analogy. The document is not about DNS.
rig is a diagnostic tool, but it queries a mapping database hierarchy and does not discover network paths.
IPv6 EIDs are mentioned only in passing in the implementation section.
UDP port 4342 is mentioned only in a definition. UDP is just the transport.

gaps.name: LISP-DDT (Locator/ID Separation Protocol Delegated Database Tree)
gaps.why: The document is about LISP and LISP-DDT, but the taxonomy has a LISP tag only under routing and no DDT tag. I have tagged LISP, which is not in the taxonomy as shown, so please verify the id.

RFC8113.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP): Shared Extension Message & IANA Registry for Packet Type Allocations
RFC8113.summary: Defines a shared LISP extension message type (type 15) with sub-types, and creates IANA registries for LISP packet types and shared-extension sub-types, updating RFC 6830.

LISP.why: The document extends LISP by defining a shared extension message type and sub-type mechanism, and updates RFC 6830.
LISP.quote: This document specifies a Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) shared message type for defining future extensions and conducting experiments

rejected.why: The registries are created for LISP packet types, but the document is about the LISP protocol extension mechanism, not IANA process or stewardship generally; the IANA section is boilerplate-like.

RFC8114.title: Delivery of IPv4 Multicast Services to IPv4 Clients over an IPv6 Multicast Network
RFC8114.summary: Specifies a stateless IPv4-in-IPv6 encapsulation and address-mapping scheme (mB4 and mAFTR) so IPv4 multicast receivers can get IPv4 multicast over an IPv6 multicast tree, mainly for DS-Lite deployments.

multicast.why: The document defines multicast distribution tree construction, IGMP/MLD interworking, PIMv4/PIMv6 interworking and multicast address mapping. No more specific multicast child tag covers the whole solution.
multicast.quote: This document specifies a generic solution for the delivery of IPv4 multicast services to IPv4 clients over an IPv6 multicast network.

IPv6 transition.why: It is an IPv4/IPv6 coexistence mechanism that delivers IPv4 service across an IPv6-only network using stateless encapsulation and IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses. It is a DS-Lite multicast extension.
IPv6 transition.quote: The solution is particularly useful for the delivery of multicast service offerings to customers serviced by Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite).

DS-Lite.why: It extends DS-Lite (B4/AFTR) with multicast-capable mB4 and mAFTR elements, so DS-Lite readers will want it.
DS-Lite.quote: This document specifies an extension to the DS-Lite model to deliver IPv4 multicast services to IPv4 clients over an IPv6 multicast-enabled network.

IGMP.why: The mB4 translates IGMP reports into MLD reports. A substantial part of the document specifies this interworking and the version mismatches in Appendix B.
IGMP.quote: The IGMP-MLD Interworking function combines the IGMP/MLD Proxying function and the address-synthesizing operations.

MLD.why: The mB4 generates MLD reports toward the IPv6 network with synthesized addresses, so MLD behaviour is a core part of the specification.
MLD.quote: The mB4 performs the host portion of the MLD protocol on the upstream interface.

PIM-SM.why: The mAFTR's PIMv6-to-PIMv4 interworking and its shared-tree to shortest-path-tree switching are specified in detail and rely on PIM-SM procedures.
PIM-SM.quote: The mAFTR MUST interwork PIM Join/Prune messages for (*,G6) and (S6,G6) on their corresponding (*,G4) and (S4,G4).

SSM.why: The document defines SSM and ASM prefix types (SSM_mPrefix64) and per-mode behaviour, and recommends SSM.
SSM.quote: This document describes a stateless translation mechanism that supports either Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) or Any-Source Multicast (ASM) operation.

rejected.why: Reconsidered but kept above as secondary.
IPv4-in-IPv6 encapsulation (RFC 2473) is used for the data path, but the document is not about generic tunnelling.
IPTV appears only as a use case in Appendix A, not as the subject of the document.
Mentioned only as another deployment context in the Introduction.
Only referenced as a possible way to provision the prefixes (RFC 8115).
IPv4-embedded address mapping is part of the solution, but the transition and multicast tags cover it better.

RFC8115.title: DHCPv6 Option for IPv4-Embedded Multicast and Unicast IPv6 Prefixes
RFC8115.summary: Defines the DHCPv6 option OPTION_V6_PREFIX64 that carries the ASM, SSM and unicast IPv6 prefixes used to build IPv4-embedded IPv6 multicast and unicast addresses for IPv4 multicast service continuity over IPv6.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies a new DHCPv6 option, its format, and client behaviour, so DHCPv6 readers need it.
DHCPv6.quote: This document defines a DHCPv6 option [RFC3315] that carries the IPv6 prefixes to be used for constructing these IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses.

IPv6 transition.why: The option supports IPv4/IPv6 multicast transition by supplying prefixes for IPv4-embedded IPv6 address synthesis, usable with DS-Lite, A+P and other techniques.
IPv6 transition.quote: Several solutions (e.g., [RFC8114]) are proposed for the delivery of multicast services in the context of transition to IPv6.

rejected.why: Multicast addressing is the context, but the document specifies a DHCP option, not multicast routing or group membership.
DS-Lite is only mentioned as one use context; the document does not specify or extend it.
SSM prefix ranges are referenced for the option's fields, but SSM itself is not the subject.
IPv6 addressing is used via RFC 6052 mapping, but the document is about the DHCPv6 option, and the more specific transition tag covers the subject.
Prefix64 terminology and the RFC 7051 discovery note relate to NAT64, but the document does not specify NAT64 translation.

RFC8116.title: Security Threats to the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol Version 2 (OLSRv2)
RFC8116.summary: Informational analysis of security threats to OLSRv2 (jittering, hop count/limit, wormholes, sequence numbers, indirect jamming, identity and link spoofing) and how RFC 7183 integrity protection mitigates them.

OLSR.quote: analyzes common security threats to the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol version 2 (OLSRv2) and describes their potential impacts on Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) operations

RFC8117.title: Current Hostname Practice Considered Harmful
RFC8117.summary: Informational RFC describing how current hostname practice leaks identifying information via DHCP, reverse DNS, mDNS, LLMNR, DNS-SD and NetBIOS, and sketching randomized hostnames as a privacy remedy.

privacy.why: The document is a privacy threat analysis of hostname disclosure and proposes randomized hostnames as mitigation.
privacy.quote: This current practice can significantly compromise your privacy, and something should change in order to mitigate these privacy threats.

hostnames.why: Hostname naming practices and their consequences are the central subject.
hostnames.quote: There is a long established practice of giving names to computers. In the Internet protocols, these names are referred to as "hostnames"

mDNS.why: mDNS is analysed as a protocol that leaks hostnames, with its own section.
mDNS.quote: Multicast DNS (mDNS) is defined in [RFC6762]. It enables hosts to send DNS queries over multicast

DNS-SD.why: DNS-SD is analysed for hostname leakage through SRV records.
DNS-SD.quote: the publication of a service also forces the publication of the hostname due to a chain of dependencies.

DHCP.why: DHCP hostname/FQDN leakage is analysed and mitigations are referenced.
DHCP.quote: A DHCP query can disclose the "hostname."

rejected.why: Reverse PTR lookup is one leak vector, but the document is not about DNS itself.
Covered in one short subsection as a leaking protocol only; not a main subject.
Mentioned only in passing as sharing DHCP's issues.
Mentioned only as limiting the usefulness of reverse lookups in IPv4.

gaps.name: LLMNR (Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution)
gaps.why: Has its own subsection as a hostname-leaking protocol, but the taxonomy has no LLMNR tag.

RFC8118.title: The application/pdf Media Type
RFC8118.summary: Updates the IANA registration of the application/pdf media type (obsoleting RFC 3778), giving an overview of PDF, its ISO subset standards, versions, implementations, fragment identifier syntax, and security considerations.

media types.why: The document exists to update the application/pdf media type registration, so readers of media type registrations would look for it here.
media types.quote: This document updates the registration of "application/pdf", a media type registration previously defined in [RFC3778], using the registration template defined in [RFC6838]

URI.why: A substantial section defines the URI fragment identifier syntax and parameters (page, zoom, search, etc.) for PDF.
URI.quote: A fragment identifier for PDF has one or more parameters, separated by the ampersand (&) or pound (#) character.

rejected.why: The document is about a media type registration, not MIME body structure or encodings; the media types tag is the more specific fit.
XMP and XFDF are mentioned only in passing; the document is not about XML usage.
PDF/UA is mentioned as one subset standard in a list, not a substantial subject of the document.
PDF is exchanged over the web, but the document does not address web architecture.

gaps.name: PDF (Portable Document Format)
gaps.why: The document is largely an overview of the PDF format and its ISO subsets (PDF/A, PDF/X, PDF/E, PDF/UA, PDF/VT), but the taxonomy has no tag for PDF or document formats.

RFC8119.title: SIP "cause" URI Parameter for Service Number Translation
RFC8119.summary: Updates RFC 4458 by defining a new SIP "cause" URI parameter value (380, "Service number translation") for retargeting by service access number translation, and gives guidance on using the parameter with the History-Info header field.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP by defining a new predefined value for the SIP URI "cause" parameter and specifies how proxies, application servers and UAS handle it with History-Info.
SIP.quote: A new value for the "cause" URI parameter of the 'sip:' or 'sips:' URI schemes is defined for the "Service number translation" use case.

rejected.why: The motivation is interworking with ISUP called IN number parameters, but the document specifies only a SIP URI parameter value and History-Info guidance, not a gateway or interworking mechanism.
It does not define ISUP encapsulation or SIP-ISUP interworking; ISUP is only cited as background.
The "cause" parameter is a SIP URI parameter, but the document is about SIP retargeting semantics, not URI syntax in general.
The IANA section only adds a reference to an existing registry row; it is boilerplate.
The ABNF is only a quoted summary of existing grammar from RFC 4458, not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: SIP History-Info / request history information
gaps.why: Much of the document is guidance on using the History-Info header field (RFC 7044) with the "cause" parameter. The taxonomy has no specific tag for it, so it falls under SIP.

RFC8120.title: Mutual Authentication Protocol for HTTP
RFC8120.summary: RFC 8120 specifies the Mutual authentication scheme for HTTP, a PAKE-based password authentication framework providing true mutual client/server authentication with its message flows, realms, sessions, host validation and IANA registries.

HTTP authentication.why: The document defines a new HTTP authentication scheme (Mutual) using WWW-Authenticate/Authorization/Authentication-Info, registered in the HTTP Authentication Schemes registry, as an alternative to Basic and Digest.
HTTP authentication.quote: This document specifies an authentication scheme for the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) that is referred to as either the Mutual authentication scheme

PAKE.why: The protocol is a PAKE framework: key exchange tweaked by the password, with verification of the shared key. The concrete algorithm is in a companion RFC, but the framework is specified here.
PAKE.quote: the authentication scheme proposed in this document is a general framework for using password-based authenticated key exchange (PAKE) and similar stronger cryptographic primitives with HTTP

rejected.why: TLS is only the substrate. The document defines host validation using existing channel bindings (tls-unique, tls-server-end-point) but no new TLS mechanism.
HOBA is mentioned only as an alternative non-password scheme in the introduction.
Cookies appear only in passing, as a comparison and for the public-suffix blacklist.
PBKDF2 is only used as a default key derivation function in Section 12.2. The document is not about it.
HMAC is only a building block inside PBKDF2 in the default functions.
Section 9 uses RFC 7613 profiles for string preparation, which is a minor supporting detail.

RFC8121.title: Mutual Authentication Protocol for HTTP: Cryptographic Algorithms Based on the Key Agreement Mechanism 3 (KAM3)
RFC8121.summary: Specifies four KAM3-based (ISO 11770-4, APKAS-AMP) augmented PAKE algorithms, using MODP and elliptic-curve groups, for the HTTP Mutual authentication protocol (RFC 8120), and registers their tokens.

PAKE.why: The document defines the K_c1, K_s1 and J functions of an augmented PAKE (APKAS-AMP / ISO KAM3) in discrete-log and elliptic-curve settings. This is the core content.
PAKE.quote: The algorithms are based on augmented password-based authenticated key exchange (augmented PAKE) techniques.

HTTP authentication.why: It supplies the cryptographic algorithms and IANA-registered tokens for the HTTP Mutual authentication scheme. Readers of HTTP authentication schemes would want it.
HTTP authentication.quote: This document specifies algorithms for use with the Mutual authentication protocol for the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) [RFC8120]

rejected.why: The P-256 and P-521 curves are used as groups for the PAKE, but the document is not about elliptic-curve cryptography in its own right.
SHA-256 and SHA-512 are only the hash function H, used as a building block.
HTTP is the host protocol, and the document's subject is the authentication algorithms, which HTTP authentication covers.
The key exchange is part of the PAKE, which is the more specific tag.
The MODP groups come from RFC 3526 (IKE), but the document does not concern IKE.

RFC8122.title: Connection-Oriented Media Transport over the Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol in the Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC8122.summary: Defines the SDP 'TCP/TLS' protocol identifier and the 'fingerprint' attribute for certificate hashes, so connection-oriented media can run over TLS with self-signed certificates, and obsoletes RFC 4572 by clarifying multiple fingerprints.

SDP.why: The document extends SDP with a new proto value and a new attribute, and specifies their use in offer/answer and advertised sessions.
SDP.quote: It defines the SDP protocol identifier, 'TCP/TLS'. It also defines the syntax and semantics for an SDP 'fingerprint' attribute

TLS.why: It specifies how certificates are chosen, presented and validated for TLS media connections, using fingerprints. This is new usage guidance for TLS, not just reliance on it.
TLS.quote: This specification defines a mechanism that allows self-signed certificates to be used securely, provided that the integrity of the SDP description is assured.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport under TLS. The setup/connection procedures come from RFC 4145 and are not changed here.
X.509 certificates are used and their identity matching is described, but the document does not profile X.509. It only hashes and matches certificates.
SIP is mentioned as a carrier of SDP and in security discussion, but the document does not specify or extend SIP.
SHA-256 and other hash functions are only named as fingerprint algorithms. The document does not specify them.
RTP is mentioned only in passing. The document explicitly does not define secure RTP over a connection-oriented channel.

RFC8123.title: Requirements for Marking SIP Messages to be Logged
RFC8123.summary: Informational INSIPID requirements document for a "log me" marker in SIP messages, so that SIP entities across networks and trust domains can log signaling for debugging and regression testing.

SIP.why: The document specifies requirements for a new marking mechanism in SIP messages, processed by SIP intermediaries, endpoints, B2BUAs and gateways, and crossing network boundaries. It is about SIP signaling deployment and extension.
SIP.quote: This document describes the requirements for adding an indicator to the SIP Protocol Data Unit (PDU) or a SIP message that marks the PDU as a candidate for logging.

rejected.why: Inter-operator SIP traversal is the scenario, but the document is about a logging marker, not peering or provisioning between providers.
UUID is only mentioned as a possible test case identifier drawn from the Session-ID. It is not a subject of the document.
Logging is the purpose, but the document concerns SIP message marking and uses the SIP Common Log Format. It does not cover the syslog protocol.
The trust domain and privacy points are security considerations of the marker, not a treatment of operational security practices.
Debugging and regression testing are the use case, but the document specifies a SIP marker, not OAM mechanisms.

RFC8124.title: The Session Description Protocol (SDP) WebSocket Connection URI Attribute
RFC8124.summary: Defines the SDP media-level attribute "websocket-uri" that carries the WebSocket connection URI, with offer/answer procedures for applications (e.g., BFCP, MSRP, SIP) using WebSocket as transport.

SDP.why: The document defines a new SDP attribute and specifies offer/answer procedures, multiplexing category and IANA registration for it.
SDP.quote: This section defines a new SDP media-level attribute, "websocket-uri", which can appear in any of the media sections.

WebSocket.why: The attribute conveys the ws/wss URI used to open WebSocket connections, and the document specifies client procedures for the handshake and setup roles; readers of WebSocket would want it.
WebSocket.quote: Applications that use SDP for negotiation and WebSocket as a transport protocol can use this specification to advertise the WebSocket client connection URI.

rejected.why: BFCP is used only as the example application; the attribute is explicitly BFCP-independent.
SIP is mentioned as one user of WebSocket transport and for offerless INVITE, but the document is not about SIP.
Only cited as another application using WebSocket transport.
TLS is merely the security substrate for wss; nothing new is defined about its use.
HTTP is only the handshake substrate of WebSocket.
The ws/wss URI is defined in RFC 6455; this document only carries it in an SDP attribute.

RFC8125.title: Requirements for Password-Authenticated Key Agreement (PAKE) Schemes
RFC8125.summary: RFC 8125 is a CFRG informational document that reviews types of password-authenticated key agreement (PAKE) schemes and sets requirements and recommendations for designers of new schemes.

PAKE.why: The whole document reviews PAKE types (balanced/augmented, encrypted/unencrypted public keys, two-party/group) and gives requirements for PAKE schemes.
PAKE.quote: Password-Authenticated Key Agreement (PAKE) schemes are interactive protocols that allow the participants to authenticate each other and derive shared cryptographic keys

rejected.why: J-PAKE is only mentioned as an example of a PAKE that sends unencrypted public keys; the document does not specify or analyse it.
Section 4.2 discusses mapping to curve points for ECC-based PAKEs, but it is a short sub-topic within the PAKE requirements.
TLS and IPsec are named only as protocols that might use a PAKE as a building block.
The document covers key agreement within PAKE, so the more specific PAKE tag covers it.

RFC8126.title: Guidelines for Writing an IANA Considerations Section in RFCs
RFC8126.summary: BCP 26 (obsoletes RFC 5226) gives guidance to specification authors on writing IANA Considerations sections: creating and updating registries, choosing registration policies, and the role of designated experts.

IANA.why: The whole document is about writing IANA Considerations sections, registry creation, registration policies and designated experts, which is the IANA registries subject.
IANA.quote: This document defines a framework for the documentation of these guidelines by specification authors, in order to assure that the provided guidance for the IANA Considerations is clear

rejected.why: Designated experts and IESG approval touch IETF procedure, but the subject is IANA registry guidance, which the IANA tag covers.
It guides how RFC text is written for IANA, but is not about RFC format or publication itself.
DNS names appear only as an example of hierarchical allocation.
TLS registries are cited only as examples of policies.
Media types are mentioned only as an example of a registry.

RFC8127.title: Mobile Access Gateway Configuration Parameters Controlled by the Local Mobility Anchor
RFC8127.summary: Defines a new Proxy Mobile IPv6 mobility option (LMA-Controlled-MAG-Session-Params) carried in PBA messages, letting the LMA enforce re-registration and heartbeat timer parameters on MAGs.

PMIPv6.why: The document extends PMIPv6 with a new mobility option and sub-options, and specifies LMA and MAG behaviour for it.
PMIPv6.quote: This specification defines a new extension, LMA-Controlled-MAG-Session-Params, to Proxy Mobile IPv6.

rejected.why: IPv6 is only the substrate; mobility header alignment is merely referenced from RFC 8200.
PMIPv6 is the protocol extended; Mobile IPv6 only supplies the Mobility Options registry.
IANA actions are boilerplate registrations, not the subject of the document.
Central configuration of MAG parameters is done via a PMIPv6 option, not a management protocol or architecture.

RFC8128.title: IETF Appointment Procedures for the ICANN Root Zone Evolution Review Committee
RFC8128.summary: This IAB memo defines how the IETF selects its one appointee to ICANN's Root Zone Evolution Review Committee (RZERC), covering qualifications, term length, nominations, selection, timeframe and mid-term vacancies.

IETF process.why: The whole document is an administrative procedure for an IETF/IAB appointment: public call for nominations, eligibility, selection, timeline and vacancies. It is IETF procedure, not a technical protocol.
IETF process.quote: This memo outlines the process by which the IETF makes an appointment to the ICANN Root Zone Evolution Review Committee (RZERC).

rejected.why: The RZERC reviews changes to the DNS root zone, but the document specifies no DNS technology. It only sets out how a committee member is appointed.
NomCom members are mentioned only as eligible nominees. The document does not describe NomCom procedures, and the IAB makes the selection.
The parent tag is implied by IETF process, so it is not listed separately.

RFC8129.title: Authentication Indicator in Kerberos Tickets
RFC8129.summary: Updates RFC 4120 by defining the AD-AUTHENTICATION-INDICATOR Kerberos authorization data type (ad-type 97), carried in AD-CAMMAC, which conveys the strength of a client's initial authentication to application services for policy decisions.

Kerberos.why: The document extends Kerberos with a new authorization data type carried in service tickets issued by the KDC, so Kerberos readers need it.
Kerberos.quote: This document updates RFC 4120, as it specifies an extension in the Kerberos protocol.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only used to define the one-line SEQUENCE OF UTF8String type and its module; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
The generic authentication topic is implied by the Kerberos tag and the document is Kerberos-specific, so it is not tagged separately.
UTF8String is just the string type used in the ASN.1 definition, not a subject of the document.
Authorization data is the carrier mechanism within Kerberos tickets; the document does not specify an authorization or access-control framework.
Pre-authentication mechanisms are only mentioned as background; they are not specified here.

RFC8130.title: RTP Payload Format for the Mixed Excitation Linear Prediction Enhanced (MELPe) Codec
RFC8130.summary: Defines the RTP payload format for the MELPe (STANAG 4591) narrowband speech codec at 2400, 1200 and 600 bps, including bit packing, comfort noise, packet loss concealment, media type registration and SDP mapping.

RTP payload format.why: The document's purpose is an RTP payload format for a specific codec, covering framing, bit packing, multiple frames per packet and media type registration.
RTP payload format.quote: This document describes how compressed Mixed Excitation Linear Prediction Enhanced (MELPe) speech as produced by the MELPe codec may be formatted for use as an RTP payload.

rejected.why: SDP is used only to map the media type parameters (rtpmap, fmtp, offer/answer). That is a standard part of any payload format, not the subject of the document.
The document defines a payload format for the codec, not the codec itself. MELPe is defined in STANAG 4591, and the taxonomy has no MELPe-specific tag. The RTP payload format tag fits better.
RTP is the substrate, and the document only specifies a payload format for it. The more specific RTP payload format tag covers it.
The media type registration is boilerplate that accompanies a payload format. It is not the subject of the document.
SRTP appears only in Security Considerations boilerplate.
Section 3.4 is a short standard congestion control considerations section. It is not a substantial part of the document.

gaps.name: MELPe codec
gaps.why: The taxonomy's codec children have no tag for MELP/MELPe (NATO STANAG 4591) narrowband speech coding. Readers looking for this codec would find it only through the RTP payload format tag.

RFC8131.title: RSVP-TE Signaling Procedure for End-to-End GMPLS Restoration and Resource Sharing
RFC8131.summary: Informational RFC reviewing RSVP-TE signaling procedures for GMPLS end-to-end restoration LSPs (1+R, 1+1+R), ASSOCIATION-based resource sharing, and make-while-break/make-before-break LSP reversion in non-packet transport networks; no new extensions defined.

GMPLS.why: The document is about GMPLS end-to-end recovery: restoration LSP association, resource sharing and reversion in non-packet transport networks.
GMPLS.quote: the Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) end-to-end recovery scheme needs to employ a restoration Label Switched Path (LSP) while keeping resources for the working and/or protecting LSPs reserved

RSVP-TE.why: The document specifies how existing RSVP-TE objects (ASSOCIATION, PROTECTION, SESSION_ATTRIBUTE SE flag) are used for restoration, sharing and reversion signaling. It adds no new extensions but reviews the signaling procedures in detail.
RSVP-TE.quote: the restoration LSP is set up with an ASSOCIATION object that has the Association Type set to "Recovery"

rejected.why: GMPLS is the more specific subject; MPLS is only the parent and background.
RSVP-TE is the specific tag under it, so the parent is implied and not chosen separately.
OSPF-TE is mentioned only in the introduction as part of the GMPLS protocol set.
RSVP-TE is the more specific tag, so RSVP is not chosen separately.

RFC8132.title: PATCH and FETCH Methods for the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)
RFC8132.summary: Defines three new CoAP methods, FETCH, PATCH and iPATCH, for retrieving and modifying parts of a resource, with their semantics, caching, error handling and IANA code assignments.

CoAP.why: The document extends CoAP with new request methods, specifying their semantics, response codes, option handling and error conditions.
CoAP.quote: This specification defines the new CoAP methods, FETCH, PATCH, and iPATCH, which are used to access and update parts of a resource.

rejected.why: PATCH for HTTP (RFC 5789) and HTTP SEARCH are only background and inspiration. The document specifies CoAP methods, not HTTP.
JSON Patch and JSON Merge Patch appear only as example payload formats and Content-Format registrations. The document is not about JSON.
DTLS is mentioned only in the Security Considerations as a way to protect FETCH payloads.
Caching behaviour for FETCH and PATCH is defined for CoAP, not HTTP.

RFC8133.title: The Security Evaluated Standardized Password-Authenticated Key Exchange (SESPAKE) Protocol
RFC8133.summary: Describes SESPAKE, an elliptic-curve password-authenticated key exchange protocol with key confirmation, attempt counters, point-generation method and GOST-based test vectors.

PAKE.why: The document specifies a new password-authenticated key exchange protocol, so it belongs under PAKE.
PAKE.quote: The SESPAKE protocol provides password-authenticated key exchange for usage in systems for protection of sensitive information.

GOST.why: Point generation uses GOST R 34.11-2012 and the test vectors and curve parameters are GOST-based, which is a substantial part of the document.
GOST.quote: The following test examples are made for the protocol implementation that is based on the Russian national standards GOST R 34.10-2012

rejected.why: PBKDF2 is only used as the function F to derive a value from the password, not specified or analysed here.
HMAC is only used for key confirmation MACs, so it is a building block and not the subject.
Elliptic curves are the underlying group of the protocol, but the document is about the PAKE, not elliptic curve cryptography as such.
The protocol is similar in style to SPAKE2 but is a distinct protocol, so SPAKE2 does not apply.
PAKE is the more specific tag and already sits under key management.

RFC8134.title: Management Incident Lightweight Exchange (MILE) Implementation Report
RFC8134.summary: Collection of implementation reports from vendors, consortiums and researchers for IODEF, RID and related incident-sharing standards from the INCH and MILE working groups, with implementation tips.

IODEF.why: Most implementations and the Implementation Guide concern IODEF v1/v2, its XSD, code generators and libraries.
IODEF.quote: implemented one or more of the standards published from the INCH and MILE working groups

RID.why: The RID agent implementation and Deep Secure RID/HTTPS support are reported, so RID readers would want this.
RID.quote: The code implements the Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID) described in RFC 6545 [RFC6545] and the Transport of RID over HTTP/ TLS protocol

rejected.why: Only mentioned as an output format of AirCERT; not a focus.
XML schema and code generators are used for IODEF, but XML is the substrate, not the subject.
Surevine and Deep Secure use XMPP as a transport; the document is not about XMPP.
Parent of IODEF and RID, which are tagged instead.
n6 uses JSON natively, but this is incidental.
TLS is only the transport mechanism in the implementations described.

gaps.name: Structured threat intelligence sharing (STIX/TAXII, ROLIE)
gaps.why: The document mentions these exchange standards, but the taxonomy has no tag for them.

RFC8135.title: Complex Addressing in IPv6
RFC8135.summary: An April 1st parody RFC proposing complex (real plus imaginary, floating-point) addressing in IPv6, mapping two IEEE 754 64-bit values into a 128-bit address, with jokes about clouds, avian carriers, square pi and Santa Claus.

humor.why: The document is an April 1st parody, with whimsical content throughout (duct tape, flat earth, Santa Claus, square pi). The humor tag fits best.
humor.quote: Complex addressing is considered unsafe, as division by 0 still provides Not a Number (NaN) values.

IPv6.why: The joke is built on IPv6 addressing and defines a mapping of the 128-bit IPv6 address. Readers browsing IPv6 addressing would find it relevant.
IPv6.quote: The 128-bit IPv6 address is divided into two 64-bit parts, where the upper half holds the real part of the address

rejected.why: IPv6 is the more specific tag for the 128-bit address mapping. The addressing topic would only be a parent of CIDR, multihoming and the like, which the document does not address seriously.
DNS is mentioned only as a joke about square addresses and root servers. The document does not specify or analyse it.
Mobile IP is cited in passing as motivation for floating addresses, and the document does not address mobility protocols.
Token Ring and RPR appear only in a throwaway joke about round addresses.

RFC8136.title: Additional Transition Functionality for IPv6
RFC8136.summary: An April 1 humor RFC that parodies IPv6 transition work by requiring IPv4 nodes to set the RFC 3514 "evil bit" and defining an IPv6 security flag via source-address parity and a hop-by-hop User Security Flag Option with a privacy bit.

humor.why: The document is an April 1st parody extending the evil bit to IPv6, with jokes such as treating all IPv4 traffic as a DDoS attack.
humor.quote: all IPv4 nodes MUST set the security flag defined by [RFC3514] to 1.
humor.section: 2. Required Function of All IPv4 Nodes

IPv6.why: It proposes IPv6 address-based flag semantics and a new hop-by-hop option for IPv6 packets, and discusses interface identifier selection. The subject is IPv6, even though the proposal is satirical.
IPv6.quote: the Security Flag bit for an IPv6 packet is simply the parity of the source address of the packet.

rejected.why: The title mentions transition, but the document only jokes about it. It specifies no real transition mechanism.
Happy Eyeballs is mentioned only as the algorithm that would favour IPv6 as a side effect. The document is not about it.
SLAAC is mentioned only as one way to choose an interface identifier so the parity comes out right. The document does not address SLAAC itself.
DHCPv6 is mentioned only in passing, as one way an address might be assigned.
The privacy flag is a joke extension and the document contains no real privacy analysis.

RFC8137.title: IEEE 802.15.4 Information Element for the IETF
RFC8137.summary: Informational RFC requesting an IEEE 802.15.4 Payload Information Element allocation for the IETF, defining the IETF IE subtype format and creating an IANA registry of IETF IE subtype IDs.

6LoWPAN.why: The document concerns IEEE 802.15.4 as a constrained link layer for IETF protocols (6TiSCH, 6lo, CoRE), defining the IETF IE and its subtype format. 6LoWPAN is the tag that covers IP over constrained link layers such as 802.15.4.
6LoWPAN.quote: IETF protocols will need to insert information in the 802.15.4 frames; the 802.15.4 standard enables that by including one or more payload IEs

rejected.why: 6TiSCH is named as a beneficiary WG that needs the IE, but the document does not specify anything about 6TiSCH itself.
The document creates an IANA registry for subtype IDs, but this is boilerplate-level; the main body is about the IE format and allocation request.
CoRE is only mentioned as a possible user of the IE.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.15.4 Information Elements
gaps.why: The document is about IEEE 802.15.4 IEs and their IETF allocation, but the taxonomy has no 802.15.4-specific tag; 6LoWPAN is the nearest fit.

RFC8138.title: IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (6LoWPAN) Routing Header
RFC8138.summary: Defines the 6LoWPAN Routing Header (6LoRH) dispatch type in Page 1, giving compressed forms of the RPL Source Routing Header, RPL Packet Information and IP-in-IP encapsulation for RPL route-over LLNs.

6LoWPAN.why: The document extends the 6LoWPAN adaptation layer with a new routing header dispatch and compression formats.
6LoWPAN.quote: This specification introduces a new IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (6LoWPAN) dispatch type for use in 6LoWPAN route-over topologies

RPL.why: Compresses RPL data-plane artifacts (RPI, SRH) and defines how RPL supplies root and instance context; readers of RPL would want it.
RPL.quote: this specification defines a method to compress the RPL Option (RFC 6553) information and Routing Header type 3 (RFC 6554)

header compression.why: Core purpose is header compression of routing headers, RPI and IP-in-IP on constrained links; no more specific child tag fits since it is not ROHC/CRTP/IPHC.
header compression.quote: An extensible compression technique is required that simplifies IP-in-IP encapsulation when it is needed and optimally compresses existing routing artifacts found in RPL LLNs.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as motivating context (frame size limits); the document does not specify 6TiSCH.
Defines a compressed IP-in-IP 6LoRH, but the document is about 6LoWPAN compression, not the IP-in-IP tunnelling protocol itself.
IPv6 headers are what gets compressed, but the document is about the 6LoWPAN layer, not IPv6 itself.
ICMPv6 errors are mentioned only in management considerations.
IANA registries are created but that is boilerplate-level apparatus.

RFC8139.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Appointed Forwarders
RFC8139.summary: RFC 8139 clarifies and updates the TRILL Appointed Forwarder mechanism, adding E-L1CS FS-LSP appointments, inhibition optimizations, Port-Shutdown messages and FGL-VLAN mapping consistency checks; it obsoletes RFC 6439.

TRILL.why: The whole document specifies TRILL link-level behaviour: forwarder appointment, inhibition, Port-Shutdown messages and new APPsub-TLVs.
TRILL.quote: This document clarifies and updates the Appointed Forwarder mechanism.

rejected.why: IS-IS is the substrate for TRILL's LSPs and Hellos. The document uses E-L1CS FS-LSPs but does not specify IS-IS itself.
The document deals with bridged LANs and VLANs only as the environment for TRILL, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
Multiple ports on the same link are handled, but this is not link aggregation in the IEEE 802.1AX sense.
TRILL is a routing-bridge protocol, but the document concerns native-frame handling at the edge rather than routing in general.

gaps.name: TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a TRILL tech tag only under routing (id 'TRILL'), and I used an id that does not exist in the list: the entry is 'TRILL' and appears in the taxonomy as a child of routing. The listed id is 'TRILL' written 'TRILL: transparent interconnection of lots of links'. I could not verify the exact id string against the taxonomy, so the tag above needs checking.

RFC8140.title: The Arte of ASCII: Or, An True and Accurate Representation of an Menagerie of Thynges Fabulous and Wonderful in Ye Forme of Character
RFC8140.summary: An April 1st humorous RFC presenting ASCII-art drawings of mythical creatures, structures and security items, with whimsical commentary and parody of RFC conventions.

humor.why: The document is an April 1st joke RFC consisting of ASCII art and parody sections (Morality Considerations, Manageability), so it belongs on the humor page.
humor.quote: This document supplies a number of representations of all manner of things (both elemental and hypothetical) supplied by some of our best collectors of curios

ASCII.why: ASCII as a medium for drawings is the document's central subject, a satirical treatment of ASCII art in RFCs. Readers browsing ASCII would plausibly want it, though it is not a technical specification.
ASCII.quote: Amongst Gutenberg's better known discoveries were the ten point font, the Courier New Font (which he is supposed to have found growing in a hedgerow close to his cottage), and the ASCII character set.

rejected.why: PCE is mentioned only in a joke about unicorns in the Traffic Engineering Database; the document is not about it.
SDN is only a passing punchline in the Unicorn section.
It pokes fun at RFC format changes (SVG, RFC 2119 debates), but it does not address RFC format or publication in substance.
The IANA Considerations section is a joke suggestion for a colour registry. It is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: ASCII art
gaps.why: The document is about drawing pictures in plain-text ASCII, which the taxonomy covers only through the ASCII character set tag.

RFC8141.title: Uniform Resource Names (URNs)
RFC8141.summary: RFC 8141 defines the canonical URN syntax (NID, NSS, r-/q-/f-components), URN-equivalence rules, URI conformance, and the procedures for defining and registering URN namespaces with IANA, obsoleting RFCs 2141 and 3406.

URN.why: The document specifies URN syntax, equivalence, and namespace definition/registration; it is the core URN specification.
URN.quote: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) is a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) that is assigned under the "urn" URI scheme and a particular URN namespace

rejected.why: URN is the more specific child; the document is about URNs, not generic URI syntax, which it relies on (RFC 3986).
Registration procedures for NIDs are part of the URN namespace mechanism, but the document is not about IANA registries generally; the IANA section is boilerplate-like.
ABNF is only the notation used to express the syntax.
Document explicitly does not allow non-ASCII characters directly; it only mentions percent-encoding and UTF-8.

RFC8142.title: GeoJSON Text Sequences
RFC8142.summary: Defines the GeoJSON text sequence format, a specialization of JSON text sequences (RS-prefixed, LF-terminated GeoJSON texts), and registers the application/geo+json-seq media type.

GeoJSON.why: The document specifies a sequence format for GeoJSON objects, extending GeoJSON usage for large geographic datasets.
GeoJSON.quote: A GeoJSON text sequence is any number of GeoJSON [RFC7946] texts, each encoded in UTF-8 [RFC3629], preceded by one ASCII [RFC20] record separator (RS) character

JSON.why: The format is a specialization of JSON text sequences (RFC 7464) and adds constraints to it, so readers of JSON-based formats would want it.
JSON.quote: This document describes a specialization of JSON text sequences.

media types.why: The document registers a new media type, application/geo+json-seq, as a key deliverable alongside the format.
media types.quote: The MIME media type for GeoJSON text sequences is "application/ geo+json-seq" (which uses the suffix established in [RFC8091]).

rejected.why: UTF-8 is only the required encoding of the texts, not a subject of the document.
The ASCII record separator character is used as a delimiter only; the document is not about ASCII.
The IANA section is just the media type registration boilerplate; the media types tag covers it.

gaps.name: GeoJSON / geographic data formats
gaps.why: The taxonomy has GeoJSON under data formats > JSON, so it is covered; no gap beyond that.

RFC8143.title: Using Transport Layer Security (TLS) with Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP)
RFC8143.summary: Updates RFC 4642 to require NNTP implementations to follow TLS BCP 195, preferring implicit TLS on port 563, disabling TLS compression, dropping mandatory RC4, requiring SNI and RFC 6125 certificate verification, and adding human-factors guidance.

NNTP.why: The document revises how NNTP uses TLS (STARTTLS vs implicit TLS, ports, capabilities, AUTHINFO SASL). It updates the NNTP-over-TLS spec, so NNTP readers need it.
NNTP.quote: NNTP implementations and deployments SHOULD prefer implicit TLS, and therefore use strict TLS configuration

TLS.why: A substantial part of the document gives TLS deployment guidance for NNTP: versions, cipher suites, compression, SNI, certificate verification and SSL stripping. It does not define a new TLS extension, but readers of TLS deployment guidance would want it.
TLS.quote: NNTP implementations and deployments MUST follow the best current practices documented in [BCP195]

rejected.why: Netnews article format is mentioned only in passing, for the Path header !! diag-match. The document is about the transport protocol, so NNTP is the more specific tag.
AUTHINFO SASL with EXTERNAL is mentioned only briefly as a way to authenticate after TLS. The document does not specify SASL.
The prohibition on RC4 cipher suites is one bullet in the update list. The document is not about RC4.
Certificate validation per RFC 5280 and RFC 6125 is referenced, but the document does not profile certificates.
The document concerns NNTP over TLS, but it updates an existing binding with security guidance. It does not define a new transport mapping, and NNTP covers it.

RFC8144.title: Use of the Prefer Header Field in Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV)
RFC8144.summary: Defines how WebDAV clients use the HTTP Prefer header (return=minimal, return=representation) to shape server responses, and registers the new "depth-noroot" preference, updating RFC 7240.

WebDAV.why: The document specifies how Prefer behaves for WebDAV methods (PROPFIND, REPORT, PROPPATCH, MKCOL, MKCALENDAR) and defines depth-noroot for the Depth header, so it is an extension of WebDAV.
WebDAV.quote: defines how the Prefer header field (RFC 7240) can be used by a Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) client to request that certain behaviors be employed by a server

HTTP.why: It extends use of the HTTP Prefer header field, updates RFC 7240, extends return=representation to 412 responses, and registers a new preference in the HTTP preferences registry.
HTTP.quote: Section 4 of this specification defines the "depth-noroot" preference that can be used with HTTP methods that support the Depth header field.

rejected.why: CalDAV is not in the taxonomy as a tag with that id. Its methods (MKCALENDAR, calendar-query) and examples are used, but the document is not about CalDAV itself. CalDAV is listed under calendaring, but the calendaring tag was not chosen.
The WebDAV request and response bodies are XML, but XML is only the encoding. The document defines nothing new about XML.
CardDAV report types are mentioned only as candidates for return=minimal. The document does not specify CardDAV.
The conditional requests (If-Match, ETag) in section 3.2 are about state-changing requests, not caching.

RFC8145.title: Signaling Trust Anchor Knowledge in DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC)
RFC8145.summary: Specifies two optional mechanisms (an EDNS edns-key-tag option and special _ta- Key Tag queries) by which validating DNSSEC resolvers signal their trust anchor Key Tags to servers so zone operators can monitor key rollovers.

DNSSEC.why: The document is about DNSSEC trust anchors, Key Tags and monitoring key rollovers. It defines signaling for validators.
DNSSEC.quote: This document specifies two different ways for validating resolvers to signal to a server which keys are referenced in their chain of trust.

EDNS.why: It defines a new EDNS(0) option (code 14), including its format and use rules by queriers and responders. EDNS readers would want it.
EDNS.quote: The edns-key-tag option is encoded as follows:

rejected.why: This is the parent of the chosen tags, so it is implied. The document is specific to DNSSEC and EDNS.
The only IANA content is a single EDNS option code registration. That is boilerplate and not the subject.
The Privacy Considerations section discusses fingerprinting risk. That is a minor part of the document and not its subject.

RFC8146.title: Adding Support for Salted Password Databases to EAP-pwd
RFC8146.summary: Updates EAP-pwd (RFC 5931) with new password preprocessing techniques (salted SHA, UNIX crypt, scrypt, PBKDF2, with SASLprep/OpaqueString) and a modified Commit payload so salted password databases can be used.

EAP.why: The document extends the EAP-pwd method: new preprocessing codes, protocol and payload modifications to the ID and Commit exchanges.
EAP.quote: EAP-pwd needs to be able to support them.

scrypt.why: Defines how scrypt parameters are encoded in the salt field and used as a preprocessing technique; recommended for new deployments.
scrypt.quote: The scrypt function takes several parameters:

PBKDF2.why: Defines PBKDF2 parameter encoding and use as an EAP-pwd preprocessing technique.
PBKDF2.quote: The PBKDF2 function requires two parameters:

PRECIS.why: Specifies OpaqueString (and SASLprep) preprocessing of passwords prior to hashing, a substantive part of the document.
PRECIS.quote: applying the Preparation and Enforcement steps of the OpaqueString profile in [RFC7613] to the password.

rejected.why: Dragonfly PAKE is the underlying mechanism of EAP-pwd; the document does not specify or change it.
Parent of scrypt and PBKDF2, which were chosen as more specific.
Only referenced as the basis of EAP-pwd; document is not about the Dragonfly exchange itself.
SHA-1/256/512 are used as salting hash functions but the document is not about the SHA family.
RFC 7616 Digest is mentioned only to explain that it cannot be supported.

RFC8147.title: Next-Generation Pan-European eCall
RFC8147.summary: Specifies how IP-based emergency calling (SIP) carries Pan-European next-generation eCall vehicle data (MSD) and a PSAP/vehicle metadata/control XML object, registering service URNs, media types, and a SIP INFO package.

eCall.why: The whole document defines NG-eCall: MSD transport, control block, service URNs sos.ecall.*, and test calls.
eCall.quote: This document describes how to use IP-based emergency services mechanisms to support the next generation of the Pan-European in-vehicle emergency call service

SIP.why: Defines a new SIP INFO package and the use of Call-Info, INVITE and INFO for eCall data exchange, which SIP readers would want.
SIP.quote: An INFO package is defined (in Section 14.9) to enable these MIME types to be carried in SIP INFO requests, per [RFC6086].

rejected.why: The document registers media types, but that is a means of carrying eCall data and not the subject.
The control block is XML, but XML is only the encoding.
The MSD uses ASN.1 PER defined by CEN. The document does not define or specify ASN.1 modules.
The more specific child tag eCall fits, so the parent is implied.
Location is carried in the MSD and PIDF-LO, but it is only incidental data and not the subject.
The document explicitly says it does not address cellular-specific details.

RFC8148.title: Next-Generation Vehicle-Initiated Emergency Calls
RFC8148.summary: Specifies how IP-based emergency calling carries vehicle crash data (VEDS) and metadata/control objects for next-generation Automatic Crash Notification calls, extending the NG eCall specification, with new MIME type, action values, registries and a SIP INFO package.

eCall.why: The document is an extension of next-generation eCall for vehicle-initiated emergency calls (ACN), defining VEDS data, control actions and an INFO package. It fits the eCall tag's vehicle emergency calling scope.
eCall.quote: This document describes how to use IP-based emergency services mechanisms to support the next generation of emergency calls placed by vehicles

SIP.why: Defines a new SIP INFO package and the use of Call-Info, INVITE and INFO for call setup and mid-call data. This is a substantial SIP extension, though it is not the main subject.
SIP.quote: This document also registers an INFO package (in Section 14.7) to enable NG-ACN-related data blocks to be carried in SIP INFO requests

rejected.why: The eCall child tag fits more specifically, so the parent is implied.
The document registers application/EmergencyCallData.VEDS+xml, but this is a registration that supports the main subject, not the focus.
VEDS and the control objects are XML, but XML is only the encoding.
Routing and location queries are mentioned only in passing; the IVS relies on the MNO for them.
PIDF-LO location appears only in the example. The document is not about location formats.
The registries are created for this document's own subject and are not a general IANA topic.

RFC8149.title: RSVP Extensions for Reoptimization of Loosely Routed Point-to-Multipoint Traffic Engineering Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC8149.summary: Defines RSVP-TE extensions (a tree re-evaluation flag, a "Preferable P2MP-TE Tree Exists" PathErr sub-code, and an S2L_SUB_LSP_FRAG fragment identifier object) for reoptimizing loosely routed P2MP-TE LSPs.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE signaling with a new Attribute Flag, a PathErr sub-code and a new object for P2MP-TE LSP reoptimization and fragmentation.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document defines Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) [RFC2205] [RFC3209] signaling extensions for reoptimizing loosely routed Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) Traffic Engineering (TE) Label Switched Paths

rejected.why: MPLS is the general context, and the document's specific subject is RSVP-TE signalling, which is a more specific tag.
GMPLS is mentioned only as an applicable network type, and nothing in the document is specific to it.
PCE is mentioned only in passing, as the case where loose routing is not used.
Base RSVP is the substrate. The extensions are RSVP-TE specific, so RSVP-TE is the better fit.
RSVP-TE is the more specific tag under it.
P2MP LSPs are MPLS traffic-engineering constructs, not IP multicast routing.

gaps.name: P2MP TE LSPs / LSP reoptimization
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for point-to-multipoint TE LSPs or make-before-break reoptimization. RSVP-TE is the closest fit.

RFC8150.title: MPLS Transport Profile Linear Protection MIB
RFC8150.summary: Defines the MPLS-LPS-MIB SMIv2 module for configuring and monitoring MPLS-TP linear protection domains (PSC and APS modes), including tables, textual conventions and notifications.

MIB.why: The document's purpose is to define a MIB module (MPLS-LPS-MIB) in SMIv2 with tables, textual conventions, notifications and compliance statements.
MIB.quote: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols.

MPLS-TP.why: The managed subject is MPLS-TP linear protection switching (RFC 6378 PSC mode and RFC 7271 APS mode) for LSPs, so MPLS-TP readers need it.
MPLS-TP.quote: it defines objects for managing Multiprotocol Label Switching - Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) linear protection.

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the MIB tag sits under SNMP and covers the document.
The module references MPLS OAM identifiers (RFC 7697) and MEs, but only to associate MEs with protection domains; it does not define OAM mechanisms.
MPLS-TP is the more specific tag and is already chosen.
Not a YANG model; it is an SMIv2 MIB.
The document references the MPLS TE MIB only for context; it is about protection switching, not TE.

gaps.name: MPLS-TP linear protection (PSC/APS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MPLS-TP; the subject is covered only by the broader MPLS technology tag.

RFC8151.title: Use Cases for Data Center Network Virtualization Overlay Networks
RFC8151.summary: Informational NVO3 working group document describing use cases for data center network virtualization overlays: large numbers of virtual networks, interconnection with external networks and WAN VPNs, and DC applications such as multi-technology, multi-zone and virtual data centers.

overlay networks.why: The whole document is about NVO3 data-plane network virtualization overlays and their use cases in data centers.
overlay networks.quote: The goal of data center Network Virtualization over Layer 3 (NVO3) networks is to decouple the communication among tenant systems from DC physical infrastructure networks

data center networking.why: The use cases are data-center scale multi-tenant networking: many virtual networks, VM mobility, vDCs and multi-zone DCs.
data center networking.quote: This document describes Network Virtualization over Layer 3 (NVO3) use cases that can be deployed in various data centers and serve different data-center applications.

VPN.why: A substantial section covers interconnecting NVO3 virtual networks with provider WAN VPNs, including the RFC 4364 options a, b and c at the DC gateway.
VPN.quote: an enterprise customer wants to use a Service Provider (SP) WAN VPN [RFC4364] [RFC7432] to interconnect its sites with an NVO3 virtual network in a DC site.
VPN.section: 3.2. DC NVO3 Virtual Network and SP WAN VPN Interconnection

rejected.why: IPsec tunnels are used for customer access to the vGW, but only as a security mechanism the use cases rely on; the document does not specify or analyse IPsec.
VXLAN is mentioned only as an example encapsulation to be interworked at a gateway; the document is not about it.
NVGRE is mentioned only as an example encapsulation; the document is not about it.
BGP/MPLS IP VPNs are referenced for interconnection options, but the document is about NVO3 use cases, so the parent VPN tag is the better fit.
BGP is used for route distribution in the interconnection scenarios but is not the subject of the document.
NAT is a gateway function listed in passing.

RFC8152.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE)
RFC8152.summary: Defines COSE, the CBOR-based format for signatures, MACs, encryption and cryptographic key representation, including header parameters, algorithms, KDFs, key distribution methods and IANA registries.

COSE.why: The document specifies COSE itself: message structures, headers, algorithms, and keys.
COSE.quote: This document defines the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) protocol.

CBOR.why: COSE is defined as security services for CBOR, with CBOR encoder restrictions (Section 14) and CBOR tags assigned. This is a substantial secondary aspect, but the document is about COSE rather than CBOR.
CBOR.quote: There is a need for the ability to have basic security services defined for this data format.

rejected.why: COSE is modelled on JOSE and compared against it, but the document does not specify JOSE.
CoAP is used for content-format identification and as a motivating example. It is not specified here.
ECDSA is one algorithm that COSE profiles, not the subject of the document.
AES modes (GCM, CCM, key wrap) are algorithms COSE uses. The document is not about AES.
ChaCha20/Poly1305 is one algorithm registered for COSE, not the subject.
HMAC is one MAC algorithm that COSE uses, not the subject.
EdDSA is a signature algorithm COSE uses, not the subject.

RFC8153.title: Digital Preservation Considerations for the RFC Series
RFC8153.summary: IAB informational document giving guidance on how the RFC Editor, in its archivist role, should preserve the RFC Series (OAIS-based lifecycle, metadata, canonical format, PDF/A-3 with embedded XML, migration, costs) and recommending a preservation approach.

RFC series.why: The whole document concerns how the RFC Series is archived, its formats (plain text, XML, PDF/A-3), metadata and the RFC Editor's archivist role, which is squarely the RFC Series subject.
RFC series.quote: It provides guidance on when and how to preserve RFCs and describes the tools required to view or re-create RFCs as necessary.

rejected.why: Canonical XML is discussed as a format to be preserved, but the document is not about XML usage itself; RFCXML is the format in question only incidentally.
The xml2rfc vocabulary is mentioned as something to archive, but the document does not specify or discuss the vocabulary.
Plain-text ASCII-only format is discussed as the historical canonical format, but only as context for archival tension, not as the subject.
IANA is only named in boilerplate, with no actions required.
Copyright and IPR are mentioned briefly, but are not the focus.
The history of the Internet is cited as a reason to archive, but the document is about preservation practice, not history.

gaps.name: Digital preservation / archiving
gaps.why: The document is about digital preservation (OAIS, bitstream vs content preservation, PDF/A-3), which has no taxonomy tag; RFC series is the closest fit.

RFC8154.title: Parallel NFS (pNFS) Small Computer System Interface (SCSI) Layout
RFC8154.summary: Defines the pNFS SCSI layout type (LAYOUT4_SCSI), which lets NFSv4.1 clients do direct I/O to SCSI block storage. It specifies volume identification, extents, and fencing via SCSI persistent reservations, and how NFSv4 semantics are enforced.

NFS.why: The document specifies a new pNFS layout type for NFSv4.1, including its XDR structures, layout operations, error handling and NFSv4 semantics enforcement. It is an NFS extension.
NFS.quote: The Small Computer System Interface (SCSI) layout type is defined in this document as an extension to pNFS to allow the use of SCSI-based block storage devices.

rejected.why: iSCSI is mentioned only as one of several SCSI transports (alongside FCP and SAS) and in the security discussion. The document does not specify or extend it.
FCP is named only as an example storage protocol. The document is not about Fibre Channel transports.
XDR is used to describe the layout structures, but this is only the encoding mechanism and not the subject of the document.
IPsec appears only in the Security Considerations, as a pointer for IP-based storage protocols.
The NFS tag sits under storage and fits more specifically, so the parent is implied.

gaps.name: SCSI block storage access / pNFS layout types
gaps.why: The document centres on SCSI persistent reservations, SCSI device identification and block extents for direct storage access. The taxonomy has no tag for SCSI itself or for pNFS layouts as a separate subject. NFS is the closest fit.

RFC8155.title: Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) Server Auto Discovery
RFC8155.summary: Defines three mechanisms (S-NAPTR service resolution, DNS-SD/mDNS, and an IANA-assigned anycast address) for TURN clients to auto-discover TURN servers, and updates RFC 5766 to relax mandatory STUN authentication for network-provided servers.

TURN.why: The document extends TURN with server discovery and updates RFC 5766's authentication requirement.
TURN.quote: This document describes three such mechanisms for TURN server discovery.

DNS-SD.why: One of the three mechanisms defines DNS-SD service names for TURN, a substantial section.
DNS-SD.quote: The <Service> portion of the TURN service instance name MUST be "_turn._udp" or "_turn._tcp" or "_turns._udp" or "_turns._tcp"

mDNS.why: Specifies mDNS queries and gratuitous announcements for TURN discovery.
mDNS.quote: A TURN client can proactively discover TURN servers being advertised in the site by multicasting a PTR query

anycast.why: Defines anycast-based discovery, with IANA-assigned IPv4 and IPv6 anycast addresses and 300 Try Alternate redirection.
anycast.quote: IP anycast can also be used for TURN service discovery.

DNS.why: Service resolution via S-NAPTR records in the DNS is one of the three mechanisms.
DNS.quote: An S-NAPTR lookup with the 'RELAY' application service and the desired protocol tag is made

rejected.why: DHCP is only used to learn the access network domain name; it is not extended.
WebRTC is the motivating use case but not the subject.
STUN authentication is relaxed, but the document concerns TURN and does not specify STUN.
(D)TLS is a security mechanism recommended in the Security Considerations, not the subject.
Mentioned only in the Security Considerations.
The more specific DNS-SD tag and the TURN tag cover this.

RFC8156.title: DHCPv6 Failover Protocol
RFC8156.summary: Defines the DHCPv6 failover protocol, which lets two DHCPv6 servers share lease bindings over TCP so either can take over clients' leases after server failure or network partition. It covers messages, options, connection management, binding updates, the endpoint state machine, and DNS update coordination.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies new DHCPv6 messages, options, status codes and server state machine for failover. It is an extension of DHCPv6.
DHCPv6.quote: This document defines a DHCPv6 failover protocol, which is a mechanism for running two DHCPv6 servers [RFC3315] with the capability for either server to take over clients' leases

rejected.why: Section 9 only explains how failover partners coordinate DHCP-driven DNS updates. It defines no new DNS update protocol.
TCP is only the substrate for the failover connection. The document adds nothing new to TCP.
TLS is only mentioned in Security Considerations as an optional way to secure the connection.
The document concerns address and prefix leasing through DHCPv6, not IPv6 itself.
