Sections 5.5.3 and 9 only carry DNS names and update status. They do not specify DNS behaviour.

RFC8157.title: Huawei's GRE Tunnel Bonding Protocol
RFC8157.summary: Informational RFC specifying Huawei's GRE Tunnel Bonding Protocol, a control and data plane that bonds a DSL GRE tunnel and an LTE GRE tunnel between a home gateway and an aggregation point to increase capacity and reliability.

GRE.why: The document defines a new control protocol and data-plane use of GRE (Key and Sequence Number extensions, new protocol type 0xB7EA) to bond tunnels. GRE readers would want it.
GRE.quote: In GRE Tunnel Bonding, two GRE tunnels, one per network connection, are set up and bonded together to form a single GRE tunnel for a subscriber.

DSL.why: Hybrid DSL/LTE access is the core use case. DSL sync rate, bandwidth and bypass handling are part of the protocol.
DSL.quote: This document focuses on the use case where a DSL (Digital Subscriber Line) connection and an LTE (Long Term Evolution) connection are bonded together.

cellular.why: The LTE link, with its PGW, PDP context and 3GPP authentication, is half of the bonded access. The document covers integration with the cellular network.
cellular.quote: The HG gets the DSL WAN interface IP address (D) from the Broadband Remote Access Server (BRAS) via the Point-to-Point Protocol over Ethernet (PPPoE) and gets the LTE WAN interface IP address (E)

rejected.why: GRE is the more specific child tag and is already chosen.
PPPoE is only mentioned as how the DSL address is obtained.
DHCP is only used to give the HG its C address over the tunnel. The document does not specify it.
ANCP is mentioned only as an optional way to detect DSL bandwidth. It is not specified here.
The RFC 2697 colour marker is used to split traffic between the tunnels. The document is not about QoS architecture.
IPsec is mentioned only as an optional way to enhance security, in Security Considerations.
DNS is only used to resolve the HAAP group's domain name.

gaps.name: Hybrid access / link bonding
gaps.why: The document is about bonding heterogeneous access links such as DSL and LTE, with per-packet offload and reordering. The taxonomy has no tag for hybrid access or bonding.

RFC8158.title: IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Information Elements for Logging NAT Events
RFC8158.summary: Defines new IPFIX Information Elements, event types and templates that NAT44/NAT64/CGN devices use to log NAT events (session/BIB create/delete, quota, threshold, port block allocation) to a Collector.

IPFIX.why: The document registers new IPFIX Information Elements and defines IPFIX templates for NAT events, extending the IPFIX information model.
IPFIX.quote: This document details the IPFIX IEs that MUST be logged by a NAT device that supports NAT logging using IPFIX

CGN.why: Logging of CGN events (port block allocation, quotas, per-subscriber limits) is a major use case, aligned with RFC 6888 requirements.
CGN.quote: This document provides the information model to be used for logging the NAT events, including Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) events.

NAT.why: The subject matter is NAT operations: sessions, BINDs, address/port pool exhaustion and thresholds. NAT readers would want this logging spec.
NAT.quote: Network operators require NAT devices to log events like creation and deletion of translations and information about the resources that the NAT device is managing.

rejected.why: Syslog is mentioned only as the alternative encoding handled by the companion document NAT-LOG; this RFC uses IPFIX.
NAT64 templates are included, but the document is about logging, not NAT64 itself. NAT covers it.
TLS/DTLS appears only as a security recommendation in Security Considerations.
RFC 7659 is only referenced for natInstanceID; this is not a MIB module.
The IANA registrations are the IPFIX IE definitions themselves, not about IANA registry guidance in general.

RFC8159.title: Keyed IPv6 Tunnel
RFC8159.summary: Specifies a keyed IPv6 tunnel for Ethernet attachment circuits based on L2TPv3 directly over IPv6 without the L2TPv3 control plane, with a mandatory 64-bit cookie, static 1:1 address-to-circuit mapping, fragmentation and OAM guidance.

L2TP.why: The document profiles L2TPv3 data-plane encapsulation (session ID, cookie, L2-specific sublayer) over IPv6 without the control plane, and extends cookie requirements.
L2TP.quote: This document describes a tunnel encapsulation for Ethernet over IPv6 with a mandatory 64-bit cookie

Ethernet.why: It defines Ethernet frame transport handling (FCS retention, VLAN tag treatment) and recommends Ethernet OAM (CFM, Y.1731) for the tunnels.
Ethernet.quote: The ingress router encapsulates the entire Ethernet frame, without the preamble and Frame Check Sequence (FCS) in L2TPv3

rejected.why: IPv6 is the substrate for the encapsulation; the document does not specify or extend IPv6 itself.
Parent of GRE and IP-in-IP; a more specific child (L2TP) is already chosen, and L2TP sits under link layer.
Uses pseudowire VCCV and FCS retention specs by reference, but the document is not about pseudowire emulation itself.
BFD is only recommended as an optional OAM tool for failure detection, not specified here.
Better ECMP load balancing is cited as a motivation, not a subject of the document.
VPN spoofing is mentioned in Security Considerations only; it is not a provider-provisioned VPN specification.
PMTU discovery is recommended in passing in the fragmentation section; the document is not about it.

RFC8160.title: IUTF8 Terminal Mode in Secure Shell (SSH)
RFC8160.summary: RFC 8160 defines a new SSH pty-req terminal mode opcode (42, IUTF8) indicating that terminal I/O uses UTF-8, and registers it with IANA.

SSH.why: The document extends the SSH connection protocol's terminal modes encoding with a new opcode, so it is about SSH.
SSH.quote: This document specifies a new opcode in the Secure Shell terminal modes encoding.

rejected.why: UTF-8 is only the encoding the terminal mode signals; the document defines nothing about the encoding itself.
Unicode is mentioned only in the security considerations, and the document does not address Unicode usage.
The IANA registry addition is boilerplate for the SSH opcode and does not make the document about IANA.
Terminal modes are a pty concept, but the document does not specify or discuss Telnet.

RFC8161.title: Benchmarking the Neighbor Discovery Protocol
RFC8161.summary: Defines benchmarking procedures (baseline and scaling tests) and the NDP-MAX-NEIGHBORS metric for measuring how many IPv6 neighbors a router's Neighbor Discovery implementation can sustain.

neighbor discovery.why: The document's whole subject is measuring the scaling of IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and its neighbor cache, so the neighbor discovery page is where readers would look.
neighbor discovery.quote: This document provides benchmarking procedures for the Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP).

benchmarking.why: It is a BMWG benchmarking methodology document specifying test setup, procedures and reported results for a device under test.
benchmarking.quote: Benchmarking procedures include a Baseline Test and an NDP Scaling Test.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the environment, and the document is about NDP specifically. The more specific child tag, neighbor discovery, covers it.
Benchmarking is the more specific fit for lab device-testing methodology. The document does not define active or passive network measurement protocols.
NDP messages are ICMPv6, but the document does not discuss ICMP itself.

RFC8162.title: Using Secure DNS to Associate Certificates with Domain Names for S/MIME
RFC8162.summary: Experimental RFC defining the SMIMEA DNS resource record, which associates S/MIME certificates with email addresses via DNSSEC-validated DNS lookups, modelled on DANE TLSA and the OpenPGP binding.

DANE.why: The document extends DANE to S/MIME by defining the SMIMEA record, which uses the TLSA wire format and semantics for certificate association via DNSSEC.
DANE.quote: describes how to use secure DNS to associate an S/MIME user's certificate with the intended domain name, similar to the way that DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE)

S/MIME.why: The document's purpose is to help S/MIME MUAs find and authenticate user certificates, and it states mandatory-to-implement behaviour for S/MIME MUAs.
S/MIME.quote: S/MIME [RFC5751] messages often contain a certificate (some messages contain more than one certificate).

rejected.why: DNSSEC validation is required for SMIMEA answers, but it is the security substrate. The document defines nothing new about DNSSEC itself.
The document defines a new RR type, but DANE is the more specific tag for it. The DNS record is a DANE mechanism.
The document concerns email security key discovery, which S/MIME and DANE already cover. The email address mapping is only a detail.
Internationalized local-parts are discussed in Section 4, but only as a limitation of the experiment. The document does not specify EAI.
RFC 7929 is cited as a similar mechanism, but this document does not address OpenPGP.
Certificates are the payload being associated. The document does not profile X.509.

RFC8163.title: Transmission of IPv6 over Master-Slave/Token-Passing (MS/TP) Networks
RFC8163.summary: Defines how IPv6 packets are encapsulated in MS/TP (RS-485 building automation) frames, with a LoWPAN_IPHC-based adaptation layer, SLAAC interface identifiers, link-local addressing, and address mapping.

6LoWPAN.why: The document is an IPv6-over-constrained-link adaptation profile built on 6LoWPAN encapsulation, IPHC compression and ND optimization. It is an IPv6 over X specification in the 6lo style.
6LoWPAN.quote: The general approach is to adapt elements of the 6LoWPAN specifications ([RFC4944], [RFC6282], and [RFC6775]) to constrained wired networks

SLAAC.why: The abstract names forming link-local and statelessly autoconfigured addresses as a core deliverable. Sections 6 and 7 define the MS/TP interface identifier and link-local address.
SLAAC.quote: This section defines how to obtain an IPv6 Interface Identifier.

rejected.why: Header compression here is 6LoWPAN IPHC, not ROHC.
Defines the SLLA/TLLA option format for MS/TP and uses RFC 6775 ARO, but this is a minor detail of the adaptation.
CRC-32K and COBS appear only in informative appendices describing the BACnet MS/TP frame.
Parent concept; the more specific tags fit better.
That tag covers RFC 2507 IPHC over PPP, not LOWPAN_IPHC.

gaps.name: BACnet MS/TP
gaps.why: The document is about IPv6 over the Master-Slave/Token-Passing building automation link layer (RS-485); the taxonomy has no BACnet or building automation tag.

RFC8164.title: Opportunistic Security for HTTP/2
RFC8164.summary: Experimental RFC describing how "http" URIs can be served over TLS and HTTP/2 using HTTP Alternative Services and Opportunistic Security, with a new "http-opportunistic" well-known URI, to mitigate passive pervasive monitoring.

HTTP.why: The document extends HTTP behaviour: it defines how clients use Alt-Svc to send http-scheme requests over an encrypted connection, and defines a well-known resource and client rules.
HTTP.quote: This document describes a use of HTTP Alternative Services [RFC7838] to decouple the URI scheme from the use and configuration of underlying encryption.

HTTP/2.why: The mechanism is specified for HTTP/2 (h2), which carries the explicit scheme. The title names HTTP/2, and the examples use HTTP/2 frames.
HTTP/2.quote: allows an "http" URI [RFC7230] to be accessed using HTTP/2 and Transport Layer Security (TLS)

web security.why: The document is a web platform security mechanism. It covers the mixed content problem, security indicators, downgrade attacks and the relationship to https.
web security.quote: Opportunistic Security does not provide the same guarantees as using TLS with "https" URIs, because it is vulnerable to active attacks

rejected.why: TLS is only the encryption substrate. The document defines nothing new about TLS itself, apart from not presenting client certificates.
JSON is only the encoding of the http-opportunistic resource, so the document is not about JSON.
The document uses http URIs and a well-known URI, but it is not about URI syntax or schemes.
Pervasive monitoring is the motivation, but the document is not a privacy threat model. Its privacy considerations are a short boilerplate-style section.
Caching of the well-known resource and of alternative services is mentioned only in passing.

gaps.name: Opportunistic Security / Alt-Svc (HTTP Alternative Services)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for opportunistic encryption or Alt-Svc. HTTP is the closest fit.

RFC8165.title: Design Considerations for Metadata Insertion
RFC8165.summary: An IAB-originated informational document advising that protocols should let end hosts add metadata themselves rather than having middleboxes insert metadata that restores information removed by encryption and data minimization, using RFC 7871 (EDNS client subnet) and RFC 7239 (Forwarded) as examples.

privacy.why: The document is a privacy design-considerations piece on data minimization and metadata restoration in response to pervasive surveillance, which is the privacy topic.
privacy.quote: designs that share metadata only by explicit actions at the host are preferable to designs in which middleboxes insert metadata

rejected.why: EDNS(0) and RFC 7871 are used as a worked example of the design pattern, but the document does not specify or extend EDNS.
DNS client subnet is only an illustrative example; the document is not about DNS protocol behaviour.
The Forwarded HTTP Extension is cited as an example of metadata insertion; the document does not define or extend HTTP.
STUN is mentioned as a way for hosts to learn their reflexive address, not as a subject of the document.
The broader security topic is too general; the document is specifically about privacy, which has its own tag.
It gives design advice, but the central subject is metadata privacy rather than general architectural principles.

RFC8166.title: Remote Direct Memory Access Transport for Remote Procedure Call Version 1
RFC8166.summary: Specifies RPC-over-RDMA version 1, a transport binding for ONC RPC on RDMA-capable transports, covering message framing, credits, chunks for direct data placement, error handling, Upper-Layer Binding requirements and RPCSEC_GSS use; obsoletes RFC 5666.

RDMA.why: The whole document defines a protocol over RDMA: credits, RDMA Send/Read/Write usage, segments and chunks, memory registration.
RDMA.quote: This document specifies a protocol for conveying Remote Procedure Call (RPC) messages on physical transports capable of Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA).

RFC8167.title: Bidirectional Remote Procedure Call on RPC-over-RDMA Transports
RFC8167.summary: Describes how RPC-over-RDMA transport endpoints carry ONC RPC Calls and Replies in both directions on one connection (needed for NFSv4.1 callbacks), covering credits, receive buffers, XIDs, chunks and retransmission.

RDMA.why: The document specifies reverse-direction operation on RPC-over-RDMA transports, including RDMA credit accounting, Receive buffer management and chunk use.
RDMA.quote: This document describes how RPC transport endpoints capable of Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) convey RPCs in both directions on a single connection.

ONC RPC.why: The document defines RPC direction, Requester/Responder roles, XID handling and retransmission for ONC RPC in the reverse direction.
ONC RPC.quote: The Open Network Computing Remote Procedure Call (ONC RPC) protocol as described in [RFC5531] is architected as a message-passing protocol

NFS.why: NFSv4.0 and 4.1 callback/backchannel operation is the motivating use case, discussed in Section 3 and the ULB considerations.
NFS.quote: Reverse-direction RPC transactions are necessary for the operation of version 4.1 of the Network File System (NFS), and in particular, of Parallel NFS (pNFS)

rejected.why: TCP is mentioned only as the alternative backchannel connection for NFS, not specified or extended here.
The document is about bidirectional operation over an existing mapping (RFC 8166), not defining a new transport binding; it explicitly does not update RFC 8166.
Credit-based flow control is covered, but it is RDMA Receive-buffer flow control, not congestion control.

RFC8168.title: DHCPv6 Prefix-Length Hint Issues
RFC8168.summary: Standards Track document giving client and server guidance on handling the DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation prefix-length hint in Solicit, Advertise, Renew and Rebind messages.

DHCPv6.why: The whole document specifies how DHCPv6 prefix delegation clients and servers should handle the prefix-length hint across the message exchange.
DHCPv6.quote: DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation allows a client to include a prefix-length hint value in the IA_PD option to indicate a preference for the size of the prefix

rejected.why: IPv6 prefixes are the thing delegated, but the document is about DHCPv6 protocol behaviour, not IPv6 addressing itself.
DHCPv6 is the more specific child tag and covers this document.
Prefix sizes are discussed only as a DHCPv6 option field; there is no addressing architecture content.
Renumbering is mentioned as a consequence of choosing among Renew/Rebind outcomes, but the document is not about renumbering procedures.

RFC8169.title: Residence Time Measurement in MPLS Networks
RFC8169.summary: Defines a new MPLS G-ACh (RTM) that accumulates per-node residence time of PTP/NTP timing packets along an RSVP-TE LSP, with capability advertisement in OSPF/IS-IS/BGP-LS and RSVP-TE signalling extensions.

MPLS.why: The document specifies a new MPLS G-ACh channel and message format carried over LSPs, extending MPLS OAM-style mechanisms.
MPLS.quote: This document defines a new Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) value and an associated Residence Time Measurement (RTM) message that can be used in a Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) network

PTP.why: The RTM mechanism exists to support PTP one-step/two-step transparent-clock behaviour across an MPLS domain, including a PTP sub-TLV.
PTP.quote: allows for a more accurate determination of the delay to be taken into account when applying the value included in a Precision Time Protocol event message

RSVP-TE.why: Substantial part defines RSVP-TE extensions: RTM_SET TLV, attribute flag and new error codes.
RSVP-TE.quote: the egress node MUST include an initialized RRO [RFC3209] and LSP_ATTRIBUTES object where the RTM_SET Attribute Flag is set
RSVP-TE.section: 4.4. RSVP-TE Control-Plane Operation to Support RTM

rejected.why: NTP is only listed as a possible carried timing packet type; the document is about PTP-oriented residence time.
Only a capability sub-TLV is defined for advertisement; the document is not about OSPF itself.
Just a sub-TLV for capability advertisement; not the subject.
BGP-LS used only to carry a capability TLV.
Residence time is a timing-sync aid; RFC 6374 delay measurement is cited only as insufficient.
G-ACh is an OAM channel but RTM is for time synchronization, not OAM.

RFC8170.title: Planning for Protocol Adoption and Subsequent Transitions
RFC8170.summary: IAB informational document summarizing principles for designing protocols to ease future transitions and describing the components of a good transition plan, with case studies (ECN, IDN, IPv6, HTTP).

internet architecture.why: The document gives architectural guidance on extensibility, coexistence vs. flag day, and translator placement across the protocol stack, which is a cross-protocol Internet architecture matter.
internet architecture.quote: This document attempts to summarize some basic principles to enable future transitions, and it also summarizes what makes for a good transition plan.

rejected.why: IPv6 is one case study (Appendix A.3); the document is about transitions generally, not IPv6/IPv4 mechanisms.
Only one illustrative case study among several.
ECN deployment is a brief case study, not the subject.
IDNA transition is a case study only.
HTTP versioning and upgrade is a case study; the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
Gives guidance for evaluating transition proposals but is not about IETF procedures.

gaps.name: Protocol transition and extensibility planning
gaps.why: The document's main subject (protocol adoption, transition plans, extensibility) has no dedicated tag; internet architecture is the nearest fit.

RFC8171.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Edge Directory Assistance Mechanisms
RFC8171.summary: Specifies Push (ESADI-based) and Pull (RBridge Channel-based) directory assistance mechanisms for TRILL edge switches to reduce ARP/ND and unknown-unicast flooding and detect forged addresses, plus a TRILL ES-IS variant for end-station support.

TRILL.why: The whole document defines TRILL protocol extensions: Push Directory servers, Pull Directory messages over RBridge Channel, new IS-IS flags, and TRILL ES-IS.
TRILL.quote: This document describes mechanisms for providing directory service to TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) edge switches.

rejected.why: ARP/ND messages are intercepted and answered using directory data, but the document does not specify or extend ARP; it is the traffic being optimized.
TRILL ES-IS is a variant of TRILL IS-IS and IS-IS sub-TLVs are used, but the document does not specify IS-IS itself; it is substrate for TRILL.
IPv6 ND is intercepted and answered from the directory, but the document does not define ND behavior.
MAC addresses and native frames are involved, but the document is about TRILL campus directory mechanisms, not IP over Ethernet.
DNS is mentioned only as an analogy for primary/secondary servers.
This covers LDAP/X.500-style directory access; the TRILL directory is a specific address-mapping service within TRILL, not that subject.

gaps.name: TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a TRILL tech entry at 'routing > TRILL' per the listing, but I used the id 'TRILL' as shown; if the intended id differs the document's primary subject is TRILL directory assistance, ESADI and RBridge Channel, which have no finer-grained tags.

RFC8172.title: Considerations for Benchmarking Virtual Network Functions and Their Infrastructure
RFC8172.summary: Informational BMWG memo describing additional considerations (hardware, configuration, testing strategies, shared resources, new benchmarks, coverage matrix, power) when benchmarking virtualized network functions and their infrastructure compared with physical devices.

benchmarking.why: The whole document is about benchmarking methodology for VNFs and their infrastructure, extending BMWG's black-box benchmarking (throughput, latency) to virtualized environments.
benchmarking.quote: This memo investigates additional methodological considerations necessary when benchmarking VNFs instantiated and hosted in general- purpose hardware

energy management.why: A section addresses measuring power consumption of the infrastructure, mentioning IPMI energy measurement. It is small, but readers of energy monitoring would want it.
energy management.quote: Both maximum power consumption and dynamic power consumption (with varying load) would be useful.

rejected.why: Service function chain is only referenced as a configuration parameter via RFC 7498; the document is not about SFC.
Considered because it covers performance metrics (RFC 6049, PDV, reordering), but the document is about benchmarking methodology, which benchmarking covers more specifically.
SDN benchmarking draft is only cited as an example of using the 3x3 matrix; not a subject of the document.
Power consumption is a brief benchmarking metric, not a discussion of environmental impact of Internet infrastructure.

gaps.name: Network Function Virtualization (NFV)
gaps.why: The document is centrally about VNFs and NFV infrastructure, but the taxonomy has no NFV/virtualization tag.

RFC8173.title: Precision Time Protocol Version 2 (PTPv2) Management Information Base
RFC8173.summary: Defines the read-only PTPBASE-MIB SNMP module for monitoring IEEE 1588-2008 Precision Time Protocol clocks (ordinary, boundary, transparent), including clock data sets, port data sets and counters.

PTP.why: The MIB exposes PTP clock, port and data-set state, so the document is about managing PTP.
PTP.quote: it defines objects for managing networks using the Precision Time Protocol (PTP), specified in IEEE Std. 1588-2008.

MIB.why: The document is a normative SMIv2 MIB module definition (PTPBASE-MIB) with textual conventions, tables and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module in a manner that is both compliant to the Structure of Management Information version 2 (SMIv2)

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines a module, not SNMP itself, and MIB is the more specific tag.
NTP is mentioned only as a time source enumeration value and in abbreviations; the document is not about it.
Parent of PTP, already implied by the PTP tag.
Ethernet appears only as a transport type identity and encapsulation value.
Pseudowire and MPLS appear only as encapsulation type identities.
No YANG is involved; the module is SMIv2 only.

RFC8174.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words
RFC8174.summary: BCP 14 update clarifying that RFC 2119 requirement key words (MUST, SHOULD, MAY, etc.) have their defined meanings only when in all capitals, and adding NOT RECOMMENDED to the boilerplate.

terminology.why: The document defines how requirements-language key words are interpreted in IETF documents, which is the terminology subject (requirements language).
terminology.quote: only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings

IETF process.why: As a BCP updating BCP 14, it sets authoring practice for IETF specifications, which is IETF process guidance.
IETF process.quote: Authors who follow these guidelines should incorporate this phrase near the beginning of their document

rejected.why: It concerns the use of requirements language in specifications, not the format, style or publication of the RFC series itself.

RFC8175.title: Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP)
RFC8175.summary: RFC 8175 specifies DLEP, a TCP-based session protocol (with UDP multicast discovery) by which radio modems report link characteristics and destination events to attached routers.

DLEP.why: The document defines DLEP in full: signals, messages, data items, session state machine and IANA registries.
DLEP.quote: This document introduces a new protocol called the Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP), which provides a bidirectional, event-driven communication channel between the router and the modem

rejected.why: TCP is only the reliable transport carrying DLEP messages; the document does not extend or specify TCP.
TLS is a recommended protection for the session, not something the document defines. It only adds a Use-TLS flag in connection points.
UDP multicast carries discovery signals only as substrate; nothing new is specified about UDP.
DLEP is relevant to mobile networks, but the DLEP tag in this taxonomy is not shown; the document is not about MANET routing protocols themselves.
IPv6 addresses appear as data items and link-local use is recommended, but the document is not about IPv6.
The IANA section creates DLEP registries, which is boilerplate-like and not the main subject.

RFC8176.title: Authentication Method Reference Values
RFC8176.summary: Establishes an IANA registry for "amr" (Authentication Methods References) claim values used in JWTs/OpenID Connect ID Tokens and defines an initial set of values such as pwd, otp, fpt, mfa.

authentication.why: The document defines identifiers for authentication methods (password, OTP, biometrics, smart card, etc.) that identity providers report. This is about authentication across protocols, with no specific protocol tag that fits better.
authentication.quote: This specification establishes a registry for Authentication Method Reference values and defines an initial set of Authentication Method Reference values.

JWT.why: The document defines values for a registered JWT claim and a registry tied to that claim. Readers of JWT claims would want it.
JWT.quote: The "amr" (Authentication Methods References) claim is defined and registered in the IANA "JSON Web Token Claims" registry

rejected.why: OAuth 2.0 is mentioned only as context, and the document says it is not for authentication. The document defines claim values, not OAuth behaviour.
The 'otp' value only references the HOTP and TOTP specifications. The document does not specify one-time password systems.
The IANA registry is the mechanism for the values. The document is about the authentication method values, not IANA registry guidance in general.
OpenID Connect is the context in which the claim is used, but the document does not define a federation framework.

gaps.name: OpenID Connect
gaps.why: The amr claim is used in OpenID Connect ID Tokens. The taxonomy has no OpenID Connect tag, and only the generic federated authentication tag is close.

RFC8177.title: YANG Data Model for Key Chains
RFC8177.summary: Defines the ietf-key-chain YANG module, a data model for key chains (key IDs, key strings, send/accept lifetimes, crypto algorithms) used for routing protocol authentication and graceful key rollover.

YANG.why: The document specifies a new YANG module (ietf-key-chain) with tree, features, typedefs and examples; readers of YANG models would look for it.
YANG.quote: This document describes the key chain YANG [YANG-1.1] data model.

key management.why: A substantial part addresses symmetric key provisioning, lifetimes and graceful key rollover, including AES key wrap protection of stored keys.
key management.quote: By properly overlapping the send and accept lifetimes of multiple key chain elements, key strings and algorithms may be gracefully updated.

rejected.why: Only the access protocol for the module and the example encoding; the document does not specify or extend NETCONF.
AES Key Wrap is only an optional feature for protecting key strings, not a main subject.
HMAC algorithms are merely identities listed in the module, not specified or analysed.
TCP-AO is mentioned only as an example of key derivation use, not the subject.
Key chains support routing protocol authentication, but the document defines a key data model rather than an authentication mechanism; key management fits better.
Mentioned only as an example consumer of key IDs.

RFC8178.title: Rules for NFSv4 Extensions and Minor Versions
RFC8178.summary: Defines the rules for extending the NFSv4 protocol family: creating minor versions, adding optional features to existing minor versions via XDR extension, interaction between minor versions, and correcting protocol flaws.

NFS.why: The whole document governs how NFSv4 evolves: minor versions, extensions and corrections. It updates RFC 5661 and RFC 7862, so NFS readers would expect to find it.
NFS.quote: This document describes the rules relating to the extension of the NFSv4 family of protocols.

ONC RPC.why: Much of the document (Section 4) sets out the rules for extending NFSv4's XDR definitions compatibly. The taxonomy groups XDR with ONC RPC.
ONC RPC.quote: The XDR extension approach allows an XDR description to be extended in a way that retains the structure of all previously valid messages.

rejected.why: The document sets protocol-versioning rules for NFSv4 and does not describe general IETF procedures, even though it governs how Proposed Standards extend NFSv4.
Section 2 only defines a few terms used in the document, such as feature statuses and version variants. It is not a glossary or a requirements-language document.
The more specific NFS tag already covers this subject, so the parent is not tagged.

RFC8179.title: Intellectual Property Rights in IETF Technology
RFC8179.summary: BCP 79 sets out IETF policy on patent/IPR disclosure by contributors and participants, licensing declarations, handling of failures to disclose, and how working groups weigh encumbered technologies; it obsoletes RFC 3979 and 4879 and updates RFC 2026.

IPR.why: The whole document defines IETF patent/IPR disclosure and licensing policy, which is exactly the IPR subject.
IPR.quote: This document sets out the IETF policies concerning IPR related to technology worked on within the IETF.

rejected.why: The document is part of the IETF process, but it is about IPR in particular, and IPR is the more specific tag under internet governance.
It touches alternate streams and the ban on IPR text in RFCs, but it is not about RFC format or publication.
Section 1 defines terms, but only to support the IPR policy.

RFC8180.title: Minimal IPv6 over the TSCH Mode of IEEE 802.15.4e (6TiSCH) Configuration
RFC8180.summary: BCP defining the minimal 6TiSCH configuration: IEEE 802.15.4 TSCH schedule, EB contents, link-layer security keys, RPL with OF0 settings, join metric, and implementation recommendations for IPv6 over TSCH.

6TiSCH.why: The whole document specifies the baseline 6TiSCH configuration: TSCH schedule, EB frames, join behaviour, and link-layer settings.
6TiSCH.quote: This document describes a minimal mode of operation for an IPv6 over the TSCH mode of IEEE 802.15.4e (6TiSCH) network.

RPL.why: A full section specifies RPL settings: OF0 parameters, rank computation, mode of operation, Trickle, packet contents, and hysteresis.
RPL.quote: When RPL is used, nodes MUST implement the non-storing mode of operation

rejected.why: 6LoWPAN framework is used unmodified and only referenced, not specified or extended here.
IPv6 is the carried network layer, not the subject of the document.
The IoT context is background only. The specific 6TiSCH tag covers the document.
Key distribution and join security are explicitly out of scope; the document only sets link-layer keys.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.15.4 TSCH (Time-Slotted Channel Hopping) link layer
gaps.why: The document's main body configures TSCH schedules, EBs, and timeslot templates; the taxonomy has no 802.15.4/TSCH tag apart from 6TiSCH.

RFC8181.title: A Publication Protocol for the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI)
RFC8181.summary: Defines the RPKI publication protocol, an XML-over-CMS-over-HTTP request/response protocol by which CA engines publish, withdraw and list RPKI objects at a publication repository.

RPKI.why: The document specifies a protocol within the RPKI for publishing certificates and other objects to repositories, so RPKI readers need it.
RPKI.quote: This document defines a protocol for publishing Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) objects.

rejected.why: XML is only the message encoding; the document is not about XML usage in general.
CMS is the signing wrapper reused from RFC 6492; nothing new is defined about CMS.
HTTP is only the transport; the document registers a media type but does not extend HTTP.
The IANA registration of application/rpki-publication is boilerplate-level; the document is not about media type rules.
The BPKI is mentioned for client authentication but is not defined here; RPKI is the more specific fit.
SHA-256 is only used for the object hash attribute.

RFC8182.title: The RPKI Repository Delta Protocol (RRDP)
RFC8182.summary: Specifies RRDP, an HTTPS-based RPKI repository distribution protocol using Update Notification, Snapshot and Delta XML files designed for scaling and CDN caching, as an alternative to rsync.

RPKI.why: The document defines a new protocol for publishing and retrieving RPKI objects between repositories and Relying Parties, which is RPKI infrastructure.
RPKI.quote: This document specifies a new RPKI Repository Delta Protocol (RRDP) for this purpose.

HTTP caching.why: A large part of the design (immutable snapshot/delta files, Cache-Control for notification files, cache lifetimes) concerns caching over HTTP.
HTTP caching.quote: it enables the use of Content Distribution Networks (CDNs) or other caching infrastructures for the retrieval of these files.

rejected.why: HTTPS is only the transport for RRDP; the document defines no new HTTP semantics or extensions.
CDNs are mentioned as a way to distribute the files, but the document does not address CDN interconnection; HTTP caching fits better.
The file formats are XML with a RELAX NG schema, but XML is merely the encoding used.
TLS is only the security mechanism for HTTPS; the HTTPS considerations just point to existing BCPs.
Version 4 UUIDs are used as session identifiers but the document defines nothing new about UUIDs.
The SIA extension is added to resource certificates, but the document does not profile certificates in its own right.

RFC8183.title: An Out-of-Band Setup Protocol for Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Production Services
RFC8183.summary: Defines a small XML-based out-of-band setup protocol for exchanging BPKI trust anchors and configuration (handles, service URIs, publication referrals) between RPKI parents/children and publishers/repositories.

RPKI.why: The document specifies the setup protocol for RPKI provisioning and publication services, including its messages, BPKI trust anchor exchange and publication referrals.
RPKI.quote: a small XML-based out-of-band protocol used to set up relationships between parents and children in the RPKI provisioning protocol [RFC6492] and between publishers and repositories

rejected.why: X.509 certificates are exchanged as key material, but the document does not profile X.509; it only describes cross-certification usage.
CMS is used to sign authorization tokens and underlying protocol messages, only as a mechanism.
XML is the encoding of the messages (with a RELAX NG schema); the document is not about XML usage generally.
The BPKI is discussed, but the document is about RPKI setup; the PKI is the mechanism for key exchange, not the subject in itself.
Base64 is just the encoding for certificates in the messages.
HTTP URLs are only service endpoints named in messages; HTTP is not specified or extended.

gaps.name: RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has RPKI only as a child of routing security, but I used the id RPKI which exists as a tech under routing security; no gap in coverage.

RFC8184.title: Dual-Homing Protection for MPLS and the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Pseudowires
RFC8184.summary: Informational framework describing PW dual-homing local protection using a Dual-Node Interconnection PW between dual-homing PEs, with one-side and two-side scenarios, for MPLS and MPLS-TP pseudowires.

pseudowire.why: The whole document is a framework for pseudowire dual-homing protection, including PE architecture and failure scenarios for service PWs and the DNI-PW.
pseudowire.quote: A Dual-Node Interconnection (DNI) PW is used between the dual-homing PE nodes to carry traffic when a failure occurs in the AC or PW side.

MPLS-TP.why: The document addresses MPLS-TP PW protection, complements MPLS-TP linear protection, and is in the pals work on MPLS-TP pseudowires.
MPLS-TP.quote: describe the framework and mechanism of MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) linear protection, which can provide protection for the MPLS Label Switched Path (LSP) or pseudowire (PW)

rejected.why: LDP signalling is only mentioned as the basis of existing PW redundancy mechanisms. This document does not specify or extend it.
RFC 7275 is cited only for state synchronization. The document is about PW protection, not L2VPN services.
MPLS is the substrate. The more specific pseudowire and MPLS-TP tags cover the subject.

RFC8185.title: Dual-Homing Coordination for MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Pseudowires Protection
RFC8185.summary: Defines the MPLS-TP Dual-Homing Coordination (DHC) message, carried in a new G-ACh channel type over a DNI-PW, that lets dual-homing PEs exchange PW status and switchover requests for local protection of static MPLS-TP pseudowires.

MPLS-TP.why: The document extends MPLS-TP with a new G-ACh channel type and DHC message for protecting static MPLS-TP pseudowires, building on MPLS-TP linear protection.
MPLS-TP.quote: A new G-ACh channel type is defined for the dual-homing coordination between the dual-homing PEs of MPLS-TP PWs.

pseudowire.why: The mechanism protects pseudowires against AC, PE and PSN failures using a DNI-PW and service PW status exchange, so pseudowire readers would expect it.
pseudowire.quote: This document proposes a dual-homing coordination mechanism for static MPLS-TP PWs

rejected.why: Covered by the more specific MPLS-TP child tag.
LDP is only referenced for PW IDs (RFC 8077); the document is for static PWs without a dynamic control plane.
OAM is relied on to determine PW and DNI-PW state but is out of scope for this document.
No VPN service is discussed; this is PW protection.

RFC8186.title: Support of the IEEE 1588 Timestamp Format in a Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP)
RFC8186.summary: Extends OWAMP and TWAMP so endpoints can negotiate and use the IEEE 1588v2 (PTP) timestamp format instead of NTP, using a new Modes bit and a redefined Z field in the Error Estimate.

TWAMP.why: The document extends TWAMP control and test protocols with timestamp format negotiation and a new Modes bit.
TWAMP.quote: this document proposes optional extensions to Control and Test protocols to support use of the IEEE 1588v2 timestamp format as an optional alternative to the NTP timestamp format.

OWAMP.why: The same extension is specified for OWAMP, with its own negotiation rules and test packet changes.
OWAMP.quote: Timestamp Format Negotiation in OWAMP Connection Setup

rejected.why: PTP's timestamp format is borrowed, but the document does not specify or extend PTP itself.
NTP is the existing timestamp format being given an alternative. The document does not specify or extend NTP.
The parent topic is implied by the OWAMP and TWAMP tags.

RFC8187.title: Indicating Character Encoding and Language for HTTP Header Field Parameters
RFC8187.summary: RFC 8187 specifies an RFC 2231-compatible profile for encoding non-ASCII character data and language information (ext-value, UTF-8 percent-encoding) in HTTP header field parameters, and obsoletes RFC 5987.

HTTP.why: The document defines an extension for HTTP header field parameters and gives guidelines for HTTP header field definitions, so HTTP readers would want it.
HTTP.quote: This document specifies an encoding suitable for use in HTTP header fields that is compatible with a simplified profile of the encoding defined in RFC 2231.

internationalization.why: A substantial part of the document covers character encoding and language tagging of text in protocol elements. No more specific child tag fits, because UTF-8, language tags and character sets are only used here, not defined or profiled in their own right.
internationalization.quote: Producers MUST use the "UTF-8" ([RFC3629]) character encoding.

rejected.why: RFC 2231 is discussed only as the basis for comparison. The document defines an HTTP encoding, not a MIME one.
UTF-8 is mandated as the encoding but is defined elsewhere. The document is not about UTF-8 itself.
Language tags are only referenced for the optional language field in ext-value. The document does not specify or profile them.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the grammar.
Percent-encoding comes from RFC 3986 and is used as a mechanism here. The document is not about URIs.
Digest authentication's username* parameter is mentioned only in the implementation report as one user of the encoding.

RFC8188.title: Encrypted Content-Encoding for HTTP
RFC8188.summary: Defines the "aes128gcm" HTTP content coding, which encrypts HTTP message payloads in fixed-size AEAD_AES_128_GCM records, with HKDF-derived keys and nonces and a header carrying salt, record size and key id.

HTTP.why: The document extends HTTP with a new content coding, registers it in the HTTP Content Coding Registry, and discusses range requests, PUT and header leakage. Readers of HTTP extensions would want it.
HTTP.quote: This document specifies a content coding (see Section 3.1.2 of [RFC7231]) for HTTP to serve these and other use cases.

AES.why: A substantial part of the document specifies AES-128-GCM record encryption, including nonce construction, key derivation and data encryption limits.
AES.quote: indicates that a payload has been encrypted using Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) as identified as AEAD_AES_128_GCM

rejected.why: Appendix A only maps the format onto JWE for comparison. The document does not specify or extend JOSE.
TLS is mentioned only as a contrast, since it protects just the channel, and as a size-hiding mitigation. The document is not about TLS.
HMAC-SHA-256 and HKDF are used as building blocks for key and nonce derivation. The document does not specify them.
The document explicitly says key management is not described.
Caching of partial messages is mentioned only in passing in the security considerations.
SHA-256 is only the hash used inside HKDF.

RFC8189.title: Multi-Cost Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO)
RFC8189.summary: Extends the ALTO protocol (RFC 7285) so Filtered Cost Map and Endpoint Cost Services can return multiple cost metrics per request as array values, and adds extended constraint tests with OR-combinations and testable cost types.

ALTO.why: The whole document specifies extensions to the ALTO protocol: multi-cost maps, new capabilities (max-cost-types, testable-cost-type-names) and input parameters (multi-cost-types, or-constraints).
ALTO.quote: This document defines a new service that allows an ALTO Client to retrieve several cost metrics in a single request for an ALTO filtered cost map and endpoint cost map.

rejected.why: ALTO messages are JSON-encoded, but JSON is only the encoding substrate; the document does not define a JSON format in its own right.
Requests are HTTP POSTs, but HTTP is only the transport and nothing new is defined about HTTP.
The IRD capabilities are extended, but this is ALTO resource description, not general service discovery.
The IANA section only says nothing is registered, so it is boilerplate.

gaps.name: ALTO (Application-Layer Traffic Optimization)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has ALTO under applications, and I'm using it as the tag id. If it were missing, this RFC would have no fitting tag, since it extends ALTO cost maps and the Endpoint Cost Service.

RFC8190.title: Updates to the Special-Purpose IP Address Registries
RFC8190.summary: BCP updating RFC 6890 so the IANA IPv4 and IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries replace the "Global" column with "Globally Reachable" and correcting several registry entries (limited broadcast, Teredo, Unique-Local).

addressing.why: The document is about IP address architecture: special-purpose address blocks and the meaning of global reachability. No more specific addressing child tag fits.
addressing.quote: This memo updates the definition of "global" from [RFC6890] for the IPv4 and IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries

IANA.why: The document's operative content is changes to IANA registries (renamed columns, corrected entries), so readers of IANA registry topics would want it.
IANA.quote: The "Global" columns in the IPv4 Special-Purpose Address Registry

rejected.why: IPv6 registry entries are edited, but the document is about the special-purpose address registries generally, not the IPv6 protocol or its deployment.
IPv4 registry entry is edited, but the document is about address registries as a whole, not IPv4 lifecycle.
Teredo's registry entry gets a footnote change, but the document does not specify or analyse Teredo.
Teredo and 6to4 entries are only touched for footnote edits; transition mechanisms are not the subject.

gaps.name: Special-purpose IP address registries
gaps.why: The document is about IANA's IPv4/IPv6 special-purpose address registries and the 'globally reachable' definition. The taxonomy has only the general addressing tag, with no narrower tag for reserved or special-use IP address blocks.

RFC8191.title: Home Network Prefix Renumbering in Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6)
RFC8191.summary: Defines an optional PMIPv6 extension in which the LMA uses Update Notification messages to push a renumbered Home Network Prefix to the MAG and MN, covering soft and hard session-connectivity modes.

PMIPv6.why: The document extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 with LMA-initiated HNP renumbering using UPN/UPA messages, so it belongs on the PMIPv6 page.
PMIPv6.quote: a solution to support HNP renumbering is proposed, as an optional extension of the PMIPv6 specification.

rejected.why: The document is about renumbering the HNP inside PMIPv6 rather than general site renumbering procedures. The PMIPv6 tag covers it more specifically.
Router Advertisements with Prefix Information Options are used to announce the new HNP to the MN, but this is only the mechanism, not the subject.
DHCP is mentioned as an alternative way of configuring the address, but the document does not specify or extend it.
MIPv6 is referenced only as a comparison for how a home agent notifies of prefix changes. The document is about PMIPv6.
The DNS record update is explicitly out of scope.
SLAAC is used by the MN to configure the new HoA, but the document does not address it as a subject.

RFC8192.title: Interface to Network Security Functions (I2NSF): Problem Statement and Use Cases
RFC8192.summary: Problem statement and use cases for I2NSF, a standard interface for controlling and monitoring vendor-diverse, often virtualized, hosted network security functions (firewalls, IPS/IDS, etc.) from customers and security controllers.

I2NSF.why: The whole document defines the problem and use cases for the Interface to Network Security Functions, so the I2NSF tag fits as the main subject.
I2NSF.quote: What is needed is a standardized interface to control and monitor the rule sets that NSFs use to treat packets traversing through these NSFs.

rejected.why: SDN is discussed as a context (Section 3.6) but the document is about the NSF interface, not SDN itself. The I2NSF tag sits under firewall, not SDN.
DOTS is mentioned only as an adjacent DDoS signalling effort and an out-of-scope item.
DDoS mitigation appears as one use case, not as a main subject of the document.
Dynamic key distribution to NSFs is one challenge among nine, which is not substantial enough for a tag.
Policy provisioning is the context, but the document does not specify policy information models.

RFC8193.title: Information Model for Large-Scale Measurement Platforms (LMAPs)
RFC8193.summary: Defines the protocol-independent LMAP Information Model for Measurement Agents, covering preconfiguration, configuration, instructions, logging, capability/status, and reporting objects exchanged with Controllers and Collectors.

LMAP.why: The whole document defines the information model for LMAP Measurement Agents, Controllers and Collectors.
LMAP.quote: This Information Model applies to the Measurement Agent within an LMAP framework.

rejected.why: The YANG data model implementing this information model is in RFC 8194; this document only references it.
LMAP is under this topic, but the more specific LMAP tag fits. The document does not define measurement metrics or methods; the measurement protocols are out of scope.
UUIDs are only used as an identifier base type, not specified or profiled here.
RFC 3339 is only cited as the datetime format for the notation, not the subject.
TLS is only mentioned as the way certificates are retrieved for Channels; it is not specified or extended here.

RFC8194.title: A YANG Data Model for LMAP Measurement Agents
RFC8194.summary: Defines YANG modules (common, control, report) modelling LMAP Measurement Agents, their control by Controllers and result reporting to Collectors, based on the LMAP Information Model.

YANG.why: The document's main body is three YANG modules with tree diagrams, so it belongs on the YANG page.
YANG.quote: This document defines a data model for Large-Scale Measurement Platforms (LMAPs).  The data model is defined using the YANG data modeling language.

LMAP.why: It models the LMAP control and report data structures exchanged between Measurement Agents, Controllers and Collectors.
LMAP.quote: The LMAP framework has three basic elements: Measurement Agents (MAs), Controllers, and Collectors.

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the protocol used to access the modules; the document defines nothing new about it.
It is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an alternative access protocol.
LMAP is the more specific child tag and already covers this topic.
It appears only as boilerplate in Security Considerations.
It appears only as boilerplate in Security Considerations.
It is mentioned only in passing as a way to carry logging information.

RFC8195.title: Use of BGP Large Communities
RFC8195.summary: Informational RFC giving operators examples of how to organize BGP Large Communities into informational and action categories (location, relation, selective NO_EXPORT, prepending, LOCAL_PREF, route server control).

BGP communities.why: The whole document is about operator use of BGP Large Communities, including informational and action community schemes.
BGP communities.quote: this document presents examples of how operators might utilize BGP Large Communities to achieve various goals.

route server.why: A dedicated section shows how Large Communities control route server prefix distribution, which is relevant to readers of the route server subject.
route server.quote: An example BGP Large Communities policy that enables client-controlled prefix distribution for a route server operating as AS 64511 is outlined as follows:

rejected.why: Parent of BGP communities, which is the more specific fit. The document is about community usage, not BGP in general.
The actions (prepending, LOCAL_PREF) are traffic-engineering functions, but only as BGP community policy and not MPLS/TE-style traffic engineering.
The Security Considerations section only points to RFC 7454. The document's main body is not about operational security.

RFC8196.title: IS-IS Autoconfiguration
RFC8196.summary: Specifies IS-IS autoconfiguration for plug-and-play networks: default configuration, System ID self-generation, a new Router-Fingerprint TLV, and duplicate System ID detection and resolution.

IS-IS.why: The whole document extends IS-IS with autoconfiguration: default config, System ID generation, a new Router-Fingerprint TLV, and duplicate System ID resolution.
IS-IS.quote: This document specifies mechanisms for IS-IS [RFC1195] [ISO_IEC10589] [RFC5308] to be autoconfiguring.

rejected.why: RFC 7503 (OSPFv3 Autoconfiguration) is only cited as inspiration for the design. This document does not specify OSPFv3.
The document addresses one protocol, IS-IS, so the specific technology tag fits better than a general routing topic.
Both IPv4 and IPv6 deployments are supported, but IPv6 is not what the document is about.
PPP is mentioned only as an example of an interface type that gets autoconfigured as point-to-point.
HMAC-MD5 authentication is recommended only as an option, via RFC 5304. The document does not address it in its own right.

RFC8197.title: A SIP Response Code for Unwanted Calls
RFC8197.summary: Defines the SIP 607 (Unwanted) response code and the sip.607 feature-capability indicator so called parties can flag unwanted calls and providers can use that as input to call filtering.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new response code and a feature-capability indicator, and specifies how SIP entities handle them.
SIP.quote: This document defines the 607 (Unwanted) SIP response code, allowing called parties to indicate that the call or message was unwanted.

spam.why: The purpose is user feedback to combat unsolicited calls and messages (voice spam), analogous to email spam buttons, though the tag is under email.
spam.quote: an increasing number of calls are unwanted [RFC5039]: they might be fraudulent or illegal telemarketing

rejected.why: The document references SIP Identity for authenticating caller identity in security considerations only. The document does not define STIR mechanisms.
Telephone numbers and tel URIs are mentioned only in passing when explaining caller identity.
TLS is only recommended as protection against spoofed responses in Security Considerations.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate for the response code and feature-capability, not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Unwanted calls / robocall mitigation
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for telephony call-abuse or robocall handling outside of email spam. The nearest tag, spam, sits under email.

RFC8198.title: Aggressive Use of DNSSEC-Validated Cache
RFC8198.summary: RFC 8198 updates RFC 4035 to let DNSSEC-validating resolvers synthesize negative answers from cached NSEC/NSEC3 ranges and positive answers from cached wildcards, improving performance, privacy and DoS resilience.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document specifies how validating resolvers use NSEC/NSEC3 and wildcard records from the cache, and it updates RFC 4035. This is DNSSEC validation and denial-of-existence behaviour.
DNSSEC.quote: This document specifies the use of NSEC/NSEC3 resource records to allow DNSSEC-validating resolvers to generate negative answers within a range and positive answers from wildcards.

rejected.why: DNS is the parent of DNSSEC and is implied. Negative caching is a DNS topic, but the document's specific subject is DNSSEC-validated records, so the more specific tag fits.
This is about DNS caching, not web caching, so it does not fit.
Privacy is mentioned as a benefit (fewer leaked queries), but the document is not a privacy analysis.
Mitigation of random QNAME attacks is a side benefit only, not the document's subject.

RFC8199.title: YANG Module Classification
RFC8199.summary: RFC 8199 defines a two-dimensional taxonomy for classifying YANG modules: abstraction layer (network element vs. network service) and origin type (standard, vendor-specific, user-specific).

YANG.why: The whole document is about categorizing YANG modules, covering network element and service modules and their origin types, so readers of the YANG subject would want it.
YANG.quote: This document describes a set of concepts and associated terms to support consistent classification of YANG modules.

rejected.why: NETCONF is mentioned only in passing as the configuration protocol that IESG encourages alongside YANG. The document does not specify or analyse it.
RFC 8049 is cited as an example of a network service module. The document is not about L3VPN.
The document does define terms, but they are specific to YANG modules. The YANG tag covers that better than the generic terminology topic.
Orchestrators and service-to-element decomposition are mentioned, but the document does not address SDN architecture.

RFC8200.title: Internet Protocol, Version 6 (IPv6) Specification
RFC8200.summary: RFC 8200 is the Internet Standard specification of IPv6, defining the basic header, extension headers and options, fragmentation, packet size rules, and upper-layer protocol issues, and obsoleting RFC 2460.

IPv6.why: The document is the core IPv6 specification: header format, extension headers, fragmentation, and upper-layer issues.
IPv6.quote: This document specifies version 6 of the Internet Protocol (IPv6).  It obsoletes RFC 2460.

rejected.why: ICMPv6 is specified in RFC 4443; here it is only referenced for error messages and the pseudo-header checksum.
Path MTU Discovery is specified in RFC 8201; this document only recommends implementing it.
AH and ESP are specified in other RFCs; this document only covers their ordering relative to other extension headers.
The Traffic Class field's use for Diffserv and ECN is only referenced, with the definitions left to RFC 2474 and RFC 3168.
IPv4 is mentioned only for comparison with IPv6, not as a subject of the document.
IPv6 addressing is explicitly specified separately in RFC 4291.

RFC8201.title: Path MTU Discovery for IP version 6
RFC8201.summary: Specifies Path MTU Discovery for IPv6, using ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages, PMTU caching, aging and packetization-layer behaviour; obsoletes RFC 1981.

PMTUD.why: The whole document specifies IPv6 Path MTU Discovery: requirements, PMTU storage, purging stale values and packetization layer actions.
PMTUD.quote: This document defines a standard mechanism for a node to discover the PMTU of an arbitrary path.

rejected.why: The document is about IPv6 PMTUD, but PMTUD is the more specific tag and IPv6 is implied as the context.
ICMPv6 Packet Too Big is the signalling mechanism relied upon; the message is defined in RFC 4443, not here.
TCP is discussed as an example packetization layer (MSS, retransmission), but the document does not specify TCP.
Referenced only for the destination cache model and proxy ND; not the subject.
Mentioned only as an example of a transport user in Section 5.5.

RFC8202.title: IS-IS Multi-Instance
RFC8202.summary: RFC 8202 specifies IS-IS Multi-Instance, an extension adding an Instance Identifier TLV so a router can run multiple IS-IS instances, each with multiple topology-specific LSDBs, on shared circuits; it obsoletes RFC 6822.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with a new IID-TLV, instance-specific adjacencies, and per-topology Update Processes. It is squarely about the IS-IS protocol.
IS-IS.quote: This document describes a mechanism that allows a single router to share one or more circuits among multiple Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) routing protocol instances.

rejected.why: Only mentioned in relation to the BFD-Enabled TLV using the ITID instead of the MTID. This is a minor interaction, not the subject.
The new multicast MAC addresses are for LAN circuits, but the document is not about IP over Ethernet.
The IANA section only registers a TLV and two MAC addresses. This is boilerplate, not the subject.

RFC8203.title: BGP Administrative Shutdown Communication
RFC8203.summary: Updates RFC 4486 to let a BGP speaker include a short UTF-8 freeform Shutdown Communication (up to 128 octets) in Cease NOTIFICATION messages with Administrative Shutdown or Administrative Reset subcodes.

BGP.why: The document extends the BGP Cease NOTIFICATION message encoding and updates RFC 4486, so it is a BGP protocol extension and operations document.
BGP.quote: specifying a mechanism to transmit a short freeform UTF-8 [RFC3629] message as part of a Cease NOTIFICATION message [RFC4271] to inform the peer why the BGP session is being shutdown or reset.

rejected.why: UTF-8 is only the encoding used for the message string; the document does not define anything new about UTF-8.
Syslog is mentioned only as a suggested reporting method and in security considerations; the document is not about it.
Security considerations are boilerplate-like and the document is about a BGP signalling mechanism, not operational security practice.
The IANA section only adds a reference to existing registry entries; it is not the subject of the document.

RFC8204.title: Benchmarking Virtual Switches in the Open Platform for NFV (OPNFV)
RFC8204.summary: Describes OPNFV VSPERF contributions to BMWG benchmarking of virtual switches on general-purpose hardware, covering test setup, configuration parameters, deployment scenarios and coverage of the 3x3 benchmark matrix.

benchmarking.why: The whole document defines benchmarking methodology considerations, configuration parameters, deployment scenarios and test coverage for vSwitch performance, extending BMWG work.
benchmarking.quote: This memo describes the contributions of the Open Platform for NFV (OPNFV) project on Virtual Switch Performance (VSPERF)

rejected.why: The document is device benchmarking in a lab (BMWG), which the benchmarking tag covers more specifically. It only references IPPM metrics.
The vSwitch forwards Ethernet frames and RFC 2889 is about LAN switching. The document is not about Ethernet protocol or OAM.
Virtual switches and NFV infrastructure are the subject. The document does not address programmable control planes.
TCP and UDP only appear as traffic types in the tests, not as the document's subject.

gaps.name: NFV / virtual switch benchmarking (OPNFV VSPERF)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for network function virtualization or virtual switches, so readers looking for NFV infrastructure would not find this RFC under a specific subject.

RFC8205.title: BGPsec Protocol Specification
RFC8205.summary: RFC 8205 specifies BGPsec, a BGP extension that adds an optional non-transitive BGPsec_PATH attribute carrying per-AS digital signatures, with capability negotiation, signature generation, and validation procedures using RPKI router certificates.

BGPsec.why: The document is the core BGPsec protocol specification: capability, BGPsec_PATH attribute, signing and validation.
BGPsec.quote: BGPsec is implemented via an optional non-transitive BGP path attribute that carries digital signatures produced by each AS that propagates the UPDATE message.

rejected.why: BGPsec is the more specific child tag; BGP is the base protocol being extended.
RPKI router certificates and ROAs are relied on for keys and origin validation, but the document does not specify RPKI itself.
Router certificates are profiled in RFC 8209; this document only uses their SKI and public key.
The signature algorithm is specified in RFC 8208; only a brief operational note on the ECDSA random number appears here.
pCount=0 for route servers is discussed, but the document is not about route servers.

RFC8206.title: BGPsec Considerations for Autonomous System (AS) Migration
RFC8206.summary: Standards-track document specifying how BGPsec signs updates (double signing with pCount=0) to support AS migration as described in RFC 7705, updating RFC 8205.

BGPsec.why: The document extends BGPsec signing behavior (pCount=0 double signatures, iBGP signing) to support AS migration, and updates RFC 8205.
BGPsec.quote: discusses considerations and methods for supporting and securing a common method for Autonomous System (AS) migration within the BGPsec protocol

RPKI.why: A substantial section covers route origin validation and ROA requirements during migration, with keys provisioned for both ASNs.
RPKI.quote: for each ROA that authorizes the old ASN (e.g., AS64510) to originate a prefix, a new ROA MUST also be created that authorizes the replacing ASN

rejected.why: BGP and the RFC 7705 AS_PATH migration mechanisms are the background; the document's normative content concerns BGPsec signatures.
Route reflectors are mentioned only briefly, requiring transparent reflection of updates; not a subject of the document.
Parent of BGPsec and RPKI, which are tagged more specifically.

RFC8207.title: BGPsec Operational Considerations
RFC8207.summary: RFC 8207 is a BCP collecting operational considerations for deploying BGPsec: router certificates and keys, incremental deployment, edge sites, routing policy for validation states, route servers, and confederations.

BGPsec.why: The whole document gives operational guidance for deploying BGPsec path validation, covering keys, policy, route servers and partial deployment.
BGPsec.quote: BGPsec is a new protocol with many operational considerations that this document attempts to describe.

RPKI.why: Substantial parts cover RPKI distribution and maintenance, router certificates published in the RPKI, Ghostbusters records, and origin validation per RFC 6811/7115.
RPKI.quote: BGPsec relies on widespread propagation of the RPKI [RFC6480].

rejected.why: BGP is the base protocol BGPsec secures. The document is about BGPsec operation, not BGP itself.
There is one paragraph on BGPsec-aware route servers and pCount 0. That is too small a share of the document for a tag.
Route reflectors and confederations get brief mentions on BGPsec enablement, not substantial coverage.
NTP is mentioned only as the common way to keep router clocks correct.
The subject is covered more specifically by BGPsec and routing security, so the generic operational tag adds nothing.

RFC8208.title: BGPsec Algorithms, Key Formats, and Signature Formats
RFC8208.summary: Specifies the ECDSA P-256/SHA-256 algorithm suite, key formats, and signature formats for BGPsec router certificates, certification requests and UPDATE messages, updating RFC 7935, with an IANA algorithm suite registry and example signed UPDATEs.

BGPsec.why: The document defines the cryptographic algorithms, key and signature formats for BGPsec, creates the BGPsec Algorithm Suite registry, and gives example BGPsec UPDATE messages.
BGPsec.quote: specifies the algorithms, algorithm parameters, asymmetric key formats, asymmetric key sizes, and signature formats used in BGPsec (Border Gateway Protocol Security)

ECDSA.why: Mandates ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256 and specifies the public key encoding and signature format for it, which ECDSA readers would want.
ECDSA.quote: The signature algorithm used MUST be the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) with curve P-256 [RFC6090] [DSS].

RPKI.why: It updates the RPKI algorithm profile (RFC 7935) for BGPsec router certificates and certification requests used by RPKI CAs.
RPKI.quote: This document updates RFC 7935 ("The Profile for Algorithms and Key Sizes for Use in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure").

rejected.why: BGP is the carrier of the UPDATE messages; the document is about BGPsec's cryptography, not BGP operations or policy.
Certificate formats are used (SubjectPublicKeyInfo) but the certificate profile itself is in RFC 8209; X.509 is the substrate here.
SHA-256 is merely selected as the hash; the document does not address the SHA family.
Section 5 only anticipates future algorithm transitions generically; nothing about post-quantum cryptography.
The registry creation is boilerplate-level IANA section, specific to BGPsec rather than IANA guidance.

RFC8209.title: A Profile for BGPsec Router Certificates, Certificate Revocation Lists, and Certification Requests
RFC8209.summary: Defines a profile of RPKI resource EE certificates (BGPsec Router Certificates), their certification requests, and RP validation rules, binding ASNs to router public keys for BGPsec path validation, and updates RFC 6487.

BGPsec.why: The document specifies the router certificates that BGPsec path validation relies on, including EKU, certificate requests and validation procedures. It is a core BGPsec building block.
BGPsec.quote: This document defines a standard profile for X.509 certificates used to enable validation of Autonomous System (AS) paths in the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)

RPKI.why: It extends the RPKI with a new resource certificate type, profiled as differences from RFC 6487, and defines RP validation for it.
RPKI.quote: This document extends the RPKI; therefore, this document updates the RPKI Resource Certificates Profile (RFC 6487).

X.509.why: A substantial part of the document is an X.509 certificate profile: subject naming, EKU, extension requirements and request profile.
X.509.quote: This document defines a profile for X.509 end entity (EE) certificates [RFC5280] for use in the context of certification of Autonomous System (AS) paths

rejected.why: BGP is the context. The document profiles certificates and does not specify BGP protocol behaviour.
X.509 and RPKI are the more specific tags that apply, so the parent PKI tag is not needed.
The ASN.1 module only defines an EKU OID in an appendix and is not the document's subject.
The OID assignments in IANA Considerations are boilerplate and not the subject.

RFC8210.title: The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) to Router Protocol, Version 1
RFC8210.summary: Specifies version 1 of the RPKI-to-Router protocol, by which routers fetch validated ROA prefix-origin data and BGPsec router keys from a trusted cache, adding the Router Key PDU, timing parameters and version negotiation, and updating RFC 6810.

RPKI.why: The whole document defines the RPKI-Router protocol that delivers RPKI validated ROA data and router keys from caches to routers for route origin validation.
RPKI.quote: routers need a simple but reliable mechanism to receive cryptographically validated Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) [RFC6480] prefix origin data and router keys from a trusted cache.

rejected.why: BGP is the consumer of the validated data, but the document does not specify or extend BGP itself.
Router Key PDUs carry BGPsec router keys, but BGPsec path validation is not specified here; the document only delivers keys.
SSH is one optional transport option (subsystem rpki-rtr), a substrate rather than the subject.
TLS is one optional transport with certificate-identity rules, but nothing new is defined for TLS.
TCP and its authentication options (MD5, TCP-AO) are only transport substrates for the protocol.
Section 9 lists transports, but this is a minor part of the document and the main subject is the RPKI-Router protocol itself.

RFC8211.title: Adverse Actions by a Certification Authority (CA) or Repository Manager in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI)
RFC8211.summary: Informational threat analysis of how deletion, suppression, corruption, modification, revocation and injection of RPKI repository objects by a CA or repository manager can adversely affect an INR holder's resources and relying-party routing decisions, across four CA/publication-point outsourcing scenarios.

RPKI.why: The whole document analyses RPKI objects (CA certs, manifests, CRLs, ROAs, router certs) and how adverse actions affect RP validation.
RPKI.quote: analyzes actions by or against a Certification Authority (CA) or an independent repository manager in the RPKI that can adversely affect the Internet Number Resources

rejected.why: Router certificates and BGPsec_PATH validation are discussed only as one object type affected; the document is not about BGPsec itself.
Parent of RPKI, which is the more specific tag; implied.
Certificates are the substrate of the RPKI objects; the document does not specify or profile X.509.
Only mentioned as the encapsulation of signed objects.
Route origin validation outcomes are discussed, but the document concerns RPKI repository threats, not BGP operation.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as the IRR alternative.

RFC8212.title: Default External BGP (EBGP) Route Propagation Behavior without Policies
RFC8212.summary: RFC 8212 updates RFC 4271 so a BGP speaker neither imports nor exports routes on EBGP sessions unless an explicit Import or Export Policy is configured, reducing route leaks and misconfiguration impact.

BGP.why: The document modifies BGP-4 (RFC 4271) decision process and route dissemination behavior for EBGP sessions by default, which is BGP protocol policy and operations.
BGP.quote: Routes contained in an Adj-RIB-In associated with an EBGP peer SHALL NOT be considered eligible in the Decision Process if no explicit Import Policy has been applied.

rejected.why: Motivated by route leaks and improving default routing security, but the document specifies a BGP protocol behavior change rather than a security mechanism like RPKI or BGPsec; BGP tag is the more specific fit.
Not mentioned or used; the document only concerns default policy behavior.
Considered because it improves default operator safety, but the content is a normative protocol change to BGP rather than operational practice guidance.

RFC8213.title: Security of Messages Exchanged between Servers and Relay Agents
RFC8213.summary: RFC 8213 requires DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 relay agents and servers to support IPsec (ESP in transport mode with encryption) to secure relay-to-relay and relay-to-server messages, and it replaces Section 21.1 of RFC 3315.

DHCP.why: The document specifies security requirements for DHCP relay-to-server traffic and is about DHCP operation. It covers DHCPv4 and DHCPv6, and DHCP is the parent tag of DHCPv6, so the parent fits both.
DHCP.quote: For DHCPv4 [RFC2131], this specification REQUIRES relay and server implementations to support IPsec encryption of relay-to-server communication
DHCP.section: 3. Security of Messages Exchanged between Servers and Relay Agents

IPsec.why: The core content is an IPsec profile: selectors, transport mode, ESP algorithms, IKEv2 key management and security policy for DHCP relay and server traffic.
IPsec.quote: Relay agents and servers MUST use IPsec in transport mode and use Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP).
IPsec.section: 3. Security of Messages Exchanged between Servers and Relay Agents

rejected.why: The document covers both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 equally, so the parent DHCP tag is the better fit.
ESP is the mode mandated within the IPsec profile. The document does not define anything new about ESP itself.
IKEv2 with pre-shared secrets is only recommended for key management, in one row of the profile. That is not a substantial part of the document.
UDP ports 67 and 547 are named only as selectors. They are a substrate detail.
Pervasive monitoring is the motivation, but the document specifies an IPsec mechanism and not privacy considerations in general.

RFC8214.title: Virtual Private Wire Service Support in Ethernet VPN
RFC8214.summary: Specifies how EVPN is used to provide point-to-point VPWS services over MPLS/IP, using per-EVI Ethernet A-D routes, a new EVPN Layer 2 Attributes extended community, and Single-Active/All-Active multihoming without PW signaling.

EVPN.why: The document defines EVPN-VPWS: BGP route usage, a new extended community, multihoming and failure handling for point-to-point services over EVPN.
EVPN.quote: This document describes how EVPN can be used to support VPWS in MPLS/IP networks.

pseudowire.why: Section 5 compares EVPN-VPWS with LDP-signalled pseudowires and the document replaces PW signalling for P2P Ethernet services, so pseudowire readers will want it.
pseudowire.quote: EVPN for VPWS eliminates the need for the traditional way of PW signaling for P2P Ethernet services

rejected.why: BGP is the control-plane substrate; the document adds an extended community for EVPN but does not extend BGP generally.
MPLS is the data-plane transport used; the document is not about MPLS itself.
VPWS is an L2VPN service, but the more specific EVPN tag already covers it.
VXLAN is mentioned only as an alternative encapsulation, with the label set to the VNI.
LDP is mentioned only in the comparison to traditional PW signalling.

RFC8215.title: Local-Use IPv4/IPv6 Translation Prefix
RFC8215.summary: RFC 8215 reserves the IPv6 prefix 64:ff9b:1::/48 for local use by IPv4/IPv6 translation mechanisms, explaining the choice of prefix length and value and giving deployment and checksum-neutrality guidance.

IPv6 transition.why: The document is about a reserved address prefix for coexistence of multiple IPv4/IPv6 translation mechanisms, which is a generic IPv6/IPv4 transition topic not tied to one specific child technology.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document reserves 64:ff9b:1::/48 for local use within domains that enable IPv4/IPv6 translation mechanisms.

addressing.why: The document's main body is about choosing and reserving an IPv6 prefix (length, value, aggregation, routing use), which is IP address architecture and allocation.
addressing.quote: The IANA has added the following entry to the "IANA IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registry"

rejected.why: The prefix is explicitly technology-agnostic; stateful NAT64 (RFC 6146) is only cited as one example mechanism.
RFC 7915 is mentioned as an example algorithm in the checksum neutrality section, but the document does not specify or extend it.
The IANA registry entries are boilerplate-like consequences of the reservation, not the subject of the document.
