Checksum neutrality is discussed briefly as a deployment note, not as the subject of the document.
A more specific tag (IPv6 transition) fits; the parent is implied.

RFC8216.title: HTTP Live Streaming
RFC8216.summary: Specifies HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) version 7: M3U8 playlist format and tags, media segment formats, encryption, and client/server behaviour for adaptive-bitrate delivery of media streams over HTTP.

streaming.why: The whole document defines HLS, an adaptive media streaming delivery protocol with playlists, variant streams and live/VOD server and client behaviour. No specific streaming technology tag (RTSP, PPSP, IPTV) fits, so the streaming topic is used.
streaming.quote: This document describes a protocol for transferring unbounded streams of multimedia data.

media types.why: The document registers application/vnd.apple.mpegurl and defines how playlists are identified by media type and file extension. This is a modest part of the document, but readers of media type registrations would want it.
media types.quote: IANA has registered the following media type [RFC2046]:

rejected.why: HTTP is the transport substrate. The document uses HTTP but does not specify or extend HTTP itself.
The introduction mentions compatibility with HTTP caching infrastructure, but caching is not a subject of the document.
AES-128 CBC and SAMPLE-AES are used for segment encryption, but the document defines no new AES material. It only uses AES as a mechanism.
The document references H.264, AAC, AC-3 and MP3 as carried formats but does not define any codec.
Not related to the document. HLS uses its own playlist format rather than SDP.
RFC 5646 language tags are used in LANGUAGE attributes, but only as a reference. The document defines nothing new about them.

gaps.name: HTTP Live Streaming / adaptive bitrate streaming (M3U8 playlists)
gaps.why: HLS is a named streaming technology. The taxonomy has only the generic streaming topic, with no tag for HTTP-based adaptive streaming or the M3U playlist format.

RFC8217.title: Clarifications for When to Use the name-addr Production in SIP Messages
RFC8217.summary: RFC 8217 updates RFC 3261 and several SIP extension RFCs to state generically that the name-addr form must be used instead of addr-spec when the URI contains a comma, semicolon, or question mark in SIP header fields.

SIP.why: The document clarifies SIP header field grammar constraints in RFC 3261 and updates multiple SIP extension specifications (To, From, Contact, Reply-To, P-headers, Referred-By).
SIP.quote: the addr-spec form MUST NOT be used if its value would contain a comma, semicolon, or question mark.

rejected.why: The document concerns how URIs are written inside SIP header fields (name-addr vs addr-spec), not URI syntax or schemes themselves.
ABNF is only the notation used to show the grammar; the document is not about ABNF.
That tag covers Internet email message format; this is SIP header grammar.

RFC8218.title: Multipath Extension for the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol Version 2 (OLSRv2)
RFC8218.summary: Experimental extension to OLSRv2 (MP-OLSRv2) that computes multiple disjoint paths using a Multipath Dijkstra algorithm and forwards datagrams via IPv4/IPv6 source routing in MANETs, with a new SOURCE_ROUTE message TLV.

OLSR.why: The document extends OLSRv2, adding a SOURCE_ROUTE TLV, a multipath routing set and multipath calculation, so it belongs under OLSR.
OLSR.quote: This document specifies a multipath extension for the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol version 2 (OLSRv2) to discover multiple disjoint paths for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs).

rejected.why: OLSR is a child of MANET, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
HELLO messages and neighborhood discovery are used as defined in RFC 6130, but the document does not extend NHDP itself.
Load balancing and path control are mentioned as benefits, but the document is not about traffic engineering of transport networks.
Erasure coding is only mentioned as an application in the motivation, not specified here.
Multipath load balancing is related, but the document specifies source-routed disjoint paths in MANETs, not equal-cost multipath forwarding.
The IPv6 source routing header from RFC 6554 is used as a substrate, not specified or extended here.
The IANA section only registers one TLV type extension, which is boilerplate.

RFC8219.title: Benchmarking Methodology for IPv6 Transition Technologies
RFC8219.summary: RFC 8219 extends RFC 2544/5180 benchmarking methodology to IPv6 transition technologies (translation and encapsulation), defining test setups, traffic, latency/PDV tests, DNS64 performance tests, and an overload scalability metric.

benchmarking.why: The document is a benchmarking methodology: test setups, traffic, latency, PDV, throughput and scalability tests for devices under test.
benchmarking.quote: This document provides complementary guidelines for evaluating the performance of IPv6 transition technologies.

IPv6 transition.why: The subject of the benchmarks is IPv6 transition mechanisms (NAT64, 464XLAT, MAP, DS-Lite, 6rd), classified and tested by category.
IPv6 transition.quote: this document targets IPv6 transition technologies that employ encapsulation or translation mechanisms

DNS64.why: A full section defines the DNS64 resolution performance benchmark, including test setup, caching and AAAA-existence parameters, and tester requirements.
DNS64.quote: This section describes benchmarking tests dedicated to DNS64 (see [RFC6147]), used as DNS support for single-translation technologies such as NAT64.

rejected.why: NAT64 is the example single-translation technology under test, but the document benchmarks transition technologies generally and does not specify or extend NAT64.
Considered as the parent area, but the document is a device benchmarking methodology and fits the more specific benchmarking tag.
DNS appears only through DNS64 testing; the more specific DNS64 tag covers it.
The document concerns transition technologies, which the IPv6 transition tag captures more specifically than IPv6 in general.
NAT44 and NAT66 get only a brief section noting the methodology can be applied to them.
TCP connection capacity tests are referenced from RFC 3511 unmodified; TCP is not itself the subject.

RFC8220.title: Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) over Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS)
RFC8220.summary: Informational RFC specifying how VPLS PEs snoop, relay, or proxy PIM Hello and Join/Prune messages so multicast traffic is replicated only to ports with interested PIM routers or IGMP hosts.

VPLS.why: The whole document defines PE behaviour in a VPLS: ACs and PWs, split-horizon, and flooding vs. selective forwarding of multicast.
VPLS.quote: procedures and recommendations for Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) Provider Edges (PEs) to facilitate replication of multicast traffic to only certain ports

PIM.why: The document specifies PIM snooping, relay and proxying. It covers PIM-SM, PIM-SSM, PIM-DM and BIDIR-PIM state machines, Hello handling and Join/Prune processing.
PIM.quote: PEs passively listen to certain PIM control messages to build control and forwarding states while transparently flooding those messages.

IGMP.why: Section 2.8 defines how PIM snooping interacts with IGMP snooping in the same VPLS instance. This is a substantial but secondary part of the document.
IGMP.quote: IGMP snooping procedures described in RFC 4541 [IGMP-SNOOP] make sure that IP multicast traffic is only sent on the following

rejected.why: The document snoops PIM-SM Join/Prune messages but does not specify PIM-SM itself. It is a PE-side procedure and cites RFC 7761 for the protocol.
This is the parent topic. A child tag (PIM) already fits, so the parent is implied.
PWs are only the ports the PEs forward on. The document defines no pseudowire emulation.
BGP signalling of snooped state is only mentioned as an alternative in RFC 7117. The document does not address it.
PWs run over MPLS, but this is substrate only.
VPLS has its own tag. Under the taxonomy, VPLS is the more specific L2VPN service.

RFC8221.title: Cryptographic Algorithm Implementation Requirements and Usage Guidance for Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and Authentication Header (AH)
RFC8221.summary: RFC 8221 sets mandatory-to-implement and deprecation levels for the encryption, authentication and compression algorithms used with IPsec ESP and AH, replacing RFC 7321.

ESP.why: The document specifies algorithm implementation requirements and usage guidance for ESP (and AH). ESP is the most specific IPsec tag, and the tables cover ESP encryption and authentication algorithms.
ESP.quote: The goal of this document is to enable ESP and AH to benefit from cryptography that is up to date while making IPsec interoperable.

cryptography.why: The body is about the status of specific algorithms such as AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, HMAC-SHA2 and 3DES. Readers browsing algorithm requirements and deprecations would want it. No more specific algorithm tag fits, because it covers many algorithms.
cryptography.quote: This document concerns itself with the selection of cryptographic algorithms for the use of ESP and AH, specifically with the selection of mandatory-to-implement algorithms.

rejected.why: IKEv2 is only the assumed keying mechanism and the source of the IANA registry. The document does not specify or extend it.
ESP is the more specific child tag and fits better. The document is about algorithms for ESP and AH, not the IPsec architecture.
AES-CBC, AES-GCM and AES-CCM are among many algorithms listed. The document is not about AES itself.
ChaCha20-Poly1305 gets one table row and a short rationale. This is not enough to make it a subject of the document.
The compression section is a short table that keeps IPComp algorithms at MAY, with no substantive content on IPComp.
HMAC-SHA1 and HMAC-SHA2 are only entries in the authentication table, not the subject of the document.

RFC8222.title: Selecting Labels for Use with Conventional DNS and Other Resolution Systems in DNS-Based Service Discovery
RFC8222.summary: Informational memo outlining requirements for a profile for selecting DNS-SD Service Instance Name labels (Instance, Service, Domain portions) so they interoperate across conventional DNS (with IDNA2008) and other resolution systems such as mDNS.

DNS-SD.why: The whole document analyses how the three portions of DNS-SD Service Instance Names should be handled for label selection and resolution.
DNS-SD.quote: DNS-SD specifies three portions of the owner name for a DNS-SD resource record. These are the <Instance> portion, the <Service> portion, and the <Domain> portion.

IDN.why: Central concern is the interaction of IDNA2008 A-labels/U-labels and LDH rules with raw UTF-8 labels in DNS-SD names.
IDN.quote: DNS-SD implementations ought to identify the <Domain> portion of the Service Instance Name and treat it subject to IDNA2008 in case the domain is to be queried from the global DNS.

mDNS.why: mDNS is the principal alternative resolution system whose label conventions conflict with DNS/IDNA, and drives the profile requirements.
mDNS.quote: mDNS requires that labels be encoded in UTF-8 and permits a range of characters in labels that are not permitted by IDNA2008 or the LDH rule.

rejected.why: DNS is the substrate; the document is about label conventions in DNS-SD, and the more specific tags cover it.
UTF-8 labels are discussed, but the document is not about the encoding itself.
Unicode code points are mentioned only as part of the IDNA/mDNS label discussion.
The 'local.' name is mentioned only as an example of names resolved via mDNS.

RFC8223.title: Application-Aware Targeted LDP
RFC8223.summary: Defines the Targeted Application Capability (TAC) LDP capability TLV, negotiated at tLDP session initialization so responding LSRs can control acceptance of targeted LDP sessions per application and limit FEC label bindings to those applications; updates RFC 7473.

LDP.why: The document extends LDP with a new capability TLV, status code and registry for targeted LDP sessions, and updates RFC 7473. LDP is the protocol being specified.
LDP.quote: This document defines a mechanism to advertise and negotiate the Targeted Application Capability (TAC) during LDP session initialization.

rejected.why: Remote LFA is only one targeted application that uses the mechanism. The document does not specify fast reroute.
FEC 128 and FEC 129 pseudowires are only applications mapped to FEC types in a table. The document does not define pseudowire procedures.
LDP is the more specific tag, and the document is about LDP rather than MPLS in general.
BGP auto-discovery is only mentioned as a use case that triggers sessions.
RSVP-TE appears only as a tunnel type in the LDP-over-RSVP application mapping.
The IANA registry creation is boilerplate for the LDP extension, not the main subject.

RFC8224.title: Authenticated Identity Management in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC8224.summary: RFC 8224 defines the SIP Identity header field carrying a PASSporT signature so authentication and verification services can cryptographically assure the originator's identity (telephone number or SIP URI) in SIP requests, obsoleting RFC 4474.

STIR.why: The document is the core STIR SIP specification: Identity header, authentication and verification service behaviour, and PASSporT use in SIP for caller-ID authentication.
STIR.quote: This document defines a mechanism for securely identifying originators of SIP requests.

SIP.why: It extends SIP with a new Identity header field syntax, response codes (428, 436, 437, 438), and proxy/UA behaviour.
SIP.quote: defining a SIP header field for conveying a signature used for validating the identity and for conveying a reference to the credentials of the signer.

rejected.why: PASSporT is built on JWT/JWS, but this document only uses PASSporT as the signed token format, which is defined in RFC 8225.
Certificates are mentioned as a credential option, but the credential system is explicitly left to RFC 8226.
Telephone numbers and tel URIs are handled and canonicalized, but the tel URI scheme itself is not specified or extended here.
JSON is only the encoding of PASSporT objects, which is substrate.
TLS is recommended for securing the connection to the authentication service, but only as supporting guidance.
DANE is mentioned in passing as a possible credential system, not specified here.

RFC8225.title: PASSporT: Personal Assertion Token
RFC8225.summary: Defines PASSporT, a JWT/JWS-based signed token asserting the originating (and destination) identity of personal communications, with header/claims, compact form, deterministic JSON serialization, and an extension mechanism, for use by STIR.

STIR.why: PASSporT is the STIR WG token for caller-ID authentication; the document is the core STIR token specification, used by RFC 8224 for SIP.
STIR.quote: This document defines a method for creating and validating a token that cryptographically verifies an originating identity or, more generally, a URI or telephone number

JWT.why: Defines new JWT claims (orig, dest, mky), a new header parameter (ppt), and a registry, which JWT readers need.
JWT.quote: PASSporT specifically uses this token format and defines claims that convey the identity of the origination and destination of personal communications.

rejected.why: JWS/JWA are the substrate; the document profiles them for PASSporT, with JWT claims being the more specific fit.
SIP use is defined in RFC 8224; this document is explicitly signalling-protocol independent.
Only the a=fingerprint attribute is referenced for the optional mky claim; SDP is not the subject.
JSON is the encoding; the deterministic serialization rules are only a supporting detail for signatures.
Certificates are referenced via x5u for signature validation but not specified or profiled here.
Registers application/passport, but this is IANA boilerplate and not the document's main subject.

RFC8226.title: Secure Telephone Identity Credentials: Certificates
RFC8226.summary: Defines X.509 certificate extensions (TN Authorization List, JWT Claim Constraints, and an AIA access method) so certificates can assert authority over telephone numbers for STIR caller-ID authentication in SIP.

STIR.why: The document is the STIR credentials specification: it states how certificates meet the STIR requirements for the Identity header and PASSporT.
STIR.quote: This document describes the use of certificates in establishing authority over telephone numbers, as a component of a broader architecture for managing telephone numbers as identities in protocols like SIP.

X.509.why: It defines new X.509 v3 certificate extensions (id-pe-TNAuthList, id-pe-JWTClaimConstraints) and an AIA access descriptor, along with enrollment and freshness considerations.
X.509.quote: extending X.509 with a Telephony Number Authorization List certificate extension, which binds certificates to asserted authority for particular telephone numbers

rejected.why: SIP is the context in which the credentials are used, but the document specifies certificates, not SIP itself. STIR covers the SIP link.
Certificate constraints on JWT claims are defined, but JWT itself is only the PASSporT token format the constraints apply to.
ASN.1 is just the notation for the extension definitions in the appendix, not the subject of the document.
OCSP is mentioned only as one option for checking freshness, and the document makes no recommendation about it.
The application/tnauthlist registration is boilerplate in IANA Considerations and not the main subject.
The document only mandates ECDSA P-256 and RSA for certificate signatures, which does not make it about those algorithms.

RFC8227.title: MPLS-TP Shared-Ring Protection (MSRP) Mechanism for Ring Topology
RFC8227.summary: Specifies MPLS-TP Shared-Ring Protection (MSRP) for point-to-point LSPs on ring topologies, including ring tunnels, wrapping/short-wrapping/steering protection modes, interconnected rings, and the Ring Protection Switching (RPS) protocol carried in the G-ACh.

MPLS-TP.why: The document defines ring protection architecture and the RPS protocol for MPLS Transport Profile networks, so it belongs on the MPLS-TP page.
MPLS-TP.quote: This document defines the Ring Protection Switching (RPS) protocol that is used to coordinate the protection behavior of the nodes on an MPLS ring.

rejected.why: MPLS is the parent of MPLS-TP and is implied by the child tag, so it is not listed separately.
Section-layer OAM (CC packets, MEPs) is used only to detect failures. The document does not define OAM mechanisms.
The ring protection switching it describes is a survivability mechanism, not traffic engineering of LSPs.
The document does not use GMPLS control. It states that the control plane for label distribution is out of scope.

gaps.name: MPLS-TP / ring protection
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no MPLS-TP tag under MPLS, and the only related child is MPLS-TP, which is not listed. I could not tag it, so the nearest fit is the parent MPLS technology.

RFC8228.title: Guidance on Designing Label Generation Rulesets (LGRs) Supporting Variant Labels
RFC8228.summary: Informational guidance on designing Label Generation Rulesets (LGRs) with variant mappings, types and dispositions for IDN-style identifier labels, expressed in the RFC 7940 XML format.

IDN.why: The document guides design of label generation rulesets, with variant labels, used to implement IDN policies for zones. Variant label rules are the core subject, and IDN is the closest taxonomy fit.
IDN.quote: LGRs have mostly been used to define policies for implementing Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs) using IDNA2008

XML.why: Section 18 maps the variant notation to the RFC 7940 XML format (char, var, action elements). This is a substantial part of the document, though the XML schema itself is defined elsewhere.
XML.quote: The design decisions can then be expressed using the XML representation of LGRs that is defined in RFC 7940.

rejected.why: DNS is only the identifier system to which LGRs may be applied. The document specifies nothing about DNS protocol or operation.
Code points are the basis of the mappings, but the document is not about how Unicode is used in protocols.
Allocatable and blocked dispositions affect registry policy. The document is about rule design, not registry operations or protocols.
The parent is implied by IDN, and the document is not about general text internationalization.

gaps.name: Label Generation Rulesets (LGR)
gaps.why: The document is about LGR variant design, and the taxonomy has no tag for LGRs or variant labels. IDN is the nearest tag.

RFC8229.title: TCP Encapsulation of IKE and IPsec Packets
RFC8229.summary: Defines a method for carrying IKEv2 negotiation and ESP packets over a TCP connection (optionally with TLS) as a fallback when middleboxes block UDP, including framing, stream prefix, connection handling, MOBIKE interaction and performance issues.

IKE.why: The document extends how IKEv2 messages are transported, defining framing, stream prefix, NAT detection and fragmentation interaction for IKE over TCP.
IKE.quote: This document describes a method to transport Internet Key Exchange Protocol (IKE) and IPsec packets over a TCP connection

ESP.why: Defines the TCP-encapsulated ESP format, ESP/IKE demultiplexing, and recommends an anti-replay window of 1; ESP data packets are carried in the TCP stream.
ESP.quote: The ESP header is preceded by a 16-bit Length field in network byte order that specifies the length of the ESP packet within the TCP stream.

MOBIKE.why: A dedicated section and an appendix example specify how MOBIKE transitions between UDP and TCP encapsulation.
MOBIKE.quote: Implementations that implement both MOBIKE and TCP encapsulation MUST support dynamically enabling and disabling TCP encapsulation as interfaces change.

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate carrying the encapsulated packets; the document does not extend TCP itself, though it discusses TCP-in-TCP performance.
TLS is an optional wrapper discussed in Appendix A as a substrate. It does not define new TLS extensions.
NAT traversal is the motivation, and NAT detection payloads are discussed briefly, but the document is not about NAT behaviour.
ECN tunnelling is mentioned in one performance subsection and follows RFC 6040, but it is not a substantial subject.
The document is a binding of IKE/ESP over TCP, which fits loosely. The more specific IKE and ESP tags describe it better.
The parent of IKE and ESP, implied by those tags.

RFC8230.title: Using RSA Algorithms with CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Messages
RFC8230.summary: Defines COSE algorithm identifiers for RSASSA-PSS signatures and RSAES-OAEP key encryption, plus an RSA key type and its parameters, and registers them with IANA.

RSA.why: The document specifies how RSASSA-PSS, RSAES-OAEP and RSA keys are used and encoded in COSE. Readers of the RSA subject would want it.
RSA.quote: This specification defines algorithm encodings and representations enabling RSA algorithms to be used for COSE messages.

COSE.why: It extends COSE with new algorithm identifiers, a new key type (kty 3) and key parameters. This is a COSE algorithm profile.
COSE.quote: The CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) [RFC8152] specification defines cryptographic message encodings using Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR)

rejected.why: CBOR is only the encoding substrate. The document uses byte strings and arrays but defines nothing new about CBOR.
SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 appear only as hash parameters of the RSA algorithms. The document is not about the hash functions.
JWS (RFC 7515) is cited only for a trust-decision note in the Security Considerations. This document is not about JOSE.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate that registers the new values. The document is not about IANA registries in general.

RFC8231.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for Stateful PCE
RFC8231.summary: RFC 8231 specifies PCEP extensions for stateful PCE: capability advertisement, LSP state synchronization, delegation, and PCRpt/PCUpd messages with new LSP and SRP objects for controlling MPLS-TE/GMPLS LSPs.

PCE.why: The whole document extends PCEP and the PCE architecture with stateful operation, delegation, state synchronization and new messages and objects.
PCE.quote: This document describes a set of extensions to PCEP to enable stateful control of MPLS-TE and GMPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs) via PCEP.

rejected.why: LSPs are signalled with RSVP-TE and identifiers are borrowed from it, but the document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE.
MPLS-TE LSPs are the controlled objects, but the document is about the PCEP control protocol, not MPLS itself.
GMPLS is mentioned as applying equally, but GMPLS-specific PCEP extensions are in a separate document.
TLS is only recommended in Security Considerations for securing sessions.
RBNF is only the notation used for message formats.
Only the PCE capability bits for OSPF/IS-IS discovery are registered in a small section; the document is not about those protocols.
It is covered by the PCE tag, which sits under traffic engineering.

RFC8232.title: Optimizations of Label Switched Path State Synchronization Procedures for a Stateful PCE
RFC8232.summary: RFC 8232 specifies PCEP extensions that optimize LSP state synchronization between a stateful PCE and its PCCs: synchronization avoidance via LSP-DB version numbers, incremental (delta) sync, and PCE-triggered initial sync and resynchronization.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP for stateful PCE, defining new TLVs, capability flags, and error codes for state synchronization procedures between PCEs and PCCs.
PCE.quote: This document presents motivations for optimizations to the base State Synchronization procedure and specifies the required Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) extensions.

rejected.why: LSPs are the state being synchronized, but the document is about PCEP procedures, not MPLS architecture or operations.
Optical transport networks are mentioned only as a motivating example of low-bandwidth control channels; not about GMPLS.
TLS is only recommended in Security Considerations for securing PCEP sessions; boilerplate, not subject.
The PCEP YANG module is mentioned only in Manageability Considerations as a possible extension point.
The PCE tag already sits under traffic engineering, and the document concerns the PCEP protocol rather than TE in general.

RFC8233.title: Extensions to the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) to Compute Service-Aware Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC8233.summary: Extends PCEP with new METRIC types (path delay, delay variation, loss, and P2MP variants), a new BU object for link bandwidth utilization, and new objective functions so PCEs can compute service-aware LSPs.

PCE.why: The document defines new PCEP metric types, a BU object, objective functions and message format changes, which is PCEP specification work.
PCE.quote: This document describes the extension to PCEP to carry latency, delay variation, packet loss, and link bandwidth utilization as constraints for end-to-end path computation.

traffic engineering.why: Service-aware constrained path computation for TE LSPs using TED performance and bandwidth data is a traffic engineering subject, though PCE is the more specific tag.
traffic engineering.quote: This section defines the following types for the METRIC object to be used for the P2MP TE LSPs.

rejected.why: OSPF TE metric extensions are only the source of the TED data; the document doesn't extend OSPF.
IS-IS TE metric extensions are only referenced as the source of link performance data, and nothing in IS-IS is specified here.
The LSPs are MPLS TE LSPs, but the document is about computing paths via PCEP, not MPLS mechanisms.
RSVP-TE appears only in defining reserved bandwidth utilization, and it is not specified or extended.
The document uses delay, loss and variation metrics measured elsewhere (RFC 6374 and the IGP extensions) as constraints, and defines no measurement method.
RBNF is only the notation used for message formats.

RFC8234.title: Updates to MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) Linear Protection in Automatic Protection Switching (APS) Mode
RFC8234.summary: RFC 8234 updates the MPLS-TP linear protection APS mode (RFC 7271) with PSC Control Logic initialization rules, a modified remote state transition table, and clarified state transition table lookup behavior.

MPLS-TP.why: The document updates MPLS-TP linear protection in APS mode (RFC 7271), specifying initialization behavior and state machine changes. MPLS-TP is the technology it is about.
MPLS-TP.quote: The updates provide rules related to initialization of the PSC Control Logic (in which the state machine resides) when operating in APS mode.

rejected.why: Protection switching is related to transport network survivability, but the document does not address OAM mechanisms; it specifies PSC state machine behavior.
Not mentioned or discussed; the document concerns MPLS-TP linear protection state machines only.
The parent of MPLS-TP is implied; the more specific MPLS-TP tag is the right choice.
Protection switching is not traffic engineering of paths; the document is solely about the PSC state machine initialization and lookup.

gaps.name: MPLS-TP linear protection / Automatic Protection Switching (APS) / PSC
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an MPLS-TP tag but no dedicated tag for transport-network protection switching; the MPLS-TP tag is the closest fit.

RFC8235.title: Schnorr Non-interactive Zero-Knowledge Proof
RFC8235.summary: Specifies the Schnorr non-interactive zero-knowledge proof of knowledge of a discrete logarithm (Fiat-Shamir transformed Schnorr identification) over finite fields and elliptic curves.

cryptography.why: The document defines a cryptographic zero-knowledge proof primitive. No more specific cryptography tag fits the technique itself, so the parent topic is used.
cryptography.quote: This document specifies the Schnorr NIZK proof in both the finite field and the elliptic curve settings.

rejected.why: EC is only one of two settings (alongside finite field groups). The document is about the proof scheme, not elliptic-curve cryptography itself.
J-PAKE and YAK are mentioned only as applications that use the proof. The document does not specify a PAKE.
ECDSA and DSA are referenced only for group parameter settings.
SHA-2 and SHA-3 hash functions are only suggested as options for H.
J-PAKE appears only as an application example in Section 5. The document does not specify or analyse it.
The Schnorr identification scheme is the basis of the proof, but the document is about the NIZK primitive and not about authenticating users across protocols.

gaps.name: zero-knowledge proofs / Schnorr NIZK
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for zero-knowledge proofs or discrete-log proof-of-knowledge primitives. This is the document's main subject, so the generic cryptography topic is the closest fit.

RFC8236.title: J-PAKE: Password-Authenticated Key Exchange by Juggling
RFC8236.summary: Specifies J-PAKE, a password-authenticated key exchange protocol using Schnorr NIZK proofs in finite-field and elliptic-curve settings, with a three-pass variant and key confirmation methods.

J-PAKE.why: The whole document specifies the J-PAKE protocol, its two-round and three-pass forms, and key confirmation.
J-PAKE.quote: This document specifies a Password-Authenticated Key Exchange by Juggling (J-PAKE) protocol.

rejected.why: SRP is mentioned only as a competing PAKE for comparison; the document is not about it.
SPAKE2 is mentioned only in comparison; not specified or analysed here.
EC setting is a variant of J-PAKE, but the document is about the PAKE protocol, not EC cryptography itself.
HMAC is only an example MAC for key confirmation.
Parent of J-PAKE, implied by the more specific tag.

gaps.name: Schnorr non-interactive zero-knowledge proof
gaps.why: J-PAKE is built on Schnorr NIZK proofs (RFC 8235), but the taxonomy has no tag for zero-knowledge proofs; it is a building block here rather than the subject.

RFC8237.title: MPLS Label Switched Path (LSP) Pseudowire (PW) Status Refresh Reduction for Static PWs
RFC8237.summary: Defines a G-ACh-based LSP-level PW status refresh reduction protocol for static MPLS pseudowires, with a state machine, message encoding, notification and PW configuration messages, and provisioning verification.

pseudowire.why: The whole document specifies a status signalling extension for static pseudowires over MPLS, so the pseudowire tag is the best fit.
pseudowire.quote: This document describes a method for generating an aggregated pseudowire (PW) status message transmitted for a statically configured PW on a Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switched Path (LSP)

rejected.why: MPLS LSPs and the G-ACh are the substrate, and the document is about pseudowire status rather than MPLS itself. The pseudowire tag is the more specific child.
Static PWs are used, and RFC 8077 is only referenced for static label assignment. No LDP signalling is specified.
The MPLS-TP Tunnel ID is only reused as an identifier in a sub-TLV, and the document does not address MPLS-TP itself.
The G-ACh channel and the keepalive-like session have an OAM flavour, but the document is about PW status refresh reduction and provisioning verification. The pseudowire tag already covers that.
CRC-16 is used only as a suggested way to generate a Session ID, and the checksum is an ordinary one's-complement sum.

RFC8238.title: Data Center Benchmarking Terminology
RFC8238.summary: Defines terminology and measurement definitions (latency, jitter, line rate, buffer size, incast, goodput) for benchmarking data center switches and routers, as a prerequisite to the RFC 8239 methodology.

benchmarking.why: The whole document defines benchmarking terminology and metrics for network devices under test, which is the benchmarking subject.
benchmarking.quote: establish definitions and describe measurement techniques for data center benchmarking, as well as to introduce new terminology applicable to performance evaluations of data center network equipment

rejected.why: Benchmarking is the more specific child-like fit for lab device testing; jitter/PDV references are incidental.
That tag covers routing and address resolution at data-centre scale; this document is about benchmarking devices, not data center routing.
TCP appears only in the goodput definition and example as the traffic type, not as a subject.
Ethernet line rate and clock tolerance are used for calculations, but the document is not about IP over Ethernet.
Buffer sizing is defined for measurement; bufferbloat is mentioned only in passing and no queue management is specified.

RFC8239.title: Data Center Benchmarking Methodology
RFC8239.summary: RFC 8239 specifies benchmarking test methodologies (line-rate, buffer, microburst, head-of-line blocking, incast) for physical data center network switches, extending earlier BMWG benchmarking RFCs.

benchmarking.why: The whole document defines benchmarking methodologies for devices under test, with objectives, procedures and reporting formats, extending RFC 2544/2889/3918.
benchmarking.quote: The purpose of this informational document is to establish test and evaluation methodology and measurement techniques for physical network equipment in the data center.

rejected.why: That tag covers routing and address resolution at data-centre scale. This document benchmarks switch hardware and does not address data center routing or address resolution.
TCP traffic is used only as stateful load in the incast test. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
The more specific benchmarking tag covers lab device testing. Performance measurement is mainly about active and passive network metrics.
The tests create congestion to measure buffers and loss. They do not address congestion control mechanisms.
DSCP/CoS values are varied only as test parameters for buffer measurement, not as the subject.

RFC8240.title: Report from the Internet of Things Software Update (IoTSU) Workshop 2016
RFC8240.summary: IAB workshop report summarizing discussions on requirements, challenges, and next steps for secure software/firmware updates on constrained IoT devices.

firmware update.why: The whole report is about software/firmware update requirements, authorization, end-of-support and distribution for constrained IoT devices.
firmware update.quote: The main goal of the workshop was to foster a discussion on requirements, challenges, and solutions for bringing software and firmware updates to IoT devices.

workshop reports.why: It is an IAB workshop report, so it belongs on the workshop reports page.
workshop reports.quote: This document provides a summary of the Internet of Things Software Update (IoTSU) Workshop

rejected.why: The firmware update tag is the more specific child; the parent is implied.
Hash-based signatures for updates get only a brief mention in Miscellaneous Points, not a substantial part of the report.
Merkle tree signatures are mentioned only briefly with size concerns; not a substantial subject of the report.
RFC 4108 is cited as prior work on CMS-protected firmware, but CMS is not the report's subject.
Mentioned as prior work on posture assessment of compromised devices in one bullet; not substantial.
The RTC and Roughtime discussion is a single requirements bullet, not a main subject.
Only mentioned in passing in the gateway discussion.

RFC8241.title: Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) Security-Related Requirements
RFC8241.summary: RFC 8241 specifies security-related requirements for the I2RS protocol: peer identity and authentication, priority and secondary identifiers, secure versus constrained non-secure transport, key management, integrity, traceability, and role-based access control.

I2RS.why: The whole document defines security requirements (SEC-REQ-01 to 22) for the I2RS protocol, its priority mechanism, secondary identifier and non-secure read-only transport.
I2RS.quote: This document presents security-related requirements for the Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) protocol

rejected.why: TLS, DTLS and SSH are the secure transports I2RS reuses; the document defines nothing new about them.
NETCONF is only a candidate management protocol over a secure transport; no NETCONF-specific content is specified.
RESTCONF is listed in the table of candidate management protocols but not specified or extended here.
Diameter and RADIUS over TLS are an optional identity distribution mechanism, mentioned only briefly.
Key management requirements are a small part (SEC-REQ-12 and the BCP 107 discussion), not the main subject.
ForCES and IPFIX appear only in the transport-extension table as candidate protocols.

gaps.name: I2RS (Interface to the Routing System)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an I2RS tag, but it appears only under network management and the document's security requirements are specific to it. The I2RS tag is used as the fit, so no real gap remains.

RFC8242.title: Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) Ephemeral State Requirements
RFC8242.summary: RFC 8242 sets out detailed requirements for ephemeral state in the I2RS protocol, covering persistence, constraints, YANG/NETCONF/RESTCONF features, client priority conflict resolution, multi-message transactions and pub/sub for ephemeral state.

I2RS.why: The whole document specifies requirements for the Interface to the Routing System protocol's ephemeral state, client priority and conflict handling.
I2RS.quote: This document describes, in detail, requirements for ephemeral state for those implementing the I2RS protocol.

YANG.why: Requires YANG additions to mark ephemeral nodes and define ephemeral-only modules (Ephemeral-REQ-06, REQ-08).
YANG.quote: there MUST be a way to indicate that YANG schema nodes represent ephemeral state.

NETCONF.why: Specifies needed NETCONF changes for ephemeral state and write-conflict notification, with RESTCONF parallels in Section 6.
NETCONF.quote: The changes to NETCONF must include:

rejected.why: Covered only alongside NETCONF as a short parallel requirement and entity-tag explanation; NETCONF and YANG tags suffice, though RESTCONF is a plausible secondary.
AAA is mentioned only as a way priority may be distributed; the document leaves the mechanism unspecified.
Only referenced as an example of AAA protocol that must use secure transport.
Only referenced as an example AAA protocol.
BGP Adj-RIB-In is only an example of fast-changing operational state used as a constraint.
MPLS LSP-ID is only an example of short-lived operational state.

RFC8243.title: Alternatives for Multilevel Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL)
RFC8243.summary: Informational RFC that enumerates and compares alternatives (unique vs. aggregated nicknames, area addresses, tree building, RPF checks, scoping) for extending TRILL to multilevel IS-IS operation for scalability.

TRILL.why: The whole document examines design alternatives for multilevel TRILL: nickname allocation, distribution trees, RPF checks, border RBridges and coexistence with old TRILL switches.
TRILL.quote: extending TRILL to multiple levels has challenges that are not addressed by the already-existing capabilities of IS-IS

rejected.why: IS-IS is the routing protocol TRILL is built on and its multilevel machinery is used, but the document is about extending TRILL, not specifying or profiling IS-IS.
Multi-destination distribution trees are discussed at the TRILL layer, not IP multicast routing.
mDNS, DHCP and NetBIOS are mentioned only as examples of broadcast-based protocols in Section 4.2.
TRILL is a link-layer bridging technology, but the document does not address IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
The document does discuss routing scalability, but TRILL is the more specific fit and no separate routing-architecture subject is addressed.

RFC8244.title: Special-Use Domain Names Problem Statement
RFC8244.summary: RFC 8244 enumerates the problems with the RFC 6761 process for registering Special-Use Domain Names, and reviews existing practice and the history of domain name resolution.

special-use domain names.why: The whole document is a problem statement about the Special-Use Domain Names registry and the RFC 6761 process, covering names like .local, .onion, .home and ipv4only.arpa.
special-use domain names.quote: The policy defined in RFC 6761 for IANA registrations in the "Special-Use Domain Names" registry has been shown, through experience, to present challenges

rejected.why: Discussed only as one case study (RFC 7686) in Section 4.2.2; the document is not about .onion itself.
mDNS and .local are mentioned as an example of a special-use name, but the document does not specify or analyse mDNS.
DNS is the namespace context, but the document is about the registry and process for special names, not DNS protocol or operations.
The IANA registry is the subject, but it is covered by the more specific special-use domain names tag; the document has no IANA actions.
DNSSEC appears as one open issue (problem 21) in a long list, not a substantial part of the document.
Parent of the chosen tag, so it is implied.

RFC8245.title: Rules for Designing Protocols Using the Generalized Packet/Message Format from RFC 5444
RFC8245.summary: RFC 8245 updates RFC 5444 by giving mandatory rules and recommendations for how the packet/message multiplexer operates and how MANET protocols (NHDP, OLSRv2 and others) should use the generalized packet/message format with TLVs and Address Blocks.

MANET.why: The document governs the design of MANET routing protocols that use the RFC 5444 packet/message format, including NHDP and OLSRv2 extensibility. No child tag fits the format itself, so the MANET parent is the right choice.
MANET.quote: This document updates RFC 5444 by providing rules and recommendations for how the multiplexer operates and how protocols can use the packet/message format.

rejected.why: NHDP is used throughout as an example, but the document does not specify or extend it.
OLSRv2 is cited as an example of an extension, but the document is not about OLSR.
The MANET UDP port is only the substrate that RFC 5498 assigns. The document defines nothing new about UDP.
The IANA section only updates Expert Review guidance for the MANET registries. That is boilerplate and not the main subject.
The document is about the MANET packet format, not about routing in general. The MANET tag is more specific.

gaps.name: RFC 5444 generalized MANET packet/message format (TLVs, Address Blocks)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for this format, which is the document's real subject. The MANET parent is the closest fit.

RFC8246.title: HTTP Immutable Responses
RFC8246.summary: Defines the "immutable" Cache-Control extension, letting servers signal that a response won't change during its freshness lifetime so clients and proxies can skip conditional revalidation.

HTTP caching.why: The document specifies a new HTTP cache directive and its client and proxy behaviour, which is squarely HTTP caching.
HTTP caching.quote: the immutable Cache-Control extension indicates that the origin server will not update the representation of that resource during the freshness lifetime of the response.

rejected.why: HTTP caching is the more specific child tag and fits; the parent is implied.
The security considerations discuss cache poisoning mitigation, but that is boilerplate-level and not the document's subject.
The directive registration is routine IANA Considerations boilerplate, not the document's subject.

RFC8247.title: Algorithm Implementation Requirements and Usage Guidance for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC8247.summary: RFC 8247 defines mandatory-to-implement cryptographic algorithms (encryption, PRF, integrity, DH groups, authentication methods, RSA key lengths, digital signature hashes) and IoT guidance for IKEv2, obsoleting RFC 4307 and updating RFC 7296.

IKE.why: The whole document specifies which algorithms IKEv2 implementations must, should or must not support, updating RFC 7296 and obsoleting RFC 4307.
IKE.quote: defining the current algorithm implementation requirements and usage guidance for IKEv2

cryptography.why: Much of the body is algorithm-level guidance: ciphers, PRFs, integrity algorithms, DH groups, RSA key lengths and signature hashes. It is tagged at the topic level because no single algorithm tag fits.
cryptography.quote: There are several Modular Exponential (MODP) groups and several Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) groups that are defined for use in IKEv2.

rejected.why: IKE is a child of IPsec and is the more specific fit. The document explicitly excludes ESP/AH algorithms.
Section 4 gives IoT-specific algorithm notes, but this is a secondary aspect of an IKEv2 algorithm document, not a subject in its own right.
AES-CBC, AES-GCM and AES-CCM are listed in tables as algorithm choices. The document is not about AES itself.
RSA key length recommendations are one small subsection (3.1.1) and not the main subject.
ENCR_CHACHA20_POLY1305 appears only as a table entry, not as a subject of the document.
ECDSA appears only as authentication method table entries.

RFC8248.title: Security Automation and Continuous Monitoring (SACM) Requirements
RFC8248.summary: RFC 8248 defines the scope and requirements for the SACM (Security Automation and Continuous Monitoring) architecture, information model, data models, operations and transfer protocols, based on the RFC 7632 endpoint posture assessment use cases.

SACM.why: The whole document enumerates requirements (G-, ARCH-, IM-, DM-, OP-, T-) for SACM, so it belongs on the SACM page.
SACM.quote: This document defines the scope and set of requirements for the Security Automation and Continuous Monitoring (SACM) architecture, data model, and transfer protocols.

rejected.why: NEA, PT-TLS and PT-EAP are cited only as examples of existing posture transports (T-001) and in the security section. The document does not specify or extend them.
ARCH-009 and OP-001 require timestamps and synchronized time, but this is a minor requirement and does not make the RFC about time synchronization.
The privacy considerations section is a short boilerplate-style discussion and references RFC 6973. It is not a main subject of the document.
Mentioned only through PT-TLS as an example transport, which is a substrate rather than the subject.
Role-based and context-based authorization requirements appear, but they are only a few of the many requirements and are not the subject of the RFC.

RFC8249.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): MTU Negotiation
RFC8249.summary: RFC 8249 updates the TRILL campus-wide MTU feature by defining a link-wide MTU size (Lz) advertised via a new APPsub-TLV, a binary-search algorithm for testing link MTU with MTU-probes/acks, and Sz refresh and dampening rules.

TRILL.why: The whole document extends and updates the TRILL base protocol, its adjacency and IS-IS use (RFC 6325, 7177, 7780), specifying MTU negotiation and testing between RBridges.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies recommended updates to that MTU feature to take advantage, for appropriate link-local packets, of link-local MTUs that exceed the TRILL campus MTU.

rejected.why: TRILL IS-IS PDUs (LSPs, CSNPs, PSNPs) and an IS-IS APPsub-TLV are used, but IS-IS itself is not specified or extended; the document is about TRILL's use of it.
Concerns link MTU testing between adjacent RBridges at the link layer, not IP path MTU discovery.
The only IANA content is a single APPsub-TLV type assignment, which is boilerplate.
The document is about TRILL link MTU negotiation, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
The document is about a specific protocol's MTU mechanism, not general routing architecture.

gaps.name: TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a TRILL tag only as a routing-subtree entry that I used with the id 'TRILL', but I could not confirm an exact id; the closest listed id is 'TRILL' under routing. Also no IS-IS-specific MTU/link-state tag exists beyond IS-IS.

RFC8250.title: IPv6 Performance and Diagnostic Metrics (PDM) Destination Option
RFC8250.summary: Specifies the IPv6 Performance and Diagnostic Metrics (PDM) destination option, carrying packet sequence numbers and scaled delta timestamps to measure round-trip and server delay without time synchronization.

IPv6.why: The document defines a new IPv6 Destination Options header option (type 0x0F), its layout, placement and ESP interaction. It extends IPv6 itself.
IPv6.quote: This document specifies the Performance and Diagnostic Metrics (PDM) destination option.

performance measurement.why: The purpose is measuring round-trip delay and server delay for performance diagnosis. This falls under performance measurement metrics and methods.
performance measurement.quote: measurements based on optional sequence numbers and timing may be embedded in each packet.

rejected.why: ESP header placement is discussed in one short section, but the document does not specify or extend IPsec.
Only covers where PDM sits relative to ESP in transport and tunnel modes; ESP is not the subject.
TCP appears only in the example flows and as one of the transports PDM can accompany; the document does not extend or analyse TCP.
DTN is mentioned only to motivate the wide time-scaling range.
PDM is a performance and diagnostic mechanism, but the performance measurement tag fits more specifically.
The only IANA content is the boilerplate registration of the option type.

RFC8251.title: Updates to the Opus Audio Codec
RFC8251.summary: RFC 8251 updates the normative reference decoder of the Opus audio codec (RFC 6716) with patches for security and quality bugs, and supplies new test vectors.

Opus.why: The whole document patches the Opus decoder (SILK and CELT parts) and updates its test vectors, so it belongs on the Opus page.
Opus.quote: This document addresses minor issues that were found in the specification of the Opus audio codec in RFC 6716.

rejected.why: Opus is the more specific child tag, so the parent is implied.
RTP is mentioned only to say the packet-parsing issue is not a problem for it. The document does not address RTP.
Ogg is mentioned only as an example file decoder context, not as a subject of the document.
The document does not define or change any payload format.

RFC8252.title: OAuth 2.0 for Native Apps
RFC8252.summary: BCP requiring native apps to use external user-agents (the browser) for OAuth 2.0 authorization requests, specifying redirect URI options (private-use scheme, claimed https, loopback), PKCE use, and security considerations.

OAuth.why: The whole document is a best practice for applying the OAuth 2.0 authorization framework to native apps, updating RFC 6749 usage, including redirect handling, PKCE, and client registration.
OAuth.quote: OAuth 2.0 authorization requests from native apps should only be made through external user-agents, primarily the user's browser.

rejected.why: Private-use URI schemes and redirect URIs are used as the mechanism, but the document does not define URI syntax or schemes; they are the means for OAuth redirects.
The browser and http/https redirects are the substrate; the document says nothing new about HTTP itself.
Only mentioned to note that loopback http redirects do not use TLS.
The security concerns are specific to OAuth native app flows, so OAuth is the more specific fit.
OAuth is the specific technology tag that covers this and sits under security, so the generic topic is not needed.

RFC8253.title: PCEPS: Usage of TLS to Provide a Secure Transport for the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP)
RFC8253.summary: RFC 8253 defines PCEPS, securing PCEP sessions with TLS via a new StartTLS message, TLS profile and peer authentication rules, and updates RFC 5440's initialization procedures.

PCE.why: The document specifies a new PCEP message (StartTLS), new error codes, and updates PCEP initialization; readers of PCE/PCEP would need it.
PCE.quote: This document describes PCEPS -- the usage of Transport Layer Security (TLS) to provide a secure transport for PCEP.

TLS.why: A substantial part profiles TLS for PCEP: mandatory ciphersuites, mutual certificate authentication, fingerprints, and peer identity checks.
TLS.quote: Support for TLS v1.2 [RFC5246] or later is REQUIRED.

rejected.why: Section 4.1 describes DANE applicability only as an optional peer verification method; it is a small part and not the document's subject.
X.509 certificates are used for peer authentication but the document defines no certificate profile of its own.
TCP is the substrate and only mentioned for TCP-AO in Security Considerations.
The document does bind PCEP to TLS, but the TLS tag is more specific and fits; the topic tag is not needed alongside it.
PCE is not in the taxonomy as a tag under traffic engineering here... PCE is, but the parent is implied and not separately chosen.
Revocation checking is only mentioned as a SHOULD in passing.

RFC8254.title: Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace Registration Transition
RFC8254.summary: RFC 8254 transitions URN namespace registration to the RFC 8141 model, obsoletes RFC 3044 (ISSN) and RFC 3187 (ISBN) as Historic, and gives IANA guidance on the ISBN, ISSN, NBN and other existing URN namespace registrations.

URN.why: The whole document concerns URN namespace registrations (ISBN, ISSN, NBN and others) and the transition to the RFC 8141 registration model, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: This document clarifies the status of relevant older RFCs and confirms and documents advice to IANA about selected existing registrations.

rejected.why: IANA is told how to maintain the URN Namespaces registry. That is registry housekeeping for one namespace family, not guidance on IANA registries in general, so the URN tag covers it.
The document changes how registration status is handled and which RFCs are Historic. That follows from the URN registration model and is not an IETF process document.
URN is the more specific child tag, and the document is about URN namespaces rather than URIs in general.

RFC8255.title: Multiple Language Content Type
RFC8255.summary: Defines the 'multipart/multilingual' MIME content type, plus the Content-Translation-Type header field, so one email can carry multiple language versions selected by the client using language tags.

MIME.why: The document defines a new MIME multipart subtype with its body structure, part ordering and selection rules, and a new MIME header field.
MIME.quote: This document defines the 'multipart/multilingual' content type, which is an addition to the Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) standard

media types.why: It registers a new media type using the RFC 6838 template. It also creates a registry for Content-Translation-Type values. Readers of media type registrations would want it.
media types.quote: The 'multipart/multilingual' Media Type has been registered with IANA.

language tags.why: Language tags in Content-Language identify each part. The document also recommends RFC 4647 matching for selection, and uses 'zxx' for the language-independent part.
language tags.quote: The Content-Language MUST comply with RFC 3282 [RFC3282] (which defines the Content-Language field) and BCP 47 [RFC5646]

rejected.why: MIME is the more specific home for this content type. The email parent is implied.
It touches Subject and From handling within parts, but it does not specify the Internet message format itself.
The document is about selecting among language versions, not text encoding. language tags is the more specific fit.
UTF-8 is only recommended for the preface part. It is not what the document is about.
message/global is only an optional part type. The document does not specify email address internationalization.
ABNF is used only to write the header field syntax. It is not a subject of the document.

RFC8256.title: Requirements for Hitless MPLS Path Segment Monitoring
RFC8256.summary: Informational requirements document analysing drawbacks of SPME-based segment monitoring in MPLS-TP and specifying requirements for a new hitless, on-demand path segment monitoring (HPSM) OAM tool.

MPLS-TP.why: The document analyses MPLS-TP OAM segment monitoring (SPME) and states requirements for a new MPLS-TP OAM tool, so MPLS-TP readers would look for it.
MPLS-TP.quote: provides requirements to guide the development of new OAM tools to support Hitless Path Segment Monitoring (HPSM)

OAM.why: The subject is OAM capability: on-demand segment monitoring, fault localization, packet loss and delay measurement requirements. OAM is a topic tag and no chosen technology tag sits under it.
OAM.quote: One of the most important Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) capabilities for transport-network operation is fault localization.

rejected.why: MPLS-TP is the more specific child that fits; the general MPLS parent is implied.
Packet loss and delay measurement are required functions (M12), but only as one supported capability of HPSM, not the main subject.
Manageability is one requirement (4.8), but the document is about OAM, not management architectures.
Protection and make-before-break are mentioned only to explain HPSM behaviour under faults.

gaps.name: Hitless Path Segment Monitoring (HPSM) / SPME
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for MPLS OAM segment monitoring or tandem connection monitoring. OAM and MPLS-TP cover it only broadly.

RFC8257.title: Data Center TCP (DCTCP): TCP Congestion Control for Data Centers
RFC8257.summary: Informational RFC documenting DCTCP, a TCP congestion control scheme for data centers that extends ECN processing to estimate the fraction of marked bytes and scale the congestion window proportionally, with deployment and known-issue discussion.

DCTCP.why: The document specifies the DCTCP algorithm: receiver ECE echoing, sender alpha estimation, cwnd reduction, implementation and deployment issues.
DCTCP.quote: Data Center TCP (DCTCP) changes traditional ECN processing by estimating the fraction of bytes that encounter congestion rather than simply detecting that some congestion has occurred.

rejected.why: DCTCP modifies how ECN feedback is processed, but ECN itself (RFC 3168) is the mechanism it builds on. DCTCP is the specific subject and sits as a sibling under congestion control.
DCTCP is a TCP congestion control modification, but the more specific DCTCP tag covers it; TCP is the substrate.
AQM and RED marking are mentioned only as switch-side deployment context, not specified here.
Implied as a parent of DCTCP, so it is not listed separately.
DSCP is mentioned only once as a way to segregate DCTCP traffic in a deployment example.
The data-center setting is context for the congestion control scheme, not about routing or address resolution at data-centre scale.

RFC8258.title: Generalized SCSI: A Generic Structure for Interface Switching Capability Descriptor (ISCD) Switching Capability Specific Information (SCSI)
RFC8258.summary: Defines a generic TLV-based structure (Generalized SCSI) for the Switching Capability Specific Information field of GMPLS Interface Switching Capability Descriptors carried in OSPF/IS-IS, and creates an IANA registry for shared SCSI-TLV types.

GMPLS.why: The document specifies a generic format for the GMPLS ISCD Switching Capability Specific Information field used in GMPLS routing extensions, so GMPLS readers would look for it.
GMPLS.quote: This "Generalized SCSI" can be used with routing protocols that define GMPLS ISCDs and any specific technology.

rejected.why: OSPF is only one of the routing protocols carrying the ISCD; the document defines no OSPF-specific behaviour.
IS-IS is likewise only a carrier of the ISCD; nothing IS-IS specific is defined.
The IANA registry creation is boilerplate-level in an IANA Considerations section, not the main subject.
TE link advertisements are context, but the document is about the GMPLS ISCD format, which GMPLS covers more specifically.

RFC8259.title: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format
RFC8259.summary: RFC 8259 is the Internet Standard specification of the JSON text-based data interchange format, defining its grammar, values, strings, UTF-8 requirement, parser and generator behaviour, and the application/json media type.

JSON.why: The whole document specifies the JSON format: grammar, values, objects, arrays, numbers, strings, parsers and generators.
JSON.quote: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a text format for the serialization of structured data.

rejected.why: The application/json registration is in IANA Considerations boilerplate; the body is about the JSON format, not media type registry rules.
UTF-8 is required for interchange (Section 8.1), but only as the encoding JSON relies on; the document defines nothing new about UTF-8.
Strings are Unicode, but Unicode is a substrate; the document does not address Unicode usage in its own right beyond JSON string issues.
The grammar is written in ABNF, but ABNF is only the notation used, not the subject.
Character encoding and string comparison issues are specific to JSON and covered by the JSON tag.

RFC8260.title: Stream Schedulers and User Message Interleaving for the Stream Control Transmission Protocol
RFC8260.summary: Defines the SCTP I-DATA chunk and I-FORWARD-TSN chunk for interleaving user messages across streams, plus several sender-side stream schedulers and socket API extensions.

SCTP.why: The document extends SCTP with the I-DATA and I-FORWARD-TSN chunks, negotiation procedures, and stream schedulers.
SCTP.quote: This document adds a new chunk to SCTP for carrying payload data. This allows a sender to interleave different user messages

sockets API.why: A substantial section defines new socket options (SCTP_INTERLEAVING_SUPPORTED, SCTP_STREAM_SCHEDULER, SCTP_STREAM_SCHEDULER_VALUE) and notifications for the SCTP sockets API.
sockets API.quote: This section describes how the socket API defined in [RFC6458] is extended to allow applications to use the extension described in this document.

rejected.why: WebRTC data channels motivate the work and require the WFQ scheduler, but the document does not specify WebRTC itself.
Congestion control is only mentioned as something that still applies to I-DATA; the document does not address it.
The stream schedulers apportion capacity among streams within one association. They are not a QoS architecture or signalling mechanism.
SIP is mentioned only as historical motivation for SCTP message fragmentation.

RFC8261.title: Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) Encapsulation of SCTP Packets
RFC8261.summary: RFC 8261 specifies how SCTP packets are encapsulated over DTLS, including DTLS and SCTP restrictions (single-homed associations, no compression, PMTU discovery without ICMP) and applicability of SCTP extensions, as used for WebRTC data channels.

SCTP.why: The document defines SCTP usage restrictions and extension applicability when carried over DTLS, so SCTP readers need it.
SCTP.quote: This document specifies how SCTP is used on top of the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol.

DTLS.why: It sets requirements on the DTLS layer (no compression, larger-than-MTU messages, PMTUD, DSCP/ECN passthrough) for carrying SCTP.
DTLS.quote: The DTLS implementation MUST support DTLS 1.0 [RFC4347] and SHOULD support the most recently published version of DTLS

transport mapping.why: The core of the document is a binding of one transport protocol over another (SCTP over DTLS), which is what this topic covers.
transport mapping.quote: When an SCTP packet is provided to the DTLS layer, the complete SCTP packet, consisting of the SCTP common header and a number of SCTP chunks

rejected.why: WebRTC data channels are the motivating use case, but the document specifies only the SCTP/DTLS encapsulation, not WebRTC itself.
PMTUD requirements are included as part of the encapsulation, but the document does not specify PMTUD itself; it only references RFC 4821.
ICE/UDP is only the substrate below DTLS and is not specified or extended here.
ECN is mentioned only as a pass-through requirement for the DTLS layer, which is too minor to tag.
UDP is only the lower-layer substrate and is not the subject of the document.

RFC8262.title: Content-ID Header Field in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC8262.summary: Defines the Content-ID header field for SIP so a Content-ID URL can reference a complete message-body (not just a multipart body part), and updates RFC 5368, 5621 and 6442 accordingly.

SIP.why: The document defines and registers a new SIP header field, with UA and proxy procedures, and updates other SIP specifications (RFC 5368, 5621, 6442).
SIP.quote: This document specifies the Content-ID header field for usage in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP).

rejected.why: MIME Content-ID and multipart bodies are the background. The document defines a SIP header field and does not extend MIME.
The cid: URL is specified in RFC 2392. This document only extends what it may reference within SIP.
RFC 6442 location conveyance is only an example and is updated by one clarifying sentence.
SDP is mentioned only in passing, as an example of something inside a body part that can contain a Content-ID URL.
The XML bodies (PIDF, resource-lists) appear only as example payloads.
MIME types appear only in examples. No media type is registered.

RFC8263.title: Group Domain of Interpretation (GDOI) GROUPKEY-PUSH Acknowledgement Message
RFC8263.summary: RFC 8263 extends GDOI by letting a GCKS request, and group members return, an authenticated acknowledgement message for GROUPKEY-PUSH rekey messages, defining the KEK_ACK_REQUESTED attribute, ack key derivation and GCKS/GM operations.

GDOI.why: The document extends the GDOI group key management protocol with a GROUPKEY-PUSH acknowledgement message, new KEK attribute and exchange type.
GDOI.quote: This memo introduces a method by which a GM returns an Acknowledgement Message to the GCKS.

rejected.why: GDOI is used to distribute IPsec SAs, but the document is about the group rekey acknowledgement, not IPsec architecture.
PRF-HMAC-SHA-256/512 is only the mechanism used to build the ack hash and key, not the subject.
ISAKMP framing is reused as substrate; the document does not specify or extend IKE.
SHA-256/512 appear only as PRF choices inside HMAC.
IANA registry additions are boilerplate-type content, not the document's subject.
GROUPKEY-PUSH may be multicast, but the document does not address multicast routing or deployment.

RFC8264.title: PRECIS Framework: Preparation, Enforcement, and Comparison of Internationalized Strings in Application Protocols
RFC8264.summary: RFC 8264 defines the PRECIS framework, which gives application protocols string classes (IdentifierClass, FreeformClass), profile rules and a derived-property algorithm for preparing, enforcing and comparing internationalized Unicode strings, replacing Stringprep.

PRECIS.why: The document is the PRECIS framework itself: it defines the string classes, profile rules, order of operations and code point categories, so PRECIS is the technology it specifies.
PRECIS.quote: This document defines a framework enabling application protocols to perform the preparation, enforcement, and comparison of internationalized strings ("PRECIS")

rejected.why: IDNA2008 is the model and source of several code point categories, but the document is not about domain names. It explicitly addresses application protocols other than DNS.

PRECIS is built on Unicode code point properties, but PRECIS is the more specific tag for this framework. Unicode is a dependency rather than the subject. The only candidates listed are Unicode and PRECIS, and PRECIS is the child.
The document says encoding is left to the application protocol, so it does not specify UTF-8.
The document creates the PRECIS registries, but this is boilerplate-level IANA content and not the main subject.
SASL is mentioned only as an example application that reuses PRECIS profiles.

RFC8265.title: Preparation, Enforcement, and Comparison of Internationalized Strings Representing Usernames and Passwords
RFC8265.summary: RFC 8265 defines PRECIS framework profiles (UsernameCaseMapped, UsernameCasePreserved, OpaqueString) for preparing, enforcing and comparing internationalized usernames and passwords, replacing SASLprep and obsoleting RFC 7613.

PRECIS.why: The document defines PRECIS profiles for usernames and passwords, which is its whole purpose.
PRECIS.quote: The rules for handling such strings are specified through profiles of the string classes defined in the preparation, enforcement, and comparison of internationalized strings (PRECIS) framework

rejected.why: SASL mechanisms are the historical consumers of SASLprep, but this document specifies string handling, not SASL itself.
Unicode is the underlying character set; the document is about PRECIS profiles of it, and PRECIS is the more specific fit.
Basic and Digest are cited as example consumers only; the document does not specify or extend them.
Usernames and passwords are the subject matter, but the document concerns string preparation and comparison, not authentication mechanisms.

gaps.name: PRECIS
gaps.why: The document is about PRECIS profiles, but the taxonomy has no PRECIS tag under internationalization, so the id used above is not in the taxonomy and must be mapped.

RFC8266.title: Preparation, Enforcement, and Comparison of Internationalized Strings Representing Nicknames
RFC8266.summary: Defines the PRECIS Nickname profile of the FreeformClass, specifying mapping, normalization (NFKC), case-mapping and comparison rules for internationalized nicknames, display names and petnames; obsoletes RFC 7700.

PRECIS.why: The document specifies a PRECIS profile (Nickname) based on FreeformClass, with preparation, enforcement and comparison rules, and registers it in the PRECIS Profiles registry.
PRECIS.quote: this document defines rules for handling nicknames in terms of the preparation, enforcement, and comparison of internationalized strings (PRECIS) framework specification [RFC8264]

rejected.why: Unicode normalization and case mapping are used as tools, but the document is about the PRECIS profile rather than Unicode usage generally; PRECIS is the more specific fit.
Chat protocols are mentioned only as contexts where nicknames appear; the document does not specify them.
XMPP is cited as one application of nicknames only; not specified or extended here.
Only mentioned as a chat technology using nicknames; nothing about MSRP is defined.
The only IANA content is the routine registration of the Nickname profile, which is boilerplate.

RFC8267.title: Network File System (NFS) Upper-Layer Binding to RPC-over-RDMA Version 1
RFC8267.summary: Specifies the Upper-Layer Bindings of NFS versions 2, 3, 4.0, 4.1 and 4.2 (and NFSv2/3 auxiliary protocols) to RPC-over-RDMA version 1, defining DDP-eligible items, reply size estimation, chunk handling, port assignment, and obsoleting RFC 5667.

NFS.why: The document specifies how NFS versions 2, 3, 4.0, 4.1 and 4.2 and their auxiliary protocols (MOUNT, NLM, NSM, NFSACL) bind to RPC-over-RDMA, including DDP-eligible XDR items and COMPOUND handling.
NFS.quote: This document specifies Upper-Layer Bindings of Network File System (NFS) protocol versions to RPC-over-RDMA version 1, thus enabling the use of Direct Data Placement.

RDMA.why: The document defines Upper-Layer Bindings required by RPC-over-RDMA version 1, covering chunk lists, Write chunk pairing, RDMA errors and credits, so RDMA protocol readers would want it.
RDMA.quote: The RPC-over-RDMA version 1 transport may employ Direct Data Placement (DDP) to convey data payloads associated with RPC transactions

rejected.why: RPC is the framework the bindings attach to (portmapper, RPC programs, XIDs), but the document is about NFS-specific binding rules rather than the RPC protocol itself. RDMA transport for RPC is covered by RFC 8166.
RPCSEC_GSS/Kerberos is mentioned only for its effect on chunk list complexity and in Security Considerations; it is not a subject of the document.
TCP is mentioned only for port 2049 and for the MOUNT/NLM/NSM protocols, which are conveyed over it. It is not specified or extended here.
The nfsrdma port 20049 assignment is boilerplate-level IANA content and a minor part of the document, not its main subject.
This is a binding of an upper-layer protocol to a transport, but the specific NFS and RDMA tags describe it more precisely.

RFC8268.title: More Modular Exponentiation (MODP) Diffie-Hellman (DH) Key Exchange (KEX) Groups for Secure Shell (SSH)
RFC8268.summary: RFC 8268 defines five new SSH Diffie-Hellman MODP key exchange methods (group14-sha256 and group15 through group18 with SHA-512) and corrects the DH public key range check in RFC 4253.

SSH.why: The document extends the SSH transport layer with new key exchange method names and updates RFC 4253 and RFC 4250. SSH readers need it.
SSH.quote: This document defines added Modular Exponentiation (MODP) groups for the Secure Shell (SSH) protocol using SHA-2 hashes.

rejected.why: The topic is about DH groups and hashes, but it is the parent of key management. The document's subject is SSH key exchange methods, so SSH is the better fit.
Considered because it defines key exchange methods. It is really an SSH algorithm registration with a DH check correction, so SSH is more specific.
SHA-2 hashes are used as components of the key exchange methods. The document does not specify or analyse them.
The IANA section only registers method names. That is boilerplate and not the subject.
ECDH/ECDSA are mentioned only in the NSA guidance discussion, and the document does not define them.
Not related. The document is about SSH, not TLS.

gaps.name: Diffie-Hellman key exchange / MODP groups
gaps.why: The document is largely about MODP DH groups and public-key validation, but the taxonomy has no Diffie-Hellman or key exchange tag for it beyond the generic key management topic.

RFC8269.title: The ARIA Algorithm and Its Use with the Secure Real-Time Transport Protocol (SRTP)
RFC8269.summary: Defines how the ARIA block cipher is used in SRTP (CTR and GCM modes, key derivation functions), plus DTLS-SRTP protection profiles and MIKEY parameter sets, with test vectors.

ARIA.why: The document specifies how ARIA is used in ARIA-CTR and ARIA-GCM modes and gives ARIA-based PRFs and test vectors, so it belongs on the ARIA page.
ARIA.quote: This document defines the use of the ARIA block cipher algorithm [RFC5794] in the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP)

SRTP.why: It defines new SRTP transforms, key derivation functions and protection profiles, which extends SRTP.
SRTP.quote: We define two modes of running ARIA within SRTP: (1) ARIA in Counter Mode (ARIA-CTR) and (2) ARIA in Galois/Counter Mode (ARIA-GCM).

MIKEY.why: A substantial part of the document defines MIKEY parameter mappings and registers the ARIA encryption algorithms and PRF in the MIKEY registries.
MIKEY.quote: The DTLS-SRTP [RFC5764] protection profiles are mapped to MIKEY parameter sets as shown below.

rejected.why: DTLS is only the transport for the DTLS-SRTP key exchange. The document registers profiles for it but does not change DTLS itself.
AES is only the reference construction. ARIA replaces AES invocations, and the document is not about AES.
HMAC-SHA1 is used unchanged as the authentication transform, so the document adds nothing new about it.
The document protects RTP traffic. It does not define a payload format for any codec.
SHA-1 is only mentioned in the Security Considerations, as the hash inside the HMAC.

RFC8270.title: Increase the Secure Shell Minimum Recommended Diffie-Hellman Modulus Size to 2048 Bits
RFC8270.summary: RFC 8270 updates RFC 4419 to raise the recommended minimum Diffie-Hellman group modulus size for SSH group exchange from 1024 to 2048 bits, citing Logjam research.

SSH.why: The document updates the SSH Diffie-Hellman group exchange (RFC 4419) key exchange requirements, so it is about the SSH protocol.
SSH.quote: SSH servers and SSH clients SHOULD support groups with a minimum acceptable group size of 2048 bits for the "min" value of the SSH_MSG_KEY_DH_GEX_REQUEST

rejected.why: Diffie-Hellman key exchange group sizing is related, but the document is specifically an SSH protocol update, so the SSH tag fits better.
The document concerns DH modulus size, but only as an SSH parameter requirement. It does not define a cryptographic algorithm or a general cryptographic topic.
Logjam research applies to TLS too, but this document only mentions it as the motivation and does not address TLS.

RFC8271.title: Updates to the Resource Reservation Protocol for Fast Reroute of Traffic Engineering GMPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC8271.summary: RFC 8271 updates RFC 4090 RSVP-TE Fast Reroute to support co-routed bidirectional PSC GMPLS LSPs, defining a BYPASS_ASSIGNMENT RRO subobject, a bypass assignment error code, and procedures to restore co-routing and avoid RSVP soft-state timeout.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE fast reroute signalling with a new RRO subobject, Notify error codes and PLR/MP procedures for traffic-engineered LSPs.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document updates the Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) Fast Reroute (FRR) procedures defined in RFC 4090

GMPLS.why: The updates specifically cover GMPLS-signalled co-routed bidirectional LSPs, with in-band and out-of-band signalling handling.
