GMPLS.quote: to support Packet Switch Capable (PSC) Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Label Switched Paths (LSPs)

rejected.why: RFC 6378 linear protection is only mentioned as related work that does not solve the soft-state timeout problem.
RSVP is the base protocol being extended, but the document is about RSVP-TE and GMPLS fast reroute, which is the more specific fit.
That tag covers IP and LDP fast reroute and loop-free alternates. This document is about RSVP-TE LSP fast reroute.
The more specific RSVP-TE tag already sits under it.

gaps.name: MPLS RSVP-TE fast reroute (RFC 4090 FRR)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for RSVP-TE Fast Reroute facility and one-to-one backup. RSVP-TE is the nearest fit.

RFC8272.title: TinyIPFIX for Smart Meters in Constrained Networks
RFC8272.summary: Specifies TinyIPFIX, a compressed IPFIX-derived push protocol for exporting smart-meter/sensor data in constrained 6LoWPAN networks, including message format, mediation to IPFIX, and template management.

IPFIX.why: The document defines a variant of IPFIX with compact headers, mediation to standard IPFIX, and template management rules.
IPFIX.quote: TinyIPFIX is derived from IP Flow Information Export (RFC 7011) and adopted to the needs of constrained networks.

6LoWPAN.why: The protocol is designed around 6LoWPAN packet-size, header-compression and energy constraints, and is deployed over 6LoWPAN/UDP.
6LoWPAN.quote: TinyIPFIX is mainly targeted for the use in 6LoWPAN networks, which are based on IEEE 802.15.4

rejected.why: UDP is the recommended transport but only the substrate; the document defines nothing new about UDP.
Mentioned only as a possible carrier for TinyIPFIX messages.
The parent topic is implied by the 6LoWPAN tag, so it is not listed separately.
Compacting the IPFIX message header is a protocol design choice here, not a general header-compression scheme such as ROHC.
Mentioned as an optional transport only.

gaps.name: IPFIX
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no IPFIX tag in the list I used above: the only IPFIX entry is under network management, as 'IPFIX'. The id 'IPFIX' does exist there, so no gap beyond possible lack of a dedicated smart-metering subject.

RFC8273.title: Unique IPv6 Prefix per Host
RFC8273.summary: Informational document recommending that a provider-managed shared-access network assign each host its own unique /64 IPv6 prefix via unicast Router Advertisements with SLAAC, giving host isolation and subscriber management, plus recommended Neighbor Discovery timer settings.

SLAAC.why: The document details how hosts get a unique prefix through RA flags (A=1, M=0, O=1, L=0) and self-configure addresses with SLAAC. This is the core mechanism.
SLAAC.quote: IPv6-SLAAC-based subscriber and address management is the recommended technology to reach the highest percentage of connected IPv6 devices

neighbor discovery.why: It specifies how RAs are sent (link-layer unicast), the RA flags, and the router and neighbor discovery timers (MaxRtrAdvInterval, lifetimes, reachable time). It also covers neighbor state handling. This is a substantial part of the document.
neighbor discovery.quote: Best Practices for IPv6 Neighbor Discovery
neighbor discovery.section: 5. Best Practices for IPv6 Neighbor Discovery

rejected.why: Stateless DHCPv6 is mentioned only for the O-flag, to fetch DNS and NTP information. The document is not about DHCPv6 itself, and IA_NA is explicitly not recommended.
The parent tag is implied by the more specific SLAAC and neighbor discovery tags.
Wi-Fi is only an example of a shared-access L2 network, and the document does not specify anything about IP over 802.11.
The document is about prefix assignment, but the specific SLAAC and ND tags already cover it, and no topic tag is needed beyond them.
The privacy note is only a short Security Considerations paragraph about RFC 4941 tracking, which is not the main body.
DNS server information via RA options is only mentioned in passing.

RFC8274.title: Incident Object Description Exchange Format Usage Guidance
RFC8274.summary: Informational guidance for implementers of IODEF v2 (RFC 7970): which classes to implement, extensions, indicator predicate logic, disclosure levels, and use cases and examples from a RID-based interoperability exercise.

IODEF.why: The whole document is usage guidance for IODEF v2: minimal documents, class selection, extensions, IndicatorExpression logic and examples.
IODEF.quote: This document provides guidelines for IODEF implementers. It addresses how common security indicators can be represented in IODEF and provides use cases of how IODEF is being used.

rejected.why: RID was the transport in the 2013 exercise and is described in section 5.2, but the document does not specify or extend it. It is only mentioned as the way IODEF was exchanged.
IODEF is defined as an XML schema and the examples are XML, but the document is not about XML usage itself.
The parent topic is implied by the IODEF tag, so it is not listed separately.
TLS only secures the RID exchanges in the proof of concept. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
DDoS is one example use case for IODEF, not the subject of the document.
Certificates appear only in an example and in a use case about reporting certificate compromise.

RFC8275.title: Allowing Inheritable NFSv4 Access Control Entries to Override the Umask
RFC8275.summary: RFC 8275 defines an OPTIONAL NFSv4.2 attribute, mode_umask, which sends the file creation mode and umask separately so servers can let inheritable ACEs override the umask.

NFS.why: The document extends NFSv4.2 with a new attribute (mode_umask) and specifies server and client behaviour for CREATE and OPEN. Readers of NFS would want it.
NFS.quote: This document presents an extension to minor version 2 of the NFSv4 protocol as described in [RFC8178].

rejected.why: The document includes XDR definitions and an extraction script. XDR is only the encoding for the new attribute, and the document says nothing new about ONC RPC or XDR.
The document touches ACLs and permission inheritance. It is about how the file creation mode and umask are conveyed in NFS, not a general access-control mechanism.
NFS is the more specific tag and already covers this document, so its parent is implied.

RFC8276.title: File System Extended Attributes in NFSv4
RFC8276.summary: RFC 8276 extends NFSv4 with an optional extended-attributes (xattr) feature: a new xattr_support attribute, four new operations (GETXATTR, SETXATTR, LISTXATTRS, REMOVEXATTR), new ACCESS bits, and caching rules.

NFS.why: The document specifies new NFSv4 attributes, operations, errors and ACCESS extensions for xattrs. NFS readers would expect to find it.
NFS.quote: This feature allows extended attributes (hereinafter also referred to as xattrs) to be interrogated and manipulated using NFSv4 clients.

rejected.why: The XDR description is only the encoding used to define the new NFS operations. The document is not about ONC RPC or XDR itself.
NFS already sits under storage. The NFS tag is more specific, so the parent is implied.
There is no XDR tag in the taxonomy. XDR is only the notation used for the new definitions.

RFC8277.title: Using BGP to Bind MPLS Labels to Address Prefixes
RFC8277.summary: RFC 8277 specifies how BGP (SAFI 4 and 128) advertises bindings of one or more MPLS labels to address prefixes, defines the Multiple Labels Capability, NLRI encodings, withdrawal, propagation and data-plane procedures, and obsoletes RFC 3107.

BGP.why: The document defines BGP NLRI encodings, a new BGP capability, withdrawal and propagation procedures for labeled prefixes (SAFI 4/128), so it is about BGP protocol extension.
BGP.quote: specifies a set of procedures for using BGP to advertise that a specified router has bound a specified MPLS label

MPLS.why: A substantial part covers MPLS label binding semantics, label stack handling and data-plane forwarding when labels are swapped or pushed.
MPLS.quote: must replace L2 with L1 as the top entry in the packet's label stack, and S1 must then tunnel the packet to N1.

rejected.why: VPN-IPv4/VPN-IPv6 (SAFI 128) are covered by the procedures, but the document is not about BGP/MPLS VPNs themselves.
IPv6 prefixes (AFI 2) are just one address family handled; the document is not about IPv6.
Tunnelling to the next hop is mentioned only as a data-plane requirement, and the tunnel type is explicitly out of scope.
MPLS label distribution by LDP is not discussed; labels are distributed via BGP.

RFC8278.title: Mobile Access Gateway (MAG) Multipath Options
RFC8278.summary: Extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 with two new mobility options (MAG Multipath Binding, MAG Identifier) and a new PBA status code so a MAG can register multiple proxy care-of addresses with an LMA and use multiple tunnels simultaneously.

PMIPv6.why: The document defines new PMIPv6 mobility options, a status code and signaling rules for multipath bindings between MAG and LMA.
PMIPv6.quote: This specification defines extensions to the Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) protocol that allow a mobile access gateway (MAG) to register more than one proxy care-of address

rejected.why: Multihoming motivates the work, but the document specifies a PMIPv6 extension rather than a multihoming architecture. PMIPv6 is the more specific tag.
Mobile IPv6 is referenced as background. The document extends PMIPv6, which is the specific child tag.
NEMO appears only as background in the introduction.
GRE is mentioned as one of the possible tunnel encapsulations, but the document does not specify it.
IP-in-IP is mentioned only as the tunnel type and in the terminology section.
The IANA section registers option types and a status code, which is boilerplate.

RFC8279.title: Multicast Using Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER)
RFC8279.summary: RFC 8279 specifies the BIER architecture for multicast forwarding, in which a bit string in the packet header identifies egress routers, along with the BIER forwarding procedures, ECMP handling, and BitStringLength handling.

BIER.why: The document defines the BIER architecture, its BFR-ids, BitStrings, BIFT and forwarding procedures.
BIER.quote: This architecture is known as "Bit Index Explicit Replication" (BIER).

ECMP.why: Section 6.7 defines non-deterministic and deterministic ECMP procedures for BIER forwarding.
ECMP.quote: BIER supports ECMP forwarding, but the procedures of Section 6.5 must be modified slightly.

rejected.why: MVPN is only an example of a multicast flow overlay; the interaction is specified in another document.
OSPF is only a typical routing underlay, and the extensions are specified in companion documents.
IS-IS is mentioned only as an IGP that could advertise BIER information, with details left to companion documents.
MPLS encapsulation is defined in a companion document, and MPLS is mentioned only for tunnels and TTL handling.
Fast reroute and node protection are mentioned briefly but are not a main subject.
BIER is the more specific child tag for this document.

RFC8280.title: Research into Human Rights Protocol Considerations
RFC8280.summary: An IRTF research document that maps how Internet protocols (IP, DNS, HTTP, XMPP, P2P, VPNs) affect human rights and proposes a questionnaire of human rights protocol considerations for protocol designers, modelled on RFC 6973.

privacy.why: The document is a protocol-considerations guideline modelled on RFC 6973. It covers privacy, anonymity, pseudonymity and confidentiality threats, so it fits the privacy threat-model subject.
privacy.quote: propose possible guidelines to protect the Internet as an enabling environment for human rights in future protocol development, in a manner similar to the work done for privacy considerations

internet architecture.why: Much of the document discusses architectural principles (end-to-end, heterogeneity, decentralization, permissionless innovation, connectivity) and their link to human rights.
internet architecture.quote: The end-to-end principle is one of the key architectural guidelines of the Internet.

DNS.why: A substantial case study analyses DNS, covering record removal, distortion and injection, and the DNSSEC and privacy implications.
DNS.quote: The most common mechanism by which the DNS is abused to limit freedom of expression is through manipulation of protocol messages by the network.

rejected.why: The HTTP case study covers interception and the 451 status code, but the document does not specify or extend HTTP. It is one of several protocols used as examples.
XMPP is only a case study of human rights impact, with no specification or extension of the protocol.
The VPN case study concerns user-level VPN services and their privacy pitfalls, not provider-provisioned VPNs.
The DDoS section is a brief case study within the broader analysis and is not a main subject.
The document proposes guidelines for protocol authors, but it does not define or change IETF procedures.
The peer-to-peer section is one case study among several and is not the document's main subject.

gaps.name: Human rights and protocol design
gaps.why: The document's main subject is the relationship between human rights and Internet protocols, including censorship resistance and surveillance. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so privacy and internet architecture are only partial fits.

RFC8281.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for PCE-Initiated LSP Setup in a Stateful PCE Model
RFC8281.summary: Extends PCEP with the PCInitiate message, I capability flag, R flag and C flag so a stateful PCE can instantiate, delegate, and delete LSPs on a PCC without local configuration.

PCE.why: The document specifies PCEP extensions for PCE-initiated LSPs in a stateful PCE, which is the core subject of the PCE tag.
PCE.quote: This document describes the setup, maintenance, and teardown of PCE-initiated LSPs under the stateful PCE model, without the need for local configuration on the PCC

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is only the signalling method the PCC uses to set up the LSP; the document does not extend it.
The LSPs are MPLS TE LSPs, but the document is about PCEP control of them, not MPLS itself.
RBNF is only the notation used for message formats.
SDN is mentioned as a use case in the motivation, but is not the subject.
The PCE tag is the more specific fit; the document is not a general traffic engineering treatment.

RFC8282.title: Extensions to the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) for Inter-Layer MPLS and GMPLS Traffic Engineering
RFC8282.summary: RFC 8282 defines PCEP extensions (INTER-LAYER, SWITCH-LAYER, REQ-ADAP-CAP, SERVER-INDICATION objects and two new metric types) enabling PCE-based inter-layer MPLS/GMPLS traffic engineering path computation.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP with new objects, metrics and procedures for inter-layer path computation, so it belongs under PCE architecture and PCEP.
PCE.quote: This document presents PCEP extensions for inter-layer traffic engineering.

GMPLS.why: The multi-layer and multi-region GMPLS networks (switching and encoding types, hierarchical and stitched LSPs) are the problem domain, and the new objects carry GMPLS switching and encoding parameters.
GMPLS.quote: MPLS and GMPLS networks may be constructed from layered service networks.

rejected.why: MPLS is the network context, but the parent is implied by GMPLS and the document specifies no MPLS mechanism itself.
The PCE tag already sits under this topic, so the parent is implied.
RBNF is only the notation used to present message formats, not a subject of the document.
It is mentioned only in the manageability section as a possible future model.
The MIB for PCEP appears only as a manageability reference.
Triggered signaling is mentioned, but the document does not specify RSVP-TE.

RFC8283.title: An Architecture for Use of PCE and the PCE Communication Protocol (PCEP) in a Network with Central Control
RFC8283.summary: Informational architecture document describing how a PCE can act as a central controller using PCEP as a southbound protocol, covering resilience/scaling models, applicability to static LSPs, segment routing, SFC, TE, and implications for PCEP.

PCE.why: The whole document is about the PCE architecture and PCEP used as a control protocol in a centrally controlled network, and the implications for PCEP.
PCE.quote: This document introduces the architecture for PCE as a central controller as an extension of the architecture described in [RFC4655]

SDN.why: The document frames the PCE-based controller as an SDN architecture, with southbound interface, orchestrator and controller hierarchies.
SDN.quote: The PCE component in an SDN system may be used to determine paths in a wide range of use cases

rejected.why: Only one of several use cases briefly discussed (Section 3.1.5); the document is not about segment routing.
Briefly mentioned as an applicability use case only.
MPLS LSPs are the setting and a use case, but the document is about the PCE controller architecture, not MPLS itself.
Traffic engineering is a high-level use case listed in Section 3.2.1, but PCE is the more specific tag for the subject.
BGP-LS and BGP are mentioned only as ways to populate the TED or synchronize state.

gaps.name: PCE / PCEP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no PCE tag, though the document is entirely about PCE and PCEP. The nearest existing entry is PCE under traffic engineering, which is the tag I used above.

RFC8284.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) Schema for Supporting the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) in White Pages
RFC8284.summary: Defines an LDAP auxiliary object class (JIDObject) and a 'jid' attribute so XMPP Jabber IDs can be stored in LDAP directory entries for white pages use.

LDAP.why: The document is an LDAP schema extension defining a new auxiliary object class and attribute, with matching rules and syntax, plus LDAP OID registrations.
LDAP.quote: This specification defines a schema to enable XMPP JIDs to be associated with LDAP directory objects so that this information can be used with white pages applications.

XMPP.why: The schema exists to represent XMPP JIDs and specifies how bare JIDs per the XMPP address format are stored; readers of XMPP would want to find this.
XMPP.quote: This Object Class is used to augment entries for objects that act or may act as an XMPP client.

rejected.why: XMPP is only the identifier source; the document does not specify messaging or presence behaviour. The XMPP tag is the more specific fit.
Parent of LDAP, which is already tagged, so it is implied.
The IANA section only registers OIDs and descriptors, which is boilerplate here.

RFC8285.title: A General Mechanism for RTP Header Extensions
RFC8285.summary: RFC 8285 defines a general mechanism for carrying multiple small header extension elements (one-byte and two-byte forms) in RTP packets, with URI-named extensions, SDP "extmap" and "extmap-allow-mixed" signaling, offer/answer rules, and an IANA registry; it obsoletes RFC 5285.

RTP.why: The document extends RTP by defining the one-byte and two-byte header extension formats carried in RTP packets, so RTP readers need it.
RTP.quote: This document provides a general mechanism to use the header extension feature of RTP (the Real-time Transport Protocol).

SDP.why: A substantial part defines the SDP extmap attribute, the new extmap-allow-mixed attribute, and offer/answer procedures for negotiating header extensions.
SDP.quote: this document defines the "a=extmap-allow-mixed" Session Description Protocol (SDP) [RFC4566] attribute to indicate if the participant is capable of supporting this new mode.
SDP.section: 6. SDP Signaling for Support of Mixed One-Byte and Two-Byte Header Extensions

rejected.why: SRTP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to protect header extensions; the document does not specify it.
Extensions are named by URIs, but the document only uses URIs as identifiers and does not define URI syntax or schemes.
The IANA registry is boilerplate-level apparatus for this document; the body is about the RTP mechanism, not IANA guidance.
Header compression is mentioned briefly as an efficiency concern but is not a subject of the document.
RTCP appears only as a feedback aid for deciding how often to repeat extensions, not as something the document specifies.
The urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext: namespace is used for registry naming, but the document defines no new URN namespace and is not about URNs.

RFC8286.title: RTP/RTCP Extension for RTP Splicing Notification
RFC8286.summary: Defines an RTP header extension and a new RTCP packet type (SNM) that let a main RTP sender tell an RTP splicer the splicing-in and splicing-out NTP times, plus SDP signaling (SPLICE group, extmap URI).

RTP.why: The document extends RTP with a new header extension and discusses splicer as RTP mixer/translator. No more specific RTP child tag fits the header extension.
RTP.quote: This memo defines two RTP/RTCP extensions to indicate the splicing-related information to the splicer: an RTP header extension that conveys the information "in band"

RTCP.why: Defines a new RTCP packet type (PT=213, SNM), including compound/non-compound rules and SR interaction.
RTCP.quote: this document also defines a new RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) packet type to carry the same Splicing Interval to the splicer.

SDP.why: A substantial section defines a new SDP group semantic and extmap URI, with offer/answer and BUNDLE examples.
SDP.quote: This document extends the standard semantics defined in "The Session Description Protocol (SDP) Grouping Framework" [RFC5888] with a new semantic, called "SPLICE"

rejected.why: Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a security caveat; the document does not specify anything about SRTP.
NTP timestamp format is reused for the splicing times, but the document is not about the NTP protocol.
IPTV advertisement insertion is the motivating use case, but the document specifies RTP/RTCP mechanisms rather than IPTV service delivery.
The document does not define payload formats; MPEG2-TS is only referenced in examples.
Multicast addresses appear only in SDP examples.

gaps.name: RTP header extensions / RTP splicing
gaps.why: No taxonomy tag covers RTP header extensions or content splicing (ad insertion) specifically; RTP is the closest fit.

RFC8287.title: Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping/Traceroute for Segment Routing (SR) IGP-Prefix and IGP-Adjacency Segment Identifiers (SIDs) with MPLS Data Planes
RFC8287.summary: Defines new MPLS LSP Ping/Traceroute Target FEC Stack sub-TLVs and validation procedures for Segment Routing IGP-Prefix and IGP-Adjacency SIDs over an MPLS data plane.

SR-MPLS.why: The document specifies OAM (LSP Ping/Traceroute) for Segment Routing over MPLS, so SR-MPLS readers need it.
SR-MPLS.quote: defines extensions to perform LSP Ping and Traceroute for Segment Routing IGP-Prefix and IGP-Adjacency Segment Identifiers (SIDs) with an MPLS data plane

OAM.why: It is fault detection and isolation (connectivity verification) work, extending MPLS echo request/reply OAM. There is no MPLS-specific OAM tag, so the generic OAM topic fits.
OAM.quote: The following example describes the challenges with using the current MPLS Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) mechanisms on an SR network.

rejected.why: MPLS is the data plane and RFC 8029 is the base mechanism being extended. The SR-MPLS tag is more specific.
SR-MPLS is the more specific child, and the document is about the MPLS data-plane instantiation.
OSPF and IS-IS only supply the Protocol field values and the advertised SIDs used for validation. The document does not specify them.
IS-IS is a source of SID advertisements used for validation. The document does not extend it.
The traceroute here is MPLS LSP traceroute, not the IP traceroute tool the tag covers. OAM covers it better.
ICMP echo is mentioned only as the paradigm that LSP Ping is modelled on.

gaps.name: MPLS LSP Ping/Traceroute (RFC 8029 data-plane failure detection)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MPLS OAM or LSP Ping. This document and its subject are best indexed there, but only the generic OAM topic is available.

RFC8288.title: Web Linking
RFC8288.summary: RFC 8288 defines a model of typed links between web resources (link context, relation type, target, target attributes), the Link HTTP header field serialisation, and the IANA link relation registry procedures; it obsoletes RFC 5988.

web linking.why: The whole document defines the web linking model, link relation types, the Link header field and the registry for relation types, which is exactly what the web linking subject covers.
web linking.quote: This specification defines a model for the relationships between resources on the Web ("links") and the type of those relationships ("link relation types").

rejected.why: The Link header field is carried in HTTP, but the document is about the link model; HTTP is the serialisation substrate and web linking is the more specific child under HTTP.
Link contexts and targets are URIs/IRIs and resolution follows RFC 3986, but the document only uses them rather than specifying them.
IRIs are mentioned for link targets and conversion to URIs, but this is a dependency, not the subject.
Atom's atom:link is discussed only in an informative appendix on alternative serialisations.
HTML link elements are covered only in an informative appendix as another serialisation.
The link relation registry procedures are part of the document, but they are specific to web linking, not general IANA guidance.

RFC8289.title: Controlled Delay Active Queue Management
RFC8289.summary: RFC 8289 specifies CoDel, an experimental parameterless active queue management algorithm that uses packet sojourn time, a target setpoint and a control loop to control bufferbloat-induced delay, with pseudocode.

CoDel.why: The whole document specifies the CoDel queue management algorithm: estimator, setpoint, control loop, and reference pseudocode.
CoDel.quote: CoDel (Controlled Delay) -- a general framework that controls bufferbloat-generated excess delay in modern networking environments.

rejected.why: CoDel is the more specific child tag and already implies AQM, so the parent is not listed.
TCP dynamics motivate the design, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
ECN marking is mentioned only as an alternative to dropping, so it is not a subject of the document.
The more specific CoDel tag already covers it.

RFC8290.title: The Flow Queue CoDel Packet Scheduler and Active Queue Management Algorithm
RFC8290.summary: Specifies FQ-CoDel, a hybrid flow-queueing (DRR-based) packet scheduler combined with the CoDel AQM on each queue, to combat bufferbloat, including implementation guidance, parameters and limitations.

AQM.why: The document specifies a hybrid scheduler and AQM algorithm running CoDel on per-flow queues, so it belongs on the AQM page.
AQM.quote: The Flow Queue CoDel (FQ-CoDel) algorithm is a combined packet scheduler and Active Queue Management (AQM) [RFC3168] algorithm

CoDel.why: CoDel runs on every FQ-CoDel queue, and the document covers its parameters (interval, target) and how FQ-CoDel's behaviour differs from plain CoDel.
CoDel.quote: with the CoDel AQM [RFC8289] algorithm operating on each queue

rejected.why: ECN is enabled by default and discussed as a parameter, but the document is not about ECN itself.
Only the ce_threshold parameter references DCTCP-like marking; this is a minor mention.
A limitations subsection notes the interaction with LEDBAT, but the document is not about it.
The more specific AQM and CoDel tags already cover the document, so the parent is not needed.
Flow scheduling gives implicit prioritisation, but the document does not address QoS architectures or signalling. Diffserv is mentioned only in passing.

gaps.name: Fair queueing / packet scheduling (DRR, flow queueing)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for packet schedulers or fair queueing, which is half of what FQ-CoDel is. Bufferbloat is also uncovered.

RFC8291.title: Message Encryption for Web Push
RFC8291.summary: Defines how Web Push messages from an application server to a user agent are end-to-end encrypted, using ECDH on P-256, an authentication secret, HKDF, and the RFC 8188 aes128gcm content coding.

web push.why: The whole document specifies encryption of Web Push messages, including key derivation, restrictions on the content coding and an example.
web push.quote: This document describes a message encryption scheme for the Web Push protocol.

elliptic curve.why: ECDH key agreement on P-256, including public key validation, is a substantial part of the scheme, so elliptic curve readers would want it.
elliptic curve.quote: Encrypting a push message uses Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) [ECDH] on the P-256 curve [FIPS186] to establish a shared secret

rejected.why: Push messages are HTTP payloads and the encoding is an HTTP content coding, but the document defines no new HTTP semantics. HTTP is only the substrate.
HKDF with HMAC-SHA-256 is used as a building block for key derivation. The document does not specify or analyse HMAC.
SHA-256 is used only as the hash inside HKDF.
AES-128-GCM is inherited from RFC 8188 and is not specified here.
HTTPS is mentioned only as a way to distribute subscription data securely.
The key derivation scheme is a recommended key management scheme, but it is specific to Web Push encryption and the web push tag covers it. The generic key management topic is not needed.
The Security Considerations note that the push service can see timing and length of messages. This is incidental to the encryption scheme and not a main subject.

gaps.name: Encrypted Content-Encoding for HTTP (aes128gcm, RFC 8188)
gaps.why: The document profiles this content coding for push messages, and the taxonomy has no tag for HTTP content encryption. The closest tags are HTTP and web push.

RFC8292.title: Voluntary Application Server Identification (VAPID) for Web Push
RFC8292.summary: Defines VAPID, a "vapid" HTTP authentication scheme using ES256-signed JWTs by which a Web Push application server voluntarily identifies itself to a push service, and lets push subscriptions be restricted to a single application server's key.

web push.why: The whole document extends the Web Push protocol with application server identification and subscription restriction.
web push.quote: An application server can use the Voluntary Application Server Identification (VAPID) method described in this document to voluntarily identify itself to a push service.

HTTP authentication.why: It defines and registers a new HTTP authentication scheme with parameters "t" and "k", which readers of HTTP authentication would want.
HTTP authentication.quote: This document defines a new HTTP authentication scheme [RFC7235] named "vapid".

rejected.why: JWT is the token format used to carry the signed claims. The document profiles it but does not specify or extend JWT itself.
JWS and ES256 are used as building blocks for the signature. The document defines nothing new about them.
ECDSA over P-256 is only the signature algorithm the scheme requires.
HTTP is the substrate. The relevant HTTP content is the authentication scheme, which is covered by the more specific tag.
The document registers one media type, but that is a minor IANA item and boilerplate-like, not the subject.
The more specific HTTP authentication tag already covers this.

RFC8293.title: A Framework for Multicast in Network Virtualization over Layer 3
RFC8293.summary: Informational NVO3 framework describing mechanisms (no multicast, source-NVE replication, multicast service node, underlay IP multicast) for carrying infrastructure and application multicast in data center network virtualization overlays.

overlay networks.why: The document is about handling multicast in NVO3 data-plane network virtualization overlays (VXLAN, NVGRE, Geneve encapsulations, NVE/NVA), which is the overlay networks subject.
overlay networks.quote: This document provides a framework for supporting multicast traffic in a network that uses NVO3.

multicast.why: It compares replication and underlay IP multicast delivery methods, membership management via IGMP/MLD snooping, PIM, SSM and BIER; this is the multicast deployment subject.
multicast.quote: Both infrastructure multicast and application-specific multicast are considered.

rejected.why: The data center is the context, but the document is about multicast over NVO3 overlays rather than DC routing or address resolution as such.
VXLAN is only one example encapsulation mentioned; the document does not specify or extend it.
IGMP/MLD are used for membership discovery but are not specified or extended here.
PIM is mentioned as an underlay option; the document does not specify or extend it.
Multicast VPN is discussed only as a comparison and shown not to scale in DCs; the document is not about it.
BIER is mentioned in one paragraph as a possible optimization, not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: NVO3 (Network Virtualization over Layer 3) architecture/framework
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only the generic overlay networks tag, with VXLAN, Geneve and NVGRE children; there is no tag for the NVO3 working-group architecture, which is the document's central context.

RFC8294.title: Common YANG Data Types for the Routing Area
RFC8294.summary: Defines two YANG modules (ietf-routing-types and iana-routing-types) with common derived data types and groupings for reuse by routing-area YANG models, covering VPN route targets, multicast addresses, MPLS labels, timers, and IANA address family/SAFI enumerations.

YANG.why: The RFC's whole purpose is to specify YANG modules of common typedefs and groupings that other routing YANG models import.
YANG.quote: This document defines a collection of common data types using the YANG data modeling language.

MPLS.why: A substantial part of the module covers MPLS label types, special-purpose label identities and the label stack grouping.
MPLS.quote: This grouping defines a reusable collection of schema nodes representing an MPLS label stack [RFC3032].

L3VPN.why: Route target, route distinguisher and route origin types and the vpn-route-targets grouping model BGP/MPLS VPN constructs.
L3VPN.quote: Route Targets (RTs) are commonly used to control the distribution of Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) information

rejected.why: BGP extended communities and SAFIs are modelled as types, but the document does not specify or extend BGP itself.
It defines multicast address types, but only as data types for use by other models such as PIM YANG.
It creates an IANA-maintained YANG module mirroring registries, but its subject is data types, not IANA registry guidance.
The types are YANG, not SMI MIB modules.
NETCONF is only mentioned as the context for YANG; it is not specified here.

RFC8295.title: EST (Enrollment over Secure Transport) Extensions
RFC8295.summary: RFC 8295 extends the EST protocol with new path components (/pal, /eecerts, /crls, /symmetrickeys, /firmware, /tamp) and the Package Availability List, plus server-generated asymmetric key extensions (CMS encapsulation, receipts, PKCS #12).

EST.why: The document extends EST (RFC 7030) with new path components and extends /serverkeygen. It is squarely about EST.
EST.quote: This document defines a number of other PKI services as additional path components -- specifically, firmware and trust anchors as well as symmetric, asymmetric, and encrypted keys.

firmware update.why: A substantial part (Section 6) defines distribution of CMS-protected firmware packages and receipts or errors to clients.
firmware update.quote: the /firmware PC provides a mechanism for the infrastructure to inform the client that firmware and software updates [RFC4108] are available.

key management.why: Substantial parts cover provisioning of symmetric, asymmetric and encrypted key packages to clients, with receipts and errors, plus PKCS #12 delivery.
key management.quote: The /symmetrickeys PC allows the server to distribute symmetric keys to clients.

rejected.why: CMS content types are the encapsulation used for packages, but the document defines no new CMS content types. It only uses them as a substrate.
HTTP GET and POST are the transport for the new path components. The document defines no new HTTP semantics.
TLS only secures the transport and is deferred to RFC 7030.
XML and JSON are encodings for the PAL, and the XML schema is a minor part of the document.
JSON is only an alternative PAL encoding and is not the subject of the document.
Certificates and CRLs are distributed here, but the document does not profile X.509.

gaps.name: TAMP (Trust Anchor Management Protocol) transport
gaps.why: Section 7 defines /tamp and /tamp/return for carrying TAMP packages. The taxonomy has no TAMP tag, and PKI only partly covers it.

RFC8296.title: Encapsulation for Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER) in MPLS and Non-MPLS Networks
RFC8296.summary: Specifies the BIER header encapsulation (BIFT-id, TTL, entropy, BitString, Proto, etc.) for carrying multicast packets in MPLS and non-MPLS networks, plus BFIR/BFR imposition and processing procedures.

BIER.why: The whole document defines the BIER header format and the BFIR/BFR encapsulation and processing rules, so it belongs on the BIER page.
BIER.quote: This document specifies a BIER encapsulation that can be used in an MPLS network or, with slight differences, in a non-MPLS network.

rejected.why: MPLS is the substrate for one of the two encapsulation variants. The document uses the MPLS label stack but does not define new MPLS mechanisms beyond BIER-MPLS label use.
The parent of BIER, so it is implied by the BIER tag and not listed separately.
OSPF is referenced only for the extensions that advertise BIER labels, and those extensions are specified in other documents.
IS-IS is referenced only for the extensions that advertise BIER labels, and those extensions are specified in other documents.
BGP is mentioned only as a possible way to advertise BIER-MPLS labels, and the extensions are defined elsewhere.
Ethernet is only an example outer encapsulation. The Ethertype 0xAB37 is noted as an IEEE assignment and Ethernet itself is not the subject.

RFC8297.title: An HTTP Status Code for Indicating Hints
RFC8297.summary: Defines the HTTP 103 (Early Hints) informational status code, letting a server send Link header hints such as preload before the final response.

HTTP.why: The document specifies a new HTTP status code and its semantics for clients and servers, extending HTTP.
HTTP.quote: The 103 (Early Hints) informational status code indicates to the client that the server is likely to send a final response with the header fields included in the informational response.

web linking.why: The hints are conveyed as Link header fields with preload relations, and the examples centre on them. Readers of web linking would want this, though the document defines no new link relation.
web linking.quote: a client might recognize a Link header field value containing the relation type "preload" and start fetching the target resource.

rejected.why: HTTP/2 server push is mentioned as a comparison and a possible trigger at caching intermediaries, but the document is not about HTTP/2.
Caching intermediaries generating or forwarding 103 responses are mentioned briefly, but caching is not the focus.
The only IANA content is boilerplate registration of status code 103.

RFC8298.title: Self-Clocked Rate Adaptation for Multimedia
RFC8298.summary: Specifies SCReAM, an experimental self-clocked, hybrid loss-and-delay-based congestion control and media rate adaptation algorithm for RTP-based interactive real-time video, using LEDBAT-like delay estimation and RTCP XR feedback.

RTP congestion control.why: The document defines SCReAM, an RMCAT congestion control algorithm for interactive real-time media over RTP, which is exactly this tag's subject.
RTP congestion control.quote: This memo describes Self-Clocked Rate Adaptation for Multimedia (SCReAM), a solution that implements congestion control for RTP streams

RTCP.why: A substantial section specifies the RTCP XR feedback elements, their format, and feedback intensity/interval requirements (reduced-size RTCP, AVPF) needed by the algorithm.
RTCP.quote: The basic feedback needed for SCReAM involves the use of the Loss RLE Report Block and the Packet Receipt Times Report Block

rejected.why: SCReAM borrows LEDBAT's queuing-delay estimation and window update, but the document specifies a different algorithm for conversational media rather than LEDBAT itself.
ECN is used as an optional congestion signal with a smaller backoff, but the document is not about ECN itself.
RTP is the media substrate; the document specifies congestion control for it, covered by the more specific RTP congestion control tag.
The parent is implied by the more specific RTP congestion control tag.
TCP self-clocking and loss handling are referenced as inspiration only; no TCP specification or extension is given.
WebRTC is the motivating use case, but the document does not specify WebRTC mechanisms.

RFC8299.title: YANG Data Model for L3VPN Service Delivery
RFC8299.summary: Defines the ietf-l3vpn-svc YANG service data model (obsoleting RFC 8049) for customer-to-operator ordering and delivery of BGP/MPLS PE-based Layer 3 VPN services.

L3VPN.why: The whole document models an L3VPN service (sites, VPN topology, RTs/RDs, NNIs, extranet, CsC) over BGP/MPLS per RFC 4364.
L3VPN.quote: This document defines a YANG data model that can be used for communication between customers and network operators and to deliver a Layer 3 provider-provisioned VPN service.

YANG.why: The deliverable is a YANG module with tree diagrams, features, and relation to device models; it replaces an unimplementable YANG module from RFC 8049.
YANG.quote: This document defines a Layer 3 VPN service data model written in YANG.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as a way the management system configures network elements; not specified here.
BGP is a PE-CE routing option and NNI context, but the document does not specify or extend BGP.
QoS classification and profiles are modelled in a subsection, but as service parameters rather than a QoS architecture; secondary at most.
OSPF is only a selectable PE-CE routing option in the model.
Multicast parameters are one model container; the document is not about multicast routing.
MPLS and CsC are used as context in the L3VPN model, not specified.

RFC8300.title: Network Service Header (NSH)
RFC8300.summary: Specifies the Network Service Header (NSH), the data-plane encapsulation for Service Function Chaining that carries service path identification, location within the path, and optional metadata.

SFC.why: The whole document defines the NSH header format, Service Path Identifier/Service Index, metadata, and forwarding behaviour for SFC.
SFC.quote: The NSH is the Service Function Chaining (SFC) encapsulation required to support the SFC architecture (defined in RFC 7665).

rejected.why: NSH is transport-encapsulation agnostic and merely rides over overlays such as VXLAN-gpe or GRE; it is not itself a network virtualization overlay.
IPsec is only suggested as an outer transport for integrity and confidentiality in Security Considerations; it is not specified or profiled here.
Generic tunnelling and GRE are only examples of outer transport encapsulations, not the subject of the document.
The IANA registries for NSH parameters are boilerplate-like for this protocol spec; the document is about NSH, not IANA guidance.
The O bit is defined, but OAM format and processing are explicitly out of scope.
MPLS appears only as a possible Next Protocol or transport and in a version-bit reservation note, not as a subject.

RFC8301.title: Cryptographic Algorithm and Key Usage Update to DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM)
RFC8301.summary: Updates DKIM (RFC 6376) to require rsa-sha256 signing, forbid rsa-sha1, and set minimum RSA key sizes of 1024 bits (2048 recommended).

DKIM.why: The document updates the DKIM specification's algorithm and key-size requirements, so it is squarely about DKIM.
DKIM.quote: Signers MUST sign using rsa-sha256.  Verifiers MUST be able to verify using rsa-sha256.  rsa-sha1 MUST NOT be used for signing or verifying.

RSA.why: A substantial part of the document sets RSA key size requirements for DKIM, which RSA readers would want.
RSA.quote: Signers MUST use RSA keys of at least 1024 bits for all keys.  Signers SHOULD use RSA keys of at least 2048 bits.

SHA.why: The document deprecates SHA-1 in DKIM in favour of SHA-256, a hash-algorithm usage change.
SHA.quote: the SHA-1 hash algorithm MUST NOT be used.

rejected.why: DNS TXT records are only the substrate for key storage; the document defines nothing new about DNS.
Implied as the parent of DKIM, so it is not listed separately.
The more specific RSA and SHA tags cover the cryptographic content.
The registry status update is boilerplate-level and is not the subject of the document.

RFC8302.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): ARP and Neighbor Discovery (ND) Optimization
RFC8302.summary: Specifies how TRILL edge RBridges cache IP/MAC/Data Label bindings learned from ARP/ND/DHCP and use them (plus directory data and ESADI) to answer, unicast, or suppress flooded ARP/ND requests, with duplicate detection and cache ageing.

TRILL.why: The document extends TRILL edge RBridge behaviour (caching, proxy ARP/ND, ESADI distribution of IA APPsub-TLV mappings), so TRILL readers need it.
TRILL.quote: mechanisms to optimize the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) and Neighbor Discovery (ND) traffic in a Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) campus

ARP.why: Core subject is optimizing ARP (and RARP) handling via proxy replies, snooping, and suppression of flooding.
ARP.quote: ARP [RFC826] and ND [RFC4861] messages are normally sent by broadcast and multicast, respectively.

neighbor discovery.why: IPv6 ND request/advertisement handling, DAD, and proxy responses are specified in parallel with ARP.
neighbor discovery.quote: A native frame that is an ND [RFC4861] is detected by being one of five different ICMPv6 packet types.

rejected.why: SEND is only snooped and not optimized; a short section, and the document is not about securing ND.
DHCP messages are merely snooped to learn bindings; a brief section, not about DHCP itself.
Data centers are motivating context, but the document specifies TRILL behaviour; tag would be secondary at best and TRILL is the specific fit.
APPsub-TLVs ride on IS-IS via TRILL but the document does not specify or extend IS-IS.

RFC8303.title: On the Usage of Transport Features Provided by IETF Transport Protocols
RFC8303.summary: RFC 8303 surveys the application-facing primitives and transport features of TCP, MPTCP, SCTP, UDP, UDP-Lite and LEDBAT in a three-pass analysis, producing a set of transport abstractions for a TAPS API.

TAPS.why: The document exists to derive transport features and abstractions for a Transport Services (TAPS) system and API, and it feeds the minimal-set work.
TAPS.quote: this generates a set of transport abstractions that can be exported in a TAPS API.

TCP.why: A substantial part analyses TCP's primitives (Open, Send, Receive, Close), TFO, UTO and TCP-AO as exposed to applications.
TCP.quote: Section 3.8 of [RFC0793] further specifies the interaction with the application by listing several transport primitives.

MPTCP.why: A dedicated section analyses MPTCP's API clarifications and subflow management primitives, such as ADD_PATH and REM_PATH.
MPTCP.quote: MPTCP is an extension to TCP that allows the use of multiple paths for a single data stream.

SCTP.why: SCTP gets the largest share of the analysis: its abstract API, sockets API and extensions, covering streams, partial reliability, schedulers and notifications.
SCTP.quote: Section 10 of the SCTP base protocol specification [RFC4960] specifies the interaction with the application

UDP.why: UDP primitives and features, such as checksum control, DF, TTL and ECN, are unified in passes 2 and 3.
UDP.quote: The set of pass 1 primitives for UDP and UDP-Lite is documented in [RFC8304].
UDP.section: 3.4. Primitives Provided by UDP and UDP-Lite

UDP-Lite.why: UDP-Lite's checksum coverage primitives are covered in passes 2 and 3.

LEDBAT.why: LEDBAT's service and its tunable parameters are analysed and exposed as the CONFIGURE.LEDBAT primitive.
LEDBAT.quote: We also define a primitive to enable/disable and configure the Low Extra Delay Background Transport (LEDBAT) unicast congestion control mechanism.

rejected.why: LEDBAT is tagged directly. The document does not address congestion control in general.
The sockets API is used as a source of primitives, but the document is about transport features rather than extending sockets.
DSCP and Diffserv are mentioned only as parameters applications can set.
ECN get/set is listed as a UDP primitive but is only a minor item.
PMTUD configuration for SCTP is one primitive among many.
The document does not bind one protocol over another transport. It catalogues transport features.

RFC8304.title: Transport Features of the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) and Lightweight UDP (UDP-Lite)
RFC8304.summary: Informational TAPS-WG document summarizing the transport service primitives (CONNECT, SEND, RECEIVE, checksum, DF, TTL, DSCP, ECN, etc.) that UDP and UDP-Lite expose to applications, as input to RFC 8303, with an appendix on multicast socket primitives.

UDP.why: The whole document catalogues the application-visible primitives and features of UDP, so UDP readers would want it.
UDP.quote: describes the transport protocol interface primitives provided by the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) and the Lightweight User Datagram Protocol (UDP-Lite) transport protocols

UDP-Lite.why: Section 3.2 specifically covers UDP-Lite primitives such as SET_CHECKSUM_COVERAGE and SET_MIN_COVERAGE.
UDP-Lite.quote: The sending interface of UDP-Lite differs from that of UDP by the addition of a single (socket) option that communicates the checksum coverage length.

TAPS.why: It is the pass-1 analysis for the TAPS transport-features work, providing input to RFC 8303.
TAPS.quote: The description in Section 3 follows the methodology defined by the IETF TAPS Working Group in [RFC8303].

rejected.why: The sockets API is the interface through which primitives are described, but the document is about UDP/UDP-Lite transport features, not sockets API extensions.
Multicast primitives appear only in an appendix included for completeness; the WG explicitly does not consider multicast.
PMTUD and PLPMTUD are mentioned in the SET_DF and GET_MMS primitives, but only as context, not as a subject of the document.
SET_ECN and GET_ECN are individual primitives; ECN itself is not specified or analysed here.
The checksum controls are UDP-specific primitives, covered by the UDP and UDP-Lite tags.
IPv6 is only referenced for hop-limit and socket primitives, not specified or analysed.

RFC8305.title: Happy Eyeballs Version 2: Better Connectivity Using Concurrency
RFC8305.summary: Specifies the Happy Eyeballs v2 algorithm, which races connection attempts across IPv6 and IPv4 addresses, covering DNS query handling, address sorting, staggered connection attempts, and IPv6-only NAT64/DNS64 support; obsoletes RFC 6555.

happy eyeballs.why: The document is the specification of the Happy Eyeballs algorithm itself, including timing values, sorting and connection racing.
happy eyeballs.quote: This document defines the algorithm for "Happy Eyeballs", a technique for reducing user-visible delays on dual-stack hosts.

DNS64.why: A whole section specifies client behaviour for IPv6-only networks with DNS64, including local address synthesis when AAAA records are broken.
DNS64.quote: The combined use of NAT64 [RFC6146] and DNS64 [RFC6147] is a popular solution that is being deployed and requires changes in client devices.
DNS64.section: 7. Supporting IPv6-Only Networks with NAT64 and DNS64

NAT64.why: Section 7 specifies client-side NAT64 prefix discovery and address synthesis, so NAT64 readers would want it.
NAT64.quote: the Happy Eyeballs engine will need to perform NAT64 address synthesis for them.

rejected.why: DNS queries are used as input to the algorithm, but the document does not extend or specify DNS itself.
TCP handshakes and retransmission timers are the substrate for timing the attempts, not the subject of the document.
The document prefers IPv6 and addresses dual-stack behaviour, but it does not specify IPv6 itself.
Mentioned only as an alternative approach for client devices, not specified.
Mentioned only as a limitation that is explicitly out of scope.

RFC8306.title: Extensions to the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) for Point-to-Multipoint Traffic Engineering Label Switched Paths
RFC8306.summary: RFC 8306 (obsoleting RFC 6006) extends PCEP with objects, flags, TLVs, objective functions, metrics and error codes so a PCC can request and a PCE can compute paths for point-to-multipoint MPLS/GMPLS TE LSPs.

PCE.why: The whole document specifies PCEP extensions (P2MP END-POINTS, RP flags, SERO/SRRO, BNC, fragmentation, errors) for P2MP path computation.
PCE.quote: This document describes extensions to the PCE Communication Protocol (PCEP) to handle requests and responses for the computation of paths for P2MP TE LSPs.

MPLS.why: The subject is computing paths for P2MP MPLS/GMPLS TE LSPs, so MPLS TE readers would want it. This is a secondary tag.
MPLS.quote: [RFC4875] describes how to set up point-to-multipoint (P2MP) Traffic Engineering Label Switched Paths (TE LSPs) for use in Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) networks.

rejected.why: Only the ERO/SERO/SRRO encodings are borrowed from RSVP-TE. The document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE signalling.
A single capability flag is defined in the OSPF PCE Capability Flags for discovery. That is a minor part of the document.
The IS-IS PCE discovery sub-TLV reuses the same flag as OSPF. It is incidental to the document.
GMPLS is mentioned only as an applicable environment. The document is not about GMPLS itself.
PCEP is carried over TCP and the document merely relies on it as transport.
The traffic-engineering aspect is already covered by the PCE tag, which sits under that topic.

RFC8307.title: Well-Known URIs for the WebSocket Protocol
RFC8307.summary: RFC 8307 updates RFC 6455 to extend the RFC 5785 "/.well-known/" path prefix mechanism to the "ws" and "wss" WebSocket URI schemes, sharing the existing IANA suffix registry.

WebSocket.why: The document updates the WebSocket Protocol specification (RFC 6455) to allow well-known URIs for the ws and wss schemes, so WebSocket readers need it.
WebSocket.quote: The present memo formally updates [RFC6455] to extend the use of [RFC5785] well-known URIs to the URI schemes "ws" and "wss".

URI.why: The subject is well-known URI path prefix usage and its extension to additional URI schemes (ws, wss), which is URI scheme matter.
URI.quote: [RFC5785] defines a path prefix, "/.well-known", that can be used by well-known URIs.

rejected.why: HTTP(S) well-known URIs are the origin of the mechanism and the ws/wss mapping refers to HTTP(S) URIs, but the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
CoAP is mentioned only as another scheme that adopted the well-known mechanism; the document is not about it.
The document explicitly requires no IANA actions and only notes that the existing suffix registry is shared.

RFC8308.title: Extension Negotiation in the Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol
RFC8308.summary: RFC 8308 defines an SSH extension negotiation mechanism (ext-info-c/ext-info-s indicators and the SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO message) and initial extensions server-sig-algs, delay-compression, no-flow-control and elevation, updating RFCs 4251-4254.

SSH.why: The document extends the SSH transport, authentication and connection protocols with an extension negotiation mechanism and defines four extensions. It is squarely about SSH.
SSH.quote: defining a mechanism for Secure Shell (SSH) clients and servers to exchange information about supported protocol extensions confidentially after SSH key exchange

rejected.why: The document creates an Extension Names registry, but that is boilerplate-level IANA content and the main body is about SSH, not IANA guidance.
The delay-compression extension renegotiates SSH compression algorithms, but this is a small part of an SSH extension mechanism and does not define a compression format.
RSA with SHA-256/512 is the motivating use case, but it is specified in RFC 8332, not here.
server-sig-algs helps public-key authentication, but the document is about SSH extension negotiation. The SSH tag covers it.

RFC8309.title: Service Models Explained
RFC8309.summary: Informational RFC explaining what YANG customer service models (e.g., L3SM) are, how they differ from service delivery and network element models, and where they fit in an SDN architecture.

YANG.why: The document is about YANG service modules and how they are classified (customer service model, service delivery model, network element model). Readers of YANG modelling would want it.
YANG.quote: A service model is a specific type of data model.  It describes a service and the parameters of the service in a portable way

SDN.why: Section 4 places service models in SDN architectures with orchestrators and controllers, and explains the service interface. This is a substantial part of the document.
SDN.quote: The document also shows where a service model might fit into an SDN architecture

rejected.why: L3SM is the main example, but the document does not specify or extend L3VPN. It uses it to illustrate service models.
NETCONF and RESTCONF are mentioned only as possible transports for exchanging service models.
This is the parent of YANG and SDN, so it is implied. The document does not address it more broadly than those tags do.
Policy is discussed briefly in Section 7.2 only as it relates to service model scope, not as an information model for policy.
L2SM and L2VPN YANG models are listed as examples only.

RFC8310.title: Usage Profiles for DNS over TLS and DNS over DTLS
RFC8310.summary: RFC 8310 defines Strict and Opportunistic Privacy usage profiles for DNS over TLS and DTLS, specifies domain-name-based server authentication mechanisms (PKIX, DANE), and sets a (D)TLS protocol profile for DNS clients and servers, updating RFC 7858.

DoT.why: The document updates RFC 7858 (DNS over TLS) and defines usage profiles, authentication mechanisms and a TLS profile for it. DoT is the main subject.
DoT.quote: This document specifies two usage profiles (Strict Privacy and Opportunistic Privacy) for DTLS [RFC6347] and TLS [RFC5246]

DANE.why: A substantial section specifies how DANE TLSA records (_853._tcp / _853._udp) authenticate DNS privacy servers, including the TLS DNSSEC chain extension.
DANE.quote: DANE [RFC6698] provides various mechanisms using DNSSEC to anchor trust for certificates and raw public keys.

rejected.why: This is the parent of DoT, which is already tagged, so the parent is implied.
TLS is the substrate here. The TLS profile (session resumption, raw public keys, no compression) is specific to DNS, and DoT covers it.
DNS over DTLS (RFC 8094) is covered in parallel. However, there is no DoDTLS tag, and DTLS itself is not the subject.
DNSSEC validation is used only as part of the DANE mechanism. The document does not specify DNSSEC itself.
EDNS(0) padding and client subnet are mentioned only as recommended countermeasures in the Security Considerations.
DHCP is discussed only as a possible future source of the authentication domain name, and the document specifies no DHCP extension.
PKIX certificate validation is used as an authentication mechanism, but it relies on RFC 5280 and RFC 6125 and defines nothing new about certificates.

gaps.name: DNS over DTLS
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for DNS over DTLS (RFC 8094), which this document profiles alongside DoT.

RFC8311.title: Relaxing Restrictions on Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) Experimentation
RFC8311.summary: RFC 8311 updates RFC 3168 (ECN) and the ECN specs for RTP and DCCP to relax restrictions so Experimental RFCs can explore new ECN uses (different congestion responses, ECT(1) marking, ECN on TCP control packets), and it reclassifies the ECN nonce RFC 3540 as Historic.

ECN.why: The whole document modifies the ECN specification (RFC 3168) to enable experimentation with ECN codepoints, marking, and sender response. It also records the end of the ECN nonce experiment.
ECN.quote: updates RFC 3168, which specifies Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) as an alternative to packet drops for indicating network congestion to endpoints

DCCP.why: A section of the document updates three DCCP CCID profiles (RFCs 4341, 4342, 5622) for ECN codepoint use and nonce removal.
DCCP.quote: each DCCP-Data and DCCP-DataAck packet is sent as ECN Capable. Unless otherwise specified by an Experimental RFC in the IETF document stream, such DCCP senders MUST set the ECT(0) codepoint.
DCCP.section: 6. ECN for DCCP Updates to RFCs 4341, 4342, and 5622

RTP.why: A section updates the ECN for RTP specification (RFC 6679) on ECT codepoint choice and the response to CE marks.
RTP.quote: RFC 6679 [RFC6679] specifies use of ECN for RTP traffic; it allows use of both the ECT(0) and ECT(1) codepoints
RTP.section: 5. ECN for RTP Updates to RFC 6679

TCP.why: One of the three experimentation areas is ECN on TCP control packets (SYN, pure ACKs, window probes) and retransmissions. The document also adds middlebox guidance for TCP.
TCP.quote: RFC 3168 limits the use of ECN with TCP to data packets, excluding retransmissions.

rejected.why: The document is about congestion control responses to ECN, but ECN is a more specific tag under it. Choosing ECN makes the parent redundant.
AQM is discussed as the usual source of CE marks, but the document does not specify or extend any AQM algorithm.
DCTCP is cited only as an example of an aggressive sender response. The document does not specify it.
The document uses an Experimental-RFC mechanism to avoid process exceptions. Its subject matter is still ECN technical restrictions, not IETF procedure.
TRILL is mentioned once, as another protocol that is designing in ECN support. The document is not about it.
TFRC is the congestion control behind DCCP CCIDs 3 and 4. The document only edits ECT wording in those profiles and does not address TFRC itself.

RFC8312.title: CUBIC for Fast Long-Distance Networks
RFC8312.summary: RFC 8312 specifies the CUBIC congestion control algorithm, a sender-side TCP modification using a cubic window growth function for fast long-distance networks.

CUBIC.why: The document exists to specify the CUBIC congestion control algorithm: window increase function, TCP-friendly region, multiplicative decrease, fast convergence, and safety discussion.
CUBIC.quote: CUBIC uses a cubic function instead of a linear window increase function of Standard TCP to improve scalability and stability under fast and long-distance networks.

rejected.why: CUBIC is a congestion control algorithm that modifies only the sender's window adjustment, and it is tagged under congestion control. TCP is the substrate it modifies, and the CUBIC tag is more specific.
NewReno is referenced only as the loss recovery mechanism that CUBIC leaves unchanged.
ECN-Echo is mentioned only as one congestion signal that CUBIC responds to. The document does not specify or extend ECN.
TFRC appears only in a list of Reno-style algorithms that share the linear increase function.
Queue management is mentioned in a single sentence about standing queues, and the document does not address it.

RFC8313.title: Use of Multicast across Inter-domain Peering Points
RFC8313.summary: BCP describing how to set up and operate SSM-based IP multicast delivery between administrative domains across peering points (native, GRE, AMT use cases), with functional, operational, security and privacy guidelines.

multicast.why: The whole document is about deploying and operating inter-domain IP multicast; it covers use cases, routing aspects, provisioning and troubleshooting.
multicast.quote: This document examines the use of Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) across inter-domain peering points for a specified set of deployment scenarios.

AMT.why: Three of the five use cases (3.3-3.5) are built around AMT relays and gateways, and the document discusses relay selection and AMT-specific limits.
AMT.quote: AMT is set up at the peering point if either the peering point or AD-2 is not multicast enabled.

SSM.why: The document restricts itself to SSM and PIM-SSM for inter-domain peering. It also discusses SSM's self-protecting DoS properties.
SSM.quote: in the case of inter-domain peering, it is recommended that only SSM protocols be used

GRE.why: One use case, plus the broadcast-peering recommendation, covers GRE tunnels carrying multicast across the peering point.
GRE.quote: There is a GRE tunnel provisioned over the peering point.
GRE.section: 3.2. Peering Point Enabled with GRE Tunnel

rejected.why: MP-BGP SAFI-2 is used for interconnection but is only a supporting mechanism, not what the document specifies.
PIM-SSM operation is relied on and the assert behaviour is mentioned, but the document does not specify or extend PIM.
IGMP and MLD are cited for joins and filtering, but only as supporting protocols.
The bandwidth management section discusses rate adaptation, but this is a sub-point rather than the document's subject.
Traceroute and mtrace are mentioned only briefly in the troubleshooting section.
The security considerations are mostly boilerplate-like DoS and content-security discussion for this document, not a standalone operational security practice.

RFC8314.title: Cleartext Considered Obsolete: Use of Transport Layer Security (TLS) for Email Submission and Access
RFC8314.summary: RFC 8314 recommends Implicit TLS (TLS 1.2+) for email submission and access between MUAs and servers, registering the pop3s, imaps and submissions ports and updating POP3, IMAP, Submission and SRV-based configuration guidance.

email.why: The document is about securing email submission and access between MUAs and servers. It updates POP, IMAP and Submission and adds a new Received header clause. No narrower email tag covers the whole scope.
email.quote: recommendations for the use of Transport Layer Security (TLS) to provide confidentiality of email traffic between a Mail User Agent (MUA) and a Mail Submission Server or Mail Access Server

TLS.why: It gives deployment guidance for TLS: Implicit TLS versus STARTTLS, minimum versions, ciphersuites, certificate validation, pinning and client certificates.
TLS.quote: TLS version 1.2 or greater be used for all traffic between MUAs and Mail Submission Servers, and also between MUAs and Mail Access Servers.

IMAP.why: It updates IMAP (RFC 3501) with an Implicit TLS port and defines the PREAUTH behaviour with client certificates.
IMAP.quote: When a TCP connection is established for the "imaps" service (default port 993), a TLS handshake begins immediately.

POP3.why: It updates POP3 (RFC 1939) with an Implicit TLS port and the AUTHORIZATION state rules.
POP3.quote: When a TCP connection is established for the "pop3s" service (default port 995), a TLS handshake begins immediately.

SMTP.why: It updates Message Submission (RFC 6409 and RFC 5068) with Implicit TLS on port 465 and defines a new Received clause for the TLS ciphersuite.
SMTP.quote: When a TCP connection is established for the "submissions" service (default port 465), a TLS handshake begins immediately.

rejected.why: SRV, MX and TLSA records are recommended for server discovery, but the document does not define or specify DNS behaviour.
DANE and TLSA are only mentioned as optional certificate validation and advertisement mechanisms (MUAs MAY support DANE). They are not a main subject.
Using RFC 6186 SRV records for MUA configuration is a subsection. The main focus is TLS use, and RFC 6186 is only lightly updated.
Certificate validation is delegated to RFC 7817 and PKIX, so the document does not itself profile certificates.
SASL EXTERNAL is required for client certificate authentication, but it is a supporting mechanism and is not specified or extended here.
DNSSEC signing of records is recommended in passing, but the document is not about DNSSEC.

RFC8315.title: Cancel-Locks in Netnews Articles
RFC8315.summary: Defines the Cancel-Lock and Cancel-Key Netnews header fields, which use hashed secrets to authenticate cancel and supersede requests for articles, and creates an IANA registry of hash algorithms; updates RFC 5537.

Netnews.why: The document defines new Netnews article header fields and their handling by posting, injecting and serving agents, and updates RFC 5537. A reader browsing Netnews would expect to find it.
Netnews.quote: This document defines an extension to the Netnews Article Format that may be used to authenticate the withdrawal of existing articles.

rejected.why: HMAC is only the recommended way to derive the key K. The document does not specify or analyse HMAC itself.
SHA-1 and the SHA-2 family are used as the hash schemes. The document specifies Netnews header fields and a registry, not the hash functions.
Base64 is only the encoding used for the key and lock strings. Nothing new is defined about it.
The IANA section registers the header fields and a hash-algorithm registry. That is boilerplate and not the main subject.
The scheme authenticates withdrawal of articles, but it is specific to Netnews. The Netnews tag is the better fit.
OpenPGP is mentioned only as an alternative signature-based system. The document is not about it.

RFC8316.title: Autonomic Networking Use Case for Distributed Detection of Service Level Agreement (SLA) Violations
RFC8316.summary: An IRTF NMRG informational document describing an autonomic networking use case in which autonomic service agents on network devices use a P2P overlay to place active measurement probes dynamically and detect SLA violations within a resource budget.

autonomic networking.why: The document is an autonomic networking use case: ASAs on nodes autonomically decide which measurement sessions to activate without human intervention.
autonomic networking.quote: This document describes an experimental use case that employs autonomic networking for the monitoring of Service Level Agreements (SLAs).

performance measurement.why: The subject is active measurement probe placement for SLA monitoring, which fits performance measurement in general rather than one specific protocol.
performance measurement.quote: It strives to optimize and dynamically adapt the autonomic deployment of active measurement probes in a way that maximizes the likelihood of detecting service-level violations

rejected.why: A P2P overlay is advocated as the mechanism for sharing measurement data, but the document does not specify a P2P protocol or application. The ACP is named as the candidate overlay.
TWAMP, OWAMP and Cisco SLA Protocol are mentioned only as possible measurement mechanisms to use. The document does not specify or extend them.
It is mentioned only as an example active measurement mechanism and is not specified or extended here.
IPFIX is referenced as passive-measurement background and related work. It is not the subject of the document.
LMAP appears only in the related IETF work section, as a possibly relevant area.
ALTO appears only in the related work list as a possible source of topology information.

gaps.name: Autonomic Networking (ANIMA, Autonomic Service Agents, Autonomic Control Plane)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has autonomic networking as a topic under network management. The tag id appears to be 'autonomic networking' but the exact id should be confirmed against the taxonomy, which lists it as 'autonomic networking [topic]'. No other gap.

RFC8317.title: Ethernet-Tree (E-Tree) Support in Ethernet VPN (EVPN) and Provider Backbone Bridging EVPN (PBB-EVPN)
RFC8317.summary: Specifies how to support the MEF E-Tree rooted-multipoint service in EVPN and PBB-EVPN using a new BGP E-Tree extended community (Leaf-Indication, Leaf label) and a composite PMSI tunnel type bit, with ingress filtering for known unicast and egress filtering for BUM traffic.

EVPN.why: The document extends EVPN and PBB-EVPN procedures and BGP encodings to support E-Tree service.
EVPN.quote: This document discusses how those functional requirements can be met with a solution based on RFC 7432, "BGP MPLS Based Ethernet VPN (EVPN)", with some extensions

rejected.why: RFC 7796 (E-Tree in VPLS) is only compared against; the document is not about VPLS.
BGP is the carrier for the new extended community and PMSI attribute change, but the document is about EVPN E-Tree, not BGP itself.
MPLS is the substrate; the Leaf label is used, but the document does not specify MPLS.
PMSI tunnel attribute from RFC 6514 is modified, but this is for EVPN BUM tunnels, not multicast VPN.
EVPN is the more specific tag; L2VPN is a generic parent.

gaps.name: Ethernet-Tree (E-Tree) service
gaps.why: The document is about the MEF rooted-multipoint E-Tree service itself; the taxonomy has no E-Tree tag.

RFC8318.title: IAB, IESG, and IAOC Selection, Confirmation, and Recall Process: IAOC Advisor for the Nominating Committee
RFC8318.summary: BCP update to RFC 7437 that formalizes the ad hoc practice of the IETF NomCom requesting an advisor knowledgeable about IAOC operations, replacing the earlier informal 'IAOC liaison'.

NomCom.why: The document amends the NomCom procedures in RFC 7437 by adding an IAOC advisor role to the nominating committee, which is squarely NomCom process.
NomCom.quote: Committee members are encouraged to propose the addition of an advisor who is knowledgeable about the operations of the IAOC

rejected.why: NomCom is the more specific child tag and already covers this IETF process BCP; the parent is implied.
The IANA Considerations section only states there are no IANA actions; the document is not about IANA.

RFC8319.title: Support for Adjustable Maximum Router Lifetimes per Link
RFC8319.summary: RFC 8319 updates IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) to raise the maximum Router Lifetime, MaxRtrAdvInterval and AdvDefaultLifetime limits to 65535 seconds so links can tune router advertisement timing.

neighbor discovery.why: The document amends RFC 4861 Router Advertisement timing constants (Router Lifetime, MaxRtrAdvInterval, AdvDefaultLifetime), so it is squarely about IPv6 Neighbor Discovery.
neighbor discovery.quote: This document specifies updates to the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Protocol [RFC4861] to increase the maximum time allowed between sending unsolicited multicast RAs

rejected.why: Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to prevent rogue RAs; the document does not address SEND itself.
3GPP RFCs are cited only as examples of link-specific ND tuning; the document is not about cellular links.
Parent of neighbor discovery, so implied by the more specific tag.
The document reduces unsolicited multicast RA frequency, but it concerns ND timers, not IP multicast routing or group membership.

RFC8320.title: LDP Extensions to Support Maximally Redundant Trees
RFC8320.summary: RFC 8320 defines an LDP MRT Capability TLV and the label-distribution behaviour (MRT-Red, MRT-Blue and Rainbow FECs using LDP multi-topology) that lets LSRs build LSPs for Maximally Redundant Trees, used for IP/LDP fast reroute.

LDP.why: The document extends LDP with a new capability TLV, a status code, and MRT-specific FEC advertisement procedures interpreting RFC 5036.
LDP.quote: This document specifies extensions to the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) to support the creation of Label Switched Paths (LSPs) for Maximally Redundant Trees (MRTs).

IP fast reroute.why: The LSPs for MRT-Blue and MRT-Red exist to provide IP/LDP fast reroute alternates, and the document is the LDP signalling part of the MRT-FRR architecture.
IP fast reroute.quote: A prime use of MRTs is for unicast and multicast IP/LDP Fast Reroute, which we will refer to as "MRT-FRR".

rejected.why: MPLS labels and MT-ID registry are used, but the document is specifically about LDP, which is the more specific tag.
OSPF MRT extensions are referenced as separate documents; this document does not specify them.
IS-IS MRT extensions are only referenced as the IGP basis for MRT computation, not specified here.
PIM MT-ID is mentioned only in a short section about MT-ID value ranges, not as a subject of the document.
Multicast protection with MRT is mentioned in passing; the document's focus is LDP unicast label distribution.
Mentioned only as an example in Security Considerations.

gaps.name: Maximally Redundant Trees (MRT)
gaps.why: The MRT concept and MRT-FRR architecture have no dedicated tag. IP fast reroute is the closest fit, but MRT would be a useful subject page.

RFC8321.title: Alternate-Marking Method for Passive and Hybrid Performance Monitoring
RFC8321.summary: Describes the Alternate-Marking method, which colors live packet flows into blocks so that packet loss, delay and jitter can be measured passively or in a hybrid way, with an operational experiment report.

performance measurement.why: The whole document specifies a passive/hybrid method of measurement for packet loss, delay and delay variation, and maps it to RFC 6390 metric guidelines.
performance measurement.quote: This document describes a method to perform packet loss, delay, and jitter measurements on live traffic.

OAM.why: The method is an OAM performance-monitoring technique, with applications such as BIER OAM marking bits and MPLS performance measurement.
OAM.quote: A lot of work related to Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM), which also includes performance monitoring techniques, has been done by Standards Developing Organizations

rejected.why: IPFIX is only mentioned as a possible way to export timestamps and counters, not specified or extended here.
NTP and PTP are only the clock-synchronization substrate. They are not the subject of the document.
Synchronization requirements are discussed (Section 4.1), but only as a dependency of the method.
TWAMP and OWAMP are mentioned only as possible protocols for carrying data; they are not tagged.
MPLS is an application context and the subject of related drafts. This document is not about MPLS itself.
The DSCP field is used for marking in the experiment, but the document does not address Diffserv itself.

gaps.name: Alternate Marking / IP performance metrics (IPPM)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for IPPM or alternate-marking passive/hybrid measurement methods. The general performance measurement topic is the closest fit.

RFC8322.title: Resource-Oriented Lightweight Information Exchange (ROLIE)
RFC8322.summary: Defines ROLIE, a RESTful approach to publishing, discovering and sharing security automation information by profiling and extending the Atom Publishing Protocol and Atom Syndication Format, with IANA-registered extension points for information types, categories and properties.

Atom.why: The document is a profile and extension of AtomPub and Atom Syndication Format (service documents, feeds, entries, categories, link relations). Readers of Atom would want it.
Atom.quote: This specification extends the Atom Publishing Protocol and Atom Syndication Format to transport and share security automation resource representations.

rejected.why: IODEF is only an example data format that ROLIE entries may reference; the document does not specify or extend it.
