TLS is only the transport security mechanism; Section 5.3 gives usage requirements but defines nothing new about TLS.
HTTP is the substrate for AtomPub; no HTTP semantics are defined or extended.
XML is the encoding used for the Atom elements and namespaces, not the subject.
Incident reports are one example of information shared, but the document is about a general security-automation exchange mechanism, not incident handling. RID is only touched on for compatibility.
Link relations (service, collection, paging) are used within Atom feeds, but the document does not define a link relation framework.
ROLIE URN sub-namespace registrations are IANA boilerplate-level apparatus, not a URN namespace specification.

gaps.name: Security automation information sharing
gaps.why: The document's actual subject, publishing and exchanging security automation content such as vulnerabilities, indicators and checklists, has no matching tag in the taxonomy; the closest ones, security and incident response, are too general or too narrow.

RFC8323.title: CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol) over TCP, TLS, and WebSockets
RFC8323.summary: Specifies how to carry CoAP over TCP, TLS and WebSockets, including message framing, CSM/Ping/Pong/Release/Abort signalling, BERT block-wise extension, Observe changes, four new URI schemes and TLS binding.

CoAP.why: The document defines a new transport binding for CoAP, with framing, signalling, and updates to the Observe and block-wise extensions.
CoAP.quote: This document outlines the changes required to use CoAP over TCP, TLS, and WebSockets transports.

transport mapping.why: It is a classic X-over-TCP/TLS/WebSocket binding, with a layering model and message framing for a reliable byte stream.
transport mapping.quote: this document defines how to transport CoAP over TCP, CoAP over TLS, and CoAP over WebSockets.

WebSocket.why: Section 4 and the Appendix specify the CoAP-over-WebSockets subprotocol, its handshake, and the coap+ws/coaps+ws URI schemes. Readers of WebSocket subprotocols would want it.
WebSocket.quote: the WebSocket Protocol [RFC6455] may be used to transport CoAP requests and responses

URI.why: It defines and registers coap+tcp, coaps+tcp, coap+ws and coaps+ws, and updates the URI decomposition and composition algorithms.
URI.quote: This document introduces four additional URI schemes for identifying CoAP resources

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate. The document does not extend or profile TCP itself.
TLS only secures the connection. The document follows RFC 7925 and RFC 7525 guidance and defines no new TLS mechanism, apart from ALPN identifier registration.
The HTTP Upgrade handshake is only the mechanism that sets up the WebSocket connection.
UDP is discussed only as the alternative transport that CoAP normally uses.
NAT binding timeouts are cited as motivation only.
DTLS is mentioned only as the secure transport CoAP uses over UDP, not as a subject of this document.

RFC8324.title: DNS Privacy, Authorization, Special Uses, Encoding, Characters, Matching, and Root Structure: Time for Another Look?
RFC8324.summary: An Independent Submission by Klensin that surveys tensions between contemporary expectations and the original DNS design (matching, IDN variants, privacy, CLASS, special names, root structure, RRTYPE extensions, transport) and asks whether to replace the DNS or limit its role.

DNS.why: The whole document analyses the DNS design, its protocol limits (multi-type queries, CLASS, loose synchronization, RRTYPEs, transport, inverse lookup, root servers) and whether it should be replaced.
DNS.quote: This document asks the question of whether it is time to either redesign and replace the DNS to match contemporary requirements and expectations

IDN.why: Sections 3.2-3.4 discuss IDNA2003/2008, normalization, case folding, variants and homograph issues as major stresses on DNS matching.
IDN.quote: Matching Part II: Non-ASCII ("Internationalized") Domain Name Labels

special-use domain names.why: A dedicated section discusses special names and private namespaces, citing RFC 6761 and RFC 8244; the title also names special uses.
special-use domain names.quote: "special names" -- labels or pseudo-labels, often in TLD positions, that signal that the full name should not be subject to normal DNS resolution

rejected.why: Query privacy is discussed in one short subsection (3.5) as a patch-versus-design concern, not as a main subject; it mentions RFC 7858 and RFC 7816 only in passing.
DNSSEC appears only as an example of deployment and zone-cut stress, not as a subject of the document.
EDNS(0) is cited for UDP buffer size and deployment issues, not specified or analysed in its own right.
The document is about the DNS specifically, not architectural principles of the Internet in general.
The more specific DNS tag already covers the document, so the parent is implied.

gaps.name: DNS root server system and root zone governance
gaps.why: Sections 3.10 and 3.12 discuss root server distribution and centrally controlled root as a policy and technical topic, and the taxonomy has no tag for the root or DNS governance.

RFC8325.title: Mapping Diffserv to IEEE 802.11
RFC8325.summary: Specifies recommended mappings between Diffserv DSCP markings (per RFC 4594 service classes) and IEEE 802.11 User Priorities/Access Categories, covering downstream and upstream handling and related security guidance.

Diffserv.why: The document maps Diffserv service classes and DSCPs to 802.11 UP/AC and recommends handling of DSCP markings at the wireless edge.
Diffserv.quote: This document specifies a set of mappings from Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) to IEEE 802.11 User Priority (UP)

WiFi.why: It concerns IP QoS over IEEE 802.11 WLANs, including EDCA access categories, the QoS Map element and AP behaviour.
WiFi.quote: This document is applicable to the use of Differentiated Services that interconnect with IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs

rejected.why: Parent of Diffserv, which is the more specific tag and is already chosen.
Mentioned only as an example tunnel for upstream packets, not specified or extended.
RFC 7561 is mentioned only to explain a conflict with GSMA mappings, and the document is not about PMIPv6.
The security section gives QoS-abuse mitigation advice, but this is a minor part of a mapping specification.
The GSMA/IPX mapping is mentioned only to exclude it; the document explicitly excludes 3G/4G.

RFC8326.title: Graceful BGP Session Shutdown
RFC8326.summary: Defines the well-known BGP community GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN and the operational procedure using it (lowering LOCAL_PREF) to reduce packet loss when EBGP sessions are deliberately shut down for maintenance.

BGP communities.why: The document's core deliverable is a new well-known BGP community and its use by routing policy; readers of BGP communities would want it.
BGP communities.quote: This document standardizes a new well-known BGP community, GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN, to signal the graceful shutdown of paths.

BGP.why: It specifies operational procedures for gracefully shutting down EBGP sessions, including policy and convergence behaviour, which is BGP operations.
BGP.quote: The goal of this procedure is to retain the paths to be shut down between the peers, but with a lower LOCAL_PREF value

rejected.why: Maintenance operations are discussed, but the subject is BGP routing procedure, which is covered by the BGP tags.
Route reflectors appear only in explaining path hiding and in an informative appendix, not as the document's subject.
The security considerations only note abuse for inbound traffic engineering, which is boilerplate-level.
The document concerns BGP convergence during planned shutdown, not fast-reroute mechanisms.

RFC8327.title: Mitigating the Negative Impact of Maintenance through BGP Session Culling
RFC8327.summary: A BCP describing BGP Session Culling: tearing down BGP sessions ahead of lower-layer maintenance, either voluntarily via administrative shutdown or involuntarily via IXP packet filters on TCP port 179.

BGP.why: The document specifies an operational practice for BGP sessions: administrative shutdown, Hold Timer expiry and convergence. This is BGP operations.
BGP.quote: BGP Session Culling is the practice of ensuring BGP sessions are forcefully torn down before maintenance activities on a lower-layer network commence

operational security.why: It gives operator and IXP practice for maintenance, including packet-filter design and hardware caveats. This is infrastructure operational practice, but it is not mainly about security.
operational security.quote: the Caretaker of the fabric could choose to cull BGP sessions on behalf of the Operators connected to the fabric.

rejected.why: BGP runs over TCP port 179 and the filters match it, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
IEEE 802.1AX is mentioned only as a hardware limitation for filters, not as a subject.
The packet filters are ACLs used for session culling, not a study of firewalls or middlebox traversal.
The topic is general, and the operational-practice content is better covered by the more specific tags.

RFC8328.title: Policy-Based Management Framework for the Simplified Use of Policy Abstractions (SUPA)
RFC8328.summary: Informational framework describing SUPA, a policy-based management approach that defines generic policy information models (GPIM, EPRIM) and derives generic YANG data models to express network-wide policy rules for controllers and network elements.

policy management.why: The document is a policy-based management framework built on generic and ECA policy information models, which is the core of the policy-based network management topic.
policy management.quote: The GPIM defines concepts and terminology needed by policy management independent of the form and content of the policy rule.

YANG.why: A substantial part of the framework is about deriving base policy YANG data models from the information models and the process for creating them.
YANG.quote: both the GPIM and the combination of the GPIM and the EPRIM are translated into generic YANG modules.

rejected.why: NETCONF is mentioned only in the YANG definition and in the Security Considerations pointer. The document does not specify or extend it.
Controllers and orchestrators appear in the architecture, but the document is about policy models and not SDN control-plane separation.
Declarative or intent-based policy is explicitly out of scope, and no autonomic mechanisms are described.

RFC8329.title: Framework for Interface to Network Security Functions
RFC8329.summary: RFC 8329 defines the I2NSF framework and reference model (consumer-facing, NSF-facing and registration interfaces), threats from externally provided NSFs, and the ECA flow security policy structure for network security functions.

I2NSF.why: The document is the I2NSF framework itself: reference model, interfaces, policy structure, registration and capability negotiation.
I2NSF.quote: This document describes the framework for Interface to Network Security Functions (I2NSF) and defines a reference model (including major functional components) for I2NSF.

rejected.why: Parent of I2NSF; implied by the I2NSF tag, and the document is not about firewalls themselves, only listing them as NSF types.
SDN and NFV are the deployment environment, not the subject of the document.
ACL YANG is only referenced for comparison in Section 7.3; no model is defined here.
IPFIX is mentioned only as a source of registration categories, not specified or extended.
RFC 5575 flow specification packet matching types are cited for reuse only.
DOTS and syslog are mentioned only as other protocols that may provide monitoring functionality.

RFC8330.title: OSPF Traffic Engineering (OSPF-TE) Link Availability Extension for Links with Variable Discrete Bandwidth
RFC8330.summary: Defines a new Availability SCSI-TLV (Generalized SCSI) for GMPLS OSPF-TE to advertise <availability, bandwidth> pairs for links with variable discrete bandwidth such as microwave and copper.

GMPLS.why: The extension is a GMPLS ISCD Generalized SCSI-TLV carried in GMPLS OSPF-TE LSAs, so GMPLS readers need it.
GMPLS.quote: This document defines a new type of Generalized Switching Capability-Specific Information (SCSI) TLV to extend the Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) routing protocol.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF-TE LSAs with a new TLV and specifies its processing procedures.
OSPF.quote: A node that has link(s) with variable discrete bandwidth attached should include an <availability, bandwidth> information list in its OSPF-TE LSA messages.

rejected.why: The signaling extension is defined in a separate draft. This document covers only OSPF advertisement.
PCE is mentioned only as a possible consumer of the flooded information. Path computation is out of scope.
The document is about OSPF-TE advertisement, which the GMPLS and OSPF tags already cover. It does not address TE in general.
The document specifies Opaque LSAs in OSPFv2 only.

RFC8331.title: RTP Payload for Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (SMPTE) ST 291-1 Ancillary Data
RFC8331.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for carrying SMPTE ST 291-1 ancillary data (timecode, captions, AFD) from SDI video, with the video/smpte291 media type and its SDP parameters and offer/answer rules.

RTP payload format.why: The document's purpose is to define a new RTP payload format, including header fields, timestamp and marker bit rules for ANC data.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo describes a Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) payload format for the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (SMPTE) ancillary space (ANC) data

SDP.why: Substantial sections define SDP mapping, DID_SDID/VPID_Code fmtp parameters, FID grouping and offer/answer behaviour for this payload.
SDP.quote: The optional parameters VPID_Code and DID_SDID, when present, are included in the "a=fmtp" attribute line of SDP

media types.why: The document registers a new media type video/smpte291 with full template and parameters.
media types.quote: This RTP payload format is identified using the "video/smpte291" media type, which is registered in accordance with RFC 4855

rejected.why: RTP is the transport the payload format is built for; the more specific RTP payload format tag covers this, and the RTP protocol itself is not extended.
ANC data is not an audio/video codec; it is ancillary metadata carried alongside video.
Only mentioned in the Security Considerations boilerplate as an applicable profile.
ABNF is used only to define one parameter's syntax; it is not the subject.
The payload is for real-time professional video interchange, not about streaming delivery or operations.

gaps.name: SMPTE SDI ancillary data / professional video
gaps.why: The document is about carrying SMPTE ST 291-1 ancillary data from serial digital interfaces over IP; the taxonomy has no tag for professional broadcast video or SDI.

RFC8332.title: Use of RSA Keys with SHA-256 and SHA-512 in the Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol
RFC8332.summary: RFC 8332 updates RFCs 4252 and 4253 to define the SSH public key algorithms rsa-sha2-256 and rsa-sha2-512, which use existing RSA keys with SHA-256/SHA-512 signatures for server and client authentication.

SSH.why: The document extends the SSH transport and authentication protocols with new public key algorithm names, encodings, negotiation and client authentication behaviour.
SSH.quote: define new public key algorithms for use of RSA keys with SHA-256 and SHA-512 for server and client authentication in SSH connections

RSA.why: The document specifies RSA signature use with SHA-2 and discusses key size and PKCS#1 v1.5 padding and verification, which is relevant to readers of RSA.
RSA.quote: Signing and verifying using these algorithms is performed according to the RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 scheme in [RFC8017] using SHA-2 [SHS] as hash.

SHA.why: The new algorithms are defined by moving from SHA-1 to SHA-2 hashes (SHA-256 and SHA-512) in SSH signatures.
SHA.quote: For the algorithm "rsa-sha2-256", the hash used is SHA-256. For the algorithm "rsa-sha2-512", the hash used is SHA-512.

rejected.why: The document concerns SSH host and user key algorithms, not a public key infrastructure.
It touches SSH user authentication only; SASL is not involved.
The IANA registry update is boilerplate, so it is not evidence for this tag.
Authentication is addressed only through SSH, and the SSH tag already covers it.

RFC8333.title: Micro-loop Prevention by Introducing a Local Convergence Delay
RFC8333.summary: Defines a router-local mechanism for link-state IGPs that delays the RIB/FIB update after a single local link-down event (ULOOP_DELAY_DOWN_TIMER) to prevent local transient micro-loops, working alongside Fast Reroute.

routing architecture.why: The document specifies a loop-free convergence mechanism for link-state IGPs (micro-loop prevention), a cross-protocol routing design matter rather than a single protocol. No specific IGP tag fits since it applies to both OSPF and IS-IS generically.
routing architecture.quote: This document describes a mechanism for link-state routing protocols that prevents local transient forwarding loops in case of link failure.

IP fast reroute.why: The mechanism is motivated by and designed to preserve FRR protection (LFA, RLFA, MRT, TE FRR). A substantial part of the document discusses FRR inefficiency caused by micro-loops.
IP fast reroute.quote: it may only be used for planned maintenance or when Fast Reroute (FRR) protects the traffic during the time between the link failure and the IGP convergence.

rejected.why: OSPF is only cited as one IGP whose timers (MinLSInterval) the mechanism builds on; the document is not specific to OSPF.
IS-IS is mentioned only for its LSP generation timer; the mechanism is protocol-agnostic across link-state IGPs.
An RSVP-TE tunnel appears only in an example of FRR inefficiency; the document is not about RSVP-TE.
LDP is mentioned only as the label distribution in the example network, not as a subject of the document.
TE tunnels and IGP shortcut appear only in one illustrative example.

gaps.name: micro-loop / transient forwarding loop avoidance (loop-free convergence)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for IGP convergence and micro-loop prevention (RFC 5715, oFIB, PLSN); it is covered only by the broad routing architecture tag.

RFC8334.title: Launch Phase Mapping for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)
RFC8334.summary: Defines an EPP extension mapping (launch namespace) for domain registry launch phases such as sunrise, landrush and claims, covering applications, trademark validation, claims notices, status values, and extended check/info/create/update/delete commands.

EPP.why: The document specifies a new EPP extension that adds launch-phase elements to the EPP domain mapping commands and responses.
EPP.quote: This document describes an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) extension mapping for the provisioning and management of domain name registrations and applications

rejected.why: XML is only the encoding and schema language of EPP; the document does not define anything new about XML itself.
EPP is the more specific child tag and is already chosen, so the parent is implied.
The document concerns registry provisioning, not DNS protocol or resolution behaviour.
The IANA section only registers the namespace, schema and EPP extension. It is boilerplate and not the main subject.
RDAP is not discussed. The document covers provisioning, not registration data access.

gaps.name: Trademark Clearinghouse / launch phases (sunrise, landrush, claims)
gaps.why: Domain registry launch processes and trademark claims handling have no specific tag. The nearest fit is the domain registration branch (EPP).

RFC8335.title: PROBE: A Utility for Probing Interfaces
RFC8335.summary: Defines PROBE, a ping-like diagnostic that uses new ICMPv4/ICMPv6 Extended Echo Request and Reply messages, carrying an Interface Identification Object, to query a probed interface's status via a proxy node, and updates RFC 4884.

ICMP.why: The document specifies new ICMP message types (Extended Echo Request/Reply) for ICMPv4 and ICMPv6, their processing rules, and updates RFC 4884's list of extensible ICMP messages.
ICMP.quote: It sends an ICMP Extended Echo Request message from a local interface, called the probing interface, to a proxy interface.

traceroute.why: PROBE is a PING-like path and interface diagnostic utility; the traceroute and path discovery tools tag is the closest fit for diagnostic utilities, and the appendix describes the application.
traceroute.quote: This document describes a network diagnostic tool called PROBE.

rejected.why: ARP table state is consulted and reported, but only as a data source, not specified or extended.
The IPv6 Neighbor Cache is consulted for reachability state, but the document does not define neighbor discovery behaviour.
Interface name and if-index come from RFC 7223 but only by reference; the document is not about the data model.
The tool is an operational diagnostic, but the more specific ICMP tag already fits.
IANA registrations are boilerplate to the protocol definition.

RFC8336.title: The ORIGIN HTTP/2 Frame
RFC8336.summary: Defines the HTTP/2 ORIGIN frame, which lets a server tell clients which origins a connection is authoritative for, and relaxes the DNS check for connection coalescing.

HTTP/2.why: The document extends HTTP/2 with a new frame type and specifies its syntax, processing, Origin Set and coalescing and authority behaviour.
HTTP/2.quote: This document defines a new HTTP/2 frame type ([RFC7540], Section 4) called ORIGIN

rejected.why: TLS certificates and SNI are used to establish authority, but the document defines nothing new about TLS.
The document relaxes the need to consult DNS for authority, but it does not specify DNS protocol or operations.
The HTTP/2 tag is more specific; the 421 status code is only referenced.
Certificate checks are mentioned as a requirement that still applies, not as the subject.
The security considerations discuss risks, but the document is a protocol extension, not a web security mechanism.
Mentioned only as a possible mitigation in Security Considerations.

RFC8337.title: Model-Based Metrics for Bulk Transport Capacity
RFC8337.summary: Experimental IPPM framework defining Model-Based Metrics, which derive IP diagnostic tests (traffic patterns and statistical criteria) from TCP models to assess whether a path or subpath can meet a Target Transport Performance for bulk transport capacity.

performance measurement.why: The document defines a new class of IP performance metrics and test methodology (test streams, statistical criteria, SPRT, validation) for measuring path capacity. This is the core subject.
performance measurement.quote: Model-Based Metrics nominally yield pass/fail evaluations of the ability of standard transport protocols to meet the specific performance objective over some network path.

TCP.why: Test streams and the run-length criteria derive from Reno-style TCP models (slowstart, AIMD, delayed ACK, TSO bursts). Section 4.1 analyses TCP properties in depth, so TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: Mathematical TCP models are used to determine traffic parameters and subsequently to design traffic patterns that mimic TCP

congestion control.why: The model of congestion control response to loss and ECN marks drives target_run_length. The standing queue tests also address AQM and bufferbloat behaviour at bottlenecks.
congestion control.quote: Assume the transport protocol is using standard Reno-style Additive Increase Multiplicative Decrease (AIMD) congestion control

rejected.why: Standing queue tests check that bottlenecks behave progressively, but AQM is only a property being tested for, not the subject.
ECN CE marks are counted alongside losses in the statistical criteria, but ECN itself is not specified or extended.
The tests are for in situ and path measurement, not benchmarking methodology for devices, although bench testing is mentioned.
LMAP is only referenced for security considerations. The document is not about large-scale measurement platforms.
SCTP appears only as an example of a self-clocked protocol, with no substantive treatment.

gaps.name: IPPM / IP performance metrics (bulk transport capacity)
gaps.why: The taxonomy's performance measurement topic fits only generally. There is no specific tag for IPPM metrics frameworks such as one-way loss, reordering and capacity metrics.

RFC8338.title: Signaling Root-Initiated Point-to-Multipoint Pseudowire Using LDP
RFC8338.summary: Specifies LDP signaling for root-initiated point-to-multipoint pseudowires, defining new P2MP PW Upstream and P2P PW Downstream FEC elements, a capability TLV, typed wildcard handling, and a wildcard PMSI tunnel type (updating RFC 7385).

pseudowire.why: The whole document defines how P2MP pseudowires are set up and maintained, including FEC elements, status handling, and interface parameters.
pseudowire.quote: This document specifies a mechanism to signal Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) Pseudowire (PW) trees using LDP.

LDP.why: The document extends LDP with new FEC types, a P2MP PW Capability TLV, typed wildcard FEC formats and label mapping procedures.
LDP.quote: this document defines a new Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC), TLVs, parameters, and status codes to facilitate LDP signaling and maintaining P2MP PWs.

rejected.why: Mentioned as the service context for P2MP PWs, but the document is about PW signaling rather than L2VPN services themselves. Pseudowire is the more specific fit.
Only one of two options for the transport P2MP LSP. The document does not specify RSVP-TE.
PMSI tunnel types come from the BGP multicast VPN specifications, but they are reused here. The document does not address MVPN.
Multicast traffic is carried by the PW, but the document specifies PW signaling, not multicast routing.
MPLS LSPs serve as the substrate. The document does not define MPLS itself.

RFC8339.title: Definition of P2MP PW TLV for Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping Mechanisms
RFC8339.summary: Defines a new P2MP Pseudowire sub-TLV for the MPLS LSP Ping Target FEC Stack TLV, so operators can verify data-plane connectivity of P2MP pseudowires carried over P2MP MPLS LSPs.

pseudowire.why: The document is about identifying and testing P2MP pseudowires with a new LSP Ping sub-TLV, so the pseudowire page fits.
pseudowire.quote: This document describes a mechanism to verify connectivity of Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) Pseudowires (PWs) using LSP Ping.

OAM.why: It extends LSP Ping, an MPLS OAM mechanism, for data-plane failure detection and connectivity verification.
OAM.quote: Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping is a widely deployed Operation, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) mechanism in MPLS networks.

MPLS.why: It extends MPLS LSP Ping (RFC 8029) with a new Target FEC Stack sub-TLV and uses MPLS label stacks and GAL/ACH encapsulation.
MPLS.quote: This document defines a new P2MP Pseudowire sub-TLV for the Target Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) Stack for P2MP PWs.

rejected.why: VPLS is only mentioned as the service whose instance the AGI identifies. The document is not about VPLS.
P2MP RSVP-TE is only one way to set up the transport LSP, so it is background.
mLDP is only an alternative way to set up the transport LSP, and the document does not extend LDP.
The P2MP trees carry multicast traffic, but the document does not address IP multicast routing.

gaps.name: LSP Ping / MPLS OAM
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MPLS LSP Ping or MPLS OAM as a technology. The closest fits are the generic OAM topic and MPLS.

RFC8340.title: YANG Tree Diagrams
RFC8340.summary: RFC 8340 (BCP 215) documents the syntax of YANG module tree diagrams, including node notation, usage guidelines for RFCs, and the representation of YANG schema mount trees.

YANG.why: The whole document defines the notation for graphically representing YANG data models, so YANG readers would look for it.
YANG.quote: This document captures the current syntax used in YANG module tree diagrams.

rejected.why: RFC 8040 is only referenced for the yang-data statement; the document says nothing about the RESTCONF protocol.
Not discussed. The document is about diagram notation, not the configuration protocol.
ietf-ospf appears only as an example module mounted in a schema mount diagram.
RFC 7407 (SNMP configuration model) is used only as a source of example diagrams.

RFC8341.title: Network Configuration Access Control Model
RFC8341.summary: RFC 8341 defines NACM, an access control model and YANG module (ietf-netconf-acm) that restricts which NETCONF and RESTCONF users may invoke protocol operations, access datastore nodes, and receive notifications, obsoleting RFC 6536.

NETCONF.why: The document specifies the access control model for NETCONF, covering protocol operations, datastore access and notifications, with detailed per-operation rules (edit-config, copy-config, commit, etc.).
NETCONF.quote: There is a need for standard mechanisms to restrict NETCONF or RESTCONF protocol access for particular users to a preconfigured subset of all available NETCONF or RESTCONF protocol operations and content.

RESTCONF.why: A substantial part of the document maps RESTCONF HTTP methods to NACM access operations (Table 1) and describes request URI handling.
RESTCONF.quote: Support for the RESTCONF protocol has been added.  The RESTCONF operations are similar to the NETCONF operations

YANG.why: The document defines the ietf-netconf-acm YANG module, with the default-deny-write and default-deny-all extensions, and handles YANG 1.1 action and notification statements.
YANG.quote: The NACM procedures and data model have been updated to support new data modeling capabilities in version 1.1 of the YANG data modeling language.

rejected.why: The document is about access control and authorization. However, the NETCONF tag is more specific, and the taxonomy has no more specific authorization child that fits, so I did not add this topic tag.
RADIUS is mentioned only as a possible external source of group names. The document does not specify or extend it.
SSH appears only as the mandatory secure transport, in Security Considerations.
TLS appears only as the secure transport for RESTCONF, in Security Considerations.
HTTP methods are mapped to access operations, but HTTP is the RESTCONF substrate and the document specifies nothing new about it.
XML is the encoding of NETCONF content and the examples. It is not the subject of the document.

RFC8342.title: Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA)
RFC8342.summary: Defines the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) for YANG/NETCONF/RESTCONF, adding <intended> and <operational> datastores, origin metadata, and updating RFC 7950 XPath and action context rules.

YANG.why: The document defines the datastore architecture binding YANG data models to management protocols, specifies two YANG modules (ietf-datastores, ietf-origin), and updates RFC 7950.
YANG.quote: The revised architectural model of datastores supports additional datastores for systems that support more advanced processing chains converting configuration to operational state.

NETCONF.why: The datastore model extends and refines the NETCONF datastore concept (<running>, <candidate>, <startup>), and substantial text discusses NETCONF behaviour and operations.
NETCONF.quote: The NETCONF <get> operation returns the contents of <running> together with the operational state.

rejected.why: RESTCONF is a protocol the architecture applies to, but the document does not specify or extend it; it is mentioned only as a consumer of the model.
Parent of the chosen tags, so it is implied.
BGP appears only as a fictional example data model in Appendix C.
I2RS is mentioned only as inspiration for the example ephemeral datastore in Appendix B.
XML is used only for example snippets and as the encoding, not as a subject.
DHCP is mentioned only as a source of learned configuration in the examples.

RFC8343.title: A YANG Data Model for Interface Management
RFC8343.summary: Defines the ietf-interfaces YANG module for configuring and monitoring network interfaces (NMDA-compliant), including mapping to IF-MIB, and obsoletes RFC 7223.

YANG.why: The document's core content is a YANG module (ietf-interfaces) with config and state data for interfaces, which other modules augment.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model [RFC7950] for the management of network interfaces.

MIB.why: A whole section maps YANG nodes to IF-MIB objects (ifIndex, ifName, counters), and the module has an if-mib feature; useful to MIB readers migrating to YANG.
MIB.quote: If the device implements the IF-MIB [RFC2863], each entry in the "/interfaces/interface" list in the operational state is typically mapped to one ifEntry.

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the access protocol and appears in examples and error handling; the document defines a data model, not NETCONF itself.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as an access protocol.
Only the IF-MIB mapping is discussed; the document does not specify SNMP itself, so the MIB tag covers it.
Ethernet, bonding and VLAN modules are informative examples in appendices, not the subject.
Parent of the chosen YANG and MIB tags, so it is implied.

RFC8344.title: A YANG Data Model for IP Management
RFC8344.summary: Defines the NMDA-compliant YANG module ietf-ip, which augments the ietf-interfaces model with per-interface IPv4/IPv6 configuration and operational state (addresses, neighbor caches, autoconfiguration), obsoleting RFC 7277.

YANG.why: The document's whole purpose is a new YANG module (ietf-ip) with its tree, features and typedefs.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model [RFC7950] for management of IP implementations.

IPv6.why: A substantial part of the model covers IPv6 settings: address status, MTU, forwarding, duplicate address detection and autoconfiguration. Readers of the IPv6 subject would want it.
IPv6.quote: The data model covers configuration of per-interface IPv4 and IPv6 parameters as well as mappings of IP addresses to link-layer addresses.

IPv4.why: Half the model manages IPv4 per-interface parameters, including addresses, netmasks, MTU, forwarding and the ARP cache.
IPv4.quote: The data model defines two containers per interface -- "ipv4" and "ipv6", representing the IPv4 and IPv6 address families.

MIB.why: A full section maps the YANG data nodes to IP-MIB objects, which is relevant to readers of MIB modules.
MIB.quote: If the device implements the IP-MIB [RFC4293], each entry in the "ipv4/address" and "ipv6/address" lists is mapped to one ipAddressEntry

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the protocol used to access the model, in examples and Security Considerations. The document does not specify it.
The neighbor list models the Neighbor Cache, but the document does not specify or extend neighbor discovery. It only exposes the cache's state.
The autoconf container configures SLAAC parameters, but this is a small part of the model and the document does not define SLAAC.
The IPv4 neighbor list represents the ARP cache, but ARP itself is only referenced.
The YANG and MIB tags already cover the subject more specifically.

RFC8345.title: A YANG Data Model for Network Topologies
RFC8345.summary: Defines the abstract base YANG data models (ietf-network and ietf-network-topology, plus NMDA-state companions) for representing network inventories and layered topologies of nodes, links and termination points, to be augmented by technology-specific models.

YANG.why: The RFC's core content is a set of YANG modules (ietf-network, ietf-network-topology and state companions) and design decisions about modelling topologies, so YANG readers would want it.
YANG.quote: This document defines an abstract (generic, or base) YANG data model for network/service topologies and inventories.

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the protocol used to access the data; mentioned in Security Considerations as a transport, not specified here.
Only referenced as an access protocol in Security Considerations; the document defines nothing about it.
I2RS is the originating working group and a use context, but the document does not specify the I2RS interface itself.
OSPF and IS-IS are only examples of network types that augmenting models may cover; this document is protocol-independent.
SDN controller overlays appear as a use case, but the document is a data model, not about SDN as a subject.
Identifiers use the inet:uri type, but this is a modelling choice, not a document about URIs.

gaps.name: Network topology / inventory modelling
gaps.why: The document is about abstract network topologies, layering (underlay/overlay) and inventories, which has no dedicated taxonomy tag; YANG is the nearest fit.

RFC8346.title: A YANG Data Model for Layer 3 Topologies
RFC8346.summary: Defines the ietf-l3-unicast-topology YANG module, which augments the RFC 8345 generic network topology model with Layer 3 unicast node, link, prefix and termination-point attributes and notifications, plus a non-NMDA companion module and an illustrative OSPF extension.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module (plus a companion state module and an example module) that augments the generic topology model, so readers of YANG models would look for it.
YANG.quote: This document introduces a YANG [RFC7950] [RFC6991] data model for Layer 3 (L3) network topologies, specifically Layer 3 Unicast.

rejected.why: OSPF appears only in a non-normative example module in Appendix B showing how the model can be extended. The document does not specify or profile OSPF.
NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the access protocols for the data, mentioned in the definitions and Security Considerations. The document defines nothing about them.
IS-IS is only named as another possible extension of the model. Nothing about it is specified.

I2RS is the sponsoring working group and appears only in the module metadata. The taxonomy has an I2RS tag, but the document defines a topology data model and not an interface to the routing system, so I did not tag it.
JSON is used only to encode the example instance data in Appendix C.
The model describes L3 topology information but is explicitly separate from routing protocol configuration and does not address routing architecture.

gaps.name: Network topology data models
gaps.why: The document is about a topology data model (L3 topologies, building on RFC 8345). The taxonomy has no tag for network topology modelling beyond the generic YANG tag.

RFC8347.title: A YANG Data Model for the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP)
RFC8347.summary: Defines the ietf-vrrp YANG module, a data model for configuring, monitoring and receiving notifications from VRRP versions 2 and 3, augmenting the ietf-interfaces and ietf-ip models.

VRRP.why: The data model covers VRRP v2 and v3 configuration, state, statistics and notifications, so VRRP readers would want it.
VRRP.quote: This document describes a data model for the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP).  Both versions 2 and 3 of VRRP are covered.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a new YANG module with tree diagrams, identities, groupings, augments and notifications.
YANG.quote: This document introduces a YANG data model [RFC6020] [RFC7950] for the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP)

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an access protocol in Security Considerations; the document does not specify NETCONF.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible access protocol.
RFC 2787 and RFC 6527 are referenced as sources for the module, but this document defines a YANG model, not a MIB.
The model has IPv6 address-family branches, but IPv6 itself is not the subject.
Used only for the example instance data in the appendix.
The more specific YANG tag already covers this.

RFC8348.title: A YANG Data Model for Hardware Management
RFC8348.summary: Defines the YANG modules ietf-hardware and iana-hardware (plus a non-NMDA ietf-hardware-state) for managing hardware components, state and sensors on a single server, with mappings to ENTITY-MIB, ENTITY-SENSOR-MIB and ENTITY-STATE-MIB.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG data model (ietf-hardware and iana-hardware modules) for hardware management.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model [RFC7950] for the management of hardware on a single server.

MIB.why: Three sections map the YANG nodes to ENTITY-MIB, ENTITY-SENSOR-MIB and ENTITY-STATE-MIB objects, so readers of MIB modules would want it.
MIB.quote: each entry in the "/hardware/component" list in the operational state is mapped to one EntPhysicalEntry.

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in Security Considerations as access protocols for the model.
The parent topic is implied by the YANG tag.
The uuid leaf uses the yang:uuid type, but the document is not about UUIDs.
The energy-object identity is a single class value, not an energy management topic.
The MIBs are referenced for mapping only, and the document does not specify SNMP.

RFC8349.title: A YANG Data Model for Routing Management (NMDA Version)
RFC8349.summary: Specifies the NMDA-compliant core YANG routing data model (ietf-routing, IPv4/IPv6 unicast routing modules and an IPv6 router advertisements submodule) providing RIBs, routes and control-plane protocol building blocks, obsoleting RFC 8022.

YANG.why: The document's main body is YANG modules defining a routing management data model, including NMDA conformance and augmentation guidance.
YANG.quote: This document specifies three YANG modules and one submodule. Together, they form the core routing data model that serves as a framework for configuring and managing a routing subsystem.

routing architecture.why: Defines generic routing framework components (routes, RIBs, control-plane protocol pseudo-protocols) used as a basis for protocol models.
routing architecture.quote: the core routing data model introduces several generic components of a routing framework: routes, RIBs containing lists of routes, and control-plane protocols.
routing architecture.section: 4. The Design of the Core Routing Data Model

neighbor discovery.why: The ietf-ipv6-router-advertisements submodule models IPv6 Neighbor Discovery router advertisement configuration parameters, a substantial part of the document.
neighbor discovery.quote: augments the schema tree of IPv6 interfaces with definitions of the following variables as required by Section 6.2.1 of [RFC4861]

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the access protocol for the modules and used in examples; the document does not specify or extend it.
IPv6 is an address family handled by the model; the neighbor discovery tag covers the specific IPv6 content.
RIP appears only as an illustrative example module in Appendix C, not as the subject.
This is a YANG model, not a MIB module or SMI work.
JSON is used only for example instance data encoding.

RFC8350.title: Alternate Tunnel Encapsulation for Data Frames in Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP)
RFC8350.summary: Experimental extension to CAPWAP that lets a WTP tunnel station data frames to an Access Router using an alternate encapsulation (CAPWAP, GRE, PMIPv6-UDP, L2TP, IP-in-IP, GTP-U), defining new message elements and sub-elements for advertisement, configuration and failure reporting.

CAPWAP.why: The document extends CAPWAP with new message elements (types 54, 55, 1062) and registries for alternate data tunnels, so it belongs on the CAPWAP page.
CAPWAP.quote: This document defines an extension to the CAPWAP protocol that supports this capability and refers to it as alternate tunnel encapsulation.

rejected.why: GRE is one of several selectable alternate encapsulations, with a GRE Key element. The document does not specify or extend GRE itself.
PMIPv6-UDP is only one of the tunnel types the document lets the WTP use. Nothing new is defined about PMIPv6.
DTLS is used only as the CAPWAP data-channel protection policy, which is defined in RFC 5415. Nothing new is defined about DTLS.
L2TP and L2TPv3 are only reserved tunnel-type values, and no L2TP-specific elements are defined.
UDP-Lite is only a transport option for the CAPWAP data tunnel, so it is a substrate and not the subject.
The document concerns CAPWAP data tunnels specifically. The CAPWAP tag is the better fit, and the generic tunneling topic adds little.

RFC8351.title: The PKCS #8 EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo Media Type
RFC8351.summary: Registers the application/pkcs8-encrypted media type for BER-encoded PKCS #8 EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo, including a password-mapping parameter that specifies the charset used to turn password text into octets.

media types.why: The document's whole purpose is a media type registration, with a full registration template and a new optional parameter.
media types.quote: This document registers the application/pkcs8-encrypted media type for the EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo type of PKCS #8.

PKI.why: The registered type carries a PKCS #8 encrypted private key, a PKI artifact that readers of PKI material would want to find.
PKI.quote: An instance of this media type carries a single encrypted private key [RFC5958] BER-encoded as a single EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo value.

PRECIS.why: The password-mapping parameter defines special values using PRECIS profiles, along with charsets and Unicode normalization, to map password text to octets.
PRECIS.quote: *precis      Preparation, Enforcement, and Comparison of Internationalized Strings (PRECIS) password profile, i.e., OpaqueString from Section 4 of [RFC7613]

rejected.why: PKCS #5 password-based encryption is cited as the context for the password, but the document does not specify or profile PBKDF2.
The value is BER-encoded, but the document does not define any ASN.1 module or encoding rules. It only references the existing type.
The parameter uses charsets and the IANA Character Sets registry, but it only defines password-mapping special values. It does not register or define charsets.
The document is about mapping a password to octets for existing PKCS #5 schemes, not about hashing or key derivation functions.

gaps.name: PKCS #8 / private key information syntax
gaps.why: The document is about the PKCS #8 EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo format for private keys. The taxonomy has no tag for PKCS formats or private key storage, so PKI is only an approximate fit.

RFC8352.title: Energy-Efficient Features of Internet of Things Protocols
RFC8352.summary: Informational overview of energy-saving challenges and techniques for constrained IoT devices, covering link-layer radio duty cycling, power save in 802.11/BLE/802.15.4/DECT ULE, and the impact on 6LoWPAN, RPL and CoAP.

IoT.why: The document is a guidance/overview for energy efficiency of constrained-device protocol stacks, which is the IoT topic. No child technology captures the energy-efficiency theme as a whole.
IoT.quote: describes the challenges for energy-efficient protocol operation on constrained devices and the current practices used to overcome those challenges

CoAP.why: Section 6 examines CoAP's energy-saving features (observe, proxies, sleepy node support, timers), a substantial part of the document.
CoAP.quote: Energy efficiency is part of the CoAP protocol design.  CoAP uses a fixed-length binary header of only four bytes

6LoWPAN.why: Section 4 analyses 6LoWPAN fragmentation, header compression and 6LoWPAN-ND for energy impact.
6LoWPAN.quote: 6LoWPAN affects the energy-efficiency problem in three aspects

RPL.why: Section 5 covers RPL control traffic and energy-aware metrics.
RPL.quote: The amount of RPL control traffic can be tuned by setting the Trickle [RFC6206] algorithm parameters

energy management.why: The central subject is energy consumption of networked devices, matching the energy management topic.
energy management.quote: it is necessary to optimize the energy consumption of the constrained devices

rejected.why: 802.11 power save is one example among several radios, not the focus.
TSCH is mentioned briefly as an 802.15.4e mode; not a substantive subject.
Mentioned only in the data compression discussion as encryption for CoAP.
TCP RTO is mentioned briefly for CoAP over TCP; not a subject.
The document is about device battery energy, not environmental impact of Internet infrastructure.
Not a taxonomy id; 6LoWPAN covers the adaptation layer.

gaps.name: Radio duty cycling / low-power link-layer energy saving
gaps.why: Core of the document (MAC/RDC, BLE, 802.15.4, DECT ULE power save) has no specific taxonomy tag.

RFC8353.title: Generic Security Service API Version 2: Java Bindings Update
RFC8353.summary: RFC 8353 updates the Java language bindings for GSS-API v2 (obsoleting RFC 5653), adding an output token to GSSException so error tokens can be sent to the peer and removing the stream-based GSSContext methods.

GSS-API.why: The whole document defines the Java classes and interfaces (GSSManager, GSSContext, GSSName, GSSException) for the GSS-API, so GSS-API readers would look for it.
GSS-API.quote: This document specifies Java language bindings for the Generic Security Services Application Programming Interface (GSS-API) version 2.

rejected.why: Kerberos v5 is only mentioned as an example mechanism the API can plug in; the document does not specify it.
SPNEGO is mentioned once as an example of why error tokens matter. It is not specified or extended here.
ASN.1 DER is only the encoding used for the Oid class; the document does not specify ASN.1 itself.
The GSS-API tag is more specific and already covers the authentication and per-message protection services described.

RFC8354.title: Use Cases for IPv6 Source Packet Routing in Networking (SPRING)
RFC8354.summary: Informational RFC describing use cases for Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) in small offices, access networks, data centers, CDNs and core networks.

SRv6.why: The whole document presents deployment use cases for Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6), so the SRv6 page is the right place for it.
SRv6.quote: This document illustrates some use cases for Segment Routing in an IPv6-only environment.

rejected.why: SRv6 is the more specific child tag and already covers the SPRING architecture here.
Data centers are only one of five use-case sections, and the section does not deal with data-center routing itself.
The CDN section only gives a cache-hierarchy example of steering with segment lists. It does not address CDN interconnection.
Traffic engineering is mentioned only as the general capability these scenarios need. It is not the subject.
IPv6 is the substrate for SRv6, and SRv6 is the more specific tag.
DOCSIS is mentioned only as an example of an access-network pipe. The document does not specify or analyse it.

RFC8355.title: Resiliency Use Cases in Source Packet Routing in Networking (SPRING) Networks
RFC8355.summary: Informational SPRING WG document describing use cases and requirements for Segment Routing network resiliency: path protection, management-free and managed local protection (fast reroute), micro-loop avoidance, and coexistence of these techniques.

segment routing.why: The document states requirements on the SPRING/segment routing architecture for resiliency; it is the SPRING use-case document, not specific to MPLS or SRv6 data planes.
segment routing.quote: identifies and describes the requirements for a set of use cases related to Segment Routing network resiliency on Source Packet Routing in Networking (SPRING) networks

IP fast reroute.why: Most of the document covers local protection with precomputed backup paths (bypass and shortest-path-based repair, sub-50 ms) in the IP fast reroute framework, with link/node/SRLG protection.
IP fast reroute.quote: commonly referred to as local protection techniques or fast-reroute techniques [RFC5286] [RFC5714]

rejected.why: Only cited as an example of a liveness-check mechanism; the document explicitly leaves the mechanism out of scope.
Micro-loop avoidance is a section, but the more specific segment routing and IP fast reroute tags cover the document.
Disjoint paths and explicit backup path constraints appear, but the focus is resiliency rather than traffic engineering.
A PW is used only as an example service being path protected.
ECMP/UCMP is mentioned only as one way of using the two paths in the path protection example.

gaps.name: Network resiliency / micro-loop avoidance
gaps.why: The document covers path protection and micro-loop avoidance during convergence, but the taxonomy has no tag for general routing resiliency or micro-loop avoidance.

RFC8356.title: Experimental Codepoint Allocation for the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP)
RFC8356.summary: RFC 8356 updates RFC 5440 by reserving experimental-use codepoint ranges in the PCEP message, object, and TLV IANA sub-registries, and describes how implementations handle unknown experimental elements.

PCE.why: The document is about PCEP codepoint registries and sets aside experimental message, object and TLV ranges. It also specifies how PCEP speakers react to unknown experimental elements.
PCE.quote: This document updates [RFC5440] by changing the allocation policies for these three registries to mark some of the codepoints as assigned for Experimental Use.

rejected.why: The IANA registry changes are the subject matter, but the document is about PCEP's own registries rather than IANA process or guidance in general. The PCE tag is the more specific fit.
Stateful MPLS-TE and GMPLS LSP control is mentioned only as background in the introduction.
It is mentioned only in passing as background context.

RFC8357.title: Generalized UDP Source Port for DHCP Relay
RFC8357.summary: Extends DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 so relay agents can use a non-standard UDP source port upstream, defining a DHCPv4 Source Port sub-option and a DHCPv6 Relay Source Port option so replies can be routed statelessly back to that port.

DHCP.why: The document extends DHCPv4 relay behaviour with a new Relay Agent Information sub-option and changes server and relay behaviour.
DHCP.quote: This document defines an extension to the DHCP protocols that allows a relay agent to use any available source port for upstream communications.

DHCPv6.why: It defines a new DHCPv6 option (OPTION_RELAY_PORT) and specifies cascaded relay and server behaviour for DHCPv6, so DHCPv6 readers need it.
DHCPv6.quote: The "Relay Source Port Option" is a new DHCPv6 option.

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport. The document changes which DHCP port relays use and does not define anything about UDP itself.
Only a brief deployment note says firewall rules may need updating. It is not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC8358.title: Update to Digital Signatures on Internet-Draft Documents
RFC8358.summary: Updates RFC 5485 so that CMS detached signatures on Internet-Drafts handle UTF-8 text, HTML and EPUB formats, registering new CMS content type OIDs and defining text/XML canonicalization rules before signing.

CMS.why: The document specifies CMS SignedData detached signatures with new eContentType values and OIDs for Internet-Draft formats, extending CMS usage.
CMS.quote: The CMS is used to construct the detached signatures for Internet-Drafts.

UTF-8.why: The motivating change is handling non-ASCII UTF-8 text in Internet-Drafts, with a new content type and canonicalization rules covering BOM handling.

RFC series.why: It concerns the publication and signing conventions for Internet-Drafts by the IETF Secretariat, following RFC 7997 non-ASCII practices.
RFC series.quote: This document updates the handling of digital signatures on Internet-Drafts that contain non-ASCII characters in a text file.

rejected.why: Only referenced for its text-file canonicalization conventions; the document is not about FTP.
Used for OID definitions and background on DER; not the subject of the document.
The .p7s suffix follows S/MIME conventions, but only incidentally; the document is about CMS detached signatures.
NVT-ASCII is borrowed for canonicalization; Telnet is not a subject.
XML canonicalization is mentioned briefly as one file format case, not the focus.
The IANA OID registrations are boilerplate-level; not the main subject.

RFC8359.title: Network-Assigned Upstream Label
RFC8359.summary: Defines a special "all-ones" Unassigned Upstream Label in the GMPLS RSVP-TE UPSTREAM_LABEL object so a node can ask the downstream node to assign a symmetric label for a bidirectional LSP, with a wavelength-setup use case for IP over optical networks.

GMPLS.why: The document extends GMPLS signalling (updating RFC 3471, 3473, 6205) for bidirectional LSPs, including lambda labels on optical networks.
GMPLS.quote: a Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Resource reSerVation Protocol with Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) mechanism that enables the network to assign an upstream label

RSVP-TE.why: The procedures are specified as RSVP-TE Path/Resv/PathErr/ResvErr message processing, so RSVP-TE readers would want this RFC.
RSVP-TE.quote: The upstream node will continue to signal the Unassigned Upstream Label in the Path message even after it receives an appropriate symmetric label in the Resv message.

rejected.why: Plain RSVP is only the base the RSVP-TE extension builds on; the document is about the GMPLS RSVP-TE mechanism.
Parent of GMPLS, so it is implied. The document is specifically about GMPLS.
The RSVP-TE tag already covers this, and the document does not address traffic engineering in general.
The IANA section registers a new subregistry, but that is boilerplate and not the main subject.

RFC8360.title: Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Validation Reconsidered
RFC8360.summary: RFC 8360 specifies an alternative RPKI certificate validation procedure using new OIDs and Verified Resource Sets, so overclaiming CA certificates are accepted for the intersection of their resources rather than rejected, with amended ROA and BGPsec router certificate validation.

RPKI.why: The whole document defines a modified RPKI validation algorithm, with new OIDs, VRS sets and amended ROA validation. RPKI readers need it.
RPKI.quote: This document specifies an alternative to the certificate validation procedure specified in RFC 6487 that reduces aspects of operational fragility in the management of certificates in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI)

X.509.why: It defines an alternative X.509 resource certificate profile, with new certificate policy and extension OIDs (RFC 3779 extensions) and amended path validation.
X.509.quote: This document defines an alternative profile for X.509 PKIX Resource Certificates.

rejected.why: Only an added constraint on BGPsec router certificate validation is given in 4.2.6. The document is not about BGPsec path validation itself.
ASN.1 modules are included only as apparatus for the new OIDs. The document is not about ASN.1.
BGP is only the context for route origin validation. The document does not specify BGP.
The parent of RPKI is implied by the RPKI tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC8361.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Centralized Replication for Active-Active Broadcast, Unknown Unicast, and Multicast (BUM) Traffic
RFC8361.summary: RFC 8361 specifies centralized replication of BUM traffic in TRILL active-active access, using unicast encapsulation to a distribution tree root and a modified RPF check to avoid drops with pseudo-nicknames; it updates RFC 6325 and defines new R and C nickname flags.

TRILL.why: The document extends the TRILL base protocol (updates RFC 6325) with centralized replication, a changed RPF calculation, and new Nickname Flags APPsub-TLV bits.
TRILL.quote: all ingress RBridges send BUM traffic to a centralized node, which MUST be a distribution tree root, using unicast TRILL encapsulation.

rejected.why: IS-IS is only the control-plane substrate; the document merely adds flags to a TRILL APPsub-TLV.
MC-LAG/DRNI are mentioned as LAALP examples but the document is not about link aggregation itself.
BUM replication is within TRILL distribution trees at layer 2, not IP multicast routing.
The flag bit assignments are boilerplate IANA considerations, not the subject.

gaps.name: TRILL
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists TRILL as a tech under routing, but my tag id list must exist exactly; 'TRILL' is present as a tech ('TRILL: transparent interconnection of lots of links'), so no real gap here.

RFC8362.title: OSPFv3 Link State Advertisement (LSA) Extensibility
RFC8362.summary: RFC 8362 defines TLV-based Extended LSAs for OSPFv3, new LSA types, TLVs and sub-TLVs, a prefix N-bit option, malformed-LSA handling, and backward-compatibility/migration mechanisms, updating RFC 5340 and RFC 5838.

OSPFv3.why: The whole document specifies an extension to OSPFv3: Extended LSA types, TLVs, sub-TLVs, prefix options, and migration rules. It updates RFC 5340 and RFC 5838.
OSPFv3.quote: This document extends the LSA format by encoding the existing OSPFv3 LSA information in Type-Length-Value (TLV) tuples and allowing advertisement of additional information with additional TLVs.

rejected.why: The parent tag is implied by OSPFv3. The document concerns only OSPFv3 and mentions OSPFv2 just as an analogy.
Segment Routing is mentioned only as a motivating use of the N-bit. The document does not specify it.
IPv6 prefixes are carried in the LSAs, but the document is about OSPFv3 routing extensions, not IPv6 itself.
The IANA section creates TLV registries, but that is boilerplate for this OSPFv3 protocol document.
Not discussed.

RFC8363.title: GMPLS OSPF-TE Extensions in Support of Flexi-Grid Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing (DWDM) Networks
RFC8363.summary: Defines OSPF-TE extensions for GMPLS to advertise available frequency slots (a new Flexi-Grid-LSC ISCD switching type, a Frequency Availability Bitmap SCSI sub-TLV, and a flexi-grid port label restriction type) in flexi-grid DWDM networks.

GMPLS.why: The document extends GMPLS routing (ISCD, SCSI, label restrictions) for flexi-grid optical networks, which is optical/transport GMPLS control.
GMPLS.quote: this document describes the Open Shortest Path First - Traffic Engineering (OSPF-TE) extensions in support of GMPLS control of networks that include devices that use the new flexible optical grid.

OSPF.why: It specifies new OSPF-TE Opaque LSA content (ISCD switching capability, SCSI sub-TLV, Port Label Restrictions type) for OSPF.
OSPF.quote: This section defines the GMPLS OSPF-TE extensions in support of advertising the available frequency ranges for flexi-grid DWDM links.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as the signalling counterpart (RFC 7792); this document covers routing, not signalling.
OSPF-TE is the vehicle, but the document is about GMPLS optical routing extensions; GMPLS already covers it.
Parent topic implied by OSPF/GMPLS; no need to list separately.
RSA architecture is referenced via RFC 7698, but PCE is not specified here.

gaps.name: Flexi-grid / WSON / SSON optical networking (DWDM frequency slots)
gaps.why: The document's core subject, spectrum-switched optical networks with flexible-grid frequency slots, has no dedicated tag; GMPLS is the nearest fit.

RFC8364.title: PIM Flooding Mechanism (PFM) and Source Discovery (SD)
RFC8364.summary: Defines the PIM Flooding Mechanism (PFM), a generic TLV-based hop-by-hop flooding mechanism in PIM, and a Group Source Holdtime TLV that floods active multicast source information so receivers can join SPTs without PIM registers, RPs or shared trees.

PIM-SM.why: The document extends PIM-SM with a new PIM message type (PFM) and source discovery procedure replacing register/RP/shared-tree operation, so PIM-SM readers would want it.
PIM-SM.quote: This document defines a new mechanism that provides a way to support PIM-SM without the need for PIM registers, RPs, or shared trees.

rejected.why: The mechanism is built on top of SSM parts of PIM-SM and recommends SSM for some cases, but the document does not specify or extend SSM itself.
Implied as the parent of PIM-SM; the more specific child tag is chosen.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a way to authenticate link-local PIM messages; boilerplate.
IANA registry creation is just the registration section, not the main subject.

RFC8365.title: A Network Virtualization Overlay Solution Using Ethernet VPN (EVPN)
RFC8365.summary: Specifies how EVPN (BGP-based Ethernet VPN) serves as a network virtualization overlay for data centers using VXLAN, NVGRE and MPLS over GRE encapsulations, including route construction, multihoming split-horizon/mass withdrawal procedures, multicast, and DCI via gateways or ASBRs.

EVPN.why: The whole document extends and profiles EVPN for IP-based overlay encapsulations, with new multihoming procedures and route constructions.
EVPN.quote: This document specifies how Ethernet VPN (EVPN) [RFC7432] can be used as a Network Virtualization Overlay (NVO) solution

VXLAN.why: VXLAN is a main encapsulation analysed, with VNI-to-EVI mapping, route encoding and local-bias split-horizon procedures defined for it.
VXLAN.quote: VXLAN encapsulation is based on UDP, with an 8-byte header following the UDP header.

NVGRE.why: NVGRE is analysed alongside VXLAN for EVPN route construction and multihoming procedures.
NVGRE.quote: [RFC7637] encapsulation is based on GRE encapsulation, and it mandates the inclusion of the optional GRE Key field, which carries the VSID.

data center networking.why: The document addresses multi-tenant data-center overlays, NVE placement in hypervisor/ToR, and data-center interconnect.
data center networking.quote: an NVO is a solution to address the requirements of a multi-tenant data center, especially one with virtualized hosts

rejected.why: BGP is the control-plane substrate for EVPN; the document does not extend BGP itself beyond EVPN routes.
MPLS over GRE is a short section using RFC 4023 as is, with no new GRE specification.
Only mentioned as applicable, with the work deferred to a separate document.
A child tag (VXLAN, NVGRE) already fits, and the specific encapsulation tags are more precise.
EVPN is the more specific tag for this document.
PIM tunnel types are only referenced as PMSI options in the multicast section.

RFC8366.title: A Voucher Artifact for Bootstrapping Protocols
RFC8366.summary: Defines the "voucher" artifact, a YANG-modelled JSON document CMS-signed by a device manufacturer's MASA, used to securely assign a pledge device to an owner domain in bootstrapping protocols.

autonomic networking.why: The voucher is the core artifact of ANIMA secure bootstrapping (BRSKI and related), and the document is about secure device onboarding to a domain. No BRSKI-specific document is defined here, so the parent topic fits.
autonomic networking.quote: This document defines a strategy to securely assign a pledge to an owner using an artifact signed, directly or indirectly, by the pledge's manufacturer.

YANG.why: A substantial part of the document is the ietf-voucher YANG module, tree diagram and its yang-data use, which readers of YANG models would want.
YANG.quote: Following is a YANG [RFC7950] module formally describing the voucher's JSON document structure.

CMS.why: Defines the CMS SignedData encoding of the voucher, a new content type (eContentType 40), and signing and certificate inclusion rules.
CMS.quote: A CMS-signed voucher, the default type, contains a ContentInfo structure with the voucher content.

media types.why: Registers a new media type and file extension for the voucher format.
media types.quote: registers the media type "application/voucher-cms+json" and the filename extension ".vcj".

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding of the YANG-defined data, a substrate.
Mentioned only as a possible consumer and in the YANG security boilerplate; not specified here.
The pinned domain certificate is conveyed, but the document does not profile X.509.
The voucher is a trust assignment mechanism, but the document does not define or profile PKI itself.
BRSKI is a separate document that uses this voucher; this RFC only defines the artifact.
Clock sensitivity is discussed in Security Considerations only; NTP is not the subject.

gaps.name: secure device onboarding / zero-touch bootstrapping
gaps.why: The voucher supports bootstrapping of devices into a domain (ownership assignment, MASA, pledge), but the taxonomy has only autonomic networking and BRSKI as nearby tags, not a general bootstrapping subject.

RFC8367.title: Wrongful Termination of Internet Protocol (IP) Packets
RFC8367.summary: An April 1st parody RFC that treats packet filtering and discarding by routers and middleboxes as "wrongful termination" and "discrimination" against packets by color, age, origin, length, IP version and flags, recommending that every device be an "Equal Opportunity Device".

humor.why: The document is dated 1 April and frames packet dropping as discrimination and wrongful termination, using terms such as 'senior packets' and 'reverse discrimination'. It is a whimsical April 1st RFC.
humor.quote: this memo recommends that every router and middlebox be an Equal Opportunity Device, which does not discriminate on the basis of actual or perceived rate, color, age

rejected.why: Filtering by firewalls and middleboxes is the premise of the joke. The document does not specify or analyse firewall mechanisms in earnest.
Section 3.5 jokes about networks rejecting IPv6 packets, but this is one of six parody scenarios. The document is not about IPv6 specification, addressing or deployment.
RFC 4115 color-aware metering is mentioned only as a premise for the color-based termination joke. The document does not address Diffserv.
Traceroute and OSPF Hello are cited only as examples of uses for low-TTL packets in a satirical recommendation.
IPv4 appears only in the TTL, minimum-length and More Fragments flag scenarios. The document does not address IPv4 itself.

RFC8368.title: Using an Autonomic Control Plane for Stable Connectivity of Network Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM)
RFC8368.summary: Informational ANIMA document describing how to use a (generalized) Autonomic Control Plane to give network OAM stable, secure in-band connectivity free of circular dependencies, covering NOC attachment, IPv4-only NMS workarounds via SIIT/NAT64, path-selection policies and encryption.

autonomic networking.why: The whole document is about using the ANIMA Autonomic Control Plane (GACP) for stable OAM connectivity, which is the autonomic networking subject.
autonomic networking.quote: how to integrate OAM processes with an autonomic control plane in order to provide stable and secure connectivity for those OAM processes

OAM.why: The document addresses the OAM circular dependency problem and how NOC/NMS-driven OAM gets stable connectivity, so OAM readers would want it.
OAM.quote: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM), as per BCP 161 [RFC6291], for data networks is often subject to the problem of circular dependencies

SIIT.why: A substantial section recommends SIIT with explicit address mappings (RFC 7757) to connect IPv4-only NMS hosts to the IPv6-only GACP.
SIIT.quote: some form of IP/ICMP translation of packets between IPv4 and IPv6 is necessary. The basic mechanisms for this are in [RFC7915]

rejected.why: Mentioned as part of the ANI, but the document does not specify or extend it.
Only noted as an alternative workaround to SIIT; SIIT is the preferred focus.
Cited as already supporting part of the host-stack multipath requirements, but only as an example; details are out of scope.
DNS naming schemes are suggested as a tool for path policies, but DNS is a supporting mechanism, not the subject.
TLS/DTLS with GACP credentials is only mentioned as a way to encrypt data-plane connections.
The GACP is IPv6-only, but the document is not about IPv6 specification, addressing or deployment as such.

gaps.name: Autonomic Control Plane (ACP) / GRASP / ANIMA
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an 'autonomic networking' topic, but it is not shown as a listed tag in the taxonomy. The closest listed tag is 'autonomic networking' under network management, which is used here. ACP and GRASP have no specific technology tags.

RFC8369.title: Internationalizing IPv6 Using 128-Bit Unicode
RFC8369.summary: April 1st humor RFC proposing 128-bit Unicode code points to be used as IPv6 addresses, with emoji/imoji addressing, multicast via high bit, and a Unicode-based replacement for DNS.

humor.why: An April 1st parody RFC with whimsical claims such as reducing global warming and Martian addresses called Bogons. The humor series is the main subject fit.
humor.quote: Assuming ISO and the Unicode Consortium follow the practices of the IETF, the next Unicode code point size will be 128 bits.

IPv6.why: The joke proposal redefines IPv6 addressing, textual notation, multicast and routing, so readers of IPv6 would expect to find it.
IPv6.quote: it seems only natural to use Unicode code points for IPv6 addresses, and vice versa.

Unicode.why: The satirical proposal is to expand the Unicode code point space to 128 bits and define UTF-128. It is also about emoji code points.
Unicode.quote: Unicode [Unicode] is currently limited to 1,114,112 code points, encoded in various encoding formats (e.g., UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32).

rejected.why: The document proposes replacing DNS with a fictional CPURS. It does not specify or analyse DNS.
Multicast is a short joke section (high-order bit marks multicast) and not a substantial treatment.
IRIs are mentioned only in passing to motivate single-character URIs.
NAT appears only as a passing joke about translating private code points inside applications.
UTF-8 is only listed as an existing encoding. The document defines UTF-128, which is a different encoding.

RFC8370.title: Techniques to Improve the Scalability of RSVP-TE Deployments
RFC8370.summary: Defines two RSVP-TE scaling techniques, Refresh-Interval Independent RSVP (RI-RSVP) and Per-Peer Flow Control, signalled via new CAPABILITY object bits, to reduce LSR processing needed to maintain LSP state.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE signalling with refresh-independent state maintenance, per-peer flow control and new capability bits, to scale RSVP-TE LSP deployments.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document defines two techniques, Refresh-Interval Independent RSVP (RI-RSVP) and Per-Peer Flow Control, that cut down the number of processing cycles required to maintain LSP state.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the more specific fit, and the document concerns TE LSP signalling. RSVP refresh-reduction (RFC 2961) is built upon rather than itself specified.
LSPs and LSRs are the context, but the subject is RSVP-TE signalling scalability, which the more specific tag covers.
The CAPABILITY object comes from the GMPLS graceful restart RFC 5063. The document is not about GMPLS.
RSVP-TE is the tag chosen under traffic engineering, so the parent is implied.

RFC8371.title: Mobile Node Identifier Types for MIPv6
RFC8371.summary: Defines new identifier type numbers (IPv6 address, IMSI, P-TMSI, EUI-48, EUI-64, GUTI, DUID) for the Mobile Node Identifier option of Mobile IPv6 (RFC 4283), registering them in IANA, with a non-normative appendix on RFID types.

Mobile IPv6.why: The document extends the Mobile IPv6 Mobile Node Identifier option with new identifier subtypes and registers them, so it belongs under Mobile IPv6.
Mobile IPv6.quote: This document defines additional identifier type numbers for use with the mobile node identifier option for Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6) as defined by RFC 4283.

rejected.why: DUID is only referenced as one identifier type; the document does not specify or extend DHCPv6.
Mentioned only as an AAA protocol where the identifiers are used; not the subject.
IMSI, P-TMSI and GUTI come from 3GPP, but the document only borrows their formats as identifiers; it does not address cellular networks.
The IANA section merely registers values in the existing subtype registry; it is boilerplate here.
The IPv6 address is used as one identifier type, but the document is not about IPv6 addressing itself.
RFID/IoT material is only in a non-normative appendix and is not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC8372.title: MPLS Flow Identification Considerations
RFC8372.summary: Informational RFC discussing considerations for designing MPLS flow identification, chiefly to enable in-band/passive loss and delay performance monitoring of user traffic in MPLS networks.

MPLS.why: The document is about identifying flows in MPLS networks: LSP types, label stack, special-purpose labels, data-plane and control-plane constraints. MPLS readers would want it.
MPLS.quote: This document discusses the aspects that need to be considered when developing a solution for MPLS flow identification.

performance measurement.why: Loss and delay measurement considerations (passive and hybrid methods on live user traffic) drive the whole document, in Sections 2 and 3.
performance measurement.quote: The key application that needs this is in-band performance monitoring of MPLS flows when MPLS is used to encapsulate user data packets.

rejected.why: ECMP is discussed as a complicating factor for batch-marked loss accounting, but the document does not specify or analyse ECMP itself.
The solution is framed as an OAM application, but the document deals specifically with flow identification and performance measurement. The performance measurement tag covers it better.
RSVP-TE is cited only as an example of how point-to-point LSPs are created.
MPLS-TP is mentioned only in passing as an example of a point-to-point LSP type.
Pseudowires appear only as an example of a layer in the label stack that may need identification.

RFC8373.title: Negotiating Human Language in Real-Time Communications
RFC8373.summary: Defines the SDP media-level attributes 'hlang-send' and 'hlang-recv' so callers and callees can negotiate spoken, written or signed human language per media stream during session setup, especially for emergency calls and call centers.

SDP.why: The document's core content is two new SDP media attributes with offer/answer semantics and IANA registration in the SDP att-field registry.
SDP.quote: This document defines new Session Description Protocol (SDP) media-level attributes so that when establishing interactive communication sessions ("calls"), it is possible to negotiate

language tags.why: The attribute values are BCP 47 language tags, and the document covers sign-language versus spoken/written tag interpretation and matching. This is a substantial part of the design.
language tags.quote: each value MUST be a list of one or more language tags per [BCP47], separated by white space.

SIP.why: It defines handling when no language is in common, using SIP rejection codes and a new Warning code 308 registered in the SIP parameters registry.
SIP.quote: the SIP response has SIP response code 488 (Not Acceptable Here) or 606 (Not Acceptable) [RFC3261] and a Warning header field

rejected.why: Emergency calls are the main motivating use case, but the mechanism is general to all SDP-negotiated calls and defines no emergency-specific protocol.
RTP appears only in the example m= lines as the media transport; the document says nothing about RTP itself.
Deaf, hard-of-hearing and sign-language users motivate the work, but the document is about language negotiation and leaves UI and accessibility issues out of scope.
It concerns language selection in sessions, not the internationalization of text in protocols.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here and do not make the document about IANA.
