gaps.name: Human language negotiation / language preference in communications
gaps.why: The document's central subject, matching users' spoken, written and signed language needs to callee capabilities, has no dedicated tag. It is only partly covered by SDP and language tags.

RFC8374.title: BGPsec Design Choices and Summary of Supporting Discussions
RFC8374.summary: Informational document recording the design rationale, decisions and discussions behind the initial draft of the BGPsec protocol (later RFC 8205), with notes on how the final specification differs.

BGPsec.why: The whole document is the design rationale for BGPsec: signing, validation, algorithm agility, incremental deployment and interaction with BGP features.
BGPsec.quote: The goal of the BGPsec effort is to enhance the security of BGP by enabling full Autonomous System (AS) path validation based on cryptographic principles.

RPKI.why: RPKI router certificates, ROAs, SKI inclusion and RPKI data skew are discussed substantially as design inputs to BGPsec.
RPKI.quote: Route origin validation using Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) [RFC6482] [RFC6811] is necessary and complements AS path attestation based on signed updates.

rejected.why: BGP is the substrate being secured; the document is about BGPsec, a child under routing security, and BGP features are discussed only as interactions.
The algorithm choice (ECDSA P-256 vs RSA-2048) is a brief design decision, not a main subject.
Route reflectors and confederations are mentioned only briefly, as deployment considerations.
Communities are discussed only in deciding they are not signed.

RFC8375.title: Special-Use Domain 'home.arpa.'
RFC8375.summary: RFC 8375 designates 'home.arpa.' as a special-use domain name for residential homenets, specifies DNS resolver and server behaviour for it, and updates HNCP (RFC 7788) to use it instead of '.home'.

special-use domain names.why: The document's core purpose is registering 'home.arpa.' as a special-use domain name, with RFC 6761 considerations and IANA registry entries.
special-use domain names.quote: This document registers the domain 'home.arpa.' as a special-use domain name [RFC6761] and specifies the behavior that is expected from the Domain Name System

home networking.why: The domain is the default name for homenets, and the document updates HNCP's default domain. Home networking readers need it.
home networking.quote: 'home.arpa.' is designated for non-unique use in residential home networks.

DNSSEC.why: A substantial part covers the insecure delegation, the lack of a trust anchor, and DS-query handling for the zone.
DNSSEC.quote: Recursive resolvers at sites using 'home.arpa.' MUST transparently support DNSSEC queries

rejected.why: DNS is the substrate. The tag is implied by the specific child tag (special-use domain names), and the document specifies no new DNS protocol feature.
Mentioned only in passing as a way resolver addresses are supplied to clients.
The IANA registry actions are boilerplate for the special-use registration and are not the main subject.
HNCP's naming and service discovery is mentioned only in the quoted text being updated. The document is not about service discovery.
Not mentioned or relevant. The document states that no special resolution protocol is required.

RFC8376.title: Low-Power Wide Area Network (LPWAN) Overview
RFC8376.summary: Informational overview of LPWAN technologies (LoRaWAN, NB-IoT, Sigfox, Wi-SUN FAN) considered by the IETF lpwan WG, with a gap analysis of existing IETF protocols (IPv6, 6LoWPAN, ROHC, CoAP, etc.) for running IP over LPWANs.

LPWAN.why: The whole document is an overview of LPWAN technologies and the gaps for running IP over them.
LPWAN.quote: Low-Power Wide Area Networks (LPWANs) are wireless technologies with characteristics such as large coverage areas, low bandwidth, possibly very small packet and application-layer data sizes

rejected.why: Not in this taxonomy position as a tag I can use confidently; LPWAN id above is also not in the taxonomy, see correction below.

RFC8377.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Multi-Topology
RFC8377.summary: Specifies TRILL extensions for IS-IS multi-topology (RFC 5120) routing of unicast and multi-destination traffic, including an explicit MT Label, per-topology adjacency, distribution trees and address learning.

TRILL.why: The whole document extends the TRILL protocol with multi-topology: topology-labelled data packets, per-topology adjacency, forwarding tables, distribution trees and ESADI. It updates RFC 6325 and RFC 7177.
TRILL.quote: extensions to the IETF TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) protocol [RFC6325] [RFC7177] [RFC7780] to support multi-topology routing

rejected.why: IS-IS multi-topology (RFC 5120) is the basis the document builds on, and it uses MT TLVs. The document is about TRILL's use of it, not about IS-IS itself. The TRILL tag fits better.
The labels are Ethertype-based, but the document is about TRILL campus routing, not IP over Ethernet.
BFD over TRILL is mentioned only as an example of RBridge Channel traffic that is sent in topology zero.
The document is about a specific protocol extension, not general routing architecture.

gaps.name: TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a TRILL tag that must be used to describe this document, but it is a parent routing entry whose children are not listed in the taxonomy. I used the id from the taxonomy as shown, 'TRILL', but the taxonomy lists the tag as 'TRILL' under routing.

gaps.name: IS-IS multi-topology (MT routing)
gaps.why: The document specifies per-topology routing built on IS-IS MT. The taxonomy has an IS-IS tag, but no tag for multi-topology routing itself.

RFC8378.title: Signal-Free Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Multicast
RFC8378.summary: Experimental RFC defining a signal-free LISP multicast mechanism in which receiver ETRs register replication lists in the LISP mapping system and source ITRs unicast-replicate and encapsulate multicast traffic across a non-multicast core, including SSM/ASM handling, multihoming and replication engineering via RTRs.

LISP.why: The document specifies a LISP extension: use of the mapping system, Map-Register/Map-Request/Map-Notify, LCAF encodings and RTRs for multicast interconnection.
LISP.quote: a signal-free mechanism can be used to allow traffic to flow between sites. The mechanism described in this document uses unicast replication and encapsulation

multicast.why: It is about interconnecting multicast trees (SSM and ASM) between sites, with receiver detection via IGMP/PIM and replication; readers of multicast would want it.
multicast.quote: a signal-free mechanism can be used to create an overlay that will allow multicast traffic to flow between sites and connect the multicast trees

rejected.why: PIM is used at sites for tree building but the document does not specify or extend it; it deliberately avoids extending PIM over the overlay.
A section discusses SSM trees, but only as one case of the LISP mechanism; the document is not about SSM itself.
IGMP is only used for receiver detection at sites, not specified or extended.
The overlay is a LISP multicast overlay, not a data-plane network virtualization encapsulation like VXLAN/Geneve.
Unicast encapsulation is a LISP data-plane mechanism; the document is not about generic tunnelling.

gaps.name: LISP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no LISP tag in the list I was able to use; LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol) is in the taxonomy under routing as 'LISP', so no gap in practice.

RFC8379.title: OSPF Graceful Link Shutdown
RFC8379.summary: Defines OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 sub-TLVs (plus a BGP-LS TLV) to advertise a link as gracefully shut down so both ends divert traffic, with procedures per link type and applications.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 with new sub-TLVs and procedures for graceful link shutdown.
OSPF.quote: This document describes the protocol extensions to disseminate graceful-link-shutdown information in OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.

OSPFv3.why: A substantial part specifies the OSPFv3 encoding in the E-Router-LSA and its procedures.
OSPFv3.quote: The Graceful-Link-Shutdown sub-TLV is carried in the Router-Link TLV as defined in [RFC8362] for OSPFv3.

rejected.why: BGP-LS TLV is defined briefly, but the document is about OSPF; BGP is only the carrier to external entities.
TE metrics and controller rerouting appear in procedures and applications, but the document is not about TE itself.
Only one application scenario (sham links, CE-PE); not the subject.
LSPs are mentioned in the application use cases only.

RFC8380.title: Directory-Assisted Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) Encapsulation
RFC8380.summary: Specifies how non-RBridge nodes (TRILL Encapsulating Nodes) can perform TRILL encapsulation using directory assistance (pull directory/ES-IS), including source nickname handling, benefits in data centers, and security considerations.

TRILL.why: The whole document extends TRILL by defining the TRILL Encapsulating Node, how it sets ingress nicknames and interacts with edge RBridges.
TRILL.quote: non-RBridge nodes performing TRILL encapsulation with assistance from a directory service and specifies a method for them to do so

rejected.why: Data center is the motivating context and benefits are discussed, but the document specifies a TRILL mechanism; the TRILL tag is the more specific fit.
Ethernet frames and bridged LANs are the substrate; the document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
IS-IS Hellos are snooped by TRILL-ENs but the document does not specify or extend IS-IS.
The directory is the TRILL pull directory defined in RFC 8171; this document only uses it, not defining directory access.

RFC8381.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Vendor-Specific RBridge Channel Protocol
RFC8381.summary: RFC 8381 defines a Vendor-Specific RBridge Channel protocol for TRILL, letting organizations identified by OUI/CID send their own typed messages over the RBridge Channel facility, and specifies its packet format and error codes.

TRILL.why: The document extends TRILL by defining a new RBridge Channel protocol (0x008) with its packet format, VERR error handling and error-response rules.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies a method to send vendor-specific messages over the RBridge Channel facility.

rejected.why: BFD is mentioned only as the first user of the basic RBridge Channel, in Security Considerations. This document is not about it.
The Ethertype and Ethernet MAC addresses are used for framing only. The document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
The IANA section registers one channel protocol value and one error-code subregistry. That is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
Vendor diagnostic messages are mentioned only as an example use. The document does not define OAM mechanisms.

RFC8382.title: Shared Bottleneck Detection for Coupled Congestion Control for RTP Media
RFC8382.summary: Experimental RFC specifying a measurement-based shared bottleneck detection mechanism (OWD skewness, variability, oscillation and loss statistics plus a flow-grouping algorithm) for coupling congestion controllers of RTP media flows.

congestion control.why: The document defines how to detect flows sharing a bottleneck so that coupled congestion controllers can combine their control; this is congestion control subject matter. No more specific child tag (e.g. RTP congestion control) fits as it is not itself a rate control algorithm.
congestion control.quote: This mechanism relies on some form of Shared Bottleneck Detection (SBD); here, a measurement-based SBD approach is described.

RTP congestion control.why: It is an RMCAT work product supporting coupled congestion control for interactive RTP media, so readers of that subject would want it, although it specifies detection rather than a controller.
RTP congestion control.quote: RTP Media Congestion Avoidance Techniques (RMCAT) congestion control algorithms will help confirm the default parameter choice.

performance measurement.why: A large part of the document defines how to measure and summarise OWD and loss statistics (mean, skewness, MAD, oscillation) from continuous measurements.
performance measurement.quote: The cleanest signal is obtained by using One-Way Delay (OWD)

rejected.why: RTP media is the application context, and RTCP is only the feedback carrier; the document does not specify or extend RTP itself.
It relies on RTCP feedback defined elsewhere (RTCP-CC-FEEDBACK) and defines no new RTCP behaviour.
ECN is only mentioned as a possible future signal.
RFC 6817 is cited only for clock skew discussion.

gaps.name: Shared bottleneck detection
gaps.why: The document's core subject has no dedicated tag; congestion control is the closest parent.

RFC8383.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Address Flush Message
RFC8383.summary: RFC 8383 specifies the TRILL Address Flush message, an RBridge Channel protocol message that lets a TRILL switch ask other switches to flush MAC address reachability learned from decapsulated TRILL Data packets, to speed convergence.

TRILL.why: The whole document defines a new TRILL RBridge Channel message, its TLV encodings and processing rules, which extends the TRILL protocol.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies a message by which a TRILL switch can explicitly request other TRILL switches to flush certain MAC reachability learned through the decapsulation of TRILL Data packets.

rejected.why: The document deals with MAC address learning and VLANs, but only as the data that TRILL flushes. Its subject is TRILL, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
RFC 4762 is cited only as an example of a similar MAC flush mechanism. The document does not cover VPLS.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate and are not the subject of the document.
The more specific TRILL tag already covers this document, and the parent tag is implied.

gaps.name: RBridge Channel
gaps.why: The message is a protocol carried over the RBridge Channel (RFC 7178), but the taxonomy has no separate tag for it, so TRILL is the closest fit.

RFC8384.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) Smart Endnodes
RFC8384.summary: Defines TRILL Smart Endnodes, which let endnodes learn endnode-table entries and encapsulate/decapsulate TRILL frames using the attached edge RBridge's nickname, with a Smart-Hello mechanism, data-packet processing rules and multihoming handling.

TRILL.why: The whole document extends the TRILL protocol with Smart Endnodes, new APPsub-TLVs, and edge RBridge forwarding behaviour.
TRILL.quote: This document addresses the problem of the size and freshness of the endnode learning table in edge Routing Bridges (RBridges)

rejected.why: TRILL IS-IS TLVs are reused as the Smart-Hello encoding, but the document does not specify or extend IS-IS routing. Smart Endnodes do not even send LSPs.
Native Ethernet frames and MAC addresses are the substrate. The document is about TRILL edge behaviour, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
Section 6 covers active-active multihoming of a Smart Endnode, but this is TRILL edge multihoming and not IP multihoming architecture. It is a small part of the document.
The IANA section only registers two APPsub-TLV types, which is boilerplate.

RFC8385.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) Transparent Transport over MPLS
RFC8385.summary: Informational RFC describing two models (VPLS and VPTS/TIR) for interconnecting multiple TRILL sites, and multiple tenants, across an MPLS provider network using pseudowires.

TRILL.why: The whole document is about carrying TRILL across MPLS, defining the VPTS/TIR model with virtual TRILL switches, adjacency, distribution trees and nicknames.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies methods to interconnect multiple TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) sites with an intervening MPLS network

VPLS.why: One of the two models uses VPLS emulated LANs between TRILL sites, and the VPTS model is compared and contrasted against VPLS in depth.
VPLS.quote: Use of VPLS [RFC4762] [RFC4761] to interconnect TRILL sites requires no changes to a VPLS implementation

pseudowire.why: TIRs are interconnected via pseudowires, and packet processing between pseudowires is specified in its own section.
pseudowire.quote: The VPTS model uses PPP or Ethernet pseudowires for MPLS encapsulation as specified in [RFC7173]

rejected.why: MPLS is the provider substrate; the document specifies TRILL/VPLS/pseudowire usage over it rather than MPLS itself.
TRILL's IS-IS control messages are just forwarded or used for adjacency; nothing new about IS-IS is specified.
The framework is referenced for terminology, but the document is specifically about VPLS and a TRILL service variant.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a recommendation.
ECMP is mentioned in one sentence on unicast forwarding and is not a subject of the document.

RFC8386.title: Privacy Considerations for Protocols Relying on IP Broadcast or Multicast
RFC8386.summary: Informational guidance for designers of protocols using IP broadcast or multicast, describing privacy risks (message frequency, persistent identifiers, hostnames, correlation, configurability) and recommended mitigations.

privacy.why: The whole document is a set of privacy considerations for protocol designers, covering tracking, identifiers and correlation.
privacy.quote: designers of protocols that make use of broadcast or multicast messages need to take special care when designing their protocols

multicast.why: The document is about the characteristics and use of IP broadcast and multicast, including address types and scopes, and how they affect privacy. It does not specify multicast routing, so this is secondary.
multicast.quote: Broadcast and multicast messages have a large (and, to the sender, unknown) receiver group by design.

rejected.why: mDNS is cited as an example of a protocol using multicast and as a source of message-suppression practice. The document does not specify or extend it.
DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 are mentioned only as examples of protocols that use broadcast or multicast.
Mentioned only as having separate privacy extensions in a referenced draft.
Hostnames leaking personal information is discussed as one example. The document is not about hostname conventions, and RFC 8117 covers that.
UUIDs appear only as an example of a persistent identifier.
Only referenced in Security Considerations via RFC 5374. The document gives no group key management content.

RFC8387.title: Practical Considerations and Implementation Experiences in Securing Smart Object Networks
RFC8387.summary: Informational memo from the LWIG working group describing challenges in securing resource-constrained smart object devices, a self-generated-identity deployment model with signed data objects, implementation experiences with ECC/RSA libraries on 8-bit and ARM microcontrollers, and design trade-offs (layering, freshness, symmetric vs asymmetric crypto).

IoT.why: The whole document addresses security guidance, provisioning and implementation experience for constrained IoT devices; no more specific IoT technology tag is the main subject.
IoT.quote: This memo describes challenges associated with securing smart object devices in constrained implementations and environments.

elliptic curve.why: A large part of the memo benchmarks ECDSA sign operations across curves and libraries on constrained hardware and recommends ECC and Curve25519/Ed25519 over RSA.
elliptic curve.quote: It is clearly observable that for similar security levels, elliptic curve public-key cryptography outperforms RSA.

CoAP.why: CoAP is the running example for the deployment model and the prototype (pub-sub broker, resource directory, data-object security in CoAP payloads).
CoAP.quote: Our discussion uses this protocol as an example, but the conclusions may apply to other similar protocols.

rejected.why: ECDSA performance is measured, but the document does not specify or profile ECDSA; the parent elliptic curve tag covers the cryptographic content.
Provisioning via self-generated identities is discussed, but it is a deployment model rather than a key management protocol specification.
DTLS, IPsec, HIP and TLS are only compared as layering options in the trade-off discussion, not specified or extended.
JOSE/COSE signatures are used in the example application only as the signing format; the document is not about them.
Cryptographic-quality randomness is noted as a requirement in a bullet and summary item, but it is not a substantial part of the document.
The document is generally about security, but the more specific IoT tag fits better and ancestors are implied by chosen tags.

gaps.name: Constrained-device cryptographic library implementation experience
gaps.why: The core of the memo is benchmarking crypto libraries (Relic, TinyECC, Wiselib, NaCl) on 8-bit and Cortex-M microcontrollers, which has no dedicated taxonomy tag beyond the general IoT and elliptic curve tags.

RFC8388.title: Usage and Applicability of BGP MPLS-Based Ethernet VPN
RFC8388.summary: Informational guide to applying BGP MPLS-based EVPN (RFC 7432) in a three-PE, three-CE multihoming scenario, covering provisioning, route usage, MAC- vs MPLS-based forwarding, and traffic optimizations such as proxy ARP and IRB.

EVPN.why: The whole document is a deployment and applicability guide for EVPN. It covers provisioning, route types, forwarding models and optimizations.
EVPN.quote: This document discusses the usage and applicability of BGP MPLS-based Ethernet VPN (EVPN) in a simple and fairly common deployment scenario.

rejected.why: BGP only carries the EVPN NLRI here. The document does not specify or extend BGP.
MPLS labels and LSPs are the data-plane substrate for EVPN. The document does not define anything new about MPLS.
VPLS appears only in a short comparison explaining why EVPN was chosen.
Proxy ARP/ND is an EVPN optimization discussed within the EVPN context. The document is not about ARP itself.
EVPN is the more specific tag and already sits under VPN. L2VPN generally is not the subject.

RFC8389.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Mapping of Address and Port with Encapsulation (MAP-E)
RFC8389.summary: Defines an SMIv2 MIB module (MAP-E-MIB) for monitoring MAP-E Border Relays and Customer Edges, with a mapping rule table and invalid-packet security check counters.

MIB.why: The document's sole content is a MIB module in SMIv2, with tables, textual conventions and conformance groups, so MIB readers would look for it.
MIB.quote: This document defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with monitoring MAP-E devices.

MAP.why: The managed objects cover MAP-E mapping rules (BMR/FMR, PSID, EA length) and security check counters, so the document is about operating MAP-E.
MAP.quote: Mapping of Address and Port with Encapsulation (MAP-E) [RFC7597] is a stateless, automatic tunneling mechanism for providing an IPv4 connectivity service

rejected.why: SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines objects, not SNMP protocol behaviour. MIB is the more specific tag.
MAP is a child of this topic, so the parent is implied and is not listed separately.
The softwire tag is a general tunnelling tag, and MAP is the more specific fit.
RFC 7598 is referenced only for the F-flag semantics, and the document does not define or extend DHCPv6.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations boilerplate.
AES is mentioned only in Security Considerations boilerplate, in the SNMPv3 USM reference.

RFC8390.title: RSVP-TE Path Diversity Using Exclude Route
RFC8390.summary: Defines new Diversity subobjects for the RSVP-TE eXclude Route Object (XRO) and Explicit Exclusion Route Subobject (EXRS), using client, PCE (Path Key) or network-assigned (Path Affinity Set) identifiers so a new LSP can be signalled diverse from a reference LSP whose path is not fully known.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE signalling with new XRO/EXRS subobjects, processing rules, and error sub-codes for LSP path diversity. It updates RFC 4874.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document specifies two new diversity subobjects for the RSVP eXclude Route Object (XRO) and the Explicit Exclusion Route Subobject (EXRS).

GMPLS.why: The GMPLS UNI overlay model is the main motivating scenario, with EN/CN examples throughout. The mechanisms apply to GMPLS networks.
GMPLS.quote: Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) User-Network Interface (UNI), where the core node may perform path computation [RFC4208].

PCE.why: One of the three identifier types is a PCE-allocated Path Key, which nodes may resolve through a PCE. The document describes how PCE path computation uses it.
PCE.quote: the PCE is consulted and the Path Key, as defined in [RFC5520], can be used in RSVP signaling as the identifier to ensure diversity.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is the more specific tag for this document. The traffic engineering parent is implied.
LSPs are the subject, but the document is specific to RSVP-TE signalling and GMPLS, not MPLS architecture or encapsulation.
L1VPN Port Information Tables are mentioned only in passing as a translation aid.
The document only touches on security in the boilerplate Security Considerations section.

RFC8391.title: XMSS: eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme
RFC8391.summary: Specifies WOTS+ one-time signatures and the XMSS and XMSS^MT stateful hash-based signature schemes, with parameter sets, XDR formats and IANA registries.

XMSS.why: The document exists to specify XMSS, XMSS^MT and WOTS+, the stateful hash-based signature scheme, with algorithms, parameters and formats.
XMSS.quote: This note specifies Winternitz One-Time Signature Plus (WOTS+), a one-time signature scheme; XMSS, a single-tree scheme; and XMSS^MT, a multi-tree variant of XMSS.

rejected.why: LMS is only mentioned as a different, separately specified scheme in the introduction.
SPHINCS is mentioned only as a stateless scheme that could be built on this modular description; it is not specified here.
SHA2 and SHAKE are used to instantiate the hash functions, so they are a building block, not the subject.
XDR is used only to define the signature and key formats.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-like and only enumerate the parameter sets defined in the body.
Post-quantum security is a motivation, but the more specific hash-based signatures subtree fits better.

RFC8392.title: CBOR Web Token (CWT)
RFC8392.summary: Defines CBOR Web Token (CWT), a compact CBOR-encoded claims set format derived from JWT and protected with COSE, including registered claims, a CWT CBOR tag, creation/validation procedures, and IANA registrations.

CBOR.why: CWT is a CBOR-based data structure: claim keys are CBOR map keys, values are CBOR types, and the document defines a new CBOR tag (61) and rules on tag use.
CBOR.quote: The claims in a CWT are encoded in the Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR)

COSE.why: Creating and validating a CWT is defined as a sequence of COSE sign, MAC and encrypt operations, including nesting. It is a security token format built on COSE.
COSE.quote: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) is used for added application-layer security protection.

JWT.why: The document is the CBOR counterpart of JWT and reuses its claim semantics. Readers of the JWT page would want it, and JWT is the closest security-token tag.
JWT.quote: CWT is derived from JSON Web Token (JWT) but uses CBOR rather than JSON.

rejected.why: JWS and JWE are only mentioned as background for JWT; CWT uses COSE instead.
OAuth is only named as a place where JWT is used, and this document does not specify any OAuth behaviour.
CoAP appears only as a Content-Format registration and as a transport for the tokens. The document does not specify CoAP behaviour.
The document was produced in the ace working group, but its text does not describe the ACE framework.
The application/cwt registration is boilerplate-level IANA content, not the main subject.
IoT is cited as motivation for a compact encoding only. The document is not guidance for constrained devices.

RFC8393.title: Operating the Network Service Header (NSH) with Next Protocol "None"
RFC8393.summary: Defines a new NSH Next Protocol value 0x00 ("None") so Service Function Chaining nodes can send metadata-only NSH packets, with processing rules, backward compatibility, use cases (per-SFP/per-flow metadata, SFI coordination, OAM) and rate-limit guidance.

SFC.why: The document extends the NSH by defining Next Protocol "None" and specifies processing rules for SFC nodes handling metadata-only packets.
SFC.quote: This document describes a network that supports Service Function Chaining (SFC) using the Network Service Header (NSH) with no payload data and carrying only metadata.

rejected.why: OAM is one illustrative use case in Section 6.4, and the document explicitly does not define an OAM mechanism, so it is not a substantial subject.
Section 7 covers rate limiting of generated packets, but this is a brief operational consideration, not congestion control as a subject.
The NSH is carried in tunnels over an underlay, but the document concerns the NSH and SFC, not data-plane virtualization overlays.
The IANA registration is boilerplate here and not the subject of the document.

RFC8394.title: Split Network Virtualization Edge (Split-NVE) Control-Plane Requirements
RFC8394.summary: Informational NVO3 document describing VM lifecycle events and the functionality and high-level requirements for a hypervisor-to-External-NVE control-plane protocol in Split-NVE, and assessing IEEE 802.1Q VDP against those requirements.

overlay networks.why: The document specifies requirements for the control plane between tNVE and nNVE in NVO3 network virtualization overlays. Overlay networks is the closest tag for data-center network virtualization edges.
overlay networks.quote: one or more control-plane protocols between a hypervisor and its associated External NVE(s) are used by the hypervisor to distribute its virtual-machine networking state

rejected.why: The context is data-center network virtualization, but the document concerns NVE control signaling, not routing or address resolution at DC scale.
VDP and VLAN tags are used over Layer 2, but the document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
Overlay encapsulation is offloaded to the nNVE, but no specific encapsulation is discussed.
Separating control from the NVE has an SDN flavour, but the document does not address SDN as such.
IGMP is mentioned only as an example for migration optimization.
UUID is mentioned only as a VSI ID format in the appendix.

gaps.name: Edge Virtual Bridging / VDP (IEEE 802.1Q VSI Discovery and Configuration Protocol)
gaps.why: Section 5 and Appendix A assess VDP as the hypervisor-to-NVE protocol, but the taxonomy has no tag for IEEE 802.1Q EVB or VDP.

gaps.name: Network virtualization (NVO3) architecture and Split-NVE requirements
gaps.why: The taxonomy covers overlay encapsulations but has no tag for NVO3 control-plane or NVE architecture.

RFC8395.title: Extensions to BGP-Signaled Pseudowires to Support Flow-Aware Transport Labels
RFC8395.summary: Extends BGP-signaled VPLS/L2VPN pseudowires by defining T and R flags in the Layer2 Info Extended Community Control Flags so PEs can signal use of flow labels (flow-aware transport) for ECMP load balancing, updating RFC 4761.

pseudowire.why: The document is about flow-aware transport labels for pseudowires, specifying how PEs signal flow label usage for PWs.
pseudowire.quote: This document defines protocol extensions required to synchronize flow label states among Provider Edges (PEs) when using the BGP-based signaling procedures.

L2VPN.why: The signaling extends BGP-based VPLS/L2VPN (RFC 4761, RFC 6624) and applies to point-to-point L2VPNs; the Layer2 Info Extended Community is an L2VPN construct.
L2VPN.quote: A PE that wishes to send a flow label in a PW packet MUST include in its VPLS BGP NLRI a Layer2 Info Extended Community using Control Flags field with T = 1.

rejected.why: BGP is the signaling substrate; the document only defines new flags in an extended community used by L2VPN signaling and does not change BGP itself.
ECMP load balancing is the motivation for the flow label, but the document is about signaling flow label presence, not ECMP mechanisms.
The flow label is an MPLS label stack entry, but MPLS is the underlying PSN and is not specified here.
The signaling is carried in VPLS NLRI, but the document extends the generic PW/L2VPN signaling rather than VPLS service behavior; the pseudowire and L2VPN tags cover it.
LDP signaling is only mentioned as the RFC 6391 predecessor; this document concerns BGP signaling.

RFC8396.title: Managing, Ordering, Distributing, Exposing, and Registering Telephone Numbers (MODERN): Problem Statement, Use Cases, and Framework
RFC8396.summary: Informational problem statement and framework for the MODERN WG describing how telephone numbers are acquired, managed and retrieved via Internet-based registry/registrar/CSP mechanisms, with actors, data types and use cases.

domain registration.why: The framework models registry, registrar and assignee roles for telephone numbers, analogous to domain registration, with acquisition, management and retrieval interfaces.
domain registration.quote: allocating, managing, and resolving TNs in an IP environment

ENUM.why: ENUM and its limits are the motivating background, and the framework addresses telephone number data and resolution beyond it. It is discussed but not specified here.
ENUM.quote: ENUM [RFC6116] created a DNS-based mechanism for translating TNs into URIs

rejected.why: SIP is only used as an example of service data (SIP URI) and REGISTER; the document is not about SIP.
STIR certificates are mentioned as credentials in use cases, but the document is not about caller-ID authentication.
RDAP/WEIRDS is cited as a candidate for reuse but is not specified or profiled here.
WHOIS is mentioned only as an analogy for administrative data.
DNS is used as an analogy for registry/registrar structure, not the subject.
The document is about number administration, not the tel URI scheme.

gaps.name: Telephone number administration / numbering resources
gaps.why: The document is about acquiring, managing and retrieving telephone number assignments (registries, registrars, number portability), which has no dedicated taxonomy tag.

RFC8397.title: Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) Multilevel Using Unique Nicknames
RFC8397.summary: Specifies the unique-nickname approach to TRILL multilevel operation over multilevel IS-IS, including unicast and multi-destination routing, nickname allocation, and the new NickBlockFlags APPsub-TLV.

TRILL.why: The whole document extends TRILL for multilevel campuses: nickname management, distribution trees, and a new APPsub-TLV.
TRILL.quote: This document specifies a unique nickname approach. This approach gives unique nicknames to all TRILL switches across the multilevel TRILL campus.

rejected.why: Multilevel IS-IS is the substrate the TRILL extensions build on. The document defines a TRILL APPsub-TLV, not a change to IS-IS itself.
The document does touch scalability, but the TRILL tag is the more specific fit.
The Security Considerations section is boilerplate-level and the document is not about securing routing.

RFC8398.title: Internationalized Email Addresses in X.509 Certificates
RFC8398.summary: Defines the SmtpUTF8Mailbox otherName form for X.509 subjectAltName/issuerAltName to carry internationalized email addresses, with matching rules, IDNA2008 requirements, and name constraint handling, updating RFC 5280.

X.509.why: The document defines a new GeneralName otherName form for X.509 certificates, updates RFC 5280 name constraints, and includes an ASN.1 module.
X.509.quote: defines a new name form for inclusion in the otherName field of an X.509 Subject Alternative Name and Issuer Alternative Name extension

EAI.why: The whole purpose is representing internationalized email addresses (RFC 6531 Mailbox with UTF-8 local-parts) in certificates, so EAI readers would want it.
EAI.quote: allows a certificate subject to be associated with an internationalized email address

IDN.why: A dedicated section requires IDNA2008 conformance and specifies A-label/U-label conversion for comparison and name constraints.
IDN.quote: all email address domains in X.509 certificates MUST conform to IDNA2008 [RFC5890] (and avoid any "mappings" mentioned in that document)

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation for the module in the appendix; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
SMTP's Mailbox syntax is referenced for the address format, but the document does not specify or extend SMTP.
UTF8String encoding is used, but the document is not about the UTF-8 encoding.
ABNF is used only as a notation convention.
The more specific X.509 tag applies, so the parent PKI tag is not listed.
Internet message format is referenced for address syntax but not specified here.

RFC8399.title: Internationalization Updates to RFC 5280
RFC8399.summary: Updates RFC 5280 (X.509 PKI certificate profile) to align its internationalized name handling with IDNA2008 and to support internationalized email addresses (SmtpUTF8Mailbox) in certificates, including name constraint changes.

X.509.why: The document is a set of formal updates to the RFC 5280 X.509 certificate and CRL profile, changing name constraints and GeneralName processing rules.
X.509.quote: The updates to RFC 5280 described in this document provide alignment with the 2008 specification for Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs) and add support for internationalized email addresses in X.509 certificates.

IDN.why: Specifies how IDNs (U-labels/A-labels, IDNA2008) are encoded, compared and displayed in certificates, replacing IDNA2003 rules.
IDN.quote: To accommodate IDNs, U-labels are converted to A-labels.

EAI.why: Adds support for internationalized email addresses (SmtpUTF8Mailbox) in certificates, with matching and display rules.
EAI.quote: If the local-part of the internationalized email address cannot be represented in ASCII, then the internationalized email address is placed in the otherName choice of GeneralName

rejected.why: DNS names appear only as certificate name forms; the document does not specify DNS protocol behaviour.
Unicode and UTF-8 are only the character basis for U-labels and the SmtpUTF8Mailbox encoding (BOM prohibition); the document does not address Unicode usage itself.
IRIs are mentioned only in a reference list inside the replaced Introduction text; no IRI rules change.
X.509 is the more specific tag and already covers the PKI profile being updated.
The more specific IDN and EAI tags cover the internationalization content.

RFC8400.title: Extensions to RSVP-TE for Label Switched Path (LSP) Egress Protection
RFC8400.summary: RFC 8400 defines RSVP-TE extensions (an Egress Protection subobject in the SERO and related PLR/egress procedures) for locally protecting the egress nodes of P2P and P2MP TE LSPs using backup LSPs to a backup egress node.

RSVP-TE.why: The document specifies new RSVP-TE signalling (SERO Egress Protection subobject, flags, PLR and egress behaviours) for protecting TE LSP egress nodes.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document describes extensions to Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) for locally protecting the egress node(s) of a Point-to-Point (P2P) or Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) Traffic Engineered (TE) Label Switched Path (LSP).

rejected.why: LSPs and labels are the setting, but the document's subject is RSVP-TE signalling, the more specific tag.
L3VPN is only the example application in Section 6; the document is not about L3VPN.
BFD is mentioned as a failure-detection mechanism, and detection is explicitly out of scope.
This is MPLS/RSVP-TE local protection, not IP or LDP fast reroute, although it builds on RFC 4090 fast reroute.
BGP is only the out-of-band channel for service labels; the document does not specify it.
The more specific RSVP-TE technology tag already covers this topic.

RFC8401.title: Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER) Support via IS-IS
RFC8401.summary: Defines IS-IS extensions (BIER Info sub-TLV and BIER MPLS Encapsulation sub-sub-TLV) to advertise BIER domain/subdomain information, BFR-ids and label ranges for BIER multicast forwarding.

BIER.why: The document specifies how BIER subdomains, BFR-ids, and encapsulation label ranges are signalled, so BIER readers need it.
BIER.quote: This document defines IS-IS extensions to support multicast forwarding using the Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER) architecture.

IS-IS.why: It defines new IS-IS sub-TLVs, procedures for multi-topology handling, misconfiguration logging and flooding reduction, extending the IS-IS protocol.
IS-IS.quote: This document presents necessary extensions to the currently deployed IS-IS for IP [RFC1195] to support distribution of information necessary for operation of BIER domains

rejected.why: MPLS label encapsulation is used for BIER label ranges, but the document does not specify MPLS itself; it only references MPLS label values.
Parent of BIER, which is already tagged and implies it.
IANA registry creation is boilerplate here and not the main subject.

RFC8402.title: Segment Routing Architecture
RFC8402.summary: RFC 8402 defines the Segment Routing architecture: source-routing with ordered segment lists (SIDs), IGP and BGP segments, binding segments, and instantiation over MPLS (SR-MPLS) and IPv6 (SRv6) data planes.

segment routing.why: The document is the core architecture specification for Segment Routing, defining segments, SIDs, SR domains and policies.
segment routing.quote: This document defines the architecture for Segment Routing, including definitions of basic objects and functions and a description of the overall design.

SR-MPLS.why: A substantial part defines SR-MPLS behavior: SRGB/SRLB labels, FIB entries, anycast SID label handling, and security considerations for the MPLS data plane.
SR-MPLS.quote: SR can be directly applied to the MPLS architecture with no change to the forwarding plane [SR-MPLS].  A segment is encoded as an MPLS label.

SRv6.why: The document defines the SRv6 instantiation: SIDs as IPv6 addresses, SRH processing, FIB entries, and SRv6 security considerations.
SRv6.quote: SR can be applied to the IPv6 architecture with a new type of routing header called the SR Header (SRH) [IPv6-SRH].

rejected.why: MPLS is the data plane that SR-MPLS reuses unchanged; the more specific SR-MPLS tag covers the relevant content.
IGP extensions for SR are defined in other documents; here IS-IS is only referenced as an advertisement mechanism.
BGP prefix and peering segments are described briefly, but the BGP extensions are defined elsewhere; this RFC is not about BGP itself.
IPv6 is the data plane for SRv6; the SRv6 tag is the more specific fit, and the SRH itself is defined in a separate document.
SR Policies can be used for TE, but the document is a general architecture and not a TE specification.
The Anycast-SID is discussed, but only as one SR segment type, not as anycast addressing in its own right.

RFC8403.title: A Scalable and Topology-Aware MPLS Data-Plane Monitoring System
RFC8403.summary: Informational RFC describing a topology-aware MPLS Path Monitoring System (PMS) that uses Segment Routing label stacks to send self-addressed probes for data-plane continuity checks, connectivity verification and fault localization within a single IGP domain.

segment routing.why: The monitoring system is built on SR label stacks (Node-SIDs, Adj-SIDs) steering probes along monitored segments, so SR is central to how it works.
segment routing.quote: Segment-based routing enables a scalable and simple method to monitor data-plane liveliness of the complete set of paths belonging to a single domain.

OAM.why: The document describes an OAM system for MPLS data-plane continuity checks, connectivity verification and fault localization; no more specific OAM tech tag exists in the taxonomy.
OAM.quote: The MPLS monitoring system adds features to the traditional MPLS ping and Label Switched Path (LSP) trace, in a very complementary way.

MPLS.why: It concerns MPLS LSP data-plane monitoring, label stacks and MPLS topology awareness, including monitoring LDP and RSVP-TE LSPs.
MPLS.quote: The system applies to the monitoring of non-SR LSPs like Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) as well as to the monitoring of SR LSPs

rejected.why: BFD and S-BFD are only listed as packet types the PMS could use for continuity checks; the document does not specify or extend them.
MPLS traceroute from RFC 8029 is used as a tool, but the document explicitly introduces no new path-trace features.
ECMP is discussed as a consideration when steering probes, but the document is not about ECMP forwarding itself.
Delay comparison with IPPM systems appears only in an implementation report mention; the focus is liveness and continuity monitoring.
ICMP is just one possible probe packet type, not specified here.
The document is about SR-based monitoring over MPLS, but segment routing is the more fitting broad tag and nothing SR-MPLS-specific is specified beyond using labels.

RFC8404.title: Effects of Pervasive Encryption on Operators
RFC8404.summary: Informational RFC cataloguing network operator, hosting, and enterprise monitoring/management/security practices that depend on cleartext and how increased encryption (TLS, IPsec, QUIC) affects them, to inform protocol development.

operational security.why: The document is a catalogue of operator and enterprise security-monitoring, troubleshooting and management practices and how encryption affects them.
operational security.quote: discusses current security and network operations as well as management practices that may be impacted by the shift to increased use of encryption

privacy.why: Balancing pervasive-monitoring mitigation and user privacy against network manageability is the document's central theme.
privacy.quote: RFC 7258 discusses the critical need to protect users' privacy when developing IETF specifications

TLS.why: Substantial discussion of TLS 1.3 visibility, SNI, ALPN, interception and decryption by monitoring tools, and their effects on operators.
TLS.quote: ALPN is a TLS extension that may be used to indicate the application protocol within the TLS session.

IPFIX.why: A dedicated section covers IPFIX and how encryption limits the information elements that can be exported.
IPFIX.quote: While the deployment of encryption has no direct effect on the use of IPFIX, certain defined IEs may become unavailable

performance measurement.why: Passive performance monitoring, application performance monitoring and PDM are discussed throughout as affected by encryption.
performance measurement.quote: Passive measurement of some metrics will be impossible with encryption that prevents inferring-packet correspondence across multiple observation points

rejected.why: IPsec is one of the encryption types whose effect on visibility is discussed (2-tuple vs 5-tuple), but the document does not specify or analyse it.
A short subsection notes that SFC classifiers lose visibility, but the document is not about SFC.
DDoS mitigation and fingerprinting are mentioned in sections, but only as one of many monitoring practices.
HTTP header insertion, caching and HTTP/2 are mentioned as affected practices, not subject matter.
CDNs are mentioned as complicating monitoring, but only in passing.
End-to-end principle is referenced, but the document focuses on operational practices rather than architectural principles.

gaps.name: Pervasive encryption / pervasive monitoring
gaps.why: The document's core subject is the effect of widespread encryption on network operations; the taxonomy has no tag for encryption's impact or pervasive monitoring (closest are privacy and operational security).

RFC8405.title: Shortest Path First (SPF) Back-Off Delay Algorithm for Link-State IGPs
RFC8405.summary: Defines a standard SPF back-off delay algorithm (a three-state FSM with timers and default parameters) for link-state IGPs such as IS-IS and OSPF, to reduce computational churn and micro-loops during convergence.

routing architecture.why: The document specifies a cross-protocol IGP convergence/SPF scheduling algorithm that applies to IS-IS, OSPF and OSPFv3 alike. It is not specific to one protocol, so the general routing architecture topic (convergence and scalability) fits best.
routing architecture.quote: This document defines a standard algorithm to temporarily postpone or "back off" link-state IGP Shortest Path First (SPF) computations.

rejected.why: OSPF is one of the IGPs the algorithm applies to, but the document does not specify or extend OSPF itself. It is cross-IGP.
IS-IS is only one of the IGPs the algorithm applies to. The document is not about IS-IS specifically.
OSPFv3 is mentioned only as an example IGP the algorithm applies to.
Fast Reroute/LFA is mentioned only as a protocol that reacts to SPF computation. The document is not about it.
BGP is mentioned only as a subsystem that reacts to IGP route changes.
LDP is mentioned only as a subsystem reacting to IGP route changes.

gaps.name: IGP convergence / SPF scheduling
gaps.why: The document is about timing of SPF computation in link-state IGPs generally and micro-loop mitigation. No dedicated tag exists for IGP convergence, so the closest general topic, routing architecture, was used.

RFC8406.title: Taxonomy of Coding Techniques for Efficient Network Communications
RFC8406.summary: An IRTF NWCRG informational document that defines recommended terminology and a high-level taxonomy for Network Coding and erasure-correcting (FEC) coding concepts, aligned with RMT and FECFRAME RFCs.

FEC.why: The whole document defines terminology for erasure-correcting codes, network coding, linear/block/sliding-window codes, FEC schemes, and FEC payload IDs, which is the FEC/network coding subject.
FEC.quote: A code for the Packet Erasure Channel (only).  These codes are also called "Application-Level FECs" to highlight that they have been designed for use

rejected.why: Only cited as an existing framework whose terminology is aligned with; the document does not specify or extend FECFRAME.
RMT, FLUTE/ALC and NORM are referenced for terminology alignment only; the document is not about reliable multicast transport.
The document is a glossary, but the subject is network coding terms; the specific FEC tag fits better, and the terminology tag is for glossaries of general terminology.
RTP packets are only mentioned as an example of a Source Packet or Symbol.
No specific code families such as LDPC or Raptor are defined; only generic linear and random linear coding are covered.

gaps.name: Network Coding
gaps.why: The document is about Network Coding (recoding at intermediate nodes, RLC, sliding window codes), which is broader than the FEC tag. The taxonomy has no dedicated tag, although the FEC tag's description does mention network coding.

RFC8407.title: Guidelines for Authors and Reviewers of Documents Containing YANG Data Models
RFC8407.summary: BCP giving authors and reviewers guidelines for writing, documenting and reviewing YANG data modules in IETF documents (module naming, XPath, data types, NMDA transition, security/IANA sections), obsoleting RFC 6087.

YANG.why: The whole document is guidance on writing and reviewing YANG modules: identifiers, types, augments, deviations, NMDA operational state, and a module template.
YANG.quote: This document defines a set of usage guidelines for documents containing YANG 1.1 [RFC7950] and YANG 1.0 [RFC6020] data models.

rejected.why: NETCONF is the protocol whose servers use the YANG modules. The document gives no NETCONF protocol specification, only YANG authoring guidance.
RESTCONF is mentioned alongside NETCONF as a consumer of the modules. It is not specified or profiled here.
The IANA section only registers the ietf-template module. It is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
XPath usage inside YANG is covered, but that is part of the YANG guidance and not about XML as a format.
The document touches on I-D and RFC documentation requirements. It is mainly YANG module authoring guidance, not IETF process.
The parent of YANG is implied. No separate broader tag is needed.

RFC8408.title: Conveying Path Setup Type in PCE Communication Protocol (PCEP) Messages
RFC8408.summary: RFC 8408 extends PCEP with a PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY TLV and a PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV so a PCEP session can support multiple TE path setup methods, defining the RSVP-TE type and related error codes and an IANA registry.

PCE.why: The document specifies new PCEP TLVs, procedures and error codes for conveying path setup type between PCC and PCE, so it is about PCEP.
PCE.quote: This document proposes an extension to the PCE Communication Protocol (PCEP) to allow support for different path setup methods over a given PCEP session.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is only the one path setup type that the document assigns a code (PST 0) and treats as the default. The document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE.
Segment routing is mentioned only as an example of a future path setup type, in an informative reference to another draft. This document does not define it.
The paths are LSPs, but the document is about PCEP signalling, not MPLS.
The paths are TE paths, but the document is about the PCEP extension. The PCE tag already covers it and sits under traffic engineering.
The IANA registry creation is boilerplate for this protocol extension, not the document's subject.

RFC8409.title: The Entity Category Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) Attribute Types
RFC8409.summary: Defines two SAML metadata entity attributes (entity category and entity category support), whose URI values label entities as members of, or supporters of, categories, for use in federated identity metadata.

federated authentication.why: The document defines SAML entity attributes used in identity federation metadata for attribute release policy and IdP discovery. This is cross-domain federated authentication, and it is the closest fit in the taxonomy.
federated authentication.quote: These category membership claims MAY be used by a relying party to provision policy for release of attributes from an identity provider

XML.why: Much of the document specifies how the attributes are encoded in XML metadata (EntityDescriptor, Extensions, EntityAttributes), with XML examples.
XML.quote: the entity category attribute MUST be encoded as a SAML 2.0 Attribute element with @NameFormat urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:attrname-format:uri

rejected.why: Attribute values are URIs, but the document only uses URIs as opaque identifiers. It does not specify URI syntax or schemes.
Category claims may inform attribute release policy, but the document defines labelling of entities, not access control.
The Security Considerations mention chains of trust and metadata signing, but only as boilerplate. The body is not about PKI.
The document has no IANA actions.

gaps.name: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) and SAML metadata
gaps.why: The document is about SAML metadata entity attributes. The taxonomy has no SAML tag, and federated authentication is only an approximate fit.

RFC8410.title: Algorithm Identifiers for Ed25519, Ed448, X25519, and X448 for Use in the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure
RFC8410.summary: Specifies ASN.1 object identifiers and encodings for Ed25519, Ed448, X25519 and X448 public keys, private keys and signatures for use in X.509 certificates.

Curve25519.why: The document defines OIDs and encodings for X25519 and X448 key agreement and the curve25519/curve448 keys.
Curve25519.quote: This document specifies algorithm identifiers and ASN.1 encoding formats for elliptic curve constructs using the curve25519 and curve448 curves.

EdDSA.why: It defines identifiers, public key, private key and signature encodings for EdDSA (Ed25519/Ed448).
EdDSA.quote: The signature algorithms covered are Ed25519 and Ed448.

X.509.why: It profiles X.509 certificate SubjectPublicKeyInfo, keyUsage bits and signature fields for these algorithms.
X.509.quote: Certificates conforming to [RFC5280] can convey a public key for any public key algorithm.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is the notation used for the OIDs and module, but the document is about algorithm identifiers in X.509, not ASN.1 itself.
Parent of the chosen Curve25519 and EdDSA tags, so it is implied.
The ASN.1 module mentions S/MIME capabilities and key wrap, but CMS is not the subject.
Parent of X.509, which is already tagged.

RFC8411.title: IANA Registration for the Cryptographic Algorithm Object Identifier Range
RFC8411.summary: Informational RFC in which DigiCert's donated OID range 1.3.101.100-127 is transferred to IANA, the existing assignments (X25519, X448, Ed25519, Ed448) are listed, and a "Specification Required" policy is set for a new "SMI Security for Cryptographic Algorithms" registry.

IANA.why: The document's purpose is to create an IANA registry, transfer control of the OID range to IANA, and set its allocation policy. Readers of the IANA registries subject would expect to find it.
IANA.quote: IANA has created the "SMI Security for Cryptographic Algorithms" registry within the SMI-numbers registry.

EdDSA.why: The range was donated to register the OIDs for the Edwards-curve algorithms (id-EdDSA25519 and id-EdDSA448), and the registry table lists them. The document only registers identifiers and does not specify the algorithms, so the role is secondary.
EdDSA.quote: allowed for the Edwards Elliptic Curve key agreement [RFC7748] and signature [RFC8032] algorithms to be defined with encodings that are smaller

rejected.why: OIDs are used with ASN.1, but the document defines no ASN.1 modules or encoding rules. ASN.1 is only the context.
The identifiers are for use in the X.509 PKI, but that profile is specified in RFC 8410. This document only manages the OID range.
X25519 and X448 appear only as registry entries. The curves themselves are not specified or discussed.
The document is only about OID registration. It says nothing about elliptic-curve cryptography itself.
The document registers algorithm identifiers but does not address cryptographic algorithms, modes, or parameters.

gaps.name: Object identifier (OID) registries / SMI numbers
gaps.why: The document is about an OID arc, the "SMI Security for Cryptographic Algorithms" registry, and its allocation policy. The taxonomy has no OID-specific tag, so IANA is the closest fit.

RFC8412.title: Software Inventory Message and Attributes (SWIMA) for PA-TNC
RFC8412.summary: RFC 8412 defines SWIMA, a set of PA-TNC attributes and message exchanges (requests, inventory and event responses, subscriptions, errors) letting NEA endpoints report installed software inventory to a NEA Server.

NEA.why: The document extends PA-TNC within the NEA architecture; NEA is the nearest subject, but it is not in the taxonomy (see gaps), so this tag is invalid and I use the closest available tag instead.
NEA.quote: providing specific attributes and message exchanges to allow endpoints to report their installed software inventory information to a NEA Server

RFC8413.title: Framework for Scheduled Use of Resources
RFC8413.summary: Informational framework describing an architecture for time-scheduled reservation of TE resources for LSPs, using a stateful PCE with a time-based TED and LSP database, including multi-domain considerations.

PCE.why: The architecture centres on a PCE holding scheduled TED and LSP-DB state, driving PCEP Initiate/Update, synchronizing between PCEs, and multi-domain computation (BRPC, H-PCE).
PCE.quote: the computing entity normally known as a Path Computation Element (PCE) [RFC4655] needs access to a database of available links and nodes

traffic engineering.why: The document is about scheduled reservation of TE resources and LSP planning, which is traffic engineering of transport networks.
traffic engineering.quote: Time-Scheduled (TS) reservation of TE resources can be used to provide resource booking for TE-LSPs

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is only mentioned as one way TE-LSPs are signaled. The document specifies nothing about it.
LSPs are the subject of the reservations, but the document does not address MPLS architecture or encapsulation.
GMPLS is mentioned only in passing and in references. It is not a focus.
BGP-LS is used only as a way to export TED information to the PCE, so BGP is substrate.
SDN is mentioned once as an alternative provisioning paradigm, not as a subject.
The document is about resource booking for LSPs, not QoS architectures or signalling.

RFC8414.title: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata
RFC8414.summary: Defines a JSON metadata format and well-known URI by which OAuth 2.0 clients discover an authorization server's endpoints and capabilities, with optional signed metadata and an IANA registry of metadata names.

OAuth.why: The whole document specifies OAuth 2.0 authorization server metadata, its endpoints, grant types, and client authentication methods; it extends the OAuth framework.
OAuth.quote: This specification defines a metadata format that an OAuth 2.0 client can use to obtain the information needed to interact with an OAuth 2.0 authorization server

service discovery.why: The document defines a discovery mechanism (well-known URI derived from the issuer identifier) for locating authorization server endpoints and capabilities.
service discovery.quote: The metadata for an authorization server is retrieved from a well-known location as a JSON [RFC8259] document, which declares its endpoint locations

rejected.why: Signed metadata is carried as a JWT, but JWT is a mechanism relied upon, not the subject of the document.
JSON is only the encoding for the metadata document.
Metadata is fetched with a plain HTTP GET; HTTP is substrate and nothing new is defined about it.
TLS requirements appear only in Security Considerations boilerplate-style text; no new TLS mechanism.
Mentioned only as one way to discover the issuer; out of scope.
JWS/JWK are used for signing metadata and key publication but are not specified or extended here.

RFC8415.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)
RFC8415.summary: RFC 8415 is the consolidated DHCPv6 specification, covering client/server/relay message exchanges, DUIDs, identity associations, address assignment, prefix delegation, stateless operation, options and reconfigure authentication, and it obsoletes RFC 3315 and several follow-up RFCs.

DHCPv6.why: The whole document specifies DHCPv6: messages, client, server and relay behavior, options, DUIDs, IAs, prefix delegation and stateless mode.
DHCPv6.quote: This document describes the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6): an extensible mechanism for configuring nodes with network configuration parameters, IP addresses, and prefixes.

rejected.why: DHCPv6 is described as operating alongside or instead of SLAAC, but SLAAC is not specified here.
DHCPv6 is the subject; IPv6 itself is only the environment, and DHCPv6 is the more specific tag.
UDP is only the transport for DHCP messages, with fixed ports 546 and 547.
IPsec is mentioned only for protecting relay-to-server messages, by reference to RFC 8213.
HMAC-MD5 is used inside RKAP, but the document is not about HMAC.
DHCP (v4) is explicitly out of scope, and DHCPv6 is the more specific child tag.

RFC8416.title: Simplified Local Internet Number Resource Management with the RPKI (SLURM)
RFC8416.summary: Defines SLURM, a JSON-format local override file letting an RPKI Relying Party filter validated ROA payloads and BGPsec assertions and add local ones before sending them to routers via the RPKI-Router protocol.

RPKI.why: The document specifies local filters and additions to RPKI validated data (VRPs, router keys) at the Relying Party, so it belongs on the RPKI page.
RPKI.quote: SLURM allows an operator to create a local view of the global RPKI by generating sets of assertions.

BGPsec.why: A substantial part defines BGPsec filters and locally added BGPsec assertions (ASN, SKI, router public key) for path validation.
BGPsec.quote: A BGPsec Assertion that matches any configured BGPsec Filter MUST be removed from the RP's output.

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding for SLURM files; the document defines no new JSON format of general interest beyond its own schema.
BGP origin validation is the use context, but the document specifies RPKI Relying Party overrides, not BGP behaviour.
Base64 is used only to encode SKI and keys; the document is not about it.
Router certificate SKI and public key formats are referenced but not specified here.

RFC8417.title: Security Event Token (SET)
RFC8417.summary: Defines the Security Event Token (SET), a JWT-based data structure with new claims (events, toe, txn) for conveying security and identity events, along with profile requirements and guidance on preventing confusion with other JWTs.

secevent.why: The document defines the SET itself, the core subject of the secevent area: security event tokens and their event delivery format, including claims and profile requirements.
secevent.quote: This specification defines an extensible Security Event Token (SET) data structure, which can be exchanged using protocols such as HTTP.

JWT.why: A SET is a JWT; the document profiles JWT claims, registers new JWT claims (events, toe, txn), and a +jwt suffix, and discusses confusion with other JWTs such as ID Tokens and access tokens.
JWT.quote: This specification profiles the use of JWT for the purpose of issuing SETs.

rejected.why: JWS and JWE are only used optionally to sign/encrypt the SET; the document does not specify or extend JOSE.
SCIM appears only as a non-normative example event; the document does not define SCIM behaviour.
Access tokens are discussed only to prevent confusion with SETs; the document is not about OAuth.
TLS is only a transport and integrity mechanism cited in Security Considerations.
Registers application/secevent+jwt and the +jwt suffix, but this is IANA boilerplate rather than the main subject.
JSON is only the encoding substrate of the claims set.

RFC8418.title: Use of the Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Key Agreement Algorithm with X25519 and X448 in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC8418.summary: Specifies how to use ephemeral-static ECDH key agreement with X25519 and X448 in CMS enveloped-data, authenticated-data and authenticated-enveloped-data content types, including KDFs (ANSI-X9.63-KDF, HKDF), algorithm identifiers, and SMIMECapabilities.

CMS.why: The document defines how KeyAgreeRecipientInfo fields are populated in the CMS EnvelopedData, AuthenticatedData and AuthEnvelopedData content types.
CMS.quote: This document describes the conventions for using Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key agreement using curve25519 and curve448 [CURVES] in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)

Curve25519.why: The document specifies the use of X25519 and X448 key agreement, including key sizes and object identifiers.
Curve25519.quote: Using curve25519 with Diffie-Hellman key agreement is referred to as "X25519".  Using curve448 with Diffie-Hellman key agreement is referred to as "X448".

rejected.why: S/MIME is only touched via the SMIMECapabilities attribute section; the document is about CMS key agreement, not S/MIME messages.
HKDF is used as a KDF but HMAC itself is not what the document is about.
AES key wrap is referenced as the key-encryption algorithm only; the document does not specify it.
Certificates are only referenced for carrying the recipient's static public key, with the details deferred to RFC 8410.
ASN.1 is the notation for the module in the appendix, not the subject of the document.
Parent of Curve25519, which is already chosen as the more specific tag.

RFC8419.title: Use of Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA) Signatures in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC8419.summary: Specifies conventions for using EdDSA (Ed25519 and Ed448, PureEdDSA only) signatures in the CMS signed-data content type, including algorithm identifiers, digest algorithms, and signed-attribute handling.

EdDSA.why: The document profiles EdDSA (Ed25519 and Ed448) for use as a signature algorithm, specifying OIDs, PureEdDSA-only use, and signature encoding.
EdDSA.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA) [RFC8032] for curve25519 [CURVE25519] and curve448 [CURVE448]

CMS.why: It defines how SignedData and SignerInfo fields (digestAlgorithms, signatureAlgorithm, signedAttributes) are populated when EdDSA is used, so CMS readers need it.
CMS.quote: with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) [RFC5652] signed-data content type

rejected.why: SHA-512 and SHAKE256 are mandated as digest algorithms, but only as supporting identifiers; the document is not about the hash family.
ASN.1 is used to express OIDs and algorithm identifiers, but only as the notation, not as the subject.
Public key OIDs are taken from RFC 8410 for certificates, but the document is about CMS signatures, not certificate profiles.
The curves are the basis of Ed25519/Ed448, but the document concerns signatures, not Curve25519/448 key agreement; EdDSA is the more specific tag.
Random number generation is mentioned only in Security Considerations boilerplate.

RFC8420.title: Using the Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA) in the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC8420.summary: Defines a new "Identity" hash value in the IKEv2 SIGNATURE_HASH_ALGORITHMS notification so that EdDSA (Ed25519/Ed448) signatures, which need no prehashing, can be negotiated for IKEv2 authentication.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 signature authentication negotiation with a new Identity hash value in the IKEv2 Hash Algorithms registry.
IKE.quote: we define a new value in the SIGNATURE_HASH_ALGORITHMS notification to indicate that no hashing is performed.

EdDSA.why: It specifies how EdDSA (Ed25519, Ed448) is used in IKEv2, including prohibiting the prehashed variants.
EdDSA.quote: Ed25519 and Ed448 are only defined with the "Identity" hash and MUST NOT be sent to a receiver that has not indicated support

rejected.why: RFC 8410 OIDs are only repeated in an appendix for convenience; the document is not about certificates.
Ed25519 and Ed448 are signature schemes covered by EdDSA; the document does not address Curve25519/448 key exchange.
IKE is a child of IPsec and is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
The appendix just repeats OIDs from RFC 8410 and does not define ASN.1 modules.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-level; the document is not about registry guidance.

RFC8421.title: Guidelines for Multihomed and IPv4/IPv6 Dual-Stack Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE)
RFC8421.summary: BCP giving guidelines for adjusting ICE candidate priorities (local/type preference) so connectivity checks are fairly intermingled across IPv4/IPv6 families and across reliable/unreliable interfaces in multihomed and dual-stack hosts, speeding ICE completion when paths are broken.

ICE.why: The whole document is guidance on how ICE candidate priorities and checklists should be computed, refining RFC 8445 behaviour.
ICE.quote: This document provides guidelines on how to make Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) conclude faster in multihomed and IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack scenarios where broken paths exist.

happy eyeballs.why: The document applies Happy Eyeballs-style fairness between IPv6 and IPv4 to ICE checks and discusses how ICE pacing overrides RFC 8305 timing; a substantial part of the motivation.
happy eyeballs.quote: This enables implementations to follow the intent of "Happy Eyeballs: Success with Dual-Stack Hosts" [RFC8305].

multihoming.why: A full section is devoted to multihomed ICE recommendations, deprioritizing unreliable interfaces.
multihoming.quote: Applications should take special care to deprioritize network interfaces known to provide unreliable connectivity when operating in a multihomed environment.

rejected.why: Dual-stack is the setting, but the document is about ICE check ordering rather than a transition mechanism; happy eyeballs is tagged more specifically.
ICE is used with offer/answer but SDP is not specified or extended here.
RTP/RTCP components are only mentioned regarding component IDs in the priority formula.
Parent of ICE, implied by the ICE tag.
IPv6 candidates are mentioned as one address family, but the document does not address IPv6 itself.

RFC8422.title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS) Versions 1.2 and Earlier
RFC8422.summary: RFC 8422 specifies ECC-based key exchange (ECDHE) and ECDSA/EdDSA authentication cipher suites, extensions, and data structures for TLS 1.2 and earlier, obsoleting RFC 4492.

TLS.why: Defines new TLS cipher suites, the Supported Elliptic Curves and Point Formats extensions, and handshake message changes for TLS 1.2 and earlier.
TLS.quote: This document describes key exchange algorithms based on Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) for the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol.

elliptic curve.why: Specifies ECDHE, named curves (NIST curves, x25519, x448), point formats, public key validation and ECDH computations.
elliptic curve.quote: the use of the ECDHE key agreement scheme with ephemeral keys to establish the TLS premaster secret

ECDSA.why: ECDSA is a major authentication mechanism, including signature encoding in ServerKeyExchange and CertificateVerify.
ECDSA.quote: All ECDSA computations MUST be performed according to ANSI X9.62 or its successors.

EdDSA.why: Adds EdDSA (Ed25519/Ed448) authentication to TLS, with the Intrinsic hash value and signing rules.
EdDSA.quote: To represent ed25519 and ed448 in the signature_algorithms extension, the value shall be (8,7) and (8,8), respectively.

Curve25519.why: Adds x25519 and x448 key exchange to TLS, including their point encoding and all-zero shared secret check.
Curve25519.quote: An ECDHE key exchange using X25519 (curve x25519) goes as follows

rejected.why: Only mentioned incidentally in IANA (DTLS-OK flag); the document targets TLS.
ECDHE_RSA uses RSA signatures, but RSA is just a signature mechanism relied on, not the subject.
Certificates are referenced for ECC key encoding via other RFCs; the document does not define a certificate profile.
AES cipher suites are listed in a table, but AES is defined elsewhere and not the subject.
IANA registry updates are boilerplate-like and secondary to the main body.
Used only for the ECDSA signature encoding; it is a substrate, not the subject.

RFC8423.title: Reclassification of Suite B Documents to Historic Status
RFC8423.summary: Reclassifies ten Suite B-related Informational RFCs (profiles of IPsec, TLS, S/MIME, SSH, CMC and certificates for NSA Suite B algorithms) to Historic because NSA moved to the CNSA Suite.

cryptography.why: The document is about the retirement of the Suite B cryptographic algorithm suite profiles and the transition to CNSA. No specific algorithm tag fits, so the cryptography topic applies directly.
cryptography.quote: This document reclassifies the RFCs related to the United States National Security Agency (NSA) Suite B cryptographic algorithms as Historic

IPsec.why: Several of the reclassified RFCs (4869, 6379, 6380) are IPsec Suite B suites and profiles. The document discusses their impact on IPsec.
IPsec.quote: RFC 4869 adds four pre-defined suites based upon Suite B specifications.

TLS.why: The TLS Suite B profiles (RFC 5430, 6460) are being made Historic, and the document discusses their referencing documents.
TLS.quote: RFC 7525 ... observes that the Suite B profile of TLS 1.2 uses different ciphersuites.

rejected.why: The S/MIME Suite B RFCs are among those reclassified, but the document does not discuss S/MIME beyond listing them.
RFC 6239 is only listed, with no substantive treatment of SSH.
RFC 5759 (certificate profile) is covered only in passing.
The document does change RFC status, but its subject is the Suite B suite rather than the status process in general.

RFC8424.title: Extensions to RSVP-TE for Label Switched Path (LSP) Ingress Fast Reroute (FRR) Protection
RFC8424.summary: Experimental RFC defining RSVP-TE extensions (a new INGRESS_PROTECTION object) so a backup ingress can locally protect the ingress node of a P2P or P2MP TE LSP, extending fast reroute to the ingress.

RSVP-TE.why: The document defines a new RSVP-TE object, subobjects, and PATH/RESV procedures for ingress protection of TE LSPs.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document describes extensions to Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) for locally protecting the ingress node of a Point-to-Point (P2P) or Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP)

IP fast reroute.why: The document is about fast reroute protection of the LSP ingress. It builds on RFC 4090 PLR behaviour, though it is MPLS TE FRR rather than IP/LDP FRR, so this tag is a loose fit.
IP fast reroute.quote: It extends the Fast Reroute (FRR) protection for transit nodes of an LSP to the ingress node of the LSP.

rejected.why: MPLS LSPs are the context, but the specific subject is RSVP-TE signalling, which is a more specific fit for the tags chosen.
BFD is only mentioned as an example failure-detection method. Detection is explicitly out of scope.
The parent topic is implied by RSVP-TE, so listing it separately would be redundant.
RFC 6378 linear protection is mentioned only as background, to say it cannot protect the ingress.
RSVP-TE is the more specific child and is already tagged.

gaps.name: MPLS TE fast reroute (RFC 4090 FRR for LSP tunnels)
gaps.why: The taxonomy's only FRR tag is for IP and LDP fast reroute. There is no tag for RSVP-TE/MPLS TE link, node and ingress protection.

RFC8425.title: IANA Considerations for IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Prefix Information Option Flags
RFC8425.summary: Creates an IANA registry for the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Prefix Information Option flags (L, A, R, reserved bits) and updates RFC 4861 to point to it.

neighbor discovery.why: The whole document concerns the Neighbor Discovery Prefix Information Option flags and updates RFC 4861 Section 4.6.2, so it belongs under IPv6 neighbor discovery.
neighbor discovery.quote: IANA has created a new registry for IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Prefix Information Option flags.

rejected.why: The document's registry is for a specific ND option's flags. It is an IANA action on a protocol, not about IANA registry policy or stewardship in general.
RFC 6275 defines the R flag, but this document only cites it in the registry and does not specify or extend Mobile IPv6.
A parent of neighbor discovery, which is the more specific tag and already covers it.
The registry is hosted in the ICMPv6 parameters page, but the document is not about ICMP.

RFC8426.title: Recommendations for RSVP-TE and Segment Routing (SR) Label Switched Path (LSP) Coexistence
RFC8426.summary: Informational RFC describing options for letting Segment Routing LSPs coexist with RSVP-TE LSPs, focusing on keeping the TE database's bandwidth accounting consistent, and detailing a solution that reduces Maximum-Reservable-Bandwidth by measured SR traffic.

RSVP-TE.why: The document's core problem is RSVP-TE bandwidth accounting and path computation when SR traffic shares links. It describes adjusting RSVP-TE reservable and unreserved bandwidth and preemption behaviour.
