RSVP-TE.quote: RSVP-TE is not aware of how much bandwidth is being consumed by SR services on the network links

segment routing.why: The document is about introducing and migrating to SR LSPs alongside RSVP-TE, covering SR traffic measurement and its effect on the TED.
segment routing.quote: Operators are looking to introduce services over Segment Routing (SR) Label Switched Paths (LSPs) in networks running Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) LSPs.

rejected.why: Parent of RSVP-TE; implied by the RSVP-TE tag, so not listed separately.
IGP-TE advertisements of bandwidth are discussed, but only as the mechanism carrying TED data; no IS-IS specification.
OSPF TE is only cited as an IGP-TE flooding mechanism; the document is not about OSPF.
DS-TE is mentioned briefly for bandwidth constraints models, which is not a substantial part of the document.
The document discusses SR LSPs generally and cites the SR architecture, with no specific SR-MPLS dataplane content.
LSPs are the subject, but RSVP-TE and segment routing tags cover it more specifically.

RFC8427.title: Representing DNS Messages in JSON
RFC8427.summary: Defines a general JSON format for representing DNS messages, resource records, paired query/response objects, and streams of them, intended to be profiled by applications such as logging and passive DNS.

DNS.why: The document defines how DNS message fields, resource records and RDATA are represented, so it is about DNS message data and belongs on the DNS page.
DNS.quote: This document describes a general format for DNS message data in JSON.

JSON.why: It specifies a JSON-based data format with object members, number and string encoding rules, and a media type, so readers of JSON formats would want it.
JSON.quote: This document uses JSON to describe DNS messages.  It also defines how to describe a paired DNS query and response and how to stream DNS objects.

rejected.why: It registers application/dns+json, but that is IANA boilerplate for the format rather than the main subject.
HEX members use base16 from RFC 4648 only as an encoding mechanism; the document defines nothing new about base16.
A-label form is mentioned only for name encoding; IDN is not the document's subject.
DNSSEC RR types such as RRSIG and NSEC appear only in a list of RDATA members and are not analysed.
The DOH working group is mentioned only in the acknowledgements; the document does not specify DNS over HTTPS.
RFC 3339 timestamps are used for the dateString member, but the document does not define date formats.

RFC8428.title: Sensor Measurement Lists (SenML)
RFC8428.summary: RFC 8428 defines SenML, a data model and JSON, CBOR, XML and EXI serializations (with media types, unit and label registries, and fragment identifiers) for carrying simple sensor measurements and actuation commands from constrained devices.

SenML.why: The document specifies the SenML format itself, including its data model, labels, units registry and media types.
SenML.quote: This specification defines a format for representing simple sensor measurements and device parameters in Sensor Measurement Lists (SenML).

CBOR.why: A full section defines the CBOR serialization with integer labels and registers its media types, so CBOR readers would want it.
CBOR.quote: The CBOR [RFC7049] representation is equivalent to the JSON representation, with the following changes:

JSON.why: The JSON serialization is the primary representation, defined with its own section and examples.
JSON.quote: The root JSON value consists of an array with one JSON object for each SenML Record.

XML.why: It defines an XML representation with a RelaxNG schema and an EXI form generated from an XSD.
XML.quote: A SenML Pack or Stream can also be represented in XML format as defined in this section.

media types.why: It registers eight media types, including the streaming SenSML variants, and gives the rationale for having both.
media types.quote: This document registers media types for each serialization format of SenML (JSON, CBOR, XML, and EXI)

rejected.why: CoAP is only a transport; the document assigns Content-Format IDs but does not specify or extend CoAP.
HTTP is only a carrier used in the examples.
CDDL is used to describe the schema in one informative section; the document is not about CDDL.
URNs are recommended for naming sensors, but the document does not define URN namespaces.
6LoWPAN is mentioned only as a constrained network where small payloads help.
The parent tag is implied by the SenML and CoAP-related child tags.

gaps.name: SenML
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no SenML tag under IoT or data formats, although SenML is the core subject of this RFC. The id I used, 'SenML', is not in the taxonomy as shown. The closest fit is the SenML [tech] node, which the listing does not include; this is a likely taxonomy gap.

RFC8429.title: Deprecate Triple-DES (3DES) and RC4 in Kerberos
RFC8429.summary: BCP that deprecates the triple-DES and RC4 Kerberos encryption and checksum types, moves RFC 4757 to Historic, and updates RFC 3961 and RFC 4120 to stop recommending triple-DES.

Kerberos.why: The document changes the status of Kerberos encryption and checksum types and updates the Kerberos specifications RFC 3961 and RFC 4120. Kerberos readers need it.
Kerberos.quote: the deprecation process should begin for their use in Kerberos

RC4.why: It deprecates the RC4 Kerberos enctypes. Section 5 analyses their weaknesses: statistical biases, unsalted MD4 password hash and NTLM key reuse.
RC4.quote: Kerberos implementations and deployments SHOULD NOT implement or deploy the RC4 encryption type RC4-HMAC(23).

DES.why: It deprecates the triple-DES Kerberos enctypes. Section 6 analyses their weaknesses: the weak string2key function and the 64-bit block size.
DES.quote: Triple-DES is based on the single-DES primitive, simply using additional key material and nested encryption.

rejected.why: AES is named only as the secure alternative that is already widely supported. The document does not specify or profile it.
PBKDF2 is mentioned only as the string2key function of modern enctypes, in contrast to the weak ones. The document is not about it.
MD4 and RSA-MD5 appear only in passing as weak components. The document is not about MD4 or MD5.
The Kerberos GSS mechanism SGN_ALG and SEAL_ALG values are deprecated in one paragraph. That is not enough to make the document about GSS-API.
RC4 in TLS is cited only as background evidence for RC4's weakness (RFC 7465).

RFC8430.title: RIB Information Model
RFC8430.summary: Specifies an information model for the router Routing Information Base (RIB), covering routing instances, RIBs, routes, nexthops, read/write operations and notifications, as the basis for the I2RS RIB YANG data model.

I2RS.why: The document is the I2RS information model for programmatically reading and writing the router RIB, which is the core of the Interface to the Routing System.
I2RS.quote: The IETF's I2RS WG used this document to design the I2RS RIB data model.

rejected.why: The document defines an information model, not a YANG module; the YANG data model is in RFC 8431.
NETCONF and RESTCONF are mentioned only in Security Considerations as access protocols for derived data models.
RBNF is only the notation used for the grammar, not the subject.
The RIB model is about a router interface and data model, not routing architecture or scalability principles in general.
Multicast nexthop replication is a brief example (Section 7.3), not a main subject.
Tunnel nexthops are one part of the nexthop grammar, not the document's subject.

gaps.name: Routing Information Base (RIB) information model
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the RIB, RIB manager or FIB programming. The I2RS tag covers it only partly.

RFC8431.title: A YANG Data Model for the Routing Information Base (RIB)
RFC8431.summary: Defines the ietf-i2rs-rib YANG module, a data model for the Routing Information Base (routes, nexthops, RPCs, notifications) aligned with the I2RS RIB information model.

YANG.why: The document's main body is a YANG module with tree diagrams, RPCs and notifications for RIB manipulation.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model for the Routing Information Base (RIB) that aligns with the Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) RIB information model.

I2RS.why: The model is the I2RS RIB data model, used by I2RS clients and agents to read and write RIB state.
I2RS.quote: The Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) [RFC7921] provides read and write access to the information and state within the routing process

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only mentioned as access protocols in Security Considerations; the document does not specify them.
MPLS label operations appear as nexthop data nodes, but the document does not specify MPLS itself.
GRE, VXLAN and NVGRE are only tunnel types listed in nexthop encapsulation, not subjects of the document.
The RIB model is covered by I2RS and YANG, so the generic routing topic is not needed.
This is a YANG model, not an SNMP MIB.

gaps.name: Routing Information Base (RIB)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for RIB or nexthop data modelling in general; I2RS and YANG cover it only partially.

RFC8432.title: A Framework for Management and Control of Microwave and Millimeter Wave Interface Parameters
RFC8432.summary: Informational CCAMP framework describing use cases, requirements and a gap analysis for a YANG data model to manage and control microwave/millimeter-wave radio link interfaces in microwave nodes.

YANG.why: The document frames requirements and gap analysis for a new YANG data model for radio link interfaces that augments the RFC 8343 interface model.
YANG.quote: This document describes the required characteristics and use cases for control and management of radio link interface parameters using a YANG data model.

SDN.why: A dedicated section covers SDN-based control of radio links, including operation modes selected by an SDN controller.
SDN.quote: One of the main drivers for applying SDN from an operator perspective is simplification and automation of network provisioning as well as end-to-end network service management.

network management.why: Much of the document covers management use cases (configuration, inventory, performance, fault) for microwave nodes, which is general network management rather than one protocol.
network management.quote: The use cases involve configuration management, inventory, status and statistics, performance management, fault management, and troubleshooting and root cause analysis.

rejected.why: NETCONF is mentioned only as an example management protocol in Security Considerations and as a collection option. The document is not about it.
The SNMP IF-MIB is cited only as the predecessor of the YANG interface model.
Ethernet interfaces are related to the radio link terminal in the model, but the document does not address Ethernet itself.
Wi-Fi and 3/4/5G are explicitly declared out of scope.
Historical performance counters are one use case, but they are covered under general management rather than as a measurement methodology.

gaps.name: Microwave and millimeter wave radio link interfaces
gaps.why: The document is about point-to-point microwave radio backhaul equipment, and the taxonomy has no tag for fixed microwave or radio link technology.

RFC8433.title: A Simpler Method for Resolving Alert-Info URNs
RFC8433.summary: Informational RFC describing a finite-state-machine-based algorithm for resolving SIP Alert-Info "alert" URNs into a chosen alerting signal, as a more efficient alternative to the RFC 7462 algorithm.

SIP.why: The document specifies how a SIP user agent processes the Alert-Info header field in INVITE requests and provisional responses to choose ring and ringback tones. It is SIP call-signalling deployment and implementation guidance.
SIP.quote: a UA is often required to select an alerting signal that renders only a subset of the information in the Alert-Info header field(s)

URN.why: A large part of the document covers the "alert" URN namespace: its hierarchical alert-ind-parts, prefix/ancestor relationships, private extensions, and how URNs are mapped to symbols and resolved.
URN.quote: the Alert-Info values can be URNs in the "alert" URN namespace that specify features of the call or of the signal

rejected.why: The document concerns Alert-Info alerting signals, not SIP event packages, presence, or XCAP.
The SIP tag is more specific and already covers the real-time call signalling subject.
Despite the formal-looking FSM and symbol construction, no formal syntax notation is specified or defined.

RFC8434.title: Requirements for Parallel NFS (pNFS) Layout Types
RFC8434.summary: Defines the requirements that every pNFS layout type must meet to work within the pNFS framework of NFSv4.1 (control protocol, fencing, access control, attribute consistency), and updates RFC 5661.

NFS.why: The whole document specifies requirements on pNFS layout types, which are part of NFSv4.1, and updates RFC 5661. NFS readers would want it.
NFS.quote: The concept of "layout type" has a central role in the definition and implementation of Parallel NFS (pNFS)

rejected.why: The SCSI and block layouts are mentioned only as examples of existing layout types. The document does not cover iSCSI.
NFSv4.1 runs on RPC, but the document says nothing about RPC itself.
The NFS tag is more specific. The block layout discussion is only an example of a layout type.
Security requirements such as fencing and access enforcement are part of the NFS layout requirements and do not make this a general security document.

gaps.name: pNFS (Parallel NFS) layout types

RFC8435.title: Parallel NFS (pNFS) Flexible File Layout
RFC8435.summary: Defines the pNFS flexible file layout type, which lets clients do I/O to NFSv3/NFSv4.x storage devices under loose or tight coupling with the metadata server, and adds client-side mirroring, fencing, error and statistics reporting.

NFS.why: The whole document extends NFSv4.1/4.2 pNFS with a new layout type (LAYOUT4_FLEX_FILES), including its XDR, locking models, mirroring, LAYOUTRETURN/LAYOUTERROR/LAYOUTSTATS usage and layout recall.

rejected.why: RPC and XDR are the substrate. XDR structures are defined only for the NFS layout, and RPC credentials are used for fencing. The document does not specify RPC itself.
RPCSEC_GSS and Kerberos GSS-API appear only in the Security Considerations, where the document says they are not supported for the loosely coupled model.
This is the parent topic of NFS. NFS is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
LDAP is mentioned only as an example source of uid ranges for synthetic ids, so the document is not about it.
Kerberos appears only in passing in the security discussion.

gaps.name: pNFS (Parallel NFS) layout types
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an NFS tag but nothing for pNFS layout types and client-side mirroring. NFS covers the document well enough, but a narrower tag would help readers browsing pNFS.

RFC8436.title: Update to IANA Registration Procedures for Pool 3 Values in the Differentiated Services Field Codepoints (DSCP) Registry
RFC8436.summary: Updates RFC 2474 to change the IANA registration policy for DSCP Pool 3 (xxxx01) to Standards Action and remove its experimental/local use, motivated by the need for a codepoint for the Lower Effort PHB.

Diffserv.why: The document modifies the Diffserv DSCP codepoint space and its registry policy defined in RFC 2474, so readers of Diffserv would want it.

rejected.why: The DS field sits in IPv4/IPv6 headers, but the document does not specify or change either protocol.
The DS field sits in IPv6 headers, but the document does not specify or change IPv6.

RFC8437.title: IMAP UNAUTHENTICATE Extension for Connection Reuse
RFC8437.summary: Defines the IMAP UNAUTHENTICATE command, which returns an IMAP connection to not-authenticated state so an administrative client can reuse it for multiple user identities, and updates the IMAP state machine and extension interactions.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP with a new command and capability, revises the IMAP state machine, and specifies interactions with other IMAP extensions.

SASL (including EXTERNAL) is used and its security layer terminated on UNAUTHENTICATE, but the document does not specify or extend SASL.

The IANA section only registers the capability, which is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC8438.title: IMAP Extension for STATUS=SIZE
RFC8438.summary: Defines the IMAP STATUS=SIZE capability, adding a SIZE data item to the STATUS command to return a mailbox's total storage size in one command.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP with a new capability and STATUS data item, with formal syntax and examples. It is squarely an IMAP extension.

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax; the document is not about it.

The IANA section only registers the capability. That is boilerplate and not the subject.

RFC8439.title: ChaCha20 and Poly1305 for IETF Protocols
RFC8439.summary: Defines the ChaCha20 stream cipher, the Poly1305 authenticator, and the combined AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 construction for IETF protocols, with test vectors and implementation and security advice; obsoletes RFC 7539.

ChaCha20.why: The whole document specifies ChaCha20, Poly1305 and their AEAD composition, with test vectors and implementation advice. This is exactly the ChaCha20 and Poly1305 tag.
ChaCha20.quote: This document defines the ChaCha20 stream cipher as well as the use of the Poly1305 authenticator, both as stand-alone algorithms and as a "combined mode"

rejected.why: AES is mentioned only as the incumbent cipher that ChaCha20 is compared against, in the introduction and in the Appendix B performance table. The document does not specify or profile it.
IPsec and TLS are named only as example consumers of the AEAD. The document defines no IPsec or TLS usage.
IKEv2 appears only in the section explaining why no PRF is specified. The document does not profile IKE.
HMAC is mentioned only in the PRF discussion, as a contrast with Poly1305.
DES is mentioned only in passing, as an example block cipher for generating nonces, and 3DES as the slow fallback cipher in the introduction. The document is not about it.

RFC8440.title: IMAP4 Extension for Returning MYRIGHTS Information in Extended LIST
RFC8440.summary: Defines the LIST-MYRIGHTS IMAP extension, adding a MYRIGHTS return option to the extended LIST command so clients get mailbox ACL rights along with LIST results in one command.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP's LIST command with a new return option and capability, so it belongs on the IMAP page.
IMAP.quote: This document defines an extension to the Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) LIST command that allows the client to request the set of rights

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation for the one-line formal syntax. The document is not about it.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate for the new capability and option. The document is not about IANA guidance.
IMAP is the more specific tag, so the parent email tag is implied.

RFC8441.title: Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/2
RFC8441.summary: Defines the Extended CONNECT method for HTTP/2 (SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL and the :protocol pseudo-header) and uses it to run the WebSocket Protocol over a single HTTP/2 stream, updating RFC 6455.

WebSocket.why: The document specifies a new opening handshake for WebSockets over HTTP/2 and updates RFC 6455.
WebSocket.quote: This document defines a mechanism for running the WebSocket Protocol (RFC 6455) over a single stream of an HTTP/2 connection.

HTTP/2.why: It extends HTTP/2 with a new SETTINGS parameter, the :protocol pseudo-header and Extended CONNECT semantics.
HTTP/2.quote: This document adds a new SETTINGS parameter to those defined by [RFC7540], Section 6.5.2.

rejected.why: The HTTP/2 child tag is more specific and covers the CONNECT method extension.
TCP is only the substrate. The document maps stream closure to TCP closure by analogy but specifies nothing about TCP.
Security requirements are only referenced by pointing to RFC 7540 and RFC 8164. TLS is not specified here.
The CONNECT tunnel is a mechanism for the HTTP/2 extension. It is not IP-level tunnelling.

RFC8442.title: ECDHE_PSK with AES-GCM and AES-CCM Cipher Suites for TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2
RFC8442.summary: Defines four new TLS 1.2/DTLS 1.2 cipher suites combining ECDHE_PSK key exchange with AES-GCM and AES-CCM AEAD algorithms, and registers their code points.

TLS.why: The document's sole purpose is to define new TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 cipher suites, including negotiation restrictions on TLS versions. DTLS is a child of TLS, but the suites are defined for both, so the parent tag covers it.
TLS.quote: This document defines several new cipher suites for version 1.2 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol and version 1.2 of the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol.

AES.why: The cipher suites are built on AES-GCM and AES-CCM AEAD algorithms, and the security considerations discuss their security levels and nonce uniqueness. This is a substantial part of what the suites are.
AES.quote: The AEAD algorithms considered in this document are AES-GCM and AES-CCM.

rejected.why: The suites are defined for both TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 with no DTLS-specific mechanism, so the parent TLS tag is the better fit.
ECDHE is the key exchange, but the document only references RFC 5489 and RFC 8422 for it and defines nothing new about elliptic curve cryptography.
The key exchange is reused from RFC 5489 and not specified here; the document only combines existing pieces into cipher suites.
IoT is mentioned only as a motivating PSK deployment scenario, not as the subject of the document.
The IANA section only registers the code points for the new cipher suites, which is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
SHA-256 and SHA-384 only appear in the cipher suite names as the hash for the PRF and are not discussed.

RFC8443.title: Personal Assertion Token (PASSporT) Extension for Resource Priority Authorization
RFC8443.summary: Defines a new PASSporT extension ("rph" claim, ppt value "rph") that lets a STIR authentication service cryptographically sign assertions of authorization for values in the SIP Resource-Priority header, with SIP authentication and verification behavior.

STIR.why: The document extends PASSporT and STIR with a new ppt type and specifies Authentication Service and Verification Service behavior for SIP, so it belongs on the STIR page.
STIR.quote: This specification documents an extension to PASSporT and the associated STIR mechanisms to provide a function to cryptographically sign the SIP 'Resource-Priority' header field.

SIP.why: A substantial part specifies SIP-specific usage tied to the SIP Resource-Priority header (RFC 4412) and INVITE handling, including stripping the header on failed verification.
SIP.quote: The verification service MUST extract the value associated with the "auth" key in a full-form PASSPorT with a "ppt" value of "rph".

JWT.why: It defines a new JWT claim, registered in the JWT Claims registry, and the claim's structure is the core of the document.
JWT.quote: This specification defines a new JSON Web Token claim for "rph" that provides an assertion for information in the SIP 'Resource-Priority' header field.

rejected.why: Signature generation follows RFC 8225 and the JOSE machinery is only the underlying mechanism; nothing new is defined about JWS/JWK.
Certificates are used for signing authority but no certificate profile is defined.
Resource priority serves NS/EP communications, but the document explicitly leaves usage out of scope and does not address emergency calling.
JSON is just the encoding of the claim.
The authorization is of the Resource-Priority header via STIR; the STIR tag is more specific and covers it.
IANA registrations are boilerplate-like and not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Resource-Priority / communications resource prioritization (RFC 4412)
gaps.why: The document is about authorizing the SIP Resource-Priority header for priority communications (NS/EP), and the taxonomy has no tag for resource priority or priority services.

RFC8444.title: OSPFv2 Extensions for Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER)
RFC8444.summary: Defines OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV sub-TLVs (BIER Sub-TLV and BIER MPLS Encapsulation Sub-TLV) to advertise BIER information, plus inter-area propagation rules by ABRs.

BIER.why: The document specifies how BIER sub-domain, BFR-id, label range and BitString length information is advertised in OSPFv2 for BIER.
BIER.quote: This document describes the OSPF protocol extension (from RFC 2328) that is required for BIER with MPLS encapsulation

rejected.why: MPLS is only the encapsulation BIER uses; the document defines labels for BIER advertisement, not anything about MPLS itself.
RFC 8401 is the IS-IS counterpart, referenced only for the BIER Algorithm registry.
Parent of BIER, which is already tagged and implies it.
The document covers OSPFv2 only.

RFC8445.title: Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE): A Protocol for Network Address Translator (NAT) Traversal
RFC8445.summary: RFC 8445 specifies ICE, the UDP NAT traversal protocol that gathers candidate addresses, pairs them and runs STUN connectivity checks to select a working path, obsoleting RFC 5245.

ICE.why: The whole document specifies ICE: candidate gathering, prioritization, checklists, connectivity checks, nomination, restarts, keepalives and lite/full implementations.
ICE.quote: This document describes a protocol for Network Address Translator (NAT) traversal for UDP-based communication. This protocol is called Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE).

STUN.why: The document defines new STUN attributes and a new error code (487 Role Conflict), and specifies STUN client and server procedures for connectivity checks.
STUN.quote: ICE extends STUN with the attributes: PRIORITY, USE-CANDIDATE, ICE-CONTROLLED, and ICE-CONTROLLING.

TURN.why: Relayed candidates, TURN permissions and channels are specified as part of ICE procedures, so TURN readers would want this.
TURN.quote: A successful Allocate response will provide the agent with a server-reflexive candidate (obtained from the mapped address) and a relayed candidate

rejected.why: NAT is the problem ICE addresses, but the NAT tag covers NAT behaviour and deployment. ICE is covered by the more specific NAT traversal tags.
SDP offer/answer is only one example of a candidate exchange. The SDP encoding is defined in a separate usage document.
SIP is mentioned only as a typical signaling usage, and SIP and SDP procedures were deliberately removed from this document.
RTP and RTCP are the data streams ICE carries, which gives the component concept. The document does not specify RTP.
The document treats IPv6 candidate gathering and address selection, but only as a detail of ICE.
Pacing of STUN transactions is discussed, but this is not congestion control as a subject.

RFC8446.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3
RFC8446.summary: Specifies TLS 1.3, including the handshake, record protocol, alerts, key schedule, PSK resumption, 0-RTT with anti-replay, and compliance requirements, obsoleting TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246).

TLS.why: The document is the TLS 1.3 protocol specification itself, covering handshake, record layer, extensions and compliance.
TLS.quote: This document specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol.

rejected.why: DTLS is only mentioned in passing, for example in the cookie discussion. The document specifies TLS over a reliable stream.
HKDF and HMAC are used as primitives in the key schedule and the Finished message. They are not the subject.
Certificates are used for authentication, but certificate validation is explicitly out of scope.
OCSP status is carried in a CertificateEntry extension. This is a minor part of the document.
AES-GCM and ChaCha20 cipher suites are listed, but the document defines no algorithm and only names the suites.
ECDHE groups are used in key exchange, but the document is not about elliptic-curve cryptography.

RFC8447.title: IANA Registry Updates for TLS and DTLS
RFC8447.summary: Updates IANA registries for TLS and DTLS: renames registries, changes registration policies to Specification Required, adds a Recommended column and notes, and defines the designated expert process.

TLS.why: The whole document modifies TLS/DTLS registries (ExtensionType, cipher suites, supported groups, certificate types, etc.) and updates several TLS RFCs. TLS readers need it. DTLS is a child of TLS, but the document treats TLS and DTLS registries together, so TLS is the fitting tag.
TLS.quote: IANA has made changes to a number of IANA registries related to Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS).

IANA.why: It changes registration policies, defines the designated expert pool and review process, and adds registry notes. This is substantive IANA registry guidance.
IANA.quote: Values with the first byte in the range 0-254 (decimal) are assigned via Specification Required [RFC8126].

rejected.why: DTLS is mentioned in the title, but the registry changes apply to TLS and DTLS jointly and no DTLS-specific content is defined.
Cipher suite tables list AES-GCM/CCM suites only as registry entries marked Recommended; the document is not about the cipher.
ChaCha20-Poly1305 suites appear only in the Recommended list, not as a subject of the document.
Supported groups such as secp256r1 and x25519 are marked Recommended in a registry; the document does not address elliptic curve cryptography itself.
The designated expert procedure is registry administration, which fits IANA better than general IETF process.

RFC8448.title: Example Handshake Traces for TLS 1.3
RFC8448.summary: Informational document giving example TLS 1.3 handshake traces (1-RTT, 0-RTT resumption, HelloRetryRequest, client authentication, compatibility mode) with all keys and intermediate values so implementations can be verified.

TLS.why: The whole document consists of TLS 1.3 handshake traces with key schedule values for testing implementations, so it belongs on the TLS page.
TLS.quote: This document includes examples of TLS 1.3 handshakes.  Private keys and inputs are provided so that these handshakes might be reproduced.

rejected.why: x25519 is used for the key exchange in the traces, but the document does not specify or analyse the curve.
RSA certificates and keys appear as test inputs, not as a subject of the document.
An ECDSA P-256 certificate is used in one example, only as a test input.
HKDF/HMAC computations are displayed as intermediate values, but the document is not about them.
Certificates are embedded in the traces without any discussion of certificate profiles.
The document covers only TLS 1.3 over stream transport, not DTLS.

RFC8449.title: Record Size Limit Extension for TLS
RFC8449.summary: Defines the TLS "record_size_limit" extension letting endpoints negotiate the maximum protected record size they will receive, replacing and deprecating the max_fragment_length extension from RFC 6066.

TLS.why: The document specifies a new TLS extension, updates RFC 6066, and deprecates max_fragment_length, so it belongs on the TLS page.
TLS.quote: An extension to Transport Layer Security (TLS) is defined that allows endpoints to negotiate the maximum size of protected records that each will send the other.

rejected.why: The extension is valid in DTLS and the document discusses PMTU, but the document is about TLS as a whole. DTLS is only a secondary mention.
Constrained devices motivate the extension, but the document defines a general TLS extension and not IoT guidance.
Mentioned only to say the record size limit is independent of PMTU. It is not the subject of the document.
The code point registration is boilerplate-level IANA content and does not make the document about IANA.

RFC8450.title: RTP Payload Format for VC-2 High Quality (HQ) Profile
RFC8450.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for carrying SMPTE ST 2042-1 VC-2 High Quality profile wavelet video, including packet types, header fields, reassembly, and the video/vc2 media type with SDP mapping.

RTP payload format.why: The document exists to define how VC-2 HQ video is packetized in RTP, including payload header, fragmentation and reassembly.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo specifies an RTP payload format for the video coding standard Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers ST 2042-1:2017 [VC2], also known as VC-2

codecs.why: VC-2 is a video codec and the document describes its media format and constraints on streams, so codec readers would want it. No specific codec child tag exists for VC-2.
codecs.quote: The VC-2 codec is a wavelet-based codec intended primarily for professional video use with high bit-rates and only low levels of compression.

rejected.why: RTP is the transport the payload format plugs into; the more specific RTP payload format tag already covers this.
SDP mapping is a short routine section of media type parameters, not a substantial subject of the document.
The video/vc2 registration is standard boilerplate for a payload format, not about media type registry rules.
The FEC section only points to RFC 5109 and gives packet-type priority; it's a brief consideration.
Congestion control section just refers to RFC 3550, 8083 and 8085; it's boilerplate considerations.
UDP is only referenced as substrate in congestion guidance.

gaps.name: VC-2 (SMPTE ST 2042-1) video codec
gaps.why: No specific codec tag exists for the VC-2 wavelet video codec, which is the subject of the payload format.

RFC8451.title: Considerations for Selecting RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Extended Report (XR) Metrics for the WebRTC Statistics API
RFC8451.summary: Informational RFC that selects RTCP SR/RR/XR metrics and defines identifiers for them in the W3C WebRTC getStats() statistics API.

RTCP.why: The document surveys and selects RTCP SR/RR/XR metrics and their report blocks for exposure in WebRTC stats; this is RTCP feedback and extended reports.
RTCP.quote: It provides a list of RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Sender Report (SR), Receiver Report (RR), and Extended Report (XR) metrics

WebRTC.why: Defines identifiers for the WebRTC statistics API, so it is about browser real-time media monitoring.
WebRTC.quote: we provide rationale for choosing additional RTP metrics for the WebRTC getStats() API

performance measurement.why: A large part of the document discusses loss, discard, burst/gap, jitter buffer and repair performance metrics and their use for quality estimation.
performance measurement.quote: The metrics are classified into 3 categories as follows: network impact metrics, application impact metrics, and recovery metrics.

rejected.why: RTCP is the child tag and implies RTP; the document is about RTCP metrics rather than RTP itself.
SDP is only mentioned as the negotiation mechanism for XR use.
Repair mechanisms such as FEC are mentioned only as the source of post-repair metrics.
Frame types are discussed only to motivate frame impairment metrics.

RFC8452.title: AES-GCM-SIV: Nonce Misuse-Resistant Authenticated Encryption
RFC8452.summary: Specifies AES-GCM-SIV, two nonce misuse-resistant AEAD algorithms (AEAD_AES_128_GCM_SIV and AEAD_AES_256_GCM_SIV) built on AES counter mode and the POLYVAL authenticator, with security bounds and test vectors.

AES.why: The document defines new AES-based authenticated encryption modes (key derivation, AES-CTR, POLYVAL tag), so it belongs under the AES block cipher and its modes.
AES.quote: This memo specifies two nonce misuse-resistant AEADs: AEAD_AES_128_GCM_SIV and AEAD_AES_256_GCM_SIV.

rejected.why: The AES tag is the more specific child covering this algorithm and its modes, so the parent is implied.
POLYVAL is a polynomial authenticator, not HMAC; it is not about hash-based MACs.
The IANA registration of AEAD algorithm IDs is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
Per-nonce key derivation is an internal part of the construction, not a key management protocol.

gaps.name: Authenticated encryption (AEAD)
gaps.why: The document is about nonce misuse-resistant AEAD constructions in the RFC 5116 format. The taxonomy has no AEAD tag; AES is the closest fit.

RFC8453.title: Framework for Abstraction and Control of TE Networks (ACTN)
RFC8453.summary: Informational framework for ACTN, defining a three-tier architecture (CNC, MDSC, PNC), topology abstraction types, virtual network services and access points for abstracting and controlling multi-domain TE networks.

traffic engineering.why: The document is about abstraction, virtualization and control of TE networks, including abstract topologies, VN provisioning and path computation across domains.
traffic engineering.quote: This document provides a framework for Abstraction and Control of TE Networks (ACTN) to support virtual network services and connectivity services.

SDN.why: The framework is an SDN-style hierarchical controller architecture (CNC/MDSC/PNC) with open programmable interfaces.
SDN.quote: One of the main drivers for Software-Defined Networking (SDN) [RFC7149] is a decoupling of the network control plane from the data plane.

rejected.why: PCE is mentioned as a possible PNC implementation and for path computation requests, but the document does not specify or extend PCE/PCEP.
YANG service models are referenced for mapping interfaces, but the document defines no models.
Only cited as an example of control plane separation; not the subject.
Mentioned only as an example TE network technology.
Policy is discussed in the manageability section but not as an information model; it is a minor part of the document.
VNS is compared to VPN models only briefly; ACTN is not provider-provisioned VPN specification.

gaps.name: ACTN / network abstraction and virtual network services
gaps.why: No taxonomy tag covers TE network abstraction, virtualization and network slicing, which is the core of the document.

RFC8454.title: Information Model for Abstraction and Control of TE Networks (ACTN)
RFC8454.summary: RFC 8454 defines an information model for the ACTN (Abstraction and Control of TE Networks) CMI and MPI interfaces, specifying VN and TE primitives, objects, and their mappings.

traffic engineering.why: The document models TE tunnels, TE topology, path computation, and virtual network control over TE networks, which is the traffic engineering subject area. No specific TE technology tag fits as the main subject.
traffic engineering.quote: This document provides an information model for Abstraction and Control of TE Networks (ACTN).

SDN.why: ACTN's hierarchical controller architecture (CNC, MDSC, PNC) with northbound and southbound interfaces is a programmable control-plane model. The document defines the primitives exchanged between the controllers.
SDN.quote: The ACTN reference architecture [RFC8453] identifies a three-tier control hierarchy comprising the following

rejected.why: Path Compute primitives are defined, but PCEP and the PCE architecture are not specified. PCEP objective functions are only reused by reference.
YANG TE topology is only referenced for the implementation. This document is a protocol-neutral information model.
RFC 3209 is cited only for setup/holding priority and affinity semantics, not as a subject.
RFC 4427 recovery types are reused by reference, but the document is not about GMPLS.
Virtual networks here are ACTN customer VNs, not provider-provisioned VPN technologies such as L3VPN or L2VPN.
LSPs and MPLS are mentioned only as a layer protocol example and are not the subject.

gaps.name: ACTN (Abstraction and Control of TE Networks)
gaps.why: The document is specifically about ACTN, with its CNC/MDSC/PNC architecture and CMI/MPI interfaces, and the taxonomy has no ACTN tag. Readers browsing for ACTN would expect to find it.

RFC8455.title: Terminology for Benchmarking Software-Defined Networking (SDN) Controller Performance
RFC8455.summary: Defines terminology (metrics, test setup terms, reference topologies) for benchmarking SDN controller control-plane performance, scalability, security and reliability, extending RFC 7426 and companion to RFC 8456.

benchmarking.why: The document is a BMWG benchmarking terminology: defines metrics such as path provisioning time/rate, capacity and failover time, plus test setups, for controller benchmarking.
benchmarking.quote: This document defines terminology for benchmarking a Software-Defined Networking (SDN) controller's control-plane performance.

SDN.why: The subject device is the SDN controller; the document extends SDN terminology (northbound/southbound interfaces, proactive/reactive flow provisioning, cluster mode).
SDN.quote: Software-Defined Networking (SDN) is a networking architecture in which network control is decoupled from the underlying forwarding function

rejected.why: Benchmarking is the more specific fit for lab device-under-test methodology; this is not active/passive network performance measurement.
Not about policy-based management information models.
No OAM mechanisms are defined; the document is about benchmarking terms.
Security and DoS handling appear only as benchmark categories, not as the document's subject.

RFC8456.title: Benchmarking Methodology for Software-Defined Networking (SDN) Controller Performance
RFC8456.summary: Defines black-box benchmarking methodologies for SDN controller performance, scalability, security and reliability, with an OpenFlow appendix illustrating the tests.

benchmarking.why: The document is a benchmarking methodology BMWG document defining tests, measurements and reporting formats for SDN controllers.
benchmarking.quote: This document defines methodologies for benchmarking the control-plane performance of Software-Defined Networking (SDN) Controllers.

SDN.why: The device under test is the SDN controller, with northbound/southbound interfaces; readers of the SDN subject would want this.
SDN.quote: The SDN Controller is a core component in the SDN architecture that controls the behavior of the network.

rejected.why: Benchmarking is the more specific fit for lab-based device methodology; this is not active/passive network metrics.
Only mentioned as an OpenFlow transport and a SYN-flood DoS example.
Encrypted connections are only a connection setup option; nothing is defined about TLS.
DoS handling is one test among many, not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: OpenFlow

RFC8457.title: IMAP "$Important" Keyword and "\Important" Special-Use Attribute
RFC8457.summary: Defines the IMAP "$Important" message keyword and the "\Important" special-use mailbox attribute, and creates an IANA registry for IMAP mailbox name attributes.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP with a new keyword and a new special-use LIST attribute, and creates a registry of IMAP mailbox attributes.
IMAP.quote: defines a new message keyword, "$Important", to apply to messages that are considered important for the user by some externally defined criteria

rejected.why: It creates an IMAP-specific registry, but that is boilerplate-like registry work. The document is about IMAP, not IANA policy in general.

IMAP is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
ABNF is used only to write one syntax line.

RFC8458.title: Using National Bibliography Numbers as Uniform Resource Names
RFC8458.summary: RFC 8458 obsoletes RFC 3188 and defines how National Bibliography Numbers are used as URNs, including syntax, assignment, resolution, and a revised RFC 8141-compliant NBN URN namespace registration (version 4).

URN.why: The document specifies and registers the NBN URN namespace, defining its syntax, assignment, lexical equivalence and resolution. URN is the most specific fitting tag.

ABNF is used only as the notation for the NSS syntax. The document is not about ABNF.

gaps.name: Persistent identifiers / digital preservation (national bibliography numbers)
gaps.why: The document is about persistent library identifiers, which are central to library and digital-preservation communities. The taxonomy has only the handle system for persistent identifiers, and URN covers only the namespace mechanism.

RFC8459.title: Hierarchical Service Function Chaining (hSFC)
RFC8459.summary: Experimental architecture RFC defining hierarchical Service Function Chaining, decomposing a large SFC domain into upper-level and lower-level subdomains bridged by Internal Boundary Nodes, with options for restoring upper-level NSH paths.

SFC.why: The whole document is an SFC architecture extension: hierarchical domains, IBNs, classifiers, SFPs and NSH handling. It belongs on the SFC subject page.

RFC8460.title: SMTP TLS Reporting
RFC8460.summary: Defines SMTP TLS Reporting (TLSRPT): a DNS TXT policy record and JSON report format, delivered by email or HTTPS, for sending MTAs to report STARTTLS, DANE and MTA-STS failures and successes to recipient domains.

SMTP.why: The document specifies reporting about SMTP MTA-to-MTA STARTTLS sessions, including report delivery by SMTP with new headers and a multipart/report type. It is an SMTP security companion to MTA-STS.
SMTP.quote: this document defines a mechanism for sending domains to report on failures at multiple stages of the MTA-to-MTA conversation.

TLS.why: The reports cover TLS negotiation and certificate validation failures (expired, host mismatch, untrusted) for SMTP sessions, so TLS deployment readers would want it.
TLS.quote: The STARTTLS extension to SMTP [RFC3207] allows SMTP clients and hosts to establish secure SMTP sessions over TLS.

DANE.why: It defines DANE-specific result types (tlsa-invalid, dnssec-invalid, dane-required) and reports applied TLSA records, adding reporting for DANE for SMTP.

media types.why: It registers new media types (tlsrpt+json, tlsrpt+gzip), the +gzip suffix, and a report-type registry for multipart/report.
media types.quote: application/tlsrpt+json

JSON.why: A substantial part of the document defines the JSON report schema and its fields.
JSON.quote: The report is composed as a plaintext file encoded in the Internet JSON (I-JSON) format [RFC7493].

rejected.why: The TXT record at _smtp._tls is only the policy discovery mechanism, not a new DNS feature.
The document borrows DMARC concepts (rua, TXT policy) but is not about DMARC reporting.
DKIM signing is required for reports sent by email, but it is only a security mechanism the document relies on.
HTTPS POST is just one of two delivery transports and nothing new is defined for HTTP.
gzip compression is used for reports; the +gzip suffix is registered, but the document is not about the gzip format itself.
The reports concern transport encryption, not sender domain authentication or anti-spoofing.

gaps.name: MTA-STS (SMTP MTA Strict Transport Security)
gaps.why: The document is a companion to MTA-STS and reports its policy failures, but the taxonomy has no MTA-STS tag. The nearest tags are SMTP and TLS.

RFC8461.title: SMTP MTA Strict Transport Security (MTA-STS)
RFC8461.summary: Defines MTA-STS, a mechanism where recipient domains publish via DNS TXT record and HTTPS well-known policy file their support for authenticated TLS on SMTP MX hosts and whether senders should refuse delivery on failure.

SMTP.why: The document specifies how sending MTAs discover and apply policies to secure SMTP delivery, including STARTTLS enforcement and MX candidate traversal.
SMTP.quote: mechanism enabling mail service providers (SPs) to declare their ability to receive Transport Layer Security (TLS) secure SMTP connections

TLS.why: Specifies certificate validation and TLS requirements for SMTP, with SNI and minimum TLS version guidance, so TLS readers would find it relevant.
TLS.quote: whether sending SMTP servers should refuse to deliver to MX hosts that do not offer TLS with a trusted server certificate

DANE.why: Positions MTA-STS as an alternative to DANE for SMTP and defines the interaction and trade-offs between them.
DANE.quote: senders who implement MTA-STS validation MUST NOT allow MTA-STS Policy validation to override a failing DANE validation

rejected.why: HTTPS is only the policy-fetch substrate; the document does not extend HTTP semantics.
A TXT record is used for policy signalling, but no new DNS behaviour is defined.
Certificate validation relies on existing PKIX rules and defines nothing new about certificates.
ABNF is only the notation used to specify the record and policy syntax.
MTA-STS protects transport security between MTAs, not sender domain authentication or anti-spoofing.

RFC8462.title: Report from the IAB Workshop on Managing Radio Networks in an Encrypted World (MaRNEW)
RFC8462.summary: IAB/GSMA workshop report on managing mobile radio networks (bandwidth optimization, congestion, caching, CDNs, regulation) as encrypted traffic grows, with suggested principles and follow-up work.

workshop reports.why: The document is a report of an IAB workshop, summarizing sessions, discussions and outcomes.
workshop reports.quote: The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) and GSM Association (GSMA) held a joint workshop on Managing Radio Networks in an Encrypted World (MaRNEW)

cellular.why: Central subject is managing radio access networks and mobile operator traffic, including 3GPP PCC-QoS and 5G.
cellular.quote: solutions for bandwidth optimization on mobile networks for encrypted content, as current solutions rely on unencrypted content

congestion control.why: Congestion control, AQM, ECN, ConEx, Sprout and PCC are a substantial part of the suggested solutions.
congestion control.quote: Congestion Control: Many attendees cited congestion control as a key issue.

privacy.why: User privacy versus network management is a core theme, with a dedicated session on user choice and privacy.
privacy.quote: New solutions should not introduce new ways for information to be discovered and attributed to individual users.

CDN.why: A full session covers CDNs, caching of encrypted content, Keyless SSL and blind caching.
CDN.quote: there is a need to place caches near the user at the edge of the mobile network

rejected.why: TCP limitations and MTG TCP options are discussed, but only as part of a broader transport evolution discussion; the document does not specify TCP.
Mentioned briefly as a view from QUIC engineers; not a subject of the report.
Encryption is the backdrop and Keyless SSL is mentioned, but TLS itself is not discussed in depth.
FQ-CoDel and AQM are listed as suggestions, but only in brief; congestion control covers them.
Mentioned as one suggestion in a list, not a substantial subject.
The workshop concerns architectural implications of encryption, but the report is mainly about specific network management issues, so the workshop reports tag fits better.

gaps.name: Encryption impact on network operators / pervasive encryption
gaps.why: The report's central theme is how increasing encryption affects network management, which no taxonomy tag covers directly.

RFC8463.title: A New Cryptographic Signature Method for DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM)
RFC8463.summary: Adds the Ed25519-SHA256 signing algorithm to DKIM (updating RFC 6376), defining the signature/key syntax, the DNS key record k=ed25519, verifier requirements, and an example.

DKIM.why: The document extends and updates DKIM with a new signature algorithm and key type, and requires verifiers to implement it.
DKIM.quote: This document adds a new signing algorithm, Ed25519-SHA256, to "DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) Signatures" (RFC 6376).

EdDSA.why: The new DKIM algorithm is Ed25519, an EdDSA variant. The document specifies how it is used for DKIM signatures and keys.
EdDSA.quote: It signs the hash with the PureEdDSA variant Ed25519, as defined in RFC 8032, Section 5.1

rejected.why: Ed25519 uses the Curve25519 curve, but the document is about the EdDSA signature use, not Curve25519 key agreement. EdDSA is the more specific tag.
DKIM public keys are published in DNS TXT records, but DNS is only the substrate. The document defines nothing new about DNS beyond a key-record tag value.
SHA-256 is only the hash used within the algorithm and is not what the document is about.
RSA is mentioned only as the existing algorithm being supplemented, and the document does not address it.
This parent tag is implied by DKIM, so it is not listed separately.
ABNF is used only to express the syntax additions.

RFC8464.title: A URN Namespace for Device Identity and Mobile Equipment Identity (MEID)
RFC8464.summary: Registers the formal URN namespace '3gpp2' and a 'meid' NSS for 3GPP2 Mobile Equipment Identity values, specifying syntax, assignment, and security/privacy guidance.

URN.why: The document is a URN namespace registration with syntax, assignment and resolution details, so it belongs on the URN page.
URN.quote: This document defines a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for the Third Generation Partnership Project 2 (3GPP2) and a Namespace Specific String (NSS) for the Mobile Equipment Identity (MEID).

rejected.why: MEID is a 3GPP2 identifier, but the document only defines a URN for it. It does not cover the cdma2000 packet-data network.
RFC 5626 Instance ID use is mentioned only in passing and is specified in RFC 8465, not here.
ABNF is only the notation used for the syntax definition.
The IANA registration is boilerplate for the namespace registration and not the subject of the document.
The privacy considerations are a short section about the MEID. The document is not about privacy in its own right.

RFC8465.title: Using the Mobile Equipment Identity (MEID) URN as an Instance ID
RFC8465.summary: Specifies how the 3GPP2 MEID URN is used as the SIP "+sip.instance" Instance ID (RFC 5626/5627), with UAC, UAS and registrar procedures and privacy constraints.

SIP.why: The document defines SIP UAC, UAS and registrar procedures for using the MEID URN as the sip.instance Instance ID, including GRUU obfuscation. It profiles SIP outbound/GRUU behaviour.
SIP.quote: specifying how the 3GPP2 MEID URN is used in the "+sip.instance" Contact header field parameter for outbound behavior

URN.why: The document is about using a specific URN namespace (3GPP2 MEID) as an identifier, so URN readers would want it, although the URN is defined in RFC 8464.
URN.quote: how the Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace reserved for the Third Generation Partnership Project 2 (3GPP2) identities and its Namespace Specific String (NSS)

cdma2000.why: The use cases concern 3GPP2 (cdma2000-family) mobile devices, IMS registration and handover between the circuit-switched and IP domains.
cdma2000.quote: 3GPP2 defines High Rate Packet Data (HRPD) with high data rates, and it dispenses with the 1x Circuit Switched (1xCS) infrastructure.

rejected.why: UUID is the default Instance ID that the MEID URN is an alternative to. The document is not about UUID.
TLS is mentioned only as a security mechanism in Security Considerations.
Emergency sessions and PSAP are only one use case for including the MEID, not the subject of the document.
Privacy handling of the MEID is covered in the procedures and Security Considerations, but the document is not a privacy analysis.
cdma2000 fits the 3GPP2 context better than generic cellular.

RFC8466.title: A YANG Data Model for Layer 2 Virtual Private Network (L2VPN) Service Delivery
RFC8466.summary: Defines the ietf-l2vpn-svc YANG customer service model for configuring provider-provisioned L2VPN services (VPWS, VPLS, EVPN) including sites, accesses, QoS, BUM, OAM, and NNIs.

YANG.why: The document's core deliverable is a YANG service data model module (ietf-l2vpn-svc).
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model that can be used to configure a Layer 2 provider-provisioned VPN service.

L2VPN.why: The model covers L2VPN service delivery, VPWS and VPLS service types, topologies, and site attachment.
L2VPN.quote: The YANG data model defined in this document includes support for point-to-point Virtual Private Wire Services (VPWSs) and multipoint Virtual Private LAN Services (VPLSs)

rejected.why: VPLS is one service type the model supports, not specified here; L2VPN is the better fit.
EVPN is listed as a service type option only.
NETCONF/RESTCONF are only how the model might be used.
BGP signalling is referenced for service types; the document does not specify BGP.
Pseudowires are underlying technology; the model abstracts them.
QoS parameters are a part of the service model, not an architecture or signalling.
VXLAN is only an encapsulation option in the model.

RFC8467.title: Padding Policies for Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS(0))
RFC8467.summary: Experimental RFC that lists padding policies for the EDNS(0) Padding option (RFC 7830), discusses their trade-offs, and recommends block-length padding (128-octet query blocks, 468-octet response blocks) for encrypted DNS transports.

EDNS.why: The document specifies how the EDNS(0) Padding option should be used, including its ordering among options and padding lengths. It is squarely about an EDNS option.
EDNS.quote: RFC 7830 specifies the "Padding" option for Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS(0)) but does not specify the actual padding length for specific applications.

DNS privacy.why: The purpose of the padding policies is to hamper size-based correlation of encrypted DNS messages. Readers of the encrypted and privacy-preserving DNS subject would want this document, though it does not define DoT or DoH itself.
DNS privacy.quote: Padding DNS messages is useful only when transport is encrypted using protocols such as DNS over Transport Layer Security

rejected.why: DNS over TLS is only cited as one encrypted transport where padding is useful. The document defines nothing new about DoT.
It appears only in a note that validating clients may change observed message size patterns. The document is not about DNSSEC.
DNS over DTLS is only mentioned as an example of an encrypted transport. It is not a subject of the document.
The document is about a specific DNS privacy mechanism, not general protocol privacy threat models. It is better covered by the DNS privacy tag.

RFC8468.title: IPv4, IPv6, and IPv4-IPv6 Coexistence: Updates for the IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) Framework
RFC8468.summary: RFC 8468 updates the IPPM framework (RFC 2330) to cover IPv6 in the definitions of Type-P and standard-formed packets, deprecates the minimal IP packet, and discusses how NAT, IPv4-IPv6 translation, encapsulation and header compression affect measurement.

performance measurement.why: The document's purpose is to update the IPPM framework for active performance measurement, covering Type-P packets and standard-formed packets.
performance measurement.quote: This memo updates the IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) framework defined by RFC 2330 with new considerations for measurement methodology and testing.

IPv6.why: A substantial part defines IPv6 standard-formed packet criteria and the effects of IPv6 extension headers on measurement.
IPv6.quote: For an IPv6 packet (as specified in [RFC8200] and any future updates) to be standard-formed, the following criteria are REQUIRED:

IPv6 transition.why: A whole section addresses how IPv4-IPv6 translation and coexistence affect measurement methodology, as the title also indicates.
IPv6 transition.quote: The definition and execution of measurements within the context of the IPPM framework is challenged whenever such translation mechanisms are present along the measurement path.
IPv6 transition.section: 6. NAT, IPv4-IPv6 Transition, and Compression Techniques

rejected.why: NAT is discussed as a factor affecting latency measurements, but the document is not about NAT behaviour itself.
6LoWPAN and ROHC are explicitly excluded from the standard-formed packet evaluation, so the document does not address them.
ROHC is only mentioned as out of scope for standard-formed packets.
OWAMP and TWAMP appear only as references in the Security Considerations section.
In situ OAM and the PDM destination option are mentioned briefly as measurement use cases, but they are not the subject of the document.

RFC8469.title: Recommendation to Use the Ethernet Control Word
RFC8469.summary: RFC 8469 updates RFC 4448 to recommend that Ethernet pseudowires use the control word, avoiding misidentification of Ethernet PW payloads as IP packets by LSRs, which causes ECMP misordering.

pseudowire.why: The document updates the Ethernet pseudowire encapsulation (RFC 4448) to recommend using the PW control word. This is squarely about pseudowire emulation.
pseudowire.quote: The pseudowire (PW) encapsulation of Ethernet, as defined in [RFC4448], specifies that the use of the control word (CW) is optional.

ECMP.why: The motivating problem is wrong ECMP path selection and packet misordering. Section 5 covers ECMP options (FAT PW, entropy labels) for Ethernet PWs.
ECMP.quote: In the absence of a PW CW, an Ethernet PW packet can be misidentified as an IP packet by a label switching router (LSR) selecting the ECMP path

rejected.why: MPLS is the substrate carrying the PWs. The document is about PW encapsulation, not MPLS itself.
Ethernet frames are the payload being emulated. The document does not address IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
It is mentioned only as a mitigation example, in a single sentence.
It is touched on only as a mitigation (a TE path that avoids load balancing), not as a subject of the document.

RFC8470.title: Using Early Data in HTTP
RFC8470.summary: Defines the Early-Data HTTP header field and the 425 (Too Early) status code, and gives client, server and intermediary rules for mitigating replay of HTTP requests sent in TLS 1.3 early data (0-RTT).

HTTP.why: The document extends HTTP with a new request header field and a new status code, and specifies client, server and intermediary behaviour for HTTP requests sent in early data.
HTTP.quote: The Early-Data header field is included in requests that might have been forwarded by an intermediary prior to the completion of the TLS handshake with its client.
HTTP.section: 5. Extensions for Early Data in HTTP

TLS.why: A substantial part of the document concerns deployment guidance for TLS 1.3 early data (0-RTT): replay risk, rejecting early data at the TLS layer, and how HTTP interacts with the handshake.
TLS.quote: A server can limit the amount of early data with the "max_early_data_size" field of the "early_data" TLS extension.
TLS.section: 3. Supporting Early Data in HTTP Servers

rejected.why: The 425 status code is only noted as not cacheable by default, which is incidental and not the subject of the document.
HTTP over QUIC 0-RTT is mentioned only as a case the advice also applies to, and the document specifies nothing about QUIC.
HTTP/2 is cited only as an example of a multiplexed protocol, and the document does not specify or extend it.
ABNF is only used to write the one-line Early-Data syntax, so it is notation and not a subject of the document.
The replay mitigations are specific to HTTP and TLS early data, which the HTTP and TLS tags already cover. The document does not define a web-platform security mechanism such as HSTS.

RFC8471.title: The Token Binding Protocol Version 1.0
RFC8471.summary: RFC 8471 specifies version 1.0 of the Token Binding protocol, in which a client proves possession of a per-server key pair over TLS-exported keying material so that security tokens can be cryptographically bound to the TLS layer to prevent export and replay.

token binding.why: The document defines the Token Binding message format, key parameters, binding establishment and bound-token validation, which is the subject of the token binding tag.
token binding.quote: The Token Binding protocol allows client/server applications to create long-lived, uniquely identifiable TLS bindings spanning multiple TLS sessions and connections.

rejected.why: TLS is the substrate: the protocol uses TLS exporters (RFC 5705) and a negotiation extension defined in RFC 8472. This document defines no new TLS extension itself, apart from registering an exporter label.
Carrying the Token Binding message in HTTP is specified in RFC 8473, not in this document.
Cookies are only an example of a token that can be bound. The document does not address them.
OAuth tokens are mentioned only as an example of bearer tokens that can be bound.
ECDSA and RSA signatures are used as signing algorithms for the proof of possession. The document does not specify or profile them.
The Privacy Considerations section is short and covers only this protocol's identifiers. It is not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC8472.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Extension for Token Binding Protocol Negotiation
RFC8472.summary: Defines the TLS "token_binding" extension used in ClientHello/ServerHello to negotiate Token Binding protocol version and key parameters for TLS 1.2 and earlier.

token binding.why: The document exists to negotiate Token Binding version and key parameters, so readers of the token binding subject need it. The tag is defined as TLS token binding.
token binding.quote: This document specifies a new TLS [RFC5246] extension to accomplish this negotiation without introducing additional network round trips in TLS 1.2 and earlier versions.

rejected.why: The document defines a new TLS extension, which could justify the TLS tag. But the extension exists for Token Binding, which is the more specific subject. TLS is the substrate.
Token Binding is used with HTTP, but this document does not address HTTP.
The extension registration is boilerplate-level IANA content, not the subject of the document.

RFC8473.title: Token Binding over HTTP
RFC8473.summary: Specifies how Token Binding messages are carried in HTTP over TLS via the Sec-Token-Binding request header, plus the Include-Referred-Token-Binding-ID response header for federated sign-on redirects, with key-pair scoping, security and privacy guidance.

token binding.why: The whole document defines Token Binding over HTTP: the Sec-Token-Binding header, provided and referred bindings, and federation use cases.
token binding.quote: This document describes a collection of mechanisms that allow HTTP servers to cryptographically bind security tokens (such as cookies and OAuth tokens) to TLS connections.

rejected.why: HTTP is the carrier; the document registers two header fields but is not about HTTP semantics itself. The token binding tag is the right home.
TLS is the substrate and the Token Binding TLS extension is defined in RFC 8472, not here. Only EKM and renegotiation interactions are covered.
Cookies are an example of a token to bind and a scoping reference point; the document does not extend cookie mechanics.
OAuth and OpenID Connect tokens are examples of tokens bound in federation; the document does not specify them.
Federated sign-on is a use case for referred bindings, but the document is about binding tokens, not a federation framework.
base64url encoding of the message is just an encoding detail.

RFC8474.title: IMAP Extension for Object Identifiers
RFC8474.summary: RFC 8474 defines the IMAP OBJECTID extension, adding server-assigned persistent identifiers (MAILBOXID, EMAILID, THREADID) for mailboxes and messages, with new response codes, STATUS/FETCH items and SEARCH keys, so clients can reuse cached data after renames or moves.

IMAP.why: The document is an IMAP extension: it defines the OBJECTID capability, MAILBOXID response code, STATUS attribute, EMAILID/THREADID FETCH items and SEARCH keys, and it updates RFC 3501.
IMAP.quote: This document updates RFC 3501 (IMAP4rev1) with persistent identifiers on mailboxes and messages to allow clients to more efficiently reuse cached data

rejected.why: UUIDs are only listed as one idea for generating identifiers in the appendix. The ObjectID format is a restricted base64url-style string, so the document is not about UUIDs.
JMAP is mentioned only as a data model the extension is designed to stay compatible with. The document does not specify anything about JMAP.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax section.
Sieve appears only in a future-considerations note about fileinto by MAILBOXID. Nothing about Sieve is specified.
The base64url character set is borrowed for ObjectID characters. The document does not define or use the Base64 encoding itself.
References, In-Reply-To and Subject are mentioned only as possible inputs to server threading logic. The document does not specify message format.

RFC8475.title: Using Conditional Router Advertisements for Enterprise Multihoming
RFC8475.summary: Informational RFC describing how conditional Router Advertisements (deprecating or restoring PA prefixes via preferred lifetime based on uplink status) can solve common IPv6 enterprise multihoming scenarios with two ISP uplinks, for hosts lacking RFC 6724 Rule 5.5 support.

multihoming.why: The whole document addresses enterprise multihoming with provider-assigned IPv6 prefixes: uplink selection by source address and host source address selection.
multihoming.quote: using more than one ISP (and address space assigned by those ISPs) introduces the problem of assigning IP addresses to hosts

neighbor discovery.why: The solution is a conditional use of Router Advertisements and PIO/RDNSS lifetimes, a substantial extension of RA behaviour under IPv6 neighbor discovery.
neighbor discovery.quote: Deprecating addresses by sending an RA with preferred_lifetime set to 0 in the corresponding Prefix Information option (PIO)
neighbor discovery.section: 3.1.2. Source Address Selection and Conditional RAs

SLAAC.why: Address deprecation via preferred lifetime relies on SLAAC semantics, which are discussed (valid vs preferred lifetime, deprecated address use).
SLAAC.quote: Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) [RFC4862] and Router Advertisements (RAs) [RFC4861] are the most suitable mechanisms for signaling network topology changes to hosts
SLAAC.section: 3.1.2. Source Address Selection and Conditional RAs

rejected.why: VRRP mastership is only used as one possible trigger for conditional RAs; the document does not specify or extend VRRP.
BGP is mentioned only as the burden of PI space, which this document avoids.
NAT is mentioned only for comparison with IPv4 multihoming; the point is solving multihoming without translation.
Too broad; more specific tags (multihoming, neighbor discovery, SLAAC) apply.
The RDNSS option lifetime is mentioned only briefly; DNS itself isn't the subject.

gaps.name: Source Address Dependent Routing / enterprise multihoming
gaps.why: The taxonomy's multihoming topic fits adequately, but source-address-based uplink selection and policy routing has no dedicated tag.

RFC8476.title: Signaling Maximum SID Depth (MSD) Using OSPF
RFC8476.summary: Defines OSPFv2/OSPFv3 extensions (Node MSD TLV in the RI LSA and Link MSD sub-TLVs) for advertising Maximum SID Depth so controllers can tell whether a Segment Routing SID stack is supportable.

OSPF.why: The document specifies new OSPF TLVs and sub-TLVs for both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3, so it extends OSPF.
OSPF.quote: This document defines an extension to OSPF used to advertise one or more types of MSDs at node and/or link granularity.

segment routing.why: The MSD advertised is the SID stack depth a node can impose on SR paths, so the document is about a Segment Routing capability.
segment routing.quote: When Segment Routing (SR) paths are computed by a centralized controller, it is critical that the controller learn the Maximum SID Depth (MSD)

rejected.why: The document covers OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 equally, so the parent OSPF tag fits better than the OSPFv3 child.
BGP-LS is only mentioned as another way to carry MSD to controllers. It is defined elsewhere.
PCEP MSD signalling is only referenced as related work. This document does not specify it.
MPLS label depth is mentioned only as a non-SR use case, and the document does not specify MPLS.
The IANA section only registers TLV types, which is boilerplate.
The document is data-plane agnostic and does not specify SR over MPLS.

RFC8477.title: Report from the Internet of Things (IoT) Semantic Interoperability (IOTSI) Workshop 2016
RFC8477.summary: IAB workshop report on IoT semantic interoperability, summarizing discussions on information/data/interaction models, formal modelling languages, translation between data models, handling change, and cross-SDO collaboration.

IoT.why: The whole report concerns IoT application-layer semantic interoperability, data models and gateways across IoT ecosystems; the IoT topic is the best fit.
IoT.quote: The main goal of the workshop was to foster a discussion on the different approaches used by companies and Standards Developing Organizations (SDOs) to accomplish interoperability at the application layer.

YANG.why: YANG is discussed as a formal data-modelling language for documentation, code generation (pyang) and design-time translation, though it is one of several languages compared.
YANG.quote: The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) uses YANG to define data and interaction models.

rejected.why: The document is a workshop report, but the tag's description is for reports from IAB/IRTF workshops; it is a plausible fit and arguably should be included as secondary. Chosen against only because the IoT subject content is the primary focus.
Only appears indirectly (CoMI, REST); not discussed as a subject.
Appears only as a position paper title in the appendix, not discussed in the body.
MIB modules are only mentioned as an example of a data model.
JSON Schema is mentioned only as OCF's formal language; not a subject of the report.
XML Schema mentioned only as formats used by OMA and Bluetooth SIG; not the subject.

gaps.name: IoT semantic interoperability / data and information models
gaps.why: The report is about information models, data models and interaction models for IoT and their translation; the taxonomy has only generic IoT and YANG tags for this.

RFC8478.title: Zstandard Compression and the application/zstd Media Type
RFC8478.summary: Informational RFC describing the Zstandard (zstd) lossless compression format (frames, blocks, FSE and Huffman entropy coding, dictionaries) and registering the application/zstd media type and the zstd HTTP content coding.

zstd.why: The whole document specifies the Zstandard compression format, its frames, blocks, entropy coding and dictionary format.
zstd.quote: Zstandard, or "zstd" (pronounced "zee standard"), is a data compression mechanism, akin to gzip [RFC1952].

media types.why: The document registers the application/zstd media type, which is a stated purpose, though a small part of the text.
media types.quote: The 'application/zstd' media type identifies a block of data that is compressed using zstd compression.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as an analogy for zstd; the document does not specify or extend gzip.
The HTTP content coding registration is a single IANA entry; HTTP is not the subject.
MIME is the transport context for the media type; the document defines nothing new about MIME itself.
The parent topic is implied by the zstd tag, so listing it separately is unnecessary.
xxHash-64 is used as an optional content checksum, but the document is not about checksums.

RFC8479.title: Storing Validation Parameters in PKCS#8
RFC8479.summary: Defines a PKCS#8 (RFC 5208/5958) private-key attribute, ValidationParams (hash OID plus seed), so RSA/DSA keys generated with the FIPS 186-4 Shawe-Taylor algorithm can carry the data needed to validate their primes.

key management.why: The document defines how private keys are stored with the data needed to validate them. That is private-key storage and handling, which fits key management better than any narrower cryptography tag.
key management.quote: describes a method of storing parameters needed for private-key validation in the Private-Key Information Syntax Specification as defined in PKCS#8 format

ASN.1.why: The document specifies a new ASN.1 attribute structure with a DER encoding. It also gives a normative-style ASN.1 module in Appendix A.

RSA.why: The attribute targets validation of RSA (and DSA) key primes, and the example is an RSA key. RSA is the main key type addressed.
RSA.quote: RSA or DSA private keys generated using the Shawe-Taylor prime generation algorithm described in [FIPS186-4] allow for parameter validation

rejected.why: The ASN.1 module imports from the PKIX common types, but the document is about PKCS#8 private keys, not X.509 certificates.
PKCS#8 private-key syntax is not about the public key infrastructure for certificates and trust. The PKIX module is only an import.
SHA2-384 is only recommended as the hash for interoperability. The document does not specify or analyse the SHA family.
The document does not address post-quantum cryptography.

gaps.name: PKCS#8 / asymmetric key packages (private-key information syntax)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for private-key container formats such as PKCS#8 and RFC 5958 Asymmetric Key Packages. Readers looking for these formats have no subject page to find this RFC under.

RFC8480.title: 6TiSCH Operation Sublayer (6top) Protocol (6P)
RFC8480.summary: Defines the 6top Protocol (6P), a link-local request/response/confirmation protocol carried in 802.15.4 IEs by which 6TiSCH neighbours negotiate adding, deleting, relocating, counting, listing and clearing TSCH schedule cells, and sets requirements for Scheduling Functions.

6TiSCH.why: The document specifies 6P, the 6top sublayer protocol of 6TiSCH, including message formats, transactions, SeqNum handling and SF requirements.
6TiSCH.quote: enables distributed scheduling in 6TiSCH networks.  6P allows neighbor nodes to add/delete Time-Slotted Channel Hopping (TSCH) cells to/on one another.

rejected.why: Not discussed; 6P schedules cells between neighbours and does not involve routing.
6P is carried in 802.15.4 Information Elements at the MAC sublayer, not in 6LoWPAN adaptation.
Parent topic of 6TiSCH, already implied by the 6TiSCH tag.
IANA registries are created, but that is boilerplate for the protocol and not the document's subject.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.15.4 TSCH scheduling
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for TSCH or IEEE 802.15.4 link-layer scheduling in its own right; 6TiSCH is the closest fit.

RFC8481.title: Clarifications to BGP Origin Validation Based on Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI)
RFC8481.summary: RFC 8481 updates RFC 6811 by clarifying that routers must evaluate and set RPKI origin validation state on all BGP routes from any source, and must not apply origin-validation policy unless the operator configures it.

RPKI.why: The document clarifies RPKI-based BGP prefix origin validation behaviour (updating RFC 6811), which is the core of the RPKI and route origin validation subject.
RPKI.quote: all prefixes should have their validation state set and that policy must not be applied without operator configuration

BGP.why: It specifies BGP router behaviour for route evaluation, redistribution into BGP, and policy application, so BGP operators would look for it.
BGP.quote: A router MUST evaluate and set the validation state of all routes in BGP coming from any source (e.g., eBGP, iBGP, or redistribution

rejected.why: RFC 8097's origin validation state extended community is mentioned only to say its automatic policy actions must not be applied without configuration; the document does not specify communities.
The parent is implied by the RPKI tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC8482.title: Providing Minimal-Sized Responses to DNS Queries That Have QTYPE=ANY
