RFC8482.summary: RFC 8482 gives guidance for DNS responders and initiators on answering QTYPE=ANY queries with minimal responses (a subset of RRsets, a synthesized HINFO record, or a best guess), reducing amplification and processing cost, and updates RFC 1034 and 1035.

DNS.why: The document specifies resolver and server behaviour for ANY queries and updates RFC 1034/1035, so it is squarely about DNS protocol behaviour.
DNS.quote: A DNS responder that receives an ANY query MAY decline to provide a conventional ANY response or MAY instead send a response with a single RRset

rejected.why: RRSIG inclusion is mentioned only as a compatibility requirement; the document is not about signing or validation.
Amplification reduction is a motivation, but the document specifies DNS response behaviour, not DDoS mitigation or signalling.
UDP is only the transport where amplification occurs; nothing new is defined about UDP usage.
The DO bit is mentioned only in passing; no EDNS mechanism is specified.

RFC8483.title: Yeti DNS Testbed
RFC8483.summary: Describes the Yeti DNS testbed, an experimental non-production DNS root server system, its infrastructure (distribution masters, Yeti-Root zone signing, IPv6-only servers) and operational experience including fragmentation, zone transfer and KSK rollover findings.

DNS.why: The document is about a DNS root server testbed: root zone distribution, priming, hints files, zone transfers, and server software behaviour.
DNS.quote: Yeti DNS is an experimental, non-production root server testbed that provides an environment where technical and operational experiments can safely be performed

DNSSEC.why: Substantial parts cover multi-signer ZSK/KSK schemes, RFC 5011 trust anchor updates, and three KSK rollover experiments with large DNSKEY responses.
DNSSEC.quote: Is it practical to sign the Yeti-Root zone using multiple, independently operated DNSSEC signers and multiple corresponding Zone Signing Keys (ZSKs)?

IPv6 transition.why: A major study area is IPv6-only root operation, IPv6 fragmentation, and serving IPv4-only end-users via dual-stack resolvers.
IPv6 transition.quote: Are there negative operational effects in the use of IPv6-only Yeti-Root servers, compared to the use of servers that are dual-stack?

rejected.why: EDNS(0) is mentioned only in connection with priming response size, not specified or extended.
IPv6 is the operating environment and fragmentation is observed, but the document does not specify or extend IPv6 itself; IPv6 transition covers the coexistence angle.
A TCP MSS issue is noted as a side finding in fragmentation; the document is not about TCP.
Security Considerations are boilerplate-like and the main body is not about operational security practices.
One server name uses IDNA punycode, which is incidental.

gaps.name: DNS root server system / root zone operations
gaps.why: The document is primarily about a root server testbed and root zone management, but the taxonomy has no root-server-specific tag; DNS is the closest fit.

RFC8484.title: DNS Queries over HTTPS (DoH)
RFC8484.summary: Defines DNS over HTTPS (DoH), a protocol mapping each DNS query-response pair onto an HTTP exchange, including the application/dns-message media type, GET/POST usage, caching interaction, and privacy/operational considerations.

DoH.why: The document specifies DoH itself, so the DoH tag is the primary and most specific fit.
DoH.quote: This document defines a protocol for sending DNS queries and getting DNS responses over HTTPS. Each DNS query-response pair is mapped into an HTTP exchange.

media types.why: The document defines and registers a new media type, application/dns-message, in Section 6 and the IANA registration. Readers of media type registrations would want it.
media types.quote: Definition of the "application/dns-message" Media Type

HTTP caching.why: A substantial section specifies how DNS TTLs interact with HTTP caching: freshness lifetime, the Age header, and stale-while-revalidate. This is new guidance for HTTP caching readers.
HTTP caching.quote: The assigned freshness lifetime of a DoH HTTP response MUST be less than or equal to the smallest TTL in the Answer section of the DNS response.

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate DoH runs over. The document profiles its use but does not define new HTTP semantics.
TLS only provides the security layer through https. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
DoH sits under DNS privacy and is more specific. DNS is only the payload being carried.
HTTP/2 is recommended as the minimum version for performance, but the document does not specify or extend it.
DNSSEC is mentioned only in Security Considerations, as an independent and compatible protocol.
URI Templates are used to configure the DoH server, but the document defines nothing new about URIs.

RFC8485.title: Vectors of Trust
RFC8485.summary: Defines Vectors of Trust, a mechanism for conveying multi-dimensional trust information (identity proofing, credential usage/management, assertion presentation) about a federated identity transaction, with OpenID Connect claim bindings and a components registry.

federated authentication.why: The document defines how an IdP conveys trust levels about an identity transaction to an RP, which is cross-domain federated authentication. It defines trust frameworks, trustmarks, and vector components for this.
federated authentication.quote: Vectors of Trust is meant to be a flexible and reusable framework for communicating authentication data between networked parties in an identity federation protocol.

JWT.why: It defines new JWT claims (vot, vtm) carried in OpenID Connect ID tokens and registers them in the JWT Claims registry. Readers of JWT would want these claims.
JWT.quote: the IdP MUST send the vector as a string within the "vot" (vector of trust) claim in the ID token.

OAuth.why: It adds the vtr request parameter and vot/vtm token introspection response fields, extending OAuth and OpenID Connect.
OAuth.quote: the client MAY request a partial set of acceptable VoT values with the "vtr" (vector of trust) claim request as part of the request object.

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding for the ID token payload and the vtr array. The document defines nothing new about JSON.
The more specific federated authentication tag fits better, since the subject is IdP-to-RP assertions.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as the in-transit protection.
JOSE signing of ID tokens is only the mechanism that binds the vector to the assertion. The document does not specify anything new about it.
The registry creation is boilerplate-style, and the document's main body is not about IANA stewardship.

gaps.name: OpenID Connect / digital identity assurance (levels of assurance, trust frameworks)
gaps.why: The document is about expressing identity assurance via vectors of trust, and OpenID Connect and identity assurance have no dedicated tag in the taxonomy.

RFC8486.title: Ambisonics in an Ogg Opus Container
RFC8486.summary: Defines two new Ogg Opus channel mapping families (2 and 3) for carrying Ambisonics, reserves experimental families 240-254, and updates RFC 7845 on channel mapping table format and unknown families.

Ogg.why: The document extends the Ogg encapsulation of Opus with new channel mapping families and updates RFC 7845's mapping table and unknown-family handling. Ogg readers need it.
Ogg.quote: This document extends the Ogg Opus format by defining two new channel mapping families for encoding Ambisonics.

Opus.why: It extends Opus with Ambisonics channel layouts, demixing matrices and downmixing, and adds to the Opus Channel Mapping Families registry.
Opus.quote: This document defines an extension to the Opus audio codec to encapsulate coded Ambisonics using the Ogg format.

rejected.why: Opus and Ogg are the more specific tags that fit, so the parent is implied.
The registry additions are boilerplate-level IANA considerations. The body is not about IANA guidance.
The document registers no media types.

gaps.name: Ambisonics
gaps.why: The document is about Ambisonics channel layouts (ACN ordering, SN3D normalization, mixed-order and non-diegetic stereo). The taxonomy has no spatial audio tag.

RFC8487.title: Mtrace Version 2: Traceroute Facility for IP Multicast
RFC8487.summary: Specifies Mtrace2, a UDP-based IP multicast traceroute facility (IPv4 and IPv6) defining Query/Request/Reply TLV formats, router and client behaviour, and diagnosis uses.

multicast.why: The document defines a multicast path-tracing tool that requires multicast router support, and covers PIM-SM, Bidirectional PIM, PIM-DM and IGMP/MLD proxy behaviour. No narrower multicast tag is about the tool itself.
multicast.quote: This document describes the IP multicast traceroute facility, named Mtrace version 2 (Mtrace2).

traceroute.why: Mtrace2 is a traceroute and path discovery facility for multicast. It traces hop by hop from receiver to source and is used to find loss and configuration problems.
traceroute.quote: Unlike unicast traceroute, Mtrace2 requires special implementations on the part of routers.

rejected.why: PIM is the multicast routing protocol whose state Mtrace2 consults, and Section 6 gives per-protocol considerations. The document does not specify or extend PIM.
UDP is only the transport for Mtrace2 messages. The document does not define anything new about how UDP is used.
The IF-MIB and IP Multicast MIB are referenced only as sources for counter values, and no MIB is defined.
Packet loss, rate and delay estimation are secondary diagnostic uses of the tool. The document is not a measurement-methodology specification.
ICMP port unreachable is mentioned only for unsupported routers.

RFC8488.title: RIPE NCC's Implementation of Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Certificate Tree Validation
RFC8488.summary: Informational RFC describing how the RIPE NCC RPKI Validator performs top-down validation of RPKI certificate trees, with an object fetcher (rsync/RRDP) and local object store, independent of retrieval mechanism.

RPKI.why: The whole document specifies relying-party validation of the RPKI tree: TAL fetching, manifest/CRL selection, ROA and certificate validation, and object store handling.
RPKI.quote: This document describes an approach to validating the content of the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) certificate tree, as it is implemented in the RIPE NCC RPKI Validator.

rejected.why: RPKI is the more specific child tag; X.509 PKIX is used as the underlying certificate profile only.
Certificate validation follows RFC 6487/5280, but the document is about RPKI tree validation, not the X.509 profile.
Validation results may feed routing decisions, but the document does not address BGP.
RPKI is the specific child tag and already covers this.
The fetcher uses https/http fallback and RRDP only as a retrieval mechanism.

gaps.name: RRDP (RPKI Repository Delta Protocol)
gaps.why: The document supports RRDP as a retrieval mechanism, but the taxonomy has no tag for it and it is not the subject here.

RFC8489.title: Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)
RFC8489.summary: RFC 8489 specifies STUN, the NAT traversal tool protocol, obsoleting RFC 5389: message format, Binding method, transports, DNS discovery, authentication mechanisms, attributes, and IANA registries.

STUN.why: The document defines and updates the STUN protocol itself: message structure, Binding method, attributes, authentication, and registries.
STUN.quote: Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) is a protocol that serves as a tool for other protocols in dealing with NAT traversal.

rejected.why: ICE is described only as one STUN usage and defined in RFC 8445; this document does not specify it.
TURN is only mentioned as relay extensions to STUN in RFC 5766.
DTLS is a transport STUN runs over; the document defines nothing new about DTLS.
TLS is only a substrate for STUN, with ciphersuite guidance following BCP 195.
DNS SRV is used for server discovery, which is a minor procedure rather than a DNS subject.
HMAC-SHA1 and HMAC-SHA256 are used for message integrity, but the document does not define HMAC.

RFC8490.title: DNS Stateful Operations
RFC8490.summary: Defines a new DNS OPCODE (DSO) for TLV-based stateful operations within persistent DNS-over-TCP/TLS sessions, with Keepalive, Retry Delay and Encryption Padding TLVs, session timers and lifecycle, updating RFC 1035 and 7766.

DNS.why: The document extends the DNS protocol with a new OPCODE, RCODE, message format and session semantics, and updates RFC 1035 and RFC 7766.
DNS.quote: This document defines a new DNS OPCODE for DNS Stateful Operations (DSO) with a value of 6.

rejected.why: DNS-over-TLS is one of the two transports DSO runs over, and the document defines no new DoT mechanism beyond early-data notes.
TCP is the substrate. The delayed-ACK and Nagle discussion is guidance for DSO implementations, not a TCP specification.
EDNS(0) is discussed only as the contrast case (DSO avoids it and obsoletes edns-tcp-keepalive within sessions). The document does not extend EDNS.
DNS-SD push notifications are a motivating use case, but the document does not define them.
TLS is only the secure transport. The 0-RTT early-data considerations are DSO-specific and do not define TLS behaviour.
The Encryption Padding TLV is a minor part of a document whose focus is session management, not privacy-preserving DNS transport.

RFC8491.title: Signaling Maximum SID Depth (MSD) Using IS-IS
RFC8491.summary: Defines IS-IS sub-TLVs (Node MSD and Link MSD) for advertising Maximum SID Depth per node/link, creates the IANA "IGP MSD-Types" registry, and defines the Base MPLS Imposition MSD type for Segment Routing controllers.

IS-IS.why: The document specifies new IS-IS sub-TLVs (Node MSD in the Router CAPABILITY TLV, Link MSD in reachability TLVs), so it extends IS-IS.
IS-IS.quote: This document defines an extension to IS-IS used to advertise one or more types of MSDs at node and/or link granularity.

segment routing.why: MSD exists to let controllers verify SID stack depth for SR paths, so SR readers would want this RFC.
segment routing.quote: When Segment Routing (SR) paths are computed by a centralized controller, it is critical that the controller learn the Maximum SID Depth (MSD)

rejected.why: BGP-LS is mentioned only as a way MSD is later exported; MSD over BGP-LS is defined in another document.
PCEP MSD signalling is defined elsewhere and only referenced as background.
MPLS label imposition depth is the meaning of the Base MPLS Imposition type, but the document does not specify MPLS itself.
The BMI-MSD type concerns MPLS labels, but the document is a general SR/IS-IS advertisement mechanism and does not define SR-MPLS behaviour.
The IANA registry creation is boilerplate-level here, not the main subject.

RFC8492.title: Secure Password Ciphersuites for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC8492.summary: Defines TLS-PWD, new TLS ciphersuites and handshake extensions that use the dragonfly password-authenticated key exchange for certificateless authentication with low-entropy passwords, including protected usernames.

TLS.why: The document extends TLS with new ciphersuites, handshake message changes, and extensions (pwd_protect, pwd_clear, password_salt) for TLS 1.2 and 1.3.
TLS.quote: This memo defines several new ciphersuites for the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol to support certificateless, secure authentication using only a simple, low-entropy password.

Dragonfly.why: The document specifies how the dragonfly PAKE is used in TLS, including Password Element derivation by hunting-and-pecking, commit generation, and shared secret computation.
Dragonfly.quote: The key exchange underlying TLS-PWD is the "dragonfly" password-authenticated key exchange (PAKE) as defined in [RFC7664].

rejected.why: The parent of Dragonfly, which is the more specific tag, so it is implied.
ECC and FFC groups are only the mathematical setting for the key exchange. The document does not define new curves.
HMAC is only used to instantiate the random function and the salted password base.
Mentioned only as a motivating use case in the introduction.
Mentioned only in an IANA registry column, not specified in the document.
AES-GCM and AES-CCM appear only as the bulk ciphers named in the ciphersuites. AES-SIV is used only to protect the username.
Used only for password and username string preparation through the OpaqueString profile, which is a minor dependency.

RFC8493.title: The BagIt File Packaging Format (V1.0)
RFC8493.summary: Specifies BagIt v1.0, a hierarchical filesystem layout convention (bag declaration, data payload directory, manifests, tag files, fetch file) for packaging, storing and transferring digital content with checksum-based integrity validation.

rejected.why: RFC 3986 is only used for percent-encoding and absolute URLs in fetch.txt; the document does not define URI syntax or schemes.
MIME is mentioned only as a serialized archival format that BagIt is contrasted with; the document is not about MIME.
SHA-256/512 and SHA-1 are named as checksum algorithms manifests may use, but the document does not specify or analyse them; they are a mechanism it relies on.
MD5 is permitted for backward compatibility and used in examples, and md5sum quirks are noted, but the document is not about MD5.
An ABNF section describes the file formats, but this is notation applied to the document's own syntax, not a subject of the document.
UTF-8 is the recommended encoding for tag files, and Unicode normalization is discussed in non-normative interoperability notes, but the document is not about these encodings.
The bag declaration names a tag-file character encoding from the IANA registry, but this is a minor parameter and not the document's subject.

gaps.name: BagIt / digital preservation file packaging
gaps.why: The document defines a filesystem-based packaging and archival format with manifests and checksum integrity for digital preservation and transfer. The taxonomy has no tag for file packaging, archival formats, or digital preservation, so it gets no tags.

RFC8494.title: Multicast Email (MULE) over Allied Communications Publication (ACP) 142
RFC8494.summary: Defines MULE, an application protocol that carries Internet Mail between MTAs over ACP 142 P_MUL reliable multicast, using a BSMTP-like compressed payload, and describes gatewaying with SMTP and which SMTP extensions are supported.

SMTP.why: MULE is an alternate MTA-to-MTA transfer mechanism alongside SMTP. The document specifies gatewaying to and from SMTP and the status of each ESMTP extension, so SMTP readers would want it.
SMTP.quote: MULE reuses the ESMTP extension framework defined in [RFC5321].

email.why: The document defines a new email transport and relaying architecture for MTAs, covering gateways and DSN error handling. This is broader than SMTP alone.
email.quote: MULE is an electronic mail transport of Internet Mail messages [RFC5322] over an ACP 142 P_MUL network.

reliable multicast.why: The protocol is built around reliable multicast under EMCON conditions, with fixed multicast groups and P_MUL PDUs. It is an application over a reliable multicast transport.
reliable multicast.quote: P_MUL [ACP142A] is a transport protocol for reliable multicast in bandwidth-constrained and delayed acknowledgement environments

rejected.why: MIME messages are the payload being carried, but the document does not specify MIME.
zlib is only used to compress the payload, and the document defines nothing new about it.
BER and ASN.1 appear only as the wrapper encoding borrowed from STANAG 4406. The document does not specify ASN.1 itself.
UDP is the substrate under P_MUL, and the document defines nothing new about its usage.
The document mentions X.400 and STANAG 4406 only for similarity of the wrapper, not to specify interworking.
S/MIME is mentioned only in the Security Considerations as end-to-end protection advice.

gaps.name: ACP 142 / P_MUL
gaps.why: The document is about transport of mail over this military reliable multicast protocol. The taxonomy has no tag for ACP 142 or P_MUL itself, so reliable multicast is the closest fit.

RFC8495.title: Allocation Token Extension for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)
RFC8495.summary: Defines an EPP extension that lets clients pass an Allocation Token credential in check, info, create and transfer commands to authorize allocation of a specific object (e.g., a domain name) from the registry server.

EPP.why: The document specifies a new EPP extension mapping, with command elements, error handling and an XML schema, so it belongs on the EPP page.
EPP.quote: an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) extension for including an Allocation Token in "query" and "transform" commands

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are only the encoding and formal syntax for the EPP extension; the document is not about XML usage itself.
The parent topic is implied by the EPP tag, and the document is specific to EPP.
The examples use domain names, but the document specifies registry provisioning, not DNS protocol or resolver behaviour.
The Allocation Token is a credential, but the document is about an EPP mapping and not about authorization as a general subject.
The IANA section only registers the XML namespace, schema and EPP extension; this is boilerplate and not the subject.

RFC8496.title: P-Charge-Info: A Private Header Field (P-Header) Extension to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC8496.summary: Documents the existing deployed SIP private header field P-Charge-Info, which carries a billing identifier for the party to be charged in INVITE requests, and registers it with IANA.

SIP.why: The document specifies a SIP private header field extension, with procedures at UAs and proxies, syntax, and trust and security rules.
SIP.quote: P-Charge-Info, a private SIP header field, to provide simple billing information

rejected.why: The header field registration is only boilerplate IANA action; the document is not about IANA registries in general.
ABNF is only used to write the syntax of the header field.
tel and SIP URIs are only used as the value of the header field, not specified or extended here.
TLS is mentioned only as one option for protecting the SIP connection in Security Considerations.
PSTN gateways are mentioned as insertion points and use cases, but no interworking mechanism is specified.

RFC8497.title: Marking SIP Messages to Be Logged
RFC8497.summary: RFC 8497 defines a "logme" parameter on the SIP Session-ID header field to mark SIP dialogs for diagnostic logging end to end, and specifies how UAs, proxies and B2BUAs insert, echo, remove and log the marker.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new Session-ID header parameter and specifies behaviour of SIP UAs, proxies and B2BUAs for marking and logging dialogs.
SIP.quote: This document describes an indicator for the SIP protocol that can be used to mark signaling as being of interest to logging.

rejected.why: SDP appears only in logging and masking of crypto attributes; the document does not specify or extend SDP.
Not about presence or instant messaging extensions; it is general SIP signalling marking.
Logging of SIP messages is referenced using SIP CLF, not the syslog protocol, which is not specified here.
Privacy considerations are a boilerplate-style section; the document's main body is not about privacy.
The Session-ID UUID is used as a test case identifier but UUIDs are not the subject of the document.

RFC8498.title: A P-Served-User Header Field Parameter for an Originating Call Diversion (CDIV) Session Case in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC8498.summary: RFC 8498 updates RFC 5502 by defining the "orig-cdiv" parameter for the SIP P-Served-User header field, which conveys the originating-after-call-diversion session case in 3GPP IMS, and it also fixes the header's ABNF.

SIP.why: The document extends a SIP private header field. It specifies new parameter semantics, proxy behaviour, ABNF corrections and call flows for call diversion in SIP.
SIP.quote: This document updates RFC 5502 by defining a new P-Served-User header field parameter, "orig-cdiv".

rejected.why: The ABNF is corrected here, but only as a way to specify the header syntax. The document is not about ABNF itself.
The document registers header field parameters, but this is boilerplate IANA Considerations and not the subject of the document.
The Trust Domain and security discussion is incidental. The document does not address authentication.
The document is motivated by 3GPP IMS, but it specifies a SIP header parameter and not IP over 3GPP systems.

gaps.name: IMS (3GPP IP Multimedia Subsystem) / SIP private headers
gaps.why: The document concerns P-headers for the 3GPP IMS core, including S-CSCF and AS behaviour. The taxonomy has no tag for IMS or SIP P-headers, so SIP is the closest fit.

RFC8499.title: DNS Terminology
RFC8499.summary: RFC 8499 is a BCP that collects and updates current definitions of DNS terminology (names, resolvers, servers, zones, wildcards, registration model, DNSSEC terms), obsoleting RFC 7719.

DNS.why: The whole document defines DNS terms: names, RCODEs, resource records, servers and clients, zones, wildcards. DNS readers would look here for terminology.
DNS.quote: This document gives current definitions for many of the terms used in the DNS in a single document.

DNSSEC.why: Sections 10 and 11 define signed zones, NSEC/NSEC3, validation, KSK/ZSK, trust anchors and the secure/insecure/bogus/indeterminate states. This is a substantial part of the document.
DNSSEC.quote: Most DNSSEC terms are defined in [RFC4033], [RFC4034], [RFC4035], and [RFC5155]. The terms that have caused confusion in the DNS community are highlighted here.

terminology.why: The document is a glossary of DNS terms, so readers browsing terminology would expect it.
terminology.quote: This document contains a collection of a wide variety of DNS-related terms, organized loosely by topic.

rejected.why: Section 9 defines registry, registrar, registrant, EPP, WHOIS and RDAP. These are only brief term definitions within a larger glossary, so I did not tag registration, EPP, RDAP or WHOIS.
mDNS is defined in a single glossary entry and is not the subject of the document.
IDN has one short glossary entry pointing to other RFCs.
EDNS and OPT appear only as brief glossary entries.
The 'Host name' entry is one term among many, not a treatment of host naming.
The parent tag is implied by DNS. The 'Naming system' entry is only a framing definition.

RFC8500.title: IS-IS Routing with Reverse Metric
RFC8500.summary: Defines the IS-IS Reverse Metric TLV, carried in IIH PDUs, which lets a router signal neighbors (or the DIS on a LAN) to add a metric offset to the inbound link metric, so traffic can be shifted away from a link during maintenance.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with a new TLV, a sub-TLV registry, and procedures for point-to-point links, LANs (DIS/pseudonode), and multi-topology IS-IS.
IS-IS.quote: This document defines the IS-IS "Reverse Metric" mechanism that allows an IS-IS node to send a Reverse Metric TLV through the IS-IS Hello (IIH) PDU

rejected.why: LDP/IGP synchronization is a use case (Section 3.4), but the document defines nothing new about LDP itself.
A TE metric sub-TLV is included, but the document is about IS-IS metric signalling, not traffic engineering in its own right.
MPLS networks are only the deployment context.
BGP VPN prefixes are mentioned only as an example in the distributed forwarding scenario.
Authentication is only a brief recommendation in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
Syslog and SNMP traps are mentioned in one operational hint only.

gaps.name: IS-IS
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no IS-IS tag in the form I needed to cite, so please check the id. The taxonomy lists IS-IS as a tech under routing, and I used it. If it is not accepted, use routing.

RFC8501.title: Reverse DNS in IPv6 for Internet Service Providers
RFC8501.summary: Informational analysis of approaches ISPs can use to provide reverse DNS (PTR in IP6.ARPA) for customers in IPv6, where prepopulating every address is infeasible, covering negative responses, wildcards, dynamic DNS, delegation and on-the-fly generation.

DNS.why: The whole document is about operating reverse DNS zones (PTR records, wildcards, delegation, on-the-fly generation) for IPv6; an operational DNS topic.
DNS.quote: This document analyzes different approaches and considerations for ISPs in managing the IP6.ARPA zone.

DNS update.why: Section 2.3 and its six subsections evaluate dynamic DNS updates (hosts, gateways, DHCP, RADIUS populated) as a main alternative, including TSIG and scaling concerns.
DNS update.quote: One way to ensure that forward and reverse records match is for hosts to update DNS servers dynamically once interface configuration is complete

IPv6.why: The problem is IPv6-specific address scale and deployment by ISPs, including SLAAC and prefix delegation, so IPv6 deployment readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: Since 2^^80 possible addresses could be configured in a single /48 zone alone, it is impractical to write a zone with every possible address entered

rejected.why: DNSSEC is mentioned only as a scaling/load consideration for wildcard and on-the-fly signing; the document is not about it.
DHCPv6 is used as a source of data and for DNS options, but is not specified or extended here.
RADIUS accounting is only one possible data source for populating zones in a single subsection.
SLAAC is mentioned as the reason hostnames cannot be associated with addresses, not as a subject.
The document concerns PTR records and naming of addresses, not host naming conventions or host tables.
Prefix delegation is background; the document is about reverse DNS, not address architecture.

RFC8502.title: L2L3 VPN Multicast MIB
RFC8502.summary: Defines two SMIv2 MIB modules (a textual-conventions module and a table module) describing P-tunnel type, identifier and PMSI Tunnel attribute information for monitoring multicast in BGP/MPLS L2 and L3 VPNs.

MIB.why: The document's sole purpose is to define MIB modules (L2L3-VPN-MULTICAST-TC-MIB and L2L3-VPN-MULTICAST-MIB) in SMIv2.
MIB.quote: it describes two MIB modules that will be used by other MIB modules for monitoring and/or configuring Layer 2 and Layer 3 Virtual Private Networks that support multicast

MVPN.why: The managed objects model P-tunnels and PMSI Tunnel attributes of multicast VPNs (RFC 6513/6514/7117), so readers of multicast VPN would want this MIB.
MVPN.quote: Throughout this document, we will use the term "L2L3VpnMCast network" to mean a BGP/MPLS L2 and L3 VPN that supports multicast.

rejected.why: SNMP is the access protocol for the MIB; the document defines data modules, not SNMP itself. The MIB tag sits under SNMP and is the more specific fit.
PMSI Tunnel attribute is carried in BGP A-D routes, but the document defines no BGP procedures; it only models the attribute.
PIM tree types appear only as enumerated P-tunnel types, not as subject matter.
RSVP-TE P2MP LSP is just one enumerated tunnel type.
RFC 7117 multicast in VPLS is referenced as background; the document is not about VPLS.
Multicast VPN is the more specific tag for this document's subject.

RFC8503.title: BGP/MPLS Layer 3 VPN Multicast Management Information Base
RFC8503.summary: Defines the BGP-MPLS-LAYER3-VPN-MULTICAST-MIB module, an SNMP MIB for configuring and monitoring multicast VPNs (MVPN) on PE routers, including MVRFs, PMSIs, advertisement statistics, multicast routes and next hops.

MVPN.why: The MIB's subject is multicast VPN on BGP/MPLS L3VPN PEs: PMSIs, MVRFs, C-multicast routes, BGP-MVPN.
MVPN.quote: describes managed objects to configure and/or monitor Multicast communication over IP Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) supported by the Multiprotocol Label Switching/Border Gateway Protocol

MIB.why: The document is a SMIv2 MIB module definition with tables, notifications and conformance statements.
MIB.quote: This document defines BGP-MPLS-LAYER3-VPN-MULTICAST-MIB, a MIB module for monitoring and/or configuring MVPNs on PEs.

rejected.why: BGP is used for C-multicast routing in BGP-MVPN but the document is a MIB for MVPN, not BGP itself.
SNMP is only the access protocol for the MIB; the MIB tag covers the subject.
PIM is one of two C-multicast signalling options referenced by objects, not specified or extended here.
MVPN is the more specific tag under VPN for this multicast MIB; L3VPN itself is only the base.
The MVPN tag is more specific and already sits under it.

RFC8504.title: IPv6 Node Requirements
RFC8504.summary: RFC 8504 is a BCP applicability statement defining which IPv6 specifications hosts and routers must, should or may implement, covering the IP layer, addressing, configuration, DNS, mobility, security and management.

IPv6.why: The whole document specifies the implementation requirements for IPv6 nodes, covering the IPv6 specification, extension headers, addressing and deployment.
IPv6.quote: This document defines requirements for IPv6 nodes.

neighbor discovery.why: A substantial section details ND requirements: router discovery, NUD, redirects, RS backoff and fragmentation rules.
neighbor discovery.quote: Neighbor Discovery MUST be supported with the noted exceptions below.

SLAAC.why: Covers SLAAC, DAD, stable IIDs and privacy extensions as node requirements.
SLAAC.quote: Hosts MUST support IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration.

DHCPv6.why: DHCPv6 address and other-configuration requirements appear in several sections, including anonymity profiles and relay agents.
DHCPv6.quote: all hosts SHOULD implement address configuration via DHCPv6.

rejected.why: IPsec requirements (SHOULD support RFC 4301, ESP, IKEv2) take up one section, but the document is not about IPsec.
Section 7 sets stub-resolver requirements, but DNS is only one small part of the document.
ICMPv6 gets a brief MUST line, which is not enough to make it a subject of the document.
Mobility is a MAY in a short section, so it is not a subject of the document.
MLDv2 is covered in a short subsection, which is not enough to tag it.
PMTUD is covered in one short subsection of requirements.

RFC8505.title: Registration Extensions for IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (6LoWPAN) Neighbor Discovery
RFC8505.summary: RFC 8505 updates 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery (RFC 6775) with an Extended Address Registration Option (EARO), Transaction ID, ROVR, extended duplicate address messages and new capability bits, supporting mobility, proxy registration, and Routing Registrars in low-power networks.

6LoWPAN.why: The document is an update to 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery, modifying the ARO, DAR/DAC messages and the 6CIO for IPv6 over low-power wireless networks.
6LoWPAN.quote: This specification updates 6LoWPAN ND [RFC6775] to simplify and generalize registration in 6LoWPAN Routers (6LRs).

neighbor discovery.why: It extends IPv6 ND NS/NA messages with registration options and defines proxy ND by Routing Registrars, so IPv6 neighbor discovery readers would want it.
neighbor discovery.quote: The EARO includes a sequence counter called the Transaction ID (TID), which is used to determine the latest location of a registering mobile device.

rejected.why: RPL is referenced (TID compatible with Path Sequence, RPL root as registering node), but the document does not specify or extend RPL.
Parent of neighbor discovery; implied, not tagged separately.
New ICMPv6 codes for DAR/DAC are defined, but they are a detail of the ND registration, not a subject about ICMP itself.
Privacy addresses and SLAAC are mentioned only as context for multiple registrations.
IANA registry creation is boilerplate here and not the main body subject.
Mentioned only as a service enabled by the follow-on AP-ND draft.

RFC8506.title: Diameter Credit-Control Application
RFC8506.summary: RFC 8506 specifies the Diameter Credit-Control application (CCR/CCA commands, AVPs, state machines, failure handling) for real-time prepaid credit authorization, obsoleting RFC 4006.

Diameter.why: The whole document defines a Diameter application: new commands (CCR/CCA, code 272), AVPs, Application-Id 4, state machines and failure procedures.
Diameter.quote: This document specifies a Diameter application that can be used to implement real-time credit-control for a variety of end-user services

rejected.why: Diameter is the specific AAA tag and is more specific than the AAA framework parent, so only Diameter is tagged.
Section 11 only sketches RADIUS prepaid interworking and defers the full translation to another document. RADIUS is not a substantial part of the document.
SIP appears only as a service example and in an appendix flow. The document is not about SIP.
The IANA Considerations are boilerplate registry actions, so they are not evidence for this tag.
The Privacy Considerations section is a single section of the document, not its main subject.

gaps.name: Diameter
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no Diameter tag even though it lists Diameter under AAA, so I could not use it exactly. The document's subject is the Diameter protocol, so the Diameter id I submitted is not a valid taxonomy id. It should be replaced with the Diameter id listed under AAA in the security hierarchy.

RFC8507.title: Simple Internet Protocol (SIP) Specification
RFC8507.summary: Historic republication of Steve Deering's 1992 Simple Internet Protocol (SIP) draft, an IPng candidate that is a 64-bit-address successor to IPv4 and a precursor of IPv6, specifying its header, addresses, fragmentation and source routing, and the ICMP/IGMP/transport changes needed.

IPng.why: The document is the specification of SIP, one of the historic IPng candidate protocols, published for the historical record.
IPng.quote: The Simple Internet Protocol was the basis for one of the candidates for the IETF's Next Generation (IPng) work that became IPv6.

rejected.why: SIP is an ancestor of IPv6, but the document specifies a different, historic protocol, not IPv6 itself.
IPv4 is the baseline SIP is compared against; the document does not specify or extend IPv4.
Here SIP means Simple Internet Protocol, not Session Initiation Protocol. The real-time communications SIP tag does not apply.
ICMP changes for SIP are described, but only as one part of the new protocol. IPng covers the document better.
IGMP changes are a short section of the new protocol's specification, not the document's subject.
Path MTU Discovery is relied on by SIP but is not the subject of the document.

RFC8508.title: IMAP REPLACE Extension
RFC8508.summary: Defines the IMAP REPLACE and UID REPLACE commands, which atomically replace an existing message in a mailbox with a new one, and describes how they interact with other IMAP extensions.

IMAP.why: The document specifies a new IMAP command (REPLACE/UID REPLACE), its semantics, state-diagram impacts, formal syntax and interactions with other IMAP extensions.
IMAP.quote: This document defines an IMAP ([RFC3501]) extension to facilitate the replacement of an existing message with a new one.

rejected.why: Sieve IMAP events are mentioned in one short subsection about interaction, but the document is not about Sieve.
MIME appears only in example message content, not as a subject of the document.
Message headers appear only in example literals and are not a subject of the document.
ABNF is only the notation used in the formal syntax section, not the document's subject.

RFC8509.title: A Root Key Trust Anchor Sentinel for DNSSEC
RFC8509.summary: Specifies a DNSSEC-validating resolver mechanism using special sentinel labels (root-key-sentinel-is-ta/not-ta-<key-tag>) that lets users and researchers determine whether a root zone KSK is in a resolver's trust anchor store, for measuring readiness for a root KSK rollover.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document defines a DNSSEC trust-anchor sentinel mechanism for validating resolvers, including special SERVFAIL processing tied to trust anchor state and root KSK rolls.
DNSSEC.quote: allow an end user and third parties to determine the trusted key state for the root key of the resolvers that handle that user's DNS queries

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific child tag and already covers the DNS resolver behaviour; the parent is implied.
The document reserves leftmost labels, not domain names or TLDs, and explicitly says this is not best practice.
The CD bit is only a precondition for sentinel processing; the document defines nothing new about EDNS.
Web fetches are used only in the example test; the mechanism does not rely on the web.

RFC8510.title: OSPF Link-Local Signaling (LLS) Extensions for Local Interface ID Advertisement
RFC8510.summary: Defines a new OSPF link-local signaling (LLS) TLV (type 18) carrying the Local Interface ID in Hello and DD packets, so neighbors learn the Remote Interface ID during neighbor discovery, with backward compatibility to RFC 4203.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF with a new LLS TLV and specifies its use alongside the existing Link Local TE Opaque LSA mechanism.
OSPF.quote: This document describes the extensions to OSPF link-local signaling (LLS) to advertise the Local Interface ID.

rejected.why: RFC 4203 is referenced for the existing Link Local/Remote Identifier mechanism, but this document is not about GMPLS.
The TE Link Local LSA is discussed only as the prior mechanism being improved on.
The IANA section is only a TLV code point allocation, which is boilerplate here.
The document concerns OSPFv2 (Extended Link Opaque LSA, Router-LSA), not OSPFv3.

RFC8511.title: TCP Alternative Backoff with ECN (ABE)
RFC8511.summary: Experimental RFC defining ABE, a sender-side change to TCP congestion control that reduces cwnd/ssthresh by a smaller factor (0.8) on ECN-Echo than on packet loss, as permitted by RFC 8311, to improve throughput over AQM-managed short queues.

ECN.why: The document changes the TCP sender's reaction to ECN CE feedback, updating the RFC 3168 response as allowed by RFC 8311.
ECN.quote: this document specifies a sender-side change to TCP where receipt of a packet with the ECN-Echo flag SHOULD trigger the TCP source to set the slow start threshold (ssthresh) to 0.8 times the FlightSize

TCP.why: It specifies a modification to TCP congestion window and ssthresh reduction in congestion avoidance.
TCP.quote: This specification changes the congestion control algorithm of an ECN-Capable TCP transport protocol by changing the TCP-sender response

AQM.why: Motivated by and evaluated against AQM (CoDel, PIE) bottlenecks, with discussion of how ECN marks signal a short controlled queue; a substantial part of the rationale.
AQM.quote: ABE improves TCP's average throughput when routers use AQM-controlled buffers that allow only for short queues.

rejected.why: Used as an evaluation environment only; the document does not specify or extend CoDel.
Mentioned as an AQM used in experiments, not specified or changed here.
Referenced for its beta_loss value and test results, but the recommendation applies to standard TCP (Reno) congestion control.
Used as a baseline in evaluation; the document does not specify NewReno.
Mentioned only as a contrasting example of a more detailed ECN response.

RFC8512.title: A YANG Module for Network Address Translation (NAT) and Network Prefix Translation (NPT)
RFC8512.summary: Defines the ietf-nat YANG module for configuring and monitoring NAT44, NAPT, NAT64, CLAT, SIIT, EAM, NPTv6 and Destination NAT, with examples.

YANG.why: The document's core deliverable is a YANG module with tree diagram and module source for NAT management.
YANG.quote: This document defines a data model for Network Address Translation (NAT) and Network Prefix Translation (NPT) capabilities using the YANG data modeling language

NAT.why: The model covers NAT44/NAPT behaviour, mappings, port allocation, filtering, timers and limits, so NAT readers would want it.
NAT.quote: Traditional NAT is defined in [RFC2663], while Carrier Grade NAT (CGN) is defined in [RFC6888].

CGN.why: Port quotas, port-set allocation, and limits follow RFC 6888 CGN requirements, with CGN examples in the appendix.
CGN.quote: In order to comply with CGN deployments in particular, the NAT YANG module allows limiting the number of external ports per subscriber

NAT64.why: NAT64 is a major translation mode modelled, with prefixes and stateless mode configuration.

SIIT.why: SIIT and EAM are explicitly modelled with features and prefix mapping lists.
SIIT.quote: Stateless IP/ICMP Translation (SIIT) [RFC7915], Explicit Address Mappings (EAM) for SIIT [RFC7757]

464XLAT.why: CLAT parameters are modelled, with a CLAT configuration example.

rejected.why: Only the management protocol through which the model is accessed; not specified here.
Relationship to NATV2-MIB is discussed briefly, but the document is a YANG model, not a MIB.
Handled by separate RFC 8513; only mentioned as an extension.
Explicit dynamic mappings via PCP are declared out of scope.
Parent of specific tags already chosen (NAT64, SIIT, 464XLAT).
MAP-E is referenced only for PSID port-set algorithm.

gaps.name: NPTv6 (IPv6-to-IPv6 Network Prefix Translation)
gaps.why: The document models NPTv6 (RFC 6296), but the taxonomy has no NPTv6 tag; NAT is the nearest fit.

RFC8513.title: A YANG Data Model for Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite)
RFC8513.summary: Defines the ietf-dslite YANG module for configuring and monitoring DS-Lite AFTR and B4 elements, augmenting the interfaces and NAT YANG modules.

DS-Lite.why: The module models DS-Lite AFTR and B4 parameters, policies, mappings and notifications, so DS-Lite readers need it.
DS-Lite.quote: This document defines a YANG module for the Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite) Address Family Transition Router (AFTR) and Basic Bridging BroadBand (B4) elements.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module (ietf-dslite) with a tree diagram and examples.
YANG.quote: This document defines a data model for DS-Lite [RFC6333], using the YANG data modeling language [RFC7950].

rejected.why: The module augments the NAT YANG module (RFC 8512) for the AFTR's NAPT44, but NAT itself is not specified here. DS-Lite is the subject.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only as access protocols in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
Softwires are the tunnel mechanism DS-Lite uses. The document adds nothing about softwires beyond DS-Lite, so DS-Lite is the more specific tag.
This is a YANG model, not an SNMP MIB.

RFC8514.title: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) - SAVEDATE Extension
RFC8514.summary: Defines the IMAP SAVEDATE capability, adding a "save date" message attribute (time saved in the current mailbox) with FETCH support and new SEARCH keys.

IMAP.why: The document is an IMAP extension that adds a capability, a FETCH data item and SEARCH keys, so it belongs on the IMAP page.
IMAP.quote: This document extends the Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) [IMAP4rev1] with a new capability called "SAVEDATE".

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax. The document does not specify or discuss it.
IMAP is the more specific tag, and its ancestor email is implied.
The save date reuses the existing IMAP date-time syntax. It does not define a new date format.

RFC8515.title: URN Namespace for ETSI Documents
RFC8515.summary: Registers the "etsi" URN Namespace Identifier with IANA for identifying ETSI-published resources, such as YANG module namespaces, and describes how ETSI manages assignments under it.

URN.why: The document's whole purpose is registering a new URN namespace (NID) and defining its assignment, syntax and resolution policy, so readers of the URN subject need it.
URN.quote: The Namespace Identifier (NID) "etsi" for Uniform Resource Names (URNs) will be used to identify resources published by ETSI.

rejected.why: YANG module namespaces are only given as example URNs (urn:etsi:yang:...); the document does not specify or discuss YANG itself.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-level; the document is about the URN namespace, not IANA registry guidance.
URN is the more specific tag that fits; URI is its parent and implied.

RFC8516.title: "Too Many Requests" Response Code for the Constrained Application Protocol
RFC8516.summary: Defines CoAP response code 4.29 "Too Many Requests", which a server uses to tell a client to reduce its request rate, with Max-Age as the back-off period, and specifies server and client behaviour.

CoAP.why: The document extends CoAP with a new response code and specifies how CoAP servers and clients must behave when it is used.
CoAP.quote: This document defines a new CoAP response code for a server to indicate that a client should reduce the rate of requests.

rejected.why: HTTP 429 is mentioned only as the analogue of the new CoAP code. The document does not specify or extend HTTP.
DTLS is cited only in Security Considerations as an underlying security mechanism.
The code signals request-rate back-off at the application layer. The document does not address transport congestion control.
The only IANA content is the registration of one response code, which is boilerplate.
CoAP is the specific technology tag and is already chosen. The document gives no general IoT guidance.

RFC8517.title: An Inventory of Transport-Centric Functions Provided by Middleboxes: An Operator Perspective
RFC8517.summary: Informational independent-stream RFC that inventories operator-motivated, transport-layer-aware middlebox functions (measurement, NAT, firewall, DDoS scrubbing, PEPs, network coding, MPTCP proxies, prioritization, shaping) to inform transport protocol design.

TCP.why: The document is about middlebox functions that observe and act on TCP fields (sequence numbers, SACK, timestamps, handshake state, PEPs), so TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: This document primarily focuses on devices that observe and act on information carried in the transport layer, and especially information carried in TCP packets.

NAT.why: NAT is one of the main middlebox functions inventoried, with its dependence on transport port fields and its role in IPv6 transition.
NAT.quote: Network Address Translators (NATs) allow multiple devices to share a public address by dividing the transport-layer port space among the devices.

firewall.why: Firewalls and the way they track transport state are covered in a dedicated section, and DDoS scrubbing sits alongside them.
firewall.quote: Firewalls are pervasive and essential components that inspect incoming and outgoing traffic.

transport.why: The document aims to inform the design of new transport protocols with respect to middlebox visibility and operator needs.
transport.quote: A primary goal is to provide information to the Internet community to aid understanding of what might be gained or lost by decisions

MPTCP.why: Network-assisted bandwidth aggregation with MPTCP proxies and Conversion Points gets its own section.
MPTCP.quote: One of the approaches uses Multipath TCP (MPTCP) proxies [TCP-CONVERT] to forward traffic along multiple paths.

rejected.why: DDoS scrubbing is covered in only one short subsection (3.3) and the document does not specify a mitigation mechanism, so it is not a main subject.
Section 2 covers passive measurements of loss, RTT and reordering, but only as a list of what middleboxes can observe. It does not define metrics or methods.
Diffserv appears only in a brief mention in 3.8 with one reference.
Congestion responsiveness is discussed briefly as something middleboxes infer or enforce, not as the document's subject.
RFC 7498 and a use-case draft are cited only as background on service functions.
Network coding and FECFRAME are mentioned briefly in 3.6 as an example function and are not developed.

gaps.name: middleboxes / performance-enhancing proxies
gaps.why: The document is fundamentally an inventory of middlebox functions, including PEPs, and the taxonomy has no tag for middleboxes in general.

RFC8518.title: Selection of Loop-Free Alternates for Multi-Homed Prefixes
RFC8518.summary: RFC 8518 updates the IP Fast Reroute LFA base specification (RFC 5286) by giving explicit inequalities and selection rules for loop-free alternates to multi-homed prefixes, including OSPF external prefixes via ASBRs, the IS-IS ATT bit, MAX_METRIC links, and multi-topology cases.

IP fast reroute.why: The whole document concerns computing loop-free alternates for IP fast reroute, updating RFC 5286.
IP fast reroute.quote: This document provides explicit inequalities that can be used to evaluate neighbors as potential alternates for MHPs.

OSPF.why: Section 4.2 gives detailed OSPF-specific rules for ASBR selection (type 5/7, RFC1583Compatibility, forwarding address) with dedicated inequalities.
OSPF.quote: This document provides detailed criteria for evaluating potential alternates for external prefixes advertised by OSPF ASBRs

IS-IS.why: Covers IS-IS ATT bit handling for LFA computation of default routes, plus IS-IS MAX_METRIC and MT IS-IS considerations.
IS-IS.quote: a node can consider a default route is being advertised from the border L1/L2 router where the ATT bit is set and can do LFA computation

rejected.why: The document addresses specific LFA computation rather than general routing architecture.
ECMP MHP cases are discussed, but only as examples within LFA selection; the document explicitly does not alter ECMP handling.
External prefixes are redistributed into the IGP via ASBRs; BGP is not involved.
MAX_METRIC is used by operators for TE, but the document is about LFA eligibility, not TE mechanisms.

RFC8519.title: YANG Data Model for Network Access Control Lists (ACLs)
RFC8519.summary: Defines YANG 1.1 data models (ietf-access-control-list, ietf-packet-fields, ietf-ethertypes) for configuring and monitoring ordered Access Control Lists whose entries match packet headers and apply forwarding/logging actions.

YANG.why: The document's core content is a set of YANG modules for ACLs, with groupings, features, identities and augmentation examples.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG 1.1 data model [RFC7950] for the configuration of ACLs.

firewall.why: ACLs are packet-filtering rules used in firewalls; the model covers match criteria and permit/deny/reject actions. It also compares itself to Linux nftables firewall filters.
firewall.quote: An ACL is a user-ordered set of rules that is used to filter traffic on a networking device.

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the access protocol for the data; it appears in examples and Security Considerations, not as subject.
This is a YANG model, not an SNMP MIB module.
TCP header fields are matched on, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
IPv6 header fields are matched in the model, but IPv6 is not the subject.
Ethernet header matching and the ethertype module are model contents, but the document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
Mentioned only as an example of a future augmentation of the matches container.
Network ACLs are packet filters, not authorization or access-control policy for users.

RFC8520.title: Manufacturer Usage Description Specification
RFC8520.summary: Specifies Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD): an architecture, YANG modules, DHCP options, LLDP TLV, X.509 extensions and signing so IoT devices can signal intended network access to a MUD manager for access control.

MUD.why: The whole document defines MUD: architecture, MUD URL, file model, and emission mechanisms.
MUD.quote: The goal of MUD is to provide a means for end devices to signal to the network what sort of access and network functionality they require

YANG.why: Defines the ietf-mud and ietf-acldns YANG modules augmenting the ACL model; a substantial part of the document.
YANG.quote: This memo specifies two YANG modules, IPv4 and IPv6 DHCP options

DHCP.why: Defines new DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options (161 and 112) with client and server behavior for carrying the MUD URL.
DHCP.quote: The IPv4 MUD URL client option has the following format:

X.509.why: Defines id-pe-mud-url and id-pe-mudsigner certificate extensions with an ASN.1 module.
X.509.quote: This section defines an X.509 non-critical certificate extension that contains a single URL that points to an online Manufacturer Usage Description
X.509.section: 11. The Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD) URL X.509 Extension

rejected.why: CMS is used as the signature format for MUD files, but the document only uses it and adds a content-type OID; it is not about CMS.
MUD files are fetched over HTTPS, but HTTP is just the substrate.
JSON is the serialization format for the MUD file, not the subject.
The IPv6 option is covered with DHCP generally; DHCP covers both versions.
EAP/TEAP is mentioned only as one way to carry the certificate with the MUD URL.
DNS names are used in ACLs and DNS is a default permitted service, but the document does not specify DNS itself.

gaps.name: LLDP (Link Layer Discovery Protocol)
gaps.why: The document defines a new LLDP vendor-specific TLV for the MUD URL, and the taxonomy has no LLDP tag.

RFC8521.title: Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) Object Tagging
RFC8521.summary: RFC 8521 is a BCP that updates RFC 7484 by defining a practice of appending service provider tags (hyphen plus an IANA-registered identifier) to RDAP object handles so clients can bootstrap entity and similar queries to the authoritative server, and creates an IANA bootstrap registry for those tags.

RDAP.why: The whole document extends RDAP bootstrapping with object tagging, defines a new bootstrap registry and an rdapConformance extension value. RDAP readers would want it.
RDAP.quote: This document updates RFC 7484 by describing an operational practice that can be used to add structure to RDAP identifiers

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding of RDAP responses and of the bootstrap registry. The document defines nothing about JSON.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations as protection for the connection to IANA, which is boilerplate.
EPP is cited only for the roidType syntax that the provider identifiers follow. The document is not about EPP.
RFC 3986 is cited only to justify choosing the hyphen-minus as an unreserved character. The document does not address URIs.
The document creates an IANA registry, but that sits in the IANA Considerations and the registration procedure. The main subject is the RDAP tagging practice.
RDAP is the more specific tag under it, so the parent is not listed.

RFC8522.title: Looking Glass Command Set
RFC8522.summary: Specifies a uniform HTTP/JSON API (under /.well-known/looking-glass) for Network Looking Glass services, with ping, traceroute, show route, show bgp and router-listing commands returning JSend-formatted responses.

HTTP APIs.why: The document defines a REST-style API on HTTP with well-known URI, query parameters, status codes and JSON responses, which is a convention for building an API on HTTP.
HTTP APIs.quote: A client issues a query using the HTTP GET method to request specific resources from the server.

BGP.why: A substantial part of the command set exposes BGP routing table, summary and neighbor information from routers, so BGP operators would want it.
BGP.quote: Display a matching record from the BGP routing table.

traceroute.why: Defines a traceroute diagnostic command as part of the API, along with ping.
traceroute.quote: Trace the path from the executing router to the destination host and list all intermediate hops.

rejected.why: JSON and JSend are only the response encoding, not the subject.
Considered since it is router querying, but BGP, traceroute and HTTP APIs tags fit more specifically; it is read-only diagnostic access.
Ping output is merely an example of command output, not specified.
Mentioned only as one possible server-to-router method and output format.
Media types are referenced for the format parameter but the document does not register any.
URI templates and a well-known URI are used, but the document is not about URIs themselves.

gaps.name: Looking Glass
gaps.why: The document is about Looking Glass services for routing/network diagnostics, and the taxonomy has no tag for that specific subject.

RFC8525.title: YANG Library
RFC8525.summary: Defines the ietf-yang-library YANG module, which lets a network management server expose its YANG modules, datastores and datastore schemas (NMDA-aware) with a content-id for client caching, obsoleting RFC 7895.

YANG.why: The document specifies a YANG module that reports which YANG modules, submodules, features and deviations a server implements, so it belongs on the YANG page.
YANG.quote: This document defines the YANG module "ietf-yang-library" that provides this information.

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the access protocols. The document mentions the :yang-library:1.1 capability and notifications, but it does not specify NETCONF.
This is a parent topic, and the more specific YANG tag already sits under it.
SSH appears only in the Security Considerations boilerplate as a NETCONF transport.
TLS appears only in the Security Considerations boilerplate.
XML namespaces and the XML examples are only incidental encoding.

gaps.name: NMDA (Network Management Datastore Architecture)
gaps.why: The document is built around NMDA datastores and datastore schemas, and the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC8526.title: NETCONF Extensions to Support the Network Management Datastore Architecture
RFC8526.summary: RFC 8526 extends NETCONF with new <get-data> and <edit-data> operations and augments <lock>, <unlock>, <validate> to support the NMDA, defining the ietf-netconf-nmda YANG module and requiring YANG library support.

NETCONF.why: The document specifies new NETCONF operations (<get-data>, <edit-data>) and augmentations to existing ones, and updates RFC 6241.
NETCONF.quote: This document extends the NETCONF protocol defined in [RFC6241] in order to support the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA)

YANG.why: A substantial part is a new YANG module and a requirement that servers implement the YANG library, updating RFC 7950.
YANG.quote: These changes are defined in the new "ietf-netconf-nmda" YANG [RFC7950] module.

rejected.why: Datastore architecture is network management, not SDN control-plane separation.
Only NETCONF is extended; RESTCONF is not mentioned in the body.
XML is merely the encoding used for NETCONF messages in examples.
SSH is only the mandatory transport mentioned in Security Considerations boilerplate.
Not about SNMP MIB modules; YANG modules are different.

gaps.name: Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA)
gaps.why: The document implements NMDA in NETCONF, but the taxonomy has no tag for datastore architecture; the broad network management topic is implied by NETCONF.

RFC8527.title: RESTCONF Extensions to Support the Network Management Datastore Architecture
RFC8527.summary: RFC 8527 extends RESTCONF (RFC 8040) to support the Network Management Datastore Architecture by adding /ds datastore resources, a with-origin query parameter, with-defaults behaviour on the operational datastore, and requiring the YANG library.

RESTCONF.why: The document updates RFC 8040 with new datastore resources, a new query parameter and capability URNs.
RESTCONF.quote: This document extends the RESTCONF protocol defined in [RFC8040] in order to support the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA)

rejected.why: YANG library and ietf-datastores are used and required, but the document defines no YANG module or modelling language change; it is about RESTCONF resources.
NMDA is shared with NETCONF, but this document only extends RESTCONF.
RESTCONF runs over HTTP, which is only the substrate.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as the secure transport.
JSON identityref encoding is only referenced for path encoding.

gaps.name: Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA)
gaps.why: The document is substantially about supporting NMDA datastores (operational, running, intended) and origin metadata, but the taxonomy has no NMDA tag.

RFC8528.title: YANG Schema Mount
RFC8528.summary: Defines the YANG schema mount mechanism, a mount-point extension and the ietf-yang-schema-mount module, for attaching whole YANG data models at a mount point in a parent schema.

YANG.why: The document defines a new YANG extension and a YANG module for composing data models. Readers of the YANG subject would want it.
YANG.quote: This document defines a mechanism that adds the schema trees defined by a set of YANG modules onto a mount point defined in the schema tree in another YANG module.

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the protocols through which the data is accessed. The document specifies nothing new about them.
The document is about YANG, not SNMP MIBs.
TLS appears only in the Security Considerations boilerplate.
SSH appears only in the Security Considerations boilerplate.
The YANG tag is more specific, and the parent is implied.

RFC8529.title: YANG Data Model for Network Instances
RFC8529.summary: Defines the ietf-network-instance YANG module for managing network instances (VRFs and VSIs) on a device, with schema mount points and interface-binding augmentations.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG data model (ietf-network-instance), with module code, tree diagrams and JSON examples.
YANG.quote: This document defines a network instance module. This module can be used to manage the virtual resource partitioning that may be present on a network device.

VPN.why: The model manages VRF and VSI instances, the device-level construct behind L3VPN and L2VPN, with well-known mount points for L3VPN, L2VPN and combined types. It does not specify VPN protocols, so the parent tag fits better than L3VPN or L2VPN.
VPN.quote: The network instance container is used to represent VRFs and VSIs. VRFs and VSIs are commonly used to isolate routing and switching domains

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the access protocols named in Security Considerations. The document does not specify them.
It only provides mount points and a placeholder for L3VPN models. The BGP/MPLS L3VPN technology itself is defined elsewhere.
L2VPN appears only as a type of NI that future models may augment. The document does not define it.
OSPF appears only in the example of a mounted module under a VRF. The document does not define or profile it.
This is a YANG model, not a MIB or SMI module.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as the transport under RESTCONF.

RFC8530.title: YANG Model for Logical Network Elements
RFC8530.summary: Defines the ietf-logical-network-element YANG module (NMDA-compliant) for managing logical resource partitioning (logical routers/systems) on a network device, using schema mount and interface assignment to LNEs.

YANG.why: The RFC's main content is a new YANG module and its tree, augmentations, and examples for LNEs, so it belongs on the YANG page.
YANG.quote: This document defines an NMDA-compliant YANG module [RFC6020] to support the creation of logical network elements (LNEs) on a network device.

rejected.why: NETCONF is only a management protocol the model may be accessed through. The document does not specify or extend it.
RESTCONF is mentioned only as an access protocol, mainly in Security Considerations.
This is a YANG model, not a SNMP MIB module. SNMP is mentioned only in passing.
OSPF appears only in the example mounted modules, not as a subject of the document.
VRFs and network instances are mentioned only as context. They are covered in RFC 8529, not here.
The YANG tag already covers this document. It is a data model, not general management architecture.

gaps.name: YANG Schema Mount / logical network elements (virtualized device partitioning)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for logical systems, logical routers or virtual device partitioning, or for YANG schema mount. The YANG tag is the closest fit.

RFC8531.title: Generic YANG Data Model for Connection-Oriented Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) Protocols
RFC8531.summary: Defines a generic, technology-independent YANG data model (ietf-connection-oriented-oam) for managing connection-oriented OAM protocols, based on CFM concepts (MD/MA/MEP), with RPCs for continuity check, connectivity verification and traceroute, notifications, and extension examples for TRILL and MPLS-TP.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module with tree diagrams, RPCs and notifications, extensible by technology-specific models.
YANG.quote: This document presents a base YANG data model for connection-oriented Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) protocols.

OAM.why: The model abstracts OAM constructs (MD, MA, MEP, continuity check, connectivity verification, traceroute, nested OAM workflows), so OAM readers would want it.
OAM.quote: It provides a technology-independent abstraction of key OAM constructs for such protocols.

rejected.why: TRILL OAM is only an illustrative extension example in Section 7; the document does not specify TRILL.
MPLS-TP is only an illustrative extension example; the document does not specify MPLS-TP.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in Security Considerations as the access mechanisms for the module.
The traceroute RPC is one part of the OAM model, not a document about traceroute and path discovery tools.
This is a YANG model, not a MIB module.
CFM from IEEE 802.1Q is the conceptual basis, but the document does not address Ethernet OAM itself.

RFC8532.title: Generic YANG Data Model for the Management of Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) Protocols That Use Connectionless Communications
RFC8532.summary: Defines a generic YANG data model (ietf-connectionless-oam plus ietf-lime-time-types) for managing connectionless OAM protocols, covering test points, tools, continuity check and path discovery data, with BFD and LSP Ping extension examples.

YANG.why: The document's core deliverable is a YANG module and a time-types module, plus augment/schema-mount guidance for extending them.
YANG.quote: This document presents a base YANG Data model for the management of Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) protocols that use connectionless communications.

OAM.why: The model abstracts OAM constructs such as test points, continuity check, path discovery and session statistics, so OAM readers would want it.
OAM.quote: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) are important networking functions that allow operators to: monitor network communications

rejected.why: BFD is only used as an illustrative extension example in Section 6; the document is not about BFD itself.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only as the access mechanisms in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
Delay and jitter statistics groupings are included, but they are a minor part of a generic OAM model.
NTP and PTP timestamp formats are only referenced as identity types in the model, not specified or analysed.
RFC 8029 LSP ping attributes are only used as test-point address types and an extension example.
ICMP ping appears only as an example tool and in references.

RFC8533.title: A YANG Data Model for Retrieval Methods for the Management of Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) Protocols That Use Connectionless Communications
RFC8533.summary: Defines a YANG module (ietf-connectionless-oam-methods) with technology-independent on-demand RPC operations (continuity-check, path-discovery) for retrieving connectionless OAM data, extensible for technology-specific OAM tools like ping and traceroute.

YANG.why: The document's main body is a YANG module defining RPC operations and a data hierarchy, so YANG data modelling is its core subject.
YANG.quote: This document presents an on-demand retrieval method YANG data model for OAM protocols that use connectionless communication.

OAM.why: The model manages OAM functions (continuity check, path discovery) for connectionless OAM protocols, so readers of the OAM subject would want it.
OAM.quote: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) are important networking functions that allow operators to:

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the protocol the RPCs run over; the document does not specify or extend it.
Path discovery corresponds to traceroute, but the document defines a generic RPC model, not the traceroute tool.
ICMP ping is cited as an example technology-specific mapping and an appendix augment, not specified here.
IPFIX appears only as an export option in an illustrative appendix example.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as an access protocol.
Mentioned only in the introduction as a well-known fault verification tool; the model does not cover it.

RFC8534.title: Explicit Tracking with Wildcard Routes in Multicast VPN
RFC8534.summary: RFC 8534 clarifies explicit tracking in BGP/MPLS Multicast VPN with wildcard S-PMSI A-D routes and defines a new LIR-pF flag in the PMSI Tunnel attribute so one wildcard route can request per-flow Leaf A-D responses.

MVPN.why: The whole document updates MVPN procedures for explicit tracking, S-PMSI/Leaf A-D routes and the PTA flags, so the MVPN page is where readers would look.
MVPN.quote: The base Multicast VPN (MVPN) specifications (RFCs 6513 and 6514) provide procedures to allow a multicast ingress node to invoke "explicit tracking"

rejected.why: BGP is the carrier of the MVPN routes, and the document specifies no general BGP behaviour. Its only BGP-level addition is a PTA flag, which is MVPN-specific.
P-tunnels and MPLS labels appear, but only as context for MVPN procedures.
BIER is mentioned only as an example of a non-6514 tunnel type that needs its own specification.
MVPN is the more specific tag and already sits under the multicast area, so the parent is not tagged.

RFC8536.title: The Time Zone Information Format (TZif)
RFC8536.summary: Specifies the binary TZif time zone information file format (versions 1-3), its use with TZDIST, and registers the application/tzif and application/tzif-leap media types.

time zones.why: The whole document defines the TZif time zone data format, its fields, versions, truncation, and interoperability, which is the subject of the time zones tag.
time zones.quote: This document specifies the Time Zone Information Format (TZif) for representing and exchanging time zone information, independent of any particular service or protocol.

media types.why: Registers application/tzif and application/tzif-leap, and the body also describes when each should be used in MIME entities and TZDIST capabilities.
media types.quote: This document defines two media types [RFC6838] for the exchange of data utilizing the Time Zone Information Format.

rejected.why: iCalendar is only mentioned in the introduction as another time zone format; TZif is a different binary format.
HTTP is used only in the TZDIST example and Accept header usage; the document does not extend HTTP.
TLS is only mentioned in Privacy Considerations as a protection mechanism for transmission.
ASCII is used for the magic number and TZ string encoding, but the document is not about ASCII.
Only the parent of time zones; the specific child tag fits better, and the document is not about calendaring generally.

RFC8537.title: Updates to the Fast Reroute Procedures for Co-routed Associated Bidirectional Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC8537.summary: Updates RFC 4090 fast reroute and RFC 7551 association procedures so co-routed associated bidirectional RSVP-TE LSPs keep co-routing after failure, via coordinated bypass tunnel assignment and unique Extended Association IDs.

RSVP-TE.why: The document specifies RSVP-TE fast reroute and association signaling procedures (BYPASS_ASSIGNMENT, Extended ASSOCIATION Object) for bidirectional LSPs, which is the RSVP-TE signalling subject.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document updates the fast reroute procedures defined in [RFC4090] to support both single-sided and double-sided provisioned associated bidirectional LSPs.

IP fast reroute.why: Fast reroute with bypass tunnels, PLR/MP roles, and revertive behavior is the core subject. The taxonomy's fast reroute tag covers IP and LDP fast reroute, so it is a loose fit for MPLS RSVP-TE FRR, but it is the closest match and readers of fast reroute would want this.
IP fast reroute.quote: The fast reroute procedures can ensure that for the co-routed LSPs, traffic flows on co-routed paths in the forward and reverse directions after fast reroute.

rejected.why: The document concerns MPLS TE LSPs, but its subject is RSVP-TE signalling, which is the more specific tag; MPLS-TP is only background.
It reuses RFC 8271 GMPLS fast reroute mechanisms, but its subject is associated bidirectional LSPs without GMPLS extensions.
MPLS-TP is mentioned only as motivation for co-routed bidirectional LSPs and is not specified here.
The RSVP-TE tag already sits under traffic engineering and covers it.

RFC8538.title: Notification Message Support for BGP Graceful Restart
RFC8538.summary: RFC 8538 updates BGP Graceful Restart (RFC 4724) so that graceful restart procedures apply on receipt of NOTIFICATION messages or Hold Time expiry, adding an "N" capability flag and a Cease "Hard Reset" subcode to request full session reset.

BGP.why: The document extends the BGP Graceful Restart capability, adds a new Cease subcode, and modifies receiving-speaker rules; it is squarely about BGP protocol behaviour.
BGP.quote: This document updates RFC 4724 by defining an extension that permits the Graceful Restart procedures to be performed when the BGP speaker receives a BGP NOTIFICATION message

rejected.why: TCP session termination is mentioned only as the trigger in BGP procedures; the document is not about TCP.
The document concerns a specific BGP mechanism, not general routing architecture or scalability.
IANA registry creation is boilerplate-level; the main body is about BGP behaviour.
The stale timer security note is minor and in Security Considerations; not the document's subject.

RFC8539.title: Softwire Provisioning Using DHCPv4 over DHCPv6
RFC8539.summary: Defines a DHCPv6 option (OPTION_S46_BIND_IPV6_PREFIX) and a DHCPv4 option (OPTION_DHCP4O6_S46_SADDR) so DHCP 4o6 clients can report their softwire source IPv6 address to the server, and updates RFC 7598 to let OPTION_S46_BR be used outside container options.

DHCPv6.why: The document defines a new DHCPv6 option, updates RFC 7598 (DHCPv6 softwire options) and specifies client and server behaviour over DHCPv4-over-DHCPv6 transport.
DHCPv6.quote: This memo defines a DHCPv6 option to convey IPv6 parameters for establishing the softwire tunnel

softwire.why: The document provisions IPv4-over-IPv6 softwires (lightweight 4over6 and MAP-E), including the BR address and the binding between the IPv4 address and the IPv6 tunnel source address.
softwire.quote: This document describes a mechanism for dynamically provisioning softwires created using DHCP 4o6

rejected.why: The more specific DHCPv6 tag covers the DHCP side, so the parent is implied.
MAP-E is only an example deployment. The document does not specify MAP.
Lightweight 4over6 is mentioned only as a context reference and is not the subject.
Implied by the softwire tag, which already sits under it.
The privacy considerations are a brief boilerplate-like subsection and do not make the document about privacy.
Shared IPv4 addresses are mentioned only briefly in Section 7.6.

gaps.name: DHCPv4-over-DHCPv6 (DHCP 4o6)
gaps.why: The document centres on DHCP 4o6 transport (RFC 7341) but the taxonomy has no specific tag for it. It is covered here only by the DHCP and DHCPv6 tags.

RFC8540.title: Stream Control Transmission Protocol: Errata and Issues in RFC 4960
