RFC8540.summary: RFC 8540 compiles errata and issues found in the SCTP specification (RFC 4960), giving problem descriptions, old/new text deltas and rationale for fixes to the protocol, congestion control, and CRC32c code.

SCTP.why: The whole document specifies corrections to SCTP, covering chunks, association setup, shutdown, heartbeats, SACK handling and the abstract API.
SCTP.quote: This document is a compilation of issues found since the publication of RFC 4960 in September 2007, based on experience with implementing, testing, and using the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP)

rejected.why: Many sections fix cwnd, ssthresh and partial_bytes_acked rules, but these are SCTP-specific behaviours covered under the SCTP tag, not a general congestion-control subject.
Sections 3.5, 3.10 and 3.46 fix the CRC32c sample code, but only as C type and portability corrections, not as work on CRC polynomials.
Section 3.40 only updates references to RFC 8311 in an appendix, which is a minor part of the document.
The ICMP handling fixes (3.36, 3.37) are small SCTP appendix corrections, not ICMP itself.
The IANA text for chunk types, chunk flags and port registration is only a small part of the document.

RFC8541.title: Impact of Shortest Path First (SPF) Trigger and Delay Strategies on IGP Micro-loops
RFC8541.summary: Informational RFC analysing how mismatched SPF trigger and SPF delay strategies (two-step vs exponential back-off) across vendors in a link-state IGP network cause transient micro-loops, motivating a standardized SPF back-off delay.

routing architecture.why: The document is about convergence behavior and micro-loops in link-state IGP routing, a routing design/scalability concern not specific to OSPF or IS-IS alone. It analyses SPF delay and trigger strategies across implementations.
routing architecture.quote: This document analyzes the impact of using different link state IGP implementations in a single network with respect to micro-loops.

rejected.why: OSPF is cited only as one of the link-state IGPs the analysis applies to; the document does not specify or extend it.
IS-IS is mentioned as an example IGP and for its optional route computation optimizations, but the document is protocol-agnostic and not about IS-IS itself.
Micro-loop mitigation (RFC 6976, RFC 8333) is referenced briefly, but the document does not address fast reroute or loop-free alternates.
The tables are illustrative timelines of convergence, not performance measurement methods or metrics.

gaps.name: IGP convergence / micro-loops / SPF back-off delay
gaps.why: The document is specifically about link-state IGP convergence timers and micro-loop avoidance; the taxonomy has no tag for IGP convergence, so it is covered only by the broad routing architecture tag.

RFC8542.title: A YANG Data Model for Fabric Topology in Data-Center Networks
RFC8542.summary: Defines YANG modules that augment the RFC 8345 network topology model to represent data-center fabrics (PODs) as nodes, with fabric attributes and fabric port termination points.

YANG.why: The document's content is YANG modules (ietf-dc-fabric-types, ietf-dc-fabric-topology and a non-NMDA state module) augmenting the RFC 8345 topology models.
YANG.quote: this document defines a YANG data model [RFC6020] [RFC7950] for a possible view of the fabric-based data-center topology

data center networking.why: The model describes data-center fabric topology: spine/leaf roles, gateway modes, inter-fabric connections and tunnel options, so readers of data-center networking would want it.
data center networking.quote: A data-center (DC) network can be composed of single or multiple fabrics, which are also known as Points Of Delivery (PODs).

rejected.why: VXLAN is only one of the fabric types and the source of the VNI range referenced in the model. The document does not specify or extend it.
Overlay technologies (VXLAN, Geneve, VLAN) are only enumerated as fabric types. The document does not cover overlay encapsulation itself.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in the Security Considerations as the access protocols for the model.
The model is a product of the I2RS WG and is described as an application of the I2RS topology model. It does not specify the I2RS interface to the routing system.
TRILL is only listed as one identity value for the fabric type, so the document is not about TRILL.
The model is meant for use by a network controller, but SDN is not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Network topology data models (RFC 8345 augmentations)
gaps.why: The document is an augmentation of the generic network/network-topology YANG model, and the taxonomy has no tag for topology modelling beyond YANG.

RFC8543.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Organization Mapping
RFC8543.summary: Defines an EPP object mapping for "organization" entities (registrars, resellers, privacy proxies, DNS operators), with attributes, commands, XML schema and a new IANA role-type registry.

EPP.why: The document specifies a new EPP object mapping with check, info, create, delete and update commands, so it belongs on the EPP page.
EPP.quote: This document describes an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) mapping for provisioning and management of organization objects stored in a shared central repository.

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are only the notation used to specify the mapping. The document is not about XML usage itself.
The IANA section creates a role registry, but that is boilerplate for this mapping. The main body is not about IANA registries.
The parent of EPP. EPP is the more specific tag, and the mapping is an EPP extension.
DNS operators appear only as one organization role type. The document does not specify DNS behaviour.

RFC8544.title: Organization Extension for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)
RFC8544.summary: Defines an EPP extension (orgext) that lets domain, host, contact and future objects be associated with organization entities (reseller, privacy proxy, etc.) via role-tagged IDs in create, update and info commands.

EPP.why: The document specifies an EPP extension with new elements for create, update and info commands and an XML schema, so it belongs under EPP.
EPP.quote: This document describes an extension to Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) object mappings that is designed to support assigning an organization to any existing object

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are only the encoding for the extension's elements. The document is not about XML usage as such.
The parent topic is implied by the EPP tag, so it is not listed separately.
The XML namespace and EPP extension registry entries are boilerplate and not the document's subject.
The internationalization section is boilerplate inherited from the EPP mappings.
Domain names are the example objects, but the document does not specify DNS behaviour.

RFC8545.title: Well-Known Port Assignments for the One-Way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP) and the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP)
RFC8545.summary: RFC 8545 reassigns the UDP well-known ports 861 and 862 from the OWAMP and TWAMP control protocols to the OWAMP-Test and TWAMP-Test protocols. It also clarifies that standards-track OWAMP and TWAMP consist of both a control protocol and a test protocol, and it updates RFCs 4656 and 5357.

OWAMP.why: The document updates the OWAMP specification (RFC 4656) and changes how OWAMP-Test receiver ports are used and negotiated, so OWAMP readers need it.
OWAMP.quote: to reallocate the well-known ports for the UDP test protocols that compose necessary parts of their respective Standards Track protocols (OWAMP and TWAMP)

TWAMP.why: The document updates RFC 5357. It changes the TWAMP-Test receiver port, amends the Section 3.5 port negotiation text, and clarifies what TWAMP and TWAMP Light consist of.
TWAMP.quote: A Control-Client that supports the use of the allocated TWAMP-Test Receiver Port (Section 7) MAY request to use that port number in the Request-TW-Session command.

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the OWAMP and TWAMP tags, so it is not listed separately.
UDP is the transport for the test protocols. The document reassigns port numbers and does not specify UDP or its usage.
TCP carries the control protocols and is only the substrate here.
The port reassignment is recorded in the IANA Considerations section, which is boilerplate. The document is about OWAMP and TWAMP port use, not IANA registry policy.
Section 5.3 only notes that varying the source port still allows measurement of different ECMP paths. This is a minor side remark.
LMAP is cited only in the Security Considerations section, so it is not a subject of the document.

RFC8546.title: The Wire Image of a Network Protocol
RFC8546.summary: An IAB informational document defining the "wire image", the information a protocol exposes to on-path non-participants, and discussing how encryption, integrity protection and protocol invariants affect engineering of that exposure and ossification.

internet architecture.why: The document is an IAB architectural abstraction about what protocols expose to the network path, how that affects protocol design, ossification and in-network functions. No narrower tag fits.
internet architecture.quote: This document defines the wire image, an abstraction of the information available to an on-path non-participant in a networking protocol.

privacy.why: A substantial part concerns information radiated to observers, fingerprinting and inference from timing and size metadata, and the privacy effects of encrypting headers.
privacy.quote: improve end-to-end privacy by reducing information radiation

rejected.why: QUIC and its invariants are used as examples of minimising the wire image, but the document specifies nothing about QUIC.
TCP is used as an example of a protocol whose wire image is writable and used by network functions. The document is not about TCP.
TLS 1.3 is cited only as an example of increasing encryption deployment. It is not the subject.
ECN bits are mentioned only as an example of signals observed in TCP's wire image.

gaps.name: protocol ossification / wire image / path signals
gaps.why: The document is about protocol evolvability, ossification and the exposure of signals to on-path devices. The taxonomy has no tag for protocol design principles or ossification other than the general internet architecture tag.

RFC8547.title: TCP-ENO: Encryption Negotiation Option
RFC8547.summary: RFC 8547 defines TCP-ENO, a new TCP option (kind 69) that lets two endpoints negotiate a TCP encryption protocol (TEP) during connection setup, with fallback to plain TCP, roles, a negotiation transcript and session ID requirements for TEPs.

TCP.why: The document specifies a new TCP option, its SYN/non-SYN forms, handshake behaviour, SYN data handling and interaction with TCP Fast Open. It is a TCP extension.
TCP.quote: The TCP Encryption Negotiation Option (TCP-ENO) addresses both of these problems through a new TCP option kind providing out-of-band, fully backward-compatible negotiation of encryption.

rejected.why: tcpcrypt is a separate TEP specified in a companion document. This RFC only defines the negotiation framework and does not specify it.
TLS is mentioned only as an existing mechanism and a comparison (STARTTLS, future TLS revisions). The document is not about TLS.
The document is about encryption negotiation at the TCP layer, which is covered by the more specific TCP tag. Its security discussion is general and not a topic in its own right.
The TCP option kind and TEP identifier registry creation is boilerplate IANA Considerations and not the subject of the document.
The document does not carry one protocol over another transport. It extends TCP itself.
DANE appears only as a possible future use of endpoint authentication, not as part of the specification.

gaps.name: TCP-level encryption / opportunistic security
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for transport-layer encryption negotiation apart from the specific tcpcrypt tag. TCP is the closest fit, but readers interested in TCP encryption negotiation have no dedicated subject.

RFC8548.title: Cryptographic Protection of TCP Streams (tcpcrypt)
RFC8548.summary: Specifies tcpcrypt, a TCP encryption protocol used with TCP-ENO, covering ECDHE key exchange, session resumption, AEAD-protected framing, rekeying and keep-alive.

tcpcrypt.why: The document is the tcpcrypt specification itself.
tcpcrypt.quote: This document describes tcpcrypt, an extension to TCP for cryptographic protection of session data.

rejected.why: tcpcrypt is the more specific tag under TCP; TCP is the substrate and its ancestor is implied.
HMAC/HKDF is used as a building block for key derivation, not the subject of the document.
AEAD_AES_GCM is one of the negotiated ciphers, but the document is not about AES.
AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 is just one listed cipher option.
Curve25519 is a mandatory key-agreement scheme, but it is used rather than specified here.
Not mentioned or used; tcpcrypt is a separate protocol.

gaps.name: TCP-ENO (TCP Encryption Negotiation Option)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the negotiation option that tcpcrypt depends on. It is specified in the companion RFC 8547, not here.

RFC8549.title: Export of BGP Community Information in IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX)
RFC8549.summary: Defines nine new IPFIX Information Elements for exporting BGP Standard, Extended and Large Community information alongside flow records, enabling traffic accounting at BGP community granularity.

IPFIX.why: The document defines new IPFIX Information Elements (bgpCommunity, bgpSourceCommunityList, etc.) and an encoding example, so it extends IPFIX.
IPFIX.quote: this document extends the existing BGP-related IEs to enable IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) to export BGP community information

BGP communities.why: The export of Standard, Extended and Large Community values is the document's subject, and readers of BGP communities would want it. It defines no new community attributes.
BGP communities.quote: including the BGP Standard Communities [RFC1997], BGP Extended Communities [RFC4360], and BGP Large Communities [RFC8092]

rejected.why: BGP is the source of the community data, and the document defines nothing new about BGP itself. BGP communities is the more specific fit.
It is mentioned only as an alternative that this mechanism does not replace.
PCE and SDN controllers are named as consumers of the exported data in the use case, but the document does not specify them.
Traffic engineering is the motivating use case, but the document specifies IE definitions rather than TE mechanisms.
The IPFIX information model is a different mechanism from SNMP MIBs.

RFC8550.title: Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) Version 4.0 Certificate Handling
RFC8550.summary: Specifies X.509 certificate handling requirements for S/MIME v4.0 agents: CRLs, certificate choices, email addresses in certificates, path validation, signature algorithms and key sizes, and PKIX extensions; obsoletes RFC 5750.

S/MIME.why: The document is the S/MIME v4.0 certificate handling specification, companion to the message specification, so S/MIME readers need it.
S/MIME.quote: This document specifies conventions for X.509 certificate usage by Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) v4.0 agents.

X.509.why: It profiles X.509 certificate and CRL use: certificate choices, path validation, basic constraints, key usage, subjectAltName and extended key usage extensions.
X.509.quote: S/MIME agents MUST use PKIX certificates to validate public keys as described in [RFC5280]

rejected.why: CMS is the underlying message format whose data types are reused. The document does not specify it; RFC 8551 does.
ECDSA is only listed among the signature algorithms required for certificate and CRL verification. It is not the document's subject.
EdDSA is only listed among the signature algorithms required for certificate and CRL verification. It is not the document's subject.
Internationalized email addresses are required in certificates, but only by reference to RFC 8398. The subject is certificate handling, not address internationalization.
Covered by the more specific X.509 tag.
OCSP appears only in a passing mention in the appendix.

RFC8551.title: Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) Version 4.0 Message Specification
RFC8551.summary: RFC 8551 specifies S/MIME version 4.0, defining how to sign, envelope, authenticate-envelope and compress MIME entities using CMS, the application/pkcs7-mime and application/pkcs7-signature media types, mandatory algorithms, and obsoletes RFC 5751.

S/MIME.why: The whole document is the S/MIME v4.0 message specification, covering message formats, creation, algorithm requirements and media types.
S/MIME.quote: S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) provides a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data.

CMS.why: A large part of the document profiles CMS content types (SignedData, EnvelopedData, AuthEnvelopedData, CompressedData), attributes and SignerInfo options for S/MIME.
CMS.quote: This specification defines how to create a MIME body part that has been cryptographically enhanced according to the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)

rejected.why: MIME is the substrate S/MIME secures. The document registers application/pkcs7-* media types but is about S/MIME security, and S/MIME is already a child of CMS.
The IANA registrations for pkcs7-mime and pkcs7-signature are boilerplate-like updates, not the main subject.
S/MIME can be used with any MIME transport, and the document is about secure message formats, not email architecture.
AES-GCM and AES-CBC are mandated as algorithm choices, but the document does not specify AES itself.
Certificate handling is explicitly out of scope and left to RFC 8550.
The ASN.1 module appendix is supporting apparatus and is unchanged from earlier versions.

RFC8552.title: Scoped Interpretation of DNS Resource Records through "Underscored" Naming of Attribute Leaves
RFC8552.summary: BCP defining the underscored-node-name convention for scoping DNS RRsets under a parent domain and creating the IANA "Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Names" registry with initial entries.

DNS.why: The document specifies a DNS naming convention for scoping resource record sets and discusses its interaction with wildcards and RR types.
DNS.quote: some services use an operational convention for defining specific interpretations of an RRset by locating the records in a DNS branch under the parent domain

IANA.why: A major part of the document defines the new registry, its entry fields, expert review guidance and initial contents.
IANA.quote: this document establishes the "Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Names" registry with IANA

rejected.why: Underscored names are reserved node labels under parent domains, not special-use top-level domain names.
Mentioned only as an example and as a registry entry; the document is not about DKIM.
TLSA entries appear only in the initial registry table; DANE is not the subject.
Only a reference in the table of initial entries (TXT _tcp/_udp); not about service discovery.
The Enumservices registry gets only a pointer note; ENUM is not the topic.

RFC8553.title: DNS Attrleaf Changes: Fixing Specifications That Use Underscored Node Names
RFC8553.summary: BCP that updates many RFCs and the SRV and URI RR specifications and RFC 8145 so that their underscored DNS node names are registered in the IANA "Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Names" registry defined by RFC 8552.

DNS.why: The document is about DNS underscored node names and how TXT, SRV and URI RRsets use them. It changes the DNS SRV and URI RR specifications.
DNS.quote: The use of underscored node names is specific to each RR TYPE that is being scoped.

IANA.why: A large part of the document aligns existing specifications with a single IANA registry and gives registration template text. It creates no new registry, but readers of IANA registry guidance would want it.
IANA.quote: The SRV RRset 'protocol' (global) underscored node name SHOULD be registered in the IANA "Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Names" registry

rejected.why: Only RFC 8145's _ta- query names are touched, and the change is registry alignment rather than DNSSEC mechanics.
Underscored attribute-leaf names are not reserved special-use domain names in the sense of that tag.
SRV records support service location, but the document is about node-name registration and not discovery mechanics.
SPF, DKIM and DMARC appear only as updated documents that use TXT underscored names.

gaps.name: Underscored attribute-leaf DNS node names (AttrLeaf)
gaps.why: The document is about underscored DNS node-name scoping and its IANA registry. The taxonomy has no specific tag for it, so DNS is the nearest fit.

RFC8554.title: Leighton-Micali Hash-Based Signatures
RFC8554.summary: RFC 8554 specifies the Leighton-Micali one-time signature (LM-OTS), the LMS Merkle-tree signature scheme and the hierarchical HSS scheme, which are stateful hash-based signatures that stay secure against quantum computers.

LMS.why: The whole document defines LM-OTS, LMS and HSS: their formats, algorithms, parameter sets, IANA registries and test cases.
LMS.quote: This note describes the Leighton and Micali adaptation [USPTO5432852] of the original Lamport-Diffie-Winternitz-Merkle one-time signature system

rejected.why: XMSS (RFC 8391) is only compared with HSS in Section 10. It is not specified here.
SHA-256 is the hash function used as a building block. The document does not specify or analyse the SHA family.
The post-quantum motivation is real, but the more specific LMS tag covers the document, so the parent is implied.
XDR is used only to define the message formats, and XDR is not an ASN.1 tag. It is a substrate, not a subject.
The IANA Considerations section creates registries, but it is boilerplate and the main body is not about IANA.

RFC8555.title: Automatic Certificate Management Environment (ACME)
RFC8555.summary: Specifies ACME, a JSON-over-HTTPS protocol using JWS-signed requests by which a CA and applicant automate account setup, domain control validation (http-01, dns-01), certificate issuance and revocation.

ACME.why: The document defines the ACME protocol itself: accounts, orders, authorizations, challenges, issuance and revocation.
ACME.quote: This document describes a protocol that a CA and an applicant can use to automate the process of verification and certificate issuance.

rejected.why: Certificates are the objects issued, but the document does not profile X.509; it manages their issuance.
JWS is the signing substrate for requests; ACME only registers two header parameters, so it is not about JOSE.
HTTP/HTTPS is the transport; ACME is an application built on it, not an extension of HTTP.
The dns-01 challenge uses a TXT record, but DNS is only a validation mechanism, with no new DNS behaviour defined.
JSON is only the message encoding.
Registers application/pem-certificate-chain in IANA Considerations, which is boilerplate and not the document's subject.

RFC8556.title: Multicast VPN Using Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER)
RFC8556.summary: Specifies how Multicast VPN (MVPN) uses BIER as a P-tunnel type, defining the PMSI Tunnel Attribute encoding for BIER, label assignment, explicit tracking via LIR/LIR-pF flags, and data-plane encapsulation/disposition.

MVPN.why: The document defines MVPN procedures: PTA construction in x-PMSI and Leaf A-D routes, explicit tracking, segmentation, and VRF disposition.
MVPN.quote: This document specifies the protocol and procedures that allow MVPN to use BIER as the method of carrying multicast traffic over a service provider's backbone network.

BIER.why: The document defines a new BIER tunnel type for MVPN, with BIER sub-domain, BFR-id and BFR-prefix encoding and BIER encapsulation/disposition at BFIR/BFER.
BIER.quote: Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER) ([RFC8279]) is an architecture that provides optimal multicast forwarding through a "multicast domain"

rejected.why: BGP route attributes (PTA, A-D routes) are the signalling vehicle, but the document is about MVPN/BIER use, not BGP itself.
BGP/MPLS VPNs are the base for MVPN, but the document is specifically about multicast; MVPN is the more specific fit.
Upstream-assigned MPLS labels are used for demultiplexing, but MPLS is a supporting mechanism rather than the subject.
Implied as the parent of BIER; the more specific tech tag covers it.
BIDIR-PIM is mentioned only as out of scope.

RFC8557.title: Deterministic Networking Problem Statement
RFC8557.summary: Problem statement documenting industry needs for Deterministic Networking (DetNet): multi-hop IP/MPLS paths for flows with bounded latency and ultra-low loss, and the open issues in topology, flow characterization, centralized/distributed path setup, and packet replication/elimination.

DetNet.why: The whole document is the DetNet problem statement, so the DetNet tag fits directly.
DetNet.quote: This paper documents the needs in various industries to establish multi-hop paths for characterized flows with deterministic properties.

rejected.why: A PCE is cited as one option for centralized path computation, but the document does not specify or extend PCE/PCEP.
RSVP-TE is mentioned as a possible distributed setup mechanism that might be extended. The document does not specify it.
The document says time synchronization need not be addressed by an IETF working group, so it is out of scope.
TE models are mentioned only in passing, and DetNet is the more specific tag for this subject.
The document deals with deterministic guarantees rather than QoS architectures or signalling, and DetNet covers it more specifically.

RFC8558.title: Transport Protocol Path Signals
RFC8558.summary: IAB document discussing implicit signals that on-path network elements infer from cleartext transport headers (e.g., TCP handshake), the effect of transport encryption removing them, and recommending explicit, intentional, integrity-protected path signals instead.

transport.why: The document is about transport-protocol signals visible to the path and the options for explicit transport/path signalling across transports; it is not specific to one transport.
transport.quote: This document discusses the nature of signals seen by on-path elements examining transport protocols, contrasting implicit and explicit signals.

internet architecture.why: An IAB architectural discussion of end-to-end principles versus on-path network element functions, with design principles for protocol designers in Section 4.
internet architecture.quote: While the architecture of the Internet may be best realized by end-to-end protocols [RFC1958], there are cases such as the use of Network Address Translators

rejected.why: TCP's handshake is the example of implicit signals, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
NATs and firewalls are examples of on-path consumers of signals; NAT behaviour itself is not the subject.
Mentioned only in passing (connection-id) as an example of an encrypted transport.
Firewall pinholes are an illustrative example, not the subject of the document.
Privacy is touched on in Security Considerations only; the main body is about path signals.
IPv6 hop-by-hop headers are mentioned as one option only.

gaps.name: Path signals / on-path element visibility (PLUS)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is explicit path signalling and the effects of encrypting transport headers on middleboxes, which no taxonomy tag covers directly.

RFC8559.title: Dynamic Authorization Proxying in the Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) Protocol
RFC8559.summary: Updates RFC 5176 and RFC 5580 to enable realm-based proxying of RADIUS CoA-Request and Disconnect-Request packets using Operator-Name, and defines a new Operator-NAS-Identifier attribute for routing to the NAS in the visited network.

RADIUS.why: The document specifies RADIUS dynamic authorization proxying, defines a new RADIUS attribute (Operator-NAS-Identifier), and updates RADIUS RFCs 5176 and 5580.
RADIUS.quote: RFC 5176 defines Change-of-Authorization (CoA) and Disconnect Message (DM) behavior for RADIUS.

rejected.why: RADIUS is the specific AAA protocol tagged; the AAA framework parent is implied and not the document's own subject.
Diameter is only mentioned in the title of a referenced RFC (5580); the document is not about it.
The IANA section merely allocates one attribute code point; it is boilerplate here.
Not discussed; the document concerns CoA proxying, not authentication methods.

RFC8560.title: Seamless Integration of Ethernet VPN (EVPN) with Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) and Their Provider Backbone Bridge (PBB) Equivalents
RFC8560.summary: Specifies how EVPN and PBB-EVPN PEs interoperate with existing VPLS and PBB-VPLS PEs in the same MPLS/IP network, covering capability discovery, unicast forwarding, MAC mobility and multicast without changes to VPLS PEs.

EVPN.why: The document defines EVPN PE behaviour for coexisting with VPLS PEs, including PBB-EVPN, so it is about EVPN.
EVPN.quote: The EVPN PEs MUST advertise both the BGP VPLS auto-discovery (A-D) route as well as the BGP EVPN Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag (IMET) route

VPLS.why: VPLS and PBB-VPLS interworking is the other half of the document, including PW setup to VPLS PEs and MAC flush handling.
VPLS.quote: The procedures for forwarding state setup and unicast operation on the VPLS PE are per [RFC8077], [RFC4761], and [RFC4762].

rejected.why: BGP carries the EVPN and VPLS A-D routes, but it is only the signalling substrate here. Nothing new is defined about BGP itself.
Pseudowires are set up between EVPN and VPLS PEs, but the document relies on existing PW procedures and does not specify pseudowire emulation.
L2VPN is the parent of the VPLS and EVPN tags chosen, so it is implied.
MPLS is the underlying network the services run over, not the subject of the document.
LDP-signalled PWs are referenced only through RFC 8077 and RFC 4762, and the document adds nothing about LDP.

RFC8561.title: A YANG Data Model for Microwave Radio Link
RFC8561.summary: Defines YANG modules for managing microwave/millimeter-wave radio link terminals and carrier terminations, plus a generic interface protection module and microwave types, augmenting the ietf-interfaces model.

YANG.why: The document's main content is three YANG modules (microwave radio link, interface protection, microwave types) with tree diagrams and module code.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model for control and management of radio link interfaces and their connectivity to packet (typically Ethernet) interfaces

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only mentioned as the access protocols in Security Considerations; the document does not specify or extend them.
IANA ifType values are registered, but the document defines YANG modules and not MIB modules.
Ethernet interfaces are only the packet side that the radio link terminal serves; the document does not deal with Ethernet itself.
The subject is the microwave radio link, but the taxonomy has no medium-specific tag for it. The YANG tag fits better, and the missing subject is listed under gaps.
This is implied as the parent of YANG. No broader network management subject is addressed beyond the YANG data model.

gaps.name: Microwave/millimeter wave radio links
gaps.why: The document is about managing microwave radio link interfaces (carrier terminations, XPIC, MIMO, adaptive coding and modulation, link protection), and the taxonomy has no tag for radio or microwave transmission.

RFC8562.title: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for Multipoint Networks
RFC8562.summary: RFC 8562 extends BFD (RFC 5880) to multipoint/multicast networks, defining MultipointHead and MultipointTail session types, demultiplexing, state machine changes, and replacement text for base-spec procedures.

BFD.why: The document specifies and updates BFD with new session types, state machine behaviour, and replacement procedures for RFC 5880.
BFD.quote: This document describes extensions to the Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) protocol for its use in multipoint and multicast networks.

rejected.why: Multicast and point-to-multipoint paths are the environment BFD runs over. The document does not specify multicast routing or group membership.
Multicast VPN fast failover is only cited as a motivating use case and is defined in another document.
TESLA appears only in Security Considerations as a possible future authentication approach, and the document says it is out of scope.
Multipoint LSPs are one kind of path BFD runs over. The document does not specify MPLS itself.
BFD uses UDP port 3784 as a substrate. The document defines nothing new about UDP.
NETCONF is mentioned once as a way to send a notification. The document is not about it.

RFC8563.title: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) Multipoint Active Tails
RFC8563.summary: RFC 8563 extends Multipoint BFD (RFC 8562) with active tail behaviour, letting tails notify the head of lost multipoint connectivity via unsolicited, multipoint-poll, or composite-poll mechanisms, with new state variables and session type MultipointClient.

BFD.why: The document specifies BFD protocol extensions for multipoint active tails, including new state variables, session type, and procedures for polling and packet handling.
BFD.quote: This application of BFD is an extension to Multipoint BFD [RFC8562], which allows tails to notify the head of the lack of multipoint connectivity.

rejected.why: Multipoint paths (IP multicast, P2MP MPLS) are only the environment BFD runs over; the document does not specify multicast routing or membership.
Point-to-multipoint MPLS is mentioned only as an example of a multipoint path, not specified here.
BFD is a fault detection mechanism, but the specific BFD tag is the better fit; no separate OAM subject is addressed.

RFC8564.title: Support of Point-to-Multipoint Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) in Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL)
RFC8564.summary: Specifies support for point-to-multipoint BFD in TRILL by defining a new RBridge Channel message (0x007, P2MP BFD Control), demultiplexing rules using Data Label, and tail tracking, updating RFCs 7175 and 7177.

BFD.why: The document extends BFD to multipoint operation over TRILL, specifying the BFD Control packet carriage, session demultiplexing and tail tracking.
BFD.quote: Point-to-multipoint (P2MP) Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) is designed to verify multipoint connectivity. This document specifies the support of P2MP BFD in Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL).

TRILL.why: The document defines a new TRILL RBridge Channel message and updates the TRILL adjacency (RFC 7177) and BFD support (RFC 7175) specifications.
TRILL.quote: a new RBridge Channel message (P2MP BFD Control), whose protocol code point is 0x007, is specified in this document.
TRILL.section: 4. A New RBridge Channel Message for P2MP BFD

rejected.why: TRILL multicast is the setting for P2MP BFD, but the document does not address multicast routing or group membership itself.
The RBridge Channel Protocols sub-TLV in LSPs announces capability, but IS-IS is only the substrate and the document does not specify IS-IS.
BFD is a fault-detection mechanism, but the specific BFD tag fits better and OAM is not addressed as a topic in its own right.

RFC8565.title: Hypertext Jeopardy Protocol (HTJP/1.0)
RFC8565.summary: April 1st humorous RFC defining HTJP, a pseudo-protocol that inverts HTTP so clients send HTTP responses and servers reply with the HTTP requests that would elicit them.

humor.why: Published 1 April as a whimsical parody protocol modelled on the Jeopardy game show, so it belongs in the humorous RFCs.
humor.quote: The Hypertext Jeopardy Protocol (HTJP) inverts the request/response semantics of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP).

HTTP.why: The whole document defines alternative conventions on HTTP/1.1 messages. It also covers the Host header, the Date header, caches and proxies, and a new Anti-HTJP-Nonce header.
HTTP.quote: HTJP is just HTTP with some alternative conventions.

rejected.why: TLS 1.3 is mentioned only as the way to secure HTJPS. The document defines nothing new about it.
Caches are discussed only briefly, to say that HTJP support in them is poor. The document is not about caching.
An Authorization header appears only in a security example. The document does not specify an authentication scheme.

RFC8567.title: Customer Management DNS Resource Records
RFC8567.summary: An April 1st joke RFC defining four new DNS resource record types (PASSWORD, CREDITCARD, SSN, SSNPTR) for storing customer credentials, payment and identity data in the DNS to supposedly aid CPE management.

humor.why: Published 1 April as a parody; the proposal to put passwords, credit card numbers and SSNs in public DNS is satirical, so it belongs in the humorous RFCs.
humor.quote: This document describes four new DNS resource record types for encoding customer information in the DNS.

DNS.why: The document specifies new DNS resource record types with RDATA wire formats and discusses related RR types, so it is about DNS resource records.
DNS.quote: This document introduces four new RRs to assist in the management of customer data by ISPs.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is only recommended in Security Considerations for data integrity; the document is not about it.
CPE management is the stated motivation, but the document defines no management protocol or practice.
The CREDITCARD RR stores payment data, but it is a joke record and defines no payment protocol.
TLSA is mentioned only in the survey of related RR types.

RFC8568.title: Network Virtualization Research Challenges
RFC8568.summary: IRTF NFVRG informational document surveying open research challenges in network virtualization (NFV, SDN, slicing, service composition, placement, testing, security) and mapping them to possible IETF/IRTF work.

SDN.why: Network virtualization with NFV and SDN is the core subject. The document covers SDN architectures (ONF, RFC 7426, ITU-T) and SDN control of NFV. It has no more specific tag for NFV, so the SDN topic fits best.
SDN.quote: The Software-Defined Networking (SDN) paradigm pushes the intelligence currently residing in the network elements to a central controller implementing the network functionality through software.

SFC.why: Section 4.6 is devoted to service composition and SFC, including the SFC architecture and gaps in SFC management and reliability.
SFC.quote: For a given service, the abstracted view of the required service functions and the order in which they are to be applied is called "Service Function Chaining" (SFC)

performance measurement.why: Metrics, IPPM, and VNF benchmarking and testing are a substantial part of the challenges discussed.
performance measurement.quote: There is a pressing need to define metrics and associated protocols to measure the performance of NFV.

rejected.why: Benchmarking of VNFs (RFC 8172) is covered only as a subsection. Performance measurement is the better fit.
MANO and orchestration are discussed, but the document is not about management protocols or operations practice. SDN already covers the orchestration and control themes.
NETCONF, RESTCONF and ForCES are mentioned only as examples of SDN southbound protocols.
IoT appears only as a slicing use case in Section 4.5.2, not as a subject of the document.
5G slicing is discussed at a high level only. The document does not address IP over 3GPP systems.
VXLAN is mentioned in passing as a possible tunneling protocol for forwarding graphs.

gaps.name: Network Function Virtualization (NFV)
gaps.why: The document is mainly about NFV, ETSI NFV architecture and VNFs, and the taxonomy has no NFV or network virtualization tag.

gaps.name: Network slicing
gaps.why: Section 4.5 covers 5G network slicing and virtual network operators, and no tag exists for it.

RFC8569.title: Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) Semantics
RFC8569.summary: Specifies the CCNx 1.0 information-centric networking protocol semantics: Interest and Content Object messages, name-based forwarding with PIT/FIB/Content Store, validation, matching rules, and the Interest Return control message, independent of wire encoding.

ICN.why: The entire document specifies CCNx, an ICN protocol: hierarchical name-based forwarding, PIT, Content Store, and Interest/Content Object matching.
ICN.quote: This document describes the core concepts of the Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) architecture and presents a network protocol based on two messages: Interests and Content Objects.

rejected.why: ABNF is only used to express the message grammar; the document is not about the notation.
Certificates may be embedded or linked for key validation, but the document does not profile X.509.
HMAC-SHA256 is one of the supported validation algorithms, mentioned in passing, not the subject.
ECDSA and RSA are listed as signature options for validation, not specified or profiled here.
The Content Store caching is CCNx-specific, not web caching.
The ccnx: URI scheme is defined in a separate draft; this document only references it.

RFC8570.title: IS-IS Traffic Engineering (TE) Metric Extensions
RFC8570.summary: Defines new IS-IS TE sub-TLVs (link delay, min/max delay, delay variation, loss, residual/available/utilized bandwidth) for distributing network-performance metrics, with advertisement threshold and stability rules; obsoletes RFC 7810.

IS-IS.why: The document specifies new sub-TLVs for IS-IS Extended IS Reachability TLVs and their advertisement behaviour, so it belongs on the IS-IS page.
IS-IS.quote: This document describes extensions (hereafter called "IS-IS TE Metric Extensions") to the Extended IS Reachability TLV defined in [RFC5305]

traffic engineering.why: The metrics extend IS-IS TE to support constrained path computation (CSPF) and path selection by performance. Traffic engineering is a substantial part of the subject, and no more specific child tag fits.
traffic engineering.quote: The data distributed by IS-IS TE Metric Extensions can be used to set up, fail over, and fail back data paths

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is cited only as a protocol that can use the distributed data to set up paths. The document does not specify or extend it.
The equivalent OSPF TE specification (RFC 7471) is mentioned only as a comparison in the appendix. This document does not cover OSPF.
Measuring network performance is explicitly out of scope. The document covers only how the results are distributed.
ALTO is mentioned once as a possible consumer of the data, and the document does not address it.
GMPLS appears only in background references, such as forwarding adjacencies and the RFC 4203 base extensions. It is not the subject of the document.
BGP-LS advertisement of these metrics is covered in a separate document (RFC 8571) that is only listed as an informative reference.

RFC8571.title: BGP - Link State (BGP-LS) Advertisement of IGP Traffic Engineering Performance Metric Extensions
RFC8571.summary: Defines seven new BGP-LS Link Attribute TLVs (delay, min/max delay, delay variation, loss, residual/available/utilized bandwidth) to carry IS-IS and OSPF TE performance metric extensions into BGP-LS, with mappings to IGP sub-TLVs.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP-LS, the BGP mechanism for distributing link-state information, with new Link Attribute TLVs. No dedicated BGP-LS tag exists, so BGP is the closest fit.
BGP.quote: New BGP-LS Link Attribute TLVs are required in order to carry the Traffic Engineering Metric Extensions defined in [RFC8570] and [RFC7471].

rejected.why: The OSPF TE metric sub-TLVs are defined in RFC 7471. This document only maps them into BGP-LS, so OSPF is the source of the data and not the subject.
The IS-IS TE metric sub-TLVs are defined in RFC 8570. This document only references them for the mapping and does not specify or extend IS-IS.
The TE metrics are the payload being carried. The document defines only BGP-LS encodings and does not address traffic engineering mechanisms.
The delay, loss and bandwidth metrics are measured and defined elsewhere. This document only gives them a transport encoding.

gaps.name: BGP-LS (BGP - Link State)
gaps.why: The document is about BGP-LS TLV extensions for link-state and TE information distribution. The taxonomy has no BGP-LS tag, so BGP is used as the nearest fit.

RFC8572.title: Secure Zero Touch Provisioning (SZTP)
RFC8572.summary: Defines Secure Zero Touch Provisioning (SZTP), a bootstrapping method for devices in factory-default state to securely get redirect or onboarding information (boot image, config, scripts) from removable storage, DNS, DHCP or RESTCONF bootstrap servers, with YANG modules, a bootstrap server API and DHCP options.

autonomic networking.why: The document is about secure zero-touch bootstrapping of devices. The closest taxonomy fit is the autonomic networking area, where BRSKI also sits. It is a broad topic tag and no more specific tag fits.
autonomic networking.quote: This document defines Secure Zero Touch Provisioning (SZTP), a bootstrapping strategy enabling devices to securely obtain bootstrapping data

YANG.why: It specifies two new YANG modules (conveyed-info and bootstrap-server) and an example device model. The data models are a substantial part of the document.
YANG.quote: This section defines a YANG 1.1 [RFC7950] module that is used to define the data model for the conveyed information artifact

RESTCONF.why: It defines a RESTCONF-based bootstrap server API with the get-bootstrapping-data and report-progress RPCs. This is a substantial part of the document.
RESTCONF.quote: The API is defined as that produced by a RESTCONF [RFC8040] server that supports the YANG 1.1 [RFC7950] module defined in this section.

DHCP.why: It defines the new OPTION_V4_SZTP_REDIRECT and OPTION_V6_SZTP_REDIRECT options, which carry redirect information. DHCP is also one of the sources of bootstrapping data.
DHCP.quote: This section defines two DHCP options: one for DHCPv4 and one for DHCPv6.

CMS.why: All three artifacts are CMS structures, signed and encrypted. The document defines how they are layered, and registers new CMS content types.
CMS.quote: The conveyed information artifact is a Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) structure, as described in [RFC5652]

rejected.why: NETCONF is only what the provisioned device is later managed with. The document does not specify or extend it.
DNS is one source of bootstrapping data, using TXT and SRV records under _sztp. That is a modest use of existing records and a name registration, not a DNS specification.
Owner certificates and path validation are used as a mechanism. The document does not profile X.509.
TLS is only the transport and authentication substrate for bootstrap server connections.
HTTP is only the substrate under RESTCONF.

gaps.name: Zero touch provisioning / device bootstrapping
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for secure device onboarding. Only BRSKI under autonomic networking is nearby, so this subject has no specific home.

RFC8573.title: Message Authentication Code for the Network Time Protocol
RFC8573.summary: RFC 8573 deprecates MD5-based packet authentication in NTP and requires AES-CMAC (RFC 4493) with a 128-bit key as the MAC for NTP authentication, updating RFC 5905.

NTP.why: The document updates how NTP packets are authenticated, changing the MAC from MD5 to AES-CMAC. It is a change to the NTP specification.
NTP.quote: AES-CMAC as specified in RFC 4493 [RFC4493] MUST be computed over all fields in the NTP header and any extension fields

AES.why: The replacement MAC is AES-CMAC, an AES-based mode. The document specifies its use and key size and gives its motivation (nonce-free, hardware support).
AES.quote: The MAC key for NTP MUST be an AES-128 key that is 128 bits in length

MD5.why: A core part of the document is deprecating MD5 as the NTP MAC, which is relevant to readers of MD5 security status.
MD5.quote: this is not a secure MAC and therefore MUST be deprecated

rejected.why: HMAC is not specified or discussed; the document only cites RFC 6151, which covers HMAC-MD5, as a reference for MD5 weakness.
The generic topic tag is not needed because the more specific NTP and AES tags cover the subject.
Keys are shared out of band and only the key size and triplet format are mentioned. This is not key management in its own right.

RFC8574.title: cite-as: A Link Relation to Convey a Preferred URI for Referencing
RFC8574.summary: Defines and registers the "cite-as" link relation type, which lets a web resource point to a preferred URI (persistent identifier, version URI, profile, or publication-level URI) for referencing, and distinguishes it from "bookmark" and "canonical".

web linking.why: The document's sole purpose is to define and register a new typed link relation under the Web Linking framework (RFC 8288), including comparison with existing relations such as alternate, canonical and bookmark.
web linking.quote: A link with the "cite-as" relation type indicates that, for referencing the link context, use of the URI of the link target is preferred

rejected.why: The document concerns which URI to prefer for citation, but it does not specify URI syntax, schemes or resolution; URIs are the objects being linked, not the subject.
Examples use the HTTP Link header and redirects, but HTTP is only the delivery substrate; nothing new is defined about HTTP itself.
The examples use <link> elements in HTML, but HTML is only a carrier for the link relation and is not what the document is about.
The IANA section merely registers the relation name; this is boilerplate and not evidence of subject.
RFC 4287 is cited only for the existing 'alternate' and 'related' relations in the comparison; the document is not about Atom.

gaps.name: Persistent identifiers (DOI, ARK, PURL) for citation
gaps.why: The motivating scenarios concern persistent identifiers for scholarly and archival resources, and the taxonomy has no general persistent-identifier tag (only the handle system).

RFC8575.title: YANG Data Model for the Precision Time Protocol (PTP)
RFC8575.summary: Defines the ietf-ptp YANG module for configuring and retrieving state of IEEE 1588-2008 Precision Time Protocol clocks and data sets, NMDA-compliant.

YANG.why: The document's main body is a YANG module and its tree hierarchy modelling PTP data sets.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model for the configuration of devices and clocks using the Precision Time Protocol (PTP)

PTP.why: The module models PTP clock and port data sets (default-ds, current-ds, parent-ds, port-ds, transparent clock data sets), so PTP readers would want it.
PTP.quote: This document defines a YANG data model for the configuration of IEEE Std 1588-2008 devices and clocks as well as retrieval of the state data

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the protocols through which the module is accessed; mentioned mainly in the introduction and security considerations.
Existing PTP MIBs (RFC 8173) are mentioned only as background; the document defines a YANG model, not a MIB.
SNMP appears only in discussing prior MIB work, not as a subject of this document.
The parent topic is implied by the PTP tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC8576.title: Internet of Things (IoT) Security: State of the Art and Challenges
RFC8576.summary: IRTF T2TRG informational overview of IoT security: thing lifecycle, threats, state of the art, and open challenges (constraints, bootstrapping, group security, software update, privacy, quantum resistance, etc.).

IoT.why: The whole document covers IoT security architecture, lifecycle, threats and challenges for constrained devices; the IoT topic fits directly.
IoT.quote: This document presents an overview of important security aspects for the Internet of Things.

firmware update.why: A substantial section covers secure firmware/software update challenges and SUIT work for IoT devices.
firmware update.quote: Software updates for IoT devices are therefore required not only for new functionality but also to eliminate security vulnerabilities
firmware update.section: 5.4. Secure Software Update and Cryptographic Agility

privacy.why: Dedicated section on IoT privacy threats (identification, localization, profiling, linkage), plus privacy as a threat in Section 3.
privacy.quote: Ziegeldorf [Ziegeldorf] defines privacy in IoT as a threefold guarantee

post-quantum.why: A section addresses quantum threats to IoT cryptography and migration to quantum-resistant algorithms.
post-quantum.quote: This situation would require us to move to quantum-resistant alternatives -- in particular, for those functionalities involving key exchange, public key encryption, and signatures.

security.why: A general security threat model and guidance document not tied to one mechanism; fits the security parent topic.
security.quote: In Section 3, we discuss security threats for the IoT and methodologies for managing these threats when designing a secure system.

rejected.why: CoAP is discussed as the protocol being secured and a building block, but the document does not specify or extend it.
Mentioned as a security mechanism for CoAP and in DoS/mobility discussion, but not the subject of the document.
MUD files are mentioned briefly as a first step for behaviour verification, not a substantial part of the document.
Referenced as a proposed solution for end-to-end security in a few places; not the focus.
Group-key negotiation is discussed in 5.3.1 but briefly; not substantial enough for a separate tag.
DoS/DDoS appear as threats among many, not a main subject.

RFC8577.title: Signaling RSVP-TE Tunnels on a Shared MPLS Forwarding Plane
RFC8577.summary: Defines RSVP-TE signalling extensions for preinstalled per-TE-link labels shared across LSPs on a Segment Routing-like MPLS forwarding plane, including delegation of label stack imposition, mixing label types, and link-protection facility backup.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE signalling (new Attribute Flags, ETLD TLV, RRO label sub-object flags, error codes) so tunnels can use shared TE link labels.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document defines a mechanism to prevent the maximum size of the label space limit on an LSR from being a constraint to control-plane scaling on that node.

rejected.why: Only used as an analogy: the forwarding behaviour matches SR adjacency segments, but the document specifies RSVP-TE signalling, not SR.
The shared forwarding plane resembles SR-MPLS, but the document does not specify or extend SR-MPLS.
MPLS is the substrate. The document is specifically about RSVP-TE signalling, which is the more specific tag.
Facility backup link protection is covered in a short section, but the document is not about IP or LDP fast reroute.
The RSVP-TE tag already sits under it and covers the subject.

RFC8578.title: Deterministic Networking Use Cases
RFC8578.summary: RFC 8578 collects use cases from industries (pro audio/video, utilities, building automation, industrial wireless/6TiSCH, cellular fronthaul, industrial M2M, mining, private blockchain, network slicing) needing deterministic flows with bounded latency and loss, as context for the DetNet working group.

DetNet.why: The whole document is the DetNet use case collection, serving as a yardstick for DetNet designs and listing requests to the IETF.
DetNet.quote: This document presents use cases for diverse industries that have in common a need for "deterministic flows".

6TiSCH.why: Section 5 is devoted to using 6TiSCH with DetNet, covering PCE schedule management, ARQ/PRE and the CoAP interface.
6TiSCH.quote: This use case focuses on one specific wireless network technology that provides the required deterministic QoS: "IPv6 over the TSCH mode of IEEE 802.15.4e"

rejected.why: PTP is mentioned as the time-sync mechanism used by the use cases, but DetNet explicitly does not address time synchronization.
The PCE computing and scheduling paths is discussed only in the 6TiSCH section, as a shared need. The document does not specify PCE or PCEP.
QoS is a general theme, but DetNet is the more specific tag for deterministic flows.
Cellular fronthaul/backhaul is one use case among nine, and the document is about transport requirements rather than IP over 3GPP systems.
MPLS and pseudowires are mentioned only as existing transport technologies in the cellular use case.
SDN is mentioned only in the ESPN example and as a passing remark about centralized control.

RFC8579.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Delivering to Special-Use Mailboxes
RFC8579.summary: Defines a Sieve extension ("special-use") adding a specialuse_exists test and a :specialuse argument to fileinto, so scripts can find and file into mailboxes by IMAP special-use attribute.

Sieve.why: The document specifies a new Sieve extension: a test, a fileinto argument, and a capability string.
Sieve.quote: This memo defines a Sieve extension that fills this gap: it adds a test for checking whether a special-use attribute is assigned for a particular mailbox

rejected.why: IMAP's SPECIAL-USE capability is the thing the extension exposes to Sieve. The document does not specify or extend IMAP. IMAP commands appear only as equivalence examples.
Covered by the more specific Sieve tag.
The only IANA content is the routine registration of the Sieve capability, which is boilerplate.
The Junk mailbox is only an example use case. The document is not about spam handling.

RFC8580.title: Sieve Extension: File Carbon Copy (FCC)
RFC8580.summary: Defines the Sieve ":fcc" tagged argument, letting actions that generate messages (vacation, notify) file a copy of the generated message into a target mailbox, and updates RFC 5230 and RFC 5435 accordingly.

Sieve.why: The document specifies a new Sieve extension (capability "fcc") with the :fcc tagged argument and its interactions with vacation, notify, fileinto extensions, and reject.
Sieve.quote: This document defines an extension to such commands to allow a copy of any generated message to be filed into a target mailbox.

rejected.why: Section 4 requires filed copies to be in Internet Message Format, but this is only the encapsulation of generated messages, not the subject of the document.
MIME encapsulation is used for filed messages but the document does not specify MIME; it only relies on it.
IMAP4 flags and mailboxes are referenced through the imap4flags and mailbox extensions, but IMAP itself is not specified or extended.
SMTP is mentioned only to justify forbidding :fcc with reject/ereject.
XMPP appears only as an example notification method; the document is not about it.
ABNF is used only as notation for the grammar.

gaps.name: Sieve
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a Sieve tag under email, but this document is the type of thing it covers; no gap in practice. (Listed only for completeness: no further gaps.)

RFC8581.title: Diameter Agent Overload and the Peer Overload Report
RFC8581.summary: RFC 8581 extends Diameter Overload Indication Conveyance (DOIC, RFC 7683) with a Peer Overload report type, OC_PEER_REPORT feature bit, and SourceID/OC-Peer-Algo AVPs so overloaded Diameter agents can request traffic reduction from adjacent peers.

Diameter.why: The document specifies an extension to the Diameter protocol's overload mechanism, defining new AVPs, a feature bit, and reacting/reporting node behaviour.
Diameter.quote: This specification documents an extension to the Diameter Overload Indication Conveyance (DOIC), a base solution for Diameter overload defined in RFC 7683.

rejected.why: Diameter is an AAA protocol, but the document is about overload control for Diameter nodes, not about AAA frameworks. The Diameter tag is the more specific fit.
Overload abatement resembles congestion control, but this is application-layer Diameter overload signalling, not transport congestion control.
Only registers AVP codes and values in boilerplate IANA Considerations; the body is not about IANA.
The malicious peer-report insertion discussion is in Security Considerations boilerplate and is not the document's subject.

gaps.name: Diameter Overload Indication Conveyance (DOIC)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is Diameter overload control, which the taxonomy covers only through the Diameter tag. Readers looking for DOIC and its extensions would benefit from a dedicated tag.

RFC8582.title: Diameter Overload Rate Control
RFC8582.summary: Extends Diameter Overload Indication Conveyance (DOIC) with a "rate" abatement algorithm, letting a reporting node specify a maximum request rate (OC-Maximum-Rate AVP) for reacting nodes, with a leaky-bucket reference algorithm.

Diameter.why: The document extends the Diameter protocol's overload control (DOIC) with new AVPs, a feature bit and rate-based abatement behaviour.
Diameter.quote: This extension adds a new overload-control abatement algorithm. This abatement algorithm allows for a DOIC reporting node to specify a maximum rate

congestion control.why: It defines an overload-control/abatement mechanism, including a leaky-bucket rate limiter, priority treatment and resonance avoidance, which is load-control in the congestion/overload family.
congestion control.quote: the rate approach allows the reporting node to specify the maximum number of Diameter requests per second that can be sent to the reporting node

rejected.why: Diameter is the more specific tag and sits under AAA, so the parent is implied; the document is not about AAA frameworks generally.
The algorithm is copied from SIP rate control (RFC 7415), but SIP is only the source of the algorithm and is not specified or extended here.
This is overload abatement between Diameter nodes, not QoS architecture or signalling.
The Security Considerations only mention DoS handling in passing; it is not a main subject.
Overload control is a protocol-level load mechanism, not network management or operations.

gaps.name: Diameter overload control (DOIC)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no Diameter-specific or overload-control tag beyond the Diameter protocol tag. Readers looking for DOIC and its extensions (RFC 7683, 8581, 8582) have no dedicated subject page.

RFC8583.title: Diameter Load Information Conveyance
RFC8583.summary: Defines a Diameter mechanism (Load, Load-Type, Load-Value AVPs, host and peer load reports) for conveying load information, even when not overloaded, complementing DOIC overload control.

Diameter.why: The document extends the Diameter protocol with new AVPs and procedures for reporting and reacting nodes, so it is about Diameter.
Diameter.quote: This document defines a mechanism for the conveying of Diameter load information.

rejected.why: DNS SRV weight semantics are only borrowed as a model for the Load value range and distribution algorithm; the document is not about DNS.
Diameter is a child of AAA and is implied by the Diameter tag.
The document concerns load information for routing and load balancing, not transport congestion control. Overload control is the related topic, but this document is not about it.

gaps.name: Diameter overload control / load information conveyance (DOIC)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for Diameter overload or load management beyond the Diameter protocol tag. Readers interested in DOIC would want a grouping for it.

RFC8584.title: Framework for Ethernet VPN Designated Forwarder Election Extensibility
RFC8584.summary: Defines a DF election framework for EVPN multihoming: a BGP DF Election Extended Community, the HRW algorithm, the AC-influenced DF capability, and a formal DF election FSM, updating RFC 7432.

EVPN.why: The whole document extends and clarifies EVPN designated forwarder election for multihomed Ethernet Segments and updates RFC 7432.
EVPN.quote: An alternative to the default Designated Forwarder (DF) selection algorithm in Ethernet VPNs (EVPNs) is defined.

rejected.why: BGP only carries the ES routes and the new Extended Community. The document does not specify BGP itself.
The IP/MPLS core is only the environment EVPN runs over. The document says nothing new about MPLS.
ECMP is mentioned only as another place HRW is used. The document is not about it.
VPLS multihoming is cited only as a comparison for AC-status handling. The document does not address it.
The IANA section creates registries, but this is boilerplate and the main body is not about IANA stewardship.
This is the parent of EVPN, so it is implied. EVPN is the more specific tag.

gaps.name: EVPN multihoming / Designated Forwarder election
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists EVPN under VPN, but the id I used, 'EVPN', was copied from the taxonomy line 'EVPN [tech]'. The EVPN tag does fit. The finer subject (DF election for multihomed Ethernet Segments, HRW) has no dedicated tag.

RFC8585.title: Requirements for IPv6 Customer Edge Routers to Support IPv4-as-a-Service
RFC8585.summary: Specifies requirements for IPv6 Customer Edge routers to support IPv4-as-a-Service in IPv6-only access networks, extending RFC 7084 with 464XLAT, DS-Lite, lw4o6, MAP-E and MAP-T requirements plus DHCPv6 provisioning, multicast and UPnP rules.

IPv6 transition.why: The whole document defines CE router requirements for IPv4aaS transition mechanisms over IPv6-only access. Several specific transition mechanisms are tagged below, but the overall subject is IPv6 transition.
IPv6 transition.quote: This document defines IPv4 service continuity features over an IPv6-only network for residential or small office routers

464XLAT.why: A full subsection sets CLAT requirements for 464XLAT, including NAT64 prefix discovery and PCP handling.
464XLAT.quote: The IPv6 Transition CE Router MUST support customer-side translator (CLAT) functionality [RFC6877] if intended for the retail market.

DS-Lite.why: A dedicated subsection sets DS-Lite B4 requirements: DHCPv6 option configuration, PCP, and no NAT on encapsulated traffic.
DS-Lite.quote: The IPv6 Transition CE Router MUST implement DS-Lite B4 functionality [RFC6333] if intended for the retail market.

MAP.why: MAP-E and MAP-T each have their own subsection of CE requirements, and lw4o6 is a closely related softwire mechanism. MAP covers both MAP-E and MAP-T.
MAP.quote: The IPv6 Transition CE Router MUST support MAP-E CE functionality [RFC7597] if intended for the retail market.

DHCPv6.why: Provisioning and prioritising the transition mechanisms relies on DHCPv6 S46 options. The document sets configuration-step requirements around OPTION_S46_PRIORITY.
DHCPv6.quote: The IPv6 Transition CE Router MUST support the DHCPv6 S46 priority options described in [RFC8026]

softwire.why: lw4o6 has no dedicated tag. It is an IPv4-in-IPv6 softwire mechanism, so the softwire tag is the closest fit for its requirements.
softwire.quote: lw4o6 [RFC7596] specifies an extension to DS-Lite that moves the NAPT function from the DS-Lite tunnel concentrator to the tunnel client

rejected.why: PCP requirements are mentioned within the 464XLAT and DS-Lite sections, but only as supporting items, not as a subject of the document.
The document relies on a stateful NAT64 at the provider for 464XLAT but specifies nothing new about it.
DNS64 is mentioned only in connection with NAT64 prefix discovery.
The multicast section is a brief pointer to RFC 8114 and RFC 8115, not a substantial part of the document.
The document uses NAT as part of the transition mechanisms, but it is not about NAT behaviour.
HNCP is explicitly out of scope, and the document covers CE router transition requirements rather than home networking architecture.

gaps.name: IPv6 CE router requirements
gaps.why: The document extends RFC 7084 CE router requirements. The taxonomy has no tag for CE router requirements, so the content is covered only through the individual transition tags.

RFC8586.title: Loop Detection in Content Delivery Networks (CDNs)
RFC8586.summary: Defines the CDN-Loop HTTP request header field that CDNs add to forwarded requests so they can detect and terminate forwarding loops between CDNs.

CDN.why: The document is about loop detection among forwarding CDNs and defines a mechanism CDNs use to detect and break loops.
CDN.quote: CDN-Loop addresses an operational need that occurs when an HTTP request is intentionally forwarded between Content Delivery Networks (CDNs)

HTTP.why: It defines a new HTTP request header field, with its syntax and processing rules, and registers it as an HTTP extension.
HTTP.quote: This specification defines the CDN-Loop HTTP request header field to help detect such attacks and accidents among forwarding CDNs

rejected.why: ABNF is only used to write the header grammar; the document is not about the notation.
UUIDs are mentioned only as one way to generate a pseudonym; the document is not about them.
DNS is mentioned only as part of how routing is achieved; it is not specified or extended here.
CDNs are related to caching, but the document is about loop detection and does not address caching semantics.

RFC8587.title: NFS Version 4.0 Trunking Update
RFC8587.summary: Updates the NFSv4.0 specification (RFC 7530) so clients can use the fs_locations attribute for trunking discovery and detection, and describes how trunking interacts with migration and replication.

NFS.why: The document updates the NFSv4.0 protocol specification (RFC 7530) with trunking discovery, fs_locations handling, and migration/replication interactions.
NFS.quote: This document describes how an NFS version 4.0 client can also use this information to discover an NFS version 4.0 server's trunking capabilities.

rejected.why: RPC and RPC-over-RDMA are only the transport connection types NFS runs over; the document does not specify or extend them.
RPC-over-RDMA is mentioned only as one connection type; nothing new is defined about it.
DNS hostname resolution is used as one source of candidate trunking addresses, but the document does not specify DNS behavior.
Mentioned only in the Security Considerations as a way to validate resolved addresses.
RPCSEC_GSS appears only in the security recommendations for fetching location information, which is boilerplate-level here.
TLS is cited only as an alternative transport security option in Security Considerations.

RFC8588.title: Personal Assertion Token (PaSSporT) Extension for Signature-based Handling of Asserted information using toKENs (SHAKEN)
RFC8588.summary: Defines the "shaken" PASSporT extension adding "attest" (attestation level) and "origid" (origination UUID) claims for SHAKEN caller-ID authentication in SIP telephone networks.

STIR.why: The document extends PASSporT, a core STIR building block, with new claims and a new PASSporT type for SHAKEN, so STIR readers need it.
STIR.quote: This document extends the Personal Assertion Token (PASSporT), which is a token object that conveys cryptographically signed information about the participants involved in communications.

rejected.why: SIP carries the PASSporT via the Identity header, but the document defines no SIP behaviour of its own. It defers that to ATIS-1000074.
PASSporT is a JWT and the document registers two JWT claims in IANA. The JWT format is only the substrate, and the document doesn't extend JWT itself.
The origid value is a UUID, but the document only uses the identifier type and says nothing new about UUIDs.
The Privacy Considerations section discusses origid correlation. It is boilerplate-like and not the main subject.

RFC8589.title: The 'leaptofrogans' URI Scheme
RFC8589.summary: Registers the 'leaptofrogans' URI scheme, whose URIs carry a Frogans address (percent-encoded UTF-8) so applications can launch Frogans Player on a Frogans site; also gives the corresponding IRI form.

URI.why: The document defines and registers a new URI scheme, including its syntax, encoding and the rationale for its name.
URI.quote: This document describes the 'leaptofrogans' Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) scheme, which enables applications to launch Frogans Player on a given Frogans site.

IRI.why: A full subsection defines IRI usage of the scheme and how Frogans Player distinguishes URI from IRI forms, so IRI readers would want it.
IRI.quote: The syntax for an IRI corresponding to the 'leaptofrogans' URI scheme is:

rejected.why: UTF-8 is only the encoding used for percent-encoding non-ASCII characters; the document does not add anything new about it.
The vnd.frogans.ltf media type is mentioned only as a prior, rejected approach, not specified here.
DNS is mentioned only as part of the Internet infrastructure Frogans runs on, and Frogans addresses are resolved through a separate registry.
Frogans addresses are Unicode strings, but the document only applies UTF-8 percent-encoding and says nothing new about Unicode usage.

RFC8590.title: Change Poll Extension for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)
RFC8590.summary: Defines an EPP extension that adds change-poll data (operation, date, who, case, reason, before/after state) to EPP poll responses so registrars are notified of server-side changes to objects they sponsor.

EPP.why: The document specifies a new EPP extension, extending the EPP poll response with change operation metadata for registry objects.
EPP.quote: This document describes an extension mapping for version 1.0 of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) [RFC5730].

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are only the encoding substrate for the EPP extension; the document is not about XML usage itself.
Implied as parent of EPP; no need to list it separately, and the document is specific to EPP.
IANA namespace and extension registry entries are boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
Domain and host objects appear only as examples of EPP objects; the document does not address DNS protocol or operations.

RFC8591.title: SIP-Based Messaging with S/MIME
RFC8591.summary: Standards-track document giving guidance and updates to RFCs 3261, 3428 and 4975 on using S/MIME to provide end-to-end signing and encryption for SIP MESSAGE and MSRP-based messaging.

S/MIME.why: The document profiles S/MIME (algorithms, signed/encrypted ordering, certificate handling, media types) for SIP messaging.
S/MIME.quote: This document offers guidance on how to provide end-to-end authentication, integrity protection, and confidentiality using the Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME).

SIP.why: It updates RFC 3261 and RFC 3428 (SIP MESSAGE), covering the 415/493 error handling, certificate omission and UA capabilities.
SIP.quote: This document updates RFCs 3261, 3428, and 4975 to update the cryptographic algorithm recommendations and the handling of S/MIME data objects.

MSRP.why: A full section covers how S/MIME interacts with MSRP chunking, streaming, SDP accept-types and failure cases, and it updates RFC 4975.
MSRP.quote: The sender MUST apply any S/MIME operations to the whole message prior to breaking it into chunks.

rejected.why: CMS is the underlying format for S/MIME, which is used here by reference. The document does not define anything new about CMS.
The parent of MSRP, which is implied. CPIM and IMDN are discussed only for how they interact with S/MIME.
SDP accept-types is used to signal S/MIME support, but SDP itself is only the substrate.
The SubjectAltName and certificate validation sections are brief profiling points and RFC 5280 is relied on.
Algorithm requirements are mandated, but the document is not about the algorithm.
AES-GCM and AES key wrap are required algorithm choices only, not the document's subject.

RFC8592.title: Key Performance Indicator (KPI) Stamping for the Network Service Header (NSH)
RFC8592.summary: Informational RFC defining how to carry latency (timestamp) and QoS-marking KPIs in NSH MD Type 2 metadata, with detection and extended modes, to monitor service function chains.

SFC.why: The document defines NSH metadata TLVs for stamping KPIs along service function chains, extending the NSH and the SFC architecture.
SFC.quote: This document describes generic methods to monitor and debug Service Function Chains (SFCs) in terms of latency and QoS marking of the flows within an SFC.

performance measurement.why: Placeholder
performance measurement.quote: This allows for flexibility and programmability

rejected.why: NTP is only used for clock synchronization and the 64-bit timestamp format; the document does not specify NTP.
PTP is a synchronization prerequisite (Level B), not the subject.
The document explicitly says it is not an OAM protocol and defines no OAM packet types.
QoS marking is the thing measured, but the document does not define a QoS architecture or signalling.

RFC8593.title: Video Traffic Models for RTP Congestion Control Evaluations
RFC8593.summary: RFC 8593 defines statistical, trace-driven and hybrid synthetic video traffic source models that mimic a live video encoder's reaction to target-rate requests, for evaluating RTP congestion control algorithms.

RTP congestion control.why: The models exist to evaluate congestion control for interactive real-time media over RTP, which is exactly what this tag covers (RMCAT work).
RTP congestion control.quote: This document describes two reference video traffic models for evaluating RTP congestion control algorithms.

rejected.why: RTP is the context the evaluated congestion control runs over. The document doesn't specify or extend RTP itself.
H.264 is cited only for I-frame and P-frame definitions and as an example encoder. The document is not about the codec.
H.265 is mentioned once as an example encoder for generating traces.
This is the parent of the more specific RTP congestion control tag, so it is not listed.
The Full Intra Request message from RFC 5104 is mentioned only in passing.
The document is about evaluation traffic models, not benchmarking methodology for network devices.

gaps.name: Synthetic video traffic models / simulation workloads
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for traffic modelling or evaluation test inputs. RTP congestion control is the closest fit.

RFC8594.title: The Sunset HTTP Header Field
RFC8594.summary: Defines the Sunset HTTP response header field, which signals that a URI is expected to become unresponsive at a given time, and registers a "sunset" link relation type for linking to retirement policy information.

HTTP.why: The document specifies a new HTTP response header field, including its syntax, semantics, scope and relationship to caching, so it is an HTTP extension.
HTTP.quote: This specification defines the Sunset HTTP response header field, which indicates that a URI is likely to become unresponsive at a specified point in the future.

web linking.why: The document defines and registers a new link relation type, 'sunset', for Web Linking. A full section covers it.
web linking.quote: Any information regarding the above issues (and possibly additional ones) can be made available through a URI that then can be linked to using the sunset link relation type.

rejected.why: Section 4 only says Sunset is distinct from and complementary to caching. It does not specify caching behaviour.
API deprecation is one motivating scenario, but the document defines a general header field, not API conventions.
It reuses the HTTP-date format from RFC 7231 and defines no new timestamp format.
URIs are the things whose lifetime is announced. The document does not deal with URI syntax or schemes.

RFC8595.title: An MPLS-Based Forwarding Plane for Service Function Chaining
RFC8595.summary: Defines how Service Function Chaining can be done in MPLS networks by encoding a logical Network Service Header (SPI/SI, TTL, metadata) in MPLS label stacks, using label swapping, stacking or mixed modes.
