SFC.why: The whole document specifies an MPLS-based forwarding plane for SFC, mapping NSH fields (SPI, SI, TTL, metadata) to label stack entries, with SFC proxy and control-plane considerations.
SFC.quote: This document describes how SFC can be achieved in an MPLS network by means of a logical representation of the NSH in an MPLS label stack.

MPLS.why: It defines new MPLS label stack encodings and label swapping/stacking procedures, and the IANA allocates extended special-purpose labels (MLI, MPI) for metadata.
MPLS.quote: The fields of these two label stack entries are encoded as follows

rejected.why: SR-MPLS for SFC is mentioned as a use case but is explicitly deferred to another document and not discussed further.
The entropy label section touches on ECMP load balancing but is a minor usage note, not the document's subject.
Mentioned only as an analogy in the implementation notes about VRF label lookup.
Tunnels between SFFs are the substrate; the encoding is independent of the tunnelling technology.
BGP control plane for NSH SFC is only referenced as an external document and not specified here.

RFC8596.title: MPLS Transport Encapsulation for the Service Function Chaining (SFC) Network Service Header (NSH)
RFC8596.summary: Describes an MPLS transport encapsulation for the SFC Network Service Header, using an SFF Label at the bottom of the MPLS label stack to indicate the NSH and select among SFFs at the destination node.

SFC.why: The document defines how the SFC Network Service Header is carried between Service Function Forwarders, a new transport encapsulation for NSH.
SFC.quote: This allows SFC packets using the NSH to be forwarded between SFFs over an MPLS network.

MPLS.why: It specifies MPLS label stack construction, label allocation, TTL handling and processing at the destination node for the SFF label, so MPLS readers would want it.
MPLS.quote: The encapsulation is a standard MPLS label stack [RFC3032] with an SFF Label at the bottom of the stack, followed by an NSH

rejected.why: Section 3 discusses ECMP considerations only briefly. It is not a substantial part of the document.
The SFF label is only compared to a pseudowire label. The document does not specify pseudowires.
Section 4 has only a short mention of GAL-based MPLS OAM. It is not substantial.
NETCONF, BGP and PCEP are mentioned only as possible ways to advertise labels, and the document puts that out of scope.
VPN labels are used only as an analogy for the SFF label.

RFC8597.title: Cooperating Layered Architecture for Software-Defined Networking (CLAS)
RFC8597.summary: Informational independent-stream RFC describing CLAS, an SDN architecture that separates service-stratum control functions from transport-stratum control functions, with deployment scenarios, use cases and challenges.

SDN.why: The whole document defines an SDN architecture, layering controllers into service and transport strata with planes and inter-controller communication, so the SDN topic page is the right home.
SDN.quote: This document describes an approach called Cooperating Layered Architecture for Software-Defined Networking (CLAS), wherein the control functions associated with transport are differentiated from those related to services

rejected.why: ACTN and TE information exchange are mentioned only as a use case and a reference; the document is not about TE.
PCE is named once as an example of a resource computation function, not specified or analysed.
QoS linking between strata is mentioned as an example only; it is not a QoS architecture or signalling document.
The management plane is one component of the architecture, but the document is about SDN layering, not network management practice.
It is an SDN control architecture for operator networks, not about Internet architectural principles.

RFC8598.title: Split DNS Configuration for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC8598.summary: Defines two IKEv2 Configuration Payload attributes, INTERNAL_DNS_DOMAIN and INTERNAL_DNSSEC_TA, so a VPN responder can assign split-DNS internal domains and DNSSEC trust anchors to an initiator in split-tunnel configurations.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with new Configuration Payload attribute types, defining their exchange, formats and IANA allocation.
IKE.quote: This document defines two Configuration Payload Attribute Types (INTERNAL_DNS_DOMAIN and INTERNAL_DNSSEC_TA) for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2 (IKEv2).

DNS.why: Specifies split-DNS behaviour: which domains the client must resolve via internal servers, how to map servers to domains, and cache and forwarding cleanup rules.
DNS.quote: These domains are intended to be resolved using non-public DNS servers that are only reachable through the IPsec connection.

DNSSEC.why: A substantial part of the document defines how DNSSEC trust anchors (DS data) are conveyed and the whitelist and security policy for accepting them.
DNSSEC.quote: The INTERNAL_DNSSEC_TA attribute type is used to convey a DNSSEC trust anchor for such a domain.

rejected.why: IPsec is the connection context, but the document extends IKEv2 specifically, so the IKE child tag fits better.
TLSA records are mentioned only when discussing the risk of trust anchor overrides, not specified or profiled.
IDNA A-labels are used only as the encoding of the domain name field.
This tag covers provider-provisioned VPNs (L3VPN and similar), whereas this document concerns remote-access IPsec VPN configuration.
The configuration attributes are analogous to DHCP configuration but DHCP is not discussed.

RFC8599.title: Push Notification with the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC8599.summary: Defines how a SIP proxy uses a Push Notification Service to wake suspended SIP UAs for binding-refresh REGISTERs and incoming requests, via new SIP URI parameters (pn-provider, pn-prid, pn-param, pn-purr), feature-capability indicators and a 555 response code.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with new URI parameters, feature-capability indicators, a 555 response code, and UA/proxy behaviour for REGISTER and dialog requests.
SIP.quote: This document describes how a Push Notification Service (PNS) can be used to wake a suspended Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) User Agent (UA) with push notifications

web push.why: It specifies how RFC 8030 web push and VAPID are used as a PNS (pn-provider=webpush), and the proxy acts as the application server. This is a substantial part of the document, but web push is one of several PNS types it profiles.
web push.quote: When Generic Event Delivery Using HTTP Push is used, the PNS-related URI parameters are set as described below.

rejected.why: HTTP push is only the mechanism of one PNS; the document is not about HTTP itself.
VAPID's JWT use is mentioned only in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate-level evidence.
TLS is only mentioned as a required security mechanism for SIP signaling.
NAT bindings are mentioned as a side effect of the REGISTER, not a subject of the document.
The registration event package and SUBSCRIBE refresh are mentioned in passing only.

gaps.name: Push Notification Service (PNS) for mobile apps
gaps.why: The central subject is push notification services such as APNs and FCM used to wake suspended apps. The taxonomy only has web push, which covers one of the PNS types.

RFC8600.title: Using Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) for Security Information Exchange
RFC8600.summary: Defines XMPP-Grid, an applicability statement for using XMPP publish-subscribe and service discovery to exchange security incident reports (illustrated with IODEF) among CSIRTs and network security platforms.

XMPP.why: The document is an applicability statement for XMPP: it specifies required XEPs (pubsub, disco), offline messaging, and XMPP-specific security guidance for the grid.
XMPP.quote: a method for using the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) [RFC6120] to collect and distribute security incident reports and other security-relevant information

IODEF.why: IODEF is the worked example payload throughout, with pubsub#type set to the IODEF namespace, and the work targets CSIRT incident exchange. It is an illustrative format rather than the core subject.
IODEF.quote: this document uses IODEF as one such example format that can be published and consumed using XMPP

rejected.why: TLS is only the required transport security mechanism; nothing new is defined about it.
SASL mechanisms (SCRAM, EXTERNAL) are only referenced as authentication options inherited from XMPP core.
The parent topic is implied by IODEF, and IODEF is already chosen as the more specific tag.
XEP-0030 service discovery is used within the workflow, but it is XMPP-specific and a small part of the document.
XML is only the encoding of stanzas and payloads.
DHCP is mentioned only as an example platform role in the security section.

RFC8601.title: Message Header Field for Indicating Message Authentication Status
RFC8601.summary: Specifies the Authentication-Results email header field, which carries results of message authentication checks (DKIM, SPF, iprev, SMTP AUTH, etc.) from border/delivery MTAs to MUAs and filters within a trust boundary, and defines the associated IANA registries.

email authentication.why: The document defines a common framework for reporting results of email authentication methods. It covers the subject broadly rather than one method, so the parent topic fits.
email authentication.quote: specifies a message header field called "Authentication-Results" for use with electronic mail messages to indicate the results of message authentication efforts

message format.why: It defines a new trace header field with ABNF, placement and ordering rules, and registers it in the message header field registry.
message format.quote: It is a structured header field as defined in "Internet Message Format" [MAIL], and thus all of the related definitions in that document apply.

DKIM.why: It specifies DKIM result values and property reporting, and registers the new header.a and header.s properties.
DKIM.quote: DKIM is represented by the "dkim" method and is defined in [DKIM].

SPF.why: It specifies how SPF results are reported (smtp.mailfrom, smtp.helo) and adds a policy result.
SPF.quote: SPF uses the "spf" method name.  The result values for SPF are defined in Section 2.6 of [SPF]

rejected.why: SMTP is the context, and SMTP AUTH is only one reported method. The document does not extend or specify SMTP itself.
The iprev method uses PTR and A/AAAA lookups, but DNS is only a substrate. The document defines nothing new about DNS.
EAI guidance is included, but only as incidental UTF-8 and U-label allowances scattered through the text.
DMARC is only listed among the methods. The document has no DMARC-specific content.
The registry sections are boilerplate-style registry maintenance. They support the main subject and do not make it an IANA guidance document.
ABNF is only used as the notation for the grammar. It is not a subject of the document.

RFC8602.title: Update to the Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP) IANA Registry Rules regarding Postal Addresses
RFC8602.summary: Updates the TRIP IANA registry rules (RFC 3219) so that postal addresses are no longer collected for TRIP Attributes and ITAD Number registrations, and removes previously collected addresses, for privacy.

TRIP.why: The document amends the registration rules for TRIP Attributes and ITAD Numbers defined in RFC 3219, so it is about TRIP registries. TRIP readers would need to find it.
TRIP.quote: This memo updates the IANA registry rules for the Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP) protocol, by no longer requiring that postal addresses be included in contact information.

rejected.why: The document is an IANA registry rule change, but it concerns only TRIP registries. It is not general IANA guidance or stewardship, and the TRIP tag is more specific.
Privacy is the stated motivation for dropping postal addresses, but the document is not a privacy threat model or considerations document. It is a narrow registry rule update.

RFC8603.title: Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite Certificate and Certificate Revocation List (CRL) Profile
RFC8603.summary: Defines the NSA's CNSA Suite profile of RFC 5280 X.509 v3 certificates and v2 CRLs, mandating P-384 ECDSA/ECDH or RSA-3072/4096 keys, SHA-384 signatures, and specific extension requirements for CA and end-entity certificates.

X.509.why: The whole document is a profile of RFC 5280 X.509 certificates and CRLs, specifying required fields, extensions and criticality for CNSA Suite certificates.
X.509.quote: This document specifies a base profile for X.509 v3 Certificates and X.509 v2 Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs)

rejected.why: P-384 ECDSA/ECDH keys are required, but the document profiles certificate fields and does not specify the cryptography itself.
RSA-3072/4096 keys and sha384WithRSAEncryption are mandated for certificates, but RSA is not the subject; the document only selects parameters for certificate use.
ECDSA appears as a signature option with OIDs and encoding, which is certificate profiling and not a specification of ECDSA.
SHA-384 is required for signatures, but the document does not specify or analyse the hash family.
X.509 is the more specific child tag and is already chosen, so the PKI parent is implied.
ASN.1 encoding of integers and OIDs is incidental to the certificate profile.

RFC8604.title: Interconnecting Millions of Endpoints with Segment Routing
RFC8604.summary: Informational RFC describing a Segment Routing design (multi-domain, SRGB sub-ranges, anycast and binding SIDs, PCE-driven SR policies) to interconnect massive-scale data centers and aggregation networks with small forwarding tables.

segment routing.why: The whole document is a large-scale SR design: SRGB allocation, anycast and binding SIDs, compressed SR policies, and the scaling arithmetic.
segment routing.quote: This document describes an application of Segment Routing to scale the network to support hundreds of thousands of network nodes

SR-MPLS.why: The design uses MPLS label SIDs (SRGB ranges, label stacks of segment lists), so SR-MPLS readers would want it.
SR-MPLS.quote: This document describes an application of SR over the MPLS data plane. SR does not introduce any changes in the MPLS data plane.

PCE.why: The control plane section describes an SR PCE computing multi-domain paths via PCEP, using BGP-LS for topology.
PCE.quote: It then automatically sends a PCEP request to an SR PCE for an SRTE policy that provides reachability information for node Z

rejected.why: BGP and BGP-LS are used as the intra-DC protocol and topology feed, but the document does not specify or extend them.
DC interconnection is the use case, but the content is about SR scaling, not data-centre routing and address resolution.
ECMP is discussed only as a brief benefit in 8.4, not a substantial subject.
TI-LFA is mentioned in one sentence and is defined in a separate document.
SR TE policies appear, but the PCE tag and the segment routing tag cover this more specifically.
IS-IS and OSPF are used as per-domain SR instances but not specified or extended here.

gaps.name: segment routing (SR) architecture and SR policy
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists "segment routing" as a tech under routing, but the id I used must match exactly; if the taxonomy id is "segment routing" it fits, but there is no tag for SR policy or inter-domain SR design specifically.

RFC8605.title: vCard Format Extensions: ICANN Extensions for the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP)
RFC8605.summary: Defines a new vCard property (CONTACT-URI) and parameter (CC) so RDAP entity responses can meet ICANN's Temporary Specification for gTLD registration data.

RDAP.why: The document extends RDAP entity representation to implement the ICANN operational profile, so RDAP readers would want it.
RDAP.quote: requirements that cannot currently be met by the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP, [RFC7483]) without extending the underlying vCard [RFC6350] specification

vCard.why: It defines a new vCard property (CONTACT-URI) and parameter (CC) and registers them in the vCard registries.
vCard.quote: This document includes specifications for an additional vCard property and an additional vCard parameter

rejected.why: URIs are only the value type of CONTACT-URI; the document defines nothing new about URIs.
RDAP's JSON encoding is not discussed; vCard is used in jCard form only via RDAP and not addressed here.
The parent is implied by RDAP, which is the more specific tag.
The IANA registrations are routine boilerplate for the new property and parameter.
ABNF is only the notation used for format definitions.
The privacy aspects are limited to a brief note in Security Considerations and the redaction rationale; not a subject in its own right.

gaps.name: vCard
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a vCard tech tag, so I tagged it above; but I listed it before checking the ids. It is present in the taxonomy as 'vCard' under applications.

RFC8606.title: ISDN User Part (ISUP) Cause Location Parameter for the SIP Reason Header Field
RFC8606.summary: Updates RFC 3326 by adding a "location" parameter to the SIP Reason header field to carry the Q.850 ISUP release location when interworking SIP with the PSTN.

SIP.why: The document extends the SIP Reason header field with a new parameter and registers it in the SIP parameters registry, so it is a SIP extension.
SIP.quote: This document adds a location value parameter to the reason-extension parameter defined in [RFC3326] so that the [Q.850] location value can be interworked from the PSTN.

PSTN interop.why: It addresses ISUP-to-SIP interworking at gateways, carrying Q.850 release location from the PSTN into SIP. No child tag fits: SIP-T is ISUP encapsulation, not this.
PSTN interop.quote: The purpose of this parameter is to hold the location of the call release so that it can be transported from the originating PSTN entity to the SIP entity

rejected.why: The document concerns mapping a Q.850 location value into a Reason parameter, not ISUP encapsulation in SIP.
ABNF is only used to define the parameter syntax; the document is not about the notation.
The IANA section is a routine parameter registration, which is boilerplate.
Not relevant; the registration is a SIP header parameter, not a media type.
The ISUP location indicates network position of call release, not physical location; the Privacy section says so explicitly.

RFC8607.title: Calendaring Extensions to WebDAV (CalDAV): Managed Attachments
RFC8607.summary: RFC 8607 extends CalDAV so that attachments to iCalendar events and tasks can be uploaded to and managed by the server via POST actions, with new iCalendar parameters (SIZE, FILENAME, MANAGED-ID), a Cal-Managed-ID header, and WebDAV properties.

CalDAV.why: The document is a CalDAV extension defining managed attachment operations, preconditions and properties.
CalDAV.quote: This specification adds an extension to the Calendaring Extensions to WebDAV (CalDAV) to allow attachments associated with iCalendar data to be stored and managed on the server.

iCalendar.why: Section 4 defines new iCalendar ATTACH property parameters (SIZE, FILENAME, MANAGED-ID), which iCalendar readers would want.
iCalendar.quote: This specification defines the following new iCalendar property parameters to be added to the "Parameters" registry

rejected.why: WebDAV is the base of CalDAV and supplies properties and preconditions, but CalDAV is the more specific tag; the document is not about WebDAV itself.
The extension uses HTTP POST, GET, Prefer and Content-Disposition as substrate, though it documents non-best-practice use. It does not define HTTP semantics, so it is not tagged.
Content-Type is used for attachments, but no media type is registered.
Parent of the chosen tags, so it is implied and not listed separately.
XML is only the encoding for WebDAV property definitions, so it is not a subject of the document.

RFC8608.title: BGPsec Algorithms, Key Formats, and Signature Formats
RFC8608.summary: Specifies the signature algorithm (ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256), algorithm suite IDs, key formats and signature formats used by BGPsec, updates RFC 7935, obsoletes RFC 8208, and includes example BGPsec UPDATE messages.

BGPsec.why: The whole document defines the algorithm suites, key and signature formats for BGPsec, with example BGPsec UPDATE messages. It also creates the BGPsec Algorithm Suites registry.
BGPsec.quote: specifies the algorithms, algorithm parameters, asymmetric key formats, asymmetric key sizes, and signature formats used in BGPsec (Border Gateway Protocol Security)

RPKI.why: It profiles algorithms and key formats for RPKI CAs and BGPsec router certificates, and updates the RPKI algorithm profile RFC 7935. The IANA registry sits in the RPKI group.
RPKI.quote: used by Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Certification Authorities (CAs) and BGPsec (Border Gateway Protocol Security) speakers

ECDSA.why: The one signature algorithm defined is ECDSA P-256. The document specifies its key encoding and signature format for BGPsec use.
ECDSA.quote: The signature algorithm used MUST be the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) with curve P-256 [RFC6090] [DSS].

rejected.why: Router certificates and SubjectPublicKeyInfo are used, but the certificate profile itself is in RFC 8209 and RFC 7935. This document only specifies the algorithms and key formats.
BGP UPDATE messages carry the signatures, but the document does not specify BGP itself. BGPsec is the more specific tag.
SHA-256 is mandated only as the hash paired with ECDSA. The document is not about the SHA family.
The IANA registry creation is boilerplate-level apparatus here. The main body is about algorithms and formats.
ECDSA is the more specific tag and already covers the elliptic curve use.

RFC8609.title: Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) Messages in TLV Format
RFC8609.summary: Specifies the TLV packet format and type/value encodings for CCNx (Content-Centric Networking) Interest, Content Object and Interest Return messages, including validation TLVs and IANA registries.

ICN.why: The document specifies the wire encoding of CCNx, an information-centric networking protocol, so the ICN subject page is the right home.
ICN.quote: Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) is a network protocol that uses a hierarchical name to forward requests and to match responses to requests.

rejected.why: The CCNx URI scheme is defined in a separate document; here names are only encoded as TLV segments.
Certificates are carried as DER-encoded TLV values but no certificate profile is defined.
HMAC-SHA256 is just one listed validation algorithm type, not the subject of the document.
Elliptic curve signature types are only entries in the validation type table.
CRC32C is one validation type among several, not a document subject.
UDP is only mentioned as a possible overlay transport in Security Considerations.

RFC8610.title: Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL): A Notational Convention to Express Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) and JSON Data Structures
RFC8610.summary: RFC 8610 defines CDDL, a notational language for describing CBOR (and JSON) data structures, covering its syntax, control operators, prelude, matching semantics, JSON use, and extended diagnostic notation.

CDDL.why: The whole document specifies CDDL: groups, types, occurrence, controls, sockets, generics, prelude and matching rules.
CDDL.quote: a notational convention to express Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) data structures (RFC 7049)

CBOR.why: CDDL's data model is CBOR's. The document covers representation types, tags, and Appendix G, which extends CBOR diagnostic notation.
CBOR.quote: A formal definition of CDDL ... CBOR data structures [RFC7049] is defined.

rejected.why: CDDL can describe JSON structures (Appendix E), but this is a side effect. JSON is a data model the language targets, not the subject.
CDDL syntax is inspired by ABNF and the grammar is written in it (Appendix B). ABNF is only used as a notation here.
The CDDL Control Operators registry is boilerplate-level IANA content, not the main subject.
YANG is mentioned only as precedent for choosing XSD regular expressions.

gaps.name: CDDL (Concise Data Definition Language)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has CDDL only as a child of CBOR. I assumed it lives there; if it's not in the taxonomy as an id, it needs checking. The data-definition and schema-language aspect also matters for JSON users.

RFC8611.title: Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping and Traceroute Multipath Support for Link Aggregation Group (LAG) Interfaces
RFC8611.summary: Extends MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute (RFC 8029) with an LSR Capability TLV, LAG description flag, and interface index sub-TLVs so the tools can discover and exercise individual LAG member links (L2 ECMP).

MPLS.why: The document specifies new TLVs, sub-TLVs and procedures for MPLS LSP Ping/Traceroute data-plane failure detection, updating RFC 8029.
MPLS.quote: extensions to the MPLS Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping and Traceroute mechanisms as specified in RFC 8029

link aggregation.why: The core purpose is diagnosing individual LAG member links, covering LAG behaviour under MPLS OAM, including the L2-switch-in-between issues in the appendix.
link aggregation.quote: discover and exercise specific paths of Layer 2 (L2) Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) over Link Aggregation Group (LAG) interfaces

ECMP.why: The document extends multipath discovery to L2 ECMP via multipath information per member link, building on the L3 ECMP coverage of LSP traceroute.
ECMP.quote: Link Aggregation Groups (LAGs), as defined in [IEEE802.1AX], provide Layer 2 (L2) ECMP

rejected.why: The subject is OAM in general, but the more specific MPLS tag covers LSP Ping/Traceroute here.
The generic traceroute tool tag is about IP path discovery tools, whereas this document extends MPLS LSP traceroute specifically.
LDP appears only as an example network in Figure 1; the document isn't about LDP.
The IANA registry creations are boilerplate; the body isn't about IANA guidance.

gaps.name: MPLS LSP Ping/Traceroute (RFC 8029 data-plane failure detection)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for MPLS OAM or LSP Ping; only the generic MPLS and OAM tags exist.

RFC8612.title: DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) Requirements
RFC8612.summary: RFC 8612 specifies the requirements for the DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) signal and data channel protocols, which let clients request and coordinate DDoS attack mitigation.

DOTS.why: The whole document is a requirements specification for the DOTS protocols (general, signal channel, data channel, security, data model).
DOTS.quote: This document defines the requirements for the Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) protocols enabling coordinated response to DDoS attacks.

rejected.why: TLS/DTLS is only the required security substrate (SEC-002/003); the document defines no TLS-specific extension.
UDP is the preferred signal channel transport, but the document is not about UDP itself or its usage guidelines.
Section 3 is a brief congestion considerations section, not a substantial treatment of congestion control as a subject.
SIG-011 requires NAT traversal and cites NAT BCPs, but this is one requirement, not the subject of the document.
SIG-002 requires sub-PMTU messages and a fallback PMTU assumption, a minor point.
This is the parent topic of DOTS. The DOTS tag is the more specific fit, so the parent is implied.

RFC8613.title: Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments (OSCORE)
RFC8613.summary: Defines OSCORE, an application-layer end-to-end security protocol for CoAP (and CoAP-mappable HTTP) using compressed COSE objects, with security context derivation, message protection rules, proxy and HTTP handling, and updates to RFC 7252.

OSCORE.why: The document specifies OSCORE itself: its option, security context, protected fields, processing and header compression.
OSCORE.quote: This document defines the Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments (OSCORE) security protocol, protecting CoAP and CoAP-mappable HTTP requests and responses end-to-end

CoAP.why: The document extends and updates CoAP, defining a new option, option classes (inner/outer), Observe, Block-wise and proxy processing. Readers of CoAP want it. It sits above OSCORE in the hierarchy, but the update to RFC 7252 and the CoAP option handling justify listing it separately.
CoAP.quote: Although an optional functionality of CoAP, OSCORE alters CoAP options processing and IANA registration.  Therefore, this document updates RFC 7252.

rejected.why: COSE is the object format OSCORE builds on, but this document defines OSCORE, not COSE itself.
HTTP is used only as a transport hop for OSCORE messages via a header field. The document does not extend HTTP semantics.
(D)TLS is mentioned for comparison and as an optional hop-by-hop complement, not specified here.
CBOR is only the underlying encoding via COSE and CDDL.
HKDF/HMAC is used for key derivation but is not the subject of the document.
Section 9 defines an 'osc' link attribute, but it is a minor part of the document.

RFC8614.title: Updated Processing of Control Flags for BGP Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS)
RFC8614.summary: RFC 8614 updates RFC 4761 BGP VPLS so that mismatched Control Word (C-bit) and Sequence (S-bit) flags in the Layer2 Info Extended Community no longer always block pseudowire setup, and specifies the behaviour for mixed-mode, P2MP LSP transport and multihoming cases.

VPLS.why: The whole document revises BGP VPLS signalling behaviour defined in RFC 4761, specifying how PEs treat C-bit and S-bit mismatches.
VPLS.quote: This document updates the meaning of the Control Flags field in the "Layer2 Info Extended Community" used for BGP Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS)

rejected.why: BGP is only the signalling substrate for VPLS NLRI; the document does not change BGP itself.
Pseudowires and the control word are discussed, but the subject is the VPLS control flags in BGP signalling, not pseudowire emulation in general.
P2MP LSPs are mentioned as transport for VPLS in one section, but the document is not about MPLS.
ECMP is mentioned only as motivation for the control word.
LAG bundles are mentioned only as motivation for the control word.
Multihoming is discussed for VPLS and refers to the VPLS multihoming draft, not EVPN.

RFC8615.title: Well-Known Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs)
RFC8615.summary: Defines the "/.well-known/" path prefix for well-known locations in HTTP, HTTPS, WS and WSS URIs, the IANA Well-Known URI registry and its registration procedure, and a new "Well-Known URI Support" column in the URI schemes registry; obsoletes RFC 5785.

URI.why: The document defines a reserved URI path prefix, the rules for registering well-known URI names, and how URI schemes declare support in the scheme registry. This is URI syntax and scheme registration.
URI.quote: This memo defines a path prefix for "well-known locations", "/.well-known/", in selected Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.

HTTP.why: It updates the http and https scheme definitions to reserve the /.well-known/ space. Its security section covers HTTP origin interaction, so HTTP readers would want it.
HTTP.quote: This specification updates the "http" [RFC7230] and "https" [RFC7230] schemes to support well-known URIs.

rejected.why: robots.txt is mentioned only as an example of site-wide metadata that could use the mechanism. The document does not specify or change it.
Section 4 gives security guidance for well-known resources, but the document is not mainly about web platform security mechanisms.
Cookies appear only in mitigation advice in the security considerations.
It creates a registry and registration policy, but this is specific to well-known URIs and is covered by the URI tag.
ws and wss are only listed as schemes that can use well-known URIs; the update is defined in RFC 8307.
A more specific tag (URI) already fits, so the broad parent is not needed.

RFC8616.title: Email Authentication for Internationalized Mail
RFC8616.summary: RFC 8616 updates SPF, DKIM and DMARC to specify whether internationalized domain names (U-labels vs A-labels) and UTF-8 local parts are used when authenticating internationalized (EAI) email.

EAI.why: The document is about how email authentication works with internationalized mail (EAI), clarifying U-label/A-label and UTF-8 local-part handling.
EAI.quote: Internationalized mail [RFC6530] (generally called "EAI" for Email Address Internationalization) allows U-labels in SMTP sessions [RFC6531] and message header fields [RFC6532].

SPF.why: It updates RFC 7208, specifying IDN representation in EHLO/MAIL FROM, macro expansion and SPF records.
SPF.quote: All U-labels MUST be converted to A-labels before being used for an SPF validation.

DKIM.why: It updates RFC 6376, changing dkim-safe-char and the form of IDNs in DKIM-Signature tags.
DKIM.quote: IDNs in the d=, i=, and s= tags of a DKIM-Signature header field MUST be encoded as A-labels.  This rule is relaxed only for internationalized message header fields

DMARC.why: It updates RFC 7489 on handling IDNs in the RFC5322.From domain and on rua/ruf addresses.
DMARC.quote: all U-labels in the domain are converted to A-labels before further processing.

rejected.why: IDNs and U-/A-labels are the subject matter, but the document only specifies how mail authentication protocols treat them and does not define IDNA itself.
The parent topic is implied by the SPF, DKIM and DMARC tags.
DNS holds the published records, but the document only says that strings in DNS records stay ASCII and that lookups use A-labels. It doesn't change DNS.
SMTPUTF8 and the EHLO and MAIL FROM identities are mentioned, but only as inputs to SPF.
UTF-8 appears in the ABNF extension for dkim-safe-char, but the document is not about the encoding.
ABNF is only the notation used for one rule.

RFC8617.title: The Authenticated Received Chain (ARC) Protocol
RFC8617.summary: Defines the experimental Authenticated Received Chain (ARC) protocol, in which mail handlers add signed ARC header sets (AAR, AMS, AS) so downstream receivers can see earlier authentication assessments, with sealing and validation procedures and DMARC-related use cases.

ARC.why: The whole document specifies ARC: its header fields, sealer and validator actions, and chain validation status.
ARC.quote: The Authenticated Received Chain (ARC) protocol provides an authenticated "chain of custody" for a message

DMARC.why: A substantial part covers using ARC to inform DMARC local policy overrides and DMARC reporting, so DMARC readers would want it.
DMARC.quote: Authenticated Received Chains allow DMARC processors to consider authentication assessments provided by other ADMDs.

rejected.why: ARC borrows DKIM signature syntax and algorithms, but DKIM is the substrate. The document does not extend DKIM itself.
SPF is mentioned only as an authentication mechanism that intermediaries break. The document does not specify or change it.
ARC adds new header fields, but the document is about the authentication mechanism, not the general Internet message format.
It only registers enhanced status code 5.7.29 and discusses SMTP responses in passing. SMTP is not the subject.
Section 4.1.4 is a short note that EAI changes are inherited from DKIM and Authentication-Results. That is too minor for a tag.
Mailing lists appear as one use case. The document does not specify mailing list protocols.

RFC8618.title: Compacted-DNS (C-DNS): A Format for DNS Packet Capture
RFC8618.summary: Defines C-DNS, a CBOR-based block-structured format for compactly storing DNS query/response packet captures with transport metadata, plus guidance on matching, PCAP reconstruction, and IANA registries.

DNS.why: The document specifies a format for capturing and storing DNS queries and responses, including DNS message fields, flags, RR data and name handling. DNS operators and tooling readers would look for it under DNS.
DNS.quote: This document describes a data representation for collections of DNS messages.

CBOR.why: The format is defined as CBOR maps and arrays, with a CDDL schema and a section on why CBOR was chosen. It also gives guidance on canonical CBOR use.
CBOR.quote: The format uses CBOR [RFC7049].

packet capture.why: The document is a DNS packet capture file format. It covers collection, Q/R matching, and conversion back to PCAP.
packet capture.quote: The format is designed for efficient storage and transmission of large packet captures of DNS traffic

rejected.why: CDDL is only used to describe the schema in Appendix A; the document does not specify or extend CDDL.
DoH and DoT/DTLS appear only as transport values recorded in a flag field, not as subjects of the document.
EDNS fields (OPT RR, version, UDP size) are recorded as data, but the document does not specify EDNS.
The Privacy Considerations section is boilerplate-like, and the anonymisation flags are a minor part of the format.
General-purpose compression tools are only benchmarked in an appendix; the document does not define a compression format.
The DO, CD and AD flag bits are merely recorded fields; the document is not about DNSSEC.

gaps.name: packet capture
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists a 'packet capture' tag under network management, but I have no basis to use it in my chosen tags list beyond what I submitted; if it is considered invalid, the document's subject of DNS traffic capture formats lacks a more specific tag.

RFC8619.title: Algorithm Identifiers for the HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF)
RFC8619.summary: Assigns ASN.1 object identifiers and an ASN.1 module for HKDF (RFC 5869) used with SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, so HKDF can be named in CMS and S/MIME protocols.

cryptography.why: The document is about identifying a key derivation function (HKDF) and its hash variants. No specific HKDF tag exists, so the cryptography topic is the best fit. It is not about a particular key management protocol.
cryptography.quote: This document assigns algorithm identifiers to the HKDF algorithm when used with three common one-way hash functions.

ASN.1.why: A substantial part of the document is an ASN.1 module and object identifier assignments, which is of interest to readers of ASN.1 modules.
ASN.1.quote: This section contains the ASN.1 module for the HKDF algorithm identifiers.

rejected.why: CMS is only the motivating consumer of the identifiers. The document does not extend or profile CMS.
SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 are only the hash functions HKDF is paired with. The document does not specify them.
HMAC is the building block inside HKDF. The document is not about HMAC itself.
The OIDs sit in the S/MIME arc and registries and include SMIME-CAPS, but the document is not about secure email.
The IANA section only records the OID assignments, which is boilerplate here.
HKDF is a key derivation function, but the document only assigns identifiers and does not address key establishment or provisioning.

gaps.name: HKDF (HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function)
gaps.why: The document is about HKDF algorithm identifiers, and the taxonomy has no tag for key derivation functions or HKDF. Readers looking for HKDF would not find it under cryptography.

gaps.name: Object identifiers (OIDs) for algorithms
gaps.why: OID assignment for cryptographic algorithms is a recurring RFC subject with no dedicated tag.

RFC8620.title: The JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP)
RFC8620.summary: RFC 8620 specifies JMAP, a JSON-over-HTTP protocol for clients to query, fetch, modify and synchronise data objects, with batching, result references, binary blob upload/download, and push notifications of state changes.

JMAP.why: The document is the core JMAP specification: session resource, standard methods, binary data and push.
JMAP.quote: The JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP) is used for synchronising data, such as mail, calendars, or contacts, between a client and a server.

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate JMAP runs over; the document defines a protocol on top and not HTTP semantics or extensions.
JSON/I-JSON is only the data encoding for the protocol; the document does not define a JSON format in its own right.
Push subscriptions reuse RFC 8030/8291 to deliver StateChange notifications. This is a JMAP mechanism that depends on Web Push, not a specification of it.
It uses problem details and is an API on HTTP, but it defines its own protocol and not conventions for HTTP APIs in general.
Mail is only an example data type. The mail data model is defined in separate specifications.
TLS is required as transport security only.

RFC8621.title: The JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP) for Mail
RFC8621.summary: RFC 8621 specifies the JMAP data model and methods for mail: Mailboxes, Threads, Emails, search snippets, Identities, email submission, and vacation responses.

JMAP.why: The whole document defines the JMAP mail capability, its data types and methods.
JMAP.quote: This document specifies a data model for synchronising email data with a server using the JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP).

rejected.why: The data model is designed to be compatible with IMAP and shares keywords and roles, but IMAP itself is not specified or extended here.
Email submission maps to SMTP envelopes and extensions, but SMTP is only the underlying mechanism, not the subject.
The Email object parses RFC 5322 headers, but the document does not define the message format. It only exposes it through JMAP.
The document represents MIME body structure, but it relies on MIME rather than defining it.
JSON is only the encoding for the JMAP messages.
The document registers no media types.

gaps.name: JMAP (JSON Meta Application Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists JMAP only as a child of email, so the id is not in the taxonomy as a standalone tag. The closest valid tag is the JMAP entry under email, which is written 'JMAP'.

RFC8622.title: A Lower-Effort Per-Hop Behavior (LE PHB) for Differentiated Services
RFC8622.summary: RFC 8622 defines the Lower-Effort (LE) Per-Hop Behavior for Differentiated Services, recommends DSCP 000001 for it, obsoletes RFC 3662, and updates RFC 4594 and RFC 8325 to use the new codepoint.

Diffserv.why: The document specifies a new Diffserv PHB, its recommended DSCP, deployment and re-marking rules, and updates to other Diffserv configuration RFCs.
Diffserv.quote: This document defines a Differentiated Services (DS) per-hop behavior [RFC2474] called "Lower-Effort Per-Hop Behavior" (LE PHB)

rejected.why: ECN is only recommended for use with LE packets in a single paragraph; the document is not about ECN.
LEDBAT is mentioned only as a suggested background transport for domains that map LE to BE. The tag set has no standalone entry for it beyond the congestion control parent.
The multicast section covers replication concerns for LE traffic, but it is a secondary consideration and the document is not about multicast routing.
This is the parent of Diffserv, so it is implied by the Diffserv tag.
RFC 8325 (Diffserv to 802.11 mapping) is updated only in a table entry; the document is not about Wi-Fi.
The DSCP assignment sits in the IANA Considerations section, which is boilerplate evidence, and the document is not about IANA registry policy.

RFC8623.title: Stateful Path Computation Element (PCE) Protocol Extensions for Usage with Point-to-Multipoint TE Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC8623.summary: Extends PCEP stateful PCE (RFC 8231/8281) to support P2MP TE LSPs, defining new capability flags, LSP object flags, P2MP-LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLVs, the S2LS object, message extensions and fragmentation.

PCE.why: The whole document specifies PCEP extensions for stateful PCE with P2MP TE LSPs: PCRpt, PCUpd, PCInitiate, S2LS object, and capability flags.
PCE.quote: provides extensions required for the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) so as to enable the usage of a stateful PCE capability in supporting P2MP TE LSPs

rejected.why: RSVP-TE P2MP signalling (RFC 4875) is referenced for identifiers and make-before-break, but the document defines PCEP extensions, not RSVP-TE.
P2MP TE LSPs are the managed objects, but the document is about PCEP, not MPLS itself.
GMPLS is mentioned only as a context where the LSPs apply.
RBNF is only the notation used for message formats.
OSPF and IS-IS PCE discovery capability bits are added, but only as a small part of the document.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations as the transport security mechanism.

gaps.name: PCE (Path Computation Element) / PCEP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a PCE tech tag under traffic engineering, but the tag id I used (PCE) does not appear in the taxonomy; the closest ids are 'PCE' under traffic engineering. See below.

RFC8624.title: Algorithm Implementation Requirements and Usage Guidance for DNSSEC
RFC8624.summary: Specifies mandatory-to-implement and recommended cryptographic algorithms for DNSSEC signing, validation, and DS/CDS digests, obsoleting RFC 6944.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document sets DNSKEY and DS/CDS algorithm requirements for DNSSEC signers and validators, plus rollover guidance.
DNSSEC.quote: This document defines the current algorithm implementation requirements and usage guidance for DNSSEC.

rejected.why: ECDSA and EdDSA are discussed only as DNSSEC algorithm choices; the document is not about elliptic-curve cryptography itself.
GOST is only mentioned as a deprecated DNSSEC algorithm (MUST NOT sign, MAY validate).
ED25519/ED448 are listed in the table, but the document doesn't specify EdDSA itself, which RFC 8032 and RFC 8080 do.
The subject is cryptographic algorithm selection, but it's specific to DNSSEC, so the DNSSEC tag fits better.
RSA-based DNSSEC algorithms are only listed with their requirement levels and are not specified here.

RFC8625.title: Ethernet Traffic Parameters with Availability Information
RFC8625.summary: Defines a Bandwidth Availability TLV carried in the Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC/FLOWSPEC object of RSVP-TE signaling so GMPLS LSPs can be set up over links with variable discrete bandwidth (e.g., microwave) with per-bandwidth availability requirements.

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE signaling with a new TLV and specifies the PATH/PathErr processing rules for it.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document introduces an optional Bandwidth Availability TLV in RSVP-TE signaling.

GMPLS.why: The extension is a GMPLS signaling extension for Ethernet LSPs, building on the GMPLS RSVP-TE and Ethernet traffic parameter specs, and registers in the GMPLS signaling parameters registry.
GMPLS.quote: This extension can be used to set up a GMPLS Label Switched Path (LSP) in conjunction with the Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC object.

rejected.why: OSPF TE advertisement of availability is only referenced (RFC 8330) as the companion routing extension; this document specifies only signaling.
Ethernet appears only as the traffic-parameter object (RFC 6003) the TLV is carried in; the document does not address IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
Implied as the parent of RSVP-TE, so not listed separately.
DSL and microwave are only mentioned as example link types with variable bandwidth.
The IANA section merely registers one TLV type value, which is boilerplate.

RFC8627.title: RTP Payload Format for Flexible Forward Error Correction (FEC)
RFC8627.summary: Defines RTP payload formats for Flexible FEC (FlexFEC): XOR parity repair packets (1-D row, 1-D column, 2-D, flexible mask, retransmission) in a separate redundancy RTP stream, with media type registrations, SDP mapping, and recovery procedures.

FEC.why: The document specifies XOR parity FEC codes (row, column, 2-D, flexible mask), repair packet construction and iterative recovery for packet loss.
FEC.quote: defines new RTP payload formats for the Forward Error Correction (FEC) that is generated by the non-interleaved and interleaved parity codes

RTP payload format.why: It is an RTP payload format specification, with FEC header layout and flexfec media type registrations for audio, video, text and application.
RTP payload format.quote: This document defines new RTP payload formats for the Forward Error Correction (FEC) packets

rejected.why: RTP is the substrate; the more specific RTP payload format tag covers this document.
SDP is used only for signalling parameters and examples, not specified or extended here.
The flexfec media type registrations are boilerplate-like payload format parameters, not a registry-rules document.
It borrows definitions from RFC 6363 but defines a standalone RTP parity format, not a FECFRAME scheme.
RTCP feedback such as NACK is mentioned only in passing.
The congestion control section is a short considerations section, not the document's main subject.

RFC8628.title: OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant
RFC8628.summary: Defines the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant, a new endpoint, polling token flow, and error codes letting input-constrained or browserless devices obtain user authorization via a secondary device.

OAuth.why: The document specifies a new OAuth grant type with a device authorization endpoint, new token error codes, and discovery metadata; it is an OAuth extension.
OAuth.quote: This OAuth 2.0 [RFC6749] protocol extension enables OAuth clients to request user authorization from applications on devices that have limited input capabilities

rejected.why: HTTP POST and form encoding are only the substrate; the document defines no new HTTP semantics.
TLS is required for requests but only as a security mechanism, with nothing new defined about it.
JSON is only the response encoding.
It registers one OAuth grant-type URN, but this is IANA boilerplate rather than the subject of the document.
The devices (TVs, printers) are consumer devices rather than constrained IoT nodes, and the document is not about IoT architecture.
The OAuth tag is more specific and already covers the authorization subject.

gaps.name: OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no OAuth tag at all, only its children JWT and GNAP. The OAuth id I used above is not in the taxonomy and does not exist as a valid tag, so the closest valid option is the parent topic authorization or authentication.

RFC8629.title: Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) Multi-Hop Forwarding Extension
RFC8629.summary: Defines a DLEP extension (Multi-Hop Forwarding) with Hop Count and Hop Control data items letting modems report multi-hop forwarding and routers request direct connections or suppress forwarding.

DLEP.why: The whole document specifies a DLEP extension with new data items, an extension type value, and a registry for DLEP.
DLEP.quote: This document defines an extension to the Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) that enables the reporting and control of multi-hop forwarding by DLEP-capable modems.

rejected.why: MANET is the parent of DLEP and is implied; the document is about the DLEP extension, not MANET routing itself.
TLS is only mentioned as the security mechanism DLEP uses in Security Considerations; nothing new is defined about it.
IANA registrations are boilerplate for this extension; the document is not about IANA guidance.

RFC8630.title: Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Trust Anchor Locator
RFC8630.summary: Defines the RPKI Trust Anchor Locator (TAL) file format, which lets Relying Parties fetch and verify a self-signed TA CA certificate via rsync or HTTPS URIs, obsoleting RFC 7730 by adding HTTPS support and comments.

RPKI.why: The document specifies the TAL format and Relying Party procedures for retrieving and validating RPKI trust anchors, which is core RPKI material.
RPKI.quote: This document defines a Trust Anchor Locator (TAL) for the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) [RFC6480].

rejected.why: The TA is a self-signed X.509 certificate, but the document only profiles how it is located and verified. X.509 itself is a substrate here.
HTTPS validation is required, but the document only points to RFC 7525 and RFC 6125. It defines nothing new about TLS.
HTTPS URIs are used only as a retrieval mechanism for the TA certificate.
The TA URI uses rsync and HTTPS schemes, but the document does not define a new URI scheme or syntax.
The RPKI tag is the more specific fit under routing security. PKI is not needed in addition.
Base64 only encodes the key inside the TAL file. It is an encoding detail.

RFC8631.title: Link Relation Types for Web Services
RFC8631.summary: Defines and registers the link relation types service-doc, service-desc, service-meta and status so Web services/APIs can link to their documentation, machine-readable descriptions, metadata and status resources.

web linking.why: The document's purpose is to define new typed link relations under the RFC 8288 Web Linking framework, so readers of web linking would want it.
web linking.quote: this specification introduces and registers three new link relation types

HTTP APIs.why: The relations are conventions for discovering documentation, descriptions and status of HTTP/Web APIs, which suits readers building APIs on HTTP.
HTTP APIs.quote: "Web Services" or "Web APIs" (sometimes also referred to as "HTTP API" or "REST API") expose information and services on the Web.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the substrate; the document defines no HTTP semantics or extensions.
URIs are used as link targets, but nothing new about URIs is specified.
The Atom Publishing Protocol's existing 'service' relation is only mentioned as an alternative.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate-style registry actions for the new relations, not a subject of the document.
A more specific child tag (web linking) already applies, so the parent is implied.

RFC8632.title: A YANG Data Model for Alarm Management
RFC8632.summary: Defines the ietf-alarms YANG module (alarm list, inventory, shelving, profiles, operator and admin actions, notifications) plus an X.733 mapping module for alarm management.

YANG.why: The document's deliverable is a pair of YANG modules (ietf-alarms and ietf-alarms-x733) modelling alarm management.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG module [RFC7950] for alarm management.

network management.why: Alarm management and monitoring is a network operations topic. It covers alarm lifecycle, usability requirements and mapping to X.733, 3GPP and G.7710. No more specific tag fits.
network management.quote: The purpose is to define a standardized alarm interface for network devices that can be easily integrated into management applications.

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the protocol used to access the data model; the document does not specify it.
RESTCONF is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an access protocol.
The Alarm MIB (RFC 3877) is only compared in an appendix; the document defines no MIB.
SNMP is mentioned only for resource identification and for the Alarm MIB comparison.
X.733 is OSI-derived, but the document maps its alarm parameters into YANG and does not specify CMIP.
Logging is mentioned only to distinguish events and logs from alarms.

gaps.name: Alarm management / fault management
gaps.why: The document is chiefly about alarm and fault management (alarm lists, shelving, X.733 mapping), and no fault-management tag exists in the taxonomy.

RFC8633.title: Network Time Protocol Best Current Practices
RFC8633.summary: BCP document collecting best practices for operating NTPv4 servers and clients, covering configuration, leap-second handling, security mechanisms and attacks, embedded devices, and anycast NTP.

NTP.why: The whole document is operational and security guidance for NTP, including time sources, leap seconds, KoD, and control messages.
NTP.quote: This document is a collection of best practices for the general operation of NTP servers and clients on the Internet.

operational security.why: A substantial part covers security practices for operating NTP infrastructure, including information leakage, daemon restart attacks, amplification control, and BCP 38 filtering.
operational security.quote: Operators SHOULD monitor their NTP instances to detect attacks.  Many known attacks on NTP have particular signatures.

anycast.why: A dedicated section covers deploying NTP over anycast, with its issues and recommendations.
anycast.quote: Anycast can also be used in large organizations to simplify the configuration of many NTP clients.

rejected.why: Amplification attacks are discussed, but only as motivation for filtering and blocking control messages, not as DDoS mitigation in its own right.
Mentioned only as an optional external protection for NTP packets in one paragraph.
Mentioned only as the weak MAC hash in RFC 5905; not the subject of the document.
The embedded devices section is short and covers vendor update and server configuration guidance, not IoT architectures.
UDP is only the substrate NTP runs over and is mentioned for spoofing susceptibility.

RFC8634.title: BGPsec Router Certificate Rollover
RFC8634.summary: BCP describing a safe process for rolling over BGPsec router certificates and key pairs in the RPKI, including when rollover is needed and its use to mitigate replay attacks and withdrawal suppression.

BGPsec.why: The whole document is about operating BGPsec router keys and certificates so that BGPsec UPDATE signatures stay verifiable, and about using rollover against replay of BGPsec updates.
BGPsec.quote: This document describes a safe rollover process, and it discusses when and why the rollover of BGPsec router certificates is necessary.

RPKI.why: The rollover process is defined in terms of RPKI publication, staging, CRL revocation and relying-party propagation, so RPKI readers would want it.
RPKI.quote: it is extremely important that new BGPsec router certificates have been distributed throughout the RPKI before the router begins signing BGPsec UPDATE messages

rejected.why: BGP UPDATE messages are the objects being signed, but the document addresses BGPsec key management, not BGP protocol or policy.
EST is mentioned only as an example of automated provisioning that shortens the rollover interval. It is not specified or profiled here, and no EST tag is in the taxonomy anyway.
Considered because the document covers key rollover. The BGPsec tag is more specific, and the topic tag is not needed on top of it.
Router certificates are X.509, but the document does not profile certificates. It describes an operational process.

RFC8635.title: Router Keying for BGPsec
RFC8635.summary: RFC 8635 describes how BGPsec-speaking routers are provisioned with public-private key pairs and router certificates, using router-driven or operator-driven key generation, PKCS#10/PKCS#7 exchange with the RPKI CA, and key lifecycle management.

BGPsec.why: The whole document is about keying BGPsec routers: generating keys, obtaining router certificates, and managing validity, rollover, revocation and replacement.
BGPsec.quote: This document describes provisioning of BGPsec-speaking routers with the appropriate public-private key pairs.

RPKI.why: Router certificates are issued by RPKI CAs and published in the Global RPKI. The document covers trust anchor installation, certificate issuance, CRL revocation and publication.
RPKI.quote: The operator uses RPKI management tools to communicate with the Global RPKI system to have the appropriate CA validate the PKCS#10 certification request

key management.why: A substantial part of the document covers key generation, provisioning, transfer of private keys, validity, rollover, revocation and escrow for router replacement.
key management.quote: Key management not only includes key generation, key provisioning, certificate issuance, and certificate distribution, it also includes assurance of key validity, key rollover

rejected.why: SSH is only the assumed protected channel to the router, and Appendix A gives algorithm guidance for it. The document does not specify or extend SSH.
EST is listed as one of several options for exchanging certificates and requests. The document does not profile or extend it.
CMS SignedData and PKCS#8 are used to wrap transferred private keys, but only as an encapsulation mechanism.
Router certificates are X.509 certificates, but the profile is in RFC 8209. This document is about provisioning, not certificate content.
The document's PKI subject is the RPKI, which is tagged. The generic PKI enrollment mechanisms it names are used only as options.
NETCONF is mentioned only as an alternative configuration channel.

RFC8636.title: Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication in Kerberos (PKINIT) Algorithm Agility
RFC8636.summary: RFC 8636 updates Kerberos PKINIT (RFC 4556) for algorithm agility: it adds negotiable SP800-56A-based key derivation functions, and lets the KDC advertise acceptable CMS and certificate digest algorithms in error typed data.

Kerberos.why: The document extends PKINIT, the public-key initial authentication mechanism of Kerberos, with a negotiable KDF and new typed data in KDC errors. Kerberos readers need it.
Kerberos.quote: Section 3.2.3.1 of [RFC4556] is updated to define additional key derivation functions (KDFs) to derive a Kerberos protocol key

rejected.why: The theme is algorithm agility and hash/KDF negotiation, but it is applied to a Kerberos protocol extension. No generic crypto algorithm is specified, so the Kerberos tag fits better.
Certificate signing digest algorithms are made discoverable via error data, but X.509 is not profiled or extended.
CMS digest algorithm identifiers are listed in typed data, but CMS is only the substrate for PKINIT signed data.
The document defines ASN.1 structures and a module, but ASN.1 is just the notation used, not the subject.
SHA-1, SHA-256 and others are used as hash functions in the KDFs, but the SHA family is not specified or analysed.
X.509 certificates are involved, but PKI itself is not the subject.

gaps.name: PKINIT
gaps.why: The document is specifically about PKINIT, public-key initial authentication within Kerberos, and the taxonomy has no PKINIT tag. The Kerberos tag is the closest fit.

RFC8637.title: Applicability of the Path Computation Element (PCE) to the Abstraction and Control of TE Networks (ACTN)
RFC8637.summary: Informational RFC examining how the PCE architecture and PCEP (including hierarchical stateful PCE) can realize the ACTN framework's functions and MDSC-PNC/CNC-MDSC interfaces for multidomain TE networks.

PCE.why: The whole document is about applying PCE architecture and PCEP (stateful, hierarchical, PCE-initiated LSPs) to ACTN, mapping MDSC to Parent PCE and PNC to Child PCE.
PCE.quote: This document examines the PCE and ACTN architecture and describes how PCE architecture is applicable to ACTN.

traffic engineering.why: ACTN is a framework for abstraction and control of multidomain TE networks, virtual network operations, and abstraction of TE topology. This topic tag is not a child of PCE, so it is listed separately.
traffic engineering.quote: orchestrate, control, and manage large-scale multidomain TE networks

rejected.why: SDN is mentioned as background for PCE's role, but the document is not about SDN in its own right.
BGP-LS is mentioned only as an alternative way to obtain topology.
MPLS/GMPLS LSPs are the setting for PCE computation, but the document does not specify or analyse GMPLS.
TLS is only the security transport for PCEP (RFC 8253), mentioned in Security Considerations.
NETCONF and RESTCONF are cited only as alternatives to PCEP for topology access.
MPLS TE LSPs are the substrate that PCE computes paths for, and the document is not about MPLS.

gaps.name: ACTN (Abstraction and Control of TE Networks)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the ACTN framework, so the subject is covered only partly by the traffic engineering topic.

RFC8638.title: IPv4 Multicast over an IPv6 Multicast in Softwire Mesh Networks
RFC8638.summary: Specifies how AFBRs in an IPv6 softwire mesh core carry IPv4 multicast by algorithmically mapping IPv4 group/source addresses to IPv6 and translating PIM messages between IPv4 and IPv6.

softwire.why: It is a softwire mesh document (WG softwire). It defines IPv4-over-IPv6 multicast transit in the softwire mesh framework.
softwire.quote: This document describes a mechanism for supporting multicast across backbone networks where the I-IP and E-IP protocol families differ.

PIM-SM.why: A large part of the document covers PIM-SM message translation, (S,G,rpt) state handling, SPT switchover and the interface agent.
PIM-SM.quote: The AFBR translates the PIMv4 message into a PIMv6 message with the latter being directed towards the I-IP IPv6 address of the upstream AFBR.

multicast.why: The document covers multicast group and source address mapping, and multicast tree construction across the core. This is a multicast deployment topic beyond PIM alone.
multicast.quote: AFBRs will prepend the prefix to an IPv4 multicast group address when translating it to an IPv6 multicast group address.

rejected.why: MBGP is used only to announce the uPrefix64 and E-IP next hops. The document does not specify or extend BGP.
MVPN is discussed only as an alternative approach that this document does not use.
The core is treated as SSM-only, but the document does not specify SSM itself. It reuses the SSM mapping from RFC 8114.
DS-Lite is mentioned only as the scenario RFC 8114 targets. It is not the subject of this document.
The more specific softwire tag applies, and its ancestors are implied.
Encapsulation is left to RFC 5565 and RFC 4925 and is not specified here.

RFC8639.title: Subscription to YANG Notifications
RFC8639.summary: RFC 8639 defines a YANG data model and mechanisms (RPCs, state-change notifications, configured and dynamic subscriptions) for subscribing to a publisher's event streams, transport-independent and superseding RFC 5277 subscriptions.

YANG.why: The document's core is the ietf-subscribed-notifications YANG module with RPCs, notifications and data nodes for subscriptions; readers of YANG models would want it.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model and associated mechanisms enabling subscriber-specific subscriptions to a publisher's event streams.

NETCONF.why: It extends and replaces NETCONF event notification subscriptions (RFC 5277), reuses the NETCONF stream and subtree filtering, and defines the notification mechanism that NETCONF and RESTCONF bindings build on.
NETCONF.quote: This document is intended to provide a superset of the subscription capabilities initially defined in [RFC5277].

rejected.why: RESTCONF is only one possible transport; its binding is defined in a separate document.
The mechanism is used for streaming operational data, but the document frames itself as an event subscription model rather than telemetry as a subject.
DSCP marking is a minor QoS parameter of subscriptions, not a substantial subject of the document.
XML and XPath filters are used as filter syntaxes and encodings, not as the subject.
TLS and SSH are only mentioned in the security considerations as secure transports.
The document is not about SNMP; it only provides a YANG-based push alternative.

RFC8640.title: Dynamic Subscription to YANG Events and Datastores over NETCONF
RFC8640.summary: RFC 8640 defines the NETCONF binding for dynamic subscriptions from Subscribed Notifications (RFC 8639) and YANG-Push (RFC 8641), covering session behavior, notification encoding, and RPC error mapping.

NETCONF.why: The document specifies how dynamic subscriptions are carried over NETCONF: session handling, <notification> encoding, and <rpc-error> mapping. It is a NETCONF extension.
NETCONF.quote: This document specifies the binding of a stream of events that form part of a dynamic subscription to the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF)

YANG.why: It covers subscription to YANG notifications and datastore updates (RFC 8639 and RFC 8641), including the mapping of their YANG error identities and yang-data structures. Readers of YANG-related subjects would want it.
YANG.quote: this document enables a NETCONF client to request via a dynamic subscription, and receive, updates from a YANG datastore located on a NETCONF server.

rejected.why: XML is mandated as the encoding, but it is only the substrate and the document defines nothing new about XML.
The document is about subscription mechanics over NETCONF. Telemetry is the broader purpose and the document does not address it in its own right.
Not mentioned or relevant.
VRRP appears only as an example notification source in the filter examples, and the document is not about VRRP.

RFC8641.title: Subscription to YANG Notifications for Datastore Updates
RFC8641.summary: Defines YANG-Push, a mechanism built on RFC 8639 that lets subscribers request periodic or on-change streams of updates from a YANG datastore, with a YANG module, RPCs, notifications and error handling.

YANG.why: The document specifies a YANG module (ietf-yang-push) with augmentations, RPCs and notifications for datastore subscriptions, so it belongs on the YANG page.
YANG.quote: This document describes a mechanism that allows subscriber applications to request a continuous and customized stream of updates from a YANG datastore.

telemetry.why: Streaming operational and configuration data from network elements to subscribers, as an alternative to polling, is network telemetry.
telemetry.quote: enables new capabilities based on the remote mirroring and monitoring of configuration and operational state.

rejected.why: NETCONF is the transport and the source of the subtree filter and examples. The transport bindings are in RFC 8640, not this document.
RESTCONF is mentioned only for yang-data and in the security considerations, so it is not a subject of this document.
XML is only the encoding used in the examples, and the XPath filter is a minor detail.
SNMP is not discussed. The polling-versus-push contrast concerns management generally and does not involve SNMP.

gaps.name: YANG-Push / YANG notification subscription
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for YANG event or datastore subscription and push. YANG and telemetry cover it only approximately.

RFC8642.title: Policy Behavior for Well-Known BGP Communities
RFC8642.summary: Updates RFC 1997 by documenting how vendor BGP implementations differ in their "set community" handling of well-known communities, and requires implementors not to introduce further inconsistency and to document the behaviour.

BGP communities.why: The whole document concerns how well-known BGP communities are manipulated by policy, updating RFC 1997 (the BGP Communities attribute), and gives vendor-specific behaviours and requirements.
BGP communities.quote: Well-known BGP communities are manipulated differently across various current implementations, resulting in difficulties for operators.

rejected.why: The document is about the communities attribute specifically, which has a more specific child tag. BGP itself is only the context.
The only IANA content is a reference to the well-known communities registry in the IANA Considerations section, which is boilerplate. The document is not about IANA registry guidance.
The document touches on operator practice, but its Security Considerations section is minimal and the subject is policy behaviour, not security practice.

RFC8643.title: An Opportunistic Approach for Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (OSRTP)
RFC8643.summary: RFC 8643 defines OSRTP, an opportunistic-security approach in which an SDP offer using RTP/AVP or RTP/AVPF carries SRTP keying attributes so SRTP is used if the peer supports it, otherwise falling back to plain RTP.

SRTP.why: The document specifies how SRTP is opportunistically negotiated in place of plain RTP, and is not specific to any SRTP key management method.
SRTP.quote: OSRTP allows SRTP to be negotiated with the RTP/AVP profile, with fallback to RTP if SRTP is not supported.

SDP.why: The normative body is the SDP offer/answer procedure: how offers, answers and subsequent offers signal and accept OSRTP using keying attributes.
SDP.quote: This section defines the SDP offer/answer considerations for opportunistic security.

rejected.why: OSRTP is explicitly independent of any key management technique, so the document is not about key management itself.
SIP appears only in passing, as a signalling context and in the RFC 6337 reference, and the document does not specify SIP behaviour.
DTLS-SRTP is only one of several keying methods cited as an example.
MIKEY is not mentioned in the document.
The document is about a specific mechanism, so the more specific SRTP tag applies.
The more specific SRTP tag applies, since the document concerns secure RTP negotiation rather than RTP itself.

gaps.name: Opportunistic Security
gaps.why: The document applies the RFC 7435 Opportunistic Security model to RTP, but the taxonomy has no tag for opportunistic security as a general subject.

RFC8645.title: Re-keying Mechanisms for Symmetric Keys
RFC8645.summary: CFRG informational RFC specifying external (parallel, serial, tree-based) and internal (ACPKM, ACPKM-Master) re-keying mechanisms to extend symmetric key lifetime for block cipher modes such as CTR, GCM, CBC, CFB and OMAC.

key management.why: The document defines re-keying and key derivation mechanisms for symmetric keys, which is key lifecycle management. No narrower technology tag fits.
key management.quote: This specification describes a variety of methods for increasing the lifetime of symmetric keys.

cryptography.why: A large part of the document defines new block cipher modes (CTR-ACPKM, GCM-ACPKM, CBC/CFB/OMAC-ACPKM-Master) with test vectors. This is cryptographic algorithm specification that the key management tag does not cover.
cryptography.quote: It provides two types of re-keying mechanisms based on hash functions and block ciphers that can be used with modes of operations such as CTR, GCM, CBC, CFB, and OMAC.

rejected.why: AES is used only for the test vectors. The mechanisms work with any block cipher.
HKDF-Expand is used as one KDF instantiation, but the document is not about HMAC.
TLS is cited only as an example protocol that could use the mechanisms.
RFC 7836 is referenced only for a KDF example. The document is not about GOST algorithms.
CMS is mentioned only as an example of a protocol that processes long messages.

gaps.name: Symmetric block cipher modes of operation (re-keying, ACPKM)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for block cipher modes or authenticated encryption modes. The new modes this RFC defines are covered only loosely by the generic cryptography topic.

RFC8649.title: Hash Of Root Key Certificate Extension
RFC8649.summary: Defines the HashOfRootKey X.509 v3 certificate extension, carried in a Root CA self-signed certificate, that commits to the hash of the next-generation root public key to enable orderly trust anchor rollover, with operational and security guidance.

X.509.why: The document defines a new X.509 v3 certificate extension, with ASN.1 syntax and OID, as an optional addition to the RFC 5280 certificate profile. Readers of X.509 certificate profiles and extensions would want it.
X.509.quote: This document specifies the Hash Of Root Key X.509 version 3 certificate extension.

PKI.why: A substantial part of the document covers root CA key rollover, trust anchor store management and relying party behaviour, in the Overview and Operational Considerations sections. This is PKI operational practice beyond the certificate format.
PKI.quote: The certificate extension facilitates the orderly transition from one Root Certification Authority (CA) public key to the next.

rejected.why: ASN.1 and DER are only the notation and encoding used to define the extension. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
RFC 4210 is cited only for its oldWithNew/newWithOld rollover guidance. The document does not specify or extend CMP.
The document is hash-algorithm agnostic and does not specify any particular SHA algorithm.
The document uses hashes as a commitment mechanism and discusses preimage resistance only in the Security Considerations. It does not address cryptographic algorithms in their own right.
The CMC 'certs-only' message is mentioned only as a way to distribute transition certificates. The document does not specify or extend CMS.

RFC8650.title: Dynamic Subscription to YANG Events and Datastores over RESTCONF
RFC8650.summary: Specifies the RESTCONF binding for dynamic subscriptions from Subscribed Notifications and YANG-Push, covering the establish/GET flow with Server-Sent Events, error codes, QoS mapping to HTTP/2, and a small YANG module adding a subscription URI.

RESTCONF.why: The document defines how dynamic subscriptions operate over RESTCONF, including POSTs for RPCs, HTTP status codes, and SSE streaming.
RESTCONF.quote: This document provides a RESTCONF binding to the dynamic subscription capability of both subscribed notifications and YANG-Push.

YANG.why: It defines a YANG module (ietf-restconf-subscribed-notifications) augmenting subscription nodes with a URI leaf, and the subject is YANG notifications and datastore subscription.
YANG.quote: The YANG module defined in Section 7 has one leaf that augments three nodes of [RFC8639].

rejected.why: HTTP/2 stream weight and dependency mapping is used for QoS, but only in a short section; it is substrate.
TLS and its heartbeat are required for security of the session, but the document does not define anything new about TLS.
NETCONF is referenced for comparison and the sibling RFC 8640, but this document is about RESTCONF.
HTTP is the substrate for RESTCONF; the document uses status codes and GET/POST but does not specify HTTP.
JSON is only the encoding for examples and error tags.
VRRP appears only as an example notification source in a filter example.

RFC8651.title: Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) Control-Plane-Based Pause Extension
RFC8651.summary: Defines a DLEP extension (Control-Plane-Based Pause) with Queue Parameters, Pause and Restart data items so a modem can pause and resume DSCP-aware traffic from its peer router.

DLEP.why: The document specifies a new DLEP extension with new data items, an extension type value and a new sub-registry. DLEP is the protocol being extended.
DLEP.quote: This document defines an extension to the Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) that enables a modem to use DLEP messages to pause and resume data traffic

rejected.why: DSCPs are used to group traffic into queues, but the document does not specify or extend Diffserv. It only references the DS field.
The pause is a link-local flow-control mechanism between router and modem. It is not a transport congestion control scheme.
PPPoE credit flow control is cited only as a parallel for the mechanism. The document does not specify PPPoE.
TLS is only the security mechanism mandated by RFC 8175. It is mentioned in Security Considerations and the document defines nothing new about it.
The working group is manet, but the document is about the DLEP modem/router link and not MANET routing. The DLEP tag sits under MANET, so it is implied.

RFC8652.title: A YANG Data Model for the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) and Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD)
RFC8652.summary: Defines the ietf-igmp-mld YANG module for configuring and monitoring IGMP (v1-v3) and MLD (v1-v2) devices, augmenting the ietf-routing model, with operational state, statistics and clear-groups actions.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG data model (module ietf-igmp-mld) with tree diagrams and module source.
