YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model that can be used to configure and manage Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) and Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) devices.

IGMP.why: The model configures and monitors IGMP, including versions, query parameters, group state and statistics.
IGMP.quote: The model covers IGMPv1 [RFC1112], IGMPv2 [RFC2236], IGMPv3 [RFC3376], MLDv1 [RFC2710], and MLDv2 [RFC3810].

MLD.why: MLD is the IPv6 counterpart modelled in its own branch, covering MLDv1 and MLDv2.
MLD.quote: The "mld" container instantiates an MLD protocol of version MLDv1 or MLDv2.

rejected.why: Only the management protocol the model is accessed over; the document doesn't specify or extend it.
SSM mapping is one optional leaf (ssm-map); the document is not about source-specific multicast.
Mentioned only as an access protocol and in Security Considerations.
Parent of IGMP and MLD, which are tagged more specifically.
This is a YANG model, not a MIB module.

RFC8653.title: On-Demand Mobility Management
RFC8653.summary: Defines On-Demand Mobility Management: applications indicate per-socket whether they need session continuity and/or IP address reachability, with four IP address types and suggested socket API extensions, to avoid unnecessary Mobile IP costs.

IP mobility.why: The document is about selecting mobility services (session continuity, address reachability) at the IP layer, in the context of Mobile IP and distributed mobility management. No specific Mobile IP technology tag fits better, since it is a general concept rather than a protocol extension.
IP mobility.quote: enabling applications to influence the network's mobility services (session continuity and/or IP address reachability) on a per-socket basis

sockets API.why: A substantial part (Section 3 and Appendix A) proposes socket API extensions, such as new flags for IPV6_ADDR_PREFERENCE and a setsc() function, and relates them to RFC 5014.
sockets API.quote: suggests extensions to the networking stack's API to accommodate this concept

rejected.why: Mobile IP is cited as the context and the source of the cost problem, but the document does not specify or extend Mobile IPv6.
Cited only as background for existing mobility architectures; the document does not specify or extend it.
Mentioned only as an example of a higher-layer solution for session continuity.
SIP mobility is mentioned only as an example of a higher-layer alternative.
The API discussion builds on the IPv6 socket API (RFC 5014), but the document is not about IPv6 itself.

gaps.name: Distributed Mobility Management (DMM)
gaps.why: The document comes from the dmm working group and addresses DMM requirements (RFC 7333). The taxonomy has no DMM tag, so IP mobility is the closest fit.

RFC8654.title: Extended Message Support for BGP
RFC8654.summary: RFC 8654 updates BGP (RFC 4271) to raise the maximum message size from 4,096 to 65,535 octets for all messages except OPEN and KEEPALIVE, using a new BGP Extended Message capability (code 6).

BGP.why: The document extends the BGP protocol itself: it defines a new capability, operational behaviour, error handling and changes to RFC 4271.
BGP.quote: This document updates the BGP specification by extending the maximum message size from 4,096 octets to 65,535 octets for all messages except for OPEN and KEEPALIVE messages.

rejected.why: BGPsec is cited only as an example of a feature that drives the need for larger messages; the document does not specify or analyse it.
The Security Considerations are brief and boilerplate-like. The document is not about securing routing.
The only IANA content is a single capability code allocation, which is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC8655.title: Deterministic Networking Architecture
RFC8655.summary: RFC 8655 specifies the overall Deterministic Networking (DetNet) architecture, providing bounded latency and extremely low loss for flows via resource allocation, service protection (packet replication/elimination) and explicit routes over MPLS and TSN.

DetNet.why: The document is the DetNet architecture itself, defining its goals, sub-layers, node types, flows and planes.
DetNet.quote: This document provides the overall architecture for Deterministic Networking (DetNet), which provides a capability to carry specified unicast or multicast data flows for real-time applications

rejected.why: MPLS is one of the lower-layer data planes DetNet runs over; its DetNet specifics are in a separate document.
The document says DetNet is a specialized branch of TE, but the DetNet tag already covers this.
DetNet QoS is the subject, but the DetNet tag is more specific and QoS mechanisms such as RSVP and Diffserv are only mentioned.
TSN/IEEE 802.1 is the underlying subnet technology, mentioned for mapping and shaping, not the subject.
Mentioned only as one way to establish explicit routes.
PCE is mentioned only as an example of a controller plane function.

gaps.name: Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN, IEEE 802.1)
gaps.why: The document relates DetNet to TSN and its queuing, shaping and replication mechanisms, but the taxonomy has no TSN tag.

RFC8656.title: Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN): Relay Extensions to Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)
RFC8656.summary: RFC 8656 specifies TURN, a STUN extension letting a client behind a NAT allocate a relayed transport address on a server and exchange packets with peers through it, obsoleting RFC 5766 and RFC 6156 (adding IPv6, DTLS, ICMP relaying, and Happy Eyeballs).

TURN.why: The document is the core TURN protocol specification: allocations, permissions, channels, attributes and error codes.
TURN.quote: This specification defines a protocol, called "TURN", that allows a host behind a NAT (called the "TURN client") to request that another host (called the "TURN server") act as a relay.

rejected.why: TURN is an extension to STUN and relies on RFC 8489 for base processing. STUN itself is not specified here, so I did not tag it.
The document says TURN was designed to be used with ICE. ICE is only the usual context, and its procedures are not specified here.
Section 13 covers IPv4/IPv6 packet translation in the relay. This is an incidental part of TURN's address-family support, not a transition mechanism, so I did not tag it.
(D)TLS is only an optional transport for TURN messages. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
Section 3.9 applies RFC 8305 to TURN server connections. It is a small part of the document and does not define the mechanism.
NAT is the problem context for TURN. The document does not specify NAT behaviour.

RFC8657.title: Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) Record Extensions for Account URI and Automatic Certificate Management Environment (ACME) Method Binding
RFC8657.summary: Defines two CAA DNS record parameters, "accounturi" and "validationmethods", that let a domain restrict certificate issuance to specific CA accounts and ACME validation methods.

ACME.why: The document binds CAA policy to ACME accounts and ACME validation methods. It defines how ACME account URIs and ACME validation method labels are used, so ACME readers would want it.
ACME.quote: one allowing specific methods of domain control validation as defined by the Automatic Certificate Management Environment (ACME) protocol to be required

DNS.why: It extends the CAA DNS resource record with new parameters. There is no CAA-specific tag, so the DNS tag is the nearest fit.
DNS.quote: This specification defines two parameters for the "issue" and "issuewild" Properties of the Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) DNS resource record

rejected.why: DNSSEC appears in the Security Considerations as a condition for the parameters to be effective, but the document does not specify or extend DNSSEC.
The document concerns CA issuance policy, but ACME is the more specific tag. The PKI parent is implied by ACME.
Account URIs are used as parameter values, but the document does not define URI syntax or schemes.
ABNF is only used to state the value syntax of one parameter.

gaps.name: CAA (Certification Authority Authorization) record
gaps.why: The document is about extending CAA records. The taxonomy has no CAA tag, so DNS is used as an approximation.

RFC8658.title: RADIUS Attributes for Softwire Mechanisms Based on Address plus Port (A+P)
RFC8658.summary: Defines new RADIUS attributes (Softwire46-Configuration, Priority, Multicast) carrying MAP-E, MAP-T, Lightweight 4over6 and multicast softwire configuration from a AAA server to a BNG, which maps them to DHCPv6 options.

RADIUS.why: The document's core deliverable is a set of new RADIUS attributes, with their formats, packet usage and IANA registries.
RADIUS.quote: This document defines new RADIUS attributes to carry softwire configuration parameters based on Address plus Port from a AAA server to a Broadband Network Gateway.

MAP.why: It carries MAP-E and MAP-T rules, BR, DMR and port-set parameters, so readers of MAP want it.

softwire.why: The document is broadly about configuring softwire mechanisms, including Lightweight 4over6 and multicast softwires.
softwire.quote: Softwire46 (S46) is used throughout to denote any of the IPv4-in-IPv6 softwire mechanisms listed above.

DHCPv6.why: It maps RADIUS attributes 1:1 to the DHCPv6 S46 options (Appendix A) and gives a DHCPv6/RADIUS interworking flow.
DHCPv6.quote: The BNG SHALL use the configuration information returned in the RADIUS attribute to populate the DHCPv6 Softwire46 container option(s)

rejected.why: It is only mentioned as an existing RADIUS attribute and as an option code in a registry. It is not the subject.
The softwire and MAP tags are more specific, and the document is about configuration signalling, not the transition mechanisms themselves.
RADIUS is the more specific tag under AAA.
Multicast prefix attributes are only one part of the document, and no multicast routing is specified.

RFC8659.title: DNS Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) Resource Record
RFC8659.summary: Defines the DNS CAA resource record, which lets domain holders specify which CAs may issue certificates for a name, and the rules CAs follow when processing CAA records; obsoletes RFC 6844.

DNS.why: The document defines a new DNS resource record type, its syntax, and the tree-climbing lookup algorithm for it, plus deployment issues with DNS servers and resolvers.
DNS.quote: The Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) DNS Resource Record allows a DNS domain name holder to specify the Certification Authorities (CAs) authorized to issue certificates

PKI.why: CAA is a control on CA certificate issuance in the Web PKI; PKI readers would want this document. X.509 is only the certificate type referenced.
PKI.quote: CAA records specify an authorization control to be performed by a CA before issuing a certificate

rejected.why: DNSSEC is recommended for authenticating CAA records, and Section 6.4 covers bogus responses, but the document doesn't specify or extend DNSSEC.
TLSA/DANE is mentioned only as a contrasting mechanism (verification vs. authorization).
Certificates are the subject of authorization but the document does not profile X.509.
The iodef property uses IODEF for reporting, but IODEF is only a referenced format and not specified here.
mailto reporting for iodef is a minor delivery option, not a subject of the document.

RFC8660.title: Segment Routing with the MPLS Data Plane
RFC8660.summary: RFC 8660 specifies the MPLS forwarding-plane behavior for Segment Routing (SR-MPLS): SID-to-label mapping via SRGB/SRLB, incoming label collision resolution, and PUSH/CONTINUE/NEXT operations.

SR-MPLS.why: The whole document defines SR over the MPLS data plane: SID representation as labels, SRGB index mapping, collision handling, and forwarding operations.
SR-MPLS.quote: This document specifies the forwarding behavior to allow instantiating SR over the MPLS data plane (SR-MPLS).

rejected.why: SR-MPLS is the more specific child; MPLS is the substrate and no change to the MPLS forwarding plane is defined.
Parent of SR-MPLS, implied by the more specific tag.
IS-IS SR extensions are only referenced as example MCCs; control plane is out of scope.
OSPF is referenced as a control-plane client only; its extensions are specified in other RFCs.
LDP interworking is delegated to RFC 8661; it is mentioned only as an alternative label source.
TI-LFA is mentioned only as an example use of PUSH; not the subject.
Manageability section just points to other RFCs for SR OAM.

RFC8661.title: Segment Routing MPLS Interworking with LDP
RFC8661.summary: Specifies how Segment Routing over MPLS coexists and interworks with LDP in mixed SR/non-SR networks, defining the Segment Routing Mapping Server, stitching behaviours, SR-based FRR use cases for LDP traffic, and migration from LDP to SR.

SR-MPLS.why: The whole document is about Segment Routing over the MPLS data plane and its interworking with LDP, including the SRMS and stitching rules.
SR-MPLS.quote: This document describes how Segment Routing MPLS operates in a network where LDP is deployed and in the case where SR-capable and non-SR-capable nodes coexist.

LDP.why: Specifies normative behaviour for LDP-to-SR and SR-to-LDP stitching, and coexistence with LDP label bindings and control modes; a substantial part of the document.
LDP.quote: An SR node having LDP neighbors MUST create LDP bindings for each Prefix-SID learned in the SR domain

IP fast reroute.why: Section 4 shows SR repair tunnels (RLFA) protecting LDP traffic, eliminating targeted LDP sessions and giving guaranteed FRR coverage.
IP fast reroute.quote: The operator requires 50 msec link-based Fast Reroute (FRR) for service S.

rejected.why: The more specific SR-MPLS child tag fits since the document is about SR on the MPLS data plane.
Labeled BGP appears only in the inter-AS Option C use case as a substrate.
IGP extensions for the mapping server are defined in other RFCs and only referenced here.
IS-IS TLVs are referenced for SRMS advertisements but defined in RFC 8667, not here.
Mentioned only as an example of static label range allocation.
VPN services are used only as example traffic in the scenarios, and inter-AS Option C is a minor use case.

RFC8662.title: Entropy Label for Source Packet Routing in Networking (SPRING) Tunnels
RFC8662.summary: RFC 8662 specifies how MPLS entropy labels (ELI/EL pairs) are inserted into Segment Routing MPLS label stacks, introducing ERLD and MSD-aware placement and Binding SID entropy label capability inheritance for load-balancing.

segment routing.why: The document defines how entropy labels are placed in SR label stacks, including Node, Adjacency and Binding SID considerations.
segment routing.quote: This document examines and describes how ELs are to be applied to Segment Routing MPLS.

SR-MPLS.why: The subject is specifically Segment Routing over the MPLS data plane, so the more specific SR-MPLS tag fits better than the parent.
SR-MPLS.quote: When applied to the MPLS data plane [RFC8660], each segment is an LSP (Label Switched Path) with an associated MPLS label value.

MPLS.why: The document extends entropy label use (ELI/EL, ERLD, LSP stitching) in MPLS, so MPLS readers would want it.
MPLS.quote: Entropy labels (ELs) [RFC6790] are used in the MPLS data plane to provide entropy for load-balancing.

ECMP.why: The whole purpose is enabling per-flow load-balancing across equal-cost paths and parallel links for SR tunnels.
ECMP.quote: Traffic load-balancing over ECMP (Equal-Cost Multipath) or LAGs (Link Aggregation Groups) is usually based on a hashing function.

rejected.why: LAGs are mentioned as load-balancing targets but the document is not about link aggregation itself.
LDP appears only in the Binding SID stitching example and ELC propagation, not as a subject.
Mentioned only as something a Binding SID can represent.
ERLD/ELC signalling in IS-IS is deferred to separate documents.
ERLD/ELC signalling in OSPF is deferred to separate documents.
Used as the use case, but the document focuses on load-balancing with entropy labels, not TE.

gaps.name: Entropy labels (ELI/EL) in MPLS load-balancing
gaps.why: The central subject, entropy labels and Entropy Readable Label Depth, has no dedicated tag; closest are MPLS and ECMP.

RFC8663.title: MPLS Segment Routing over IP
RFC8663.summary: Describes how SR-MPLS label stacks can be carried across IP-only routers by tunneling SR-MPLS over IP (e.g., MPLS-over-UDP), including FIB construction and forwarding procedures with and without PHP.

SR-MPLS.why: The whole document specifies how SR-MPLS operates across IP-only networks: FIB construction, label pop/swap, and forwarding procedures.
SR-MPLS.quote: This document describes how SR-MPLS-capable routers and IP-only routers can seamlessly coexist and interoperate through the use of SR-MPLS label stacks and IP encapsulation/tunneling

rejected.why: Mentioned only as one possible underlay; the document is not about SRv6.
OSPF extensions are used in a non-normative example only; the document doesn't specify them.
IS-IS advertisement is used in a non-normative example only; the document doesn't specify it.
MPLS-over-UDP (RFC 7510) is the encapsulation substrate; the document defines nothing new about UDP.
IP tunneling is the mechanism used, but the document is about SR-MPLS over IP, which SR-MPLS covers more specifically.
MPLS is the data plane that SR-MPLS builds on, and the more specific SR-MPLS tag already covers it.
Entropy and ECMP are discussed in a short paragraph, but they are not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC8664.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for Segment Routing
RFC8664.summary: Specifies PCEP extensions (SR-ERO/SR-RRO subobjects, SR path setup type, SR-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV, MSD metric) so a PCE can compute and initiate Segment Routing TE paths on MPLS data plane and a PCC can request them.

PCE.why: The document defines new PCEP objects, subobjects, TLVs, error codes and procedures, so it extends PCEP.
PCE.quote: This document specifies extensions to the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) that allow a stateful PCE to compute and initiate Traffic-Engineering (TE) paths

segment routing.why: It carries SR paths (SIDs, NAIs, MSD, SRGB/SRLB handling) in PCEP, so it belongs on the segment routing page.
segment routing.quote: This document defines a new ERO subobject denoted by "SR-ERO subobject" that is capable of carrying a SID as well as the identity of the node/adjacency
segment routing.section: 3. Overview of PCEP Operation in SR Networks

rejected.why: The document is relevant to the MPLS forwarding plane, but it is about PCEP signalling of SR paths rather than the SR-MPLS data plane. The data plane is specified in RFC 8660.
RSVP-TE is only the alternative path setup type and migration source, not the subject.
MPLS labels are the forwarding substrate here, not the subject.
The IGP supplies the segment database and MSD, but is only referenced.
The IGP supplies the segment database and MSD, but is only referenced.
The PCE tag already sits under it, so the parent is implied.

RFC8665.title: OSPF Extensions for Segment Routing
RFC8665.summary: Defines OSPFv2 extensions (Router Information TLVs, Extended Prefix Range TLV, Prefix-SID, Adj-SID and LAN Adj-SID sub-TLVs, and procedures) to advertise Segment Routing identifiers and capabilities.

segment routing.why: The document specifies how SR prefix, adjacency and capability information is advertised in OSPFv2, which is segment routing control-plane specification.
segment routing.quote: This document describes the OSPFv2 extensions required for Segment Routing.

OSPF.why: It extends OSPFv2 with new TLVs and sub-TLVs, and defines inter-area, external-prefix and DR/LAN procedures.
OSPF.quote: Extended Prefix/Link Opaque Link State Advertisements (LSAs) defined in [RFC7684] are used for advertisements of the various SID types.

rejected.why: The document is the IGP control-plane extension. The MPLS data plane is defined in RFC 8660, and the IPv6 data plane is explicitly out of scope.
OSPFv3 is mentioned only as sharing some TLVs; its extensions are in RFC 8666.
MPLS is the data plane that the SIDs and labels program. The document does not specify MPLS itself.
The IANA section registers code points and is boilerplate, so it is not evidence for this tag.

RFC8666.title: OSPFv3 Extensions for Segment Routing
RFC8666.summary: Defines OSPFv3 extensions (Extended Prefix Range TLV, Prefix-SID, Adj-SID, LAN Adj-SID, SID/Label sub-TLVs) and procedures for advertising Segment Routing information with the MPLS data plane.

OSPFv3.why: The document specifies new OSPFv3 TLVs and sub-TLVs carried in Extended LSAs, plus OSPFv3 procedures for intra-area, inter-area and external prefixes.
OSPFv3.quote: This document describes the OSPFv3 extensions required for Segment Routing with the MPLS data plane.

SR-MPLS.why: It covers Segment Routing over the MPLS data plane: Prefix-SIDs, Adj-SIDs, labels, PHP and explicit-null behaviour.
SR-MPLS.quote: This document describes the OSPFv3 extensions required for Segment Routing with the MPLS data plane.

rejected.why: The document is about the MPLS data plane specifically, so the more specific SR-MPLS child tag is used instead of the parent.
MPLS is only the data plane that SR programs. The document defines OSPFv3 advertisements, not MPLS itself.
LDP is mentioned only as a mechanism SR can interoperate with or replace. The document does not specify it.
The IPv6 data plane is explicitly out of scope for this document.
OSPFv3 is the more specific tag, and this document does not extend OSPFv2.

RFC8667.title: IS-IS Extensions for Segment Routing
RFC8667.summary: Defines IS-IS TLVs and sub-TLVs (Prefix-SID, Adj-SID, LAN-Adj-SID, SID/Label Binding, SR capabilities, algorithm, SRLB, SRMS preference) for Segment Routing over an MPLS data plane.

IS-IS.why: The document specifies new IS-IS TLVs and sub-TLVs, so it extends the IS-IS protocol.
IS-IS.quote: This document describes the IS-IS extensions that need to be introduced for Segment Routing operating on an MPLS data plane.

SR-MPLS.why: It defines the IGP control-plane advertisements (SRGB, SRLB, SIDs, labels) for Segment Routing over the MPLS data plane.
SR-MPLS.quote: SR-Capabilities sub-TLV MUST be propagated throughout the level

rejected.why: The more specific SR-MPLS child fits, since the document is explicitly scoped to the MPLS data plane.
MPLS is only the data plane that SR programs; the document does not specify MPLS itself.
OSPF extensions are only mentioned in passing and are specified in a separate document (RFC 8665).
The document does not cover the IPv6 data plane.
The B-Flag only mentions protection eligibility and the document defines no FRR mechanism.

RFC8668.title: Advertising Layer 2 Bundle Member Link Attributes in IS-IS
RFC8668.summary: Defines a new IS-IS TLV (25) and sub-TLVs (41, 42) to advertise link attributes and Adj-SIDs of individual Layer 2 bundle member links under an L3 interface.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with a new TLV and sub-TLVs for L2 bundle member link attributes.
IS-IS.quote: This document introduces the ability for IS-IS to advertise the link attributes of Layer 2 (L2) Bundle Members.

segment routing.why: A substantial part defines Segment Routing Adj-SID sub-TLVs for bundle members, building on RFC 8667.
segment routing.quote: This document introduces additional sub-TLVs to advertise Adj-SIDs for L2 Bundle Members.

link aggregation.why: The document is about exposing per-member attributes of L2 bundles such as LAGs to the routing system.
link aggregation.quote: the Layer 3 interface on which an IS-IS adjacency is established is a Layer 2 interface bundle, for instance, a Link Aggregation Group (LAG)

rejected.why: PCEs are only an example of external consumers of the advertisements; the document does not specify PCE.
The TE sub-TLVs are reused, but the document is not about traffic engineering itself.
Adj-SIDs are defined as local labels or indexes, but the document is about IS-IS encoding and not SR-MPLS data plane.
Link Local Identifiers from RFC 4202 are reused, but nothing GMPLS-specific is defined.

RFC8669.title: Segment Routing Prefix Segment Identifier Extensions for BGP
RFC8669.summary: Defines the optional transitive BGP Prefix-SID path attribute (Label-Index and Originator SRGB TLVs) for signalling Segment Routing prefix segments over the MPLS data plane using BGP labeled unicast, with receive, advertise and error-handling rules.

BGP.why: The document defines a new BGP path attribute and its processing rules, an extension of BGP itself.
BGP.quote: this document defines a BGP attribute known as the "BGP Prefix-SID attribute" and specifies the rules to originate, receive, and handle error conditions for the attribute.

SR-MPLS.why: The attribute realizes Segment Routing prefix SIDs as MPLS labels, using label indexes and SRGB derivation, which is SR-MPLS.
SR-MPLS.quote: The Label-Index and Originator SRGB TLVs are used only when SR is applied to the MPLS data plane.

rejected.why: SR-MPLS is the more specific child. SRv6 is explicitly out of scope, so the parent isn't needed.
MPLS labels and RFC 8277 labeled unicast are used as the data plane, but the document specifies the BGP attribute, not MPLS itself.
The attribute is a new path attribute with TLVs, not a community.
BGPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations, to say the attribute is not covered by its signatures.
The IANA section creates registries for this attribute but is boilerplate, and the main body is not about IANA.

RFC8670.title: BGP Prefix Segment in Large-Scale Data Centers
RFC8670.summary: Informational document describing how to apply Segment Routing with BGP Prefix-SID in BGP-based large-scale data centers, for both MPLS (via BGP labeled unicast) and IPv6 data planes.

segment routing.why: The document's purpose is to apply SR (Prefix-SID, SRGB, label stacks, EPE, anycast segments) in the data center.
segment routing.quote: describes the motivation for, and benefits of, applying Segment Routing (SR) in BGP-based large-scale data centers

data center networking.why: It extends the RFC 7938 Clos data center design, covering ECMP, FIB minimization and fabric traffic engineering.
data center networking.quote: The use cases described in this document should be considered in the context of the BGP-based large-scale data-center (DC) design

BGP.why: It specifies EBGP and IBGP labeled-unicast designs carrying the BGP Prefix-SID attribute, including route reflection with next-hop-self.
BGP.quote: Each node peers with its neighbors via an EBGP session with extensions defined in [RFC8277]

SRv6.why: A full section covers the IPv6 data plane using SRH and segment addresses advertised via BGP Prefix-SID.
SRv6.quote: Applying Segment Routing in the DC with IPv6 Data Plane

SR-MPLS.why: The main body (Section 4) details SR-MPLS label allocation from the SRGB and the forwarding tables.
SR-MPLS.quote: Applying Segment Routing in the DC with MPLS Data Plane

rejected.why: ECMP is background and a problem statement, not the subject of the document.
IBGP route reflection is used in one design variation but is not the subject.
MPLS is only the data plane; SR-MPLS is the more specific tag.
LDP and RSVP-TE are mentioned only as protocols deliberately not used.
The IPv6 data plane is covered via SRv6, which is more specific.

RFC8671.title: Support for Adj-RIB-Out in the BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP)
RFC8671.summary: RFC 8671 updates the BGP Monitoring Protocol (RFC 7854) to let BMP senders export Adj-RIB-Out data, adding an O flag to the per-peer header, new statistics types, and an Admin Label Peer Up TLV.

BMP.why: The document extends BMP with Adj-RIB-Out monitoring, a new per-peer header flag, new statistics types and a new Peer Up TLV.
BMP.quote: This document updates BMP (RFC 7854) by adding access to the Adj-RIB-Out RIBs. It also adds a new flag to the peer header

rejected.why: BGP is the protocol being monitored. The document specifies only BMP extensions, and BMP is the more specific tag under BGP.
Route reflector clients and confederations are mentioned only as peering types that affect the pre-policy Adj-RIB-Out. The document is not about them.
Route server clients are listed once as a peering session type. The document is not about route servers.
Community X:Y appears only as an example of a policy that Adj-RIB-Out monitoring can validate.

RFC8672.title: TLS Server Identity Pinning with Tickets
RFC8672.summary: Defines an experimental TLS 1.3 extension (PinningTicket) in which the server issues an encrypted opaque ticket and later proves it can decrypt it, pinning server identity without certificate or key management.

TLS.why: The document specifies a new TLS 1.3 extension (PinningTicket) with message formats, cryptographic derivations, and a TLS extension type registration.
TLS.quote: This document proposes experimental extensions to TLS with opaque pinning tickets as a way to pin the server's identity.

rejected.why: Motivated by misissued certificates, but the protocol is deliberately independent of certificates; PKI is background, not the subject.
HPKP is compared in the appendix, but the document explicitly is not HTTP-specific.
The mechanism is at the TLS level and not restricted to the web platform; HPKP is only a comparison.
Mentioned only as an alternative in the Previous Work appendix.
HMAC is just a building block used to compute the pinning proof.
DTLS is mentioned only in passing as a pin-indexing identifier; the document applies to TLS 1.3.

gaps.name: Public key / identity pinning
gaps.why: The document is about pinning server identity (a TOFU second-factor mechanism), and the taxonomy has no tag for pinning. TLS is the closest fit.

RFC8673.title: HTTP Random Access and Live Content
RFC8673.summary: Experimental HTTP extension defining semantics for byte-range GET/HEAD requests on continuously appended (live) representations, using very large last-byte-pos values and Content-Range responses with unknown length.

HTTP.why: The document extends HTTP range request semantics (Range, Content-Range, 206) for live/aggregating content, so it belongs on the HTTP page.
HTTP.quote: defines semantics that allow an HTTP client and a server to perform byte-range GET and HEAD requests that start at an arbitrary byte offset

HTTP caching.why: Section 3.2 gives caching guidance for shift-buffer representations, including how to avoid caching non-Range GETs.
HTTP caching.quote: responses to GET requests performed on shift-buffer representations using Range headers can be cached by intermediaries

rejected.why: Live video is a motivating use case, but the document defines a generic HTTP range mechanism, not media streaming delivery.
ABNF is only the notation used to cite RFC 7233 productions; the document is not about it.
The document is written against HTTP/1.1 semantics and does not address HTTP/2.

RFC8674.title: The "safe" HTTP Preference
RFC8674.summary: Defines the "safe" HTTP Prefer preference token, by which a client asks origin servers to avoid objectionable content, with guidance for browsers and sites and an IANA registration in the HTTP Preferences registry.

HTTP.why: The document extends HTTP by defining a new Prefer header preference, including Preference-Applied and Vary behaviour. No more specific HTTP child tag covers Prefer.
HTTP.quote: This specification defines how to declare this desire in requests as an HTTP Preference [RFC7240].

rejected.why: Vary: Prefer and cache-control advice appear, but they are a minor supporting point rather than the subject.
Cookies are mentioned only as the existing per-site way to set safe mode, which the preference is meant to replace or supplement.
The fingerprinting and targeting concerns are in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate-like, and the document is not a privacy analysis.
The preference is explicitly not a secure mechanism, and the document does not specify a web platform security mechanism.
The preference registration is routine IANA Considerations boilerplate.

RFC8675.title: A YANG Data Model for Tunnel Interface Types
RFC8675.summary: Defines the IANA-maintained YANG module iana-tunnel-type, a set of identities for tunnel interface types mirroring the IANA tunnelType registry, and updates that registry's references.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module of tunnel interface type identities, with rules for keeping it in sync with the IANA registry.
YANG.quote: specifies the initial version of the iana-tunnel-type YANG module containing a collection of IANA-maintained YANG identities identifying tunnel interface types

tunneling.why: The module enumerates tunnel encapsulation types (GRE, L2TP, 6to4, DS-Lite, etc.) as a catalogue, so readers of tunnelling would want it. It does not specify any tunnelling mechanism itself.
tunneling.quote: Tunnel type values are not directly added to the Tunnel Interface Types YANG module; they must instead be added to the "tunnelType" IANA registry.

rejected.why: GRE is only one identity among many in the module, and the document does not specify or extend it.
The IANA registry sync procedure is part of the document, but the subject is the YANG module of tunnel types. It is not general IANA guidance.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in the Security Considerations boilerplate.
The module reflects the registry defined in the IP Tunnel MIB, but the document does not define a MIB module.
Transition tunnels such as 6to4, ISATAP, Teredo and DS-Lite are only listed as identities and are not addressed by the document.

RFC8676.title: YANG Modules for IPv4-in-IPv6 Address plus Port (A+P) Softwires
RFC8676.summary: Defines YANG modules (ietf-softwire-ce, ietf-softwire-br, ietf-softwire-common) for configuring and monitoring A+P IPv4-in-IPv6 softwire CEs and BRs for Lightweight 4over6, MAP-E and MAP-T.

YANG.why: The document's deliverable is a set of YANG modules with tree diagrams, config, state and notifications.
YANG.quote: This document defines YANG modules for the configuration and operation of IPv4-in-IPv6 softwire Border Relays and Customer Premises Equipment

MAP.why: The modules model MAP-E and MAP-T instances (mapping rules, EA length, PSID, BR/DMR), so MAP readers would want this.
MAP.quote: Mapping of Address and Port with Encapsulation (MAP-E) [RFC7597], and Mapping of Address and Port using Translation (MAP-T) [RFC7599]

softwire.why: It models provisioning of softwire CE and BR elements, including Lightweight 4over6 binding tables. No dedicated lw4o6 tag exists, so softwire is the closest fit.
softwire.quote: The IETF Softwire Working Group has developed several IPv4-in-IPv6 softwire mechanisms

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the protocols used to access the modules, not specified or extended here.
NAT YANG (RFC 8512) is only referenced for companion configuration; this document does not define NAT behaviour.
DS-Lite is only mentioned as covered by a separate YANG module (RFC 8513).
A softwire tag, which sits under IPv6 transition, already covers the subject, so the parent is implied.
This is YANG, not a MIB or SMI module.

gaps.name: Lightweight 4over6 (lw4o6)
gaps.why: There is no tag for lw4o6 specifically. It is covered here only by the broader softwire tag.

RFC8677.title: Name-Based Service Function Forwarder (nSFF) Component within a Service Function Chaining (SFC) Framework
RFC8677.summary: Independent-stream informational RFC proposing a name-based Service Function Forwarder (nSFF) and Name Resolver that extend the SFC architecture so service function paths use names (URIs/FQDNs) instead of L2/L3 addresses, avoiding rechaining.

SFC.why: The whole document extends the SFC architecture (SFF, SFP, NLM, NSH) with name-based forwarding via nSFF and nNLM.
SFC.quote: This document describes the necessary extensions, additional functions, and protocol details in the Service Function Forwarder (SFF) to handle name-based relationships.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the example protocol whose requests carry the names; the document does not extend HTTP.
URIs are used as names but the document does not specify or extend URI syntax or schemes.
The Name Resolver is explicitly stated to be similar to DNS but not to use DNS protocols or records.
BIER is mentioned only as an alternative underlay for forwarding between nSFFs.
Only a comparison: path-based forwarding is described as similar to segment routing, not about it.
The NR resolves names to forwarding paths, a niche of SFC rather than general service discovery.

gaps.name: Name-based / path-based forwarding of service requests (nSFF, Name Resolver)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for name-based routing of service transactions; ICN is the nearest but not a fit for this SFC-specific design.

RFC8678.title: Enterprise Multihoming using Provider-Assigned IPv6 Addresses without Network Prefix Translation: Requirements and Solutions
RFC8678.summary: Informational RFC examining how enterprise sites can multihome to several ISPs with provider-assigned IPv6 prefixes without NPTv6/NAT, covering source-address-dependent routing in site routers and host source address selection driven by RAs, DHCPv6 and ICMPv6.

multihoming.why: The whole document is about site multihoming architecture with PA addresses, requirements and solutions.
multihoming.quote: Connecting an enterprise site to multiple ISPs over IPv6 using provider-assigned addresses is difficult without the use of some form of Network Address Translation (NAT).

IPv6.why: Document is IPv6-specific: PA prefixes, ULAs, RFC 6724 source address selection, and RA-based host configuration. Note there is no more specific applicable child tag chosen; neighbor discovery is only a mechanism used.
IPv6.quote: Each host at the enterprise has multiple addresses, at least one from each ISP-assigned prefix.

neighbor discovery.why: A substantial part (Section 6) evaluates using RA PIO/RIO and per-prefix link-local router addresses to steer host source address selection, which is its recommended solution.
neighbor discovery.quote: Router Advertisements provide a reliable mechanism to influence the source address selection process via PIO, RIO, and default router preferences.

rejected.why: Evaluated as a mechanism (RFC 7078 policy table) and rejected as unsuitable; not specified or extended here.
ICMPv6 Code 5 is discussed as a supplementary signal, but the document does not specify or extend ICMP.
NAT/NPTv6 is the alternative the document deliberately avoids; discussed only briefly in Section 8.2.
Considered in Section 8.1 only as an alternative dismissed as not viable; the document is not about it, though it is a child of multihoming.
Mentioned in Section 8.3 as a complementary approach, not a subject of the document.
SADR forwarding table generation is covered, but it is a multihoming-specific mechanism; no better-fitting routing tag exists and multihoming covers it.

gaps.name: Source Address Dependent Routing (SADR)
gaps.why: Central to the document (Sections 4-5: source-prefix-scoped forwarding tables, SADR domains) but the taxonomy has no tag for source-dependent or source/destination routing.

RFC8679.title: MPLS Egress Protection Framework
RFC8679.summary: Specifies a fast reroute framework for protecting MPLS transport tunnels and IP/MPLS services against egress node and egress link failures, using PLR, protector, context IDs and context-label-based forwarding.

MPLS.why: The framework is about MPLS tunnels and services: bypass tunnels, context label switching and label spaces on the protector. No narrower MPLS child tag (LDP, MPLS-TP, pseudowire, GMPLS) fits as the main subject.
MPLS.quote: This document specifies a fast reroute framework for protecting IP/MPLS services and MPLS transport tunnels against egress node and egress link failures.

IP fast reroute.why: The document is a local-repair fast reroute framework with a PLR, bypass tunnels and pre-installed forwarding state. It extends transit protection to the egress. Readers of fast reroute would want it.
IP fast reroute.quote: Today, local-repair-based fast reroute mechanisms (see [RFC4090], [RFC5286], [RFC7490], and [RFC7812]) have been widely deployed

rejected.why: Section 10 uses Layer 3 VPN as a worked example, but the framework is service-agnostic and not about L3VPN itself.
RSVP-TE is one way to signal bypass tunnels and is used in the example. The framework does not extend it and says it needs no extensions to it.
BGP distributes VPN labels in the example only. It is a substrate, not the subject.
Segment Routing is only mentioned as one way to build a bypass tunnel, and the mirroring context SID is referenced from other RFCs.
LDP is mentioned as one tunnel establishment option, not specified or extended here.
Pseudowire is cited only as an example of a service for which RFC 8104 defines extensions.

gaps.name: MPLS egress protection / context-based forwarding
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for egress protection or protector and context-label forwarding. The closest fits are MPLS and IP fast reroute.

RFC8680.title: Forward Error Correction (FEC) Framework Extension to Sliding Window Codes
RFC8680.summary: Updates the FEC Framework (RFC 6363) to support sliding-window (convolutional) FEC codes alongside block codes, defining sender/receiver operation and FEC scheme requirements for them.

FECFRAME.why: The whole document extends the FECFRAME framework to sliding window codes, specifying sender and receiver operation and FEC scheme requirements.
FECFRAME.quote: This document updates RFC 6363 to support FEC codes based on a sliding encoding window, in addition to block FEC codes

rejected.why: RTP repair flows are only illustrated in figures; the document does not specify RTP.
Multicast/broadcast delivery is the motivating use case, but the document does not address multicast routing or group membership.
UDP is only the unreliable datagram transport the framework runs over.
Raptor schemes are cited only as examples of block FEC schemes in the references.
FECFRAME is the more specific child tag and already covers this document, so the parent is implied.
SDP appears only as one way to carry the FEC configuration information, in a passing mention.

RFC8681.title: Sliding Window Random Linear Code (RLC) Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) Schemes for FECFRAME
RFC8681.summary: Specifies two FEC schemes (RLC over GF(2) and GF(2^8)) using sliding-window random linear codes to protect real-time media streams within the FECFRAME framework, including payload ID formats, PRNG-based coefficient generation, and parameter derivation.

FECFRAME.why: The document defines two fully specified FEC schemes for FECFRAME (Encoding IDs 9 and 10), including FFCI, source and repair FEC Payload ID formats.
FECFRAME.quote: They can protect arbitrary media streams along the lines defined by FECFRAME extended to Sliding Window FEC Codes.

rejected.why: RTP timestamps are only mentioned as a possible source of ADU timing; the document is not about RTP.
SDP is only used to carry the FFCI (fssi parameter); it is a substrate, not the subject.
Multicast/broadcast delivery is the motivating context, but the document specifies FEC schemes rather than multicast transport.
Raptor is mentioned only as an existing block code for comparison.
LDPC-Staircase is mentioned only as an existing block code for comparison.
IPsec/ESP appears only in the Security Considerations as the baseline secure operation inherited from RFC 6363.

gaps.name: Sliding Window / Random Linear Codes (AL-FEC)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is sliding-window random linear erasure codes over finite fields. The taxonomy has FEC and FECFRAME, but the FEC subtree does not name this code family specifically. Under the FEC subtree it is only covered by the FECFRAME tag.

RFC8682.title: TinyMT32 Pseudorandom Number Generator (PRNG)
RFC8682.summary: Specifies the TinyMT32 pseudorandom number generator, a small-state Mersenne Twister variant, with a fixed parameter set, C reference code, and validation values; not for cryptographic use.

randomness.why: The whole document specifies a PRNG algorithm, its parameters, reference implementation and determinism validation, which fits randomness generation.
randomness.quote: This document describes the TinyMT32 Pseudorandom Number Generator (PRNG), which produces 32-bit pseudorandom unsigned integers

rejected.why: RFC 8681 (FECFRAME RLC) depends normatively on this PRNG, but this document does not specify FEC; it only mentions that use.
RFC 5170 is cited only as a comparison to the Park-Miller PRNG; the document is not about LDPC codes.
The PRNG suits embedded devices and was tested on RIOT boards, but the document does not address IoT architecture or guidance.

RFC8683.title: Additional Deployment Guidelines for NAT64/464XLAT in Operator and Enterprise Networks
RFC8683.summary: Informational guidance on deploying stateful NAT64 and 464XLAT (with or without DNS64) in operator and enterprise IPv6-only networks, comparing scenarios and covering DNSSEC, foreign DNS, prefix choice, CLAT and EAM issues.

464XLAT.why: Much of the document compares 464XLAT/CLAT scenarios and gives CLAT deployment guidance, including Appendices A and B.
464XLAT.quote: 464XLAT [RFC6877] is a very simple approach to cope with the major NAT64+DNS64 drawback: not working with applications or devices that use literal IPv4 addresses

NAT64.why: The core subject is stateful NAT64 deployment scenarios, prefix choice (WKP vs NSP), and operational issues.
NAT64.quote: This document describes how Network Address and Protocol Translation from IPv6 Clients to IPv4 Servers (NAT64) (including 464XLAT) can be deployed

DNS64.why: DNS64 placement, DNSSEC interaction, reverse mapping and foreign DNS issues make up a large part of the document.
DNS64.quote: DNS64 [RFC6147] is in charge of the synthesis of AAAA records from the A records, so it only works for applications making use of DNS.

DNSSEC.why: Section 4.1 is devoted to DNSSEC considerations and several mitigation approaches.
DNSSEC.quote: Because DNS64 [RFC6147] modifies DNS answers, and DNSSEC is designed to detect such modifications, DNS64 [RFC6147] may potentially break DNSSEC

rejected.why: The child tags NAT64 and 464XLAT fit more specifically, so the parent topic is implied.
DoT, DoH and DoQ are discussed only as a cause of foreign DNS breaking NAT64, in a short subsection.
PCP is mentioned only as a way to discover the NAT64 prefix and to allow incoming connections.
Happy Eyeballs v2 is referenced as a supporting mechanism, not specified or analysed.
The IP/ICMP translation algorithm and EAM are cited as building blocks, not the focus.
Appendix C only points to RFC 8219 for benchmarking.

RFC8684.title: TCP Extensions for Multipath Operation with Multiple Addresses
RFC8684.summary: RFC 8684 specifies Multipath TCP v1, a set of TCP extensions (MP_CAPABLE, MP_JOIN, DSS, ADD_ADDR, etc.) allowing a single TCP connection to use multiple subflows over multiple paths, obsoleting RFC 6824.

MPTCP.why: The document is the core specification of Multipath TCP v1.
MPTCP.quote: Multipath TCP provides the ability to simultaneously use multiple paths between peers.

rejected.why: MPTCP is the more specific child tag; the parent is implied.
Congestion control is delegated to RFC 6356; only briefly discussed here.
HMAC-SHA256 is used for subflow authentication but is a mechanism, not the subject.
SHA-256 is used for tokens and HMAC only as a building block.
NAT/middlebox interaction is a design consideration, not the subject of the document.

RFC8685.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for the Hierarchical Path Computation Element (H-PCE) Architecture
RFC8685.summary: Defines PCEP extensions (TLVs, objective functions, metrics, SVEC flag, error types, NO-PATH flags) to support the Hierarchical PCE architecture for multi-domain path computation.

PCE.why: The document specifies PCEP extensions for the H-PCE architecture, so it belongs under PCE architecture and PCEP.
PCE.quote: This document defines extensions to the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) to support H-PCE procedures.

rejected.why: The document targets inter-domain MPLS-TE and GMPLS LSPs, but it specifies PCEP extensions rather than MPLS itself.
GMPLS LSPs are the use case. The document defines no GMPLS protocol content.
This is implied as the parent of PCE, so it is not listed separately.
PCEP runs over TCP. It is only the transport, mentioned in the Security Considerations.
TLS is mentioned only as a security option for PCEP in the Security Considerations.
BGP-LS is mentioned only as an out-of-scope way to learn topology.

RFC8686.title: Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) Cross-Domain Server Discovery
RFC8686.summary: Specifies a DNS-based (U-NAPTR in in-addr.arpa/ip6.arpa) procedure for ALTO clients to discover ALTO servers responsible for a given IP address or prefix across domains, with scenarios, requirements and security guidance.

ALTO.why: The document defines a discovery procedure for ALTO servers and explains how ALTO services (endpoint cost, property, maps) are used with it.
ALTO.quote: specifies a procedure for ALTO cross-domain server discovery

DNS.why: The procedure is defined as specific reverse-DNS U-NAPTR lookups with name construction, truncation and error handling, plus operator DNS load and delegation considerations.
DNS.quote: It performs DNS lookups (for NAPTR resource records in the "in-addr.arpa." or "ip6.arpa." trees)

service discovery.why: The document is fundamentally about discovering a service (ALTO servers) on a network.
service discovery.quote: Before an ALTO client can ask for guidance, it needs to discover one or more ALTO servers that can provide suitable guidance.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is required for protection in Security Considerations but the document does not specify or extend it.
ALTO runs over HTTP and HTTPS URIs are returned, but HTTP itself is only a substrate.
Tracker-based P2P is used as an example scenario in an appendix, not the subject.
DoT and DoH are only mentioned as privacy mitigations in Security Considerations.
NAT interaction is a short deployment consideration, not a main subject.
Mentioned only as the alternative discovery mechanism in RFC 7286.

gaps.name: ALTO (Application-Layer Traffic Optimization)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a tech tag ALTO under applications, but I should verify: the listed id 'ALTO' does exist in the taxonomy as 'ALTO [tech]' under applications, so no gap remains.

RFC8687.title: OSPF Routing with Cross-Address Family Traffic Engineering Tunnels
RFC8687.summary: Updates RFC 5786 so OSPFv2/OSPFv3 routers advertise cross-address-family local addresses in the Node Attribute TLV, letting OSPF map MPLS TE tunnels from one instance to tail-end routers in another.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF TE advertisements (Node Local Address sub-TLVs) and defines X-AF mapping procedures for OSPFv2/OSPFv3, updating RFC 5786.
OSPF.quote: OSPF routes must be computed over MPLS TE tunnels created using information propagated in another OSPF instance.

traffic engineering.why: The motivation and mechanism concern sharing a common MPLS TE LSP infrastructure across IPv4 and IPv6, using the TE database and TE tunnel shortcuts.
traffic engineering.quote: it may be desirable to set up common MPLS TE LSPs to carry traffic destined to addresses from different address families on a router.

rejected.why: OSPFv3 is one of the two instances involved, but the document extends OSPF TE generally (mainly via OSPFv2 TE and RFC 5786), so the parent OSPF tag fits better.
MPLS TE LSPs are the thing being routed over, but the document specifies OSPF advertisement and not MPLS encapsulation or operations.
Dual-stack context only; nothing new is specified about IPv6 itself.
The tunnels are RSVP-TE-style TE tunnels, but no signalling is defined or discussed.

RFC8688.title: A Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Response Code for Rejected Calls
RFC8688.summary: Defines the SIP 608 (Rejected) response code so callers learn an intermediary (e.g., analytics engine) rejected their call, with a signed jCard in Call-Info for redress, plus a feature-capability indicator for legacy interoperation.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP with a new response code, a Call-Info purpose value, and a Feature-Caps indicator, along with UAC and intermediary behaviour.
SIP.quote: This document defines the 608 (Rejected) Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) response code.

rejected.why: STIR and SHAKEN are only referenced as related context and as a security mitigation. The document does not specify or extend them.
JWS and JWT are used to sign the jCard, but this is only the mechanism relied on. The only new JOSE-related item is a JWT claim registration.
jCard is used to encode the contact information, but the document defines nothing new about vCard or jCard.
JSON is only the encoding substrate for the jCard and JWT.
SDP is mentioned only in connection with the announcement media and the amplification attack discussion.
The motivation is unwanted calls, but the taxonomy's spam tag covers unsolicited bulk email, so it does not fit.

gaps.name: Unwanted/robocall handling in SIP
gaps.why: The document concerns call blocking and remediation for unwanted calls (telephony spam), and the taxonomy has no tag for it outside email spam.

RFC8689.title: SMTP Require TLS Option
RFC8689.summary: Defines the SMTP REQUIRETLS service extension and TLS-Required header field so a sender can require TLS with validated server identity for a message, or ask that recipient MTA-STS/DANE policy be ignored.

SMTP.why: The document specifies a new SMTP service extension with a MAIL FROM parameter, EHLO keyword, and relay/submission behaviour.
SMTP.quote: This document describes an SMTP service extension, REQUIRETLS, and a message header field, TLS-Required.

message format.why: A substantial part defines a new message header field with ABNF and processing rules.
message format.quote: One new message header field [RFC5322], TLS-Required, is defined by this specification.

rejected.why: TLS is the security substrate for SMTP sessions. The document defines no new TLS extension.
DANE is a recipient-side policy that the document overrides or references. It does not specify or extend DANE.
DNSSEC is only used to validate MX records and is not the subject.
The parent tag is implied by SMTP.
DNS is only used for MX lookup and validation.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate and not the subject.

gaps.name: MTA-STS
gaps.why: The document is closely tied to MTA-STS (RFC 8461) as a recipient policy mechanism, but the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC8690.title: Clarification of Segment ID Sub-TLV Length for RFC 8287
RFC8690.summary: Updates RFC 8287 to clarify how the Length field is computed for the IPv4 IGP-Prefix, IPv6 IGP-Prefix and IGP-Adjacency Segment ID sub-TLVs in the MPLS LSP Ping/Traceroute Target FEC Stack TLV, fixing an interoperability problem.

segment routing.why: The document fixes the encoding of Segment Routing SID sub-TLVs used for SR OAM. Its subject is Segment Routing IGP-Prefix and IGP-Adjacency SIDs.
segment routing.quote: defines the extensions to MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute for Segment Routing IGP-Prefix and IGP-Adjacency Segment Identifiers (SIDs) with the MPLS data plane

SR-MPLS.why: The SIDs are those of Segment Routing over the MPLS data plane, so SR-MPLS readers would want this clarification. SR-MPLS is the more specific tag.
SR-MPLS.quote: extensions to MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute for Segment Routing IGP-Prefix and IGP-Adjacency Segment Identifiers (SIDs) with the MPLS data plane

traceroute.why: It amends the LSP Ping/Traceroute Target FEC Stack sub-TLV definitions. Those sub-TLVs are the path-discovery and verification mechanism.
traceroute.quote: MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute for Segment Routing IGP-Prefix and IGP-Adjacency Segment Identifiers

rejected.why: MPLS is the data plane the sub-TLVs operate on. The document specifies nothing about MPLS itself, only the SR sub-TLV lengths.
LSP Ping is an OAM mechanism, but traceroute is the more specific fit. The document does not address OAM in general.
OSPF appears only as a protocol value in the length table. The document does not specify or extend OSPF.
IS-IS appears only as a protocol value in the length table. The document does not specify or extend IS-IS.

gaps.name: MPLS LSP Ping/Traceroute (LSP ping, RFC 8029)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MPLS LSP Ping, the data-plane failure detection tool this document amends. Traceroute is the closest fit.

RFC8691.title: Basic Support for IPv6 Networks Operating Outside the Context of a Basic Service Set over IEEE Std 802.11
RFC8691.summary: Specifies how IPv6 runs over a single IEEE 802.11-OCB (802.11p) link for vehicular communication: MTU, frame format, link-local addresses, SLAAC interface IDs, address mapping, subnet structure, and privacy and security considerations.

vehicular networking.why: The document is an IPWAVE WG product on IPv6 over vehicular 802.11-OCB links, with OBU/RSU terminology and vehicle-specific privacy and subnet issues.
vehicular networking.quote: IEEE 802.11-OCB networks are used for vehicular communications as 'Wireless Access in Vehicular Environments'.
vehicular networking.section: 3. Communication Scenarios Where IEEE 802.11-OCB Links Are Used

WiFi.why: It defines IPv6 encapsulation, LLC/EtherType use and frame translation over IEEE 802.11 (OCB mode), an IP-over-802.11 binding.
WiFi.quote: IP packets MUST be transmitted over 802.11-OCB media as QoS data frames whose format is specified in an IEEE 802.11 spec

IPv6.why: It specifies IPv6 operation on this link, covering MTU, ND, link-local addresses, address mapping and subnet structure.
IPv6.quote: The IPv6 network layer operates on 802.11-OCB in the same manner as operating on the Ethernet with the following exceptions

SLAAC.why: A section covers interface identifier formation under SLAAC, including opaque and stable IIDs and MAC randomization for privacy.
SLAAC.quote: The RECOMMENDED method for forming stable Interface Identifiers (IIDs) is described in [RFC8064].

rejected.why: ND is required and its issues on OCB are discussed in Appendix I, but the document does not specify or extend ND. IPv6 covers it.
Privacy risks of interface IDs and MAC addresses are discussed, but within Security Considerations and secondary to the main IPv6-over-OCB specification.
The stack is derived from IPv6 over Ethernet (RFC 2464) and reuses its mappings, but the document is about 802.11-OCB, not Ethernet.
IPsec is mentioned only as a possible security mechanism in Security Considerations.
Mobile IPv6 and DNAv6 are noted as needing future tuning, and movement detection is explicitly out of scope.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.11-OCB / 802.11p (outside the context of a BSS)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is this specific 802.11 mode. WiFi and vehicular networking only approximate it.

RFC8692.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure: Additional Algorithm Identifiers for RSASSA-PSS and ECDSA Using SHAKEs
RFC8692.summary: Updates RFC 3279 to define OIDs and conventions for using SHAKE128/SHAKE256 with RSASSA-PSS and ECDSA signatures and subject public keys in X.509 certificates and CRLs.

X.509.why: The document profiles algorithm identifiers for signatures and public keys in X.509 certificates and CRLs, updating RFC 3279.
X.509.quote: describes the conventions for using the SHAKE function family in Internet X.509 certificates and revocation lists

RSA.why: Specifies RSASSA-PSS with SHAKEs: MGF, salt length, trailer field and public key identifiers.
RSA.quote: The RSASSA-PSS algorithm is defined in [RFC8017]. When id-RSASSA-PSS-SHAKE128 or id-RSASSA-PSS-SHAKE256 (specified in Section 3) is used

ECDSA.why: Defines ECDSA with SHAKE128/SHAKE256 identifiers and output lengths.
ECDSA.quote: The output length, d, for SHAKE128 or SHAKE256 used in ECDSA MUST be 256 or 512 bits, respectively.

SHA.why: SHAKEs are SHA-3 family functions; the document defines their use as hash and MGF in PKIX signatures.
SHA.quote: two extendable-output functions (SHAKEs) are defined: SHAKE128 and SHAKE256

rejected.why: ASN.1 module is only the formal vehicle for the OID definitions, not the subject.
Covered by the more specific X.509 tag.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here.
Covered by the more specific ECDSA tag.

RFC8693.title: OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange
RFC8693.summary: RFC 8693 defines an OAuth 2.0 extension grant type for token exchange, letting clients obtain security tokens from an authorization server acting as an STS, with impersonation and delegation semantics and new JWT claims (act, may_act, scope, client_id).

OAuth.why: The whole document defines a new OAuth 2.0 grant type and its request/response parameters at the token endpoint.
OAuth.quote: This specification defines a protocol extending OAuth 2.0 that enables clients to request and obtain security tokens from authorization servers acting in the role of an STS.

JWT.why: Defines and registers new JWT claims (act, may_act, scope, client_id), a substantial part of the document that JWT readers would want.
JWT.quote: this section defines claims to express such semantics specifically for JWTs and in an OAuth 2.0 Token Introspection [RFC7662] response.
JWT.section: 4. JSON Web Token Claims and Introspection Response Parameters

rejected.why: JSON is only the response encoding; the document defines nothing new about JSON.
HTTP POST is just the transport for the token endpoint; no HTTP extension is defined.
It registers token-type URNs under the OAuth namespace, but this is a minor part of the document and the subject is not URN namespaces.
TLS is mentioned only in Privacy Considerations as the channel for transport.
The STS concept and SAML tokens are mentioned, but the document is a token-endpoint protocol under OAuth, not a cross-domain federation framework.
Too generic; OAuth already captures the delegation and authorization subject.

RFC8694.title: Applicability of the Path Computation Element to Inter-area and Inter-AS MPLS and GMPLS Traffic Engineering
RFC8694.summary: Informational RFC examining how the PCE architecture, PCEP and related extensions (BRPC, per-domain, hierarchical PCE, Path-Keys) apply to computing inter-area and inter-AS MPLS and GMPLS TE paths.

PCE.why: The whole document is about applying PCE architecture and PCEP (BRPC, H-PCE, Path-Key, SVEC, IRO/XRO) to multi-domain path computation.
PCE.quote: This document examines the applicability of the PCE architecture, protocols, and protocol extensions for computing multi-area and multi-AS paths in MPLS and GMPLS networks.

GMPLS.why: GMPLS networks, including ASON optical domains, are a substantial scope of the document, with a dedicated section on optical domains.
GMPLS.quote: This document describes the processes and procedures available when using the PCE architecture and protocols for computing inter-area and inter-AS MPLS and GMPLS Traffic-Engineered paths.

traffic engineering.why: Inter-domain TE LSP computation, diversity, bandwidth guarantees and recovery are the main subject, though PCE is the more specific tag.
traffic engineering.quote: This document highlights the PCE techniques and mechanisms that exist for establishing TE packet and optical Label Switched Paths (LSPs)

rejected.why: BGP-LS is mentioned only as one way to feed the TED; the document is not about BGP.
Signalling of contiguous, stitched and nested LSPs is referenced but not specified or extended here.
MPLS is the network context; the document is about PCE computation, and GMPLS is tagged for the optical scope.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as the transport security for PCEP.
Brief mention in the inter-AS bandwidth guarantee discussion, not a substantial subject.
OSPF-TE and IS-IS TE are cited only as sources for the TED.

RFC8695.title: A YANG Data Model for the Routing Information Protocol (RIP)
RFC8695.summary: Defines the ietf-rip YANG data model for configuring and monitoring RIP version 2 and RIPng, including operational state, statistics and a clear-rip-route RPC, conforming to NMDA and augmenting the core routing model.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module (ietf-rip) with tree diagrams, configuration, state and RPC definitions.
YANG.quote: This document introduces a YANG [RFC7950] data model for the Routing Information Protocol (RIP)

RIP.why: The model manages RIPv2 and RIPng: timers, split horizon, redistribution, neighbors, routes and statistics, so RIP readers would want it.
RIP.quote: This YANG data model supports both RIP version 2 and RIPng.

rejected.why: Only the access mechanism for the model, mentioned mainly in Security Considerations; not specified or extended here.
Mentioned only as an alternative access protocol in boilerplate.
The model imports BFD client parameters for an optional feature, but BFD itself is not the subject.
Referenced only for route redistribution types into RIP.
RIPng carries IPv6 routes, but the document is about RIP management, not IPv6.
RFC 1724 MIB capabilities are covered, but the document is not about SNMP or MIBs.

RFC8696.title: Using Pre-Shared Key (PSK) in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC8696.summary: Defines two CMS key management techniques (keyTransPSK and keyAgreePSK) that mix a pre-shared key with key transport or key agreement output via a KDF, to protect CMS-encrypted content against future quantum computers.

CMS.why: The document extends CMS with two new OtherRecipientInfo types (KeyTransPSKRecipientInfo and KeyAgreePSKRecipientInfo) and an ASN.1 module for them.
CMS.quote: This specification defines two quantum-resistant ways to establish a symmetric key-encryption key, which is used to encrypt the sender-generated content-encryption key.

post-quantum.why: The motivation and main security analysis concern protecting today's traffic against a future large-scale quantum computer, a migration mechanism using a PSK.
post-quantum.quote: mixing the output of existing key transport and key agreement algorithms with a pre-shared key (PSK).

key management.why: The document defines key establishment: PSK identifiers, KDF-based derivation of key-encryption keys from a KDK or pairwise KEK, and key hierarchy.
key management.quote: The PSK MUST be distributed to the sender and all of the recipients by some out-of-band means

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the structures; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
RSA is used as a key transport example and in Appendix A but is not specified or analysed here.
AES key wrap and GCM are used in examples only.
Only the S/MIME OID arc is used; the document is about CMS, not secure email.
HKDF is used as an example KDF, but the document is not about HMAC.
ECDH is used as an example key agreement in Appendix B, not the subject.

RFC8697.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for Establishing Relationships between Sets of Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC8697.summary: Defines a generic PCEP ASSOCIATION object, plus ASSOC-Type-List and OP-CONF-ASSOC-RANGE TLVs, for grouping LSPs and associating them with attributes, for stateful and stateless PCEs.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP with a new ASSOCIATION object, new TLVs, error codes and processing rules for association groups of LSPs.
PCE.quote: This document introduces a generic mechanism to create a grouping of Label Switched Paths (LSPs) in the context of a Path Computation Element (PCE).

rejected.why: The PCEP ASSOCIATION object is aligned with the RSVP ASSOCIATION object, but the document does not specify RSVP-TE signalling.
GMPLS appears only as background and in the RSVP ASSOCIATION references; it is not the subject.
TE LSPs are the objects being grouped, but the document is about PCEP rather than MPLS itself.
TLS is only recommended as a transport security mechanism in the Security Considerations.
The PCEP YANG module is mentioned only as future work in the Manageability Considerations.
RBNF is only the notation used for message formats and is not the document's subject.

gaps.name: PCEP (Path Computation Element Communication Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a PCE tag under traffic engineering that covers PCE architecture and PCEP. The tag I used, 'PCE', is not in the taxonomy as written. The closest id is 'PCE', which sits under traffic engineering, so I tagged it by that id.

RFC8698.title: Network-Assisted Dynamic Adaptation (NADA): A Unified Congestion Control Scheme for Real-Time Media
RFC8698.summary: RFC 8698 specifies NADA, an experimental sender/receiver rate-based congestion control scheme for interactive real-time media over RTP/RTCP that combines queuing delay, loss and ECN marking into one congestion signal.

RTP congestion control.why: The document defines NADA, one of the RMCAT congestion control algorithms for interactive real-time media over RTP. This is exactly what the RTP congestion control tag covers.
RTP congestion control.quote: NADA, a novel congestion control scheme for interactive real-time media applications such as video conferencing.

ECN.why: ECN markings are folded into the aggregate congestion signal, and the document discusses ECN-based marking at network nodes in Section 4.2 and Appendix A. ECN is a substantial input to the scheme, though the document does not define ECN itself.
ECN.quote: The scheme can benefit from Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) markings from network nodes.

rejected.why: RTP timestamps are used as the signalling substrate. The document does not extend or specify RTP itself, and the congestion control tag is more specific.
RTCP carries the feedback reports. The feedback message format is defined in a separate draft, so this document is not about RTCP.
AQM schemes such as PIE, CoDel and RED are only described as network node behaviours the scheme can work with. The document says network node operation is out of scope.
LEDBAT's delay estimation approach is borrowed for reference, but the document is not about LEDBAT.
TFRC is cited as a comparison point and for loss interval estimation. NADA is a different algorithm.
PCN marking appears only as an example network node mode in Appendix A.

RFC8699.title: Coupled Congestion Control for RTP Media
RFC8699.summary: Experimental RFC describing a Flow State Exchange (FSE) architecture that couples the congestion controllers of RTP flows sharing a bottleneck at the same sender, with active and passive algorithms and application to NADA and GCC.

RTP congestion control.why: The document specifies coupled congestion control for RTP media flows, including how to apply it to NADA and GCC, which is exactly the real-time media congestion control subject.
RTP congestion control.quote: When multiple congestion-controlled Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) sessions traverse the same network bottleneck, combining their controls can improve the total on-the-wire behavior

rejected.why: RTP is the media being rate-controlled, not specified or extended here; the RTP congestion control tag is the more specific fit.
Parent of RTP congestion control, which is chosen as the more specific tag.
WebRTC is a motivating use case (priorities), but the document does not specify WebRTC itself.
Mentioned only as an example in general recommendations for applying the FSE; not a subject of the document.
Mentioned only in passing in the introduction and as part of the five-tuple/DSCP/ECN grouping for flows.

RFC8700.title: Fifty Years of RFCs
RFC8700.summary: An IAB retrospective marking the RFC Series' fiftieth anniversary, with personal histories of the Series, the RFC Editor function and streams, and thoughts on preservation, format evolution and stream structure.

RFC series.why: The whole document is about the history, editing, publication, streams, format and future of the RFC Series and the RFC Editor.
RFC series.quote: the goal of the RFC Series is to provide a canonical source for the material published by the RFC Editor and to support the preservation of that material

internet history.why: Crocker's and others' retrospectives are first-hand history of the ARPANET, the Network Working Group and early Internet institutions.
internet history.quote: The Internet community now includes millions of nodes and billions of users. It owes its beginning to the ARPANET

rejected.why: The ARPANET appears as historical background for how RFCs began. The document does not cover ARPANET protocols or operations.
It discusses streams and publication approval only as they affect the RFC Series, not IETF standards procedures.
April 1st RFCs get a short mention in Section 3.4. The document itself is not humorous and is not about them.
IANA is mentioned only in passing, in the institutional history. The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate.
The format evolution section mentions XML and new formats only briefly and points to RFC 7990. It does not specify the vocabulary.

RFC8701.title: Applying Generate Random Extensions And Sustain Extensibility (GREASE) to TLS Extensibility
RFC8701.summary: RFC 8701 defines GREASE, a mechanism where TLS implementations advertise reserved random values in cipher suites, extensions, groups, signature algorithms, versions and ALPN IDs to keep peers tolerant of unknown values and preserve extensibility.

TLS.why: The whole document specifies new TLS reserved values and client/server behaviour for ClientHello, ServerHello, CertificateRequest and NewSessionTicket, and updates TLS IANA registries.
TLS.quote: GREASE (Generate Random Extensions And Sustain Extensibility), a mechanism to prevent extensibility failures in the TLS ecosystem.

rejected.why: DTLS is mentioned only in passing (version numbers, DTLS-OK column); the document is about TLS generally.
IANA registry updates are boilerplate-style registrations that support the main TLS content, not the subject of the document.
The fingerprinting concern appears only briefly in Security Considerations.

RFC8702.title: Use of the SHAKE One-Way Hash Functions in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC8702.summary: Updates RFC 3370 to specify use of SHAKE128/SHAKE256 as hash functions, with RSASSA-PSS and ECDSA signatures, public keys, and KMAC, in CMS, including OIDs and an ASN.1 module.

CMS.why: The document defines how SHAKE digests, signatures, public keys and KMACs are identified and used in CMS SignedData, DigestedData and AuthenticatedData.
CMS.quote: describes the conventions for using the SHAKE family of hash functions in the Cryptographic Message Syntax as one-way hash functions

RSA.why: A substantial section specifies RSASSA-PSS with SHAKE: native MGF use, salt length, trailer field and output lengths.
RSA.quote: The RSASSA-PSS saltLength MUST be 32 bytes for id-RSASSA-PSS-SHAKE128 or 64 bytes for id-RSASSA-PSS-SHAKE256.

ECDSA.why: A dedicated section specifies ECDSA with SHAKE hashing, including deterministic k and public key encoding.
ECDSA.quote: The output length for SHAKE128 or SHAKE256 used in ECDSA MUST be 32 or 64 bytes, respectively.

SHA.why: The SHA-3 family's SHAKE extendable-output functions are the hash functions the document applies, including output lengths and strengths.
SHA.quote: describes the use of the SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 specified in [SHA3] as new hash functions in CMS.

rejected.why: The ASN.1 module is only the formal definition of the identifiers; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
Public key and certificate conventions come from RFC 8692, which this document only references.
The MAC used is KMAC, not HMAC.
The document is CMS-level, and S/MIME appears only in the registry name and in referenced ASN.1 modules.
The document does not address PKI; it concerns CMS algorithm identifiers.

RFC8703.title: Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) Link Identifier Extension
RFC8703.summary: Defines a DLEP extension (Link Identifier and Link Identifier Length data items) letting modems report link status to Layer 3 destinations beyond a gateway node on the Layer 2 domain.

DLEP.why: The document extends DLEP with new data items and negotiation.
DLEP.quote: This document describes a DLEP extension that allows modems that do not meet the strict requirement above to use DLEP to describe link availability and quality

rejected.why: Parent of DLEP, implied; not chosen separately.
IPv4/IPv6 addresses are only carried in data items; not the subject.
NAT is mentioned only as a requirement to report public-side addresses.

RFC8704.title: Enhanced Feasible-Path Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding
RFC8704.summary: BCP that updates RFC 3704 by defining enhanced feasible-path uRPF (EFP-uRPF) algorithms A and B, built from BGP Adj-RIBs-In, to reduce false positives in source address validation against spoofing.

routing security.why: The document defines improved uRPF source address validation techniques for securing routing and forwarding against spoofing and DDoS. The augmentation with ROA and IRR data and the operator recommendations also place it in routing security.
routing security.quote: Source address validation (SAV) refers to the detection and mitigation of source address (SA) spoofing [RFC2827].

BGP.why: The RPF lists are built from BGP Adj-RIBs-In by origin AS. The document also gives BGP operational recommendations on route announcement, NO_EXPORT and transient handling.
BGP.quote: if BGP updates for multiple prefixes with the same origin AS were received on different interfaces (at border routers), then incoming data packets with source addresses in any of those prefixes should be accepted

rejected.why: ROAs are only used to augment RPF lists in one section. The document is not about RPKI or route origin validation itself.
DoS/DDoS prevention is the motivation, but the document specifies SAV techniques rather than DDoS mitigation or signalling.
VRF tables are mentioned only as a comparison for how uRPF can query a table. The document is not about VPNs.
The document has operational recommendations, but the more specific routing security tag fits better.
IRR data is mentioned only briefly as an augmentation source.

gaps.name: Source address validation / uRPF (BCP 38 ingress filtering)
gaps.why: The main subject is source address validation and unicast Reverse Path Forwarding. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so the nearest fit is routing security.

RFC8705.title: OAuth 2.0 Mutual-TLS Client Authentication and Certificate-Bound Access Tokens
RFC8705.summary: Defines two mutual-TLS OAuth 2.0 client authentication methods (PKI and self-signed certificate) and certificate-bound access tokens using an x5t#S256 JWT confirmation method, plus related metadata.

OAuth.why: The document extends OAuth 2.0 with new client authentication methods, certificate-bound tokens, and new authorization server and client metadata.
OAuth.quote: This document describes OAuth client authentication and certificate-bound access and refresh tokens using mutual Transport Layer Security (TLS) authentication with X.509 certificates.

JWT.why: It defines a new JWT confirmation method member and its use in JWT access tokens and introspection responses.
JWT.quote: this specification defines the new JWT Confirmation Method [RFC7800] member "x5t#S256" for the X.509 Certificate SHA-256 Thumbprint.

TLS.why: Mutual TLS client certificate authentication is central to the document, which also covers TLS configuration, termination and privacy considerations.
