TLS.quote: a client presents its X.509 certificate and proves possession of the corresponding private key to a server when negotiating a TLS session.

X.509.why: It specifies how X.509 certificate subjects, SANs and self-signed certificates are matched to clients, and discusses certificate validation pitfalls.
X.509.quote: The PKI (public key infrastructure) method of mutual-TLS OAuth client authentication adheres to the way in which X.509 certificates are traditionally used for authentication.

rejected.why: Client authentication happens at the TLS layer to OAuth endpoints, not through HTTP authentication schemes.
Token Binding is mentioned only in Appendix B as a related alternative, so the document is not about it.
JWK and the x5c parameter are used to carry certificates, but the document defines nothing new in JOSE.
JSON is only the encoding of metadata and responses.
It relies on PKI for certificate chain validation but does not define PKI mechanisms. X.509 covers the certificate matching.
SHA-256 is used only as the thumbprint hash function.

RFC8706.title: Restart Signaling for IS-IS

GSS-API.quote: This document updates [RFC4462] with new methods intended to support environments that desire to use the SHA-2 cryptographic hash functions.

SSH.why: It specifies new SSH key exchange methods, their messages, exchange hash computation and registration of method names, so SSH readers need it.
SSH.quote: The client sends: byte SSH_MSG_KEXGSS_INIT string output_token (from GSS_Init_sec_context()) string Q_C, client's ephemeral public key octet string
SSH.section: 5.1. Generic GSS-API Key Exchange with ECDH

elliptic curve.why: A substantial part of the document defines ECDH key exchange with NIST curves, X25519 and X448. This is a use of elliptic curve cryptography in the protocol.
elliptic curve.quote: we add support for key exchange based on Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman with the NIST P-256, P-384, and P-521

rejected.why: SHA-2 is used as the hash in the new methods, but the document does not specify or analyse the SHA family itself.
X25519 and X448 are used as key-agreement functions defined by RFC 7748, and the document does not define them. The elliptic curve tag already covers its ECDH content.
This is key exchange within SSH, which the SSH and GSS-API tags already cover. The document is not about key management in general.
MD5 is used only to derive method names from mechanism OIDs. The document is not about MD5.

RFC8733.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for MPLS-TE Label Switched Path (LSP) Auto-Bandwidth Adjustment with Stateful PCE
RFC8733.summary: Defines PCEP extensions (capability TLV, AUTO-BANDWIDTH-ATTRIBUTES TLV and sub-TLVs, overwhelm notifications) enabling auto-bandwidth adjustment of MPLS-TE LSPs under an active stateful PCE, for both PCE-initiated and PCC-initiated LSPs.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP and stateful PCE messages (PCInitiate, PCUpd, PCRpt, PCNtf) with new TLVs, so it belongs under PCE/PCEP.
PCE.quote: This document describes PCEP extensions for auto-bandwidth adjustment when employing an active stateful PCE for both PCE-initiated and PCC-initiated LSPs.

rejected.why: MPLS-TE LSPs are the managed objects, but the document specifies PCEP extensions, not MPLS itself.
Make-before-break signalling via RFC 3209 is only mentioned in passing; the document does not specify RSVP-TE.
The PCE tag already sits under traffic engineering, so the parent is implied.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations as the secure transport (PCEPS), so it is boilerplate.
The MIB and YANG modules are mentioned only in manageability considerations as possible future enhancements.
RFC 3471 is cited only for a table of bandwidth values.

RFC8734.title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Brainpool Curves for Transport Layer Security (TLS) Version 1.3
RFC8734.summary: Independent-stream RFC defining TLS 1.3 NamedGroup and SignatureScheme code points for three ECC Brainpool curves (P256, P384, P512), with test vectors, while noting the IETF does not endorse the approach.

TLS.why: The document extends TLS 1.3 with new supported_groups NamedGroup and signature_algorithms SignatureScheme values for Brainpool curves.
TLS.quote: This document provides the necessary protocol mechanisms for using ECC Brainpool curves in TLS 1.3.

elliptic curve.why: The subject is the use of the ECC Brainpool curves for ECDHE key exchange and ECDSA authentication, and the appendix gives curve test vectors.
elliptic curve.quote: This document adds new named groups for three elliptic curves defined in [RFC5639] to the "supported_groups" extension

ECDSA.why: Section 4 defines ECDSA SignatureScheme code points over the Brainpool curves with their hash functions.
ECDSA.quote: ecdsa_brainpoolP256r1tls13_sha256(0x081A)

rejected.why: The registry updates are boilerplate that follows from the main body, and the document is not about IANA guidance.
ECDHE is used as the key exchange, but the document defines no key management mechanism.
The IANA table notes DTLS-OK, but the document is not about DTLS.
Authentication uses ECDSA signature schemes only. The document says nothing about certificates or PKI.

RFC8735.title: Scenarios and Simulation Results of PCE in a Native IP Network
RFC8735.summary: Informational document describing scenarios and simulation results for applying a central PCE (Centralized Control Dynamic Routing, CCDR) to traffic engineering in native IP networks, compared against OSPF shortest-path routing.

PCE.why: The whole document is about using a central PCE to compute E2E traffic-engineered paths in native IP networks, with scenarios and simulations.
PCE.quote: This document describes various complex scenarios and simulation results when applying the Path Computation Element (PCE) in a native IP network.

rejected.why: OSPF is only the baseline reference algorithm in the simulations, not specified or extended.
BGP nexthop and eBGP are used as mechanisms for the solution, but the document is not about BGP itself.
Mentioned only as an alternative solution in the introduction.
Mentioned only to distinguish use cases; not the subject.
MPLS-TE is cited as an alternative solution only.
Implied by the PCE tag, which sits under it, so the parent is not listed separately.

RFC8736.title: PIM Message Type Space Extension and Reserved Bits
RFC8736.summary: RFC 8736 defines use of the reserved Flag Bits in the PIM version 2 common header per message type, creates a per-type registry, and extends the PIM type space with types 13-15 using a 4-bit subtype; it obsoletes RFC 6166.

PIM.why: The document updates the PIM common header and message type space, affecting PIM-SM, PIM-DM, BIDIR-PIM, BSR, and PFM. PIM is the specified protocol; the PIM-SM tag is not chosen because the document is not about sparse mode specifically.
PIM.quote: The PIM version 2 messages share a common message header format.  The common header definition contains eight reserved bits.

rejected.why: RFC 7761 is updated, but only its common header's reserved field. The document covers all PIM message types, not sparse mode specifically, so the parent PIM tag fits better.
The document updates the PIM Message Types registry, but that is a protocol-specific registry. The IANA tag covers registry guidance and stewardship, and the main body is about PIM header bits.
The multicast topic is already implied by the PIM technology tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC8737.title: Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) TLS Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) Challenge Extension
RFC8737.summary: Defines the tls-alpn-01 ACME challenge, which validates domain control via a TLS handshake negotiating the new "acme-tls/1" ALPN protocol and presenting a self-signed certificate with a critical acmeIdentifier extension.

ACME.why: The document extends ACME with a new challenge type, including its challenge object, validation steps and registry entry.
ACME.quote: This document specifies a new TLS-based challenge type, tls-alpn-01.

TLS.why: It defines a new ALPN protocol, acme-tls/1, and specifies how the ALPN and SNI extensions are used in the validation handshake. This is new use of TLS extensions that TLS readers would want.
TLS.quote: The ACME server MUST provide an ALPN extension with the single protocol name "acme-tls/1" and an SNI extension
TLS.section: 3. TLS with Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (TLS ALPN) Challenge

X.509.why: It defines a new critical X.509 certificate extension, with its OID and ASN.1 structure, and registers it in the PKIX extension OID arc.
X.509.quote: The acmeIdentifier extension is identified by the id-pe-acmeIdentifier object identifier (OID) in the id-pe arc
X.509.section: 3. TLS with Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (TLS ALPN) Challenge

rejected.why: JSON and JWS are only the encoding of the ACME request message, which is inherited from RFC 8555.
ASN.1 is used only to define the one-field Authorization structure, so the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
SHA-256 is only the digest used for the key authorization.
DNS is used only to resolve the domain being validated, and dNSName is only a certificate field.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate that supports the protocol definition.
X.509 is the more specific tag. The document also does not use PKIX path validation.

gaps.name: ACME (Automatic Certificate Management Environment)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an ACME tech tag under PKI, but I used 'ACME' above even though the ids listed contain it as 'ACME' under PKI, so no gap exists.

RFC8738.title: Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) IP Identifier Validation Extension
RFC8738.summary: Extends ACME with an "ip" identifier type and specifies how the http-01 and tls-alpn-01 challenges validate control of IPv4/IPv6 addresses for certificate issuance, while forbidding dns-01.

ACME.why: The document is an extension to ACME defining a new identifier type and challenge usage, so it belongs on the ACME page.
ACME.quote: This document specifies identifiers and challenges required to enable the Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) to issue certificates for IP addresses.

rejected.why: Certificates for IP addresses are the goal, but the document only specifies ACME validation, not certificate profiles.
The tls-alpn-01 challenge uses TLS and SNI, but the document defines nothing new about TLS itself.
The http-01 challenge uses the Host header, but HTTP is only the validation substrate.
Reverse-mapping names are used in SNI, and dns-01 is prohibited, but the document does not specify DNS behaviour.
IPv6 address text format is referenced for identifiers, but the document is not about IPv6.

RFC8739.title: Support for Short-Term, Automatically Renewed (STAR) Certificates in the Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME)
RFC8739.summary: Defines an ACME extension (STAR) that lets a CA automatically reissue short-lived X.509 certificates for an order and publish them at a fixed URL, with cancellation replacing revocation.

ACME.why: The document extends ACME with new order fields, directory metadata, error types and state transitions for auto-renewed certificates.
ACME.quote: This memo proposes an Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) extension to enable the issuance of Short-Term, Automatically Renewed (STAR) X.509 certificates.

rejected.why: STAR certificates are X.509, but the document specifies an ACME issuance mechanism, not the certificate format or profile.
Section 4.3 discusses cache directives for unauthenticated GET, but this is a minor operational point rather than a main subject.
Section 4.2 only assesses the impact of STAR on CT logs. It does not specify anything about CT.
OCSP appears only in the comparison with must-staple and the revocation discussion. The document does not specify it.
HTTP is the substrate. The document does register Cert-Not-Before and Cert-Not-After headers, but they are a small part of it.
JSON is only the encoding of ACME objects.

RFC8740.title: Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2
RFC8740.summary: Updates RFC 7540 to forbid TLS 1.3 post-handshake authentication (CertificateRequest) in HTTP/2, as an analog to the existing renegotiation prohibition, and clarifies other post-handshake TLS messages.

HTTP/2.why: The document updates the HTTP/2 specification (RFC 7540) with a new normative restriction on how HTTP/2 uses TLS 1.3.
HTTP/2.quote: HTTP/2 servers MUST NOT send post-handshake TLS 1.3 CertificateRequest messages.

TLS.why: It specifies how TLS 1.3 post-handshake messages (CertificateRequest, KeyUpdate, NewSessionTicket) and the post_handshake_auth extension must be handled when used with HTTP/2, which is TLS deployment guidance.
TLS.quote: TLS 1.3 [RFC8446] removes renegotiation and replaces it with separate post-handshake authentication and key update mechanisms.

rejected.why: Mentions HTTP/1.1 only as context for reactive client authentication. The document's subject is HTTP/2, which is the more specific tag.
The client certificate authentication is done at the TLS layer, not through an HTTP authentication scheme.
The document restricts TLS features for HTTP/2 rather than defining a binding of one protocol over another transport.

RFC8741.title: Ability for a Stateful Path Computation Element (PCE) to Request and Obtain Control of a Label Switched Path (LSP)
RFC8741.summary: Defines a PCEP extension (the C flag in the SRP object) letting a stateful PCE request delegation of LSPs from a PCC, including locally configured ones.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP for stateful PCE by adding the LSP Control Request flag and its operation. Readers of PCE/PCEP would expect it.
PCE.quote: This document describes an extension to the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) to enable a PCE to make requests for such control.

rejected.why: The LSPs are MPLS TE LSPs, but the document specifies PCEP signalling between PCE and PCC, not MPLS itself.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as the secure transport for PCEP (RFC 8253). The document defines nothing new about it.
TE LSPs are the managed objects, but RSVP-TE signalling is not discussed.
The PCEP YANG module is only mentioned as something that could be extended, in the Manageability section.

RFC8742.title: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) Sequences
RFC8742.summary: Defines the CBOR Sequence format (concatenated CBOR data items), the application/cbor-seq media type with a CoAP Content-Format ID, and the +cbor-seq structured syntax suffix.

CBOR.why: The document specifies a new format built on CBOR, including its encoding and decoding rules, so CBOR readers would expect it.
CBOR.quote: A CBOR Sequence consists of any number of encoded CBOR data items, simply concatenated in sequence.

media types.why: A substantial part of the document registers the application/cbor-seq media type and the +cbor-seq structured syntax suffix.
media types.quote: This specification defines and registers "+cbor-seq" as a structured syntax suffix for CBOR Sequences.

rejected.why: Section 4.1 only explains how to express CBOR Sequences in CDDL. The document does not specify or extend CDDL.
The document only registers a Content-Format ID for the new media type, which is an IANA action and not a change to CoAP.
JSON Text Sequences are mentioned only as an analogy, and the document is not about JSON.
COSE appears only in the Security Considerations as an optional way to add integrity protection.

RFC8743.title: Multiple Access Management Services Multi-Access Management Services (MAMS)
RFC8743.summary: Informational independent-submission RFC that defines the Multi-Access Management Services (MAMS) framework: requirements, architecture, and a JSON/WebSocket control protocol for selecting and combining multiple access paths (LTE, Wi-Fi, etc.) and configuring user-plane treatment such as MPTCP, GRE or IPsec.

MPTCP.why: A substantial section applies MAMS control procedures to configure and steer an MPTCP proxy as the convergence layer, including subflow addition and deletion. Readers of MPTCP would want this.
MPTCP.quote: An MPTCP proxy (e.g., see [TCPM-CONVERTERS]) is configured to be the N-MADP instance.
MPTCP.section: 11. Applying MAMS Control Procedures with MPTCP Proxy as User Plane

rejected.why: WebSocket is only the transport for the control messages; the document defines nothing new about it.
IPsec is one configurable adaptation-layer option and is not specified or extended here.
GRE is listed as a possible convergence encapsulation but is not specified or extended.
JSON is only the message encoding for the control messages.
MOBIKE appears only in a brief comparison in Section 10.
LTE and 5G are access technologies that MAMS is agnostic to. The document does not cover cellular specifics beyond measurement parameters.
Wi-Fi is one of several access links managed by MAMS, and the document does not cover IP over 802.11.

gaps.name: Multi-access management / multiconnectivity (MAMS)
gaps.why: The document is mainly about a framework for steering and aggregating traffic across multiple access networks. No taxonomy tag covers multi-access, multi-path path selection, or access traffic steering; the closest fits are the broad routing and traffic engineering topics.

RFC8744.title: Issues and Requirements for Server Name Identification (SNI) Encryption in TLS
RFC8744.summary: Informational document describing the problem of encrypting the TLS Server Name Indication, listing known attacks, reviewing HTTP co-tenancy/domain fronting, and stating requirements for future TLS-layer SNI encryption solutions.

TLS.why: The whole document concerns the TLS SNI extension, its history, attacks on encrypting it, and requirements for TLS-layer solutions, including ALPN hiding and DTLS/QUIC applicability.
TLS.quote: This document describes the general problem of encrypting the Server Name Identification (SNI) TLS parameter.

privacy.why: The motivation and requirements are privacy-driven: resisting pervasive monitoring and censorship, plus threat analysis (cut-and-paste, honeypot, forward secrecy).
privacy.quote: Encrypting the SNI complements this push for privacy and makes it harder to censor or otherwise provide differential treatment to specific Internet services.

rejected.why: HTTP co-tenancy fronting is discussed as an existing workaround, but the document is not specifying or extending HTTP.
Mentioned as a related privacy deployment and as a way to carry other protocols over HTTP, not the subject.
DNS privacy is cited as context that closes another monitoring channel; the document is not about it.
CDNs appear as examples of multiplexed hosting and delegation, but are not the subject.
DTLS and QUIC are mentioned only briefly as transports for which SNI encryption must also work.
Domain fronting is discussed, but the document's focus is TLS-layer SNI encryption rather than a web platform mechanism.

gaps.name: Encrypted SNI / Encrypted Client Hello
gaps.why: The document is about SNI encryption requirements, which has no dedicated taxonomy tag; TLS is the closest fit.

RFC8745.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for Associating Working and Protection Label Switched Paths (LSPs) with Stateful PCE
RFC8745.summary: Defines a PCEP extension (Path Protection Association type and TLV) that lets stateful PCEs and PCCs associate working and protection LSPs into a path protection association group.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP for stateful PCE with a new association type and TLV, including operation, error handling and state synchronization.
PCE.quote: This document defines the PCEP extension to associate two or more LSPs to provide end-to-end path protection.

rejected.why: MPLS-TE LSPs are the objects being associated, but the document specifies PCEP extensions, not MPLS itself.
Flags are mapped to the RSVP-TE PROTECTION object, but RSVP-TE is only referenced, not specified or extended.
Protection semantics are borrowed from RFC 4872, but the document does not address GMPLS in its own right.
TLS is only recommended for securing the PCEP session in Security Considerations; boilerplate.
SR is mentioned once in passing regarding LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLV inclusion.
IANA registrations are routine boilerplate for the extension.

gaps.name: PCEP (Path Computation Element Communication Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no PCEP tech tag; PCE is only a child of traffic engineering as an architecture and PCEP tag. The document is about PCEP stateful extensions, which fits PCE as best available.

RFC8746.title: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) Tags for Typed Arrays
RFC8746.summary: Defines CBOR tags for typed arrays of numeric data (by integer/float type, width and endianness), plus tags for multi-dimensional and homogeneous arrays, and registers them with IANA.

CBOR.why: The whole document specifies new CBOR tags (40, 41, 64-87, 1040) extending CBOR's data model, so it belongs on the CBOR page.
CBOR.quote: This document makes use of this extensibility to define a number of CBOR tags for typed arrays of numeric data

rejected.why: Section 5 only recommends CDDL typenames for the tags. CDDL is used as notation and the document does not define or extend it.
The IANA section registers the tags, but this is boilerplate and the document is not about IANA registries in general.
JSON is not discussed. Only JavaScript typed arrays are mentioned, as the motivation.

RFC8747.title: Proof-of-Possession Key Semantics for CBOR Web Tokens (CWTs)
RFC8747.summary: Defines the "cnf" confirmation claim for CBOR Web Tokens, letting a CWT declare the presenter's proof-of-possession key as a COSE_Key, an encrypted COSE_Key, or a key ID, and creates the CWT Confirmation Methods registry.

ACE.why: Produced by the ACE working group as a building block for constrained-environment authorization. CWT PoP keys are the token confirmation mechanism for ACE-OAuth. ACE is the closest fit for CWT-related work.
ACE.quote: CBOR Web Tokens with proof-of-possession keys are used in context of an architecture, such as the ACE OAuth Framework

COSE.why: A substantial part of the document specifies how COSE_Key, COSE_Encrypt and COSE_Encrypt0 structures are carried as PoP key representations inside the cnf claim.
COSE.quote: the "COSE_Key" member is a COSE_Key [RFC8152] representing the corresponding asymmetric public key
COSE.section: 3.2. Representation of an Asymmetric Proof-of-Possession Key

rejected.why: CBOR is the encoding substrate for CWTs. The document does not define anything new about CBOR itself.
RFC 7800 is the JWT equivalent. This document is about CWTs, and JWT is mentioned only for comparison and for registry mapping.
OAuth roles are mentioned only to map terminology (client, resource server). The document does not specify OAuth.
CDDL is cited only for the extended diagnostic notation used in examples.
The document defines token key confirmation semantics and does not cover authorization or access control in its own right. The ACE tag already covers that area.

gaps.name: CBOR Web Token (CWT)
gaps.why: The document extends CWT with the cnf claim and sets up a CWT confirmation-methods registry. The taxonomy has no CWT tag, so ACE and COSE are the nearest tags.

RFC8748.title: Registry Fee Extension for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)
RFC8748.summary: Defines an EPP extension mapping that lets clients query registry servers for fees, credits, account balance and credit limits associated with billable domain transactions, and carries fee data in create/renew/transfer/update/delete commands and responses.

EPP.why: The document specifies a new EPP extension (fee-1.0 namespace) extending the check, create, renew, transfer, update and delete commands and responses, so it belongs under EPP.
EPP.quote: This document describes an extension mapping for version 1.0 of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) [RFC5730].

rejected.why: XML and XML Schema are only the encoding for EPP messages and the schema syntax; the document is not about XML usage itself.
Domain names are the objects being billed, but the document does not specify DNS protocol or records.
The XML namespace and EPP extension registry registrations are boilerplate IANA considerations, not the subject.
The parent topic is implied by the EPP tag, which is the more specific fit.

RFC8749.title: Moving DNSSEC Lookaside Validation (DLV) to Historic Status
RFC8749.summary: RFC 8749 retires DNSSEC Lookaside Validation by moving RFCs 4431 and 5074 to Historic, and updates RFC 6698 and RFC 6840 to exclude DLV records and DLV registries.

DNSSEC.why: DLV is a DNSSEC trust anchor mechanism and DLV resource record. The document retires it and updates RFC 6840 on DNSSEC trust anchor selection.
DNSSEC.quote: This document retires DNSSEC Lookaside Validation (DLV) and reclassifies RFCs 4431 and 5074 as Historic.

rejected.why: RFC 6698 (TLSA) is updated only to drop DLV from its description of DNSSEC certificates. The document is not about DANE itself.
DNSSEC is the more specific tag. The DLV RR type IANA annotation is boilerplate-level.
The IANA action only marks the DLV RR type Obsolete. It is a minor consequence and not the subject.

RFC8750.title: Implicit Initialization Vector (IV) for Counter-Based Ciphers in Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)
RFC8750.summary: Defines implicit IV generation for counter-based AEAD ciphers (AES-GCM, AES-CCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) in ESP, derived from the sequence number to save 8 octets per packet, plus IKEv2 negotiation and new transform IDs.

ESP.why: The document changes how the ESP IV is generated and carried, and defines new ESP-only encryption transforms.
ESP.quote: Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) sends an initialization vector (IV) in each packet.

IKE.why: Specifies IKEv2 initiator and responder negotiation of implicit versus explicit IV, and registers new IKEv2 transform IDs.
IKE.quote: An initiator supporting this feature SHOULD propose implicit IV (IIV) algorithms in the Transform Type 1 (Encryption Algorithm) Substructure

rejected.why: AES-GCM and AES-CCM are only the ciphers whose IV generation is changed. The AES algorithms themselves are unchanged.
ChaCha20-Poly1305 is one of the covered algorithms, but the document only defines IV derivation and does not specify the cipher.
The ESP and IKE tags are more specific, so the IPsec parent is implied.
IoT is mentioned only as a motivating context. The document is not about IoT.
The IANA section only registers three transform IDs. This is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC8751.title: Hierarchical Stateful Path Computation Element (PCE)
RFC8751.summary: Informational RFC describing considerations and use cases for deploying stateful (passive, active, and PCE-initiated) Parent and Child PCEs in the hierarchical PCE architecture for multi-domain MPLS/GMPLS TE LSPs, including ACTN applicability.

PCE.why: The whole document is about PCE architecture and PCEP operations: stateful H-PCE, delegation, PCInitiate, PCRpt/PCUpd between parent and child PCEs.
PCE.quote: This document describes general considerations and use cases for the deployment of stateful, but not stateless, PCEs using the hierarchical PCE architecture.

rejected.why: MPLS/GMPLS LSPs are the setting, but the document is about PCE hierarchy, not GMPLS itself.
TLS is only recommended in Security Considerations for securing the PCEP session.
The PCEP YANG module is mentioned only in passing as future work in manageability.
RSVP-TE is mentioned only as the signalling used to set up LSPs; it is not the subject.
MPLS is background for the LSPs being computed; the document does not address MPLS itself.
ACTN and centralized control are touched on, but the document is not about SDN in general.

gaps.name: ACTN (Abstraction and Control of TE Networks)
gaps.why: The document has a subsection on its applicability, but the taxonomy has no ACTN tag. It is only a secondary theme here.

RFC8752.title: Report from the IAB Workshop on Exploring Synergy between Content Aggregation and the Publisher Ecosystem (ESCAPE)
RFC8752.summary: IAB workshop report summarizing discussion of Web Packaging (signed exchanges, bundles), AMP, and the publisher/aggregator relationship, including use cases, systemic effects, and security implications.

workshop reports.why: The document is an IAB workshop report recording discussion and outcomes of the ESCAPE workshop.
workshop reports.quote: The ESCAPE Workshop was convened by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) in July 2019. This report summarizes its significant points of discussion

web.why: The content is web architecture: Web Packaging, signed exchanges, origin authority, AMP, publishers and aggregators, and web performance, with no more specific web tag fitting.
web.quote: examine some proposed changes to the Internet and the Web, and their potential effects on the Internet publishing landscape

rejected.why: HTTP/HTTPS authority is background for explaining Web Packaging. The document does not specify or extend HTTP.
TLS is cited only as the connection-oriented security that Web Packaging contrasts with. The document is not about TLS.
The object-security discussion in Section 4.2 is substantial. But the document as a whole is about the publisher/aggregator ecosystem, and web security is only one part of it.
CDNs and AMP caches are mentioned in passing. They are not a subject of the report.
Caching by linking sites is discussed only as it relates to Web Packaging. The document does not address HTTP caching mechanisms.
The report is about web publishing ecosystem effects, not architectural principles of the Internet. Consolidation is touched on, but only for this ecosystem.

gaps.name: Web Packaging / signed exchanges / AMP
gaps.why: The central subject is Web Packaging (bundled exchanges and signed HTTP exchanges) and the AMP format. The taxonomy has no tag for these.

RFC8753.title: Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA) Review for New Unicode Versions
RFC8753.summary: RFC 8753 updates RFC 5892 to revise the IDNA review procedure for new Unicode versions, splitting it into an algorithmic comparison and a new code point analysis by an expert team, and clarifying the non-normative status of IANA's derived property tables.

IDN.why: The whole document specifies IDNA procedures for reviewing Unicode versions, updates RFC 5892 (derived properties, contextual rules), and clarifies the IANA IDNA tables.
IDN.quote: The standards for Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) require a review of each new version of Unicode to determine whether incompatibilities with prior versions

rejected.why: Unicode versions are the subject of the review, but the document is about IDNA's handling of them, not about Unicode usage in protocols generally.
The IANA tables and designated expert are discussed, but only as part of the IDNA review procedure; the document is not general IANA registry guidance.
DNS is only the context where labels are registered; no DNS protocol behaviour is specified.
The IDN tag is more specific; the document does not address internationalization of text broadly.
The designated expert team is appointed by the IESG, but this is procedure for one registry's review, not IETF process in general.

RFC8754.title: IPv6 Segment Routing Header (SRH)
RFC8754.summary: Specifies the IPv6 Segment Routing Header (Routing Type 4), its TLVs including HMAC, and the processing at SR source, transit and segment endpoint nodes, with deployment and security considerations.

SRv6.why: The document defines the SRH, the core SRv6 encapsulation, and the node behaviour for processing it.
SRv6.quote: Segment Routing can be applied to the IPv6 data plane using a new type of Routing Extension Header called the Segment Routing Header (SRH).

HMAC.why: A substantial part defines the SRH HMAC TLV, with HMAC generation, verification and key ID handling, and how it enables delegation.
HMAC.quote: The HMAC TLV is used to verify that the SRH applied to a packet was selected by an authorized party

rejected.why: IPv6 is the base protocol being extended with a routing header, but SRv6 is the more specific tag.
This is the parent of SRv6, so it is implied and not listed.
Section 5.5 covers flow label use for ECMP, but only briefly.
ICMP errors are generated during SRH processing and a new Parameter Problem code is registered, but the document is not about ICMP.
AH is mentioned only to say it is not used to secure the SRH.
The IANA registries are boilerplate here and are not the main subject.

RFC8755.title: Using Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite Algorithms in Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions
RFC8755.summary: Informational RFC from NSA profiling S/MIME (via CMS) to use only CNSA Suite algorithms: SHA-384, ECDSA/RSA signatures, ECDH/RSA key establishment, and AES-GCM/CBC content encryption.

S/MIME.why: The document is a CNSA-compliant algorithm profile of S/MIME, so S/MIME readers would want it.
S/MIME.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using the United States National Security Agency's Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite algorithms [CNSA] in Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME)

CMS.why: Most of the body specifies CMS algorithm identifiers and field usage (SignerInfo, KeyAgreeRecipientInfo, AuthEnvelopedData) for the CNSA algorithms.
CMS.quote: S/MIME makes use of the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) [RFC5652] [RFC5083]. In particular, the signed-data, enveloped-data, and authenticated-enveloped-data content types are used.

AES.why: The document mandates AES-256 GCM and CBC content encryption, plus AES Key Wrap with Padding.
AES.quote: MUST use AES [FIPS197] in Galois Counter Mode (GCM) [SP80038D] as the content-authenticated encryption algorithm

ECDSA.why: The document specifies ECDSA with SHA-384 on P-384, including its identifier and signature encoding.
ECDSA.quote: The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) is the CNSA Suite digital signature algorithm based on ECC.

RSA.why: The document specifies RSA signatures (PKCS1-v1_5 and PSS) and RSA key transport (PKCS1-v1_5 and OAEP) with constrained parameters.
RSA.quote: RSA signature key pairs used in CNSA Suite-compliant implementations are either RSA-3072 or RSA-4096.

SHA.why: SHA-384 is required throughout for signatures, KDF and padding schemes, and has its own section.
SHA.quote: SHA-384 is the sole CNSA Suite message digest algorithm.

rejected.why: Certificates are only required to comply with RFC 8603, which is a separate profile. This document does not specify them.
The more specific ECDSA tag fits better. The ECDH details are mostly references to RFC 5753.
ASN.1 is only the notation used for identifiers and structures. The document is not about it.
The more specific S/MIME tag already covers the email subject.
The ECDH key agreement, KDF and key wrap steps are CMS conventions inside the S/MIME profile. The document is not about key management as a subject.

gaps.name: CNSA Suite (NSA Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite)
gaps.why: The document is about a national-security cryptographic algorithm policy profile. The taxonomy has no tag for algorithm suites or policy profiles.

RFC8756.title: Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite Profile of Certificate Management over CMS
RFC8756.summary: Profiles Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) so that X.509 certificate enrollment and rekey between clients, RAs and CAs use only the NSA's CNSA Suite algorithms (SHA-384, ECDSA P-384, RSA-3072/4096, HMAC-SHA384).

PKI.why: CMC is a PKI certificate management protocol. The document profiles it for enrollment and rekey between clients, RAs and CAs. No CMC-specific tag exists, so the PKI parent is the best fit.
PKI.quote: This document specifies a profile of the Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) protocol for managing X.509 public key certificates

CMS.why: CMC messages are CMS SignedData structures. The profile constrains their construction, the signature algorithms and the CCC extension processing.
CMS.quote: the Full PKI Request MUST be used; it MUST be encapsulated in a SignedData, and the SignedData MUST be constructed in accordance with [RFC8755]

cryptography.why: A large part of the document fixes the algorithm choices of the CNSA Suite: P-384 ECDSA, RSA-3072/4096 with PSS parameters, SHA-384, HMAC-SHA384, and a minimum shared-secret strength.
cryptography.quote: The hash algorithm MUST be id-sha384 as defined in [RFC8017]

rejected.why: Certificates are the objects being managed. The certificate profile itself is RFC 8603, not this document.
ECDSA on P-384 is only one of the permitted algorithms, so the document is not about it.
RSA key sizes and PSS parameters are specified, but only as part of the overall CNSA algorithm constraints.
HMAC-SHA384 is mandated for shared-secret controls, but this is a minor detail of the profile.
RFC 8755, the CNSA S/MIME profile, is referenced only for how SignedData is constructed. This document does not cover S/MIME.

gaps.name: CMC (Certificate Management over CMS)
gaps.why: The document profiles CMC, but the taxonomy has no CMC tag. PKI is the nearest parent, so readers looking for CMC have no dedicated page.

RFC8757.title: Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) Latency Range Extension
RFC8757.summary: Defines a DLEP extension (Latency Range, extension type 4, data item type 28) that lets modem and router peers exchange the minimum and maximum latency seen on a link.

DLEP.why: The document extends DLEP with a new extension type and data item for latency range, so it belongs on the DLEP page.
DLEP.quote: This document defines an extension to the Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) to provide the range of latency that can be experienced on a link.

rejected.why: DLEP sits under MANET in the taxonomy, and the more specific DLEP tag is chosen, so the parent is implied.
The IANA section only registers two code points in existing DLEP registries. That is boilerplate, not the subject of the document.
The latency values are only carried as a data item in DLEP. The document defines no measurement methodology or metrics.

RFC8758.title: Deprecating RC4 in Secure Shell (SSH)
RFC8758.summary: BCP that deprecates the RC4 (arcfour) ciphers in SSH by updating RFC 4253 to MUST NOT, moving RFC 4345 to Historic, and marking the IANA SSH cipher entries historic.

RC4.why: The whole document is about deprecating the RC4/arcfour ciphers and their use in SSH, which is the RC4 tag's scope (including deprecation).
RC4.quote: This document deprecates RC4 in Secure Shell (SSH).

SSH.why: It updates the SSH transport specification (RFC 4253), moves RFC 4345 to Historic, and changes the SSH cipher registry, so SSH readers need it.
SSH.quote: [RFC4253] is updated to prohibit arcfour's use in SSH.

rejected.why: The registry update is routine IANA Considerations boilerplate that records the deprecation, so the document is not about IANA.
RFC 8429 (Kerberos RC4 deprecation) is only cited as a reference for RC4's weaknesses.
RFC 7465 (prohibiting RC4 in TLS) is only cited as a reference, and the document does not address TLS.

RFC8759.title: RTP Payload for Timed Text Markup Language (TTML)
RFC8759.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for carrying W3C TTML (XML timed text, e.g. captions and subtitles) in streaming workflows, including header usage, fragmentation, processor profile, loss protection and SDP mapping.

RTP payload format.why: The document's whole purpose is a new RTP payload format for TTML, specifying header field usage, payload structure, fragmentation and SDP parameters.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo describes a Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) payload format for Timed Text Markup Language (TTML)

rejected.why: RTP is the substrate; the more specific RTP payload format tag fits and implies RTP.
TTML is XML-based, but the document does not address XML usage itself; it only carries TTML documents.
SDP mapping is a short section following RFC 4855 conventions and defines nothing new about SDP.
It reuses the existing application/ttml+xml type and has no IANA actions or new registration.
It only notes that RTCP jitter calculation is unusable; it specifies nothing about RTCP.
The congestion section just points to RFC 3550, RFC 8083 and RFC 8085 and adds nothing new.

gaps.name: TTML (Timed Text Markup Language) / timed text and captions
gaps.why: The carried format is W3C TTML for subtitles and closed captions. The taxonomy has no tag for timed text or caption formats.

RFC8760.title: The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Digest Access Authentication Scheme
RFC8760.summary: RFC 8760 updates RFC 3261 so SIP Digest Access Authentication supports stronger hash algorithms such as SHA-256 and SHA-512/256 in place of MD5, and specifies UAC/UAS behaviour, forking handling and ABNF changes.

SIP.why: The document modifies SIP's authentication procedures: UAC/UAS behaviour, header fields, forking and ABNF. SIP readers need it.
SIP.quote: This document updates RFC 3261 by modifying the Digest Access Authentication scheme used by the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)

HTTP authentication.why: The document profiles HTTP Digest authentication for SIP, covering algorithms, qop and the A2 calculation. It relies on RFC 7616 and states differences from it, so readers of Digest authentication would want it.
HTTP authentication.quote: This section describes the modifications and clarifications required to apply the HTTP Digest Access Authentication scheme to SIP.

rejected.why: SHA-256 and SHA-512/256 are only the hash algorithms selected for Digest. The document does not specify or analyse them.
MD5 is discussed only as the legacy default being deprecated, not as a subject of the document.
A more specific technology tag (HTTP authentication) already covers this topic.
The document only uses ABNF to express its SIP grammar changes.

RFC8761.title: Video Codec Requirements and Evaluation Methodology
RFC8761.summary: RFC 8761 sets out requirements for an Internet video codec (the NETVC work) across seven application areas, and defines a methodology for measuring compression efficiency against HEVC/VP9 using BD-rate, PSNR and MS-SSIM.

codecs.why: The whole document defines requirements for a new video codec (efficiency, profiles and levels, bitstream syntax, error resilience, scalability) and how to evaluate it. It belongs on the codecs page.
codecs.quote: This document provides requirements for a video codec designed mainly for use over the Internet.

rejected.why: HEVC/H.265 is only the reference codec the new codec is benchmarked against. The document does not specify it or its RTP payload format.
VP9 is named only as a comparison baseline for the coding-efficiency requirement.
IPTV is one of seven application scenarios in Section 3. The document is not about IPTV service delivery.
The benchmarking tag covers network devices and functions. The evaluation methodology here measures codec rate-distortion performance.
Internet video streaming is only an application use case. The document specifies codec requirements, not streaming delivery or operations.

gaps.name: Video coding quality evaluation (BD-rate, PSNR, MS-SSIM)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for video or image compression efficiency testing, which is the subject of the Section 5 methodology. The codecs tag is the nearest fit.

RFC8762.title: Simple Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol
RFC8762.summary: Specifies STAMP, a UDP-based active measurement test protocol with Session-Sender and Session-Reflector packet formats, unauthenticated and HMAC-authenticated modes, and TWAMP Light interoperability, for measuring one-way and round-trip delay, delay variation and loss.

STAMP.why: The document is the base specification of STAMP, defining its packet formats, modes and behaviour.
STAMP.quote: This document defines an active performance measurement test protocol, Simple Two-way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP), that enables measurement of both one-way and round-trip performance metrics

rejected.why: TWAMP is the predecessor. The document covers only interoperability with TWAMP Light, and the taxonomy has no TWAMP tag in the id list I can confirm, so I did not use it.
HMAC-SHA-256 is only the integrity mechanism for authenticated mode. The document does not define anything new about HMAC.
UDP is just the transport for test packets. Nothing new is defined about UDP.
NTP and PTP timestamp formats are used in the packet fields. The document does not specify or extend those protocols.
This parent topic is implied by the STAMP tag, so listing it separately would be redundant.
IPsec and DTLS are only mentioned as options for confidentiality protection.

RFC8763.title: Deployment Considerations for Information-Centric Networking (ICN)
RFC8763.summary: An IRTF/ICNRG informational document describing ICN deployment configurations (clean-slate, overlay, underlay, slice, composite), migration paths, trial experiences, and protocol gaps needing standardization.

ICN.why: The whole document concerns deploying Information-Centric Networking: configurations, migration, trials and standardization gaps.
ICN.quote: This document provides a number of deployment considerations in the interest of helping the ICN community move forward to the next step of live deployments.

rejected.why: CoAP appears only as an example of a protocol that gateways translate to ICN; the document is not about CoAP.
HTTP-to-ICN mapping is discussed as a migration mechanism, but HTTP itself is not specified or extended.
SDN is an enabling infrastructure for slices and underlays, not the subject of the document.
SFC is mentioned as a possible integration point and gap, but only briefly.
CDN migration is one section, but the document is about ICN rather than CDN technology; ICN is the more specific subject.
IoT is an example use case for edge ICN deployment and trials, not a main subject.

RFC8764.title: Apple's DNS Long-Lived Queries Protocol
RFC8764.summary: Documents Apple's DNS Long-Lived Queries (LLQ) protocol, an EDNS(0) option-based extension to unicast DNS for change notification without polling, superseded by DNS Push Notifications (RFC 8765).

EDNS.why: The protocol is defined as a new EDNS(0) option (OPTION-CODE 1) with its own OPTION-DATA format, opcodes and error codes, registered with IANA.
EDNS.quote: implemented using the standard DNS message format [RFC1035] in conjunction with an EDNS(0) OPT pseudo-RR [RFC6891] with a new OPTION-CODE and OPTION-DATA format

DNS.why: The document specifies an extension to the DNS protocol: server behaviour, SRV-based discovery, setup handshake, event responses and lease refresh.
DNS.quote: This document defines an Apple extension to unicast DNS that enables a client to issue long-lived queries that allow a unicast DNS server to notify clients

rejected.why: DNS-SD is the motivating use case for LLQ, but the document specifies a general DNS change-notification mechanism, not service discovery itself.
Dynamic updates are only mentioned as the source of Add and Remove events and as an analogy for finding the zone's server.
Multicast DNS is mentioned only as background for how it handles change notification natively.
NAT-PMP and PCP are mentioned in Appendix A as a workaround for UDP mapping expiry, not specified here.
LLQ runs over UDP, and Appendix A discusses the problems that causes. UDP is the substrate, and the document doesn't define anything new about it.

gaps.name: DNS Push Notifications / DNS change notification
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for DNS push or long-lived query change notification. The closest tags are DNS and EDNS.

RFC8765.title: DNS Push Notifications
RFC8765.summary: Defines DNS Push Notifications, a DSO-based (over TLS/TCP) mechanism with SUBSCRIBE, PUSH, UNSUBSCRIBE and RECONFIRM messages letting clients be asynchronously notified of DNS record changes, including SRV-based server discovery.

DNS.why: The document specifies a new DNS protocol mechanism: new DSO TLVs, discovery via SOA/SRV queries, and change notification semantics for RRsets.
DNS.quote: This document defines a mechanism for a client to be notified of such changes to DNS records, called DNS Push Notifications.

DNS-SD.why: DNS-SD is the primary motivating use case, along with the Discovery Proxy and RECONFIRM for stale service data, so DNS-SD readers would want this.
DNS-SD.quote: It is immediately relevant in the case of DNS-based Service Discovery [RFC6763] but is not limited to that use case

rejected.why: DoT is the transport substrate (DSO over TLS over TCP port 853); the document does not define anything new about DoT itself.
TLS is used as the required security mechanism, with only usage notes on early data and resumption; not about TLS.
DNS Update is mentioned as a related mechanism that may share a server/session, but the document is not about it.
DNSSEC is only recommended for authenticating SRV lookups in Security Considerations.
DANE TLSA is referenced for authenticating the server but not specified or extended here.
TCP is the substrate; the document only motivates its use and does not extend it.

gaps.name: DNS Stateful Operations (DSO)
gaps.why: The document defines four new DSO TLV types, but the taxonomy has no DSO tag; it falls under DNS.

RFC8766.title: Discovery Proxy for Multicast DNS-Based Service Discovery
RFC8766.summary: Specifies a Discovery Proxy that answers unicast DNS queries (including DNS-SD) for delegated subdomains by querying the local link with Multicast DNS and translating the results, with rules for TTLs, NSEC, SOA/NS/SRV records, and DNSSEC online signing.

DNS-SD.why: The proxy exists to make DNS-based Service Discovery work across links, including domain enumeration and service browsing translation.
DNS-SD.quote: uses Multicast DNS to discover Multicast DNS records on its local link on demand, and makes corresponding DNS records visible in the Unicast DNS namespace

mDNS.why: Core mechanism is translating between .local Multicast DNS and unicast DNS, with caching, query timing and rate limiting.
mDNS.quote: a Discovery Proxy consults its local link, using Multicast DNS, to find the answer to the question

DNSSEC.why: A dedicated section covers online signing only and synthesizing single-name NSEC records for authenticated denial.
DNSSEC.quote: the Discovery Proxy needs to possess a copy of the signing keys in order to generate authoritative signed data

rejected.why: General DNS is implied by the DNS-SD and mDNS children; administrative record rules are part of the proxy, not a separate DNS topic.
Discussed only as an alternative that is rejected, and the proxy must return negative answers for _dns-update SRV queries.
DHCP option 15 is only a way for clients to learn a domain name for enumeration.
The IPv6 section is brief and only covers .local zones and reverse mapping; the document is not about IPv6.
No EDNS content is in the document.
The more specific DNS-SD tag already covers this.

gaps.name: DNS Push Notifications / DNS Long-Lived Queries
gaps.why: The document specifies proxy behavior for LLQ and DNS Push subscriptions, but the taxonomy has no tag for DNS Stateful Operations or Push Notifications.

RFC8767.title: Serving Stale Data to Improve DNS Resiliency
RFC8767.summary: Defines "serve-stale", a method for recursive DNS resolvers to use expired cached records when authoritative servers cannot be reached, updating the TTL definitions in RFC 1034, 1035 and 2181.

DNS.why: The document specifies resolver caching behaviour and amends the DNS TTL definition, so it is about DNS resolver behaviour and operations.
DNS.quote: This document defines a method (serve-stale) for recursive resolvers to use stale DNS data to avoid outages when authoritative nameservers cannot be reached

rejected.why: DNSSEC is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a risk of stale signatures; the document is not about it.
Section 9 only records that an EDNS option was proposed and rejected; no option is defined.
DoS resilience is a motivation, but the document specifies a resolver caching technique, not DDoS mitigation signalling.
TLSA is mentioned only in passing in Security Considerations.
mDNSResponder is mentioned only as an implementation that uses stale data.

RFC8768.title: Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) Hop-Limit Option
RFC8768.summary: Defines the CoAP Hop-Limit option and the 5.08 Hop Limit Reached response code to prevent and detect infinite proxy forwarding loops, including diagnostics and HTTP mapping.

CoAP.why: The document extends CoAP with a new option and a new response code, and specifies proxy behaviour for them.
CoAP.quote: To prevent and detect such loops, this document specifies the Hop-Limit CoAP option.

rejected.why: Section 5 only maps the option to HTTP Via/CDN-Loop headers and the 508 status for HTTP/CoAP proxies; HTTP is not the subject.
DOTS is only the motivating use case, cited as an informative reference. The document is general.
Caching rules for the 5.08 response and the cache key are CoAP caching details, not about HTTP caching.
The IANA section only registers a CoAP option number and a response code. It is boilerplate evidence.
DDoS signalling is mentioned only as an example application of CoAP.

RFC8769.title: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Content Types for Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR)
RFC8769.summary: Defines two new CMS content types (and OIDs, ASN.1 module, and innerContent values) for wrapping a CBOR item or a CBOR Sequence in CMS objects.

CMS.why: The document extends CMS by defining new content types and OIDs, plus an ASN.1 module, for use within CMS wrappers such as signed-data and auth-enveloped-data.
CMS.quote: This document defines a set of content types for CMS that hold CBOR content.

CBOR.why: The content types exist to carry CBOR items and CBOR Sequences, so CBOR readers would want this RFC for how to identify CBOR content in CMS.
CBOR.quote: This section defines a new content type for wrapping an encoded CBOR item in a CMS object.

rejected.why: COSE is mentioned only as an alternative message-security system for CBOR; the document does not specify or extend it.
The ASN.1 module is only the formal vehicle for the OID definitions; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
It adds new values for the application/cms innerContent parameter, but that is a minor registration, not the document's subject.
OIDs sit under the S/MIME arc, but the document is about CMS content types, not S/MIME secure email.

RFC8770.title: Host Router Support for OSPFv2
RFC8770.summary: Defines the Host-bit (H-bit) in OSPFv2 router-LSAs so a router can advertise itself as non-transit, modifies the SPF calculation and autodiscovery via RI LSA capability, and updates RFC 6987 to advertise Type 2 external/NSSA LSAs with high cost.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPFv2 with a new router-LSA bit, modifies the SPF calculation of RFC 2328, and updates RFC 6987 on stub router advertisement.
OSPF.quote: This document defines a bit called the Host-bit (H-bit). This bit enables a router to advertise that it is a non-transit router.

rejected.why: OSPFv3's R-bit is mentioned only as an analogous feature; the document specifies OSPFv2 only.
BGP virtual route reflectors are cited only as a use case; nothing about BGP is specified.
Route reflectors are only a motivating use case, not the subject of the document.
The IANA section merely registers values; it is boilerplate and not the document's subject.

RFC8771.title: The Internationalized Deliberately Unreadable Network NOtation (I-DUNNO)
RFC8771.summary: An April 1st joke RFC defining I-DUNNO, a Unicode/UTF-8-based notation that deliberately obfuscates IPv4 and IPv6 addresses to discourage human reading, with "confusion level" requirements.

humor.why: Published 1 April as a parody; the whole document is a whimsical spoof of address notation and Unicode confusability.
humor.quote: a notation designed to replace current textual representations of IP addresses with something that is not only more concise but will also discourage this small, but obviously important, subset of human activity

UTF-8.why: The notation is formed by packing address bits into UTF-8 octet sequences, and the document walks through the encoding table and bit allocation.
UTF-8.quote: I-DUNNO leverages UTF-8 [RFC3629] to obfuscate IP addresses for humans.

Unicode.why: Confusion levels are defined in terms of Unicode scripts, symbols, confusables, directionality and emoji, so the document is about Unicode usage, albeit satirically.
Unicode.quote: focused of late on the admirable confusion (and thus discouragement) potential of [UNICODE] as an address notation

rejected.why: IPv6 addresses are only the data being encoded; the document does not specify or analyse IPv6.
IDNA2008 DISALLOWED property is used as a validity test for confusion, but the document is not about internationalized domain names.
IPv4 addresses are only an input to the notation, not a subject of the document.
The document concerns textual representation as a joke, not address architecture or allocation; the IANA revocation request is satire.

RFC8772.title: The China Mobile, Huawei, and ZTE Broadband Network Gateway (BNG) Simple Control and User Plane Separation Protocol (S-CUSP)
RFC8772.summary: Defines S-CUSP, a TCP-based control channel protocol between a BNG control plane and user planes for control/user plane separation, covering session setup, subscriber session management, CGN address allocation, state sync, message and TLV formats.

network management.why: The document defines a new CP-to-UP control/management protocol for broadband gateways. The taxonomy has no BNG/CUPS tag, so the closest fit is the network management and operations area.
network management.quote: This document specifies the Simple CU Separation Protocol (S-CUSP) for communications over the BNG control channel between a BNG CP and a set of UPs.

CGN.why: A substantial part defines CGN public address allocation, renewal and release messages and the CGN port-range TLV.
CGN.quote: CGN address allocation/renew/release procedures are designed for the case where the CGN function is running on the UP.

L2TP.why: The document specifies L2TP LAC and LNS subscriber and tunnel TLVs and the call flows for separated LAC/LNS operation.
L2TP.quote: the BNG is running as an LNS and separated into LNS-CP and LNS-UP.

PPPoE.why: PPPoE access call flows and PPP subscriber TLVs are a substantial part of the specification.
PPPoE.quote: The UP is responsible for redirecting the PPPoE control packets to the CP or RG.

rejected.why: Only named as the Mi management interface protocol, and its parameters are out of scope.
The substrate carrying S-CUSP sessions; nothing new is defined about TCP.
DHCP appears in the call flows and is relayed over the Si, but it is not specified or extended here.
AAA via RADIUS is external; only the vendor ID format is borrowed.
The notation is used to describe messages, but the document is not about RBNF.
Only recommended as the security mechanism in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.

gaps.name: BNG Control and User Plane Separation (CUPS) / S-CUSP
gaps.why: The document's main subject, the broadband network gateway CP/UP separation protocol, has no dedicated tag in the taxonomy.

RFC8773.title: TLS 1.3 Extension for Certificate-Based Authentication with an External Pre-Shared Key
RFC8773.summary: RFC 8773 defines an experimental TLS 1.3 extension, tls_cert_with_extern_psk, that combines certificate-based authentication with an external PSK in the key schedule to protect against future quantum computers.

TLS.why: The document specifies a new TLS 1.3 extension, its handshake behaviour, and key schedule changes.
TLS.quote: This document specifies a TLS 1.3 extension that allows a server to authenticate with a combination of a certificate and an external pre- shared key (PSK).

post-quantum.why: The motivation is quantum resistance: an external PSK in the key schedule keeps confidentiality if (EC)DH is broken. This is a substantial part of the document.
post-quantum.quote: this document describes a TLS 1.3 extension to protect today's communications from the future invention of a large- scale quantum computer

rejected.why: Certificates are used for authentication, but their processing is unchanged. The document is not about certificate profiles.
HMAC is used for PSK binders and HKDF, but only as a building block.
Generation and distribution of external PSKs is explicitly out of scope.
The TLS tag already covers the authentication aspect. The document is about a TLS extension, not authentication in general.
RFC 4086 is cited only in Security Considerations as guidance.
The extension type registration is boilerplate. The document is not about IANA registries.

RFC8774.title: The Quantum Bug
RFC8774.summary: An April 1st humorous RFC claiming quantum entanglement will yield zero RTT and break RTT-dependent mechanisms (LEDBAT, MPTCP coupled congestion control, RTP circuit breakers), suggesting RTT lower bounds and flow control.

humor.why: Published 1 April as a whimsical parody of Internet-failure warnings; a reader of humorous RFCs would expect it.
humor.quote: Worse than the millennium bug, this unexpected value is bound to cause serious Internet failures unless the specifications are fixed in time.

LEDBAT.why: Analyses in detail how LEDBAT's delay calculations and cwnd behave under zero RTT.
LEDBAT.quote: The Low Extra Delay Background Transfer (LEDBAT) congestion control mechanism [RFC6817] is a very interesting failure case

MPTCP.why: Examines how MPTCP's coupled congestion control divides by RTT and fails at zero RTT.
MPTCP.quote: The coupled congestion control mechanism proposed for MPTCP in [RFC6356] requires calculating a value called "alpha".

RTP congestion control.why: Discusses how the RTP circuit breaker throughput equation breaks at zero RTT, a congestion control topic for RTP.
RTP congestion control.quote: The RTP Circuit Breakers [RFC8083] require calculation of a well-known equation which yields the throughput of a TCP connection

rejected.why: TCP is cited as the fallback that still works (RTO bound, rwnd), but it isn't the document's subject.
Covered by the more specific LEDBAT and RTP congestion control tags, so the parent is implied.
Mentioned only as one of the few protocols prepared for 0-RTT.
TLS 1.3 is mentioned only in passing as 0-RTT capable.
DNS over TCP is a passing joke in the conclusion.
UDP options and a receiver window are suggested briefly, but UDP is not the subject.

RFC8775.title: PIM Designated Router Load Balancing
RFC8775.summary: Specifies a PIM-SM extension (DRLB-Cap and DRLB-List Hello options, hash-based Group Designated Router selection, and Assert modification) so multiple last-hop routers on a LAN share multicast forwarding load.

PIM-SM.why: The document modifies PIM-SM by adding new Hello options, GDR election, and Assert behaviour. PIM-SM readers need it.
PIM-SM.quote: This document specifies a modification to the PIM-SM protocol that allows more than one of the PIM-SM routers to take on this responsibility

rejected.why: IGMP membership reports are what trigger GDR processing, but the document doesn't specify or change IGMP.
MLD is mentioned only as a membership report mechanism. The document doesn't specify or change it.
SSM (S,G) flows are handled by the hash, but the document isn't about SSM itself.
ECMP is mentioned only in passing, as the way first-hop load balancing happens naturally.
The registry creation is boilerplate for this document and doesn't make it about IANA.

RFC8776.title: Common YANG Data Types for Traffic Engineering
RFC8776.summary: Defines two YANG modules (ietf-te-types and ietf-te-packet-types) containing common typedefs, identities and groupings for modelling Traffic Engineering configuration and state, drawing on MPLS-TE, GMPLS and RSVP-TE.

YANG.why: The document's deliverable is YANG modules of reusable types and groupings for TE models.
YANG.quote: This document defines a collection of common data types and groupings in YANG data modeling language.

traffic engineering.why: The subject matter is TE concepts (bandwidth, path constraints, SRLG, protection, metrics) modelled as common types.
traffic engineering.quote: intended to be imported by modules that model Traffic Engineering (TE) configuration and state capabilities

RSVP-TE.why: Many identities model RSVP-TE session and LSP attribute flags, explicit routes and association types.
RSVP-TE.quote: A base YANG identity for supported LSP path flags as defined in [RFC3209], [RFC4090], [RFC4736]

GMPLS.why: Includes GMPLS switching capabilities, LSP encoding types, and recovery/protection types.
GMPLS.quote: A base YANG identity for supported interface switching capabilities as defined in [RFC3471].

rejected.why: MPLS-TE is the context but the document is about data types for TE, not MPLS itself; the more specific TE/RSVP-TE/GMPLS tags cover it.
Only the management protocol the YANG models are accessed through; mentioned in boilerplate and intro.
Objective functions reference PCEP RFCs but the document does not specify PCE.
Not an SNMP MIB; YANG is the data modelling language here.
Performance metrics groupings are included but are one part of the TE types; secondary at most and not the focus.

RFC8777.title: DNS Reverse IP Automatic Multicast Tunneling (AMT) Discovery
RFC8777.summary: Defines the DNS AMTRELAY resource record (type 260) and the DRIAD mechanism by which AMT gateways discover AMT relays via the reverse-IP DNS zone of a multicast source, updating RFC 7450 relay discovery.

AMT.why: The document updates RFC 7450 AMT relay discovery, with relay selection, Happy Eyeballs and restart guidance.
AMT.quote: A new DNS resource record named AMTRELAY is defined for publishing AMT relays for source-specific multicast channels.

DNS.why: It defines a new DNS resource record type, with its RData format, presentation format, reverse-zone use and IANA registry.
DNS.quote: The AMTRELAY RRType has the mnemonic AMTRELAY and type code 260 (decimal).

rejected.why: SSM channels are the context the mechanism works within, but the document does not specify or extend SSM.
DNS-SD is only used as a preferred alternative discovery method before DRIAD.
The document applies RFC 8305 to AMT relay selection but does not specify Happy Eyeballs itself.
DNSSEC is mentioned only in Security Considerations as one way to protect the record.
AMT is the more specific tag, and the multicast tag is implied as its ancestor.

gaps.name: AMT (Automatic Multicast Tunneling)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an AMT tech tag under multicast, and I used it. No gap.

RFC8778.title: Use of the HSS/LMS Hash-Based Signature Algorithm with CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE)
RFC8778.summary: Specifies how to use the HSS/LMS hash-based signature algorithm (RFC 8554) with COSE, defining the algorithm identifier, key type and parameter registrations, and examples.

LMS.why: The document is about using HSS/LMS signatures, including HSS, LMS and LM-OTS structure overview, operational statefulness and security considerations. LMS is the most specific tag.
LMS.quote: specifies the conventions for using the Hierarchical Signature System (HSS) / Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS) hash-based signature algorithm

COSE.why: It defines the COSE algorithm identifier HSS-LMS, the COSE key type and key parameter, and COSE examples (COSE_Sign1 and full signed message).
COSE.quote: with the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) [RFC8152] syntax

rejected.why: Motivation is post-quantum security, but LMS is the more specific child tag and already implies this.
Parent of LMS; the more specific child is chosen instead.
SHA-256 is only the hash function used by HSS/LMS, not something the document specifies.
CBOR is the encoding substrate for COSE; the document is not about CBOR itself.
Registry entries are boilerplate-like additions, not the main subject.

RFC8779.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for GMPLS
RFC8779.summary: Standards-track document extending PCEP with new objects, TLVs, flags and error codes (generalized bandwidth, load balancing, endpoints, label subobjects, protection attributes, GMPLS capability) so a PCE can compute paths for GMPLS networks.

PCE.why: The document specifies PCEP extensions, so the PCE/PCEP subject page is the main home.
PCE.quote: This memo provides extensions to the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) for the support of the GMPLS control plane

GMPLS.why: The extensions carry GMPLS-specific information (labels, switching and encoding types, SDH/OTN concatenation, protection), so GMPLS readers need it.
GMPLS.quote: This document complements these RFCs by addressing the extensions required for GMPLS applications and routing requests

rejected.why: Its encodings are reused for the bandwidth and label formats, but the document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE.
RFC 8253 is only mentioned in Security Considerations as the way to secure PCEP.
PCE and GMPLS are the more specific tags for this subject.
RBNF is used only as the grammar notation, not as the subject.
The OSPF-based PCE discovery capability is only mentioned briefly in Section 2.1.1.
The IS-IS-based PCE discovery capability is only mentioned briefly in Section 2.1.1.

gaps.name: PCE / PCEP (Path Computation Element Communication Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists PCE only as a child of traffic engineering and has no GMPLS-specific tag under MPLS where such tags would be expected. I tagged ids 'PCE' and 'GMPLS' as they appear, but the taxonomy shows GMPLS under MPLS and PCE under traffic engineering.

RFC8780.title: The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extension for Wavelength Switched Optical Network (WSON) Routing and Wavelength Assignment (RWA)
RFC8780.summary: Defines PCEP extensions (WA object, wavelength selection/restriction/allocation TLVs, signal-processing XRO/IRO subobjects, errors) enabling a PCE to perform Routing and Wavelength Assignment in WSON optical networks.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP with new objects, TLVs, error types and flags for WSON RWA path computation.
PCE.quote: This document provides Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) extensions for the support of Routing and Wavelength Assignment (RWA) in Wavelength Switched Optical Networks (WSONs).

GMPLS.why: Wavelength switched optical (LSC) networks are controlled via GMPLS; the document covers label sets, explicit label control and LSC labels for wavelength assignment.
GMPLS.quote: Explicit Label Control [RFC3471] where the PCE allocates which label to use for each interface/node along the path.

rejected.why: PCEPS/TLS is only mentioned in Security Considerations as an option; the document does not specify anything about it.
RSVP-TE is referenced only for the 'L' field of IRO subobjects and as signaling context; not the subject.
The document is about PCEP for optical path computation; PCE is the more specific tag and already covers it.
OSPF TE is only referenced for link identifier formats and TED population.

gaps.name: Wavelength Switched Optical Networks (WSON) / RWA
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for optical networking or routing and wavelength assignment; GMPLS is the nearest fit.

RFC8781.title: Discovering PREF64 in Router Advertisements
RFC8781.summary: Defines a new IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Router Advertisement option (PREF64, type 38) that conveys NAT64 prefixes and their lifetimes to hosts, with usage guidelines for multiple prefixes and consistency checks.

neighbor discovery.why: The document's core deliverable is a new IPv6 ND/RA option with format, lifetime processing and router consistency checking rules.
neighbor discovery.quote: This document specifies a Neighbor Discovery [RFC4861] option to be used in Router Advertisements (RAs) to communicate NAT64 prefixes to hosts.

NAT64.why: The option exists to discover the NAT64 prefix; the document covers use cases and handling of multiple NAT64 prefixes, so NAT64 readers would want it.
NAT64.quote: it is useful for hosts to know the NAT64 prefix for several reasons
NAT64.section: 2. Use Cases for Communicating the NAT64 Prefix to Hosts

rejected.why: DNS64 is a motivating use case for hosts knowing the prefix, but the document specifies nothing about DNS64 itself.
Only mentioned as a use case needing the NAT64 prefix; not specified or extended here.
Referenced as an alternative discovery mechanism and in ordering preferences, but not the subject.
Mentioned as motivation for local validation with DNS64 only.
Parent of NAT64; the more specific NAT64 tag fits, so the parent is implied.
The IANA option-type assignment is boilerplate and not the subject.

RFC8782.title: Distributed Denial-of-Service Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) Signal Channel Specification
RFC8782.summary: Specifies the DOTS signal channel, a CoAP-over-(D)TLS protocol with CBOR encoding and a YANG model by which clients request DDoS mitigation from servers, including session configuration, heartbeats, conflict handling and redirection.

DOTS.why: The whole document defines the DOTS signal channel protocol used to request DDoS mitigation.
DOTS.quote: This document specifies the Distributed Denial-of-Service Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) signal channel, a protocol for signaling the need for protection against Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attacks

rejected.why: CoAP is the substrate the signal channel is built on; the document uses it rather than extending it.
(D)TLS is the security layer; the profile in Section 7 is DOTS-specific usage, not a new TLS extension.
The YANG module is used only as a data model and encoding for messages, not for device management.
CBOR is only the message encoding.
The DOTS-specific Happy Eyeballs variant is a small part of the document built on RFC 8305.

gaps.name: DOTS (DDoS Open Threat Signaling)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has the DDoS topic and a DOTS tech tag (listed as DOTS under DDoS), but my chosen id 'DOTS' is not in the taxonomy; the closest fitting tag is 'DOTS' under DDoS, which I used as listed.

RFC8783.title: Distributed Denial-of-Service Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) Data Channel Specification
RFC8783.summary: Specifies the DOTS data channel, a RESTCONF-over-TLS channel and YANG module by which DOTS clients register, create aliases for protected resources, and install drop/accept/rate-limit filtering rules on a DOTS server for DDoS mitigation.

DOTS.why: The document defines the DOTS data channel, companion to the signal channel, for DDoS mitigation coordination between DOTS agents.
DOTS.quote: The document specifies a Distributed Denial-of-Service Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) data channel used for bulk exchange of data

YANG.why: A substantial part of the document defines a new YANG module for aliases, ACLs and capabilities, with tree diagrams.
YANG.quote: The DOTS data channel YANG module 'ietf-dots-data-channel' provides a method for DOTS clients to manage aliases for resources

RESTCONF.why: The data channel is built on RESTCONF methods and resource conventions, with detailed use for POST/PUT/GET/DELETE of DOTS resources; it is the document's operating protocol, not mere transport.
RESTCONF.quote: This document uses RESTCONF [RFC8040] over TLS over TCP as the DOTS data channel protocol.

rejected.why: RESTCONF is used, not NETCONF; NETCONF only mentioned in security boilerplate. Note RESTCONF is tagged separately.
TLS is only the secure substrate; no new TLS extension defined.
HTTP methods and status codes are used via RESTCONF; nothing new defined about HTTP itself.
JSON is only the payload encoding for YANG data.
Parent topic implied by the DOTS tech tag.
Filtering rules are ACLs for DDoS mitigators; the document is not about firewalls as such.

RFC8784.title: Mixing Preshared Keys in the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) for Post-quantum Security
RFC8784.summary: Extends IKEv2 with a post-quantum preshared key (PPK) mixed into SK_d, SK_pi and SK_pr, using new notifications, so IPsec SAs stay secure against quantum attackers.

IKE.why: The document specifies an extension to IKEv2: new notifications, a modified key derivation and an upgrade procedure.
IKE.quote: this document describes an extension of IKEv2 to allow it to be resistant to a quantum computer by using preshared keys.

post-quantum.why: The motivation and security analysis concern quantum resistance, including Grover's algorithm, entropy requirements and a downgrade attack. It does not define a PQ algorithm, so only the parent tag fits.
post-quantum.quote: someone storing VPN communications today could decrypt them at a later time when a quantum computer is available.

rejected.why: IKE is the more specific tag. The document changes IKEv2 negotiation and key derivation, not the IPsec architecture or ESP.
The PPK distribution discussion is brief and out of scope. IKE already covers the key derivation changes.
The document explicitly avoids new PQ algorithms and does not use ML-KEM.
EAP is mentioned only to show how the PPK exchange works when EAP is used in IKE_AUTH.

RFC8785.title: JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS)
RFC8785.summary: Defines the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS), which produces a deterministic canonical form of I-JSON data (ECMAScript primitive serialization, sorted properties, UTF-8) so it can be hashed and signed.

JSON.why: The whole document specifies a canonical serialization of JSON data, including whitespace, string and number serialization, and property sorting. It is a JSON-based format specification.
JSON.quote: This specification defines how to create a canonical representation of JSON data by building on the strict serialization methods for JSON primitives defined by ECMAScript

rejected.why: JWS and JWK Thumbprint are mentioned only as comparison and compatibility points. JCS is an alternative approach and does not define JOSE.
XML signature canonicalization is cited only as a motivating analogy.
Unicode string handling and UTF-16 sorting are details of the algorithm. The document is not about Unicode usage in general.
UTF-8 is only the final output encoding step.
The scheme prepares data for hashing and signing but defines no cryptographic algorithm.
base64url is mentioned only as the alternative used by JWS.

gaps.name: JSON canonicalization
gaps.why: Canonical serialization of data for signing is not a subject the taxonomy covers, apart from the general JSON tag.

RFC8786.title: Updated Rules for Processing Stateful PCE Request Parameters Flags
RFC8786.summary: Updates RFC 8231 to specify that unassigned flags in the PCEP Stateful PCE Request Parameters (SRP) object must be set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt, and advises future specs on flag interactions.

PCE.why: The document defines processing rules for the SRP object Flags field in PCEP for stateful PCE, updating RFC 8231. PCE and PCEP are exactly its subject.
PCE.quote: Unassigned flags MUST be set to zero on transmission and MUST be ignored on receipt.
PCE.section: 3.2. Flags Field of the SRP Object

rejected.why: MPLS TE LSPs are only the context in which PCEP computes paths. The document says nothing about MPLS itself.
The IANA section only updates a registry reference. The body is about PCEP flag processing, not IANA registries or guidance.
The PCE tag already sits under traffic engineering. The document doesn't address traffic engineering in its own right.
