RFC8787.title: Location Source Parameter for the SIP Geolocation Header Field
RFC8787.summary: Defines the "loc-src" parameter for the SIP Geolocation header field so an entity adding a locationValue (mainly for emergency calling) can identify itself by hostname, updating RFC 6442.

SIP.why: The document extends the SIP Geolocation header field (updating RFC 6442) with a new header field parameter and registers it in the SIP parameters registry.
SIP.quote: This document defines the "loc-src" parameter so that the entity adding the locationValue to the Geolocation header field can identify itself using its hostname.

geolocation.why: It concerns conveyance of location information and how a recipient chooses among multiple locationValues, so geolocation readers would want it.
geolocation.quote: Knowing the identity of the entity that added the location to the message allows the recipient to choose which location to consider first

emergency services.why: Emergency calling architectures (3GPP, ETSI) motivate the parameter, so emergency services readers would find it relevant.
emergency services.quote: The primary intent of the "loc-src" parameter in this specification is for use in emergency calling.

rejected.why: PIDF-LO is only referenced in an example; the document does not specify or extend it.
TLS is mentioned only as hop-by-hop protection in the example and security considerations.
The document refers to the trust domain of RFC 3325 for identity but does not deal with caller-ID authentication.
The example uses an https location URI from a LIS, but HELD is not specified or discussed.

RFC8788.title: Eligibility for the 2020-2021 Nominating Committee
RFC8788.summary: A one-time BCP interpreting NomCom volunteer eligibility rules for the 2020-2021 cycle after IETF 107 was cancelled, counting only in-person meetings IETF 102-106.

NomCom.why: The document exists solely to set NomCom volunteer eligibility for the 2020-2021 cycle, modifying the BCP 10 rules.
NomCom.quote: Members of the IETF community must have attended at least three of the last five in-person IETF meetings in order to volunteer.

rejected.why: NomCom is the more specific child tag and already implies the parent.
The document discusses the cancelled IETF 107 meeting only as context for the eligibility rule, not as a report of a workshop.

RFC8789.title: IETF Stream Documents Require IETF Rough Consensus
RFC8789.summary: A BCP updating RFC 2026 to require that the IETF never publish IETF Stream RFCs without establishing IETF rough consensus, closing the path for non-consensus Informational/Experimental publication.

IETF process.why: The document changes IETF standards-process rules (updating RFC 2026) about when IESG may approve documents for publication, which is IETF process procedure.
IETF process.quote: The IETF MUST NOT publish RFCs on the IETF Stream without establishing IETF rough consensus for publication.

rejected.why: It touches RFC streams (IETF, IRTF, Independent), but the subject is the IETF consensus requirement for approval, not RFC format, style, or publication mechanics.
The child tag IETF process fits more specifically, so the parent is not listed.

RFC8790.title: FETCH and PATCH with Sensor Measurement Lists (SenML)
RFC8790.summary: Defines two new media types (application/senml-etch+json and +cbor) and their semantics for using CoAP FETCH, PATCH and iPATCH methods with SenML-represented resources, including fragment identification and extensibility.

SenML.why: The document extends SenML with Fetch and Patch Pack formats, defining selection and update semantics over SenML Records.
SenML.quote: This document defines new media types for the CoAP FETCH, PATCH, and iPATCH methods for resources represented using the SenML data model.

CoAP.why: It specifies how the CoAP FETCH and (i)PATCH methods are used with SenML payloads, including error codes and Content-Format registrations.
CoAP.quote: The CoAP [RFC7252] FETCH, PATCH, and iPATCH methods [RFC8132] enable accessing and updating parts of a resource or multiple resources with one request.

rejected.why: The document registers two media types, but that is the vehicle for the SenML/CoAP specification rather than the subject itself; the registration is IANA boilerplate.
JSON is only one of the two encodings of the new media types; it is a substrate, not the subject.
CBOR is only the binary encoding for the media type; it is a substrate, not the subject.
Fragment identification reuses the SenML 'rec' scheme and does not define new URI mechanisms.

RFC8791.title: YANG Data Structure Extensions
RFC8791.summary: Defines the YANG extension statements "structure" and "augment-structure" for modelling abstract data structures (not config/state), and updates YANG tree diagram notation to display them.

YANG.why: The document specifies new YANG extensions (module ietf-yang-structure-ext) for defining and augmenting abstract data structures, and extends YANG tree diagram format.
YANG.quote: This document defines a new YANG extension statement called "structure", which is similar to but more flexible than the "yang-data" extension

rejected.why: Only appears in an example of rpc-error; the document is not about NETCONF.
Mentioned only as the origin of the yang-data extension (RFC 8040), not specified here.
XML is used only for an encoding example in the appendix.
JSON is used only for an encoding example in the appendix.
IANA section is boilerplate module registration.

RFC8792.title: Handling Long Lines in Content of Internet-Drafts and RFCs
RFC8792.summary: RFC 8792 defines two backslash-based strategies (single and double) for folding long lines in text content of Internet-Drafts and RFCs, with self-describing headers enabling automated unfolding, plus a Bash script implementing them.

RFC series.why: The document addresses how RFC and Internet-Draft authors handle over-long lines in sourcecode/artwork inclusions, which is a matter of RFC format and style conventions.
RFC series.quote: each line of an RFC (and hence of an Internet-Draft) must be limited to 72 characters

rejected.why: YANG modules and tree diagrams are only cited as examples of content that may need folding; the document is not about YANG.
xml2rfc <sourcecode> and <artwork> elements are the target context, but the document defines a plain-text folding method, not XML usage.
It references the xml2rfc vocabulary elements but does not specify or extend that vocabulary.
ABNF is mentioned only as an example of content that may be included in documents.
JSON is mentioned only as example content that may be folded.

gaps.name: Line folding of text content in documents
gaps.why: The backslash line-wrapping conventions (single and double backslash strategies) are a document authoring/tooling subject with no specific taxonomy tag; RFC series is the closest fit.

RFC8793.title: Information-Centric Networking (ICN): Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) and Named Data Networking (NDN) Terminology
RFC8793.summary: An IRTF ICNRG informational glossary defining terms used in the CCNx and NDN information-centric networking architectures, with a sketch of the ICN big picture and usage semantics.

ICN.why: The whole document defines terminology for ICN architectures (CCNx and NDN): Interest/Data packets, PIT, FIB, Content Store, naming and data-centric security.
ICN.quote: Information-Centric Networking (ICN) is a novel paradigm where network communications are accomplished by requesting named content instead of sending packets to destination addresses.

rejected.why: It is a glossary, but the subject is ICN. The ICN tag is more specific, and the terminology topic is about glossaries and requirements language generally.
DTN is mentioned only to say ICN data nodes differ from DTN data nodes.
ICN names are discussed, but as a feature of ICN architecture rather than general name resolution. ICN already covers this.
SHA256 appears only as an example of how a Packet ID is computed.
Data-centric security terms are defined, but they are part of the ICN vocabulary and not a separate security subject.

RFC8794.title: Extensible Binary Meta Language
RFC8794.summary: Defines EBML, a binary XML-like container format (variable-size integers, element IDs/sizes, element types, header, versioning, EBML Schema in XML) used by Matroska and WebM, plus IANA registries for element IDs and DocTypes.

Matroska.why: EBML is the binary container foundation for Matroska and WebM; the taxonomy has no EBML tag, and the Matroska container tag is the closest place for readers of audio/video container formats.
Matroska.quote: EBML is used by the multimedia container, Matroska [Matroska].

rejected.why: EBML is only modeled on XML; the EBML Schema is an XML document, but the RFC does not specify XML usage in protocols.
ABNF is used only to define the path attribute syntax.
The document defines a generic container meta-format, not codecs.
CRC-32 is a global element, but the document is not about CRC polynomial choice.
UTF-8 is merely one element type.
The registries are boilerplate-like and secondary to the format specification.

gaps.name: EBML (Extensible Binary Meta Language)
gaps.why: There is no tag for generic binary container or meta formats. EBML is also the basis for Matroska and WebM, so readers would look for it under a data formats or container tag.

RFC8795.title: YANG Data Model for Traffic Engineering (TE) Topologies
RFC8795.summary: Defines the ietf-te-topology YANG data model, a technology-agnostic base model for representing, retrieving and manipulating Traffic Engineering topologies (nodes, links, TTPs, connectivity matrices, overlay/underlay) that technology-specific models can augment.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module and its tree structure, plus guidance for writing augmentations. YANG model readers would look for it.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model [RFC7950] for representing, retrieving, and manipulating TE topologies.

traffic engineering.why: The model describes TE nodes, TE links, TEDs, and multi-layer/abstract TE topologies. It is about traffic engineering of packet and transport networks, and no more specific child tag fits.
traffic engineering.quote: A TE topology is the topology on which path computational algorithms are run to compute TE paths.

rejected.why: Only the access protocol for the data model, mentioned in Security Considerations; the document does not specify NETCONF.
GMPLS attributes (ISCDs, switching capability) are referenced by the model, but the document is not about GMPLS itself.
OSPF-TE and IS-IS appear only as TED information sources in an enumeration.
This is a YANG model, not a MIB module.
Topology exposure to clients has an SDN flavour, but the document does not frame itself as SDN.
Path computation runs over this topology, but PCE or PCEP is not specified.

RFC8796.title: RSVP-TE Summary Fast Reroute Extensions for Label Switched Path (LSP) Tunnels
RFC8796.summary: RFC 8796 updates RFC 4090 facility backup FRR for RSVP-TE LSPs, adding Extended ASSOCIATION objects (B-SFRR-Ready/Active) so PLR and MP signal bypass-tunnel groups of protected LSPs together, reducing signaling and processing during fast reroute.

RSVP-TE.why: The document specifies new RSVP-TE signaling extensions (Extended ASSOCIATION objects, Path/Resv procedures) for fast reroute of TE LSPs.
RSVP-TE.quote: This document updates RFC 4090 for the Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) Traffic Engineering (TE) procedures defined for facility backup protection.

IP fast reroute.why: Fast reroute facility bypass protection with PLR/MP behaviour is the core subject; readers of the fast reroute page would want it.
IP fast reroute.quote: The updates include extensions that reduce the amount of signaling and processing that occurs during Fast Reroute (FRR)

rejected.why: MPLS LSPs are the setting, but the document's content is RSVP-TE signaling, which is a more specific tag.
The ASSOCIATION object is borrowed from GMPLS recovery RFCs, but the document does not address GMPLS itself.
The RSVP-TE tag already sits under it and covers the subject.

RFC8797.title: Remote Direct Memory Access - Connection Manager (RDMA-CM) Private Data for RPC-over-RDMA Version 1
RFC8797.summary: Defines an optional RDMA-CM Private Data message format exchanged by RPC-over-RDMA version 1 peers at connection setup to advertise inline thresholds and remote invalidation support, and creates an IANA registry for Private Data format identifiers; updates RFC 8166.

RDMA.why: The document specifies connection-time Private Data for RDMA transports, covering RDMA Send/Receive, remote invalidation and STags. It is about RDMA protocol usage.
RDMA.quote: This document specifies the format of Remote Direct Memory Access - Connection Manager (RDMA-CM) Private Data exchanged between RPC-over-RDMA version 1 peers

ONC RPC.why: It extends and updates RFC 8166, the RPC-over-RDMA transport for ONC RPC, which readers of ONC RPC would want.
ONC RPC.quote: The RPC-over-RDMA version 1 transport protocol [RFC8166] enables payload data transfer using Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) for upper-layer protocols based on Remote Procedure Calls

rejected.why: NFS is only the motivating upper-layer protocol (larger NFSv4 messages); the document does not specify NFS.
It is mentioned only in Security Considerations as protecting Private Data on iWARP; not the subject.
The registry creation is boilerplate-level; the main body is not about IANA stewardship.
It is about connection-setup data for one transport, not a mapping of one protocol over another transport.

gaps.name: RDMA-CM Private Data / RPC-over-RDMA
gaps.why: The taxonomy has RDMA under storage, but this is close to a transport binding for RPC. An 'RPC-over-RDMA' tag would fit better.

RFC8798.title: Additional Units for Sensor Measurement Lists (SenML)
RFC8798.summary: RFC 8798 registers additional primary unit names in the IANA SenML Units registry and creates a new Secondary Units registry for units derived by linear scale/offset from primary units.

SenML.why: The document extends SenML by adding new units and defining a secondary units registry, so it is squarely about SenML.
SenML.quote: This short document registers a number of additional unit names in the IANA registry for units in SenML.

rejected.why: The registries are the means of delivering SenML units, but the document is about SenML units, not IANA stewardship or registry guidance generally.
SenML is a media type but the document only adds unit names to a SenML registry, not media type registration rules.
SenML encodes in JSON but the document does not deal with the encoding.

RFC8799.title: Limited Domains and Internet Protocols
RFC8799.summary: Independent-stream informational RFC that surveys "limited domains" (controlled environments) in Internet protocols, gives examples and a taxonomy, discusses standardizing limited-domain protocols, and outlines functional requirements for secure domain membership.

internet architecture.why: The document analyzes how limited domains challenge the idea of universal interoperability and end-to-end transparency in the Internet architecture, and argues some protocols should be standardized with limited scope.
internet architecture.quote: there is a noticeable trend towards network-specific and local requirements, behaviors, and semantics

security.why: A substantial part of the document sets out functional requirements for domain identity, secure enrollment, peer and role verification, and trust boundaries.
security.quote: domain membership operations should be cryptographically secured; a domain without such security cannot be reliably protected from attack.

rejected.why: Cited as one example of a limited-domain solution, not the subject of the document.
Used as an example of domain-specific semantics (DSCP); only a passing illustration.
One item in a list of limited-domain solutions; the document is not about SFC.
Mentioned as an example of a domain-scoped technology only.
IPv6 extension headers are discussed as examples, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Briefly cited as an example of a security domain; not a focus.

gaps.name: Limited domains / controlled environments
gaps.why: The document's central subject has no dedicated tag; internet architecture is the closest fit.

RFC8800.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extension for Label Switched Path (LSP) Diversity Constraint Signaling
RFC8800.summary: Defines a PCEP extension introducing a Disjoint Association type (with DISJOINTNESS-CONFIGURATION/STATUS TLVs, new objective functions and error codes) so a PCC can tell a PCE that a group of LSPs must have diverse paths.

PCE.why: The RFC extends PCEP with a new association type, TLVs, objective functions (MSL/MSS/MSN) and error codes for disjoint path computation by a PCE.
PCE.quote: This document specifies a PCEP extension to signal that a set of LSPs in a particular group should use diverse (disjointed) paths

rejected.why: LSPs are the objects being computed, but the document is about PCEP signalling, not MPLS architecture or operations.
Mentioned only in passing as a network type; not a subject of the document.
Only recommended in Security Considerations for securing PCEP sessions (PCEPS); boilerplate, not subject.

The PCEP YANG module is only referenced informatively in Manageability Considerations.

RFC8801.title: Discovering Provisioning Domain Names and Data
RFC8801.summary: Defines a Router Advertisement option (PvD Option) carrying an FQDN PvD ID to identify explicit provisioning domains, plus retrieval of PvD Additional Information as JSON via HTTPS at /.well-known/pvd.

neighbor discovery.why: The core of the document is a new IPv6 Router Advertisement (Neighbor Discovery) option, with router and host behavior.
neighbor discovery.quote: This document defines a mechanism for explicitly identifying PvDs through a Router Advertisement (RA) option.

multihoming.why: The motivation and use cases are host multihoming across multiple PvDs, with a dedicated operational section on enabling multihoming.
multihoming.quote: PvDs allows hosts to manage connections to multiple networks and interfaces simultaneously

media types.why: Registers the application/pvd+json media type used for the Additional Information object.
media types.quote: This document registers the media type for PvD JSON text, "application/pvd+json".

rejected.why: HTTP over TLS is only the retrieval substrate for the JSON object; nothing new is defined about HTTP itself.
JSON is the encoding of the Additional Information; the document defines keys but is not about JSON as a format.

TLS is only used to secure the fetch, and no new TLS mechanism is defined.
The PvD ID is an FQDN, and DNS server usage per PvD is discussed, but DNS itself is not the subject.
IPv6 is the general context. The specific Neighbor Discovery tag fits better.

gaps.why: The document's main subject is provisioning domains, and the taxonomy has no tag for them or for the multiple-PvD architecture of RFC 7556.

RFC8802.title: The Quality for Service (Q4S) Protocol
RFC8802.summary: Describes Q4S, an experimental application-level protocol using HTTP-like syntax and SDP bodies to negotiate and monitor end-to-end latency, jitter, bandwidth and packet loss, and to raise alerts and recoveries when constraints are violated.

performance measurement.why: The protocol is an active end-to-end measurement protocol with defined latency, jitter, bandwidth and packet loss methods. It is compared directly with OWAMP/TWAMP.
performance measurement.quote: The Quality for Service (Q4S) protocol provides a mechanism to negotiate and monitor latency, jitter, bandwidth, and packet loss, and to alert whenever one of the negotiated conditions is violated.

QoS.why: It covers QoS constraint negotiation, qos-levels, alerts to an Actuator or policy server, and recovery. These are QoS signalling and monitoring concerns, though the protocol itself only measures and alerts.
QoS.quote: Q4S enables applications to become reactive under e2e network quality changes.

rejected.why: Q4S borrows HTTP syntax and status codes but states it is not an HTTP extension.
SDP is only the container for quality constraints. The document defines new SDP attributes for Q4S, but the media descriptions are unused and the document is not about SDP in the offer/answer sense.
OWAMP and TWAMP are discussed only for comparison, and the document does not specify or extend them.
TCP and UDP are the transports Q4S runs over, and the document defines nothing new about them.
RTP/RTCP are mentioned only as protocols Q4S could be used alongside or as alternative measurement procedures.
The Reno/CUBIC discussion in 7.8 only explains how to adjust constraints for TCP throughput and does not address congestion control.

RFC8803.title: 0-RTT TCP Convert Protocol
RFC8803.summary: Specifies the 0-RTT TCP Convert Protocol, by which a Transport Converter proxy lets clients use TCP extensions such as Multipath TCP towards servers that do not support them, using TLVs carried in the SYN payload.

TCP.why: The Convert Protocol is a TCP proxy mechanism that handles TCP option negotiation (WS, SACK, Timestamp, TFO, TCP-AO) and sends data in SYNs. It is about TCP extensions and their deployment.
TCP.quote: This document specifies an application proxy, called Transport Converter, to assist the deployment of TCP extensions such as Multipath TCP.

MPTCP.quote: As a sample applicability use case, this document specifies how the Convert Protocol applies for Multipath TCP.

rejected.why: SOCKSv5 is compared in Section 3 as the closest existing proxy protocol, but the document specifies a different protocol and does not extend or profile SOCKS.
TLS is only mentioned as running end-to-end through the converter and as a possible authentication option. The document does not specify anything about TLS.
PCP is mentioned as a way for a client to create mappings for incoming connections. The document says that defining TLVs for this is out of scope.
Address sharing and preservation modes are discussed, but the subject is the TCP converter proxy rather than NAT behaviour.
The document defines a new application-layer protocol carried in the TCP bytestream and SYN payload. It does not map an existing protocol onto TCP.
The IANA registries it creates are standard boilerplate for a new protocol, not a subject of the document.

RFC8804.title: Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI) Request Routing Extensions
RFC8804.summary: Defines CDNI Metadata Interface and Footprint & Capabilities Advertisement extensions (Redirect Target capability and Fallback Target metadata) for Open Caching request routing between upstream and downstream CDNs, and registers two CDNI payload types.

CDN.why: The whole document specifies CDN Interconnection interface extensions for request routing redirect and fallback targets between uCDN and dCDN.
CDN.quote: This document defines extensions to the CDNI Metadata Interface (MI) and the Footprint & Capabilities Advertisement interface (FCI).

rejected.why: DNS CNAME redirection is one redirect mechanism used, but the document defines no new DNS behaviour or records.

Payload type registration is boilerplate-level IANA considerations, not the main subject.
ECS is only referenced for routing decisions and privacy; nothing new is defined.
URI syntax is referenced for constructing Location URLs but is not the subject.

RFC8805.title: A Format for Self-Published IP Geolocation Feeds
RFC8805.summary: Documents a deployed CSV-based "geolocation feed" format by which network operators self-publish mappings of IP prefixes to coarse location (country, region, city), with consumer guidance on integrity, authority verification, and refresh.

geolocation.why: The whole document defines a format for publishing and consuming IP geolocation information, including privacy trade-offs of location granularity.
geolocation.quote: a network operator can publish a mapping of IP address prefixes to simplified geolocation information, colloquially termed a "geolocation feed"

RFC8806.title: Running a Root Server Local to a Resolver
RFC8806.summary: Informational document describing how a DNS recursive resolver operator can run a local, DNSSEC-validated copy of the root zone on the same host to improve resilience and prevent snooping, obsoleting RFC 7706.

RFC8807.summary: Defines an EPP extension that lets clients use passwords longer than 16 characters at login and lets servers return login security events (password/certificate expiry, insecure TLS cipher/protocol, etc.) in the login response.

RFC8811.summary: RFC 8811 describes the architecture for DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS): the client, server and gateway components, their relationships, sessions, and signaling modes. It specifies no protocol.

RFC8812.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) and JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) Registrations for Web Authentication (WebAuthn) Algorithms
RFC8812.summary: Registers RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 (SHA-1/256/384/512) and ECDSA with secp256k1 (ES256K) algorithm identifiers and the secp256k1 curve in the IANA COSE and JOSE registries, for use by WebAuthn and CTAP.

RFC8813.summary: Updates RFC 5480 to state that keyEncipherment and dataEncipherment key usage bits MUST NOT be set in certificates whose SubjectPublicKeyInfo uses id-ecPublicKey, id-ecDH or id-ecMQV.

RFC8814.title: Signaling Maximum SID Depth (MSD) Using the Border Gateway Protocol - Link State
RFC8814.summary: Defines two new BGP-LS Attribute TLVs (Node MSD, Link MSD) so BGP-LS speakers can advertise Maximum SID Depth values to controllers for Segment Routing path computation.

rejected.why: The OSPF MSD extensions are defined in RFC 8476. This document only carries that information in BGP-LS.

RFC8815.summary: BCP recommending deprecation of Any-Source Multicast (ASM) for interdomain use in favour of Source-Specific Multicast (SSM), with guidance for vendors, operators and application developers.

SSM.why: The document's central recommendation is to use SSM instead of ASM between domains, and it details SSM's advantages and deployment.
SSM.quote: It recommends the use of Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) for interdomain multicast applications and recommends that hosts and routers in these deployments fully support SSM.

multicast.why: The document is about the choice of multicast service model and interdomain multicast deployment, which is a general multicast matter and not tied to a single protocol. It also covers ASM, MSDP, Embedded-RP and BIDIR-PIM, which have no child tag.
multicast.quote: This document recommends deprecation of the use of Any-Source Multicast (ASM) for interdomain multicast.

PIM-SM.quote: The most commonly deployed ASM routing protocol is Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM), as detailed in [RFC7761].

MSDP.why: MSDP is the interdomain ASM source discovery mechanism whose scalability, security and fragility problems motivate the deprecation.

MLD.why: MLDv2 is the IPv6 counterpart to IGMPv3 and is recommended alongside it for SSM host and router support.
MLD.quote: This document recommends that all hosts, router platforms, and security appliances used for deploying multicast support the components of IGMPv3 [RFC3376] and MLDv2 [RFC3810]

rejected.why: PIM-SM is the more specific child tag and fits better. BIDIR-PIM is only discussed as a reason not to deprecate intradomain ASM.
It is only mentioned as the recommended alternative to ASM for service discovery in Section 4.4. The document is not about it.
Embedded-RP and IPv6 multicast addresses are mentioned, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
This tag covers group key management. The document only mentions SSM's intrinsic source-control security.

RFC8821.summary: Defines the CCDR architecture for traffic engineering in native IP networks, using multiple BGP sessions with a PCE as central controller and identifying the PCEP extensions needed to push BGP peer, next-hop route and prefix information to routers.

IPv4 and IPv6 are just payload types carried in the encapsulation.

RFC8823.title: Extensions to Automatic Certificate Management Environment for End-User S/MIME Certificates
RFC8823.summary: Defines an ACME "email" identifier type and "email-reply-00" challenge, using challenge/response emails signed with DKIM or S/MIME, so ACME can issue end-user S/MIME certificates.

ACME.why: The document extends ACME with a new identifier type and challenge type, so it belongs on the ACME page.
ACME.quote: This document specifies identifiers and challenges required to enable the Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) to issue certificates for use by email users that want to use S/MIME.

S/MIME.why: The purpose is to issue S/MIME certificates. It also covers signing-only versus encryption-only certificates and key usage.
S/MIME.quote: Section 3 defines extensions for issuing end-user S/MIME [RFC8550] certificates.

rejected.why: DKIM is used to sign the challenge and response emails, but the document does not specify or extend it.
Email is the transport for the challenge. The document is about certificate issuance, not email architecture.
It constrains the header fields of the challenge and response messages, but only to serve the validation protocol.
It touches CSR contents and subjectAltName, but does not profile X.509 certificates.
Internationalized addresses are mentioned briefly, but this is not a main subject.
ACME and S/MIME are the more specific tags; PKI as a parent is implied.

RFC8824.title: Static Context Header Compression (SCHC) for the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)
RFC8824.summary: Defines how to apply SCHC header compression to CoAP headers and options, including asymmetric request/response handling, CoAP extensions (Block, Observe, No-Response) and OSCORE inner/outer compression.

SCHC.why: The document specifies SCHC Rules for compressing CoAP headers, which is the core of the SCHC framework's application to CoAP.
SCHC.quote: this document defines how to compress Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) headers using the Static Context Header Compression and fragmentation (SCHC) framework.

CoAP.why: Detailed compression of CoAP header fields and options (Uri-Path, Block, Observe, No-Response) makes CoAP readers interested in this document.
CoAP.quote: CoAP header structure differs from IPv6 and UDP, since CoAP uses a flexible header with a variable number of options

OSCORE.why: A substantial part of the document covers compression of OSCORE-protected messages with inner and outer rules, including OSCORE option field splitting and examples.
OSCORE.quote: SCHC needs two Rules to compress the CoAP header. A first Rule focuses on the Inner header.

rejected.why: The more specific SCHC tag covers this; the generic header compression topic is not the better fit.
UDP/IPv6 compression is only referenced from RFC 8724 as context; this document does not address it.
Mentioned only as an example encryption layer in a figure; not a subject of the document.
Motivating environment; the SCHC tag is more specific.

RFC8825.title: Overview: Real-Time Protocols for Browser-Based Applications
RFC8825.summary: RFC 8825 is an applicability statement that serves as the roadmap to the WebRTC protocol suite, grouping functions and naming the specifications WebRTC endpoints must implement.

WebRTC.why: The document is the overview and roadmap of the WebRTC protocol suite and says which specifications compliant WebRTC implementations must follow.
WebRTC.quote: This document gives an overview and context of a protocol suite intended for use with real-time applications that can be deployed in browsers

rejected.why: SIP is mentioned only as a possible inter-server signalling protocol and as a gateway target. The document does not specify or profile it.
RTP and SRTP are named as the required media transport, but their details are delegated to RFC 8834 and others, so the document is not about them.
ICE and Trickle ICE are cited as required components and as a deployment note, but they are specified in other RFCs.
SDP offer/answer is referenced as a principle for connection management. The document does not define or extend it.
HTTPS and WebSockets appear only as the application-to-server signalling substrate.
XMPP and Jingle are mentioned only as examples of possible signalling between servers.

RFC8826.title: Security Considerations for WebRTC
RFC8826.summary: RFC 8826 defines the threat model for WebRTC (browser-based real-time communications) and analyzes threats around local device access, communications consent verification, media security, and privacy.

WebRTC.why: The whole document is a security threat analysis of WebRTC, so the WebRTC page is where readers would look for it.
WebRTC.quote: This document defines the WebRTC threat model and analyzes the security threats of WebRTC in that model.

web security.why: A substantial part covers the browser threat model, same-origin policy, CORS and cross-origin consent, and how WebRTC fits into the web platform's security.
web security.quote: Users can safely visit arbitrary web sites and execute scripts provided by those sites.

privacy.why: The document has a dedicated privacy section on call correlation, fingerprinting and IP location privacy, which fits the privacy topic.
privacy.quote: they can also represent a privacy threat in settings where the user wishes to be anonymous.

rejected.why: ICE is used as the consent-verification handshake, but the document only analyzes it in a short section and does not specify or extend it.
WebSockets appears only as background for consent verification and masking in the SOP discussion.
SRTP and DTLS-SRTP are mentioned as the existing media security mechanisms, but this document does not specify them.
The parent topic is implied by the more specific tags chosen, and the document is not general security guidance.
HTTP and HTTPS appear only as the signalling substrate and in attack scenarios.
NAT traversal is touched on only through ICE consent and TURN IP-hiding, not as a main subject.

RFC8827.title: WebRTC Security Architecture
RFC8827.summary: Defines the WebRTC security architecture: trust model, consent and device permissions, DTLS-SRTP communications security, IP location privacy, and an IdP-based peer authentication mechanism using a new SDP "identity" attribute.

WebRTC.why: The whole document is the security architecture for WebRTC, covering browser permissions, consent, media security and peer identity.
WebRTC.quote: This document defines the security architecture for WebRTC, a protocol suite intended for use with real-time applications that can be deployed in browsers

SDP.why: Defines a new SDP attribute with syntax and offer/answer rules, and registers it with IANA. SDP readers need this.
SDP.quote: The SDP "identity" attribute is a session-level attribute that is used by an endpoint to convey its identity assertion to its peer.

authentication.why: A substantial part of the document specifies IdP-based peer identity assertion, verification and identity formats across Authenticating Party, IdP and Relying Party.
authentication.quote: it is desirable for the endpoint (i.e., the browser) to be able to directly identify the endpoint on the other side without trusting the signaling service

rejected.why: DTLS and DTLS-SRTP are the substrate for keying media. The document mandates them but does not specify or extend them.
SRTP is required for media protection, but this document does not define or profile it.
ICE is used for consent verification and is referenced, not specified or extended here.
IP location privacy is covered in sections 6.4 and 9.2, but it is part of the WebRTC architecture and the WebRTC tag already covers it.
OAuth is mentioned only as an example IdP technology. The document defines a generic IdP interface instead.
Origin and mixed-content issues are discussed, but only as they apply to WebRTC permissions, so the WebRTC tag is the better fit.

RFC8828.title: WebRTC IP Address Handling Requirements
RFC8828.summary: Defines four modes governing which IP addresses WebRTC implementations expose to web applications (and routing/proxy behaviour), balancing privacy against media performance, with implementation and application guidance.

WebRTC.why: The whole document specifies WebRTC implementation requirements for address gathering and exposure, so it belongs under WebRTC.
WebRTC.quote: This document provides information and requirements for how IP addresses should be handled by Web Real-Time Communication (WebRTC) implementations.

privacy.why: A substantial part of the document analyses privacy leaks (VPN, private addresses, fingerprinting, correlation across browsing contexts) and the trade-offs in mitigating them.
privacy.quote: This document summarizes the concerns and makes recommendations on how WebRTC implementations should best handle the trade-off between privacy and media performance.

rejected.why: ICE is the mechanism that gathers candidates, but the document does not extend or profile it; it only constrains which addresses are exposed.
Only mentioned as a technique used by ICE for address discovery; not specified or extended.
Referenced as a relay and in application guidance, but the document does not define anything about TURN itself.
NAT is background to the private-address exposure concern, not a subject addressed in its own right.
Mentioned only as an example of proxies that lack UDP support.
Already covered by the WebRTC tag; the document is about address exposure, not traversal techniques.

RFC8829.title: JavaScript Session Establishment Protocol (JSEP)
RFC8829.summary: RFC 8829 specifies JSEP, the mechanism by which JavaScript controls WebRTC session establishment through the RTCPeerConnection API, defining offer/answer handling, SDP generation and parsing rules, ICE gathering control, and the state machine.

WebRTC.why: The document is a core WebRTC specification defining the signaling-plane control interface for browser real-time media.
WebRTC.quote: how the W3C Web Real-Time Communication (WebRTC) RTCPeerConnection interface [W3C.webrtc] is used to control the setup, management, and teardown of a multimedia session

SDP.why: Much of the document (Section 5) specifies how SDP offers and answers are constructed, parsed and applied, including a:-line profiles for JSEP.
SDP.quote: JSEP's session descriptions use Session Description Protocol (SDP) syntax for their internal representation.

ICE.why: Substantial content on ICE gathering, trickling, candidate policy, pool, restart and versions as exposed through the API.
ICE.quote: JSEP decouples the ICE state machine from the overall signaling state machine.

rejected.why: SIP is mentioned as one possible signaling protocol and for forking, but JSEP is signaling-agnostic and does not specify SIP.
RTP/RTCP handling is controlled via transceivers and SDP attributes but the document does not specify RTP itself.
DTLS fingerprints and roles are negotiated in SDP, but DTLS is a substrate and not the subject.
Data channels over SCTP/DTLS appear only as an m= section to be generated.
STUN/TURN servers are only configuration parameters for ICE gathering.
Covered by the more specific ICE tag; the document only uses ICE for NAT traversal.

RFC8830.title: WebRTC MediaStream Identification in the Session Description Protocol
RFC8830.summary: Defines the SDP media-level "msid" attribute that associates RTP streams/media descriptions with WebRTC MediaStreams and MediaStreamTracks, with offer/answer procedures.

SDP.why: The document defines a new SDP attribute, its syntax, mux category and offer/answer procedures, so it is about SDP.
SDP.quote: This document defines a new SDP [RFC4566] media-level "msid" attribute.

WebRTC.why: The mechanism exists to map WebRTC MediaStream/MediaStreamTrack identifiers into SDP signaling for the WebRTC API.
WebRTC.quote: signal the association between the SDP concept of "media description" and the Web Real-Time Communication (WebRTC) concept of MediaStream/MediaStreamTrack

rejected.why: RTP streams and SSRCs are the things being associated, but the document does not specify or extend RTP.
The IANA section registers an SDP attribute, not a media type.
ABNF is only used to write the attribute grammar.
ICE is mentioned only in passing in the discussion of when packets can flow.

RFC8831.title: WebRTC Data Channels
RFC8831.summary: Specifies WebRTC data channels: how SCTP over DTLS over ICE/UDP is used as a generic peer-to-peer non-media data transport between browsers, including requirements, SCTP extensions, PPIDs, and channel open/transfer/close.

WebRTC.why: The document defines the WebRTC data channel mechanism, a core part of the WebRTC architecture.
WebRTC.quote: This document specifies the non-media data transport aspects of the WebRTC framework.

SCTP.why: Specifies which SCTP extensions (reconfiguration, partial reliability, interleaving) must be supported and how streams, PPIDs and association management are used for data channels.
SCTP.quote: The following SCTP protocol extensions are required:

rejected.why: DTLS is the encapsulation substrate for SCTP; the document relies on RFC 8261 and defines nothing new about DTLS.
ICE is only the lower layer providing NAT traversal; not specified here.
Media is sent with SRTP and explicitly not specified here; only mentioned for coexistence.
The data channel API merely mirrors WebSocket's API; the protocol is not addressed.
PMTU discovery is a requirement handled via RFC 4821 references, a minor aspect of the document.
Congestion control is a requirement but the document defers to SCTP's own mechanism and specifies nothing new.

RFC8832.title: WebRTC Data Channel Establishment Protocol
RFC8832.summary: Specifies the Data Channel Establishment Protocol (DCEP), a two-way handshake using DATA_CHANNEL_OPEN and DATA_CHANNEL_ACK messages over SCTP to open symmetric WebRTC data channels, and creates the IANA registries for it.

WebRTC.why: DCEP is a WebRTC data channel component. A reader browsing WebRTC would expect to find it there.
WebRTC.quote: The Data Channel Establishment Protocol (DCEP) is designed to provide, in the WebRTC data channel context [RFC8831], a simple in-band method for opening symmetric data channels.

SCTP.why: The protocol is built on SCTP streams, stream identifiers and stream resets. It uses an SCTP PPID for demultiplexing and registers that PPID. This is substantial SCTP usage, and SCTP readers would want it.
SCTP.quote: The Data Channel Establishment Protocol is a simple, low-overhead way to establish bidirectional data channels over an SCTP association

rejected.why: DTLS is only the secure substrate. The document sets the odd/even stream rule from the DTLS client/server role, but it defines nothing new for DTLS.
The protocol field only reuses the WebSocket Subprotocol Name Registry for label strings. The document is not about WebSocket.
Labels and protocol strings are UTF-8 encoded, but this is only an encoding detail.
The IANA section creates DCEP registries, but that is boilerplate for this protocol document, not a document about IANA.

RFC8833.title: Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) for WebRTC
RFC8833.summary: Defines two TLS ALPN labels, "webrtc" and "c-webrtc", identifying WebRTC DTLS sessions (DTLS-SRTP and SCTP data channels) and, for c-webrtc, a promise to keep media confidential from other applications, and registers them with IANA.

WebRTC.why: The document defines WebRTC-specific identifiers and the media confidentiality semantics for browser real-time sessions, including the browser-enforced isolation of media from the signaling application.
WebRTC.quote: This document specifies two Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) labels for use with Web Real-Time Communication (WebRTC).

TLS.why: The document defines new ALPN protocol IDs for the TLS ALPN extension and registers them. This is new use of the TLS extension mechanism, which TLS readers need.
TLS.quote: Identifying WebRTC protocol usage with Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) [RFC7301] enables an endpoint to positively identify WebRTC uses and distinguish them from other DTLS uses.

DTLS.why: The labels are negotiated in DTLS sessions and identify DTLS-SRTP and data channel uses, so DTLS readers would want it. The ALPN extension is used with DTLS here.
DTLS.quote: The "webrtc" label identifies regular WebRTC: a DTLS session that is used to establish keys for the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP)

rejected.why: SRTP keys come from the DTLS session, but the document does not specify or extend SRTP. It only references DTLS-SRTP.
SCTP carries the data channels over DTLS, but it is only the substrate and is not specified here.
ICE is mentioned only to say it is not covered by the identifier.
The IANA section registers two ALPN IDs. That is boilerplate and the document is not about IANA process.
The media confidentiality promise concerns access control between applications and browsers, not protocol privacy considerations in general. WebRTC and TLS cover it better.

RFC8834.title: Media Transport and Use of RTP in WebRTC
RFC8834.summary: Specifies which RTP and RTCP features, profiles, extensions, robustness and congestion-control mechanisms WebRTC endpoints must or should support for media transport.

WebRTC.why: The document defines WebRTC's media transport requirements, so readers of the WebRTC subject would expect it.
WebRTC.quote: This memo describes the media transport aspects of the WebRTC framework.

RTP.why: The document profiles RTP for WebRTC. It covers the profile choice, sessions, multiplexing, SSRC and CNAME handling, and header extensions.
RTP.quote: The Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) [RFC3550] is REQUIRED to be implemented as the media transport protocol for WebRTC.

RTCP.why: A substantial part covers RTCP: reduced-size RTCP, feedback messages (FIR, PLI, NACK, TMMBR), CNAMEs and XR monitoring.
RTCP.quote: RTCP is a fundamental and integral part of RTP and MUST be implemented and used in all WebRTC endpoints.

SRTP.why: The document mandates the secure RTP/SAVPF profile with SRTP and SRTCP for all WebRTC media.
SRTP.quote: WebRTC endpoints MUST NOT send packets using the basic RTP/AVP profile or the RTP/AVPF profile; they MUST employ the full RTP/SAVPF profile

rejected.why: SDP is the signaling mechanism the document refers to, but it defines nothing new about SDP.
The document mandates the RTP circuit breaker and refers to congestion control requirements, but it is not about congestion control algorithms. RFC 8836 covers those.
ICE is mentioned only as the source of transport addresses.
DTLS-SRTP keying is only referenced for the security mechanism and is not specified here.
The document only points to RFC 8854 for FEC recommendations.
The document points to other RFCs for codec payload formats and defines none itself.

RFC8835.title: Transports for WebRTC
RFC8835.summary: Specifies the data transport protocols required of WebRTC endpoints, including NAT/firewall traversal (ICE, STUN, TURN), IPv4/IPv6 handling, SCTP-over-DTLS data channels, SRTP media transport, and DSCP-based media prioritization.

WebRTC.why: The whole document defines the transport requirements for WebRTC endpoints and browsers.
WebRTC.quote: This document describes the data transport protocols used by Web Real-Time Communication (WebRTC)

ICE.why: ICE is the primary middlebox mechanism, with mandated full implementation, ICE-TCP candidates and Happy Eyeballs for ICE.
ICE.quote: ICE [RFC8445] MUST be supported.  The implementation MUST be a full ICE implementation, not ICE-Lite.

TURN.why: Substantial discussion of mandatory TURN modes (TCP, TLS, IPv6 extensions) and optional TURN TCP candidates with rationale.

Diffserv.why: Section 4.2 covers DSCP marking, handling of blocked DSCPs, and single-DSCP rules for SCTP and TCP.
Diffserv.quote: Implementations SHOULD attempt to set QoS on the packets sent, according to the guidelines in [RFC8837].

rejected.why: SCTP over DTLS is mandated but its encapsulation and details are defined in other RFCs; only a brief requirement here.
Secure RTP media transport is referenced and delegated to RFC 8834 and RFC 8827.
TLS/DTLS are used as substrate and referenced, not specified or extended here.
Only a single SHOULD pointing to RFC 8421; not a substantial part of the document.
UDP and TCP are assumed system-provided interfaces, not the subject.
Section 3.3 on temporary addresses is short; it is address selection for ICE rather than IPv6 in its own right.

RFC8836.title: Congestion Control Requirements for Interactive Real-Time Media
RFC8836.summary: Informational RFC setting out requirements for congestion control algorithms for interactive point-to-point real-time media over RTP (WebRTC), and explaining why TFRC does not meet them.

RTP congestion control.why: The whole document defines requirements for congestion control of interactive real-time media over RTP, which is exactly this tag's subject.
RTP congestion control.quote: This document describes a set of requirements that can be used to evaluate other congestion control mechanisms in order to figure out their fitness for this purpose

TFRC.why: Section 3 analyses TFRC and TFRC-SP and concludes they cannot meet the requirements, so TFRC readers would want it.
TFRC.quote: TFRC's biggest deficiency is that it only considers loss events as a congestion indication.

rejected.why: RTP is the media transport the requirements assume. The document does not specify or extend it.
RTCP is mentioned as the usual feedback backchannel, but only as one requirement item. The document does not define RTCP behaviour.
WebRTC is the motivating use case and is cited, but the document is about congestion control, not WebRTC architecture.
Only one requirement says the algorithm should be stable with AQM. AQM is not a subject of the document.
ECN is listed once as an example of an available congestion signal. The document does not address it.
The more specific child tag RTP congestion control already applies.

RFC8837.title: Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) Packet Markings for WebRTC QoS
RFC8837.summary: Recommends default DSCP packet markings that web browsers should apply to WebRTC media (RTP) and data channel traffic, mapped from flow type and application priority.

WebRTC.why: The document specifies browser behaviour for marking WebRTC media and data channel traffic, so WebRTC readers need it.
WebRTC.quote: This document provides the recommended DSCP values for web browsers to use for various classes of Web Real-Time Communication (WebRTC) traffic.

Diffserv.why: It defines a mapping of flows to Diffserv code points (EF, AF, LE, DF) and per-hop behaviour recommendations.
Diffserv.quote: The DSCP values for each flow type of interest to WebRTC based on application priority are shown in Table 1.

rejected.why: RTP streams are the traffic being marked, but the document does not specify or extend RTP.
It gives DSCP rules for SCTP associations carrying data channels, but SCTP itself is not specified or extended.
Diffserv is the more specific child tag and already covers the QoS aspect.
Congestion control is mentioned only briefly, as a consumer of application priority and as a reset requirement when the DSCP changes.

RFC8838.title: Trickle ICE: Incremental Provisioning of Candidates for the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) Protocol
RFC8838.summary: Defines Trickle ICE, an extension to ICE (RFC 8445) allowing candidates to be exchanged incrementally while connectivity checks proceed, including half trickle, end-of-candidates, and checklist handling.

ICE.why: The whole document specifies modifications to ICE procedures: checklists, pairing, pruning, end-of-candidates, restarts, and ICE-lite interaction.
ICE.quote: an extension to the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) protocol that enables ICE agents to begin connectivity checks while they are still gathering candidates

rejected.why: SDP is only used for examples; the usage is defined in RFC 8840.
SIP is mentioned only as a using protocol defined elsewhere (RFC 8840).
STUN is a candidate gathering mechanism, not the subject.
TURN is a candidate gathering mechanism, not the subject.
XMPP is only cited as a using protocol via XEP-0176.
Parent of ICE, implied by the ICE tag.

RFC8839.title: Session Description Protocol (SDP) Offer/Answer Procedures for Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE)
RFC8839.summary: RFC 8839 specifies how ICE is used with SDP offer/answer: the SDP attributes (candidate, ice-ufrag, ice-pwd, ice-lite, ice-mismatch, ice-pacing, ice-options, remote-candidates), initial and subsequent exchange procedures, SIP considerations, and IANA registries; it obsoletes RFC 5245 and RFC 6336.

ICE.why: The document specifies the SDP offer/answer usage of ICE, including candidate exchange, restart, nomination alignment and the ICE options registry.
ICE.quote: This document describes Session Description Protocol (SDP) Offer/Answer procedures for carrying out Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) between the agents.

SDP.why: It defines new SDP attributes and the offer/answer procedures that use them, so readers of SDP and offer/answer would want it.
SDP.quote: This specification defines eight new SDP attributes -- the "candidate", "remote-candidates", "ice-lite", "ice-mismatch", "ice-ufrag", "ice-pwd", "ice-pacing", and "ice-options" attributes.

SIP.why: A substantial section covers SIP latency guidelines, forking, preconditions, third-party call control, and ALG/SBC interactions.
SIP.quote: When ICE is used with SIP, forking may result in a single offer generating a multiplicity of answers.

rejected.why: STUN is the mechanism for connectivity checks, defined elsewhere (RFC 8445/5389); this document only requires agents to be ready to receive Binding requests.
RTP and RTCP appear only as components of the data stream (candidates for component IDs and the rtcp attribute). The document does not specify them.
It is the broader topic, but the ICE tag is more specific and already covers the document.
Relayed candidates are mentioned only in the rel-addr description, so TURN is not a subject here.
The IANA section registers SDP attributes and ICE option subregistries. It is boilerplate-like and does not make the document about IANA.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the attribute grammar.

RFC8840.title: A Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Usage for Incremental Provisioning of Candidates for the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (Trickle ICE)
RFC8840.summary: Defines how Trickle ICE is used with SIP: candidates are trickled in SIP INFO requests via a new "trickle-ice" Info Package, with a new application/trickle-ice-sdpfrag media type, SDP "end-of-candidates" attribute and SIP option tag, plus discovery of support and Half Trickle fallback.

ICE.why: The document specifies how Trickle ICE, the incremental candidate provisioning extension of ICE, is used with SIP, including the end-of-candidates attribute and candidate delivery procedures.
ICE.quote: This document defines usage semantics for Trickle ICE with the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP).

SIP.why: It defines a SIP Info Package, a SIP option tag, dialog establishment procedures for trickling, and capability discovery via OPTIONS/GRUU.
SIP.quote: This document defines a new Info Package as specified in [RFC6086] for use with Trickle ICE together with the corresponding media type, SDP attribute, and SIP option tag.

SDP.why: It defines a new SDP attribute with offer/answer procedures and a pseudo-SDP body grammar (sdpfrag) for INFO requests.
SDP.quote: This section defines the new SDP media-level and session-level [RFC4566] "end-of-candidates" attribute.

media types.why: A new media type is registered and its grammar is defined in Section 9, a substantial part of the document.
media types.quote: This document defines the new media type "application/trickle-ice-sdpfrag" in accordance with [RFC6838].

rejected.why: STUN is only used by ICE connectivity checks and is mentioned in passing; the document does not specify it.
TURN appears only in terminology and a figure, not as a subject of the document.
RTP/RTCP multiplexing considerations are brief guidance on candidate trickling, not about RTP itself.
ABNF is only used to write the body grammar.

RFC8841.title: Session Description Protocol (SDP) Offer/Answer Procedures for Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) over Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) Transport
RFC8841.summary: Defines the SDP proto values UDP/DTLS/SCTP and TCP/DTLS/SCTP, the sctp-port and max-message-size attributes, and SDP offer/answer procedures for negotiating SCTP-over-DTLS associations.

SDP.why: The document defines new SDP proto values and attributes and the offer/answer procedures for them, so it is an SDP extension.
SDP.quote: This specification defines the following new Session Description Protocol (SDP) protocol identifiers (proto values): "UDP/DTLS/SCTP" and "TCP/DTLS/SCTP".

SCTP.why: It specifies how SCTP associations over DTLS are described, established and closed via SDP, which readers of SCTP would want.
SCTP.quote: SCTP association on top of a DTLS association on top of UDP

DTLS.why: It covers DTLS association negotiation and its interaction with SCTP and TCP connections for SCTP-over-DTLS.
DTLS.quote: A DTLS association is managed according to the procedures in [RFC8842]. Hence, the SDP "setup" attribute is used to negotiate the (D)TLS roles

rejected.why: The webrtc-datachannel fmt value is only an example and registry entry. Data channel negotiation is left to other RFCs.
ICE candidate handling is discussed in one subsection, but only as a NAT consideration.
TCP is only a substrate, used with RFC 4571 framing and RFC 4145 connection management.
UDP is only the transport substrate for DTLS.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-like registration for the new SDP values.

RFC8842.title: Session Description Protocol (SDP) Offer/Answer Considerations for Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) and Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC8842.summary: Defines SDP offer/answer procedures for negotiating and establishing DTLS associations (and TLS connections), introduces the "tls-id" SDP attribute, and updates RFC 5763 and RFC 7345.

SDP.why: The document defines a new SDP attribute and the offer/answer procedures for it, so it belongs on the SDP page.
SDP.quote: This document defines a new SDP media-level attribute, "tls-id".

DTLS.why: The core subject is when and how a new DTLS association is established via signalling, including the criteria for a new association.
DTLS.quote: defines the Session Description Protocol (SDP) offer/ answer procedures for negotiating and establishing a Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) association.

ICE.why: A dedicated section covers ICE candidates, ICE restart and ufrag changes in relation to DTLS association establishment.
ICE.quote: When a new DTLS association is established over an unordered transport, in order to disambiguate any packets associated with the newly established DTLS association

rejected.why: SIP is the signalling protocol carrying the offers (forking, offerless INVITE are covered briefly), but the document is not about SIP itself.
RFC 5763 DTLS-SRTP is updated, but only the generic offer/answer text is changed; SRTP itself is not specified.
TLS is covered in a short section on using tls-id, but the document does not define TLS behaviour; the TLS extension is in RFC 8844.
RTP media is only an example DTLS usage; nothing is specified about RTP.
UDPTL-over-DTLS (T.38) is updated only by reference to the common procedures.

RFC8843.title: Negotiating Media Multiplexing Using the Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC8843.summary: Defines the SDP 'BUNDLE' grouping extension and 'bundle-only' attribute for negotiating a single transport for multiple m= sections via offer/answer, plus a new RTCP SDES MID item and RTP header extension, and updates RFCs 3264, 5888 and 7941.

SDP.why: The document's core is an SDP grouping extension, a new attribute, and offer/answer procedures; it updates RFC 3264 and RFC 5888.
SDP.quote: This specification defines a new Session Description Protocol (SDP) Grouping Framework extension called 'BUNDLE'.

RTP.why: Substantial parts cover a single RTP session per bundle, SSRC/MID/PT association of streams to m= sections, RTP/RTCP multiplexing, and the MID SDES item and header extension.
RTP.quote: This specification defines a new RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Source Description (SDES) item and a new RTP header extension.

ICE.why: A dedicated section defines how ICE candidates, checks and attributes apply to a BUNDLE transport.
ICE.quote: This section describes how to use the BUNDLE grouping extension together with the ICE mechanism [RFC8445].

rejected.why: SIP is only the usual carrier of SDP; the document is about SDP and not SIP.
A short section gives rules for DTLS use inside a bundle, but DTLS is not what the document is about.
SRTP and DTLS-SRTP are only mentioned for protocol identification and security; nothing new is defined for them.
The MID SDES item is defined here, but the tag was not chosen since the RTP tag covers it. RTCP in the taxonomy centres on feedback, reports and XR.
WebRTC and JSEP are mentioned only in the note about the inconsistency; the document is not about WebRTC.

RFC8844.title: Unknown Key-Share Attacks on Uses of TLS with the Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC8844.summary: RFC 8844 describes unknown key-share attacks on DTLS-SRTP with SDP fingerprints and WebRTC/SIP identity bindings, and defines two TLS extensions (external_id_hash, external_session_id) to mitigate them, updating RFC 8122.

TLS.why: The document defines two new TLS extensions and their handshake validation rules, which is new TLS functionality that readers of TLS need.
TLS.quote: The "external_id_hash" TLS extension carries a hash of the identity assertion that the endpoint sending the extension has asserted to its peer.

DTLS.why: The attacks and the extensions apply to DTLS-SRTP handshakes, and the document addresses DTLS-specific usage.
DTLS.quote: This document describes unknown key-share attacks on the use of Datagram Transport Layer Security for the Secure Real-Time Transport Protocol (DTLS-SRTP).

SDP.why: The fingerprint attack and the external_session_id extension depend on the SDP fingerprint and tls-id attributes. The document updates RFC 8122, which is SDP-based.
SDP.quote: This solution relies on the unique identifier given to DTLS sessions using the SDP "tls-id" attribute [DTLS-SDP].

SRTP.why: DTLS-SRTP key agreement is the system under attack, and the mitigations harden it.
SRTP.quote: Further use with Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) [DTLS] and the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) [SRTP] is defined as DTLS-SRTP [DTLS-SRTP].

WebRTC.why: Section 3 analyses the attack on WebRTC identity assertions and defines how to compute the hash for them.
WebRTC.quote: WebRTC identity (see Section 7 of [WEBRTC-SEC]) and SIP identity [SIP-ID] both provide a mechanism that binds an external identity to the certificate fingerprints

STIR.why: The document specifies how to compute external_id_hash for PASSporT and SIP identity bindings, which are STIR caller-ID mechanisms.
STIR.quote: Where the compact form of PASSporT [PASSPORT] is used, it MUST be expanded into the full form.

rejected.why: SIP identity is a binding mechanism the attack targets, and 3PCC is discussed. The document does not specify or extend SIP itself.
JSON is only the encoding of WebRTC identity assertions that get hashed.
SHA-256 is simply the hash chosen for the binding. The document defines nothing new about SHA.
ICE is mentioned once as an additional constraint on the attacker and is not a subject of the document.
The generic security topic is implied by the more specific TLS tag.

RFC8845.title: Framework for Telepresence Multi-Streams
RFC8845.summary: Defines the CLUE framework for telepresence: Media Providers advertise captures, capture scenes, simultaneous transmission sets and encoding groups, and Consumers configure which multiple streams to receive, alongside SIP/SDP signaling.

telepresence.why: The whole document specifies the CLUE telepresence multi-stream framework: captures, scenes, encoding groups, advertisements and configure messages.
telepresence.quote: This document defines a framework for a protocol to enable devices in a telepresence conference to interoperate.

rejected.why: SIP and SDP offer/answer are the session setup substrate; CLUE is used in addition to them and does not extend SIP itself.
Individual encoding parameters are carried in SDP, but the document defines no SDP extension.
RTP carries the media streams but is not specified or extended here.
The telepresence tag sits under it and is more specific; XCON is only referenced for security considerations.
xCard is used only for the person-information attribute, a minor use.
The data model XML schema is defined in the companion RFC 8846, not here.

RFC8846.title: An XML Schema for the Controlling Multiple Streams for Telepresence (CLUE) Data Model
RFC8846.summary: Defines the XML schema for the CLUE data model describing telepresence scenarios (media captures, capture scenes, encoding groups, simultaneous sets, people), used in CLUE protocol messages, with IANA registries and a media type.

telepresence.why: The CLUE data model describes multi-stream telepresence captures, scenes and encodings, which is the subject of the telepresence tag.
telepresence.quote: The document defines a coherent structure for information associated with the description of a telepresence scenario.

XML.why: The core deliverable is an XML schema with extensibility rules and a registered +xml media type.
XML.quote: This document provides an XML schema file for the definition of CLUE data model types.

rejected.why: Mentioned only in passing; the document does not define SDP content.
Streams are sent via RTP but the document does not specify RTP.
xCard is imported for person and scene info, but only as a reused component.
It registers application/clue_info+xml, but that is boilerplate IANA registration, not the main subject.
Parent of telepresence, so it is implied by that tag.
Only referenced in the endpoint definition; not specified here.

RFC8847.title: Protocol for Controlling Multiple Streams for Telepresence (CLUE)
RFC8847.summary: RFC 8847 specifies the CLUE application protocol (XML messages options, optionsResponse, advertisement, ack, configure, configureResponse, with state machines, versioning and extensions) by which telepresence endpoints describe and negotiate multi-stream sessions over the CLUE data channel.

telepresence.why: The document defines the CLUE protocol itself, its messages and state machines, for Media Providers and Consumers in telepresence sessions.
telepresence.quote: The Controlling Multiple Streams for Telepresence (CLUE) protocol is an application protocol conceived for the description and negotiation of a telepresence session.

media types.why: The document registers a new media type for CLUE messages, a modest but real part of the document.
media types.quote: This section registers the "application/clue+xml" media type.

rejected.why: CLUE messages ride on SCTP-over-DTLS, but this is only the substrate, specified in RFC 8850.
Used only as the transport security for the data channel; nothing new is defined about it.
XML is the message encoding; the document defines a CLUE schema but is not about XML usage in general.
Mentioned as having limitations that CLUE addresses, and signaling details are in RFC 8848, not here.
SIP session establishment is delegated to RFC 8848; this document is not about SIP.
Streams are sent via RTP, but RTP is only referenced as the media transport.

RFC8848.title: Session Signaling for Controlling Multiple Streams for Telepresence (CLUE)
RFC8848.summary: RFC 8848 specifies how CLUE telepresence signalling works with SIP and SDP: a new SDP grouping semantic and SIP media feature tag, offer/answer procedures, CLUE data channel use, BUNDLE multiplexing and example call flows.

telepresence.why: The whole document defines session signalling for CLUE multi-stream telepresence calls.
telepresence.quote: specifies how the CLUE protocol and the CLUE data channel are used in conjunction with each other and with existing signaling mechanisms

SDP.why: Defines a new SDP group semantic, label usage on m= lines, and offer/answer procedures for CLUE-controlled media.
SDP.quote: This section defines a new SDP Grouping Framework [RFC5888] extension called 'CLUE'.

SIP.why: Defines a new SIP media feature tag and SIP INVITE/UPDATE usage to set up CLUE calls.
SIP.quote: The "sip.clue" media feature tag [RFC3840] indicates support for CLUE in SIP [RFC3261] calls.

rejected.why: Uses the WebRTC data channel as a substrate for CLUE messages; not about WebRTC itself.
SCTP over DTLS is only the data channel transport.
CaptureID in RTP/RTCP is defined in RFC 8849; this document only requires its use.
Mentioned only as a cost motivating BUNDLE.
Required in Security Considerations only; boilerplate-level reliance.
Telepresence tag is the more specific fit for CLUE.

RFC8849.title: Mapping RTP Streams to Controlling Multiple Streams for Telepresence (CLUE) Media Captures
RFC8849.summary: Defines how RTP streams are used and mapped to CLUE telepresence Media Captures, including a new RTCP CaptureID SDES item and RTP header extension identifying the constituent capture of a switched MCC.

telepresence.quote: This document describes how the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) is used in the context of the Controlling Multiple Streams for Telepresence (CLUE) protocol.

RTP.why: It defines a new RTP header extension and a new RTCP SDES item, and discusses RTP topologies and SSRC usage.
RTP.quote: this document defines an RTP header extension and SDES item that includes the captureID of the original MC

rejected.why: SDP is used to label and negotiate the streams, but the document does not specify or extend SDP.
SRTP and DTLS-SRTP are mandated in the Communication Security section, but they are not the subject of the document.
The new SDES item is an RTCP element, but the document's focus is the CLUE mapping, so RTP covers it.
DTLS is only a keying mechanism required for security.

RFC8850.title: Controlling Multiple Streams for Telepresence (CLUE) Protocol Data Channel
RFC8850.summary: Defines how to realize a CLUE data channel for carrying CLUE protocol messages using WebRTC data channels (SCTP over DTLS), including SCTP option constraints and SDP m=line/dcmap attribute values, and registers the "clue" subprotocol.

telepresence.why: The document specifies the data channel used by the CLUE telepresence protocol.
telepresence.quote: transporting CLUE protocol messages [RFC8847] between two CLUE entities

SDP.quote: defines how to (1) construct the SDP media description ("m=" line) for describing the SCTPoDTLS association used to realize a CLUE data channel

WebRTC.why: The document profiles the WebRTC data channel for CLUE, setting ordering, reliability, PPID and stream reset behavior.
WebRTC.quote: defines how to use the WebRTC data channel mechanism [RFC8831] to realize a data channel

rejected.why: SCTP is the substrate. The document only selects options for it, such as ordered delivery, no partial reliability and PPID 51, and defines no new SCTP behavior.
DTLS is only the transport under SCTP and the document adds nothing new about it.
CLUE entities are SIP UAs, but SIP session signalling is out of scope and handled in RFC 8848.
The tag telepresence is more specific and already covers the CLUE subject.

RFC8851.title: RTP Payload Format Restrictions
RFC8851.summary: Defines the SDP "a=rid" media-level attribute and codec-agnostic restrictions (max-width, max-fps, max-br, depend, etc.) on RTP streams, with offer/answer procedures, interaction with VP8/H.264 fmtp parameters, and an IANA registry; updates RFC 4855.

SDP.why: The document defines a new SDP attribute, a=rid, with its grammar, offer/answer rules and a registry. This is an SDP extension.

RTP.why: The restrictions apply to RTP streams and payload formats. They bind to streams through the RTP stream identifier SDES item, so RTP readers would want this document.
RTP.quote: unambiguously identify the RTP streams within an RTP session and restrict the streams' payload format parameters in a codec-agnostic way

rejected.why: It restricts payload formats generically and interacts with VP8 and H.264 parameters. It does not define a payload format for any codec.
H.264 format parameters appear only as illustrative interaction examples in a non-normative section.
VP8 parameters are discussed only as an example of how they interact with rid restrictions.
The RtpStreamId SDES item is defined in RFC 8852. This document only uses it.

RFC8852.title: RTP Stream Identifier Source Description (SDES)
RFC8852.summary: Defines two new RTCP SDES items, RtpStreamId and RepairedRtpStreamId, plus RTP header extension forms, for uniquely identifying RTP streams and linking redundancy streams to the streams they repair.

RTCP.quote: This document defines and registers two new Real-time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP) Stream Identifier Source Description (SDES) items.

rejected.why: SDP is referenced for mapping streams to media descriptions, but the document defines nothing in SDP.
Motivated by simulcast and MSID, but the document does not specify WebRTC itself.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here and not the main subject.
Redundancy streams are only referenced for identification; no loss-recovery scheme is defined.

RFC8853.title: Using Simulcast in Session Description Protocol (SDP) and RTP Sessions
RFC8853.summary: Defines how to do simulcast (multiple encoded versions of one media source sent as separate RTP streams) and a new SDP media-level attribute "a=simulcast" using RIDs, with offer/answer rules, RTP-level identification, and middlebox behaviour.

RTP.why: It describes how simulcast RTP streams are identified (RtpStreamId, MID) and how mixers and selective forwarding middleboxes handle them (Section 6).

rejected.why: WebRTC is mentioned only as a context where the mechanism works; the document is not about WebRTC.
RTCP SDES items are used to carry RtpStreamId, but they are defined in RFC 8852, not here.
SDP offer/answer is used, but SIP signalling is not discussed.
Payload formats such as H.264, VP8 and RED appear only in examples and are not specified here.

Bitrate adaptation gets one short section that only assumes a congestion-control mechanism and does not define one.

RFC8854.title: WebRTC Forward Error Correction Requirements
RFC8854.summary: Provides guidance and requirements on which Forward Error Correction mechanisms WebRTC implementations should use for audio and video, how to negotiate them in SDP, and when to apply FEC adaptively.

FEC.why: The whole document is about choosing, negotiating and adaptively applying FEC schemes (separate stream, redundant encoding, in-band FEC, Flexible FEC) for packet loss recovery.
FEC.quote: This specification provides guidance on which FEC mechanisms to use, and how to use them, for WebRTC implementations.

rejected.why: RTP is the media transport FEC is applied to, but the document does not specify RTP itself.
It recommends existing payload formats (RFC 2198 redundancy, Flexible FEC) but defines none.
SDP offer/answer is used to signal FEC support, but nothing new is defined for SDP.
Opus in-band FEC is recommended for use, but the document is not about the codec.
AMR built-in FEC is referenced as a mechanism, but the codec is not the subject.
SRTP appears only in Security Considerations as the ordering of FEC and encryption.

RFC8855.title: The Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP)
RFC8855.summary: RFC 8855 specifies the Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP), used between floor participants/chairs and floor control servers to manage access to shared conference resources, obsoleting RFC 4582 and adding UDP/DTLS transport support.

BFCP.quote: This document specifies the Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP). BFCP is used between floor participants and floor control servers, and between floor chairs

The XCON framework is referenced for scope and floor creation, but the document does not specify it.
TLS/DTLS is used as the security mechanism with cipher suite requirements, but nothing new is defined about TLS.
DTLS is the security substrate for BFCP over UDP, not the subject of the document.
UDP is the transport used for the unreliable mode, not specified or extended in its own right.
The SDP offer/answer negotiation for BFCP is defined in RFC 8856 and only referenced here.
NAT traversal (ICE, STUN keepalives) is mentioned as a motivation and recommendation, but is not the subject.

RFC8856.title: Session Description Protocol (SDP) Format for Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP) Streams
RFC8856.summary: Defines SDP offer/answer procedures, m= line proto values and new SDP attributes (floorctrl, confid, userid, floorid, bfcpver) for negotiating BFCP streams over TCP/UDP with TLS/DTLS and ICE, obsoleting RFC 4583.

BFCP.why: The document is the SDP signalling format for BFCP streams, extending how BFCP connections are established and negotiated.
BFCP.quote: This document defines the Session Description Protocol (SDP) offer/answer procedures for negotiating and establishing Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP) streams.

SDP.why: It defines new SDP media-level attributes, new proto values and offer/answer procedures, so SDP readers need it.
SDP.quote: This section defines the SDP 'floorctrl' media-level attribute.

rejected.why: ICE is only considered for how it interacts with BFCP proto values; the document does not specify ICE.
DTLS is used as a security substrate, and generic procedures are delegated to RFC 8842.
TLS is used as a substrate; the document defines no new TLS extension.
SIP is mentioned only as one way to carry SDP.
BFCP is a child of conferencing and is already tagged, so the parent is implied.
TCP connection management uses the RFC 4145 setup and connection attributes, so TCP is only the transport.

RFC8857.title: The WebSocket Protocol as a Transport for the Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP)
RFC8857.summary: Defines the "bfcp" WebSocket subprotocol for carrying BFCP messages over WebSocket (WS/WSS), with SDP proto values, offer/answer procedures using websocket-uri, and authentication guidance.

BFCP.why: The document extends BFCP with a new transport binding, so BFCP readers need it.
BFCP.quote: This document specifies the use of Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP) as a new WebSocket subprotocol enabling a reliable transport mechanism between BFCP entities

The HTTP Upgrade handshake is only the substrate used to establish WebSocket.
TLS only secures WSS. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
Cookies are mentioned only as an authorization option in the authentication section.
HOBA is cited only as a possible way to overcome weaknesses in other authentication schemes.
TCP is only the underlying transport.

gaps.name: BFCP (Binary Floor Control Protocol)
