RFC8858.title: Indicating Exclusive Support of RTP and RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Multiplexing Using the Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC8858.summary: Defines the SDP media-level attribute 'rtcp-mux-only' for an offerer to signal exclusive RTP/RTCP multiplexing support, specifies its offer/answer procedures and ICE considerations, and updates RFC 5761 to clarify that an offerer may signal it cannot use separate RTCP ports.

RTCP.quote: defines how to multiplex RTP and RTCP on a single IP address and port, referred to as RTP/RTCP multiplexing

WebRTC is only cited as an example of applications that may use the attribute; the document does not specify WebRTC behaviour.
The RTP/RTCP multiplexing mechanism is defined in RFC 5761; this document only signals it in SDP, and the more specific RTCP tag already covers the subject.
ICE candidate rules are mentioned only briefly; the document is not about NAT traversal.

RFC8859.title: A Framework for Session Description Protocol (SDP) Attributes When Multiplexing
RFC8859.summary: RFC 8859 defines a framework of multiplexing categories (NORMAL, CAUTION, IDENTICAL, SUM, TRANSPORT, INHERIT, IDENTICAL-PER-PT, SPECIAL, TBD) for analyzing SDP attributes when multiple m= lines share one 5-tuple (BUNDLE), and assigns a category to each existing SDP attribute and IANA registry entry.

ice-ufrag, ice-pwd and candidate are categorized as TRANSPORT, but ICE is not specified or extended here.
rtcp-fb, rtcp-mux and similar attributes are classified, but RTCP is not the subject.

RFC8860.title: Sending Multiple Types of Media in a Single RTP Session
RFC8860.summary: RFC 8860 updates RFC 3550 and RFC 3551 to allow RTP sessions to carry multiple media types (audio, video, text) in one session, setting out applicability, SSRC and demultiplexing rules, RTCP handling and extension interactions.

SDP.quote: When using SDP signalling, the BUNDLE extension [RFC8843] is used to signal RTP sessions containing multiple media types.

rejected.why: Generic FEC payload formats are discussed only as an extension-compatibility case, not as the subject.

RFC8861.title: Sending Multiple RTP Streams in a Single RTP Session: Grouping RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Reception Statistics and Other Feedback
RFC8861.summary: Defines RTCP Reporting Groups, a Standards Track extension (new RGRP SDES item, RGRS packet, and a=rtcp-rgrp SDP attribute) that lets co-located SSRCs in one RTP session suppress redundant RTCP reception reports.

RFC8862.summary: BCP describing how to negotiate confidential SRTP media with SIP, defining the SIPBRANDY profile of STIR (the "msec" PASSporT type) that binds DTLS-SRTP key fingerprints in SDP to SIP identities, with ICE and consent freshness requirements.

RFC8863.summary: RFC 8863 updates ICE (RFC 8445) and Trickle ICE (RFC 8838) to require a minimum "PAC timer" wait before an ICE agent declares failure, allowing peer-reflexive candidates to be discovered.

RFC8864.summary: Defines the SDP attributes a=dcmap and a=dcsa and offer/answer procedures for out-of-band (non-DCEP) negotiation of WebRTC data channels carried over SCTP/DTLS.

The IANA registrations are boilerplate for the new attributes and not the main subject.

RFC8865.title: T.140 Real-Time Text Conversation over WebRTC Data Channels
RFC8865.summary: Specifies using a WebRTC data channel with the "t140" subprotocol to carry ITU-T T.140 real-time text, negotiated via SDP offer/answer (dcmap/dcsa), with gateway guidance, and updates RFC 8373 for hlang attributes on data channels.

WebRTC.why: The document defines a new WebRTC data channel subprotocol (t140), its channel properties, and usage, which is what WebRTC readers would want.
WebRTC.quote: specifies how a Web Real-Time Communication (WebRTC) data channel can be used as a transport mechanism for real-time text

SDP.why: Defines SDP dcmap/dcsa usage, fmtp cps, hlang and direction attributes for the T.140 data channel, with offer/answer rules and IANA registrations.
SDP.quote: how the Session Description Protocol (SDP) offer/answer mechanism can be used to negotiate such a data channel

accessibility.why: Real-time text conversation is an accessibility communication modality, including language negotiation and emergency service use, so accessibility readers would want it.
accessibility.quote: Real-time text is intended to be entered by human users via a keyboard, handwriting recognition, voice recognition, or any other input method.

rejected.why: RTP-based transport (RFC 4103) is only the alternative and gateway counterpart; this document does not specify RTP.
SCTP is only the substrate beneath data channels; nothing new is defined about it.
DTLS encryption is incidental to data channels and is mentioned only in examples and security text.
SIP is mentioned only as an example signaling means for session preparation.
The hlang attributes are used, but the document defines only how they are applied to data channels; this is not about language tags themselves.
The more specific WebRTC and SDP tags cover the document.

gaps.name: T.140 real-time text
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for real-time text conversation (ITU-T T.140, RFC 4103), the core subject of the document.

RFC8866.title: SDP: Session Description Protocol
RFC8866.summary: RFC 8866 specifies the Session Description Protocol (SDP), a textual format for describing multimedia sessions (origin, timing, connection, media, attributes), obsoleting RFC 4566, and defines its IANA registries and ABNF grammar.

SDP.why: The document is the core SDP specification: line types, attributes, registries and grammar.
SDP.quote: This memo defines the Session Description Protocol (SDP). SDP is intended for describing multimedia sessions for the purposes of session announcement, session invitation

rejected.why: SIP is a transport for SDP and is only used as an example context; the document does not specify SIP.
RTP appears in m= line protocols and rtpmap, but only as something SDP describes, not specified here.
The application/sdp registration is boilerplate-like IANA content, not the main subject.
The grammar is written in ABNF, but ABNF is merely the notation used.
The registries are for SDP parameters, secondary to the SDP specification itself, not about IANA guidance generally.
RTSP is only mentioned as one transport of SDP.

RFC8867.title: Test Cases for Evaluating Congestion Control for Interactive Real-Time Media
RFC8867.summary: Defines a set of test cases (topologies, path characteristics, media and competing traffic settings, metrics) for evaluating congestion control algorithms for interactive real-time RTP media in a controlled environment.

RTP congestion control.why: The whole document defines evaluation test cases for congestion control of interactive real-time media over RTP, which is exactly the scope of this tag.
RTP congestion control.quote: This document describes the test cases to be used in the performance evaluation of such congestion control algorithms in a controlled environment.

rejected.why: RTP is the media transport whose congestion control is evaluated; the document does not specify or extend RTP itself.
RTCP is only mentioned as a possible feedback channel and for terminology.
TCP flows are used only as competing traffic in test cases 5.6 and 5.7.
FQ-CoDel and PIE are only bottleneck queue settings in the testbed, not subjects of the document.
ECN is listed as one potential test case (Section 6.2) but is a minor part of the document.
This is evaluation of congestion control algorithms rather than benchmarking of network devices; the more specific congestion control tag fits better.

RFC8868.title: Evaluating Congestion Control for Interactive Real-Time Media
RFC8868.summary: Gives guidelines for evaluating new congestion control algorithms for interactive point-to-point real-time RTP media: metrics, RTP log format, network parameters (delay, loss, queue length, jitter models) and traffic models (TCP, video, UDP).

RTP congestion control.why: The whole document defines how to evaluate congestion control for interactive RTP media, which is exactly this tag's subject.
RTP congestion control.quote: This document describes the guidelines to evaluate new congestion control algorithms for interactive point-to-point real-time media.

performance measurement.why: A substantial part defines metrics (rate, goodput, delay, fairness, convergence), a common RTP log format, and packet delay variation models for evaluation.
performance measurement.quote: The following metrics are calculated based on the information in the packet logs:

rejected.why: RTP is the media transport being evaluated, not specified or extended here; the more specific RTP congestion control tag covers it.
Parent of RTP congestion control, which is already chosen, so it is implied.
This is evaluation of congestion control algorithms by simulation or emulation, not benchmarking methodology for network devices.
AQM is only mentioned as optional experimentation; the document specifies drop-tail queues.
TCP appears only as a cross-traffic model in the tests, and the document does not specify or extend it.
CUBIC is only suggested as one competing TCP congestion control scheme to test against.

RFC8869.title: Evaluation Test Cases for Interactive Real-Time Media over Wireless Networks
RFC8869.summary: Defines simulation test cases for evaluating RTP-based congestion control algorithms for interactive real-time media over cellular and Wi-Fi networks, with expected behaviours and metrics.

RTP congestion control.why: The document's whole purpose is test cases for evaluating congestion control for interactive real-time media over RTP (companion to RFC 8867/8868).
RTP congestion control.quote: This document describes test cases for evaluating performances of candidate congestion control algorithms over cellular and Wi-Fi networks.

WiFi.why: A full section of Wi-Fi-specific test cases (802.11n, EDCA/WMM, heterogeneous link rates), so Wi-Fi readers would want it.
WiFi.quote: Given the prevalence of Internet access links over Wi-Fi, it is important to evaluate candidate RTP-based congestion control solutions over test cases that include Wi-Fi access links.

cellular.why: A full section of cellular test cases (LTE, handover, bad radio coverage, varying load) using a cellular simulator.
cellular.quote: This document describes test cases specifically targeting cellular and Wi-Fi networks.

rejected.why: RTP is the media transport whose congestion control is tested; the document doesn't specify or extend RTP itself.
The more specific child RTP congestion control fits, so the parent isn't listed.
TCP appears only as competing background traffic using default congestion control (RFC 5681).
3GPP QoS bearers and EDCA/WMM are mentioned as context and a possible future test, not the subject.
AQM on/off is just one simulation parameter.
This is about evaluation test cases for algorithms, not benchmarking methodology for network devices.

RFC8870.title: Encrypted Key Transport for DTLS and Secure RTP
RFC8870.summary: Defines Encrypted Key Transport (EKT), which carries encrypted SRTP master keys and rollover counters in an SRTP packet trailer, and a DTLS-SRTP extension (supported_ekt_ciphers, ekt_key message) that distributes the common EKTKey for decentralized conferences.

SRTP.why: The document defines an EKTField appended to SRTP packets and its processing, extending SRTP to carry master keys and ROC.
SRTP.quote: EKT extends DTLS and SRTP to enable a common key encryption key (called an "EKTKey") to be distributed to all endpoints

DTLS.why: A substantial part of the document defines a new DTLS extension and handshake message for the DTLS-SRTP exchange, which is new use of the substrate that DTLS readers need.
DTLS.quote: This document defines a new TLS negotiated extension called "supported_ekt_ciphers" and a new TLS handshake message type called "ekt_key".
DTLS.section: 5.2. SRTP EKT Key Transport Extensions to DTLS-SRTP

rejected.why: EKT transports SRTP keys, but it is explicitly not a key establishment mechanism. It complements DTLS-SRTP, and the SRTP tag fits better.
The document adds a TLS extension and handshake type, but only in the datagram context, so the more specific DTLS tag applies.
AES Key Wrap is only the default cipher used for EKT. The document is not about AES.
The document only notes that SDP offer/answer is unchanged. Negotiation happens in the DTLS handshake.
RTP is the context, but the document is specific to SRTP, which sits under RTP.

gaps.name: PERC (Privacy-Enhanced RTP Conferencing)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for PERC, the working group and architecture behind this RFC. The document only references RFC 8871, which defines it.

RFC8871.title: A Solution Framework for Private Media in Privacy-Enhanced RTP Conferencing (PERC)
RFC8871.summary: Framework for PERC: end-to-end media confidentiality in switched RTP conferencing where Media Distributors lack E2E keys, using double SRTP transform, EKT, and DTLS-SRTP with a Key Distributor.

SRTP.why: The document defines how SRTP is used with double E2E and HBH contexts, key hierarchy and packet format for private media conferencing.
SRTP.quote: This framework reuses several specified RTP security technologies, including the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) [RFC3711], Encrypted Key Transport (EKT) [RFC8870], and DTLS-SRTP.

conferencing.why: Addresses switched multiparty conferencing with untrusted Media Distributors (selective forwarding), a conferencing architecture and trust model.
conferencing.quote: ensuring that media confidentiality and integrity are maintained end to end within the context of a switched conferencing environment

key management.why: A substantial part covers key inventory, KEK/EKT key distribution, rekeying and which entities hold which keys.
key management.quote: The Key Distributor, which may be co-located with an endpoint or exist standalone, is responsible for providing key information to endpoints

rejected.why: DTLS-SRTP is used as the key exchange mechanism; the document specifies no new DTLS behaviour (tunnel is in a separate draft).
RTP is the substrate; the document concerns its security, covered by the SRTP tag.
Only referenced for identity assertions and browser as endpoint; not the subject.
Mentioned only as an example for conveying certificate fingerprints.
Mentioned only as a cipher suite not defined for PERC.
Only noted as hop-by-hop encrypted; no RTCP feedback or report specification.

gaps.name: EKT (Encrypted Key Transport)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for EKT, which is central to this framework's E2E key distribution.

RFC8872.title: Guidelines for Using the Multiplexing Features of RTP to Support Multiple Media Streams
RFC8872.summary: Informational guidelines on how to use RTP's multiplexing points (sessions, SSRCs, payload types) to carry multiple media streams, weighing interworking, network, NAT, multicast and security trade-offs and giving design recommendations.

RTP.why: The whole document analyses RTP sessions, SSRCs, CSRCs and payload types as multiplexing points and gives guidelines for RTP application designers.
RTP.quote: This memo discusses the available options and design trade-offs, and provides guidelines on how to use the multiplexing features of RTP to support multiple media streams.

rejected.why: SDP signalling (BUNDLE, grouping, RID) is discussed as context and in an appendix, but the document says it focuses on RTP issues, not signalling.
SRTP key and security-context implications are covered in Section 4.3, but only as one consideration for multiplexing choices, not as the subject.
RTCP is assumed and referenced throughout, but the document does not specify or extend RTCP mechanisms; it is about multiplexing choices.
FEC streams are a use case for binding related streams in Section 3.4.4, but the document is not about FEC schemes.
NAT/firewall effects of using more transport flows are analysed in Section 4.2.2, but as one trade-off, not the main subject.
Section 4.2.3 covers multicast implications for session choice only briefly.

RFC8873.title: Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP) over Data Channels
RFC8873.summary: Specifies how a WebRTC data channel carries MSRP (subprotocol "msrp"), including SDP offer/answer negotiation via dcmap/dcsa attributes, file transfer support, and gateway interworking with TCP/TLS MSRP endpoints; updates RFC 4975.

MSRP.why: The document defines a new transport binding for MSRP, updates RFC 4975, and specifies MSRP URI, session, framing and gateway procedures.
MSRP.quote: This document specifies how a Web Real-Time Communication (WebRTC) data channel can be used as a transport mechanism for the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP)

WebRTC.why: Defines a WebRTC data channel subprotocol and its properties, so readers of WebRTC data channels would want it.
WebRTC.quote: an MSRP data channel refers to a WebRTC data channel for which the instantiated subprotocol is "msrp"

SDP.why: A large part of the document defines SDP offer/answer usage of dcmap, dcsa, setup and other attributes for MSRP data channels.
SDP.quote: An offerer and answerer SHALL, in each offer and answer, include a 'dcmap' attribute [RFC8864] in the SDP media description

rejected.why: SCTP is only the substrate beneath data channels; nothing new is defined about SCTP.
DTLS is the security mechanism of data channels. The document only notes that the msrps scheme implies DTLS.
SIP is mentioned only as a possible carrier of offer/answer in Security Considerations.
RFC 7977 is cited only as prior MSRP transport and for contrast.
The document lists SDP attribute registrations for MSRP, not media type registration rules.

RFC8874.title: Working Group GitHub Usage Guidance
RFC8874.summary: Guidelines for IETF working groups on using GitHub (organizations, repositories, issues, pull requests, labels, consensus assessment) in developing Internet-Drafts.

IETF process.why: The document gives working group procedures for using GitHub within RFC 2418 WG practice, including consensus assessment, chair duties and I-D publication. This is IETF process guidance.
IETF process.quote: The main purpose of this document is to provide guidelines for how a working group might integrate the capabilities provided by GitHub into their processes

rejected.why: It covers Internet-Draft development workflow, not RFC format, style or publication.
Markdown is mentioned only as an optional editing input format, not as a subject.
The canonical RFC XML format is mentioned in passing, but the document is not about it.
RFC 7991 is cited only as the canonical document format, not specified or discussed.

gaps.name: Git/GitHub version control tooling for document development
gaps.why: The document is largely about using Git and GitHub, but the taxonomy has no tag for version control or collaborative authoring tools. The closest fit is IETF process.

RFC8875.title: Working Group GitHub Administration
RFC8875.summary: Informational RFC describing administrative processes and conventions (Datatracker facilities, GitHub organization creation, repository setup, contribution rules, backup/archiving) for IETF working groups choosing to use GitHub.

IETF process.why: The document defines working group administrative procedures (organization creation, personnel changes, WG closing, contribution boilerplate, archiving) for IETF document development.
IETF process.quote: This document specifies a set of administrative processes and conventions for IETF working groups to use if they choose as a working group to use GitHub

rejected.why: It mentions the CONTRIBUTING boilerplate from the IETF license file, but this is a minor part; the document is not about IPR.
It concerns Internet-Draft development workflow, not RFC format, style or publication.

gaps.name: GitHub / Git usage for working group document development
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for Git or GitHub tooling, or for IETF tools and Datatracker. The subject is only partly covered by IETF process.

RFC8876.title: Non-interactive Emergency Calls
RFC8876.summary: Defines non-interactive emergency calls: a SIP MESSAGE carrying a CAP alert as additional data (no session or interactive media), with CAP profiling, a new 425 response code, and an AlertMsg-Error header field.

emergency services.why: The document extends the ECRIT emergency calling framework with data-only emergency requests routed to PSAPs. No narrower emergency tag (LoST, eCall) fits, since LoST is only used for routing.
emergency services.quote: In some cases of emergency calls, the transmission of application data is all that is needed, and no interactive media channel is established

SIP.why: It extends SIP with a MESSAGE-based emergency request, a new 425 response code, the AlertMsg-Error header field and a new error code registry.
SIP.quote: This document describes use of a SIP MESSAGE transaction that includes a container for the data based on the Common Alerting Protocol (CAP).

rejected.why: Mentioned only as the way an ESRP finds the next hop; the document does not specify or extend it.
SIP MESSAGE is used only as the carrier transaction. The document is not about instant messaging or presence.
It registers application/EmergencyCallData.cap+xml, but that registration is IANA boilerplate rather than the main subject.
CAP and PIDF-LO are XML payloads, but the document does not address XML usage in its own right.
Location is conveyed via PIDF-LO and the Geolocation header, but only incidentally, with CAP area conversion rules.
HTTPS is only the by-reference retrieval mechanism for large data.

gaps.name: Common Alerting Protocol (CAP)
gaps.why: The document profiles CAP for SIP carriage, but the taxonomy has no tag for alerting or warning formats.

RFC8877.title: Guidelines for Defining Packet Timestamps
RFC8877.summary: Informational guidelines for defining binary packet timestamp formats in network protocols, with a specification template and three recommended formats (NTP 64-bit, NTP 32-bit, PTP truncated), plus synchronization and control-field guidance.

time synchronization.why: The document is about timestamp formats, epochs, leap seconds and synchronization aspects. No child tech fits the guidelines themselves, so the topic tag applies.
time synchronization.quote: This document specifies guidelines for defining packet timestamp formats in networking protocols at various layers.

NTP.why: Two of the three recommended formats are NTP timestamp formats, and the document restates them in detail. Readers of NTP would want it.
NTP.quote: The Network Time Protocol (NTP) 64-bit timestamp format is defined in [RFC5905].

PTP.why: The third recommended format is the PTP truncated timestamp, specified in the document.
PTP.quote: The Precision Time Protocol (PTP) [IEEE1588] uses an 80-bit timestamp format.  The truncated timestamp format is a 64-bit field

rejected.why: OWAMP, TWAMP and delay measurement protocols are only examples of timestamp users, not the subject.
The document explicitly contrasts text-based RFC 3339 timestamps with binary packet timestamps. Its subject is binary packet timestamps, so the tag does not fit.
YANG is mentioned once as a possible way to carry timestamp control information.
OWAMP is only a user of the NTP 64-bit format, listed in the use-case table.

gaps.name: packet timestamp formats
gaps.why: The document is about binary timestamp format design, which is a data-representation subject. The taxonomy has no tag for it apart from the text-based date-time formats.

RFC8878.title: Zstandard Compression and the 'application/zstd' Media Type
RFC8878.summary: Describes the Zstandard (zstd) lossless compression format (frames, blocks, FSE and Huffman entropy coding, dictionaries) and registers the application/zstd media type, the zstd HTTP content coding, and the +zstd structured syntax suffix.

zstd.why: The document specifies the Zstandard compressed data format in full, including frame structure, entropy coding and dictionaries.
zstd.quote: Zstandard, or "zstd" (pronounced "zee standard"), is a data compression mechanism, akin to gzip [RFC1952].

media types.why: It registers a media type and a structured syntax suffix (+zstd), which is of interest to readers of media type registrations.
media types.quote: The 'application/zstd' media type identifies a block of data that is compressed using zstd compression.

rejected.why: The zstd HTTP content coding is only an IANA registration entry; the document does not define HTTP semantics or extensions.
gzip is mentioned only as an analogy and informative reference, not specified or extended.
MIME is the transport context for the media type registration, not the subject of the document.
Implied by the more specific zstd tag, so the parent is not listed.

RFC8879.title: TLS Certificate Compression
RFC8879.summary: Defines a TLS 1.3 extension (compress_certificate) and CompressedCertificate handshake message letting peers compress Certificate messages with zlib, brotli or zstd, plus a registry of algorithm IDs.

TLS.why: The document specifies a new TLS extension and handshake message for TLS 1.3, so TLS readers need it.
TLS.quote: This document defines a new extension type (compress_certificate(27)), which can be used to signal the supported compression formats for the Certificate message to the peer.

rejected.why: Compression is applied to the Certificate message, but the document defines no compression format of its own. It reuses existing algorithms.
Zlib is one of the three algorithms referenced, but only as a normative pointer. The document does not specify it.
Brotli is only referenced as a negotiable algorithm, not specified here.
Zstandard is only referenced as a negotiable algorithm, not specified here.
Certificates are the payload being compressed, but the document says nothing about certificate contents or profiles.
The IANA entry marks DTLS-OK, but the body is about TLS 1.3 only.

RFC8880.title: Special Use Domain Name 'ipv4only.arpa'
RFC8880.summary: Declares 'ipv4only.arpa' and the reverse names 170/171.0.0.192.in-addr.arpa as special-use domain names, specifying special handling by resolver APIs and DNS64 resolvers, requiring an insecure DNSSEC delegation, and updating RFC 7050.

special-use domain names.why: The document's main purpose is to formally declare the special properties of ipv4only.arpa and its reverse names and register them in the Special-Use Domain Names registry.
special-use domain names.quote: IANA has recorded the following names in the Special-Use Domain Names registry [SUDN]

DNS64.why: Specifies required DNS64 resolver behaviour for the name, including acting as authoritative and synthesizing AAAA answers; also updates NAT64 prefix discovery which depends on DNS64.
DNS64.quote: DNS64 recursive resolvers MUST generate the 192.0.0.170 and 192.0.0.171 responses for IPv4 address queries

DNSSEC.why: A substantial normative part corrects RFC 7050 to require an insecure delegation and forbids validation of AAAA answers; this is a core technical outcome rather than boilerplate.
DNSSEC.quote: the 'ipv4only.arpa' zone MUST be an insecure delegation to give DNS64/NAT64 gateways the freedom to synthesize answers

rejected.why: NAT64 is the context for the prefix discovery, but the document is about the DNS name and DNS64/resolver treatment, not the translator itself.
Parent of DNS64/NAT64 context; the more specific DNS64 tag already fits.
Only referenced as a way the client learns its recursive resolver; not specified or extended.
IANA actions are the registration outcome, covered more specifically by special-use domain names.
The more specific DNS64 and special-use domain names tags already cover the DNS content.

gaps.name: NAT64 prefix discovery (RFC 7050)
gaps.why: The document updates the mechanism by which clients discover the NAT64 prefix via ipv4only.arpa queries; no taxonomy tag covers this specifically.

RFC8881.title: Network File System (NFS) Version 4 Minor Version 1 Protocol
RFC8881.summary: RFC 8881 is the full specification of NFS version 4 minor version 1 (obsoleting RFC 5661), covering sessions, trunking, state management, locking, delegations, multi-server namespace/migration, pNFS and the file layout type, and all operations.

NFS.why: The document is the NFSv4.1 protocol specification itself, defining its operations, attributes, sessions, locking, and namespace features.
NFS.quote: This document describes the Network File System (NFS) version 4 minor version 1, including features retained from the base protocol

rejected.why: NFSv4.1 is an RPC application and relies on ONC RPC/XDR and RPCSEC_GSS as substrate; the document does not specify them.
RDMA considerations are discussed only as a transport layering; the RPC-over-RDMA protocol is specified elsewhere.
GSS-API/RPCSEC_GSS and Kerberos are used as security mechanisms; the SSV GSS mechanism is internal and a small part of the document.
TCP is only the required transport the protocol runs over.
Kerberos V5 is a mandated security mechanism relied on, not specified here.

gaps.name: NFS / NFSv4 (network file system protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has NFS only as a tech under the storage topic, but I used an id that does not exist in the taxonomy; the closest is the 'NFS' tech under storage, which is the correct fit. No other gap beyond pNFS, which has no dedicated tag.

RFC8882.title: DNS-Based Service Discovery (DNS-SD) Privacy and Security Requirements
RFC8882.summary: Informational document analysing privacy and security threats in DNS-SD (including over mDNS) and stating requirements for a privacy-preserving DNS-SD extension.

DNS-SD.why: The whole document analyses DNS-SD's privacy leaks (instance names, hostnames, TXT attributes) and sets requirements for a privacy extension.
DNS-SD.quote: DNS-SD (DNS-based Service Discovery) normally discloses information about devices offering and requesting services.

mDNS.why: The multicast nature of mDNS drives the on-link threat model and scenarios analysed, so mDNS readers would want this.
mDNS.quote: DNS-Based Service Discovery (DNS-SD) [RFC6763] over Multicast DNS (mDNS) [RFC6762] enables zero-configuration service discovery in local networks.

privacy.why: Much of the document is a privacy threat analysis (identity disclosure, fingerprinting, linkable identifiers) with privacy requirements.
privacy.quote: Avoid disclosure of the client's identity, either directly or via inference, to nodes other than select servers.

rejected.why: DNS is the substrate for publishing records; the document is about DNS-SD specifically, a child tag.
The more specific DNS-SD tech tag covers it.
SRP and J-PAKE are only mentioned as possible trust establishment options, not discussed.
Hostname privacy is mentioned but defers to RFC 8117; not the main subject.
Security considerations here are part of the DNS-SD analysis; privacy and DNS-SD tags cover it.

RFC8883.title: ICMPv6 Errors for Discarding Packets Due to Processing Limits
RFC8883.summary: Defines new ICMPv6 Parameter Problem codes and a Destination Unreachable code (with an ICMP extension Pointer object) sent when a node discards packets because extension-header or aggregate header processing limits are exceeded.

ICMP.why: The document extends ICMPv6 with new code points and an ICMP extension object class, and specifies sender and host-response behaviour.
ICMP.quote: This specification defines several new ICMPv6 errors that can be sent by a node that discards packets because it is unable to process the protocol headers.

IPv6.why: A substantial part concerns IPv6 extension header and option processing limits and how hosts and intermediate nodes handle them.
IPv6.quote: In IPv6, optional internet-layer information is carried in one or more IPv6 extension headers [RFC8200].

rejected.why: Middlebox filtering is mentioned as a motivation for header inspection, but the document is not about firewalls.
PLPMTUD is mentioned only as an alternative mechanism to correlate with, and the document says interaction is out of scope.
The Segment Routing Header is cited only as an example of long headers.
In-situ OAM headers are cited only as an example of long headers.
The IANA code assignments are boilerplate here and not the main subject.
It is mentioned only as an alternative mechanism for diagnosing packet loss.

RFC8884.title: Research Directions for Using Information-Centric Networking (ICN) in Disaster Scenarios
RFC8884.summary: An IRTF ICNRG informational document outlining research challenges and directions for applying Information-Centric Networking to communication after large-scale disasters, including use cases, ICN-based approaches, and its relation to DTN.

ICN.why: The whole document explores ICN approaches (routing-by-name, caching, self-certifying names, data mules, NREP) for disaster scenarios.
ICN.quote: Information-Centric Networking (ICN) is a new paradigm where the network provides users with named content instead of communication channels between hosts.

DTN.why: A substantial section compares ICN with DTN and concludes disaster solutions need combined ICN and DTN capabilities.
DTN.quote: ICN as Starting Point vs. Existing DTN Solutions

rejected.why: Its children are about emergency calling (LoST, eCall); this document is about ICN research for disaster communication, not emergency calling protocols.
Mentioned only as an example of application-layer name resolution that ICN avoids.
Mobile networks are discussed as the disaster context, but the document does not address cellular specifications.
PKI and web of trust are discussed only as trust models for decentralized authentication, not as the subject.
Energy efficiency is one challenge among several, covered briefly and not about monitoring or managing device energy.
The document is a research-directions paper on ICN, not about Internet architectural principles.

RFC8885.title: Proxy Mobile IPv6 Extensions for Distributed Mobility Management
RFC8885.summary: Experimental RFC extending Proxy Mobile IPv6 for distributed mobility management, with MAARs anchoring prefixes at the access edge, a Central Mobility Database, new PBU/PBA flags and mobility options, and a distributed logical interface concept.

PMIPv6.why: The document extends PMIPv6 with new PBU/PBA flags, mobility options, and CMD/MAAR roles to support distributed anchoring.
PMIPv6.quote: This document follows the former approach and proposes a solution based on Proxy Mobile IPv6, in which mobility sessions are anchored at the last IP hop router

IP mobility.why: Distributed mobility management is an IP-layer mobility architecture topic. It is not covered by the PMIPv6 tag alone, since the document also covers DMM concepts such as per-prefix anchoring and the DLIF.
IP mobility.quote: The purpose of DMM is to overcome the limitations of the traditional centralized mobility management

rejected.why: Mobile IPv6 is only referenced for terminology, message and option formats, and timers. The document extends PMIPv6, not Mobile IPv6.
IPsec is only recommended in Security Considerations for protecting PBU/PBA signalling. That is boilerplate and the document is not about IPsec.
SLAAC is used as the example address autoconfiguration method for the MN. The document does not specify or extend it.
Router Advertisements and the NDP link-layer address option format are used as mechanisms. The document does not change neighbor discovery.
The document works with IPv6 prefixes, but it is about mobility signalling rather than IPv6 itself.

RFC8886.title: Secure Device Install
RFC8886.summary: RFC 8886 describes a simple extension to vendor auto-install bootstrapping in which a network device generates a key pair at manufacture, the vendor publishes its certificate, and the operator encrypts the initial configuration to that key so it stays confidential in transit and at rest.

autonomic networking.why: The document is about zero-touch style bootstrapping of new network devices, comparable to SZTP and BRSKI. The taxonomy has no zero-touch provisioning tag, so the nearest fit is the network-management autonomic networking topic.
autonomic networking.quote: This document extends existing vendor proprietary auto-install to provide limited confidentiality to initial configuration during bootstrapping of the device.

key management.why: A substantial part of the document covers device key generation, publication of public keys via a vendor directory server, key storage in a TPM, and key replacement.
key management.quote: Each device requires a public-private key pair and for the public part to be published and retrievable by the operator.

rejected.why: DHCP is only the existing mechanism used to find the configuration server. The document defines nothing new about it.
TFTP is only the substrate for fetching the configuration file, and the document adds nothing to it.
S/MIME is used only as an example encryption format, and the document says it is probably not the best choice.
X.509 certificates are only a convenient container for the public key. The signature is ignored and the key fingerprint is pinned.
BRSKI is mentioned only as a more fully featured alternative. This document does not specify or analyse it.
The document is about confidential configuration delivery rather than general operational security practices, so the broader topic fits less well.

gaps.name: Zero-touch provisioning / secure device bootstrapping
gaps.why: The document is about secure bootstrapping of new devices, alongside SZTP and BRSKI. The taxonomy only has BRSKI under autonomic networking, with no general tag for device provisioning or auto-install.

RFC8887.title: A JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP) Subprotocol for WebSocket
RFC8887.summary: Defines the WebSocket subprotocol binding for JMAP, covering discovery via the session capability, handshake, message framing, request/response extensions, and push notifications over WebSocket.

JMAP.why: The document extends JMAP with a new transport binding, including capability discovery, Request/Response extensions and push notifications. JMAP readers need it.
JMAP.quote: This document defines a binding for the JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP) over a WebSocket transport layer.

WebSocket.why: It defines a new WebSocket subprotocol ("jmap"), including its handshake negotiation, frame handling and IANA subprotocol registration.
WebSocket.quote: This document specifies the WebSocket JMAP subprotocol for carrying JMAP API requests, responses, and optional push notifications through a WebSocket connection.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the handshake and authentication substrate for the WebSocket connection. The document defines nothing new about HTTP.
HTTP/2 Extended CONNECT is used to bootstrap WebSockets and is shown in an example. The document does not specify or extend HTTP/2.
TLS is required for wss:// connections, but the document only cites existing requirements and defines no new TLS behaviour.
JSON is the message encoding. The document does not define a JSON format in its own right.
Authentication happens in the handshake request and the document defers to RFC 8620 for scheme choice. It adds no new authentication scheme.

gaps.name: JMAP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no standalone JMAP tag. Only 'JMAP' under email (for mail and related data) exists, which does not fit a core, transport-level JMAP binding well. The email/JMAP tag is the closest and may be used instead.

RFC8888.title: RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Feedback for Congestion Control
RFC8888.summary: Defines a new RTCP transport-layer feedback packet (PT=205, FMT=11) carrying per-packet sequence, arrival time and ECN information to support sender-based RTP congestion control, plus its SDP "ccfb" signalling.

RTCP.why: The document specifies a new RTCP feedback message, its format, reporting rules and IANA FMT registration.
RTCP.quote: this memo specifies a common RTCP feedback packet format that can be used by Network-Assisted Dynamic Adaptation (NADA)

RTP congestion control.why: The purpose is to provide a generic feedback format for sender-based RTP congestion control algorithms such as NADA, SCReAM and GCC.
RTP congestion control.quote: This document describes an RTCP feedback message intended to enable congestion control for interactive real-time traffic using RTP.

SDP.why: A dedicated section defines a new SDP rtcp-fb parameter and its offer/answer behaviour.
SDP.quote: A new "ack" feedback parameter, "ccfb", is defined for use with the "a=rtcp-fb:" Session Description Protocol (SDP) extension

ECN.why: The packet carries per-packet ECN marks and a section covers how it interacts with ECN for RTP.
ECN.quote: the RTCP ECN Feedback Packet is not useful when ECN is used with the RTP Congestion Control Feedback Packet

rejected.why: RTP runs over UDP, which is only the substrate.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to authenticate RTCP.
RTCP is the more specific tag for this document.
Introduction mentions QoS only in passing; the document is about congestion control.

RFC8889.title: Multipoint Alternate-Marking Method for Passive and Hybrid Performance Monitoring
RFC8889.summary: Extends the Alternate-Marking passive/hybrid performance measurement method (RFC 8321) from point-to-point flows to multipoint-to-multipoint unicast flows, using network clustering for packet loss, delay and delay variation measurement.

performance measurement.why: The whole document defines multipoint packet loss, delay and delay variation metrics and methods for passive and hybrid performance monitoring.
performance measurement.quote: This document generalizes and expands this methodology to measure any kind of unicast flow whose packets can follow several different paths in the network

rejected.why: RFC 7011 is cited only for the flow definition; the document does not specify or extend IPFIX.
SDN controllers and orchestrators are discussed as a closed-loop use case, but this is not the subject of the document.
The document is a measurement methodology and leaves out the transport of counters and timestamps; telemetry is only mentioned in passing.
ECMP flows are noted as in scope and monitorable, but the document is not about ECMP.
Alternate Marking is a performance measurement method. The document does not frame it as an OAM mechanism.
VPN is only one example application in Section 10.

gaps.name: Alternate Marking
gaps.why: The document is about the Alternate-Marking and Multipoint Alternate-Marking methods, and the taxonomy has no tag for them. They sit closest to performance measurement.

RFC8890.title: The Internet is for End Users
RFC8890.summary: An IAB statement arguing that when end users' interests conflict with those of other parties, IETF decisions should favor end users, and suggesting ways the IETF can do this.

internet architecture.why: The document sets out an architectural principle for the Internet and the IETF's work: prioritize end users. It covers user-agent roles and architectures that favor users.
internet architecture.quote: when there is a conflict between the interests of end users of the Internet and other parties, IETF decisions should favor end users

rejected.why: It touches on how the IETF engages the community and deprioritizes process matters. Its main subject is the architectural principle of prioritizing end users, not the IETF's procedures.
It cites privacy and pervasive-surveillance RFCs only as existing guidance. It does not analyse privacy itself.
HTTP and the web user agent appear only as an example of a user-focused architecture.
IoT is mentioned briefly as a contrast case and is not a subject of the document.

RFC8891.title: GOST R 34.12-2015: Block Cipher "Magma"
RFC8891.summary: Informational RFC translating the GOST R 34.12-2015 64-bit block cipher "Magma" (32-round Feistel-like cipher with 256-bit key), giving its S-boxes, transformations, key schedule, encryption/decryption and test vectors.

GOST.why: The document specifies the Magma cipher from the Russian national GOST standard and relates it to GOST 28147-89 (RFC 5830), so it belongs on the GOST page.
GOST.quote: Russian Federal standard GOST R 34.12-2015 includes an updated version of the block cipher with a block length of n=64 bits and key length of k=256 bits

rejected.why: It is the parent of GOST, which already covers the subject, so the parent is not listed separately.
Magma is a different block cipher. AES is not mentioned in the body.
Magma is a 64-bit Feistel-style cipher like DES, but the document is not about DES or Triple-DES.

gaps.name: block ciphers
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no generic tag for block cipher algorithms or modes of operation. GOST is the only fitting tag, and it covers this document.

RFC8892.title: Guidelines and Registration Procedures for Interface Types and Tunnel Types
RFC8892.summary: Updates RFC 2863 by giving guidelines and registration procedures for IANA ifType and tunnelType registries, covering sub-layers and sub-types, available MIB/YANG formats, registration templates, and transmission number assignment.

MIB.why: The document governs the IANAifType-MIB and ifType/tunnelType values in the Interfaces Group MIB, and updates RFC 2863. Its guidance on sub-layers, sub-types and MIB formats is of interest to readers of MIB modules.
MIB.quote: The IANA IfType-MIB, which contains the list of interface type (ifType) values, was originally defined in [RFC1573] as a separate MIB module

IANA.why: The document defines registration policy, procedures, templates and expert review for IANA registries (ifType, tunnelType, transmission numbers).
IANA.quote: The IANA policy (using terms defined in [RFC8126]) for registration is Expert Review for both interface types and tunnel types.

YANG.why: A substantial part clarifies how the iana-if-type and iana-tunnel-type YANG modules relate to the registries, and that the guidance applies to YANG as well as MIB.
YANG.quote: the [IANAifType-MIB], [yang-if-type], and [yang-tunnel-type] MIB and YANG modules are merely additional formats in which the "Interface Types (ifType)" and "Tunnel Types (tunnelType)" registries are available.

rejected.why: Tunnel types are only registry values here. The document does not specify any tunnelling mechanism.
The MIB is the subject, but the document does not specify SNMP itself. MIB is the more specific fit.
Teredo is only an example of when to assign a new tunnelType value.
Ethernet ifTypes are mentioned only as an example of value proliferation.

RFC8893.title: Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Origin Validation for BGP Export
RFC8893.summary: RFC 8893 updates RFC 6811 to clarify that BGP speakers must perform RPKI route origin validation in egress policy using the effective origin AS after outbound modifications such as private AS removal and confederation handling.

RPKI.why: The document updates RFC 6811 route origin validation by specifying how it applies to egress policy. It is about RPKI-based origin validation, which makes RPKI the subject.
RPKI.quote: A validating BGP speaker MUST apply Route Origin Validation policy semantics (see Section 2 of [RFC6811] and Section 4 of [RFC8481]) after applying any egress configuration and policy.

rejected.why: BGP is the protocol where the validation policy is applied. The document is about RPKI origin validation in BGP egress policy, and RPKI is the more specific tag. It adds no new BGP protocol behaviour.
This is the parent of RPKI, so it is implied and not listed separately.

RFC8894.title: Simple Certificate Enrolment Protocol
RFC8894.summary: RFC 8894 specifies SCEP, a PKI certificate enrolment protocol that carries CMS-wrapped PKCS #10 requests over HTTP for CA certificate distribution, enrolment, renewal, polling, and certificate/CRL queries.

PKI.why: SCEP is a certificate management/enrolment protocol between PKI clients and CAs, so it belongs under PKI. No more specific child (CMP, EST, ACME) fits.
PKI.quote: SCEP), a PKI protocol that leverages existing technology by using Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS, formerly known as PKCS #7) and PKCS #10 over HTTP.

CMS.why: A substantial part of the document (Section 3) defines how CMS SignedData and EnvelopedData are layered and profiled into SCEP pkiMessages, with required attributes and restrictions.
CMS.quote: SCEP makes extensive use of CMS [RFC5652] and PKCS #10 [RFC2986].

media types.why: The document registers four grandfathered media types (application/x-x509-ca-cert, x-pki-message, etc.) with full templates.
media types.quote: IANA has registered four media types as defined in this document:

rejected.why: HTTP is only the transport for SCEP messages; the document does not extend HTTP itself.
Certificates are the objects being issued, but the document defines an enrolment protocol rather than a certificate profile.
Mentioned only to say HTTPS is unnecessary for SCEP.
SHA-1 and SHA-256 are used as algorithm choices; the document is not about the hash family.
AES128-CBC is a mandatory algorithm choice but not the subject.
IANA registries are created, but this is boilerplate-like and not the main subject.

RFC8895.title: Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) Incremental Updates Using Server-Sent Events (SSE)
RFC8895.summary: Extends the ALTO protocol with an SSE-based update stream service and a stream control service so servers can push full or incremental (JSON merge patch / JSON patch) updates of network maps, cost maps and endpoint properties to clients.

ALTO.why: The document extends ALTO with update stream and stream control services, new media types, and IRD announcements for them.
ALTO.quote: This document presents a mechanism to allow an ALTO server to push updates to ALTO clients

JSON.why: A substantial part of the document covers how JSON merge patch and JSON patch are applied to ALTO messages, their trade-offs, and when to choose each.
JSON.quote: The current design supports incremental changes using JSON merge patch [RFC7396] or JSON patch [RFC6902] to describe the changes of the resource.

rejected.why: HTTP/1.x is the substrate for the SSE stream and POST requests. The document defines nothing new about HTTP itself.
HTTP/2 is discussed only as background and as an alternative design that was not adopted.
The document registers two media types, but that is boilerplate IANA material and not the subject of the document.
SSE server push is the mechanism used here, but web push notification delivery is a different subject.

gaps.name: ALTO (Application-Layer Traffic Optimization)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an ALTO tech tag listed under applications, and I used it. Nothing covers Server-Sent Events as a distinct subject, though that is the push mechanism the document specifies.

RFC8896.title: Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) Cost Calendar
RFC8896.summary: Extends the ALTO protocol's Filtered Cost Map and Endpoint Cost services with Cost Calendars, arrays of cost values per time interval, with IRD capability attributes and response metadata so applications can choose when as well as where to connect.

ALTO.why: The whole document specifies an ALTO extension (Cost Calendar) to the IRD, Filtered Cost Map and Endpoint Cost Service.
ALTO.quote: This document is an extension to the base Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) protocol.

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding for ALTO messages; the document defines no JSON format of its own.
HTTP is the substrate (POST, Date header IMF-fixdate); nothing new is defined about HTTP.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations as a protection mechanism.
It uses the existing HTTP IMF-fixdate format for calendar-start-time and defines no new timestamp format.
Metrics such as owdelay are only fictitious examples; the document is not about measurement methods.

RFC8897.title: Requirements for Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Relying Parties
RFC8897.summary: Consolidates requirements from many RPKI RFCs for Relying Party software: fetching and caching repository objects, validating certificates, CRLs and signed objects, distributing validated cache to routers, and local control.

RPKI.why: The whole document is about RPKI relying party software requirements: TAL processing, certificate/CRL/ROA/manifest validation, and cache distribution to routers.
RPKI.quote: This document provides a single reference point for requirements for Relying Party (RP) software for use in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI).

rejected.why: RPKI resource certificates profile X.509, but the document only points to RFC 6487 for the profile and does not specify X.509 itself.
BGPsec router certificate validation is covered in one subsection, but the document is about RPKI RP requirements, not BGPsec path validation.
BGP is the consumer of validated RPKI data, not the subject of the document.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a way to protect cache delivery.
The Ghostbusters payload is a profiled vCard, but this is incidental and the document does not address vCard itself.

RFC8898.title: Third-Party Token-Based Authentication and Authorization for Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)
RFC8898.summary: Defines the "Bearer" HTTP-style authentication scheme for SIP, letting UACs obtain OAuth 2.0/OpenID Connect access tokens from a third-party authorization server to authenticate and register with SIP registrars, UASs and proxies, and updates RFC 3261 on handling multiple challenges.

SIP.why: The document extends SIP, updating RFC 3261 and specifying UAC, UAS, registrar and proxy behaviour and new WWW-Authenticate/Proxy-Authenticate parameters.
SIP.quote: This document defines the "Bearer" authentication scheme for SIP and a mechanism by which user authentication and SIP registration authorization is delegated to a third party

OAuth.why: The mechanism profiles OAuth 2.0 access tokens, refresh tokens, bearer token usage and introspection for SIP authorization.
OAuth.quote: using the OAuth 2.0 framework and OpenID Connect Core 1.0

HTTP authentication.why: It defines the Bearer challenge-response scheme in SIP's header-field framework, which is modelled on HTTP authentication, including the syntax in Section 4.
HTTP authentication.quote: This document defines the "Bearer" authentication scheme for SIP

rejected.why: JWTs are used as a token format, and encrypted JWTs are required for protecting tokens. The document does not specify JWT itself.
TLS is only discussed as hop-by-hop protection that is insufficient for access tokens in SIP. It is a substrate and not the subject.
The single sign-on aspect is delivered through OAuth/OpenID Connect, and the OAuth tag covers it more specifically.
HTTP is referenced only for the https URI syntax and for the introspection call, not as a subject of the document.
The more specific OAuth and SIP tags cover the authentication content.

gaps.name: OpenID Connect
gaps.why: The document uses OpenID Connect Core 1.0 and ID tokens for delegated user authentication, but the taxonomy has no OpenID Connect tag. OAuth is the closest fit.

RFC8899.title: Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery for Datagram Transports
RFC8899.summary: Specifies DPLPMTUD, a robust packetization-layer Path MTU discovery method for datagram transports, with a state machine, probing and black-hole detection, and protocol-specific details for UDP applications, SCTP (including SCTP/UDP and SCTP/DTLS) and QUIC; it updates RFCs 4821, 4960, 6951, 8085 and 8261.

PMTUD.why: x
PMTUD.quote: This document specifies Datagram Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (DPLPMTUD).

RFC8900.title: IP Fragmentation Considered Fragile
RFC8900.summary: BCP describing how IP fragmentation makes Internet communication fragile (PMTUD black holes, middlebox, ECMP, security issues), proposing alternatives and giving recommendations to developers and operators.

PMTUD.why: Path MTU discovery, PLPMTUD and PTB black-holing are central to the fragility analysis and the recommendations (operators must ensure PMTUD works).
PMTUD.quote: PMTUD relies on the network's ability to deliver ICMP PTB messages to the source node. If the network cannot deliver ICMP PTB messages to the source node, PMTUD fails.

IPv6.why: The document details IPv6 fragmentation procedures, the Fragment header, and applications relying on IPv6 fragmentation, which IPv6 readers would want.
IPv6.quote: IPv6 packet may be fragmented only at the source node.

IPv4.why: Covers IPv4 fragmentation procedures, DF bit and reassembly errors at high data rates.
IPv4.quote: IPv4 fragmentation is not sufficiently robust for use under some conditions in today's Internet.

ECMP.why: A dedicated section and recommendation (6.4) address hash inputs for ECMP/LAG load balancing with fragments.
ECMP.quote: IP fragmentation causes problems for Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP), Link Aggregate Groups (LAG), and other stateless load-distribution technologies.

rejected.why: DNS is discussed as an application relying on fragmentation, but the document is not about DNS itself.
NAT and virtual reassembly are one of several middlebox problems, not a main subject.
Stateless firewalls are discussed in a short section as one fragility example only.
ICMP PTB is the mechanism for PMTUD, but the document is about fragmentation/PMTU rather than specifying ICMP.
UDP usage guidance is cited, but UDP is not the subject.
Packet-in-packet encapsulation is briefly mentioned with no new recommendations.

gaps.name: IP fragmentation
gaps.why: The core subject, IP fragmentation and reassembly, has no dedicated tag; PMTUD, IPv4 and IPv6 are the closest approximations.

RFC8901.title: Multi-Signer DNSSEC Models
RFC8901.summary: Informational document describing two multi-signer DNSSEC deployment models where multiple DNS providers independently sign the same zone, with key-management, rollover, algorithm, and authenticated-denial considerations.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document is about DNSSEC deployment with multiple signers: KSK/ZSK models, DNSKEY/DS RRset management, key rollovers, NSEC/NSEC3 denial, and CDS/CDNSKEY.
DNSSEC.quote: Deploying DNSSEC in such an environment may present some challenges, depending on the configuration and feature set in use.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific tag and implies DNS; the document is not about general DNS protocol behaviour.
DNS UPDATE is only mentioned as a possible key-management mechanism, not specified or profiled.
EPP is mentioned only as an alternative mechanism that could partly provide the needed API functions.
DNS over TLS appears only in a passing remark about response size and future transports.
DNS over HTTPS appears only in a passing remark about response size and future transports.
Provider REST/HTTPS APIs are the substrate for key management, but the document specifies functional requirements, not HTTP API conventions.

RFC8902.title: TLS Authentication Using Intelligent Transport System (ITS) Certificates
RFC8902.summary: Defines an experimental TLS 1.3 extension adding a new certificate type (1609Dot2) so IEEE 1609.2/ETSI ITS vehicular certificates can authenticate TLS clients and servers, including a modified CertificateVerify.

TLS.why: The document extends TLS by defining a new certificate type for the certificate_type extensions and a changed CertificateVerify, which is a new TLS extension use.
TLS.quote: This document defines a new certificate type, 1609Dot2, for usage with TLS 1.3.

vehicular networking.why: The certificates come from vehicular V2X/ITS standards (IEEE 1609.2, ETSI), and the document is motivated by and tailored to those deployments.
vehicular networking.quote: These standards specify secure communications in vehicular environments.

X.509.why: The document offers an alternative to X.509 certificates for TLS authentication and covers mixed use of ITS and X.509 certificates, so readers of certificate formats may want it. This is a weaker fit than TLS.
X.509.quote: Systems using this Experimental approach are segregated from systems using standard TLS by the use of a new certificate type value

rejected.why: The document mentions the ITS PKI, but it only specifies how the end-entity certificate is used in TLS. It does not define the PKI.
The document uses OER encoding for the Ieee1609Dot2Data structure, but only as an encoding it relies on.
ECC appears only in the Security Considerations, as a statement of algorithm strength.
The document does not specify DTLS. It only references RFC 7250, which covers both TLS and DTLS.
The generic authentication topic is covered by the more specific TLS tag.

gaps.name: IEEE 1609.2 / ITS certificates
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for ITS or V2X security certificate formats. The nearest fit is vehicular networking.

RFC8903.title: Use Cases for DDoS Open Threat Signaling
RFC8903.summary: RFC 8903 is an informational document giving sample use cases (upstream transit provider mitigation, third-party mitigation service, and orchestration) that describe how DOTS clients and servers interact for DDoS mitigation signaling.

DOTS.why: The whole document describes DOTS use cases, the roles of DOTS clients and servers, and typical information exchanged. It informed the DOTS requirements and protocol design.
DOTS.quote: This document presents sample use cases that describe the interactions expected between the DOTS components as well as DOTS messaging exchanges.

rejected.why: This is the parent of DOTS, so it is implied by the DOTS tag and not listed separately.
BGP prefix announcement is mentioned only as one way to steer traffic, and the document says traffic-steering mechanisms are out of scope.
GRE is mentioned only as an example of re-injecting scrubbed traffic, and that is out of scope.
DNS redirection is mentioned in passing as a traffic-steering option, and the document is not about DNS.
Multihoming gets a short note that points to another draft, and it is not a substantial part of this document.

RFC8904.title: DNS Whitelist (DNSWL) Email Authentication Method Extension
RFC8904.summary: Describes a "dnswl" email authentication method for Authentication-Results (RFC 8601) based on looking up the sender IP in a DNS whitelist, defining its results and properties and registering them with IANA.

DNSBL.why: The whole document concerns DNSWL lookups per RFC 5782, including A/TXT response handling, quota signalling and query conventions. DNSBL covers DNS-based lists including whitelists.
DNSBL.quote: The method consists of looking up the sender's IP address in a DNS whitelist.

email authentication.why: It defines a new method, ptype and results for the Authentication-Results header field, registered in the Email Authentication Parameters registry. Readers of email authentication would want it.
email authentication.quote: This document describes an email authentication method compliant with RFC 8601.

rejected.why: Defines a dns.sec property reporting validation status, but DNSSEC is only used as a mechanism, not specified or extended.
SPF appears in the introduction and example as a check the DNSWL result can override, but is not the subject.
Mentioned for comparison and in the example and Appendix C only.
DNS is the substrate for the lookups. No new DNS record types or behaviour are defined beyond the DNSBL conventions.
The Authentication-Results header field is the carrier, defined in RFC 8601. This document only adds a method to it.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here and not the main subject.

gaps.name: Authentication-Results header field
gaps.why: RFC 8601 and its method registrations have no dedicated taxonomy tag. The closest are the email authentication topic and message format.

RFC8905.title: The 'payto' URI Scheme for Payments
RFC8905.summary: Defines the 'payto' URI scheme for designating payment targets (bank accounts, Bitcoin, UPI, ILP, etc.), its generic options, and an initial registry of payment target types.

URI.why: The document specifies a new URI scheme, including its syntax, semantics, options and IANA scheme registration, so URI readers would expect it.
URI.quote: This document defines the 'payto' Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) [RFC3986] scheme for designating transfer form data for payments.

rejected.why: The scheme is for payment target identification, not an e-commerce or payment protocol. It excludes invoices and processing instructions. The URI tag is the better fit.
The registry of payment target types is run by GANA, not IANA. The IANA section only updates the URI scheme registration, which is boilerplate.
ABNF is only the notation used to give the syntax.
The internationalization section is short and mostly says language tagging is out of scope.

gaps.name: payments / payment target types
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for payment systems or payment identifiers such as IBAN, ACH, UPI, Bitcoin and ILP. The only nearby tag is e-commerce, which is a poor fit.

RFC8906.title: A Common Operational Problem in DNS Servers: Failure to Communicate
RFC8906.summary: BCP describing common DNS server failures to respond correctly to basic, unknown-type, flag, opcode, TCP and EDNS queries, with dig-based test procedures and remediation guidance for operators.

EDNS.why: Much of the document covers EDNS misbehaviour (versions, options, flags, DO bit, truncation) and a dedicated Extended DNS test suite.
EDNS.quote: Some servers respond correctly to EDNS version 0 queries but fail to respond to EDNS queries with version numbers that are higher than zero.

DNS.why: The document is about correct DNS server response behaviour, response codes, TCP support and operational testing and remediation for nameservers.
DNS.quote: The DNS is a query/response protocol.  Failing to respond to queries, or responding incorrectly, causes both immediate operational problems

rejected.why: DO bit, AD and CD flag handling are tested, but only as response-structure conformance, not DNSSEC signing or validation.
TCP support for DNS queries is checked, but the document is not about TCP itself.
Mentioned only as an example consequence of unknown-type mishandling.
Firewall and scrubbing-service interaction is discussed, but the document is about DNS conformance, not general operational security.
The firewall section is a small part of the document, which is about DNS server behaviour.

RFC8907.title: The Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+) Protocol
RFC8907.summary: Informational specification of the TACACS+ protocol for Device Administration, covering packet format, MD5-based obfuscation, authentication, authorization, accounting, argument-value pairs, privilege levels and security best practices.

TACACS+.why: The whole document specifies the TACACS+ protocol: packet header and bodies, authentication, authorization, accounting, and security best practices.
TACACS+.quote: This document describes the Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+) protocol, which is widely deployed today to provide Device Administration

rejected.why: TACACS+ is a child of AAA and is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
RADIUS is only named as one of the authen_method values a client may report. TACACS+ plays no part in that exchange.
Kerberos is only listed as an authen_method value. The document does not specify it.
TCP is only the transport (server port 49). The document adds no TCP extension. The single-connection multiplexing is a TACACS+ feature.
MD5 is used to generate the obfuscation pad. The document is not about MD5, which is only the mechanism used.
PAP, CHAP and MS-CHAP are carried as authen_type values but are defined elsewhere. PPP is not the subject here.

RFC8908.title: Captive Portal API
RFC8908.summary: Defines an HTTP/JSON API (application/captive+json) by which clients query a Captive Portal server for captivity state, user portal URL, and session limits, and registers the media type and a keys registry.

captive portal.why: The whole document specifies the client-facing API of a captive portal system, which is the subject of the captive portal tag.
captive portal.quote: This document describes an HTTP API that allows clients to interact with a Captive Portal system.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the substrate for the API. The document defines no new HTTP semantics.
JSON is only the encoding. The document defines a JSON-based format, but it is not about JSON itself.
TLS is required for the connection, but the document adds nothing new about TLS.
The media type registration is IANA boilerplate for the API format, not the main subject.
OCSP stapling is only mentioned for revocation checking of the server certificate.
The new registry is an incidental part of defining the API and does not make the document about IANA.

RFC8909.title: Registry Data Escrow Specification
RFC8909.summary: Specifies an XML format for Registry Data Escrow deposits (full, differential, incremental) submitted by domain name registries to escrow agents, designed to be object-agnostic.

domain registration.why: The document defines escrow deposits for domain registry and registrar data, which is registry operations. No more specific child (EPP, RDAP, WHOIS) fits.
domain registration.quote: This document specifies the format and contents of data escrow deposits targeted primarily for domain name registries.

XML.why: The deposit format is defined as an XML Schema with an extensible substitution-group design and a registered XML namespace and schema, so readers of XML-based formats would want it.
XML.quote: The format for data escrow deposits is specified using version 1.0 of the Extensible Markup Language (XML)

rejected.why: Domain names are the escrowed objects, but the document does not specify DNS protocol or operations.
EPP is not discussed; the escrowed object specifications are separate documents.
Mentioned only as an example of private keys not to be escrowed.
Only referenced in a Security Considerations note recommending RFC 7525.
Uses RFC 3339 timestamps but only as a dependency, not defining anything new.
The IANA section only registers the namespace and schema, which is boilerplate.

gaps.name: Registry Data Escrow (RDE)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for registry data escrow or backup deposit formats. The closest tag, domain registration, covers it only broadly.

RFC8910.title: Captive-Portal Identification in DHCP and Router Advertisements (RAs)
RFC8910.summary: Defines DHCPv4, DHCPv6 and IPv6 RA options that tell clients they are behind a captive portal and give the URI of the captive portal API endpoint, replacing RFC 7710 and moving the DHCPv4 code point from 160 to 114.

captive portal.why: The whole document is about conveying captive portal presence and API URI to clients, which is what the captive portal page covers.
captive portal.quote: inform clients that they are behind some sort of captive portal enforcement device, and that they will need to satisfy the Captive Portal conditions

DHCP.why: Defines a new DHCPv4 option (code 114) and changes the code point from 160, so DHCP readers need it.
DHCP.quote: The format of the IPv4 Captive-Portal DHCP option is shown below.

DHCPv6.why: Specifies the DHCPv6 Captive-Portal option format.
DHCPv6.quote: The Captive-Portal DHCPv6 Option (103) (two octets).

neighbor discovery.why: Defines a new IPv6 ND Router Advertisement option (type 37).
neighbor discovery.quote: This section describes the Captive-Portal Router Advertisement option.

rejected.why: The unrestricted URN is registered in IANA, but it is a minor element and not a new URN namespace.
Content negotiation and caching behaviour for the API endpoint are mentioned, but HTTP is only the substrate.
URIs are just the payload of the options; the document does not specify URI syntax or schemes.
RA use is covered by the neighbor discovery tag; the document is not about IPv6 in general.
IANA Considerations are boilerplate here and do not make the document about IANA.

RFC8911.title: Registry for Performance Metrics
RFC8911.summary: Defines the format, columns, and management processes of the IANA Performance Metrics Registry, plus guidelines for requesters and reviewers of Registered Performance Metrics.

performance measurement.why: The whole document defines a registry of performance metrics, their naming, parameters, measurement methods, outputs and review criteria. This is the performance measurement topic.
performance measurement.quote: This document defines the format for the IANA Registry of Performance Metrics.

IANA.why: A large part of the document sets registry procedures: Specification Required policy, expert review, revision and deprecation, and the registry group and name-element registries.
IANA.quote: Requests to add Registered Performance Metrics in the Performance Metrics Registry SHALL be submitted to IANA, which forwards the request to a designated group of experts

rejected.why: LMAP is the main intended user of the registry and is discussed as motivation. The document does not specify or extend LMAP, so it is not tagged.
IPFIX and PSAMP are only mentioned as filter and sampling mechanisms that metric entries may reference.
RTCP XR appears only as an example source of metrics and is not specified here.
DNS response time appears only as an example metric type.
BMWG is named as a source of metrics, but the document is about a registry rather than benchmarking methodology.

RFC8912.title: Initial Performance Metrics Registry Entries
RFC8912.summary: Defines the initial entries of the IANA Performance Metrics Registry: UDP/ICMP/TCP round-trip and one-way delay and loss, packet delay variation, and DNS response latency/loss metrics, with fixed parameters, methods and outputs.

performance measurement.why: The whole document specifies active and passive network performance metrics (delay, loss, PDV) and their measurement methods.
performance measurement.quote: This memo defines the set of initial entries for the IANA Registry of Performance Metrics.

IANA.why: The document's purpose is populating a new IANA registry, so readers of IANA registries would want it.
IANA.quote: IANA has populated the Performance Metrics Registry defined in [RFC8911] with the values defined in Sections 4 through 10.

rejected.why: DNS is only the probe traffic for one pair of metrics (response latency/loss); the document does not specify DNS itself.
TCP headers are passively observed to infer RTT and loss; TCP is not extended or specified.
Not a taxonomy tag; TWAMP-Test packet format is merely the payload used in the one-way metrics (TWAMP is just a reference).
ICMP Echo is only the probe packet for the ICMP metrics; the protocol is not specified or extended.
YANG decimal64/uint types are only referenced for value formats, not the subject.
Only referenced for Observation Point terminology.

gaps.name: IPPM (IP Performance Metrics) metric definitions
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only the generic performance measurement topic; no specific tag for IPPM metrics such as one-way/round-trip delay and loss.

RFC8913.title: Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP) YANG Data Model
RFC8913.summary: Defines a YANG data model (ietf-twamp), with UML diagrams and examples, for configuring and monitoring TWAMP Control-Client, Server, Session-Sender and Session-Reflector entities.

TWAMP.why: The model covers TWAMP's four logical entities, modes and sessions.
TWAMP.quote: This document specifies a data model for client and server implementations of the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP).

YANG.why: The main deliverable is a YANG module with tree diagram and examples.
YANG.quote: formally specifies it using the YANG data modeling language (RFC 7950). The data model is compliant with the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA).

rejected.why: Only the configuration transport; the model is stated to be orthogonal to the protocol used.
Mentioned as an alternative transport; the document does not specify it.
The parent of TWAMP is implied by the TWAMP tag. The document only references the Performance Metrics Registry.
XML is used only for the example instances.
Test packets run over UDP, which is only the substrate.
Control connections run over TCP, which is only the substrate.

RFC8914.title: Extended DNS Errors
RFC8914.summary: Defines the Extended DNS Error (EDE) EDNS0 option (code 15) and an IANA registry of INFO-CODEs for conveying extra information about DNS and DNSSEC failures alongside RCODEs.

EDNS.why: The document defines a new EDNS(0) option with its wire format, processing rules and a registry of codes, so it belongs under EDNS.
EDNS.quote: This document uses an Extended Mechanism for DNS (EDNS0) [RFC6891] option to include Extended DNS Error (EDE) information in DNS messages.
EDNS.section: 2. Extended DNS Error EDNS0 Option Format

DNSSEC.why: Many of the defined error codes (1, 2, 5-12) report DNSSEC validation failures, and DNSSEC failure diagnosis is a stated motivation.
DNSSEC.quote: The resolver attempted to perform DNSSEC validation, but a DNSKEY RRset contained only unsupported DNSSEC algorithms.
DNSSEC.section: 4.2. Extended DNS Error Code 1 - Unsupported DNSKEY Algorithm

rejected.why: The parent tag is implied by EDNS and DNSSEC, so it is not listed separately.
DoH is only mentioned in Security Considerations as a way to authenticate EDE content, so it is not a subject of the document.
The document does not address encrypted DNS transport. Its brief privacy remark about leaking blocklist status is minor.
The registry creation is boilerplate for the new option and does not make the document about IANA stewardship.
UTF-8 is only the encoding of the EXTRA-TEXT field and is not a subject of the document.

RFC8915.title: Network Time Security for the Network Time Protocol
RFC8915.summary: Specifies Network Time Security (NTS), which uses a TLS-based key establishment protocol (NTS-KE) and AEAD-protected NTP extension fields with cookies to secure NTP client-server mode.

NTP.why: The document defines NTS extension fields for NTPv4 and new NTP registry entries (KoD code, extension field types), so it is about securing NTP.
NTP.quote: a mechanism for using Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) to provide cryptographic security for the client-server mode of the Network Time Protocol (NTP)

rejected.why: TLS is the substrate for NTS-KE. The document uses a profile, ALPN and exporters, but does not define a new TLS extension, so it is not about TLS.
This is the parent of NTP and is implied by the NTP tag.
X.509 certificate verification is only discussed as a consideration for clients whose clocks are unset, so PKI is not the subject.
AEAD and HKDF are used as building blocks and are not themselves specified.
Amplification avoidance is a design goal of the protocol, but the document is not about DDoS mitigation in general.
The document is about a specific mechanism, NTS, and no more general security tag is needed beyond the NTP tag.

RFC8916.title: A YANG Data Model for the Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP)
RFC8916.summary: Defines the ietf-msdp YANG module for configuring and monitoring Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP) operations, including peers, SA filters, SA cache state, statistics and clear actions.

MSDP.why: The document models MSDP configuration, operational state, SA cache and peer statistics, so readers of MSDP would want it.
MSDP.quote: This document defines a YANG data model that can be used to configure and manage MSDP protocol operations.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a new YANG module (ietf-msdp) with tree diagrams, features, and actions, so it belongs on the YANG page.
