YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model for the configuration and management of Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP) protocol operations.

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only mentioned as access protocols in Security Considerations. The document doesn't specify or extend them.
PIM-SM is referenced only as context for RP and RPF terms. The model for PIM is explicitly out of scope.
MSDP runs over TCP, and the model configures the TCP connection source and MD5 authentication. This is substrate use, not a new TCP specification.
BGP is referenced only for peer-as verification semantics. The model does not cover BGP.
JSON is used only for the example data trees in the appendix.

RFC8917.title: The LoST-Validation Straightforward-Naming Authority PoinTeR (S-NAPTR) Application Service Tag
RFC8917.summary: Registers the 'LoST-Validation' S-NAPTR application service tag and describes how LoST clients use it, via NAPTR DNS records, to discover servers designated for location validation, updating RFC 5222.

LoST.why: The document extends LoST server discovery with a new service tag for validation servers and updates RFC 5222.
LoST.quote: This tag can appear in a Naming Authority Pointer (NAPTR) Domain Name System (DNS) record to assist clients of the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) Protocol

service discovery.why: The core content is a U-NAPTR/DDDS-based discovery procedure for finding the right LoST server, with fallback rules. No S-NAPTR/DDDS tag exists, so the general service discovery tag fits.
service discovery.quote: An entity needing to perform location validation using LoST performs the discovery procedure as described in [RFC5222], except that the 'LoST- Validation' service tag is used

rejected.why: NAPTR records are only the mechanism for discovery. The document defines a service tag and does not specify DNS protocol behaviour.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a recommendation, not the subject.
Context is emergency services, but the LoST tag is more specific and sits under it, so the parent is implied.
The registry addition is routine IANA action for the tag, not guidance on IANA registries.
HTTP/HTTPS URL schemes are mentioned only in passing.

gaps.name: S-NAPTR / U-NAPTR / DDDS application service tags
gaps.why: The document is about a tag in the S-NAPTR registry and the DDDS discovery procedure. The taxonomy has no tag for NAPTR/DDDS, so service discovery is the closest fit.

RFC8918.title: Invalid TLV Handling in IS-IS
RFC8918.summary: Clarifies that IS-IS PDUs containing disallowed or invalid TLVs/sub-TLVs must not be rejected (TLVs ignored), with special handling for LSP purges, and corrects the POI TLV registry entry, updating RFCs 5305 and 6232.

IS-IS.why: The whole document specifies correct IS-IS behavior for handling invalid or disallowed TLVs, updates IS-IS RFCs, and corrects an IS-IS registry entry.
IS-IS.quote: TLVs in a PDU (other than LSP purges) that are disallowed MUST be ignored and MUST NOT cause the PDU itself to be rejected by the receiving IS.

rejected.why: Purge authentication is discussed only as background for purge handling. The document makes no security changes.
The IANA actions are minor boilerplate: a reference and a POI registry entry correction. The document is not about IANA guidance.
Not a taxonomy tag. TLV encoding is the substrate for IS-IS, and the document is about IS-IS handling of it.

RFC8919.title: IS-IS Application-Specific Link Attributes
RFC8919.summary: Defines IS-IS Application-Specific Link Attributes (ASLA) sub-TLV and an Application-Specific SRLG TLV, with application identifier bit masks, so RSVP-TE, SR Policy and LFA can use distinct or shared link attribute values, plus migration guidance.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with a new sub-TLV (type 16) and a new TLV (238) for application-specific link attributes. It also gives deployment and migration rules for IS-IS routers.
IS-IS.quote: This document introduces new link attribute advertisements that address both of these shortcomings.

traffic engineering.why: The attributes being made application-specific are TE link attributes: bandwidth, admin groups, TE metrics and SRLGs. Their use by RSVP-TE and other TE applications is the document's core concern.
traffic engineering.quote: Advertisement of link attributes by the Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) protocol in support of traffic engineering (TE) was introduced by [RFC5305]

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is one of the applications identified by a bit in the mask. The document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE signalling.
SR Policy is only an application consuming the attributes. The document does not define segment routing.
LFA is only an application identified by a bit. The document does not specify fast reroute.
The IANA registries it creates are boilerplate for the protocol extension, not the document's subject.

RFC8920.title: OSPF Application-Specific Link Attributes
RFC8920.summary: Defines the Application-Specific Link Attributes (ASLA) sub-TLV for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 so that link attributes originally defined for RSVP-TE can be advertised per application (RSVP-TE, SR Policy, LFA), with deployment and migration guidance.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 with a new ASLA sub-TLV in the Extended Link Opaque LSA and E-Router-LSA.
OSPF.quote: This document introduces new link attribute advertisements in OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 that address both of these shortcomings.

OSPFv3.why: A substantial part of the document specifies OSPFv3 code points and encodings, including the E-Router-LSA and the IPv6 interface address sub-TLVs.
OSPFv3.quote: The ASLA sub-TLV is a sub-TLV of the OSPFv2 Extended Link TLV [RFC7684] and OSPFv3 Router-Link TLV [RFC8362].

traffic engineering.why: The attributes being re-advertised are TE link attributes (SRLG, TE metric, delay, bandwidth, admin group) shared among TE applications.
traffic engineering.quote: Existing traffic-engineering-related link attribute advertisements have been defined and are used in RSVP-TE deployments.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is one of the applications whose link attributes are discussed, but the document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE signalling.
SR Policy is named only as an application using the link attributes. The document does not define segment routing.
LFA is an example application that uses the attributes. The document does not specify fast reroute mechanisms.
The companion IS-IS document (RFC 8919) is referenced for the application bit registry, but this document is about OSPF.

RFC8921.title: Dynamic Service Negotiation: The Connectivity Provisioning Negotiation Protocol (CPNP)
RFC8921.summary: Defines CPNP, a generic client/server protocol (default over DTLS/UDP) for dynamically negotiating service parameters such as connectivity provisioning, with quotation/offer/accept messages, state machines and timers.

QoS.why: The negotiated CPP clauses cover QoS guarantees, capacity and availability, and the protocol is a service/SLA negotiation signalling mechanism. This is the nearest taxonomy fit for the connectivity-provisioning negotiation theme, though a loose one.
QoS.quote: CPNP uses the CPP template to encode connectivity provisioning clauses that are subject to negotiation.

network management.why: The document specifies an automated Customer-Provider service provisioning and order-management protocol, which falls under network operations and management. Its server logging and order-handling guidelines also sit here.
network management.quote: CPNP is a tool that introduces automation to the service negotiation and activation procedures, thus fostering the overall service provisioning process.

rejected.why: DTLS is only the default secure transport and is not specified or extended here.
NETCONF is named only as a way to provision the network after negotiation, which is out of scope.
RBNF is only the notation used to define the messages.
COPS-SLS and COPS-PR are mentioned only as prior proposals and are not specified here.
YANG models for L3VPN and L2VPN appear only as use-case context.
VPN services are one example use case, not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Service negotiation / SLA negotiation protocol
gaps.why: The document is about dynamic Customer-Provider service negotiation (the quotation/offer/accept model), and the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC8922.title: A Survey of the Interaction between Security Protocols and Transport Services
RFC8922.summary: Informational survey of security protocols (TLS, DTLS, SRTP, QUIC, gQUIC, tcpcrypt, MinimaLT, CurveCP, IPsec, WireGuard, OpenVPN) and their interfaces to transports and applications, to support Transport Services (TAPS) work.

TAPS.why: The survey exists to inform the Transport Services architecture and API, identifying the security-protocol interfaces a Transport Services system must expose.
TAPS.quote: Its goal is to supplement efforts to define and catalog Transport Services by describing the interfaces required to add security protocols.

TLS.why: TLS and DTLS are surveyed as the generic application payload security protocols, with their transport dependencies and interfaces analysed.
TLS.quote: TLS (Transport Layer Security) [RFC8446] is a common protocol used to establish a secure session between two endpoints.

IPsec.why: IPsec is one of the surveyed packet security protocols and appears in the interface comparison.
IPsec.quote: IKEv2 [RFC7296] and ESP [RFC4303] together form the modern IPsec protocol suite that encrypts and authenticates IP packets

QUIC.why: IETF QUIC and gQUIC are surveyed as transport-layer security protocols combining transport and security.
QUIC.quote: QUIC is a new standards-track transport protocol that runs over UDP, loosely based on Google's original proprietary gQUIC protocol

tcpcrypt.why: tcpcrypt is surveyed, including its dependency on TCP-ENO.
tcpcrypt.quote: Tcpcrypt [RFC8548] is a lightweight extension to the TCP protocol for opportunistic encryption.

SRTP.why: SRTP with DTLS-SRTP and ZRTP is surveyed as the application-specific security protocol.
SRTP.quote: Secure RTP (SRTP) is a profile for RTP that provides confidentiality, message authentication, and replay protection

rejected.why: Covered in a brief subsection, but the parent TLS tag adequately represents the (D)TLS survey content.
The more specific protocol tags apply, so the parent topic is implied.
TAPS and QUIC/tcpcrypt tags already sit under this topic.
UDP is only the substrate beneath several surveyed protocols, not the document's subject.
TCP is the substrate for TLS and tcpcrypt; only the tcpcrypt dependency is discussed.
WireGuard and OpenVPN are mentioned as VPN protocols, but this is not provider-provisioned VPN content.

gaps.name: WireGuard / OpenVPN / MinimaLT / CurveCP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tags for these non-IETF security protocols, which the survey describes and compares.

RFC8923.title: A Minimal Set of Transport Services for End Systems
RFC8923.summary: Informational TAPS document that derives and recommends a minimal set of transport features (from the RFC 8303 superset) that end systems and transport systems should expose to applications, independent of TCP/UDP/SCTP.

TAPS.why: The document defines the minimal set of transport features for a transport system, input to the TAPS API. This is exactly the Transport Services architecture subject.
TAPS.quote: This document recommends a minimal set of Transport Services offered by end systems and gives guidance on choosing among the available mechanisms and protocols.

rejected.why: SCTP features are analysed as a source of transport features, but the document does not specify or extend SCTP.
TCP is the baseline for one-sided implementation of the minimal set, but the document is not about TCP itself.
UDP and UDP-Lite are surveyed as sources of features and fallbacks. The document does not specify them.
LEDBAT appears only as one feature in the list (capacity profile), so it is not a subject of the document.
The Berkeley sockets API is mentioned only as a comparison point, and this document is not about sockets API extensions.
MPTCP appears only through the 'Disable MPTCP' feature.

RFC8924.title: Service Function Chaining (SFC) Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) Framework
RFC8924.summary: Informational framework for OAM of Service Function Chaining, defining a layering model, OAM components (SF, SFC, classifier), functions, gap analysis, and candidate tools.

SFC.why: The whole document is an OAM framework for service function chaining, covering SFs, SFFs, classifiers, SFPs and the NSH O bit.
SFC.quote: This document provides a reference framework for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) [RFC6291] of SFC.

OAM.why: It defines connectivity, continuity, trace and performance-measurement OAM functions and does a gap analysis of OAM tools. Readers of the OAM subject would want it.
OAM.quote: SFC OAM messages should be encapsulated with the necessary SFC header and with OAM markings when testing the SFC component.

rejected.why: BFD and S-BFD are only candidate tools discussed in one short subsection, not specified or extended here.
ICMP is only a candidate connectivity tool in Section 7.1, not the subject.
Performance measurement is one function among several. OWAMP and TWAMP are only mentioned as existing tools.
NETCONF appears only in the manageability table as an existing mechanism.
Overlay layers are described only as part of the layering model. VXLAN is a mere example.

RFC8925.title: IPv6-Only Preferred Option for DHCPv4
RFC8925.summary: Defines DHCPv4 option 108 (IPv6-Only Preferred) letting IPv6-only-capable hosts forgo IPv4 addresses on NAT64-enabled IPv6-mostly networks, with client/server behavior and an update to RFC 2563.

DHCP.why: The document defines a new DHCPv4 option, specifies client and server behavior, and updates RFC 2563 (Auto-Configure option). DHCPv4 is the main subject.
DHCP.quote: This document specifies a DHCPv4 option to indicate that a host supports an IPv6-only mode and is willing to forgo obtaining an IPv4 address

IPv6 transition.why: The option exists to enable incremental IPv6-only deployment with NAT64/464XLAT. It has a dedicated section on transition technology considerations. NAT64 is only assumed, not specified, so the parent topic fits better than a child tag.
IPv6 transition.quote: IPv6-mostly (or IPv4-on-demand) segments where IPv6-only hosts coexist with legacy dual-stack devices.

rejected.why: NAT64 is assumed as the network-provided translation service, but the document does not specify or extend it.
464XLAT is only mentioned as one way a host can be IPv6-only capable, not specified here.
DNS64 is mentioned only in passing as part of the network's IPv6-only service.
The option is DHCPv4-only; DHCPv6 is not addressed.
The document concerns IPv4 address configuration via DHCPv4 and avoiding IPv4 addresses, but IPv4 itself is not the subject. DHCP is the better fit.

RFC8926.title: Geneve: Generic Network Virtualization Encapsulation
RFC8926.summary: RFC 8926 specifies Geneve, a UDP-based, extensible TLV-option tunnel encapsulation for data-center network virtualization overlays, including header format, options processing, deployment and security guidance.

Geneve.why: The document defines the Geneve encapsulation protocol, its header, options and deployment considerations.
Geneve.quote: This document describes Geneve, an encapsulation protocol designed to recognize and accommodate these changing capabilities and needs.

rejected.why: Mentioned as a predecessor and transition peer, but not specified or profiled here.
Only referenced as a prior encapsulation; not the subject.
Substrate transport for Geneve; the document does not define new UDP behaviour beyond using it, though it covers checksum use.
Recommended only as an external security mechanism in Security Considerations.
Motivates source-port entropy but ECMP itself is not the subject.
Parent of Geneve, implied by the Geneve tag.

RFC8927.title: JSON Type Definition
RFC8927.summary: Experimental Independent Submission defining JSON Type Definition (JTD), a JSON-based schema language for describing JSON message shape, enabling code generation and portable validation with standardized error indicators.

JSON.why: The document specifies a schema format for JSON documents, with syntax, validation semantics and error indicators. It is a JSON-based format and a JSON schema language, so JSON readers would look for it.
JSON.quote: This document describes a schema language for JSON [RFC8259] called JSON Type Definition (JTD).

rejected.why: CDDL is only used to describe JTD's syntax and in a comparison appendix. The document does not specify or extend CDDL.
CDDL's CBOR side is not relevant. JTD is JSON-only.
The timestamp type simply refers to RFC 3339. The document does not define anything new about date-time formats.
The document has no media type registration and no IANA actions.

gaps.name: JSON schema language / data definition languages
gaps.why: JTD is a schema and validation language for JSON. The taxonomy has no tag for schema languages beyond JSON itself and CDDL, which is specific to the CBOR/JSON tags.

RFC8928.title: Address-Protected Neighbor Discovery for Low-Power and Lossy Networks
RFC8928.summary: Specifies Address-Protected Neighbor Discovery (AP-ND), extending 6LoWPAN ND registration (RFC 8505) with a Crypto-ID in the ROVR field, new CIPO and NDP Signature options, and ECC signature proof of address ownership in LLNs.

6LoWPAN.why: The document extends 6LoWPAN ND registration with Crypto-ID ownership proof, 6LR/6LBR flows, and a new 6CIO capability bit.
6LoWPAN.quote: This document updates the IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (6LoWPAN) Neighbor Discovery (ND) protocol defined in RFCs 6775 and 8505.

SEND.why: Secure ND is a close analogue, so the document compares itself with SEND and reuses its nonce option. SEND is the nearest tag for secured ND, though it has no dedicated tag.
SEND.quote: it protects the owner of an address against address theft and impersonation attacks in a Low-Power and Lossy Network (LLN)

SAVI.why: The mechanism enforces source address validation by registration state, as an alternative to SAVI snooping.
SAVI.quote: provides the same conceptual benefit as Source Address Validation Improvement (SAVI) [RFC7039] in that only the owner of an IPv6 address may source packets with that address

rejected.why: The document builds on IPv6 ND, but its focus is the 6LoWPAN registration extension. The more specific 6LoWPAN tag already covers it.
ECDSA is used as one signature scheme, and the document does not define it. The document is about the ND extension.
Ed25519 is an optional Crypto-Type used here, not the subject of the document.
Hash functions serve as building blocks for the Crypto-ID and signatures, and are not what the document is about.
IPv6 is the base protocol. The more specific ND and 6LoWPAN tags apply instead.
The IANA registries it creates are boilerplate and not the main subject.

RFC8929.title: IPv6 Backbone Router
RFC8929.summary: RFC 8929 updates RFCs 6775 and 8505 to define the 6LoWPAN Backbone Router (6BBR), which provides IPv6 Neighbor Discovery proxy services (routing and bridging proxy) over a backbone to federate multiple wireless LLNs into a single multi-link subnet, using registrations with a Binding Table.

neighbor discovery.why: The document specifies ND proxy operation on the backbone, EARO in NS(DAD)/NA, and DAD handling, extending IPv6 ND.
neighbor discovery.quote: enable proxy services for IPv6 Neighbor Discovery by Routing Registrars called "Backbone Routers"

6LoWPAN.why: It builds on and updates 6LoWPAN ND (RFC 6775/8505): 6LN/6LR/6LBR roles, registration, EDAR/EDAC, applicable to LLNs.
6LoWPAN.quote: A 6LoWPAN Node (6LN) registers all of its IPv6 addresses using NS messages with an Extended Address Registration Option (EARO)

rejected.why: Wi-Fi APs are a use case (6BBR collocated with AP), but the document is not about IP over 802.11 itself.
RPL is mentioned only as an example route-over mesh protocol in a non-normative note.
The document concerns multi-link subnets, not IPv4/IPv6 coexistence.
SAVI is only mentioned as a related non-normative approach and a security benefit.
DAD is used from RFC 4862, but the document does not specify address autoconfiguration.
LLNs and IoT are the context, but the document's focus is ND proxying on the backbone.

gaps.name: Multi-Link Subnet (MLSN) / ND proxy
gaps.why: The document is about federating links into one subnet with ND proxies. Taxonomy only has neighbor discovery, and the multihoming and addressing topics do not fit.

RFC8930.title: On Forwarding 6LoWPAN Fragments over a Multi-Hop IPv6 Network
RFC8930.summary: Specifies generic rules for forwarding 6LoWPAN fragments across route-over multi-hop networks without per-hop reassembly, and describes the Virtual Reassembly Buffer technique using RFC 4944 formats.

6LoWPAN.why: The whole document defines 6LoWPAN Fragment Forwarding and VRB, extending the fragmentation behaviour of RFC 4944 for constrained link layers.
6LoWPAN.quote: This document provides generic rules to enable the forwarding of an IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (6LoWPAN) fragment over a route-over network.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the payload carried by 6LoWPAN. The document is about link-adaptation fragmentation below IP, not IPv6 itself.
RPL is only mentioned in passing for compressed-form artifacts. The document does not specify or analyse it.
MPLS label swapping is cited only as an analogy for forwarding fragments by state lookup.
RFC 8201 appears only as background on limiting fragmentation. The document does not address PMTUD.
The Security Considerations mention firewalls only briefly. They are not a substantial subject of the document.
The 6LoWPAN tech tag is more specific than this topic. Its ancestors are implied, so the topic is not listed separately.

gaps.name: 6LoWPAN fragment forwarding / Virtual Reassembly Buffer
gaps.why: The 6LoWPAN tag covers this only in part. The taxonomy has no tag for fragmentation or fragment forwarding in constrained networks.

RFC8931.title: IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (6LoWPAN) Selective Fragment Recovery
RFC8931.summary: RFC 8931 updates RFC 4944 with a 6LoWPAN fragment forwarding and selective end-to-end fragment recovery protocol (RFRAG and RFRAG-ACK dispatch types) with ECN-based congestion control for route-over LLN meshes.

6LoWPAN.why: The document defines new 6LoWPAN dispatch types and headers for fragment forwarding and recovery, updating the 6LoWPAN fragmentation of RFC 4944.
6LoWPAN.quote: This document updates RFC 4944 with a protocol that forwards individual fragments across a route-over mesh and recovers them end to end

congestion control.why: Windowing, ack requests, ECN echo and an appendix on congestion control are a substantial part of the protocol. The general congestion control topic fits because the ECN support is carried in the 6LoWPAN headers and the mechanism itself is left to implementations.
congestion control.quote: This document also adds an ECN mechanism that can be used to protect the network by adapting the size of the window, the size of the fragments, and/or the inter-frame gap.

rejected.why: ECN bits are carried and echoed, but how ECN is marked at the IP/LoWPAN level is explicitly out of scope; it is a feature of the document, not its subject.
RPL is only mentioned as the routing protocol of the LLN mesh and in the parameter-tuning discussion.
6TiSCH is referenced for the architecture and Track concept, but the document does not specify anything about it.
The label-switching analogy is used to explain Datagram_Tag swapping, but the document does not concern MPLS.
TCP congestion avoidance is only a model and informative reference.
Firmware update is a motivating use case, not what the document specifies.

RFC8932.title: Recommendations for DNS Privacy Service Operators
RFC8932.summary: BCP giving operational, policy and security recommendations for operators of DNS privacy services (recursive resolvers offering encrypted DNS), covering wire, data-at-rest and onward data handling, plus a framework for a Recursive operator Privacy Statement.

DNS privacy.why: The whole document is guidance for operating privacy-preserving DNS resolvers, covering transport, data handling, and privacy statements.
DNS privacy.quote: operational, policy, and security considerations for DNS recursive resolver operators who choose to offer DNS privacy services

DoT.why: Substantial recommendations on operating DoT: profiles, authentication, padding, ports, ALPN, TLS proxy limits.
DoT.quote: DNS privacy services that offer DoT need to provide credentials that will be accepted by the client's trust model

DoH.why: Has a dedicated section of operator recommendations for DoH services.
DoH.quote: Clients must be able to forgo the use of HTTP cookies [RFC6265] and still use the service.

DNSSEC.why: A section requires DNSSEC validation and explains encryption does not replace it.
DNSSEC.quote: All DNS privacy services must offer a DNS privacy service that performs Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) validation.

rejected.why: Covered by the more specific DNS privacy tag; ancestors are implied.
TLS is the substrate for DoT/DoH; only profile guidance is referenced, nothing new about TLS.
EDNS padding and ECS are mentioned as recommendations, but the document does not specify or extend them.
Mentioned only as an example for certificate automation.
The operational guidance is specific to DNS privacy, which is the better-fitting tag.

gaps.name: IP address pseudonymization/anonymization of traffic logs
gaps.why: Appendix B surveys techniques for anonymizing IP addresses in DNS logs and captures; no taxonomy tag covers data anonymization.

RFC8933.title: Update to the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) for Algorithm Identifier Protection
RFC8933.summary: Updates RFC 5652 (CMS) to require the same digest algorithm for message content and signed attributes and to recommend including the CMSAlgorithmProtection attribute, protecting algorithm identifiers against substitution attacks.

CMS.why: The document is a direct update to CMS (RFC 5652), modifying its sections 5.3, 5.4, 5.6 and 14 for signed-data and authenticated-data.
CMS.quote: This document updates the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) specified in RFC 5652 to ensure that algorithm identifiers in signed-data and authenticated-data content types are adequately protected.

rejected.why: X.509 certificates are mentioned only as a comparison for how algorithm identifiers are protected by signing; the document does not specify or profile them.
S/MIME is not discussed in the body; it appears only in the title of an informative reference.
SHA-256 and SHA-512 are used only as examples of digest algorithms in the attack discussion.
RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 and RSASSA-PSS are mentioned in Security Considerations only as examples of how signature schemes handle digest identifiers.
The Time-Stamp Protocol is touched on only in a compatibility note, and the document is not about PKI.

RFC8934.title: PCE Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for Label Switched Path (LSP) Scheduling with Stateful PCE
RFC8934.summary: Defines PCEP extensions for stateful PCE (new capability flags, SCHED-LSP-ATTRIBUTE and SCHED-PD-LSP-ATTRIBUTE TLVs, error codes) to compute, activate, and delete LSPs based on scheduled start times, durations, periodic repeats, elastic ranges and grace periods.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP and stateful PCE procedures with scheduling TLVs, capability bits, and error values, so it belongs under PCE/PCEP.
PCE.quote: this document defines a set of needed extensions to PCEP used for stateful PCEs so as to enable LSP scheduling for path computation and LSP setup/deletion

rejected.why: LSPs are the managed object, but the document specifies PCEP extensions, not MPLS itself.
Covered by the PCE tag, which sits under it. The scheduled TE resource framework is RFC 8413, not this document.
Only recommended for clock synchronization when relative time is used; it is not the subject.
PCEPS and TCP-AO appear only in Security Considerations as boilerplate-level references.
Mentioned once in the Introduction as a possible use case, not addressed in the document.
Mentioned once in the Introduction as a possible use case, not addressed in the document.

RFC8935.title: Push-Based Security Event Token (SET) Delivery Using HTTP
RFC8935.summary: Defines push-based delivery of Security Event Tokens (SETs) via HTTP POST over TLS to a recipient endpoint, with 202 success and 400 JSON error responses and an IANA registry of SET error codes.

secevent.why: The document specifies SET delivery, with SET Transmitter and Recipient behaviour, responses and an error code registry. This is the core of secevent.
secevent.quote: This specification defines a mechanism by which a transmitter of a Security Event Token (SET) [RFC8417] can deliver the SET to an intended SET Recipient

rejected.why: HTTP POST is the transport. The document defines a delivery profile and does not extend HTTP itself.
TLS is mandated as the secure transport, but nothing new is defined about TLS.
The SET is a JWT, but JWT is defined elsewhere (RFC 7519 and RFC 8417) and is only the payload encoding here.
DANE is mentioned only as an option for validating the server certificate.
JSON is used for the error response body. It is an encoding detail.
The document defines one specific delivery endpoint and error format. It does not describe general conventions for building APIs on HTTP.

RFC8936.title: Poll-Based Security Event Token (SET) Delivery Using HTTP
RFC8936.summary: Defines poll-based delivery of Security Event Tokens (SETs) via HTTP POST over TLS, including long/short polling, acknowledgement and error reporting, as the counterpart to push-based delivery in RFC 8935.

secevent.why: The whole document specifies delivery of Security Event Tokens by polling, an alternative to push delivery in RFC 8935.
secevent.quote: This specification defines how a stream of Security Event Tokens (SETs) [RFC8417] can be transmitted to an intended SET Recipient using HTTP [RFC7231] over TLS.

rejected.why: HTTP POST is only the transport for SET delivery. The document defines no HTTP extension or semantics.
TLS is the required secure transport, and the document defines nothing new about its use.
JSON is only the encoding of the poll requests and responses.
SETs are JWTs, but this document only transports them and defines nothing about JWT.
OAuth bearer tokens are mentioned only as an option in the security considerations.
DANE appears only as an option for validating the server certificate.

RFC8937.title: Randomness Improvements for Security Protocols
RFC8937.summary: RFC 8937 (CFRG) describes a construction that wraps a CSPRNG with a keyed PRF derived from a signature by a long-term private key, so security protocols such as TLS keep good randomness even when the CSPRNG is weak or broken.

randomness.why: The whole document specifies a randomness wrapper (G') that improves CSPRNG output, which is the core subject of the randomness tag.
randomness.quote: This document describes a way for security protocols implementations to augment their CSPRNGs using long-term private keys.

rejected.why: TLS is the motivating example and Section 5 applies the wrapper to it, but the document defines nothing new about TLS. The construction is generic.
The document requires a deterministic signature, such as RFC 6979 ECDSA, and compares itself to RFC 6979 in Section 9. It does not specify or extend ECDSA.
HKDF is used as the Extract/Expand instantiation. HKDF is a building block here, not the subject.
The long-term private key is used only to seed randomness. The document does not address key establishment, provisioning or storage.
The document does not address post-quantum cryptography.

RFC8938.title: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) Data Plane Framework
RFC8938.summary: Informational framework for the DetNet data plane, describing service and forwarding sub-layers, PREOF, IP and MPLS data plane considerations, aggregation, and controller plane requirements.

DetNet.why: The whole document is the DetNet data plane framework, covering sub-layers, metadata, PREOF, aggregation and controller plane considerations.
DetNet.quote: This document provides an overall framework for the Deterministic Networking (DetNet) data plane.

rejected.why: DetNet MPLS data plane is discussed, but the normative specification is in a separate document. MPLS is a forwarding substrate here.
Mentioned only as one possible distributed controller plane option.
PCEP is listed only as an example of a centralized provisioning mechanism.
Explicit routes and resource reservation are discussed, but they are covered by DetNet as a whole and are not the subject of a separate topic.
Cited only as an example of an encapsulation or protection mechanism.
SRv6 and MPLS segment routing are mentioned in passing as options.

RFC8939.title: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) Data Plane: IP
RFC8939.summary: RFC 8939 specifies the DetNet data plane for IP hosts and routers, using existing IP 6-tuple and higher-layer header fields for flow identification and forwarding-sub-layer service without any DetNet-specific encapsulation.

DetNet.why: The whole document defines the DetNet IP data plane: flow identification, forwarding and traffic treatment procedures for DetNet flows.
DetNet.quote: This document specifies the DetNet data plane operation for IP hosts and routers that provide DetNet service to IP-encapsulated data.

rejected.why: IPv4 and IPv6 header fields are used for flow matching, but the document does not specify or extend IPv6 itself.
DSCP is one of the 6-tuple fields and CoS uses standard DSCP, but Diffserv is only relied on, not specified or extended.
QoS is discussed as a DetNet service property, but the document does not define a QoS architecture or signalling.
AH/ESP SPI is matched for flow identification, but IPsec itself is not the subject.
MPLS is mentioned only as an alternative sub-network or in referenced companion documents.
Only a brief recommendation against ECMP for a single DetNet flow.

RFC8940.title: Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Session-Id Derivation for EAP Subscriber Identity Module (EAP-SIM), EAP Authentication and Key Agreement (EAP-AKA), and Protected EAP (PEAP)
RFC8940.summary: Updates RFC 5247 Appendix A to define EAP Session-Id derivation for EAP-SIM and EAP-AKA fast reconnect, clarifies full-authentication derivation, and defines Session-Id for PEAP.

EAP.why: The document specifies exported Session-Id derivation for the EAP methods EAP-SIM, EAP-AKA and PEAP, and updates the EAP key management framework.
EAP.quote: RFC 5247 is updated to define and clarify EAP Session-Id derivation for multiple Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) methods.

rejected.why: EAP-SIM uses GSM triplets, but the document is about EAP Session-Id derivation, not GSM authentication or interworking.
PEAP uses TLS random values for Session-Id, but TLS is only the substrate and nothing new is defined for it.
ERP is the motivation for the Session-Id definitions, but the document does not specify or extend ERP.
The document is not about IP over 3GPP systems; AKA and SIM are only the EAP methods whose Session-Id is defined.

RFC8941.title: Structured Field Values for HTTP
RFC8941.summary: Defines Structured Fields: a set of typed data structures (Lists, Dictionaries, Items, Parameters) with strict parsing and serialization algorithms for defining new HTTP header and trailer fields.

HTTP.why: The document specifies a common syntax and handling rules for new HTTP fields, extending HTTP's field machinery.
HTTP.quote: intended to make it easier and safer to define and handle HTTP header and trailer fields, known as "Structured Fields"

rejected.why: ABNF is used as notation to describe syntax, not the subject of the document.
JSON is discussed only in the FAQ as an alternative that was rejected.
Base64 is used only to encode Byte Sequences, as a substrate.
HTTP/2 and HPACK are mentioned only in passing as an encoding context.
This is about field syntax, not API conventions.

RFC8942.title: HTTP Client Hints
RFC8942.summary: Defines the Client Hints framework for HTTP, including the Accept-CH response header by which servers opt in to receiving proactive content negotiation request headers, plus guidelines for creating such headers and their privacy and caching implications.

HTTP.why: The document extends HTTP with a new response header field and a framework for request header fields, including Vary interaction and opt-in persistence per origin.
HTTP.quote: This document defines an Accept-CH response header that servers can use to advertise their use of request headers for proactive content negotiation

content negotiation.why: Client Hints is a mechanism for proactive content negotiation, motivated by shortcomings of user-agent sniffing and traditional negotiation headers.
content negotiation.quote: Client Hints, a framework that enables servers to opt-in to specific proactive content negotiation features, adapting their content accordingly

rejected.why: Vary handling for cacheable responses is discussed briefly, but the document is not about caching.
Cookies are only mentioned as an alternative technique and as data cleared with opt-in preferences.
Fingerprinting and privacy are a motivation and are covered in the Security Considerations, but the document is not a privacy threat-model document.
ABNF is only the notation used for the header definition.

RFC8943.title: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) Tags for Date
RFC8943.summary: Defines and registers two CBOR tags for calendar dates without time: tag 1004 (RFC 3339 full-date text string) and tag 100 (integer days since 1970-01-01).

CBOR.why: The document defines new CBOR tags for dates and registers them in the CBOR tags registry, so it is about CBOR extensions.
CBOR.quote: This specification defines a CBOR tag for a text string representing a date without a time.

date-time formats.why: It specifies date representations (RFC 3339 full-date and days since epoch) and how to compare them. Readers of date and time formats would want it.
date-time formats.quote: The tagged text string is represented as specified by the RFC 3339 [RFC3339] "full-date" production.

rejected.why: This tag is about time zone data distribution. The document only notes that dates have no time zone.
The document only registers tags in an IANA registry. That is boilerplate, not the subject.
CDDL is not used or discussed in the document.

RFC8944.title: A YANG Data Model for Layer 2 Network Topologies
RFC8944.summary: Defines the ietf-l2-topology YANG module (plus a non-NMDA companion state module) augmenting the RFC 8345 generic network and topology models with Layer 2 attributes for networks, nodes, links and termination points.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module and its companion state module, augmenting the RFC 8345 topology models.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model for Layer 2 network topologies.

I2RS.why: Produced by the I2RS WG and motivated by I2RS use cases, where nodes expose topology to a controller.
I2RS.quote: within the context of Interface to the Routing System (I2RS), nodes within the network can use the data model to capture their understanding of the overall network topology

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the access protocols mentioned in Security Considerations; the document defines no protocol behaviour.
VXLAN appears only as an encapsulation type and VNI field in the model; the document is not about VXLAN itself.
The model describes Layer 2 topology attributes, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
TRILL is only an encapsulation identity; its own YANG model is explicitly out of scope.
JSON is used only for the example instance data encoding.
The lag and member-link-tp leaves are minor attributes, not a substantial part of the document.

gaps.name: Network topology data models
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for network topology modelling (RFC 8345 and its technology-specific augmentations), which is the real subject of this RFC beyond YANG.

RFC8945.title: Secret Key Transaction Authentication for DNS (TSIG)
RFC8945.summary: RFC 8945 specifies TSIG, a shared-secret HMAC-based transaction authentication mechanism for DNS messages (queries, responses, dynamic updates, zone transfers), obsoleting RFC 2845 and RFC 4635 and fixing a MAC/time check ordering flaw.

DNS.why: The document defines the TSIG meta resource record type, new RCODEs (BADSIG, BADKEY, BADTIME, BADTRUNC) and the server and client processing rules for DNS messages. It is a DNS protocol extension and has no more specific DNS child tag.
DNS.quote: This document describes a protocol for transaction-level authentication using shared secrets and one-way hashing.

rejected.why: DNSSEC appears only as a comparison in Section 10.2 ('Why Not DNSSEC?') and as a contrast for glue records. TSIG is a separate, symmetric-key mechanism.
Authenticating dynamic updates is one use case, but the document specifies TSIG generally, covering zone transfers and responses too. RFC 2136 is only referenced.
HMAC is the keyed-hash mechanism TSIG relies on, and the document specifies no new HMAC construction. It only picks algorithm names and truncation rules for TSIG.
SHA-1 and the SHA-2 variants appear only as algorithm choices in the TSIG algorithm table. The document is not about the hash functions.
gss-tsig is listed as an optional algorithm name and defined in RFC 3645, not in this document.

RFC8946.title: Personal Assertion Token (PASSporT) Extension for Diverted Calls
RFC8946.summary: Extends PASSporT with a "div" type/claim indicating a call was diverted from its original destination, and a "div-o" type with an "opt" claim nesting a PASSporT, with SIP authentication and verification procedures; updates RFC 8224.

STIR.why: The document defines a new PASSporT extension and the STIR authentication and verification service behaviour for diverted calls, and updates RFC 8224.
STIR.quote: This specification extends PASSporT to include an indication that a call has been diverted from its original destination to a new one.

SIP.why: A substantial part covers SIP behaviour: Identity header fields, retargeting, 3xx redirection, and History-Info interaction. It also updates RFC 8224 to allow Identity headers in 3xx responses.
SIP.quote: This section specifies SIP-specific usage for the "div" PASSporT type and its handling in the SIP Identity header field "ppt" parameter value.

rejected.why: PASSporT is built on JWT, and two JWT claims are registered. The document is about call diversion, not JWT itself.
JSON is only the encoding substrate for the claims.
Credentials and certificates are referenced, but only as the signing mechanism defined elsewhere.
JWS signing is relied on but not specified or extended.

gaps.name: PASSporT
gaps.why: The document is about PASSporT extensions, but the taxonomy has no PASSporT tag. STIR is the nearest fit.

RFC8947.title: Link-Layer Address Assignment Mechanism for DHCPv6
RFC8947.summary: Defines two new DHCPv6 options, IA_LL and LLADDR, that let a client (a hypervisor or an IoT device) request, renew and release blocks of locally unique link-layer (MAC) addresses from a DHCP server.

DHCPv6.why: The RFC extends DHCPv6 with the new IA_LL and LLADDR options, and specifies the Solicit/Request/Renew/Release handling for them. DHCPv6 is the protocol being extended, not just a substrate.
DHCPv6.quote: This document proposes a new mechanism that extends DHCPv6 operation to handle link-layer address assignments.

rejected.why: The RFC assigns MAC addresses, but it does not cover IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM. IEEE 802 addresses are only the thing being allocated.
DHCPv6 is the more specific child tag. The document does not extend DHCPv4.
IoT is mentioned as a use case, but the document is not about IoT architecture or constrained devices.
It is referenced only for informing neighbors after an address change, which is a minor point.
This topic covers IP address architecture. The document is about link-layer addresses, and DHCPv6 is already tagged.

gaps.name: IEEE 802 MAC address assignment (SLAP, IEEE 802c)
gaps.why: The document is about allocating locally administered MAC addresses and summarises the IEEE 802c SLAP quadrants. The taxonomy has no tag for link-layer address assignment.

RFC8948.title: Structured Local Address Plan (SLAP) Quadrant Selection Option for DHCPv6
RFC8948.summary: Defines the DHCPv6 QUAD option (OPTION_SLAP_QUAD) letting clients or relays indicate preferred IEEE 802c SLAP quadrants for local MAC address assignment under the RFC 8947 link-layer address assignment mechanism.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies a new DHCPv6 option and the client/relay/server procedures that use it, extending RFC 8947 link-layer address assignment.
DHCPv6.quote: A new DHCPv6 option (QUAD) is defined for this purpose.

rejected.why: The MAC address space and IEEE 802c are the subject matter, but the document specifies a DHCPv6 option, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
The DHCPv6 child tag is the more specific fit; the document does not address DHCPv4.
IoT devices are only an example scenario for choosing quadrants, not the subject of the document.
Wi-Fi devices are used as a motivating scenario only; nothing about IP over 802.11 is specified.
MAC address randomization privacy is mentioned as a use case, but the document does not analyse privacy threats.

gaps.name: Structured Local Address Plan (SLAP) / IEEE 802 MAC address assignment
gaps.why: The document is about assigning local MAC addresses from IEEE 802c SLAP quadrants. The taxonomy has no tag for MAC address management, and the nearest link-layer tags are medium-specific.

RFC8949.title: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR)
RFC8949.summary: RFC 8949 is the Internet Standard specification of CBOR, a compact binary data format with a JSON-based extensible data model, encoding rules, tags, deterministic encoding, JSON conversion guidance, and diagnostic notation, obsoleting RFC 7049.

CBOR.why: The document is the core specification of CBOR: major types, tags, serialization, deterministic encoding, and diagnostic notation.
CBOR.quote: The Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format whose design goals include the possibility of extremely small code size, fairly small message size

JSON.why: CBOR's data model derives from JSON, and Section 6 gives substantial advice on converting between CBOR and JSON, which JSON readers would want.
JSON.quote: The underlying data model is an extended version of the JSON data model [RFC8259].

rejected.why: Only compared with CBOR in Appendix E as an alternative serialization; the document is not about ASN.1.
The application/cbor and +cbor registrations are in IANA Considerations boilerplate, not the main subject.
Only a Content-Format registration and a design-inspiration acknowledgement; CoAP is not the subject.
Text strings use UTF-8 as an encoding substrate; the document does not define anything new about UTF-8.
Constrained-node suitability is a design goal, but the document is a general data format specification.
Only mentioned for Extended Diagnostic Notation in RFC 8610; not specified here.

RFC8950.title: Advertising IPv4 Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI) with an IPv6 Next Hop
RFC8950.summary: RFC 8950 (obsoleting RFC 5549) extends MP-BGP AFI/SAFI definitions so IPv4 and VPN-IPv4 NLRI can be advertised with an IPv6 next hop, defines the Extended Next Hop Encoding BGP capability, and gives usage examples for IPv4 over IPv6 core and IPv4 unicast/multicast VPNs.

BGP.why: The document extends MP-BGP next-hop encoding and defines a new BGP capability (Extended Next Hop Encoding), so it is squarely about BGP protocol extensions.
BGP.quote: This document specifies the extensions necessary to allow the advertising of IPv4 NLRI or VPN-IPv4 NLRI with a next-hop address that belongs to the IPv6 protocol.

L3VPN.why: A substantial part covers VPN-IPv4 NLRI (SAFI 128) with an IPv6 next hop, i.e. BGP/MPLS L3VPN over an IPv6 core.
L3VPN.quote: The extensions defined in this document may be used for support of IPv4 VPNs over an IPv6 backbone.

MVPN.why: The document newly allows AFI/SAFI <1/129> (multicast VPN) to use an IPv6 next hop, which MVPN readers will want.
MVPN.quote: The extensions defined in this document may be used for support of IPv4 multicast VPNs over an IPv6 backbone.

IPv6 transition.why: The motivation is IPv4 islands across an IPv6 core (softwire mesh), which is an IPv4/IPv6 coexistence mechanism.
IPv6 transition.quote: establish connectivity between 'islands' of networks of one address family type across a transit core of a differing address family type.

rejected.why: IPv6 is only the address family of the next hop; the document is not about IPv6 specification, addressing or deployment per se.
Softwire Mesh Framework and problem statement are cited as motivation and a usage scenario, but the document specifies BGP encoding, not a softwire mechanism.
Route reflectors are mentioned briefly in Operations regarding passing next hops unchanged, not a main subject.
MPLS appears only through the BGP/MPLS VPN context; the document does not address MPLS itself.

RFC8951.title: Clarification of Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST): Transfer Encodings and ASN.1
RFC8951.summary: RFC 8951 updates RFC 7030 (EST) by deprecating Content-Transfer-Encoding headers in favour of plain base64 bodies, correcting the ASN.1 module for CSR attributes, and clarifying error message content types.

EST.why: The whole document amends the EST specification: endpoint encoding, CSR attributes response, and error handling.
EST.quote: This document updates RFC 7030: Enrollment over Secure Transport to resolve some errata that were reported and that have proven to cause interoperability issues

ASN.1.why: A substantial part fixes ASN.1 syntax for CsrAttrs and provides a normative ASN.1 module (Appendix A).
ASN.1.quote: [errata4384] is closed by correcting the ASN.1 Module in Section 4.

Base64.why: Core change is replacing Content-Transfer-Encoding with plain base64 bodies, including whitespace tolerance rules.
Base64.quote: require the POST request and payload response of all endpoints using base64 encoding, as specified in Section 4 of [RFC4648]

rejected.why: EST runs over HTTP and the document cites HTTP rules on Content-Transfer-Encoding, but it does not extend HTTP itself.
MIME Content-Transfer-Encoding is being deprecated for EST, not specified; MIME is background.
CMC and CMS structures are referenced as payloads but not specified or changed.
Secure transport is the substrate only; nothing new about TLS is defined.
Certificates are the enrolled objects but the document does not profile them.

RFC8952.title: Captive Portal Architecture
RFC8952.summary: Describes the captive portal architecture: components (user equipment, provisioning service, API server, enforcement device, signal), identifier properties, and workflows, using DHCP/RA provisioning and an HTTP API.

captive portal.why: The whole document specifies the architecture, components, identity and workflow of captive portals.
captive portal.quote: This document describes a captive portal architecture.

rejected.why: DHCP/RA is only a provisioning mechanism for the API URI, defined in RFC 8910, not specified here.
The API is only required to exist; details are explicitly out of scope and defined in RFC 8908.
TLS is only used to secure the API and validate certificates.
IPv6 RAs and addresses are mentioned only incidentally.
Mentioned only as a requirement not to break DNSSEC validation.

RFC8953.title: Coordinating Attack Response at Internet Scale 2 (CARIS2) Workshop Report
RFC8953.summary: Report of the CARIS2 workshop on scaling attack response and incident prevention/detection as session encryption becomes ubiquitous, covering breakouts on protocol adoption, preventative protocols, incident response coordination, and monitoring/measurement.

workshop reports.why: The document is a report of a community workshop, matching the workshop reports topic.
workshop reports.quote: The Coordinating Attack Response at Internet Scale (CARIS) 2 workshop [CARISEvent], sponsored by the Internet Society, took place on 28 February and 1 March 2019

incident response.why: The workshop's central theme is scaling and coordinating incident response, with discussion of IoC sharing, trust, and taxonomies.
incident response.quote: Incident response coordination currently does not scale.

rejected.why: IODEF is only one of several formats discussed for adoption; the document does not specify or analyse it in depth.
MUD is discussed in a breakout, but the document is not about MUD itself. It is a minor part of the report.
TLS and QUIC are mentioned as the encryption trend motivating the workshop, not as subjects of the document.
Privacy is a recurring consideration, but the document is not a privacy threat-model or considerations document.
DANE is mentioned only as an example of limited adoption.
IPv6 is mentioned in adoption and address reputation discussions but is not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Threat information sharing (STIX, MISP, IoCs, taxonomies)
gaps.why: The workshop discusses sharing of indicators of compromise and taxonomies for threat and attack description, which the taxonomy covers only partly under incident response.

RFC8954.title: Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) Nonce Extension
RFC8954.summary: Updates RFC 6960 by redefining the OCSP Nonce extension to require nonce lengths of 1 to 32 octets, with 32 required for new clients, and updates the ASN.1 definitions accordingly.

OCSP.why: The whole document revises the OCSP Nonce extension and updates RFC 6960, so it belongs on the OCSP page.
OCSP.quote: This document specifies the updated format of the Nonce extension in the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) request and response messages.

rejected.why: RFC 5280 is cited only for the extension model. The document is about OCSP messages, not certificate profiles.
The document gives ASN.1 definitions for the nonce, but ASN.1 is only the notation used and is not the subject.
The nonce must come from a strong PRNG, but this is a single requirement that points to RFC 4086. The document is not about randomness.
OCSP is already covered by its own tag, which sits under PKI, so the parent is implied.

RFC8955.title: Dissemination of Flow Specification Rules
RFC8955.summary: Defines the BGP Flow Specification NLRI encoding (SAFI 133/134) for IPv4 and VPNv4 traffic filter rules, plus extended communities for traffic filtering actions, validation, and ordering; obsoletes RFC 5575 and RFC 7674.

BGP flowspec.why: The document is the core specification of BGP Flow Specification: NLRI components, operators, validation, ordering and traffic filtering action communities.
BGP flowspec.quote: defines a Border Gateway Protocol Network Layer Reachability Information (BGP NLRI) encoding format that can be used to distribute (intra-domain and inter-domain) traffic Flow Specifications

L3VPN.why: A substantial section defines the VPNv4 flowspec address family with Route Distinguisher and VRF import via route targets, plus the rt-redirect action.
L3VPN.quote: This document defines an additional BGP NLRI type (AFI=1, SAFI=134) value, which can be used to propagate Flow Specification in a BGP/MPLS VPN environment.
L3VPN.section: 8. Dissemination of Traffic Filtering in BGP/MPLS VPN Networks

rejected.why: The more specific child BGP flowspec applies, so the parent is implied.
DoS/DDoS mitigation is a motivating application, but the document specifies the encoding and actions, not DDoS mitigation methods.
DSCP matching and marking are components/actions, but the document is not about Diffserv itself.
RFC 6811 and BGPsec are mentioned only as possible mitigations in Security Considerations.
Route reflection is mentioned only in passing as reusable infrastructure and for originator ID.
IPv6 flowspec is defined in RFC 8956; this document covers only IPv4 and VPNv4.

RFC8956.title: Dissemination of Flow Specification Rules for IPv6
RFC8956.summary: RFC 8956 extends BGP Flow Specification (RFC 8955) to IPv6, defining IPv6 NLRI component types, ordering, validation, a redirect-IPv6 extended community, and IANA registry updates.

BGP flowspec.why: The whole document defines IPv6 extensions to BGP Flow Specification: component types, ordering, validation, actions and registry changes.
BGP flowspec.quote: It specifies new Border Gateway Protocol [RFC4271] encoding formats to enable "Dissemination of Flow Specification Rules" [RFC8955] for IPv6.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the packet type being matched, not the subject. The document extends BGP flowspec and does not specify IPv6 itself.
BGP is the carrier, and the BGP flowspec tag is the more specific fit under it.
SAFI 134 and VRF redirect are mentioned, but only as part of the flowspec extension.
ICMPv6 type and code are only fields that the flowspec components match on.
The registry updates are boilerplate-style IANA considerations, not the main subject.

RFC8957.title: Synonymous Flow Label Framework
RFC8957.summary: Defines Synonymous Flow Labels (SFLs), MPLS labels that mimic existing labels while triggering additional per-flow actions (such as packet counting for performance measurement) at the egress LER, including label stack usage, TTL/TC handling, aggregation and ECMP considerations.

MPLS.why: The document specifies a new MPLS label-stack technique for flow identification, including how SFLs are placed in the stack and processed at egress LSRs.
MPLS.quote: labels that mimic the behavior of other MPLS labels provide the identification service

performance measurement.why: The main motivating use of SFLs is per-flow packet loss measurement. The document discusses how ECMP can invalidate such measurements.
performance measurement.quote: in a Performance Monitoring (PM) application, the agreed action could be recording the receipt of the packet by incrementing a packet counter

rejected.why: There is a short section on ECMP effects and entropy labels. It is a side consideration, not the subject of the document.
Pseudowires are used only as an example of an application label, so the document is not about pseudowire emulation.
IPFIX is mentioned only as one possible action an SFL could trigger. The document does not specify or extend it.
VPNs appear only as a multipoint-to-point example of source-specific SFLs.
The document describes flow identification, not an OAM mechanism. Measurement is only one use of it.

RFC8958.title: Updated Registration Rules for URI.ARPA
RFC8958.summary: BCP update to RFC 3405 removing the IETF URI tree requirement for URI.ARPA registrations, requiring instead that schemes be permanent registrations under BCP 35.

URI.why: The document sets the rules for which URI schemes may be inserted into URI.ARPA, tied to URI scheme registration status. Readers of URI scheme topics would want it.
URI.quote: All registrations in URI.ARPA MUST now be for schemes that are permanent registrations, as described in BCP 35.

DNS.why: URI.ARPA is a DNS zone used by DDDS for URI scheme resolution. The document governs which schemes go into that zone.
DNS.quote: procedures for requesting that a URI scheme be inserted into the URI.ARPA zone

rejected.why: The document is entirely instructions to IANA, but its subject is URI.ARPA registration eligibility. It is not general IANA registry guidance or stewardship.
Not about media type registration; the registries concerned are URI schemes.

gaps.name: DDDS (Dynamic Delegation Discovery System) / URI.ARPA
gaps.why: RFC 3405 defines DDDS Part Five and the URI.ARPA assignment procedures. The taxonomy has no DDDS or NAPTR tag, so DNS is the nearest fit.

RFC8959.title: The "secret-token" URI Scheme
RFC8959.summary: Registers the provisional "secret-token" URI scheme, which makes bearer/API tokens easy to identify so accidental disclosure (e.g., in source repositories) can be detected.

URI.why: The document defines and registers a new URI scheme with its syntax, so it belongs on the URI page.
URI.quote: The "secret-token" URI scheme identifies a token that is intended to be a secret.

rejected.why: Bearer token usage per RFC 6750 is only an example of where the tokens might be carried. The document does not specify or extend OAuth.
The Authorization header example is illustrative only. The document adds nothing to HTTP authentication schemes.
ABNF is only the notation used to define the scheme's syntax.
The document is about identifying tokens so they are not leaked. It does not define an authentication mechanism.
The scheme registration is boilerplate-level IANA action. The document is not about IANA registries.
UTF-8 is used only to encode disallowed characters before percent-encoding.

RFC8960.title: A YANG Data Model for MPLS Base
RFC8960.summary: Defines the ietf-mpls YANG module, a base data model that augments the RFC 8349 routing RIB model with MPLS forwarding data (labels, NHLFEs, label blocks, MPLS-enabled interfaces) and a native MPLS RIB instance.

YANG.why: The document's deliverable is a YANG module with tree diagram and module text, so YANG data models are its core subject.
YANG.quote: This document contains a specification of the MPLS base YANG data model.

MPLS.why: The model covers MPLS label forwarding: NHLFE, label stacks, label blocks, MPLS interfaces and the native MPLS RIB, so MPLS readers would want it.
MPLS.quote: serves as a base framework for configuring and managing an MPLS switching subsystem on an MPLS-enabled router

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only mentioned as access protocols in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
SR Adj-SIDs and the SRGB appear only as examples of native MPLS routes and in the appendix, not as the subject.
RSVP-programmed routes and fast reroute are cited only as examples or references. Future augmenting modules would cover them.
LDP is named only as a module that may later augment this one.
IS-IS appears only as the route source in the appendix example.
JSON is only the encoding of the appendix instance example.

RFC8961.title: Requirements for Time-Based Loss Detection
RFC8961.summary: BCP defining high-level, protocol-agnostic requirements for last-resort time-based loss detection (retransmission timeouts) for unicast Internet communication, covering initial RTO, RTT/feedback-time sampling, congestion response, and exponential backoff.

congestion control.why: The requirements tie loss detection to congestion response and exponential backoff for network safety. This is transport-general guidance, not specific to TCP, so the congestion control topic fits.
congestion control.quote: Loss detected by the RTO mechanism MUST be taken as an indication of network congestion and the sending rate adapted using a standard mechanism

TCP.why: The document generalises TCP's RTO (RFC 6298) and discusses TCP RTO practice and spurious-retransmission detection throughout. It is a TCPM product, but it is protocol-agnostic, so TCP is secondary.
TCP.quote: For example, TCP's RTO [RFC6298] would satisfy this requirement due to its use of an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA)

rejected.why: Cited only as an example of a protocol with its own RTO; the document does not specify or analyse SCTP.
Mentioned only in passing as a protocol with its own time-based loss detection.
Used only as an example of feedback time (cache miss versus hit) and of a simple loss detector.
The more specific congestion control tag already covers the subject, and the document is about loss detection rather than a particular transport.
The QUIC loss detection draft is cited only as a reference to recent proposals.

gaps.name: Loss detection / retransmission timeout (RTO)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is time-based loss detection and RTO computation. The taxonomy has no tag for loss detection or recovery outside FEC and congestion control.

RFC8962.title: Establishing the Protocol Police
RFC8962.summary: An April 1st parody RFC that "establishes" the Protocol Police, a secret body selected by NomCom to enforce IETF standards, with jokes about layer violations, traffic imprisonment, and morality sections.

humor.why: The document is an April 1st satire of IETF culture, published 1 April 2021. It is a whimsical document and belongs on the humor page.
humor.quote: For possibly the first time in IETF history, words like "SHALL" and "MAY" are used in this document in their real and enforceable sense.

rejected.why: The text says NomCom selects the Protocol Police, but only as a joke. It does not address NomCom procedures.
It mentions NTP eras only in passing, as a joke. It does not specify or analyse NTP.
It mentions XMPP once, as a punchline about reachability. It does not address the protocol.
The document makes fun of how the IETF treats compliance. It does not describe or change any real process.
The IANA Considerations section is a joke request for a registry of criminal networks. That is boilerplate and not the document's subject.
Section 2 is a joke on the requirements language. The document is not about terminology.

RFC8963.title: Evaluation of a Sample of RFCs Produced in 2018
RFC8963.summary: An independent-stream study of a random sample of 20 RFCs from 2018 (compared with 2008 and 1998 samples) that measures delays from first draft to publication, AUTH48 and copy editing, and compares Semantic Scholar citation counts and web references with deployment.

IETF process.why: The document analyses the IETF standards process: working group time, IETF Last Call and IESG review, and the stages of RFC production, including AUTH48. It uses Datatracker data to measure where delays arise.
IETF process.quote: the author attempts to understand the delays involved in publishing an idea in the IETF or through the Independent Stream, from the first individual draft to the publication of the RFC

RFC series.why: A substantial part covers RFC Editor production, copy editing, AUTH48 delays, the Independent Stream and the Independent Submissions Editor bottleneck, plus the citation impact of RFCs.
RFC series.quote: The RFC production, from approval by the IESG to publication, including the AUTH48 reviews.

rejected.why: RFC 8446 and other TLS documents are only sample items whose process history is reviewed. The document does not address the protocol itself.
CUBIC (RFC 8312) is one sampled RFC, discussed for its delay and citation count and not as a subject of the document.
RFCs 8471 and 8472 are only entries in the sample, so the subject is not treated in its own right.
RFC 8468 (IPPM) is one sampled RFC, mentioned only for its process history.
The IANA considerations are boilerplate. The brief remark that IANA does not cause publication delays is not a main subject.
This is an individual study of the RFC production process, not a report from a workshop.

gaps.name: Publication delay and citation metrics for RFCs
gaps.why: The document is about measuring RFC production delays and citation impact. The taxonomy has no tag for process metrics or bibliometrics, so IETF process and RFC series are only approximate fits.

RFC8964.title: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) Data Plane: MPLS
RFC8964.summary: Specifies the DetNet data plane over an MPLS PSN, defining the d-CW, S-Label, F-Label and A-Label encapsulation, PREOF processing, OAM indication, flow aggregation, and CoS/QoS handling, reusing pseudowire and MPLS-TE mechanisms.

DetNet.why: The document defines the DetNet data plane encapsulation and service/forwarding sub-layer behaviour over MPLS, which is the core DetNet subject.
DetNet.quote: This document specifies the Deterministic Networking (DetNet) data plane when operating over an MPLS Packet Switched Network.

MPLS.why: It specifies an MPLS label-stack encapsulation (S-Label, F-Labels, A-Label) and how MPLS LSRs, LSPs and MPLS-TE are used to carry DetNet flows.
MPLS.quote: The purpose of this document is to describe the use of the MPLS data plane to establish and support DetNet flows.

pseudowire.why: The service sub-layer is built on existing pseudowire encapsulations, including the control word, S-Label analogous to PW label, and VCCV-based OAM.
pseudowire.quote: The DetNet Control Word (d-CW) conforms to the Generic PW MPLS Control Word (PWMCW) defined in [RFC4385].

rejected.why: Mentioned as one possible way to signal and allocate label resources, but the document does not specify or extend it.
MPLS-TE LSPs are reused for the forwarding sub-layer, but the document does not address traffic engineering in its own right.
CoS via MPLS Diffserv is referenced in a short section, but it is not a substantial subject of the document.
OAM indication is a brief section using existing VCCV mechanisms, with DetNet OAM deferred to other work.
Only mentioned in passing, to say that ECMP use for DetNet flows is not recommended.
YANG models are referenced only as a possible future controller-plane mechanism.

gaps.name: DetNet (Deterministic Networking)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has DetNet as a tech under routing, but the data plane over MPLS is the document's central subject. I used the DetNet id, which exists, so this is a small gap. A narrower tag for DetNet data planes or PREOF (packet replication, elimination and ordering) would help readers.

RFC8965.title: Applicability of the Babel Routing Protocol
RFC8965.summary: Informational document describing the properties, limitations, and successful deployment niches (heterogeneous, overlay, mesh, small unmanaged networks) of the Babel distance-vector routing protocol.

Babel.why: The whole document analyses the applicability, properties, extensions and limitations of the Babel routing protocol.
Babel.quote: This document describes a number of niches where Babel has been found to be useful and that are arguably not adequately served by more mature protocols.

rejected.why: Pure wireless mesh deployments are discussed in one subsection, but the document is about Babel, not MANET routing as such; OLSR and AODV are only comparisons.
OSPF and IS-IS are mentioned only as contrasting mature protocols, not specified or analysed.
EIGRP is cited only as the origin of the feasibility mechanism Babel uses.
RIP is a point of comparison for small networks, not a subject of the document.
Babel-DTLS and Babel-MAC appear only in Security Considerations as references to other documents.
The tag covers data-plane virtualization overlays such as VXLAN; Babel's use over tunnel overlays is a deployment scenario, not that subject.

RFC8966.title: The Babel Routing Protocol
RFC8966.summary: RFC 8966 specifies version 2 of the Babel routing protocol, a loop-avoiding distance-vector protocol for wired and wireless mesh networks, covering its operation, TLV encoding and IANA registries, and obsoleting RFC 6126 and RFC 7557.

Babel.why: The document is the core specification of the Babel routing protocol, so it belongs on the Babel page.
Babel.quote: Babel is a loop-avoiding, distance-vector routing protocol that is robust and efficient both in ordinary wired networks and in wireless mesh networks.

rejected.why: Babel works in wireless mesh networks, but the document specifies a general routing protocol rather than MANET routing as such. The Babel tag is the more specific fit.
Babel packets are carried in UDP datagrams. UDP is only the transport substrate here.
Babel control traffic runs over IPv6 or IPv4 and carries routes for both. The document does not specify IPv6 itself.
RIP is mentioned only as a comparison point for distance-vector routing, not as a subject of the document.
The IANA Considerations section creates Babel registries, but it is boilerplate relative to the main body and is not the document's subject.
EIGRP is referenced only as the source of the feasibility condition and as an alternative protocol, not as a subject of the document.

RFC8967.title: MAC Authentication for the Babel Routing Protocol
RFC8967.summary: Defines a MAC-based cryptographic authentication extension for the Babel routing protocol, with packet counters, indices and challenge/reply TLVs for replay protection, obsoleting RFC 7298.

Babel.why: The document extends Babel with new TLVs (MAC, PC, Challenge Request/Reply) and neighbour/interface table changes, so it is about Babel.
Babel.quote: This document describes a cryptographic authentication mechanism for the Babel routing protocol that has provisions for replay avoidance.

routing security.why: It secures a routing protocol against spoofing and replay attacks, which is what routing security covers.
routing security.quote: An attacker can redirect traffic to itself or to a different node in the network, causing a variety of potential issues.

HMAC.why: HMAC-SHA256 is the mandatory-to-implement MAC algorithm, and the document specifies how the MAC is computed with it.
HMAC.quote: Every implementation MUST implement HMAC-SHA256 as defined in [RFC6234] and Section 2 of [RFC2104]

rejected.why: Keyed BLAKE2s is only a SHOULD-implement algorithm option, not a main subject.
UDP is only the substrate. Its port and address fields feed the pseudo-header.
RFC 8968 (Babel over DTLS) is mentioned only as an alternative approach.
PBKDF2, bcrypt and scrypt appear only as advice in Security Considerations.
A more specific routing security tag and the Babel tag already cover this.

gaps.name: Babel
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no Babel tag. Under routing there is a Babel entry in the taxonomy list, so if it does not exist as written, the Babel protocol itself has no fitting tag.

RFC8968.title: Babel Routing Protocol over Datagram Transport Layer Security
RFC8968.summary: Specifies how to secure the Babel routing protocol by protecting unicast Babel packets with DTLS, including connection initiation, transmission/reception rules, MTU handling, and a registered UDP port.

Babel.why: The document extends and profiles Babel with a security mechanism, changing how Babel sends and receives TLVs, so it belongs on the Babel page.
Babel.quote: The Babel Routing Protocol does not contain any means to authenticate neighbours or provide integrity or confidentiality for messages sent between them.

DTLS.why: It specifies how DTLS is used: client/server role selection, mutual authentication, replay protection, minimum version, and overhead handling. This is a new application profile of DTLS, not mere substrate use.
DTLS.quote: This document specifies a mechanism to prevent such attacks using Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS)

rejected.why: The document concerns DTLS specifically. TLS is mentioned only for Appendix A optimizations, such as raw public keys and the cached information extension.
This is the topic parent of the matching topic, but the document is not about routing security in general. It secures one protocol, so the more specific tags suffice.
UDP is only the transport substrate. The IANA port registration is boilerplate-like and defines nothing new about UDP.
The MTU section only adjusts packet sizes for DTLS overhead. It does not concern path MTU discovery.

RFC8969.title: A Framework for Automating Service and Network Management with YANG
RFC8969.summary: Informational framework describing how layered YANG service, network and device models are integrated to automate service and network management life cycles, with L3VPN, VN and event-based telemetry examples.

YANG.why: The whole document is about layering and integrating YANG service, network and device models, including schema mount and module classification.
YANG.quote: This document describes a framework for service and network management automation that takes advantage of YANG modeling technologies.

SDN.why: The framework is an SDN-style orchestrator/controller architecture for automated service delivery and closed-loop control.
SDN.quote: SDN techniques are meant to automate the overall service delivery procedures and typically rely upon standard data models.

telemetry.why: Covers telemetry-driven closed loops, YANG-Push subscriptions and ECA policies for performance monitoring and service assurance.
telemetry.quote: allow the NETCONF server to send updates only when the value exceeds a certain threshold for the first time
telemetry.section: 5.3. Event-Based Telemetry in the Device Self Management

rejected.why: NETCONF/RESTCONF are only the transport the YANG modules are accessed over. The document does not specify or extend them.
The L3VPN service and network models are an example used for illustration. The document is not about L3VPN protocol itself.
OAM models are mentioned for service diagnosis, but only as one part of the framework, not a main subject.
Policies and ECA are mentioned briefly, but they are not the document's focus.
Closed-loop and self-management ideas appear in passing, and the document does not address autonomic networking as a subject.

gaps.name: Service models / service and network management automation framework
gaps.why: The document is about service models and life-cycle automation across service, network and device layers. The taxonomy has no tag for service models, so it falls back on YANG and SDN.

RFC8970.title: IMAP4 Extension: Message Preview Generation
RFC8970.summary: Specifies an IMAP extension (PREVIEW capability and FETCH data item, with a LAZY modifier) letting clients request a server-generated short text preview of a message.

IMAP.why: The document defines a new IMAP capability, FETCH attribute and modifier, so it is an extension to IMAP.
IMAP.quote: allows a client to request a server-generated abbreviated text representation of message data that is useful as a contextual preview of the entire message

rejected.why: MIME is referenced for body parts and text/plain, but the document does not specify or extend it.
Previews are encoded in UTF-8, but this is only a substrate requirement.
ABNF is used only to write the formal syntax.
The IANA section only registers the capability, which is boilerplate.
The document is about IMAP access and does not concern Internet message headers or addressing.

RFC8971.title: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for Virtual eXtensible Local Area Network (VXLAN)
RFC8971.summary: Describes how to run BFD asynchronous mode over point-to-point VXLAN tunnels between VTEPs using a Management VNI, including encapsulation, addressing and reception rules.

BFD.why: The document specifies how BFD control packets are encapsulated, sent and validated for VXLAN tunnels, so it is BFD usage.
BFD.quote: This document describes the use of the Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) protocol in point-to-point Virtual eXtensible Local Area Network (VXLAN) tunnels

VXLAN.why: It defines a Management VNI and VXLAN encapsulation of BFD monitoring VTEP-to-VTEP continuity, which is of interest to VXLAN readers.
VXLAN.quote: BFD control messages MUST be sent using the Management VNI, which acts as the control and management channel between VTEPs.

rejected.why: EVPN is mentioned only as another use of VXLAN encapsulation in the introduction. The document is not about it.
UDP is only the transport for the outer VXLAN and inner BFD packets. Nothing new is defined about it.
