Data centers are the motivating deployment, but the document specifies a BFD mechanism, not data-center routing or address resolution.
The inner Ethernet frame format is part of the encapsulation, but the document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.

RFC8972.title: Simple Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol Optional Extensions
RFC8972.summary: RFC 8972 defines optional TLV extensions to STAMP (Extra Padding, Location, Timestamp Information, Class of Service, Direct Measurement, Access Report, Follow-Up Telemetry, HMAC), a STAMP Session Identifier, and related IANA registries, updating RFC 8762.

STAMP.why: The whole document specifies extensions to STAMP and updates RFC 8762 with a Session Identifier; STAMP readers need it.
STAMP.quote: This document describes optional extensions to Simple Two-way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP) that enable measurement of performance metrics.

rejected.why: Only referenced for wire compatibility; the document is about STAMP, and TWAMP is not in the taxonomy anyway.
HMAC is used as a mechanism for the HMAC TLV, which is a STAMP extension; the document does not specify HMAC itself.
Implied as the parent of STAMP; the STAMP tag is more specific.
The CoS TLV tests DSCP mapping but the document does not specify Diffserv.
Mentioned only as a clock synchronization source value in a registry.
The IANA subregistries are boilerplate-like registrations for the STAMP extensions, not the main subject.

RFC8973.title: DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) Agent Discovery
RFC8973.summary: Specifies how DOTS clients (and Call Home DOTS servers) discover peer DOTS agents using DHCPv4/DHCPv6 options, S-NAPTR service resolution, and DNS-SD.

DOTS.why: The whole document defines discovery of DOTS agents, including Call Home, so it belongs on the DOTS page.
DOTS.quote: This document specifies mechanisms to configure DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) clients with their DOTS servers.

DHCPv6.why: Defines new DHCPv6 options OPTION_V6_DOTS_RI and OPTION_V6_DOTS_ADDRESS plus client behaviour.
DHCPv6.quote: The DHCPv6 DOTS Reference Identifier option is used to configure the name of the DOTS server

DHCP.why: Defines new DHCPv4 options 147 and 148 and client behaviour.
DHCP.quote: The DHCPv4 DOTS Address option can be used to configure a list of IPv4 addresses of a peer DOTS agent.

DNS-SD.why: A whole section defines DNS-SD service names and records for DOTS discovery.
DNS-SD.quote: The <Service> portion of the DOTS service instance name MUST be "_dots-signal._udp"

DNS.why: Section 6 defines S-NAPTR/SRV-based service resolution with new application service and protocol tags.
DNS.quote: a resolution mechanism based on S-NAPTR resource records in the DNS

rejected.why: Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a mitigation.
Mentioned only in passing in Security Considerations.
Parent topic implied by DNS-SD tag.
Only the authentication substrate for DOTS sessions; nothing new defined.
PKIX reference identifiers are used but not specified.

gaps.name: DOTS (DDoS Open Threat Signaling)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a DOTS tech tag under DDoS (DOTS), which exists, so no gap in practice; however, the ids I used must match exactly.

RFC8974.title: Extended Tokens and Stateless Clients in the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)
RFC8974.summary: RFC 8974 introduces an extended token length (TKL) encoding for CoAP and an Extended-Token-Length capability option, and gives guidance for stateless CoAP clients and intermediaries that serialize per-request state into tokens.

CoAP.why: The document extends CoAP's message format (TKL field), defines a new signaling option, and gives guidance on stateless CoAP clients and proxies. It updates RFC 7252 and RFC 8323.
CoAP.quote: this document additionally introduces a new, optional CoAP protocol extension for extended token lengths.

rejected.why: Cited only in Security Considerations as a model for nonce handling. The document is not about OSCORE.
CoJP in 6TiSCH is mentioned only as an example use case.
CoAP over WebSockets is only a transport whose message format is updated in an appendix. The document does not define anything about WebSocket itself.
AES-CCM is recommended only for encrypting serialized state in Security Considerations. The document does not address it in its own right.
The document is about CoAP, which is tagged directly. Constrained-node context alone does not make it about IoT in general.
CoAP over TCP is only a transport whose message format is updated. The document says nothing about TCP itself.

RFC8975.title: Network Coding for Satellite Systems
RFC8975.summary: An informational IRTF NWCRG document describing use cases and research challenges for applying network coding (linear packet combinations, FEC) above the network layer in satellite communication systems.

satellite.why: The whole document concerns satellite communication systems: their ground-segment topology and use cases such as gateway handover, hybrid access and varying channel conditions.
satellite.quote: The objective is to contribute to a larger deployment of Network Coding techniques in and above the network layer in satellite communication systems.

FEC.why: Network coding here means linear-combination packet erasure coding for loss recovery. The use cases are about repairing packet losses without retransmission.
FEC.quote: Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) (also called "Application-Level FEC") operates above the link layer and targets packet-loss recovery.

DTN.why: A research-challenge subsection covers network coding in the DTN stack and its integration with the IETF DTN architecture.
DTN.quote: Network Coding enables E2E reliable communications over a DTN with potential adaptive re-encoding

rejected.why: Section 3.2 is a reliable multicast use case, but it is one of six use cases and NORM and FLUTE are only mentioned for comparison.
Section 4.1 raises the interaction between coding and congestion control, but only briefly and it defers to another draft.
The DVB-based ground segment is only background topology. The document is not about IP over DVB links.
Service function chaining is mentioned in passing as a virtualization research challenge.
NORM is cited only as an alternative that is limited to block coding.
RFC 6363 and RFC 8681 are cited only as references. The document does not specify or profile FECFRAME.

gaps.name: Network coding
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for network coding in general (linear packet combinations, inter-flow and intra-flow coding). FEC is the closest fit.

RFC8976.title: Message Digest for DNS Zones
RFC8976.summary: Defines the ZONEMD DNS resource record, which carries a cryptographic message digest over a zone's data, with procedures for calculating and verifying it (SIMPLE scheme, SHA384/SHA512), and is meant to be used with DNSSEC.

DNS.why: The document defines a new DNS RR type (ZONEMD, type 63), including its wire and presentation formats and IANA registries. It also covers zone content handling by name servers.
DNS.quote: This document describes a protocol and new DNS Resource Record that provides a cryptographic message digest over DNS zone data at rest.

DNSSEC.why: Digest calculation and verification are closely tied to DNSSEC. The document covers placeholder records so NSEC/NSEC3 are correct, RRSIG handling, canonical ordering, and validation steps. Readers of DNSSEC would want it.
DNSSEC.quote: When used in combination with DNSSEC, ZONEMD allows recipients to verify the zone contents for data integrity and origin authenticity.

rejected.why: SHA-384 and SHA-512 are only the hash algorithms used. The document does not specify or analyse them.
TSIG and similar channel-security mechanisms are mentioned only as alternative approaches.
TLS-based zone transfer and DoH appear only in the discussion of alternative approaches.
ZONEMD acts like a checksum without DNSSEC, but this is a zone-level cryptographic digest rather than the Internet checksum topic.

RFC8977.title: Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) Query Parameters for Result Sorting and Paging
RFC8977.summary: Defines RDAP query parameters (count, sort, cursor) and response metadata elements (sorting_metadata, paging_metadata) so clients can control sorting and paging of large search result sets.

RDAP.why: The document extends RDAP search queries with new parameters and response elements, and registers RDAP extensions (paging, sorting).
RDAP.quote: This document describes RDAP query extensions that allow clients to specify their preferences for sorting and paging result sets.

rejected.why: Paging and sorting are REST API conventions, but the document is specific to RDAP queries rather than a general HTTP API convention.
JSONPath expressions are used to describe sorted fields and Appendix A lists operators, but the document does not specify JSONPath.
RDAP responses are JSON, which is only the encoding substrate here.
RFC 8288 links are used in the metadata, but only as a mechanism the document relies on.
jCard/vCard properties are referenced as sort fields only.
RDAP is the modern replacement, but the document does not cover WHOIS or legacy directory services.

RFC8978.title: Reaction of IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) to Flash-Renumbering Events
RFC8978.summary: Informational document describing how IPv6 SLAAC hosts keep using stale prefixes after flash-renumbering events (e.g., CE router reboot with DHCPv6-PD), and recommending operational mitigations such as stable prefixes and shorter PIO lifetimes.

SLAAC.why: The whole document analyses SLAAC behaviour (PIO lifetimes, RFC 4862 rules on valid lifetime) under flash renumbering and suggests SLAAC parameter tweaks.
SLAAC.quote: hosts on the local network may continue using stale prefixes for an unacceptably long time (on the order of several days), thus resulting in connectivity problems.

renumbering.why: Flash renumbering and the deprecation of old prefixes is the central subject, and the operational mitigations address renumbering in general.
renumbering.quote: there are several scenarios that may lead to the so-called "flash-renumbering" events, where a prefix employed by a network suddenly becomes invalid

DHCPv6.why: A dedicated section covers DHCPv6-PD and SLAAC interaction, including PIO lifetimes that outlast the PD lease, which RFC 8415 forbids.
DHCPv6.quote: the interaction between the two protocols is largely unspecified.

rejected.why: RFC 4861 RA/PIO defaults are discussed, but the document is about SLAAC behaviour, not about specifying or extending Neighbor Discovery.
CE routers are the main scenario, but the document is about SLAAC prefix lifetimes generally and not home network architecture.
Implied as the ancestor of SLAAC and renumbering, so it is not listed separately.

RFC8979.title: Subscriber and Performance Policy Identifier Context Headers in the Network Service Header (NSH)
RFC8979.summary: Defines two NSH variable-length Context Headers, Subscriber Identifier and Performance Policy Identifier, that carry opaque subscriber and performance policy identifiers to Service Functions for policy enforcement in an SFC domain.

SFC.why: The document specifies new NSH Context Headers, their structure, use and processing by NSH-aware nodes in service function chaining.
SFC.quote: These Variable-Length Context Headers can be carried in the Network Service Header (NSH) and are used to inform Service Functions (SFs)

rejected.why: Privacy is discussed (obfuscated, non-persistent identifiers), but only as a consideration of the header design, not the document's main subject.
The document registers two NSH metadata types, but this is boilerplate IANA Considerations and not the document's subject.
3GPP mobile networks are given as an applicable use case, but the document does not specify anything about cellular networks.
Performance policy identifiers relate to QoS, but the document defines opaque identifiers and does not specify a QoS architecture or signalling.
NAT appears only as motivation for carrying subscriber identity past a NAT boundary. The document is not about NAT.

RFC8980.title: Report from the IAB Workshop on Design Expectations vs. Deployment Reality in Protocol Development
RFC8980.summary: IAB workshop report summarizing discussions on how protocol deployments (DNS, email, web/CDN, BGP, IoT, etc.) diverged from design expectations, with focus on centralization, threat models and possible follow-up actions.

workshop reports.why: The document is a report of an IAB workshop, summarizing discussions and conclusions.
workshop reports.quote: The Design Expectations vs. Deployment Reality in Protocol Development Workshop was convened by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) in June 2019.

internet architecture.why: The workshop addresses architectural trends such as centralization and consolidation and their effect on the Internet's design principles.
internet architecture.quote: Document architectural principles, e.g., (re)application of the end-to-end principle.

privacy.why: Privacy and surveillance consequences of centralization, and the call for a new threat model, are substantial themes.
privacy.quote: concentrated, centralized deployment models present risks to user choice, privacy, and future protocol evolution.

rejected.why: DNS is one of several case studies of concentration, not the document's subject.
DoH is cited as an example of differing aspirations in standardization; the document does not address the protocol itself.
BGP is mentioned as a case study of limited deployment of improvements, not specified or analysed.
DNSSEC is compared to WebPKI as an adoption example only.
CDNs appear as an example of web centralization, not a subject of the report.
MUD is mentioned once as an example of user control for IoT.

gaps.name: Centralization / consolidation of Internet deployments
gaps.why: The central theme of the report; no taxonomy tag covers centralization or deployment-reality analysis beyond the general architecture tag.

RFC8981.title: Temporary Address Extensions for Stateless Address Autoconfiguration in IPv6
RFC8981.summary: RFC 8981 specifies temporary IPv6 addresses with randomized interface identifiers for SLAAC, to limit address-based activity correlation, and obsoletes RFC 4941.

SLAAC.why: The whole document extends SLAAC with temporary address generation, lifetimes, regeneration and DAD handling.
SLAAC.quote: This document describes an extension to IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration that causes hosts to generate temporary addresses with randomized interface identifiers

privacy.why: The motivation and problem statement are about privacy threats from stable identifiers, and the document is a privacy mitigation.
privacy.quote: Changing addresses over time limits the window of time during which eavesdroppers and other information collectors may trivially perform address-based network-activity correlation

rejected.why: The parent of SLAAC, so it is implied and not listed separately.
Router Advertisements and DAD are used as inputs, but the document is not about neighbor discovery.
HMAC-SHA-256 is only one suggested option for the PRF, not a subject of the document.
The document cites RFC 4086 for random number generation but does not specify randomness requirements.
Mentioned only as an example of a device affected by many addresses.
Mentioned only to forbid HMAC-MD5 and to note the flaw in RFC 4941.

RFC8982.title: Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) Partial Response
RFC8982.summary: RFC 8982 defines an RDAP query extension, the "fieldSet" parameter, with "subsetting_metadata" and basic field sets (id, brief, full), letting clients request partial responses from RDAP servers.

RDAP.why: The document extends RDAP with a new query parameter, response metadata, and an rdapConformance identifier, so it is squarely about RDAP.
RDAP.quote: This document describes an RDAP query extension that allows clients to specify their preference for obtaining a partial response.

rejected.why: Partial responses are a general REST concept, but the document specifies an RDAP-specific extension rather than general HTTP API conventions.
RDAP responses are JSON, but JSON is only the encoding substrate.
HTTP is the transport RDAP runs over; the document defines no new HTTP semantics.
Links per RFC 8288 are used in the metadata but are not the subject of the document.
WHOIS is only mentioned in passing as a comparison in the appendix.

RFC8983.title: Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) Notification Status Types for IPv4/IPv6 Coexistence
RFC8983.summary: RFC 8983 defines two new IKEv2 notification status types, IP4_ALLOWED and IP6_ALLOWED, which let a responder tell an initiator which address families it allows, and updates RFC 7296 with the rules for using them.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with new notify status types and updates RFC 7296 with initiator and responder behaviour for them.
IKE.quote: This document specifies new Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) notification status types to better manage IPv4 and IPv6 coexistence

IPv6 transition.why: The new notifications manage IPv4/IPv6 coexistence and dual-stack address assignment, so readers of the IPv4/IPv6 coexistence subject would want this RFC.
IPv6 transition.quote: allowing the responder to signal to the initiator which address families are allowed

rejected.why: 3GPP PDP-context cause codes are the motivating example. The document says the new types are not specific to 3GPP, and it defines nothing about cellular networks.
IKEv2 is the protocol being extended and is tagged as IKE. The document says nothing about ESP, AH or IPsec policy.
The registry update is boilerplate in the IANA Considerations section and is not the subject of the document.
The document only signals which address families are allowed. It does not specify IPv6 itself.
IKEv2 configuration attributes are used for address assignment, but the document does not cover DHCP.

RFC8984.title: JSCalendar: A JSON Representation of Calendar Data
RFC8984.summary: RFC 8984 defines JSCalendar, a JSON data model and representation for calendar events, tasks and groups, intended as a successor to iCalendar, with IANA registries and a media type.

JSCalendar.why: The document specifies the JSCalendar format itself, including its objects, properties, recurrence rules, and registries.
JSCalendar.quote: This specification defines a data model and JSON representation of calendar data that can be used for storage and data exchange in a calendaring and scheduling environment.

rejected.why: JSON (I-JSON) is only the encoding substrate. The document defines a calendar data model, not a JSON format in general.
iCalendar is the format JSCalendar aims to succeed and map from. It is not specified or extended here.
The document defines TimeZone objects, but only as a mapping of iCalendar VTIMEZONE inside JSCalendar. It does not address time zone data distribution.
The media type registration is IANA boilerplate for the format. The body does not address media type rules.
The more specific JSCalendar tag under calendaring already covers this document, so the parent is implied.

RFC8985.title: The RACK-TLP Loss Detection Algorithm for TCP
RFC8985.summary: Specifies RACK-TLP, a time-based TCP loss detection algorithm (Recent Acknowledgment plus Tail Loss Probe) using per-segment timestamps and SACK, as an alternative to DupAck counting.

TCP.why: The document specifies a new TCP loss detection and recovery algorithm, including timers, probes and SACK/DSACK use. It is a TCP extension.
TCP.quote: This document presents RACK-TLP, a TCP loss detection algorithm that improves upon the widely implemented duplicate acknowledgment (DupAck) counting approach

rejected.why: The document explicitly decouples loss detection from congestion control and does not modify it. It only discusses the interaction (Section 9.3).
NewReno is not discussed; the document is about SACK-based loss detection, not NewReno fast recovery.
QUIC is mentioned only in passing as another transport that could implement RACK-TLP (Section 9.5).
ECMP is mentioned only as a cause of packet reordering.

gaps.name: TCP loss detection and recovery (RACK, TLP, SACK-based)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for TCP loss recovery. TCP covers it, but readers looking for loss recovery algorithms would find it useful to have a specific tag.

RFC8986.title: Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) Network Programming
RFC8986.summary: Defines the SRv6 Network Programming framework: SID format (LOC:FUNCT:ARG), the base set of SRv6 endpoint behaviors (End, End.X, End.DT*, End.DX*, End.B6.*, flavors PSP/USP/USD), SR Policy headend behaviors (H.Encaps*), and the IANA SRv6 Endpoint Behaviors registry.

SRv6.why: The whole document specifies SRv6 SIDs, endpoint behaviors and headend behaviors, so SRv6 is the central subject.
SRv6.quote: This document defines the SRv6 Network Programming concept and specifies the base set of SRv6 behaviors that enables the creation of interoperable overlays with underlay optimization.

L3VPN.why: Several behaviors (End.DX4/DX6/DT4/DT6/DT46) are defined to realise BGP/MPLS L3VPN service over SRv6, equivalent to per-CE and per-VRF labels.
L3VPN.quote: One of the applications of the End.DT6 behavior is the L3VPNv6 use case where a FIB lookup in a specific tenant table at the egress PE is required.

EVPN.why: End.DX2, End.DX2V, End.DT2U and End.DT2M are defined for EVPN VPWS, flexible cross-connect, and BUM/E-Tree use cases.
EVPN.quote: One of the applications of the End.DT2U behavior is the EVPN Bridging Unicast [RFC7432].

rejected.why: SRv6 is the more specific child tag and it fits; the parent is implied.
IPv6 is the substrate carrying the SRH and SIDs; the document is about SRv6 behaviors, not IPv6 itself.
BGP and BGP-LS are only mentioned in a brief illustrative control-plane section whose specification is out of scope.
TI-LFA is only mentioned as an application of the USD flavor and H.Encaps, not specified here.
End.BM binds to an SR-MPLS policy, but the document is not about SR-MPLS itself.
The registry creation is boilerplate-level IANA considerations; the body is about SRv6 behaviors.

RFC8987.title: DHCPv6 Prefix Delegating Relay Requirements
RFC8987.summary: Specifies functional requirements for DHCPv6 relay agents acting as delegating relays with prefix delegation, addressing known operational problems (dropped messages, state loss, multiple prefixes, duplicate DUIDs, loops) and covering routing, service continuity and operations.

DHCPv6.why: The whole document specifies requirements for DHCPv6 relays doing prefix delegation (IA_PD, IAPREFIX, Leasequery use), so it belongs on the DHCPv6 page.
DHCPv6.quote: This document provides a set of requirements for devices implementing a relay function for use with prefix delegation.

rejected.why: DHCPv6 is the more specific child tag and is the one that applies.
The document is about DHCPv6 relays. IPv6 is only the network layer they run on, and DHCPv6 is the more specific tag.
Prefix delegation is covered by the DHCPv6 tag. The document does not address IP address architecture or allocation in its own right.
Requirement O-3 only recommends that some time synchronization protocol be used and does not specify NTP.
IPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations, as the way to secure traffic per RFC 8213.
This is a passing reference to RFC 4778 in Security Considerations, not a subject of the document.

RFC8989.title: Additional Criteria for Nominating Committee Eligibility
RFC8989.summary: Defines a fixed-duration process experiment under RFC 3933 that adds alternative eligibility paths (WG chair/secretary, RFC authorship, online attendance) for IETF NomCom volunteers and recall petition signatories, temporarily varying RFC 8713.

NomCom.why: The whole document modifies NomCom volunteer eligibility criteria, and thereby recall petition eligibility, which is the NomCom procedures subject.
NomCom.quote: temporarily updates the criteria for qualifying volunteers to participate in the IETF Nominating Committee

rejected.why: NomCom is the more specific child tag and the document is about NomCom eligibility, so the parent is implied.
Fewer face-to-face meetings for sustainability is mentioned only as motivation, not as the subject.
RFC authorship counts as an eligibility criterion, but the document does not address RFC format, style or publication.

gaps.name: IETF process experiments (RFC 3933)
gaps.why: The document is a process experiment with a defined term and evaluation, and no taxonomy tag covers process experiments specifically. IETF process covers it only broadly.

RFC8990.title: GeneRic Autonomic Signaling Protocol (GRASP)
RFC8990.summary: Specifies GRASP, a generic signaling protocol for autonomic nodes and Autonomic Service Agents to discover peers, synchronize state (including flooding), and negotiate parameters, with CBOR/CDDL message formats and an external security substrate such as the ACP.

autonomic networking.why: GRASP is the core signaling protocol of the Autonomic Networking Infrastructure, defined for ASAs. The document is about autonomic networking.
autonomic networking.quote: enables autonomic nodes and Autonomic Service Agents to dynamically discover peers, to synchronize state with each other, and to negotiate parameter settings with each other

rejected.why: CBOR is only the encoding for messages. The document defines nothing new about CBOR.
CDDL is only used to describe the message syntax. The document does not specify CDDL.
GRASP discovery is for objectives and peers, and the document is about the whole protocol. The autonomic networking tag already covers it. SLP and DNS-SD appear only in the comparison appendix.
TCP and UDP are only the transports GRASP uses.
GRASP specifies no security of its own and relies on the ACP, described in another document.
The IANA registries and assignments are boilerplate here, not the subject of the document.

RFC8991.title: GeneRic Autonomic Signaling Protocol Application Program Interface (GRASP API)
RFC8991.summary: Conceptual API for Autonomic Service Agents to call a GRASP protocol module, covering registration, discovery, negotiation, synchronization and flooding, asynchronous models, data structures and error codes.

autonomic networking.why: The document defines the API by which autonomic service agents use GRASP, the signalling protocol of the autonomic networking framework (ASA, ACP). No GRASP-specific tag exists, so the autonomic networking topic is the best fit.
autonomic networking.quote: Such an API is needed for Autonomic Service Agents (ASAs) calling the GRASP protocol module to exchange Autonomic Network messages with other ASAs.

rejected.why: CBOR only encodes objective values and GRASP messages. The document does not specify or extend it.
CDDL is cited only as the data definition language for GRASP. The document does not define anything about it.
BRSKI is mentioned only as an autonomic infrastructure component in the introduction and references.
The API is for autonomic agents, not a sockets API extension, though it is an application programming interface.
The API has no explicit security features. It relies on the ACP trust model, and the security considerations are boilerplate.

gaps.name: GRASP (GeneRic Autonomic Signaling Protocol)
gaps.why: The document is about the API for GRASP, but the taxonomy has no GRASP tag. Only the broader autonomic networking topic is available.

RFC8992.title: Autonomic IPv6 Edge Prefix Management in Large-Scale Networks
RFC8992.summary: Informational document defining two GRASP objectives (PrefixManager and PrefixManager.Params) for autonomic IPv6 edge prefix management in large ISP networks, with an IPv4 extension, to validate the Autonomic Networking Infrastructure design.

autonomic networking.why: The document is a use case of the Autonomic Networking Infrastructure, defining GRASP objectives and PrefixManager ASA behaviour, and validating ANI components.
autonomic networking.quote: This document defines two autonomic technical objectives for IPv6 prefix management at the edge of large-scale ISP networks

addressing.why: The subject matter is IP prefix allocation and delegation, including pool management and aggregation, with an IPv4 extension.
addressing.quote: how to make IPv6 prefix management at the edges of large-scale networks as autonomic as possible

rejected.why: DHCPv6-PD is only compared against and used as a complement; the document does not specify or extend it.
CBOR and CDDL are only the encoding for the objective definitions.
Only referenced as the secure bootstrap mechanism that the devices rely on.
IPv6 is the address family being managed, but the document is not about the IPv6 protocol itself; addressing is the more specific fit.
YANG is mentioned only as an alternative way to express the parameters.
The ancestor is implied if a child applies, and the document is not about general network management.

gaps.name: Autonomic Networking / GRASP (ANIMA)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an 'autonomic networking' topic only under network management, and my 'autonomic networking' tag id may not exist exactly as written. GRASP itself has no tech tag, so documents about it and its objectives have no precise home.

RFC8993.title: A Reference Model for Autonomic Networking
RFC8993.summary: RFC 8993 defines a reference model for Autonomic Networking in managed networks, describing the autonomic node, the Autonomic Networking Infrastructure (ANI), its security/trust bootstrapping, Autonomic Service Agents, and management and coordination aspects.

autonomic networking.why: The whole document is the architectural reference model for autonomic networking: nodes, ANI, ASAs, and coordination.
autonomic networking.quote: This document describes a reference model for Autonomic Networking for managed networks.

rejected.why: BRSKI is referenced for enrollment (RFC 8995) but is specified elsewhere; this document only summarizes its role.
The PKI/domain certificate and MASA are described briefly as trust infrastructure, but details are defined in BRSKI; not a substantial part of the document.
SNMP and NETCONF are mentioned only as traditional management methods that may coexist with autonomic functions.
Intent is discussed as a high-level policy concept but only as a research topic in a short section.
The ACP is described as an overlay, but the document explicitly says the term is not used in the common data-plane virtualization sense.

gaps.name: GRASP (GeneRic Autonomic Signaling Protocol) / ACP (Autonomic Control Plane)
gaps.why: The document is built around the ANI, GRASP, and ACP, but the taxonomy only has an 'autonomic networking' topic under network management (and BRSKI); no specific tags for GRASP or ACP.

RFC8994.title: An Autonomic Control Plane (ACP)
RFC8994.summary: RFC 8994 specifies the Autonomic Control Plane (ACP), a self-creating, certificate-authenticated, hop-by-hop encrypted IPv6 overlay (using GRASP discovery, IPsec/DTLS secure channels, ULA addressing and RPL routing) serving as a virtual out-of-band channel for autonomic functions and OAM.

autonomic networking.why: The document defines the ACP, the core infrastructure of the ANIMA autonomic networking work.
autonomic networking.quote: Autonomic functions need a control plane to communicate, which depends on some addressing and routing.

RFC8995.title: Bootstrapping Remote Secure Key Infrastructure (BRSKI)
RFC8995.summary: RFC 8995 specifies BRSKI, a protocol for zero-touch secure bootstrapping of new devices (pledges) using manufacturer IDevID certificates, a join proxy, a domain registrar and MASA-issued vouchers, with optional EST enrollment, aimed at the Autonomic Control Plane.

BRSKI.why: The document defines the BRSKI protocol: pledge, join proxy, registrar, MASA, voucher-request, audit-log and status telemetry.
BRSKI.quote: The Bootstrapping Remote Secure Key Infrastructure (BRSKI) protocol provides a solution for secure zero-touch (automated) bootstrap of new (unconfigured) devices

rejected.why: TLS is the substrate for the BRSKI-EST and BRSKI-MASA connections; the document defines nothing new about TLS.
Defines a MASA URL certificate extension and relies on IDevID certificates, but the document is about bootstrapping rather than certificate profiles.
Defines a voucher-request YANG module, but it is a small part; the voucher format is in RFC 8366.
HTTP is only the transport for the REST operations.
The result is a bootstrapped key infrastructure, but the document is about the BRSKI bootstrap protocol, which is covered by the more specific BRSKI tag.
mDNS/DNS-SD proxy discovery is only a non-normative appendix option.

gaps.name: EST (Enrollment over Secure Transport) and voucher artifacts
gaps.why: BRSKI extends EST and relies on vouchers, but the taxonomy has no tag for EST here beyond the BRSKI entry, so readers of those subjects won't find it.

RFC8996.title: Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1
RFC8996.summary: BCP document that formally deprecates TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 and DTLS 1.0, forbids negotiating them, updates RFC 7525 and many other RFCs that referenced those versions, and marks the older RFCs Historic.

TLS.why: The document's whole purpose is to deprecate TLS 1.0 and 1.1 and set deployment guidance (minimum TLS 1.2), updating the TLS BCP 195.
TLS.quote: TLS 1.0 MUST NOT be used.  Negotiation of TLS 1.0 from any version of TLS MUST NOT be permitted.

DTLS.why: DTLS 1.0 is deprecated alongside TLS and RFC 6347 is updated to forbid negotiating it, which is a substantial part of the document.
DTLS.quote: Implementations MUST NOT negotiate DTLS version 1.0 [RFC4347] [RFC6347].

rejected.why: SHA-1 weakness is cited as a reason in Section 3, but the document is not about the SHA family itself.
Only boilerplate mention; the document has no IANA actions.
SIP RFCs appear in the list of updated RFCs, but the document does not address SIP.
It marks RFCs Historic and obsoletes others, but this is a technical deprecation, not process.

RFC8997.title: Deprecation of TLS 1.1 for Email Submission and Access
RFC8997.summary: RFC 8997 updates RFC 8314 to raise the minimum TLS version for email submission and access between MUAs and servers from TLS 1.1 to TLS 1.2, following the deprecation of TLS 1.0/1.1.

TLS.why: The document sets TLS version requirements (minimum TLS 1.2) and deprecates TLS 1.1 for email use, which is TLS deployment guidance.
TLS.quote: MUAs MUST implement TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] or later, e.g., TLS 1.3 [RFC8446].

email.why: It updates RFC 8314's recommendations for email submission and access (MUA to submission/access servers), so email readers would expect it.
email.quote: the use of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol to provide confidentiality of email between a Mail User Agent (MUA) and a Mail Submission Server or Mail Access Server

rejected.why: Submission is covered only through RFC 8314's general text; the document specifies no SMTP-specific behaviour.
Mail access is mentioned generically; nothing IMAP-specific is defined.
Mail access is mentioned generically; nothing POP3-specific is defined.
The more specific TLS tag already applies.

RFC8998.title: ShangMi (SM) Cipher Suites for TLS 1.3
RFC8998.summary: Specifies two TLS 1.3 cipher suites (SM4-GCM/CCM with SM3), the SM2 signature scheme and SM2 curve group for TLS 1.3, as a non-IETF-endorsed profile for use in China.

TLS.why: Defines new TLS 1.3 cipher suites, signature scheme and named group, and a handshake profile with registrations in TLS registries.
TLS.quote: This document specifies how to use the ShangMi (SM) cryptographic algorithms with Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol version 1.3.

cryptography.why: Document defines use of the SM2/SM3/SM4 national algorithms, including AEAD_SM4_GCM and AEAD_SM4_CCM definitions and test vectors. No specific SM tag exists, so the parent topic fits.
cryptography.quote: SM2 for authentication, SM4 for encryption, and SM3 as the hash function.

rejected.why: SM2 curve parameters are given, but the document is about the SM suite as a whole, and the cryptography tag already covers it.
RFC 5116 style and GCM/CCM modes are borrowed, but SM4 is used instead of AES.
Certificate requirements are only a few profile rules, not a substantial subject.
The IANA table marks the suites DTLS-OK as No, so DTLS is not addressed.
The registrations are boilerplate IANA Considerations, not the main body.

gaps.name: ShangMi (SM) algorithms: SM2, SM3, SM4
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for Chinese national cryptographic algorithms, so readers of that subject would find no page; the only fit is the generic cryptography topic.

RFC8999.title: Version-Independent Properties of QUIC
RFC8999.summary: RFC 8999 defines the version-independent invariant properties of the QUIC transport protocol: long and short header layouts, connection IDs, the Version field, and Version Negotiation packets.

QUIC.why: The whole document specifies the invariant packet format, connection ID and version negotiation behaviour of QUIC, so it belongs on the QUIC page.
QUIC.quote: This document defines the properties of the QUIC transport protocol that are common to all versions of the protocol.

rejected.why: QUIC runs over UDP datagrams, but UDP is only the substrate and the document defines nothing new about UDP.
TLS is mentioned only in Appendix A as an assumption that may not hold for all QUIC versions. The document is not about TLS.
The document describes QUIC's own invariants. It does not define a binding of another protocol onto a transport.

RFC9000.title: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport
RFC9000.summary: RFC 9000 specifies the core QUIC version 1 transport protocol: streams, flow control, connections, handshake, address and path validation, connection migration, termination, packet and frame formats, and error codes.

QUIC.why: The document is the core specification of the QUIC transport protocol.
QUIC.quote: QUIC is a secure general-purpose transport protocol.  This document defines version 1 of QUIC

rejected.why: TLS is integrated via the companion QUIC-TLS document; this RFC only uses it for the handshake.
UDP is only the substrate carrying QUIC packets.
Congestion control and loss detection are in QUIC-RECOVERY; this document only references them.
ECN support and validation is a subsection of QUIC, not the subject of the document.
Datagram size and DPLPMTUD are one section applying existing mechanisms to QUIC.
HTTP/3 is an application protocol over QUIC, mentioned only incidentally.

RFC9001.title: Using TLS to Secure QUIC
RFC9001.summary: RFC 9001 specifies how TLS 1.3 is used to secure QUIC: carrying TLS handshake messages in CRYPTO frames, deriving packet and header protection keys, key update, 0-RTT handling, AEAD usage limits, and QUIC-specific TLS adjustments.

QUIC.why: The document specifies QUIC's security: packet protection, header protection, key update, Initial secrets and Retry integrity. QUIC readers need it.
QUIC.quote: This document describes how QUIC [QUIC-TRANSPORT] is secured using TLS [TLS13].

TLS.why: It defines a new TLS extension and QUIC-specific TLS adjustments (no EndOfEarlyData, no middlebox compatibility mode, no post-handshake auth, no KeyUpdate), so it is about TLS usage and extensions.
TLS.quote: The quic_transport_parameters extension is carried in the ClientHello and the EncryptedExtensions messages during the handshake.

rejected.why: AES is used for header protection and AEAD, but only as a primitive; the document is not about AES.
ChaCha20-Poly1305 header protection is defined, but it is one of the cipher suites and does not make the document about ChaCha20.
DTLS is mentioned only in a reference title. It is not the subject.
Considered because TLS is carried over QUIC, but this is a security integration and is covered by the QUIC and TLS tags.
Referenced only as an example of a 0-RTT profile. It is not the subject.
HKDF is used for key derivation, but there is no tag for HKDF and the document is not about HMAC.

RFC9002.title: QUIC Loss Detection and Congestion Control
RFC9002.summary: Specifies QUIC's loss detection (RTT estimation, packet/time thresholds, probe timeout) and a NewReno-style congestion controller with persistent congestion, ECN response and pacing.

QUIC.why: The whole document specifies QUIC's loss recovery and congestion control machinery, so QUIC readers need it.
QUIC.quote: This document describes loss detection and congestion control mechanisms for QUIC.

congestion control.why: Defines slow start, recovery, congestion avoidance, persistent congestion, and pacing for QUIC.
congestion control.quote: This document specifies a sender-side congestion controller for QUIC similar to TCP NewReno [RFC6582].

NewReno.why: The specified controller is a NewReno-style algorithm with slow start, recovery period and congestion avoidance states.
NewReno.quote: The NewReno congestion controller described in this document has three distinct states, as shown in Figure 1.

ECN.why: Specifies the endpoint's congestion response to ECN-CE counts and discusses ECN misreporting.
ECN.quote: QUIC treats a Congestion Experienced (CE) codepoint in the IP header as a signal of congestion.

rejected.why: Used only as a comparison point for the algorithms; the document does not specify or extend TCP.
Mentioned only as an alternative a sender may choose; not specified.
Substrate for QUIC only.
Referenced for key discarding and handshake confirmation only; not the subject.

RFC9003.title: Extended BGP Administrative Shutdown Communication
RFC9003.summary: Extends the BGP Cease NOTIFICATION Administrative Shutdown/Reset subcodes so a UTF-8 Shutdown Communication of up to 255 octets can be sent, updating RFC 4486 and obsoleting RFC 8203.

BGP.why: The document extends the BGP Cease NOTIFICATION message with a shutdown communication field, which is a BGP protocol extension and operational mechanism.
BGP.quote: specifying a mechanism to transmit a short free-form UTF-8 [RFC3629] message as part of a Cease NOTIFICATION message [RFC4271]

rejected.why: UTF-8 is only the encoding of the message string. The document does not define or profile UTF-8 itself.
Syslog is mentioned only as one way an implementation may report received messages. The document does not specify or extend it.
Privacy appears only as a brief data-minimization note in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
The document cites Unicode security issues only in Security Considerations and in the UTF-8 requirement. It is not about Unicode usage.

RFC9004.title: Updates for the Back-to-Back Frame Benchmark in RFC 2544
RFC9004.summary: RFC 9004 updates the Back-to-Back Frame benchmark procedure of RFC 2544, adding a corrected DUT buffer-time calculation, search algorithm requirements, repetition and reporting rules for lab benchmarking of network devices.

benchmarking.why: The document is a BMWG benchmarking methodology update defining test procedure, calculations and reporting for the Back-to-Back Frames benchmark.
benchmarking.quote: This memo updates the procedures of the test to measure the Back-to-Back Frames benchmark of RFC 2544, based on further experience.

rejected.why: The document is about lab benchmarking of devices under test, which is covered by the more specific benchmarking tag, not live network performance metrics.
RFC 5180 is only mentioned in the introduction as an implicit update to RFC 2544. The document does not address IPv6.
Link-layer technology is only used to compute the Max Theoretical Frame Rate. The document is not about Ethernet.
NFV and virtual switch (VSPERF) testing is only the context for the experience that motivated the update. The document does not address SDN.

RFC9005.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extension for Associating Policies and Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC9005.summary: RFC 9005 defines a new PCEP Policy Association Type, with a POLICY-PARAMETERS-TLV, so that PCEP peers can associate LSPs with operator-configured policies through the generic ASSOCIATION object.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP by adding a new Association Type, a new TLV and new error values, so it is about PCE and PCEP.
PCE.quote: This document specifies a PCEP extension to associate one or more LSPs with policies using the generic association mechanism.

rejected.why: The LSPs are the objects being grouped, but the document does not specify MPLS itself.
RSVP-TE is only mentioned as one way the LSPs may be signalled.
Segment routing is only mentioned as another way the LSPs may be set up.
TLS is only recommended in the Security Considerations to secure the PCEP session.
Policy definitions are explicitly out of scope; the document only carries an association to a policy.
The PCEP YANG module is only referenced under Manageability Considerations.

RFC9006.title: TCP Usage Guidance in the Internet of Things (IoT)
RFC9006.summary: Informational guidance for implementing and using TCP on constrained IoT devices in Constrained-Node Networks, covering MSS, ECN, single-MSS stacks, options, delayed ACKs, RTO, initial window, connection management, and a survey of small TCP stacks.

TCP.why: The whole document is about TCP implementation choices (options, delayed ACKs, RTO, IW, SACK, TFO) and usage in constrained environments.
TCP.quote: This document provides guidance on how to implement and use the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) in Constrained-Node Networks (CNNs)

IoT.why: Document targets Constrained-Node Networks and IoT devices, with IoT-specific traffic patterns and device constraints; readers of IoT guidance would want it.
IoT.quote: Such environments require a lightweight TCP implementation and may not make use of optional functionality.

rejected.why: ECN is discussed in one subsection as a recommended feature but is not the document's subject.
CoAP over TCP is mentioned as an example use case, not specified or extended here.
Congestion control topics are covered as TCP features; the more specific TCP tag fits and no congestion-control mechanism is defined.
6LoWPAN is mentioned for MTU context only.
TLS is only recommended in Security Considerations as a substrate.
Middlebox NAT timeouts are discussed only as a connection lifetime concern.

RFC9007.title: Handling Message Disposition Notification with the JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP)
RFC9007.summary: Defines a JMAP data model and the MDN/send and MDN/parse methods for sending and parsing Message Disposition Notifications (read receipts) for email, plus an "mdn" capability and a new error code.

JMAP.why: The document extends JMAP for Mail with a new capability, MDN object type, and the MDN/send and MDN/parse methods.
JMAP.quote: This document specifies a data model for handling Message Disposition Notifications (MDNs) (see RFC 8098) in the JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP)

rejected.why: JMAP is the more specific tag; the document is about the JMAP data model. Email is the subject of the data, but the JMAP tag covers it.
MDN headers like Message-ID are referenced, but the document does not specify message format.
JSON is only the encoding used by JMAP, not the subject.
Only the $mdnsent keyword case-sensitivity is mentioned; not about IMAP.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate for the capability and error code.

gaps.name: Message Disposition Notification (MDN)
gaps.why: The document is about handling MDNs (read receipts) in JMAP, but the taxonomy has no MDN tag; it is only loosely covered by email. JMAP is also absent from the taxonomy, so the tag above is not valid.

RFC9008.title: Using RPI Option Type, Routing Header for Source Routes, and IPv6-in-IPv6 Encapsulation in the RPL Data Plane
RFC9008.summary: RFC 9008 analyzes the 24 RPL data-plane flows in Storing and Non-Storing modes to determine when the RPI option, RH3 source routing header, and IPv6-in-IPv6 encapsulation are required, and updates RFC 6553 (new RPI Option Type 0x23), RFC 6550 (DODAG Configuration flag) and RFC 8138.

RPL.why: The document specifies and updates RPL data-plane behaviour: RPI option type, DIO DODAG Configuration flag, and per-flow header use in Storing and Non-Storing modes.
RPL.quote: This document updates RFC 6553 by adding a change to the RPI Option Type.

tunneling.why: A large part of the analysis is when IPv6-in-IPv6 encapsulation is needed and to whom it is addressed; this is part of the tunnelling subject, though IPv6 tunnelling has no more specific tag.
tunneling.quote: Most of the use cases described herein require the use of IPv6-in-IPv6 packet encapsulation.

rejected.why: RFC 8138 compression is referenced and updated for decompression, but the document is about RPL data-plane headers, not 6LoWPAN itself.
Relies on RFC 8200 extension header rules, but does not specify IPv6 itself.
Encapsulation is used throughout, but it is IPv6-in-IPv6 analysis in an RPL context, not a spec of IP-in-IP; the tunneling parent fits better and is only a secondary tag.
IANA actions are boilerplate for this document.
RFC 6040 is only mentioned in one sentence.
Mentioned in a single table note only.

RFC9009.title: Efficient Route Invalidation
RFC9009.summary: RFC 9009 describes problems with RPL's No-Path DAO route invalidation in Storing mode and specifies a new Destination Cleanup Object (DCO) message, with DCO-ACK and a Transit Information 'I' flag, for proactive downstream route invalidation.

RPL.why: The document extends RPL with a new control message (DCO/DCO-ACK), a new Transit Information flag, and new rules for route invalidation in Storing mode.
RPL.quote: this document specifies a new proactive route invalidation message called the "Destination Cleanup Object" (DCO), which fulfills requirements for optimized route invalidation messaging.

rejected.why: 6LoWPAN terms (6LR, 6LBR) and the EARO status value are only referenced; the document does not specify anything about 6LoWPAN itself.
LLNs are the setting, but the document is about RPL route invalidation. The RPL tag is the more specific fit.
RPL control messages are carried as ICMPv6 messages, but that is only the substrate and the document defines nothing new about ICMP.
The IANA registries are boilerplate here and are not the main body of the document.

RFC9010.title: Routing for RPL (Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks) Leaves
RFC9010.summary: RFC 9010 specifies how a 6LoWPAN ND router (6LR) injects RPL routes on behalf of RPL-unaware leaf hosts, with root-proxied EDAR/EDAC, updated RPL Target option, DODAG Configuration flag, RPL Status, and multicast via MLD.

RPL.why: The document updates RFC 6550 (RPL Target option, DODAG Configuration option, Status) and defines RPL-unaware-leaf route injection, DAO/DCO operation.
RPL.quote: This document specifies how the router injects the host routes in the RPL domain on behalf of the RUL.

6LoWPAN.why: It updates RFC 6775 and RFC 8505 (ARO/EARO status range, R flag in NA) and relies on 6LoWPAN ND registration as the host-to-router interface; readers of 6LoWPAN ND need it.
6LoWPAN.quote: Using the 6LoWPAN ND Address Registration mechanism, the RUL signals that the router must inject a host route for the Registered Address.

rejected.why: Classical IPv6 ND is background; the document is about 6LoWPAN ND registration, which falls under the 6LoWPAN tag.
MLDv2 is proxied in Section 10 but unchanged ('This specification does not change MLD'); it is a mechanism used, not the subject.
Mentioned only as a reason to use the registered 6LR; not specified or extended here.
IANA registry changes are boilerplate-like and secondary to the protocol content.
Not relevant; 6LoRH compression appears only in the appendix example.
IPv6 is the substrate; nothing new about IPv6 itself is specified.

RFC9011.title: Static Context Header Compression and Fragmentation (SCHC) over LoRaWAN
RFC9011.summary: Defines a profile of SCHC (RFC 8724) header compression and fragmentation for LoRaWAN, specifying RuleID/FPort mapping, IID computation, fragmentation modes, parameters, timers and message formats.

LoRaWAN.why: The document is the SCHC adaptation over LoRaWAN, specifying how IPv6 is carried over LoRaWAN using FPort, device classes and addressing.
LoRaWAN.quote: This document defines a profile of SCHC (RFC 8724) for use in LoRaWAN networks and provides elements such as efficient parameterization and modes of operation.

SCHC.why: It profiles SCHC compression and fragmentation (ACK-on-Error uplink, ACK-Always downlink, tile sizes, timers, formats), so SCHC readers need it.
SCHC.quote: This document describes the parameters and modes of operation when SCHC is used over LoRaWAN networks.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the payload being compressed; the document does not specify IPv6 itself. IID computation is a minor part.
AES-128 CMAC is used only for IID derivation and LoRaWAN encryption; the document is not about the cipher.
LPWAN is the parent of SCHC and LoRaWAN; ancestors are implied by the child tag.
A topic tag is not given directly when a technology tag under it (SCHC) is chosen.
Multicast downlink is mentioned briefly as a No-ACK mode, but it is not a substantial subject.

RFC9012.title: The BGP Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute
RFC9012.summary: RFC 9012 defines the BGP Tunnel Encapsulation path attribute (replacing RFC 5512/5566), with sub-TLV encodings for tunnel types (VXLAN, NVGRE, L2TPv3, GRE, MPLS-in-GRE), tunnel selection procedures, extended communities, and error handling.

BGP.why: The document specifies a new BGP path attribute, its TLVs, extended communities, decision-process impact, and error handling.
BGP.quote: This document defines a BGP path attribute known as the "Tunnel Encapsulation attribute", which can be used with BGP UPDATEs of various Subsequent Address Family Identifiers

tunneling.why: Substantial part of the document concerns signalling tunnel types and building encapsulation headers (GRE, L2TPv3, IP-in-IP, MPLS-in-UDP).
tunneling.quote: provide information needed to create tunnels and their corresponding encapsulation headers

overlay networks.why: Defines VXLAN and NVGRE Encapsulation sub-TLVs and VNI/VSID handling procedures, relevant to network virtualization overlay readers.
overlay networks.quote: Defining Encapsulation sub-TLVs for a number of tunnel types not discussed in [RFC5512]: Virtual eXtensible Local Area Network (VXLAN)

rejected.why: MPLS label stack and embedded labels are handled via sub-TLVs, but the document is not about MPLS itself.
EVPN is one of the AFI/SAFIs that may carry the attribute and Appendix A touches RFC 8365, but it is not the subject.
The Prefix-SID sub-TLV reuses RFC 8669 content, only a small part of the document.
GRE encapsulation sub-TLV is defined, but GRE is a tunnel type signalled, not specified here.
L2TPv3 sub-TLV only signals session ID and cookie; L2TP is not specified.
Only mentioned as deprecated code points from RFC 5566.

RFC9013.title: OSPF Advertisement of Tunnel Encapsulations
RFC9013.summary: Defines a new OSPF Router Information LSA TLV (Tunnel Encapsulations) and sub-TLVs for advertising the tunnel types a router can decapsulate, for both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF (v2 and v3) with a new RI LSA TLV and a new sub-TLV registry.
OSPF.quote: defines how to advertise, in OSPF Router Information Link State Advertisements (LSAs), the list of tunnel encapsulations supported by the tunnel decapsulator

rejected.why: Applies to both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 equally; it is not specific to OSPFv3, so the parent OSPF tag fits.
Tunnel types and several sub-TLVs are reused from the BGP Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute (RFC 9012), but the document does not specify BGP.
Tunnels are the subject of advertisement, but the document defines no tunnel encapsulation itself, only capability signalling in OSPF.
Softwire mesh is cited as a use case and for security considerations only.
RLFA repair tunnels are mentioned only as one motivating example.

RFC9014.title: Interconnect Solution for Ethernet VPN (EVPN) Overlay Networks
RFC9014.summary: Specifies data center interconnect (DCI) solutions using gateways to connect EVPN-based network virtualization overlays to WAN L2VPNs (VPLS, PBB-VPLS, EVPN, PBB-EVPN), defining the Interconnect Ethernet Segment, gateway EVPN route processing and Unknown MAC Route use.

EVPN.why: The document extends EVPN procedures (I-ES, UMR, route processing on GWs) for DC interconnect, so it is about EVPN.
EVPN.quote: this document describes how EVPN routes are processed on Gateways (GWs) that interconnect EVPN-Overlay and EVPN-MPLS networks, as well as the Interconnect Ethernet Segment (I-ES), to provide multihoming.

VPLS.why: Substantial sections specify interconnecting EVPN-overlay with VPLS and PBB-VPLS WANs, including PW handling and multihoming.
VPLS.quote: VPLS Interconnect for EVPN-Overlay Networks

rejected.why: VXLAN is a data plane encapsulation used in the overlay and VNI translation, not the subject of the document.
Overlays are the networks being interconnected, but the document's subject is the EVPN interconnect solution; the overlay encapsulations are only used.
Considered as parent of VPLS/EVPN, but a more specific child tag fits, so parent is implied.
BGP is the control plane carrying EVPN routes but is not specified or extended here.
MPLS is a substrate for PWs and EVPN-MPLS, not the subject.
PWs are used in the handoff and VPLS interconnect but the document does not specify pseudowire emulation itself.

gaps.name: Data Center Interconnect (DCI)
gaps.why: The document's central subject is DCI with gateways; the taxonomy has only a general 'data center networking' tag focused on routing and address resolution within the data center.

RFC9015.title: BGP Control Plane for the Network Service Header in Service Function Chaining
RFC9015.summary: RFC 9015 defines a BGP control plane for service function chaining: a new SFC AFI/SAFI with Service Function Instance and Service Function Path routes, the SFP attribute, and related extended communities, used with the NSH.

SFC.why: The whole document specifies a control plane for service function chaining and the NSH SPI/SI, including SFIR, SFPR, classifier and SFF operation.
SFC.quote: This document describes the use of BGP as a control plane for networks that support service function chaining.

BGP.why: It extends BGP with a new AFI/SAFI, a new path attribute (SFP attribute), extended communities and a registry set. Readers of BGP would want it.
BGP.quote: The document introduces a new BGP address family called the "Service Function Chain (SFC) Address Family Identifier / Subsequent Address Family Identifier"

BGP flowspec.why: A section defines a new BGP FlowSpec action extended community to instruct SFC classifiers.
BGP flowspec.quote: defining a new action Extended Community called "Flow Specification for SFC Classifiers", identified by the value 0x0d.

rejected.why: MPLS label stacks are an optional data-plane representation of SPI/SI, not the subject.
RTs and RDs are borrowed from BGP/MPLS VPNs, but the document is not about VPN service.
It defines extended communities only as a mechanism; the document is not about communities in general.
NAT64 appears only as example service function types in the registry.

RFC9016.title: Flow and Service Information Model for Deterministic Networking (DetNet)
RFC9016.summary: Informational DetNet document defining the flow and service information model (App-flow, DetNet flow and service attributes, and join/leave/modify operations) for IP and MPLS DetNet data planes.

DetNet.why: The whole document specifies the information model for DetNet flows and services, including attributes, requirements and operations.
DetNet.quote: This document describes the flow and service information model for Deterministic Networking (DetNet). These models are defined for IP and MPLS DetNet data planes.

rejected.why: DetNet MPLS is one of the data planes the model covers, but the document only lists S-Label and F-Label stack identification attributes. It does not specify MPLS.
The document says it does not specify a data model. The DetNet YANG model is in a separate draft.
Resource allocation is mentioned only in passing. The document is an information model and does not cover traffic engineering mechanisms.
TSN and IEEE 802.1Qcc are used as the basis for the model, but the document does not address IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
IP flow identification fields come from RFC 8939 and are only listed as attributes. The document does not specify IP.

RFC9017.title: Special-Purpose Label Terminology
RFC9017.summary: RFC 9017 recommends terminology for MPLS Special-Purpose Labels (base, extended, composite SPLs), renames the IANA registry accordingly, and clarifies handling of the Entropy Label Indicator when it follows the Extension Label, updating RFCs 3032 and 7274.

MPLS.why: The document is about MPLS special-purpose label terminology and label-stack handling (XL, ELI), updating MPLS label stack encoding RFCs 3032 and 7274.
MPLS.quote: This document discusses and recommends terminology that may be used when MPLS Special-Purpose Labels (SPLs) are specified and documented.

rejected.why: It renames one IANA registry, but the subject is MPLS label terminology, not IANA registry guidance generally; the IANA section is boilerplate-like.
The document is terminology, but specific to MPLS SPLs; the MPLS tag fits the subject better. The terminology topic is for general glossaries and requirements language.
Mentioned only to state that the GMPLS Special-Purpose Generalized Label Values registry is unchanged.
RFC 8595 is cited only as the first user of eSPLs, as background.

RFC9018.title: Interoperable Domain Name System (DNS) Server Cookies
RFC9018.summary: RFC 9018 updates RFC 7873 to specify an interoperable construction of DNS Server Cookies (SipHash-2-4 based, versioned format), Client Cookie construction guidance, Server Secret rollover, and creates an IANA registry of Server Cookie methods.

EDNS.why: DNS Cookies are an EDNS(0) option (the COOKIE option). The document specifies how to construct Client and Server Cookies carried in that option, and no more specific DNS tag fits.
EDNS.quote: DNS Cookies, as specified in [RFC7873], are a lightweight DNS transaction security mechanism

rejected.why: EDNS is the more specific child that fits the COOKIE option, so the parent is implied.
The Server Cookie is a MAC, but it is built with SipHash-2-4, not HMAC.
Interoperability across anycast server sets is the motivation. The document does not address anycast addressing or operation itself.
The IANA registry it creates is boilerplate-level apparatus for the main subject. The document is not about IANA guidance.
It is only mentioned as another DNS security feature. The document is not about DNSSEC.
Server clock synchronisation is mentioned only as a requirement in the security considerations.

gaps.name: DNS Cookies
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no DNS Cookies tag. EDNS is the closest, but readers looking for DNS Cookies would want a dedicated tag.

RFC9019.title: A Firmware Update Architecture for Internet of Things
RFC9019.summary: RFC 9019 defines terminology and an architecture for secure firmware updates of IoT devices, covering the roles, bootloader integration, device types, and the motivation for a transport-agnostic manifest format (SUIT).

firmware update.why: The whole document is the SUIT firmware update architecture for IoT: stakeholders, firmware consumer, status tracker, bootloader, manifests and example flows.
firmware update.quote: this document provides the motivation for the standardization of a manifest format as a transport-agnostic means for describing and protecting firmware updates.

rejected.why: CoAP is only mentioned as one of several possible application-layer transports; the architecture is transport-agnostic.
TEEs and TEEP are mentioned only briefly in relation to personalization data; the document is not about TEEP.
The CBOR-based manifest serialization is in a separate document; it is only a reference here.
Mentioned only in a single sentence recommending post-quantum signatures for ROM bootloaders.
The parent topic is implied by the firmware update tag, so it is not listed separately.
Mentioned only as one possible way to discover servers.

RFC9020.title: YANG Data Model for Segment Routing
RFC9020.summary: RFC 9020 defines three YANG modules for Segment Routing configuration and operational state: a generic SR module, a common types/groupings module for IGP extensions, and an SR-MPLS data plane module.

YANG.why: The document's deliverable is a set of YANG modules with tree diagrams, module code, and configuration examples.
YANG.quote: This document defines three YANG data models [RFC7950].

segment routing.why: The modules model SR configuration and state: SRGB, SRLB, Prefix-SIDs, Adj-SIDs, and SID collision notifications.
segment routing.quote: The first one is for Segment Routing (SR) [RFC8402] configuration and operation.

SR-MPLS.why: One of the three modules, ietf-segment-routing-mpls, is dedicated to the SR-MPLS data plane, and the appendix examples use it.
SR-MPLS.quote: The third YANG data model defines a module that is intended to be used on network elements to configure or operate the SR MPLS data plane [RFC8660].

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only mentioned as access protocols in Security Considerations. The document defines no NETCONF behaviour.
The more specific SR-MPLS tag covers the MPLS data-plane content.
The document says it does not define IGP extensions. IS-IS appears only in system-id typedefs and references.
The document does not define OSPF extensions. OSPF is mentioned only in references and a router-id typedef.
XML is used only for the configuration examples in the appendix.
JSON is used only for the configuration examples in the appendix.

RFC9021.title: Use of the Walnut Digital Signature Algorithm with CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE)
RFC9021.summary: Specifies how to use the WalnutDSA quantum-resistant signature algorithm with COSE, defining algorithm identifiers, a new COSE key type and its parameters, and IANA registrations.

COSE.why: The document defines a new COSE signature algorithm, key type and key parameters, so COSE readers would want it.
COSE.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using the Walnut Digital Signature Algorithm (WalnutDSA) [WALNUTDSA] for digital signatures with the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) syntax

post-quantum.why: WalnutDSA is a post-quantum signature scheme, and the motivation and security analysis centre on quantum resistance.
post-quantum.quote: WalnutDSA is a lightweight, quantum-resistant digital signature algorithm.

rejected.why: CBOR is only the encoding substrate used by COSE; the document does not define anything new about CBOR.
SHA-2 is merely the hash used in hash-then-sign; the document is not about it.
RFC 4086 is cited only in Security Considerations boilerplate-style guidance.
The registry entries are routine IANA Considerations and do not make the document about IANA.
Hash-based schemes are mentioned only for comparison; WalnutDSA is group-theoretic.
Constrained devices are mentioned as motivation, but the document does not address IoT architecture or guidance.

RFC9022.title: Domain Name Registration Data (DNRD) Objects Mapping
RFC9022.summary: Defines the XML and CSV object mappings (domain, host, contact, registrar, IDN table reference, NNDN, EPP parameters, policy, header) for domain name registry data escrow deposits under the Registry Data Escrow specification.

domain registration.why: The document is about registry and registrar data held in domain registries and how it is escrowed. It builds on the EPP domain, host and contact object mappings. No EPP-specific tag fits better, because it does not extend EPP itself.
domain registration.quote: This document specifies the format, contents, and semantics of Domain Name Registration Data (DNRD) escrow deposits for a domain name registry.

CSV.why: A whole CSV model is specified, with file definitions, field elements, checksums and parent/child cascade rules. It is a substantial part of the document.
CSV.quote: This document defines two different models that can be used to deposit data escrow objects: XML and CSV (comma-separated values).

XML.why: The document defines XML Schema-based object formats and namespaces, and the CSV model is itself described through XML. This is a major part of the specification.
XML.quote: The XML model includes all the deposit information (metadata and data) in an XML document.

rejected.why: EPP mappings are the basis for the escrowed object attributes, but the document does not specify or extend EPP. It only reuses EPP types.
IDN table references and variants are handled as escrow objects, but the document does not define IDN mechanisms such as IDNA or label validity.
DS and key data are escrowed per RFC 5910, but only as data fields. DNSSEC itself is not the subject.
Registrar WHOIS server URLs appear as a data field only.
DNS is the context for the registry data, but the document is not about DNS protocol or operations.
The optional CRC32 or SHA-256 integrity check for CSV files is a minor convention, not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Registry Data Escrow (RDE)
gaps.why: The document's main subject is registry data escrow deposits (full, differential and incremental), and the taxonomy has no tag for it. 'domain registration' is the closest fit.

RFC9023.title: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) Data Plane: IP over IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN)
RFC9023.summary: Informational RFC specifying how the DetNet IP data plane operates over an IEEE 802.1 TSN sub-network, mapping DetNet IP flows to TSN Streams and using FRER inside the sub-network.

DetNet.why: The whole document is the DetNet IP data plane over a TSN sub-network, covering flow-to-stream mapping, TSN node requirements and service protection.
DetNet.quote: This document specifies the Deterministic Networking IP data plane when operating over a Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) sub-network.

rejected.why: The TSN sub-network is IEEE 802.1 bridged Ethernet. The document is about DetNet mapping onto it, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
The document talks about IP generally and does not address IPv6 specifically.
It is mentioned once, only as an example of a control plane protocol that differs from MSRP.
The tag is for IETF's Message Session Relay Protocol. The MSRP here is IEEE 802.1's Multiple Stream Registration Protocol, mentioned in passing.
The document covers latency and congestion protection through sub-network mechanisms, but the subject is DetNet, which is more specific.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) and FRER
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for TSN or Frame Replication and Elimination for Reliability (IEEE 802.1CB). They are central to the document, but DetNet covers it adequately.

RFC9024.title: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) Data Plane: IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking over MPLS
RFC9024.summary: Specifies the DetNet MPLS data plane procedures for interconnecting IEEE 802.1 TSN networks across a DetNet MPLS network, treating TSN Streams as App-flows mapped by a service proxy at edge nodes.

DetNet.why: The document is a DetNet data plane specification defining how TSN Streams map to DetNet flows over MPLS, including edge node and service proxy procedures.
DetNet.quote: This document specifies the Deterministic Networking data plane when Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) networks are interconnected over a DetNet MPLS network.

rejected.why: The DetNet MPLS data plane is defined in RFC 8964; this document only uses MPLS as the substrate and defines TSN-specific edge procedures.
PW encapsulations and T-PE/S-PE concepts are borrowed from RFC 8964/3985 but not specified or extended here.
TSN is IEEE 802.1 bridging, but the document is about DetNet interconnection of TSN, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
MPLS-TE LSPs and RSVP-TE are mentioned only as underlying mechanisms and in a control-plane comparison.
L2VPN is only mentioned as a conceptual parallel to the service.

gaps.name: Time-Sensitive Networking (IEEE 802.1 TSN)
gaps.why: The document is substantially about interworking with TSN (Stream identification, FRER), but the taxonomy has no tag for TSN.

RFC9025.title: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) Data Plane: MPLS over UDP/IP
RFC9025.summary: Specifies how the DetNet MPLS data plane encapsulation is carried over a UDP/IP packet switched network, based on MPLS-in-UDP, mapping it to the DetNet IP data plane.

DetNet.why: The whole document defines DetNet data plane operation, flow identification and provisioning for MPLS over UDP/IP.
DetNet.quote: This document specifies use of the MPLS DetNet encapsulation over an IP network.

MPLS.why: The document concerns DetNet MPLS encapsulation (S-Labels, F-Labels, d-CW) and how it is carried over UDP/IP, so MPLS readers would want it.
MPLS.quote: It maps the MPLS data plane encapsulation described in [RFC8964] to the DetNet IP data plane defined in [RFC8939].

UDP.why: Defines how UDP headers and source ports are used to identify DetNet flows in MPLS-over-UDP encapsulation.
UDP.quote: The headers for each outgoing packet MUST be formatted according to the configuration information and as defined in [RFC7510], and the UDP Source Port value MUST be set

rejected.why: The encapsulation works with IPv4, IPv6 and SRv6, but the document is not about IPv6.
Mentioned once as a compatible IPv6 SRH environment, not a subject of the document.
It is a carrying of MPLS over UDP, but the specific tags MPLS and UDP fit better and it is not an X-over-transport binding in that sense.
DSCP is a provisioned field only; QoS treatment is inherited from the DetNet IP data plane.

RFC9026.title: Multicast VPN Fast Upstream Failover
RFC9026.summary: Defines MVPN extensions for fast upstream failover: downstream PEs consider P-tunnel status (including a new BGP BFD Discriminator attribute using multipoint BFD) in UMH selection, and a new Standby PE community enables standby C-multicast routes and hot/warm/cold root standby.

MVPN.why: The whole document extends BGP/MPLS multicast VPN procedures (UMH selection, C-multicast routes, standby upstream PE).
MVPN.quote: This document defines Multicast Virtual Private Network (VPN) extensions and procedures that allow fast failover for upstream failures

BFD.why: A substantial part defines how P2MP BFD sessions are set up and used via a new BGP BFD Discriminator attribute to monitor P-tunnels.
BFD.quote: The P-tunnel status may be derived from the status of a multipoint BFD session [RFC8562] whose discriminator is advertised along with an x-PMSI A-D Route.

rejected.why: BGP is the carrier of the new attribute and community, but the subject is multicast VPN failover; the BGP-specific tag is less fitting than MVPN.
P2MP RSVP-TE tunnels are only one way to determine tunnel status, covered briefly in 3.1.3.
Fast reroute is mentioned only as an interacting mechanism; this is MVPN upstream PE failover, not LFA/FRR.
BGP/MPLS IP VPNs are the context, but the document is about multicast in them, covered by MVPN.
MPLS P-tunnels are substrate only.
PIM state on PE-CE is mentioned incidentally; the document is not about PIM.

RFC9027.title: Assertion Values for Resource Priority Header and SIP Priority Header Claims in Support of Emergency Services Networks
RFC9027.summary: Defines new "esnet.x" assertion values for the PASSporT "rph" claim and a new "sph" claim protecting the SIP Priority header value "psap-callback", to secure emergency call origination and PSAP callback.

STIR.why: Extends the PASSporT/STIR framework with new claim values and a new claim for signing SIP priority headers; this is STIR caller-identity assertion work.
STIR.quote: This document adds new assertion values for a Resource Priority Header ("rph") claim and a new SIP Priority Header ("sph") claim

emergency services.why: The whole purpose is protecting emergency call origination and PSAP callback priority markings, so emergency services readers would want it.
emergency services.quote: in support of the security of emergency services networks for emergency call origination and callback

rejected.why: SIP header fields (Resource-Priority, Priority) are the things being signed, but the document specifies PASSporT claims rather than SIP itself; STIR covers it.
The sph claim is registered in the JWT Claims registry, but that is IANA boilerplate; PASSporT is merely built on JWT.
Claims are JSON objects but JSON is only the encoding substrate.
The only IANA action is a single claim registration, not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: PASSporT (Personal Assertion Token) extensions
gaps.why: The document extends PASSporT with new claims; the taxonomy has only STIR as a broader parent, no PASSporT-specific tag.

RFC9028.title: Native NAT Traversal Mode for the Host Identity Protocol
RFC9028.summary: Specifies Native ICE-HIP, a NAT traversal mode for the Host Identity Protocol that uses HIP messages (UPDATE-based connectivity checks, control and data relay servers, UDP encapsulation) in place of STUN/TURN.

HIP.why: The document extends HIP with new parameters, relay registration, connectivity checks and mobility handling for NAT traversal.
HIP.quote: this document specifies an alternative NAT traversal mode referred to as "Native ICE-HIP" that employs the HIP messaging format instead of STUN or TURN

ICE.why: It adapts ICE candidate gathering, prioritization, checklists and nomination, and Appendix B details the differences from ICE, so ICE readers would want it.
ICE.quote: This specification builds heavily on the ICE methodology, so it is recommended that the reader is familiar with the ICE specification [RFC8445]

rejected.why: ESP is the data plane that HIP uses; the document only handles its UDP encapsulation and SPIs, and does not specify ESP itself.
The document explicitly avoids STUN and TURN and replaces them with HIP messages.
The Data Relay Server is similar to TURN, but TURN is not used or specified.
NAT is the problem being solved, but the document is about HIP traversal mechanisms; the NAT traversal topic is covered by the ICE tag.
Appendix E only gives brief guidance on DNS lookups of HIP hosts, which is not a substantial part of the document.
UDP is only the encapsulation substrate for HIP and ESP.

RFC9029.title: Updates to the Allocation Policy for the Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS) Parameters Registries
RFC9029.summary: Updates RFC 7752 by changing the IANA allocation policy for the BGP-LS Parameters registries from Specification Required to Expert Review and replacing the guidance to designated experts.

BGP.why: The document changes the registration policy for the BGP-LS (a BGP extension) parameter registries and the expert guidance, which concerns IDR WG BGP-LS operation. No narrower BGP tag fits.
BGP.quote: This document updates [RFC7752] by changing the allocation policy for all of the registries to "Expert Review" and updating the guidance to the designated experts.

IANA.why: The document is essentially an IANA registry allocation policy and designated-expert guidance change, which is IANA registry stewardship.
IANA.quote: IANA has changed the assignment policy for each of these registries to "Expert Review".

rejected.why: Only a brief DoS note on the registry in Security Considerations; not about securing routing.
Expert guidance involves WG chair and AD checks, but it is about registry allocation, which IANA covers better.
