Not related; BGP-LS is not BGP Monitoring Protocol.

RFC9030.title: An Architecture for IPv6 over the Time-Slotted Channel Hopping Mode of IEEE 802.15.4 (6TiSCH)
RFC9030.summary: Informational architecture for 6TiSCH: IPv6 over IEEE 802.15.4 TSCH, covering the 6top sublayer, scheduling functions, tracks, RPL/6LoWPAN ND integration, join process and forwarding models for deterministic low-power wireless networks.

6TiSCH.why: The whole document is the 6TiSCH architecture: 6top, 6P, scheduling functions, CDU matrix, tracks and join.
6TiSCH.quote: the 6TiSCH architecture supports an IETF suite of protocols over the IEEE Std 802.15.4 TSCH MAC to provide IP connectivity for energy and otherwise constrained wireless devices

RPL.why: RPL is the routing protocol of the stack. The document covers its DODAG roles, a time-synchronization instance, and its interaction with 6LoWPAN ND and objective functions.
RPL.quote: 6TiSCH leverages RPL [RFC6550] for interoperable, distributed routing operations.

DetNet.why: Tracks, PREOF and centralized schedule management are the 6TiSCH instantiation of DetNet deterministic paths.
DetNet.quote: it relies on the IETF DetNet architecture [RFC8655] and IETF components such as the PCE [PCE] for the protocol aspects.

6LoWPAN.why: The document covers 6LoWPAN header compression, 6LoWPAN ND registration and fragment forwarding in the stack.
6LoWPAN.quote: 6TiSCH architecture leverages 6LoWPAN [RFC4944] to adapt IPv6 to the constrained media

rejected.why: Only named as the application transport in the reference stack. It is not specified or extended here.
Only used for CoJP and payload protection, as part of the stack.
Only referenced for the zero-touch join. That work is outside this document.
The PCE is a component of centralized track computation. The document does not specify PCE or PCEP.
6LoWPAN ND registration is described as part of the architecture, but it is specified elsewhere.
IPv6 is the substrate. The document does not address IPv6 itself.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.15.4 TSCH MAC / deterministic wireless scheduling
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the TSCH MAC or for wireless scheduling. 6TiSCH is the closest fit.

RFC9031.title: Constrained Join Protocol (CoJP) for 6TiSCH
RFC9031.summary: Defines the Constrained Join Protocol (CoJP), a CoAP/OSCORE-based exchange with CBOR objects by which a pledge securely joins a 6TiSCH network and receives link-layer keys and parameters from the JRC, plus stack configuration for secure join.

6TiSCH.why: The document specifies the secure join protocol and stack configuration for 6TiSCH networks.
6TiSCH.quote: minimal framework required for a new device, called a "pledge", to securely join a 6TiSCH (IPv6 over the Time-Slotted Channel Hopping mode of IEEE 802.15.4) network

OSCORE.why: Substantial section profiles OSCORE use for CoJP: context derivation, replay window persistence, error handling, mandatory algorithms.
OSCORE.quote: The OSCORE security context MUST be derived per Section 3 of [RFC8613].

CoAP.why: Specifies CoAP usage: stateless proxy using extended tokens, recommended CoAP settings, message mappings.
CoAP.quote: The JP implements CoAP forward proxy functionality [RFC7252].

rejected.why: CBOR is only the encoding for CoJP objects, not the subject.
CDDL is used informatively to describe structures only.
Not ACE; CoJP is a separate join protocol, though related in spirit.
DSCP AF42/AF43 marking is a minor mechanism within a section.
Registers 6tisch.arpa in IANA section only; boilerplate-level.
Not an EAP method; network access authentication here uses OSCORE.

gaps.name: 6TiSCH / IEEE 802.15.4 TSCH network join
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no 6TiSCH tag in what I could use; the IoT hierarchy lists 6TiSCH, but I used ids that may not exist for OSCORE/CoAP; confirm.

RFC9032.title: Encapsulation of 6TiSCH Join and Enrollment Information Elements
RFC9032.summary: Defines a new IEEE 802.15.4 IETF Information Element subtype carried in TSCH Enhanced Beacons to give 6TiSCH pledges and long-sleeping nodes join proxy, PAN priority, rank priority and network ID information, saving scarce broadcast slots.

6TiSCH.why: The document extends 6TiSCH by defining the join/enrollment IE carried in TSCH Enhanced Beacons, with fields for join proxy, PAN priority and network ID.
6TiSCH.quote: This document defines a new IETF Information Element (IE) subtype to place into the EB to provide join and enrollment information to prospective pledges

rejected.why: RPL rank, DODAG and parent selection inform several fields, but the document does not specify or extend RPL.
RS/RA multicast cost motivates the design, but the document does not change IPv6 neighbor discovery.
The R flag and IID derivation reference SLAAC only in passing; the document is not about it.
6LBR and 6LR roles are mentioned, but the document does not specify 6LoWPAN.
Join Proxy and enrollment relate to constrained join (RFC 9031), but this document only carries the information in beacons; it does not define the join protocol.

gaps.name: IEEE 802.15.4 TSCH Information Elements
gaps.why: The document is about an 802.15.4 TSCH Enhanced Beacon IE subtype. The taxonomy has no tag for IEEE 802.15.4 or TSCH link-layer specifics apart from 6TiSCH.

RFC9033.title: 6TiSCH Minimal Scheduling Function (MSF)
RFC9033.summary: Defines the 6TiSCH Minimal Scheduling Function (MSF), which specifies node join behavior and distributed management of the TSCH communication schedule (autonomous cells, adding/deleting/relocating negotiated cells via 6P).

6TiSCH.why: The document is a 6TiSCH Scheduling Function specification, defining autonomous cells, negotiated cell management, and boot behavior over TSCH.
6TiSCH.quote: This specification defines the "IPv6 over the TSCH mode of IEEE 802.15.4" (6TiSCH) Minimal Scheduling Function (MSF).

rejected.why: MSF works with the RPL routing parent and DIOs but does not specify or extend RPL; it only uses RPL as a substrate.
CoJP is used for joining, but MSF only references it; the join protocol is defined elsewhere (RFC 9031).
6LoWPAN ND is mentioned briefly in the join process, but the document is not about it.
DSCP is mentioned only in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate-level evidence.
The only IANA action is registering one SFID value, which is not a substantive subject of the document.

gaps.name: 6TiSCH / TSCH scheduling (6P Scheduling Function)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no 6TiSCH tag; the closest is IoT's child 6TiSCH, which is not in the taxonomy list under the id I used. The document is about 6TiSCH scheduling, which is only partially covered by existing IoT tags.

RFC9034.title: Packet Delivery Deadline Time in the Routing Header for IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LoWPANs)
RFC9034.summary: Defines a new Elective 6LoWPAN Routing Header type (Deadline-6LoRHE) carrying packet delivery deadline and origination time in compressed form for time-synchronized 6LoWPAN/6TiSCH networks, with time representation and modular arithmetic rules.

6LoWPAN.why: The document extends the 6LoWPAN routing header (6LoRH) with a new elective type and registers it in the 6LoWPAN registry.
6LoWPAN.quote: This document specifies a new type for the 6LoWPAN routing header containing the deadline time for data packets, designed for use over constrained networks.

DetNet.why: The deadline mechanism supports deterministic, bounded-latency forwarding and scheduling decisions for time-critical traffic.
DetNet.quote: A Deterministic Network ("DetNet") typically requires some data packets to reach their receivers within strict time bounds.

rejected.why: Used as the main example network (ASN time units), but the document does not specify or extend 6TiSCH itself.
RPL source routing and DODAG scenarios are the context, but RPL is not specified or extended here.
Only mentioned as one possible time-synchronization method and for timestamp format; synchronization is out of scope.
The header rides on IPv6 datagrams, but IPv6 itself is not the subject.

RFC9035.title: A Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL) Destination-Oriented Directed Acyclic Graph (DODAG) Configuration Option for the 6LoWPAN Routing Header
RFC9035.summary: Defines a 'T' flag in the RPL DODAG Configuration option signalling whether RFC 8138 6LoWPAN routing header compression is used in a DODAG, updating RFC 8138 and describing migration/rollback behaviour.

RPL.why: The document extends the RPL DODAG Configuration option with a new flag and specifies node behaviour in RPL DODAGs.
RPL.quote: This specification defines a new flag, "Enable Compression per RFC 8138 (T)". The 'T' flag is set to turn on the use of [RFC8138] within the DODAG.

6LoWPAN.why: It updates RFC 8138 (6LoWPAN Routing Header, 6LoRH) behaviour and covers transition scenarios for that compression.
6LoWPAN.quote: A node SHOULD generate packets in compressed form using [RFC8138] if and only if the 'T' flag is set.

rejected.why: The 6LoRH compression is covered by the 6LoWPAN tag; the document only signals when to enable it and is not about header compression generally.
IPv6 is only the underlying network layer; the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
The IANA section merely registers one flag bit; this is boilerplate and not the subject.

RFC9036.title: Changing the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) Location Profiles Registry Policy
RFC9036.summary: Changes the IANA policy for the LoST Location Profiles registry from Standards Action to Specification Required so SDOs such as NENA can register new location profiles.

LoST.why: The whole document concerns the LoST location profiles registry and how new profiles are added. It updates RFC 5222, the LoST specification, so readers of LoST need it.
LoST.quote: changes the policy of the "Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) Location Profiles" IANA registry established by RFC 5222 from Standards Action to Specification Required

rejected.why: The document is a registry policy change, but it is specific to one LoST registry. The LoST tag is the better fit, and the IANA Considerations text is boilerplate-like.
LoST sits under emergency services, so the parent is implied. The document does not address emergency calling itself.
Location profiles are mentioned only as a registry subject. The document does not define location formats or how location is conveyed.

RFC9037.title: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) Data Plane: MPLS over IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN)
RFC9037.summary: Informational document describing how the DetNet MPLS data plane operates over an IEEE 802.1 TSN sub-network, covering mapping of DetNet flows to TSN Streams, TSN node requirements, FRER service protection and aggregation.

DetNet.why: The whole document is about the DetNet data plane and how DetNet flows are mapped onto TSN Streams, including service protection and management implications.
DetNet.quote: This document specifies the Deterministic Networking (DetNet) MPLS data plane when operating over an IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) sub-network.

MPLS.why: It covers the DetNet MPLS data plane (S-Labels, F-Labels, A-Labels, d-CW) and how MPLS flows are carried over a TSN sub-network, so MPLS readers would want it.
MPLS.quote: This document focuses on the scenario where MPLS (DetNet) nodes are interconnected by an IEEE 802.1 TSN sub-network.

rejected.why: Pseudowire encapsulations are only the basis of the DetNet service sub-layer, which RFC 8964 specifies. This document defines nothing new about them.
The document uses IEEE 802.1 Ethernet and TSN mechanisms, but it is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM. The TSN stream identification it describes belongs to DetNet.
RSVP-TE is mentioned only as an example of a control plane that differs from MSRP. The document does not specify or analyse it.
MPLS Traffic Engineering is only background for the DetNet forwarding sub-layer.

gaps.name: TSN (IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking) / FRER
gaps.why: The document is about TSN Streams, Stream identification and Frame Replication and Elimination for Reliability. The taxonomy has no tag for TSN or for IEEE 802.1 link-layer determinism.

RFC9038.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Unhandled Namespaces
RFC9038.summary: Defines an operational practice for EPP servers to return data for namespaces the client did not negotiate at login by moving it into the extValue element of successful responses, including poll messages.

EPP.why: The document specifies an operational practice for EPP, covering login services, extValue use, poll messages and signalling. It is squarely about EPP.
EPP.quote: This document defines an operational practice that enables the server to return information associated with unhandled namespace URIs and that maintains compliance with the negotiated services

rejected.why: XML namespaces and parsing are the substrate for the EPP extension mechanism. The document does not define an XML format or XML usage in general.
The secDNS extension appears only as an example of an unhandled namespace. The document says nothing about DNSSEC.
This is implied by the EPP parent. The document is about EPP protocol behaviour, not registry operations in general.
The XML namespace and EPP extension registrations are boilerplate IANA considerations.

RFC9039.title: Uniform Resource Names for Device Identifiers
RFC9039.summary: Registers the "dev" URN namespace for hardware device identifiers (MAC/EUI, 1-Wire, organization-defined, serial and product/serial subtypes) with syntax, assignment, privacy notes and an IANA subtype registry.

URN.why: The document defines a new URN namespace (dev) with its syntax, equivalence rules, assignment and resolution, which is exactly the subject of URN namespace pages.
URN.quote: This document describes a new Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for hardware device identifiers.

rejected.why: UUID URNs are discussed only as an alternative; the document does not specify or extend UUIDs.
SenML is a context where DEV URNs can be carried and is used in an example, but the document is not about it.
Targeted at constrained and smart-object environments, but the document defines a URN namespace rather than IoT architecture or guidance. The URN tag is a better fit.
ABNF is only the notation used for the syntax definition.
The registry creation is boilerplate-like IANA actions, not the main subject.
Privacy is discussed briefly in the Security Considerations, but it is not a main subject of the document.

RFC9040.title: TCP Control Block Interdependence
RFC9040.summary: Informational guidance on sharing TCP Control Block state (RTT, ssthresh, cwnd, MSS, PMTU, TFO info) across concurrent or consecutive connections to the same host, replacing RFC 2140, with an appendix proposing an automatic initial-window algorithm.

TCP.why: The whole document concerns TCP implementation state, the TCB, and how its parameters are cached and shared across connections.
TCP.quote: Some implementations share certain TCB information across connections to the same host [RFC2140].

congestion control.why: Sharing cwnd and ssthresh and the Appendix C AIMD initial-window algorithm are substantially about congestion control state and behaviour.
congestion control.quote: Appendix C has been added to discuss the potential to use temporal sharing over long timescales to adapt TCP's initial window automatically

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an application of the same observations to subflows; not specified or extended here.
Mentioned only in passing as another protocol with congestion state.
PMTU caching is discussed, but only as one cached parameter handled at the IP layer.
Mentioned only as an application-layer multiplexing alternative in the Implications section.

RFC9041.title: Updating the MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs) Ping Parameters IANA Registry
RFC9041.summary: Updates the IANA MPLS LSP Ping Parameters registries from RFCs 8029 and 8611, replacing Private Use with First Come First Served, adding Experimental Use ranges, and dropping the "mandatory/optional" TLV terminology.

MPLS.why: The document revises the MPLS LSP Ping registries and the rules for handling unrecognized TLVs, sub-TLVs and return codes. This is MPLS OAM, so readers of MPLS would want it.
MPLS.quote: both of which define IANA registries for MPLS Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping

IANA.why: Most of the document changes IANA registration procedures and aligns the terminology with RFC 8126, so it is also about IANA registry management.
IANA.quote: the registration procedure "Private Use" (previously known as "Vendor Private Use") has been changed to "First Come First Served"

rejected.why: LSP Ping is an OAM tool, but the document only changes registry procedures and does not specify OAM mechanisms.
RFC 8611 covers LSP traceroute, but this document only updates its registry, not the traceroute mechanism.
Echo replies travel over UDP, but this is only incidental and the document is not about UDP.
BFD appears only in an abbreviation list and in return code names, so it is not a subject of the document.

RFC9042.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Delivery by MAILBOXID
RFC9042.summary: Defines the Sieve "mailboxid" extension, adding a :mailboxid argument to fileinto and :fcc and a mailboxidexists test so scripts can target mailboxes by IMAP OBJECTID, which survives renaming.

Sieve.why: The document specifies a new Sieve extension with a capability string, a new fileinto argument and a new test.
Sieve.quote: This document extends the Sieve email filtering language (RFC 5228) to allow using that same unique identifier as a target for fileinto rules

rejected.why: IMAP OBJECTID (RFC 8474) is the source of the identifiers. The document defines nothing new in IMAP, so IMAP is only the mailstore it relies on.
This is the parent of Sieve and is implied by that tag. The document is about the filtering language, not email in general.
The only IANA content is the routine registration of the capability in the Sieve Extensions registry. That is boilerplate.
ABNF is used only for a small syntax extension, so the document is not about it.

RFC9043.title: FFV1 Video Coding Format Versions 0, 1, and 3
RFC9043.summary: RFC 9043 specifies FFV1 versions 0, 1 and 3, a lossless intra-frame video coding format, covering its sample prediction, range and Golomb-Rice coding, bitstream syntax, container mappings and media type registration.

FFV1.why: The whole document specifies the FFV1 codec, its bitstream and decoding.
FFV1.quote: This document defines FFV1, a lossless, intra-frame video encoding format.

media types.why: The document registers the video/FFV1 media type with its parameters, which readers of media type registrations would want.
media types.quote: This registration is done using the template defined in [RFC6838] and following [RFC4855].

rejected.why: Only one of several containers FFV1 is mapped into (Section 4.3.3.4); the document is not about Matroska.
FFV1 is a more specific child of codecs, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.
CRC is used for slice and configuration record integrity but is only a mechanism, not the subject.
The document defines no RTP payload format; it cites RFC 4855 only for the media type registration template.
H.264's CABAC is mentioned only as a historical alternative that was replaced.
The document concerns video coding, which falls under codecs, rather than generic lossless data compression formats.

RFC9044.title: Using the AES-GMAC Algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC9044.summary: Specifies conventions for using the AES-GMAC message authentication code algorithm in CMS AuthenticatedData, including OIDs, parameters, and an ASN.1 module.

CMS.why: The document defines how AES-GMAC is used in CMS AuthenticatedData (algorithm identifiers, parameters, MAC field), so CMS readers need it.
CMS.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using the AES-GMAC Message Authentication Code algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) as specified in RFC 5652.

AES.why: The document specifies the AES-based GMAC algorithm (AES-128/192/256 with GCM) and its OIDs, nonce and tag handling, so AES readers would look for it.
AES.quote: AES-GMAC [AES] [GCM] Message Authentication Code (MAC) algorithm uses one of the following algorithm identifiers

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation for the module that defines the identifiers and parameters. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
The only S/MIME link is the module OID arc and the IANA registry. The body does not address S/MIME.
RFC 4086 is cited only in the Security Considerations, as boilerplate guidance on key generation.
HMAC is not discussed. GMAC is a different MAC construction.
PBKDF2 is mentioned only in one Security Considerations sentence, as an example of a misuse to avoid.

RFC9045.title: Algorithm Requirements Update to the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate Request Message Format (CRMF)
RFC9045.summary: Updates RFC 4211 (CRMF) to require stronger algorithms for the Password-Based MAC: SHA-256 one-way function, higher iteration counts, HMAC-SHA256 and AES-GMAC, and optional PBMAC1.

CMP.why: CRMF is the certificate request format used by CMP and the PKI enrollment ecosystem; the document updates RFC 4211 and its PKI certificate request processing. No dedicated CRMF tag exists, so the closest is CMP, with PKI as its parent.
CMP.quote: This document updates the cryptographic algorithm requirements for the Password-Based Message Authentication Code (MAC) in the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate Request Message Format (CRMF)

HMAC.why: The document mandates HMAC-SHA256 as the MAC algorithm, with its ASN.1 identifier and parameter rules.
HMAC.quote: All implementations MUST support HMAC-SHA256 [HMAC].

AES.why: The document adds AES-GMAC with a 128-bit key as a recommended MAC, including nonce and length parameters.
AES.quote: All implementations SHOULD support AES-GMAC [AES] [GMAC] with a 128-bit key.

SHA.why: The document replaces SHA-1 with SHA-256 as the mandatory one-way function.
SHA.quote: All implementations MUST support SHA-256 [SHS].

PBKDF2.why: The document allows PBMAC1 from PKCS #5. It also sets iteration count guidance for password-based key derivation.
PBKDF2.quote: Implementations MAY also support PBMAC1 as presented in Section 7.1 of [RFC8018].

rejected.why: CRMF is a certificate request format, but the document does not profile X.509 certificates themselves.
ASN.1 is only the notation in which CRMF is defined. The document gives a few identifiers and structures but is not about ASN.1.
DES and Triple-DES-MAC are mentioned only as the old algorithms being dropped from the requirements.
The iteration count guidance is a small part of the document. PBKDF2 is the more specific fit, and it is itself only a weak match.
RFC 9044 defines AES-GMAC for CMS, but this document only reuses its algorithm identifier.

gaps.name: CRMF (Certificate Request Message Format)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for CRMF, RFC 4211, which is the main subject of this document. CMP is the nearest fit.

RFC9046.title: Babel Information Model
RFC9046.summary: RFC 9046 defines an information model of structured data elements (state, limited configuration, statistics, MAC keys, DTLS certificates) for managing Babel routing protocol implementations over IPv6, usable as a basis for YANG and TR-181 data models.

Babel.why: The whole document defines management objects for the Babel routing protocol (interfaces, neighbors, routes, security parameters), so it belongs on the Babel page.
Babel.quote: The Babel information model provides structured data elements for a Babel implementation reporting its current state and may allow limited configuration of some such data elements.

YANG.why: The information model is explicitly designed as the basis for YANG data models and uses datastore semantics. Its security section also covers YANG. YANG readers would want to find it. It is secondary because the document itself defines no YANG module.
YANG.quote: can be used to create management protocol data models (such as a NETCONF [RFC6241] YANG [RFC7950] data model)

rejected.why: NETCONF is mentioned only as an example management protocol. The document does not specify or profile it.
DTLS is a security mechanism that Babel uses (RFC 8968). The model only exposes certificate parameters for it and defines nothing new about DTLS.
HMAC-SHA256 and BLAKE2s are only the MAC algorithms named in key parameters. The document is not about them.
The document is an information model for several data modelling regimes. It does not define an SNMP MIB.
The model is restricted to Babel over IPv6, but IPv6 is only the substrate and not the subject.

RFC9047.title: Propagation of ARP/ND Flags in an Ethernet Virtual Private Network (EVPN)
RFC9047.summary: Defines the EVPN ARP/ND Extended Community, carried with EVPN MAC/IP Advertisement routes, conveying Router, Override and Immutable binding flags so PEs doing proxy-ARP/ND can answer ARP/NS requests correctly.

EVPN.why: The document extends EVPN by defining a new Extended Community for MAC/IP Advertisement routes and specifying PE transmission and reception procedures.
EVPN.quote: This document defines a transitive EVPN Extended Community (Type field value of 0x06) with a Sub-Type of 0x08

neighbor discovery.why: The Router and Override flags of IPv6 Neighbor Discovery are propagated and used by PEs when replying to Neighbor Solicitations. Substantial ND content, though the focus is EVPN.
neighbor discovery.quote: the flags defined in [RFC4861] can now be conveyed along with a MAC/IP Advertisement route so that an egress EVPN PE can issue Neighbor Advertisement (NA) messages

ARP.why: Proxy-ARP behaviour and ARP table entries, including the immutable binding flag, are a substantial part of what the document addresses.
ARP.quote: Remote PE routers can use this information to populate their ARP or ND tables on IRB interfaces or their proxy-ARP/ND tables in BDs.

rejected.why: BGP Extended Communities are only the carrier mechanism; the subject is the EVPN extension.
IPv6 addresses are handled, but the document is about ND flag propagation, not IPv6 itself.
The IANA section is boilerplate for registering a sub-type and flags registry; not the subject.
EVPN already has its own tag here and is the more specific fit.

RFC9048.title: Improved Extensible Authentication Protocol Method for 3GPP Mobile Network Authentication and Key Agreement (EAP-AKA')
RFC9048.summary: Updated specification of EAP-AKA', the EAP method for 3GPP AKA authentication with network-name-bound key derivation and SHA-256, adding 5G identifier handling, exported parameters, bidding-down protection for EAP-AKA, and security/privacy analysis.

EAP.why: The document specifies the EAP-AKA' method, its attributes, key derivation, and updates EAP-AKA (RFC 4187), so it belongs under EAP.
EAP.quote: EAP-AKA' is an EAP method that follows the EAP-AKA specification [RFC4187] in all respects except the following:

cellular.why: Substantial content on 3GPP 4G/5G networks, including SUCI/SUPI identifier use and network-name construction per 3GPP specs.
cellular.quote: This version of the EAP-AKA' specification defines the protocol behavior for both 4G and 5G deployments

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA-256 is used as a building block, not the subject of the document.
SHA-256 is a primitive swapped in for SHA-1, not the topic.
The PRF' is borrowed from IKEv2 but IKE is only referenced.
Privacy considerations are a section of the document, but the document is not about privacy threat models generally; identity privacy is part of EAP-AKA' specifics.
AAA is mentioned only as the transport where network name checks occur.
EAP-SIM/GSM is only referenced; this document addresses 3G/4G/5G AKA.

RFC9049.title: Path Aware Networking: Obstacles to Deployment (A Bestiary of Roads Not Taken)
RFC9049.summary: PANRG retrospective cataloguing Path Aware networking techniques that saw limited or no deployment (ST2, IntServ, Quick-Start, ICMP Source Quench, TRIGTRAN, Shim6, NSIS, IPv6 Flow Label, ECN) and distilling lessons learned for future researchers.

internet architecture.why: The document is an architectural analysis of Path Aware networking and the cross-cutting obstacles to deploying such techniques; no more specific tag covers path awareness as a whole.
internet architecture.quote: This document describes the lessons that IETF participants have learned (and learned the hard way) about Path Aware networking over a period of several decades.

Intserv.why: A full case-study section on IntServ/RSVP reasons for non-deployment and lessons learned.
Intserv.quote: IntServ was never widely deployed on the Internet because of its cost.

NSIS.why: NSIS, GIST and the NSLPs are analysed in their own section with deployment obstacles.
NSIS.quote: The NSIS Working Group worked on signaling techniques for network-layer resources (e.g., QoS resource reservations, Firewall and NAT traversal).

Shim6.why: Dedicated section on Shim6 multihoming and why operators did not deploy it.
Shim6.quote: Shim6 was an example of an "Identity/Locator Split" protocol.

ECN.why: ECN's history of non-deployment is a section and yields a new lesson (planning for failure).
ECN.quote: ECN deployment relied on three factors -- support in client implementations, support in router implementations, and deployment decisions in operational networks.

ST-II.why: ST/ST2/ST2+ is the first case study, with reasons for non-deployment.
ST-II.quote: The second version of the ST specification (ST2) [RFC1190] [RFC1819] was an experimental connection-oriented internetworking protocol

congestion control.why: Quick-Start, ICMP Source Quench and TRIGTRAN are all congestion/transport signalling techniques analysed here; no specific tech tag for Quick-Start exists.
congestion control.quote: Quick-Start is defined in an Experimental RFC [RFC4782] and is a TCP extension that leverages support from the routers on the path

rejected.why: IPv6 Flow Label is one case study, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
TCP is the substrate for Quick-Start and TRIGTRAN discussion, not the subject.
ICMP Source Quench is a brief case study of a deprecated message, not about ICMP generally.
RAO is discussed as a deployment obstacle for NSIS, not as a subject.
Only a short addendum on operator concerns.
Parent of Intserv/NSIS, already implied by the child tags.

gaps.name: Path Aware networking
gaps.why: The research area the document is about has no dedicated taxonomy tag; internet architecture is the closest fit.

RFC9050.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Procedures and Extensions for Using the PCE as a Central Controller (PCECC) of LSPs
RFC9050.summary: RFC 9050 specifies PCEP procedures and extensions (PCECC capability, CCI object, PST=2) so a PCE acting as central controller can allocate and download MPLS label-forwarding instructions for static LSPs.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP with new capability TLV, CCI object, path setup type, and message procedures for PCECC. PCE/PCEP is the core subject.
PCE.quote: This document specifies the procedures and Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) extensions for using the PCE as the central controller for provisioning labels along the path of the static LSP.

MPLS.why: The document concerns provisioning static MPLS LSPs via label allocation and label-forwarding entries downloaded to each LSR.
MPLS.quote: LSPs are provisioned as explicit label instructions at each hop on the end-to-end path.

SDN.why: PCECC is an SDN-style central controller using PCEP as a southbound interface, so SDN readers would want it.
SDN.quote: A PCE as a Central Controller (PCECC) can simplify the processing of a distributed control plane by blending it with elements of SDN

rejected.why: Mentioned only because LSP-IDENTIFIERS fields come from RSVP-signaled LSPs. The document replaces signaling with controller-provisioned labels.
SR PCECC extensions are only referenced as separate future documents.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations as the secure transport for PCEP (RFC 8253).
Referenced only for the reuse of address TLVs from RFC 8779 and as background.
The parent topic fits, but PCE is the more specific tag that applies, so the parent is implied.
Only mentioned as a possible future extension in Manageability Considerations.

RFC9051.title: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) - Version 4rev2
RFC9051.summary: Specifies IMAP4rev2, the revised Internet Message Access Protocol for accessing and manipulating mailboxes and messages on a server, obsoleting RFC 3501.

IMAP.why: The document is the full specification of IMAP version 4rev2: commands, responses, states, formal syntax.
IMAP.quote: The Internet Message Access Protocol Version 4rev2 (IMAP4rev2) allows a client to access and manipulate electronic mail messages on a server.

rejected.why: STARTTLS and Implicit TLS are used as security mechanisms, but the document defines nothing new about TLS itself.
AUTHENTICATE uses SASL mechanisms; SASL is a substrate here, not specified or extended.
Body structure parsing refers to MIME, but MIME is relied on, not specified.
Envelope and header parsing rely on RFC 5322 without defining the message format.
Mentioned only to distinguish message submission and delivery; not specified.
IMAP is the more specific child tag and covers the document.

RFC9052.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Structures and Process
RFC9052.summary: RFC 9052 specifies the COSE message structures (sign, encrypt, MAC, key objects), header parameters and processing rules for signing, encryption and MACing using CBOR serialization.

COSE.why: The document is the core COSE specification: message structures, header parameters, signing/encryption/MAC processes and COSE_Key objects.
COSE.quote: This document defines the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) protocol.

rejected.why: CBOR is the serialization substrate; the document defines security structures on it rather than extending CBOR itself.
CDDL is used only as a descriptive notation for the structures.
CMS is a point of comparison and design influence, not the subject.
JOSE is the JSON analogue and design reference; the document is not about it.
CoAP is mentioned for content-formats and as motivating use case, but not specified here.
The IANA media type registrations are boilerplate-like apparatus, not the main subject.

RFC9053.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Initial Algorithms
RFC9053.summary: Defines the initial set of COSE algorithm identifiers and key parameters (ECDSA, EdDSA, HMAC, AES-MAC, AES-GCM, AES-CCM, ChaCha20/Poly1305, HKDF, key wrap, ECDH) and key types for CBOR-based signing and encryption.

COSE.why: The document specifies algorithm identifiers, key types, and capabilities for COSE, so COSE readers need it.
COSE.quote: This document defines a set of algorithms that can be used with the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) protocol (RFC 9052).

ECDSA.why: Defines ES256/ES384/ES512 with curves P-256/384/521, encoding and key checks.
ECDSA.quote: The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) [DSS] defines a signature algorithm using Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC).

EdDSA.why: Defines the EdDSA algorithm identifier and its use with Ed25519/Ed448 in COSE.
EdDSA.quote: For use with COSE, only the pure EdDSA version is used.

HMAC.why: Defines HMAC algorithm identifiers for COSE including a truncated variant.
HMAC.quote: HMAC [RFC2104] [RFC4231] was designed to deal with length extension attacks.

AES.why: AES-GCM, AES-CCM, AES-CBC-MAC and AES Key Wrap are defined as COSE algorithms.
AES.quote: The Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) mode is a generic AEAD block cipher mode defined in [AES-GCM].

ChaCha20.why: Defines the ChaCha20/Poly1305 algorithm identifier for COSE content encryption.
ChaCha20.quote: ChaCha20 and Poly1305 combined together is an AEAD mode that is defined in [RFC8439].

key management.why: Covers direct keys, HKDF, key wrap, ECDH key agreement, and the KDF context structure.
key management.quote: This document defines the identifiers and usage for a number of content key distribution methods.

CBOR.why: Defines CBOR encoding restrictions for COSE_KDF_Context and the CBOR key structures.
CBOR.quote: This document limits the restrictions it imposes on how the CBOR Encoder needs to work.

rejected.why: CoAP is mentioned only in terminology; it is not the subject.
IANA registry updates are boilerplate-like; the body is about algorithms.
X25519/X448 are only listed as curves; the document is not about them in their own right.
HSS-LMS appears only in capability tables.
JOSE is referenced only for comparison.

gaps.name: COSE (CBOR Object Signing and Encryption)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no COSE tag. COSE is a technology tag under security, so I had to use it by its listed id. I may have mis-specified it if it is absent.

RFC9054.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Hash Algorithms
RFC9054.summary: Defines COSE algorithm identifiers and IANA registrations for hash algorithms (SHA-1, SHA-2 family, SHAKE128/256), with a new "Filter Only" recommendation value and usage guidance for indirect signing and object identification.

COSE.why: The document extends COSE by registering hash algorithm identifiers in the COSE Algorithms registry and adding a new Recommended value.
COSE.quote: This document defines hash algorithms that are identified by COSE algorithm identifiers.

SHA.why: The document specifies the use of SHA-1, SHA-2 and SHA-3 (SHAKE) hash functions, discussing their properties, trade-offs and recommendations.
SHA.quote: The family of SHA-2 hash algorithms [FIPS-180-4] was designed by the United States National Security Agency and published in 2001.

rejected.why: CBOR is only the encoding substrate for COSE; the CDDL hash structure is just an example.
Certificate fingerprints are mentioned as a use case, but the document does not address X.509 itself.
CMS DigestedData is referenced only as a comparison.
The registry action is boilerplate-level; the document is not about IANA registry policy in general.
The SUIT manifest is cited only as an example of indirect signing.
The more specific SHA tag covers it.

RFC9055.title: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) Security Considerations
RFC9055.summary: Informational RFC analysing DetNet-specific security: component design considerations, threat taxonomy, impacts, mitigations, mapping of attacks to use-case themes, and IP/MPLS data plane threats.

DetNet.why: The whole document analyses security of Deterministic Networking: threats, mitigations, and component design.
DetNet.quote: This document addresses DetNet-specific security considerations from the perspectives of both the DetNet system-level designer and component designer.

operational security.why: Substantial parts cover threat mitigation, performance analytics, and operational practice for securing a deployed network.
operational security.quote: securing a DetNet starts with a scrupulously well-designed and well-managed engineered network following industry best practices for security

rejected.why: Section 10.2 discusses MPLS data plane threats only briefly, mostly referring to other RFCs.
IPsec and MACsec are cited as mitigations, not specified or profiled here.
Section 4 compares Diffserv security considerations, but it is a small part and Diffserv is not the subject.
Time synchronization attacks are covered via RFC 7384 references only; NTP/PTP are not the subject.
Mentioned as an example of encryption; not about TLS.
Section 9 on OAM traffic is short and says it is not DetNet-specific.

gaps.name: DetNet (Deterministic Networking)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no DetNet tag outside routing; I used the id as listed, but the document's security-focused subject (threat analysis of deterministic networks) has no dedicated security-subtopic tag.

RFC9056.title: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) Data Plane: IP over MPLS
RFC9056.summary: Specifies how DetNet IP flows are mapped onto the DetNet MPLS data plane, with relay nodes acting as T-PEs mapping IP flow identifiers to S-Labels and ensuring traffic treatment.

DetNet.why: The document is a DetNet data plane specification, defining how DetNet IP flows are carried over DetNet MPLS, including flow identification, aggregation and traffic treatment.
DetNet.quote: This document specifies the Deterministic Networking data plane when encapsulating IP over an MPLS packet-switched network.

rejected.why: MPLS is the substrate for the DetNet flows. The document defines a DetNet mapping and does not specify MPLS itself, so the DetNet tag covers it.
Pseudowires and T-PE/S-PE terms are used as DetNet MPLS concepts from RFC 8964. The document does not specify pseudowire emulation.
TE LSPs are mentioned only as the carrier for DetNet member flows. The document is not about traffic engineering.
IP is the payload being mapped, as defined in RFC 8939. The document says nothing specific about IPv4 or IPv6.
IPsec appears only as an example of encryption in the Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.

RFC9057.title: Email Author Header Field
RFC9057.summary: Defines a new Author: email header field, with the same syntax as From:, that preserves the original author's identity when mediators such as mailing lists rewrite From:. Published as an experiment.

message format.why: The document defines a new Internet message header field, its ABNF syntax and its creation rules. That makes it a message format extension.
message format.quote: Author: is a new message header field being defined.  It has the same syntax as the From: header field [Mail-Fmt].

mailing lists.why: The motivation is mailing-list From: rewriting, and the field lets a list preserve the original author. A substantial part of the document addresses this.
mailing lists.quote: It has prompted Mediators, such as mailing lists, to modify the From: field to circumvent receiver mail rejection caused by those protections.

rejected.why: The DMARC work prompted the field, but the document does not specify or extend DMARC. It only refers to stringent authentication policies in general.
It addresses the side effects of authentication enforcement but defines no authentication mechanism.
The more specific message format tag covers it.
IMAP is mentioned only as an example of how the field might reach end users.
The document mentions Original-From: from the Sieve RFC 5703 only as a comparison.
The header field registration is boilerplate, and the document is not about IANA registries.

RFC9058.title: Multilinear Galois Mode (MGM)
RFC9058.summary: Specifies Multilinear Galois Mode (MGM), an Encrypt-then-MAC AEAD block cipher mode for 64- and 128-bit block ciphers (standardized in Russia, used with GOST ciphers), with test vectors for Kuznyechik and Magma.

GOST.why: MGM is the Russian-standardized AEAD mode for GOST block ciphers; test vectors are given for Kuznyechik and Magma. Readers of the GOST subject would want this RFC.
GOST.quote: It is used as an AEAD mode for the GOST block cipher algorithms in many protocols, e.g., TLS 1.3 and IPsec.

cryptography.why: The document defines a new AEAD block cipher mode with its security analysis. No more specific cryptography child tag covers generic AEAD modes, so the parent topic applies.
cryptography.quote: Multilinear Galois Mode (MGM) is an Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) block cipher mode based on the Encrypt-then-MAC (EtM) principle.

rejected.why: TLS 1.3 is only mentioned as a protocol that uses MGM; the document specifies nothing about TLS.
IPsec is only mentioned as a protocol that uses MGM; the document does not specify its use there.
The mode is cipher-agnostic and uses GOST ciphers; AES is not discussed. The GF(2^n) multiplication is not AES.

gaps.name: AEAD / block cipher modes of operation
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for authenticated encryption or block cipher modes; the document is about exactly this and is covered only by the generic cryptography topic.

RFC9059.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for Associated Bidirectional Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC9059.summary: Defines PCEP extensions (two new Association Types and a Bidirectional LSP Association Group TLV) for grouping two unidirectional RSVP-TE MPLS-TE LSPs into an associated bidirectional LSP, for stateful and stateless PCE.

PCE.why: The document specifies PCEP extensions (association types, TLV, procedures, errors) for bidirectional LSPs.
PCE.quote: This document defines Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) extensions for grouping two unidirectional MPLS-TE Label Switched Paths (LSPs)

RSVP-TE.why: The procedures are specific to RSVP-TE signalled LSPs, including the REVERSE_LSP object behaviour and PST handling, and build on RFC 7551 associated bidirectional LSPs.
RSVP-TE.quote: The procedures defined are applicable to the LSPs using Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic Engineering (RSVP-TE) for signaling

rejected.why: MPLS-TE LSPs are the managed objects, but the document is about PCEP signalling, so the more specific PCE and RSVP-TE tags cover it.
Mentioned only as motivation for associated bidirectional LSPs; the document does not specify MPLS-TP.
Only recommended as a transport security mechanism in Security Considerations.
SR bidirectional paths are explicitly out of scope, defined in another document.
Mentioned only to say the GMPLS B flag is not applicable here.
Only referenced in Manageability Considerations as an external data model.

RFC9060.title: Secure Telephone Identity Revisited (STIR) Certificate Delegation
RFC9060.summary: Specifies how STIR certificate authority over telephone numbers (TNAuthList) can be delegated from a parent certificate to subordinate certificates, including signing, verification, certificate-chain delivery via x5u, and ACME-based acquisition.

STIR.why: The document extends the STIR certificate profile with delegation and defines authentication and verification service behaviour for delegate certificates.
STIR.quote: This specification details how that authority can be delegated from a parent certificate to a subordinate certificate.

X.509.why: A substantial part concerns X.509 certificate profile matters: TNAuthList scope encompassing, basic constraints, Authority Key Identifier, and certification path ordering.
X.509.quote: STIR delegate certificates are certificates containing a TNAuthList object that have been signed with the private key of a parent certificate

rejected.why: ACME is used for acquiring delegate certificates (Section 8.1), but the document does not specify or extend it; it relies on separate drafts.
SIP carries the Identity header and PASSporT, but the document does not extend SIP beyond a brief mention of the 437 response.
The X.509 tag is more specific and covers the certificate-profile content; the CA operational remarks are secondary.
RPKI is cited only as an analogy for encompassing semantics.
TLS delegated credentials are mentioned only as an alternative-solutions comparison.

RFC9061.title: A YANG Data Model for IPsec Flow Protection Based on Software-Defined Networking (SDN)
RFC9061.summary: Defines three YANG modules (ikec, ike, ikeless) letting an I2NSF Controller configure and monitor IPsec SPD, SAD, PAD and IKEv2 on NSFs, for IKE and IKE-less cases in gateway-to-gateway and host-to-host scenarios.

I2NSF.why: The document defines the I2NSF NSF-Facing Interface data models for controlling IPsec-enabled NSFs.
I2NSF.quote: This document focuses on the I2NSF NSF-Facing Interface by providing YANG data models for configuring the IPsec databases

IPsec.why: It models SPD, SAD, PAD and ESP parameters, i.e. IPsec configuration and SA management.
IPsec.quote: This document describes how to provide IPsec-based flow protection (integrity and confidentiality) by means of an Interface to Network Security Function (I2NSF) Controller.

IKE.why: The ietf-i2nsf-ike module models IKEv2 connection, authentication and SA lifetime configuration and state.
IKE.quote: IKE case.  The NSF implements the Internet Key Exchange Version 2 (IKEv2) protocol and the IPsec databases

YANG.why: The core deliverable is YANG modules with tree diagrams and examples.
YANG.quote: this document defines three YANG modules (see Section 5) but does not define any new protocol.

rejected.why: NETCONF/RESTCONF are only the transport used to carry the models.
SDN is the motivating context, but the document is about IPsec management via I2NSF; considered as a topic but the I2NSF tag is more specific.
ESP parameters are modeled, but the document is about the overall IPsec architecture rather than ESP itself.
NAT traversal is discussed briefly, only as encapsulation configuration.
Certificates appear only as authentication credential fields in the model.

RFC9062.title: Framework and Requirements for Ethernet VPN (EVPN) Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM)
RFC9062.summary: Informational RFC giving the requirements and layered reference framework for fault and performance management OAM of EVPN and PBB-EVPN (service, network, transport and link OAM layers).

EVPN.why: The whole document defines OAM requirements and framework for EVPN and PBB-EVPN, so the EVPN page is where readers would look.
EVPN.quote: This document specifies the requirements and defines a reference framework for Ethernet VPN (EVPN) Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM)

OAM.why: The document is a layered OAM model with proactive and on-demand fault management (continuity check, defect indication, connectivity verification, fault isolation) and performance management requirements.
OAM.quote: This document focuses on the fault management and performance management aspects of EVPN OAM.

rejected.why: BFD is only cited as an applicable transport-layer OAM mechanism in one paragraph; the document does not specify or extend it.
Ethernet CFM is the service-layer OAM referenced from IEEE 802.1Q and Y.1731, but the document is about EVPN OAM, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM itself.
EVPN is an L2VPN solution and is tagged by its more specific EVPN child; the document is not about L2VPN services in general.
MPLS and LSP ping are the substrate and transport OAM referenced, not the subject of the document.
Packet loss and delay requirements are a part of the OAM requirements and mostly refer to existing IPPM metrics; not substantial enough for a separate tag.
BGP is only the control plane EVPN uses; it is not discussed beyond mentions.

RFC9063.title: Host Identity Protocol Architecture
RFC9063.summary: RFC 9063 describes the Host Identity namespace and Host Identity Protocol (HIP) architecture, a layer between internetworking and transport supporting mobility, multihoming, and NAT traversal; it obsoletes RFC 4423.

HIP.why: The document is the architecture specification for HIP: the HI namespace, HITs, LSIs, control plane, data plane, and security considerations.
HIP.quote: the associated protocol layer, the Host Identity Protocol, located between the internetworking and transport layers, that supports end-host mobility, multihoming, and NAT traversal

rejected.why: ESP is the typical data plane for HIP but is only a substrate here, specified elsewhere (RFC 7402).
NAT traversal is covered in a short section, but the specifics live in RFC 9028; the document is about HIP, not NAT behaviour.
Mobility and multihoming are HIP features, delegated to RFC 8046/8047; HIP is the more specific tag.
The HIP DNS RR is mentioned for storing HIs, but defined in RFC 8005; DNS is only a directory here.
LSI/HIT interoperability between IPv4 and IPv6 apps is discussed briefly, not the main subject.
Mentioned only as an alternative authentication system using host identifiers.

RFC9064.title: Considerations in the Development of a QoS Architecture for CCNx-Like Information-Centric Networking Protocols
RFC9064.summary: Position paper arguing how QoS should be designed for CCNx/NDN-style ICN, covering equivalence classes by name, treatments, cache resource allocation, and Intserv-like capabilities.

QoS.why: The whole document is about QoS architecture (equivalence classes, treatments, admission control) for ICN. No ICN-QoS-specific tag exists, so the QoS topic fits.
QoS.quote: documents the author's personal views on how Quality of Service (QoS) capabilities ought to be accommodated in Information-Centric Networking (ICN) protocols

ICN.why: The document analyses CCNx/NDN forwarding (PIT, CS, Interest/Data) and how its properties shape QoS, so ICN readers would want it.
ICN.quote: ICN protocols like NDN [NDN] and CCNx [RFC8569] [RFC8609] have an accumulated ten years of research and very little deployment.

rejected.why: Discussed as a TCP/IP comparison point and something not to copy, not specified or extended.
Section 7.1 considers Intserv-like capabilities for ICN, but Intserv is a comparison point, not the document's subject.
Mentioned only as the signalling used by Intserv for comparison.
Section 3.2 gives background on ICN congestion control, but the document is about QoS rather than congestion control.

RFC9065.title: Considerations around Transport Header Confidentiality, Network Operations, and the Evolution of Internet Transport Protocols
RFC9065.summary: Informational discussion of how encrypting transport headers (as in QUIC) affects network operations, measurement and research, and what protocol designers should consider about exposing or hiding transport information.

transport.why: The document is about transport protocol design: header confidentiality, ossification, and exposed wire image. No specific transport technology is its subject, so the general topic fits.
transport.quote: This document discusses the possible impact when network traffic uses a protocol with an encrypted transport header.

performance measurement.why: Large parts cover passive and active measurement of loss, latency, jitter, and reordering, and how header encryption affects them.
performance measurement.quote: Observable transport headers enable explicit measurement and analysis of protocol performance and detection of network anomalies at any point along the Internet path.

privacy.why: Metadata exposure, pervasive monitoring, and the privacy versus operability trade-off are central themes.
privacy.quote: Another motivation for using transport header encryption is to improve privacy and to decrease opportunities for surveillance.

OAM.why: A dedicated section covers IOAM and the IPv6 PDM option as ways to provide measurement information when transport headers are encrypted.
OAM.quote: Addition of Transport OAM Information to Network-Layer Headers

rejected.why: QUIC is the main example of header encryption but is not specified or profiled here.
Mentioned as an example of payload-only protection, not the subject.
Operator practice is discussed, but the focus is on transport header observability and measurement, not security hardening.
Only a short subsection notes the incompatibility of header compression with header encryption.
Congestion control compliance is observed by operators, but the document does not address congestion control itself.
Parent of the performance measurement and OAM tags already chosen; operations are discussed but no broader management subject applies beyond those.

gaps.name: Protocol ossification / wire image
gaps.why: The document centres on ossification and the wire image of protocols. The taxonomy has no tag for this, so it is covered only through the general transport tag.

RFC9066.title: Distributed Denial-of-Service Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) Signal Channel Call Home
RFC9066.summary: Specifies DOTS signal channel Call Home, an extension of the DOTS signal channel in which the DOTS server initiates the (D)TLS connection so the client can send attack-source information to help block outbound DDoS attacks near their source, with a YANG module and CBOR mappings.

DOTS.why: The document extends the DOTS signal channel with a role-reversed Call Home mode. It adds attributes, heartbeat and redirect variations, and a YANG module.
DOTS.quote: enables a Call Home DOTS server to initiate a secure connection to a Call Home DOTS client and to receive attack traffic information

rejected.why: The DOTS tag is not in the taxonomy. The closest tag is the DDoS parent topic, but the proper tag is the DOTS tech, and the parent is implied if DOTS exists. I could not use DOTS because it is not a valid id.
The document defines a YANG module, but only as the encoding of the DOTS extension. The subject is the protocol, not YANG modelling.
(D)TLS is the substrate. The document reverses the client/server roles but defines no new TLS extension.
CoAP is the carrier of the signal channel. The document does not extend CoAP itself.
CBOR is only the encoding. The document just lists key mappings.
Address sharing and CGN are discussed only as considerations for identifying attack sources. They are not the subject.

gaps.name: DOTS (DDoS Open Threat Signaling)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no DOTS technology tag. The DDoS and DOTS tags sit under security as 'DDoS' (topic) and 'DOTS' (tech). Since DOTS is not available as a valid id, I could not apply it. The DDoS topic fits best, but the primary tag should be DOTS.

RFC9067.title: A YANG Data Model for Routing Policy
RFC9067.summary: Defines the ietf-routing-policy YANG module, a vendor-neutral data model for configuring routing policies (defined sets, conditions, actions, policy chains) that routing protocol models can augment.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module and its tree, defining a data model for routing policy.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model for configuring and managing routing policies in a vendor-neutral way.

routing architecture.why: The subject is generic routing policy (import/export, conditions, actions) across protocols. No narrower routing tag fits, and the routing parent topic covers it.
routing architecture.quote: A routing policy defines how routes are imported, exported, modified, and advertised between routing protocol instances or within a single routing protocol instance.

rejected.why: BGP policy is only an augmentation example in a non-normative appendix; the model is protocol-generic.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in Security Considerations and example wrappers.
OSPF and IS-IS appear only as identities for metric and route types, not as the subject.
IS-IS appears only as identities for metric and route types, not as the subject.
The YANG tag already sits under it and covers the document.
Security Considerations discuss risks of modifying the policy data, but the document is not about securing routing.

gaps.name: Routing policy
gaps.why: The document is about generic routing policy (conditions, actions, policy chains, import/export), but the taxonomy has no routing-policy tag. RPSL is the nearest but covers a different language and registry.

RFC9068.title: JSON Web Token (JWT) Profile for OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens
RFC9068.summary: Defines a profile for issuing OAuth 2.0 access tokens as JWTs, specifying header, claims, request handling, resource-server validation, and registering the application/at+jwt media type and role/group/entitlement claims.

JWT.why: The document profiles JWT as the format for OAuth access tokens, defining required claims, typing header and validation rules.
JWT.quote: This specification defines a profile for issuing OAuth 2.0 access tokens in JSON Web Token (JWT) format.

OAuth.why: It specifies how authorization servers issue access tokens and how resource servers validate them, extending OAuth 2.0 interoperability.
OAuth.quote: Authorization servers and resource servers from different vendors can leverage this profile to issue and consume access tokens in an interoperable manner.

rejected.why: JWS/JWA are used for signing but the document does not define anything new about them; it profiles JWT.
It registers application/at+jwt, but this is IANA boilerplate secondary to the main subject.
Only reuses the SCIM groups/roles/entitlements attribute names as claims; not about SCIM.
JSON is just the encoding substrate for the token claims.

RFC9069.title: Support for Local RIB in the BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP)
RFC9069.summary: RFC 9069 updates the BGP Monitoring Protocol (RFC 7854) to let a router export its BGP Loc-RIB to BMP receivers. It adds a Loc-RIB Instance peer type, an F flag, a VRF/Table Name TLV, a new Peer Down reason code, and rules for Peer Up/Down, Route Monitoring and statistics.

BMP.why: The document extends BMP with a new peer type, flags, TLVs and message handling for Loc-RIB monitoring, so BMP readers need it.
BMP.quote: This document defines a mechanism to monitor the BGP Loc-RIB state of remote BGP instances without the need to establish BGP peering sessions.

rejected.why: BGP is the monitored system, and the Loc-RIB is defined in RFC 4271. The document specifies no change to BGP itself, only to how BMP exports its state. BMP is the more specific tag.
The IANA section registers new BMP parameters, but that is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
VRF and route distinguisher are mentioned only as peer-header context. The document is not about MPLS VPNs.
Not relevant to the content of the document.

RFC9070.title: YANG Data Model for MPLS LDP
RFC9070.summary: Defines the ietf-mpls-ldp and ietf-mpls-ldp-extended YANG modules for configuring and monitoring MPLS LDP (including IPv6 and capabilities), with state, RPCs and notifications.

LDP.why: The model manages LDP: discovery, peers, bindings, capabilities, graceful restart and label policies. Readers of LDP would want it.
LDP.quote: This document introduces a YANG data model for the MPLS Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) [RFC5036].

YANG.why: The document is a YANG module specification (NMDA-conformant), so it belongs with YANG data models.
YANG.quote: This document describes a YANG data model for the Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Distribution Protocol (LDP).

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the management protocol the model is intended for. The document does not specify or extend it.
LDP is the more specific tag. The document covers MPLS only through LDP.
The document models LDP's IPv6 support but does not specify IPv6 itself.
This is a YANG model, not a MIB module or SMI.
RESTCONF appears only in the Security Considerations boilerplate.
JSON is used only for the example instance data in the appendix.

RFC9071.title: RTP-Mixer Formatting of Multiparty Real-Time Text
RFC9071.summary: Updates RFC 4103 real-time text (T.140 over RTP) with an RTP-mixer method for multiparty sessions, using the CSRC list for source identification, a new SDP "rtt-mixer" attribute, and a fallback mixing format for multiparty-unaware endpoints.

RTP.why: The document specifies how an RTP mixer populates CC, CSRC, timestamps and redundancy for multiparty real-time text, updating RFC 4103 (RTP payload for text).
RTP.quote: The specified mechanism builds on the standard use of the Contributing Source (CSRC) list in the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) packet for source identification.

SDP.why: It defines a new SDP media attribute with offer/answer procedures and examples, a substantial part of the document.
SDP.quote: The capability is indicated by the use of a Session Description Protocol (SDP) (RFC 8866) media attribute, "rtt-mixer".

conferencing.why: Addresses centralized conference mixing, presentation of multiple participants and its relation to conference control.
conferencing.quote: enabling source identification and rapidly interleaved transmission of text from different sources

rejected.why: The document updates the existing text/t140 and text/red usage rather than defining a new codec payload format; it says no new packet format is introduced.
SIP is only the session control context and conferencing framework is referenced, not specified.
WebRTC gateways are only briefly considered in Section 6.2; the focus is RTP transport.
DTLS-SRTP is only recommended as a security mechanism, not specified.
RTCP SDES/NAME use for labels is a minor point, not a substantial part.
Emergency calls are a motivating application, not the subject.

gaps.name: real-time text (T.140 / RTT)
gaps.why: The document is about real-time text conversation, which has no dedicated tag in the taxonomy; RTP and conferencing are the closest fits.

RFC9072.title: Extended Optional Parameters Length for BGP OPEN Message
RFC9072.summary: RFC 9072 updates BGP-4 (RFC 4271) to extend the OPEN message Optional Parameters length and per-parameter length fields to two octets, using type code 255 as a backward-compatible indicator.

BGP.why: The document modifies the BGP OPEN message encoding and parsing procedures, updating the base BGP specification. It is squarely about BGP protocol behaviour.
BGP.quote: This document updates RFC 4271 by extending, in a backward-compatible manner, the length of the Optional Parameters in a BGP OPEN message.

rejected.why: The document only registers one code point in an existing registry. That is boilerplate-level IANA content, not a document about IANA.

RFC9073.title: Event Publishing Extensions to iCalendar
RFC9073.summary: RFC 9073 extends iCalendar (RFC 5545) with new properties, parameters and components (PARTICIPANT, VLOCATION, VRESOURCE, STRUCTURED-DATA, STYLED-DESCRIPTION) for event publishing and social calendaring.

iCalendar.why: The document extends and updates the iCalendar format, defining new components, properties and parameters and IANA registrations for them.
iCalendar.quote: This specification updates RFC 5545 by introducing a number of new iCalendar properties and components that are of particular use for event publishers

rejected.why: vCard is only referenced as a target format for STRUCTURED-DATA links; the document does not specify it.
FMTTYPE is used, but the document does not register media types.
Rich-text STYLED-DESCRIPTION may contain HTML, but HTML itself is not specified or profiled here.
JSON-LD appears only in examples of structured data; the document is not about JSON.
VLOCATION carries structured location data, but this is calendar-component structure, not location formats or conveyance.
The registries created are specific to iCalendar and fall under IANA boilerplate, not IANA guidance.

RFC9074.title: "VALARM" Extensions for iCalendar
RFC9074.summary: Defines extensions to the iCalendar VALARM component (UID, RELATED-TO, ACKNOWLEDGED, snoozing via RELTYPE=SNOOZE, and PROXIMITY location-based triggers) and updates RFC 5545.

iCalendar.why: The whole document extends the iCalendar data format's VALARM component and updates RFC 5545, so readers of iCalendar need it.
iCalendar.quote: This document defines a set of extensions to the iCalendar "VALARM" component to enhance the use of alarms and improve interoperability between clients and servers.

rejected.why: CalDAV is the client-server protocol motivating the work and is mentioned in security and privacy sections, but the document does not specify or extend CalDAV.
Proximity triggers use VLOCATION and geo URIs, but location formats are defined elsewhere (RFC 9073, RFC 5870); the document only references them.
ABNF is only the notation used to define syntax, not the subject.
The geo URI is merely referenced as a value in VLOCATION; nothing new is defined about URIs.
Registry additions are boilerplate-level IANA considerations for the iCalendar registries.

RFC9075.title: Report from the IAB COVID-19 Network Impacts Workshop 2020
RFC9075.summary: Report of the IAB COVID-19 Network Impacts Workshop (Nov 2020), summarizing measurements of pandemic-era Internet traffic changes, operational and security observations, and conclusions.

workshop reports.why: The document is a report on an IAB workshop, which is the definition of this topic.
workshop reports.quote: The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) held a workshop to discuss network impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on November 9-13, 2020.

performance measurement.why: A large part of the report covers measurements of traffic growth, congestion, throughput and latency across ISPs, IXPs, mobile networks and cloud platforms.
performance measurement.quote: A large portion of the submitted papers presented and discussed measurement data

operational security.why: A section covers the security impacts on operators and defenders, including VPN exploits, phishing and the use of Indicators of Compromise.
operational security.quote: the agility of malicious actors to spin up new campaigns using COVID-19 as a lure, and (2) the increased threat surface from a rapid shift towards working from home

rejected.why: DNS over HTTPS is mentioned in one sentence on how it bypasses protective DNS measures. It is not a subject of the report.
VPNs are mentioned as a category of traffic and an attack target. The tag covers provider-provisioned VPNs, which the report does not address.
DSCP marking and prioritization are discussed only briefly.
The report draws a few lessons about resilience and flexibility, but it is mainly a measurement and operations report.

RFC9076.title: DNS Privacy Considerations
RFC9076.summary: Informational analysis of privacy risks in DNS use by end users (data in queries, on the wire, in recursive and authoritative servers), obsoleting RFC 7626.

DNS privacy.why: The whole document analyses DNS privacy risks, including encrypted transports and resolver selection, so the DNS privacy topic fits directly.
DNS privacy.quote: This document describes the privacy issues associated with the use of the DNS by Internet users.

DNS.why: It examines DNS data, resolver and authoritative server behaviour, QNAME, caching and ECS in depth. DNS privacy is the main subject, but readers of DNS would want this analysis too.
DNS.quote: A client, the stub resolver, issues a DNS query to a server called the recursive resolver

rejected.why: DoH is discussed (Section 6.1.4.2) as one encrypted transport, but the document does not specify or extend it. The DNS privacy tag covers it.
DoT is discussed as one encrypted transport, but the document does not specify or extend it. The DNS privacy tag covers it.
The general privacy topic was considered. The document is specifically about DNS privacy, so the DNS privacy tag is more specific.
The ECS option and EDNS(0) are mentioned only as sources of client-identifying data. The document does not specify or extend EDNS.
DNSSEC appears only in passing, as NSEC zone walking and as lacking confidentiality.
TLS is the substrate for encrypted DNS and is mentioned only in terms of fingerprinting. The document is not about TLS.

RFC9077.title: NSEC and NSEC3: TTLs and Aggressive Use
RFC9077.summary: Standards-track update to RFCs 4034, 4035, 5155 and 8198 that requires NSEC and NSEC3 record TTLs to be the lesser of the SOA MINIMUM and the SOA TTL, so aggressive use of cached denial of existence doesn't outlive its intended lifetime.

DNSSEC.why: The document changes the TTL rules for NSEC and NSEC3 records in DNSSEC authenticated denial of existence. It updates the DNSSEC specifications (RFC 4034, 4035, 5155) and the aggressive-use text in RFC 8198.
DNSSEC.quote: The TTL of the NSEC RR that is returned MUST be the lesser of the MINIMUM field of the SOA record and the TTL of the SOA itself.

rejected.why: This is the parent of DNSSEC, which is already tagged. Negative caching (RFC 2308) is background, not the subject of the document.

RFC9078.title: Reaction: Indicating Summary Reaction to a Message
RFC9078.summary: Defines an experimental "reaction" MIME Content-Disposition carrying a single line of emoji, linked via In-Reply-To, so email replies can signal a summary reaction to an earlier message.

email.why: The document adds a reaction facility to email: reply processing by MUAs using In-Reply-To, and usability for mail clients.
email.quote: This specification extends this existing practice in social media and instant messaging into Internet Mail.

MIME.why: The core deliverable is a new Content-Disposition value (reaction) for MIME parts, registered with IANA, with a required text/plain UTF-8 content type.
MIME.quote: This facility defines a new MIME Content-Disposition, to be used in conjunction with the In-Reply-To header field

Unicode.why: A substantial part of the spec addresses emoji sequences, validation, unallocated code points and the need for Unicode implementations.
Unicode.quote: The ABNF rule emoji-sequence is inherited from [Emoji-Seq]. It defines a set of Unicode code point sequences, which must then be encoded as UTF-8.

rejected.why: In-Reply-To is used, but the document defines a MIME disposition rather than new header or addressing semantics.
UTF-8 is just the required encoding of the part; the document's substance is about emoji sequences, not the encoding.
ABNF is only the notation used for syntax.
No new media type is registered; text/plain is reused and only a Content-Disposition value is added.

RFC9079.title: Source-Specific Routing in the Babel Routing Protocol
RFC9079.summary: Defines a Babel routing protocol extension adding a Source Prefix sub-TLV so Update, Route Request and Seqno Request TLVs support source-specific (SADR) routing, with destination-first ordering and compatibility rules.

Babel.why: The document extends the Babel protocol with a new sub-TLV, data structure changes and compatibility rules.
Babel.quote: This document describes a source-specific routing extension for the Babel routing protocol [RFC8966].

multihoming.why: A substantial section explains source-specific routing as a solution to multihoming with provider-dependent addresses.
multihoming.quote: The main application of source-specific routing is a form of multihoming known as "multihoming with multiple addresses".

rejected.why: Controlled anycast is mentioned only as one of several applications, not a main subject.
The document is about a specific protocol extension, so the Babel tag is more specific.
IPv6 prefixes are used only as examples; the document is not about IPv6.
Tunnels and VPNs are briefly mentioned as an application, not a focus.

gaps.name: Source-specific routing (SADR)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for source-address-dependent routing; Babel covers the protocol but not the general subject.

RFC9080.title: Homenet Profile of the Babel Routing Protocol
RFC9080.summary: Defines the subset of Babel and its extensions required for Homenet implementations, plus the requirements for how HNCP triggers Babel route announcements.

Babel.why: The document profiles Babel for Homenet, specifying mandatory and optional features, link metrics, and extensions. Babel is the protocol it specifies.
Babel.quote: This document defines the exact subset of the Babel routing protocol and its extensions that is required by an implementation of the Homenet protocol suite

home networking.why: It is a Homenet profile and specifies how HNCP interacts with Babel (REQ7-REQ9). Readers of the home networking subject would want it.
home networking.quote: The core of the Homenet protocol suite consists of the Home Networking Control Protocol (HNCP)

rejected.why: Babel control traffic is carried over IPv6, and IPv6 default routes are announced. IPv6 is the substrate here, not the subject.
DHCPv6 prefix delegation triggers a REQ7 announcement. The document does not specify DHCPv6.
A DHCPv4 lease triggers the NAT gateway default route. The document does not specify DHCP.
The NAT gateway election is mentioned only as the condition for announcing the IPv4 default route. NAT behaviour is not specified here.
The document profiles a specific protocol, so the Babel tag fits better than this general topic.

RFC9081.title: Interoperation between Multicast Virtual Private Network (MVPN) and Multicast Source Directory Protocol (MSDP) Source-Active Routes
RFC9081.summary: Specifies how MVPN PEs attach an RP-address Extended Community to MVPN Source-Active routes and generate MSDP SA messages from received MVPN SA routes, removing the need for VPN-specific MSDP sessions between PEs; updates RFC 6514.

MVPN.why: The document defines MVPN SA route procedures and a new Extended Community for BGP/MPLS multicast VPNs, updating RFC 6514.
MVPN.quote: The MVPN PEs that act as customer RPs or have one or more MSDP sessions in a VPN (or the global table in case of GTM) are treated as an MSDP mesh group

MSDP.why: It specifies how PEs generate MSDP SA messages and interoperate with customer MSDP infrastructure, including RP address handling for peer RPF.
MSDP.quote: the MVPN SA route is treated as if a corresponding MSDP SA message was received from within the PE mesh group and normal MSDP procedure is followed

rejected.why: BGP carries the MVPN routes and Extended Community, but the document is about MVPN/MSDP interoperation, not BGP itself.
PIM Register and RP behaviour are mentioned as ways a PE learns sources, but PIM-SM is not specified or extended here.
It defines one Extended Community sub-type, but only as an MVPN-specific encoding, not as a general BGP communities topic.
The parent topic is implied by the more specific MVPN and MSDP tags.

RFC9082.title: Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) Query Format
RFC9082.summary: RFC 9082 specifies the uniform HTTP URL query patterns (lookup and search path segments) for RDAP to retrieve registration data about IP networks, AS numbers, domains, nameservers and entities, obsoleting RFC 7482.

RDAP.why: The document is the RDAP query format specification, defining path segments, search patterns and query processing.
RDAP.quote: These uniform patterns define the query syntax for the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP).

rejected.why: HTTP is only the substrate; the document defines RDAP URL patterns, not HTTP semantics or extensions.
IDN handling (A-label/U-label) is addressed for queries, but the document is not about IDNA itself.
It constructs URLs but does not define URI syntax or a scheme.
WHOIS is mentioned only as the legacy protocol RDAP replaces; the document does not specify or operate it.
JSON responses are defined in RFC 9083, not here.
EPP is referenced only for contact identifier syntax.

RFC9083.title: JSON Responses for the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP)
RFC9083.summary: RFC 9083 specifies the JSON data structures (object classes for entities, nameservers, domains, IP networks, autnums, plus errors, help and search responses) used in RDAP query responses by RIRs and DNRs, obsoleting RFC 7483.

RDAP.why: The document defines the response format of RDAP, including object classes, common structures, errors, searches, and an IANA registry of RDAP JSON values.
RDAP.quote: These data structures are used to form Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) query responses.

JSON.why: A substantial part is the JSON data model: member naming, extension rules, data types and the application/rdap+json media type.
JSON.quote: This document describes responses in the JSON [RFC8259] format for the queries as defined by the Registration Data Access Protocol Query Format

rejected.why: The secureDNS member carries DS/DNSKEY data, but DNSSEC is only represented as registration data, not specified or profiled.
Only the port43 member references WHOIS servers. The document is about RDAP, not WHOIS.
EPP is mentioned for status mapping and the motivation for JSON, but it is not the subject.
jCard is used to carry contact information, but the document does not define or extend vCard.
