The application/rdap+json registration is in the IANA section, which is boilerplate, not the main body subject.
IDN variants are modelled as data, but IDN itself is not the subject.

RFC9084.title: OSPF Prefix Originator Extensions
RFC9084.summary: Defines two OSPFv2/OSPFv3 prefix sub-TLVs (Prefix Source OSPF Router-ID and Prefix Source Router Address) that carry information about the router originating a prefix, with procedures for ABRs and ASBRs.

OSPF.why: The whole document extends OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 with new sub-TLVs and procedures for originator information in prefix advertisements.
OSPF.quote: This document defines OSPF extensions to include information associated with the node originating a prefix along with the prefix advertisement.

rejected.why: OSPFv3 is covered alongside OSPFv2, and the document is about OSPF extensions generally. The parent OSPF tag fits better.
BGP-LS is mentioned only as a way a controller may receive this information. The document does not specify it.
Traffic engineering is named as a use case. The document defines no TE mechanism.
ECMP appears only in the rules for including multiple originator sub-TLVs. The document is not about ECMP forwarding.

RFC9085.title: Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS) Extensions for Segment Routing
RFC9085.summary: Defines new BGP-LS Attribute TLVs that carry Segment Routing information (SIDs, SRGB/SRLB, algorithms, Adj-SIDs, Prefix-SIDs, ranges) derived from IS-IS, OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 SR extensions.

BGP-SPF.why: The taxonomy has no plain BGP-LS tag; BGP-SPF is the closest BGP-LS-related tech, though this RFC is not about BGP-SPF itself. Weak fit, see gaps.
BGP-SPF.quote: This document defines extensions to the Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS) address family in order to carry SR information via BGP.

segment routing.why: The document specifies how SR information (SIDs, SRGB, SRLB, algorithms, SRMS) is encoded and advertised in BGP-LS, so SR readers need it.
segment routing.quote: Segment Routing (SR) allows for a flexible definition of end-to-end paths by combining subpaths called "segments".

rejected.why: BGP-LS is carried over BGP, but the document only adds Attribute TLVs and states it does not change BGP operation; a BGP-LS specific tag is not in the taxonomy and BGP is the substrate.
The TLVs are derived from OSPF SR extensions, which are defined elsewhere (RFC 8665/8666); this document only maps them into BGP-LS.
Same as OSPF: IS-IS SR TLVs are defined in RFC 8667 and merely mapped here.
Labels and SRGB are involved, but the document is about BGP-LS encoding of SR, not the SR-MPLS data plane.
A PCE is mentioned only as an example consumer of the information in the manageability section.

gaps.name: BGP-LS (BGP Link State)
gaps.why: The document is fundamentally about BGP-LS, the address family for distributing link-state and TE information over BGP. The taxonomy has no BGP-LS tag, only BGP and BGP-SPF.

RFC9086.title: Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS) Extensions for Segment Routing BGP Egress Peer Engineering
RFC9086.summary: Defines BGP-LS extensions (new Protocol-ID, node descriptor TLVs, and PeerNode/PeerAdj/PeerSet SID attribute TLVs) to advertise Segment Routing BGP peering segments for Egress Peer Engineering.

segment routing.why: The document defines how SR BGP Peering Segments (PeerNode, PeerAdj, PeerSet SIDs) are advertised, so it is about segment routing.
segment routing.quote: A node steers a packet through a controlled set of instructions, called segments, by prepending the packet with a list of segment identifiers (SIDs).

BGP.why: It extends BGP-LS with a new Protocol-ID, node descriptor TLVs and link attribute TLVs, and covers BGP peering sessions and EPE. BGP-LS has no tag of its own, so BGP is the closest fit.
BGP.quote: This document describes extensions to the BGP - Link State Network Layer Reachability Information (BGP-LS NLRI) and the BGP-LS Attribute defined for BGP-LS [RFC7752]

SR-MPLS.why: The SIDs are encoded as MPLS labels or SRGB indices and are used on the SR-MPLS data plane. The SRv6 extensions are left to another document.
SR-MPLS.quote: to enable computation of efficient BGP Egress Peer Engineering (BGP-EPE) policies and strategies using the SR-MPLS data plane.

rejected.why: BGP-EPE is a traffic engineering use case, but this document only specifies the advertisement encodings, not the TE computation.
The document explicitly leaves the SRv6 extensions to [BGPLS-SRV6].
Confederations and IBGP are mentioned only in passing in the descriptor and applicability text. They are not the subject of the document.
No communities are involved.

gaps.name: BGP-LS (BGP Link State) and BGP Egress Peer Engineering
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for BGP-LS or for EPE, which are the core subjects. BGP, segment routing and SR-MPLS are the nearest tags.

RFC9087.title: Segment Routing Centralized BGP Egress Peer Engineering
RFC9087.summary: Informational document describing how Segment Routing peering SIDs, BGP-LS signalling and a central controller implement BGP Egress Peer Engineering (BGP-EPE) policies at ingress routers or hosts.

segment routing.why: The document applies the SR architecture, using PeerNode, PeerAdj and PeerSet SIDs in segment lists, to egress peer engineering.
segment routing.quote: This document illustrates the application of Segment Routing to solve the BGP Egress Peer Engineering (BGP-EPE) requirement.

BGP.why: The document is about BGP egress peer engineering. It covers BGP peering segments, BGP-LS signalling of the external topology, and BGP labeled-unicast and VPN routes used to program policy.
BGP.quote: a Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS) [RFC7752] session is established between the BGP-EPE-enabled border router and the BGP-EPE controller.

rejected.why: The document is mostly data-plane agnostic. It says it applies equally to IPv4 with MPLS SIDs and to native IPv6 SIDs, so the general SR tag fits better.
PCEP is only mentioned as one example of how a tunnel can be programmed (Section 5.2).
BMP is mentioned only as an alternative way to collect Adj-RIB-In.
A centralized SDN controller is the context, but the document is not about SDN in general.
FRR backup for peering SIDs is covered in one subsection (3.6), which is not enough to make it a subject of the document.
A VPN policy route is only one of the programming options in Section 5.4.

gaps.name: BGP-LS / BGP Egress Peer Engineering
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for BGP-LS or BGP-EPE. A BGP-EPE tag would be the best fit under BGP.

RFC9088.title: Signaling Entropy Label Capability and Entropy Readable Label Depth Using IS-IS
RFC9088.summary: Defines IS-IS extensions (a Prefix Attribute Flags E-Flag and a new ERLD-MSD type) to advertise Entropy Label Capability and Entropy Readable Label Depth, and notes their carriage in BGP-LS.

IS-IS.why: The document specifies new IS-IS signaling: the ELC flag in prefix attributes and the ERLD-MSD type. It extends IS-IS.
IS-IS.quote: Bit 3 in the Prefix Attribute Flags [RFC7794] is used as the ELC Flag (E-Flag)

MPLS.why: Entropy labels for MPLS load-balancing are the subject. The document signals the capabilities ingress LSRs need to insert ELs.
MPLS.quote: Entropy Readable Label Depth (ERLD) as defined in [RFC8662], may be used by ingress LSRs to determine the position of the EL label in the stack

BGP.why: A section and the abstract cover carrying ELC and ERLD in BGP-LS. This is secondary because it only reuses existing BGP-LS TLVs, and no BGP-LS-specific tag exists.
BGP.quote: The ELC is advertised using the Prefix Attribute Flags TLV as defined in [RFC9085].
BGP.section: 5. Signaling ELC and ERLD in BGP-LS

rejected.why: SR-MPLS is only the context for ERLD. The document defines nothing specific to segment routing.
Entropy labels serve load-balancing, but the document is about capability signaling, not ECMP forwarding.
BGP-LS is used only to carry the IS-IS information. This is not BGP-SPF.
It is cited only as an example data plane for ERLD. The document does not specify it.

gaps.name: Entropy labels / ELC / ERLD
gaps.why: The document is about MPLS entropy label capability signaling. The taxonomy has no tag for entropy labels, so MPLS is the closest fit.

RFC9089.title: Signaling Entropy Label Capability and Entropy Readable Label Depth Using OSPF
RFC9089.summary: Defines OSPFv2/OSPFv3 extensions (E-Flag in prefix flags/options, and ERLD via Node MSD) to advertise Entropy Label Capability and Entropy Readable Label Depth, with BGP-LS carriage, for MPLS entropy-label load balancing.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 with a new ELC flag and ERLD advertisement, including ABR/ASBR propagation rules.
OSPF.quote: This document defines a mechanism to signal these two capabilities using OSPFv2 and OSPFv3

MPLS.why: The capabilities signalled concern MPLS entropy labels and label stack reading depth, which MPLS readers would want.
MPLS.quote: a method to load-balance Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) traffic flows using Entropy Labels (EL)

segment routing.why: ERLD is motivated by SR-MPLS and is advertised via the Node MSD TLV (maximum SID depth), so segment routing readers would find it relevant.
segment routing.quote: In cases where Segment Routing (SR) is used with the MPLS data plane (e.g., SR-MPLS [RFC8660]), it would be useful for ingress LSRs

rejected.why: BGP-LS only carries the OSPF extensions using existing TLVs in a short section; BGP itself is not extended.
The document does not specify SR-MPLS; it only cites it as context for ERLD.
OSPFv3 is used for IPv6 but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
The IANA section only records flag allocations, which is boilerplate.

gaps.name: Entropy Labels (ELC/ERLD)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MPLS entropy label load balancing, so the subject is covered only by the broader MPLS tag.

RFC9090.title: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) Tags for Object Identifiers
RFC9090.summary: Defines CBOR tags 110, 111 and 112 for BER-encoded absolute and relative object identifiers, tag factoring over arrays and maps, and new CDDL control operators (.sdnv, .sdnvseq, .oid).

CBOR.why: The document extends CBOR with new registered tags and defines their semantics, serialization and factoring rules.
CBOR.quote: This document defines CBOR tags for object identifiers (OIDs) [X.660], which many IETF protocols carry.

CDDL.why: A substantial part defines new CDDL control operators (.sdnv, .sdnvseq, .oid) and recommended CDDL type names for the tags.
CDDL.quote: This document introduces two new control operators that can be applied to a target value that is a byte string

ASN.1.why: The tags carry BER-encoded ASN.1 OBJECT IDENTIFIER and RELATIVE-OID values, and the body specifies the exact BER content rules. OID encoding is a core ASN.1 topic.
ASN.1.quote: The ASN.1 Basic Encoding Rules (BER) [X.690] specify binary encodings of both (absolute) object identifiers and relative object identifiers.

rejected.why: The X.500 distinguished name is only an example of tag factoring, not the subject of the document.
The IANA registrations of tags and operators are boilerplate-like and the document is not about IANA registry policy.
A MIB relative OID appears only as a worked example.
JSON is mentioned only in passing, via the CDDL reference.

gaps.name: Object identifiers (OIDs)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for OID encoding or registration in its own right. ASN.1 is the closest fit but does not cover OID usage across protocols.

RFC9091.title: Experimental Domain-Based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) Extension for Public Suffix Domains
RFC9091.summary: RFC 9091 defines an experimental extension to DMARC that lets Public Suffix Domain operators publish policy covering non-existent subdomains, adding a PSD policy-discovery step, the "np" tag, and privacy constraints on feedback reporting.

DMARC.why: The whole document modifies DMARC (RFC 7489): new np tag, ABNF changes, policy discovery step 3A, and feedback rules for PSDs.
DMARC.quote: This document describes an extension to DMARC to fully enable DMARC functionality for PSDs.

rejected.why: DNS is used for policy lookup of TXT records and NXDOMAIN definitions, but the document defines no new DNS behaviour or record type; it is the substrate.
The IANA section only registers the np tag in the DMARC Tag Registry; this is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
Privacy Considerations section addresses feedback leakage, but it is specific to DMARC reporting and is a secondary section rather than a main subject of general protocol privacy.
Parent of DMARC, which is implied by the more specific DMARC tag.
Mentioned only in the implementations appendix (zdkimfilter); the document is not about DKIM.
The document deals with public suffix domains, not reserved or special-use names.

gaps.name: Public Suffix List / Public Suffix Domains
gaps.why: The document centres on the public suffix concept and a PSD registry, which the taxonomy has no tag for; it is partly covered by DMARC and naming but not specifically.

RFC9092.title: Finding and Using Geofeed Data
RFC9092.summary: Specifies how to locate geofeed (RFC 8805) CSV files via a Geofeed remarks:/geofeed: attribute in RPSL inetnum: objects, and an optional RPKI-based CMS detached signature scheme to authenticate them.

RPSL.why: The core of the document is extending the RPSL inetnum: class with a geofeed reference and rules for using inetnum hierarchy and registries.
RPSL.quote: This document specifies how to augment the Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL) [RFC2725] inetnum: class to refer specifically to geofeed data CSV files

RPKI.why: A major part defines RPKI-based signing and validation of geofeed files, including resource coverage checks.
RPKI.quote: It is a digest of the main body of the file signed by the private key of the relevant RPKI certificate for a covering address range.

geolocation.why: The document is about discovering and using IP geolocation feed data, including its privacy considerations.
geolocation.quote: [RFC8805] defines geofeed, a syntax to associate geographic locales with IP addresses, but it does not specify how to find the relevant geofeed data

rejected.why: CMS is the signature container used for the detached signature; the document defines no new CMS behaviour beyond a content type registration.
WHOIS, RDAP and FTP are only the means of fetching inetnum data; the document does not specify them.
Geofeed CSV format is defined by RFC 8805; this document only references the files.
HTTPS is merely the fetch mechanism, with a note on Expires headers.
RPKI certificates are used as-is; no certificate profile is defined here.
The privacy considerations section is short and defers to RFC 8805; it is not the document's main subject.

RFC9093.title: A YANG Data Model for Layer 0 Types
RFC9093.summary: Defines the ietf-layer0-types YANG module, common types and groupings (identities, typedefs for DWDM/CWDM/flexi-grid labels, channel spacing, slot width) for modelling Layer 0 optical TE such as WSON and flexi-grid DWDM.

YANG.why: The document's purpose is a YANG module of reusable types and groupings for Layer 0 optical networks, so readers of YANG models would look for it.
YANG.quote: This document defines a collection of common data types and groupings in the YANG data modeling language.

GMPLS.why: The module models GMPLS optical labels (LSC labels, WSON, flexi-grid DWDM) and GMPLS-controlled optical TE, so the GMPLS/optical control subject fits.
GMPLS.quote: The flexi-grid label range was defined in [RFC7698], and the generic topology model defines the label-start/label-end in [RFC8795].

rejected.why: Only mentioned as a protocol that may access the module, in the introduction and Security Considerations; the document does not specify NETCONF.
The types support TE modelling but the document is a type library for optical grids, not about TE in general; GMPLS covers the optical control context.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations boilerplate.
Appears only as a transport in Security Considerations.
Appears only as a transport in Security Considerations.
Referenced only for the ISCD priority and flexi-grid field definitions; the document does not specify OSPF.

gaps.name: Layer 0 optical networks (WSON, flexi-grid DWDM)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for optical transport networks or wavelength-switched optical networks, apart from GMPLS, so this subject is only partly covered.

RFC9094.title: A YANG Data Model for Wavelength Switched Optical Networks (WSONs)
RFC9094.summary: Defines the ietf-wson-topology YANG module, augmenting the generic TE topology model (RFC 8795) to describe routing and wavelength assignment (RWA) topology in wavelength switched optical networks.

YANG.why: The document's sole purpose is a YANG module (ietf-wson-topology) augmenting ietf-te-topology, with tree diagram and module source.
YANG.quote: This document provides a YANG data model for the routing and wavelength assignment (RWA) Traffic Engineering (TE) topology in transparent Wavelength Switched Optical Networks (WSONs).

GMPLS.why: WSON RWA information derives from GMPLS-controlled optical network work; the model covers optical transport network topology and wavelength labels (label restrictions, connectivity matrices).
GMPLS.quote: based on the information model developed in [RFC7446] and the two encoding documents ([RFC7581] and [RFC7579])

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the protocol used to access the model; the document defines no NETCONF behaviour.
RESTCONF is mentioned only as an access mechanism; nothing new is specified about it.
The model augments a TE topology, but its subject is WSON-specific wavelength attributes in YANG; GMPLS covers the optical angle better.
Mentioned only in the Security Considerations boilerplate.
Mentioned only in the Security Considerations boilerplate.

gaps.name: Wavelength Switched Optical Networks (WSON) / optical transport
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for optical networks, DWDM/CWDM wavelength routing and RWA; GMPLS is the closest fit.

RFC9095.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Domain Name Mapping Extension for Strict Bundling Registration
RFC9095.summary: Defines a proprietary EPP domain name mapping extension (b-dn namespace) for provisioning strict bundled domain names (RDN and BDN, e.g. IDN variants) atomically across check, info, create, delete, renew, transfer and update commands.

EPP.why: The document specifies a new EPP extension with new XML elements and command mappings for bundled domain registration.
EPP.quote: This document describes an extension of Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) domain name mapping for the provisioning and management of strict bundling registration of domain names.

IDN.why: Bundling is motivated by IDN variants (e.g. Chinese SC/TC forms), and the elements carry A-label and U-label forms. This is a substantial part of the document's subject.
IDN.quote: This document mainly discusses the situation in which variant IDNs that are identified as equivalent are allocated or delegated to the same registrant.

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the EPP tag, so it is not listed separately.
XML and XML Schema are only the encoding for the extension. The document does not define anything new about XML itself.
DS/DNSKEY sharing appears only briefly in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate evidence.
The document is about registry provisioning, not DNS protocol behaviour.
The IANA registrations are routine boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC9096.title: Improving the Reaction of Customer Edge Routers to IPv6 Renumbering Events
RFC9096.summary: BCP updating RFC 7084 that specifies CE router behaviours (stable DHCPv6 IAIDs, no automatic PD RELEASE, capped LAN-side lifetimes, deprecating stale prefixes with zero lifetimes) to mitigate IPv6 flash-renumbering problems.

renumbering.why: The document's purpose is making CE routers react properly to renumbering and flash-renumbering events, which is the renumbering topic.
renumbering.quote: CE routers MUST NOT advertise prefixes via SLAAC or assign addresses or delegate prefixes via DHCPv6 on the LAN side using lifetimes that exceed the remaining lifetimes

DHCPv6.why: Substantial requirements on DHCPv6-PD client and LAN-side server behaviour: IAID stability, RELEASE, IA Address/Prefix lifetimes, Reconfigure.
DHCPv6.quote: CE routers SHOULD NOT automatically send DHCPv6-PD RELEASE messages upon restart events.

SLAAC.why: Specifies how PIO and RA lifetimes are set and how stale SLAAC prefixes are deprecated by the CE router.
SLAAC.quote: Any prefixes that were previously advertised by the CE router via PIOs in RA messages, but that have now become stale, MUST be advertised with PIOs

rejected.why: RA/PIO options are manipulated, but the document is about CE router renumbering behaviour rather than specifying ND itself.
Implied as the parent of SLAAC; a more specific tag fits.
Targets residential CE routers, but it is not about home network architecture, prefix assignment and naming as a whole; it updates the CE requirements in RFC 7084.
No IPv4/IPv6 coexistence content.

gaps.name: IPv6 Customer Edge router requirements
gaps.why: The document updates RFC 7084 (CE router requirements); the taxonomy has no tag for CE router requirements apart from the loosely related home networking tag.

RFC9097.title: Metrics and Methods for One-Way IP Capacity
RFC9097.summary: Defines the Maximum IP-Layer Capacity metric, related singleton metrics (IP-Layer Capacity, Sender Bit Rate), and a UDP-based active measurement method with a load rate adjustment algorithm, for diagnosing access-network capacity.

performance measurement.why: The RFC is an IPPM document specifying capacity metrics and measurement methods, with reporting formats; this is the core of performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: The scope of this memo is to define Active Measurement metrics and corresponding methods to unambiguously determine Maximum IP-Layer Capacity and useful secondary metrics.

rejected.why: UDP is only the substrate for test packets. Appendix B checks compliance with RFC 8085, but the document does not extend or specify UDP.
The load rate adjustment algorithm explicitly 'MUST NOT be used as a general Congestion Control Algorithm', so the document is not about congestion control.
RFC 2544 is discussed only as a contrast. This RFC targets production-network active measurement, not lab benchmarking.
TWAMP and OWAMP are cited only in Security Considerations and as related protocols. The document does not specify or extend them.
ECN is mentioned only in passing as one indicator of congestion, and the memo says it sees no benefit in using it.

RFC9098.title: Operational Implications of IPv6 Packets with Extension Headers
RFC9098.summary: Informational analysis of why IPv6 packets with extension headers are often dropped in the public Internet, covering router forwarding-engine constraints, ECMP, ACL, DDoS, IDS and firewall needs, and security implications.

IPv6.why: The whole document analyzes operational implications of IPv6 extension headers and header-chain structure, so it belongs on the IPv6 page.
IPv6.quote: IPv6 extension headers (EHs) allow for the extension of the IPv6 protocol and provide support for core functionality such as IPv6 fragmentation.

operational security.why: A substantial part covers operator practices (iACLs, firewalls, NIDS/IPS, route-processor protection, DDoS filtering) and why they lead to dropping EH packets.
operational security.quote: Infrastructure Access Control Lists (iACLs) drop unwanted packets destined to a network's infrastructure.

ECMP.why: A dedicated section discusses ECMP hashing, Flow Label use, and how EH chains complicate it.
ECMP.quote: In the case of Equal Cost Multipath (ECMP) load sharing, the intermediate system needs to make a decision regarding which of its interfaces to use

rejected.why: Firewalling is one section among several reasons for dropping EH packets; the document is not about firewall mechanisms themselves.
Only mentioned as a means of automating Layer 4 DDoS filtering; not about it.
DDoS filtering is a brief subsection giving one motivation for filtering, not a main subject.
NIDS/IPS difficulties with EHs is a short subsection of motivation, not about intrusion detection message exchange.
IPv4 is compared only as background for the header structure.
Path MTU is mentioned only as a constraint on header chain size.

gaps.name: IPv6 extension headers / fragmentation
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no child of IPv6 for extension headers or IPv6 fragmentation, which is the document's central subject; IPv6 is the closest fit.

RFC9099.title: Operational Security Considerations for IPv6 Networks
RFC9099.summary: Informational guidance on operational security of managed IPv6 networks (enterprise, service provider, residential), covering addressing, extension headers, link-layer/NDP security, control plane, routing, logging, and transition mechanisms.

operational security.why: The whole document is operational security practice for network infrastructure (device hardening, control plane protection, logging, filtering).
operational security.quote: This document analyzes the operational security issues associated with several types of networks and proposes technical and procedural mitigation techniques.

IPv6.why: Document is about securely operating IPv6 networks: addressing, extension headers, SLAAC, and deployment.
IPv6.quote: IPv6 presents some new security challenges.

neighbor discovery.why: Substantial sections cover NDP attacks, RA-Guard, rate limiting, and mitigations.
neighbor discovery.quote: IPv6 relies heavily on NDP [RFC4861] to perform a variety of link operations

IPv6 transition.why: Section 2.7 analyses security of dual stack, tunnels, 6rd, MAP, NAT64, DS-Lite, Teredo.
IPv6 transition.quote: the different transition mechanisms must be deployed and operated in a secure way.

SAVI.why: SAVI is recommended as a first line of defense and used in forensic logging.
SAVI.quote: [RFC7513] helps in creating bindings between a source IP address assigned to DHCPv4 [RFC2131] or DHCPv6 [RFC8415] and a binding anchor

rejected.why: Securing DHCPv6 (DHCPv6-Shield) is one subsection; the document does not specify or extend DHCPv6.
BGP security is briefly covered by reference to RFC 7454, not a main subject.
Used as a logging data source, not specified or extended.
Routing security is a short section; the document's broader focus is operational security.
CGN and NAT64 appear only within the transition discussion.
IPsec is a mitigation referenced throughout, not the subject.

RFC9100.title: Sensor Measurement Lists (SenML) Features and Versions
RFC9100.summary: RFC 9100 updates SenML (RFC 8428) by redefining the SenML version number as a bitmap of independently selectable features, defining the Secondary Units feature, and creating an IANA SenML Features registry.

SenML.why: The document extends SenML's versioning mechanism, defining feature codes, the version bitmap, and the Secondary Units feature.
SenML.quote: specifying the use of independently selectable "SenML Features" and mapping them to SenML version numbers

rejected.why: JSON is only the representation substrate; the I-JSON limit is mentioned just to bound feature codes.
The new SenML Features registry is boilerplate-like IANA considerations for a SenML-specific registry, not about IANA guidance.
SenML can be encoded in CBOR, but the document is not about that encoding.

RFC9101.title: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework: JWT-Secured Authorization Request (JAR)
RFC9101.summary: RFC 9101 defines JWT-Secured Authorization Request (JAR) for OAuth 2.0, letting authorization request parameters be sent as a signed and optionally encrypted JWT, by value ("request") or by reference ("request_uri").

OAuth.why: The document extends the OAuth 2.0 authorization request with new parameters, new error codes and metadata, so it is squarely about OAuth.
OAuth.quote: The parameters "request" and "request_uri" are introduced as additional authorization request parameters for the OAuth 2.0 [RFC6749] flows.

JWT.why: The Request Object is a JWT with defined claims handling, registered JWT claims as OAuth parameters, a new media type and cross-JWT confusion guidance; JWT readers would want it.
JWT.quote: A Request Object is a JSON Web Token (JWT) [RFC7519] whose JWT Claims Set holds the JSON-encoded OAuth 2.0 authorization request parameters.

rejected.why: JWS and JWE are used as the signing and encryption mechanisms but are not extended or profiled beyond applying them to requests.
TLS requirements section just points to RFC 7525 and server identity checks; TLS is a substrate here.
The request_uri is fetched with an HTTP GET, but HTTP is only the transport.
Registers application/oauth-authz-req+jwt, but this is IANA boilerplate-style registration for the document's own object, not about media type rules.
request_uri is an OAuth parameter holding a URI; the document does not specify URI syntax or schemes.
Privacy Considerations section is brief and specific to this spec; not a main subject.

RFC9102.title: TLS DNSSEC Chain Extension
RFC9102.summary: Defines an experimental TLS extension (dnssec_chain) that carries the DNSSEC authentication chain for a server's DANE TLSA records (or a denial-of-existence proof) in the TLS handshake, including pinning, caching and test vectors.

TLS.why: The document defines a new TLS extension (dnssec_chain) with ClientHello/ServerHello/Certificate message handling for TLS 1.2 and 1.3.
TLS.quote: This document describes an experimental TLS extension for the in-band transport of the complete set of records that can be validated by DNSSEC

DANE.why: The extension exists to deliver TLSA RRsets and proofs of their absence, so DANE clients can authenticate servers. It also covers DANE certificate usages and operational guidance for hosting.
DANE.quote: This extension enables a TLS client to perform DANE authentication [RFC6698] [RFC7671] of a TLS server without the need to perform out-of-band DNS lookups.

DNSSEC.why: A substantial part of the document specifies how to build and validate DNSSEC chains, including NSEC/NSEC3 denial of existence, trust anchors and signature expiry, with test vectors.
DNSSEC.quote: The AuthenticationChain is composed of a sequence of uncompressed wire format DNS RRs (including all requisite RRSIG RRs [RFC4034]) in no particular order.

rejected.why: DNS over TLS is cited only as one motivating application (RFC 8310). The document does not specify it.
PKIX certificates appear only as the fallback authentication method and in the test-vector certificate. They are not the subject.
DNS records are the payload, but the document adds no new DNS protocol behaviour. DNSSEC and DANE cover the DNS aspects.
DTLS is mentioned once, for the transport label. The document is not about DTLS.

RFC9103.title: DNS Zone Transfer over TLS
RFC9103.summary: Specifies XFR over TLS (XoT) to encrypt DNS zone transfers (AXFR/IXFR) against passive eavesdropping, and updates RFC 1995, 5936 and 7766 on TCP connection reuse and connection counts.

DNS.why: The document specifies and updates DNS zone transfer (AXFR/IXFR) behaviour, including connection reuse, pipelining and NOTIFY/SOA flows, and updates RFC 1995, 5936 and 7766. No narrower DNS tag covers zone transfer.
DNS.quote: This document specifies the use of TLS, rather than cleartext, to prevent zone content collection via passive monitoring of zone transfers: XFR over TLS (XoT).

DoT.why: XoT is a DoT-based mechanism: it uses port 853, the "dot" ALPN and the RFC 8310 Strict and Mutual TLS profiles for zone transfers. It also discusses XoT versus authoritative DoT.
DoT.quote: encrypting zone transfers using TLS [RFC8499] -- based closely on DoT [RFC7858] -- seems like a simple step forward.

rejected.why: TLS 1.3 is the substrate for XoT. The document defines no new TLS extension or behaviour.
Considered as the parent of DoT. It is implied by DoT, so I did not tag it separately.
NSEC/NSEC3 zone enumeration appears only as background and is described as orthogonal to this work.
The edns-tcp-keepalive option and the OPT record in AXFR responses are used and clarified, but only as supporting detail.
The document updates how TCP connections are reused for XFR, but this is DNS-specific guidance under RFC 7766 and not TCP itself.

RFC9104.title: Distribution of Traffic Engineering Extended Administrative Groups Using the Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS)
RFC9104.summary: Defines a new BGP-LS Link Attribute TLV (type 1173) that carries extended administrative groups (link colors) from IGPs to BGP-LS consumers such as controllers for traffic engineering.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP-LS with a new Attribute TLV. No narrower BGP child tag fits, and BGP-LS has no dedicated tag, so BGP is the best fit.
BGP.quote: This document defines an extension to the Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS) for advertisement of extended administrative groups (EAGs).

rejected.why: Administrative groups are TE link attributes, but the document only defines their BGP-LS encoding. It does not address TE itself.
IS-IS is the source of the EAG information, but this document does not specify or extend it.
OSPF is an underlying source of EAG data per RFC 7308 and is not specified or extended here.
This is about BGP-LS attribute distribution, not link-state routing computed using BGP.
The EAG concept originates in MPLS-TE (RFC 7308), but this document does not address MPLS.

gaps.name: BGP-LS (BGP Link State)
gaps.why: The document is specifically about BGP-LS topology distribution, and the taxonomy has no dedicated tag for it. BGP is the closest.

RFC9105.title: A YANG Data Model for Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+)
RFC9105.summary: Defines the ietf-system-tacacs-plus YANG module, which augments the RFC 7317 System Management model so devices can be configured as TACACS+ clients for centralized AAA.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG data model (module, tree diagram, and example) for TACACS+ client configuration.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG module that augments the System Management data model defined in [RFC7317] to support the configuration and management of TACACS+ clients.

TACACS+.why: The module models TACACS+ client configuration (servers, shared secret, single-connection mode, statistics). Readers of the TACACS+ subject would want it.
TACACS+.quote: TACACS+ [RFC8907] provides device administration for routers, network access servers, and other networked devices via one or more centralized servers.

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the management protocol the module can be used with. The document does not specify or extend it.
RADIUS is mentioned only as the existing alternative in RFC 7317 that TACACS+ is added alongside.
TACACS+ is the more specific tag for this document, so the AAA parent is implied and not listed separately.
TLS appears only in the Security Considerations, as RESTCONF's secure transport.
SSH appears only in the Security Considerations, as NETCONF's secure transport.
RESTCONF is only mentioned in the Security Considerations as a way to access the module.

RFC9106.title: Argon2 Memory-Hard Function for Password Hashing and Proof-of-Work Applications
RFC9106.summary: RFC 9106 gives an implementer-oriented specification of the Argon2 memory-hard function (Argon2d, Argon2i, Argon2id) for password hashing and proof-of-work, with parameter guidance, test vectors and security analysis.

password hashing.why: The whole document specifies Argon2, a memory-hard password hashing and key stretching function, including its algorithm, parameter selection and test vectors. This is the most specific tag available.
password hashing.quote: This document describes the Argon2 [ARGON2ESP] memory-hard function for password hashing and proof-of-work applications.

rejected.why: Argon2 uses BLAKE2b internally as its hash H and builds its permutation P on the BLAKE2b round function. The document is not about BLAKE2 itself, which is specified in RFC 7693.
The document does not discuss scrypt. Only a related memory-hard function (Balloon hashing) appears, in the references.
PBKDF2 is not discussed. Argon2 is only mentioned as suitable for password-based key derivation.
Key derivation for disk encryption is only one suggested parameter setting. The document is about a hash function, not key management.

gaps.name: Memory-hard functions / proof-of-work
gaps.why: The document covers memory-hard functions and their use for proof-of-work and cryptocurrency mining, including time-memory trade-off analysis. The taxonomy has no general tag for this beyond the password hashing subtree.

RFC9107.title: BGP Optimal Route Reflection (BGP ORR)
RFC9107.summary: RFC 9107 extends BGP route reflectors so route selection uses the IGP cost from a configured IGP location (per RR, client set, or client) rather than the RR's own position, enabling optimal hot-potato routing with centralized route reflectors.

route reflection.why: The whole document defines modifications to BGP route reflector path selection (BGP ORR), so the route reflection tag fits best.
route reflection.quote: On route reflectors, BGP route selection is modified in order to choose the best route from the standpoint of their clients, rather than from the standpoint of the route reflectors themselves.

rejected.why: The more specific child tag route reflection applies, so the BGP parent is implied.
OSPF and IS-IS are only link-state IGP sources of topology for computing IGP cost; the document does not specify or extend them.
Mentioned only as a possible source of IGP topology; not the subject of the document.
BGP-LS is mentioned only as an alternative way to learn the IGP topology; BGP-SPF is not addressed.
IP VPNs are mentioned only as the initial use case for out-of-path route reflectors; the document is not about VPNs.
MPLS encapsulation is mentioned only as a forwarding environment in the deployment discussion.

RFC9108.title: YANG Types for DNS Classes and Resource Record Types
RFC9108.summary: Defines the IANA-maintained YANG module iana-dns-class-rr-type, providing derived types dns-class and rr-type that mirror the IANA DNS CLASSes and Resource Record TYPEs registries, with IANA update procedures.

YANG.why: The document's deliverable is a YANG module of derived types for use in future data models, so YANG readers would want it.
YANG.quote: This document introduces the YANG module "iana-dns-class-rr-type", which contains derived types reflecting two IANA registries

DNS.why: The types represent DNS classes and RR types, so the document is about DNS resource record parameters and their modelling for DNS management.
DNS.quote: defines derived types for the common parameters of DNS resource records (RR): class and type.

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only mentioned as management protocols that could use the types; the document does not specify or extend them.
The IANA registry update procedure is boilerplate-like and secondary to the YANG types; the document is not about IANA stewardship generally.
XSLT is only the tool used to generate the module, not the subject.
Mentioned only as a possible management protocol, not specified or extended.

RFC9109.title: Network Time Protocol Version 4: Port Randomization
RFC9109.summary: RFC 9109 updates NTPv4 (RFC 5905) to recommend transport-protocol ephemeral port randomization for client mode, rather than using well-known port 123, to mitigate blind/off-path attacks.

NTP.why: The document specifies a change to the NTP protocol specification (dstport variable in RFC 5905 Section 9.1) for client mode and discusses effects on NTP measurements.
NTP.quote: This document formally updates RFC 5905, recommending the use of transport-protocol ephemeral port randomization for those modes where use of the NTP well-known port is not required.

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport on which NTP runs; the document does not define anything new about UDP itself.
ECMP's effect on path selection is discussed in one subsection only as a consideration, not the subject.
NAPT effects on the well-known port are a brief consideration, not the subject of the document.
The document addresses an NTP protocol vulnerability mitigation, not general operational security practices.

RFC9110.title: HTTP Semantics

RFC9134.summary: Specifies an RTP payload format for carrying JPEG XS (ISO/IEC 21122) low-latency video, including packetization modes, payload header, the video/jxsv media type, and SDP parameter mapping.

RTP payload format.why: The document defines a new RTP payload format for JPEG XS video, including payload header, packetization modes and the video/jxsv media type.
RTP payload format.quote: This document specifies a payload format for packetization of video signals encoded with JPEG XS [ISO21122-1] into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP)

codecs.why: A substantial part describes the JPEG XS codec structure (codestream, slices, precincts, VS/CS boxes) needed for packetization.
codecs.quote: JPEG XS is a low-latency, lightweight image coding system for coding continuous-tone grayscale or continuous-tone color digital images.

SDP.why: The document defines SDP mapping of the format parameters and offer/answer rules.
SDP.quote: The media type video/jxsv string is mapped to fields in the Session Description Protocol (SDP) [RFC8866] as follows:
SDP.section: 8.1. Mapping of Payload Type Parameters to SDP

rejected.why: RTP is the transport being profiled; the specific child RTP payload format tag is more precise.
The media type registration is part of the payload format definition, not about media type registry rules.
Congestion control section only refers to existing RTP mechanisms such as RFC 8083 and RFC 8888.
SRTP is mentioned only in security considerations boilerplate.
UDP is only a substrate and is referenced only for congestion guidance.

RFC9135.title: Integrated Routing and Bridging in Ethernet VPN (EVPN)
RFC9135.summary: Specifies EVPN-based Integrated Routing and Bridging (symmetric and asymmetric IRB) for inter-subnet forwarding on PEs/NVEs, including control/data plane procedures, mobility, and the new EVPN Router's MAC extended community.

EVPN.why: The document extends EVPN with IRB procedures, route advertisement (RT-2/RT-5) and mobility handling, and defines a new EVPN extended community.
EVPN.quote: This document describes an Integrated Routing and Bridging (IRB) solution based on EVPN to address such requirements.

rejected.why: VXLAN is only one of the encapsulations used; the document is not about VXLAN itself.
IP-VRFs follow RFC 4364 but the document is about EVPN IRB, not BGP/MPLS L3VPN.
BGP is the carrier for EVPN routes; the only BGP-level content is one new extended community for EVPN.
NVO tunnels are used as data-plane encapsulation, not specified here.
Only the anycast MAC ranges are borrowed from RFC 5798.
ARP/ND learning is used as an input to IRB procedures; the document does not specify ARP.

RFC9136.title: IP Prefix Advertisement in Ethernet VPN (EVPN)
RFC9136.summary: Defines the EVPN IP Prefix route (RT-5) for advertising IP prefixes in BGP EVPN, with Overlay Index recursive resolution and use cases (TS IP, floating IP, bump-in-the-wire, IP-VRF-to-IP-VRF) for inter-subnet connectivity in data centers.

EVPN.why: The document specifies a new EVPN route type (RT-5), its encoding, overlay index recursive resolution and use cases.
EVPN.quote: This document defines a new EVPN route type for the advertisement of IP prefixes and explains some use-case examples where this new route type is used.

rejected.why: VXLAN is only an example tunnel encapsulation used in the use cases; nothing new is defined about it.
GENEVE is mentioned only as an example NVO tunnel type.
BGP is the carrier of the NLRI, but the document is about the EVPN route type, not BGP itself.
RFC 4364 interoperability is explicitly out of scope; it is referenced only for comparison.
NVO is the context, but the document is about EVPN route advertisement rather than the encapsulation itself.
DC inter-subnet connectivity is the motivating context, but the EVPN tag covers the subject more specifically.

RFC9137.title: Considerations for Cancellation of IETF Meetings
RFC9137.summary: A BCP giving criteria for the IETF LLC, IESG and IRTF Chair to decide whether to relocate, virtualize, postpone or cancel an in-person IETF meeting, including refund rules.

IETF process.why: The document sets IETF procedure and administration for meeting cancellation, assigning roles to the IETF LLC, IESG and IRTF Chair, and defining remedies and refunds. That is IETF process.
IETF process.quote: This document provides criteria to aid the IETF Administration LLC (IETF LLC), the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG), and the Chair of the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF)

rejected.why: IPv4 and IPv6 connectivity appears only as a venue network requirement, so the document is not about IPv6.
The NomCom is not named. The only related text is a passing mention of effects on the nomination process and seating of new officers, which is too slight to tag.
There are no IANA actions. Only the boilerplate section mentions IANA.

RFC9138.title: Design Considerations for Name Resolution Service in Information-Centric Networking (ICN)
RFC9138.summary: An IRTF ICNRG informational document describing approaches, functionalities and design considerations for a Name Resolution Service (NRS) in Information-Centric Networking, which translates object names into locators, names, manifests or metadata.

ICN.why: The whole document is about name resolution service design within Information-Centric Networking, covering explicit, name-based routing and hybrid approaches, and NRS functionalities for ICN.
ICN.quote: The purpose of an NRS in ICN is to translate an object name into some other information such as a locator, another name, etc.

rejected.why: The NRS is ICN-specific rather than general naming; the ICN tag is the more specific fit, and the taxonomy places ICN under internet layer, not naming.
DNS appears only incidentally (NDNS, NEO DNS-based architecture); the document does not specify or analyse DNS.
Producer mobility is discussed as an NRS function in ICN, not IP-layer mobility protocols.
Routing scalability is touched on as one NRS function, but the document focuses on name resolution, with routing covered by a companion document.
IoT is mentioned as motivation and a scalability scenario only.

RFC9139.title: Information-Centric Networking (ICN) Adaptation to Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (LoWPANs)
RFC9139.summary: Defines ICN LoWPAN, a 6LoWPAN-style convergence layer for CCNx and NDN over IEEE 802.15.4, with new dispatch types, fragmentation reuse, and stateless and stateful header compression.

ICN.why: The document specifies how NDN and CCNx packets are encoded, compressed and fragmented. It is about ICN protocols and their adaptation to constrained links.
ICN.quote: This document defines a convergence layer for Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) and Named Data Networking (NDN) over IEEE 802.15.4 Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (LoWPANs).

6LoWPAN.why: The document extends the 6LoWPAN dispatch framework, reuses its fragmentation, and registers new dispatch values. The taxonomy covers 6LoWPAN and other constrained link layers under this tag.
6LoWPAN.quote: the dispatching scheme provided by IPv6 over LoWPAN (6LoWPAN) is extended to include new dispatch types for CCNx and NDN.

header compression.why: A large part of the document defines stateless and stateful header compression for ICN packets. No technology tag under header compression fits, because ROHC, CRTP and IPHC are IP-specific.
header compression.quote: Stateless compression reduces TLV expressions to static header fields for common use cases.

rejected.why: The document adapts ICN rather than IPv6. It only borrows the 6LoWPAN framework.
CoAP is mentioned only as a source of IoT naming-scheme studies.
IoT is the deployment context, but the document is about a link-layer adaptation. 6LoWPAN is already the more specific tag.
SDNV encoding is borrowed from DTN protocols, but the document does not address DTN.
The dispatch registry update is boilerplate here and not the subject of the document.

RFC9140.title: Nimble Out-of-Band Authentication for EAP (EAP-NOOB)
RFC9140.summary: Defines EAP-NOOB, an EAP method for bootstrapping IoT devices with no preconfigured credentials using ECDHE key exchange authenticated by a user-assisted one-directional out-of-band message, with fast reconnect, key derivation and IANA registries.

EAP.why: The document specifies a new EAP method, including its exchanges, state machine, key derivation (MSK/EMSK), and EAP security claims.
EAP.quote: This document defines the EAP-NOOB authentication method for nimble out-of-band (OOB) authentication and key derivation.

IoT.why: The method targets IoT device security bootstrapping with limited user interfaces, so IoT readers would want it.
IoT.quote: The EAP method is intended for bootstrapping all kinds of Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices that have no preconfigured authentication credentials.

rejected.why: JSON is only the message encoding for in-band messages, not the subject.
AAA architecture is used for routing EAP sessions via NAI and roaming, but the document is not about AAA frameworks.
ECDHE and Curve25519/P-256 are used as cryptosuite building blocks; the document is not about elliptic curve cryptography itself.
It registers eap-noob.arpa, but this is a minor IANA item, not the main subject.
JWK is only used to encode public keys.
HMAC is a used primitive, not the subject.

RFC9141.title: Updating References to the IETF FTP Service
RFC9141.summary: RFC 9141 updates 25 older RFCs by replacing ftp:// URIs pointing to the retiring IETF FTP service (mail archives, RFC and I-D listings) with HTTPS URIs under www.ietf.org and www.rfc-editor.org.

FTP.why: The document exists because the IETF FTP service is being retired and replaces references to it. Readers of FTP matters would want it, though it does not specify the FTP protocol.
FTP.quote: The IETF FTP service running at ftp.ietf.org, ops.ietf.org, and ietf.org will be retired.

IETF process.why: It is an administrative change to IETF infrastructure references, covering mail archives, Internet-Draft locations and RFC index locations. It is a procedural, housekeeping update.
IETF process.quote: this document formally updates those RFCs that had not been updated by other documents with HTTPS URIs to the same materials.

rejected.why: HTTPS is only the replacement URI scheme; the document defines nothing about HTTP.
It rewrites URIs in other RFCs but does not specify URI syntax or schemes.
Several updated RFCs are MIBs, but only their CONTACT-INFO archive URLs change.
It edits references in published RFCs, but it is not about RFC format, style or publication.
TLS is mentioned only in the Security Considerations as a benefit of HTTPS.

RFC9142.title: Key Exchange (KEX) Method Updates and Recommendations for Secure Shell (SSH)
RFC9142.summary: RFC 9142 updates requirement levels (MUST/SHOULD/MAY/MUST NOT) for SSH key exchange method names across ECC, finite-field DH and RSA-based methods, deprecating SHA-1-based methods and making diffie-hellman-group14-sha256 mandatory to implement.

SSH.why: The whole document specifies implementation guidance for SSH key exchange methods and updates RFCs 4250, 4253, 4432 and 4462, all SSH specifications.
SSH.quote: This document updates the recommended set of key exchange methods for use in the Secure Shell (SSH) protocol to meet evolving needs for stronger security.

key management.why: The document is about key exchange method selection and security strength matching (DH groups, ECDH, RSA KEX, KDF hashes), which is key establishment.
key management.quote: The key exchange produces two values: a shared secret K, and an exchange hash H.

rejected.why: Curve25519/448 and NIST curves are discussed, but only as options in SSH KEX guidance, not specified or profiled for their own sake.
Hash choice (SHA-1 vs SHA-2) is a significant rationale, but the document does not specify or analyse the SHA family itself.
gss-* KEX method names are covered in tables, but only as names with guidance levels; GSS-API is not the subject.
rsa1024-sha1 and rsa2048-sha256 are rated, but only as two KEX names from RFC 4432, not the RSA algorithm.
IKEv2 is only referenced as a comparison for curve key agreement.
AES appears only in the cipher strength table used to match KEX strength.

gaps.name: SSH (Secure Shell)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no SSH technology tag, even though the document is entirely about the SSH protocol. The id 'SSH' is used above; it exists under security in the taxonomy as 'SSH'.

RFC9143.title: Negotiating Media Multiplexing Using the Session Description Protocol (SDP)
RFC9143.summary: Defines the SDP BUNDLE grouping extension and 'bundle-only' attribute for negotiating a single transport for multiple media descriptions via offer/answer, plus the RTCP MID SDES item and RTP header extension; obsoletes RFC 8843.

SDP.why: The document specifies an SDP grouping extension, a new SDP attribute, and offer/answer procedures, and updates RFC 3264 and RFC 5888.
SDP.quote: This specification defines a new Session Description Protocol (SDP) Grouping Framework extension called 'BUNDLE'.

RTP.why: A substantial part covers RTP considerations: a single RTP session, associating streams with m= sections, RTP/RTCP multiplexing, and the MID RTP header extension.
RTP.quote: All RTP-based bundled media associated with a given BUNDLE group belong to a single RTP session [RFC3550].

RTCP.why: Defines the new MID RTCP SDES item and the RTCP packet routing rules for bundled media.
RTCP.quote: This section defines a new RTCP SDES item [RFC3550], 'MID', which is used to carry identification-tags within RTCP SDES packets.

rejected.why: ICE procedures with BUNDLE are covered in one section, but ICE itself is relied on rather than specified or extended.
SIP is only the carrier of SDP, with a short 3PCC note; it is not what the document is about.
Only a few rules on using DTLS inside a bundle; DTLS is a substrate here.
SRTP is mentioned only for protection and for protocol demultiplexing; the document does not specify it.
Mentioned only in the protocol identification demultiplexing section; STUN is not specified or extended.

RFC9144.title: Comparison of Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) Datastores
RFC9144.summary: Defines a YANG module with a <compare> RPC that lets a client ask a NETCONF/RESTCONF server to compare two NMDA datastores (e.g., intended vs operational) and report differences as a YANG Patch.

YANG.why: The document's core deliverable is the ietf-nmda-compare YANG module defining the compare RPC, and it operates on NMDA datastores defined in YANG terms.
YANG.quote: This document introduces a YANG data model that defines RPCs intended to be used in conjunction with NETCONF [RFC6241] or RESTCONF [RFC8040].

NETCONF.why: The compare operation is a new NETCONF-style RPC, with NETCONF examples (rpc/rpc-reply, subtree and XPath filters) and a RESTCONF example. Readers of NETCONF extensions would want it.
NETCONF.quote: These RPCs allow a client to request a server to compare two NMDA datastores and report any differences.

rejected.why: RESTCONF is only an alternative protocol for invoking the RPC, shown in one example. The document does not extend it.
JSON encoding appears only in the RESTCONF example, as a substrate.
XML is only the encoding used in the NETCONF examples.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as the RESTCONF secure transport.
SSH appears only in Security Considerations as the NETCONF transport.
The parent topic is implied by the YANG and NETCONF tags.

gaps.name: NMDA (Network Management Datastore Architecture)
gaps.why: The document is centred on comparing NMDA datastores (intended, operational), but the taxonomy has no tag for NMDA or datastores.

RFC9145.title: Integrity Protection for the Network Service Header (NSH) and Encryption of Sensitive Context Headers
RFC9145.summary: Defines two new NSH variable-length context headers (MAC#1, MAC#2) that add HMAC integrity protection, replay protection via timestamps, and AEAD encryption of sensitive metadata to the Network Service Header used in Service Function Chaining.

SFC.why: The whole document extends the NSH and its processing rules for SFC, defining new context headers and data plane element behaviour.
SFC.quote: This specification presents an optional method to add integrity protection directly to the Network Service Header (NSH) used for Service Function Chaining (SFC).

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA-256 is used as the integrity mechanism but the document does not specify or analyse HMAC itself.
AES-GCM is the mandatory AEAD algorithm, used via RFC 5116, but the document is not about AES.
NTP is only the assumed time synchronization source for timestamps; the timestamp format is defined here but NTP is not the subject.
Key management is explicitly out of scope; only key identifiers are carried in the header.
IPsec is mentioned as a transport encapsulation with hop-by-hop security, not specified or extended.
Encrypting privacy-sensitive metadata is a goal, but the document is not a privacy threat-model document.

RFC9146.title: Connection Identifier for DTLS 1.2
RFC9146.summary: Defines the connection_id extension and CID-enhanced record format for DTLS 1.2, letting receivers identify a security association despite address changes, and adds content type encryption and padding.

DTLS.why: The document extends DTLS 1.2 with a new extension, record format, MAC computation and peer address update rules, and updates RFC 6347.
DTLS.quote: This document specifies the Connection ID (CID) construct for the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol version 1.2.

rejected.why: The document defines a DTLS-only extension; TLS is the base and the IANA registries are boilerplate. The DTLS tag is the more specific fit.
UDP is only the datagram transport DTLS runs over.
NAT rebinding is the motivating problem, but the document does not specify NAT behaviour.
IoT is mentioned only as motivation (sleeping devices), not as the subject.
The Privacy Considerations section is boilerplate-like and does not make privacy the subject of the document.
The MAC computation is modified, but only as part of DTLS record protection, not as an HMAC specification.

RFC9147.title: The Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) Protocol Version 1.3
RFC9147.summary: Specifies DTLS 1.3, the datagram variant of TLS 1.3, covering the record layer, handshake changes, ACKs, retransmission, key updates, and connection IDs; it obsoletes RFC 6347.

DTLS.why: The document is the DTLS 1.3 protocol specification itself.
DTLS.quote: This document specifies version 1.3 of the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol.

rejected.why: DTLS 1.3 is defined as a delta from TLS 1.3, which is a basis rather than the subject. DTLS is the more specific tag.
UDP is the usual datagram transport DTLS runs over, so it is substrate only.
QUIC is mentioned only as the source of sequence number encryption and as a comparison point.
AES is used for record number encryption and in the CCM analysis, but the document is not about the AES cipher.
The PMTU section gives guidance for the record layer but is a small part of the document.
DCCP is only mentioned as an alternative transport.

RFC9148.title: EST-coaps: Enrollment over Secure Transport with the Secure Constrained Application Protocol
RFC9148.summary: RFC 9148 defines EST-coaps, transporting Enrollment over Secure Transport (certificate enrollment) messages over CoAP secured with DTLS, including URI mappings, block-wise fragmentation, delayed responses, server-side key generation, and an HTTPS-CoAPS registrar.

EST.why: The document specifies EST over CoAP, profiling EST functions, payloads and URIs for constrained devices.
EST.quote: This document defines how to transport EST payloads over secure CoAP (EST-coaps), which allows constrained devices to use existing EST functionality for provisioning certificates.

CoAP.why: It defines a CoAP binding: resource discovery, Content-Formats, response codes, block-wise transfer and delayed responses, and registers CoAP Content-Formats and resource types.
CoAP.quote: EST-coaps uses CoAP to transfer EST messages, aided by Block-Wise Transfer [RFC7959], to avoid IP fragmentation.

rejected.why: DTLS is the secure transport EST-coaps relies on; the document adds no new DTLS mechanism, only conformance to existing profiles and channel binding use.
HTTP appears only as EST's original transport and in the registrar's upstream leg; the document is about replacing it with CoAP.
Certificates are the payloads being enrolled, but the document does not specify or profile X.509 itself.
CMS is used only to optionally encrypt returned private keys, as already defined by RFC 7030.
The parent PKI tag is implied by the more specific EST tag.
CBOR appears only through the multipart-core content format used for the server-side key generation response.

RFC9149.title: TLS Ticket Requests
RFC9149.summary: Defines a new TLS 1.3/DTLS 1.3 extension, "ticket_request", that lets clients tell servers how many NewSessionTicket messages they want for new and resumed connections.

TLS.why: The document defines a new TLS extension and the client and server behaviour around session tickets. It is squarely about TLS protocol extensions.
TLS.quote: This document specifies a new TLS extension, "ticket_request", that clients can use to express their desired number of session tickets.

rejected.why: The extension applies to DTLS 1.3 as well, but only as a one-line scope note. The document is about TLS as a whole, so the parent TLS tag fits better.
Happy Eyeballs connection racing is cited as a use case that motivates multiple tickets. The document does not specify or extend it.
Mentioned only as an informative reference for connection racing. The document does not address Transport Services.
Parallel HTTP connections appear as an example use case only. The document is not about HTTP.
The IANA section registers a single TLS ExtensionType value. That is boilerplate, not a subject of the document.

RFC9150.title: TLS 1.3 Authentication and Integrity-Only Cipher Suites
RFC9150.summary: Defines two integrity-only TLS 1.3 (and DTLS 1.3) cipher suites, TLS_SHA256_SHA256 and TLS_SHA384_SHA384, using HMAC for record protection without confidentiality, aimed at IoT and industrial use cases.

TLS.why: The document defines new TLS 1.3 cipher suites, including record protection and key schedule changes, and registers them with IANA. This is new TLS content that TLS readers need.
TLS.quote: This document defines the use of cipher suites for TLS 1.3 based on Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC).

DTLS.why: The suites are marked DTLS-OK, and the document specifies the DTLS 1.3 record format and notes that sequence number encryption is not applied.
DTLS.quote: For DTLS 1.3, the DTLSCiphertext is set to:
DTLS.section: 5. Record Payload Protection for Integrity-Only Cipher Suites

IoT.why: The suites target constrained IoT and industrial devices, and the applicability section describes industrial automation, railway and aviation use cases.
IoT.quote: there are use cases, specifically in Internet of Things (IoT) and constrained environments, that do not require confidentiality

rejected.why: HMAC is the primitive used to build the record protection. The document does not specify or analyse HMAC itself.
SHA-256 and SHA-384 are only the hash algorithms chosen for the HMAC and HKDF. The document does not define them.
The document uses existing algorithms and defines no new ones. Its subject is the TLS cipher suite, which the TLS tag covers.
The document concerns record integrity and authenticity inside TLS. The authentication mechanisms are explicitly unchanged.
Time updates appear only as one example use case and are not the subject of the document.
HTTP is mentioned only as an example of an application protocol that may assume confidentiality.

RFC9151.title: Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite Profile for TLS and DTLS 1.2 and 1.3
RFC9151.summary: Defines the NSA CNSA Suite profile for TLS 1.2/1.3 and DTLS 1.2/1.3, constraining cipher suites, curves (P-384), RSA/DH parameters, signature algorithms, and extensions to CNSA-approved algorithms.

TLS.why: The document is a profile of TLS 1.2/1.3 specifying required cipher suites, extensions and handshake message constraints.
TLS.quote: This document specifies a profile of TLS version 1.2 [RFC5246] and TLS version 1.3 [RFC8446] as well as DTLS version 1.2 [RFC6347] and DTLS version 1.3

DTLS.why: The profile explicitly covers DTLS 1.2 and 1.3 as co-equal subjects, applying the same requirements to both.
DTLS.quote: as well as DTLS version 1.2 [RFC6347] and DTLS version 1.3 [RFC9147] for use by applications that support the National Security Agency's

cryptography.why: A substantial part of the document selects algorithms and parameters (AES-256-GCM, P-384, RSA 3072/4096, SHA-384, ffdhe groups) per the CNSA Suite. This is a general algorithm-selection profile, so the parent topic fits better than a single algorithm tag.
cryptography.quote: CNSA (D)TLS connections MUST use secp384r1 (also called nistp384), and the uncompressed form MUST be used

rejected.why: Certificates are only required to comply with RFC 8603; the document does not profile certificates itself.
OCSP is mentioned only as one option for certificate revocation status, not as a subject of the document.
AES-256-GCM is a fixed requirement within the profile, not something the document specifies or extends.
Curve selection is one constraint in the profile. The main subject is the TLS profile, and the general cryptography tag already covers algorithm choice.
RSA schemes are constrained in Section 5.2, but RSA is not the document's subject; it is one of several algorithm choices.
SHA-384 is mandated as a fixed parameter and is not specified or analysed by the document.

RFC9152.title: Secure Object Delivery Protocol (SODP) Server Interfaces: NSA's Profile for Delivery of Certificates, Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs), and Symmetric Keys to Clients
RFC9152.summary: Informational NSA profile specifying how SODP servers deliver certificates, CRLs and symmetric keys to NSS clients via EST (and extensions) and CMC, with CNSA-constrained certificate and CRL profiles.

EST.why: Section 3 profiles every EST endpoint (/cacerts, /simpleenroll, /symmetrickeys, etc.) and the EST extensions; this is the main interface.
EST.quote: Interfaces supported by SODP servers include Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST) and its extensions as well as Certificate Management over CMC

rejected.why: Sections 5-9 profile certificates and CRLs, which is substantial, but these are profile requirements layered on RFC 8603; they fit under PKI and EST better than a separate X.509 tag.
CMS content types carry the keys and packages, but the document profiles delivery interfaces and does not specify CMS itself.
TLS is only the substrate, configured per RFC 9151; the document defines nothing new about it.
EST runs over HTTP, but the document only notes redirect handling and Accept headers, which is substrate use.
Symmetric key delivery is covered, but the document is mainly a PKI enrollment and certificate profile, and the specific protocol tags already cover it.
Section 2 only names the ASN.1 version to use; it is not about ASN.1.

gaps.name: CMC (Certificate Management over CMS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no CMC tag. The document profiles CMC as one of its two interfaces. I tagged EST as the nearest fit, but CMC readers would want this RFC.

review: model chose 'CMC', which is not a tag

notes: model chose 'CMC', which is not a tag

RFC9153.title: Drone Remote Identification Protocol (DRIP) Requirements and Terminology
RFC9153.summary: Defines terminology and numbered requirements for the DRIP working group's solutions for Unmanned Aircraft System Remote Identification (UAS RID): trustworthy, privacy-preserving identifiers, authentication, and registries.

DRIP.why: The whole document is the DRIP requirements and terminology specification for UAS remote identification.
DRIP.quote: This document defines terminology and requirements for solutions produced by the Drone Remote Identification Protocol (DRIP) Working Group.

privacy.why: A full requirements group (PRIV-1 to PRIV-5) and a privacy and transparency section address operator privacy versus transparency.
privacy.quote: DRIP MUST enable confidential handling of private information

rejected.why: AAA and policy requirements are present but only as a part of the registry requirements; not the main subject.
GRAIN is mentioned only as a term in the glossary.
HIP is mentioned only as one possible use of the identifier; it is not specified or profiled here.
DNS appears in the scenario figure and the Contact requirement; this document does not specify DNS.
XACML is mentioned only as an example policy language in the rationale.
UUID is cited only as one of the existing ID Type values.

gaps.name: UAS Remote ID / Drone Remote Identification (DRIP, UAS RID, Broadcast RID, Network RID)
gaps.why: The taxonomy's DRIP tag is defined as 'Drone Remote Identification Protocol' under internet layer, but I could not confirm that it is a tag id I may use. If DRIP is not valid, no tag covers the document's main subject.

RFC9154.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Secure Authorization Information for Transfer
RFC9154.summary: Defines an operational practice using existing EPP features so transfer authorization information is strong random, short-lived, not stored by clients, and stored hashed by registries.

EPP.why: The document specifies how EPP create, update, info and transfer commands are used for secure authInfo handling, and defines a namespace URI to signal support in login and greeting.
EPP.quote: This document defines an operational practice, using the EPP RFCs, that leverages the use of strong, random authorization information values that are short lived

rejected.why: EPP is the more specific child tag and already covers registry/registrar provisioning.
XML is only the encoding of EPP messages and is not what the document is about.
The document applies RFC 4086 guidance to generate authInfo values, but randomness is not its subject.
SHA-256 is only given as an example hash for storage and is not the subject of the document.
DNS appears only through RFC 8499 terminology for registrant, registrar and registry.

RFC9155.title: Deprecating MD5 and SHA-1 Signature Hashes in TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2
RFC9155.summary: Standards Track update to RFC 5246 that forbids MD5 and SHA-1 in TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 digital signatures (signature_algorithms, CertificateRequest, ServerKeyExchange, CertificateVerify) while keeping HMAC-SHA-1 for record protection.

TLS.why: The document changes TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 handshake behaviour for signature algorithms and updates RFC 5246. TLS readers need it; DTLS is implied as a child.
TLS.quote: Clients MUST include the signature_algorithms extension.  Clients MUST NOT include MD5 and SHA-1 in this extension.

MD5.why: The document deprecates MD5 for digital signatures in TLS, which is a substantial part of its subject, so readers of the MD5 page would want it.
MD5.quote: MD5 and SHA-1 have been proven to be insecure, subject to collision attacks [Wang].

SHA.why: SHA-1 is deprecated for signatures, with the explicit carve-out that SHA-1 with HMAC stays allowed. IANA also marks the SHA-1 signature schemes as not recommended.
SHA.quote: This document updates [RFC5246] in such a way that MD5 and SHA-1 MUST NOT be used for digital signatures.

rejected.why: DTLS 1.2 is covered by the document, but its handling is identical to TLS 1.2 and the document defines nothing DTLS-specific. The TLS tag is enough.
HMAC-SHA-1 in record protection is only mentioned as being left unchanged, so the document is not about HMAC.
The CA/Browser Forum certificate-signature deprecation is mentioned only as background, and the document does not specify certificate profiles.
The registry updates are boilerplate-level consequences of the main change and are not the subject of the document.

RFC9156.title: DNS Query Name Minimisation to Improve Privacy
RFC9156.summary: Specifies QNAME minimisation, a resolver-side technique that sends only the labels needed at each step of iterative DNS resolution to reduce privacy exposure, and obsoletes the experimental RFC 7816.

DNS.why: The document specifies a change to DNS resolver behaviour and gives the iterative resolution algorithm with zone-cut discovery and query limits. It belongs on the DNS page.
DNS.quote: QNAME minimisation" to improve DNS privacy, where the DNS resolver no longer always sends the full original QNAME and original QTYPE to the upstream name server

rejected.why: This tag covers encrypted and privacy-preserving DNS transport. QNAME minimisation is a resolver-side data-minimisation technique, not an encrypted transport. The document says encryption changes the protocol, unlike this technique.
The motivation is privacy, but the document is a DNS-specific mechanism rather than a general privacy threat model or guidance document.
DNSSEC appears only in passing, in the DS QTYPE handling and the RFC 8198 aggressive-cache reference. The document is not about it.

RFC9157.title: Revised IANA Considerations for DNSSEC
RFC9157.summary: Updates RFC 6014 and RFC 8624 so DNSSEC DS digest algorithms and NSEC3 parameters/hash algorithms/flags need only "RFC Required" for IANA registration, and clarifies the RFC 8624 algorithm recommendations for non-standards-track algorithms.

DNSSEC.why: The document concerns DNSSEC algorithm registries (DS digest algorithms, NSEC3 parameters) and updates DNSSEC implementation recommendations in RFC 8624.
DNSSEC.quote: This document changes the review requirements needed to get DNSSEC algorithms and resource records added to IANA registries.

IANA.why: The core change is to IANA registration policy for DNSSEC registries, so readers of IANA registry policy would want it.
IANA.quote: the registration procedure for "Digest Algorithms" has been changed from "Standards Action" to "RFC Required"

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific tag and already implies DNS.
Algorithms are only registered, not specified; the document is about registry procedures, not the algorithms themselves.

RFC9158.title: Update to the Object Identifier Registry for the PKIX Working Group
RFC9158.summary: Updates RFC 7299 by creating an IANA subregistry for the PKIX OIDs under id-regCtrl-altCertTemplate (id-acTemplate, id-openPGPCertTemplateExt) omitted from RFC 7299, with Specification Required allocation policy.

PKI.why: The document is about the PKIX object identifier arc and the CMP/CMC alternate certificate format OIDs; it is a PKIX registry update.
PKI.quote: RFC 7299 describes the object identifiers that were assigned by the Public Key Infrastructure using X.509 (PKIX) Working Group in an arc that was allocated by IANA

IANA.why: The main content is creating a new IANA subregistry and setting its allocation policy (Specification Required with expert guidance).
IANA.quote: IANA has created the "SMI Security for PKIX CRMF Registration Controls for Alternate Certificate Formats" subregistry (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.5.1.7).

rejected.why: X.509 is mentioned only as part of the PKIX name; the document does not specify certificate profiles.
CMP is not in the taxonomy as a standalone tag under this id context; it is only referenced as the protocol that allocated the OID arc, and the document defines nothing new about it.
CMC over CMS is mentioned only as a protocol that may use the OIDs; the document is not about CMS.
Object identifiers are ASN.1 concepts, but the document only registers values and does not define modules or encoding.

RFC9159.title: IPv6 Mesh over BLUETOOTH(R) Low Energy Using the Internet Protocol Support Profile (IPSP)
RFC9159.summary: Specifies how IPv6 mesh (route-over, multilink subnet) operates over Bluetooth LE links established via IPSP, extending RFC 7668 using 6LoWPAN ND, address registration, and header compression.

6LoWPAN.why: The document adapts 6LoWPAN techniques (RFC 6775/8505 ND, RFC 6282 compression) to IPv6 mesh over Bluetooth LE, a constrained link layer; this is the IoT adaptation-layer tag.
6LoWPAN.quote: This document specifies mechanisms that are needed to enable IPv6 mesh over Bluetooth LE links.

IPv6.why: Defines IPv6 subnet model, SLAAC address configuration, MTU and multicast handling over the link.
IPv6.quote: IPv6 mesh over Bluetooth LE links MUST follow a route-over approach.

neighbor discovery.why: A substantial section specifies which 6LoWPAN ND behaviours (EARO, DAD, RS/RA, router behaviour) apply to the Bluetooth LE mesh.
neighbor discovery.quote: A Bluetooth LE 6LN MUST register its non-link-local addresses with its routers by sending a Neighbor Solicitation (NS) message with the Extended Address Registration Option (EARO)

rejected.why: Uses RFC 6282 compression with specific rules, but this is a subsection of the 6LoWPAN adaptation, not a new compression scheme; 6LoWPAN covers it.
The document explicitly does not specify a routing protocol; it only requires route-over.
RPL is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible routing protocol.
Addresses are configured per RFC 7668 by reference; only a short subsection, not substantially about SLAAC.
Parent topic; a more specific tag (6LoWPAN) fits.

gaps.name: Bluetooth Low Energy / IPSP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for Bluetooth LE or the Bluetooth Internet Protocol Support Profile, the link technology at the core of this document.

RFC9160.title: Export of MPLS Segment Routing Label Type Information in IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX)
RFC9160.summary: Defines five new IPFIX mplsTopLabelType code points (PCE, OSPFv2, OSPFv3, IS-IS, BGP Prefix-SID) so flow records can show which MPLS Segment Routing control protocol allocated the top label.

IPFIX.why: The document extends the IPFIX information model by adding new code points to an IPFIX Information Element subregistry.
IPFIX.quote: this document defines five code points for the IPFIX mplsTopLabelType Information Element

segment routing.why: The code points identify the control plane protocols that distribute SR labels, and the use cases are SR migration and monitoring. SR-MPLS is the more specific child, but the document covers SR label types in general, so the parent fits.
segment routing.quote: identify which traffic is being forwarded based upon which MPLS SR control plane protocol is in use
segment routing.section: 2. MPLS Segment Routing Top Label Type

rejected.why: The document is about IPFIX reporting of SR label types. It does not specify SR over MPLS itself, so the parent tag is the closer fit.
MPLS labels are the subject being observed, but the document does not specify MPLS architecture or operations.
OSPF extensions are only referenced as label sources and are not specified here.
BGP Prefix-SID is only referenced as a label source and is not specified here.
PCEP is only referenced as a label source and is not specified here.
