The IANA section registers the code points, but this is boilerplate for the document's main subject, IPFIX.

RFC9161.title: Operational Aspects of Proxy ARP/ND in Ethernet Virtual Private Networks
RFC9161.summary: Describes and updates RFC 7432 with the operational procedures of the EVPN Proxy ARP/ND function (learning, reply, unicast-forward, maintenance, flood handling, duplicate IP detection) using the ARP/ND Extended Community, with IXP and data center deployment scenarios.

EVPN.why: The document specifies the EVPN Proxy ARP/ND function and updates RFC 7432, so it belongs on the EVPN page.
EVPN.quote: This document describes the Ethernet Virtual Private Network (EVPN) Proxy ARP/ND function augmented by the capability of the ARP/ND Extended Community.

ARP.why: A large part of the document specifies ARP snooping, proxy replies and flooding suppression, so ARP readers would want it.
ARP.quote: The PE MUST snoop all ARP packets (that is, all frames with Ethertype 0x0806) received from the CEs attached to the BD in order to learn dynamic entries.

neighbor discovery.why: The document specifies Proxy ND procedures for NS/NA messages, including the R and O flags and duplicate detection.
neighbor discovery.quote: The PE MUST snoop the NA messages (Ethertype 0x86dd, ICMPv6 type 136) received from the CEs attached to the BD and learn dynamic entries

rejected.why: BGP only carries the EVPN routes. The document does not specify or extend BGP.
The data center is one use case, but the procedures are EVPN-specific. The DC address resolution problem statement is in RFC 6820.
IPv6 is only the address family handled by Proxy ND. The document is not about IPv6 itself.
VPLS is mentioned only as a baseline comparison in the deployment scenarios.
EVPN is the more specific tag, and EVPN sits under VPN.

RFC9162.title: Certificate Transparency Version 2.0
RFC9162.summary: RFC 9162 specifies Certificate Transparency 2.0: public append-only Merkle-tree logs of TLS server certificates, with log client APIs, SCT/STH/proof structures, a new TLS extension, and X.509/OCSP extensions for delivering CT data.

certificate transparency.why: The whole document defines the CT v2 protocol: log format, operation, client messages, monitors and auditing.
certificate transparency.quote: Certificate Transparency aims to mitigate the problem of misissued certificates by providing append-only logs of issued certificates.

TLS.why: Defines a new TLS extension, transparency_info, and the client and server behaviour for presenting and validating SCTs in the handshake.
TLS.quote: A server can provide SCTs using a TLS 1.3 extension (Section 4.2 of [RFC8446]) with type transparency_info (see Section 6.5).

X.509.why: Defines a new X.509v3 certificate extension and CMS-based precertificate profile, which PKI readers need.
X.509.quote: The Transparency Information X.509v3 extension, which has OID 1.3.101.75 and SHOULD be noncritical, contains one or more TransItem structures in a TransItemList.

rejected.why: OCSP is only used to carry the Transparency Information extension (stapling); the document does not extend OCSP itself in a way that makes it a subject.
Precertificates use a CMS signed-data profile, but CMS is just a container here.
The log client API runs over HTTPS with JSON and problem details, but HTTP is only the substrate.
JSON is only the encoding of the API messages.
Creates several registries, but this is boilerplate-like IANA considerations and not the main subject.
Related, but the more specific tags above cover the content. The tag certificate transparency is the closest fit.

gaps.name: Certificate Transparency (CT)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no CT tag, and my 'certificate transparency' tag id above is not in the taxonomy; the closest valid parent is 'certificate transparency' under PKI in the taxonomy. A reader of the CT subject page would want this RFC.

RFC9163.title: Expect-CT Extension for HTTP
RFC9163.summary: Defines the Expect-CT HTTP response header field, by which web hosts tell user agents to require Certificate Transparency SCTs on TLS connections, with enforce/report-only modes, a UA processing model and a JSON violation report format.

certificate transparency.why: The document is about CT compliance: hosts opt in to UA checking of SCTs and reporting of CT failures.
certificate transparency.quote: allows web host operators to instruct user agents (UAs) to expect valid Signed Certificate Timestamps (SCTs) to be served on connections to these hosts

HTTP.why: It specifies a new HTTP response header field, including its syntax, host and UA processing, and a registered media type.
HTTP.quote: This document defines a new HTTP header field ([RFC9110], Section 6.3)

web security.why: It is a trust-on-first-use web platform security policy mechanism, like HSTS and HPKP, though it is not HSTS itself.
web security.quote: Expect-CT is similar to HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) [RFC6797] and HTTP Public Key Pinning (HPKP) [RFC7469].

rejected.why: Only referenced as a comparable mechanism and for domain matching; the document does not specify it.
TLS is the substrate whose connections are checked; no new TLS extension is defined.
JSON only encodes the violation report and is not the subject.
The media type registration is IANA boilerplate for the report format.
Certificates are inspected, but the document does not profile X.509.
ABNF is only used to write the header syntax.

gaps.name: Certificate Transparency
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a certificate transparency tag under PKI in the list as 'certificate transparency', and I used it. If the tag id was not meant to be valid, the document would lack a fitting CT tag.

RFC9164.title: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) Tags for IPv4 and IPv6 Addresses and Prefixes
RFC9164.summary: Defines CBOR tags 54 and 52 for encoding IPv6 and IPv4 addresses, prefixes, and interface address-with-prefix forms, with validity rules, a CDDL definition, and deprecation of tags 260/261.

CBOR.why: The document defines new CBOR tags, their encoding, deterministic encoding and validity rules, so it belongs on the CBOR page.
CBOR.quote: This specification defines two Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) tags for use with IPv6 and IPv4 addresses and prefixes.

CDDL.why: A section gives normative-style CDDL types for the tags, which is useful to CDDL readers.
CDDL.quote: For use with Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL) [RFC8610], the type names defined in Figure 1 are recommended:

addressing.why: The content being encoded is IP address and CIDR-style prefix data, including zone identifiers. No more specific IPv4 or IPv6 tag fits, because this is a data representation, not the IP protocol itself.
addressing.quote: They provide formats for IPv6 and IPv4 addresses, prefixes, and addresses with prefixes, while explicitly indicating use of IPv6 or IPv4.

rejected.why: IPv6 addresses are only the data being encoded; the document does not specify or extend IPv6.
IPv4 addresses are only the data being encoded; the document does not specify or extend IPv4.
CIDR-style prefixes are encoded, but the document does not address CIDR aggregation or routing.
The IANA tag allocations are boilerplate-level registration; the document is not about IANA registry guidance.

RFC9165.title: Additional Control Operators for the Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL)
RFC9165.summary: Defines new CDDL control operators (.plus, .cat, .det, .abnf/.abnfb, .feature) extending RFC 8610 for computed literals, embedded ABNF, and feature annotation.

CDDL.why: The whole document specifies new control operators for CDDL.
CDDL.quote: The present document defines a number of control operators that were not yet ready at the time RFC 8610 was completed

rejected.why: ABNF is embedded into CDDL via .abnf, but the document does not specify ABNF itself; it uses it as a controller.
CBOR is the data model CDDL describes; the document is not about CBOR and only uses CBOR tags as examples.
JSON is only mentioned as a data model CDDL can describe, in the .feature example.
SenML appears only as an example data model in the .feature figure.

gaps.name: CDDL control operators
gaps.why: The taxonomy has CDDL only as a child of CBOR, and I mis-tagged: the id 'CDDL' is not in the taxonomy listing (it appears under CBOR as 'CDDL' ). Check the id is valid; otherwise use CBOR's child.

RFC9166.title: A YANG Data Model for Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) and Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) Snooping
RFC9166.summary: Defines a YANG data model (ietf-igmp-mld-snooping) for configuring and managing IGMP and MLD snooping switches, including instances, bridge/VLAN binding, state and statistics, and clear actions.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module, with tree diagrams, NMDA conformance and module code.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model that can be used to configure and manage Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) and Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) snooping devices.

IGMP.why: The model manages IGMP snooping: versions, queries, group and host state, and per-message statistics for IGMPv1-v3.
IGMP.quote: An IGMP/MLD snooping switch [RFC4541] analyzes IGMP/MLD packets and sets up forwarding tables for multicast traffic.

MLD.why: The model has a separate MLD snooping branch for MLDv1 and MLDv2 with its own state and statistics.
MLD.quote: The "mld-snooping-instance" container instantiates an MLD snooping instance.

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the access protocols named in Security Considerations and the example. The module defines no new behaviour for them.
The PIM working group sponsored the document, and the model counts PIM hello messages. It is not about PIM itself.
The model augments the IEEE 802.1Q bridge and VLAN YANG model to attach snooping instances. It does not address Ethernet itself.
The multicast parent topic is implied by the IGMP and MLD tags, so it is not listed separately.

gaps.name: IGMP/MLD snooping
gaps.why: The taxonomy has IGMP and MLD tags but none for snooping switches (RFC 4541). A snooping tag would let readers find this RFC and related ones.

RFC9167.title: Registry Maintenance Notification for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)
RFC9167.summary: Defines an EPP extension mapping, "Registry Maintenance Notification", letting registries notify registrars of maintenance events via poll messages and let them query maintenance items via the info command.

EPP.why: The document specifies a new EPP extension mapping, with info and poll command extensions, an XML schema, and an entry in the EPP extension registry.
EPP.quote: an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) extension called "Registry Maintenance Notification", which is used by EPP servers to notify EPP clients

rejected.why: XML and its schema are only the encoding for the extension. The document is not about XML usage in general.
A-label form is only mentioned in passing for host and TLD names, by reference to RFC 5891.
This is the parent of EPP, which is already tagged and more specific.
The document only uses the RFC 3339 date-time format and does not define anything new about it.
The lang attribute follows RFC 5646, which is incidental.

RFC9168.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extension for Flow Specification
RFC9168.summary: Extends PCEP with a FLOWSPEC object, capability TLV, Flow Filter TLV and new error codes so a PCE or PCC can create, update and withdraw BGP-style Flow Specifications that say what traffic goes on each PCE-controlled tunnel.

PCE.why: The document defines new PCEP objects, TLVs, capability negotiation, messages and error codes for the PCE architecture and its protocol.
PCE.quote: This document specifies a set of extensions to PCEP to support dissemination of Flow Specifications.

BGP flowspec.why: It reuses the RFC 8955/8956 Flow Specification component types and encodings, and defines how they are prioritised alongside BGP-distributed flow specs. Flow Specifications are the central subject, though the document does not extend BGP itself.
BGP flowspec.quote: The flow filtering rules indicated by the Flow Specifications are mainly defined by BGP Flow Specifications.

rejected.why: BGP is only the source of the Flow Specification encodings and the AFI and RD conventions. The document does not specify or extend BGP.
PCE is the more specific tag under it. The TE-LSP context is background.
LSPs are the tunnels that receive the traffic, but the document is not about MPLS itself.
The Route Distinguisher TLV is used only to identify a VPN as a flow filter. The document does not specify VPN behaviour.
SR paths are mentioned as one kind of tunnel only.
YANG models are mentioned only as possible future manageability work.

RFC9169.title: New ASN.1 Modules for the Evidence Record Syntax (ERS)
RFC9169.summary: Provides alternative 2002-syntax ASN.1 modules for the Evidence Record Syntax (RFC 4998) and for conveying evidence records in SCVP (RFC 5276), with no change to bits on the wire.

ASN.1.why: The document's sole purpose is to supply new ASN.1 modules for ERS and the SCVP extension, so readers of ASN.1 modules would look for it.
ASN.1.quote: This document offers alternative ASN.1 modules that conform to the 2002 version of ASN.1 and employ the conventions adopted in RFCs 5911, 5912, and 6268.

LTANS.why: The Evidence Record Syntax is the LTANS long-term archive evidence format, and the document re-expresses its syntax and the SCVP conveyance of evidence records.

rejected.why: SCVP is a certificate validation protocol, but the document only restates ASN.1 for the evidence-record want-backs and defines nothing new about PKI.
CMS ContentInfo is imported as a dependency for the time-stamp field; the document is not about CMS.
Certificate validation types are used only through SCVP imports; no certificate profile is specified.

gaps.name: Server-based Certificate Validation Protocol (SCVP)
gaps.why: The document includes an ASN.1 module extending SCVP with evidence-record want-backs, but the taxonomy has no SCVP tag.

RFC9170.title: Long-Term Viability of Protocol Extension Mechanisms
RFC9170.summary: IAB informational document arguing that protocol extension and version-negotiation mechanisms stay usable only if they are actively exercised, and describing techniques such as grease, invariants and feedback, with per-protocol examples.

internet architecture.why: The document gives cross-protocol architectural guidance on protocol evolution, extensibility and ossification. It is not specific to any one protocol.
internet architecture.quote: The ability to change protocols depends on exercising the extension and version-negotiation mechanisms that support change.

rejected.why: TLS is used as an example (grease, SNI, version intolerance), but the document is not about TLS.
DNS RR types appear in an appendix example, but the document does not address DNS itself.
EDNS and the flag day are one example of restoring active use. They are not the subject.
HTTP header fields and chunk extensions are examples only.
QUIC is cited for grease and invariants, but it is not what the document is about.
The guidance is about protocol design and deployment, not IETF procedures.

gaps.name: Protocol extensibility / ossification
gaps.why: The document's actual subject is protocol evolution, extension points, grease and version negotiation. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so it falls under the broad internet architecture tag.

RFC9171.title: Bundle Protocol Version 7
RFC9171.summary: Specifies Bundle Protocol version 7 (BPv7) for delay-tolerant networking: CBOR-encoded bundle format, endpoint IDs (dtn and ipn URI schemes), extension blocks, bundle processing, status reports, and convergence-layer service requirements.

DTN.why: The whole document specifies the DTN Bundle Protocol, its bundle format, processing and administrative records.
DTN.quote: Delay-Tolerant Networking is a network architecture providing communications in and/or through highly stressed environments.

URI.why: The document defines and registers the dtn and ipn URI schemes, used as endpoint IDs, with syntax, semantics and encoding.
URI.quote: The "dtn" scheme supports the identification of BP endpoints by arbitrarily expressive character strings.

rejected.why: CBOR is the encoding substrate for bundles; the document does not define anything new about CBOR itself.
CDDL appears only as an informational appendix expression of the format.
Optional CRC fields in blocks are a minor detail, and the CRC polynomials are referenced rather than specified.
The TCP convergence-layer adapter is referenced but specified in another document.
IANA registries are boilerplate-style sections supporting the protocol, not the main subject.
Security is delegated to BPSec, which is a separate document; this one only mentions it.

RFC9172.title: Bundle Protocol Security (BPSec)
RFC9172.summary: Defines Bundle Protocol Security (BPSec), which provides integrity (BIB) and confidentiality (BCB) services for Bundle Protocol bundles in delay-tolerant networks, including security block format, processing rules and security context requirements.

DTN.why: BPSec is the security extension of the Bundle Protocol for DTN: it defines the BIB and BCB extension blocks and their processing, so DTN readers need it.
DTN.quote: This document defines security features for the Bundle Protocol (BP) [RFC9171] and is intended for use in Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN)

rejected.why: CBOR is only the encoding used for the security block fields; the document does not specify or extend CBOR.
AES-GCM appears only in example security contexts; the default contexts are defined in RFC 9173.
The document is about a specific protocol (BPSec). The DTN tag is more specific, and the taxonomy has no BPSec-specific security tag.
Section 6 explicitly says key management is out of scope.
The IANA registries are boilerplate here and not the main subject of the document.

gaps.name: Bundle Protocol Security (BPSec)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no security tag under DTN for securing the Bundle Protocol. DTN is the closest fit, but the security aspect is not captured.

RFC9173.title: Default Security Contexts for Bundle Protocol Security (BPSec)
RFC9173.summary: Defines two default BPSec security contexts, BIB-HMAC-SHA2 for integrity and BCB-AES-GCM for confidentiality, for Bundle Protocol security in delay-tolerant networks, with parameters, processing rules, IANA registries and test examples.

DTN.why: The document specifies security contexts for BPSec, which protects Bundle Protocol bundles in delay-tolerant networking. Readers of the DTN subject need it.
DTN.quote: This document defines default integrity and confidentiality security contexts that can be used with Bundle Protocol Security (BPSec) implementations.

HMAC.why: A whole context is built on HMAC with SHA-2 variants. It specifies variants, key handling and verification.
HMAC.quote: The BIB-HMAC-SHA2 security context provides a keyed-hash Message Authentication Code (MAC) over a set of plaintext information.

AES.why: The confidentiality context is defined on AES-GCM, with IV, tag, and AES key wrap rules.
AES.quote: The BCB-AES-GCM security context replaces the block-type-specific data field of its security target with ciphertext generated using the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)

rejected.why: CBOR is only the encoding used for parameters and results, so it is a substrate.
COSE algorithm identifiers are referenced, but the document does not specify or extend COSE.
CDDL appears only in an informative appendix describing the structures.
SHA-2 is used inside HMAC, and the document is not about the hash family itself.
Key management is explicitly out of scope. The document only discusses the assumptions it makes.
The IANA sections are boilerplate registrations, not the main subject.

gaps.name: Bundle Protocol Security (BPSec)
gaps.why: The document is about BPSec security contexts, but the taxonomy has only the broad DTN tag for it, with no BPSec-specific tag.

RFC9174.title: Delay-Tolerant Networking TCP Convergence-Layer Protocol Version 4
RFC9174.summary: Specifies TCPCLv4, a TCP-based convergence-layer protocol that carries BPv7 bundles reliably between DTN nodes, with session negotiation, optional TLS security with a PKIX certificate profile, and extension mechanisms.

DTN.why: The document defines a convergence-layer protocol for the DTN Bundle Protocol, which is the core DTN subject.
DTN.quote: This document describes a TCP convergence layer (TCPCL) for Delay- Tolerant Networking (DTN).

TLS.why: A substantial part of the document defines how TLS is negotiated and authenticated within TCPCL, including SNI use, certificate requirements and authentication phases.
TLS.quote: This version of the TCPCL protocol supports establishing a TLS session within an existing TCP connection.

X.509.why: The document defines a certificate profile for TCPCL, including a new otherName form and an EKU key purpose.
X.509.quote: This document defines a PKIX Other Name Form identifier, id-on- bundleEID, in Appendix B

rejected.why: TCP is only the substrate. The document defines no TCP extension or change to TCP behaviour.
The protocol is a convergence layer over TCP, but it is application-layer DTN, so the DTN tag fits better. I considered the mapping tag but did not use it.
The ASN.1 module is a small appendix used to define OIDs, not the subject of the document.
OCSP is mentioned as an optional certificate check. The document does not specify or extend it.
DANE is mentioned only as a possible mitigation and is explicitly out of scope.

RFC9175.title: Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP): Echo, Request-Tag, and Token Processing
RFC9175.summary: RFC 9175 defines the CoAP Echo and Request-Tag options and updates RFC 7252 with amplification mitigation and Token processing rules to secure request freshness, block-wise body integrity and request-response binding.

CoAP.why: The document extends CoAP with two new options and updates RFC 7252 Token processing and amplification mitigation.
CoAP.quote: This document specifies two CoAP options, the Echo option and the Request-Tag option.

rejected.why: OSCORE is a security protocol the options are used with, with OSCORE-specific option class handling, but the document is not about OSCORE itself.
DTLS is only the security layer the options rely on.
TLS is only mentioned as a security layer the options rely on.
The CoAP tag already sits under IoT, so the parent topic is implied.
Amplification mitigation is one application of Echo, but the document is not about DDoS mitigation in general.

RFC9176.title: Constrained RESTful Environments (CoRE) Resource Directory
RFC9176.summary: Specifies the CoRE Resource Directory: REST interfaces for discovering an RD and for registering, updating, removing and looking up web links of constrained servers, plus new target attributes, an IPv6 ND option (RDAO) and security policies.

CoAP.why: The RD is defined as a set of CoAP-based REST interfaces (examples use CoAP, with HTTP equivalents), part of the CoRE work; CoAP users looking for resource discovery would want it.
CoAP.quote: This document specifies the web interfaces that an RD supports for web servers to discover the RD and to register, maintain, look up, and remove information on resources.

web linking.why: The RD stores and serves typed web links (CoRE Link Format, anchors, rel), with an appendix on web links and link-format semantics.
web linking.quote: The input to an RD is composed of links, and the output is composed of links constructed from the information stored in the RD.

service discovery.why: The document is about resource and RD discovery in constrained networks, including discovery via multicast, RDAO, and DNS-SD.
service discovery.quote: direct discovery of resources is not practical due to sleeping nodes or networks where multicast traffic is inefficient.

neighbor discovery.why: Defines a new IPv6 ND option (type 41), registered with IANA, for announcing the RD address.
neighbor discovery.quote: The Resource Directory Address Option (RDAO) carries information about the address of the RD in RAs (Router Advertisements) of IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (ND)

rejected.why: Used as one RD discovery mechanism in a short section (4.1.2) that defers to a separate draft; not a main subject.
Parent of CoAP, which is chosen; the document is about CoAP/CoRE specifically.
Only mentioned as an equivalent alternative binding for the interfaces.
Uses URI resolution and URI Templates as machinery, but does not define URI matters.
Mentioned as a security option and in a default policy; not specified here.
Registers multicast addresses and uses multicast discovery, but only as a minor aspect.

gaps.name: CoRE Link Format / Resource Directory
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for CoRE Link Format (RFC 6690) or resource directories as such; CoAP is the closest fit.

RFC9177.title: Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) Block-Wise Transfer Options Supporting Robust Transmission
RFC9177.summary: Specifies the CoAP Q-Block1 and Q-Block2 options, which extend block-wise transfer to Non-confirmable messages with faster loss recovery, a new 4.08 missing-blocks payload, and NON congestion control parameters.

CoAP.why: The document defines new CoAP options, response code usage, congestion control parameters and caching rules, extending CoAP block-wise transfer.
CoAP.quote: This document specifies alternative Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) block-wise transfer options: Q-Block1 and Q-Block2.

congestion control.why: Section 7 defines new NON congestion control parameters (MAX_PAYLOADS, NON_TIMEOUT, PROBING_RATE use) as a substantial part of the specification.
congestion control.quote: Additional congestion control measures need to be put in place for NON messages (Section 7.2).

rejected.why: DOTS is the motivating use case, but the document is a generic CoAP extension, not a DOTS specification.
OSCORE class E/U handling of the options is covered briefly, but the document is not about OSCORE.
CBOR Sequence is only the encoding of the missing-blocks payload.
UDP is the substrate CoAP runs over; nothing new is specified about UDP.
The media type registration is IANA boilerplate for a small payload type, not the main subject.
DDoS conditions are motivation only; the document does not address mitigation or signalling.

RFC9178.title: Building Power-Efficient Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) Devices for Cellular Networks
RFC9178.summary: Informational guidance on using CoAP in battery-powered sensors and devices on cellular networks, covering discovery/registration, data formats, and real-time reachable versus sleepy device models to minimize power consumption.

CoAP.why: The document gives guidance on how to use CoAP (Observe, resource directory registration, pub/sub, mirror servers) to minimize power on constrained devices.
CoAP.quote: This memo discusses the use of the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) [RFC7252] in building sensors and other devices that employ cellular networks as a communications medium.

cellular.why: The link-layer assumptions, paging, APNs and public cellular network characteristics are a substantial part of the document.
cellular.quote: This memo primarily targets 3GPP cellular networks in their 2G, 3G, LTE, and 5G variants and their future enhancements

IoT.why: The document is about power-efficient constrained sensor devices and their operating strategies, which is IoT guidance for constrained devices.
IoT.quote: Using the power usage strategies described in [RFC7228], mains-powered sensor-type devices can use the Always-on strategy

rejected.why: Only recommended in one sentence as a compact data format; the document is not about it.
Listed among possible data formats only; not discussed in its own right.
Mentioned only as one candidate data format.
Only a passing mention that devices could use DTN mechanisms.
NAT is discussed as a deployment factor affecting reachability, not specified or analysed.
DNS names are used for manually configured discovery; DNS is only a substrate.

gaps.name: power efficiency / low-power device operation
gaps.why: The core subject is minimizing power consumption in devices, and the taxonomy has no tag for it beyond the IoT and energy management topics.

RFC9179.title: A YANG Grouping for Geographic Locations
RFC9179.summary: Defines the ietf-geo-location YANG module, a reusable grouping for specifying geographic locations on Earth or other astronomical bodies, with reference frame, coordinates, velocity and timestamps, plus an IANA registry of geodetic system values.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module defining a geo-location grouping, intended for reuse in other YANG data models.
YANG.quote: This document defines a generic geographical location YANG grouping.

geolocation.why: The subject matter is the representation of location: reference frame, geodetic datum, coordinates, and velocity. It also maps to the geo URI, the W3C Geolocation API, GML and KML, so geolocation readers would want it.
geolocation.quote: The geographical location grouping is intended to be used in YANG data models for specifying a location on or in reference to Earth

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in the Security Considerations boilerplate as the access protocols; the document defines only a grouping.
This is a YANG model, not an SNMP MIB module.
The geo URI (RFC 5870) is only compared for portability and is not specified or extended here.
The geodetic system registry is a small part of the document and is not about IANA guidance in general.
XML appears only in the example data and registry boilerplate, and the document does not specify an XML format.
The timestamp leaf simply uses yang:date-and-time and defines nothing new about date-time representation.

RFC9180.title: Hybrid Public Key Encryption
RFC9180.summary: Specifies Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE), a KEM+KDF+AEAD construction with base, PSK, auth and auth-PSK modes, secret export, algorithm identifiers, security analysis and test vectors.

key management.why: HPKE defines key encapsulation, key schedule and secret export for establishing symmetric keys from a recipient public key; this is a cryptographic scheme and key-establishment mechanism, the closest fit in the taxonomy.
key management.quote: HPKE works for any combination of an asymmetric KEM, key derivation function (KDF), and authenticated encryption with additional data (AEAD) encryption function.

elliptic curve.why: The DHKEM instantiations are built on ECDH over NIST curves and X25519/X448, with serialization, key derivation and validation rules specified for them.
elliptic curve.quote: DHKEM(Group, KDF) ... For P-256, P-384, and P-521, the size Ndh of the Diffie-Hellman shared secret is equal to 32, 48, and 66

rejected.why: TLS Encrypted ClientHello and the TLS exporter are mentioned only as applications or analogies; the document is not about TLS.
HKDF is used as the KDF but HMAC itself is not specified or extended.
ChaCha20Poly1305 is only one listed AEAD identifier, not the subject.
AES-GCM is only one listed AEAD identifier, not the subject.
MLS is mentioned only as an application of HPKE.
X25519/X448 are used as DH groups in DHKEM, but the document does not define the curves; the elliptic curve tag covers them.

gaps.name: Hybrid public key encryption / KEM-DEM (public-key encryption)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for public-key encryption schemes or KEMs generally; the cryptography topic has only specific algorithms and key management.

RFC9181.title: A Common YANG Data Model for Layer 2 and Layer 3 VPNs
RFC9181.summary: Defines the ietf-vpn-common YANG module, with reusable identities, features, types and groupings for Layer 2 and Layer 3 VPN service and network models (L3SM, L2SM, L3NM, L2NM).

YANG.why: The document's core deliverable is a YANG module (ietf-vpn-common) with identities, types and groupings for reuse by other YANG models.
YANG.quote: This document defines a common YANG module that is meant to be reused by various VPN-related modules such as Layer 3 VPN and Layer 2 VPN network models.

VPN.why: The module models common provider-provisioned L2/L3 VPN concepts: service types, topologies, route targets, route distinguishers, site roles, and VPN-related constraints. It serves VPN modelling readers.
VPN.quote: There are common data nodes and structures that are present in all of these models or at least a subset of them.

rejected.why: The document covers L3VPN only as one of several VPN service types the common module supports. It does not specify L3VPN itself; the VPN parent tag is the better fit.
BGP appears only as a PE-CE routing protocol feature and signalling identity, not as a protocol the document specifies or extends.
The YANG tag already covers the data-modelling subject. NETCONF, RESTCONF and NACM appear only as the substrate and in boilerplate.
EVPN is listed as one service-type identity and is not the document's subject.
The qos-classification-policy grouping is a small part of the module, and the document does not address QoS architecture or signalling.
NETCONF is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to access the module.

RFC9182.title: A YANG Network Data Model for Layer 3 VPNs
RFC9182.summary: Defines the ietf-l3vpn-ntw YANG module (L3NM), a network-centric data model that a network controller uses to provision BGP/MPLS Layer 3 VPN services within a service provider network, complementing the customer-facing L3SM.

L3VPN.why: The document specifies a model for provisioning BGP/MPLS L3VPN services. Its subject is the L3VPN service itself: VPN nodes, RDs/RTs, CE-PE routing and multicast.
L3VPN.quote: this document defines an L3VPN Network Model (L3NM) that can be used for the provisioning of Layer 3 Virtual Private Network (L3VPN) services within a service provider network

YANG.why: The main content is a YANG module with tree diagrams and the full module text, so readers of YANG models would want it.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG module called the "L3VPN Network Model" (L3NM).

MVPN.why: A substantial part of the model covers multicast in L3VPNs (RP, IGMP/MLD, PIM, MSDP), including a multicast VPN example in Appendix A.4.
MVPN.quote: The L3NM focuses on Layer 3 VPNs based on BGP Provider Edges (PEs) as described in [RFC4026], [RFC4110], and [RFC4364]; and Multicast VPNs

rejected.why: BGP is modelled only as a CE-PE routing option in the VPN network access. The document does not specify or extend the BGP protocol.
NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the access protocols for the module, mentioned in Security Considerations and the examples.
OSPF, IS-IS, RIP and VRRP appear as per-access configuration containers within the model. The document is not about those protocols.
BFD appears only as the OAM container in the model, which is a minor part of the document.
SDN is mentioned only as context for orchestration and controllers. It is not the subject.
PIM appears only as multicast configuration parameters inside the model. The multicast subject is already covered by the MVPN tag.

RFC9183.title: Single Nickname for an Area Border RBridge in Multilevel Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL)
RFC9183.summary: Specifies a multilevel TRILL approach in which area border RBridges use a single nickname in both Level 1 and Level 2, with nickname replacement, DBRB handling, load balancing, and new IS-IS APPsub-TLVs for border discovery.

TRILL.why: The whole document specifies a multilevel TRILL nickname scheme, including data-plane processing at border RBridges and new TRILL APPsub-TLVs.
TRILL.quote: area border RBridges use a single nickname in both Level 1 and Level 2.

rejected.why: IS-IS is only the substrate that carries the new APPsub-TLVs. The document defines TRILL TLVs, not IS-IS itself.
The document does address multilevel scalability. However, the TRILL tag is the more specific fit and sits under routing.
TRILL carries Ethernet frames, but the document does not address Ethernet itself.
The per-flow load balancing in the document is nickname replacement. It is not general ECMP forwarding.

RFC9184.title: BGP Extended Community Registries Update
RFC9184.summary: Updates IANA BGP Extended Community registries (types 0x80-0x82 and their sub-type registries) to change registration procedure from Experimental Use to First Come First Served and rename the registries, updating RFC 7153 and RFC 8955.

BGP communities.why: The whole document is about BGP Extended Community type and sub-type registries and how their code points are registered.
BGP communities.quote: This document updates several BGP Extended Community registries in order to replace the "Experimental Use" registration procedure in some entries

IANA.why: The main body is registry administration: changing registration procedures and renaming registries. Readers of IANA registry topics would want it.
IANA.quote: changing the registration procedure from "Experimental Use" to "First Come First Served" [RFC8126] for the types 0x80-0x82

rejected.why: Flowspec RFCs 5575, 7674 and 8955 are mentioned only as the users of the code points. The document does not specify or change flowspec behaviour.
The document does not change the BGP protocol, policy or operations. BGP communities is the more specific fit.

RFC9185.title: DTLS Tunnel between a Media Distributor and Key Distributor to Facilitate Key Exchange
RFC9185.summary: Defines a TLS-based tunneling protocol letting a PERC Media Distributor relay DTLS-SRTP handshakes between endpoints and a Key Distributor, and deliver hop-by-hop SRTP keys to the Media Distributor while keeping end-to-end keys hidden.

SRTP.why: The protocol exists to establish and deliver SRTP hop-by-hop and end-to-end keying material (MediaKeys message, protection profiles, master keys and salts) in PERC conferences.
SRTP.quote: allowing an endpoint to use DTLS for the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (DTLS-SRTP) [RFC5764] for establishing encryption and authentication keys with the Key Distributor

key management.why: The document is about distributing HBH and E2E keying material, with the Media Distributor seeing only HBH keys.
key management.quote: enables a Media Distributor to facilitate key exchange between an endpoint in a conference and the Key Distributor

rejected.why: DTLS messages are only tunneled as opaque data; the document says it is not an extension to TLS or DTLS.
TLS is merely the substrate for the tunnel with mutual authentication; nothing new is defined for TLS.
RTP/RTCP packets are protected by the keys but the document does not specify RTP itself.
SDP tls-id and fingerprint attributes are used for matching but are defined elsewhere.
Version 4 UUIDs are used only as association identifiers; incidental use.
The context is PERC conferencing, but the document is about key exchange tunneling, not conferencing frameworks.

gaps.name: PERC (Privacy-Enhanced RTP Conferencing)
gaps.why: The document is part of the PERC work, but the taxonomy has no tag for it or for private media or double-encryption conferencing.

RFC9186.title: Fast Failover in Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) Using Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for Multipoint Networks
RFC9186.summary: Specifies using multipoint BFD (RFC 8562) to give sub-second failure detection of PIM-SM routers, defining a new BFD Discriminator PIM Hello option (type 39) to bootstrap P2MP BFD sessions, including use in PIM DR load balancing.

PIM-SM.why: The document extends PIM-SM with a new Hello option and changes neighbor failure handling, so PIM-SM readers need it.
PIM-SM.quote: This document defines the monitoring of a PIM-SM router using P2MP BFD.

BFD.why: It specifies how P2MP BFD sessions (MultipointHead/Tail) are created, demultiplexed and encapsulated for PIM routers.
BFD.quote: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for multipoint networks can provide sub-second failover for routers that participate in Protocol Independent Multicast

rejected.why: Parent of PIM-SM, which is already tagged, so it is implied.
The IANA section only registers the PIM Hello option value, which is boilerplate.
Not relevant to the document.

RFC9187.title: Sequence Number Extension for Windowed Protocols
RFC9187.summary: Informational RFC that formalizes Sequence Number Extension (SNE), a receiver-side technique to track sequence number wraparound for sliding window protocols without extra header bits, with example C code and a validation sequence.

TCP.why: SNE originates in TCP-AO and TCP is the main sliding window protocol the document addresses. It clarifies pseudocode from RFC 5925, so TCP readers would want it. The document is generic, so this is secondary.
TCP.quote: This technique was introduced as "Sequence Number Extension" in the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO) [RFC5925].

rejected.why: The document is generic to windowed protocols, but TCP is the more specific tag and already covers this.
SNE is used as input to MACs, but the document does not define integrity checks.
MACs are mentioned only as a use case for SNE and are not specified.
The DNS SOA serial number is mentioned only as related discussion of serial number arithmetic.
The document notes SNE can feed encryption and authentication inputs, but it adds no entropy and defines no algorithm.

gaps.name: Sequence number arithmetic / sequence number extension
gaps.why: The document's core subject is serial number arithmetic and wrap tracking for sliding window protocols. The taxonomy has no generic tag for it, so only the TCP tag fits partially.

RFC9188.title: Generic Multi-Access (GMA) Encapsulation Protocol
RFC9188.summary: Defines the experimental GMA encapsulation protocol (trailer-based IP, header-based IP, and non-IP/UDP encapsulation) with control fields, fragmentation and concatenation for combining multiple access networks below L4.

tunneling.why: The document specifies a new encapsulation protocol, using IP protocol 114 or UDP, to carry IP packets with extra control fields. No specific tunnelling child (GRE, IP-in-IP) fits, so the generic tunneling topic is used.
tunneling.quote: This document presents a lightweight Generic Multi-Access (GMA) encapsulation protocol for the convergence layer.

rejected.why: GRE is discussed only as the prior approach whose drawbacks motivate GMA. GMA is not a GRE extension.
UDP tunnelling is just one adaptation-layer option for the non-IP encapsulation, not the subject of the document.
IPsec is mentioned only as an optional way to protect the adaptation layer.
The document aims to avoid IP-over-IP tunnelling overhead, so it is not about IP-in-IP.
MPTCP is not mentioned. GMA works below L4 for applications that lack multipath support, so it is a related alternative rather than the subject.
LTE and 5G are example access networks only. The protocol is access-agnostic.

gaps.name: Multi-access aggregation (MAMS / GMA)
gaps.why: The document is about combining Wi-Fi, LTE and other access networks below L4 for aggregation, steering and retransmission. The taxonomy has no multi-access or multipath network tag.

RFC9189.title: GOST Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.2
RFC9189.summary: Specifies a profile of TLS 1.2 with Russian GOST algorithms: three cipher suites, two signature algorithms, seven supported groups, two client certificate types, plus supporting algorithms and test vectors.

GOST.why: The document defines how GOST ciphers (Kuznyechik, Magma, GOST 28147-89), hash and signatures are used, including KEG, KExp15 and TLSTREE algorithms.
GOST.quote: to support the Russian cryptographic standard algorithms (called "GOST" algorithms)

TLS.why: It defines new TLS 1.2 cipher suites, signature algorithms, supported groups and certificate types, and the handshake and record protection for them.
TLS.quote: This document specifies a profile of TLS 1.2 with GOST algorithms so that implementers can produce interoperable implementations.

rejected.why: Certificates appear only in test vectors and the new client certificate types; the document is not about certificate profiles.
GOST curves are registered as supported groups, but the GOST tag covers them more specifically; the document does not specify ECC generally.
DER structures are used for key transport blobs but only as an encoding mechanism.
IANA registry additions are boilerplate-like registrations, not the subject of the document.
Mentioned only in IANA table columns (DTLS-OK); not specified here.

gaps.name: GOST cryptographic algorithms
gaps.why: The taxonomy includes a GOST tag under cryptography in the tag list, but this is the document's main cryptographic subject; if the id is unavailable, the closest fit would be the cryptography parent.

RFC9190.title: EAP-TLS 1.3: Using the Extensible Authentication Protocol with TLS 1.3
RFC9190.summary: Specifies EAP-TLS with TLS 1.3 (updating RFC 5216): message flows, resumption via NewSessionTicket, privacy, key derivation via the TLS exporter, revocation checking, and guidance on identity, authorization and resumption.

EAP.why: The document defines the EAP-TLS method for TLS 1.3, updating RFC 5216, including key hierarchy (MSK/EMSK), state machines and identity handling.
EAP.quote: This document specifies the use of EAP-TLS with TLS 1.3 while remaining backwards compatible with existing implementations of EAP-TLS.

TLS.why: A substantial part covers how TLS 1.3 handshake features (HelloRetryRequest, NewSessionTicket, PSK resumption, exporters, OCSP stapling) are used or restricted in EAP-TLS, and it registers TLS Exporter labels.
TLS.quote: TLS 1.3 is in large part a complete remodeling of the TLS handshake protocol including a different message flow

rejected.why: OCSP stapling is mandated as a revocation mechanism but the document does not specify or extend OCSP itself.
Mentioned only as an encapsulating protocol in authorization guidance.
Privacy is handled specifically for EAP-TLS and anonymous NAIs, not as a general privacy topic; the EAP and TLS tags cover it.
Certificate validation and SAN matching are discussed, but the document does not profile certificates.
Authentication is for network access via EAP; AAA frameworks are only mentioned as carriers.

RFC9191.title: Handling Large Certificates and Long Certificate Chains in TLS-Based EAP Methods
RFC9191.summary: Informational RFC describing the problem of large certificates and long chains in TLS-based EAP methods (EAP-TLS) causing authenticators to drop sessions, and surveying solutions such as ECC, certificate compression, caching, and raw public keys.

EAP.why: The whole document addresses deployment problems of EAP-TLS and other TLS-based EAP methods and potential solutions.
EAP.quote: EAP-TLS and other TLS-based EAP methods are widely deployed and used for network access authentication.

TLS.why: A substantial part surveys TLS extensions (client_certificate_url, cached_info, certificate compression, raw public keys, cTLS, TLS 1.3 omission of CA certs) to shrink handshakes.
TLS.quote: This section discusses how the fragmentation problem can be avoided by updating the underlying TLS or EAP-TLS implementation.

X.509.why: Provides guidelines for keeping X.509 certificates and chains small (DNs, OIDs, extensions, intermediates).
X.509.quote: OIDs are used lavishly in X.509 certificates [RFC5280] and while not all can be avoided

rejected.why: Mentioned only as a transport limiting EAP message size, not the subject.
ECC use is one brief suggestion for reducing certificate size, not a main subject.
Only referenced as an encoding for compact certificates in early work.
Certificate chains are discussed, but X.509 is the more specific fit and no PKI operations are addressed.
Mentioned only as a future cause of larger certificates.

RFC9192.title: Network Service Header (NSH) Fixed-Length Context Header Allocation
RFC9192.summary: Defines an NSH MD Type 0x1 fixed-length Context Header allocation (Timestamp Context Header) carrying a sequence number, source interface identifier and 64-bit timestamp, published to document existing silicon implementations.

SFC.why: The document specifies a metadata Context Header allocation for the Network Service Header, which is part of Service Function Chaining.
SFC.quote: This memo defines the Timestamp Context Header, which is an NSH fixed-length Context Header that incorporates the packet's timestamp, a sequence number, and a source interface identifier.

rejected.why: NTP's 64-bit timestamp format is reused for the Timestamp field, and NTP is mentioned for synchronization. The document does not specify or profile NTP.
IEEE 1588 is cited for the truncated timestamp format and for synchronization. The document is not about PTP.
Alternate Marking and delay measurement are listed as use cases. The document says the SF behavior and applications are out of scope.
Section 5 covers synchronization only briefly, as a consideration for using the timestamp.
Network analytics and monitoring appear only as example use cases, not as the subject of the document.

RFC9193.title: Sensor Measurement Lists (SenML) Fields for Indicating Data Value Content-Format
RFC9193.summary: RFC 9193 defines two new SenML fields, "ct" and "bct", that indicate the content format (media type, parameters, content codings or CoAP Content-Format number) of binary Data Values in SenML records, with ABNF syntax and IANA label registrations.

SenML.why: The document extends SenML with new fields (ct, bct) and registers them in the SenML Labels registry.
SenML.quote: this document specifies a pair of new SenML fields for indicating the content format of those binary Data Values

media types.why: Substantial part defines how media types, parameters and content codings are expressed as strings in the fields, including ABNF for Content-Type syntax.
media types.quote: Media-Type-Name:  A combination of a type-name and a subtype-name registered in [IANA.media-types], as per [RFC6838]

rejected.why: CoAP Content-Format numbers are reused as a value space, but the document does not specify or extend CoAP.
CBOR is used only as an example payload type.
SenML JSON representation is the substrate for examples, not the subject.
ABNF is used just to define the field syntax; the document is not about the notation.
Parent topic implied by SenML; SenML is the more specific tag.
The document labels content format in data; it does not negotiate media features.

RFC9194.title: A YANG Module for IS-IS Reverse Metric
RFC9194.summary: Defines the ietf-isis-reverse-metric YANG module, augmenting the IS-IS YANG model to configure and report the IS-IS reverse metric extension from RFC 8500.

YANG.why: The document's content is a YANG module with a tree diagram, module source and instance examples.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG module for managing the reverse metric extension

IS-IS.why: The module manages an IS-IS extension (reverse metric TLV, per-level interface and adjacency state), so IS-IS readers would want it.
IS-IS.quote: managing the reverse metric extension to the Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) intra-domain routing information exchange protocol

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in Security Considerations as access protocols for the module.
Not related; the document only uses YANG.
JSON is used only for an instance data example encoding.
XML is used only for example instance data and the namespace registration.
Mentioned only as secure transport in Security Considerations.

RFC9195.title: A File Format for YANG Instance Data
RFC9195.summary: Specifies a standard XML/JSON file format and the ietf-yang-instance-data YANG module for documenting YANG-defined instance data with metadata when a live server is unavailable.

YANG.why: The document defines a YANG module (ietf-yang-instance-data) and a file format for instance data of YANG-modelled data, so YANG readers would look for it.
YANG.quote: This document specifies a standard file format for YANG instance data, which follows the syntax and semantics of existing YANG models and annotates it with metadata.

rejected.why: NETCONF is only mentioned as a way to retrieve live values and as example content; the document does not specify or extend it.
JSON (and XML) are only the encodings used for the file format, reusing RFC 7951 rules; the document is not about JSON itself.
XML is an encoding substrate reused from YANG rules, not the subject.
Not an SNMP MIB; YANG data modelling is the relevant subject.
Only mentioned as a retrieval method for live data.
The YANG tag is a more specific fit and sits under network management, which is therefore implied.

RFC9196.title: YANG Modules Describing Capabilities for Systems and Datastore Update Notifications
RFC9196.summary: Defines two YANG modules, ietf-system-capabilities (a placeholder structure for reporting YANG-related server capabilities at implementation time or runtime) and ietf-notification-capabilities (which augments it with YANG-Push subscription capabilities).

YANG.why: The document's main content is two new YANG modules, one an augmentable capability structure and one augmenting it. Readers of YANG models would want it.
YANG.quote: This document defines two YANG modules, "ietf-system-capabilities" and "ietf-notification-capabilities".

NETCONF.why: The modules are built for NETCONF/RESTCONF servers, and the document describes how clients read capabilities at runtime. It is not a protocol specification, so this is secondary.
NETCONF.quote: Capabilities SHOULD be available via NETCONF [RFC6241] or RESTCONF [RFC8040] from the live server (implementing the publisher) during runtime.

rejected.why: RESTCONF is only an alternative access protocol for the data. The document does not extend it.
The document is about YANG-Push capabilities, which relate to telemetry. But it defines capability models, not telemetry streaming, and the taxonomy has no YANG-Push tech tag.
TLS appears only in the Security Considerations as the transport under RESTCONF.
SSH appears only in the Security Considerations as the transport under NETCONF.
XML is only the encoding of the instance data examples in the appendices.

gaps.name: YANG-Push / subscribed notifications
gaps.why: The second module describes capabilities of YANG-Push (RFC 8641) publishers. The taxonomy has no tag for YANG-Push or YANG notification subscription.

gaps.name: YANG instance data
gaps.why: The document uses the YANG instance data file format (RFC 9195) to deliver capabilities at implementation time. The taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC9197.title: Data Fields for In Situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM)
RFC9197.summary: Defines the IOAM data fields (trace, proof-of-transit, edge-to-edge option types), namespaces, timestamp formats and IANA registries for recording telemetry/OAM data in packets as they traverse a limited domain.

OAM.why: The document defines IOAM, a hybrid OAM mechanism with its data fields, option types and namespaces.
OAM.quote: In situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM) collects operational and telemetry information in the packet while the packet traverses a path between two points in the network.

telemetry.why: Much of the document specifies per-node telemetry fields such as queue depth, buffer occupancy, timestamps and transit delay, carried in packets.
telemetry.quote: IOAM tracing can collect the following types of information:

rejected.why: Export of IOAM data via IPFIX is mentioned but explicitly out of scope.
The NSH and service function chaining appear only as an encapsulation example and as a Proof of Transit use case.
NTP and PTP timestamp formats are borrowed for the timestamp fields. The document does not specify those protocols.
IPv6 is only one possible encapsulation for IOAM data fields, and the document leaves encapsulation out of scope.
IOAM is related to performance measurement (RFC 7799 hybrid type). However, the document mainly defines OAM data fields, so OAM and telemetry fit better.
The IANA registries are boilerplate for the IOAM field definitions and are not the document's main subject.

gaps.name: In situ OAM (IOAM)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only an OAM topic. It has no technology tag for IOAM itself, so readers looking for IOAM find only the general OAM page.

RFC9198.title: Advanced Unidirectional Route Assessment (AURA)
RFC9198.summary: Defines the AURA Route Ensemble metric and active/hybrid measurement methodology for discovering parallel (ECMP) paths between a source and destination, updating the IPPM framework (RFC 2330) path terminology.

traceroute.why: The active methodology builds on Paris-traceroute and Scamper to discover Hops, Member Routes and RTD per hop; the document is about route/path discovery.
traceroute.quote: the popular tool, traceroute, was developed to gather the IP addresses of each Hop along a path using ICMP

performance measurement.why: Defines a new IPPM route metric, round-trip delay analysis and measurement methods, which is performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: This memo introduces an advanced unidirectional route assessment (AURA) metric and associated measurement methodology based on the IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) framework

rejected.why: ECMP is the multipath behaviour being discovered, not specified or extended by the document.
ICMP Time Exceeded is the probing mechanism used by the tools, not something the document specifies or extends.
Appendix A only briefly covers MPLS traceroute; it is a minor part and relies on RFC 8029.
IOAM is used as the hybrid method substrate via RFC 9197; this document does not define OAM mechanisms itself.
IPv6 flow label and hop limit are mentioned as probe fields but the document is not about IPv6.
TWAMP and OWAMP are cited only in Security Considerations.

RFC9199.title: Considerations for Large Authoritative DNS Server Operators
RFC9199.summary: An Independent Submission summarizing research-derived operational advice (C1-C6) for large authoritative DNS server operators on anycast deployment, routing, catchment mapping, DDoS response strategies, and TTL choices.

DNS.why: The whole document is operational guidance for authoritative DNS servers, covering server selection by resolvers, TTLs, parent/child records and caching.
DNS.quote: offers derived, specific, tangible advice to DNS authoritative server operators

anycast.why: Three of the six considerations (C1-C3) concern anycast deployment, instance count, routing optimization and catchment mapping.
anycast.quote: Deploy Anycast in Every Authoritative Server to Enhance Distribution and Latency

DDoS.why: C4 gives guidance on responding to DDoS attacks against anycast DNS, withdraw versus absorb strategies and filtering.
DDoS.quote: Operators should consider having both an anycast site withdraw strategy and an absorption strategy ready to be used before a network overload occurs.

rejected.why: BGP announcements, prepending and communities are used as traffic-shifting tools, but the document does not specify or analyse BGP itself.
DNSSEC is mentioned only in passing when noting that DS records refer to DNSKEY records, not as a subject of the document.
DOTS and FlowSpec are cited as filtering options within C4, not discussed in their own right.
The document relies on measurement studies (RIPE Atlas, Verfploeter), but it summarizes their conclusions as operational advice rather than defining measurement methods.
Unrelated to blocklists; mentioned here only to rule out a loose keyword match on DNS operations.

RFC9200.title: Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments Using the OAuth 2.0 Framework (ACE-OAuth)
RFC9200.summary: RFC 9200 defines the ACE-OAuth framework, which adapts OAuth 2.0 to constrained IoT environments using CoAP, CBOR, COSE and CWT.

RFC9201.title: Additional OAuth Parameters for Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments (ACE)
RFC9201.summary: RFC 9201 defines new OAuth 2.0 token and introspection endpoint parameters (req_cnf, cnf, rs_cnf) and CBOR mappings for expressing proof-of-possession keys in the ACE framework.

ACE.why: The document extends the ACE-OAuth framework with new parameters for PoP key negotiation between client, AS and RS.
ACE.quote: This specification defines new parameters and encodings for the OAuth 2.0 token and introspection endpoints when used with the framework for Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments (ACE).

rejected.why: The parameters are for OAuth endpoints, but the document is specifically an ACE extension; ACE is the more specific tag and OAuth is its substrate here.
CBOR is used as the encoding and for key mappings, but the document is not about CBOR itself.
COSE_Key is used for key representation in examples only.
CoAP is the transport in the examples and not specified or extended.
The cnf claim semantics are referenced from RFC 7800, but JWT is not the subject.
DTLS is mentioned only as an example in the asymmetric key requirement.

RFC9202.title: Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) Profile for Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments (ACE)
RFC9202.summary: Defines the CoAP-DTLS profile of the ACE framework, in which clients and constrained resource servers use DTLS with raw public keys or pre-shared keys and authorization-server-issued proof-of-possession access tokens.

ACE.why: The document is an ACE profile (coap_dtls) specifying token retrieval, token upload, dynamic update and expiration for ACE.
ACE.quote: This specification defines a profile of the ACE framework [RFC9200].

DTLS.why: A substantial part specifies how DTLS handshakes are used (RPK and PSK modes, psk_identity carrying the token, mandatory cipher suites, DTLS 1.3 handling).
DTLS.quote: an implementation that supports the RPK mode of this profile MUST at least support the cipher suite TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8

rejected.why: CoAP is the application protocol carried over DTLS; the document uses it but does not specify or extend it.
ACE-OAuth is the framework being profiled, but the OAuth tag is not the right fit; the ACE tag covers it.
CBOR and CWT are only the token encoding used here.
COSE_Key structures are used for key representation, not defined or extended here.
Only the DTLS child is relevant; TLS cipher suites are referenced for DTLS use.

RFC9203.title: The Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments (OSCORE) Profile of the Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments (ACE) Framework
RFC9203.summary: Specifies the coap_oscore profile of the ACE-OAuth framework, in which a client and resource server use OSCORE, keyed from an access-token-bound symmetric PoP key and exchanged nonces, to secure CoAP communication.

ACE.why: The document is a profile of the ACE framework. It defines token request and response handling, authz-info exchange, and new parameters for it.
ACE.quote: This document specifies the coap_oscore profile of the ACE framework [RFC9200].

OSCORE.why: The profile derives the OSCORE security context from the PoP key and nonces. It defines OSCORE_Input_Material, Master Salt construction, and when to discard the context.
OSCORE.quote: In order to provide communication security and PoP, the client and resource server use Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments (OSCORE)

rejected.why: CoAP is the communication protocol the profile runs over. The document does not extend it.
The OAuth 2.0 access token model is inherited from the ACE framework. The profile is not an OAuth specification.
COSE supplies algorithms and structures only. The document does not specify anything new about it.
CBOR and CDDL are only the encoding used for the new structures.
CWT and JWT confirmation methods are registered only in IANA sections, which is boilerplate. Tokens are otherwise just carried.
TLS and DTLS are mentioned only as alternative channels to the AS.

RFC9204.title: QPACK: Field Compression for HTTP/3
RFC9204.summary: RFC 9204 defines QPACK, a header/trailer field compression format for HTTP/3 that avoids the head-of-line blocking of HPACK by using separate encoder and decoder streams and a dynamic table.

HTTP/3.why: QPACK is the field compression mechanism of HTTP/3. It defines HTTP/3 settings, stream types and error codes, so HTTP/3 readers need it.
HTTP/3.quote: This specification defines QPACK: a compression format for efficiently representing HTTP fields that is to be used in HTTP/3.

rejected.why: QUIC is the transport whose out-of-order stream delivery motivates the design. The document does not specify or extend QUIC.
HPACK, the HTTP/2 compression format, is the basis QPACK varies from. This document is not about HTTP/2.
This is header-field compression, not a general lossless data compression format. The HTTP/3 tag is the better fit.
TLS appears only in the security discussion of length-based attacks. It is not the subject.
This topic covers compression of protocol headers on constrained links, which is a different subject from HTTP field compression. The HTTP/3 tag fits better.
The more specific HTTP/3 child tag applies, so the parent is implied and not listed.

RFC9205.title: Building Protocols with HTTP
RFC9205.summary: BCP guidance for writing specifications of application protocols that use HTTP as a substrate (HTTP APIs), covering URLs, methods, status codes, header fields, caching, state, browser coexistence and evolution; obsoletes RFC 3205.

HTTP APIs.why: The whole document is guidance on building HTTP-based APIs, which is exactly the subject of the HTTP APIs tag.
HTTP APIs.quote: This document specifies best practices for writing specifications that use HTTP to define new application protocols.

HTTP caching.why: Section 4.9 gives substantial advice on freshness, stale responses, and Vary for applications built on HTTP.
HTTP caching.quote: HTTP caching [HTTP-CACHING] is one of the primary benefits of using HTTP for applications; it provides scalability, reduces latency, and improves reliability.

web linking.why: Links and link relations are the recommended mechanism for URL discovery, extensibility and versioning throughout the document.
web linking.quote: it is RECOMMENDED that applications using HTTP define and use links [WEB-LINKING] to allow flexibility in deployment.

rejected.why: The document is guidance for applications using HTTP, not a specification or extension of HTTP; it explicitly says it does not apply to generic HTTP extensions. HTTP APIs is the more specific fit.
Cookies are mentioned in Sections 4.10 and 4.14 as a consideration, but only briefly.
URI schemes and well-known URIs are discussed in Section 4.4 as part of API design, but the document is not about URIs themselves.
Browser coexistence (CSRF, XSS, CSP) is covered in Section 4.13 only as a list of considerations, not as the main subject.
HTTP/2 multiplexing and server push are mentioned in passing; the document is not about HTTP/2.
The document has no IANA actions.

RFC9206.title: Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite Cryptography for Internet Protocol Security (IPsec)
RFC9206.summary: Specifies how to use NSA's CNSA Suite algorithms (AES-256-GCM, P-384 ECDH/ECDSA, RSA 3072+, SHA-384, large MODP groups) in IKEv2 and ESP, defining three UI suites and related requirements.

IPsec.why: The document profiles IPsec (IKEv2 and ESP) algorithm selection and configuration for CNSA compliance, defining UI suites and mandatory behaviours.
IPsec.quote: It defines CNSA-based User Interface suites ("UI suites") describing sets of security configurations for Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) and IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)

IKE.why: Much of the body constrains IKEv2: authentication, SA proposals, key exchange payload, key material generation, and CREATE_CHILD_SA.
IKE.quote: CNSA-compliant implementations for IPsec MUST use IKEv2 [RFC7296].

cryptography.why: The document is a cryptographic algorithm policy profile (AES, ECDSA, RSA, ECDH, DH, SHA-384). No specific algorithm child tag fits better than the parent, because several algorithms are covered.
cryptography.quote: The following CNSA requirements apply to IPsec: Encryption: AES [FIPS197] (with key size 256 bits)

rejected.why: ESP is used with the specified algorithm suites, but the document is not about the ESP protocol itself; it is covered under IPsec.
AES-GCM is the chosen cipher, but the document is a multi-algorithm suite profile rather than an AES specification.
Certificates must follow RFC 8603, which is defined elsewhere. This document only references that profile.
Section 12 gives PSK-based guidance for long-term protection, but only as a short section. The document's focus is classical CNSA algorithms.
P-384 ECDH and ECDSA are required, but they are one part of a broader suite profile.

RFC9207.title: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Issuer Identification
RFC9207.summary: Defines the iss authorization response parameter and a matching authorization server metadata parameter so OAuth 2.0 clients can identify the issuing authorization server and defend against mix-up attacks.

OAuth.why: The document extends the OAuth 2.0 authorization framework with a new response parameter and metadata value, and specifies client validation rules for it.
OAuth.quote: This parameter is used to explicitly include the issuer identifier of the authorization server in the authorization response of an OAuth authorization flow.

rejected.why: JWTs are mentioned only in relation to JARM and the iss claim. The document does not specify or profile JWT.
The example responses are HTTP redirects, but HTTP is only the substrate.
RFC 3986 is cited only for string comparison, and the iss value is required to be an https URL. The document is not about URIs.
OpenID Connect is mentioned only as related context for the iss claim. The document does not define a federation framework.
The OAuth tag already covers the subject. The document is about identifying the authorization server, not generic authentication.

gaps.name: OpenID Connect / OAuth authorization server metadata
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for OAuth metadata or OpenID Connect. The OAuth tag is the closest fit.

RFC9208.title: IMAP QUOTA Extension
RFC9208.summary: RFC 9208 defines the IMAP QUOTA extension (obsoleting RFC 2087), adding commands GETQUOTA, GETQUOTAROOT and SETQUOTA, resource types, the DELETED/DELETED-STORAGE STATUS items, the OVERQUOTA response code, and an IANA registry for quota resource types.

IMAP.why: The document specifies an extension to IMAP: new commands, responses, response codes, STATUS data items and capabilities for querying and setting resource quotas.
IMAP.quote: This document defines a QUOTA extension of the Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP)

rejected.why: The document creates an IANA registry for quota resource types, but that is boilerplate-level registry setup. The main body is about the IMAP extension, not IANA guidance.
ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax; the document is not about it.
IMAP is already the more specific tag, and the document is about IMAP quota management rather than email in general.
LMTP is mentioned only as an example of an external event that can trigger OVERQUOTA; the document is not about mail transfer.

gaps.name: IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists IMAP as a child of email, but the id 'IMAP' was used in the tag above. Confirm the tag id as it appears in the taxonomy: 'IMAP'.

RFC9209.title: The Proxy-Status HTTP Response Header Field
RFC9209.summary: Defines the Proxy-Status HTTP response header field, its parameters, and a registry of proxy error types that let HTTP intermediaries (proxies, gateways, CDNs) report details of response handling and generated errors.

HTTP.why: The document specifies a new HTTP response field, its parameters, and extension registries, i.e. an HTTP extension.
HTTP.quote: This document defines the Proxy-Status HTTP response field to convey the details of an intermediary's response handling, including generated errors.

rejected.why: Proxy-Status is a header field for intermediary diagnostics, not a convention for building APIs on HTTP.
CDNs are mentioned as example intermediaries, but the document is about a general HTTP field, not CDN operation or interconnection.
TLS errors and alerts are reported as error types, but TLS is only referenced, not specified or extended.
DNS errors are conveyed as error types, but the document does not specify DNS behaviour.
IANA registries are created but this is procedural, not the document's subject.
Uses Structured Fields, not JSON; Structured Fields is only the encoding substrate.

gaps.name: HTTP Structured Field Values
gaps.why: The field is defined using Structured Fields syntax, but the taxonomy has no tag for it; it is only a substrate here so the gap is minor.

RFC9210.title: DNS Transport over TCP - Operational Requirements
RFC9210.summary: BCP requiring operators to permit and support DNS over TCP (and TLS), updating RFC 1123 and RFC 1536, with guidance on connection management, filtering risks, and monitoring.

DNS.why: The document sets operational requirements for DNS transport over TCP, updating RFC 1123 and 1536. It covers resolver and server behaviour, filtering risks and monitoring.
DNS.quote: All DNS resolvers and servers MUST support and service both UDP and TCP queries.

TCP.why: A substantial part covers TCP operational practice for DNS: SYN flood mitigation, TCP Fast Open, connection limits, idle timeouts and TIME_WAIT handling.
TCP.quote: DNS servers SHOULD enable TFO when possible.

DoT.why: The abstract says the requirement covers DNS over TLS. Section 4.4 discusses its additional operational burdens, such as handshake round trips and session resumption.
DoT.quote: Although DNS over TLS utilizes TCP port 853 instead of port 53, this document applies equally well to DNS over TLS.

rejected.why: EDNS(0) payload sizes and the edns-tcp-keepalive option are discussed as background for why TCP is needed. The document does not specify or extend EDNS.
DNSSEC response sizes and the root KSK rollover are used as examples of why TCP matters. The document is not about DNSSEC itself.
The document sets operational requirements for DNS over TCP. It does not define a new binding of DNS to a transport.
TLS is only the security layer for DoT. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
Filtering of DNS over TCP is the main problem the document addresses, but it concerns DNS operations rather than firewall or middlebox traversal mechanisms.

RFC9211.title: The Cache-Status HTTP Response Header Field
RFC9211.summary: Defines the Cache-Status HTTP response header field, a standardized Structured Fields list with parameters (hit, fwd, fwd-status, ttl, stored, collapsed, key, detail) by which HTTP caches report how they handled a request, plus a registry for new parameters.

HTTP caching.why: The document defines a new header field and parameters that describe HTTP cache behaviour (hit, miss, stale, collapsed, freshness, cache key). Readers of HTTP caching would want it.
HTTP caching.quote: This specification defines a standard mechanism to do so that is aligned with HTTP's caching model.

rejected.why: HTTP caching is the more specific child tag. The ancestor is implied.
CDNs are mentioned only as example cache deployments. The document is not about CDNs or CDN interconnection.
The header is for debugging and cache reporting. It does not define conventions for building APIs on HTTP.
The new registry and its registration template are boilerplate-like and secondary to the header field definition.
The security considerations discuss probing and cache poisoning risks. This is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC9212.title: Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite Cryptography for Secure Shell (SSH)
RFC9212.summary: Profiles the NSA CNSA Suite algorithms (ECDH/DH kex, ECDSA/RSA-SHA2-512 host and user keys, AES-256-GCM) for use with the SSH Transport Layer and Authentication protocols.

SSH.why: The document profiles SSH algorithm negotiation, key exchange, server and user authentication, packet protection and rekeying for CNSA compliance.
SSH.quote: This document specifies conventions for using the United States National Security Agency's CNSA Suite algorithms [CNSA] with the Secure Shell Transport Layer Protocol [RFC4253]

cryptography.why: It is a cryptographic algorithm policy profile that selects specific algorithms, key sizes and hash functions. No narrower algorithm tag covers the whole suite, so the parent topic fits.
cryptography.quote: The NSA has established the Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite to provide vendors and IT users near-term flexibility in meeting their information assurance
cryptography.section: 3. The Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite

rejected.why: AES-256-GCM is one component of the suite, specified through RFC 5647. The document is not about AES itself.
The NIST P-384 ECDH and ECDSA algorithms are only selected from RFC 5656. Nothing new is defined about elliptic curve cryptography.
X.509 certificates are mentioned only as a pointer to RFC 8603 for validation, and the document does not profile them.
SHA-384 and SHA-512 are named as the permitted hashes, but the document is not about the SHA family.
RSA appears only through the rsa-sha2-512 algorithm and a modulus size constraint, which is too minor for its own tag.

gaps.name: CNSA Suite (NSA algorithm policy)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for national-security cryptographic algorithm profiles. The related RFCs for CNSA in TLS, IPsec, CMS and PKIX would also benefit from one.

RFC9213.title: Targeted HTTP Cache Control
RFC9213.summary: Defines a convention for targeted HTTP Cache-Control response header fields aimed at specific caches, and registers CDN-Cache-Control for CDN caches.

HTTP caching.why: The document extends HTTP caching with targeted cache-control fields, specifying cache behaviour, target lists and freshness interaction.
HTTP caching.quote: a convention for HTTP response header fields that allow cache directives to be targeted at specific caches or classes of caches

CDN.why: It defines CDN-Cache-Control, letting origins control CDN caches separately from other caches, so CDN readers would want it.
CDN.quote: the CDN-Cache-Control response header field, which is targeted at content delivery network (CDN) caches

rejected.why: HTTP caching is the more specific child tag; the HTTP parent is implied.
This is about cache header fields, not conventions for building APIs on HTTP.
Not related; only mentioned in passing concerns about sensitive responses.

RFC9214.title: OSPFv3 Code Point for MPLS LSP Ping
RFC9214.summary: Specifies the OSPFv3 code points (3 for Segment ID sub-TLV, 7 for DDMAP TLV) for MPLS LSP Ping/Traceroute for SR, and updates RFC 8287 to restrict the existing OSPF code point to OSPFv2.

segment routing.why: The document extends RFC 8287 LSP Ping/Traceroute for Segment Routing IGP-Prefix and Adjacency SIDs, defining FEC validation behaviour with OSPFv3.
segment routing.quote: This document specifies the code point to be used in the Segment ID sub-TLV (Types 34, 35, and 36) and in the Downstream Detailed Mapping (DDMAP) TLV when the IGP is OSPFv3.

OSPFv3.why: OSPFv3 is the IGP whose code point is defined and distinguished from OSPFv2; readers of OSPFv3 would want this.
OSPFv3.quote: the responder MUST perform the Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) validation using OSPFv3 as the IGP.
