OSPFv3.section: 4. OSPFv3 Protocol in Segment ID Sub-TLVs

MPLS.why: It extends MPLS LSP ping (TLV code points and registries), which is MPLS data-plane OAM.
MPLS.quote: Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switched Paths (LSPs) Ping Parameters

rejected.why: The document concerns OSPFv3 specifically, which has a more specific child tag.
IANA registry assignments are boilerplate here, not the subject of the document.
IPv6 is mentioned only as the address family indicated by sub-TLVs; the document is not about IPv6.
LSP ping is OAM, but the document is about code points under MPLS/SR rather than OAM generally.

RFC9215.title: Using GOST R 34.10-2012 and GOST R 34.11-2012 Algorithms with the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure
RFC9215.summary: Specifies encoding formats, OIDs and parameters for using GOST R 34.10-2012 signatures and GOST R 34.11-2012 hashes in X.509 certificates and CRLs, plus Russian qualified-certificate extensions and test examples.

GOST.why: The document defines how the Russian GOST signature and hash algorithms are identified and encoded for use in Internet PKI.
GOST.quote: encoding formats, identifiers, and parameter formats for the GOST R 34.10-2012 and GOST R 34.11-2012 algorithms

X.509.why: It profiles X.509 certificates and CRLs, covering key usage, qualified-certificate extensions, DN additions, and test certificates.
X.509.quote: This specification defines the contents of the signatureAlgorithm, signatureValue, signature, and subjectPublicKeyInfo fields within X.509 Certificates and Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs).

rejected.why: ASN.1 modules appear in the appendices, but they only carry the X.509 and GOST definitions. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
The GOST signature algorithm uses elliptic curves, and curve parameters are given. The focus is X.509 encoding and identifiers, and GOST is the more specific tag.
CMS is mentioned only for signature value representation. The document is not about CMS.
X.509 is the more specific child and already covers the PKI aspect.

RFC9216.title: S/MIME Example Keys and Certificates
RFC9216.summary: Defines a small set of sample X.509v3 certificates, keys and PKCS #12 objects (RSA and Ed25519 CAs, personas Alice, Bob, Carlos, Dana) for generating and testing S/MIME signed and encrypted email samples.

S/MIME.why: The certificates and keys exist to generate and test S/MIME signed and encrypted messages, so S/MIME readers would want this RFC.
S/MIME.quote: The S/MIME development community benefits from sharing samples of signed or encrypted data.

X.509.why: The body of the document consists of example X.509 certificates, including CA, cross-signed and end-entity certificates, with their policies and extensions.
X.509.quote: This document defines a small set of X.509v3 certificates ([RFC5280]) and secret keys for use when generating or operating on such samples.

rejected.why: Ed25519 keys appear in the samples, but the document does not specify or extend the algorithm. RFC 8032 does that.
RSA keys are used in the samples, but the document is not about the RSA algorithm.
CMS is the message format S/MIME uses, but the document defines no CMS structures. It only mentions the SMIMECapabilities extension.
Email is the use context for the certificates. The subject is S/MIME certificates, and the more specific S/MIME tag already covers it.
Certificates and CAs are covered by the more specific X.509 tag.
SHA-256 is used only to derive key seeds from strings.

gaps.name: PKCS #12 / PKCS #8 key containers
gaps.why: The document supplies PKCS #12 and PKCS #8 objects as test material, and the taxonomy has no tag for key container formats.

RFC9217.title: Current Open Questions in Path-Aware Networking
RFC9217.summary: An IRTF PANRG document that poses eight open research questions on path-aware networking: path property vocabulary, distribution and trust, path selection, interfaces, transport/application implications, endpoints, operation and deployment.

internet architecture.why: The document is about an architectural property of the Internet (path awareness) and the open questions in realizing it across layers and domains. No more specific tag fits.
internet architecture.quote: a path-aware internetworking architecture has two important properties: it exposes the properties of available Internet paths to endpoints

traffic engineering.why: Operating a path-aware network, where endpoints select paths and may conflict with operator intent, is a substantial theme. It touches traffic engineering and routing control. This is a weaker fit than the architecture tag.
traffic engineering.quote: Competing control inputs from path-aware endpoints and the routing control plane may lead to more difficult traffic engineering or non-convergent forwarding

rejected.why: RFC 4655 PCE is cited only as an example of an administrative, non-endpoint-exposed path interface. The document does not specify or analyse it.
ALTO is mentioned once as an example of path awareness in transport-layer terms. The document is not about it.
TLS is mentioned as an authentication layer and for its session identifiers and linkability. The document does not address the protocol itself.
BGP appears only as a contrast: hijacking attacks and inbound-oriented policies. It is not a subject of the document.
The document concerns endpoint path selection across the Internet, not routing architecture or scalability principles as such. The internet architecture tag covers it better.
Privacy appears only in brief remarks, such as linkable identifiers across paths. It is not a main subject.

gaps.name: Path-aware networking
gaps.why: The document's central subject, endpoint discovery and selection of network paths, has no dedicated tag. It is currently covered only by the broader internet architecture tag.

RFC9218.title: Extensible Prioritization Scheme for HTTP
RFC9218.summary: Defines the Priority HTTP header field, urgency and incremental priority parameters, and HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 PRIORITY_UPDATE frames as an extensible replacement for RFC 7540 stream priorities.

HTTP.why: Defines a new HTTP header field, priority parameters and registry, and server scheduling guidance. It is an HTTP extension.
HTTP.quote: This document defines the Priority header field for communicating the initial priority in an HTTP version-independent manner

HTTP/2.why: Defines an HTTP/2 setting and PRIORITY_UPDATE frame (type 0x10), and replaces RFC 7540 stream priorities.
HTTP/2.quote: The SETTINGS_NO_RFC7540_PRIORITIES HTTP/2 setting is defined by this document in order to allow endpoints to omit or ignore HTTP/2 priority signals

HTTP/3.why: Defines the HTTP/3 PRIORITY_UPDATE frame with its types, error handling and control-stream rules.
HTTP/3.quote: The HTTP/3 PRIORITY_UPDATE frame (type=0xF0700 or 0xF0701) is used by clients to signal the initial priority of a response

rejected.why: QUIC is only the transport for HTTP/3. Section 12 on retransmission scheduling mentions it, but the document defines nothing new for QUIC.
Caching is touched on briefly in Sections 5 and 14, but the document is not about caching.
CDNs appear as intermediary examples in the fairness discussion, but the document is not about CDNs.
Scavenging congestion control is mentioned only as one example of intentional unfairness.
The document defines a protocol-level priority signal, not conventions for building APIs on HTTP.

RFC9219.title: S/MIME Signature Verification Extension to the JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP)
RFC9219.summary: Defines a JMAP for Mail extension (capability urn:ietf:params:jmap:smimeverify) adding Email/get properties and Email/query filters that return server-computed S/MIME signature verification status.

JMAP.why: The document extends JMAP for Mail with new Email/get properties, Email/query filter conditions, a capability, and Email/changes interaction.
JMAP.quote: This document specifies an extension to "The JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP) for Mail" (RFC 8621) for returning the S/MIME signature verification status.

S/MIME.why: The extension is about reporting S/MIME signature and certificate verification results, defining status values (signed/verified, signed/failed) and errors. S/MIME readers would want it.
S/MIME.quote: returning the S/MIME signature verification status [RFC8551], without requiring a JMAP client to download the signature body part and all signed body parts

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding that JMAP uses. The document defines nothing new about JSON.
Certificate validation and CRL checking are referenced via RFC 5280, but the document does not specify or profile certificates.
CMS is mentioned only as a format the client would otherwise have to decode. The document does not address it.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations as the channel protection that JMAP requires.
multipart/signed is mentioned in passing. The document is about verification status, not MIME structure.

RFC9220.title: Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/3
RFC9220.summary: RFC 9220 adapts the Extended CONNECT mechanism for running WebSocket over a single HTTP/2 stream (RFC 8441) to HTTP/3, registering the SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL setting for HTTP/3 and describing stream closure mapping.

WebSocket.why: The document specifies how WebSocket is bootstrapped over HTTP/3, including closure semantics, so WebSocket readers would want it.
WebSocket.quote: defines a mechanism for running the WebSocket Protocol [RFC6455] over a single stream of an HTTP/2 connection

HTTP/3.why: It extends HTTP/3 with the Extended CONNECT setting (0x08) and defines HTTP/3-specific stream closure and error mapping for this use.
HTTP/3.quote: This document registers a new setting in the "HTTP/3 Settings" registry

rejected.why: RFC 8441's HTTP/2 mechanism is the basis being ported, but this document specifies only HTTP/3 details.
Problem details (RFC 7807) is only mentioned as an optional 501 response format.
HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, but the document is not about QUIC itself.
TCP closure behaviour is only referenced as an analogy for HTTP/3 stream closure.
The HTTP/3 tag is more specific, and the document is not about HTTP semantics in general.

RFC9221.title: An Unreliable Datagram Extension to QUIC
RFC9221.summary: Defines the QUIC DATAGRAM frame types and the max_datagram_frame_size transport parameter, which let applications send unreliable, congestion-controlled datagrams over a QUIC connection.

QUIC.why: The document specifies a new QUIC transport parameter and frame types, covering their acknowledgement, flow control and congestion control behaviour. It is a QUIC extension.
QUIC.quote: This document defines an extension to the QUIC transport protocol to add support for sending and receiving unreliable datagrams over a QUIC connection.

rejected.why: UDP is mentioned only as the transport that real-time applications used before, and as QUIC's substrate. The document does not specify or profile UDP.
TLS appears only as the security mechanism that QUIC uses. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
DTLS is cited only as the alternative that QUIC datagrams are compared against in the motivation. The document does not extend or profile it.
Datagrams simply use QUIC's existing congestion controller. The document adds no new congestion control mechanism.

RFC9222.title: Guidelines for Autonomic Service Agents
RFC9222.summary: Informational guidelines for designing Autonomic Service Agents (ASAs) in autonomic networks, covering ASA structure, interaction with ANI/ACP/GRASP, GRASP objective design, life cycle, coordination and robustness.

autonomic networking.why: The whole document is about designing ASAs for autonomic networks.
autonomic networking.quote: This document proposes guidelines for the design of Autonomic Service Agents (ASAs) in the context of an Autonomic Network (AN)

rejected.why: Not in the taxonomy as written under that id; see below.
Only referenced as the bootstrap mechanism; the document does not specify or extend it.
Used as the encoding for GRASP objective values; not the subject.
Mentioned as an example of a non-autonomic management interface the ASA must coexist with.
Only mentioned briefly for data models and YANG-to-CBOR mapping.
Mentioned only as an example of services an ASA might manage.

gaps.name: GRASP / Autonomic Service Agents
gaps.why: The document is about ASAs and GRASP objectives, but the taxonomy has no tag for GRASP or ASAs specifically. The nearest fit is the 'autonomic networking' topic under network management, which has a different id.

RFC9223.title: Real-Time Transport Object Delivery over Unidirectional Transport (ROUTE)
RFC9223.summary: Specifies ROUTE, an ALC/LCT-based protocol for robust, real-time delivery of Application Objects (e.g., DASH/CMAF segments) over unidirectional UDP/IP unicast, broadcast and multicast, with FLUTE-derived File Mode, extended FDT, and RaptorQ FEC repair flows.

ALC.why: ROUTE is defined as an ALC-based protocol instantiation with constrained LCT header usage, so ALC readers would want it.
ALC.quote: The repair protocol is based on Asynchronous Layered Coding (ALC) as defined in RFC 5775 [RFC5775]

LCT.why: Substantial part of the document constrains LCT header fields, codepoints and extensions (EXT_TOL, EXT_TIME) for ROUTE.
LCT.quote: The LCT packet header fields SHALL be used as defined by the LCT building block in RFC 5651 [RFC5651].

FLUTE.why: File Mode extends FLUTE's FDT with Extended FDT; ROUTE is aligned with and extends FLUTE for real-time media.
FLUTE.quote: This mode replicates FLUTE as defined in RFC 6726 [RFC6726] but with the ability to send static and pre-known file metadata out of band.

FECFRAME.why: Defines a FEC repair protocol with FEC transport objects and super-objects, built on FEC Framework concepts.
FECFRAME.quote: The FEC framework uses concepts of the FECFRAME work as defined in RFC 6363 [RFC6363]

Raptor.why: Repair flows use RaptorQ FEC payload IDs and OTI.
Raptor.quote: The FEC building block is used according to RFC 6330 [RFC6330], but only repair packets are delivered.

reliable multicast.why: The document is about robust one-to-many delivery over unidirectional multicast/broadcast with loss recovery; no FLUTE/ALC-specific tag alone covers the general subject, though children chosen sit under it.
reliable multicast.quote: The ROUTE protocol is suitable for unicast, broadcast, and multicast transport.

streaming.why: Targets DASH/HLS/CMAF live streaming with fast stream acquisition and low-latency delivery.
streaming.quote: The ROUTE protocol also supports chunked delivery of real-time Application Objects to enable low-latency streaming applications

rejected.why: UDP is only the substrate on which ROUTE runs.
HTTP is used for the object cache interface and Entity Mode headers, not specified here.
Package modes reuse MHTML and S/MIME; they are mechanisms, not the subject.
Mentioned only as a possible security mechanism in the abstract.
The more specific reliable multicast subtree is used; the document does not address multicast routing.
Only recommended in Security Considerations.

gaps.name: DASH / CMAF adaptive media streaming
gaps.why: Application objects are DASH/HLS segments and CMAF chunks; the taxonomy has no tag for adaptive HTTP streaming formats.

RFC9224.title: Finding the Authoritative Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) Service
RFC9224.summary: RFC 9224 specifies how RDAP clients find the authoritative RDAP server for domain names, IP addresses and AS numbers, using IANA-hosted JSON bootstrap registries and longest-match lookup; it obsoletes RFC 7484.

RDAP.why: The whole document defines the RDAP bootstrap mechanism: registry structure, matching rules and query base URLs for RDAP clients.
RDAP.quote: This document specifies a method to find which Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) server is authoritative to answer queries for a requested scope

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding for the bootstrap registries; the document does not define a general JSON format.
HTTP is the substrate for retrieving registries and queries; nothing new is defined about HTTP.
The IANA registries are the data source, but the document is about RDAP service discovery, not IANA registry guidance; the IANA section is boilerplate-like.
TLS is only mentioned as the transport for fetching the registries.
CIDR notation is only used for IPv4 prefix entries; the document is not about CIDR.
Conceptually related, but RDAP is the more specific tag for this bootstrap method and the generic topic is not needed in addition.

RFC9225.title: Software Defects Considered Harmful
RFC9225.summary: An April 1st parody RFC that "discourages" introducing software defects, giving humorous examples and best-practice rules such as "Authors MUST NOT implement bugs."

humor.why: This is an April 1st whimsical document that parodies BCP-style RFCs, so the humor subject page is where readers would look for it.
humor.quote: Authors MUST NOT implement bugs.

rejected.why: It parodies RFC conventions such as BCP language and requirements keywords, but it is not about the RFC series format or publication.
The security considerations are tongue-in-cheek and the document gives no real operational security guidance.
It uses the BCP 14 requirements keywords for comic effect only. It is not about terminology.

gaps.name: Software defects / software quality
gaps.why: The document's nominal subject is software bugs and their cost. The taxonomy has no software engineering or quality tag, but the treatment is satirical, so humor covers it.

RFC9226.title: Bioctal: Hexadecimal 2.0
RFC9226.summary: An April 1st Independent Submission proposing "bioctal", a hexadecimal alternative alphabet (0-7 then c j z w f s b v) that makes mental hex-to-binary conversion easier.

humor.why: Published 1 April as a whimsical parody proposal, with a lizard-detector security scenario and dismissed objections. It fits the humorous RFC series.
humor.quote: Bioctal restores congruence by replacing the second row with characters mnemonically related to the corresponding character in the first octave.

rejected.why: US-ASCII is only mentioned in passing when discussing sorting and symbol-change obstacles. The document is not about ASCII.
It proposes a digit alphabet, not a character set registration or use. ASCII and EBCDIC appear only in the objections.
EBCDIC is mentioned once as a joke about sorting order, and the document is not about it.
Bioctal is a hex-like numeral notation, not a textual data encoding like Base16/32/64.

gaps.name: numeral systems / number representation
gaps.why: The document proposes an alternative to hexadecimal notation. The taxonomy has no tag for number-base notation, so only humor fits.

RFC9227.title: Using GOST Ciphers in the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and Internet Key Exchange Version 2 (IKEv2) Protocols
RFC9227.summary: Defines four GOST-based (Kuznyechik and Magma, MGM mode, tree-based external rekeying) encryption transforms for IPsec ESP and IKEv2, with IANA transform IDs and test vectors.

GOST.why: The document specifies how GOST ciphers (Kuznyechik, Magma) and the GOST-based KDF are used in IETF protocols.
GOST.quote: This document defines four transforms for ESP and IKEv2 based on Russian cryptographic standard algorithms (often referred to as "GOST" algorithms).

ESP.why: It defines ESP transforms, with IV format, AAD construction for ESP and ICV handling.
ESP.quote: This document defines a set of encryption transforms for use in the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)

IKE.why: Defines IKEv2 encryption transforms, including IKEv2 AAD and key use (SK_ei/SK_er).
IKE.quote: This document defines four transforms of Type 1 (Encryption Algorithm) for use in ESP and IKEv2.

rejected.why: MGM is compared with GCM but AES is not the cipher used.
HMAC underlies the KDF but only as a building block.
Rekeying is a tree-based key derivation mechanism taken from RFC 8645; the document is about cipher transforms, not key management as a whole.
ESP and IKE are the more specific tags that cover it.

gaps.name: Multilinear Galois Mode (MGM) AEAD mode
gaps.why: The document is built on MGM, but the taxonomy has no tag for AEAD modes other than the cipher-specific ones.

RFC9228.title: Delivered-To Email Header Field
RFC9228.summary: Defines the Delivered-To email header field, which records each delivery event and address used in a message's handling sequence, for path analysis, loop detection and reply addressing; published as an Experimental RFC.

message format.why: The document defines a new Internet message header field, its syntax and its ordering rules among trace fields. This is the core subject of the message format tag.
message format.quote: The syntax of the header field is: "Delivered-To:" FWS addr-spec FWS CRLF ; addr-spec is from [Mail-Fmt]

rejected.why: SMTP supplies the envelope RCPT TO address and the trace-field model, but the document specifies a header field, not SMTP behaviour.
This is the parent of message format, which is implied by the more specific tag.
A mailing list appears in the example and in loop discussion, but the document is not about list protocols or headers.
The header field registration is boilerplate and does not make the document about IANA.
ABNF is only the notation used for the one-line syntax.

RFC9229.title: IPv4 Routes with an IPv6 Next Hop in the Babel Routing Protocol
RFC9229.summary: Defines an experimental Babel extension (new address encoding AE 4, "v4-via-v6") that lets IPv4 prefixes be announced with IPv6 next hops, so IPv4 traffic can flow over interfaces without IPv4 addresses.

Babel.why: The document specifies an extension to Babel: a new address encoding, its handling in Update and request TLVs, and backwards compatibility.
Babel.quote: This document defines an extension to the Babel routing protocol that allows announcing routes to an IPv4 prefix with an IPv6 next hop

PMTUD.why: A whole section sets out ICMPv4 origination and PMTUD requirements for routers without IPv4 addresses. That is a substantial part of the document.
PMTUD.quote: every Babel router that is able to forward IPv4 traffic MUST be able originate ICMPv4 traffic.

rejected.why: IPv6 next hops are used by the extension, but the document does not specify IPv6 itself or its deployment.
ICMPv4 is covered only as it relates to PMTUD. The document does not specify ICMP, so the narrower PMTUD tag fits better.
The document is about routing IPv4 over an IPv6 next hop, which is not a coexistence or transition mechanism like those in this subtree. It is also not a tunnelling or translation scheme.
RFC 5549 (BGP) is mentioned only as inspiration for the extension.
ARP appears only in the introductory background on neighbour resolution.

RFC9230.title: Oblivious DNS over HTTPS
RFC9230.summary: Defines Oblivious DoH, an experimental protocol that proxies HPKE-encrypted DNS-over-HTTPS messages through an Oblivious Proxy to a Target so no single server sees both client IP and query content.

oblivious DNS.why: The whole document specifies the Oblivious DoH protocol: client, proxy and target roles, message format, and HPKE encryption.
oblivious DNS.quote: This document defines Oblivious DoH, an experimental protocol built on DoH that permits proxied resolution, in which DNS messages are encrypted

media types.why: Registers a new media type that is used throughout the HTTP exchange.
media types.quote: This document registers a new media type, "application/oblivious-dns-message".

rejected.why: DoH is the substrate; the document defines a distinct protocol, and the more specific oblivious DNS tag covers it.
HTTP is only the transport for the exchange; the document does not extend HTTP semantics.
Only used for TLS-style struct encoding and connection security; not the subject.
Mentioned only as future work (OHTP); this document does not specify it.
This is the parent of the oblivious DNS tag, which is already chosen, so it is implied.
EDNS Client Subnet is mentioned only as a hint option; the document is not about EDNS.

gaps.name: HPKE (Hybrid Public Key Encryption)
gaps.why: The protocol's encryption is built on HPKE, with a mandated cipher suite, but the taxonomy has no HPKE tag.

RFC9231.title: Additional XML Security Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs)
RFC9231.summary: RFC 9231 updates the IANA "XML Security URIs" registry, listing URIs for algorithms (digest, MAC, signature, encryption, key agreement, key derivation) and KeyInfo types used with XML Signature and XML Encryption, obsoleting RFC 6931.

XML signatures.why: The whole document is a reference list of URIs identifying algorithms and key info types for XML Signature and XML Encryption.
XML signatures.quote: URIs intended for use with XML digital signatures, encryption, canonicalization, and key management.

XMSS.why: New URIs for dozens of XMSS and XMSSMT parameter sets are defined here, a substantial new part of the document.
XMSS.quote: XMSS (eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme) and XMSSMT (XMSS Multi-Tree) [RFC8391] are stateful hash-based signature schemes

ChaCha20.why: New URIs and XML usage for ChaCha20, Poly1305 and ChaCha20+Poly1305 are added in this revision.
ChaCha20.quote: ChaCha20+Poly1305 is an Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) algorithm.

EdDSA.why: Adds new XML signature URIs for the Ed25519 and Ed448 EdDSA variants.
EdDSA.quote: Identifiers for two variants, Ed25519 and Ed448, are given below.

rejected.why: The document updates a registry, but its subject is the XML security algorithm URIs, not IANA registry policy in general.
URIs are used purely as identifiers for algorithms. The document does not address URI syntax or schemes.
XML is the substrate for the signature and encryption syntax. The more specific XML signatures tag fits better.
ECDSA URIs are listed, but only as part of a broad list. They are not a focus of the document.
HMAC-based URIs are listed in passing. The document is not about HMAC itself.
RSA signature URIs are listed, but the document does not specify RSA.

RFC9232.title: Network Telemetry Framework
RFC9232.summary: RFC 9232 is an informational architectural framework for network telemetry, defining terminology, four telemetry modules (management, control, forwarding, external data), component structure, and a taxonomy mapping existing techniques such as YANG-Push, BMP, IPFIX and IOAM.

telemetry.why: The whole document defines the framework, taxonomy and terminology for network telemetry, i.e. streaming operational data from network elements.
telemetry.quote: Network telemetry is a technology for gaining network insight and facilitating efficient and automated network management.

OAM.why: The document positions telemetry relative to OAM, treats OAM as a subset, and surveys OAM for data planes such as IOAM and alternate marking.
OAM.quote: Network telemetry extends beyond the classical network Operations, Administration, and Management (OAM) techniques

rejected.why: Only surveyed as one of many example mechanisms; the document does not specify or extend it.
YANG is used as a data model example and mentioned throughout, but the document does not define models.
BMP is described briefly in an appendix as an example of control plane telemetry, not a subject of the document.
IPFIX is one surveyed technique in the appendix, not the focus.
Active/passive/hybrid measurement methods are mentioned as a taxonomy dimension, but the document is not about performance measurement itself.
Autonomic and intent-based networks are motivation only, not the subject.

gaps.name: telemetry
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists 'telemetry' only as a topic under network management. I used the id 'telemetry' as given, but a tag for IOAM or in-situ telemetry would also suit this document.

RFC9233.title: Internationalized Domain Names for Applications 2008 (IDNA2008) and Unicode 12.0.0
RFC9233.summary: RFC 9233 documents the changes between Unicode 6.0.0 and 12.0.0 and their effect on IDNA2008 derived property values. It concludes that no exceptions are added and supplies the tables IANA needs to update its IDNA registry.

IDN.why: The whole document is about IDNA2008 derived property values (PVALID, DISALLOWED, CONTEXT) for code points in internationalized domain name labels. It updates the IANA IDNA tables.
IDN.quote: This document describes the changes between Unicode 6.0.0 and Unicode 12.0.0 in the context of the current version of Internationalized Domain Names for Applications 2008 (IDNA2008).

rejected.why: Unicode versions are the subject of the analysis, but the document concerns their effect on IDNA label validity. The IDN tag covers that more precisely.
IDNs are used in DNS labels, but the document does not specify DNS protocol, records or server behaviour.
The document supplies tables for an IANA registry, but that is a boilerplate-level consequence. The subject is IDNA code point validity, not IANA registry policy.
The document is about text in domain names, which is covered by the more specific IDN tag.

RFC9234.title: Route Leak Prevention and Detection Using Roles in UPDATE and OPEN Messages
RFC9234.summary: Defines BGP Role negotiation via a new OPEN capability and the Only to Customer (OTC) path attribute so BGP speakers can prevent and detect route leaks.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP with a new capability, a new path attribute and new OPEN error handling, so it is a BGP protocol extension.
BGP.quote: This document enhances the BGP OPEN message to establish an agreement of the relationship on each eBGP session between autonomous systems

routing security.why: Its purpose is to secure inter-domain routing against route leaks caused by misconfiguration, which places it under routing security.
routing security.quote: Propagated routes are then marked according to the agreed relationship, allowing both prevention and detection of route leaks.

rejected.why: BGPsec is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a comparison. The document does not specify or extend it.
RPKI is not used or discussed. The mechanism is in-band role negotiation and does not use route origin validation.
The RS and RS-Client roles are defined, but only as two of five roles. The document is about role negotiation in general, not route server operation.
OTC is a new path attribute, not a community. Communities are mentioned only implicitly as an alternative to operator-configured marking.

gaps.name: BGP route leaks
gaps.why: Route leak definition, classification and prevention has no dedicated tag. It is covered here by BGP and routing security.

RFC9235.title: TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO) Test Vectors
RFC9235.summary: Provides test vectors for validating TCP-AO implementations (KDF and MAC for HMAC-SHA-1-96 and AES-128-CMAC-96) over IPv4 and IPv6, with and without TCP option coverage, plus a list of common implementation errors.

TCP.why: The document exists to validate implementations of TCP-AO, a TCP extension, so the TCP subject page is where readers would look for it.
TCP.quote: This document provides test vectors to validate the correct implementation of the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO) [RFC5925]

rejected.why: HMAC-SHA-1-96 is used as one of the MAC algorithms under test, but the document is about TCP-AO test vectors and does not specify or analyse HMAC.
AES-128-CMAC is a mandatory algorithm whose outputs are tested, but the document does not define or extend AES.
SHA-1 is only the hash underlying the KDF and MAC being tested; the document is not about the SHA family.
IPv6 packets are used as test inputs, but the document says nothing new about IPv6.
IPv4 packets are used as test inputs, but the document says nothing new about IPv4.
Port 179 and the DSCP value are borrowed from BGP for the test connection, but BGP is not the subject.

gaps.name: TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for TCP-AO, so the document falls back to the parent TCP tag.

RFC9236.title: Architectural Considerations of Information-Centric Networking (ICN) Using a Name Resolution Service
RFC9236.summary: An IRTF/ICNRG informational document describing how introducing a Name Resolution Service into Information-Centric Networking changes the ICN architecture and routing system, covering registration, resolution, update, protocols and routing integration.

ICN.why: The whole document is about ICN architecture when using a name resolution service, including NDN and CCNx name-based routing, producer mobility and off-path caching.
ICN.quote: This document describes the potential changes in the ICN architecture caused by the introduction of an NRS and the corresponding implication to the ICN routing system.

rejected.why: DNS is only mentioned as a possible NRS and as an analogy for security and privacy. The document does not specify or analyse DNS.
The name resolution here is specific to ICN, and ICN already covers it. The generic naming topic would add little.
The routing implications are discussed, but only in the ICN context. The ICN tag is the more specific fit.
Producer mobility is discussed in ICN terms, not as IP-layer mobility.
No encoding is specified. RESTful API use is only mentioned in passing.

RFC9237.title: An Authorization Information Format (AIF) for Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments (ACE)
RFC9237.summary: Defines the Authorization Information Format (AIF), a compact CBOR/JSON information and data model for authorization lists, with a REST-specific instantiation for ACE, plus media types and Content-Formats.

ACE.why: AIF is the authorization information format for ACE, conveying permissions from an authorization server to constrained devices.
ACE.quote: To transfer detailed authorization information from an authorization manager (such as an ACE-OAuth authorization server [RFC9200]) to a device, a compact representation format is needed.

authorization.why: The document defines an access-matrix-based authorization information model of object and permission pairs.
authorization.quote: The semantics of the authorization information defined in this document are that of an _allow-list_: everything is denied until it is explicitly allowed.

media types.why: It registers two new media types with Toid and Tperm parameters and a sub-parameter registry.
media types.quote: This specification defines media types for the generic information model, expressed in JSON (application/aif+json) or in CBOR (application/aif+cbor).

rejected.why: CBOR is only the encoding for one representation. The document does not specify CBOR itself.
CoAP supplies the explanatory examples and the method numbers, but the document does not extend or specify CoAP.
ACE-OAuth is the context in which AIF is used, but AIF is a payload format and not part of the OAuth framework. The ACE tag fits better.
JSON is an alternative encoding only, and the document defines nothing new about JSON.
CDDL is used only to write down the data model.
URI paths serve as object identifiers, but the document does not specify URI syntax or schemes.

RFC9238.title: Loading Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD) URLs from QR Codes
RFC9238.summary: Informational document defining how to encode a MUD URL (RFC 8520) in an SQRL-format QR code sticker on devices lacking in-band MUD support, with new data record M180 and guidance on MAC address, privacy and security.

MUD.why: The document extends how MUD URLs are conveyed to network enforcement points via QR codes, a new mechanism for MUD.
MUD.quote: This informational document details a protocol to load Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD) definitions from RFC 8520 for devices that do not have them integrated.

IoT.why: Motivated by constrained IoT devices that cannot be updated with firmware support; also covers crowd-sourced MUD profiles for consumer IoT devices.
IoT.quote: Most small Internet of Things (IoT) devices do not have LLDP and often have very restricted DHCP clients.

rejected.why: MUD URLs are carried in the QR code, but the document does not specify URI syntax or schemes; it only constrains the query part.
MUD files are JSON, but this is only the substrate format and not the subject of the document.
Mentioned only as an existing in-band MUD URL mechanism from RFC 8520 that this document offers an alternative to.
Cited only as an example deployment where IDevID certificate extension makes sense.
The MUD YANG model is referenced but the document does not define or extend any model.
US-ASCII is the character encoding required by SQRL fields, not the subject.

gaps.name: QR codes / SQRL (Standardized Quick Response for Logistics)
gaps.why: The document's core protocol is encoding data in QR codes using the SQRL 12N data identifier format, which has no tag in the taxonomy.

RFC9239.title: Updates to ECMAScript Media Types
RFC9239.summary: RFC 9239 obsoletes RFC 4329 and registers the text/javascript media type (plus obsolete ECMAScript aliases), defining charset parameter, encoding detection, and module handling for JavaScript/ECMAScript sources.

media types.why: The document exists to register and update media type registrations (text/javascript and obsolete aliases) and defines their parameters and usage.
media types.quote: This document describes the registration of media types for the ECMAScript and JavaScript programming languages and conformance requirements for implementations of these types.

character sets.why: A substantial part specifies the charset parameter, character encoding scheme detection (BOM, charset, UTF-8 default), and error handling for source text.
character sets.quote: If present, the value of the charset parameter MUST be a registered charset [CHARSETS]

rejected.why: UTF-8 is required as the default encoding but the document does not specify the UTF-8 encoding itself; it is covered under character encoding handling.
HTML is only referenced as the default consumer of text/javascript in script tags; the document is not about HTML.
Media types are the subject, covered by the more specific media types tag; the document does not define MIME body structure or encodings.
IANA registrations are the mechanism, but the document is about specific media types, not IANA registry guidance.

gaps.name: ECMAScript / JavaScript
gaps.why: The document is about the media types for the JavaScript programming language, but the taxonomy has no tag for programming languages or scripting.

RFC9240.title: An Extension for Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO): Entity Property Maps
RFC9240.summary: RFC 9240 extends the ALTO protocol by generalizing endpoint properties to entities in typed entity domains and by adding property map and filtered property map resources, plus new IANA registries for entity domain and property types.

ALTO.why: The whole document defines an ALTO protocol extension: entity domains, property maps, filtered property maps, and the related registries.
ALTO.quote: This document specifies an extension to the base Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) Protocol that generalizes the concept of "endpoint properties"

rejected.why: Property map messages are JSON-encoded, but JSON is only the encoding. The document does not specify anything new about JSON.
GET and POST are used to request the resources, but HTTP is only the substrate. The document defines nothing new about HTTP itself.
CIDR prefixes are used as hierarchical entity identifiers for inheritance, but the document does not specify or analyse CIDR.
Two media types are registered in the IANA section, which is boilerplate. The body is about the ALTO extension, not media type registration rules.
It creates ALTO-specific registries, which are covered by the ALTO tag. It is not general IANA guidance.

RFC9241.title: Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI) Footprint and Capabilities Advertisement Using Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO)
RFC9241.summary: Defines a new ALTO service, the CDNI Advertisement Service (with filtered and property-map variants), that carries CDNI Footprint & Capabilities Advertisement (FCI) objects between downstream and upstream CDNs.

ALTO.why: The document extends ALTO with new services, media types, a footprint type, entity domains and a property type, including filtered and property map variants.
ALTO.quote: This document defines a new Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) service, called "CDNI Advertisement Service"

CDN.why: The document implements the CDNI FCI between upstream and downstream CDNs, so it belongs on the CDN and CDN interconnection page.
CDN.quote: A CDNI Request Routing Footprint & Capabilities Advertisement interface (FCI) is needed to achieve the goals of a CDNI.

rejected.why: HTTP GET and POST are only the transport for the ALTO services. The document defines nothing new about HTTP.
JSON is only the encoding for the advertisement objects. The document does not specify a JSON format in its own right.
The media type registrations are IANA boilerplate for the new service, not the subject of the document.
ASN footprints are only a footprint type. The document says nothing about BGP.
TLS mutual authentication is mentioned only in Security Considerations.
HTTP Digest Authentication is mentioned only in Security Considerations, as a requirement inherited from RFC 8008.

RFC9242.title: Intermediate Exchange in the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC9242.summary: Defines the IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange for IKEv2, run between IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH, so large data (e.g. post-quantum key exchange public keys) can be sent with IKE fragmentation, including negotiation, key use, and authentication of the intermediate messages.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with a new exchange type, notification, and modified AUTH computation, so it belongs under IKE.
IKE.quote: This document defines a new exchange, called "Intermediate Exchange", for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2).

rejected.why: IKE is the more specific child tag; ESP/AH are not addressed.
Post-quantum key exchange is only the motivating example; the document is deliberately not tied to any use case and defines no PQ algorithm.
UDP is only the transport for IKE; the document defines nothing new about UDP usage.
PMTU and IP fragmentation are the motivation, but the document does not specify PMTU discovery.
Key derivation follows existing IKEv2 rules; the document does not define a new key management scheme. IKE already covers it.
NAT detection and port 4500 switching are mentioned in passing only.

RFC9243.title: A YANG Data Model for DHCPv6 Configuration
RFC9243.summary: Defines YANG modules (common, server, relay, client) for configuring and managing DHCPv6 elements via NETCONF/RESTCONF, with examples and extensibility guidance.

DHCPv6.why: The modules model DHCPv6 server, relay and client configuration and state, including options, pools, leases and notifications, so DHCPv6 readers need it.
DHCPv6.quote: This document defines YANG [RFC7950] modules for the configuration and management of DHCPv6 'elements' (servers, relays, and clients)

YANG.why: The document's main content is YANG modules and tree diagrams, including guidance on augmenting them, so it belongs on the YANG page.
YANG.quote: This document describes YANG data models for the configuration and management of Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the protocol used to access the modules. The document does not specify or extend it.
RESTCONF is only an alternative access protocol, mentioned in the introduction and Security Considerations.
This is a YANG model and does not define SNMP MIB modules.
IPv6 is only the environment DHCPv6 runs in. The document is about DHCPv6 configuration, not IPv6 itself.
SIP appears only in an example module for the RFC 3319 SIP server options (Appendix B).

RFC9244.title: Distributed Denial-of-Service Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) Telemetry
RFC9244.summary: RFC 9244 extends the DOTS signal channel with telemetry attributes (traffic baseline, pipe capacity, attack details, mitigation status and efficacy) exchanged between DOTS clients and servers for DDoS mitigation, and defines two YANG modules.

DOTS.why: The document is a DOTS signal channel extension.
DOTS.quote: enrich the Distributed Denial-of-Service Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) signal channel protocol with various telemetry attributes

RFC9245.title: IETF Discussion List Charter
RFC9245.summary: Defines the charter and scope of the IETF discussion mailing list, appropriate and inappropriate postings, and the moderation and appeals procedure; obsoletes RFC 3005 and updates RFC 3683.

IETF process.why: A BCP on IETF community procedure: list scope, moderator appointment by the IETF Chair, and the appeals chain to the IESG under RFC 2026.
IETF process.quote: This document defines the charter for the IETF discussion list and explains its scope.

rejected.why: That tag covers mailing list protocols, headers and management, not the policy governing one list's content.
Unsolicited bulk email is only listed as one inappropriate posting type, not a subject of the document.
The document concerns a discussion forum's policy, not email technology.

RFC9246.title: URI Signing for Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI)
RFC9246.summary: Defines a URI Signing method for CDN Interconnection as a JWT profile, specifying claims, token renewal for segmented content, CDNI metadata/logging interface extensions, and message flows for HTTP and DNS redirection.

CDN.why: The whole document specifies access authorization between CSPs, upstream and downstream CDNs, including CDNI metadata, FCI and logging interface extensions.
CDN.quote: describes how the concept of URI Signing supports the content access control requirements of Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI)

JWT.why: Defines a JWT profile with new claims (cdniuc, cdniip, cdniets, cdnistt, etc.) registered in the JWT claims registry.
JWT.quote: proposes a URI Signing method as a JSON Web Token (JWT) profile

URI.why: Specifies how a signed token is carried in URIs as path-style or form-style parameters, with URI container matching and normalization.
URI.quote: embedding a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) [RFC7519] in an HTTP or HTTPS URI

rejected.why: Cookies are only used as one transport for token renewal, not the subject.
DNS-based request routing is a flow variant, not something the document specifies about DNS.
JWS/JWE are used as building blocks; the document profiles JWT rather than extending JOSE.
Only recommended for clock synchronization.
Considered, but the specific JWT tag fits better; the access-control topic is covered by the technology tags.

gaps.name: CDNI (Content Delivery Network Interconnection)
gaps.why: The document is about CDNI, and the taxonomy's CDN tag covers CDN and CDN interconnection; no separate finer tag exists, though a mismatch is possible if CDN is not a valid id.

RFC9247.title: BGP - Link State (BGP-LS) Extensions for Seamless Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (S-BFD)
RFC9247.summary: Defines a new BGP-LS Node attribute TLV (type 1032, S-BFD Discriminators TLV) to carry S-BFD discriminators learned from IS-IS and OSPF across IGP domains via BGP.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP-LS, a BGP address family, with a new Attribute TLV on the Node NLRI. No narrower BGP child tag (such as BMP or communities) fits, so BGP is the right tag.
BGP.quote: This document defines extensions to the BGP - Link State (BGP-LS) address family to carry the S-BFD Discriminators' information via BGP.

BFD.why: The payload is S-BFD discriminators, which let an initiator set up Seamless BFD sessions to responders. The document extends how that S-BFD information is distributed, so BFD readers would want it.
BFD.quote: The S-BFD Discriminators of a node are considered a node-level attribute and are advertised as such.

rejected.why: IS-IS is only the source of the discriminator information, which is defined in RFC 7883. This document does not extend IS-IS.
OSPF is only the source of the discriminator information, which is defined in RFC 7884. This document does not extend OSPF.
The document only makes a routine code point allocation in the IANA Considerations section, which is boilerplate.
This tag is for link-state routing using BGP-LS. This document only adds a node attribute to BGP-LS and does not compute routes with it.

RFC9248.title: Interoperability Profile for Relay User Equipment
RFC9248.summary: Defines an interoperability profile for Relay User Equipment (VRS videophones) specifying SIP signaling, WebRTC-derived media, contacts, video mail, and HTTP/JSON provider-selection and configuration services between a device and a relay provider.

SIP.why: The document profiles SIP for registration, call origination, dial-around, incoming calls, emergency calls and mid-call signaling, so SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: This interoperability profile for Relay User Equipment (RUE) is a profile of the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and related media protocols

accessibility.why: The document's purpose is accessible communication via Video Relay Service for deaf, hard of hearing and speech-disabled users, including real-time text.
accessibility.quote: enables people with hearing disabilities who use sign language, such as American Sign Language (ASL), to communicate with voice telephone users through video equipment

emergency services.why: A dedicated section specifies emergency call handling with geolocation, LoST routing and additional data.
emergency services.quote: Implementations MUST conform to [RFC6881] for handling of emergency calls

vCard.why: Contact exchange uses xCard and the owner info is conveyed as xCard.
vCard.quote: Implementations MUST be able to export/import the list of contacts in xCard [RFC6351] XML format.

CardDAV.why: A section specifies how RUE uses CardDAV for contact synchronization and its configuration.
CardDAV.quote: The RUE MUST and providers MAY be able to synchronize the user's contact directory between the RUE endpoint and one maintained by the user's VRS provider using CardDAV

RTP payload format.why: Real-time text via T.140 RTP payload and RTP-mixer multiparty text are required, a substantive media part of the profile.
RTP payload format.quote: Implementations MUST support real-time text [RFC4102] [RFC4103] via T.140 media.

rejected.why: The document adopts WebRTC media specifications but is a plain SIP profile; WebRTC is a referenced substrate and gateway case only.
HTTP is used as transport for the configuration services; nothing new is defined about HTTP itself.
TLS is merely mandated as the security mechanism with no new TLS definitions.
JSON encodes configuration payloads, only a substrate.
ICE is required but only referenced, not specified or extended.
SDP conformance is mandated by reference; the document does not define SDP content beyond referencing.

gaps.name: Video Relay Service / Telecommunications Relay Service
gaps.why: The core subject, VRS and relay services for deaf users, has no dedicated tag; closest is accessibility.

RFC9249.title: A YANG Data Model for NTP
RFC9249.summary: Defines the ietf-ntp YANG module for configuring and monitoring NTPv4 (and NTPv3), covering associations, authentication keys, access rules, clock state and statistics, with usage examples and mappings to NTPv4-MIB and RFC 7317.

YANG.why: The document's main deliverable is a YANG module (ietf-ntp) with tree diagrams, module source and NETCONF examples.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model [RFC7950] that can be used to configure and manage Network Time Protocol version 4 [RFC5905].

NTP.why: The module models NTP associations, modes (unicast, broadcast, multicast, manycast), authentication, stratum and clock state, so it is about managing NTP.
NTP.quote: The data model covers configuration of system parameters of NTP such as access rules, authentication and VPN Routing and Forwarding (VRF) binding

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the protocol used to carry the model and appears in examples and Security Considerations. The document does not specify it.
The NTPv4-MIB mapping tables are a short section, and the document defines a YANG model rather than a MIB module.
HMAC-SHA algorithms appear only as identities in the module, and the document is not about them.
The ACL and access rules govern on-the-wire NTP access, not an AAA framework.
The NTP tag already sits under it and is more specific.

RFC9250.title: DNS over Dedicated QUIC Connections
RFC9250.summary: RFC 9250 specifies DNS over dedicated QUIC connections (DoQ), mapping DNS messages to QUIC streams for stub-to-recursive, recursive-to-authoritative and zone transfer use, with error codes, 0-RTT, padding and privacy guidance.

DoQ.why: The document defines DoQ: stream mapping, ALPN token, port 853, error codes and connection handling. DoQ is the dedicated tag for this subject.
DoQ.quote: This document presents a mapping of the DNS protocol over the QUIC transport [RFC9000] [RFC9001]. DNS over QUIC is referred to here as DoQ

rejected.why: QUIC is the substrate. The document defines no new QUIC mechanism, only how DNS uses it.
DoT is the model for the privacy goals and for authentication, but this document does not specify or extend it.
DoH is mentioned only for comparison and for the Message ID convention.
TLS 1.3 is used only through QUIC. The document defines no TLS extension except registering the doq ALPN ID, which is boilerplate-level.
The EDNS padding and tcp-keepalive options are used or prohibited, but the document does not define EDNS options.
DoQ is the more specific tag, so the parent DNS tag is implied and not listed.

RFC9251.title: Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) and Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) Proxies for Ethernet VPN (EVPN)
RFC9251.summary: Specifies IGMP/MLD proxy procedures on EVPN PEs, defining new BGP EVPN route types (SMET, Membership Report Synch, Leave Synch), a Multicast Flags extended community, and multihoming synchronization.

EVPN.why: The document defines new EVPN route types, extended communities and multihoming procedures for EVPN.
EVPN.quote: incorporating IGMP/MLD Proxy procedures on EVPN Provider Edges (PEs)

IGMP.why: It specifies IGMP proxy reporting, proxy querier and leave handling, including translation between IGMP reports and BGP routes.
IGMP.quote: The IGMP Proxy mechanism is used to reduce the flooding of IGMP messages over an EVPN network

MLD.why: MLD proxying is specified in parallel with IGMP, including MLD flag encoding and report reconstruction.
MLD.quote: When this document uses the term "IGMP Membership Report", the text equally applies to the MLD Membership Report.

rejected.why: BGP is the carrier for the new EVPN routes. The document does not specify BGP itself, so the EVPN tag covers the new route types.
Multicast VPN is referenced only for wildcard procedures and security considerations. The subject here is EVPN.
PIM Hello is mentioned only for detecting a multicast router on an attachment circuit.
The more specific IGMP and MLD tags cover the multicast subject.
EVPN is the more specific tag for the L2VPN service described here.

RFC9252.title: BGP Overlay Services Based on Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6)
RFC9252.summary: RFC 9252 defines BGP extensions (SRv6 L3/L2 Service TLVs, SID Information and Structure sub-TLVs, transposition scheme) to signal SRv6 Service SIDs for L3VPN, EVPN and Internet overlay services.

SRv6.why: The document defines how SRv6 Service SIDs and endpoint behaviors are signaled and used for overlay services, so SRv6 readers need it.
SRv6.quote: SRv6-based BGP services refer to the Layer 3 (L3) and Layer 2 (L2) overlay services with BGP as the control plane and SRv6 as the data plane.

EVPN.why: A major section specifies how EVPN route types 1, 2, 3 and 5 carry SRv6 Service SIDs, with label-field transposition.
EVPN.quote: BGP-Based Ethernet VPN (EVPN) over SRv6

L3VPN.why: Defines IPv4/IPv6 VPN over an SRv6 core, extending RFC 4364 and RFC 4659 with the SRv6 L3 Service TLV.
L3VPN.quote: BGP-Based L3 Service over SRv6

BGP.why: The document extends the BGP Prefix-SID attribute with new TLVs and specifies BGP error handling (treat-as-withdraw) and propagation rules.
BGP.quote: This document extends the use of the BGP Prefix-SID attribute [RFC8669] to carry SRv6 SIDs and their associated information

rejected.why: SRv6 runs over the IPv6 data plane, but the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
Multicast VPN with SRv6 is explicitly declared out of scope.
MPLS label fields are reused for transposition, but the document is not about MPLS.
EVPN and SRv6 are overlay services, but this tag covers VXLAN/Geneve/NVGRE-style encapsulations, which this document does not address.
The more specific SRv6 tag fits. This document is about SRv6, not the general segment routing architecture.

RFC9253.title: Support for iCalendar Relationships
RFC9253.summary: RFC 9253 updates the iCalendar RELATED-TO property with new temporal and ordering relation types and a GAP parameter, and defines new LINK, CONCEPT and REFID properties for linking and grouping iCalendar components.

iCalendar.why: The whole document extends the iCalendar data format with new properties, parameters, value types and RELTYPE values, and updates RFC 5545.
iCalendar.quote: This specification updates the iCalendar RELATED-TO property defined in RFC 5545 by adding new relation types and introduces new iCalendar properties (LINK, CONCEPT, and REFID)

rejected.why: The LINK property is modelled on and maps to RFC 8288 attributes, but the document defines an iCalendar property, not anything new about Web Linking itself.
CalDAV collections are mentioned as context for UID references and linking across collections, but the document does not specify or extend CalDAV.
URIs are used as property values, but the document only relies on URI syntax and defines nothing new about it.
The XML-REFERENCE value type uses XPointer, but this is a minor value type and not a substantial treatment of XML.
The parent topic is implied by iCalendar, so it should not be listed separately.

RFC9254.title: Encoding of Data Modeled with YANG in the Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR)
RFC9254.summary: Defines YANG-CBOR, the CBOR encoding rules for YANG-modelled data, including SID and name-based map keys, per-type encodings, and the application/yang-data+cbor media type.

YANG.why: The document specifies how YANG data trees, nodes and built-in types are encoded, and defines YANG Schema Item identifiers (SIDs). Readers of YANG would want it.
YANG.quote: This document defines encoding rules for YANG in the Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) (RFC 8949).

CBOR.why: It is a CBOR-based encoding that defines CBOR tags 43-47 and maps each YANG type to a CBOR major type.
CBOR.quote: The aim of this document is to define a set of encoding rules for the Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) [RFC8949], collectively called "YANG-CBOR".

rejected.why: CoAP is only mentioned as a protocol that can carry the content-formats. The document registers CoAP Content-Formats but does not specify CoAP.
NETCONF and RESTCONF are referenced only as protocols that use text-string identifiers. They are not specified here.
The JSON encoding (RFC 7951) is only a model for the name-based keys. The document does not specify JSON.
The document registers one media type, but that is IANA boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
Constrained nodes motivate the compact encoding, but the document is not about IoT architecture.

RFC9255.title: The 'I' in RPKI Does Not Stand for Identity
RFC9255.summary: Standards Track document stating that RPKI certificates attest only to authorization over Internet Number Resources, not to real-world identity of INR holders, and must not be used to authenticate real-world documents or transactions.

RPKI.why: The whole document clarifies the semantics of the RPKI: it provides authorization over INRs, not identity. Readers of the RPKI subject need this guidance.
RPKI.quote: RPKI-based credentials of INRs MUST NOT be used to authenticate real-world documents or transactions.

rejected.why: WHOIS is mentioned only as the way RIRs provide INR-to-identity mapping; the document does not specify or analyse it.
Router Keying for BGPsec is cited only as an example of RPKI growth; not the subject.
RPKI is a more specific tag that fits; the general PKI parent is implied and the document is not about PKI in general.
RFC 5280 is referenced only for the notion of public/private key; certificate profiles are not discussed.
The document is about what RPKI does not authenticate, but the RPKI tag is more specific and already covers it.

RFC9256.title: Segment Routing Policy Architecture
RFC9256.summary: Defines the Segment Routing Policy architecture: SR Policy identification, candidate paths, selection, Binding SIDs, segment types, steering of traffic (including BGP color-based steering) and failure recovery, updating RFC 8402.

segment routing.why: The whole document specifies the SR Policy construct and steering into it, updating the SR architecture RFC 8402.
segment routing.quote: SR Policy is an ordered list of segments (i.e., instructions) that represent a source-routed policy.

SR-MPLS.why: Segment types, BSID and steering behaviour are specified for the SR-MPLS data plane, including label stack handling.
SR-MPLS.quote: It applies equally to the SR- MPLS and SRv6 instantiations of segment routing.

SRv6.why: SRv6 SIDs, BSID behaviours and headend processing are covered alongside SR-MPLS.
SRv6.quote: Type B: SRv6 SID: An IPv6 address corresponding to any of the SID behaviors for SRv6

rejected.why: BGP Color extended community steering is used, but the BGP signalling is defined in other documents.
PCEP is only a way of signalling candidate paths; the document defines no PCEP extensions.
TI-LFA is mentioned in a short section on recovery; it is not the document's subject.
It is implied as the parent of the segment routing tag family in a general sense, but SR Policy is the more specific subject and no traffic engineering tag fits better.
The YANG model is only referenced, not defined here.
Only a Segment Types registry is created, which is boilerplate.

RFC9257.title: Guidance for External Pre-Shared Key (PSK) Usage in TLS
RFC9257.summary: Informational guidance on using external pre-shared keys in TLS 1.3 (and DTLS/CTLS), covering security properties, entropy, group-sharing attacks, use cases, provisioning, stack interfaces, and privacy limits.

TLS.why: The whole document is deployment guidance for external PSKs in TLS 1.3, including identity handling, stack interfaces and attacks such as rerouting and Selfie.
TLS.quote: This document provides guidance on the use of external Pre-Shared Keys (PSKs) in Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 [RFC8446].

rejected.why: Guidance is said to apply to DTLS 1.3 too, but only as a one-line scope note. The document is about TLS PSKs generally.
PAKEs are mentioned as the remedy for low-entropy PSKs, but the document does not specify or analyse them.
PSK provisioning is discussed, but it is specific to TLS PSK usage, so the TLS tag covers it.
IoT is listed as one use case among many. It is not a substantial focus.
RADIUS over TLS appears only as one example use case.
The Privacy Considerations section is short and covers PSK identity linkability within TLS. The document as a whole is not a privacy threat-model document.

RFC9258.title: Importing External Pre-Shared Keys (PSKs) for TLS 1.3
RFC9258.summary: Defines a PSK importer interface for TLS 1.3 and DTLS 1.3 that derives imported PSKs bound to a target KDF and protocol from external PSKs, with a new binder label and an IANA registry of KDF identifiers.

TLS.why: The document extends TLS 1.3 (and DTLS 1.3) with a new PSK importer mechanism, a new binder key label, and a new IANA registry of TLS KDF identifiers.
TLS.quote: this document specifies a PSK importer interface by which external PSKs may be imported and subsequently bound to a specific key derivation function (KDF) and hash function

rejected.why: DTLS 1.3 is mentioned as a target protocol, but the document is about TLS 1.3 PSK importing. It adds nothing DTLS-specific, so the parent TLS tag covers it.
The document derives keys, but it does so inside the TLS key schedule. It is not a general key management or provisioning protocol.
HKDF, which is built on HMAC, is the underlying derivation primitive. The document does not specify or profile HMAC.
QUIC is mentioned only because it uses the TLS 1.3 protocol version value. The document says nothing about QUIC itself.
SHA-256 and SHA-384 appear only as the hash functions that HKDF uses. They are not the subject of the document.

RFC9259.title: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) in Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6)
RFC9259.summary: Describes how IPv6 ping and traceroute work in SRv6 networks, defines the O-flag in the SRH to trigger telemetry/flow sampling at segment endpoints, and outlines centralized path-continuity monitoring for SRv6 paths.

SRv6.why: The whole document defines OAM for SRv6, including a new SRH O-flag and its processing at SRv6 segment endpoints.
SRv6.quote: This document describes how the existing IPv6 mechanisms for ping and traceroute can be used in an SRv6 network.

OAM.why: The document is about OAM mechanisms: ping, traceroute, hybrid OAM via the O-flag, and centralized path monitoring.
OAM.quote: the document specifies the OAM flag (O-flag) in the SRH as a marking bit in the user packets to trigger telemetry data collection

traceroute.why: A substantial part of the document (Section 2.2, Appendix A.2) covers traceroute to an IPv6 address via a segment list and to a SID.
traceroute.quote: Traceroute to a SID is used for hop-by-hop fault localization as well as path tracing to a SID.

ICMP.why: ICMPv6 echo and Time Exceeded/Destination Unreachable are the mechanisms used for SRv6 ping and traceroute, and are illustrated at length.
ICMP.quote: Appendix A illustrates the ICMPv6-based ping and UDP-based traceroute mechanisms for ping and traceroute to an SRv6 SID.

rejected.why: IPFIX is assumed only as the export mechanism; the document defines no formats or data elements for it.
Referenced only for exporting mirrored packet sections; not the document's subject.
Mentioned only as another OAM probe type to which the procedures apply.
IPv6 is the substrate; the document is about SRv6, which is more specific.
Hybrid OAM and delay computation are illustrated, but the document is not primarily a performance-measurement specification, and STAMP is only referenced.
The O-flag triggers telemetry collection, but OAM is the more fitting parent for the document's scope, which leaves export formats out of scope.

gaps.name: SRv6 (Segment Routing over IPv6) / SRH
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an SRv6 tag (under segment routing) but the document's primary subject is SRv6 OAM; if the tag did not exist, a gap would be noted. Present tags cover it adequately.

RFC9260.title: Stream Control Transmission Protocol
RFC9260.summary: RFC 9260 is the consolidated SCTP specification, obsoleting RFC 4960 and incorporating the chunk flags registry and the I bit; it defines packet formats, association setup, data transfer, congestion control, fault management and the ULP interface.

SCTP.why: The entire document specifies SCTP: chunks, association state machine, multihoming, streams, and API.
SCTP.quote: This document describes the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) and obsoletes RFC 4960.

rejected.why: SCTP congestion control is a substantial section, but it is part of the SCTP specification; the SCTP tag covers it.
Referenced only for comparison and as the basis for congestion control and RTO algorithms.
Section 7.3 only refers to existing PMTUD specifications with SCTP-specific notes.
CRC32c is used as the checksum in an appendix; the document is not about CRC polynomial selection.
Section 10 describes how SCTP handles ICMP messages, but ICMP itself is not specified.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as an option for protection.

RFC9261.title: Exported Authenticators in TLS
RFC9261.summary: RFC 9261 defines Exported Authenticators, a mechanism built on TLS/DTLS exporters that lets peers prove ownership of additional identities (X.509 certificates) after the handshake, with the proof transmitted out of band and validated by the peer.

TLS.why: The document specifies a new TLS-based mechanism: authenticator request/authenticator messages derived from TLS exporters, new exporter labels, a new handshake type and an extension registry update.
TLS.quote: enables peers to provide proof of ownership of an identity, such as an X.509 certificate. This proof can be exported by one peer

rejected.why: DTLS is covered alongside TLS as '(D)TLS' but the document is not specifically about DTLS; the TLS tag is the main home.
X.509 certificates are the identity type carried, but the document does not profile or extend X.509 itself.
Mentioned only as an example of a multiplexed protocol motivating the mechanism; not specified here.
HMAC is used for the Finished computation as a building block; the document does not address HMAC itself.
Only mentioned as an example of a secure transport for carrying authenticators.
Subject is covered more specifically by the TLS tag; the generic authentication topic is not separately needed.

RFC9262.title: Tree Engineering for Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER-TE)
RFC9262.summary: RFC 9262 specifies BIER-TE, a per-packet stateless multicast path-steering mechanism in which BIER bit positions denote topology adjacencies, with its forwarding plane, adjacency types, controller operations and bit-position optimizations.

BIER.why: The document specifies BIER-TE, an extension of BIER forwarding with new BitString semantics, BIFT adjacency types and controller operations.
BIER.quote: BIER-TE introduces a new semantic for "bit positions" (BPs). These BPs indicate adjacencies of the network topology

rejected.why: BIER-TE is described as a path steering mechanism for TE, but the document is about the BIER-based multicast forwarding mechanism itself, not general TE.
Appendix A only compares BIER-TE to SR; SR is not specified or profiled.
BIER-TE is multicast, but a more specific BIER tag fits and the parent is implied.
NETCONF, YANG and PCEP are only mentioned as possible controller-to-BFR protocols, not specified here.
BGP appears only as a possible flow overlay signalling or route-reflector mechanism.
MPLS is an encapsulation option for BIER packets and is not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: BIER (Bit Index Explicit Replication)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no BIER tag, so the document is tagged under the closest id, BIER, which the taxonomy lists under multicast. Please confirm the id.

RFC9263.title: Network Service Header (NSH) Metadata Type 2 Variable-Length Context Headers
RFC9263.summary: Defines seven NSH MD Type 2 variable-length context headers (Forwarding Context, Tenant ID, Ingress Node ID, Ingress Interface, Flow ID, Source/Destination Groups, Policy ID) for use in Service Function Paths, and creates IANA registries for them.

SFC.why: The document extends the Network Service Header with new MD Type 2 context headers for service function chaining. SFC is the tag covering the NSH.
SFC.quote: This document defines several common metadata Context Headers for use within NSH MD Type 2.

rejected.why: VXLAN VNI is only an example of a forwarding context value carried in the header. The document does not specify VXLAN.
MPLS VPN labels and entropy labels are referenced as values carried in the context headers. The document is not about MPLS.
The IANA registries are boilerplate that supports the header definitions. The document is not about IANA guidance.
The Geneve VNI is cited only as a source for the 24-bit VNI value. The document does not specify Geneve.
The IPv6 Flow Label is only a value that the Flow ID header can carry. The document does not address IPv6.
RFC 4364 is cited only for the MPLS VPN label. The document does not address L3VPN.

RFC9264.title: Linkset: Media Types and a Link Relation Type for Link Sets
RFC9264.summary: Defines two media types (application/linkset and application/linkset+json) for standalone sets of Web Links, plus the "linkset" link relation type for discovering them.

web linking.why: The document extends Web Linking (RFC 8288) with a new link relation type and standalone link set formats built on the Web Linking model.
web linking.quote: This specification also introduces a link relation type to support the discovery of sets of links.

media types.why: It defines and registers two new media types, application/linkset and application/linkset+json, and a profile parameter for them.
media types.quote: The assigned media type for this format is "application/linkset".

JSON.why: A substantial part specifies a JSON-based format (linkset object, context and target objects, attributes, JSON-LD context).
JSON.quote: This document format uses JSON [RFC8259] as the syntax to represent a set of links.

rejected.why: HTTP Link header and HTTP interactions are the substrate and context; the document does not extend HTTP itself.
The document is about link formats, not conventions for building APIs on HTTP, though the httpapi WG sponsored it.
URI references are used in links but the document does not define URI syntax or schemes.
Language tags appear only in title* handling, which is a minor detail.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here and do not make the document about IANA registries.

RFC9265.title: Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) Coding and Congestion Control in Transport
RFC9265.summary: An IRTF NWCRG informational memo discussing how FEC coding and congestion control can coexist when FEC is placed above, within, or below the transport, with research questions and recommendations.

FEC.why: The whole document analyses forward erasure correction for packet transport and its interaction with transport, including coding rates, repair symbols and reliability.
FEC.quote: FEC coding mechanisms should not hide congestion signals.  This memo offers a discussion of how FEC coding and congestion control can coexist.

congestion control.why: The document is about preserving congestion signals and fairness to non-coded flows when FEC is used. It is not about one specific congestion control algorithm, so the parent topic fits.
congestion control.quote: Since FEC coding repairs losses, blindly applying FEC may easily lead to an implementation that also hides a congestion signal from the sender.

rejected.why: TCP is used as an example of a loss-based, reliable transport. The document does not specify or extend it.
QUIC with the unreliable datagram extension is mentioned as an example. It is not a subject of the document.
ECN is mentioned only as one possible signalling method for recovered losses.
FECFRAME is only referenced as related work (RFC 8680 and RFC 8681), not discussed in the body.
Multipath is discussed generically in scope terms. MPTCP appears only as a coupled congestion control example.
Tetrys is listed only as an example of FEC below the transport.

gaps.name: Network coding
gaps.why: The document comes from the Network Coding Research Group and covers coding for network communications. The taxonomy has only FEC-related tags, and no general network coding tag.

RFC9266.title: Channel Bindings for TLS 1.3
RFC9266.summary: Defines the "tls-exporter" channel binding type based on TLS exported keying material for TLS 1.3, and updates SCRAM and GS2 SASL specs to use it as the default binding over TLS 1.3.

TLS.why: The document specifies a new channel binding for TLS using the TLS keying material exporter, and registers a TLS Exporter Label. It also covers TLS 1.3 and legacy TLS use and the triple handshake issue.
TLS.quote: defines a channel binding type, tls-exporter, that is compatible with TLS 1.3

SASL.why: A substantial section updates the default channel binding and the mandatory-to-implement binding for SCRAM and GS2 SASL mechanisms over TLS 1.3.
SASL.quote: this document updates [RFC5801], [RFC5802], and [RFC7677] to use "tls-exporter" as the default channel binding over TLS 1.3

rejected.why: GSS-API appears only as the mechanism family (GS2) whose default channel binding is updated. The document is not about GSS-API itself.
Channel binding supports authentication protocols, but the document's subject is TLS and SASL channel binding, which the more specific tags already cover.
The document uses exported keying material but does not address key establishment or provisioning. It also forbids using the binding as a secret key.

gaps.name: Channel bindings
gaps.why: The document defines a channel binding type under RFC 5056. The taxonomy has no tag for channel binding as a subject across TLS, SASL and GSS-API.

RFC9267.title: Common Implementation Anti-Patterns Related to Domain Name System (DNS) Resource Record (RR) Processing
RFC9267.summary: Informational memo describing common implementation anti-patterns in DNS resource record parsing (compression pointers, label/name lengths, NUL placement, RDLENGTH, record counts) that cause DoS and RCE, with recommended mitigations.

DNS.why: The whole document is about the DNS wire format and resource record parsing in resolver/client implementations, with violations of RFC 1035 and recommendations for correct handling.
DNS.quote: common vulnerabilities related to Domain Name System (DNS) resource record (RR) processing as seen in several DNS client implementations

rejected.why: The document is about implementation bugs in DNS parsing, not operational security practices for network infrastructure. The DNS tag covers its subject.
DoH is mentioned only in passing as another place the same flaws may occur. The document does not specify or analyse it.
DoT is mentioned only in passing as another place the same flaws may occur. The document does not specify or analyse it.
An mDNS CVE appears only in the references list. The document is not about mDNS.

RFC9268.title: IPv6 Minimum Path MTU Hop-by-Hop Option
RFC9268.summary: Defines an experimental IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option that records the minimum link MTU along the forward path and returns it to the source, to speed up and supplement Path MTU Discovery.

PMTUD.why: The option is a new Path MTU discovery mechanism that complements PMTUD, PLPMTUD and DPLPMTUD, with transport-layer behaviour for using its result.
PMTUD.quote: This document specifies a new IPv6 Hop-by-Hop Option that is used to record the Minimum Path MTU (PMTU) along the forward path

IPv6.why: It defines a new IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option, including its format, router and host processing, and its IANA type assignment, so it extends IPv6.
IPv6.quote: This document specifies a new IPv6 Hop-by-Hop (HBH) Option to record the minimum Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU)

rejected.why: ICMPv6 Packet Too Big is the existing mechanism this option works around. The document does not specify or extend ICMP.
QUIC appears only as an example of a transport that can use DPLPMTUD with the option.
UDP is mentioned only as a datagram transport that could carry the probes.
TCP is discussed only in a short example of where the option might be included.
IPsec and TLS appear only as ways to validate packets that carry the option, in the Security Considerations.
DNS and DNSSEC appear in a single bullet as a possible use case and are not the subject of the document.

RFC9269.title: Experimental Scenarios of Information-Centric Networking (ICN) Integration in 4G Mobile Networks
