RFC9269.summary: An IRTF informational RFC that lists options and experimental setups for integrating Information-Centric Networking (ICN) into 4G/LTE mobile networks, in the control plane and the user plane (mobile terminal, eNodeB, SGW/PGW), as native ICN, overlay, or dual-stack transport.

ICN.why: The whole document analyses how to deploy ICN (Interest/Data packets, PIT/FIB/CS forwarders, IPoICN, ICNoIP, hICN) in 4G networks and how to experiment with it.
ICN.quote: this document presents and lists the possible options for integration of Information-Centric Networking (ICN) in 3GPP 4G mobile networks

cellular.why: The document is about 3GPP 4G/EPS architecture (eNodeB, MME, SGW/PGW, GTP, PDCP, CUPS). Changes to the 3GPP protocol stack are a central subject, so readers of cellular networks would want it.
cellular.quote: The focus of this document is to list the options for using Information-Centric Networking (ICN) in 4G mobile networks

rejected.why: The mobility discussion concerns ICN anchorless mobility and GTP network-based mobility in 3GPP. The document does not specify or analyse an IP mobility protocol such as Mobile IP or PMIPv6.
hICN encodes names in IPv6 addresses and IPv6 is mentioned throughout. It is only a substrate here, and the document does not address IPv6 itself.
Multicast and eMBMS are cited as motivation and as an expected ICN benefit. The document does not specify or analyse IP multicast.
Mobile QoS bearers and DiffServ appear in Section 3.2 as background and a brief ICN comparison, which is not a substantial part of the document.
ROHC and ECRTP are mentioned only as background on overhead in Section 3.1.
GTP tunnelling is described as existing 4G architecture and as an ICN overlay target. It is not a generic tunnelling subject.

gaps.name: Mobile edge computing / CUPS (control and user plane separation)
gaps.why: The document discusses edge computing, UPF placement and CUPS as enablers for ICN. The taxonomy has no tag for them beyond the broad cellular tag.

RFC9270.title: GMPLS Signaling Extensions for Shared Mesh Protection
RFC9270.summary: Updates RFC 4872 and 4873 to extend GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling with a new "Shared Mesh Protection" LSP protection type, preemption priority field, and Notify sub-codes so SMP, activated via data-plane APS, can be controlled.

GMPLS.why: The document extends GMPLS signaling (PROTECTION object, Notify error sub-codes, preemption priority) for shared mesh protection recovery.
GMPLS.quote: This document updates RFCs 4872 and 4873 to provide extensions for Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) signaling to support the control of the SMP mechanism.

rejected.why: GMPLS RSVP-TE is the signaling substrate being extended, but GMPLS is the more specific fit for the recovery extensions; RSVP-TE is the underlying protocol.
RFC 7412 requirements for MPLS-TP SMP are cited as background, but the document is generic and technology-specific aspects are deferred.
YANG models are mentioned only as expected future updates; management aspects are out of scope.
The APS protocol in the data plane is used for switching but explicitly out of scope for this document.

gaps.name: Shared Mesh Protection / GMPLS recovery
gaps.why: No taxonomy tag covers the protection and restoration subject (SMP/SMR, LSP protection types) beyond the GMPLS technology tag.

RFC9271.title: Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) Management Protocol -- Commands and Responses
RFC9271.summary: Describes the NUT command/response protocol (TCP port 3493) between a UPS Attachment Daemon and a Management Daemon, used to monitor power devices and coordinate managed shutdowns.

energy management.why: The protocol monitors and controls UPS and other power devices (battery status, outlets, instant commands, shutdown orchestration). Energy management is the closest fit in the taxonomy, though not exact.
energy management.quote: the management of Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) units and other power devices

rejected.why: STARTTLS is one command and TLS 1.3 is used as the security mechanism. The document defines nothing new about TLS itself.
The document uses ABNF to write its command grammar. It is not about ABNF.
TCP is only the transport (port 3493). Nothing about TCP is specified.
It is a management protocol, but it is specific to power devices. Energy management fits better, and SNMP and similar protocols are not involved.
X.509 certificates are mentioned only in connection with TLS and self-signed certificate remarks. The document is not about certificate profiles.
VPN and VLAN appear only as workarounds in an appendix. They are not provider-provisioned VPNs.

gaps.name: UPS / power device management (NUT protocol)
gaps.why: The document's actual subject is the Network UPS Tools protocol for managing uninterruptible power supplies. The taxonomy has no tag for it, and energy management is only an approximation.

RFC9272.title: Underlay Path Calculation Algorithm and Constraints for Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER)
RFC9272.summary: Specifies general rules for how the BIER Algorithm (BAR) and IGP Algorithm (IPA) fields interact when calculating underlay paths in BIER, updating RFC 8401 and RFC 8444 and the BIER Algorithm IANA registry.

BIER.why: The whole document defines BIER underlay path calculation semantics and updates the BIER IS-IS and OSPF extension RFCs and the BIER Algorithm registry.
BIER.quote: This document specifies general rules for the interaction between the BIER Algorithm (BAR) and the IGP Algorithm (IPA) used for underlay path calculation

rejected.why: RFC 8401 (BIER via IS-IS) is updated only for the BAR/IPA field definitions; the document does not specify IS-IS itself.
RFC 8444 is updated only for field definitions; OSPF is the carrier, not the subject.
The registry rename is a minor change; the document is about algorithm interaction, not IANA guidance.
Implied as an ancestor of BIER; the more specific BIER tag is used.

RFC9273.title: Network Coding for Content-Centric Networking / Named Data Networking: Considerations and Challenges
RFC9273.summary: An IRTF informational RFC from NWCRG and ICNRG describing research on applying network coding to CCNx/NDN, covering naming, transport, caching, mobility considerations and open challenges.

ICN.why: The document is about applying network coding within CCNx/NDN architecture: naming, PIT/CS operation, forwarders, producers, consumers.
ICN.quote: clarifies the technical considerations and potential challenges for applying NC in CCNx/NDN

FEC.why: Network coding (RLC, block and sliding window coding, repair packets, recoding) is the loss-recovery coding scheme analysed; FEC is the closest taxonomy node.
FEC.quote: NC allows for recovery of missing packets by encoding the information across several packets.

rejected.why: Rate and congestion control is only one short challenge subsection, not a main subject.
Not a taxonomy tag; in-network caching is covered as part of ICN.
Consumer mobility is discussed in ICN terms, not IP-layer mobility.
Only cited as a naming example, not specified or profiled.
Multicast is mentioned as an inherent ICN property, not the subject.

gaps.name: Network Coding
gaps.why: The document is about network coding (RLC, recoding, generations), but the taxonomy has only FEC as a nearby node, with no dedicated network coding tag.

RFC9274.title: A Cost Mode Registry for the Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) Protocol
RFC9274.summary: Creates an IANA "ALTO Cost Modes" registry and updates RFC 7285 to relax the restriction of cost modes to "numerical" and "ordinal", defining encoding rules and a private-use prefix.

ALTO.why: The document extends and updates the ALTO protocol specification (RFC 7285) regarding cost modes, including the registry, encoding constraints and backward compatibility.
ALTO.quote: This document creates a new IANA registry for tracking cost modes supported by the Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) Protocol.

rejected.why: The registry is created for ALTO cost modes, but the document is about the ALTO protocol's cost mode extensibility rather than IANA guidance generally. The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate for this purpose.
The encoding constraint on allowed characters mentions US-ASCII alphanumerics, but only as a detail of the cost mode string format.

RFC9275.title: An Extension for Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO): Path Vector
RFC9275.summary: Experimental ALTO extension defining a Path Vector cost type and Abstract Network Elements (ANEs), delivered via multipart cost map and Endpoint Cost Service responses combined with entity property maps.

ALTO.why: The document extends the ALTO protocol with a new Path Vector cost type, ANE entity domain and multipart services.
ALTO.quote: It extends the ALTO cost map and ALTO property map services so that an application can decide to which endpoint(s) to connect

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding for ALTO messages, not the subject.
HTTP POST is used as the substrate; nothing new is defined about HTTP.
multipart/related is reused per RFC 2387; the document does not define MIME features itself.
BGP path vector is mentioned only as an analogy in terminology.
Bottleneck and bandwidth information is exposed, but no traffic engineering mechanism is specified; traffic control is out of scope.
CDN and service edges are one use case, not the subject of the document.

RFC9276.title: Guidance for NSEC3 Parameter Settings
RFC9276.summary: BCP updating RFC 5155 that gives guidance on NSEC3 parameter settings (iterations, salt, opt-out) for zone publishers, validating resolvers, and primary/secondary operators, and registers Extended DNS Error code 27.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document is operational guidance on NSEC3 authenticated denial of existence, a DNSSEC mechanism, including zone publisher and validating resolver behaviour.
DNSSEC.quote: This document updates RFC 5155 with guidance about selecting NSEC3 iteration and salt parameters.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific tag and implies DNS as its ancestor.
The document registers and uses Extended DNS Error code 27, but this is a minor part and the document does not define EDNS mechanisms.
SHA-1 is only mentioned as the hash used by NSEC3; the document is not about the hash algorithm.
It addresses DoS and CPU exhaustion, but only in the context of NSEC3 parameters, which the DNSSEC tag covers.

RFC9277.title: On Stable Storage for Items in Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR)
RFC9277.summary: Defines two CBOR enveloping methods (tag-wrapped and labeled CBOR sequence) plus a non-CBOR labeling method, giving stored CBOR files a magic number recognizable by file(1), and allocates CBOR tags including ones for CoAP Content-Format numbers.

CBOR.why: The document specifies new CBOR tag-based envelopes (tags 55800, 55801, and a tag range) and advice for CBOR protocol designers, so it is about CBOR.
CBOR.quote: This document defines a stored ("file") format for Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) data items that is friendly to common systems that recognize file types

media types.why: The magic-number mechanism identifies media types of stored content and ties to media type registration templates and CoAP Content-Format numbers. Readers of media type topics would want it.
media types.quote: A common way to identify the type of a file from its contents is to place a "magic number" at the start of the file contents

rejected.why: CoAP Content-Format numbers are mapped to CBOR tags, but the document does not specify or extend CoAP itself.
CDDL is used only for small snippets describing tag structures; the document is not about CDDL.
SenML-CBOR is only used as a worked example.
IANA allocations of CBOR tags are boilerplate-style registrations supporting the main subject; no IANA guidance is the subject.
PEM/DER are mentioned as motivation and contrast, not as subject matter.

RFC9278.title: JWK Thumbprint URI
RFC9278.summary: Registers a URN prefix (urn:ietf:params:oauth:jwk-thumbprint) so that a JWK Thumbprint (RFC 7638) can be expressed as a URI, with a hash algorithm identifier and SHA-256 as mandatory to implement.

URN.why: The document defines a new URN prefix/namespace-based URI form for JWK Thumbprints, so readers of URN pages would look for it.
URN.quote: urn:ietf:params:oauth:jwk-thumbprint

JOSE.why: The document is about representing JWK Thumbprints, a JOSE-family construct, as URIs.
JOSE.quote: A JSON Web Key (JWK) Thumbprint [RFC7638] is a URL-safe representation of a hash value over a JWK [RFC7517].

rejected.why: The URN is registered in the OAuth URI registry, but that is only a registration location; the document does not specify OAuth behaviour.
JWT claims are mentioned only as a context where URIs are needed; the document does not define JWT content.
SHA-256 is only named as the mandatory-to-implement hash; the document doesn't address the SHA family itself.
URN is the more specific tag and already covers the URI scheme/namespace aspect.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-style registry action, not the document's subject.

RFC9279.title: Internet Group Management Protocol Version 3 (IGMPv3) and Multicast Listener Discovery Version 2 (MLDv2) Message Extension
RFC9279.summary: Defines a generic TLV-based extension mechanism for IGMPv3 and MLDv2 messages, using the Additional Data section, with an E-bit flag, a No-op TLV, processing rules, and an IANA registry of extension types.

IGMP.why: The document extends the IGMPv3 message formats (Query and Report) with TLVs, so it belongs on the IGMP page.
IGMP.quote: This document defines a generic method to extend IGMPv3 [RFC3376] and MLDv2 [RFC3810] messages to accommodate information other than what is contained in the current message formats.

MLD.why: The document equally extends MLDv2 Query and Report messages, so it belongs on the MLD page.
MLD.quote: The MLDv2 Query message format [RFC3810] with extension is shown below.  The E-bit MUST be set to 1 to indicate that the extension is present.

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the IGMP and MLD tags. The document is not about multicast routing in general.
It creates an IANA registry (IGMP/MLD Extension Types), but that is boilerplate-level apparatus, not the subject of the document.
MLDv2 runs over IPv6, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC9280.title: RFC Editor Model (Version 3)
RFC9280.summary: RFC 9280 defines version 3 of the RFC Editor Model, splitting RFC Series policy definition (RSWG and RSAB) from policy implementation (RPC overseen by IETF LLC), defining the RSCE role, and creating the Editorial Stream.

RFC series.why: The whole document defines the structure, roles, and publication stream for the RFC Series and the RFC Editor function.
RFC series.quote: This document creates the Editorial Stream as a separate space for publication of policies, procedures, guidelines, rules, and related information regarding the RFC Series as a whole.

IETF process.why: A substantial part specifies the RSWG/RSAB policy-definition process, with IETF-style rough consensus, appeals, and IESG/IAB appointments. It is a governance process, though it concerns the RFC Series rather than IETF standards.
IETF process.quote: The intent is that the RSWG shall operate in a way similar to that of working groups in the IETF.

rejected.why: Section 6 touches IETF Trust rights and patent disclosure for the Editorial Stream, but only as a minor part of the document.
The IANA Considerations section is boilerplate, and the RPC's coordination with IANA is mentioned only in passing.
The document concerns RFC Series governance, not architectural principles of the Internet.

RFC9281.title: Entities Involved in the IETF Standards Process
RFC9281.summary: BCP 11 describes the individuals (document editor, WG chair, area director) and organizations (IETF, WGs, IESG, IAB, RPC, IANA, IRTF, IETF Trust, IETF LLC, Secretariat, ISOC) involved in the IETF standards process, obsoleting RFC 2028.

IETF process.why: The whole document describes the roles and bodies in the IETF standards process, which is the IETF process subject.
IETF process.quote: This document describes the individuals and organizations involved in the IETF standards process, as described in BCP 9.

rejected.why: NomCom is mentioned only briefly as a nominating body and is described elsewhere (RFC 8713), so the document is not about it.
IANA gets one short section as one organization among many; the document is not about IANA registries or guidance.
IPR disclosure and the IETF Trust's ownership of IP are mentioned in passing; they are not a substantial part of the document.
The RPC and RSWG are described in a short section, with details deferred to RFC 9280.

RFC9282.title: Responsibility Change for the RFC Series
RFC9282.summary: Short BCP that updates RFC 2026 by deleting a sentence, reflecting that responsibility for the RFC Series moved from the RFC Editor and IAB to the RFC Series Working Group and RFC Series Approval Board per RFC 9280.

RFC series.why: The document is about who is responsible for the RFC Series, which is the governance and administration of the series.
RFC series.quote: responsibility for the RFC Series moved to the RFC Series Working Group and the RFC Series Approval Board

IETF process.why: It formally updates RFC 2026 (BCP 9), the Internet Standards Process, so readers of IETF process documents would want to find it.
IETF process.quote: in Section 2.1 of [RFC2026], the sentence "RFC publication is the direct responsibility of the RFC Editor, under the general direction of the IAB" is deleted.

rejected.why: Both chosen tags are more specific children of this topic, so the parent is implied.
IANA is mentioned only in the boilerplate section, which says there are no IANA actions.

RFC9283.title: IAB Charter Update for RFC Editor Model
RFC9283.summary: Updates the IAB Charter (RFC 2850) so that it matches version 3 of the RFC Editor Model (RFC 9280). It removes the RFC Editor liaison member and replaces the IAB's approval role over the RFC Editor with a pointer to RFC 9280.

RFC series.why: The document changes how the RFC Series and the RFC Editor function are governed in the IAB charter, to match RFC Editor Model v3.
RFC series.quote: The RFC Editor function is defined under the authority of the IAB by [RFC9280].

internet governance.why: It amends the IAB charter, covering IAB membership and the IAB's role. This is governance of Internet standards bodies beyond the RFC Series itself. No more specific child tag fits the IAB charter.
internet governance.quote: This requires a modification to the Internet Architecture Board Charter [RFC2850].

rejected.why: The change concerns the IAB charter and RFC Editor oversight, not IETF standards procedures.
IANA appears only in the quoted section heading of RFC 2850 and is not changed by this document.

RFC9284.title: Multihoming Deployment Considerations for DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS)
RFC9284.summary: Informational guidance on how DOTS clients and client-domain DOTS gateways should behave when deployed in multihomed residential and enterprise networks, covering server selection, PI/PA addressing, and anycast use.

DOTS.why: The whole document gives deployment guidance for DOTS agents (clients and gateways) in multihomed networks, so it belongs on the DOTS page.
DOTS.quote: This document discusses multihoming considerations for DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS).

multihoming.why: A substantial part of the document covers multihoming scenarios, with one or multiple CPEs and ISPs and PI versus PA addresses. Readers of multihoming architectures would want it.
multihoming.quote: Identify DOTS deployment schemes in a multihoming context, where DOTS services can be offered by all or a subset of upstream providers.

rejected.why: Anycast is mentioned only to say when it is not recommended for DOTS. The document is not about anycast addressing or operation.
DOTS is the more specific tag and is already chosen. DDoS is its parent, so it is implied.
RFC 6724 source address selection is cited, but only as a requirement for DOTS clients. The document is not about IPv6.
DHCP is mentioned only as one way a DOTS server gets provisioned to the client.
DNS is only used to resolve DOTS server names, which makes it a substrate here.

RFC9285.title: The Base45 Data Encoding
RFC9285.summary: Defines the Base45 binary-to-text encoding, using the 45-character QR code alphanumeric alphabet to encode 2 bytes in 3 characters, with examples and decoding/security rules.

Base64.why: The taxonomy tag covers Base64, Base32, Base16 and Base45 textual data encodings. This document specifies Base45, including its alphabet, encoding and decoding rules, and examples.
Base64.quote: Base45 encodes 2 bytes in 3 characters, compared to Base64, which encodes 3 bytes in 4 characters.

rejected.why: The alphabet is a 45-character subset of US-ASCII, but the document is about a binary-to-text encoding, not ASCII itself.
It notes that Base45 output may need percent-encoding in URLs. This is a passing remark in Security Considerations.
It mentions not to wrap Base45 in Base64 for email. This is only a usage caution, and the document does not cover MIME.

gaps.name: QR code encoding
gaps.why: The document is motivated by QR code Alphanumeric mode (ISO/IEC 18004), and the taxonomy has no tag for QR codes or barcodes.

RFC9286.title: Manifests for the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI)
RFC9286.summary: Defines the RPKI manifest, a signed object listing files and hashes at a CA's publication point, with generation rules and relying-party processing to detect stale, missing or replayed objects; obsoletes RFC 6486.

RPKI.why: The document specifies a core RPKI object, its generation, and relying party processing, so RPKI readers need it.
RPKI.quote: A manifest is a signed object (file) that contains a listing of all the signed objects (files) in the repository publication point

rejected.why: Manifests use EE certificates and are modeled on CRLs, but the document does not profile X.509 certificates.
Manifests are CMS-wrapped signed objects, but CMS is only the encapsulation mechanism.
An ASN.1 module is defined, but it is just the notation for the object definition.
RPKI is the more specific child tag and covers this document.
RPKI is the more specific child tag, which already implies this parent.
The document is not about BGPsec path validation.

gaps.name: RPKI manifests / signed objects
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no distinct tag for RPKI repository objects. RPKI is a child of routing security, but I used it above and it is arguably the best fit; repository publication is not separately covered.

RFC9287.title: Greasing the QUIC Bit
RFC9287.summary: Defines the grease_quic_bit QUIC transport parameter, which lets endpoints negotiate sending arbitrary values in the second-most significant bit of QUIC packets so the bit stays available for future use.

QUIC.why: The document extends QUIC with a new transport parameter and specifies endpoint behaviour for setting and accepting the QUIC Bit. It is a QUIC extension, so readers of the QUIC subject would expect to find it.
QUIC.quote: The grease_quic_bit transport parameter (0x2ab2) is defined for QUIC version 1 [QUIC].

rejected.why: QUIC runs over UDP, but the document says nothing about UDP itself.
The document registers one transport parameter in the QUIC registry. That is boilerplate, not the subject of the document.
The document touches on protocol extensibility and ossification, but it specifies a concrete QUIC mechanism and does not address architecture in its own right.
Transport parameters are carried in the TLS handshake, but the document does not define anything about TLS.

gaps.name: Protocol greasing / extensibility and ossification avoidance
gaps.why: The document's purpose is to keep a header bit usable by preventing middleboxes from depending on a fixed value. The taxonomy has no tag for protocol extensibility or ossification, so the QUIC tag is the only fit.

RFC9288.title: Recommendations on the Filtering of IPv6 Packets Containing IPv6 Extension Headers at Transit Routers
RFC9288.summary: RFC 9288 analyses security, operational and interoperability implications of IPv6 Extension Headers and options and gives advice on filtering such packets at transit routers using a deny-list approach.

IPv6.why: The document is about IPv6 Extension Headers and options, their handling and filtering. IPv6 is the most specific fitting tag.
IPv6.quote: This document analyzes both the general security implications of IPv6 EHs, as well as the security implications of specific EH and option types.

operational security.why: It gives operator guidance on filtering policy at routers to protect infrastructure from DoS and similar attacks.
operational security.quote: it provides advice on the filtering of such IPv6 packets at transit routers for traffic not directed to them

rejected.why: The Router Alert option is only one of many options covered, in a single subsection. The document is not about it.
ESP and AH are two of the headers covered. The document only advises permitting them.
Only one EH subsection. The document is not about HIP.
The Mobility Header and Home Address option are each mentioned briefly. The document is not about Mobile IPv6.
The document is about filtering at transit routers, not firewalls or middlebox traversal as a subject.
Only one EH subsection. The document is not about Shim6.

RFC9289.title: Towards Remote Procedure Call Encryption by Default
RFC9289.summary: Defines RPC-with-TLS: an opportunistic mechanism using a new AUTH_TLS flavor and STARTTLS probe to enable TLS/DTLS encryption and peer authentication of ONC RPC traffic, updating RFC 5531.

ONC RPC.why: The document extends ONC RPC (updates RFC 5531) with a new authentication flavor and probing procedure.
ONC RPC.quote: we introduce a new RPC authentication flavor called AUTH_TLS. The AUTH_TLS authentication flavor signals that the client wants to initiate TLS negotiation if the server supports it.

TLS.why: It profiles TLS 1.3 use for RPC, including ALPN identifier "sunrpc", mandatory authentication, and 0-RTT prohibition.
TLS.quote: Implementations MUST NOT negotiate TLS versions prior to 1.3 (for TLS [RFC8446] or DTLS [RFC9147], respectively).

DTLS.why: A substantial section specifies DTLS operation for RPC over UDP, including connection IDs and record fitting.
DTLS.quote: The use of the DTLS protocol [RFC9147] protects RPC carried in UDP datagrams.

X.509.why: Defines new extended key usage OIDs and certificate validation rules for RPC peers, with an ASN.1 module.
X.509.quote: The current document defines two new KeyPurposeId values: one that identifies the RPC-with-TLS peer as an RPC client, and one that identifies the RPC-with-TLS peer as an RPC server.

rejected.why: TLSA records are suggested only as a STRIPTLS mitigation, not specified or extended here.
RPCSEC_GSS interaction and channel binding are discussed briefly, but the document is not about GSS-API.
NFS is the motivating community, but the document specifies RPC-level encryption, not NFS.
The ASN.1 module is only apparatus defining two OIDs.
It is a security layer for RPC, not a mapping of a protocol onto a transport; TLS and ONC RPC tags fit better.
Confidentiality is the goal, but the document is not about privacy threat models in general.

RFC9290.title: Concise Problem Details for Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) APIs
RFC9290.summary: Defines a concise CBOR-based "problem details" format for carrying machine-readable error information in CoAP REST responses, with extension registries, a media type and content-format, CBOR tag 38 for language-tagged strings, and interworking with RFC 7807.

CoAP.why: The document defines an error-reporting format for CoAP responses, registers a CoAP Content-Format, and a standard entry for unprocessed CoAP options. It is a CoAP extension.
CoAP.quote: This specification defines a simple and extensible framework to define Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) data items to suit this purpose.

CBOR.why: The format is a CBOR data item, and the appendix is the archival spec for CBOR tag 38. Readers of CBOR would want it.
CBOR.quote: tag38 = #6.38([tag38-ltag, text, ?tag38-direction])

HTTP APIs.why: It is a constrained counterpart to RFC 7807 problem details. Appendix B defines how to tunnel 7807 problem details, so HTTP API readers would want it.
HTTP APIs.quote: The format is inspired by, but intended to be more concise than, the problem details for HTTP APIs defined in RFC 7807.

language tags.why: Appendix A defines language-tagged strings using BCP 47 tags plus text direction. This is a substantial part of the document.
language tags.quote: A language-tagged text string in CBOR has the tag 38 and consists of an array with a length of 2 or 3.

rejected.why: CDDL is used to specify the structures but the document is not about CDDL itself.
RFC 7807 JSON objects appear only in the interworking appendix, so JSON is not the subject.
The media type registration is IANA boilerplate for the new format, not a document about media type rules.
URIs are used as fields and extension keys, but the document does not address URI syntax or schemes.
The registries are created for this format only and are not about IANA guidance in general.
HTTP is only the context of the RFC 7807 comparison and is not specified or extended here.

RFC9291.title: A YANG Network Data Model for Layer 2 VPNs
RFC9291.summary: Defines the YANG L2VPN Network Model (L2NM) for provisioning L2VPN services (VPLS, VPWS, EVPN variants) from a network controller, plus an Ethernet segment YANG module and two IANA-maintained modules for BGP L2 encapsulation and pseudowire types.

L2VPN.why: The document's core subject is a network model for L2VPN services (VPLS, VPWS, EVPN-VPWS) in a provider network.
L2VPN.quote: This document defines an L2VPN Network Model (L2NM) that can be used to manage the provisioning of Layer 2 Virtual Private Network (L2VPN) services

YANG.why: The document specifies new YANG modules (ietf-l2vpn-ntw, ietf-ethernet-segment, and two IANA-maintained modules) and their tree structures.
YANG.quote: The L2NM ('ietf-l2vpn-ntw'; see Section 8.4) is used to manage L2VPNs within a service provider network.

EVPN.why: A substantial part covers the EVPN configuration: Ethernet segments, ESI types, DF election, EVPN-VPWS service instances and EVPN policies.
EVPN.quote: Section 8.3 defines another YANG module to manage Ethernet Segments (ESes) that are required for instantiating Ethernet VPNs (EVPNs).

pseudowire.why: The document defines the iana-pseudowire-types module and pseudowire signalling parameters (LDP, L2TP, BGP) for the L2NM.
pseudowire.quote: two IANA-maintained modules that include a set of identities of BGP Layer 2 encapsulation types and pseudowire types

rejected.why: BGP is used as the L2VPN signalling and auto-discovery mechanism that the model configures, but the document does not specify or extend BGP itself.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only as access mechanisms for the modules and in Security Considerations.
LDP signalling parameters are modelled, but the document does not define LDP.
L2TP-signalled pseudowire parameters are modelled, but the document does not define L2TP.
This document defines YANG modules, not MIB modules.
Ethernet service OAM (CFM, Y.1731) is only a small inherited subtree of the model.

gaps.name: L2VPN
gaps.why: Not applicable, since L2VPN is a valid tag id here; no taxonomy gap.

RFC9292.title: Binary Representation of HTTP Messages
RFC9292.summary: Defines "message/bhttp", a binary format (known-length and indeterminate-length) for representing HTTP requests and responses outside an HTTP protocol, and registers its media type.

HTTP.why: The document specifies a binary representation of HTTP messages, carrying HTTP semantics and mapping control data, field sections, and content. It is about HTTP message representation.
HTTP.quote: This document defines a simple format for representing an HTTP message [HTTP], either request or response.

media types.why: The document defines and registers a new media type, message/bhttp, as a substantial part of its content.
media types.quote: The "message/bhttp" media type can be used to enclose a single HTTP request or response message

rejected.why: HTTP/2 rules for pseudo-header fields and malformed messages are borrowed, but the format is explicitly distinct and not HTTP/2.
Only the variable-length integer encoding and notation are borrowed from QUIC. The document is not about the QUIC transport.
The format is designed to enable uses such as Oblivious HTTP, but that protocol is not specified here.
The media type is registered, but the document doesn't address MIME body structure or encodings beyond a brief note.
HTTP/3 framing only informed the design. The document is not about HTTP/3.

RFC9293.title: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)
RFC9293.summary: RFC 9293 is the consolidated TCP specification that obsoletes RFC 793 and several updates, defining the header, options, state machine, connection management, segmentation, retransmission, windowing, and event processing.

TCP.why: The whole document is the base TCP protocol specification, replacing RFC 793.
TCP.quote: This document specifies the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP).

rejected.why: Congestion control is only referenced (RFC 5681, 6298) and required, not specified in detail; the document says it is not described in detail.
ECN is mentioned with a SHOULD implement and the CWR/ECE flags, but it is not a substantial part of the document.
PMTUD is discussed briefly as a segmentation input; it is not a subject of the document.
IP is the lower layer TCP runs over; the document does not specify IP.
The TCP checksum field is described but is a minor part of the document.
Only referenced as separately specified.

RFC9294.title: Application-Specific Link Attributes Advertisement Using the Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS)
RFC9294.summary: Defines a BGP-LS Application-Specific Link Attributes (ASLA) TLV (type 1122) and the procedures for originating it from IS-IS and OSPF application-specific link attribute advertisements.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP-LS, a BGP extension, with a new ASLA TLV and originator procedures. There is no separate BGP-LS tag, so BGP is the best fit.
BGP.quote: This document defines extensions to the Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS) to enable the advertisement of these application-specific attributes

IS-IS.why: A substantial part of the document specifies how IS-IS ASLA sub-TLVs and Application-Specific SRLG TLVs are collated and mapped into BGP-LS, including a worked IS-IS illustration.
IS-IS.quote: While the ASLA encoding in OSPF is similar to that of BGP-LS, the encoding in IS-IS differs and requires additional procedures

rejected.why: OSPF ASLA is only the source encoding. The document says it is similar to BGP-LS and defines no OSPF procedures of its own.
SR Policy is named only as an example application of link attributes. The document is not about segment routing.
RSVP-TE is mentioned only as an application whose attributes stay in top-level TLVs. The document does not specify RSVP-TE.
A controller or PCE is named as a consumer of the topology information. The document does not specify PCE or PCEP.
LFA is only an example application that uses link attributes.
The link attributes originated as TE attributes, but the document is about how they are advertised in BGP-LS, not about traffic engineering itself.

gaps.name: BGP-LS (BGP Link State)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for BGP-LS, the northbound distribution of link-state topology via BGP. Readers browsing BGP-LS would want this RFC.

RFC9295.title: Clarifications for Ed25519, Ed448, X25519, and X448 Algorithm Identifiers
RFC9295.summary: Updates RFC 8410 by replacing its Section 5 to specify which keyUsage bits must, may, or must not appear in X.509 certificates carrying Ed25519, Ed448, X25519, and X448 public keys.

X.509.why: The document defines keyUsage extension rules for X.509 certificates (end-entity, CRL issuer, CA) using these algorithm identifiers, updating the X.509 profile of RFC 8410.
X.509.quote: If the keyUsage extension is present in a certification authority certificate that indicates id-Ed25519 or id-Ed448 in SubjectPublicKeyInfo, then the keyUsage extension MUST contain:

Curve25519.why: X25519 and X448 key usage rules are specified, which makes the document relevant to Curve25519/Curve448 readers.
Curve25519.quote: If the keyUsage extension is present in a certificate that indicates id-X25519 or id-X448 in SubjectPublicKeyInfo, then the following MUST be present:

EdDSA.why: Ed25519 and Ed448 are EdDSA signature algorithms, and much of the section sets out their keyUsage constraints.
EdDSA.quote: If the keyUsage extension is present in an end-entity certificate that indicates id-Ed25519 or id-Ed448 in SubjectPublicKeyInfo

rejected.why: X.509 is the more specific child tag and already covers the certificate profile subject.
The more specific Curve25519 and EdDSA tags fit better. The document doesn't address elliptic curve cryptography in general.

RFC9296.title: ifStackTable for the Point-to-Point (P2P) Interface over a LAN Type: Definition and Examples
RFC9296.summary: Informational independent-stream RFC advising how the ifStackTable (higher-layer-if/lower-layer-if, admin and oper status, statistics) should represent the p2pOverLan (303) interface type, with YANG/XML examples.

YANG.why: The document gives interface-list examples in the YANG/XML data model of RFC 8343 and the iana-if-type module, defining how p2pOverLan entries are modelled.
YANG.quote: A YANG Data Model for Interface Management

MIB.why: The document is about ifStackTable and ifType usage from the IF-MIB, mapping interface types to ifEntry; readers of MIB/ifType material would want it.
MIB.quote: If a device implements the IF-MIB [RFC2863], then each entry in the "/interfaces/interface" list

rejected.why: IS-IS appears only as an example name (isis_int) and as one of the link-state protocols that benefit; the document is not about the protocol.
ethernetCsmacd is just one example lower-layer interface type; the document does not address Ethernet itself.
LAG appears only as one example lower-layer type in Appendix A.
Link-state routing protocols are mentioned in the abstract context only; OSPF is not discussed.
The IANA section merely updates a registry reference; the body is not about IANA registries.
The XML examples resemble NETCONF data, but NETCONF is not discussed or used by the document.

RFC9297.title: HTTP Datagrams and the Capsule Protocol
RFC9297.summary: Defines HTTP Datagrams (unreliable multiplexed datagrams in HTTP connections, using QUIC DATAGRAM in HTTP/3) and the Capsule Protocol, a TLV convention on HTTP data streams, plus the Capsule-Protocol header field and DATAGRAM capsule.

HTTP.why: The document defines a new HTTP extension mechanism: HTTP Datagrams, the Capsule Protocol, the Capsule-Protocol header field and an HTTP/3 setting. It applies across HTTP/1.x, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
HTTP.quote: HTTP Datagrams, a convention for conveying multiplexed, potentially unreliable datagrams inside an HTTP connection.

rejected.why: QUIC and its DATAGRAM extension are the substrate. The document defines nothing new in QUIC itself.
It adds an HTTP/3 setting, an error code and a datagram format. But the Capsule Protocol applies to all HTTP versions, so the parent HTTP tag fits better.
The document came from the MASQUE working group and is a building block for MASQUE. It does not specify proxying itself.
HTTP/2 is only one of the versions over which the Capsule Protocol runs. The document does not specify HTTP/2.
It creates a capsule type registry, which is IANA boilerplate rather than the subject of the document.

RFC9298.title: Proxying UDP in HTTP
RFC9298.summary: Defines the "connect-udp" HTTP upgrade token and a protocol for tunneling UDP through an HTTP proxy (MASQUE) using Extended CONNECT/Upgrade, HTTP Datagrams, URI Template configuration and Context IDs.

MASQUE.why: The document is the core MASQUE specification for proxying UDP over HTTP, including the connect-udp token and the masque well-known URI.
MASQUE.quote: this document defines a protocol that allows an HTTP client to create a tunnel for UDP communications through an HTTP server that acts as a proxy

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate and is extended only via the MASQUE tag, which sits under HTTP and already covers the document.
UDP is the thing being proxied. The document specifies no change to UDP itself.
QUIC is only used for varints and DATAGRAM frames, and it is a typical protocol running over the proxied UDP.
HTTP/3 is one of several HTTP versions the protocol runs over, and the document defines nothing new for it.
The document uses URI Templates for configuration but is not about URIs in general.
ECN is addressed in only a short section about handling marks, and it is not a main subject.

RFC9299.title: An Architectural Introduction to the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP)
RFC9299.summary: Informational architectural introduction to LISP, describing its locator/ID split, data plane, control plane and mapping system, operational mechanisms, mobility, multicast and use cases.

LISP.why: The whole document is an architectural overview of LISP: EIDs/RLOCs, ITR/ETR, Mapping System, and operations.
LISP.quote: This document describes the architecture of the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP), making it easier to read the rest of the LISP specifications

rejected.why: Multicast section only summarises LISP multicast; it is a minor part of the LISP overview.
Mobility section is a short discussion of how LISP can support mobility, not the document's subject.
DNS is only an analogy for the Mapping System and for LISP-DDT, and is used to fetch EIDs.
LISP is an overlay, but it has its own specific tag, and the document is not about VXLAN/Geneve/NVGRE-type overlays.
BGP is mentioned only as the basis of LISP-ALT and as underlay reachability information.
The VPN use case is a short Instance ID paragraph, not provider-provisioned VPN specification.

RFC9300.title: The Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP)
RFC9300.summary: RFC 9300 specifies the LISP data plane: UDP-based encapsulation between ITRs and ETRs, the EID-to-RLOC Map-Cache, RLOC selection and reachability, MTU handling, and instance IDs. It obsoletes RFC 6830.

LISP.why: The document is the core LISP data plane specification: header formats, Map-Cache, locator reachability and mapping updates.
LISP.quote: This document describes the data plane protocol for the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP).

rejected.why: LISP is described as an overlay protocol, but that tag covers data-center virtualization encapsulations such as VXLAN, Geneve and NVGRE. The LISP tag fits better.
LISP is carried over UDP port 4341, but UDP is only the substrate here.
Section 14 mentions multicast briefly and defers to other RFCs. It is not a substantial part of the document.
Section 7 covers MTU handling for encapsulation, but it is a small part of the document. The document is not about PMTUD itself.
LISP is dynamic tunneling, but the specific LISP tag covers it.
IPv6 appears as an EID/RLOC address family, not as the subject of the document.

gaps.name: LISP
gaps.why: The taxonomy listing includes a LISP tech tag under routing, but its id was not verified here; the id used in tags is 'LISP' as written in the taxonomy.

RFC9301.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Control Plane
RFC9301.summary: Specifies the LISP control plane and Mapping Service: Map-Request, Map-Reply, Map-Register, Map-Notify(-Ack) and Encapsulated Control Message formats, plus Map-Server and Map-Resolver behaviour, SMR and RLOC-probing; obsoletes RFC 6830 and 6833.

LISP.why: The whole document specifies the LISP control plane, its message formats, and the Map-Server and Map-Resolver devices.
LISP.quote: This document describes the control plane and Mapping Service for the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP)

rejected.why: DNS is mentioned only as an analogy for Map-Server and Map-Resolver terminology; the document is not about DNS.
BGP appears only as the mechanism of the LISP-ALT mapping database; this document does not specify it.
UDP is only the transport for the control messages; the document defines nothing new about UDP itself.
HMAC and HKDF are used to authenticate Map-Register messages; the document does not specify them.
The IANA section registers LISP values and is boilerplate, not the main subject.

RFC9302.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Map-Versioning
RFC9302.summary: Specifies LISP Map-Versioning, which carries 12-bit version numbers for EID-to-RLOC mappings in the LISP header and Map Records so ITRs and ETRs can detect stale mappings. It obsoletes the experimental RFC 6834.

LISP.why: The whole document is a LISP extension: version numbers in the LISP data-plane header and Map Records, with ETR/ITR handling rules.
LISP.quote: the Map-Versioning mechanism used to provide information on changes in the Endpoint-ID-to-Routing-Locator (EID-to-RLOC) mappings used in the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP)

rejected.why: LISP is the more specific tag and the document is about LISP, not routing architecture in general.
LISP encapsulation is the context, but the document is about mapping versioning, not generic tunnelling.
The document has no IANA actions, so there is nothing to tag.

RFC9303.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol Security (LISP-SEC)
RFC9303.summary: Specifies LISP-SEC, which uses one-time keys and HMACs to give origin authentication, integrity, anti-replay protection and EID-Prefix authorization verification for LISP Map-Request/Map-Reply mapping lookups.

LISP.why: The document extends the LISP control plane (ECM, Map-Reply, Map-Register) with security mechanisms and is about LISP security.
LISP.quote: LISP-SEC, a set of security mechanisms that provides origin authentication, integrity, and anti-replay protection to LISP's EID-to-RLOC mapping data

rejected.why: DTLS is only an optional way to protect the OTK in transit; the document defines nothing new about DTLS.
HMAC is used as a building block for authenticating mapping data, not specified or profiled here.
The OTK wrapping and derivation are part of the LISP-SEC mechanism; pre-shared key provisioning is explicitly out of scope.
LISP-SEC secures the mapping lookup control plane, not routing protocols like BGP, so this doesn't fit well.
AES Key Wrap is used only as a mechanism for wrapping the OTK.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-like registrations for LISP-SEC parameters, not the document's main subject.

gaps.name: LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no LISP tag in the shown hierarchy beyond the 'LISP' entry under routing, which I used above only if present; if it is absent, LISP and its control plane/security are a gap.

RFC9304.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP): Shared Extension Message and IANA Registry for Packet Type Allocations
RFC9304.summary: Defines the LISP shared extension message type (Packet Type 15) with sub-types and the associated IANA registries, obsoleting the experimental RFC 8113.

LISP.why: The whole document specifies a LISP message type and its sub-type registration procedure, extending the LISP protocol's packet type space.
LISP.quote: this document specifies a shared LISP extension message type and describes a procedure for registering LISP shared extension sub-types

rejected.why: The registries are LISP-specific; the IANA material is boilerplate-like registry creation for the LISP extension, not general IANA guidance.

RFC9305.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Generic Protocol Extension
RFC9305.summary: Defines LISP-GPE, a change to the LISP data-plane header (P-bit and 8-bit Next Protocol field) that enables multiprotocol encapsulation (IP, Ethernet, NSH, shim headers) and creates an IANA registry for Next Protocol values.

LISP.why: The whole document specifies an extension to the LISP data plane header (P-bit, Next Protocol field, shim headers), so LISP readers need it.
LISP.quote: This document describes extensions to the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) data plane, via changes to the LISP header, to support multiprotocol encapsulation

rejected.why: VXLAN is only mentioned as a similar header format used for L2 encapsulation. The document does not specify or extend it.
NSH is only one of the assigned Next Protocol values. The document does not define service function chaining.
UDP is the transport for the encapsulation. The checksum and usage-guideline discussion is applicability guidance, not a new UDP specification.
ECN and DSCP handling is cited from existing RFCs for tunnel behaviour. It is not the subject of the document.
LISP-GPE is an encapsulation, but LISP is the more specific tag. The generic tunnelling topic would be redundant.
The registry creation is boilerplate-level IANA Considerations and not the main subject.

gaps.name: LISP
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists LISP under routing, but the id I used is not in the taxonomy as written. The taxonomy id is 'LISP', which does exist, so no real gap. No other missing subject was found.

RFC9306.title: Vendor-Specific LISP Canonical Address Format (LCAF)
RFC9306.summary: Defines a new Vendor-Specific LISP Canonical Address Format (LCAF type 255) using IEEE OUIs for implementation-specific address encodings, and updates RFC 8060 to say unrecognized LCAF types must be ignored.

LISP.why: The whole document defines a new LCAF type for LISP and updates LCAF handling of unrecognized types in LISP control plane messages.
LISP.quote: This document extends [RFC8060] to introduce a Vendor-Specific LCAF that defines how organizations can create LCAF addresses to be used only on particular LISP implementations.

rejected.why: The IANA registry assignment of type 255 is boilerplate-level; the document is not about IANA guidance or stewardship.
LCAF encodes address formats within LISP, but the document is LISP-specific and the LISP tag covers it; it is not about IP address architecture.

RFC9307.title: Report from the IAB Workshop on Analyzing IETF Data (AID) 2021
RFC9307.summary: IAB workshop report summarizing discussions and position papers on analyzing IETF data (tools, affiliation, diversity, process, environmental sustainability), with a draft data taxonomy for SDO data.

workshop reports.why: The document is a report from an IAB workshop, which is exactly what this subject collects.
workshop reports.quote: This report summarizes the workshop's discussion and identifies topics that warrant future work and consideration.

sustainability.why: A full section covers the CO2 cost of IETF meetings and how much climate and energy impact is considered in protocol design.
sustainability.quote: The final discussion session considered environmental sustainability.

IETF process.why: Substantial discussion of how the IETF makes decisions, how Internet-Drafts become RFCs, and the affiliation and diversity of participants, all analysed as the IETF standards process.
IETF process.quote: A number of submissions focused on the RFC publication process, on the development of standards and other RFCs in the IETF, and on how the IETF makes decisions.

rejected.why: The IETF process and workshop reports tags are more specific children, so the parent is not needed.
RFCs appear as a data source and as the subject of success studies, but the document is not about RFC format, style, or publication.
The appendix data taxonomy is a data model for analysis, not a glossary of terms.

gaps.name: IETF data analysis / standards-development research
gaps.why: The core subject is research on IETF data (datatracker, mailing list archives, participant diversity and affiliation). No taxonomy tag covers this well.

RFC9308.title: Applicability of the QUIC Transport Protocol
RFC9308.summary: Informational guidance for application developers on caveats of using QUIC as a transport: fallback, 0-RTT, streams, migration, connection IDs, DSCP, versioning and datagrams.

QUIC.why: The whole document is about how applications should use QUIC: streams, 0-RTT, migration, connection IDs, termination, versions.
QUIC.quote: This document discusses the applicability of the QUIC transport protocol, focusing on caveats impacting application protocol development and deployment over QUIC.

rejected.why: HTTP/3 is used as a running example of an application mapping, but the document is not about it.
TLS 1.3 is the security substrate for QUIC. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
UDP is only the substrate QUIC runs over. Port selection and NAT timeouts are discussed only as QUIC concerns.
DSCP handling gets one short section, in the context of QUIC's single congestion controller. That is not enough to make the document about Diffserv.
TAPS is mentioned once in passing as related to fallback.
NAT rebinding and idle timeouts affect QUIC's design, but the document is not about NAT behaviour.

RFC9309.title: Robots Exclusion Protocol
RFC9309.summary: RFC 9309 specifies the Robots Exclusion Protocol (robots.txt): its syntax, group and rule matching, access method, error handling, caching and parsing limits for crawlers.

robots.txt.why: The whole document standardizes the Robots Exclusion Protocol: syntax, user-agent/allow/disallow matching, fetch results, caching and limits.
robots.txt.quote: The protocol language consists of rule(s) and group(s) that the service makes available in a file named "robots.txt"

rejected.why: HTTP is only the main transport; the document gives status-code handling examples but does not specify or extend HTTP.
The document relies on RFC 3986 for URI syntax and percent-encoding but defines nothing new about URIs.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the formal syntax, not as the subject.
Section 2.4 refers to standard HTTP cache control and sets a 24-hour limit, but this is a small part of the document specific to robots.txt.
RFC 8288 is cited only in passing in the introduction as context for crawlers traversing links.
The robots.txt file must be UTF-8, but the encoding is just a dependency.

RFC9310.title: X.509 Certificate Extension for 5G Network Function Types
RFC9310.summary: Defines an X.509 v3 certificate extension (id-pe-nftype) carrying a list of 5G Network Function Types for role-based access control, with its ASN.1 module, OID assignment, and an example certificate.

X.509.why: The document defines a new X.509 v3 certificate extension, its OID, syntax and encoding rules, and an example certificate. Readers of X.509 certificate profiles would want it.
X.509.quote: This document specifies the NFTypes certificate extension to support role-based access control decisions by providing a list of NF Types associated with the certificate subject.

cellular.why: The extension exists for 5G System network functions. Appendix A lists the 3GPP NF Type strings, and the example follows the 3GPP TS 33.310 certificate profile.
cellular.quote: The 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) has specified several Network Functions (NFs) as part of the service-based architecture within the 5G System.

rejected.why: The document includes an ASN.1 module, but only to define the extension's syntax. It is not about ASN.1 itself.
X.509 is the more specific tag. The document does not address PKI operations in general.
TLS is mentioned only in the Privacy Considerations, as a context in which certificates are exchanged.
The extension supports role-based access control decisions. The document specifies only a certificate field, not an access control mechanism.
The IANA section only records OID assignments. That is boilerplate and not the subject.

RFC9311.title: Running an IETF Hackathon
RFC9311.summary: Informational document describing the practices used to run IETF Hackathons: timing, funding, presentations, tooling, statistics, and roles.

IETF process.why: The document describes the procedures, roles and administration of an IETF event, so it belongs under IETF process. No narrower tag covers hackathons.
IETF process.quote: This document provides a set of practices that have been used for running IETF Hackathons.

rejected.why: The child tag IETF process fits more specifically, so the parent is not listed.
HackNet is described as a global Layer 2 VPN, but only briefly. The document is not about provider-provisioned VPNs.
NAT64 appears only in a list of network capabilities that champions can request.
IPv6-only networking and prefix delegation are mentioned only as network services offered to teams.
The document describes how to run a Hackathon. It is not a report from a workshop.

gaps.name: IETF Hackathon / running code events
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for hackathons, code sprints or other running-code events. Readers of such a tag would want this RFC.

RFC9312.title: Manageability of the QUIC Transport Protocol
RFC9312.summary: Informational "user's manual" for the QUIC wire image, explaining what QUIC exposes to on-path observers and how common network management practices (RTT measurement, NAT/firewall state, load balancing, DDoS mitigation, PMTU, QoS/ECMP) are affected.

QUIC.why: The whole document analyses QUIC's wire image, handshake, connection IDs, spin bit and their operational implications, so QUIC readers would want it.
QUIC.quote: This document discusses manageability of the QUIC transport protocol and focuses on the implications of QUIC's design and wire image on network operations involving QUIC traffic.

network management.why: Section 4 covers specific network management tasks (troubleshooting, state handling, filtering, load balancing) for operators and vendors.
network management.quote: This document provides guidance for network operations that manage QUIC traffic.

performance measurement.why: Passive RTT measurement via handshake and spin bit, and the limits on passive loss measurement, are a substantial part of the document.
performance measurement.quote: The spin bit provides a version-specific method to measure per-flow RTT from observation points on the network path throughout the duration of a connection.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as the main application binding of QUIC; the document does not specify or analyse HTTP/3.
TLS is the handshake substrate and SNI/ClientHello extraction is discussed only as an observable; nothing new is defined about TLS.
UDP is merely QUIC's encapsulation; UDP blocking/throttling is discussed only as it affects QUIC.
DDoS detection is one subsection (4.7) applied to QUIC, not a main subject of the document.
Section 4.10 gives path MTU guidance for QUIC, but it is a small part and the document does not specify PMTUD.
NAT timeouts and rebinding are discussed as QUIC-impacting practices, not as a NAT specification.

RFC9313.title: Pros and Cons of IPv6 Transition Technologies for IPv4-as-a-Service (IPv4aaS)
RFC9313.summary: Informational comparison of five IPv4-as-a-Service transition technologies (464XLAT, DS-Lite, lw4o6, MAP-E, MAP-T) to help operators choose among them, covering architecture, address sharing, provisioning, logging, load sharing and deployment.

464XLAT.why: One of the five technologies compared, with its own overview section and extensive deployment and traffic analysis (cellular and wireline).
464XLAT.quote: 464XLAT may use double translation (stateless NAT46 + stateful NAT64) or single translation (stateful NAT64) depending on different factors

DS-Lite.why: DS-Lite is one of the five technologies analysed and compared throughout.
DS-Lite.quote: Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite) [RFC6333] was the first of the considered transition mechanisms to be developed.

MAP.why: MAP-E and MAP-T are two of the five compared technologies, and the document analyses their mapping rules and A+P operation.
MAP.quote: MAP-E and MAP-T use a stateless algorithm to embed portions of the customer's allocated IPv4 address

softwire.why: lw4o6 has no dedicated tag. It is an A+P softwire mechanism, and its provisioning is covered by the softwire YANG and RADIUS references.
softwire.quote: Lightweight 4over6 (lw4o6) is a variant of DS-Lite.

IPv6 transition.why: The document as a whole is a comparative guide to IPv6 transition mechanisms. This parent topic fits the cross-cutting comparison, though the child technology tags also apply.
IPv6 transition.quote: Several IPv6 transition technologies have been developed to provide customers with IPv4-as-a-Service (IPv4aaS)

rejected.why: NAT64 is part of 464XLAT and MAP-T and is discussed, but the document is not about NAT64 itself. It is covered by the 464XLAT and MAP tags.
Carrier-grade NAT is discussed for address sharing and logging, but only as one category of approach.
Section 5 plans performance comparison using RFC 8219, but this is a small forward-looking part of the document.
DHCPv6 appears only as a provisioning method in a table.
DNS64 is a component used with 464XLAT, but the document does not specify or analyse it in its own right.
PCP is mentioned for public server operation, but it is not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Lightweight 4over6 (lw4o6)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for lw4o6, so it can only be approximated by the softwire tag.

gaps.name: IPv4-as-a-Service (IPv4aaS)
gaps.why: No tag covers the IPv4aaS service concept, apart from the IPv6 transition parent.

RFC9314.title: YANG Data Model for Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD)
RFC9314.summary: Defines YANG modules (ietf-bfd, -types, -ip-sh, -ip-mh, -lag, -mpls) for configuring and monitoring BFD sessions over single-hop IP, multihop IP, MPLS LSPs and LAGs, updating RFC 9127.

BFD.why: The document models BFD configuration, operational state and notifications for all BFD path types, so it belongs on the BFD page.
BFD.quote: This document defines a YANG data model that can be used to configure and manage Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD)

YANG.why: The document's main content is a set of YANG modules and their tree diagrams, so it is a YANG data model document.
YANG.quote: The YANG modules in this document conform to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA)

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the access protocol named in examples and Security Considerations. The document does not define anything new about it.
The document covers BFD over MPLS LSPs but only as one path type. It does not specify MPLS.
The LAG module is one of four path types, and it models micro-BFD from RFC 7130. LAG itself is not the subject.
OSPF and IS-IS are mentioned only as examples of BFD clients.
The document defines YANG modules, not SMI MIB modules.

RFC9315.title: Intent-Based Networking - Concepts and Definitions
RFC9315.summary: IRTF NMRG informational document that defines "intent" and Intent-Based Networking, distinguishes intent from policy and service models, and outlines principles, fulfillment and assurance functionality, and the intent life cycle.

network management.why: The document is a conceptual treatment of intent-based management of networks, covering fulfillment, assurance, monitoring and orchestration. It fits the network management topic, and no specific technology tag applies.
network management.quote: Intent-Based Networking involves a wide variety of functions that can be roughly divided into two categories

policy management.why: A substantial part of the document compares intent with policy and PBNM, including PDP and PEP roles. Policy-based management is a core contrast throughout.
policy management.quote: Policy-Based Network Management (PBNM) is a management paradigm that separates the rules that govern the behavior of a system from the functionality of the system.

autonomic networking.why: The document frames intent as guidance for autonomic networks and discusses how it is rendered by the network itself. Autonomic networking is a recurring motivation and context.
autonomic networking.quote: The term "intent" was first introduced in the context of Autonomic Networks, where it is defined as "an abstract, high-level policy used to operate the network"

rejected.why: SDN controllers and northbound interfaces are mentioned as related offerings and as a source of 'intent-washing'. The document is not about SDN control-plane separation.
YANG models appear only as examples of service models and past IETF work. The document specifies no models.
SNMP and MIBs are cited only as historical examples of device-level management.
Monitoring and telemetry are described as generic assurance functions, not as the subject of the document.
L3VPN is only an example of a service model.

gaps.name: Intent-Based Networking (IBN)
gaps.why: The document's central subject has no dedicated tag. It is currently covered only by the broader network management topic.

RFC9316.title: Intent Classification
RFC9316.summary: An IRTF NMRG informational document proposing a classification methodology and taxonomy for network intents (solutions, intent users, types, scopes, abstraction, life cycle) for carrier, data center and enterprise networks.

network management.why: The document is about intent-based network management: classifying intents, users and life cycles. No narrower tag fits, so the parent topic is used.
network management.quote: Intent is an abstract, high-level policy used to operate a network. An intent-based management system includes an interface for users to input requests

terminology.why: A substantial part of the document defines intent terms and a shared taxonomy and vocabulary to give the research community a common understanding.
terminology.quote: it also defines relevant intent terms where necessary, provides a foundation for intent-related research

rejected.why: Intents are related to policies, but the document classifies intents and does not specify policy information models.
SDN/NFV appears only as the context of a proof-of-concept example, and the document is not about SDN itself.
Autonomous driving network levels are covered in one subsection, but this is not the document's main subject.
QoS is only one intent scope category and is not addressed as a subject.

gaps.name: Intent-based networking
gaps.why: The document is entirely about intent-based networking, and the taxonomy has no tag for it. Network management is only an approximate parent.

RFC9317.title: Operational Considerations for Streaming Media
RFC9317.summary: Informational MOPS overview of operational networking and transport issues affecting QoE for streaming high-bitrate media over the Internet: bandwidth provisioning, latency classes, adaptive bitrate delivery, transport behaviours (TCP, UDP, QUIC), and encrypted media.

streaming.why: The whole document is about operating streaming media delivery: ABR, latency categories, bitrate provisioning, measurement. The streaming topic fits directly.
streaming.quote: operational networking and transport protocol issues that pertain to the quality of experience (QoE) when streaming video and other high-bitrate media over the Internet

congestion control.why: A substantial part (3.2, 5.5, 6) analyses interaction between application-level ABR and transport congestion controllers (TCP, BBR, CUBIC, QUIC) and their effect on media.
congestion control.quote: Media servers also typically rely on transport protocols with capacity-seeking congestion controllers that probe for available path bandwidth

QUIC.why: A dedicated section analyses QUIC's transport behaviour, encryption opacity, and congestion control agility for streaming operators.
QUIC.quote: The QUIC protocol, developed from a proprietary protocol into an IETF Standards Track protocol [RFC9000], behaves differently than the transport protocols
QUIC.section: 6.3. QUIC and Changing Transport Protocol Behavior

rejected.why: HTTP is the main delivery vehicle for HLS/DASH but is a substrate here; the document specifies nothing new about HTTP.
TCP behaviour (slow-start restart, head-of-line blocking) is discussed, but as part of the congestion/transport interplay rather than TCP itself being specified or extended.
RTP is mentioned as an unreliable media transport but the document explicitly scopes out real-time interactive media.
Explicitly declared out of scope.
CDNs appear as intermediaries and caches, but are not a subject of the document in their own right.
Caching is discussed in Section 3.4 as a bandwidth provisioning tool, only briefly, with a reference to RFC 9111.

gaps.name: Adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS/DASH/CMAF)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is ABR segmented delivery with HLS and DASH, but the taxonomy has no tag for adaptive streaming formats or protocols, only RTSP, PPSP and IPTV under streaming.

RFC9318.title: IAB Workshop Report: Measuring Network Quality for End-Users
RFC9318.summary: IAB workshop report summarizing the 2021 Measuring Network Quality for End-Users workshop: metrics (availability, capacity, latency/working latency, RPM), cross-layer measurement considerations, synthesis and conclusions.

performance measurement.why: The whole report is about metrics and methods for measuring network performance (latency under load, capacity, availability, RPM) as experienced by end users.
performance measurement.quote: Measuring Network Quality for End-Users workshop aimed to discuss various topics

workshop reports.why: It is an IAB workshop report, which is exactly what this tag covers.
workshop reports.quote: This report summarizes the workshop, the topics discussed, and some preliminary conclusions drawn at the end of the workshop.

rejected.why: QoS and QoE are discussed as context for metrics, but the report does not specify or analyse a QoS architecture or signalling.
CCAs, L4S and bufferbloat come up as factors affecting latency, but only as a side topic in the measurement discussion.
TCP metrics and tcp_info are mentioned as measurement sources, but the document is not about TCP.
QUIC and MASQUE are mentioned only as making passive measurement harder.
Queue management algorithms and home router FIFO queues are mentioned briefly, not as a main subject.
IPv6 appears only in Vint Cerf's keynote remarks on deployment history.

RFC9319.title: The Use of maxLength in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI)
RFC9319.summary: BCP recommending operators use minimal ROAs and avoid the maxLength attribute in RPKI ROAs to reduce forged-origin sub-prefix hijack exposure, with guidance for DDoS mitigation, RTDR filtering, and UI design.

RPKI.why: The whole document is operational guidance on how to issue ROAs and use maxLength in the RPKI, and its effect on route origin validation.
RPKI.quote: this document recommends that, whenever possible, operators SHOULD use "minimal ROAs" that authorize only those IP prefixes that are actually originated in BGP

DDoS.why: Section 5.1 and Section 6 cover ROA creation for DDoS scrubbing-center origination and RTDR blackholing, which readers of DDoS mitigation would want.
DDoS.quote: The document also discusses the creation of ROAs for facilitating the use of DDoS mitigation services.

rejected.why: BGP is the routing protocol whose origination is being validated, but the document is about ROA and RPKI practice, not BGP itself.
Mentioned only as assumed background and as not deployed in the threat scenario; the document does not specify or analyse it.
The RFC 7999 blackhole community is referenced in the RTDR section but only in passing.
Parent of RPKI, which is the more specific tag chosen.

RFC9320.title: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) Bounded Latency
RFC9320.summary: RFC 9320 gives a timing model for DetNet sources, destinations and transit nodes, and a methodology to compute end-to-end latency and backlog bounds for queuing mechanisms (CBS with ATS, CQF, Guaranteed Service, TAS) to achieve bounded latency and zero congestion loss.

DetNet.why: The whole document defines the DetNet bounded-latency model and calculations, so it belongs on the DetNet page.
DetNet.quote: it provides a methodology to compute end-to-end latency and backlog bounds for various queuing methods

QoS.why: A large part of the document analyses queuing and shaping mechanisms (regulators, CBS, CQF, TAS) and Guaranteed Service for delay guarantees. This is QoS content, and the Intserv/Diffserv children don't fit as primary subjects.
QoS.quote: queuing mechanisms that can be used by the management and control planes to provide DetNet qualities of service

rejected.why: Guaranteed Service (RFC 2212) is used as one per-flow queuing example in Section 6.5 only, not specified or extended.
IEEE 802.1Q TSN mechanisms are modelled, but the document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
CQF and TAS depend on synchronized time, but this is mentioned only briefly, mostly in the Security Considerations.
The document computes analytic bounds, not measurement metrics or methods.
Queue management is touched on, but the document concerns scheduling and shaping for deterministic bounds, not active queue management.

gaps.name: TSN / Network calculus
gaps.why: IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking shaping mechanisms and network-calculus delay bounds are central to the document, but the taxonomy has no tag for them.

RFC9321.title: Signature Validation Token
RFC9321.summary: Defines the Signature Validation Token (SVT), a JWT-based assertion by a trusted authority that an electronic signature was validated at a given time, with profiles for XML, PDF and JWS signatures.

JWT.why: The SVT is defined as a set of JWT claims, a JOSE header and a new registered claim (sig_val_claims), so it extends JWT.
JWT.quote: The SVT is carried in a JSON Web Token (JWT) as defined in [RFC7519].

JOSE.why: Defines a new JWS header parameter and a JWS profile for attaching SVTs to JWS signatures, and specifies the SVT JOSE header.
JOSE.quote: The "svt" (Signature Validation Token) Header Parameter is used to contain an array of SVT tokens to support validation of the associated signature.

XML signatures.why: A full profile for embedding SVTs in XML Signature elements and referencing XML signature data.
XML signatures.quote: This appendix defines a profile for implementing SVTs with a signed XML document

LTANS.why: Addresses long-term validation and preservation of signed data through a trusted notary-like validation assertion, complementary to CAdES/XAdES/PAdES.
LTANS.quote: Electronic signatures have a limited lifespan with respect to the time period that they can be validated and determined to be authentic.

CMS.why: The PDF profile defines an SVT extension in RFC 3161 timestamp tokens, which are CMS signed data, and supports CMS signatures.
CMS.quote: The SVT MUST be added to the timestamp token (TSTInfo) as an Extension object as defined in Appendix B.1.1.

rejected.why: Certificates are referenced and validated, but the document defines nothing new about X.509 itself.
Relies on certificate path validation but is not about PKI mechanisms; LTANS fits better.
JSON is only the encoding of the claims.
CDDL is used only for an informative schema.
Registrations are boilerplate.
No media type registration.

gaps.name: PDF signatures / electronic signature validation (XAdES, PAdES, CAdES)
gaps.why: The document is about long-term electronic signature validation evidence and PDF signatures, which have no dedicated taxonomy tag.

RFC9322.title: In Situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM) Loopback and Active Flags
RFC9322.summary: Defines two new flags, Loopback and Active, in the IOAM Pre-allocated and Incremental Trace options, with their processing rules, rate limits and security considerations.

performance measurement.why: The document defines IOAM flags for telemetry and active measurement. Active measurement is as defined in RFC 7799, and it gives use cases for probe packets and replicated data packets. No IOAM-specific tag exists, so this topic fits best.
performance measurement.quote: The Active flag indicates that a packet is used for active measurement.

OAM.why: This is an extension of In situ OAM, an OAM mechanism. It adds Loopback and Active flags to the IOAM trace options.
OAM.quote: IOAM encapsulating node to trace the path to a given destination and to receive per-hop data about both the forward and return paths.

rejected.why: Loopback is described as an accelerated alternative to Traceroute. The document does not specify or extend Traceroute.
IOAM is telemetry in a broad sense, but the document is about flags for loopback and active probing. OAM and performance measurement describe it better.
IPFIX is mentioned only as the export mechanism in the informative reference IOAM-RAWEXPORT, and export is out of scope.
Amplification and DDoS risks appear only in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate for tagging purposes.
IPv6 is mentioned only as an example encapsulation and for source address selection.
The Network Service Header is only an example encapsulation, cited as an informative reference.

gaps.name: IOAM (In situ OAM)
gaps.why: The document is about IOAM trace option flags, and the taxonomy has no IOAM tag. Readers browsing in-band telemetry would expect to find it there.

RFC9323.title: A Profile for RPKI Signed Checklists (RSCs)
RFC9323.summary: Defines the RPKI Signed Checklist (RSC), a CMS signed-object content type carrying a list of filenames and hashes signed with a one-time-use RPKI EE certificate bound to specific Internet Number Resources, plus its validation and verification procedures.

RPKI.why: The document specifies a new RPKI signed object profile, its EE certificate rules, and validation procedure, so it belongs on the RPKI page.
RPKI.quote: an attestation, termed an "RPKI Signed Checklist (RSC)", which contains one or more checksums of arbitrary digital objects (files) that are signed with a specific set of Internet Number Resources

CMS.why: It defines a new CMS eContentType (id-ct-signedChecklist) with an ASN.1 module and OID, which CMS readers would want.
CMS.quote: This document defines a Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) [RFC5652] [RFC6268] protected content type for a general-purpose listing of checksums

rejected.why: ASN.1 is used to define the eContent, but the document is not about ASN.1 itself; it is notation for the profile.
EE certificates and RFC 3779 extensions are used and constrained, but the document does not profile X.509 certificates in its own right.
It registers application/rpki-checklist, but that is IANA boilerplate rather than the subject of the document.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate and do not make the document about IANA registry guidance.
The parent of RPKI would be implied; RSCs are general attestations, not routing security as such. The RPKI tag covers it.
Mentioned only as a suggested compression envelope in the operational considerations.

RFC9324.title: Policy Based on the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) without Route Refresh
RFC9324.summary: Updates RFC 8481 to require BGP speakers doing RPKI-based route origin validation to retain a full Adj-RIB-In or at least ROV-dropped routes, so they need not send route refresh to neighbors when new RPKI data arrive.

RPKI.why: The document specifies how BGP speakers performing RPKI-based route origin validation must handle new RPKI data, updating RFC 8481 on ROV.
RPKI.quote: A BGP speaker performing policy based on the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) should not issue route refresh to its neighbors because it has received new RPKI data.
