BGP.why: It sets BGP speaker behaviour: Adj-RIB-In retention and avoiding route refresh requests to peers, an operational and implementation matter for BGP.
BGP.quote: If an implementation chooses not to retain the full Adj-RIB-In, it MUST retain at least routes dropped due to ROV for potential future evaluation.

rejected.why: IXP route servers are mentioned only briefly in operational recommendations, not the subject.
Mentioned only as a possible future RPKI-based policy; not addressed.
Operational guidance is given but is specific to ROV and BGP, which are covered by more specific tags.
RPKI is the more specific child tag and is already chosen.

RFC9325.title: Recommendations for Secure Use of Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS)
RFC9325.summary: BCP 9325 gives updated recommendations for the secure use of TLS and DTLS (versions, cipher suites, extensions, resumption, key limits, revocation), obsoleting RFC 7525 and updating RFCs 5288 and 6066.

TLS.why: The whole document is deployment and implementation guidance for TLS 1.2/1.3: versions, extensions (SNI, ALPN), resumption, 0-RTT, cipher suites.
TLS.quote: This document provides the latest recommendations for ensuring the security of deployed services that use TLS and DTLS.

DTLS.why: The document gives DTLS-specific version and key-usage-limit recommendations in parallel with TLS, including DTLS 1.3.
DTLS.quote: Implementations MUST support DTLS 1.2 [RFC6347].

rejected.why: Cipher suite and key length guidance is part of the TLS recommendations; the document is not about cryptographic algorithms in their own right.
AES-GCM is recommended and its nonce reuse is discussed, but only as a TLS cipher suite choice.
Revocation and OCSP stapling are one subsection of the security considerations, not a main subject.
HSTS is mentioned as a Strict TLS mechanism but is not specified or extended here.
QUIC is explicitly out of scope; it is mentioned only as a protocol that uses the TLS handshake.
HTTP is one of the application protocols that runs over TLS and is not the subject.

RFC9326.title: In Situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM) Direct Exporting
RFC9326.summary: Defines a new IOAM Option-Type, Direct Export (DEX), which triggers IOAM nodes to collect, aggregate or export telemetry data directly instead of pushing it into in-flight packets, with packet selection, rate limiting and format rules.

telemetry.why: IOAM DEX is an on-path network telemetry mechanism that triggers export and collection of operational data from network nodes. The taxonomy has no IOAM-specific tag, so the telemetry topic fits best.
telemetry.quote: This Option-Type is used as a trigger for IOAM data to be directly exported or locally aggregated without being pushed into in-flight data packets.

OAM.why: IOAM is an OAM mechanism, and the document extends it with a new option type. Readers browsing OAM would expect to find it.
OAM.quote: In situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM) is used for recording and collecting operational and telemetry information.

rejected.why: IPFIX is only mentioned in a referenced draft as one possible export format. The export format is explicitly out of scope.
The document concerns triggering telemetry export. It does not define performance metrics or measurement methods, even though it comes from the IPPM working group.
IPv6 options are only an example of an encapsulation. The document does not specify them.
The IANA registries it creates are boilerplate-level apparatus. The main body is not about IANA guidance.

gaps.name: IOAM (In situ OAM)
gaps.why: The document is about the IOAM Direct Export option type, but the taxonomy has no IOAM tag. The closest tags are telemetry and OAM.

RFC9327.title: Control Messages Protocol for Use with Network Time Protocol Version 4
RFC9327.summary: Historic RFC documenting the NTP mode 6 control message format (and mode 7 remote facility format), status words, and commands used to monitor and control NTP daemons, carried over RFC 1305 for use with NTPv4.

NTP.why: The document specifies NTP control messages (mode 6) and the mode 7 remote facility format, extending NTP's management interface. NTP readers would want it.
NTP.quote: The NTP mode 6 control messages are used by NTP management programs (e.g., ntpq) when a more robust network management facility (e.g., SNMP) is not available.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as the more robust alternative that these control messages stand in for; the document does not specify or analyse SNMP.
The messages ride directly after the UDP header, but UDP is just the substrate.
The Security Considerations discuss NTP amplification via mode 7 monlist, but that is boilerplate-section material and not the main subject of the document.
The messages serve as a management interface, but the NTP tag is the specific fit and the document is about the NTP protocol's control messages, not management architecture.

RFC9328.title: RTP Payload Format for Versatile Video Coding (VVC)
RFC9328.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for Versatile Video Coding (VVC, H.266): NAL unit packetization (single, aggregation, fragmentation), de-packetization, the video/H266 media type with SDP parameters and offer/answer rules, and use of PLI/FIR feedback.

RTP payload format.why: The document's core purpose is a new RTP payload format for a video codec, including packet structures and de-packetization.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo describes an RTP payload format for the Versatile Video Coding (VVC) specification

SDP.why: A large part of the document defines SDP mapping of the H266 parameters and offer/answer, declarative usage and multicast rules.
SDP.quote: media type parameters to be used with the Session Description Protocol (SDP) [RFC8866]

codecs.why: The document includes an overview of the VVC codec, and no specific VVC tag exists, so the codecs parent fits.
codecs.quote: VVC is reported to provide significant coding efficiency gains over High Efficiency Video Coding [HEVC]

RTCP.why: Specifies how RTCP feedback messages (PLI, FIR, SLI, RPSI) are used with VVC.
RTCP.quote: The following subsections define the use of the Picture Loss Indication (PLI) and Full Intra Request (FIR) feedback messages

rejected.why: HEVC is only the predecessor codec used for comparison; the document is about VVC.
It registers one media type (video/H266), but this is incidental to the payload format rather than about media type registry rules.
SRTP is only mentioned in security considerations as an applicable profile.
The congestion control section is brief boilerplate deferring to RTP.
AVC/H.264 RTP format is only cited as a design ancestor.

gaps.name: Versatile Video Coding (VVC / H.266)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has codec tags for H.264 and HEVC but none for VVC; a VVC codec tag would fit this document.

RFC9329.title: TCP Encapsulation of Internet Key Exchange Protocol (IKE) and IPsec Packets
RFC9329.summary: RFC 9329 specifies how to carry IKEv2 and ESP packets over a TCP connection (port 4500, "IKETCP" stream prefix) as a fallback when UDP is blocked, obsoleting RFC 8229 with clarifications on retransmission, cookies/puzzles, MOBIKE interaction and TLS use.

IKE.why: The document specifies IKE message framing over TCP, with detailed handling of retransmissions, cookies and puzzles, IKE_SA_INIT errors and NAT detection payloads.
IKE.quote: This document describes a method to transport Internet Key Exchange Protocol (IKE) and IPsec packets over a TCP connection

ESP.why: The document defines the encapsulation format of ESP packets in a TCP stream and its effects on IPsec SA processing, such as the DF bit and DSCP.
ESP.quote: involves sending both IKE packets for Security Association (SA) establishment and Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) packets over a TCP connection

MOBIKE.why: A substantial section and an appendix example cover how MOBIKE switches between UDP and TCP encapsulation.
MOBIKE.quote: When a MOBIKE-enabled Initiator changes networks, the INFORMATIONAL exchange with the UPDATE_SA_ADDRESSES notification SHOULD be initiated first over UDP before attempting over TCP.

rejected.why: TCP is only the transport substrate. The document defines no new TCP behaviour and only discusses TCP-in-TCP performance.
TLS is an optional framing layer described in an appendix. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
NAT traversal is a motivation, and the NAT detection payloads are IKE mechanics. The document does not address NAT behaviour itself.
IKE is a more specific child tag and it fits. The document covers the IKE and ESP encapsulation rather than the IPsec architecture.
UDP is the default transport that this document falls back from. It is not specified or extended here.
Tunneling ECN gets only a short subsection of performance considerations, which is not enough to make the document about ECN.

RFC9330.title: Low Latency, Low Loss, and Scalable Throughput (L4S) Internet Service: Architecture
RFC9330.summary: Describes the L4S architecture, which combines Scalable congestion controls, ECN-based signalling with ECT(1) as identifier, and Dual-Queue Coupled AQM in the network to give low queuing latency, low loss and scalable throughput, with incremental deployment guidance.

congestion control.why: The document's core subject is a new class of Scalable congestion controls (Prague, DCTCP, SCReAM) and how they coexist with Classic ones. It is not about one specific controller.
congestion control.quote: the root cause of queuing delay is in the capacity-seeking congestion controllers of senders, not in the queue itself

ECN.why: L4S redefines ECN semantics (ECT(1) identifier, CE marking not equivalent to drop). The document describes and justifies this ECN usage.
ECN.quote: It uses the Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) protocol, but it signals the very start of queue growth immediately

AQM.why: A major architectural component is the network AQM: the DualQ Coupled AQM and the per-flow FQ-CoDel alternatives.
AQM.quote: The Dual-Queue Coupled AQM was developed as a minimal complexity solution to this problem.

rejected.why: TCP and AccECN feedback are discussed as host transports, but the document is not about TCP itself.
Diffserv is compared with L4S and mentioned for NQB/EF identifiers, but it is not the subject.
DCTCP is the example Scalable control, but no DCTCP tag exists. The congestion control tag covers this.
QUIC is only one transport that could carry L4S congestion control and has native fine-grained ECN feedback. The document is not about QUIC.
QoS is discussed in comparison, but L4S addresses only queuing latency, not QoS architectures or signalling.
FQ-CoDel is mentioned as one per-flow option, but the CoDel algorithm itself is not specified or analysed.

gaps.name: L4S (Low Latency, Low Loss, Scalable throughput)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the L4S architecture itself, so readers browsing for it must find it under congestion control, ECN and AQM.

RFC9331.title: The Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) Protocol for Low Latency, Low Loss, and Scalable Throughput (L4S)
RFC9331.summary: RFC 9331 defines the L4S ECN protocol: use of the ECT(1)/CE codepoints to identify L4S traffic, the Prague requirements for Scalable congestion control transports, and the marking behaviour for network nodes (AQM), as an Experimental service.

ECN.why: The document defines an experimental ECN variant, using ECT(1) as the L4S identifier and specifying new marking and response semantics.
ECN.quote: L4S uses an Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) scheme at the IP layer that is similar to the original (or 'Classic') ECN approach

congestion control.why: The Prague L4S Requirements for Scalable congestion control are a substantial part of the document. This is the general congestion-control topic, with no more specific child tag.
congestion control.quote: it SHOULD implement a congestion control behaviour that ensures that, in steady state, the average duration between induced ECN marks does not increase as flow rate scales up

AQM.why: The document specifies how L4S AQMs classify and mark packets, including the coupling between L4S and Classic signals, and how they combine with other identifiers.
AQM.quote: the likelihood that the AQM drops a Not-ECT Classic packet (p_C) MUST be roughly proportional to the square of the likelihood

rejected.why: TCP is one example transport. The document is about the IP-layer identifier and the congestion response across transports.
QUIC is mentioned only as a transport that already gives sufficient ECN feedback.
Diffserv interaction is discussed as a complementary identifier, but the document is not about Diffserv.
DCTCP is cited as the origin of Scalable congestion control, and the document does not specify it.
IPsec and DTLS VPN anti-replay is a side issue in Section 6.2 and does not make the document about IPsec.

gaps.name: L4S (Low Latency, Low Loss, Scalable throughput)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the L4S service, which spans several RFCs (the architecture, DualQ and this identifier spec). The ECN, congestion control and AQM tags cover it only partly.

RFC9332.title: Dual-Queue Coupled Active Queue Management (AQM) for Low Latency, Low Loss, and Scalable Throughput (L4S)
RFC9332.summary: Defines the Dual-Queue Coupled AQM framework for L4S, coupling a Classic and an L4S queue so Scalable ECN-based flows get low latency and share capacity fairly with Classic flows, with normative requirements and example DualPI2 and Curvy RED algorithms.

AQM.why: The document specifies a DualQ Coupled AQM framework with normative requirements and example AQM algorithms (DualPI2, Curvy RED).
AQM.quote: This specification defines a framework for coupling the Active Queue Management (AQM) algorithms in two queues intended for flows with different responses to congestion.

ECN.why: L4S relies on ECN marking with the ECT(1)/CE identifier and distinct marking probabilities for L4S versus Classic. The document specifies how the network applies and couples ECN marking.
ECN.quote: The AQM algorithm for the low-latency (L) queue MUST be able to apply ECN marking to ECN-capable packets.

rejected.why: DCTCP is discussed as a Scalable congestion control example, but the document is about the network-side AQM, and no DCTCP tag exists anyway.
PIE is mentioned only as a related AQM; no such tag exists, and PI2 is a variant used in the appendix.
The document concerns end-system congestion controls only as context; the AQM tag is more specific.
Diffserv EF and NQB are mentioned only as comparison and optional classifiers.
Reno and CUBIC are referenced as Classic congestion controls, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
DOCSIS is cited as an example deployment and reference, not the subject of this document.

gaps.name: L4S (Low Latency, Low Loss, Scalable throughput)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no L4S tag, although this RFC is a core part of the L4S family (RFC 9330/9331/9332); it is best covered by AQM and ECN.

RFC9333.title: Minimal IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)
RFC9333.summary: Informational guidance on the minimal properties an ESP implementation must meet to interoperate with RFC 4303 ESP, with advice for constrained IoT devices on SPI, sequence number, padding, dummy packets, ICV and cipher choices.

ESP.why: The document walks through each ESP field (SPI, SN, padding, next header, ICV) giving minimal-implementation guidance, so it is about ESP itself.
ESP.quote: This document describes the minimal properties that an IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) implementation needs to meet to remain interoperable with the standard ESP as defined in RFC 4303.

rejected.why: IKEv2 and minimal IKEv2 are mentioned as the SA negotiation mechanism, but the document does not specify or extend them.
Constrained devices are the target audience, but the document is about ESP implementation; the ESP tag fits better.
A parent of ESP, so it is implied by the ESP tag.
AES modes are mentioned only as examples when choosing cipher suites. The document defers to RFC 8221 for algorithm recommendations.
Random generation is discussed only for SPI generation and cites RFC 4086. The document is not about randomness requirements.
Privacy implications of non-random SPIs and padding are discussed, but they are a side concern of ESP minimalism, not the document's subject.

RFC9334.title: Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS) Architecture
RFC9334.summary: RFC 9334 defines the RATS architecture for remote attestation: roles (Attester, Verifier, Relying Party, etc.), conceptual messages (Evidence, Endorsements, Reference Values, Attestation Results), topological patterns (Passport, Background-Check), trust model and freshness mechanisms.

remote attestation.why: The whole document is the architecture for remote attestation: Attester, Verifier and Relying Party roles, Evidence and Attestation Results, freshness and trust models.
remote attestation.quote: This document provides an architectural overview of the entities involved that make such tests possible through the process of generating, conveying, and evaluating evidentiary Claims.

rejected.why: TEEP provisioning appears only as one reference use case (Section 2.5); the document does not specify TEEP.
Network Endpoint Assessment is a use case and is mentioned once in Section 8.2 with a reference to RFC 5209; the document does not specify NEA.
JWT and CWT are listed as possible claims encodings in Section 9; the document does not define them.
X.509 certificates are mentioned as a possible carrier for Evidence and as trust anchors; the document does not profile them.
FIDO and WebAuthn appear only as a use case in Section 2.7.
This is a parent topic. A more specific tag should be chosen where one fits.

gaps.name: Remote attestation (RATS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has `remote attestation` as a tag under security, but it was not shown in the visible list. If it exists, it is the right primary tag. If it does not, the document has no fitting tag for remote attestation architecture, trust models and freshness.

RFC9335.title: Completely Encrypting RTP Header Extensions and Contributing Sources
RFC9335.summary: RFC 9335 defines Cryptex, an update to SRTP that encrypts RTP header extensions (ids, lengths, values) and CSRCs, negotiated with a new SDP a=cryptex attribute and with test vectors for AES-CTR and AES-GCM.

SRTP.why: The document updates RFC 3711 and changes the SRTP encrypted portion and encryption/decryption procedure to cover header extensions and CSRCs.
SRTP.quote: defines Cryptex as a new mechanism that completely encrypts header extensions and CSRCs

SDP.why: Defines a new SDP attribute with offer/answer and BUNDLE rules, and registers it with IANA. Readers of SDP would want it.
SDP.quote: Cryptex support is indicated via a new "a=cryptex" SDP attribute defined in this specification.

rejected.why: RTP header extensions are the subject matter, but the document's contribution is the SRTP encryption transform, so the more specific SRTP tag fits better.
AES-CTR and AES-GCM are only used for the test vectors and the existing SRTP cipher suites. The document defines nothing new about AES.
DTLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as the alternative when more of the header must be encrypted.
Privacy and fingerprinting motivate the work, but the document specifies a mechanism and is not a privacy threat analysis.

RFC9336.title: X.509 Certificate General-Purpose Extended Key Usage (EKU) for Document Signing
RFC9336.summary: Defines the id-kp-documentSigning KeyPurposeId for the X.509 Extended Key Usage extension, so certificates can be marked for signing human-consumed documents, and describes how relying parties and CAs use it.

X.509.why: The document extends the X.509 certificate profile with a new EKU KeyPurposeId and gives validation and CA guidance for it. Readers of X.509 certificates and profiles would want it.
X.509.quote: This document defines a general-purpose Document-Signing KeyPurposeId for inclusion in the Extended Key Usage (EKU) extension of X.509 public key certificates.

rejected.why: The ASN.1 module is only the formal definition of one OID. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
id-kp-emailProtection is discussed only as the existing practice this document avoids. The document does not specify or extend S/MIME.
The parent tag is implied by X.509. The document is specifically about an X.509 certificate extension value.
The OID registrations are boilerplate IANA Considerations. The document is not about IANA registry policy.
id-kp-clientAuth and TLS are mentioned only in the Security Considerations, as protocols to keep separate from document signing.

RFC9337.title: Generating Password-Based Keys Using the GOST Algorithms
RFC9337.summary: Specifies how to use PKCS #5 (PBKDF2, PBES2, PBMAC1) with the Russian GOST R 34.11-2012 HMAC and GOST R 34.12-2015 Kuznyechik/Magma ciphers to derive keys from passwords, with ASN.1 identifiers and test vectors.

GOST.why: The document profiles GOST R 34.11-2012 and GOST R 34.12-2015 (Kuznyechik, Magma) for password-based key derivation, encryption and MAC.
GOST.quote: in conjunction with the Russian national standard GOST algorithms

PBKDF2.why: The core of the document is PBKDF2 with HMAC_GOSTR3411 as the PRF, including OIDs, parameters and test vectors.
PBKDF2.quote: The DK is calculated by means of a key derivation function PBKDF2 (P, S, c, dkLen)
PBKDF2.section: 4. Algorithm for Generating a Key from a Password

rejected.why: HMAC is used as the PRF building block, but the document is not about HMAC itself.
The parent of PBKDF2; the more specific child tag is chosen.
ASN.1 is only used to express identifiers and parameter structures, not the subject of the document.
Not used; the ciphers are GOST Kuznyechik and Magma.
Password-based key derivation is covered by the more specific PBKDF2 tag.

RFC9338.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Countersignatures
RFC9338.summary: Defines the version 2 COSE countersignature algorithm, with the new header parameters (labels 11 and 12) and CBOR tag 19, replacing the flawed countersignature text removed from RFC 9052.

COSE.why: The whole document specifies countersignatures for COSE structures, updating RFC 9052, so COSE is the subject.
COSE.quote: This document defines a countersignature algorithm along with the needed header parameters and CBOR tags for COSE.

rejected.why: CBOR is the encoding substrate for COSE structures. The document only registers a CBOR tag and uses deterministic encoding, and does not specify CBOR itself.
CDDL is used only as the notation for the structures, so the document is not about it.
Group OSCORE is mentioned only as an example of a user of countersignatures.
ECDSA and EdDSA appear only as algorithms in the examples.
The IANA section registers a CBOR tag and header parameters. That is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.

RFC9339.title: OSPF Reverse Metric
RFC9339.summary: Specifies OSPF Link-Local Signaling TLVs (Reverse Metric and Reverse TE Metric) that let a router tell its neighbor which metric to advertise for the link toward it, for link maintenance and adaptive metric use cases.

OSPF.why: The document defines new OSPF LLS TLVs and procedures for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 Router-LSA and TE metric handling, so it is squarely about OSPF.
OSPF.quote: This document specifies the extensions to OSPF that enable a router to use Link-Local Signaling (LLS) to signal the metric that receiving OSPF neighbor(s) should use

rejected.why: The Reverse TE Metric TLV touches TE metrics, but this is a minor part of an OSPF extension; the document is not about TE as a subject.
The mechanism applies to both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 generally and is not specific to OSPFv3; the parent OSPF tag fits better.
RFC 8500 is only cited as the IS-IS precursor concept; the document does not address IS-IS.
YANG is mentioned only to note that the base OSPF model will be augmented; the document defines no YANG module.
The IANA section merely registers two TLV code points, which is boilerplate.

RFC9340.title: Architectural Principles for a Quantum Internet
RFC9340.summary: An IRTF QIRG informational RFC introducing quantum information concepts and laying out architectural goals and principles for a quantum internet based on entanglement distribution, Bell pairs and swapping repeaters.

internet architecture.why: The document's purpose is architectural principles, goals and an abstract network model for a quantum internet, analogous to RFC 1958 for the classical Internet.
internet architecture.quote: we attempt to lay down the framework and introduce some basic architectural principles for a quantum internet

rejected.why: Used only as an analogy in the Section 7 thought experiment, not specified or extended.
Security is one stated goal, but the document proposes no mechanism. QKD is discussed as an application only.
Discussed only as an analogy to MPLS TE in the thought experiment.
Quantum routing is mentioned briefly but is not a main subject.
OpenFlow is mentioned only in passing as an analogy for centralised signalling.

gaps.name: quantum networking / quantum internet
gaps.why: The whole document concerns quantum networks (entanglement distribution, quantum repeaters, QKD), and the taxonomy has no quantum tag.

RFC9341.title: Alternate-Marking Method
RFC9341.summary: Specifies the Alternate-Marking Method, which colors packets in alternating blocks to measure packet loss, delay and jitter on live traffic, and obsoletes the experimental RFC 8321.

performance measurement.why: The whole document defines a passive/hybrid method of measurement for IPPM performance metrics (loss, delay, delay variation), and includes RFC 6390 compliance.
performance measurement.quote: This document describes the Alternate-Marking technique to perform packet loss, delay, and jitter measurements on live traffic.

rejected.why: The method is OAM-like, but the document is framed as performance measurement; the performance measurement tag fits more specifically.
NTP is only cited as a possible clock synchronization source, not specified or extended.
IEEE 1588 PTP is only mentioned as a possible time synchronization mechanism.
TWAMP and OWAMP are only mentioned as protocols that could be extended to carry counters; the document does not specify this.
The method is measurement of live traffic, not streaming operational data from network elements, and data collection transport is out of scope.
Section 5 covers synchronization and timing requirements, but only as a prerequisite of the measurement method, not as a subject in its own right.

RFC9342.title: Clustered Alternate-Marking Method
RFC9342.summary: Standards-track RFC that obsoletes RFC 8889 and extends the Alternate-Marking performance measurement method to multipoint-to-multipoint unicast flows via network clustering, covering packet loss, delay, and delay variation measurement.

performance measurement.why: The document specifies a passive/hybrid method for measuring packet loss, delay and delay variation across multipoint networks. Performance measurement is the subject, and no specific child tag fits.
performance measurement.quote: This document generalizes and expands the Alternate-Marking methodology to measure any kind of unicast flow whose packets can follow several different paths in the network

rejected.why: RFC 7011 is cited only as inspiration for the flow definition. The document does not specify or extend IPFIX.
SDN controllers and orchestrators are mentioned as users of the method, but the document is not about SDN.
ECMP paths are said to be monitorable with the method, but this is one applicability note, not a subject of the document.
The method is a performance measurement technique. The document does not frame it as an OAM mechanism, so performance measurement is the better fit.
Telemetry is only touched on through the referenced iFIT framework. The document is a measurement methodology and leaves counter transport out of scope.

gaps.name: Alternate-Marking Method
gaps.why: The document extends a specific passive/hybrid packet-marking measurement method (RFC 9341). The taxonomy has no tag for it, so the broader performance measurement tag is used.

RFC9343.title: IPv6 Application of the Alternate-Marking Method
RFC9343.summary: Defines the AltMark IPv6 Hop-by-Hop/Destination Option carrying Alternate-Marking bits (L, D) and a FlowMonID so the passive Alternate-Marking method can measure packet loss, delay and jitter in a controlled IPv6 domain.

performance measurement.why: The document applies a passive packet loss, delay and jitter measurement method and specifies its operation, so it belongs under performance measurement.
performance measurement.quote: describes how the Alternate-Marking Method can be used as a passive performance measurement tool in an IPv6 domain

IPv6.why: It defines a new IPv6 extension header option (AltMark), with IANA allocation in the IPv6 options registry, and discusses Flow Label and extension header processing.
IPv6.quote: It defines an Extension Header Option to encode Alternate-Marking information in both the Hop-by-Hop Options Header and Destination Options Header.

rejected.why: The option is motivated by OAM, but performance measurement is the more specific tag for the document's subject.
The document calls Alternate Marking an on-path telemetry technique, but it is mainly about the measurement method and the IPv6 option.
SRH and SRv6 are mentioned only as an example of a Routing Header. The SRv6 encapsulation is left to another draft.
Time synchronization is a prerequisite and a security remark, not a subject of the document.
IPsec is only suggested for securing inter-domain links.
ECMP appears only in the discussion of Flow Label use and of clustered marking.

RFC9344.title: CCNinfo: Discovering Content and Network Information in Content-Centric Networks
RFC9344.summary: Specifies CCNinfo, an experimental traceroute-like tool for CCNx content-centric networks that discovers per-name-prefix routing paths, RTT, and in-network cache state via Request/Reply messages encoded in CCNx TLV.

ICN.why: The document defines a new protocol for Content-Centric Networking (CCNx), an ICN architecture, covering Request/Reply messages, PIT handling, and cache reporting.
ICN.quote: CCNinfo defines the protocol messages to investigate path and in-network cache conditions in CCN.

traceroute.why: CCNinfo is a traceroute-like path discovery tool for CCN, and the document positions it against IP traceroute and ICN traceroute.
traceroute.quote: IP traceroute is a useful tool for discovering the routing conditions in IP networks

OAM.why: The document is an operations and diagnostic mechanism for troubleshooting and measuring RTT, path stretch and cache hit probability. This fits OAM and path diagnostics.
OAM.quote: CCNinfo is useful to understand and debug the behavior of testbed networks and other experimental deployments of CCN systems.

rejected.why: It reports RTT and cache statistics, but the main purpose is path and cache discovery and debugging, not a performance measurement framework.
Not used or discussed; irrelevant.
The IANA section registers CCNx type values, but this is boilerplate relative to the document's subject.
The multicast traceroute RFC 8487 is only cited as a similar flow; the document is not about IP multicast.
The parent topic is implied by narrower tags and the document's diagnostic focus is already captured by OAM and traceroute.

gaps.name: Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) in-network cache and forwarding messages
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only the generic ICN tag. A dedicated CCNx tag would group RFC 8569, RFC 8609 and CCNinfo.

RFC9345.title: Delegated Credentials for TLS and DTLS
RFC9345.summary: Specifies Delegated Credentials, a TLS/DTLS 1.3 extension letting a server or client use a short-lived credential signed by its end-entity certificate, plus a new X.509 DelegationUsage extension.

TLS.why: Defines a new TLS extension and handshake behaviour for (D)TLS 1.3 server and client authentication, which is exactly the TLS extension case. DTLS is covered by the parent tag as it is a co-equal subject, and the DTLS-specific behaviour is identical.
TLS.quote: A client that is willing to use delegated credentials in a connection SHALL send a "delegated_credential" extension in its ClientHello.

X.509.why: Defines a new X.509 certificate extension, with an ASN.1 module and certificate requirements, that readers of X.509 profiles would want.
X.509.quote: This document defines a new X.509 extension, DelegationUsage, to be used in the certificate when the certificate permits the usage of delegated credentials.

rejected.why: The document covers DTLS equally with TLS but with no DTLS-specific mechanism; the TLS tag covers it. DTLS could be added as a secondary tag if the index wants DTLS pages to list it.
ASN.1 is used only to define the DelegationUsage extension module, which is a supporting encoding for the X.509 extension.
Mentioned only as a possible way to provision delegated credentials, not specified or profiled.
CDNs are only the motivating deployment setting for TLS termination, and the document does not address CDN operation.
Ed25519 is cited only as an example of a modern algorithm that delegation would allow.
The document works within the existing PKI and deliberately requires no PKI changes. Its X.509 extension is covered by the X.509 tag.

RFC9346.title: IS-IS Extensions in Support of Inter-Autonomous System (AS) MPLS and GMPLS Traffic Engineering
RFC9346.summary: Defines IS-IS extensions (Inter-AS Reachability Information TLV 141 and related sub-TLVs, plus TE Router ID sub-TLVs in the Router CAPABILITY TLV) for flooding inter-AS TE link information, adding IPv6-only support and obsoleting RFC 5316.

IS-IS.why: The document specifies new IS-IS TLVs and sub-TLVs and their flooding procedures.
IS-IS.quote: This document describes extensions to the Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) protocol to support Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) Traffic Engineering

traffic engineering.why: The purpose is to advertise inter-AS TE link information for MPLS/GMPLS TE path computation, including per-domain and BRPC/PCE scenarios.
traffic engineering.quote: It defines IS-IS extensions for the flooding of TE information about inter-AS links, which can be used to perform inter-AS TE path computation.

rejected.why: BGP is mentioned only as a possible source of configuration data and for checking misconfiguration, not specified or extended.
PCE and BRPC are used as motivating scenarios, but the document explicitly makes no change to PCE architecture or usage.
GMPLS is named in the title, but the document defines no GMPLS-specific mechanism, only IS-IS TE advertisement.
MPLS LSPs are the use case, but the document is about IS-IS advertisement, not MPLS operation.
RSVP-TE Path messages and the ERO are only cited as context for the problem statement.
IPv6-only support is added to the IS-IS TLVs, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC9347.title: Aggregation and Fragmentation Mode for Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and Its Use for IP Traffic Flow Security (IP-TFS)
RFC9347.summary: Defines an aggregation and fragmentation (AGGFRAG) payload mode for ESP, used for IP Traffic Flow Security (IP-TFS) with constant-rate fixed-size tunnel packets, optional congestion control, and an IKEv2 USE_AGGFRAG negotiation.

ESP.why: The document defines a new ESP Next Header payload type (AGGFRAG_PAYLOAD) and its processing. It is an extension of ESP.
ESP.quote: This document defines an aggregation and fragmentation (AGGFRAG) mode for ESP, as well as ESP's use for IP Traffic Flow Security (IP-TFS).

IKE.why: It defines a new IKEv2 notify message type and its negotiation for Child SAs, which IKE readers need.
IKE.quote: a new "USE_AGGFRAG" notification message enables the AGGFRAG_PAYLOAD payload on a Child SA pair.

congestion control.why: A substantial part of the document covers congestion-controlled mode, congestion information fields, TFRC-based rate calculation and circuit breakers. No more specific technology tag fits, since TFRC and ECN are only used.
congestion control.quote: IP-TFS adapts to network congestion by lowering the packet send rate to accommodate the congestion, as well as raising the rate when congestion subsides.

rejected.why: The document is about ESP and IKEv2 specifically, and those are the more specific tags. IPsec architecture is only background.
The document uses RFC 5348 rate control as a recommended algorithm but does not specify or extend it.
ECN handling is a small subsection on how to map and use ECN bits. The document is not about ECN.
Traffic flow confidentiality is the goal, but the document specifies a mechanism and is not a privacy threat-model document.
PMTUD and PLMTUD are mentioned as ways to pick the packet size and are not specified here.
The YANG and MIB documents are only referenced and are separate RFCs.

gaps.name: Traffic flow confidentiality (IP-TFS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for traffic analysis resistance or traffic flow confidentiality. This is the document's central motivation.

RFC9348.title: A YANG Data Model for IP Traffic Flow Security
RFC9348.summary: Defines the ietf-ipsec-iptfs YANG module, augmenting the RFC 9061 IPsec IKE and IKE-less models to configure and monitor IP Traffic Flow Security (IP-TFS) on IPsec tunnel SAs.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module with tree diagram, configuration and operational/statistics data, so it belongs under YANG data models.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG module [RFC7950] for the management of the IP Traffic Flow Security (IP-TFS) extensions defined in [RFC9347].

IPsec.why: The module manages IPsec tunnel-mode SAs, SPD and SAD entries with IP-TFS additions, so IPsec readers would want this document.
IPsec.quote: The IP-TFS YANG module augments the IPsec YANG module from [RFC9061].

rejected.why: IKEv2 is only the context; the module augments the IKE and IKE-less models from RFC 9061 but does not specify or extend IKE itself.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in Security Considerations as access mechanisms for the module.
ESP aggregation and fragmentation are defined in RFC 9347; this document only manages them via YANG.
A congestion-control boolean is configured and references RFC 5348, but the document is not about congestion control itself.
TLS appears only as the secure transport mentioned in Security Considerations.

RFC9349.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for IP Traffic Flow Security
RFC9349.summary: Defines a read-only SNMP MIB module (IP-TRAFFIC-FLOW-SECURITY-MIB) exposing configuration and statistics of IP-TFS (IPsec ESP aggregation/fragmentation mode), derived from the RFC 9348 YANG model.

MIB.why: The document's core content is an SMIv2 MIB module with tables, objects and conformance groups for IP-TFS.
MIB.quote: This document defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for use with network management protocols in the Internet community.

IPsec.why: The MIB manages IP-TFS, an enhancement to IPsec tunnel-mode SAs, and exposes IPsec SA statistics, so IPsec readers would want it.
IPsec.quote: managed objects for the management of IP Traffic Flow Security additions to Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) and IPsec.

rejected.why: SNMP is the access mechanism; the document defines a MIB module and tags the more specific MIB child.
The YANG model (RFC 9348) is a reference point only; this document defines no YANG.
ESP aggregation/fragmentation mode is specified in RFC 9347, not here; ESP is only the managed subject.
RFC 5348 is only referenced in a congestion control object description.
IKEv2 is mentioned in the abstract, but no IKE objects or behaviour are defined.

gaps.name: IP Traffic Flow Security (IP-TFS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IP-TFS, the ESP aggregation/fragmentation mode for traffic confidentiality, which is the subject of this MIB.

RFC9350.title: IGP Flexible Algorithm
RFC9350.summary: RFC 9350 specifies IGP Flexible Algorithm: IS-IS and OSPF extensions to advertise Flexible Algorithm Definitions (metric type, constraints), participation, and prefix/ASBR metrics so IGPs compute constraint-based paths, used with SR-MPLS Prefix-SIDs and SRv6 locators.

IS-IS.why: Defines the IS-IS FAD sub-TLV, sub-sub-TLVs, and FAPM sub-TLV, plus IS-IS-specific procedures.
IS-IS.quote: This document specifies a set of extensions to IS-IS, OSPFv2, and OSPFv3 that enable a router to advertise TLVs

OSPF.why: Defines the OSPF FAD TLV, sub-TLVs, FAPM, the EIA-ASBR LSA and FAAM for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.
OSPF.quote: The OSPF FAD TLV is advertised as a top-level TLV of the Router Information (RI) Link State Advertisement (LSA)

segment routing.why: Flex-Algorithm is tied to SR Prefix-SIDs and SRv6 locators, with forwarding procedures for both data planes.
segment routing.quote: specifies a way of using Segment Routing (SR) Prefix-SIDs and SRv6 locators to steer packets along the constraint-based paths

rejected.why: Motivated by RSVP-TE/SR-TE, but the document defines IGP-computed constrained paths, not a TE architecture.
Only the forwarding section and locator algorithm association touch SRv6; the SRv6 encoding is defined in RFC 9352.
Only Prefix-SID association and forwarding are covered; SR-MPLS itself is defined elsewhere, so the parent tag fits better.
LFA constraints for Flex-Algorithm are mentioned briefly, but are not a substantial part of the document.

RFC9351.title: Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS) Extensions for Flexible Algorithm Advertisement
RFC9351.summary: Defines BGP-LS extensions (new TLVs and sub-TLVs) to advertise IGP Flexible Algorithm Definitions and Flexible Algorithm Prefix Metrics in the BGP-LS address family.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP-LS (a BGP address family) with new Node and Prefix attribute TLVs. No BGP-LS-specific tag exists, so BGP is the closest fit.
BGP.quote: This document defines extensions to the BGP-LS address family to advertise the FAD as a part of the topology information from the network.

segment routing.why: The FAD information supports SR Policy path construction with Flex-Algo SIDs (SR-MPLS and SRv6). This is a substantial motivation for the document, though the extensions themselves are not SR-specific.
segment routing.quote: This information can then be used for setting up SR Policy paths end to end across domains by using the appropriate Flexible-Algorithm-specific SIDs

rejected.why: OSPF is the source of the advertised information (FAD, FAPM). The document defines no OSPF extensions.
IS-IS is the source of the advertised information. The document defines no IS-IS extensions.
Affinities and SRLG constraints are used, but the document is about advertising the FAD, not about traffic engineering.
RSVP-TE is mentioned only in the introduction as background.
SR-MPLS is referenced as the context for SIDs. The document defines no SR-MPLS mechanisms.

gaps.name: BGP-LS (BGP Link State) / IGP Flexible Algorithm
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for BGP-LS or for IGP Flexible Algorithm. Both are central to this document and its siblings (RFC 7752, 9085, 9294, 9350).

RFC9352.title: IS-IS Extensions to Support Segment Routing over the IPv6 Data Plane
RFC9352.summary: Defines IS-IS extensions (SRv6 Locator TLV, SRv6 Capabilities, End/End.X/LAN End.X SID sub-TLVs, SID Structure, MSD types, anycast flag) to advertise Segment Routing over IPv6 information.

SRv6.why: The document specifies how SRv6 SIDs, locators and endpoint behaviors are advertised, so SRv6 readers need it.
SRv6.quote: This document describes the IS-IS extensions required to support SR over the IPv6 data plane.

IS-IS.why: It defines new IS-IS TLVs, sub-TLVs and registries, and updates RFC 7370.
IS-IS.quote: This document specifies IS-IS extensions that allow the IS-IS protocol to encode some of these SIDs and their behaviors.

rejected.why: The parent is implied by the more specific SRv6 tag.
IPv6 is only the data plane over which SRv6 runs; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
The anycast A-flag is a small part of the document, not its subject.
IANA registry updates are boilerplate-like and not the main subject.
BGP-LS is only mentioned in passing.
IPFRR is mentioned only in the B-flag description.

RFC9353.title: IGP Extension for Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Security Capability Support in PCE Discovery (PCED)
RFC9353.summary: Defines two PCE-CAP-FLAGS bits (TCP-AO support, PCEP over TLS support) and new KEY-ID and KEY-CHAIN-NAME sub-TLVs so a PCE can advertise PCEP security capabilities via OSPF and IS-IS PCE Discovery, updating RFCs 5088, 5089, 8231 and 8306.

PCE.why: The document extends PCE Discovery and PCEP security capability advertisement, and updates several PCE RFCs. Readers of PCE and PCEP material need it.
PCE.quote: This document defines two capability flag bits in the OSPF PCE Capability Flags to indicate TCP-AO support [RFC5925] [RFC5926] and PCEP over TLS support

OSPF.why: It specifies OSPF encodings for the new flag bits and for the KEY-ID and KEY-CHAIN-NAME sub-TLVs in the Router Information LSA, and updates RFC 5088.
OSPF.quote: [RFC5088] defines a PCE Discovery (PCED) TLV carried in an OSPF Router Information Link State Advertisement (LSA)

IS-IS.why: It specifies IS-IS encodings for the new sub-TLVs in the Router CAPABILITY TLV, and updates RFC 5089.
IS-IS.quote: The KEY-ID sub-TLV MAY be present in the PCED sub-TLV carried within the IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV

rejected.why: PCEP over TLS is only a capability being advertised. The document defines nothing new about TLS itself.
TCP-AO support and key identifiers are advertised in the IGP. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
The registry changes are boilerplate that supports the protocol extension. The document's main body is not about IANA stewardship.
UTF-8 is only the encoding of the key chain name string. It is incidental to the document.
YANG appears only in references to key chain and PCEP models. The document defines no model.
The parent of PCE is implied by the PCE tag.

RFC9354.title: Transmission of IPv6 Packets over Power Line Communication (PLC) Networks
RFC9354.summary: Specifies how IPv6 packets are carried over constrained power line communication (PLC) networks (IEEE 1901.1, IEEE 1901.2, ITU-T G.9903) by adapting 6LoWPAN/6lo mechanisms for addressing, neighbor discovery, header compression and fragmentation.

6LoWPAN.why: The document is a 6lo adaptation-layer specification for PLC links, covering IID formation, ND registration, RFC 6282 header compression and RFC 4944 fragmentation, adapted to PLC media.
6LoWPAN.quote: This document specifies the transmission of IPv6 packets over those constrained PLC networks. The general approach is to adapt elements of the 6LoWPAN

rejected.why: RPL is mentioned as a suitable routing protocol and for prefix dissemination, but the document does not specify or extend it.
Section 4.4 uses RFC 6775/8505 registration, but this is applying existing 6LoWPAN ND, and the 6LoWPAN tag is the better fit.
IID derivation for SLAAC is covered, but as part of the adaptation layer. The 6LoWPAN tag covers it more precisely.
RFC 6282 is applied with a minor SAM/DAM modification for 1901.1, which is a subsection of the 6lo adaptation. The 6LoWPAN tag covers it.
The PLC/AMI constrained-device context is background. The document is a link-layer adaptation rather than IoT architecture guidance.
AODV-RPL is only cited as a routing option, and the AODV tag is not applicable.

gaps.name: Power Line Communication (PLC)
gaps.why: The document is about IPv6 over PLC links (IEEE 1901.1/1901.2, ITU-T G.9903), and the taxonomy has no link-layer tag for power line networks.

RFC9355.title: OSPF Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) Strict-Mode
RFC9355.summary: RFC 9355 defines OSPF BFD strict-mode, using an LLS B-bit and a new Local Interface IPv4 Address TLV to block OSPF adjacency formation until a BFD session is established, updating the RFC 2328 neighbor state machine.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF, updating the RFC 2328 neighbor state machine and defining LLS signalling for strict-mode adjacency formation.
OSPF.quote: augmenting the OSPF neighbor state machine with a check for BFD session up before progression from Init to 2-Way state

BFD.why: The document specifies how BFD session establishment gates OSPF adjacency formation, including BFD multi-hop for virtual links and BFD enable/disable behaviour.
BFD.quote: it will establish a BFD session with that neighbor first before bringing up the OSPF adjacency

OSPFv3.why: A substantial part of the document defines the OSPFv3 IPv4 address-family specifics and the new LLS TLV needed to support strict-mode there.
OSPFv3.quote: Implementations that support OSPF BFD strict-mode for OSPFv3 IPv4 AF instances MUST include the Local Interface IPv4 Address TLV

rejected.why: YANG is mentioned only in passing in Operations and Management Considerations, which says the base OSPF YANG module is expected to be augmented. The document defines no model.
IS-IS appears only as a pointer to similar functionality in RFC 6213. The document does not address it.
The IANA section only records the B-bit and TLV type 21 assignments. This is boilerplate and not the subject.
The document is about a specific protocol extension, not general routing architecture.

RFC9356.title: Advertising Layer 2 Bundle Member Link Attributes in OSPF
RFC9356.summary: Defines OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 sub-TLVs to advertise link attributes of individual L2 bundle member links, and specifies their advertisement via BGP-LS, updating RFC 9085.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 with a new L2 Bundle Member Attributes sub-TLV.
OSPF.quote: This document defines sub-TLVs to advertise link attribute information for each of the L2 bundle members that comprise the L3 interface on which OSPF operates.

link aggregation.why: The subject is the member links of L2 bundles such as LAG. The document advertises their attributes, so readers of link aggregation would want it.
link aggregation.quote: the L3 interface on which an OSPF adjacency is established is a L2 interface bundle, for instance, a Link Aggregation Group (LAG)

BGP.why: A section specifies BGP-LS advertisement of the OSPF information, and the document updates RFC 9085.
BGP.quote: the L2 bundle member information can now be advertised from OSPF into BGP-LS on the same lines as discussed for IS-IS

rejected.why: Adj-SID sub-TLVs are reused per member link, but the document does not define segment routing itself.
PCE is only the motivating external entity, and the document does not specify PCE.
The YANG model is mentioned only as a place where future configuration will be added.
IS-IS (RFC 8668) is cited as the earlier similar work, but this document does not cover it.
The advertised attributes support traffic engineering, but the document is about the advertisement mechanism.

RFC9357.title: Label Switched Path (LSP) Object Flag Extension for Stateful PCE
RFC9357.summary: Defines a new LSP-EXTENDED-FLAG TLV (type 64) for the PCEP LSP object, providing an extensible variable-length flag array because all 12 bits of the original LSP object Flag field are used.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP (stateful PCE, RFC 8231) with a new TLV in the LSP object, and creates an IANA registry for its flags. It is squarely about PCEP.
PCE.quote: This document defines a new LSP-EXTENDED-FLAG TLV for the LSP object for an extended Flag field.

rejected.why: GMPLS LSPs are mentioned only as the objects controlled by stateful PCE. The document does not specify anything about GMPLS.
MPLS-TE LSPs are the context for PCEP, but the document does not address MPLS itself.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations as the recommended transport protection for PCEP.
The IANA registry creation is boilerplate for this protocol extension. The document is not about IANA guidance.
The document is about PCEP, which sits under this parent, but PCE is the more specific tag.

gaps.name: PCEP (Path Computation Element Communication Protocol)
gaps.why: I tagged this RFC as PCE, which is the closest fit. The taxonomy describes PCE as 'architecture and PCEP', but it has no separate tag for stateful PCE extensions. I used PCE as the primary tag.

RFC9358.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for Establishing Relationships between Sets of Label Switched Paths and Virtual Networks
RFC9358.summary: RFC 9358 extends the PCEP association mechanism (RFC 8697) with a new VN Association type and VIRTUAL-NETWORK-TLV so sets of LSPs can be tied to a Virtual Network, supporting ACTN-style VN control in hierarchical PCE.

PCE.why: The document defines a new PCEP association type and TLV, extending PCEP between parent and child PCEs.
PCE.quote: we define a new association group called the "VN Association Group (VNAG)".  This grouping is used to define the association between a set of LSPs and a VN.

rejected.why: LSPs are the objects being grouped, but the document specifies only PCEP extensions, not MPLS itself.
TLS is only recommended in Security Considerations to secure the PCEP session; nothing new is defined about it.
The PCE tag already sits under traffic engineering and covers the subject. ACTN/VN context is framing, not a separate subject.
A PCEP YANG module is mentioned only in Manageability Considerations and is not the subject.
ASCII is only the character set suggested for the Virtual Network Identifier string.

gaps.name: ACTN (Abstraction and Control of TE Networks) / Virtual Networks
gaps.why: The document's motivation is VN control under ACTN, but the taxonomy has no ACTN tag.

RFC9359.title: Echo Request/Reply for Enabled In Situ OAM (IOAM) Capabilities
RFC9359.summary: Defines a generic container/object format for echo request/reply mechanisms letting an IOAM encapsulating node discover enabled IOAM capabilities of transit and decapsulating nodes, usable across IPv6, MPLS, SFC and BIER data planes.

OAM.why: The document specifies an OAM mechanism (IOAM capabilities discovery via echo request/reply), which belongs under OAM; no technology tag exists for IOAM itself.
OAM.quote: allowing the IOAM encapsulating node to discover the enabled IOAM capabilities of each IOAM transit and IOAM decapsulating node

telemetry.why: IOAM is in-band telemetry; the capability objects cover tracing, edge-to-edge, and direct export of operational data.
telemetry.quote: what types of IOAM tracing data can be added or exported by the transit nodes along the transport path

rejected.why: ICMPv6 Echo is explicitly not what is used; ICMP is only referenced as a possible carrier in later documents.
MPLS LSP ping is one of several data planes the generic format is intended for; the document is not about MPLS.
Mentioned only as an alternative discovery method with limitations.
One of several target data planes; not the subject.
Registries created are boilerplate-level for this document, not its subject.
TTL-increment probing is used in the operational guide, but the document is not about traceroute.

gaps.name: IOAM (In situ OAM)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no IOAM technology tag, though the entire document is about IOAM capability discovery.

RFC9360.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Header Parameters for Carrying and Referencing X.509 Certificates
RFC9360.summary: Defines COSE header parameters (x5bag, x5chain, x5t, x5u and sender variants for static-static ECDH) to carry or reference X.509 certificates in COSE messages, plus the application/cose-x509 media type.

COSE.why: The document extends COSE with new header parameters and algorithm parameters for certificates; COSE readers need it.
COSE.quote: This document extends the way that keys can be identified and transported by providing attributes that refer to or contain X.509 certificates.

X.509.why: Specifies how X.509 certificates and chains are carried, hashed and referenced, including validation and trust-anchor handling.
X.509.quote: This document defines a set of attributes that will allow applications to transport and refer to X.509 certificates in a consistent manner.

rejected.why: CBOR is only the encoding substrate; the document does not define anything new about CBOR.
It registers application/cose-x509, but that is minor boilerplate-like IANA content, not the main subject.
X.509 is the more specific fit; PKI validation is only referenced via RFC 5280.
Only mentioned as a motivating use case, with no EDHOC content in the document.
CDDL is used only to describe the structures.
Mentioned only as a use case in the introduction.

RFC9361.title: ICANN Trademark Clearinghouse (TMCH) Functional Specifications
RFC9361.summary: Describes the architecture, interfaces, processes and data formats (DNL list, SMD revocation list, LORDN, Trademark Claims Notice XML) between the ICANN Trademark Clearinghouse and domain registries and registrars during Sunrise, Trademark Claims and QLP periods.

domain registration.why: The document specifies registry/registrar processes for provisioning domain names during Sunrise and Trademark Claims periods, which is domain registration operations.
domain registration.quote: interfaces between the ICANN Trademark Clearinghouse (TMCH) and Domain Name Registries, as well as between the ICANN TMCH and Domain Name Registrars

rejected.why: EPP is only mentioned as the typical implementation of the registrar-registry ry interface, which is out of scope.
HTTPS with Basic authentication is the substrate for the interfaces; nothing new is defined about HTTP.
The TCN is XML with a schema, but XML is only the encoding.
CSV is used as the file format for lists, but the document does not define CSV itself.
CRLs and certificate validation of the TMV certificates are used, but the document does not profile X.509.
PGP signing of lists is a mechanism used, not the subject.
The document concerns domain name registration policy and not DNS protocol or operation.

gaps.name: Trademark Clearinghouse / trademark rights protection mechanisms
gaps.why: The document is about ICANN's TMCH, Sunrise and Trademark Claims services; the taxonomy has no tag for trademark or rights-protection mechanisms beyond generic domain registration.

RFC9362.title: Distributed Denial-of-Service Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) Signal Channel Configuration Attributes for Robust Block Transmission
RFC9362.summary: Defines new DOTS signal channel configuration attributes (max-payloads, non-timeout, etc.) for negotiating CoAP Q-Block1/Q-Block2 robust block transmission parameters, with a YANG module augmenting the RFC 9132 signal channel module and CBOR key mappings.

DOTS.why: The document extends the DOTS signal channel with new negotiable configuration attributes, so it belongs on the DOTS page.
DOTS.quote: This document specifies new DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) signal channel configuration parameters that can be negotiated between DOTS peers

CoAP.why: The attributes configure CoAP robust block-wise transfer parameters (RFC 9177), so CoAP readers would want it.
CoAP.quote: enable the use of Q-Block1 and Q-Block2 Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) options

YANG.why: A substantial part of the document is the ietf-dots-robust-trans YANG module augmenting ietf-dots-signal-channel.
YANG.quote: this document defines a YANG data model for representing these new DOTS signal channel configuration parameters

rejected.why: CBOR is only the encoding; the document gives CBOR key mappings but defines nothing new about CBOR itself.
The parameters come from RFC 9177's congestion-control guards, but the document only makes them configurable and does not specify congestion control.
DDoS is the motivating context, but the topic tag is covered by the more specific DOTS tag.
JSON appears only in the readability example, as a representation of YANG-modelled data.
UDP is only the transport CoAP runs over.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate and not the document's main subject.

RFC9363.title: A YANG Data Model for Static Context Header Compression (SCHC)
RFC9363.summary: Defines the ietf-schc YANG module that formally represents SCHC compression/decompression and fragmentation Rules so SCHC instances can exchange or modify them.

YANG.why: The document's purpose is to specify a YANG module (ietf-schc) with its tree and identities.
YANG.quote: This document describes a YANG data model for the Static Context Header Compression (SCHC) compression and fragmentation Rules.

SCHC.why: The model formalizes SCHC Rules (fields, matching operators, CDAs, fragmentation modes, timers), so readers of SCHC would want it.
SCHC.quote: SCHC is a compression and fragmentation mechanism for constrained networks defined in [RFC8724].

rejected.why: CoAP fields are only identities in the model; the document does not specify or extend CoAP.
NETCONF/RESTCONF are mentioned only in Security Considerations as access mechanisms.
IPv6 header fields are referenced as field identifiers only; the document is not about IPv6.
Considered as the parent of SCHC, but SCHC has its own tag under LPWAN, which is the more specific fit.
Considered but the document is about SCHC Rules, with LPWAN only as the target environment; SCHC is the more specific tag.
OSCORE option fields appear only as identities; the document does not specify OSCORE.

RFC9364.title: DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC)
RFC9364.summary: RFC 9364 is a BCP that introduces the DNSSEC core RFCs, algorithm documents, extensions and related documents in one place, and states that DNSSEC is the best current practice for origin authentication of DNS data.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document is a roadmap to DNSSEC specifications (core, algorithms, extensions such as trust anchors, NSEC3, key rollover) and declares DNSSEC a BCP.
DNSSEC.quote: Using the DNSSEC set of protocols is the best current practice for adding origin authentication of DNS data.
DNSSEC.section: 1.1. DNSSEC as a Best Current Practice

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific child tag; DNS is implied as its ancestor.
Only mentioned as a standard that relies on signed zones; the document explicitly says it does not cover such standards.
ECDSA and EdDSA are only briefly mentioned as signing algorithms adopted for DNSSEC, not the subject of the document.
GOST is mentioned in a single sentence as a little-used algorithm, not a substantial part of the document.
The IANA section only lists existing DNSSEC registries and creates none; boilerplate is not evidence.
RSA is mentioned only in passing as a popular signing algorithm.

RFC9365.title: IPv6 Wireless Access in Vehicular Environments (IPWAVE): Problem Statement and Use Cases
RFC9365.summary: Informational problem statement and use-case document for IPv6-based vehicular networking (IPWAVE), covering V2V/V2I/V2X use cases and a gap analysis of IPv6 neighbor discovery, mobility management, and security/privacy.

vehicular networking.why: The whole document is about IPv6 in vehicular (V2V, V2I, V2X) environments: use cases, architecture, and gap analysis.
vehicular networking.quote: This document discusses the problem statement and use cases of IPv6-based vehicular networking for Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS).

neighbor discovery.why: Section 5.1 analyses ND, DAD, NUD and the link model for VANETs, and security threats to ND are covered in Section 6.1.
neighbor discovery.quote: the time constraint of a wireless link has a major impact on IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (ND).

IP mobility.why: Mobility management (MIPv6, PMIPv6, NEMO, DMM) for vehicles is one of the main problem areas and has an appendix.
IP mobility.quote: The seamless connectivity and timely data exchange between two endpoints requires efficient mobility management including location management and handover.

rejected.why: RPL is discussed as a candidate routing approach for multihop V2X, but the document does not specify or profile it.
IPsec and TLS are mentioned only as possible secure channels in the security discussion, not as a subject of the document.
MANET routing and NHDP are mentioned in comparison with vehicular ND, but they are not the document's subject.
MAC address pseudonyms and tracking are discussed, but they are a sub-point of the problem statement, not a privacy threat model for the document as a whole.
IEEE 802.11-OCB is the link layer assumed, but the document does not specify IP over 802.11; that is RFC 8691.
The ancestor tag is implied by the more specific tags chosen (neighbor discovery), so it is not listed separately.

gaps.name: Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) / IPWAVE
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for ITS, DSRC/C-V2X, or the IPWAVE subject. The vehicular networking tag covers it only approximately.

RFC9366.title: Multiple SIP Reason Header Field Values
RFC9366.summary: Updates RFC 3326 so a SIP message may carry multiple Reason header field values for the same protocol when that registered protocol defines what multiple values mean.

SIP.why: The document changes the SIP Reason header field rules defined in RFC 3326, which is an extension to SIP.
SIP.quote: A SIP message MAY contain more than one Reason value (i.e., multiple Reason lines).

rejected.why: STIR's identity header error handling motivated the change, but it is only cited as an informative example. The document itself is about the SIP Reason header.

RFC9367.title: GOST Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3
RFC9367.summary: Defines four GOST cipher suites (Kuznyechik/Magma with MGM AEAD and TLSTREE re-keying), seven GOST R 34.10-2012 signature schemes, elliptic-curve groups, and a profile for TLS 1.3, with test vectors.

GOST.why: The document is about making GOST algorithms (Kuznyechik, Magma, GOST R 34.11-2012, GOST R 34.10-2012) usable in IETF protocols.
GOST.quote: This document defines the cipher suites, signature schemes, and key exchange mechanisms for using Russian cryptographic standards, called GOST algorithms, with TLS Version 1.3.

TLS.why: It registers new TLS 1.3 cipher suites, signature schemes and named groups, and specifies a TLS 1.3 profile, so TLS readers need it.
TLS.quote: This document defines four new cipher suites (the TLS13_GOST cipher suites) and seven new signature schemes (the TLS13_GOST signature schemes) for the Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

rejected.why: The curves are used as part of the GOST signature/ECDHE definitions, which GOST covers more specifically; the document is not about elliptic-curve cryptography in general.
Re-keying (TLSTREE) is part of the record protection design, not a general key management subject.
HMAC is only used as part of the TLS 1.3 key schedule and Finished computation.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here; the main body is not about IANA registries.
The cipher suites are registered as not DTLS-OK; the document covers TLS 1.3 only.

RFC9368.title: Compatible Version Negotiation for QUIC
RFC9368.summary: Defines a QUIC version negotiation mechanism (incompatible via Version Negotiation packets and compatible within one connection), a version_information transport parameter, downgrade prevention, and server deployment guidance, updating RFC 8999.

QUIC.why: The whole document specifies a QUIC extension: version negotiation, the version_information transport parameter, a new error code, and operational guidance for QUIC deployments.
QUIC.quote: This document describes a version negotiation mechanism that allows a client and server to select a mutually supported version.

rejected.why: QUIC uses TLS 1.3 for authentication of transport parameters and session resumption is mentioned, but the document defines nothing new about TLS.
QUIC runs over UDP, but this is only substrate and not discussed.
The IANA section registers a transport parameter and error code, which is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
The QUIC tag is more specific and already covers the transport-layer subject.

RFC9369.title: QUIC Version 2
RFC9369.summary: Specifies QUIC version 2, a version of QUIC nearly identical to version 1 that changes the version number, long header packet types, Initial salt, HKDF labels and Retry integrity keys to combat ossification and exercise version negotiation.

QUIC.why: The document defines a new QUIC version, its wire-image differences, version negotiation requirements and sample packet protection, so it belongs on the QUIC subject page.
QUIC.quote: This document specifies QUIC version 2, which is identical to QUIC version 1 except for some trivial details.

rejected.why: TLS is used for key derivation and session resumption as in QUIC v1, but the document defines no new TLS behaviour; it only changes QUIC labels and salts.
Mentioned only as an ALPN that can run over QUIC v2 and in Alt-Svc discussion; the document is not about HTTP/3.
DNS over QUIC is cited only as an example ALPN that works over QUIC version 2.
The ChaCha20-Poly1305 short header example in Appendix A.5 is just a test vector for QUIC v2 packet protection, not about the cipher.
HKDF labels are changed as part of QUIC key derivation, but the document is not about HMAC or HKDF itself.

RFC9370.title: Multiple Key Exchanges in the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC9370.summary: RFC 9370 extends IKEv2 to perform multiple successive key exchanges (hybrid classical and post-quantum) using IKE_INTERMEDIATE and a new IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE exchange, and renames the Transform Type 4 and related registry.

IKE.why: The document specifies new IKEv2 transform types, a new IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE exchange, notifications and key derivation changes, and updates RFC 7296.
IKE.quote: This document describes how to extend the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) to allow multiple key exchanges to take place while computing a shared secret

post-quantum.why: The motivation and the hybrid design target post-quantum migration of IKEv2 key exchange. The document is generic about algorithms but its security focus is quantum resistance.
post-quantum.quote: This method allows integration of PQC in IKEv2, while maintaining backward compatibility, to derive a set of IKE keys that is resistant to quantum-computer attacks.

rejected.why: IKEv2 is the specified protocol and sits under IPsec. The child tag IKE is more specific and already covers it.
The document is key establishment in IKE, but IKE is the more specific tag and already covers it.
Child SAs for ESP/AH are mentioned only incidentally in the CREATE_CHILD_SA discussion.
No specific post-quantum algorithm is defined or profiled. The algorithms appear as placeholders such as PQ_KEM_1.
The IANA registry changes are boilerplate-like registry updates for the IKE extension, not a document about IANA guidance.

RFC9371.title: Registration Procedures for Private Enterprise Numbers (PENs)
RFC9371.summary: Describes how IANA registers Private Enterprise Numbers (OID prefix 1.3.6.1.4.1), including requesting, modifying and deleting PENs, registry specifics, and brief overview of uses.

IANA.why: The document specifies the registration procedures (First Come First Served) and maintenance of an IANA registry, so readers of IANA registry matters would want it.
IANA.quote: This document describes how Private Enterprise Numbers (PENs) are registered by IANA.  It shows how to request a new PEN and how to modify a current PEN.

rejected.why: PENs are OIDs, but the document is about the registry procedure, not ASN.1 modules or encoding rules.
SNMP MIBs are the historical motivation for PENs only; the document does not specify SNMP.
MIB configurations are mentioned as a historical use only.
Listed as one of several protocols that use PENs in extension mechanisms; not about them.
Mentioned as an example of a protocol limiting the PEN value size; not about Diameter.
Registration is done by IANA, not through an IETF process; the document does not define one.

gaps.name: Object identifiers (OIDs) / Private Enterprise Numbers
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for OID or enterprise-number identifier registries, which are the document's actual subject. IANA is the closest fit.

RFC9372.title: L-Band Digital Aeronautical Communications System (LDACS)
RFC9372.summary: Informational overview of the L-band Digital Aeronautical Communications System (LDACS), an aeronautical cellular data link carrying IPv6 for ATN/IPS, covering its architecture, protocol stack, mobility, reliability and link-layer security, to introduce it to the IETF and RAW.

IPv6.why: The document is about carrying IPv6 over an aeronautical link and the ATN/IPS IPv6 transition, and seeks expertise on IPv6 over LDACS.
IPv6.quote: LDACS is a scheduled and reliable multi-application cellular broadband system with support for IPv6.

PMIPv6.why: PMIPv6 is the foreseen local mobility mechanism inside the LDACS access network, discussed again in Section 7.4.
PMIPv6.quote: Local mobility within the LDACS access network is realized through Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6)

LISP.why: LISP is the mobility solution ICAO asked the IETF to provide for the multilink concept, and the document gives context relative to it.
LISP.quote: global mobility between "multilink" access networks (which need not be LDACS) is implemented on top of LISP

security.why: A large part of the document covers LDACS security requirements, objectives, architecture, PKI and key establishment. The section has real content beyond boilerplate, and no more specific tag fits.
security.quote: The goal of this section is to inform the reader about the state of security in aeronautical communications

rejected.why: DTLS 1.3 is only mentioned as the ATN/IPS transport security. The document does not specify or extend it.
ROHC is mentioned only as considered for the SNP layer, in a single sentence.
Diffserv classes are used to signal QoS to the LDACS MAC, but this is a brief mention.
LDACS is a link layer, but the taxonomy has no aeronautical link tag. It is a close fit, but the document is about IPv6 over the link and its reliability rather than a generic link layer.
SNMP and NETCONF are only mentioned as possible management protocols that vendors might use.
IPsec, IKEv2 and TLS 1.3 are only noted as conceivable ground-side security options.

gaps.name: Aeronautical telecommunications (ATN/IPS, LDACS)
gaps.why: The document is about a civil aviation data link and the ATN/IPS architecture, and the taxonomy has no aeronautical or aviation communications tag.

gaps.name: Reliable and Available Wireless (RAW)
gaps.why: The document is framed for the RAW working group. The taxonomy has no tag for reliable and deterministic wireless networking.

RFC9373.title: EdDSA Value for IPSECKEY
RFC9373.summary: Assigns IPSECKEY algorithm type value 4 for EdDSA public keys in the IANA IPSECKEY registry, reusing the RFC 8080 key format, and reformats the registry.

DNS.why: The document extends the IPSECKEY DNS resource record with a new algorithm type for EdDSA public keys, which is a DNS resource record parameter matter.
DNS.quote: IPSECKEY [RFC4025] is a resource record (RR) for the Domain Name System (DNS) that is used to store public keys for use in IP security

EdDSA.why: EdDSA public keys are the new value being added, so readers of the EdDSA subject would want this.
EdDSA.quote: This document adds support for Edwards-Curve Digital Security Algorithm (EdDSA) public keys in the format defined in [RFC8080] to the IPSECKEY RR.

rejected.why: Only the RFC 8080 public key format, defined for DNSSEC, is reused. The document does not concern signing or validation.
IPsec is the consumer of the keys stored in IPSECKEY. The document specifies no IPsec behaviour.

RFC9374.title: DRIP Entity Tag (DET) for Unmanned Aircraft System Remote ID (UAS RID)
RFC9374.summary: Defines Hierarchical Host Identity Tags (HHITs) as self-asserting IPv6 addresses used as DRIP Entity Tags for UAS Remote ID, extending HIPv2/ORCHIDv2 with hierarchy, EdDSA/cSHAKE128 suite, DNS registry discovery and IANA registries.

DRIP.quote: HHITs as self-asserting IPv6 addresses, which makes them trustable identifiers for use in Unmanned Aircraft System Remote Identification (UAS RID) and tracking.

RFC9375.title: A YANG Data Model for Network and VPN Service Performance Monitoring
RFC9375.summary: Defines the ietf-network-vpn-pm YANG module, augmenting the RFC 8345 network topology model to expose performance monitoring (loss, delay, jitter, interface counters) for underlay networks and L2/L3 VPN services.

YANG.why: The document's core deliverable is a YANG data model (ietf-network-vpn-pm) augmenting the network topology model.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG module for performance monitoring (PM) of both underlay networks and overlay VPN services

performance measurement.why: The model reports one-way loss, delay, jitter with percentiles and measurement intervals; it is about network performance monitoring data, though it introduces no new metrics.
performance measurement.quote: this document defines a YANG module for both network and VPN service performance monitoring (PM).

VPN.why: A substantial part of the model covers VPN service topologies, VPN tunnel PM and VPN access interface PM for L2/L3 VPNs.
VPN.quote: The performance of VPN services is associated with the performance changes of the underlay networks that carry VPN services.

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the access methods for the model; the document defines no protocol behaviour for them.
TWAMP, OWAMP and STAMP appear only as possible PM data sources (identities); the document does not specify or extend them.
