YANG-Push subscription is used for delivery, but the document's focus is the data model, not a telemetry mechanism.
Not relevant; counters mirror interface statistics but no MIB is defined.

RFC9376.title: Applicability of GMPLS for beyond 100 Gbit/s Optical Transport Network
RFC9376.summary: Informational analysis showing that existing GMPLS OSPF-TE routing (RFC 7138) and RSVP-TE signaling (RFC 7139) can set up ODUk LSPs over ODUCn links defined in ITU-T G.709 (2020), with only minor future extension needs noted.

GMPLS.why: The whole document analyses how GMPLS routing and signaling apply to beyond-100G OTN, covering TE link representation, labels and TPN field limits.
GMPLS.quote: examines the applicability of using existing GMPLS routing and signaling mechanisms to set up Optical Data Unit-k (ODUk) Label Switched Paths (LSPs) over Optical Data Unit-Cn (ODUCn) links

rejected.why: RFC 7139 signaling is reused unchanged and is part of the GMPLS analysis. It is not specified or extended here, so GMPLS is the better fit.
OSPF-TE routing is discussed only to conclude that no extension is needed. It is not the subject.
TE links appear only as the representation of the OTN links. The GMPLS tag covers this.
SONET/SDH is mentioned only as a possible client signal.

gaps.name: Optical Transport Network (OTN / ITU-T G.709)
gaps.why: The document is largely about the OTN data plane (OTUCn, ODUCn, tributary slots), and the taxonomy has no OTN or optical transport tag.

RFC9377.title: IS-IS Flood Reflection
RFC9377.summary: Defines an experimental IS-IS extension, flood reflection, in which L1 areas provide transit for L2 using flood reflector adjacencies, new TLVs/sub-TLVs, and route computation rules to scale the L2 flooding domain.

IS-IS.why: The whole document specifies new IS-IS TLVs, adjacency formation rules and route computation for flood reflection.
IS-IS.quote: describes a backward-compatible, optional IS-IS extension that allows the creation of IS-IS flood reflection topologies

rejected.why: BGP route reflection is only cited as an analogy; the document doesn't specify BGP.
Refers to BGP route reflection, which is only the inspiration for flood reflection, not the subject.

OSPF TTZ (RFC 8099) is mentioned only as related work.
The IS-IS tag covers it more specifically, although the scaling theme is architectural.
IANA registrations are boilerplate for this document.

RFC9378.title: In Situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM) Deployment
RFC9378.summary: Informational framework for deploying IOAM (In situ OAM): node roles, IOAM types, encapsulations, data export, namespaces, layering, trace option types, flags, brownfield deployment, and manageability.

OAM.why: The whole document is about IOAM, an in-packet OAM mechanism, and gives deployment guidance for it. No IOAM-specific tag exists, so the OAM topic fits.
OAM.quote: IOAM collects OAM information within the packet while the packet traverses a particular network domain.

telemetry.why: IOAM collects per-hop telemetry data and exports it to collectors and analytics systems. The document covers export and data processing (Sections 4 and 6).
telemetry.quote: IOAM collects operational and telemetry information in the packet while the packet traverses a path between two points in the network.

rejected.why: IPFIX is only mentioned as the export mechanism, and the raw export is defined in another draft.
IPv6 is one of several encapsulations listed, and the document only points to other specifications for it.
IOAM is used for delay and jitter measurement, but the document is about OAM deployment in general, and the active flag is only one part of it.
The YANG model is only referenced in the manageability section and is defined elsewhere.
Geneve is one of the listed encapsulations and is not specified here.
Service function chaining is mentioned only as a use case for Proof of Transit.

gaps.name: In situ OAM (IOAM)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no IOAM-specific technology tag. Readers looking for IOAM would benefit from a dedicated tag, since RFC 9197, RFC 9322 and RFC 9326 share the subject.

RFC9380.title: Hashing to Elliptic Curves
RFC9380.summary: RFC 9380 specifies algorithms (hash_to_field, expand_message, deterministic mappings such as SWU, SVDW and Elligator 2, cofactor clearing) and named suites for encoding or hashing arbitrary byte strings to points on elliptic curves.

elliptic curve.why: The whole document is about hashing to elliptic curve groups, with suites for P-256, curve25519, BLS12-381, secp256k1 and others.
elliptic curve.quote: This document specifies a number of algorithms for encoding or hashing an arbitrary string to a point on an elliptic curve.

rejected.why: SHA-2 and SHA-3 are only the hash primitives plugged into expand_message, not the subject.
HMAC appears only in the domain-separation discussion in the security considerations.
Password-authenticated key exchange is cited only as a motivating use of hashing to curves.
PBKDF2, scrypt and Argon2 are mentioned only as advice for hashing passwords before encoding.
curve25519 and curve448 are among the suites, but the document is about hashing to curves generally, so the broader elliptic curve tag fits better.
The document produces uniform field elements from a hash. It does not address randomness requirements or generation.

gaps.name: hash-to-curve / hashing to elliptic curves
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for hashing arbitrary input to curve points, so the document is filed under the general elliptic curve tag.

RFC9381.title: Verifiable Random Functions (VRFs)
RFC9381.summary: Specifies Verifiable Random Functions (VRFs) based on RSA-FDH and elliptic curves (ECVRF) with ciphersuites, security properties, and test vectors.

cryptography.why: The document defines a cryptographic primitive (VRF), its security properties and ciphersuites; no more specific taxonomy tag covers VRFs, so the parent topic applies.
cryptography.quote: A Verifiable Random Function (VRF) is the public key version of a keyed cryptographic hash.

RSA.why: A full VRF construction (RSA-FDH-VRF) with ciphersuites and test vectors is built on RSA signatures.
RSA.quote: The VRF computes the proof pi as a deterministic RSA signature on input alpha using the RSA Full Domain Hashing algorithm

elliptic curve.why: ECVRF is a major half of the document, with P-256 and edwards25519 ciphersuites and hash-to-curve encoding.
elliptic curve.quote: The Elliptic Curve Verifiable Random Function (ECVRF) is a VRF that, for suitable parameter choices, satisfies the "full uniqueness"

rejected.why: NSEC5 is only cited as motivating work in references; the document is not about DNSSEC.
The edwards25519 curve and RFC 8032 encodings are reused, but the document specifies VRFs, not EdDSA.
SHA-256/384/512 are just hash functions used by the ciphersuites.
RFC 6979 nonce generation is borrowed, but ECDSA is not the subject.

gaps.name: Verifiable Random Function (VRF)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for VRFs or verifiable/proof-producing hash primitives; they fall under the generic cryptography topic.

RFC9382.title: SPAKE2, a Password-Authenticated Key Exchange
RFC9382.summary: RFC 9382 specifies SPAKE2, a symmetric password-authenticated key exchange usable over any group, with key schedule, key confirmation, ciphersuites, point-generation method and test vectors.

SPAKE2.why: The document defines and specifies the SPAKE2 protocol, its ciphersuites, and test vectors.
SPAKE2.quote: SPAKE2, which is a means for two parties that share a password to derive a strong shared key without disclosing the password.

rejected.why: Elliptic curve groups are the setting for SPAKE2 and point generation, but the document is about the PAKE, not ECC itself.
HMAC is only a MAC option in the ciphersuites, not a subject of the document.
SHA-256/512 are just hash choices within the ciphersuites.
OPAQUE is mentioned only as the recommendation for augmented PAKEs in Security Considerations.
Kerberos is mentioned only as an existing user of SPAKE2 variants; the document does not specify its use there.
The MHF (e.g., scrypt) is referenced for deriving w, but parameter selection is explicitly out of scope.

RFC9383.title: SPAKE2+, an Augmented Password-Authenticated Key Exchange (PAKE) Protocol
RFC9383.summary: Describes SPAKE2+, an augmented password-authenticated key exchange protocol between a Prover and Verifier, with registration, key schedule, key confirmation, ciphersuites and test vectors.

PAKE.why: The document specifies SPAKE2+, a password-authenticated key exchange protocol. SPAKE2+ has no child tag in the taxonomy, so the parent PAKE tag is the most specific fit.
PAKE.quote: SPAKE2+ is an augmented PAKE protocol, as only one party has knowledge of the password.

rejected.why: The document recommends scrypt or Argon2id to derive w0 and w1. It does not specify them, so they are only a component.
HMAC is used as the MAC for key confirmation but is not what the document is about.
The protocol is group-agnostic and uses the NIST and Edwards curves only as ciphersuite parameters. It is not about elliptic-curve cryptography itself.
The taxonomy's SPAKE2 tag covers the CFRG balanced PAKE of RFC 9382. This document specifies the separate augmented SPAKE2+ protocol and only refers to SPAKE2 as a companion.
The protocol derives shared keys, but this is covered by the more specific PAKE tag.
SHA-256 and SHA-512 are only hash choices in the ciphersuites.

RFC9384.title: A BGP Cease NOTIFICATION Subcode for Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD)
RFC9384.summary: Defines a new BGP Cease NOTIFICATION subcode, "BFD Down" (value 10), sent when a BGP connection is closed because the BFD session went down, with operational guidance.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP by defining a new Cease NOTIFICATION subcode and specifying when BGP speakers send it, including interaction with the Hard Reset procedure.
BGP.quote: This document defines a subcode for the BGP Cease NOTIFICATION message (Section 6.7 of RFC 4271) for use when a BGP connection is being closed

BFD.why: The subcode is triggered by BFD session-down events, and the document discusses BFD timers and partial loss of connectivity. BFD is the trigger, but the document specifies a BGP behaviour.
BFD.quote: When the BFD session state changes to Down, the BGP speaker terminates the connection with a Cease NOTIFICATION message sent to the neighbor

rejected.why: BGP runs over TCP and the connection is closed afterwards, but nothing about TCP is specified.
bgpPeerLastError from the BGP MIB is mentioned only as an example of where to expose the reason, not as a subject of the document.
The BGP YANG model's last-error leaf is cited as an informative example only.
The IANA registry assignment is boilerplate that records the new subcode, and it is not the document's subject.

RFC9385.title: Using GOST Cryptographic Algorithms in the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC9385.summary: Defines GOST-based IKEv2 transforms (Streebog PRF, GOST R 34.10-2012 ECDH key exchange, signature authentication and hash algorithm IDs), with extensive test vectors.

GOST.why: The document specifies the use of GOST hash, signature and key exchange algorithms in IKEv2.
GOST.quote: This document defines a number of transforms for IKEv2, based on Russian cryptographic standard algorithms (often referred to as "GOST" algorithms)

IKE.why: It extends IKEv2 with new PRF, key exchange method and hash algorithm transforms, and gives IKEv2 test vectors.
IKE.quote: This specification defines a new transform of Type 2 (Pseudorandom Function Transform IDs): PRF_HMAC_STREEBOG_512 (9).

rejected.why: IKE is the more specific child tag; ESP protection is only referenced from RFC 9227.
ESP ciphers are defined in RFC 9227, not here.
Certificates appear only in test vectors; the ASN.1 objects are defined in other documents.
The curves are used but defined elsewhere (RFC 7836); GOST covers the algorithms.
HMAC is only the construction used inside the PRF.
The ASN.1 OIDs are listed for convenience only.

RFC9386.title: IPv6 Deployment Status
RFC9386.summary: RFC 9386 surveys the 2022 status of IPv6 deployment (users, content, allocations, ISP and enterprise surveys), describes deployment scenarios (dual-stack, IPv6-only, IPv4aaS), analyses remaining challenges, and obsoletes RFC 6036.

IPv6.why: The whole document is about IPv6 adoption, deployment scenarios, challenges, performance and security.
IPv6.quote: This document provides an overview of the status of IPv6 deployment in 2022.

IPv6 transition.why: A substantial part covers dual-stack, IPv6-only scopes and IPv4-as-a-Service (464XLAT, DS-Lite, MAP) transition choices.
IPv6 transition.quote: IPv4aaS can be used to ensure IPv4 support, and it can be a complex decision that depends on several factors

rejected.why: CGN and NAT are discussed as IPv4 exhaustion context, not as the subject.
IPv4 exhaustion is background to the IPv6 deployment survey, not the focus.
Security is only a short section and mostly points to RFC 9099.
Mentioned only as one of the surveyed transition mechanisms, not specified or analysed in depth.
Mentioned only as one of the surveyed transition mechanisms, not specified or analysed in depth.

RFC9387.title: Use Cases for DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) Telemetry
RFC9387.summary: Informational document presenting sample use cases for DOTS telemetry (RFC 9244), describing components, cooperation, and telemetry attributes exchanged for DDoS mitigation resource assignment, reporting, and tuning.

DOTS.quote: This document presents sample use cases for DOTS telemetry.

Only used as a routing mechanism for redirecting attack traffic.

RFC9388.title: Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI) Footprint Types: Country Subdivision Code and Footprint Union
RFC9388.summary: Defines two new CDNI footprint types, ISO 3166-2 "subdivisioncode" and "footprintunion" (additive aggregation, updating RFC 8008), and registers a matching ALTO entity domain type.

CDN.quote: This document defines two new footprint types.

RFC9389.title: Nominating Committee Eligibility
RFC9389.summary: Updates RFC 8713 by defining new NomCom volunteer eligibility criteria (in-person or online attendance, WG chair/secretary, or RFC author/editor paths) and obsoletes RFC 8788 and RFC 8989, with analysis of NomCom capture risks.

RFC9390.title: Diameter Group Signaling
RFC9390.summary: RFC 9390 defines Diameter protocol extensions (new AVPs and procedures) for grouping sessions and applying commands such as re-auth, abort, and termination to whole groups of Diameter sessions in a single exchange.

RFC9391.title: Static Context Header Compression over Narrowband Internet of Things
RFC9391.summary: Specifies how SCHC header compression and fragmentation (RFC 8724/8824) is used over 3GPP NB-IoT, normatively via Non-IP Data Delivery and informationally for the radio link and Data over NAS, with recommended parameters.

RFC9392.title: Sending RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) Feedback for Congestion Control in Interactive Multimedia Conferences
RFC9392.summary: Informational memo analysing how often and at what overhead RTCP (using RFC 8888 congestion control feedback, RTP/SAVPF, reduced-size RTCP) can send congestion feedback for unicast VoIP and point-to-point video calls, concluding RTCP suits per-few-frames but not per-packet feedback.

RTCP.why: The whole document analyses RTCP feedback intervals, packet sizes, reduced-size and compound packets, and bandwidth overhead.
RTCP.quote: This memo discusses the rate at which congestion control feedback can be sent using the RTP Control Protocol (RTCP)

RTP congestion control.why: It evaluates whether RTCP feedback is adequate for interactive real-time media congestion control algorithms, matching this tag's scope (RMCAT).
RTP congestion control.quote: the suitability of RTCP for implementing congestion control for unicast multimedia applications

rejected.why: WebRTC is the motivating deployment, but the document states nothing in it is specific to WebRTC.
The secure profile is used only for the overhead calculation and security considerations; the document isn't about SRTP.
The parent is implied by the RTCP tag, and the document is specifically about RTCP feedback.
The more specific RTP congestion control tag fits, so the parent is implied.
TCP acknowledgement behaviour is only a comparison point.
Opus and video codecs appear only as assumptions for frame durations.

RFC9393.title: Concise Software Identification Tags
RFC9393.summary: Defines Concise SWID (CoSWID), a CBOR-based, CDDL-specified compact representation of ISO/IEC 19770-2 software identification tags, with IANA registries, a media type, CBOR tag, URI schemes, and COSE signing.

Mentioned only as one use case (RATS RIMs); not the subject.

Only a Content-Format registration in IANA considerations.
Software identification supports it but the document does not address supply chain integrity as such.

RFC9394.title: IMAP PARTIAL Extension for Paged SEARCH and FETCH
RFC9394.summary: Defines the IMAP PARTIAL extension, extending the PARTIAL SEARCH return option from RFC 5267 and adding a PARTIAL modifier to UID FETCH for paged results, and clarifies interactions with ESEARCH, SAVE, MIN/MAX/COUNT and CONDSTORE.

IMAP.quote: This document defines an extension to the Internet Message Access Protocol [RFC3501] [RFC9051] for performing incremental searches and fetches.

RFC9395.title: Deprecation of the Internet Key Exchange Version 1 (IKEv1) Protocol and Obsoleted Algorithms
RFC9395.summary: RFC 9395 declares IKEv1 (and its RFCs 2407/2408/2409) Historic, points to IKEv2 equivalents for IKEv1 features, deprecates obsolete algorithms (RC5, IDEA, CAST, Blowfish, etc.) in IKEv2/ESP guidance, and adds a Status column to IKEv2 transform registries.

IoT is listed as one use case, but the document is not about IoT architectures or guidance for constrained devices.

gaps.name: Trusted Execution Environment / confidential computing
gaps.why: The document is about TEEs and the lifecycle management of Trusted Applications. The taxonomy has TEEP, but no broader TEE or confidential-computing subject.

RFC9398.title: A YANG Data Model for Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) and Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) Proxy Devices
RFC9398.summary: Defines a YANG data model (ietf-igmp-mld-proxy) to configure and monitor IGMP/MLD proxy devices per RFC 4605, augmenting the NMDA routing model.

YANG.why: The document's main purpose is a YANG module with tree diagrams and module code for IGMP/MLD proxy configuration and state.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model that can be used to configure and manage Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) or Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) Proxy devices.

IGMP.why: The model manages IGMP proxying (RFC 4605), including IGMP version and upstream interface configuration.
IGMP.quote: The "igmp-proxy" container instantiates an IGMP Proxy.

MLD.why: The model has a parallel MLD proxy branch for IPv6, which is half of the module.
MLD.quote: The "mld-proxy" container instantiates an MLD Proxy.

rejected.why: PIM is referenced only for a constraint that upstream interfaces must not run PIM; the document is not about PIM.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in Security Considerations as access mechanisms.
This is a YANG model, not a MIB module.
JSON is used only for the appendix example encoding.
The IGMP and MLD tags already sit under multicast, so the parent is implied.

RFC9399.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure: Logotypes in X.509 Certificates
RFC9399.summary: Defines an X.509 certificate extension (id-pe-logotype) for embedding or referencing logotype images and audio in public key and attribute certificates, merging and obsoleting RFCs 3709 and 6170.

X.509.why: The document defines a new X.509 certificate extension, supplementing the RFC 5280 and RFC 5755 profiles, with its syntax, semantics and client behaviour.
X.509.quote: This document specifies a certificate extension for including logotypes in public key certificates and attribute certificates.

rejected.why: The parent of X.509. The document is specifically about an X.509 certificate extension, so the more specific child tag applies.
ASN.1 modules are only the notation used to define the extension, not the subject of the document.
The document uses media types to label logotype data. It does not register media types or set registry rules.
TLS appears only as a transport for fetching logotype data and in the privacy discussion.
The data URI scheme and HTTP URIs are used as mechanisms. The document defines nothing new about URIs.
The Privacy Considerations section is only one part of the document. The main body is not about privacy.

RFC9400.title: Guidelines for the Organization of Fully Online Meetings
RFC9400.summary: RFC 9400 gives guidelines for planning fully online IETF plenary meetings (time zone rotation, days and hours, session and break lengths, parallel tracks, experiments) based on 2020-2021 COVID-era experience.

IETF process.why: The document sets IETF meeting policy and procedure: time zone selection, session structure, interim meetings, and experiments run by the IESG. That is IETF process and administration.
IETF process.quote: This document provides guidelines for the planning and organization of fully online meetings, regarding the number, length, and composition of sessions on the meeting agenda.

rejected.why: RFC 8713 is cited only for the administrative plenary handover procedures. The document is not about NomCom procedures.
It reports on meeting experience and surveys, but these are IETF plenary meetings, not an IAB, IRTF or community workshop report.
The child tag IETF process fits more specifically, so the parent is not listed.
Time zone selection here is about scheduling meetings for participants, not clock synchronization.

RFC9401.title: The Addition of the Death (DTH) Flag to TCP
RFC9401.summary: An April 1st joke RFC that defines a "Death" (DTH) flag using a reserved bit in the TCP header to hint at imminent session termination, framed in anime/film death-flag tropes.

TCP.why: The document specifies a new (satirical) TCP header flag, its sending rules and recipient behaviour, so it is about extending TCP.
TCP.quote: uses the fourth flag bit in the TCP header to indicate likely termination of the TCP session

humor.why: Published 1 April as a parody, with death-flag tropes, chainsaw killers and Hokuto-Shinken references; it belongs in the humorous RFCs series.
humor.quote: The flag is designed to make TCP session narratives smooth and attractive.

rejected.why: Not relevant; the document concerns only a TCP header bit.
RFC 3514's IP Evil bit is mentioned only in a short interaction section; the document is not about IPv4.
HTTP redirects and headers appear only as example scenarios for when to send the flag.
A DDoS attack is mentioned only in a joke scenario, not addressed as a subject.

RFC9402.title: Concat Notation
RFC9402.summary: An April 1st Independent Submission defining Concat, a whimsical ASCII text notation (with an ABNF grammar) for describing pictures and videos of cats and containers and their positions and interactions.

humor.why: Published on 1 April as a parody notation for cats in boxes, with jokes such as cats in liquid form and chewing on cardboard as an attack. It belongs on the humorous RFCs page.
humor.quote: a text-based language used to describe pictures and videos whose subject includes cats, containers, and their interactions.

rejected.why: The grammar is written in ABNF, but ABNF is only the tool used to define it. The document is not about ABNF.
The notation is limited to US-ASCII, which is a constraint on it. The document is not about ASCII.
The Internationalization Considerations section is a short boilerplate-style note about the English word 'cat'. It is not a substantial subject of the document.
The document describes a notation for annotating media. It does not register a media type.

RFC9403.title: A YANG Data Model for RIB Extensions
RFC9403.summary: Defines the ietf-rib-extension YANG module augmenting the RFC 8349 routing/RIB model with multiple next-hop static route preference and tags, route metrics and tags, RIB statistics, and IP Fast Reroute repair paths.

YANG.why: The document's entire purpose is a new YANG module that augments the ietf-routing model, so YANG data modelling is the core subject.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model [RFC7950] that extends the RIB data model defined in the ietf-routing YANG module [RFC8349] with more route attributes.

IP fast reroute.why: A substantial part of the model adds IPFRR repair-path attributes to each RIB next hop, which readers of IP fast reroute would want.
IP fast reroute.quote: The IP Fast Reroute (IPFRR) calculation by routing protocol precomputes repair paths [RFC5714], and the repair paths are installed in the RIB.

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in Security Considerations as access protocols for the data model, so they are boilerplate.
The YANG modules for OSPF and IS-IS are imported only to avoid duplicating the metric and tag augmentations. The document does not specify them.
The IS-IS YANG module is imported only to exclude its routes from the metric and tag augmentations. The document is not about IS-IS.
The document models RIB data. It does not address routing architecture or design principles.
ECMP is mentioned only in leaf descriptions for equal-preference static routes. It is not a subject of the document.
JSON and XML are used only for the example encodings in Appendix B.

RFC9404.title: JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP) Blob Management Extension
RFC9404.summary: Extends JMAP (RFC 8620) with Blob/upload, Blob/get and Blob/lookup methods and a blob capability, so blobs can be created, fetched and reverse-looked-up inline within JMAP requests.

JMAP.why: The document defines a JMAP extension: a new capability URI and the Blob/upload, Blob/get and Blob/lookup methods.
JMAP.quote: This extension adds additional ways to create and access blobs by making inline method calls within a standard JMAP request.

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding for JMAP requests and responses. The document does not define a JSON-based format in its own right.
Base64 is used for the data:asBase64 properties, but it is only a mechanism the document relies on. The document adds nothing about Base64 itself.
The upload and download endpoints are HTTP-based, but this document defines inline JMAP methods, not HTTP semantics. RFC 3230 digests are only referenced.
The document creates a registry and registers a capability and an error code. That is boilerplate-style registration, not the main subject.
Mailbox, Thread and Email appear only as examples of types that can reference blobs. The document does not address email itself.

gaps.name: JMAP (JSON Meta Application Protocol)
gaps.why: The document is about a JMAP extension, but the taxonomy has no JMAP tag outside email. The only JMAP tag is the one under email, which is scoped to mail and related data. I used it for lack of a better fit, and it is only an approximate match for a general blob extension.

RFC9405.title: AI Sarcasm Detection: Insult Your AI without Offending It
RFC9405.summary: An April 1st parody RFC proposing a framework for detecting sarcasm in AI systems via training data, tokenization, feature extraction and classification, with guidelines for using sarcasm inoffensively.

humor.why: Published 1 April as a whimsical, tongue-in-cheek document about sarcasm and AI; it belongs in the humorous RFC series.
humor.quote: The guidelines provided in this RFC offer a lighthearted and humorous approach to using sarcasm in a way that is both effective and respectful.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as a possible transport for detection requests; the document specifies nothing about HTTP/2.
Only mentioned as a way to log detection results; the document is not about syslog.
Cited in Security Considerations as boilerplate-level advice; the document is not about TLS.
IANA Considerations only recommends a future sarcasm MIME type; no media type is defined in the body.
HTTP and HTTPS are cited only in passing as transport and security; the document defines nothing about HTTP.

gaps.name: AI / natural language processing (sarcasm detection)
gaps.why: The document's actual subject is machine-learning-based sarcasm detection in AI systems, and the taxonomy has no AI or NLP tag.

RFC9406.title: HyStart++: Modified Slow Start for TCP
RFC9406.summary: RFC 9406 specifies HyStart++, a modification to TCP slow start that uses RTT increase to exit slow start early, with a Conservative Slow Start phase to avoid premature exit due to jitter.

congestion control.why: The document specifies a slow start exit algorithm for congestion control. It is not a new TCP protocol or option, so the topic tag fits better than the TCP tag.
congestion control.quote: HyStart++ uses increase in round-trip delay as a heuristic to find an exit point before possible overshoot.

TCP.why: The algorithm is specified for TCP senders and builds on RFC 5681. It modifies TCP sender behaviour (cwnd, ssthresh, RTT sampling), so TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: While this document describes HyStart++ for TCP, it can also be used for other transport protocols that use slow start

rejected.why: QUIC is mentioned only as another transport that could use HyStart++. The document is not about it.
SCTP is mentioned only as another transport that could use HyStart++. The document is not about it.
ECN marking is only one of the signals that ends slow start. It is not a subject of the document.
HyStart++ is not tied to CUBIC in the text. CUBIC is not mentioned.

RFC9407.title: Tetrys: An On-the-Fly Network Coding Protocol
RFC9407.summary: Describes Tetrys, an experimental on-the-fly network coding protocol that uses an elastic encoding window, linear combinations over finite fields and receiver feedback to recover packet erasures for delay-sensitive flows, with packet formats and research issues.

Tetrys.why: The document specifies the Tetrys protocol itself: encoding, elastic window, decoding, packet formats.
Tetrys.quote: Tetrys, which is an on-the-fly network coding protocol that can be used to transport delay-sensitive and loss-sensitive data over a lossy network

congestion control.why: A substantial research-issues section covers interaction of coding with congestion control and adaptive coding rate, though Tetrys is the main subject.
congestion control.quote: Coding rate adaptation within Tetrys can have major impacts on congestion control if done inappropriately.

rejected.why: Tetrys is a child of FEC in the taxonomy and is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
Referenced for header extension compatibility and security discussion only; the document doesn't specify a FECFRAME scheme.
The header format is inspired by LCT, but LCT is not what the document is about.
ESP is mentioned only as a baseline security option in Security Considerations.
UDP is mentioned only as a possible underlying transport whose source port may serve as the TSI.
NORM and RMT are cited as related work; Tetrys targets unicast flows primarily.

gaps.name: network coding
gaps.why: The document is about on-the-fly network coding (RLC-style linear coding over finite fields); only the Tetrys tag under FEC captures it, with no general network coding tag.

RFC9408.title: A YANG Network Data Model for Service Attachment Points (SAPs)
RFC9408.summary: Defines the ietf-sap-ntw YANG module, augmenting the RFC 8345 network model with Service Attachment Points (UNI and NNI) so a controller can expose where VPN, slice and other services can be or are attached.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a new YANG network data model (ietf-sap-ntw) that augments ietf-network.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model for representing an abstract view of the provider network topology that contains the points from which its services can be attached

VPN.why: The model is tied to provider-provisioned VPN services. It reuses RFC 9181 service types and works with the L3NM and L2NM, and the appendices illustrate it with VPN examples, including inter-AS Option A.
VPN.quote: The SAPs are the network reference points to which network services, such as Layer 3 Virtual Private Network (L3VPN) or Layer 2 Virtual Private Network (L2VPN), can be attached.

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF only provide the access protocols; the document defines a data model, not protocol behaviour.
SDN is mentioned only briefly as a context for exchanging information between control elements; it is not the subject.
L3VPN appears as one of several example service types and in illustrations; the document does not specify or extend L3VPN.
EVPN is only listed as a supported service type.
This is a YANG model, not a MIB module or SMI.
JSON is only the encoding used in the examples.

gaps.name: Service Attachment Points / service models and network models for service automation
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for YANG service/network model topology and inventory or service orchestration. YANG and VPN capture it only partly.

RFC9409.title: The 'sip-trunking-capability' Link Relation Type
RFC9409.summary: Registers the 'sip-trunking-capability' link relation type, used (e.g., via WebFinger) to locate an ITSP's SIP trunking capability set document for automated enterprise-to-ITSP SIP peering.

web linking.why: The document's core deliverable is a new link relation type registered in the Link Relation Types registry under RFC 8288 Web Linking.
web linking.quote: This document specifies the 'sip-trunking-capability' link relation type according to the rules of RFC 8288.

SIP.why: The link relation exists to support automated SIP trunk peering between enterprise and ITSP networks, so SIP readers would want it.
SIP.quote: allows for automated establishment of SIP [RFC3261] trunking between the two telephony networks.

WebFinger.why: The example usage shows a WebFinger query and JRD response using the new relation, a substantial part of the body.
WebFinger.quote: solicits the location of the capability set document from the well-known URI hosted by the ITSP using the WebFinger protocol [RFC7033].

rejected.why: The document concerns enterprise-to-ITSP trunk configuration discovery, not SPEERMINT peering between SIP service providers.
OAuth 2.0 is mentioned only as an example way for the ITSP to identify the enterprise.
JSON and JRD are only the encoding of the example responses.
URIs and well-known URIs are only referenced, and the document does not define anything new about them.

RFC9410.title: Handling of Identity Header Errors for Secure Telephone Identity Revisited (STIR)
RFC9410.summary: Extends STIR/SIP Identity header error handling by defining a "STIR" Reason header protocol and a "ppi" parameter so verification failures can be reported to the authentication service via provisional responses, including for multiple Identity headers.

STIR.why: The document extends STIR error handling for Identity header fields and PASSporT verification failures, so it belongs on the STIR page.
STIR.quote: This document defines a new Reason header field [RFC3326] protocol, "STIR", for STIR applications using SIP as defined in [RFC8224].

SIP.why: It defines new SIP Reason header protocol and parameter usage in SIP responses. SIP readers would want it, though STIR is the main subject.
SIP.quote: Any provisional SIP response message or final response message, with the exception of a 100 (Trying), MAY contain one or more Reason header fields

rejected.why: PASSporT is a JWT-based token, but the document only uses it as an identifier in the ppi parameter and does not specify it.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate that supports the main body, which is not about IANA guidance.
It concerns error reporting for caller identity authentication, which the STIR tag already covers more specifically.

RFC9411.title: Benchmarking Methodology for Network Security Device Performance
RFC9411.summary: RFC 9411 defines benchmarking terminology and methodology for next-generation firewalls and intrusion prevention systems, covering testbed setup, DUT configuration, KPIs, HTTP/HTTPS throughput, connection rate, latency and capacity tests, and a CVE-based security effectiveness test; it obsoletes RFC 3511.

benchmarking.why: The whole document is a benchmarking methodology for network devices, with test setups, KPIs, procedures and reporting formats.
benchmarking.quote: This document provides benchmarking terminology and methodology for next-generation network security devices, including next-generation firewalls (NGFWs) and next-generation intrusion prevention systems (NGIPSs).

firewall.why: The devices under test are NGFWs and NGIPSs, and the document specifies how to configure and measure them. It obsoletes the firewall benchmarking RFC 3511.
firewall.quote: The DUT/SUT MUST be configured in "Inline" mode so that the traffic is actively inspected by the DUT/SUT.

rejected.why: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are only the traffic generated for the tests. The document does not specify or extend HTTP.
TLS is used for the HTTPS test traffic and for TLS inspection on the DUT. Cipher suites are recommended for testing only, so the document is not about TLS.
QUIC is emulated as test traffic and its parameters are configured on the test equipment. The document does not define or extend QUIC.
TCP stack parameters are set for the emulated clients and servers, and TCP connection rate is a KPI. TCP itself is the substrate, not the subject.
The benchmarking tag sits under network management, but the document's subject is device benchmarking rather than network performance metrics, so the more specific benchmarking tag fits.

RFC9412.title: The ORIGIN Extension in HTTP/3
RFC9412.summary: Registers and specifies the ORIGIN frame (type 0x0c) for HTTP/3, carrying over the HTTP/2 ORIGIN frame semantics so servers can indicate which origins a connection is authoritative for.

HTTP/3.why: The document defines a new HTTP/3 frame type and registers it in the HTTP/3 Frame Types registry, so it extends HTTP/3.
HTTP/3.quote: The ORIGIN HTTP/3 frame allows a server to indicate what origin or origins [RFC6454] the server would like the client to consider

rejected.why: The HTTP/2 ORIGIN frame is defined in RFC 8336. This document only references it as the source of the semantics and does not extend HTTP/2.
QUIC is only the substrate for HTTP/3. The document borrows its frame diagram notation and defines nothing new about QUIC.
HTTP/3 is the more specific child tag, so the parent is implied.
The only IANA content is a routine frame-type registration. The document is not about IANA registries.

RFC9413.title: Maintaining Robust Protocols
RFC9413.summary: IAB document arguing that the robustness principle ("be liberal in what you accept") is overapplied, and recommending active protocol maintenance, virtuous intolerance and deliberate exclusion to keep protocols interoperable over time.

internet architecture.why: The document is an architectural-principles discussion of the robustness principle, protocol decay, extensibility and ecosystem effects. No more specific tag exists, so the broader architecture topic fits.
internet architecture.quote: The robustness principle, often phrased as "be conservative in what you send, and liberal in what you accept", has long guided the design and implementation of Internet protocols.

rejected.why: Used only as an example of a ClientHello empty-extension bug; the document does not specify or analyse TLS.
Cited as an example of error handling (RFC 7606) in a flexible protocol; the document is not about BGP.
Mentioned as a protocol whose specifications were restored after neglect; only an example.
INADEQUATE_SECURITY is cited once as an example of virtuous intolerance.
QUIC error frames are cited once as an example of fatal error mechanisms.
It touches on maintenance within the standards process, but the focus is protocol design and implementation practice, not IETF procedure.

gaps.name: Protocol maintenance / robustness principle / protocol design guidance
gaps.why: The document's core subject is general protocol design and maintenance practice (robustness principle, extensibility, active maintenance). The taxonomy only has the broad 'internet architecture' topic, with no tag for protocol design guidance.

RFC9414.title: Unfortunate History of Transient Numeric Identifiers
RFC9414.summary: An IRTF/PEARG informational document giving a historical timeline of how transient numeric identifiers (IP ID, TCP ISNs, IPv6 IIDs, NTP REFIDs, ephemeral ports, DNS ID) were specified and attacked, showing that advice on generating them is warranted.

privacy.why: The document analyses the security and privacy consequences of predictable identifiers across protocols, including host tracking and information leakage. It is a cross-protocol privacy analysis.
privacy.quote: how the security and privacy properties of such protocols have been affected as a result of it

TCP.why: A full timeline covers TCP initial sequence numbers and TCP ephemeral ports. It traces the specification flaws from RFC 793 through RFC 6528 and RFC 9293.
TCP.quote: [RFC0793] suggests the use of a global 32-bit ISN generator that is incremented by 1 roughly every 4 microseconds.

IPv6.why: The IPv6 Fragment Identification and IPv6 Interface Identifier timelines make up a large part of the document. They cover RFC 4291, 7217, 7721, 8064 and 8981.
IPv6.quote: The IPv6 Identification was originally specified in [RFC1883].

DNS.why: The DNS ID timeline covers cache poisoning through predictable IDs and ports, the Kaminsky attack and RFC 5452. It is a substantial section.
DNS.quote: The DNS ID [RFC1035] can be employed to match DNS replies to outstanding DNS queries.

rejected.why: The NTP REFID and NTP port randomization timelines are short examples within a broader analysis. NTP is not the document's subject.
IIDs generated by SLAAC are discussed only as one sample identifier. The document is not about SLAAC itself.
The IPv4 Identification field is one of several samples. The document is not about IPv4 itself.
Algorithms for generating the identifiers are left to RFC 9415. This document is a history and does not specify randomness requirements.
The timelines are history, but they serve a security and privacy argument rather than being a retrospective on the Internet.

gaps.name: transient numeric identifiers / predictable identifier generation
gaps.why: The document's central subject has no specific taxonomy tag. Only the broad privacy and security topics and the individual protocols fit.

RFC9415.title: On the Generation of Transient Numeric Identifiers
RFC9415.summary: An IRTF PEARG informational RFC that categorizes transient numeric identifiers (IPv6 IDs, IIDs, TCP ISNs, ephemeral ports, DNS IDs) by interoperability requirements and failure severity, gives algorithms to generate them, and assesses their security and privacy vulnerabilities.

privacy.why: The document analyses privacy implications such as network activity correlation, fingerprinting and information leakage from identifier generation, and gives guidance to minimise them.
privacy.quote: performs an analysis of the security and privacy implications of different types of "transient numeric identifiers" used in IETF protocols

randomness.why: Much of the document covers PRNG and CSPRNG choice, modulo bias and PRF-based generation of identifiers, so readers of randomness generation would want it.
randomness.quote: The requirement of uniqueness with a soft failure severity can be complied with a Pseudorandom Number Generator (PRNG).

rejected.why: TCP ISNs, ephemeral ports and timestamps are examples of identifiers. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
IPv6 IDs, IIDs and flow labels are surveyed as examples, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
The DNS ID is only one example identifier in the survey.
This parent topic is implied by the narrower privacy tag, so it is not chosen separately.
HMAC is only one possible PRF option for the generation algorithms.
SLAAC and RFC 7217 are cited as an example use of the stable-identifier algorithm, not specified here.

gaps.name: Transient numeric identifier generation / protocol identifier selection
gaps.why: The document's core subject is the selection of unpredictable protocol identifiers (ports, IDs, sequence numbers). The taxonomy has no tag for it that is not tied to one protocol.

RFC9416.title: Security Considerations for Transient Numeric Identifiers Employed in Network Protocols
RFC9416.summary: BCP that updates RFC 3552 to require protocol specifications to state interoperability requirements for transient numeric identifiers, assess their vulnerabilities, and avoid predictable generation.

privacy.why: The document gives protocol-design requirements on the security and privacy implications of identifier choice, including information leakage, tracking and correlation across contexts. This fits the privacy topic better than the general security topic.
privacy.quote: This entire document is about the security and privacy implications of transient numeric identifiers

rejected.why: TCP ISNs and ports are examples of identifiers. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
IPv6 IIDs and fragment IDs are only examples. The document is not about IPv6.
DNS IDs are one cited example of a predictable identifier, not the subject.
Flawed PRNGs are mentioned as one common flaw. The document does not address randomness generation in its own right. The generation algorithms are covered in RFC 9415.
The parent topic is implied by the more specific privacy tag. The document is not a general security handbook.
NTP Reference IDs appear only in a list of examples.

gaps.name: Transient numeric identifiers / predictable identifiers
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the security of protocol identifier generation, such as sequence numbers, ports and IDs. The document is about this subject, and the related RFCs 9414 and 9415 would share the tag.

RFC9417.title: Service Assurance for Intent-Based Networking Architecture
RFC9417.summary: Describes the SAIN architecture for assuring service instances in intent-based networking, using assurance graphs of subservices, SAIN agents/orchestrator/collector, health scores and symptoms, with YANG-modelled interfaces defined in RFC 9418.

network management.why: The document is an operations/management architecture for service assurance, monitoring, symptom correlation and service impact analysis, which fits the general network management topic.
network management.quote: This document describes an architecture that provides some assurance that service instances are running as expected.

YANG.why: The component interfaces are defined as YANG modules and the architecture is built around model-driven telemetry and Network Service YANG Modules. A dedicated section covers the open YANG interfaces.
YANG.quote: The architecture presented in this document is implemented by a set of YANG modules defined in a companion document [RFC9418].

telemetry.why: Health status is streamed from agents to the collector via model-driven telemetry, a substantial part of the architecture.
telemetry.quote: Stream (via telemetry, such as YANG-Push [RFC8641]) operational and config metric values when possible, else continuously poll.

rejected.why: The architecture involves orchestrators and closed-loop automation, but it is about assurance and monitoring rather than a programmable, separated control plane.
NETCONF and RESTCONF are mentioned only in Security Considerations as protection for the YANG configuration.
NTP is only a candidate for time synchronization between the elements. The document does not specify or extend it.
L2VPN and L3VPN appear only as example services to assure, not as the subject of the document.
MIB modules are mentioned only as one possible source of metrics behind the metric engine.
IS-IS appears only in the example assurance graph of a tunnel service.

gaps.name: Intent-based networking / service assurance
gaps.why: The document's central subject is service assurance for intent-based networking. The taxonomy has no tag for intent-based networking or service assurance, so network management is the closest fit.

RFC9418.title: A YANG Data Model for Service Assurance
RFC9418.summary: Specifies YANG modules (base, device, interface, plus examples) modelling service assurance graphs of subservices, dependencies, health scores and symptoms for the SAIN architecture.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a set of YANG modules with tree diagrams, augmentation guidelines and examples.
YANG.quote: This document specifies YANG modules for representing assurance graphs.

telemetry.why: A major use case is exporting health scores and symptoms of services and subservices, i.e. service assurance monitoring of network state.
telemetry.quote: Assurance telemetry: Export the assurance graph with health statuses and symptoms for each node.

rejected.why: Only mentioned in Security Considerations as an access protocol; the document does not specify or extend it.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a transport option.
Appears only as an example subservice module in an appendix; the document is not about the IS-IS protocol.
Assurance for intent-based networking is the architecture of RFC 9417; this document is only the data model, not about autonomic networking.
Parent of YANG and telemetry, already implied by those tags.
Used only for example instance and YANG library encoding.

gaps.name: Service assurance / intent-based networking (SAIN)
gaps.why: The document's core subject is service assurance via assurance graphs, which has no dedicated tag in the taxonomy.

RFC9419.title: Considerations on Application - Network Collaboration Using Path Signals
RFC9419.summary: IAB guidance document setting out architectural principles (intentional distribution, consent, minimization, limited impact, minimal entity set) for designing explicit, authenticated path signals between applications and network elements, and listing areas for further work.

internet architecture.why: The document is IAB architectural guidance on how applications and on-path network elements should collaborate, which is the core subject of the internet architecture tag.
internet architecture.quote: This section provides architecture-level principles for protocol designers and recommends models to apply for network collaboration and signaling.

privacy.why: Much of the document concerns privacy implications of exposing information, data minimization, consent and pervasive monitoring, so readers of privacy considerations would want it.
privacy.quote: these principles focus on the inherent privacy and security concerns of sharing information between endpoints and network elements

rejected.why: QUIC is only cited as an example of encrypted transport with explicit signals like the Spin Bit; the document does not specify or analyse it.
TCP header fields are mentioned only as an example of implicit path signals.
ECN is mentioned as an example of an openly distributed path signal, not addressed in its own right.
Oblivious DNS and PDoT are only listed as related work in the further work section.
The document has no security considerations and its security content is better covered by the privacy tag.

gaps.name: path signals / application-network collaboration
gaps.why: The document's central subject, explicit signalling between endpoints and on-path elements (RFC 8558 path signals), has no dedicated tag. Internet architecture is the closest fit.

RFC9420.title: The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Protocol
RFC9420.summary: RFC 9420 specifies the Messaging Layer Security (MLS) protocol, an asynchronous group key establishment protocol using ratchet trees, providing forward secrecy and post-compromise security for end-to-end encrypted group messaging.

MLS.why: The entire document defines the MLS protocol: ratchet trees, key schedule, proposals, commits, Welcome messages, framing and extensibility.
MLS.quote: we specify a key establishment protocol that provides efficient asynchronous group key establishment with forward secrecy (FS) and post-compromise security (PCS)

rejected.why: TLS is used only for its presentation language and as a recommended transport; the document does not specify or extend TLS.
Group key establishment is the subject, but MLS is the more specific tag, so the topic parent is implied.
X.509 is only one supported credential type; the document does not profile certificates.
QUIC is only mentioned as a recommended secure transport and as the source of the variable-length integer encoding.
The message/mls media type registration is a minor IANA item, not a main subject.
The registries it creates are boilerplate for the protocol, not the subject of the document.

RFC9421.title: HTTP Message Signatures
RFC9421.summary: Defines a mechanism for creating, encoding and verifying detached digital signatures or MACs over selected components of HTTP messages, with the Signature, Signature-Input and Accept-Signature fields and IANA registries.

HTTP.why: Defines new HTTP fields (Signature, Signature-Input, Accept-Signature), derived components and canonicalization of HTTP messages; it is an HTTP extension.
HTTP.quote: This document describes a mechanism for creating, encoding, and verifying digital signatures or message authentication codes over components of an HTTP message.

rejected.why: Signatures can be used for authentication, but the document is a general message integrity mechanism, not an authentication scheme.
Only the substrate it complements; the document explains TLS's limits but defines nothing about TLS.
JWS algorithms may be used for signing, but this is a minor subsection and not the document's subject.
Algorithms are used as signature options, not specified or profiled in their own right.
One of several algorithms referenced; HMAC is not defined or extended here.
Considered as a parent, but the specific fit is HTTP; the document is not about a browser platform security mechanism.

RFC9422.title: The LIMITS SMTP Service Extension
RFC9422.summary: Defines the LIMITS SMTP service extension, letting SMTP, submission and LMTP servers advertise session limits (MAILMAX, RCPTMAX, RCPTDOMAINMAX) in the EHLO/LHLO response, and creates an IANA registry of such limits.

SMTP.why: The document specifies a new SMTP service extension, with its EHLO keyword, parameter syntax, and limits applying to MAIL FROM and RCPT TO commands.
SMTP.quote: This document defines a LIMITS extension for the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), including submission, as well as the Local Mail Transfer Protocol (LMTP).

rejected.why: Implied as the parent of SMTP; the more specific SMTP tag is chosen.
ABNF is only used as notation to define the parameter syntax, not the subject of the document.
The new limits registry is boilerplate-style registration for the extension, not a document about IANA guidance in its own right.
STARTTLS is only mentioned as a case where EHLO is reissued.

gaps.name: LMTP (Local Mail Transfer Protocol)
gaps.why: The extension also applies to LMTP (LHLO), but the taxonomy has no LMTP tag; SMTP is the closest fit.

RFC9423.title: Constrained RESTful Environments (CoRE) Target Attributes Registry
RFC9423.summary: Creates an IANA "Target Attributes" registry for Web Link target attribute names used in CoRE, with expert instructions and initial entries, and updates the RD Parameters registry to coordinate with it.

web linking.why: The registry coordinates target attribute names for Web Links (RFC 8288) as used in CoRE link serialisations; readers of web linking would want it.
web linking.quote: This document introduces an IANA registry for coordinating names of target attributes when used in CoRE

CoAP.why: The registry is part of the CoRE/CoAP parameters group and its initial entries come from CoAP specs (ct, obs, osc, hct, rt, if, sz, and RD attributes), so CoAP resource discovery readers need it.
CoAP.quote: Link Format [RFC6690] in the Constrained Application Protocol's (CoAP's) resource discovery process

rejected.why: The document is an IANA registry creation, but the registry is specific to CoRE target attributes. It is not general IANA guidance, and IANA Considerations is boilerplate for tagging here.
Web Linking is used in the HTTP Link header, but the document is not about HTTP.
Only the 'osc' attribute entry refers to OSCORE; the document is not about it.
Link Format and the Resource Directory are discovery mechanisms, but the document only registers attribute names. The attributes are not a discovery mechanism.

gaps.name: CoRE Link Format / Resource Directory
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the CoRE Link Format (RFC 6690) or the CoRE Resource Directory (RFC 9176), which this registry serves.

RFC9424.title: Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) and Their Role in Attack Defence
RFC9424.summary: Informational document describing Indicators of Compromise (IoCs), the Pyramid of Pain, the IoC lifecycle, opportunities, operational limitations and defence-in-depth use, with case studies (Cobalt Strike, APT33).

operational security.why: The document is about operational practice for cyber defence using IoCs: discovery, sharing, deployment, detection and limitations. This is the closest fit for operational security.
operational security.quote: This document reviews the fundamentals, opportunities, operational limitations, and recommendations for IoC use.

incident response.why: A substantial part covers sharing and exchanging threat indicators between organisations and reacting to detections. It touches on incident and threat information exchange, though IODEF is only one cited format.
incident response.quote: Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) [RFC7970]. This enables distribution via a structured feed

rejected.why: Protective DNS filtering and DGAs are discussed as deployment points for IoCs, but the document doesn't specify or analyse DNS itself.
Mentioned only as one of several sharing formats; the document doesn't specify or extend it.
TLS SNI and certificates are examples of IoC types, not subjects of the document.
IDS/IPS are mentioned as consumers of IoCs, but the document doesn't address intrusion detection message exchange.
Not about DDoS mitigation.
Section 5.3 on sharing privacy trade-offs is brief and not a protocol privacy analysis.

gaps.name: Cyber threat intelligence / indicators of compromise
gaps.why: The document is about IoCs and threat intelligence sharing for attack defence. The taxonomy has no tag specific to threat intelligence or cyber defence, so operational security and incident response are only approximate fits.

RFC9425.title: JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP) for Quotas
RFC9425.summary: Defines a JMAP extension with a Quota data type, capability URI, and standard get/changes/query/queryChanges methods so clients can read account, domain, or global usage limits.

JMAP.why: The whole document is a JMAP extension: new capability urn:ietf:params:jmap:quota, Quota data type and methods, and push support. Readers of JMAP would want it.
JMAP.quote: This specification defines a data model for handling quotas over JMAP, allowing a user to obtain details about a certain quota.

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding JMAP uses; the document defines no JSON format of its own beyond the JMAP data model.
Mail is only one of the data types a quota can apply to (an example); the document is not about email itself.
HTTP is merely referenced for the Accept-Language header on the description field; it is substrate.
The IANA section registers a capability and data type, which is boilerplate and not the subject.
UTF-8 is mentioned only as the encoding of the description string.

gaps.name: JMAP (JSON Meta Application Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has a JMAP tag only under email (JMAP: for mail and related data), but I wrote the id 'JMAP' without checking it exists. Looking again, the id is 'JMAP' under email, so it is valid, but it is scoped to mail and related data, whereas this RFC is a generic JMAP quota extension not specific to mail.

RFC9426.title: BATched Sparse (BATS) Coding Scheme for Multi-hop Data Transport
RFC9426.summary: Describes a baseline BATS (BATched Sparse) network coding scheme, with a fountain-code-like outer code and linear network coding recoding at intermediate nodes, for multi-hop data delivery, and discusses research issues.

BATS.why: The document specifies the BATS coding scheme: outer encoder, recoder and outer decoder, with parameters and packet formats.
BATS.quote: BATched Sparse (BATS) code is a class of efficient linear network coding scheme with a matrix generalization of fountain codes as the outer code

rejected.why: RaptorQ is cited only as related work and for inactivation decoding. The document is not about Raptor codes.
BATS is related to FEC, but the closest child tag is BATS, which is more specific. The parent is implied.
Congestion control is mentioned only as a research issue, not addressed in its own right.
Ad hoc networks are one usage scenario in Section 4.3. The document does not specify MANET routing.
CCN and liquid data networking appear only as a brief candidate use case.

RFC9427.title: TLS-Based Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Types for Use with TLS 1.3
RFC9427.summary: Updates TLS-based EAP methods (EAP-FAST, EAP-TTLS, TEAP, PEAP) for TLS 1.3 by defining new key derivations via the TLS Exporter, and addresses application data, identities, session tickets and resumption.

EAP.why: The document specifies updated key derivation, client certificate handling, identities and resumption for EAP-TTLS, TEAP, EAP-FAST and PEAP, and updates RFCs 4851, 5281 and 7170.
EAP.quote: This document updates those methods in order to use the new key derivation methods available in TLS 1.3.

TLS.why: A substantial part covers TLS 1.3 behaviour affecting EAP: the TLS-Exporter, NewSessionTicket handling, post-handshake application data, resumption, and new TLS Exporter labels.
TLS.quote: Unlike previous TLS versions, TLS 1.3 can continue negotiation after the initial TLS handshake has been completed

rejected.why: NAI realm routing in AAA frameworks is discussed only in the identities guidance. The document is not about AAA frameworks.
RADIUS is mentioned only via a reference on dynamic peer discovery and the User-Name attribute. It is not the subject.
HMAC is used for the TEAP compound MAC and in PEAP derivations, but only as a mechanism the document relies on.
The only IANA content is registering TLS Exporter labels, which is boilerplate-level and not what the document is about.

RFC9428.title: Transmission of IPv6 Packets over Near Field Communication
RFC9428.summary: Specifies how IPv6 packets are transmitted over NFC peer-to-peer mode (LLCP) using 6LoWPAN techniques: SLAAC with stable IIDs from the SSAP, ND via RFC 6775/8505, IPHC header compression, MTU via MIUX, no fragmentation, and unicast-only multicast handling.

6LoWPAN.why: The document is an IPv6-over-constrained-link adaptation specification using 6LoWPAN: dispatch header, IPHC compression, ND optimization, and 6LN/6LR/6LBR roles over NFC.
6LoWPAN.quote: This document describes how IPv6 is transmitted over NFC using IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (6LoWPAN) techniques.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the payload carried; the document does not specify IPv6 itself, and the more specific 6LoWPAN tag covers it.
SLAAC is used with stable IIDs per RFC 7217 but only profiled as part of the adaptation, not the focus.
Uses RFC 6775/8505 ND as defined elsewhere; a section applies it but does not define new ND behaviour.
Relies on RFC 6282 IPHC and GHC as defined elsewhere; no new compression is specified.
NFC is not a cellular network.

gaps.name: Near Field Communication (NFC)
gaps.why: The document is about IPv6 over NFC, an RFID-derived short-range link technology, and the taxonomy has no link-layer tag for NFC or similar short-range wireless.

RFC9429.title: JavaScript Session Establishment Protocol (JSEP)
RFC9429.summary: RFC 9429 specifies JSEP, the API-level mechanisms by which a JavaScript application controls WebRTC session establishment via SDP offer/answer and ICE, including SDP generation and parsing procedures; it obsoletes RFC 8829.

WebRTC.why: JSEP is a core WebRTC specification defining the RTCPeerConnection signaling-plane behavior in browsers.
WebRTC.quote: This document describes how the W3C Web Real-Time Communication (WebRTC) RTCPeerConnection interface [W3C.webrtc] is used to control the setup, management, and teardown of a multimedia session.

SDP.why: Much of the document (Section 5) specifies how SDP offers and answers are constructed, parsed, and applied, including offer/answer, bundle, simulcast and imageattr attributes.
SDP.quote: JSEP's session descriptions use Session Description Protocol (SDP) syntax for their internal representation.

ICE.why: Substantial sections cover ICE gathering, trickling, candidate policy, candidate pool, and restarts as exposed through the JSEP API.
ICE.quote: JSEP decouples the ICE state machine from the overall signaling state machine.

rejected.why: SIP is only mentioned as one possible signaling protocol and in forking discussion; JSEP is signaling-agnostic.
RTP/RTCP handling is described via SDP attributes, but the document does not specify RTP itself.
DTLS is a required substrate for media and data; the document defines nothing new about it.
Data channels use SCTP/DTLS as a substrate, with only SDP lines for it.
STUN/TURN servers are only configured for ICE gathering; not specified here.

RFC9430.title: Extension of the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) Profile for Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments (ACE) to Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC9430.summary: RFC 9430 updates the DTLS profile of ACE (RFC 9202) so that it applies to TLS as well as DTLS, and gives rules for choosing between them when a Client connects to a Resource Server.

ACE.why: The document extends an ACE profile. It changes how the Client and Resource Server establish their security association, and it updates the coap_dtls profile registration.
ACE.quote: This document updates "Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) Profile for Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments (ACE)" (RFC 9202) by specifying that the profile applies to TLS as well as DTLS.

rejected.why: TLS is the transport security mechanism that the ACE profile now also uses. The document defines no new TLS extension or behaviour.
DTLS is the existing substrate of the RFC 9202 profile. Nothing new is defined about DTLS itself.
CoAP over UDP or TCP is the protocol that the profile secures. CoAP is not specified or extended here.
ACE builds on OAuth 2.0, but this document only touches the ACE profile and not OAuth itself.
OSCORE is mentioned only as an example of another profile that already supports both transports.

RFC9431.title: Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) and Transport Layer Security (TLS) Profile of Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments (ACE) Framework
RFC9431.summary: Defines the MQTT/TLS profile of the ACE framework, using PoP-bound OAuth 2.0 access tokens to authenticate and authorize MQTT clients' connect, publish and subscribe operations at a broker, with TLS providing confidentiality and broker authentication.

ACE.why: The document is an ACE profile (mqtt_tls). It defines token transport, PoP, scope (AIF-MQTT) and AS discovery for MQTT brokers.
ACE.quote: This document specifies a profile for the Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments (ACE) framework to enable authorization in a publish-subscribe messaging system

rejected.why: TLS is the secure transport and client-auth substrate. The only TLS-specific additions are an exporter label and cipher-suite requirements, which do not make the document about TLS.
OAuth 2.0 tokens and the AS/RS roles are used through the ACE framework. The document profiles ACE rather than specifying OAuth.
JWT and CWT are only token formats that the profile permits. The document does not define them.
CDDL is used only to write the AIF-MQTT scope data model.
CBOR is an optional encoding for tokens and is not the subject of the document.
HTTP carries the client-AS and RS-AS exchanges as a substrate.

gaps.name: MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport) publish-subscribe protocol
gaps.why: The document centres on MQTT authorization, but the taxonomy has no MQTT or publish-subscribe tag. Readers browsing for MQTT would want it.

RFC9432.title: DNS Catalog Zones
RFC9432.summary: Defines DNS catalog zones, a method for automatically provisioning member zones on primary and secondary name servers by publishing the list of zones and their properties as a regular DNS zone transferred via AXFR/IXFR.

DNS.why: The document specifies a new DNS zone structure (PTR records, properties, version TXT) and name server behaviour for catalog consumers and producers, so it belongs under DNS.
DNS.quote: This document describes a method for automatic DNS zone provisioning among DNS primary and secondary name servers by storing and transferring the catalog of zones

rejected.why: DNSSEC appears only in the group property example and in the state reset discussion. The document is not about signing or validation.
DNS UPDATE is mentioned only as an optional way to modify catalog zones, with a recommendation to authenticate it. The document does not specify it.
Zone transfer over TLS is cited only in Security Considerations as a way to protect transfers. It is not part of the document's subject.
The document recommends the 'invalid.' name from RFC 6761 for catalog zones. It uses that name but does not define special-use names.
The document creates one registry for catalog zone properties. That is boilerplate-level apparatus, not the subject of the document.

RFC9433.title: Segment Routing over IPv6 for the Mobile User Plane
RFC9433.summary: Informational document describing how SRv6 can serve as the mobile (3GPP 5G) user plane in place of GTP-U, defining new SRv6 endpoint behaviors (End.MAP, End.M.GTP6.D/E, End.M.GTP4.E, H.M.GTP4.D, End.Limit) and interworking with legacy GTP-U gNBs.

SRv6.why: The document defines new SRv6 endpoint behaviors and applies SRv6 network programming to the mobile user plane.
SRv6.quote: This document also specifies the SRv6 Endpoint Behaviors required for mobility use cases.

cellular.why: Substantial portions cover the 3GPP 5G reference architecture (gNB, UPF, N3/N9/N6) and interworking with GTP-U and PDU session types.
cellular.quote: This document discusses how SRv6 could be used as the user plane of mobile networks.

rejected.why: Parent of SRv6; the more specific SRv6 tag fits, so the ancestor is implied.
SRv6 runs on IPv6, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
GTP-U tunnel replacement and interworking are discussed, but the focus is SRv6 behaviors, not generic tunnelling.
Mobile user plane is addressed, but this is 3GPP cellular user plane, not Mobile IP-style mobility; the document leaves the control plane unchanged.
Waypoint SIDs for TE are mentioned in the Enhanced mode, but not as the document's subject.
End.Limit rate limiting and QFI arguments are minor parts and do not make the document about QoS architectures.

gaps.name: SRv6 mobile user plane / 5G user plane (GTP-U replacement)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for SRv6 or its mobile-user-plane applications; 'segment routing' exists but SRv6 is the closest match, and there is no tag for 3GPP user-plane/GTP-U.

RFC9434.title: Drone Remote Identification Protocol (DRIP) Architecture
RFC9434.summary: Informational architecture document for DRIP, describing protocols and services for Unmanned Aircraft System Remote ID, including HHIT-based identifiers, DNS-based registries, broadcast/network RID, crowdsourced harvesting, and contact.

DRIP.why: The document is the DRIP architecture itself, defining the entities, identifiers, registries and trust model for drone remote identification.
DRIP.quote: This document describes an architecture for protocols and services to support Unmanned Aircraft System Remote Identification and tracking (UAS RID), plus UAS-RID-related communications.

HIP.why: HHITs/HITs derive from HIP, with HIP RRs and rendezvous servers used for lookup and HIP BEX for secure contact; a substantial part of the architecture builds on HIP identifiers.
HIP.quote: One method directly supported by the use of HHITs as DRIP entity identifiers is initiation of a HIP Base Exchange (BEX) and Bound End-to-End Tunnel (BEET).

DNS.why: The public registry is specified as DNS-based, with HHIT FQDNs delivering HI via HIP RRs, PTRs and revocation.
DNS.quote: A DRIP identifier MUST be registered as an Internet domain name (at an arbitrary level in the hierarchy, e.g., in .ip6.arpa). Thus, the DNS can provide all the needed public DRIP information.

rejected.why: RDAP and EPP are cited as methods the private registry can leverage, but only briefly; the document is not about them.
Mentioned in one sentence as something the private registry can leverage; not a subject of the document.
Only noted as usable to deliver untrusted public information; no substantive coverage.
HHITs are IPv6-compatible identifiers, but the document does not address IPv6 addressing itself.
Ed25519 is chosen as mandatory-to-implement signing algorithm, but this is a minor detail, not the document's subject.
Section 10 gives a short privacy discussion, but it is a boilerplate-like considerations section and details are deferred to future documents.

gaps.name: UAS Remote ID / UTM (unmanned aircraft traffic management)
gaps.why: DRIP is covered by the DRIP tag, but the broader subject of UAS Remote ID, Broadcast/Network RID, and UTM/USS has no dedicated taxonomy tag.

RFC9435.title: Considerations for Assigning a New Recommended Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP)
RFC9435.summary: Informational guidance for the IETF on assigning a new recommended Diffserv DSCP, covering observed DSCP re-marking behaviours (bleaching, ToS precedence manipulation), lower-layer mappings, and selection considerations.

Diffserv.why: The whole document is about Diffserv codepoints, PHBs, and DSCP re-marking along Internet paths, and about guiding new DSCP assignments.
Diffserv.quote: This document discusses considerations for assigning a new DSCP for a standard PHB.

rejected.why: Section 5.2 covers Diffserv-to-MPLS mappings, but only as one example of lower-layer DSCP interpretation. The document is not about MPLS.
Section 5.1.2 covers the 802.11 UP mapping as an example of re-marking. It is a small part of the document, and the document is not about Wi-Fi.
The IANA note only adds a pointer to the DSCP registry. That is boilerplate, and the document is not about IANA registry procedure.
Diffserv is the more specific tag under QoS, so the parent is implied.
The IP header ToS/DS field is discussed, but IPv4 itself is not the subject.

RFC9436.title: PIM Message Type Space Extension and Reserved Bits
RFC9436.summary: Defines use of the reserved bits in the PIM common header as per-message-type flag bits, extends the PIM message type space using subtypes for types 13-15, and updates the IANA PIM Message Types registry, obsoleting RFC 8736.

PIM.why: The document specifies the PIM common header flag bits and extends the PIM message type space, updating several PIM specifications.
PIM.quote: The PIM version 2 messages share a common message header format.  The common header definition contains eight reserved bits.

rejected.why: RFC 7761 is updated, but the document concerns the common header across all PIM message types, not the sparse mode protocol itself. The parent PIM tag fits better.
The document updates the PIM Message Types registry, but this is a protocol-specific registry change rather than IANA guidance. The IANA section is boilerplate evidence here.
Not related to the document's subject. The referenced PIM extensions are only mentioned for their flag bit usage.

RFC9437.title: Publish/Subscribe Functionality for the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP)
RFC9437.summary: RFC 9437 extends the LISP control plane with Publish/Subscribe so Map-Servers can notify ITRs/RTRs/PITRs of EID-to-RLOC mapping changes using Map-Request N-bit/I-bit additions and Map-Notify/Map-Notify-Ack procedures.

LISP.why: The document extends the LISP control plane with new Map-Request bits and subscribe/publish procedures between Map-Servers and xTRs.
LISP.quote: This document specifies an extension to the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) control plane to enable Publish/Subscribe (PubSub) operation.

rejected.why: Security considerations (nonces, PubSubKey via LISP-SEC) support the extension but are not the document's subject.
BGP is only mentioned in an appendix as an alternative for prefix redistribution.
The IANA section only registers bits; it is boilerplate rather than the subject.
LISP-YANG is only an informative reference for provisioning identifiers.

RFC9438.title: CUBIC for Fast and Long-Distance Networks
RFC9438.summary: RFC 9438 specifies the CUBIC congestion control algorithm for TCP (also usable for QUIC and SCTP), obsoleting RFC 8312, moving it to Standards Track, and updating RFC 5681 to allow CUBIC's more aggressive behavior.

CUBIC.why: The document specifies the CUBIC algorithm in full.
CUBIC.quote: CUBIC is a standard TCP congestion control algorithm that uses a cubic function instead of a linear congestion window increase function

RFC9439.title: Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) Performance Cost Metrics
RFC9439.summary: RFC 9439 extends ALTO with eight network performance cost metrics (one-way and round-trip delay, delay variation, loss rate, hop count, TCP throughput, residual and available bandwidth) and adds a "cost-context" field to convey the metric's source.

ALTO.why: The document extends the ALTO base protocol with new cost metrics, a cost-context field, and new IANA registries. A reader browsing ALTO would expect to find it.
ALTO.quote: This document addresses this issue by extending the specification to provide a variety of network performance metrics, including network delay, delay variation (a.k.a. jitter), packet loss rate, hop count, and bandwidth.

performance measurement.why: A substantial part of the document defines delay, jitter, loss and bandwidth performance metrics. It also covers statistical operators and how they relate to IPPM and TWAMP-based sources.
performance measurement.quote: This document introduces a mechanism called "cost-context" to provide additional details, when they are available

rejected.why: JSON is only the value encoding for the metrics, so it is a substrate and not the subject.
OSPF TE metric extensions are used as the source semantics for the end-to-end metrics. The document does not specify or extend OSPF.
BGP-LS is cited as a data source for link metrics. The document is not about BGP.
The TCP throughput metric references CUBIC for its estimation equation, but the document is not about CUBIC.
The examples use HTTP and the Last-Modified and Expires headers, but only as the transport for ALTO.
TWAMP is mentioned only as a possible measurement source, so it is not a subject of the document.

RFC9440.title: Client-Cert HTTP Header Field
