RFC9440.summary: Defines the Client-Cert and Client-Cert-Chain HTTP request header fields that a TLS-terminating reverse proxy uses to pass the client's X.509 certificate and chain to origin servers, with processing rules and deployment guidance.

HTTP.why: The document defines new HTTP header fields, with processing rules, caching (Vary) behaviour and field registrations. It is an HTTP extension.
HTTP.quote: this document describes two HTTP header fields, "Client-Cert" and "Client-Cert-Chain", which a TLS terminating reverse proxy (TTRP) adds to requests sent to the backend origin servers

rejected.why: The document relies on mutually authenticated TLS as the source of the certificate. It defines no TLS protocol change or extension.
X.509 certificates are only the payload carried in the header fields. The document does not profile them.
It has one rule about Vary and no-store for responses selected by Client-Cert. That is a small part of the document, not a substantial one.
It conveys client certificate information for access control. It defines no HTTP authentication scheme.
Base64 is only the encoding used for the Structured Field Byte Sequence.
HTTP/2 and HPACK are mentioned only in the deployment considerations on header compression and size.

RFC9441.title: Static Context Header Compression (SCHC) Compound Acknowledgement (ACK)
RFC9441.summary: RFC 9441 defines the SCHC Compound ACK message format and procedure, which carries bitmaps for several windows in one ACK in ACK-on-Error fragmentation mode. It updates RFC 8724 and extends the SCHC YANG module of RFC 9363.

SCHC.why: The document specifies an extension to SCHC fragmentation and loss recovery, replacing Section 8.4.3 of RFC 8724.
SCHC.quote: It defines a SCHC Compound ACK message format and procedure, which are intended to reduce the number of response transmissions

YANG.why: It defines a new YANG module augmenting the SCHC data model, with a full section on it.
YANG.quote: This document also extends the SCHC YANG data model defined in [RFC9363] by including a new leaf in the Ack-on-Error fragmentation mode
YANG.section: 5. SCHC Compound ACK YANG Data Model

rejected.why: LPWAN technologies are the target environment, but the parent tag is implied by SCHC and the document is not about a specific LPWAN technology.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in the Security Considerations boilerplate for the YANG module.
Sigfox is only mentioned in a list of LPWANs the mechanism could be used on.
LoRaWAN is only mentioned in a list of LPWANs the mechanism could be used on.

RFC9442.title: Static Context Header Compression (SCHC) over Sigfox Low-Power Wide Area Network (LPWAN)
RFC9442.summary: Defines the SCHC over Sigfox profile: parameter values, fragmentation modes (No-ACK, ACK-on-Error, ACK-Always), header sizes, and message formats for SCHC compression and fragmentation over the Sigfox LPWAN.

Sigfox.why: The document profiles SCHC for the Sigfox LPWAN, covering its uplink/downlink constraints and message formats.
Sigfox.quote: This document defines a profile of SCHC over Sigfox LPWAN and provides optimal parameter values and modes of operation.

SCHC.why: The document specifies SCHC fragmentation/reassembly modes, ACK formats, aborts and RuleID usage. SCHC is the framework being profiled.
SCHC.quote: This document describes the parameters, settings, and modes of operation to be used when SCHC is implemented over a Sigfox LPWAN.

rejected.why: The parent tag is implied by the more specific Sigfox and SCHC tags, so it is not listed separately.
CoAP is mentioned only as a possible context provisioning protocol, and the document says context configuration is out of scope.
NETCONF is mentioned only as a possible context provisioning protocol, and the document says context configuration is out of scope.
RESTCONF is mentioned only as a possible context provisioning protocol, and the document says context configuration is out of scope.
IPv6 appears in the architecture figure and as uncompressed packets carried over SCHC. The document is not about IPv6.
SCHC fragmentation uses ACK-based retransmission, but the document does not treat loss recovery schemes as a subject in their own right.

RFC9443.title: Multiplexing Scheme Updates for QUIC
RFC9443.summary: Updates RFC 7983 and RFC 5764 so the single-port demultiplexing scheme for DTLS, STUN, SRTP/SRTCP, ZRTP and TURN channels also covers QUIC packets, including the TURN channel overlap and the incompatibility with QUIC bit greasing.

QUIC.why: The document extends the packet demultiplexing scheme to classify QUIC packets by first byte. It also covers QUIC-specific matters such as grease_quic_bit and QUIC v2 compatibility.
QUIC.quote: to also allow QUIC [RFC9000] to be multiplexed on the same port.

RTP.why: The updated algorithm is the RTP receiver's demultiplexing scheme, covering RTP/RTCP and SRTP on a shared port. Readers of RTP would want it.
RTP.quote: defines a scheme for a Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) [RFC3550] receiver to demultiplex DTLS

TURN.why: A whole section resolves the overlap between TURN channel byte values and QUIC short-header first bytes, based on the TURN server's source address.
TURN.quote: [RFC7983] allocates the values from 64 to 79 in order to allow TURN channels to be demultiplexed

rejected.why: DTLS is one of the protocols being demultiplexed. The document defines nothing new about DTLS itself.
STUN is demultiplexed on the same port, but the document does not specify or extend it.
SRTP is one of the multiplexed protocols. The document does not change how SRTP works or how its keys are derived.
WebRTC appears only as a motivating use case, so it is not a subject of the document.
STUN and TURN are traversal tools, but the document is about packet demultiplexing, not NAT traversal.

RFC9444.title: Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) for Subdomains
RFC9444.summary: Extends ACME so a client can obtain certificates for subdomains by proving control of an ancestor domain, defining the subdomainAuthAllowed and ancestorDomain fields and a directory metadata flag.

ACME.why: The document extends ACME with new authorization, identifier and directory metadata fields for subdomain issuance, so it belongs on the ACME page.
ACME.quote: This document specifies how Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) can be used by a client to obtain a certificate for a subdomain identifier

rejected.why: DNS TXT records and domain-name terminology are used for challenges and definitions, but the document does not specify DNS itself.
Certificates are the output of ACME issuance, but the document does not profile X.509.
Covered by the more specific ACME tag; the document adds no general PKI content.
JSON is only the encoding for ACME objects.

RFC9445.title: RADIUS Extensions for DHCP-Configured Services
RFC9445.summary: Defines two new RADIUS attributes (DHCPv6-Options and DHCPv4-Options) carrying DHCP options, and updates RFC 4014 to relax the permitted RADIUS attributes in the DHCP relay agent RADIUS Attributes suboption, with an encrypted DNS provisioning example.

RADIUS.why: The document's core contribution is new RADIUS attributes, their packet usage, and a table of attributes.
RADIUS.quote: This document specifies two new RADIUS attributes: DHCPv6-Options (Section 3.1) and DHCPv4-Options (Section 3.2).

DHCP.why: It carries DHCP options in RADIUS, updates the DHCPv4 relay agent suboption of RFC 4014, and creates DHCP option registries.
DHCP.quote: The RADIUS Attributes DHCP suboption [RFC4014] enables a DHCPv4 relay agent to pass identification and authorization attributes received during RADIUS authentication to a DHCPv4 server.

DHCPv6.why: A whole attribute is dedicated to DHCPv6 options, and the document extends the DHCPv6 RADIUS option registry for relay agents.
DHCPv6.quote: This field contains a list of DHCPv6 options (Section 21 of [RFC8415]).

rejected.why: Encrypted DNS provisioning (DNR) is only the motivating example; the document does not specify encrypted DNS.
DNS resolvers are only the example service; the attributes are generic.
RADIUS is tagged more specifically.
IANA registries are boilerplate here, not the main subject.

RFC9446.title: Reflections on Ten Years Past the Snowden Revelations
RFC9446.summary: Independent-stream collection of four essays reflecting on the Snowden revelations ten years on, covering the journalistic experience, the IETF/technical community response (RFC 7258 pervasive monitoring, TLS 1.3, DoH/DoT, ACME), human rights impacts, and the history of the Crypto Wars.

privacy.why: The document is centrally about privacy and surveillance threats, the IETF's pervasive-monitoring response, and what privacy challenges remain for protocols.
privacy.quote: pervasive monitoring is an attack

security.why: Substantial parts cover the Crypto Wars, export-grade crypto, the Danvers Doctrine and IETF security posture in general, not a single mechanism.
security.quote: The IETF has long had a commitment to strong, ubiquitous encryption.

internet history.why: A retrospective on 2013 events and the longer history of government cryptography and the IETF's reaction.
internet history.quote: Now that some years have passed, it seems appropriate to reflect on that period of time

rejected.why: Discussed as an example of post-Snowden privacy work, but the document does not specify or analyse it.
TLS 1.3 and ECH are mentioned as outcomes; no TLS content is specified here.
Mentioned as an outcome of Let's Encrypt; not the subject.
Cited as an example of a human-rights-enabling protocol, only briefly.
The Crypto Wars history touches DES, DUAL_EC_DRBG and AES, but as policy history rather than algorithm content.
Describes IETF reaction (perpass, BCP 188), but the document is not about process itself.

gaps.name: Human rights and Internet protocols / pervasive surveillance policy
gaps.why: A large part of the document (Section 4) concerns human rights considerations and the HRPC research group, which has no dedicated taxonomy tag.

RFC9447.title: Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) Challenges Using an Authority Token
RFC9447.summary: Defines a generic ACME "tkauth-01" Authority Token Challenge, with a JWT-based "atc" token type, binding to the ACME account, and an HTTPS REST interface for acquiring tokens from a Token Authority, for use with identifiers such as TNAuthList.

ACME.why: The document defines a new ACME challenge type (tkauth-01), a new challenge field, and registries for ACME validation methods and token types. This is an extension of ACME.
ACME.quote: this document specifies a generic Authority Token Challenge for ACME that supports subtype claims for different identifiers or namespaces

JWT.why: A substantial part of the document defines the JWT Authority Token format, including the new "atc" claim and the use of the iss, jti and exp claims. It also registers the claim with IANA.
JWT.quote: This document specifies a tkauth-type of "atc", which contains a standard JWT [RFC7519] using a signature string defined by a JSON Web Signature (JWS)

rejected.why: HTTPS POST is only the transport for token acquisition. The document defines nothing new about HTTP itself.
TLS is only required for confidentiality in the Security Considerations, and the document adds nothing to TLS.
JWS is used to sign the token, but the document does not extend JOSE. The JWT format is the relevant subject.
The goal is issuing certificates, but the document defines no certificate profile. It specifies an ACME challenge and token.
ACME is the more specific subject, and the document is about proving eligibility through a challenge, not about PKI in general.
JSON is only the encoding of the token and request body.

gaps.name: ACME (Automated Certificate Management Environment)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an ACME tag under PKI, but this document's subject is an ACME challenge extension. Authority Token and TNAuthList profiles may warrant their own subtags.

RFC9448.title: TNAuthList Profile of Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) Authority Token
RFC9448.summary: Defines a profile of the ACME Authority Token (RFC 9447) with a new TNAuthList identifier type and tkauth-01 challenge so CAs can issue STIR certificates to VoIP providers for telephone number and SPC resources.

ACME.why: The ACME tag is not in the taxonomy list as shown? It is: ACME under PKI. The document extends ACME with a new identifier type, challenge usage, token validation and an x5u order field.
ACME.quote: This document defines a new type of identifier object called TNAuthList.

STIR.why: The profile exists to obtain STIR certificates containing the TNAuthList used to sign PASSporTs, addressing the STIR problem statement.
STIR.quote: automated and authorized creation of certificates for Voice over IP (VoIP) telephone providers to support Secure Telephone Identity (STI)

rejected.why: The Authority Token is a JWT, but the document only profiles claims for it and uses JWT as a substrate, not as the subject.
JWS is used for ACME messages and the x5u header, as a mechanism rather than the subject.
Certificates carry the TNAuthList extension, defined in RFC 8226; this document concerns issuance via ACME, not the certificate profile.
SIP carries PASSporTs but is only mentioned as background context.
HTTP is used as the transport for the token acquisition and ACME messages; nothing new is defined for HTTP.
base64url encoding is used as an encoding mechanism only.

RFC9449.title: OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP)
RFC9449.summary: Specifies DPoP, an application-level proof-of-possession mechanism that sender-constrains OAuth 2.0 access and refresh tokens using a signed JWT in a DPoP HTTP header, with nonces, key confirmation, and authorization code binding.

OAuth.why: The document is an OAuth 2.0 extension. It defines the DPoP token type, the dpop_jkt authorization request parameter, and server and client metadata.
OAuth.quote: Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP) is an application-level mechanism for sender-constraining OAuth [RFC6749] access and refresh tokens.

JWT.why: It defines the DPoP proof JWT with its claims (htm, htu, ath, nonce) and the jkt confirmation method under cnf. It also registers the new claims and the dpop+jwt type, so JWT readers need it.
JWT.quote: The value of the header is a JSON Web Token (JWT) [RFC7519] that enables the authorization server to bind issued tokens to the public part of a client's key pair.

HTTP authentication.why: It defines a new HTTP authentication scheme, DPoP, including WWW-Authenticate challenges and interaction with the Bearer scheme.
HTTP authentication.quote: A DPoP-bound access token is sent using the Authorization request header field per Section 11.6.2 of [RFC9110] with an authentication scheme of DPoP.

rejected.why: JWS and JWK are used to sign the proofs and carry the key, but the document defines no new JOSE mechanism.
TLS is relied on for message integrity and is contrasted with DPoP, but the document does not specify anything about TLS.
DPoP and DPoP-Nonce are new HTTP header fields, but HTTP is the substrate. The relevant HTTP subject is the authentication scheme, which is tagged.
The XSS discussion is incidental. The document is about OAuth token binding, not the web platform security mechanisms.
TLS token binding is only cited as an alternative that DPoP is used instead of.

RFC9450.title: Reliable and Available Wireless (RAW) Use Cases
RFC9450.summary: Informational RAW WG document describing wireless use cases (aeronautics, amusement parks, industrial, pro A/V, gaming, UAV/V2V, edge robotics, emergency vehicles) that need reliable and available, bounded-latency wireless, extending the DetNet use cases.

DetNet.why: RAW extends DetNet to wireless; the document extends the DetNet use cases (RFC 8578) and lists requirements for reliable, bounded-latency flows over wireless Tracks.
DetNet.quote: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) provides the capability to carry specified unicast or multicast data streams for real-time applications with extremely low data loss rates and bounded latency

rejected.why: Mentioned as prior work (RFC 9030, TSCH) but the document is not about 6TiSCH.
IEEE 802.11 appears in several use cases as the link technology, but the document doesn't specify or analyse IP over Wi-Fi.
QoS and Diffserv classes come up in the requirements but only in passing.
Cellular is cited as one connectivity option in the UAV and robotics use cases and is not a subject of the document.
UAV and V2V platooning is one use case among eight, not the document's focus.
Industrial IoT is mentioned only in passing.

gaps.name: RAW (Reliable and Available Wireless)
gaps.why: The document's own subject is reliable and available wireless networking, and the taxonomy has no tag for it. DetNet is the closest fit.

RFC9451.title: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) Packet and Behavior in the Network Service Header (NSH)
RFC9451.summary: Updates RFC 8300 to clarify the meaning of an NSH OAM packet and the handling of the O bit in the Network Service Header, including Next Protocol filtering and discard/forward behavior.

SFC.why: The document updates the NSH specification (RFC 8300) and defines how SFC data plane elements (SF, SFF, proxy, classifier) process the O bit.
SFC.quote: Setting this bit indicates an NSH OAM packet. Such a packet is any NSH-encapsulated packet that exclusively includes SFC OAM data.

OAM.why: The document defines what an OAM packet and SFC OAM data are in NSH and how elements must treat them, so readers of OAM mechanisms would want it.
OAM.quote: This document clarifies an ambiguity related to the definition of the Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) packet discussed in [RFC8300].

rejected.why: IPv4/IPv6 appear only as Next Protocol values of inner packets that must be discarded when the O bit is set; the document is not about IP.
MPLS is only mentioned as a Next Protocol value (0x03) in the discard rule.
Ethernet is only mentioned as a Next Protocol value (0x05) in the discard rule.

RFC9452.title: Network Service Header (NSH) Encapsulation for In Situ OAM (IOAM) Data
RFC9452.summary: Defines how IOAM data fields are encapsulated in the Network Service Header (NSH) for SFC, allocating NSH Next Protocol 0x06 and specifying the IOAM header format within NSH.

SFC.why: The document specifies a new NSH Next Protocol encapsulation for IOAM, extending the NSH, which is the SFC encapsulation.
SFC.quote: This document defines how IOAM-Data-Fields are transported as part of the Network Service Header (NSH) encapsulation [RFC8300] for the Service Function Chaining (SFC) Architecture

OAM.why: IOAM is an OAM and telemetry mechanism. The document specifies how its data is carried, so OAM readers would want it. There is no IOAM-specific tag, so the OAM topic fits best.
OAM.quote: IOAM-Data-Fields are carried as NSH payload using a Next Protocol header that follows the NSH headers.

rejected.why: IOAM collects telemetry, but the document is about encapsulation in NSH. OAM is the closer fit.
NSH is a service-plane encapsulation, not a network virtualization overlay like VXLAN or Geneve.
The only IANA content is a single code point allocation, which is boilerplate.

gaps.name: IOAM (In situ OAM)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no IOAM tag, though a family of RFCs (9197, 9322, 9326, 9378, 9452) addresses it.

RFC9453.title: Applicability and Use Cases for IPv6 over Networks of Resource-constrained Nodes (6lo)
RFC9453.summary: Informational applicability statement describing 6lo (IPv6 over constrained-node networks) link-layer technologies, guidelines for adapting the 6LoWPAN stack, deployment examples (Wi-SUN, Thread, G3-PLC, Netricity) and use cases.

6LoWPAN.why: The whole document is about applicability of 6lo/6LoWPAN adaptation layers over various constrained link layers, with guidelines for adopting the stack and deployment examples.
6LoWPAN.quote: The 6lo adaptation layers use a variation of the 6LoWPAN stack applied to each particular link-layer technology.

rejected.why: RPL is mentioned in the guidelines and deployment examples but only as a routing protocol used alongside 6lo, not the subject.
IPv6 is the network layer being adapted, but the document is about the 6lo adaptation, which is covered by the more specific tag.
6LoWPAN ND is described in a guideline paragraph only; not a substantial part of the document.
Header compression is one guideline item referencing other RFCs; not a main subject.
The 6LoWPAN tag sits under IoT, so the parent is implied.
DTLS/TLS and IPsec are only mentioned as end-to-end security options.

RFC9454.title: Update to OSPF Terminology
RFC9454.summary: Updates OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 specifications and related RFCs to replace master/slave terminology with Leader/Follower (and the MS bit with the L bit) per inclusive-language guidance, without changing protocol operation.

OSPF.why: The document edits the OSPF base specification and related OSPF RFCs, renaming terms in the Database Description process and the DD flags registry.
OSPF.quote: The base OSPFv2 specification "OSPF Version 2" [RFC2328] defines the synchronization of databases as two routers forming a "master/slave" relationship.

terminology.why: The document's purpose is a terminology change toward inclusive language, so readers browsing terminology would want it.
terminology.quote: This document updates some OSPF terminology to be in line with inclusive language used in the industry.

rejected.why: It updates RFC 5340 and RFC 5838, but only as part of a terminology change that mostly addresses OSPF as a whole. The parent OSPF tag covers it.
It updates RFC 5614, the MANET CDS flooding extension, but only to rename terms. It does not address MANET routing.
The IANA section only updates one registry entry's description. That is boilerplate, not the subject of the document.

RFC9455.title: Avoiding Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) Containing Multiple IP Prefixes
RFC9455.summary: BCP recommending that each RPKI Route Origin Authorization (ROA) contain a single IP prefix, to avoid fate-sharing problems from CA certificate changes and expiry.

RPKI.why: The document gives operational guidance on how to issue ROAs in the RPKI. Its subject is RPKI ROA issuance practice, so RPKI readers would want it.
RPKI.quote: Unless the CA has good reasons to the contrary, an issued ROA SHOULD contain a single IP prefix.

rejected.why: ROAs authorize BGP route origination, but the document is about RPKI object issuance, not the BGP protocol or its policy.
This is the parent of RPKI, which is already tagged, so the parent is implied.
RFC 3779 certificate extensions are mentioned only in passing as background for resource validity.
The advice is operational, but it concerns RPKI object management specifically, which RPKI already covers.

RFC9456.title: Updates to the TLS Transport Model for SNMP
RFC9456.summary: RFC 9456 updates the SNMP TLS Transport Model (RFC 6353) for TLS/DTLS 1.3, forbidding 0-RTT, updating the SnmpTLSFingerprint hash registry, and revising the SNMP-TLS-TM-MIB module.

SNMP.why: The document revises the SNMP TLS Transport Model, so it is about SNMP transport security and its framework.
SNMP.quote: This document updates and clarifies how the rules of [RFC6353] apply when using Transport Layer Security (TLS) or Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS)

MIB.why: It updates the SNMP-TLS-TM-MIB module, including its textual conventions, tables and conformance groups.
MIB.quote: This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to the SMIv2

TLS.why: A substantial part of the document sets rules for using TLS 1.3 and DTLS 1.3 with SNMP, covering 0-RTT, version requirements and cipher suites.
TLS.quote: TLS 1.3 implementations for SNMP MUST NOT enable the 0-RTT mode of session resumption (either sending or accepting)

rejected.why: DTLS 1.3 is covered jointly with TLS as '(D)TLS'. The document specifies how SNMP uses it, not DTLS itself, so TLS is the better fit.
It creates the 'SNMP-TLSTM HashAlgorithms' registry, but this is boilerplate-level IANA content for the MIB change, not the main subject.
X.509 certificates are mapped to security names in the MIB, but the document does not specify or profile X.509.
Hash algorithms appear only as registry values for fingerprints; the document does not define or analyse them.

RFC9457.title: Problem Details for HTTP APIs
RFC9457.summary: Defines the "problem details" object (application/problem+json and application/problem+xml) for carrying machine-readable error information in HTTP API responses, and creates an IANA registry of HTTP problem types.

HTTP APIs.why: The whole document is a convention for conveying errors in HTTP APIs, exactly what the HTTP APIs tag covers (problem details).
HTTP APIs.quote: This document defines a "problem detail" to carry machine-readable details of errors in HTTP response content to avoid the need to define new error response formats for HTTP APIs.

rejected.why: JSON is the data model and serialization used, but the document defines an error format rather than anything about JSON itself.
An XML serialization is given in an appendix, but it is secondary to the JSON model and XML is only an encoding.
The document builds on HTTP semantics (status codes, content negotiation) but does not extend HTTP itself; HTTP APIs is the more specific fit.
It registers application/problem+json and application/problem+xml, but that is IANA boilerplate rather than the subject of the document.
Problem types are identified by URIs, but the document only uses URIs and does not define URI syntax or schemes.
It creates an HTTP Problem Types registry, but this is a minor part of the document and not about IANA guidance.

RFC9458.title: Oblivious HTTP
RFC9458.summary: Defines Oblivious HTTP, a protocol that uses HPKE to encapsulate binary HTTP messages and forwards them via a relay to a gateway, so servers cannot link requests to clients.

oblivious HTTP.why: The whole document specifies Oblivious HTTP: key configuration, HPKE encapsulation of requests and responses, relay and gateway behaviour, and its security and privacy considerations.
oblivious HTTP.quote: this document defines Oblivious HTTP, a protocol for encrypting and sending HTTP messages from a client to a gateway.

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate the protocol runs over and encapsulates. The specific HTTP-related subject is covered by the more specific oblivious HTTP tag.
Oblivious DoH is only cited as the design basis and as an example of future use. The document does not specify DNS.
TLS is only the transport protection for the relay connections, and replay guidance borrows from TLS early data. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
The document registers three media types, but this is IANA boilerplate for its own formats. It is not about media type registry rules.
Privacy is the motivation, and the document has privacy considerations, but the subject is the specific protocol, which has its own tag.
The document defines two problem types, but this is a minor use of Problem Details. It does not change conventions for HTTP APIs.

gaps.name: Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE)
gaps.why: The protocol is built on HPKE encapsulation, but the taxonomy has no HPKE tag. The closest option is the general cryptography topic, which does not fit well.

RFC9459.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): AES-CTR and AES-CBC
RFC9459.summary: Specifies AES-CTR and AES-CBC (non-AEAD) content encryption algorithms and COSE algorithm identifiers for use with COSE, to be paired with a separate integrity mechanism such as a digital signature.

COSE.why: The document extends COSE by defining new algorithm identifiers, key checks and processing rules for AES-CTR and AES-CBC.
COSE.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using AES-CTR and AES-CBC as content encryption algorithms with the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) [RFC9052] syntax.

AES.why: The document is about using the AES block cipher in CTR and CBC modes, including IV handling, padding and security properties.
AES.quote: Only AES Counter (AES-CTR) mode and AES Cipher Block Chaining (AES-CBC) are discussed in this document.

rejected.why: CBOR is only the data format underlying COSE. The document defines nothing new about CBOR itself.
The SUIT manifest is cited as a motivating use case (firmware encryption), but the document does not address firmware update architecture or manifests.
The IANA section only registers six COSE algorithm identifiers, which is boilerplate-level evidence for this tag.
CMS is referenced only for its padding algorithm (RFC 5652 Section 6.3).

RFC9460.title: Service Binding and Parameter Specification via the DNS (SVCB and HTTPS Resource Records)
RFC9460.summary: Specifies the SVCB and HTTPS DNS resource record types for publishing service endpoint bindings, aliasing (including at zone apex), and connection parameters such as ALPN, port and address hints, with client and server behaviour and an HTTP mapping.

DNS.why: Defines new DNS RR types, their wire/presentation format, resolver and authoritative server behaviour, and zone structuring.
DNS.quote: This document specifies the "SVCB" ("Service Binding") and "HTTPS" DNS resource record (RR) types

HTTP.why: Section 9 defines the HTTP/HTTPS mapping, including http-to-https upgrade and interaction with Alt-Svc.
HTTP.quote: The HTTPS RR is a variation of SVCB for use with HTTP

rejected.why: DNSSEC is optional and only discussed for downgrade protection; the document is not about it.
HSTS-like upgrade behaviour is a section, but the HSTS protocol itself is only referenced.
ECH, SNI and ALPN are referenced as substrate; nothing new is defined for TLS.
ECS handling is a brief subsection, not a main subject.
A short subsection on DNS64 interaction; not about DNS64 itself.
DoT/DoH are recommended transports only.

RFC9461.title: Service Binding Mapping for DNS Servers
RFC9461.summary: Defines the SVCB mapping for the "dns" service type, letting named DNS servers advertise encrypted transports (DoT, DoH, DoQ) via _dns SVCB records, and registers the new "dohpath" SvcParamKey.

DNS.why: The document specifies a DNS resource record mapping (SVCB for the dns scheme, _dns names, SvcParamKeys, new dohpath key) for DNS servers. No narrower DNS child covers SVCB-based discovery of DNS servers.
DNS.quote: This document provides the SVCB mapping for named DNS servers, allowing them to indicate support for encrypted transport protocols.

DNS privacy.why: The purpose is to let clients discover encrypted DNS transports, with downgrade analysis. It does not define DoH, DoT or DoQ themselves, so the generic privacy tag fits better than the specific protocol tags.
DNS privacy.quote: allowing DNS servers to offer alternative endpoints and transports, including encrypted transports like DNS over TLS (DoT) [RFC7858], DNS over HTTPS (DoH) [RFC8484]

rejected.why: DoH is defined in RFC 8484. This document only adds a dohpath parameter to locate the DoH endpoint, so DoH is relied on, not specified.
DoT is only one of the transports advertised via alpn. It is not specified or extended here.
DoQ is only one of the transports advertised via alpn. It is not specified or extended here.
SVCB-based discovery is the mechanism, but the DNS tag already covers this document's subject.
URI Templates are used only to express the dohpath value. The document does not specify URI syntax.
The document explicitly does not mandate DNSSEC. It is only mentioned in the security analysis.

gaps.name: SVCB / HTTPS resource records (Service Binding)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SVCB service binding. The document is a mapping profile of that RR type.

RFC9462.title: Discovery of Designated Resolvers
RFC9462.summary: Defines DDR, which lets DNS clients discover and verify a resolver's encrypted DNS configuration (DoH/DoT/DoQ) via SVCB queries to the special-use name resolver.arpa or to a known resolver name.

DNS privacy.why: The document is about moving from unencrypted to encrypted DNS by discovering designated encrypted resolvers (DoH, DoT, DoQ). It is not a specification of any single transport, so the parent topic fits.
DNS privacy.quote: a set of mechanisms for DNS clients to use DNS records to discover a resolver's encrypted DNS configuration

special-use domain names.why: It defines and registers the new special-use domain name resolver.arpa, with its handling rules for clients, forwarders and servers. Readers of that subject would want it.
special-use domain names.quote: IANA has registered "resolver.arpa" in the "Special-Use Domain Names" registry established by [RFC6761].

rejected.why: DoH is one of the encrypted transports being discovered. The document does not specify or extend it.
DoT is a discovery target only. The document does not specify it.
DoQ is a discovery target only. The document does not specify it.
The document is about DNS, but DNS privacy and special-use domain names are more specific tags that fit.
TLS certificate validation is used to verify designation, but the document defines nothing new in TLS.
The document checks certificate SAN entries per RFC 5280 but does not profile certificates.

gaps.name: SVCB/HTTPS service binding records
gaps.why: The document builds on SVCB records for DNS servers, but the taxonomy has no tag for SVCB. It is covered only by the general DNS tag.

RFC9463.title: DHCP and Router Advertisement Options for the Discovery of Network-designated Resolvers (DNR)
RFC9463.summary: Defines DHCPv4, DHCPv6 and IPv6 Router Advertisement options that let hosts discover network-designated encrypted DNS resolvers (DoH, DoT, DoQ) via an authentication domain name, IP addresses and SVCB-style service parameters.

DHCPv6.why: Specifies a new DHCPv6 option (OPTION_V6_DNR), its format and client behaviour.
DHCPv6.quote: The DHCPv6 client MUST include OPTION_V6_DNR in an Option Request Option (ORO)

DHCP.why: Defines the DHCPv4 OPTION_V4_DNR option and client behaviour. DHCPv4 has no separate child tag, so the DHCP tag applies.
DHCP.quote: the DHCPv4 client requests the encrypted DNS resolver by including OPTION_V4_DNR in a Parameter Request List option

neighbor discovery.why: Defines a new IPv6 Router Advertisement/Neighbor Discovery option carrying resolver information.
neighbor discovery.quote: This section defines a new Neighbor Discovery option [RFC4861]: the IPv6 RA Encrypted DNS option.

DNS privacy.why: The purpose is discovery of encrypted DNS resolvers, a core DNS privacy provisioning matter. DoH, DoT and DoQ are only the discovered protocols, so the generic parent fits better than the specific tags.
DNS privacy.quote: specifies new DHCP and IPv6 Router Advertisement options to discover encrypted DNS resolvers (e.g., DNS over HTTPS, DNS over TLS, and DNS over QUIC)

rejected.why: One of the protocols the resolvers may speak; the document does not specify DoH itself.
Only a discovered protocol, not specified here.
Only a discovered protocol, not specified here.
Uses SVCB parameters and DNS terms, but the document specifies provisioning options, not DNS protocol behaviour.
PKIX validation of the resolver certificate is a substrate mechanism; nothing new is defined for TLS.
Certificate validation is referenced only to authenticate the ADN; no certificate profile is defined.

RFC9464.title: Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) Configuration for Encrypted DNS
RFC9464.summary: Defines three new IKEv2 Configuration Payload attribute types (ENCDNS_IP4, ENCDNS_IP6, ENCDNS_DIGEST_INFO) that let an IKEv2 responder assign encrypted DNS resolvers (DoH, DoT, DoQ) to an initiator, with certificate digest validation.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with new Configuration Payload attributes and specifies the exchange behaviour for them.
IKE.quote: This document specifies new Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) Configuration Payload Attribute Types to assign DNS resolvers

DNS privacy.why: The document provisions encrypted DNS resolvers (DoH, DoT, DoQ) and their authentication. It is not specific to one encrypted transport, so the parent topic fits better than any single child.
DNS privacy.quote: assigning encrypted DNS configurations to an Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) initiator

rejected.why: DoH is one of several encrypted DNS protocols the attributes can describe. The document does not specify it.
DoT is only one of the encrypted protocols that can be configured. The document does not define anything about it.
DoQ is only one of the encrypted protocols that can be configured. The document does not define anything about it.
DNS is the subject of the configuration, but the document is about delivering that configuration through IKEv2, not about DNS protocol behaviour.
TLS is the substrate for the encrypted DNS sessions. The document only validates the certificate by SPKI hash and does not define anything new about TLS.
The SPKI digest check is described as similar to DANE PKIX-EE(1) with selector SPKI(1), but DANE itself is not used.

RFC9465.title: PIM Null-Register Packing
RFC9465.summary: Defines PIM Packed Null-Register and Packed Register-Stop messages, plus a Register-Stop P-bit capability signal, so a DR and RP can carry many (source, group) records in one PIM-SM message.

PIM-SM.why: The document extends PIM-SM's Register/Null-Register/Register-Stop exchange between DR and RP with new packed message types and a capability bit.
PIM-SM.quote: This document defines a standard to send information about multiple multicast sources and groups in a single PIM message.

rejected.why: Mentioned only in the Anycast RP considerations; the document does not specify or extend MSDP.
Path MTU Discovery is only referenced briefly in fragmentation considerations; it is not what the document is about.
PIM-SM is the more specific child tag and fits better, so the parent is not listed.
Anycast-RP is covered only in a short operational note, not as a main subject.

RFC9466.title: PIM Assert Message Packing
RFC9466.summary: Defines PackedAssert messages and a PIM Hello option so PIM-SM routers can pack multiple Assert records into one message, reducing packet counts and speeding single-forwarder election on shared LANs.

PIM-SM.why: The document extends PIM-SM's Assert mechanism with new packed message encodings and a Hello option, without changing the Assert state machine. PIM-SM is the specified and extended protocol.
PIM-SM.quote: This document defines a mechanism to send and receive information for multiple IP multicast flows in a single PackedAssert message.

rejected.why: PIM-SSM is mentioned only as part of PIM-SM. The document does not specify anything about SSM.
MVPN MDT appears only as a use case example in the appendix.
DetNet over TSN is mentioned only in a use case example.
The more specific child PIM-SM fits, so the parent is not listed.
YANG is mentioned only as an example of how implementations might expose counters. The document defines no model.

RFC9467.title: Relaxed Packet Counter Verification for Babel MAC Authentication
RFC9467.summary: RFC 9467 updates the Babel MAC authentication (RFC 8967) packet counter verification rules, adding separate unicast/multicast counters and window-based replay checks to tolerate packet reordering, e.g. on Wi-Fi.

Babel.why: The document modifies the Babel MAC authentication mechanism's packet counter verification, so it is about the Babel routing protocol and its security extension.
Babel.quote: This document relaxes the packet verification rules defined in "MAC Authentication for the Babel Routing Protocol" (RFC 8967)

rejected.why: IEEE 802.11 power-saving behaviour is only the motivation for the change; the document does not specify IP over Wi-Fi.
Considered, since this is authentication of a routing protocol, but that tag's children cover RPKI/BGPsec. The Babel tag is the more specific home, and the topic tag is not directly warranted.
The window-based replay check is modelled on RFC 4303 Section 3.4.3 but ESP itself is not specified or extended.
The MAC computation is defined in RFC 8967 and is not changed here.
Generic authentication topic; the document concerns only replay protection in Babel, which the Babel tag already covers.

RFC9468.title: Unsolicited Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for Sessionless Applications
RFC9468.summary: Defines "unsolicited BFD" procedures letting a BFD session be initiated by one side only without per-session configuration on the passive side, and adds a YANG module augmenting RFC 9314 to configure it.

BFD.why: The document specifies new BFD session initiation procedures (active/passive roles, passive-side session creation, bfd.Role state variable) for single-hop BFD.
BFD.quote: we present procedures for "unsolicited BFD" that allow a BFD session to be initiated by only one side and established without explicit per-session configuration

YANG.why: A substantial part of the document is the ietf-bfd-unsolicited YANG module augmenting the RFC 9314 BFD model, with tree diagram and example.
YANG.quote: We also introduce a new YANG module to configure and manage "unsolicited BFD".

rejected.why: BGP and route server use at IXPs are motivating examples only; the document does not specify or change BGP.
IXP route server next-hop liveness is a use-case example, not the subject.
NETCONF/RESTCONF appear only as access protocols for the YANG module in Security Considerations and the example.
TLS is mentioned only in YANG security boilerplate.
Security mitigations for resource usage are a short part of the BFD procedures, not a standalone operational security subject.

RFC9469.title: Applicability of Ethernet Virtual Private Network (EVPN) to Network Virtualization over Layer 3 (NVO3) Networks
RFC9469.summary: Informational document describing how EVPN serves as the control plane for NVO3 networks, covering L2/L3 services, Geneve, multihoming, MAC mobility, BUM optimization and DCI, without introducing new procedures.

EVPN.why: The whole document analyses the applicability of EVPN: route types, multihoming, MAC mobility, IRB, DCI. EVPN is the subject.
EVPN.quote: This document describes the use of EVPN for NVO3 networks and discusses its applicability to basic Layer 2 and Layer 3 connectivity requirements

overlay networks.why: The document is framed around NVO3 data-plane network virtualization overlays (VXLAN, Geneve) and how a control plane serves them.
overlay networks.quote: NVE devices sit at the edge of the underlay network and provide Layer 2 and Layer 3 connectivity among Tenant Systems

rejected.why: BGP (MP-BGP) is the signalling substrate for EVPN routes. The document is not about BGP itself.
Geneve has a short section on EVPN signalling for it, but this is a minor part. The Geneve extensions are in a separate draft.
VXLAN is only mentioned as an example NVO3 encapsulation.
The context is data centers, but the document is about EVPN control plane applicability, not data center routing as such.
MVPN appears only as an interworking mention in the multicast and DCI sections.
EVPN is the more specific tag, so the L2VPN parent is implied.

RFC9470.title: OAuth 2.0 Step Up Authentication Challenge Protocol
RFC9470.summary: RFC 9470 defines an OAuth 2.0 step-up authentication mechanism: a resource server signals via the Bearer WWW-Authenticate challenge (insufficient_user_authentication, acr_values, max_age) that a stronger or more recent authentication is needed, and the client passes those requirements in a new authorization request.

OAuth.why: The document is an OAuth 2.0 extension: it adds a new error code and challenge parameters, defines authorization request usage, token introspection response members, and authorization server metadata use.
OAuth.quote: This document extends the collection of error codes defined by [RFC6750] with a new value, insufficient_user_authentication

rejected.why: JWT access tokens are one way to convey acr/auth_time, but the document only references RFC 9068 claims. It does not specify JWT itself.
The challenge uses the WWW-Authenticate Bearer scheme, but this is OAuth-specific. It does not define or extend a general HTTP authentication scheme.
The topic is covered by the OAuth tag. The document says it does not define the mechanics of authentication.
JSON appears only as the encoding of introspection responses and tokens, so it is substrate.
HTTP 401 responses and headers are the transport for the challenge, not the subject.

gaps.name: OpenID Connect
gaps.why: The document relies heavily on OIDC parameters (acr_values, max_age, the acr and auth_time claims), but the taxonomy has no OpenID Connect tag.

RFC9471.title: DNS Glue Requirements in Referral Responses
RFC9471.summary: RFC 9471 updates RFC 1034 to require authoritative DNS servers to include all available in-domain glue records in referral responses or set the TC flag when message size prevents it, and describes sibling and cyclic glue.

DNS.why: The document specifies authoritative server behaviour for glue in DNS referral responses and updates RFC 1034, so it is squarely about core DNS protocol behaviour.
DNS.quote: when a name server generates a referral response, it MUST include all available glue records for in-domain name servers in the additional section or MUST set TC=1

rejected.why: A DNSSEC referral appears only as an example of missing glue; the document is not about signing or validation.
EDNS(0) UDP message size is mentioned only as context for response size limits; the document does not specify or extend EDNS.
TCP is only the fallback transport used after TC=1; nothing new is defined about TCP.
UDP is just the transport whose size limits motivate the requirement; the document does not address UDP usage.

RFC9472.title: A YANG Data Model for Reporting Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) and Vulnerability Information
RFC9472.summary: Defines a YANG module augmenting the MUD model with a "transparency" extension to locate SBOMs and vulnerability information, plus a /.well-known/sbom endpoint.

MUD.why: The document is a MUD extension (the "transparency" extension registered in the MUD Extensions registry) that augments the MUD model, so MUD readers need it.
MUD.quote: This memo extends the Manufacturer User Description (MUD) YANG schema to provide the locations of software bills of materials (SBOMs) and vulnerability information

YANG.why: The document specifies a new YANG module and its tree, so it belongs under YANG data models.
YANG.quote: module: ietf-mud-transparency

supply chain integrity.why: SBOM and vulnerability discovery for software transparency fits supply chain integrity and transparency for digital artefacts.
supply chain integrity.quote: Software bills of materials (SBOMs) are descriptions of what software, including versioning and dependencies, a device contains.

rejected.why: HTTP and CoAP are only retrieval mechanisms for the SBOM; the document defines nothing new about them.
CoAP is only an optional retrieval interface and is not specified or extended here.
The well-known URI /.well-known/sbom is registered, but the document does not address URI syntax or schemes. It only uses the RFC 8615 mechanism.
The Security Considerations say the module is not necessarily accessed via NETCONF or RESTCONF.
IoT devices are the motivating use case, but the document is about SBOM discovery, not constrained-device guidance.

gaps.name: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) / vulnerability reporting
gaps.why: The document's subject is locating SBOMs and vulnerability information. The taxonomy has no SBOM tag, so the closest fit is supply chain integrity, and MUD is not in the taxonomy as a standalone tag either.

RFC9473.title: A Vocabulary of Path Properties
RFC9473.summary: An IRTF PANRG informational document that defines terminology for paths, path elements and flows, categorizes path properties, gives use cases (path selection, protocol selection, service invocation), and lists example properties such as delay, loss, capacity and MTU.

internet architecture.why: The document gives a conceptual framework for path-aware networking, an architectural change to how endpoints see and use network paths. No more specific tag exists.
internet architecture.quote: Path-aware networking, as defined in Section 1.1 of [RFC9217], describes "endpoint discovery of the properties of paths they use for communication across an internetwork

performance measurement.why: A substantial part defines observed and assessed performance properties (one-way delay, delay variation, loss, link capacity, link usage). These are tied to IPPM metrics.
performance measurement.quote: Some path properties express the performance of the transmission of a packet or flow over a link or subpath.

rejected.why: ALTO is cited only as a path-selection example and as a source of cost metrics. The document does not specify or extend it.
Service Function Chaining is referenced for service invocation but is not the subject.
BGP's MED attribute is mentioned briefly as an example of path selection.
The document defines a vocabulary, but it is domain-specific path-aware networking terminology, not a general glossary or requirements-language document.
QUIC appears only as an example of protocol availability over a path.
MPTCP is mentioned only as an example of a capability invoked through a service function.

gaps.name: path-aware networking
gaps.why: The whole document concerns path-aware networking, meaning endpoint discovery and use of path properties. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so readers must go to the broad internet architecture page.

RFC9474.title: RSA Blind Signatures
RFC9474.summary: Specifies RSABSSA, an RSA blind signature protocol (Prepare, Blind, BlindSign, Finalize) using RSA-PSS encoding so unblinded signatures verify with standard RSA-PSS, with variants, security analysis and test vectors.

RSA.why: The whole document defines a blind signature protocol built on RSA and RSA-PSS (RFC 8017), including key usage rules and RSA-specific security considerations.
RSA.quote: This document specifies an RSA-based blind signature protocol.

rejected.why: Privacy Pass is only cited as motivating context; the document does not specify it.
SHA-384 is only a hash parameter in the named variants; the document is not about the SHA family.
X.509 appears in one sentence on the OID to use for the public key; that is too minor for a tag.
Section 7.7 only says the protocol is not post-quantum ready; the document is not about post-quantum cryptography.
Randomness generation is a security consideration here, and RFC 4086 is only cited.

gaps.name: Blind signatures
gaps.why: The document is about blind signature schemes in general (Chaum-style untraceable signing). The taxonomy has no tag for digital signatures or blind signature schemes, so only RSA fits.

RFC9475.title: Messaging Use Cases and Extensions for Secure Telephone Identity Revisited (STIR)
RFC9475.summary: Defines a new "msg" PASSporT type and "msgi" JWT claim (message digest) and discusses applying STIR PASSporTs and certificates to SIP MESSAGE and MSRP-based messaging to curb spoofed or nuisance messages.

STIR.why: The document extends STIR's PASSporT with a new type and claim and explains STIR certificate use for messaging.
STIR.quote: this document defines a new "msg" PASSporT type. "msg" PASSporTs may carry a new optional JSON Web Token (JWT) [RFC7519] claim "msgi"

instant messaging.why: A substantial part covers securing text/multimedia messaging, including SIP MESSAGE and MSRP sessions, against impersonation.
instant messaging.quote: this specification explores how the PASSporT mechanism defined for STIR could be applied in providing protection for textual and multimedia messaging

rejected.why: SIP is the carrier of the Identity header and MESSAGE; the document specifies STIR extensions, not SIP itself.
MSRP sessions are discussed as a use case needing no changes; the document does not specify or extend MSRP.
The msgi claim is registered as a JWT claim, but JWT is the substrate rather than the subject.
Mentioned only as an alternative integrity mechanism for MESSAGE, not specified here.
SHA-2 algorithms are merely selected for the digest; the document is not about the hash family.
Messaging spam is motivation, but the document does not address spam filtering as its subject.

RFC9476.title: The .alt Special-Use Top-Level Domain
RFC9476.summary: Reserves the ".alt" pseudo-TLD as a special-use domain name for non-DNS alternative namespaces, and gives guidance on its use and leakage into the DNS.

special-use domain names.why: The document's purpose is to reserve .alt in the Special-Use Domain Name registry and give the RFC 6761 reservation considerations.
special-use domain names.quote: This document reserves the top-level label "alt" (short for "alternative") as a special-use domain name [RFC6761].

rejected.why: The document is about names explicitly not resolved via DNS. DNS is the context it distinguishes itself from, and the parent of the chosen tag.
Only mentioned for aggressive NSEC caching that mitigates leaked .alt queries. This is not a subject of the document.
A different special-use TLD that is not discussed. .alt is not a Tor-specific namespace.
The more specific special-use domain names tag covers it.

RFC9477.title: Complaint Feedback Loop Address Header
RFC9477.summary: Defines the CFBL-Address and CFBL-Feedback-ID email header fields that let a Message Originator tell Mailbox Providers where to send ARF/XARF complaint feedback, with DKIM-based validation rules and privacy considerations (experimental).

ARF.why: The document specifies how complaint feedback reports in ARF/XARF format are addressed, generated, and forwarded, extending the CFBL mechanism.
ARF.quote: The Feedback Message MUST be an [ARF] or [XARF] report.

DKIM.why: A substantial part of the document defines DKIM signature requirements (strict, relaxed, third-party double signing, h= coverage) for trusting the CFBL header.
DKIM.quote: If the domain is not matched by a valid [DKIM] signature or the header field is not covered by the "h=" tag, the Mailbox Provider SHALL NOT send a report message.

message format.why: It defines two new Internet message header fields with ABNF syntax and registers them as provisional message headers.
message format.quote: cfbl-address = "CFBL-Address:" CFWS addr-spec [";" CFWS report-format] CRLF

rejected.why: Too broad; more specific children (ARF, DKIM, message format) fit.
Complaint feedback loops relate to spam/abuse reporting, but the document is about the header and reporting address mechanism, not spam filtering or reputation.
HMAC is only recommended for building hard-to-forge feedback IDs; not the subject.
The From/DKIM domain alignment resembles DMARC, but DMARC is not specified or used.
One-click unsubscribe is only compared against in the introduction; not the subject.

gaps.name: Complaint Feedback Loop (CFBL)
gaps.why: The document is about complaint feedback loops for email abuse. The taxonomy has no CFBL tag, and ARF is the closest fit.

RFC9478.title: Labeled IPsec Traffic Selector Support for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC9478.summary: Defines a new IKEv2 Traffic Selector type, TS_SECLABEL, for negotiating opaque Mandatory Access Control security labels as SPD selectors (Labeled IPsec), with negotiation rules and an IANA registry entry.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with a new Traffic Selector type and specifies how it is negotiated. IKE is the most specific fitting tag, and IPsec is implied as its ancestor.
IKE.quote: This document specifies a new TS Type, TS_SECLABEL, for IKEv2 that can be used to negotiate security labels as additional selectors for the SPD

rejected.why: The tag covers security labels for networked data such as CIPSO and CALIPSO. This document carries opaque labels in IKEv2 and does not define label formats, so the subject is IKE. It is a plausible secondary tag, but the labels are only the payload.
It is the parent of IKE and is implied by the IKE tag. Listing it separately would be redundant.
The only IANA content is a single registry entry in the boilerplate section, and the document is not about IANA guidance.

RFC9479.title: IS-IS Application-Specific Link Attributes
RFC9479.summary: Defines IS-IS Application-Specific Link Attributes (ASLA) sub-TLV and an Application-Specific SRLG TLV with application identifier bit masks, so RSVP-TE, SR Policy and LFA can use distinct link attribute values; obsoletes RFC 8919.

IS-IS.why: The document specifies new IS-IS sub-TLVs and a new TLV, with encoding, processing rules, and migration guidance for IS-IS link attribute advertisements.
IS-IS.quote: This document introduces link attribute advertisements that address both of these shortcomings.

traffic engineering.why: The link attributes are TE attributes (bandwidth, admin group, TE metrics, SRLG) and the document concerns their per-application use by RSVP-TE and SR Policy.
traffic engineering.quote: Advertisement of link attributes by the Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) protocol in support of Traffic Engineering (TE) was introduced by [RFC5305]

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is one application that consumes the attributes. The document does not specify RSVP-TE itself.
SR Policy is just one of the applications identified by a bit. The document does not define segment routing.
LFA is only one application bit. The document does not specify LFA.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-like and support the IS-IS protocol extensions. They are not the document's subject.

RFC9480.title: Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) Updates
RFC9480.summary: RFC 9480 updates CMP (RFC 4210) and its HTTP transfer (RFC 6712): adds EnvelopedData in place of EncryptedValue, CMP version 3, new general message types, new EKUs, extended polling, and a /.well-known/cmp path.

CMP.why: The document exists to update CMP and its HTTP transfer.
CMP.quote: This document contains a set of updates to the syntax of Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) version 2 and its HTTP transfer mechanism.

RFC9481.title: Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) Algorithms
RFC9481.summary: RFC 9481 specifies conventions and OIDs for using cryptographic algorithms (digests, signatures, key management, encryption, MACs) with the Certificate Management Protocol, and updates the algorithm profile in Appendix D.2 of RFC 4210.

CMP.why: The document is the algorithm profile for CMP, updating RFC 4210 Appendix D.2. CMP is not a separate tag, so this is invalid; see rejected.
CMP.quote: This document describes the conventions for using several cryptographic algorithms with the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP).

RFC9482.title: Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) Transfer for the Certificate Management Protocol
RFC9482.summary: Specifies CoAP over UDP as a transfer mechanism for the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP), including URI format, discovery, block-wise transfer, announcements via Observe, and CoAP-to-HTTP proxy guidance.

CoAP.why: The document defines how CoAP is used to carry CMP: URI paths, discovery, block-wise transfer, Observe-based announcements, and a new content-format.
CoAP.quote: This document specifies the use of the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) as a transfer mechanism for the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP).

PKI.why: CMP is the PKI certificate management protocol; the document is about transferring it, so PKI readers would want it. No CMP-specific tag exists, so PKI is the closest fit.
PKI.quote: CMP defines the interaction between various PKI entities for the purpose of certificate creation and management.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the existing CMP transport that a CoAP-to-HTTP proxy interconnects with; the document doesn't specify or extend HTTP.
DTLS is only recommended for confidentiality in Security Considerations; nothing new is defined about it.
Certificates are what CMP manages, but the document does not profile or specify them.
The document is a transport binding, but the CoAP tag is more specific and is the better home; the transport mapping topic was weighed as a possible parent-level fit.
The CoAP URI path and well-known registration are details of the CoAP binding, not a new URI scheme.
The application/pkixcmp content-format registration is incidental IANA boilerplate.

gaps.name: CMP (Certificate Management Protocol)
gaps.why: The document is about CMP transfer, but the taxonomy has no CMP tag under PKI. The CMP tag exists in the taxonomy under PKI, so this is a gap only in that the tag was not chosen here.

RFC9483.title: Lightweight Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) Profile
RFC9483.summary: RFC 9483 profiles the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) and CRMF for lightweight, automated certificate enrollment, update, revocation and support operations in industrial/IoT settings, with HTTP and CoAP transfer.

CMP.why: The whole document profiles CMP operations.
CMP.quote: profiling the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP), the related Certificate Request Message Format (CRMF), and transfer based on HTTP or Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)

RFC9484.title: Proxying IP in HTTP
RFC9484.summary: Defines the "connect-ip" HTTP upgrade token and capsules (ADDRESS_ASSIGN, ADDRESS_REQUEST, ROUTE_ADVERTISEMENT) letting an HTTP client tunnel arbitrary IP packets through an HTTP server acting as an IP proxy, updating RFC 9298.

MASQUE.why: This is the MASQUE IP proxying specification (connect-ip), produced by the masque WG, and it updates the masque well-known URI registration.
MASQUE.quote: this document defines a protocol that allows an HTTP client to create an IP tunnel through an HTTP server that acts as an IP proxy.

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate (Upgrade, Extended CONNECT, datagrams). MASQUE is the more specific tag for what the document defines.
QUIC DATAGRAM frames are a transport used, but the document does not specify or extend QUIC.
VPNs appear as use-case examples only. The tag is for provider-provisioned VPNs over BGP/MPLS, which this document is not about.
The document does tunnel IP, but MASQUE is the more specific tag for this HTTP-based tunnelling.
HTTP/3 is only one of the HTTP versions carrying the tunnel and is not specified here.
ICMP is used for error signalling, but the document does not define it.

RFC9485.title: I-Regexp: An Interoperable Regular Expression Format
RFC9485.summary: Specifies I-Regexp, a restricted subset of XSD regular expressions designed for interoperable Boolean matching across regexp libraries, with ABNF syntax and mapping guidance to ECMAScript, PCRE, RE2 and Ruby.

ABNF.why: The document defines a formal syntax for a regexp flavor in ABNF. This is a formal syntax notation specification of a text format, so the closest fit is the ABNF/formal syntax tag, though the document uses ABNF rather than specifying it. Weak but best available.
ABNF.quote: An I-Regexp MUST conform to the ABNF specification in Figure 1.

rejected.why: Motivated by JSONPath work, but the document is not about JSON or JSON-based formats.
I-Regexp is a subset of XSD regexps, but the document does not address XML usage in protocols or XML-based formats.
Supports full Unicode scalar values and categories, but the document is about regexp syntax, not Unicode usage in general.
UTF-8 is only mentioned as the interchange encoding and in security considerations.
CDDL .regexp is mentioned only in acknowledgements as motivation.

gaps.name: Regular expressions (I-Regexp)
gaps.why: The document's main subject is an interoperable regular expression format, and the taxonomy has no tag for regular expressions or pattern matching.

RFC9486.title: IPv6 Options for In Situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM)
RFC9486.summary: Defines how IOAM (In situ OAM) Data-Fields are encapsulated in IPv6 hop-by-hop and destination options, with new option types and deployment requirements for IOAM domains.

IPv6.why: The document specifies new IPv6 hop-by-hop and destination option types carrying IOAM data, along with IPv6 deployment considerations (MTU, extension header handling). No more specific IPv6 child tag fits.
IPv6.quote: This document outlines how IOAM Data-Fields are encapsulated in IPv6 [RFC8200] and discusses deployment requirements

OAM.why: IOAM is an OAM mechanism for in-band diagnostics and telemetry. The document specifies its encapsulation and deployment, so readers of OAM mechanisms would want it.
OAM.quote: IOAM records operational and telemetry information in the packet while the packet traverses a path between two points in the network.

rejected.why: IOAM does record telemetry data. However, the document is about IPv6 encapsulation of IOAM fields, and the OAM tag covers the subject more directly.
ECMP appears only as a requirement that IOAM must not change forwarding behaviour. The document is not about ECMP.
MTU and PMTU are mentioned as a deployment consideration (C3). This is a minor point, and the document is not about PMTUD.
AH is mentioned only to say IOAM does not rely on it, in the Security Considerations section.
The IANA section only assigns option type codes. This is boilerplate and does not make the document about IANA.

gaps.name: IOAM (In situ OAM)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IOAM itself. This RFC and its companions (RFC 9197, RFC 9326) would be best found under a dedicated IOAM tag.

RFC9487.title: Export of Segment Routing over IPv6 Information in IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX)
RFC9487.summary: Defines eleven new IPFIX Information Elements and an IANA subregistry for exporting SRv6 data (SRH fields, segment list, active segment type, endpoint behavior, locator length), with encoding examples.

IPFIX.why: The document extends IPFIX with new Information Elements, templates and encodings for exporting SRv6 flow information.
IPFIX.quote: This document introduces new IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Information Elements (IEs) to identify a set of information related to Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6)

SRv6.why: The exported elements describe SRv6 SRH contents, segment lists, and endpoint behaviors, so SRv6 readers would want it.
SRv6.quote: data contained in a Segment Routing Header (SRH), the SRv6 control plane, and the SRv6 Endpoint behavior that traffic is being forwarded with

rejected.why: The more specific SRv6 tag applies; the parent is implied.
IPv6 and the Routing Extension Header are only the context of the exported data; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
BGP Prefix-SID, IS-IS, OSPFv3 and PCEP are only referenced as sources of segment type values, not specified.
The IANA section registers the IEs and a subregistry, but that is boilerplate for this document's subject.
No data model is defined; the elements are IPFIX information model entries.

RFC9488.title: Local Protection Enforcement in the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP)
RFC9488.summary: Updates RFC 5440 to clarify the PCEP LSPA Local Protection Desired (L) flag and defines a new Protection Enforcement (E) flag so a PCE can treat protection as mandatory, preferred or unprotected during path computation.

PCE.why: The document extends and clarifies PCEP by adding the E flag to the LSPA object and specifying PCE behaviour and backwards compatibility.
PCE.quote: This document updates RFC 5440 to clarify usage of the Local Protection Desired bit signaled in the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP).

rejected.why: The L flag originates in RSVP-TE and fast reroute, but the document specifies PCEP behaviour, not RSVP-TE signalling.
Segment Routing is used for examples (protected and unprotected SIDs), but the text says the content is agnostic to path setup type and data plane.
TLS appears only as a recommendation in the Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
Fast reroute is the motivating concept for local protection, but the document is not about fast reroute mechanisms.
BGP-LS is mentioned only as a way for the PCE to learn protection eligibility.

RFC9489.title: Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping Mechanisms for EVPN and Provider Backbone Bridging EVPN (PBB-EVPN)
RFC9489.summary: Defines four new Target FEC Stack sub-TLVs and procedures for using MPLS LSP Ping to detect data plane failures in EVPN and PBB-EVPN networks.

EVPN.why: The document specifies EVPN/PBB-EVPN-specific sub-TLVs (MAC/IP, Inclusive Multicast, Ethernet A-D, IP Prefix) and connectivity-check procedures for EVPN routes, so EVPN readers would want it.
EVPN.quote: This document describes mechanisms for detecting data plane failures using LSP Ping in MPLS-based Ethernet VPN (EVPN) and Provider Backbone Bridging EVPN (PBB-EVPN) networks.

OAM.why: The document is an OAM extension: LSP Ping echo request/reply procedures and return codes for validating the data plane against the control plane.
OAM.quote: Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping is a widely deployed Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) mechanism in MPLS networks.

MPLS.why: It extends MPLS LSP Ping (RFC 8029, RFC 6425), adding sub-TLVs to the Target FEC Stack TLV, new return codes, and G-ACh/GAL encapsulation, including P2MP P-tree handling.
MPLS.quote: Procedures for simple and efficient mechanisms to detect data plane failures using LSP Ping in MPLS networks are well defined in [RFC8029] and [RFC6425].

rejected.why: EVPN routes are advertised over BGP, but BGP is only the control-plane substrate; the document defines no BGP behaviour.
EVPN is a VPLS-like L2 service, but the document is not about VPLS.
EVPN VPWS is covered only briefly in section 4.3.3 and is not pseudowire emulation as such.
Ethernet MAC and segment concepts appear only as fields of the EVPN sub-TLVs; the document is not about Ethernet OAM or IP over Ethernet.
The IANA section only registers sub-TLV types and return codes; it is boilerplate here.

RFC9490.title: Report from the IAB Workshop on Management Techniques in Encrypted Networks (M-TEN)
RFC9490.summary: IAB workshop report summarising M-TEN discussions on how network management techniques (traffic classification, collaboration with endpoints, relays, zero-knowledge middleboxes, content filtering) can coexist with pervasive encryption.

operational security.why: The report is about network management and monitoring/security functions in encrypted networks, including SOC operations, malware detection and policy enforcement. This is the best fit among the management topics.
operational security.quote: Network management techniques need to evolve to work effectively and reliably in the presence of ubiquitous traffic encryption and to support user privacy.

privacy.why: A substantial part of the report covers user privacy, traffic obfuscation, consent and metadata exposure, and the trade-off between privacy and management.
privacy.quote: Consent for collection and measurement of metadata is an important consideration in deploying network measurement techniques.

workshop reports.why: It is an IAB workshop report.
workshop reports.quote: This document is a report on the proceedings of the workshop.

rejected.why: TLS 1.3 and Encrypted Client Hello appear only in passing as examples, so the report is not about TLS.
MASQUE is mentioned as one relay approach, but it is not a focus of the report.
Encrypted DNS appears only as an example of metadata encryption and in the ZKP demonstration.
Passive measurement and safe-measurement guidelines are discussed, but the report's main subject is management of encrypted traffic, not measurement metrics.
MUD gets one passing mention as a subset of contracts.
ECN is cited once as an example of explicit signalling.

gaps.name: encrypted traffic classification / network management in encrypted networks
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for traffic classification or visibility of encrypted traffic. Operational security is the closest, but it is imperfect.

RFC9491.title: Integration of the Network Service Header (NSH) and Segment Routing for Service Function Chaining (SFC)
RFC9491.summary: Specifies how the Network Service Header (NSH) and Segment Routing (SR-MPLS and SRv6) are combined for Service Function Chaining, including the End.NSH SRv6 behavior, SFF caching of SR state, encapsulations, and IANA assignments.

SFC.why: The document defines how NSH-based service function chaining works with SR transport, including SFF processing, SPI/SI caching and NSH encapsulation.
SFC.quote: integration of the Network Service Header (NSH) and Segment Routing (SR), as well as encapsulation details, to efficiently support Service Function Chaining (SFC)

segment routing.why: SR is a co-subject: SR segment lists steer packets between SFFs, and the document adds SR behavior for service segments.
segment routing.quote: SR is thus responsible for steering traffic through the necessary SFFs as part of the segment routing path

SRv6.why: It defines the new SRv6 End.NSH endpoint behavior, pseudocode extending RFC 8754 processing, and NSH carried after the SRH.
SRv6.quote: In the case of SRv6, the behavior described within this document is assigned the name END.NSH
SRv6.section: 4. SR-Based SFC with the Integrated NSH Service Plane

SR-MPLS.why: It specifies SR-MPLS packet processing and NSH encapsulation under MPLS label stacks, including NEXT/CONTINUE and No-PHP handling.
SR-MPLS.quote: When an SFF receives a packet destined to S and S is a local Prefix-SID associated with an SF, the SFF strips the SR segment list

rejected.why: MPLS is only the data plane under SR-MPLS; the SR-MPLS tag is the more specific fit.
IPv6 is the substrate for SRv6; the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
The IANA assignments (protocol number 145, End.NSH code point) are boilerplate-like and secondary to the main body.
NSH is a service-plane encapsulation, not a network virtualization overlay like VXLAN or Geneve.

RFC9492.title: OSPF Application-Specific Link Attributes
RFC9492.summary: Defines the OSPFv2/OSPFv3 Application-Specific Link Attributes (ASLA) sub-TLV, with application bit masks, so link attributes originally defined for RSVP-TE can carry per-application values for SR Policy, LFA and others; obsoletes RFC 8920.

OSPF.why: The document defines new OSPFv2 Extended Link and OSPFv3 Router-Link sub-TLVs and the ASLA mechanism, so it is an OSPF extension.
OSPF.quote: This document introduces link attribute advertisements in OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 that address both of these shortcomings.

rejected.why: The document covers both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 equally, so the general OSPF tag fits better than the OSPFv3 child.
RSVP-TE is the legacy user of these attributes and one application bit. The document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE signalling.
LFA is only listed as one application that consumes the attributes. The document does not specify IP fast reroute.
SR Policy is only one consuming application, and the document does not define segment routing mechanisms.
The link attributes are TE attributes, but the document is about how they are advertised per application in OSPF, not about traffic engineering itself.
GMPLS is mentioned only as an origin of some attributes, such as the SRLG in RFC 4203.

RFC9493.title: Subject Identifiers for Security Event Tokens
RFC9493.summary: Defines Subject Identifiers as JSON objects with named Identifier Formats (account, email, iss_sub, opaque, phone_number, did, uri, aliases), a new IANA registry for formats, and the JWT "sub_id" claim for use in Security Event Tokens.

secevent.why: The document is a secevent WG product defining how subjects are identified within Security Event Tokens, including a registry of identifier formats.
secevent.quote: This specification formalizes the notion of Subject Identifiers as structured information that describes a subject and named formats that define the syntax and semantics

JWT.why: Registers and specifies a new JWT claim, "sub_id", and its interaction with "sub" and "iss_sub"; a substantial part of the document.
JWT.quote: This document defines the JWT "sub_id" Claim, in accordance with Section 4.2 of [RFC7519], as a common claim that identifies the JWT Subject

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding for Subject Identifiers; the document does not specify JSON itself.
The Email Identifier Format uses email addresses as identifier values, but the document isn't about email systems.
The URI and acct formats reuse existing URI schemes as values; no new URI syntax or scheme is defined.
The registry is created for this spec's formats, but that's boilerplate-level IANA considerations, not guidance about IANA in general.
Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a way to protect transport.
The phone number format uses E.164 strings, not the tel URI scheme.

gaps.name: Security Event Tokens (SET)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for Security Event Tokens other than the secevent id, which is used here, and the JWT tag isn't in the taxonomy either; I may have used ids not present.

RFC9494.title: Long-Lived Graceful Restart for BGP
RFC9494.summary: RFC 9494 defines the BGP Long-Lived Graceful Restart capability and the LLGR_STALE and NO_LLGR well-known communities. They let stale routes be kept much longer than BGP Graceful Restart allows, as least-preferred routes. The RFC also updates RFC 6368 for PE-CE use.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP with a new capability, session-reset procedures, route selection depreferencing and deployment guidance.
BGP.quote: This document introduces a BGP capability called the "Long-Lived Graceful Restart Capability" (or "LLGR Capability").

BGP communities.why: It defines two new well-known communities, LLGR_STALE and NO_LLGR, and the rules for attaching and propagating them.
BGP communities.quote: The well-known BGP community LLGR_STALE (value: 0xFFFF0006) can be used to mark stale routes retained for a longer period of time

L3VPN.why: A substantial part of the document covers PE-CE procedures in BGP/MPLS VPNs and updates RFC 6368 on ATTR_SET handling. The Security Considerations also discuss VPN label reuse.
L3VPN.quote: Procedures When BGP Is the PE-CE Protocol in a VPN

rejected.why: MPLS is mentioned only as tunneled forwarding that makes the extension safer, and in the VPN label security discussion. The document is not about MPLS.
VPLS is cited only as an example of BGP carrying auto-discovery data.
Flowspec is cited only as an example of BGP carrying configuration-like data.
BFD is mentioned once as an optional way to check next-hop viability.
The IANA section only registers the capability code, the communities and a flags registry. That is boilerplate and not the main subject.

RFC9495.title: Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) Processing for Email Addresses
RFC9495.summary: Defines the "issuemail" CAA property tag, which lets a domain restrict which Certification Authorities may issue S/MIME-style email certificates for addresses in that domain, and specifies its syntax and processing.

PKI.why: The document is about controlling which CAs may issue certificates, specifically email-protection certificates, and how a CA must check this before issuance.
PKI.quote: This document defines a CAA Property Tag that restricts the allowed set of issuers of certificates that certify email addresses.

DNS.why: It extends the CAA DNS resource record with a new Property Tag, including its value syntax and the RRSet lookup and processing rules. Readers of CAA/DNS RR material would want it.
DNS.quote: indicates that the domain is requesting that Certification Authorities restrict the issuance of certificates that certify email addresses
