rejected.why: S/MIME certificates are only the motivating use case. The document defines no S/MIME behaviour and is about CA authorization through DNS.
The document refers to the extendedKeyUsage and subjectAltName extensions only to define which certificates count as certifying an email address. It does not profile certificates.
Email addresses are the subject of the certificates, but no email protocol or format is specified or changed.
It does not discuss DNSSEC. It relies on the RFC 8659 lookup algorithm.
It only says to convert U-Labels to A-Labels when looking up the domain. This is a minor detail.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the property value syntax.

RFC9496.title: The ristretto255 and decaf448 Groups
RFC9496.summary: Specifies the ristretto255 and decaf448 prime-order groups, built on Curve25519 and edwards448, with encoding, decoding, equality, element derivation, scalar fields, API guidance and test vectors.

elliptic curve.why: The document defines prime-order groups on Edwards curves (Curve25519, edwards448), which is elliptic-curve cryptography. No more specific child tag fits, since it is not Curve25519 key exchange or EdDSA itself.
elliptic curve.quote: This memo specifies two prime-order groups, ristretto255 and decaf448, suitable for safely implementing higher-level and complex cryptographic protocols.

rejected.why: Used as the internal representation for ristretto255, but the document specifies a new group abstraction rather than the Curve25519 ECDH/curve specification.
Mentioned only as motivation (Ed25519 validation inconsistencies); the document does not specify or extend EdDSA.
Not related; these are classical elliptic-curve groups.

RFC9497.title: Oblivious Pseudorandom Functions (OPRFs) Using Prime-Order Groups
RFC9497.summary: Specifies OPRF, VOPRF and POPRF protocols over prime-order groups (ristretto255, decaf448, NIST P-curves), including DLEQ proofs, ciphersuites, and test vectors.

cryptography.why: The document is a cryptographic protocol specification for oblivious PRFs. No specific OPRF technology tag exists, so the parent cryptography topic fits.
cryptography.quote: This document specifies an OPRF, VOPRF, and POPRF instantiated within standard prime-order groups, including elliptic curves.

elliptic curve.why: A substantial part of the document defines ciphersuites over elliptic-curve groups: serialization, hash-to-curve, input validation, and scalar generation.
elliptic curve.quote: This ciphersuite uses P-256 [NISTCurves] for the Group and SHA-256 for the hash function.

rejected.why: OPAQUE and PAKEs are named only as applications of OPRFs. The document does not specify a PAKE.
Privacy Pass is cited as a motivating application, but the document does not specify it.
The SHA hashes are only components of the ciphersuites, not the subject of the document.
OPAQUE is only an informative reference and an example use case.

gaps.name: Oblivious Pseudorandom Functions (OPRF/VOPRF/POPRF)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for OPRFs or for privacy-enhancing cryptographic protocols. The document falls back on the generic cryptography topic.

RFC9498.title: The GNU Name System
RFC9498.summary: Specifies the GNU Name System (GNS), a decentralized, censorship-resistant, privacy-preserving name resolution protocol and alternative to DNS, including record wire formats, resolution, zone revocation and cryptographic routines.

naming.why: GNS is a name system distinct from DNS; the general naming topic fits, with no specific technology tag for GNS.
naming.quote: GNS is a decentralized and censorship-resistant domain name resolution protocol that provides a privacy-enhancing alternative to the Domain Name System (DNS) protocols.

DNS.why: GNS reuses DNS record types, defines GNS2DNS delegation, BOX records for SRV/TLSA, and migration via DNS-to-GNS servers. Readers of DNS would want it as an alternative and interoperating system.
DNS.quote: A GNS2DNS record delegates resolution to DNS.

special-use domain names.why: Uses and registers .gns.alt, and discusses namespace ambiguity with special-use names (Section 9.10).
special-use domain names.quote: this document uses the suffix ".gns.alt" in compliance with [RFC9476]. ".gns.alt" is also registered in the GANA ".alt Subdomains" registry

rejected.why: Only mentions DS records optionally under GNS2DNS; not about DNSSEC.
TLSA records are boxed in BOX records, but DANE itself is not the subject.
Uses Ed25519/ECDSA for zone keys but the document is about the name system, not the curves.
EdDSA is a building block for EDKEY zones, not the subject.
DHT remote storage is explicitly out of scope; only a substrate.
Internationalization is addressed briefly (Section 8), delegating to IDNA; not a main subject.

gaps.name: GNU Name System (GNS) / petname systems / decentralized name systems
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for GNS or alternative decentralized name systems; only the generic naming topic fits.

RFC9499.title: DNS Terminology
RFC9499.summary: RFC 9499 is a BCP that consolidates current definitions of DNS terminology (names, RCODEs, resource records, servers/resolvers, zones, wildcards, registration model, DNSSEC), obsoleting RFC 8499 and updating RFC 2308.

DNS.why: The whole document defines DNS terms: names, RCODEs, RRs, servers, resolvers, zones, wildcards. A DNS reader would look for it.
DNS.quote: This document gives current definitions for many of the terms used in the DNS in a single document.

DNSSEC.why: Two full sections cover DNSSEC terms: signed zones, NSEC/NSEC3, KSK/ZSK, trust anchors, validation and secure/insecure/bogus/indeterminate states.
DNSSEC.quote: Most DNSSEC terms are defined in [RFC4033], [RFC4034], [RFC4035], and [RFC5155]. The terms that have caused confusion in the DNS community are highlighted here.

terminology.why: It is a glossary, a BCP that sets the DNS vocabulary and clarifies definitions of earlier RFCs.
terminology.quote: This document contains a collection of a wide variety of DNS-related terms, organized loosely by topic.

rejected.why: The Registration Model section defines registry, registrar and registrant, but it is one short section of a glossary. EPP, WHOIS and RDAP are only defined as terms, not specified.
EDNS and OPT are defined as single glossary entries, not the subject of the document.
DoT, DoH, DoQ and XoT are defined as terms only. The document does not specify or extend those protocols.
The 'Host name' entry is one term among many, so the document is not about hostname conventions.
IDN has a single glossary entry that points to the IDNA RFCs.
DNS is the more specific tag, and the 'Naming system' entry is only a brief introduction to it.

RFC9500.title: Standard Public Key Cryptography (PKC) Test Keys
RFC9500.summary: Publishes a set of publicly known RSA, DLP (DSA/DH/Elgamal) and ECDLP (P-256/384/521) test private keys, in C-like notation and OpenSSL encodings, so applications can recognise them as test-only keys.

cryptography.why: The document is about cryptographic key material across algorithm families. No more specific tag covers it, because it spans RSA, DLP and ECDLP.
cryptography.quote: This document provides a set of standard Public Key Cryptography (PKC) test keys that may be used wherever pre-generated keys and associated operations like digital signatures are required.

rejected.why: RSA keys are one of three families provided. The document does not specify or analyse RSA itself, so a reader of the RSA subject page would not expect it.
The P-256/384/521 keys are only one of three sets of sample data. The document is not about elliptic-curve cryptography.
ECDSA is mentioned only as an algorithm the ECDLP keys could be used with.
The keys are test keys with no certificates or infrastructure, so the document is not about PKI.
The document gives static sample keys. It does not cover key establishment, provisioning or storage.

RFC9501.title: Open Participation Principle regarding Remote Registration Fee
RFC9501.summary: BCP stating that the IETF must always offer a free option for remote meeting participation, extending the RFC 3935 open process principle and leaving implementation and finances to the IETF LLC.

IETF process.why: The document sets an IETF procedural principle on meeting participation and registration fees, extending the open process principle. This is IETF process and administration, so the topic tag fits directly.
IETF process.quote: there must be an option for free remote participation in any IETF meeting, regardless of whether the meeting has a physical presence.

rejected.why: The parent is implied by IETF process, and the document is about IETF process specifically, so the parent is not listed separately.
The IPR/copyright section is boilerplate and has no bearing on the document's subject.
The document quotes the RFC 3935 mission statement but does not define terms or a glossary.
The document discusses the IETF's financial sustainability, not environmental sustainability of Internet infrastructure.

gaps.name: IETF meetings / IETF LLC finances and administration
gaps.why: The document is about meeting registration fees and the IETF LLC's financial responsibilities. The taxonomy has only the general IETF process tag, with no specific tag for meetings or administrative finance.

RFC9502.title: IGP Flexible Algorithm in IP Networks
RFC9502.summary: Extends IGP Flexible Algorithm (RFC 9350) beyond Segment Routing so that IS-IS and OSPF can compute constraint-based paths to regular IPv4/IPv6 prefixes, defining new TLVs/sub-TLVs for participation and prefix reachability.

IS-IS.why: The document defines new IS-IS TLVs and sub-TLVs (IP Algorithm Sub-TLV, IPv4/IPv6 Algorithm Prefix Reachability TLVs) and their processing rules.
IS-IS.quote: The IS-IS IPv4 Algorithm Prefix Reachability top-level TLV is defined for advertising IPv4 Flexible Algorithm Prefix Reachability in IS-IS.

OSPF.why: New OSPFv2 TLVs and sub-TLVs for IP Flex-Algorithm participation, prefix reachability, forwarding address and ASBR metric extend OSPF.
OSPF.quote: A new sub-TLV of the OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV is defined for advertising IP Algorithm Prefix Reachability in OSPFv2

OSPFv3.why: A dedicated section defines the OSPFv3 sub-TLV and the IPFAAM sub-TLV for OSPFv3, so OSPFv3 readers would want it.
OSPFv3.quote: The OSPFv3 [RFC5340] IP Algorithm Prefix Reachability Sub-TLV is defined for advertisement of the IP Algorithm Prefix Reachability in OSPFv3.

rejected.why: The base Flex-Algorithm SR data planes are only background; this document specifically adds a non-SR IP data plane.
SRv6 locators are mentioned only for conflict handling and as contrast, not specified here.
LFA/R-LFA is only briefly mentioned in the Protection section as a restriction to the Flex-Algorithm topology.
Mentioned in passing as a restoration enhancement.
Constraint-based path computation is related, but the document is about IGP extensions, not TE architecture.

gaps.name: IGP Flexible Algorithm
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IGP Flexible Algorithm (RFC 9350), which is the core subject. IS-IS and OSPF are the closest tags, but readers browsing Flex-Algorithm would want this RFC.

RFC9503.title: Simple Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP) Extensions for Segment Routing Networks
RFC9503.summary: Defines two new STAMP TLVs (Destination Node Address and Return Path with sub-TLVs for control code, return address, SR-MPLS label stack and SRv6 segment list) extending RFC 8972 for performance measurement in Segment Routing networks.

STAMP.why: The document extends STAMP with new TLVs and registries, so STAMP readers need it.
STAMP.quote: This document specifies Simple Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP) extensions (as described in RFC 8762) for SR networks

segment routing.why: The extensions steer STAMP reply packets over SR return paths. Segment lists for SR-MPLS and SRv6 are carried in sub-TLVs, so SR readers would want it.
segment routing.quote: SR is applicable to both Multiprotocol Label Switching (SR-MPLS) and IPv6 (SRv6) forwarding planes

rejected.why: Used only as a forwarding plane for the return label stack. The document does not extend SR-MPLS. The generic segment routing tag covers it.
Only the SRv6 segment list is carried as a sub-TLV. The document does not specify SRv6 itself.
Not in the taxonomy. The interoperability section is a short note that defers to RFC 8762.
The STAMP tag already sits under it, so the parent is implied.
STAMP runs over UDP. This is substrate only.
Mentioned in a use-case example only. The document is not about ECMP.
The STAMP YANG model is only referenced informatively.

RFC9504.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for Stateful PCE Usage in GMPLS-Controlled Networks
RFC9504.summary: Specifies PCEP extensions (GMPLS-CAPABILITY flags, LSP Exclusion XRO subobject, LSP-EXTENDED-FLAG flags, new error codes) so a stateful PCE can report, update and initiate LSPs in GMPLS-controlled networks.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP and stateful PCE behaviour (capability advertisement, LSP report/update/initiation, XRO subobject, errors). PCE tag covers PCE architecture and PCEP.
PCE.quote: This document provides the extensions required for PCEP so as to enable the usage of a stateful PCE capability in GMPLS-controlled networks.

GMPLS.why: The extensions are specifically for GMPLS LSPs (switching types, G-PID, bidirectional LSPs, label control), so GMPLS readers would want it.
GMPLS.quote: extensions that are necessary in order for the deployment of stateful PCEs and the requirements for PCE-initiated LSPs in GMPLS-controlled networks

rejected.why: GMPLS signalling is referenced only as background for LSP attributes; the document is about PCEP, not RSVP-TE.
PCEPS over TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations.
YANG models are mentioned only in Manageability Considerations as future work.
RBNF is just the notation used in the appendix for message formats.
IANA registrations are boilerplate for the protocol extensions, not the subject of the document.

RFC9505.title: A Survey of Worldwide Censorship Techniques
RFC9505.summary: An IRTF PEARG informational survey of technical mechanisms (identification and interference at application, transport and routing layers) and non-technical measures that censorship regimes use to block or impair Internet traffic.

privacy.why: The survey of censorship, produced by the Privacy Enhancements and Assessments Research Group, is about threats to user access and confidentiality. The taxonomy has no censorship tag, so privacy is the closest fit.
privacy.quote: It aims to make designers, implementers, and users of Internet protocols aware of the properties exploited and mechanisms used for censoring end-user access to information.

TLS.why: A substantial subsection covers how censors exploit SNI, ESNI/ECH, and server certificates in TLS handshakes.
TLS.quote: Most of these techniques relate to the Server Name Indication (SNI) field, including censoring SNI, Encrypted SNI (ESNI), or omitted SNI.

DNS.why: DNS interference (mangling, cache poisoning, lying resolvers) is a major section of the survey.
DNS.quote: There are a variety of mechanisms that censors can use to block or filter access to content by altering responses from the DNS

BGP.why: Covers BGP prefix withdrawal and hijacking as censorship interference mechanisms.
BGP.quote: More fine-grained and potentially wide-spread censorship can be achieved with BGP hijacking, which adversarially re-routes BGP IP prefixes

rejected.why: HTTP header identification is discussed as a censor target, but the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
RST injection and packet dropping rely on TCP behaviour, but the document is not about TCP itself.
QUIC censorship is mentioned in passing in several places, but it is not a main subject.
DDoS is covered as one censor technique in a short subsection; the DDoS topic is about mitigation and signalling.
DoH and DoT are cited only as mitigations for DNS interference.
BGP hijacking is described as a censorship technique, and the document does not address routing security mechanisms.

gaps.name: Internet censorship / blocking and filtering
gaps.why: The whole document is about censorship techniques, circumvention and measurement, and the taxonomy has no censorship tag.

RFC9506.title: Explicit Host-to-Network Flow Measurements Techniques
RFC9506.summary: RFC 9506 describes protocol-independent explicit marking techniques (Spin bit, Delay bit, loss bits T/Q/L/R, ECN-echo E bit) that let endpoints expose packet loss and delay to passive on-path observers, especially for encrypted transport protocols.

performance measurement.why: The whole document defines hybrid passive/active methods for measuring packet loss and delay (RTT, half-RTT, upstream/downstream loss) on live traffic.
performance measurement.quote: Explicit Host-to-Network Flow Measurement Techniques that are specifically designed for encrypted transport protocols.

QUIC.why: The techniques are motivated by encrypted transports and build on the QUIC Spin bit. QUIC is a major application, with the Spin bit, ECN counters and Connection ID privacy discussed. The bits are not specified for QUIC itself.
QUIC.quote: reserved bits in a QUIC v1 header, as already done with the latency Spin bit

rejected.why: The E bit reports ECN-Echo feedback, but this is a small part of a document focused on loss and delay.
TCP is mentioned as an applicable protocol and in loss-detection caveats, but the document is transport-agnostic and does not specify TCP.
ConEx is cited only as a similar loss and ECN signalling mechanism, not specified or extended here.
UDP surplus space is only mentioned as a possible place for the bits.
Alternate-Marking is related to OAM, but performance measurement is the more specific tag.
The document mentions congestion controllers only in passing, and the measurement aspect dominates.

gaps.name: Alternate-Marking / hybrid passive measurement
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for Alternate-Marking or explicit path signals. This RFC is closely tied to RFC 9341 and RFC 8558, and the performance measurement topic only partly covers them.

RFC9507.title: Information-Centric Networking (ICN) Traceroute Protocol Specification
RFC9507.summary: Specifies the ICN Traceroute protocol, a management/debugging tool for CCNx and NDN that defines request and reply packet formats and forwarder and client operation for tracing paths to name prefixes.

ICN.why: The document defines a traceroute protocol for CCNx and NDN information-centric networks, specifying packet formats and forwarder behaviour over PIT/CS/FIB.
ICN.quote: This document describes the design of a management and debugging protocol analogous to the traceroute protocol of TCP/IP

traceroute.why: The protocol is a traceroute-style path discovery tool, with HopLimit-increasing requests and per-hop replies, so the traceroute subject page is relevant.
traceroute.quote: the ability to ascertain the characteristics of at least one of the available routes to a name prefix is a fundamental requirement

rejected.why: Transit delay measurement is one goal, but the document is mainly a path-discovery and debugging tool, covered by traceroute.
The tool supports management and debugging, but it is already tagged more specifically as traceroute under network management.
IP traceroute and ICMP appear only as background for comparison; the document does not specify ICMP.
Base64 is used only to encode the nonce, as an encoding substrate.

RFC9508.title: Information-Centric Networking (ICN) Ping Protocol Specification
RFC9508.summary: Specifies an ICN Ping protocol (Echo Request/Reply packet formats for CCNx and NDN, plus forwarder handling) for testing reachability and measuring RTT of names in Information-Centric Networks.

ICN.why: The whole document defines a ping protocol for CCNx and NDN networks, including packet formats and forwarder behaviour.
ICN.quote: This document proposes protocol mechanisms for a ping equivalent in ICN networks (Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) [RFC8609] and Named Data Networking (NDN) [NDNTLV]).

rejected.why: ICMP Echo is only the IP analogy used as background; the document specifies an ICN protocol, not ICMP.
Mentioned only as a companion tool needed for ICN; the document defines ping, not path discovery.
RTT measurement is a goal, but the document defines a reachability/debugging protocol and leaves measurement applications out of scope.
Ping is a management and debugging tool, but the ICN tag is more specific and no OAM-focused content beyond that is present.
Base64 is used only as a nonce encoding detail, not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: CCNx/NDN path steering
gaps.why: The document relies on the Path Label TLV from RFC 9531, but only ICN is available as a tag, so this isn't covered separately.

RFC9509.title: X.509 Certificate Extended Key Usage (EKU) for 5G Network Functions
RFC9509.summary: Defines three X.509 Extended Key Usage KeyPurposeIds (id-kp-jwt, id-kp-httpContentEncrypt, id-kp-oauthAccessTokenSigning) for certificates used by 5G Network Functions to sign JWTs, encrypt JSON in HTTP via JWE, and sign OAuth access tokens.

X.509.why: The document extends X.509 certificates by defining new EKU KeyPurposeIds and how they are included in certificates and handled by CAs.
X.509.quote: This specification defines the KeyPurposeIds id-kp-jwt, id-kp-httpContentEncrypt, and id-kp-oauthAccessTokenSigning
X.509.section: 3. Extended Key Purpose for Network Functions

cellular.why: The motivating use case is certificates for 3GPP 5G Core Network Functions and SEPPs, so readers of 5G and cellular topics would want it.
cellular.quote: The operators of 5G ("fifth generation") systems as defined by 3GPP make use of an internal PKI to generate X.509 PKI certificates

rejected.why: JWTs are only what the certificates are used to sign. The document defines nothing about the JWT format.
JWS and JWE are the usage contexts for the certified keys. The document does not specify or extend them.
OAuth 2.0 access token signing is only a purpose for one of the EKUs. The OAuth framework itself is not addressed.
The parent of X.509. The more specific X.509 tag fits.
The ASN.1 module in the appendix only defines OIDs. The document is not about ASN.1.
TLS appears only in the Privacy Considerations, as background on whether certificates are exchanged in the clear.

RFC9510.title: Alternative Delta Time Encoding for Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) Using Compact Floating-Point Arithmetic
RFC9510.summary: Experimental IRTF RFC that updates the CCNx TLV message format (RFC 8609) by adding a one-byte logarithmic (floating-point style) time code for the Interest Lifetime and Recommended Cache Time fields.

ICN.why: CCNx is an Information-Centric Networking protocol. The document changes how CCNx messages encode Interest Lifetime and Recommended Cache Time, so ICN readers would want it.
ICN.quote: This document updates RFC 8609 ("CCNx messages in TLV Format") to specify this alternative encoding.

rejected.why: The constrained-device use case is only the motivation. The document specifies a CCNx time encoding and does not address IoT architecture or guidance.
The compact time code is borrowed from RFC 9139 (ICN over LoWPANs), but this document does not specify any 6LoWPAN adaptation.
The document defines a small floating-point time code, but only as a CCNx TLV field encoding. It is not a general data format.
These are relative time offsets in CCNx messages, not Internet timestamp representations.
The document is about the encoding of time values, not about synchronizing clocks.

RFC9511.title: Attribution of Internet Probes
RFC9511.summary: RFC 9511 defines simple out-of-band (well-known probing.txt file) and in-band (URI in probe payload) techniques for active Internet measurement probes to identify their source, purpose and contact.

performance measurement.why: The document is about attributing active measurement probes, covering operational and ethical aspects of Internet measurement.
performance measurement.quote: Active measurements over the public Internet can target either collaborating parties or non-collaborating ones.

operational security.why: Helps operators investigate unsolicited probe traffic and decide how to treat it, an operational practice concern.
operational security.quote: those probes could trigger an alarm that will request some investigations by either the party receiving the probe

rejected.why: It defines a Probe Description URI and registers a well-known URI suffix, but URI syntax and schemes are not the subject.
ICMP echo requests are only carriers for the in-band URI; nothing new is specified about ICMP.
IPv6 extension headers (PadN) are used as a carrier, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
Reverse DNS is used to build the out-of-band URI, but DNS is only a substrate here.
The description file is fetched over HTTPS from a well-known path, but HTTP is just the substrate.
The well-known URI registration is boilerplate-level IANA action, not the main subject.

RFC9512.title: YAML Media Type
RFC9512.summary: Registers the application/yaml media type and the +yaml structured syntax suffix, defining fragment identifier handling and interoperability/security considerations for YAML, including its relation to JSON.

YAML.why: The document exists to register the media type for YAML and specify YAML interoperability, fragment identification and security considerations.
YAML.quote: This document registers the application/yaml media type and the +yaml structured syntax suffix with IANA.

media types.why: A substantial part is the media type and structured syntax suffix registration, so readers of media type registrations would want it.
media types.quote: this specification registers the application/yaml media type and the +yaml structured syntax suffix [MEDIATYPE].

JSON.why: A significant section covers YAML/JSON interoperability and JSON Pointer fragment identifiers evaluated on YAML graphs.
JSON.quote: When using flow collection styles (see Section 7.4 of [YAML]), a YAML document could look like JSON [JSON]; thus, similar interoperability considerations apply.

rejected.why: Fragment identifiers for YAML are defined, but the document does not specify URI syntax; URI is relied upon.
Only referenced for content negotiation terminology; not about HTTP.
Mentioned as motivation only; the document does not define media feature negotiation.
OpenAPI is cited as a use case, but the document is not about API conventions.

RFC9513.title: OSPFv3 Extensions for Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6)
RFC9513.summary: Specifies OSPFv3 extensions (SRv6 Capabilities TLV, SRv6 Locator LSA, End/End.X SID sub-TLVs, MSD types, anycast prefix option) to advertise Segment Routing over IPv6 information.

SRv6.why: The document defines how SRv6 locators, SIDs, endpoint behaviors and capabilities are advertised in the IGP; it is about SRv6 control-plane support.
SRv6.quote: This document describes the OSPFv3 extensions required to support SR over the IPv6 data plane.

OSPFv3.why: It defines a new OSPFv3 LSA (SRv6 Locator LSA), TLVs, sub-TLVs and a prefix option bit, so it extends OSPFv3.
OSPFv3.quote: This document specifies OSPFv3 extensions to support SRv6 capabilities as defined in [RFC8986], [RFC8754], and [RFC9259].

rejected.why: The more specific SRv6 child tag applies, so the parent is implied.
IPv6 is only the data plane SRv6 runs on; the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
BGP-LS is mentioned only as an informative example of a consumer of the advertised data.
IANA registry actions are boilerplate for the protocol extensions and not the subject of the document.
It is mentioned only in reference to Flexible Algorithm procedures; the document is about the IPv6 data plane.

RFC9514.title: Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS) Extensions for Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6)
RFC9514.summary: Defines BGP-LS extensions (new SRv6 SID NLRI type and TLVs) to advertise SRv6 capabilities, End.X SIDs, locators, endpoint behaviors, BGP EPE peer SIDs and SID structure, derived from IS-IS/OSPFv3 or local node.

SRv6.why: The document is about advertising SRv6 SIDs, End.X, locators and endpoint behaviors; SRv6 readers need these encodings.
SRv6.quote: This document defines extensions to BGP - Link State (BGP-LS) to advertise SRv6 segments along with their behaviors and other attributes via BGP.

BGP.why: It extends BGP-LS with a new NLRI type, new attribute TLVs and a new IANA registry, so it is a BGP protocol extension.
BGP.quote: This document defines the following new Link-State NLRI type for SRv6 SID information: SRv6 SID NLRI (type 6).

rejected.why: IS-IS SRv6 TLVs are only the source of the data that is copied into BGP-LS TLVs. The document does not extend IS-IS.
OSPFv3 SRv6 TLVs are only the source of the data that is copied into BGP-LS TLVs. The document does not extend OSPFv3.
The document does not deal with BGP communities.
The SR PCE is only mentioned as a consumer of the BGP-LS data in the manageability section.
The more specific SRv6 tag fits better, because the document is about the IPv6 data plane and not segment routing in general.
SR-MPLS is only referenced for comparison, in the appendix and in the references to RFC 9085 and RFC 9086.

gaps.name: BGP-LS (BGP Link-State) and BGP Egress Peer Engineering
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no BGP-LS or BGP-EPE tag. These are the main subject of the document, and the BGP tag only partly covers them.

RFC9515.title: Revision to Registration Procedures for Multiple BMP Registries
RFC9515.summary: Updates RFC 7854 by changing the IANA registration policy for the 32768-65530 ranges of six BMP registries from Specification Required to First Come First Served.

BMP.why: The document's whole purpose is to revise registration procedures for six BMP (BGP Monitoring Protocol) registries, updating RFC 7854. BMP readers would want to find it.
BMP.quote: IANA has revised the following registries within the BMP group:

IANA.why: The document is about IANA registry policy, changing the registration policy from Specification Required to First Come First Served.
IANA.quote: the ranges 32768-65530 whose registration procedures were "Specification Required" are revised to have the registration procedures "First Come First Served"

rejected.why: BMP monitors BGP, but the document does not specify or change BGP itself. BMP is the more specific tag.
The document revises registry policy only and does not change the IETF standards process.

RFC9516.title: Active Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) for Service Function Chaining (SFC)
RFC9516.summary: Defines requirements for active OAM in Service Function Chaining, an NSH-based Active OAM header, and an SFC Echo Request/Reply mechanism (with consistency verification and tracing) to detect and localize defects.

SFC.why: The document specifies active OAM encapsulation, Echo Request/Reply and consistency verification for SFC and the NSH, so SFC readers need it.
SFC.quote: This document defines how active Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM), per the definition of active OAM in [RFC7799], is implemented when the Network Service Header (NSH) [RFC8300] is used

OAM.why: Fault-management OAM requirements and echo/traceroute mechanisms are a substantial part of the document, though the OAM topic is not under SFC.
OAM.quote: This document defines the set of requirements for active FM OAM mechanisms to be used in an SFC architecture.
OAM.section: 3. Requirements for Active OAM in SFC

rejected.why: Only cited as an analogy for Echo Request/Reply; the document does not specify ICMP.
Mentioned only as an example of an OAM protocol that could be demultiplexed; not specified.
Tracing an SFP is a mode of the SFC echo mechanism, but the document is about SFC OAM, not the traceroute tool in general.
UDP is only the substrate for out-of-band replies.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-like apparatus for the new protocol, not the document's subject.
Mentioned only as another encapsulation and for MPLS echo analogy; out of scope.

RFC9517.title: A URN Namespace for the Data Documentation Initiative (DDI)
RFC9517.summary: Registers the "ddi" URN namespace identifier for Data Documentation Initiative resources, defining its NSS syntax (agency:resource:version) and DNS/U-NAPTR-based resolution via ddi.urn.arpa.

URN.why: The document is a formal URN namespace registration under RFC 8141, specifying syntax, assignment, lexical equivalence and resolution for the ddi NID.
URN.quote: This document describes the Namespace Identifier (NID) "ddi" for Uniform Resource Names (URNs) used to identify resources that conform to the standards published by the Data Documentation Initiative (DDI) Alliance.

DNS.why: Resolution of DDI agency identifiers is defined through DNS delegation with NAPTR and SRV records, with example zone records and a DDDS algorithm in the appendices. This is a substantial part of the document.
DNS.quote: A DNS request for a DDI agency within the domain ddi.urn.arpa is delegated by the DNS servers of the DDI Alliance to the DNS servers of the relevant DDI agency.

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used to state the URN grammar. The document is not about the notation.
DoH is mentioned only once, in Security Considerations, as an optional way to protect DNS queries.
The discovery mechanism is U-NAPTR/DDDS over DNS, specific to this namespace. The DNS tag already covers it.
DDI specifications are expressed in XML Schema, but the document only names them as the resources being identified.

RFC9518.title: Centralization, Decentralization, and Internet Standards
RFC9518.summary: An Independent Submission arguing that standards bodies have limited ability to prevent centralization of Internet functions, surveying harms and benefits of centralization and decentralization strategies, and recommending concrete steps standards efforts can take.

internet architecture.why: The document is an architectural discussion of centralization and decentralization as properties of the Internet and the role standards play in preserving decentralization.
internet architecture.quote: One of the Internet's defining features is its lack of any single point of technical, political, or economic control.

internet governance.why: Substantial parts discuss ICANN and CA/Browser Forum governance and the legitimacy of the IETF and standards bodies (Section 4.1), making it relevant to governance readers.
internet governance.quote: Often, this is through the establishment of a multi-stakeholder body, which is an institution that includes representatives of the different kinds of parties

rejected.why: DNS is used as an example of centralized naming and governance, not specified or analysed in its own right.
SMTP and email federation are used as an example of federation limits only.
XMPP is cited only as an example of voluntary federation.
RFC 9230 is cited briefly as an example of oblivious protocols limiting third parties.
Privacy appears as one benefit of intermediaries, not a main subject.
Legitimacy of the IETF is discussed in one subsection, but the document is not about IETF procedures; governance is the better fit.

gaps.name: Centralization and decentralization of Internet functions
gaps.why: The core subject is centralization/decentralization, including federation and distributed consensus; the taxonomy has no tag for it beyond the broad architecture topic.

RFC9519.title: Update to the IANA SSH Protocol Parameters Registry Requirements
RFC9519.summary: Changes the registration policy for most IANA Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol Parameters registries from IETF Review to Expert Review, and defines the designated expert review process.

SSH.why: The document updates the registries of the SSH protocol and amends the SSH RFCs 4250, 4716, 4819 and 8308. SSH readers will want it.
SSH.quote: This specification updates the registration policies for adding new entries to registries within the IANA "Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol Parameters" group of registries.

IANA.why: Its main content is IANA registration policy: moving to Expert Review and setting out the designated expert procedures.
IANA.quote: Expert Review [RFC8126] registry requests are registered after a three-week review period on the <ssh-reg-review@ietf.org> mailing list

rejected.why: The document sets registry review procedure, not the wider IETF standards process. The IANA tag covers it.
IPsec and TLS registries are mentioned only as precedent for the same policy change.
TLS registries are mentioned only as precedent for the same policy change.

RFC9520.title: Negative Caching of DNS Resolution Failures
RFC9520.summary: Updates RFC 2308, 4035 and 4697 to require resolvers to negatively cache DNS resolution failures (SERVFAIL, REFUSED, timeouts, loops, DNSSEC validation failures), with retry limits, cache durations and backoff, and limits on requerying parent zones.

DNS.why: The whole document specifies DNS resolver behaviour for caching and retrying failed resolutions, updating RFC 2308 and RFC 4697.
DNS.quote: Resolvers MUST implement a cache for resolution failures.  The purpose of this cache is to eliminate repeated upstream queries that cannot be resolved.

DNSSEC.why: It updates RFC 4035 to make caching of DNSSEC validation failures mandatory, a substantial part of the document.
DNSSEC.quote: security-aware resolvers MUST cache DNSSEC validation failures, with some restrictions.

rejected.why: Encrypted DNS transports are only listed in the terminology as possible transports; the document does not specify them.
EDNS(0) appears only in the FORMERR discussion as a common cause; the document is not about EDNS.
Retry storms and attack traffic are motivation and security considerations, not the subject; the document specifies resolver caching.
The document limits query rates through caching, but this is DNS resolver behaviour and not transport congestion control.
DNS-over-TLS is mentioned only as an example transport in terminology.

RFC9521.title: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for  Generic Network Virtualization Encapsulation (Geneve)
RFC9521.summary: Specifies how BFD asynchronous mode is used to monitor point-to-point Geneve tunnels, defining BFD packet encapsulation for Ethernet and IP payloads and demultiplexing rules at the NVE.

BFD.why: The document defines how BFD sessions are run, encapsulated, and demultiplexed over Geneve tunnels.
BFD.quote: This document describes the use of the Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) protocol [RFC5880] to enable monitoring the continuity of the path between two Geneve tunnel endpoints

Geneve.why: It specifies Geneve header field settings (O bit, C bit, Protocol Type, VNI) for BFD packets and Geneve tunnel endpoint behaviour, so Geneve readers need it.
Geneve.quote: BFD over IP over Ethernet is carried in the payload.
Geneve.section: 3. BFD Packet Transmission over a Geneve Tunnel

rejected.why: Geneve is the more specific child tag and is already chosen.
Only referenced via RFC 8971 as a similar earlier BFD mapping, not the subject of this document.
UDP is the substrate for BFD and Geneve encapsulation, with nothing new defined about it.
IPv4 and IPv6 are both used as inner and outer headers, but the document does not address either as a subject.
Ethernet frames appear only as an inner payload type, and the document does not address IP over Ethernet in its own right.
BFD is a connectivity monitoring mechanism, but the BFD tag covers it more specifically. The Geneve OAM draft is out of scope.

RFC9522.title: Overview and Principles of Internet Traffic Engineering
RFC9522.summary: RFC 9522 is an informational overview of Internet traffic engineering principles, giving terminology, a taxonomy of TE systems, a review of IETF TE techniques, recommendations, and inter-domain and operational practice notes; it obsoletes RFC 3272.

traffic engineering.why: The whole document is about traffic engineering principles, process models, taxonomy and recommendations, which is exactly the subject of the traffic engineering page.
traffic engineering.quote: This document describes the principles of traffic engineering (TE) in the Internet.

congestion control.why: A substantial part of the document covers congestion and how to combat it, including AQM, RED and ECN. It is network-side congestion management, so it fits the congestion control page.
congestion control.quote: Congestion avoidance and response schemes can include demand-side policies and supply-side policies.

PCE.why: PCE and PCEP are covered as a central component of TE systems in the SDN discussion, in multi-layer TE and in operational practice.
PCE.quote: The PCE [RFC4655] is an entity (component, application, or network node) that is capable of computing a network path or route

RSVP-TE.why: RSVP-TE is reviewed as a core TE signalling mechanism and recurs in the survivability and operations sections.
RSVP-TE.quote: RSVP-TE enables the establishment of traffic-engineered MPLS LSPs (TE LSPs), using loose or strict paths

MPLS.why: MPLS-TE, LSP protection and Diffserv-aware TE over MPLS take up large parts of the document.
MPLS.quote: MPLS is a powerful technology for Internet TE because it supports explicit LSPs

Diffserv.why: The document reviews Diffserv as a TE mechanism and has a dedicated section on TE in Diffserv environments.
Diffserv.quote: TE can complement Diffserv to improve utilization of network resources.

rejected.why: Section 7 covers inter-domain TE using BGP and BGP-LS appears in passing, but the document does not specify or extend BGP.
SR and SR Policy are described as TE mechanisms, but only as one item in a broad survey.
Mentioned as a TE technique in a short survey subsection only.
Section 4.3.2 discusses SDN and TE, but it is a sub-topic and the taxonomy tag is not warranted as a main subject.
ALTO is reviewed in one subsection as an approach relying on TE, not a main subject.
A short survey subsection describes DetNet as a branch of TE; the document is not about DetNet.

gaps.name: Internet traffic engineering
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag named "traffic engineering". It has a topic under routing, "traffic engineering [topic]: Traffic engineering of packet and transport networks". I used that id in the tags. If the id is rejected, this is the document's core subject and needs a general TE tag.

RFC9523.title: A Secure Selection and Filtering Mechanism for the Network Time Protocol with Khronos
RFC9523.summary: Describes Khronos, a watchdog companion to NTPv4 clients that randomly samples servers from a large pool and trims outliers to defend against time-shifting attacks, without changing the wire protocol.

NTP.why: The document specifies a client-side selection/filtering mechanism for NTP clients that changes the system process and defends the NTP clock against time-shifting attacks.
NTP.quote: This document describes a companion application to the NTPv4 client, named "Khronos", that is used as a "watchdog" alongside NTPv4

rejected.why: DNS is used only to gather NTP server IPs during calibration; the document doesn't define anything new about DNS.
The security content concerns the time-shifting threat model for NTP, which is already covered by the NTP tag; it isn't general operational security guidance.
Parent of NTP, so it is implied by the NTP tag.
Secure random server selection is required, but only as a brief implementation note.

RFC9524.title: Segment Routing Replication for Multipoint Service Delivery
RFC9524.summary: Defines the Segment Routing Replication segment, which lets a node replicate packets to downstream nodes, with SR-MPLS and SRv6 (End.Replicate) data-plane behaviours for multipoint service delivery.

segment routing.why: The document defines a new SR segment type and its behaviour. Both its SR-MPLS and SRv6 data planes are covered, so the parent tag fits.
segment routing.quote: The Replication segment is a new type of segment for Segment Routing (SR) [RFC8402], which allows a node

SRv6.why: It specifies the new SRv6 End.Replicate endpoint behaviour with pseudocode, OAM and ICMPv6 handling, and an IANA codepoint.
SRv6.quote: this document specifies "Endpoint with replication and/or decapsulate" behavior (End.Replicate for short) to replicate a packet

SR-MPLS.why: It specifies how Replication-SIDs are processed with MPLS labels (POP, PUSH, NEXT), which is a substantial part of the document.
SR-MPLS.quote: When the active segment is a Replication-SID, the processing results in a POP [RFC8402] operation and the lookup of the associated RS.

rejected.why: The document is about replication inside an SR domain. It explicitly puts management of IP multicast groups and tree building out of scope.
MVPN and EVPN are only use cases for the Replication segment. The document does not specify or extend them.
EVPN BUM traffic is mentioned only as a use case, not as the subject.
The ICMPv6 restrictions and ping are a small part of the document. They only constrain error-message behaviour for the new SID.
PCE is referenced only as a possible control plane in another draft. This document does not specify it.

RFC9525.title: Service Identity in TLS
RFC9525.summary: RFC 9525 specifies how TLS/DTLS clients verify application service identity against PKIX certificates (DNS-ID, IP-ID, SRV-ID, URI-ID, wildcards) and how issuers and service providers represent and request them, obsoleting RFC 6125.

TLS.why: The document defines how a TLS/DTLS client matches a server's presented identity to its reference identity, which is guidance on TLS deployment and authentication. It applies to the whole TLS family, including QUIC.
TLS.quote: This document defines procedures for how clients perform this verification.

X.509.why: It specifies which X.509 certificate name forms to use and check: subjectAltName dNSName, iPAddress, SRVName and URI. It also bans the Common Name for identifying a service.
X.509.quote: A subjectAltName entry of type dNSName as defined in [PKIX].

rejected.why: The tag X.509 is the more specific child that fits. The document deals with PKIX name forms and not with PKI architecture.
DNS names are the identifiers being matched, but the document does not specify DNS. DNS resolution is explicitly out of scope.
It is mentioned only as another context where PKIX-based certificates appear.
A-label handling is a matching detail that relies on IDNA. The document does not specify IDNA.
URI-IDs are matched using the URI syntax, but the document is not about URIs.
QUIC is only an example protocol in the TLS family.

RFC9526.title: Simple Provisioning of Public Names for Residential Networks
RFC9526.summary: Experimental protocol by which a home network's Homenet Naming Authority uses a DNS-update-based Control Channel and a TLS-protected zone-transfer Synchronization Channel to outsource publication of its Public Homenet Zone (including DNSSEC signing, DS delegation and reverse zones) to a DNS Outsourcing Infrastructure.

DNS.why: The core of the document is DNS operations: hidden-primary/secondary zone transfer (AXFR/IXFR, NOTIFY), DNS UPDATE control messages, SOA/NS template building, and authoritative outsourcing.
DNS.quote: This document describes how an HNA can instruct a DOI to publish a Public Homenet Zone on its behalf.

home networking.why: It is a homenet architecture document defining the HNA, naming of home devices, renumbering and reverse zones for residential networks.
home networking.quote: Home network owners may have devices or services hosted on their home network that they wish to access from the Internet

DNSSEC.why: The HNA must sign the zone and a dedicated section covers building the chain of trust through DS publication, CDS/CDNSKEY and key handling.
DNSSEC.quote: The HNA MUST provide the hash of the KSK via the DS RRset so that the DOI can provide this value to the parent zone.
DNSSEC.section: 6.2. Building the DNSSEC Chain of Trust

DNS update.why: The Control Channel is defined as DNS UPDATE messages used as commands to set up delegation, synchronization address and deletion.
DNS update.quote: To provide the DS RRset to initialize the DNSSEC chain of trust, the HNA MAY send a DNS update [RFC3007] message.
DNS update.section: 6.5.2. Providing Information for the DNSSEC Chain of Trust

renumbering.why: A full section gives recommendations for make-before-break and break-before-make renumbering, TTL handling, and reachability analysis for published names.
renumbering.quote: During a renumbering of the home network, the HNA IP address may be changed and the Public Homenet Zone will be updated by the HNA with new AAAA records.

rejected.why: DNS over TLS is only the transport protecting the Control and Synchronization channels; the document defines nothing new about DoT itself.
Mutually authenticated TLS is used as the security mechanism, not specified or extended here.
DHCPv6 prefix delegation is mentioned as a provisioning means, with the actual options defined in RFC 9527, not here.
JSON is used only for an optional configuration blob in an appendix; it is not the subject.
IPv6 addressing is background; the document is about publishing names in DNS, not IPv6 itself.
Privacy is discussed in a considerations section, but the document does not specify encrypted DNS transport as a subject in its own right.

RFC9527.title: DHCPv6 Options for the Homenet Naming Authority
RFC9527.summary: Defines three DHCPv6 options (Registered Homenet Domain, Forward and Reverse Distribution Manager) and a Supported Transport registry so an ISP can provision a Homenet Naming Authority with the DNS outsourcing infrastructure for a home network.

DHCPv6.why: The document's core content is new DHCPv6 option definitions, with server, client and relay behaviour, and IANA option code assignments.
DHCPv6.quote: This document defines DHCPv6 options so that a Homenet Naming Authority (HNA) can automatically set the appropriate configuration

home networking.why: It supports the homenet naming architecture. It provisions the HNA on the CPE router for residential networks, as a companion to RFC 9526.
home networking.quote: outsource the authoritative naming service for the home network

rejected.why: DNS over TLS is only the transport named in the Supported Transport bit (DomTLS). The document defines nothing new about DoT itself.
DNS zone outsourcing is specified in RFC 9526. This document only carries FQDNs and transport bits in DHCPv6 options.
TLS is only the mandated authentication and transport mechanism for the control channel. It is not what the document is about.
The IANA registries (option codes and Supported Transport) are boilerplate for the option definitions. The document is not about IANA guidance.

RFC9528.title: Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman Over COSE (EDHOC)
RFC9528.summary: RFC 9528 specifies EDHOC, a compact authenticated Diffie-Hellman key exchange built on COSE and CBOR for constrained IoT, mainly to key OSCORE, with its messages, key derivation, cipher suites, error handling and IANA registries.

EDHOC.why: The document defines the EDHOC protocol itself: messages, methods, key derivation, cipher suites, errors and registries.
EDHOC.quote: This document specifies Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman Over COSE (EDHOC), a very compact and lightweight authenticated Diffie-Hellman key exchange with ephemeral keys.

OSCORE.why: The document's main use case is keying OSCORE. Appendix A specifies how the OSCORE context is derived and how connection identifiers map to OSCORE IDs.
OSCORE.quote: a main use case is to establish an Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments (OSCORE) security context.

rejected.why: CoAP is the default transport, described in Appendix A.2. EDHOC is not bound to a particular transport, so CoAP is a substrate here.
The id is not in the taxonomy as a tag. COSE is reused as the cryptographic and identification substrate, not specified or extended beyond registering two header parameters.
CBOR is the message encoding and substrate, not the subject of the document.
EDHOC is a key exchange, but the tag already chosen sits under the same area and is the more specific fit.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-like registration material, not the document's main subject.
The document uses ECDH and EdDSA primitives as building blocks and does not specify new elliptic curve cryptography.

gaps.name: Authenticated key exchange (AKE) protocols / LAKE
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for generic authenticated key exchange protocols. There is no tag for the IETF LAKE working group's lightweight AKE work other than the IoT/constrained-environment tags.

RFC9529.title: Traces of Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman Over COSE (EDHOC)
RFC9529.summary: Informational document giving annotated example traces (test vectors) of EDHOC authenticated key exchange sessions, including OSCORE key derivation, key update, and invalid-message examples.

EDHOC.why: The whole document is traces of EDHOC sessions for testing implementations.
EDHOC.quote: EDHOC [RFC9528] is a lightweight authenticated key exchange protocol designed for highly constrained settings.

rejected.why: OSCORE parameters are derived from EDHOC output, but OSCORE itself is not specified; it is a consumer.
CBOR is the encoding of messages, used as a substrate; though invalid-encoding examples touch it, the document is not about CBOR.
Only used as a building block in EDHOC; COSE is not in the taxonomy as a tag anyway.
One of the algorithms used in the example trace, not the subject.
Certificates appear as credentials in the example but X.509 is not the subject.
EDHOC is already tagged more specifically.

gaps.name: EDHOC (Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman Over COSE)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no EDHOC tag except under ACE/IoT, and I used an id not in the taxonomy; see note.

RFC9530.title: Digest Fields
RFC9530.summary: Defines the HTTP Content-Digest, Repr-Digest, Want-Content-Digest and Want-Repr-Digest fields for integrity digests of message content and representations, creates a hash algorithm registry, and obsoletes RFC 3230.

HTTP.why: The document specifies new HTTP header and trailer fields and their semantics with respect to content and representation data. It obsoletes the HTTP Digest and Want-Digest fields from RFC 3230.
HTTP.quote: This document defines HTTP fields that support integrity digests.

rejected.why: The fields give integrity checking only. The document says it does not define authentication, authorization, or privacy.
SHA-256, SHA-512 and SHA-1 are registered as algorithm keys. The document does not specify or analyse the SHA family.
md5 is listed as a deprecated registry entry only. The document says nothing new about MD5.
TLS is mentioned only as transport-level integrity and as a complementary mitigation. It is not a subject of the document.
JSON objects appear only as example payloads in the appendices.
The registry creation is part of the HTTP field definitions. The document is not about IANA registry guidance in general.
The document uses checksums and digests as HTTP fields. It does not specify the Internet checksum or its integrity checks.

RFC9531.title: Path Steering in Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) and Named Data Networking (NDN)
RFC9531.summary: Experimental IRTF specification of path discovery and path steering for CCNx and NDN, using a path label TLV in Interest, Data and InterestReturn messages to steer Interests along previously discovered paths.

ICN.why: The document extends CCNx and NDN, the Information-Centric Networking architectures, with a path label for path discovery and steering. It defines the packet encodings and forwarder behaviour.
ICN.quote: Path steering is a mechanism to discover paths to the producers of ICN Content Objects and steer subsequent Interest messages along a previously discovered path.

rejected.why: ICN Traceroute (RFC 9507) and ICN Ping are only cited as users of path steering. This document does not specify them.
Multipath congestion control is named as one use case. The document defines no congestion control.
The mechanism steers Interests through nexthops chosen by forwarding-plane lookup, but it is an ICN forwarding extension, not IP routing architecture. ICN is the better fit.
IPsec and MACsec are mentioned only as a cost comparison for path label encryption, so the document is not about them.

RFC9532.title: HTTP Proxy-Status Parameter for Next-Hop Aliases
RFC9532.summary: Defines the next-hop-aliases HTTP Proxy-Status parameter, which carries the chain of DNS CNAME aliases and canonical names an intermediary saw while resolving the next hop.

HTTP.why: The document extends the HTTP Proxy-Status response field with a new parameter and registers it in the HTTP Proxy-Status Parameters registry. Readers of HTTP extensions would want it.
HTTP.quote: This document defines the next-hop-aliases HTTP Proxy-Status Parameter.

DNS.why: A substantial part of the document specifies how DNS CNAME chains are reported, ordered and encoded (including escaping of special characters in DNS names), and the limits of resolver APIs for obtaining them.
DNS.quote: include all alias names and canonical names received in CNAME records [DNS] during the course of resolving the next hop's hostname using DNS

rejected.why: Cookie policies are mentioned only as one motivating use of the CNAME chain; the document is not about cookies.
CONNECT-UDP proxying is cited as a context where the parameter is useful, but the document does not specify or extend it.
The Security Considerations only note that the parameter carries no DNSSEC information; DNSSEC is not a subject of the document.
Percent-encoding from RFC 3986 is used as an encoding mechanism only; the document defines nothing new about URIs.
The document defines a response-field parameter and is not about conventions for building APIs on HTTP.

RFC9533.title: One-Way and Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol Extensions for Performance Measurement on a Link Aggregation Group
RFC9533.summary: Extends OWAMP and TWAMP with new control commands and micro-session ID fields so performance (delay, jitter, loss) can be measured on each member link of a Link Aggregation Group.

TWAMP.why: The document extends TWAMP control and test protocols with a new command and new Micro-session ID packet fields.
TWAMP.quote: a new command, Request-TW-Micro-Sessions (11), is defined in this document

OWAMP.why: The document extends OWAMP with a new control command and per-member-link test procedures.
OWAMP.quote: a new command, Request-OW-Micro-Sessions (5), is defined in this document

link aggregation.why: The measurement target is the member links of a LAG. The test packets carry LAG member link identifiers, so LAG readers would want this RFC.
link aggregation.quote: This document defines extensions to the One-Way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP) and the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP) to implement performance measurement on every member link of a Link Aggregation Group (LAG).

rejected.why: Its children OWAMP and TWAMP are tagged, so the parent is implied.
RFC 8668 is only cited as the source of member link attributes. This document does not specify IS-IS.
IEEE 802.1AX is referenced for the LAG definition only, and the document is not about Ethernet.
UDP is only the substrate for the test packets. The document mentions UDP ports but defines nothing new for UDP.

RFC9534.title: Simple Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol Extensions for Performance Measurement on a Link Aggregation Group
RFC9534.summary: Extends STAMP with a Micro-session ID TLV (type 11) and procedures so performance measurement can be run per member link of a Link Aggregation Group, validating the member link on each test packet.

STAMP.why: The document defines a new STAMP TLV and micro-session test procedures, so it extends STAMP itself.
STAMP.quote: This document extends Simple Two-way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP) to implement performance measurement on every member link of a Link Aggregation Group (LAG).

link aggregation.why: The measurement is scoped to LAG member links, with member link validation. Readers interested in link aggregation behaviour would want it.
link aggregation.quote: multiple sessions (one session for each member link) need to be established between the two endpoints that are connected by the LAG

rejected.why: OWAMP and TWAMP are mentioned only as comparisons of the metrics that can be measured. The document does not extend them.
The STAMP YANG data model is cited only for configuring the mapping, and the document says that augmentation is out of scope.
RFC 8668 is mentioned only as a source of Layer 2 bundle member link attributes for steering. The document does not touch IS-IS.
The tag is implied by STAMP, which sits under it, so it should not be listed separately.
UDP is only the transport for the test packets. The document says nothing new about it.

RFC9535.title: JSONPath: Query Expressions for JSON
RFC9535.summary: RFC 9535 specifies JSONPath, a string syntax and semantics for querying JSON values with selectors, segments, filter expressions, function extensions and Normalized Paths, and registers a media type and a function-extension registry.

JSONPath.why: The document defines the JSONPath query language in full: syntax, semantics, selectors, segments, functions and normalized paths.
JSONPath.quote: JSONPath defines a string syntax for selecting and extracting JSON (RFC 8259) values from within a given JSON value.

rejected.why: JSON is the data model the queries run against, not something the document specifies. The JSONPath tag sits under JSON, so it already covers this.
ABNF is only the notation used to write the grammar.
The media type registration for application/jsonpath is IANA boilerplate, a minor part of the document.
The Function Extensions subregistry is registry apparatus and not the main subject.
XPath is discussed only as historical inspiration in an appendix.
Unicode scalar values are used for string handling, but the document is not about Unicode usage.

RFC9536.title: Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) Reverse Search
RFC9536.summary: Defines an RDAP extension for reverse search, letting clients find domains, nameservers or entities by properties of related objects (chiefly entities), with help-response discovery, property-mapping, and IANA registries.

RDAP.why: The whole document extends RDAP query capabilities, defines new path segments, help and response members, and IANA registries for reverse search.
RDAP.quote: This document describes an RDAP extension that allows servers to provide a reverse search feature based on the relationship defined in RDAP

rejected.why: Reverse WHOIS is background motivation only; the document specifies an RDAP feature.
JSONPath is used as the mapping mechanism but the document is not about JSONPath itself.
Mentioned only as a use case for registrars doing bulk updates.
HTTP is the substrate; only status codes 501/400 are used.
Privacy considerations are a section but not the main subject; the document is about the search feature.
JSON is just the encoding of RDAP responses.

RFC9537.title: Redacted Fields in the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) Response
RFC9537.summary: Defines an RDAP extension that lets servers signal and describe redacted response fields via a "redacted" member, using four redaction methods and JSONPath expressions to locate the fields.

RDAP.why: The document is an extension to RDAP that defines the "redacted" response member and the "redacted" rdapConformance identifier. It specifies how RDAP servers redact and signal fields in lookup and search responses.
RDAP.quote: This document describes an RDAP extension for specifying methods of redaction of RDAP responses and explicitly identifying redacted RDAP response fields

rejected.why: JSONPath is the default expression language used to point at redacted fields. The document does not define or extend it, and it has its own section only for client and server usage considerations. It is a substrate here.
RDAP responses are JSON, but the document does not specify JSON or a JSON format in its own right. It only adds a member to an existing response format.
jCard and vCard shape how redaction works, because of positional arrays. The document does not specify or extend them.
The RDAP tag already sits under this topic, so adding the parent would be redundant.
Redaction is motivated by privacy and server policy. The document is not a privacy threat-model or considerations document, and its Security Considerations section is minimal.

RFC9538.title: Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI) Delegation Using the Automated Certificate Management Environment
RFC9538.summary: Defines a CDNI Metadata interface object (ACMEDelegationMethod) and FCI advertisement so an upstream CDN can delegate HTTPS certificates to a downstream CDN using the ACME delegation profile of RFC 9115, for both STAR and non-STAR delegation.

CDN.why: The document extends the CDNI Metadata and FCI interfaces with a new delegation metadata object and payload type, so it belongs on the CDN/CDNI page.
CDN.quote: This document defines metadata to support delegating the delivery of HTTPS content between two or more interconnected Content Delivery Networks (CDNs).

ACME.why: A substantial part of the document concerns ACME delegation, including STAR and non-STAR certificate issuance flows between uCDN, dCDN and CA, so ACME readers would want it.
ACME.quote: this section defines the AcmeDelegationMethod object, which describes metadata for using the ACME delegation interface [RFC9115].

rejected.why: X.509 certificates are what is delegated, but the document defines nothing about certificate profiles.
TLS appears only in the Security Considerations, as guidance to follow (RFC 9325).
HTTPS content delivery is the context, but the document specifies no HTTP semantics or extensions.
The metadata objects are JSON-encoded, but JSON is only the encoding substrate.
DNS redirection and CNAME mappings are mentioned only as context, and nothing new is defined about DNS.
The only IANA action is a payload type registration, which is boilerplate.

RFC9539.title: Unilateral Opportunistic Deployment of Encrypted Recursive-to-Authoritative DNS
RFC9539.summary: Experimental RFC giving guidance for recursive resolvers and authoritative servers to unilaterally and opportunistically use DoT and DoQ on the recursive-to-authoritative hop, with a probing policy and fallback to Do53, to defend against passive monitoring.

DoT.why: The document specifies how DoT is used opportunistically between recursive resolvers and authoritative servers, including port 853, ALPN "dot", padding and connection management.
DoT.quote: A recursive resolver SHOULD implement the client side of DoT.

DoQ.why: DoQ is the other encrypted transport the document profiles for recursive-to-authoritative use, with UDP port 853 and ALPN "doq".
DoQ.quote: A recursive resolver SHOULD implement the client side of DoQ.

DNS privacy.why: The document's purpose is opportunistic encrypted DNS transport that protects query privacy. It covers more than one encrypted transport, so the parent topic is appropriate alongside the DoT and DoQ tags.
DNS privacy.quote: defend DNS query privacy against a passive network monitor

rejected.why: The document explicitly declines to pursue DoH for this use because the endpoint URL path cannot be predicted opportunistically.
TLS is the substrate for DoT. Only SNI and early-data handling are discussed, and the document defines no new TLS mechanism.
The more specific DNS privacy, DoT and DoQ tags cover the subject, and the ancestor is implied.
DANE is mentioned only in Appendix B as a possible future authentication mechanism, not as something the document specifies.
QUIC is the substrate for DoQ and is not itself specified or extended here.
Happy Eyeballs is referenced only as an analogy for how connection attempts are raced.

RFC9540.title: Discovery of Oblivious Services via Service Binding Records
RFC9540.summary: Defines the "ohttp" SVCB/HTTPS SvcParamKey to advertise Oblivious HTTP support for a service, a well-known URI for locating the Oblivious Gateway Resource, and a method to fetch its key configuration, including use with DDR/DNR for DoH resolvers.

oblivious HTTP.why: The document extends Oblivious HTTP with discovery of gateways and fetching of key configuration, so OHTTP readers need it.
oblivious HTTP.quote: This document defines a parameter that can be included in Service Binding (SVCB) and HTTPS DNS resource records to denote that a service is accessible using Oblivious HTTP

DNS.why: It defines a new SvcParamKey for SVCB and HTTPS resource records, which is a new DNS RR parameter and its use with DNS server SVCB records.
DNS.quote: This document defines a way to use DNS resource records (RRs) to advertise that an HTTP service supports Oblivious HTTP.

DNS privacy.why: A substantial part covers discovering oblivious DoH resolvers via DDR/DNR, with privacy-preserving DNS resolution and dohpath targeting attacks.
DNS privacy.quote: the presence of the "ohttp" parameter means that the DNS server being described has a DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) service [DOH] that can be accessed using Oblivious HTTP.
DNS privacy.section: 4.2. Use in DNS Server SVCB RRs

rejected.why: DoH is the service being reached obliviously and is only referenced; the document does not specify DoH itself.
HTTP is the substrate; the document uses redirects and GET but defines nothing new about HTTP.
The well-known URI registration is minor; it does not concern URI syntax or schemes.
Discovery is covered, but the more specific DNS and OHTTP tags capture it; DNS-SD is a different mechanism.
Mentioned only as a downgrade mitigation in Security Considerations.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here.

review: model chose 'well-known URI', which is not a tag

notes: model chose 'well-known URI', which is not a tag

RFC9541.title: Flush Mechanism for Customer MAC Addresses Based on Service Instance Identifier (I-SID) in Provider Backbone Bridging EVPN (PBB-EVPN)
RFC9541.summary: Extends PBB-EVPN C-MAC flush with a B-MAC/I-SID MAC/IP Advertisement route (I-SID in Ethernet Tag, MAC Mobility sequence number increment) so PEs flush customer MACs per I-SID and B-MAC when null-ES attachment circuits fail.

EVPN.why: The document extends PBB-EVPN C-MAC flush procedures using EVPN MAC/IP Advertisement routes and the MAC Mobility extended community.
EVPN.quote: PBB-EVPN defines a flush mechanism for Customer MACs (C-MACs) called "C-MAC flush"

rejected.why: BGP is the carrier of EVPN routes; no new attributes or BGP behaviour are defined.
Ethernet/G.8032 appears only as access context, not as subject matter.
PWs are only an example attachment circuit in the scenario.
MPLS is the underlying network, not what the document addresses.
EVPN is the more specific tag and is already chosen; L2VPN is its parent, so listing it would be redundant.
VPLS (RFC 4762) is only cited as an example of CE-managed redundancy.

gaps.name: PBB-EVPN / C-MAC flush
gaps.why: The document is specifically about PBB-EVPN, but the taxonomy has no PBB-EVPN tag. EVPN is the closest fit, and that tag is not in the taxonomy as given, so the EVPN tag above may be invalid.

RFC9542.title: IANA Considerations and IETF Protocol and Documentation Usage for IEEE 802 Parameters
RFC9542.summary: BCP that obsoletes RFC 7042, setting IANA assignment rules and expert review/IESG ratification procedures for MAC addresses, protocol numbers and other parameters under the IANA OUI, defining documentation values, CBOR tags for MAC addresses/OUIs, and EtherType request procedures.

Ethernet.why: The document covers EUI-48/EUI-64 MAC identifiers, EtherTypes, LSAPs/SNAP and IANA OUI assignments for Ethernet parameters.
Ethernet.quote: Some IETF protocols use Ethernet or other communication frame formats and parameters related to IEEE 802

IANA.why: Defines assignment policies, Expert Review and IESG Ratification procedures, and templates for IANA OUI-based registries.
IANA.quote: This document specifies IANA considerations for the assignment of code points under that IANA OUI, including MAC addresses and protocol identifiers

CBOR.why: Specifies CBOR tags 48 and 1048 for MAC addresses and OUIs/CIDs, a new CBOR-related definition.
CBOR.quote: IANA has assigned 48 as the CBOR tag to indicate a MAC address.

rejected.why: Modified EUI-64 interface identifiers are discussed, but only as a deprecated use of MAC identifiers.
The EUI48/EUI64 RRTYPEs are only referenced, defined in RFC 7043.
VRRP MAC blocks are listed as existing assignments only.
The LLDP TLV for MUD is mentioned only as an example of an OUI-based parameter.
This covers IEEE MAC addressing rather than IP address architecture.
The Ethernet tag is more specific and already applies.

gaps.name: IEEE 802 parameters / OUI and MAC address assignment
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MAC address identifiers, OUIs, EtherTypes, or LLDP, so the best fit is the Ethernet tag.

RFC9543.title: A Framework for Network Slices in Networks Built from IETF Technologies
RFC9543.summary: RFC 9543 defines the "IETF Network Slice" concept and a framework for requesting, controlling, and realizing network slices (SDPs, connectivity constructs, SLOs/SLEs, the Network Slice Controller, NRPs, isolation) over networks built from IETF technologies.

traffic engineering.why: The framework partitions resources in a shared TE underlay (Network Resource Partitions, filtered topologies, ACTN virtual networks) to deliver guaranteed performance. Traffic engineering is the closest fitting subject area.
traffic engineering.quote: Realization of IETF Network Slices is a mapping of the definition of the IETF Network Slice to the underlying infrastructure

VPN.why: Network slices are presented as an evolution of VPN services, with a section on enhanced VPNs and a L3VPN example. The VPN readership would want this document.
VPN.quote: traffic separation between different IETF Network Slices may be achieved using VPN technologies, such as L3VPN, L2VPN, EVPN, etc.
VPN.section: 8.2. Isolation in IETF Network Slice Realization

SFC.why: A dedicated section and an appendix example cover how ancillary CEs and service functions map onto SFC classification and forwarding.
SFC.quote: Service Function Chaining (SFC) [RFC7665] techniques can be used by a provider to instantiate such an IETF Network Slice Service.
SFC.section: 7.6. Network Slicing and Service Function Chaining (SFC)

rejected.why: The controller and orchestrator architecture resembles SDN, but the document never frames itself as SDN.
YANG is mentioned only as a possible modelling language and for future slice-service models. The document does not define any.
NETCONF, RESTCONF and PCEP appear only in a list of example interface mechanisms.
SLIs and SLOs are defined as service terms, but the document does not specify measurement methods or metrics.
PCEP is cited only as an example encoding for the slice interface.
The controller and management architecture is a substantial part, but the traffic engineering tag captures the main subject better. The management interfaces are left abstract.

gaps.name: Network slicing
gaps.why: The document is about network slicing and the IETF Network Slice, and the taxonomy has no tag for it. Traffic engineering and VPN fit only partially.

RFC9544.title: Precision Availability Metrics (PAMs) for Services Governed by Service Level Objectives (SLOs)
RFC9544.summary: Defines Precision Availability Metrics (violated/severely violated interval and packet counts, derived ratios and MTBF-like metrics) for assessing whether network services meet their SLOs, e.g., for RFC 9543 Network Slice Services.

performance measurement.why: The document defines new performance metrics (VI, SVI, VFI, VPC, SVPC, VIR, SVIR) for monitoring compliance with SLOs. This is performance measurement metrics work, with no specific measurement protocol.
performance measurement.quote: This specification introduces a new set of metrics, Precision Availability Metrics (PAMs), aimed at capturing service levels for a flow

rejected.why: A YANG data model for PAMs is only listed as future work in Section 6, not specified here.
IPFIX Information Elements for PAMs are only mentioned as future work, and IPFIX is cited only as existing flow-record state of the art.
The Interfaces Group MIB (RFC 2863) is cited only as existing interface metrics that are agnostic of service levels.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in the future-work list for a YANG model.
The document defines metrics, not OAM mechanisms, and explicitly leaves measurement methods out of scope.
RFC 3198 is cited only for the SLA and SLO definitions; the document does not address policy management models.

gaps.name: Service Level Objectives / network slice service assurance
gaps.why: The document is about SLO compliance and service availability for RFC 9543 Network Slice Services. The taxonomy has no tag for SLOs, service assurance or network slicing.

RFC9545.title: Path Segment Identifier in MPLS-Based Segment Routing Networks
RFC9545.summary: Defines the Path Segment Identifier (PSID), a local label from the egress node's SRLB placed after the last label of an SR-MPLS label stack so the egress can identify the SR path, with use cases for performance measurement, bidirectional paths, 1+1 protection and nesting.

SR-MPLS.why: The document defines a new segment type and label stack handling for SR over the MPLS data plane, so it belongs under SR-MPLS.
SR-MPLS.quote: A Path Segment Identifier (PSID) is a single label that is assigned from the Segment Routing Local Block (SRLB) of the egress node of an SR path.

performance measurement.why: Performance measurement is a main motivating use case, and a section covers passive, active and hybrid measurement with the PSID.
performance measurement.quote: A PSID can be used by the measuring points (e.g., the ingress and egress nodes of the SR path or a centralized controller) to correlate the packet counts and timestamps

rejected.why: The more specific SR-MPLS child fits, because the PSID is defined only for the MPLS data plane.
MPLS is the substrate for SR-MPLS. The document is not about MPLS itself.
Section 2.1 only gives ECMP considerations. It is a caveat, not a subject of the document.
PCEP is mentioned only for MSD and in the references, and the signalling of the PSID is out of scope.
OAM is touched on through GAL and IOAM. It is not a main subject.

RFC9546.title: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) for Deterministic Networking (DetNet) with the MPLS Data Plane
RFC9546.summary: Defines the DetNet Associated Channel Header (d-ACH) and usage principles for active OAM test packets in DetNet networks with an MPLS data plane, plus OAM interworking with TSN and DetNet IP.

DetNet.why: The whole document specifies OAM encapsulation for DetNet, including PREOF interaction and interworking with TSN and DetNet IP.
DetNet.quote: This document defines format and usage principles of the Deterministic Networking (DetNet) service Associated Channel over a DetNet network with the MPLS data plane.

OAM.why: The document is about active OAM for failure detection and performance measurement, and it describes OAM interworking models.
OAM.quote: The DetNet service Associated Channel can be used to carry test packets of active Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) protocols

MPLS.why: The d-ACH is carried with S-Label and F-Label in the MPLS data plane, building on the PW associated channel header and G-ACh channel types.
