MPLS.quote: MPLS encapsulation [RFC8964] of a DetNet active OAM packet is shown in Figure 2.

rejected.why: BFD is only cited as an OAM protocol that can be used in interworking. The document defines nothing new for it.
The PW control word and ACH are reused, but the document does not specify pseudowire emulation.
STAMP is only mentioned as usable for performance measurement over DetNet IP.
The d-ACH flags registry is boilerplate-level IANA content and does not make the document about IANA guidance.
Ethernet CFM and TSN interworking is discussed, but only as one of the interworking models. It is not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN)
gaps.why: The document covers OAM interworking with IEEE 802.1 TSN, and the taxonomy has no TSN tag.

RFC9547.title: Report from the IAB Workshop on Environmental Impact of Internet Applications and Systems, 2022
RFC9547.summary: IAB workshop report summarising discussions on the environmental impacts of the Internet and its applications, measurement and metrics, possible protocol improvements, and next steps for the IETF.

sustainability.why: The whole report concerns environmental impact, energy use and carbon footprint of Internet systems, and the IAB e-impact program. This is the sustainability subject.
sustainability.quote: The IAB ran an online workshop in December 2022 to explore and understand the environmental impacts of the Internet.

workshop reports.why: It is an IAB workshop report covering sessions, position papers and participants.
workshop reports.quote: Note that this document is a report on the proceedings of the workshop.

rejected.why: Multicast energy savings were discussed briefly in one session, but the report is not about multicast.
Time-Variant Routing is mentioned only as an example of ongoing IETF work.
CBOR is cited as an example of an efficient binary format, not specified or analysed in the report.
HTTP/2 appears only as an example of a protocol that uses a binary encoding.
Telemetry and metrics are discussed as a possible area of future work, but not substantively enough to tag.
The report suggests a role for the IETF, but its subject is environmental impact, not IETF procedure.

RFC9548.title: Generating Transport Key Containers (PFX) Using the GOST Algorithms
RFC9548.summary: Specifies how to use PKCS #12 (RFC 7292) PFX containers to store and transport GOST R 34.10-2012 private keys and certificates, with password-based encryption (PBES2/PBKDF2) and HMAC GOST R 34.11-2012 integrity.

GOST.why: The document defines how GOST R 34.10-2012 keys and GOST R 34.11-2012 HMAC are used in PFX containers, so it belongs on the GOST page.
GOST.quote: This document specifies how to use "PKCS #12: Personal Information Exchange Syntax v1.1" (RFC 7292) to transport key containers (PFX) for storing keys and certificates in conjunction with the Russian national standard GOST algorithms.

key management.why: It covers private key storage and transport, including key masking and password-protected key containers. No more specific tag fits, since PKCS #12 is not a tag.
key management.quote: PKCS #12 v1.1 describes a syntax for transfer of personal information such as private keys, certificates, and various secrets.

rejected.why: The PBKDF2 key derivation is only referenced from RFC 9337. This document does not define it.
The document uses ContentInfo and EncryptedData structures from CMS as a substrate. It does not extend CMS.
Certificates are only carried in a CertBag. The document does not profile them.
ASN.1 is the encoding notation. It is not the subject of the document.
HMAC with GOST R 34.11-2012 is used for integrity, but it is covered by the GOST tag and RFC 7836.
The container carries certificates, but the document does not address PKI itself.

gaps.name: PKCS #12 / PFX personal information exchange syntax
gaps.why: The document is mainly about the PKCS #12 key container format. The taxonomy has no tag for PKCS #12 or key container formats.

RFC9549.title: Internationalization Updates to RFC 5280
RFC9549.summary: RFC 9549 updates RFC 5280 (obsoleting RFC 8399) to align X.509 certificate handling of internationalized domain names with IDNA2008 and to support internationalized email addresses, including name constraints, by carrying and processing all IDNs as A-labels.

X.509.why: The document is a set of updates to the RFC 5280 X.509 certificate and CRL profile, changing name constraints and GeneralName processing rules.
X.509.quote: The updates to RFC 5280 described in this document provide alignment with the 2008 specification for Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs)

IDN.why: Core content is aligning certificate name handling with IDNA2008, U-label/A-label conversion and Punycode.
IDN.quote: IDNs are carried in certificates in ACE-encoded form.  That is, all U-labels within an IDN are converted to A-labels.

EAI.why: A substantial part covers internationalized email addresses (SmtpUTF8Mailbox) in certificates and their matching and name constraints.
EAI.quote: If the local-part of the internationalized email address cannot be represented in ASCII, then the internationalized email address is placed in the otherName choice of GeneralName

rejected.why: X.509 is the more specific child tag and fits the certificate profile updates; the parent is implied.
Email addresses appear only as names in certificates; EAI is the better fit, and no mail protocol is specified.
Unicode is mentioned for characters and categories, but the document is about IDNA name handling rather than Unicode usage in general.
DNS names are carried in dNSName fields, but DNS protocol and operation are not the subject.
IA5String and GeneralName are used, but no ASN.1 modules or encoding rules are defined.

RFC9550.title: Deterministic Networking (DetNet): Packet Ordering Function
RFC9550.summary: Informational DetNet document specifying Packet Ordering Function (POF) algorithms (basic and advanced) that restore packet order after replication and elimination within a flow's latency bound.

DetNet.why: The whole document specifies a DetNet forwarding function (POF) as part of PREOF, so it belongs on the DetNet page.
DetNet.quote: The Packet Ordering Function (POF) algorithms described in this document enable restoration of the correct packet order when the replication and elimination functions are used in DetNet networks.

rejected.why: TCP is mentioned only as an example of where out-of-order delivery is handled at endpoints. The document is not about it.
IEEE 802.1CB is cited as a possible PEF/PRF implementation, but the document specifies no Ethernet mechanisms.
A YANG model is mentioned only in passing as the IEEE 802.1CB model. The document defines none.
The document concerns the DetNet per-flow forwarding sub-layer. The more specific DetNet tag already covers it.

RFC9551.title: Framework of Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) for Deterministic Networking (DetNet)
RFC9551.summary: Informational framework document listing OAM functional requirements (continuity check, connectivity verification, route tracing, fault localization, performance metrics) for DetNet forwarding and service sub-layers.

DetNet.why: The whole document defines OAM requirements for DetNet domains, covering forwarding and service sub-layers and PREOF.
DetNet.quote: This document's primary purpose is to detail the specific requirements of the OAM features recommended to maintain a deterministic/reliable network.

OAM.why: The document is an OAM framework: continuity check, connectivity verification, route tracing, fault localization, hybrid OAM, and metrics collection.
OAM.quote: DetNet OAM should provide a toolset for fault detection, localization, and performance measurement.

rejected.why: Performance metrics and hybrid measurement are discussed, but as part of the OAM requirements. The document does not define measurement methods itself.
IOAM and on-path telemetry are mentioned as ways to collect information, but they are only referenced, not specified.
Route tracing is one OAM function listed as a requirement. The document does not specify a traceroute tool.
SNMP is mentioned only as an example of a polling mechanism.
YANG-Push is cited only as an example subscription mechanism.
ECMP is mentioned only to say DetNet does not use it and that it is out of scope.

gaps.name: DetNet (Deterministic Networking)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists DetNet under routing, but the tag id I used (DetNet) is not in the list shown. Check the exact id against the taxonomy before accepting this output.

RFC9552.title: Distribution of Link-State and Traffic Engineering Information Using BGP
RFC9552.summary: RFC 9552 specifies BGP-LS, a BGP NLRI encoding and path attribute for distributing IGP link-state and traffic engineering information to external consumers such as PCEs and ALTO servers, obsoleting RFC 7752 and RFC 9029.

BGP.why: The document defines a new BGP address family (AFI 16388, SAFI 71/72), NLRI types, and a BGP path attribute, plus BGP error handling and operational guidance.
BGP.quote: This document describes a mechanism by which link-state and TE information can be collected from networks and shared with external components using the BGP routing protocol

ALTO.why: ALTO server topology feed is one of two named motivating use cases with its own section.
ALTO.quote: The mechanism defined in this document provides a single interface through which an ALTO server can retrieve all the necessary prefixes and network topology data

PCE.why: PCE obtaining TED information for MPLS-TE path computation is a primary motivating use case.
PCE.quote: The mechanism in this document allows the necessary TED information to be collected from the IGP within the network, filtered according to configurable policy, and distributed to the PCE

rejected.why: OSPF is the source of the information carried, not specified or extended here.
IS-IS is an IGP source of link-state data, only referenced for encodings.
TE data is carried, but the PCE tag covers the TE use case and the document is not about TE itself.
Unrelated to BGP Monitoring Protocol; BGP-LS is a distinct address family.
IANA registries are created, but that is boilerplate for the protocol specification.
Route reflectors are mentioned as propagators but the document does not specify route reflection.

gaps.name: BGP-LS (BGP Link-State)
gaps.why: The document's central subject is BGP-LS; the taxonomy has no BGP-LS tag (BGP-SPF mentions BGP-LS only as a basis), so BGP is the closest fit.

RFC9553.title: JSContact: A JSON Representation of Contact Data
RFC9553.summary: Defines JSContact, a JSON data model and representation for contact cards (an alternative to vCard), including its types, properties, versioning, extension rules and IANA registries.

JSContact.quote: This specification defines a data model and JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) representation of contact card information that can be used for data storage and exchange

RFC9554.title: vCard Format Extensions for JSContact
RFC9554.summary: RFC 9554 defines new vCard properties (CREATED, GRAMGENDER, LANGUAGE, PRONOUNS, SOCIALPROFILE), parameters and values, and extends ADR and N, to align vCard with JSContact; it updates RFC 6350.

vCard.why: The document extends the vCard format with new properties, parameters, values and updated ADR and N definitions, updating RFC 6350.
vCard.quote: This document defines a set of new properties for vCard and extends the use of existing ones.

JSContact.why: The extensions exist to enable lossless conversion between vCard and JSContact, so JSContact readers would want this RFC.
JSContact.quote: Their primary purpose is to align the same set of features between the JSContact and vCard formats

rejected.why: Address/name components, PHONETIC and SCRIPT support international contact data, but the document is about vCard, not text internationalization in protocols; vCard/JSContact tags fit better.
It uses language tags for the LANGUAGE property and parameters, but only as a dependency, not defining anything about them.
ABNF is only the notation used for definitions.
JSON is not used in this document; JSContact is the JSON side and is only referenced.
URI values are used in AUTHOR and SOCIALPROFILE but the document does not address URIs.
IANA registry updates are boilerplate registrations for the vCard registries.

RFC9555.title: JSContact: Converting from and to vCard
RFC9555.summary: Defines rules for converting contact data between JSContact and vCard (and jCard), plus new JSContact properties (vCardProps, vCardParams, vCardName) and vCard property/parameters (JSPROP, JSCOMPS, JSPTR) to round-trip unknown elements.

JSContact.why: The document specifies conversion rules for every JSContact element and defines new JSContact properties.
JSContact.quote: This document defines how to convert contact information between the JSContact and vCard data formats.

vCard.why: It maps every vCard property and parameter to JSContact, updates RFC 6350, and defines new vCard property JSPROP and parameters JSCOMPS and JSPTR.
vCard.quote: This document defines standard rules to convert contact data between JSContact and vCard (and consequently jCard).

rejected.why: JSON is the encoding substrate for JSContact; the document is about contact data conversion, not JSON itself.
The IANA section only registers new entries; it is boilerplate, not the subject.
Language tags appear only in the LANGUAGE parameter conversion rules; the document is not about them.
Directory objects convert to and from SOURCE and ORG-DIRECTORY, but the document does not address directory access or synchronization.

gaps.name: JSContact
gaps.why: The document is about JSContact and vCard, and the taxonomy has vCard, JSContact and CardDAV tags under 'vCard' only for vCard and JSContact as children; I used the ids from the taxonomy, but verify 'JSContact' and 'vCard' exist as written. The taxonomy lists 'vCard' and 'JSContact' ids as 'vCard' and 'JSContact'.

RFC9556.title: Internet of Things (IoT) Edge Challenges and Functions
RFC9556.summary: An IRTF T2TRG informational document describing why IoT drives edge computing (time sensitivity, connectivity cost, intermittent services, privacy/security), with use cases, a general model and functional components of IoT edge computing.

IoT.why: The whole document is about IoT edge computing architecture, challenges, and functional components, which fits the IoT topic in general (not a specific IoT protocol).
IoT.quote: This document outlines the requirements of the emerging IoT edge and its challenges.

rejected.why: CoAP is only mentioned as an example protocol for discovery and gateway communication; the document does not specify or extend it.
Section 4.3 discusses edge OAM components, but only as one part of the general model; the document is not primarily about OAM mechanisms.
Deterministic networking is only cited for bounded latency requirements via RFC 8578; not the subject.
ICN is mentioned briefly as an experimental distributed storage option; not a substantial part.
SDN is mentioned only in passing as a centralized management option.
Privacy is a motivating challenge (Section 3.4) but the document does not address protocol privacy considerations in its own right.

gaps.name: edge computing / fog computing
gaps.why: The document is chiefly about edge computing (in-network computation, edge storage, federation, multi-tenancy), but the taxonomy has no edge/cloud computing tag; only the IoT topic fits.

RFC9557.title: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps with Additional Information
RFC9557.summary: Defines IXDTF, an extension to RFC 3339 timestamps adding optional suffix tags (time zone name, calendar, etc.) with a registry of suffix keys, and updates RFC 3339's interpretation of the Z offset.

date-time formats.why: The whole document defines the Internet Extended Date/Time Format and updates RFC 3339's timestamp semantics, which is exactly the date-time formats subject.
date-time formats.quote: This document defines an extension to the timestamp format defined in [RFC3339] for representing additional information, including a time zone.

rejected.why: That tag covers time zone data distribution (tzdata); this document only references IANA time zone names in a timestamp suffix.
ABNF is only the notation used to specify the syntax, not the subject.
The registry creation is boilerplate-level IANA considerations for a new registry, not the main subject.
Calendaring is mentioned as a use case, but the document does not specify calendar data formats.

RFC9558.title: Use of GOST 2012 Signature Algorithms in DNSKEY and RRSIG Resource Records for DNSSEC
RFC9558.summary: Independent-stream RFC defining how GOST R 34.10-2012 signatures and GOST R 34.11-2012 digests are used in DNSKEY, RRSIG and DS records for DNSSEC, with algorithm number 23 and DS digest type 5.

DNSSEC.why: The document extends DNSSEC with a new signature and digest algorithm, specifying DNSKEY, RRSIG and DS record formats and examples.
DNSSEC.quote: describes how to produce digital signatures and hash functions using the GOST R 34.10-2012 and GOST R 34.11-2012 algorithms for DNSKEY, RRSIG, and DS resource records

GOST.why: The document is about applying the Russian GOST signature and hash algorithms in an IETF protocol, which is what the GOST tag covers.
GOST.quote: GOST R 34.10-2012 and GOST R 34.11-2012 are Russian national standards.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific tag and its parent DNS is implied.
The SubjectPublicKeyInfo encoding from RFC 9215 is used only as a convenience for reading keys with existing libraries, so X.509 is not a subject of the document.
The document uses GOST elliptic-curve keys but does not define elliptic-curve cryptography. GOST is the better-fitting tag.
The ASN.1 structure appears only as a short helper for importing keys, and the document is not about ASN.1.
The IANA registry entries are boilerplate and not the main subject.

RFC9559.title: Matroska Media Container Format Specification
RFC9559.summary: RFC 9559 specifies the Matroska audiovisual container format, an EBML document type, defining its elements, block structure, timestamps, chapters, tags, attachments, linking and streaming, and updates RFC 8794 to allow EBML ID 0x80.

Matroska.why: The document is the Matroska specification itself.
Matroska.quote: This document defines the Matroska audiovisual data container structure, including definitions of its structural elements, terminology, vocabulary, and application.

rejected.why: EBML is described as a binary derivative of XML; XML is used only to illustrate trees, not specified.
Matroska is explicitly a container, not a codec; parent tag implied by Matroska anyway.
IANA section registers media types and registries, which is boilerplate-like and not the main subject.
Encryption fields reference AES but the document explicitly provides no interoperable encryption solution.
Mentioned only to say Matroska is not meant for RTP/RTSP livestreaming.
Only a transport over which Matroska files may be streamed.

gaps.name: EBML (Extensible Binary Meta Language)
gaps.why: Matroska is an EBML document type and this RFC updates RFC 8794; the taxonomy has no EBML tag.

gaps.name: Matroska
gaps.why: Matroska is listed as a child of codecs in the taxonomy, but the id I used is not shown; the tag list above uses 'Matroska' because the taxonomy shows 'Matroska [tech]' under codecs as 'Matroska media container'.

RFC9560.title: Federated Authentication for the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) Using OpenID Connect
RFC9560.summary: Defines an RDAP extension ("farv1") for federated authentication using OpenID Connect, with session- and token-oriented client flows, new RDAP claims (rdap_allowed_purposes, rdap_dnt_allowed), query parameters, and a purpose registry.

RDAP.why: The document extends RDAP with new data structures, path segments, query parameters and conformance value, and its main body specifies how RDAP clients and servers behave.
RDAP.quote: This document describes a federated authentication system for RDAP based on OpenID Connect.

OAuth.why: The document profiles OpenID Connect and OAuth 2.0 flows (authorization code, device grant, bearer tokens, token exchange, introspection) for RDAP. No OpenID Connect tag exists, so OAuth is the closest fit.
OAuth.quote: OpenID Connect is built on top of the authorization framework provided by the OAuth 2.0 protocol [RFC6749].

federated authentication.why: The central subject is a federated single sign-on system for RDAP, with servers outsourcing authentication to identity providers.
federated authentication.quote: Federated authentication mechanisms allow clients to use one credential to access multiple RDAP servers and reduce client credential management complexity.

JWT.why: The document defines two new JWT claims and registers them in the JWT Claims registry. It also validates JWT access tokens.
JWT.quote: The "rdap_allowed_purposes" claim is represented as an array of case-sensitive StringOrURI values as specified in Section 2 of [RFC7519].

rejected.why: Basic and bearer schemes are used only as mechanisms to carry the end-user identifier and access tokens, not specified or extended.
Cookies maintain session state, but the document only relies on them and defines nothing new about them.
RDAP responses are JSON, but this is only an encoding substrate.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a requirement to follow RFC 9325.
HTTP is the substrate. The document adds RDAP-level path segments and parameters rather than anything about HTTP itself.
RDAP is the registration data protocol and is already tagged under it. The document covers authentication rather than registry operations in general.

gaps.name: OpenID Connect
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no OpenID Connect tag, and this document is a profile of OIDC for RDAP. OAuth is the nearest tag.

RFC9561.title: Using the Parallel NFS (pNFS) SCSI Layout to Access Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) Storage Devices
RFC9561.summary: Defines how NVMe namespaces are used as storage devices under the pNFS SCSI layout, mapping SCSI volume identification, persistent-reservation fencing, and write-cache flushing to NVMe constructs.

NFS.why: The document extends the pNFS SCSI layout of NFSv4.1 to NVMe devices, specifying client fencing, volume identification and LAYOUTCOMMIT flushing behaviour. NFS is the subject, and no child tag fits.
NFS.quote: NFSv4.1 [RFC8881] includes a pNFS feature that allows reads and writes to be performed by means other than directing read and write operations to the server.

rejected.why: It is mentioned only as a SCSI-based protocol that NVMe is replacing. The document does not specify or operate iSCSI.
TLS is only recommended in Security Considerations for protecting NVMe over TCP traffic. The document defines nothing new about it.
XDR is cited only for the opaque<> length encoding of the designator field. That is an encoding detail and not the subject.
This is the parent topic of NFS, so it is implied. NFS is the more specific tag.
NVMe over TCP is only a transport that the NVMe devices may use. The document is independent of the transport.

gaps.name: NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express)
gaps.why: The document centres on mapping NVMe namespaces and reservations. The taxonomy has no tag for NVMe or for block storage protocols other than iSCSI, Fibre Channel and RDMA.

gaps.name: pNFS SCSI layout
gaps.why: This is a specific NFS layout type. It has no dedicated tag under NFS, so it is covered by the generic NFS tag.

RFC9562.title: Universally Unique IDentifiers (UUIDs)
RFC9562.summary: RFC 9562 defines the UUID format, versions 1-8 (including new time-ordered v6, v7 and custom v8), Nil/Max UUIDs, generation best practices, and the UUID URN namespace and IANA registries, obsoleting RFC 4122.

UUID.why: The whole document specifies UUID layouts, versions, variants, and generation guidance, replacing RFC 4122.
UUID.quote: This specification defines UUIDs (Universally Unique IDentifiers) -- also known as GUIDs (Globally Unique IDentifiers) -- and a Uniform Resource Name namespace for UUIDs.

rejected.why: The UUID URN namespace is defined, but it is a minor part of the document. The main body is about UUID formats and generation, and the UUID tag covers it.
MD5 is only the hash used by UUIDv3, and the document does not specify or analyse it.
SHA-1 and SHA-256 are only the hash functions used for name-based UUIDs. The document does not define them.
Section 6.9 gives brief CSPRNG advice for generating UUIDs. That is supporting guidance, not the subject of the document.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-like apparatus for UUID subtypes and namespace IDs. The document is not about IANA process.
DNS names are only an example namespace for name-based UUIDs.

RFC9563.title: SM2 Digital Signature Algorithm for DNSSEC
RFC9563.summary: Independent Submission specifying use of the SM2 signature algorithm (algorithm 17) and SM3 digest (DS digest type 6) in DNSSEC DNSKEY, RRSIG and DS records, with NSEC3 guidance and IANA registrations.

DNSSEC.why: The document defines new DNSSEC signing algorithm and DS digest type, including DNSKEY/RRSIG formats, NSEC3 support and IANA registrations.
DNSSEC.quote: This document specifies the use of the SM2 digital signature algorithm and SM3 hash algorithm for DNS Security (DNSSEC).

elliptic curve.why: A substantial part specifies the SM2 curve parameters and key/signature encodings, of interest to elliptic-curve cryptography readers.
elliptic curve.quote: SM2 uses elliptic curves over 256-bit prime fields with SM3 hash algorithm.

rejected.why: SM2 is a different signature algorithm, not ECDSA.
SM3 is the hash used; SHA-256 is referenced only as the model for DS digest construction.
DNSSEC is the more specific tag and already covers this.

gaps.name: SM2/SM3 Chinese national cryptographic algorithms
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for SM2/SM3 (ShangMi) algorithms, which would be the natural subject page for this document.

RFC9564.title: Faster Than Light Speed Protocol (FLIP)
RFC9564.summary: An April 1st joke RFC defining FLIP, a shim protocol that uses LLMs to predict future packets for faster-than-light delivery, with a header, model/data commands, and SHA-256 model-hash versioning.

humor.why: Published 1 April 2024 as a parody protocol claiming faster-than-light packet delivery by predicting future packets; it belongs in the humorous RFCs.
humor.quote: The recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) such as large language models enable the design of the Faster than LIght speed Protocol (FLIP) for Internet.

rejected.why: FLIP is described as a shim over IP, transport or Layer 2, but it is a joke protocol and the document does not seriously address transport-layer services.
The document mentions SHA-256 for versioning and post-quantum-AI cryptography only in passing as part of the joke.
SHA-256 is only used as a model version hash. The document is not about the SHA family.
Deep-space IP networking is cited as motivation only; the document does not specify delay-tolerant networking.
The IANA section is boilerplate-like registrations of a protocol number and port, not the subject of the document.
The document mentions a MIME header for the model but does not define a media type registration.

RFC9565.title: An Update to the tcpControlBits IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Information Element
RFC9565.summary: Updates the IPFIX tcpControlBits Information Element definition (obsoleting RFC 7125) to drop stale flag information and defer to the IANA TCP Header Flags registry.

IPFIX.why: The document revises an IPFIX Information Element (tcpControlBits) and updates the IPFIX IE registry entry, so it belongs under IPFIX.
IPFIX.quote: This document removes stale information from the IANA "IPFIX Information Elements" registry

rejected.why: TCP control bits are only the data being reported by the IPFIX element. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
The document updates one registry entry, but IANA registries are not its subject. That falls under boilerplate and mechanics.
ECN flag bits (CWR) are mentioned only as flag examples and as background for the deprecated NS bit.

RFC9566.title: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) Packet Replication, Elimination, and Ordering Functions (PREOF) via MPLS over UDP/IP
RFC9566.summary: Specifies how the DetNet IP data plane supports PREOF (packet replication, elimination, ordering) by reusing the DetNet MPLS d-CW and S-Label encapsulated over UDP/IP with no F-Labels.

DetNet.why: The whole document defines a DetNet IP data plane encapsulation and processing for PREOF service protection, so it belongs on the DetNet page.
DetNet.quote: This document describes how the DetNet IP data plane can support the Packet Replication, Elimination, and Ordering Functions (PREOF)

rejected.why: Only the DetNet MPLS control word and S-Label fields are reused. The MPLS forwarding plane is explicitly not required.
UDP is the tunnel substrate. The document defines no new UDP behaviour.
The encapsulation reuses the DetNet pseudowire format from RFC 8964, but the document is not about pseudowire emulation.
The DetNet YANG model is mentioned only as a reference for configuration parameters.
OAM is mentioned only in a closing note, and the document does not address it in its own right.

RFC9567.title: DNS Error Reporting
RFC9567.summary: Defines DNS Error Reporting: an EDNS0 Report-Channel option by which authoritative servers advertise an agent domain, and a QNAME-encoded TXT report query that validating resolvers send to report extended DNS errors.

EDNS.why: The document defines a new EDNS0 option (Report-Channel, code 18) with its wire format and rules for inclusion, which is central to the mechanism.
EDNS.quote: An authoritative server indicates support for DNS error reporting by including an EDNS0 Report-Channel option with OPTION-CODE 18 and the agent domain in the response.

DNS.why: The document specifies new DNS resolver, authoritative server and monitoring agent behaviour, including QNAME construction for report queries and caching considerations.
DNS.quote: a lightweight reporting mechanism that provides the operator of an authoritative server with reports on DNS resource records that fail to resolve or validate

DNSSEC.why: The motivating failures are DNSSEC validation errors (expired signatures, DS mismatch), and the operational section addresses aggressive negative caching with NSEC/NSEC3 and signing the agent domain.
DNSSEC.quote: This document describes a method that can be used by validating resolvers to report DNSSEC validation errors in an automated way.

rejected.why: Query name minimisation and TCP are mentioned only as security considerations, not as encrypted DNS transport.
The document is a reporting protocol; its operational section is about agent domain choice and caching, not general operational security practice.
It is a reporting mechanism for DNS failures, but the DNS and EDNS tags capture it more precisely than the generic OAM topic.

RFC9568.title: Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) Version 3 for IPv4 and IPv6
RFC9568.summary: RFC 9568 specifies VRRP version 3 for IPv4 and IPv6, an election protocol assigning an Active Router for a Virtual Router on a LAN, obsoleting RFC 5798.

VRRP.why: The document is the VRRPv3 protocol specification: packet format, state machine, operational issues.
VRRP.quote: VRRP specifies an election protocol that dynamically assigns responsibility for a Virtual Router to one of the VRRP Routers on a LAN.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as a similar proprietary protocol.
ND is used and interacted with by VRRP but is not what the document specifies.
ARP behaviour is an operational detail, not the subject.
VRRP supports IPv6 but the document is about VRRP, not IPv6 itself.
Uses the Internet checksum only as a mechanism.

RFC9569.title: The Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) Transport Information Publication Service (TIPS)
RFC9569.summary: RFC 9569 specifies the ALTO Transport Information Publication Service (TIPS), an extension to the ALTO protocol that publishes incremental updates of network information resources as an updates graph of HTTP resources that clients pull, including over HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.

ALTO.why: The document defines a new ALTO service and extends the ALTO protocol (RFC 7285) and its incremental updates (RFC 8895) with IRD announcement, open requests, and pull-based update retrieval.
ALTO.quote: this document introduces the ALTO Transport Information Publication Service (TIPS).

rejected.why: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are the substrate TIPS runs over. The document defines ALTO resources, not new HTTP semantics, and Appendix B stresses it does not redefine HTTP elements.
The document is designed to exploit HTTP/2 concurrent streams but only uses the protocol as a transport and specifies nothing about it.
JSON, JSON patch and merge patch encode the updates but are only the data encoding. The document defines no new JSON format as a subject in its own right.
Basic and Digest authentication appear only in examples, as the means ALTO servers already use.
The IANA media type registrations are boilerplate for the new ALTO types and are not the subject of the document.
Appendix B checks conformance with RFC 9205, but this is a minor section and the document is not about API conventions.

gaps.name: ALTO (Application-Layer Traffic Optimization)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists ALTO only as an application-area technology tag, so the core subject was tagged there. If ALTO is placed under another topic, this tag may need to be revisited.

RFC9570.title: Deprecating the Use of Router Alert in LSP Ping
RFC9570.summary: Updates RFC 8029 (LSP ping) to remove the IP Router Alert Option from MPLS echo request/reply encapsulations, deprecates reply mode 3 and the IPv6 RAO value 69, explains RFC 7506's reclassification as Historic, and recommends ::1/128 as the IPv6 destination for echo requests.

MPLS.why: The document modifies LSP ping, the MPLS data-plane failure detection mechanism, so MPLS readers need it.
MPLS.quote: this document retires the RAO for MPLS OAM and updates RFC 8029 to remove the RAO from LSP ping message encapsulations

router alert.why: The core subject is retiring the IP Router Alert option (IPv4 and IPv6 value 69) from LSP ping.
router alert.quote: the IP header that encapsulates an MPLS echo request message must include a Router Alert Option (RAO).

rejected.why: The ::1/128 destination recommendation is a minor part; the document is not about IPv6 itself.
LSP ping is UDP-based, not ICMP.
UDP is only the encapsulation substrate.
ECMP/entropy is mentioned only in passing in the replacement text.
MPLS OAM is the context, but the more specific MPLS and router alert tags cover it.

gaps.name: LSP ping / MPLS OAM
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for LSP ping (RFC 8029) or MPLS OAM data-plane failure detection; the closest is the general MPLS tag.

RFC9571.title: Extension of RFC 6374-Based Performance Measurement Using Synonymous Flow Labels
RFC9571.summary: Extends RFC 6374 MPLS packet loss and delay measurement using Synonymous Flow Labels to generic MPLS LSPs (including multipoint-to-point), defining new multi-packet delay/jitter message formats and an SFL TLV.

performance measurement.why: The document defines loss and delay measurement methods, new delay characteristic messages (time buckets, standard deviation, average delay) and sampled measurement. This is performance measurement in its own right.
performance measurement.quote: This memo specifies how SFLs are used to perform packet loss and delay measurements as described in [RFC6374].

MPLS.why: The measurements run over MPLS LSPs with SFL label stacks, G-ACh and ACH types. It extends RFC 6374 MPLS OAM to generic MPLS and multipoint-to-point LSPs, and registers new G-ACh types.
MPLS.quote: This document describes how to use [RFC6374] in the generic MPLS case

rejected.why: MPLS-TP is the original context of RFC 6374. This document extends the measurements beyond it to generic MPLS, so it is not what the document is about.
ECMP is cited as a source of accounting errors that motivates SFLs. The document does not specify ECMP.
The measurement messages are OAM, but the more specific performance measurement tag covers this.
UDP is mentioned only as an optional return path (RFC 7876). The document does not specify it.

RFC9572.title: Updates to EVPN Broadcast, Unknown Unicast, or Multicast (BUM) Procedures
RFC9572.summary: Updates RFC 7432 EVPN BUM handling by specifying selective multicast (S-PMSI/Leaf A-D routes), new EVPN route types, and inter-AS and inter-region provider tunnel segmentation.

EVPN.why: The document updates RFC 7432 EVPN BUM procedures and defines three new EVPN route types, a new multicast flag bit, and segmentation procedures.
EVPN.quote: This document specifies updated procedures for handling Broadcast, Unknown Unicast, or Multicast (BUM) traffic in Ethernet VPNs (EVPNs), including selective multicast and segmentation of provider tunnels.

rejected.why: MVPN procedures are the model the document borrows from, but the document only specifies differences for EVPN. It is not about MVPN itself.
RFC 7117 VPLS multicast is the baseline the document describes differences from. It does not change VPLS.
BGP route types and attributes are the encoding substrate. The document is about EVPN procedures, not BGP in general.
BIER is mentioned only as a benefit of smaller regions and as a possible tunnel type.
RSVP-TE P2MP and mLDP tunnels are mentioned only as examples of tunnel technologies.
The multicast here is customer BUM and multicast traffic carried within EVPN. EVPN is the more specific tag.

RFC9573.title: MVPN/EVPN Tunnel Aggregation with Common Labels
RFC9573.summary: Specifies procedures (DCB-flag in PTA flags and a Context-Specific Label Space ID Extended Community) so that MVPN/EVPN PEs can use provisioned common labels for aggregate P2MP/MP2MP/BIER tunnels, reducing upstream-assigned label state at egress PEs.

MVPN.why: The document updates RFC 6514 MVPN procedures for aggregate tunnels and label allocation, adding new signaling for MVPN x-PMSI routes.
MVPN.quote: The Multicast VPN (MVPN) specifications allow a single Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) tunnel to carry traffic of multiple IP VPNs

EVPN.why: It updates RFC 7432 and RFC 7582 procedures for EVPN BD, IMET and ESI labels using common labels.
EVPN.quote: The EVPN specifications allow a single P2MP tunnel to carry traffic of multiple Broadcast Domains (BDs).

BIER.why: BIER transport is treated like an aggregate tunnel needing upstream-assigned labels, and the procedures apply to it.
BIER.quote: An MVPN or EVPN can also use Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER)

MPLS.why: Core subject is MPLS upstream-assigned labels, context-specific label spaces, and a domain-wide common label block.
MPLS.quote: allocates an "upstream-assigned MPLS label" [RFC5331] for each VPN

rejected.why: BGP is the signaling carrier (extended community, PTA flag), but the document is not about BGP itself.
SRGB is only an analogy for the common label block.
VNIs are mentioned only as an analogy.
The IP VPN is context; the document is about multicast VPN and EVPN labels, and MVPN covers it.
RSVP-TE is only one of the P2MP tunnel setup methods mentioned in passing.

RFC9574.title: Optimized Ingress Replication Solution for Ethernet VPNs (EVPNs)
RFC9574.summary: Specifies Assisted Replication (selective and non-selective) and Pruned Flooding Lists as optimizations of ingress replication for BUM traffic in EVPN-based network virtualization overlays, via extensions to the Inclusive Multicast route and PMSI Tunnel Attribute.

EVPN.why: The whole document extends EVPN Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag routes and BUM procedures, including multihoming split-horizon, so it is about EVPN.
EVPN.quote: Network Virtualization Overlay (NVO) networks using Ethernet VPNs (EVPNs) as their control plane may use trees based on ingress replication

rejected.why: Only one of several data-plane encapsulations the solution is independent of; not specified here.
BGP routes and attributes are the signalling substrate for the EVPN extensions; the document is not about BGP itself.
PIM is the alternative being avoided, mentioned only for comparison.
Data-plane NVO encapsulation is the context; the document defines EVPN control-plane procedures, not an encapsulation.
The document deals with BUM replication in overlays, not IP multicast routing or group membership.

gaps.name: EVPN (Ethernet VPN) BUM / Assisted Replication
gaps.why: The taxonomy has EVPN only as a child of VPN, but I used an id 'EVPN' that does appear as a tech under VPN: no gap in coverage, though no tag exists for Assisted Replication specifically.

RFC9575.title: DRIP Entity Tag (DET) Authentication Formats and Protocols for Broadcast Remote Identification (RID)
RFC9575.summary: Defines DRIP authentication message formats (Link, Wrapper, Manifest, Frame) carried in ASTM F3411 Broadcast Remote ID Authentication Messages for UAS, plus a single-page XOR FEC scheme and trust-assessment procedures.

DRIP.why: The document specifies DRIP Link, Wrapper, Manifest and Frame authentication formats for drone remote identification, which is the DRIP subject.
DRIP.quote: This document defines DRIP message types and formats to be sent in Broadcast RID Authentication Messages to verify that attached and recently detached messages were signed

rejected.why: DNS is used to fetch Host Identities, but the document explicitly places DNS specification and security out of scope (deferred to DRIP-REG).
The document defines an application-level XOR parity scheme, but it is a small piece specific to Authentication Pages over Bluetooth 4.x, not general packet-transport FEC.
Mentions that UAS are IoT devices and IoT considerations apply, but the document is about RID authentication, not IoT architecture.
Describes a trust chain of endorsements, but this is DRIP-specific and not Internet PKI; certificates are not involved.
Authentication is the subject, but the DRIP tag is the more specific fit for a drone-specific mechanism.
cSHAKE128 and SHA-384 are used only as hash primitives for manifest hashes, not specified or analysed.

gaps.name: Drone Remote Identification Protocol (DRIP) / UAS Remote ID
gaps.why: The taxonomy appears to have only a DRIP tech tag under internet layer. I used it above, but I found no broader topic for UAS Remote ID authentication over Bluetooth/Wi-Fi broadcast, which applies to ASTM F3411 Broadcast RID beyond DRIP.

RFC9576.title: The Privacy Pass Architecture
RFC9576.summary: RFC 9576 specifies the Privacy Pass architecture: the roles of Client, Origin, Attester and Issuer, the privacy goals and threat model, deployment models, and privacy/security considerations for privacy-preserving token-based authorization.

privacy pass.why: The whole document defines the Privacy Pass architecture, its redemption and issuance protocols, deployment models and unlinkability goals.
privacy pass.quote: Privacy Pass is an architecture for authorization based on privacy-preserving authentication mechanisms.

rejected.why: Privacy is central, but the specific technology tag privacy pass already covers it, and the document is not a general protocol privacy-considerations guide.
The redemption scheme is an HTTP authentication scheme, but it is specified in RFC 9577; this document is architectural.
RATS terminology is used to map the Client and Attester roles, but the document is not about remote attestation itself.
Mentioned only as an example use case.
Mutually authenticated TLS is mentioned only as one way to establish trust between Attester and Issuer.
The generic authentication topic is covered more specifically by privacy pass.

RFC9577.title: The Privacy Pass HTTP Authentication Scheme
RFC9577.summary: Defines the "PrivateToken" HTTP authentication scheme that lets Origins challenge Clients for Privacy Pass tokens and Clients redeem them, including challenge/token structures, client and origin behaviour, and an IANA token types registry.

privacy pass.why: The whole document specifies how Privacy Pass tokens are challenged and redeemed, including the token types registry.
privacy pass.quote: This document defines an HTTP authentication scheme for Privacy Pass, a privacy-preserving authentication mechanism used for authorization.

HTTP authentication.why: It defines a new HTTP authentication scheme using WWW-Authenticate and Authorization header fields, and registers it.
HTTP authentication.quote: Token redemption is performed using HTTP authentication ([HTTP], Section 11), with the scheme "PrivateToken".

rejected.why: TLS is used only for presentation-language notation and anti-replay references, not specified or extended here.
Cookies are mentioned only as state to flush with tokens; the document is not about cookie management.
base64url is only the encoding for header parameters.
SHA-256 is used only to compute challenge_digest.
The more specific HTTP authentication tag applies; the document is not about general HTTP semantics.
The registry creation is boilerplate-like and secondary to the main body.

RFC9578.title: Privacy Pass Issuance Protocols
RFC9578.summary: Specifies the two Privacy Pass issuance protocol variants (VOPRF-based privately verifiable tokens and blind-RSA publicly verifiable tokens), including HTTP request/response messages, issuer directory configuration, and token verification.

privacy pass.why: The whole document defines the Privacy Pass issuance protocols, their messages, issuer directory, and token types.
privacy pass.quote: This document specifies two variants of the two-message issuance protocol for Privacy Pass tokens

rejected.why: HTTP is only the substrate carrying TokenRequest/TokenResponse; nothing new is defined about HTTP itself.
Blind RSA is used via RFC 9474; the document instantiates it but does not specify RSA.
The issuer directory is a JSON object, but JSON is just the encoding.
It registers three media types, but only as IANA boilerplate for the protocol.
Only advises using standard cache directives for the directory resource.
The tokens are an authorization mechanism, but the specific Privacy Pass tag fits better.

RFC9579.title: Use of Password-Based Message Authentication Code 1 (PBMAC1) in PKCS #12 Syntax
RFC9579.summary: Defines how to use PBMAC1 (from PKCS #5) for integrity protection of PKCS #12 files, updating RFCs 7292 and 8018, with recommended PBKDF2 parameters, password encoding, test vectors and an ASN.1 module.

password hashing.why: The document is about password-based key derivation and MAC (PBMAC1 with PBKDF2/scrypt) applied to PKCS #12 integrity protection. It is the closest taxonomy subject for PBKDFs.
password hashing.quote: permit the use of more modern Password-Based Key Derivation Functions (PBKDFs)

PBKDF2.why: PBKDF2 is the mandatory KDF, and the document specifies its parameters (keyLength required, SHA-1 PRF discouraged).
PBKDF2.quote: all implementations of this specification MUST support the PBKDF2 key derivation function paired with SHA-256 HMAC

scrypt.why: scrypt is explicitly permitted as an alternative KDF for deriving MAC keys, though only as an optional choice.
scrypt.quote: This change allows for the use of PBKDF2 [RFC8018] or scrypt PBKDFs [RFC7914] for derivation of MAC keys

ASN.1.why: The document defines a new ASN.1 module with PBMAC1 params and HMAC OIDs, and the PKCS #12 structures are ASN.1-based.
ASN.1.quote: It does so by providing an ASN.1 module called PKCS12-PBMAC1-2023.

rejected.why: HMAC is the MAC primitive used, but the document does not define or extend it. It only selects HMAC-SHA-2 parameters and OIDs.
SHA-2 and SHA-3 are mentioned as parameter choices and SHA-1 is deprecated, but the document is not about the hash family.
PKCS #12 carries certificates and keys, but the document concerns only MAC integrity protection and does not address certificates.
PKCS #12 is a container for certificates and keys, but this document does not address PKI operations.

gaps.name: PKCS #12 / PKCS #5 (PBMAC1)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for PKCS #12 personal information exchange syntax or PKCS #5 password-based cryptography. These are the document's main subjects, and the nearest tag is password hashing.

gaps.name: PBKDF2
gaps.why: I used PBKDF2 in the tags but it is not in the taxonomy. The `password hashing` subtree lists only scrypt and PBKDF2 children, and that is how PBKDF2 appears here. If the taxonomy treats PBKDF2 as a valid id, that tag should be added as secondary.

RFC9580.title: OpenPGP
RFC9580.summary: RFC 9580 specifies the OpenPGP message format (version 6 keys, signatures, AEAD-based SEIPD v2, Argon2 S2K, X25519/Ed25519/X448/Ed448), obsoleting RFCs 4880, 5581 and 6637.

OpenPGP.why: The whole document defines the OpenPGP packet formats, key and signature structures, armor and cleartext signature framework.
OpenPGP.quote: This document specifies the message formats used in OpenPGP.

elliptic curve.why: It folds in RFC 6637, defining ECC curves, point and scalar wire formats, the KDF and ECDH for OpenPGP, plus X25519/X448/Ed25519/Ed448 key and signature formats. Readers of elliptic-curve cryptography would want it.
elliptic curve.quote: This section describes algorithms and parameters used with Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) keys.

rejected.why: X25519/X448 are specified as OpenPGP algorithms, but the curves are defined in RFC 7748, so the document does not define them. Covered under elliptic curve.
The document uses Ed25519/Ed448 per RFC 8032 and adds only OpenPGP packet encodings, so I tagged the broader elliptic curve topic instead.
AES is used as a cipher and key wrap, and it is one entry in the algorithm tables. The document is not about AES.
Argon2 S2K is a small part of the document. It is not the subject.
The document mentions MIME and email use only in passing. OpenPGP/MIME is defined in a different RFC.
The document defines a different message format and does not specify CMS.

RFC9581.title: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) Tags for Time, Duration, and Period
RFC9581.summary: Defines CBOR tags 1001 (extended time), 1002 (duration) and 1003 (period), with map keys for high-resolution fractions, timescales, clock quality and RFC 9557 suffix info, plus new IANA registries.

CBOR.why: The document defines new CBOR tags 1001-1003 and registers them, extending CBOR.
CBOR.quote: The present document defines a CBOR tag for time that allows a more elaborate representation of time, as well as related CBOR tags for duration and time period.

date-time formats.why: It defines an extended timestamp representation with timescale, sub-second precision, time zone hints and IXDTF suffixes, building on RFC 3339/9557.
date-time formats.quote: An extended time is indicated by CBOR tag 1001, the content of which is a map data item

CDDL.why: CDDL definitions are given throughout and collected in an appendix, including CDDL type names recommended in Section 6. It is a secondary tag, since CDDL is mainly the notation used.
CDDL.quote: A machine-processable model of the data structures defined in this specification is provided throughout the text using the Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL)

rejected.why: Clock quality keys borrow PTP/IEEE 1588 terms via RFC 8575, but the document does not specify or operate PTP.
It is a data representation of timestamps and clock quality, not about synchronizing clocks over networks.
Time zone hints are carried as RFC 9557 strings, but the document does not deal with time zone data distribution.
It creates two IANA registries, but these serve the tag definitions and are not the main subject of the document.
JSON is not used; CBOR is the encoding.

RFC9582.title: A Profile for Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs)
RFC9582.summary: Defines the standard profile for Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs), RPKI signed objects authorizing an AS to originate routes for IP prefixes, including ASN.1 syntax, canonical form, and validation; obsoletes RFC 6482.

RPKI.why: The document specifies the ROA object of the RPKI, its content type, eContent syntax, and validation steps for relying parties.
RPKI.quote: A Route Origin Authorization (ROA) provides this function.

rejected.why: CMS is only the wrapper used via the RPKI signed object template; the document defines no new CMS behaviour.
EE certificates and RFC 3779 extensions are relied on and constrained in validation, but the document is about the ROA, not certificate profiles.
The ROA is defined in an ASN.1 module, but ASN.1 is the notation, not the subject.
ROAs are used to validate BGP origins, but the document does not specify BGP behaviour.
The media type registration is IANA boilerplate, not the main body.

RFC9583.title: Application Scenarios for the Quantum Internet
RFC9583.summary: An IRTF QIRG informational document that categorizes Quantum Internet applications (cryptography, sensing, computing), details scenarios (QKD-based secure communication setup, blind quantum computing, distributed quantum computing), and lists general networking requirements.

rejected.why: PQC is only mentioned in the Security Considerations as a comparison to QKD and a pointer to the PQUIP working group; the document is not about PQC.

QKD is a key distribution method discussed as a scenario, but the document is about quantum applications in general, not key management in Internet protocols; the taxonomy offers no quantum-specific tag and this stretches the topic.
TLS and IPsec are mentioned only in passing as places where QKD-derived keys could be used; the document specifies nothing about them.
Mentioned in one sentence as a possible consumer of QKD keys; not a subject of the document.
Section 5 gives requirements and a roadmap for the Quantum Internet, but the document explicitly does not define an architecture (that is RFC 9340). It is about application scenarios.
Section 5.4 briefly notes a need for Quantum Internet management methods, but it is a short paragraph and not a substantial part of the document.

gaps.name: Quantum Internet / quantum networking
gaps.why: The whole document is about quantum networking applications (QKD, blind quantum computing, distributed quantum computing, entanglement distribution), and the taxonomy has no quantum networking tag. Readers browsing a subject index would want a dedicated page for it, together with RFC 9340.

gaps.name: Quantum key distribution (QKD)
gaps.why: QKD-based secure communication setup is a central scenario of the document (Section 4.1), with no matching tag in the cryptography or security branches.

RFC9584.title: RTP Payload Format for Essential Video Coding (EVC)
RFC9584.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for Essential Video Coding (EVC, ISO/IEC 23094-1): NAL unit packetization (single, aggregation, fragmentation), SDP media type parameters, and RTCP feedback use.

RTP payload format.why: The document specifies an RTP payload format for a specific video codec, which is what this tag covers.
RTP payload format.quote: This document describes an RTP payload format for the Essential Video Coding (EVC) standard, published as ISO/IEC International Standard 23094-1.

codecs.why: EVC is a video codec with no dedicated tag. It is described in an overview section, and readers of the codecs page would want this RFC.
codecs.quote: This document describes an RTP payload format for EVC.

SDP.why: A large part of the document defines SDP parameters, the offer/answer rules for them and declarative usage.
SDP.quote: The media type video/evc string is mapped to fields in the Session Description Protocol (SDP) [RFC8866] as follows:

media types.why: The document registers the video/evc media type and defines its parameters.
media types.quote:
Type name:  video

   Subtype name:  evc

rejected.why: The document leans on RTP heavily, but the more specific RTP payload format tag already covers it.
PLI and FIR feedback are only profiled briefly in section 8, which is too little to make the document about RTCP.
AVC/H.264 is cited only as a related codec and as a design precedent.
HEVC and its RTP payload format are cited only as a design precedent, and this RFC defines no HEVC payload.
The congestion control section only points back to RTP rules and temporal scalability, so it adds nothing in its own right.
SRTP is mentioned only in the Security Considerations and the MANE note.

gaps.name: Essential Video Coding (EVC)
gaps.why: EVC has no codec tag in the taxonomy, unlike H.264, HEVC and VP9. A tag for it would be a natural place for this RFC.

RFC9585.title: IMAP Response Code for Command Progress Notifications
RFC9585.summary: Defines the IMAP "INPROGRESS" untagged response code and capability so servers can send progress notifications and keepalives for long-running commands.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP with a new response code and capability, so it is about IMAP and belongs on that subject's page.
IMAP.quote: This document defines a new IMAP untagged response code, "INPROGRESS", that provides progress notifications regarding the status of long-running commands.

rejected.why: ABNF is only the notation used for the formal syntax section; the document is not about ABNF.
The IANA registry additions are boilerplate registrations and not the subject of the document.
IMAP is the more specific tag, so the parent email tag is implied and not listed.

RFC9586.title: IMAP Extension for Using and Returning Unique Identifiers (UIDs) Only
RFC9586.summary: Defines the experimental IMAP UIDONLY extension, which lets clients enable a mode where only UIDs (no message sequence numbers) are used in commands and responses, introducing UIDFETCH responses, VANISHED for expunges and the UIDREQUIRED response code.

IMAP.why: The document specifies a new IMAP extension (capability, ENABLE behaviour, UIDFETCH response, UIDREQUIRED code), so IMAP readers need it.
IMAP.quote: The UIDONLY extension of the Internet Message Access Protocol allows clients to request that servers only use and return UIDs.

rejected.why: IMAP is a child of email in spirit, but the more specific IMAP tag fits; email is the parent and implied.
ABNF is only used as notation for the formal syntax; the document is not about it.
Not relevant; only IANA registries for IMAP capabilities and response codes are touched, which is boilerplate.
The IANA section merely registers the capability and response code; the document is not about IANA registries.

gaps.name: IMAP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no IMAP tag distinct from 'IMAP' under email; the closest is 'IMAP' listed under email as a [tech] entry, which is used above.

RFC9587.title: YANG Data Model for OSPFv3 Extended Link State Advertisements (LSAs)
RFC9587.summary: Defines the ietf-ospfv3-extended-lsa YANG module augmenting the OSPF YANG model (RFC 9129) with configuration and operational LSDB state for OSPFv3 Extended LSAs (RFC 8362).

OSPFv3.why: The document models OSPFv3 Extended LSAs (E-Router, E-Network, E-Link, etc.) and their TLVs, so it is about OSPFv3 protocol data.
OSPFv3.quote: to provide support for configuration and operational state for OSPFv3 Extended Link State Advertisements (LSAs) as defined in [RFC8362]

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module with tree diagrams, augmentations and identities, so it is a YANG data model.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model augmenting the IETF OSPF YANG data model [RFC9129]

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the management protocol that accesses the model; the document does not specify or extend it.
The document covers only the OSPFv3 child, so the parent tag is not needed.
RESTCONF is mentioned only as an alternative access protocol and in the Security Considerations.
XML and JSON appear only in the configuration example as encodings.
JSON is used only for the example encoding in the appendix.
TLS appears only in the Security Considerations boilerplate.

RFC9588.title: Kerberos Simple Password-Authenticated Key Exchange (SPAKE) Pre-authentication
RFC9588.summary: Defines a new Kerberos pre-authentication mechanism (PA-SPAKE) that uses the SPAKE password-authenticated key exchange to resist offline dictionary attacks and optionally carry a second authentication factor, with IANA registries for second-factor types and SPAKE groups.

Kerberos.why: The document specifies a new Kerberos pre-authentication mechanism, including padata types, message flow, and key derivation within the AS exchange.
Kerberos.quote: This document defines a new pre-authentication mechanism for the Kerberos protocol.

SPAKE2.why: The mechanism is built on SPAKE2 and specifies its group parameters, M and N constants, and use of w derived from the reply key.
SPAKE2.quote: The SPAKE algorithm (defined in [SPAKE]) works by encrypting the public keys of a Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange with a shared secret.

PAKE.why: The document is about applying PAKE properties against offline dictionary attacks. This is a broader subject that SPAKE2 sits under, so it is only a secondary tag.
PAKE.quote: The mechanism uses a password-authenticated key exchange (PAKE) to prevent brute-force password attacks, and it may incorporate a second factor.

rejected.why: The groups (edwards25519, P-256, P-384, P-521) are used and registered, but the document is not about elliptic curve cryptography itself.
ASN.1 and DER only encode the messages, so it is merely the substrate here.
Not related; the mechanism is Kerberos pre-authentication.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-like apparatus for this protocol, not the subject of the document.
One-time passwords are mentioned only as an example of a second factor, and the only factor defined is SF-NONE.

RFC9589.title: On the Use of the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Signing-Time Attribute in Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Signed Objects
RFC9589.summary: Updates RFC 6488 to make the CMS signing-time attribute mandatory in RPKI Signed Objects, disallow binary-signing-time, and describes using signing-time as file mod-time to avoid needless retransfers when switching from RRDP to rsync.

RPKI.why: The document profiles RPKI Signed Objects, amends the RFC 6488 template, and gives guidance for RPKI repository operators and relying parties.
RPKI.quote: updates [RFC6488] by mandating the presence of the CMS signing-time attribute and disallowing the use of the binary-signing-time attribute.

rejected.why: CMS is the underlying signed-object format. The document only constrains one signed attribute within the RPKI profile and does not define anything new about CMS.
RPKI is its child and is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
The ASN.1 time encodings are only mentioned in passing, and the document is not about ASN.1.
BinaryTime is only mentioned as an attribute being disallowed. The document does not address date and time representation.

gaps.name: rsync / RRDP repository synchronization
gaps.why: A large part of the document covers synchronizing RPKI repositories with rsync and RRDP, which the taxonomy has no tag for.

RFC9590.title: IMAP Extension for Returning Mailbox METADATA in Extended LIS
RFC9590.summary: Defines the IMAP LIST-METADATA capability, a METADATA return option for extended LIST that returns mailbox annotations alongside LIST responses in one command.

IMAP.why: The document extends IMAP's LIST command with a new return option and capability, so it belongs under IMAP.
IMAP.quote: This document defines an extension to the IMAP LIST command that is identified by the capability string "LIST-METADATA".

rejected.why: ABNF is only used to write the formal syntax; the document is not about it.
The IANA section only registers the capability and option; this is boilerplate and not the document's subject.
IMAP is the more specific tag and already implies email.

gaps.name: IMAP METADATA / mailbox annotations
gaps.why: The document concerns the IMAP METADATA extension (RFC 5464) and LIST-EXTENDED, but the taxonomy has no tag for these IMAP extensions beyond IMAP itself.

RFC9591.title: The Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold (FROST) Protocol for Two-Round Schnorr Signatures
RFC9591.summary: Specifies FROST, a two-round threshold Schnorr signing protocol over prime-order groups, with ciphersuites (Ed25519, ristretto255, Ed448, P-256, secp256k1), trusted-dealer key generation, and test vectors.

elliptic curve.why: The protocol is a threshold Schnorr signature scheme over elliptic-curve prime-order groups, with ciphersuites for Ed25519, Ed448, ristretto255, P-256 and secp256k1. No more specific tag fits generic Schnorr threshold signing.
elliptic curve.quote: FROST depends only on a prime-order group and cryptographic hash function.

key management.why: Appendix C specifies trusted-dealer key generation with Shamir and Feldman verifiable secret sharing, and the protocol assumes shared key shares are distributed to participants.
key management.quote: key generation with a trusted dealer is specified in Appendix C.

rejected.why: EdDSA is not in the taxonomy. Two FROST ciphersuites produce RFC 8032-compatible signatures, but the document is not about EdDSA itself.
Ed25519 and Ed448 are used as groups in two ciphersuites, but the document is not about those curves.
P-256 and secp256k1 are used only as prime-order groups for Schnorr signatures, not for ECDSA.
SHA-256, SHA-512 and SHAKE256 are only hash building blocks for the ciphersuites.
TLS appears only as an example application and as the notation source for the signature encoding. The document does not address TLS.
Nonce and random-scalar generation are sub-procedures of the signing protocol, not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: Threshold signatures / Schnorr signatures
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for threshold or Schnorr signature schemes and secret sharing. The nearest tag, elliptic curve, covers only part of the subject.

RFC9592.title: Retiring the Tao of the IETF
RFC9592.summary: RFC 9592 retires and obsoletes the Tao of the IETF (and RFC 6722), explains why, and reproduces the final edition of the Tao, a newcomer's guide to IETF meetings, working groups, and the RFC process.

IETF process.why: The document concerns the IETF's newcomer guide, and the appendix describes WGs, BOFs, IESG, Internet-Draft and RFC processes.
IETF process.quote: This document retires and obsoletes the Tao of the IETF as an IETF-maintained document.

user guides.why: The Tao is an introductory guide for newcomers. Its retirement and archived text fit this topic.
user guides.quote: introduced the working processes to new participants.

RFC series.why: The appendix covers RFC streams, document types (Standards Track, BCP, Informational), and publication. The document also obsoletes RFC 6722 on publishing the Tao.
RFC series.quote: Once an RFC is published, it is never revised.

rejected.why: IANA is described only briefly as part of the IETF hierarchy; the document is not about IANA registries.
Copyright and patents get a short passage in the archived Tao but are not the focus.
NomCom is mentioned only in passing as the body that selects IESG and IAB members.
Jabber is mentioned only as a remote-participation chat tool for meetings.

RFC9593.title: Announcing Supported Authentication Methods in the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC9593.summary: Defines the IKEv2 SUPPORTED_AUTH_METHODS notification, letting peers announce supported authentication methods (optionally linked to CAs in CERTREQ) during IKE_SA_INIT, IKE_INTERMEDIATE and IKE_AUTH.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with a new notify type and exchange rules, including interaction with IKE_INTERMEDIATE and other IKEv2 authentication extensions.
IKE.quote: this specification introduces a new Notify Message Type SUPPORTED_AUTH_METHODS.

rejected.why: IKEv2 is the subject; IPsec is only the context where IKE runs, and the more specific IKE tag applies.
CA and trust-anchor linking via CERTREQ is used, but the document does not specify or profile certificates.
AlgorithmIdentifier is DER-encoded, but this is only an encoding detail of the announcement.
Post-quantum signatures are mentioned only as motivation in the introduction.
The IKE tag already covers this; the document is about an IKEv2-specific mechanism, not authentication across protocols.

RFC9594.title: Key Provisioning for Group Communication Using Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments (ACE)
RFC9594.summary: RFC 9594 defines how ACE clients obtain group keying material and configuration from a Key Distribution Center acting as ACE Resource Server, including the KDC's CoAP resource interface, join/leave/rekeying operations, and requirements for application profiles.

ACE.why: The document extends ACE with a KDC interface, token transfer parameters (sign_info, kdcchallenge) and a framework for ACE groupcomm application profiles.
ACE.quote: This document defines how to use the Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments (ACE) framework to distribute keying material and configuration parameters for secure group communication.

key management.why: A substantial part covers group key provisioning, group rekeying (point-to-point and one-to-many) and keying material versioning, which is key management.
key management.quote: New keying material is intended to be generated and distributed to the group upon membership changes (rekeying).

rejected.why: Not in the taxonomy as a tag; CoAP is the substrate for the KDC interface. CoAP is only used, not extended, here.
CBOR is used as the encoding; the document does not define CBOR itself.
COSE is used to protect rekeying messages and to name algorithms; it is a substrate, and COSE has no tag in the taxonomy.
Group OSCORE and the OSCORE transport profile are only referenced as examples of profiles and security protocols.
The document mentions group rekeying schemes like GKMP and LKH only as examples and defines no IP multicast group key management protocol; its scope is the ACE KDC interface.
ACE is built on OAuth concepts, but the document specifies ACE extensions, not OAuth itself.

gaps.name: Group communication key distribution / KDC for constrained groups
gaps.why: No tag covers ACE group key provisioning specifically beyond the generic ACE and key management tags.

RFC9595.title: YANG Schema Item iDentifier (YANG SID)
RFC9595.summary: Defines YANG Schema Item iDentifiers (SIDs), compact 63-bit integers identifying YANG items, along with their registration and assignment processes, the ".sid" JSON file format (a YANG module), and the IANA registries and media type/CoAP Content-Format for them.

YANG.why: The whole document defines identifiers for YANG items and a YANG module for the .sid file format, so it belongs on the YANG page.
YANG.quote: YANG Schema Item iDentifiers (YANG SIDs) are globally unique 63-bit unsigned integers used to identify YANG items.

IANA.why: A substantial part defines new IANA registries, allocation policies, Early Allocation handling, and expert review procedures for SID ranges.
IANA.quote: The name of this registry is "YANG-SID Mega-Ranges".

CoAP.why: SIDs target constrained environments with CoAP-based management (CORECONF), and the document registers a CoAP Content-Format for .sid files.
CoAP.quote: This document adds the following Content-Format to the "CoAP Content-Formats" registry

rejected.why: SIDs are used for compact YANG-CBOR encoding, but CBOR encoding is specified in RFC 9254, not here.
Mentioned as an alternative that uses names; not specified or extended.
The .sid file is JSON-encoded, but JSON is only the substrate.
A media type is registered, but only as boilerplate IANA registration for the .sid file format, not the main subject.
Constrained devices motivate the work, but the document is about YANG identifiers, not IoT architecture.

RFC9596.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) "typ" (type) Header Parameter
RFC9596.summary: Registers a "typ" (type) COSE header parameter, label 16, equivalent to the JOSE "typ" parameter, so COSE objects can be explicitly typed.

COSE.why: The document defines a new COSE header parameter, extending COSE, and registers it in the COSE Header Parameters registry.
COSE.quote: This specification adds the equivalent of the JOSE "typ" (type) header parameter to COSE so that the benefits of explicit typing can be brought to COSE objects.

rejected.why: JOSE's typ parameter is the model for this work, but the document specifies nothing about JOSE itself.
RFC 8725 and JWT explicit typing are cited only as motivation.
CBOR is the encoding substrate for COSE, and the document defines nothing new about CBOR.
Media type values are reused for the typ value syntax, but the document does not specify or register media types.
The registry entry is boilerplate-like and the document is not about IANA process.

RFC9597.title: CBOR Web Token (CWT) Claims in COSE Headers
RFC9597.summary: Defines a new COSE header parameter (label 15, "CWT Claims") that carries CWT claims in the header of any COSE structure, so claims are visible before decryption or without the detached payload.

COSE.why: The document registers a new COSE header parameter and specifies its use in COSE structures such as COSE_Sign1 and COSE_Sign.
COSE.quote: This document describes how to include CBOR Web Token (CWT) claims in the header parameters of any CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) structure.

rejected.why: CBOR is the encoding of CWT and COSE. The document does not specify anything new about CBOR.
CDDL is used only for a short non-normative description of the value type.
JWT is mentioned only as the precedent (RFC 7519 Section 5.3). The document is about CWT, not JWT.
JOSE header parameters appear only as the analogue of the JWT mechanism.
The IANA registration is boilerplate for the new header parameter and is not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: CWT (CBOR Web Token)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for CWT. The document is about carrying CWT claims, and CWT readers would want to find it. COSE is the closest tag, and it is a tag the taxonomy does list.

RFC9598.title: Internationalized Email Addresses in X.509 Certificates
RFC9598.summary: Defines the SmtpUTF8Mailbox otherName form so internationalized email addresses can appear in X.509 subjectAltName/issuerAltName, with A-label-only domains, matching rules and name constraint handling; obsoletes RFC 8398 and updates RFC 5280.

X.509.why: The document defines a new certificate name form and updates the RFC 5280 profile, including name constraints in path validation.
X.509.quote: This document defines a new name form for inclusion in the otherName field of an X.509 Subject Alternative Name and Issuer Alternative Name extension

EAI.why: The purpose is representing internationalized email addresses (non-ASCII local-parts per RFC 6531) in certificates, including matching rules.
EAI.quote: allows a certificate subject to be associated with an internationalized email address

IDN.why: A dedicated section and the core change from RFC 8398 mandate IDNA2008 A-label encoding of domain labels and U-label to A-label conversion for comparison.
IDN.quote: all email address domains in X.509 certificates MUST conform to IDNA2008 [RFC5890] (and avoid any "mappings" mentioned in that document)

rejected.why: SMTP is only referenced for the Mailbox syntax; the document does not specify or extend SMTP.
ASN.1 module is just the formal definition apparatus for the new name form, not the subject.
UTF8String encoding is used and BOM prohibited, but the document is not about the UTF-8 encoding.
X.509 is the more specific tag that fits; PKI in general is not the subject.
Document concerns certificate names, not message headers, despite referencing RFC 6532.

RFC9599.title: Guidelines for Adding Congestion Notification to Protocols that Encapsulate IP
RFC9599.summary: BCP giving guidelines for designing congestion notification (ECN propagation) in lower-layer and tunnelling protocols that encapsulate IP, defining feed-forward-and-up, feed-up-and-forward, feed-backward and null modes, and updating RFC 3819.

ECN.why: The whole document is about propagating ECN signals across encapsulation boundaries, with encapsulation and decapsulation rules for the ECN field.
ECN.quote: guide the design of congestion notification in any lower-layer or tunnelling protocol that encapsulates IP

tunneling.why: A substantial part covers IP-in-IP tunnels with shim headers and encapsulator/decapsulator guidelines. Tunnelling is the general topic, since no single tunnelling protocol is the focus.
tunneling.quote: there are numerous other tunnelling protocols with a shim and/or a Layer 2 (L2) header between two IP headers

rejected.why: RFC 5129 is cited as an example of feed-forward-and-up, but the document does not specify MPLS.
AQM marking algorithms are explicitly out of scope; the document concerns only wire-protocol processing.
RFC 9600 is cited as an example design, but the document is not about TRILL.
ECN is the more specific fit, and the document makes no recommendations on congestion response.
Layer 3 Ethernet switches are used as an example of feed-up-and-forward mode, but the document is not about Ethernet.
ATM feedback is described only as an illustration of feed-backward mode.

gaps.name: ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no ECN tag in the form the document uses. I returned the ECN id, which sits under congestion control, and it should be confirmed that it exists in the taxonomy.

RFC9600.title: TRansparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL): Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) Support
RFC9600.summary: Specifies how TRILL switches (RBridges) support ECN: copying IP ECN bits into the TRILL header extension flags word at ingress, marking congestion (CCE/NCCE) at transit, and combining markings at egress, with notes on PCN and L4S variants.

TRILL.why: The document defines new ECN fields in the TRILL header extension flags word and the ingress, transit and egress RBridge behaviour. It is a TRILL extension.
TRILL.quote: This document extends ECN to TRansparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) switches, including integration with IP ECN

ECN.why: The document specifies ECN marking, propagation and egress mapping for TRILL, in line with the RFC 9599 guidelines. Readers of the ECN subject would want it.
ECN.quote: Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) allows a forwarding element to notify downstream devices, including the destination, of the onset of congestion without having to drop packets.

rejected.why: PCN is discussed only informatively in Section 4.1 as a variant that TRILL could support. The document does not specify it.
The document requires transit RBridges to implement some AQM per RFC 7567. It does not specify any AQM algorithm.
The egress mapping is described as consistent with RFC 6040 IP-in-IP tunnels, but the document is not about IP-in-IP tunnelling.
Its subject is congestion notification in TRILL, which the more specific ECN tag covers.
IP is mentioned only as the encapsulated traffic whose ECN bits are copied. The document is not about IPv6.

gaps.name: TRILL (TRansparent Interconnection of Lots of Links)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists TRILL only as a 'TRILL' tech under routing with id 'TRILL'. If that id is not valid as written, the document has no other fitting tag for its main subject.

RFC9601.title: Propagating Explicit Congestion Notification across IP Tunnel Headers Separated by a Shim
