RFC9601.summary: Updates RFC 6040 to clarify that ECN propagation rules cover IP-in-IP tunnels with shim headers, adds safe-configuration requirements for non-ECN tunnel ingresses and fragmentation/reassembly rules, and updates L2TP, GRE, Teredo and AMT with ECN text (including a new L2TP ECN Capability AVP and an AMT E flag).

ECN.why: The whole document concerns how ECN is propagated and safely handled at tunnel ingress and egress, including fragmentation and reassembly rules.
ECN.quote: made the rules for propagation of Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) [RFC3168] consistent for all forms of IP-in-IP tunnel.

tunneling.why: It defines the scope of ECN handling for generic IP-in-IP tunnels with shim headers and surveys many tunnelling protocols.
tunneling.quote: the scope of [RFC6040] includes any IP-in-IP tunnel, including those with one or more shim headers and other encapsulations between the IP headers.

L2TP.why: It updates L2TPv2 and L2TPv3 and defines a new ECN Capability AVP for negotiation between LCCEs.
L2TP.quote: The ECN Capability AVP defined here has Attribute Type 103.
L2TP.section: 6.1.1.2.1. ECN Capability AVP for Negotiation between LCCEs

GRE.why: It updates the GRE specification with safe-configuration requirements for a non-ECN ingress.
GRE.quote: The following text is appended to Section 3 of [RFC2784] as an update to the base GRE specification:
GRE.section: 6.1.2.1. Safe Configuration of a "Non-ECN" GRE Ingress

Teredo.why: It updates Teredo with a new section requiring the outer ECN field to be zeroed.
Teredo.quote: A Teredo tunnel ingress implementation that does not support ECN propagation as defined in [RFC6040] or one of its compatible predecessors

AMT.why: It updates AMT and defines a new ECN capability flag in the AMT Request message.
AMT.quote: Bit 14 of the AMT Request Message counting from 0 (or bit 7 of the Reserved field counting from 1) is defined here as the AMT Gateway ECN Capability flag (E)
AMT.section: 6.1.4.2. ECN Capability Declaration of an AMT Gateway

rejected.why: The ECN tag sits under this topic, so the parent is implied. The document is about ECN propagation, not congestion control in general.
Diffserv appears only as a related field, in the rule that ECN and DSCP handling must not be treated as one 8-bit field. The document is not about Diffserv.
IPsec is mentioned only as a prior ECN-compatible tunnel mode (RFC 4301) and as a protocol that sets up GRE tunnels.
LISP is only listed in the survey, and the document says it needs no update.
VXLAN is listed in the survey and given a recommendation, but it is not updated and is not a substantial part of the document.
UDP is the substrate of the tunnels discussed. The document adds only a passing implication for the UDP usage guidelines.

RFC9602.title: Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) Segment Identifiers in the IPv6 Addressing Architecture
RFC9602.summary: Informational RFC that explains how SRv6 SIDs relate to the IPv6 Addressing Architecture (RFC 4291) and has IANA allocate 5f00::/16 as a dedicated special-purpose prefix for SRv6 SIDs.

SRv6.why: The document is about SRv6 SIDs: their format, how transit nodes treat them, compressed SIDs, and a dedicated prefix for them.
SRv6.quote: This document explores the characteristics of SRv6 SIDs and focuses on the relationship of SRv6 SIDs to the IPv6 Addressing Architecture.

addressing.why: A large part of the document analyses SIDs against the IPv6 addressing architecture and allocates a special-purpose IPv6 address block (5f00::/16).
addressing.quote: it is desirable to allocate some address space that explicitly signals that the addresses within that space cannot be expected to comply with [RFC4291].

rejected.why: IPv6 is the data plane SRv6 runs on. The addressing aspects are covered by the more specific addressing tag, which sits under internet layer.
SRv6 is the more specific child tag, so the parent is not needed.
The IANA registry allocation is boilerplate-like for this document. The subject is SRv6 SIDs and addressing, not IANA stewardship.
DNS is mentioned only once, in a statement that global DNS should not reference addresses from this block.
The document covers only the IPv6 data plane, not MPLS.

RFC9603.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for IPv6 Segment Routing
RFC9603.summary: RFC 9603 extends PCEP to support Segment Routing over the IPv6 data plane, defining the SRv6 PCE capability sub-TLV, a new path setup type (PST=3), and SRv6-ERO and SRv6-RRO subobjects with procedures and error handling.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP (PCE architecture and protocol) with new capability, ERO/RRO subobjects, path setup type and error codes.
PCE.quote: This document outlines the necessary extensions to support SR for the IPv6 data plane within PCEP.

SRv6.why: The document is about carrying SRv6 SIDs, endpoint behaviors and SID structure in PCEP to instantiate SRv6 paths.
SRv6.quote: This document defines new subobjects "SRv6-ERO" and "SRv6-RRO" in the ERO and the RRO, respectively, to carry the SRv6 SID.
SRv6.section: 3. Overview of PCEP Operation in SRv6 Networks

rejected.why: SRv6 is the more specific child that fits; the parent is implied.
Only the RFC 8664 baseline being extended; this document is about the IPv6 data plane.
Only recommended for securing PCEP sessions in Security Considerations; boilerplate.
PCE is the more specific tag under traffic engineering, so the parent is not needed.
BGP-LS is only mentioned as a way to learn MSD topology information.
YANG models for PCEP are explicitly out of scope and only referenced.

RFC9604.title: Carrying Binding Label/SID in PCE-Based Networks
RFC9604.summary: RFC 9604 defines a PCEP TLV (TE-PATH-BINDING) and procedures so a PCC can report, or a PCE can request or allocate, binding labels/SIDs (MPLS labels or SRv6 SIDs) for RSVP-TE and SR-TE paths.

PCE.why: The document's main content is a new PCEP TLV, a new LSP object P flag, new error codes, and the PCC/PCE procedures for using them.
PCE.quote: This document specifies an extension to PCEP to manage the binding of label/SID that can be applied to SR, RSVP-TE, and other path setup types.

segment routing.why: The binding SID is an SR concept. The document covers BSIDs for SR-MPLS and SRv6 paths, including SR-ERO and SRv6-ERO handling, so the parent SR tag fits better than one child.
segment routing.quote: Segment Routing (SR) utilizes a Binding Segment Identifier (BSID)

rejected.why: SRv6 SID formats are one part of the TLV (BT=2 and 3), but the document covers SR-MPLS and SRv6 alike, so the parent segment routing tag fits better.
RSVP-TE paths are only one kind of path the binding can be attached to. The document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE signalling.
MPLS labels and label stack entries are used as binding value encodings. The document is not about MPLS itself.
TLS appears only in the Security Considerations as the PCEPS transport recommendation.
TE paths are the context, but the PCE tag is the more specific fit.

RFC9605.title: Secure Frame (SFrame): Lightweight Authenticated Encryption for Real-Time Media
RFC9605.summary: Defines SFrame, a transport-independent end-to-end authenticated encryption framing for media frames in SFU-based conference calls, including header format, key derivation, AEAD cipher suites, key management (sender keys, MLS), and an IANA registry.

SFrame.why: The document specifies SFrame itself: header, encryption schema, cipher suites and application responsibilities.
SFrame.quote: This document describes the Secure Frame (SFrame) end-to-end encryption and authentication mechanism for media frames in a multiparty conference call

MLS.why: A section defines how SFrame keys and KIDs are derived from MLS epochs, a key management option readers of MLS would want.
MLS.quote: To generate keys and nonces for SFrame, we use the MLS exporter function to generate a base_key value for each MLS epoch.

rejected.why: SFrame is contrasted with SRTP and typically runs over it, but SRTP is not specified or extended here.
SFrame is explicitly independent of RTP; RTP integration is only discussed in an informative appendix.
AES-CTR and AES-GCM are used as primitives in the cipher suites, but the document is not about AES itself.
HMAC is used to build the compound AEAD and in HKDF, as a building block only.
Key management is explicitly out of scope beyond two sample schemes; the MLS tag covers the specific scheme.
SDP is mentioned only as a possible way to negotiate SFrame parameters.

RFC9606.title: DNS Resolver Information
RFC9606.summary: Defines the RESINFO DNS resource record type and a key/value registry by which recursive resolvers publish their capabilities (QNAME minimisation, extended DNS errors, info URL) to DNS clients.

DNS.why: The document specifies a new DNS RR type (RESINFO), its query behaviour and its RDATA format, so it belongs on the DNS page.
DNS.quote: this document defines a new resource record (RR) type for DNS clients to query the recursive resolvers.

EDNS.why: The exterr key advertises which Extended DNS Error codes a resolver can return. EDE is an EDNS option, so readers of that subject would want this. This is a weaker fit than the DNS tag.
EDNS.quote: If the DNS resolver supports the EDE option defined in [RFC8914] to return additional information about the cause of DNS errors

rejected.why: The RESINFO format reuses DNS-SD TXT key/value encoding rules, but the document does not specify service discovery.
The keys help clients infer privacy properties, but the document defines no encrypted or privacy-preserving transport.
DoT, DoH and DoQ appear only in the terminology definition of encrypted DNS and as discovery context. The document does not specify them.
DNSSEC validation is only one of two suggested measures in the Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
The IANA section creates a registry, but this is boilerplate for the new RR type and does not make the document about IANA stewardship.
The resolver.arpa name is used only as a QNAME option. The document defines nothing new about special-use names.

RFC9607.title: RTP Payload Format for the Secure Communication Interoperability Protocol (SCIP) Codec
RFC9607.summary: Defines the RTP payload format and the audio/scip and video/scip media subtypes for the SCIP secure communication protocol, treating its encrypted payload as opaque, with SDP mapping and offer/answer guidance.

RTP payload format.why: The document specifies an RTP payload format for the SCIP pseudo-codec, including header field usage, clock rates and congestion considerations.
RTP payload format.quote: This document describes the RTP payload format of the Secure Communication Interoperability Protocol (SCIP).

media types.why: A substantial part of the document is the registration templates for audio/scip and video/scip, which readers of media type registrations would want.
media types.quote: The "audio/scip" and "video/scip" media subtypes have previously been registered in the "Media Types" registry

SDP.why: The document gives the SDP mapping of the media subtypes and offer/answer considerations for negotiating SCIP.
SDP.quote: The media subtype ("scip") goes in SDP "a=rtpmap" as the encoding name.

rejected.why: SRTP is only mentioned as optional additional protection. SCIP does its own payload encryption and the document does not specify SRTP.
The more specific RTP payload format tag covers the document. RTP itself is the substrate and is not extended.
SCIP is a pseudo-codec that wraps encrypted output of other codecs. The document does not define a codec, so the RTP payload format tag fits better.
RTCP feedback is only mentioned as optional because SCIP handles its own retransmission.
The congestion control section is brief and only points to existing guidance.

gaps.name: SCIP (Secure Communication Interoperability Protocol)
gaps.why: The document is about the SCIP secure voice, video and data protocol, which has no tag of its own. It is a niche, non-public application-layer protocol.

RFC9608.title: No Revocation Available for X.509 Public Key Certificates
RFC9608.summary: Defines the noRevAvail X.509 certificate extension, which signals that the CA publishes no revocation information for a certificate, and updates RFC 5280 path validation to skip revocation checking when it is present.

X.509.why: The document defines a new X.509v3 certificate extension and updates the RFC 5280 certification path validation algorithm. This is squarely X.509 certificate profile work.
X.509.quote: This specification defines the noRevAvail certificate extension so that a relying party can readily determine that the CA does not publish revocation information

rejected.why: OCSP appears only as a comparison with the ocsp-nocheck extension, and the document does not specify or extend OCSP.
ACME is mentioned only as an example of how short-lived certificates are obtained.
ASN.1 is only the notation for the extension's module, so the document is not about ASN.1.
The parent tag is implied by X.509, and the document is specifically about the X.509 certificate profile.

RFC9609.title: Initializing a DNS Resolver with Priming Queries
RFC9609.summary: BCP that specifies the priming queries a recursive DNS resolver sends to obtain the root NS RRset and root server addresses, obsoleting RFC 8109.

DNS.why: The document specifies resolver behaviour for priming queries and responses against root servers, which is core DNS resolver operation.
DNS.quote: This document describes the queries that a DNS resolver should emit to initialize its cache.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is discussed in Section 3.3, but only to note that the root-servers.net zone is unsigned. The document is not about DNSSEC.
The document recommends using EDNS0 and a reassembly size of at least 1024 octets. That is a minor use of the mechanism and defines nothing new about EDNS.
UDP and TCP are only the transports the priming query can use.

RFC9610.title: JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP) for Contacts
RFC9610.summary: Defines the JMAP data model for contacts, with AddressBook and ContactCard types (JSContact cards) and their get/changes/set/query/copy methods, filters, sorting and sharing rights.

JMAP.why: The document extends JMAP with a new capability, two data types and a new error code. Readers of the JMAP subject need it.
JMAP.quote: This specification defines a data model for synchronising contacts between a client and a server using JMAP.

JSContact.why: A ContactCard is a JSContact Card with added properties (id, addressBookIds, blobId). The document also has filters over JSContact properties and registers new JSContact properties. Readers of JSContact would want it.
JSContact.quote: a representation of a person, company, entity, or a group of such entities in JSContact Card format

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding that JMAP uses. The document does not define anything about JSON itself.
CardDAV is a different protocol for address book access. The document does not mention or specify it.
The document works with the JSContact representation, not vCard. Only the JSContact child tag fits.
The Internationalisation Considerations section is a short advisory on restricting Unicode characters. It is boilerplate-like and not the subject of the document.
The registrations are routine IANA Considerations and are not what the document is about.

RFC9611.title: Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) Support for Per-Resource Child Security Associations (SAs)
RFC9611.summary: Defines two IKEv2 notifications (SA_RESOURCE_INFO and TS_MAX_QUEUE) for negotiating multiple Child SAs with identical Traffic Selectors, each bound to a resource such as a CPU, to increase IPsec throughput.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with new notify types and negotiation rules for per-resource Child SAs, so it belongs under IKE.
IKE.quote: this document defines one Notify Message Status Types and one Notify Message Error Types payload for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)

rejected.why: IPsec is the context (Child SAs, SPD, sequence numbers), but the specified protocol work is the IKEv2 negotiation. IKE is the more specific tag.
ESP encryption and its per-SA sequence counters motivate the work, but the document does not specify or extend ESP.
It is an IKEv2 extension, but this document is not about mobility or multihoming.

RFC9612.title: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) Reverse Path for MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs)
RFC9612.summary: Defines the BFD Reverse Path TLV, an extension to MPLS LSP ping echo requests that tells the egress BFD peer which LSP to use for its BFD control packets, plus two new return codes.

BFD.why: The document extends BFD for MPLS LSPs by controlling the reverse path of a BFD session, so readers of the BFD subject need it.
BFD.quote: This document describes an extension to the MPLS Label Switched Path (LSP) echo request that allows a BFD system to request that the remote BFD peer transmit BFD control packets

MPLS.why: It defines a new MPLS LSP ping TLV and return codes and applies to traffic-engineered LSPs, so MPLS OAM readers would want it.
MPLS.quote: This document defines the BFD Reverse Path TLV as an extension to LSP ping [RFC8029]

rejected.why: RSVP-TE LSPs are mentioned only as one kind of explicit path. The document does not specify RSVP-TE.
The monitored paths are traffic-engineered LSPs, but the document is about failure detection and not about traffic engineering.
LSP ping and BFD are OAM mechanisms, but the more specific BFD and MPLS tags cover this document.
The IANA section only registers a TLV and return codes. It is boilerplate for this purpose.

gaps.name: MPLS LSP ping
gaps.why: The document extends LSP ping (RFC 8029) with a new TLV and return codes. The taxonomy has no tag for LSP ping or MPLS OAM.

RFC9613.title: Requirements for Solutions that Support MPLS Network Actions (MNAs)
RFC9613.summary: RFC 9613 specifies requirements for solutions supporting MPLS Network Actions (MNAs), covering network action indicators, ancillary data (in-stack and post-stack), and alert mechanisms in the MPLS data plane.

MPLS.why: The whole document defines requirements for extending the MPLS data plane and label stack with network action indicators and ancillary data.
MPLS.quote: This document specifies requirements for the development of MPLS Network Actions (MNAs) that affect the forwarding or other processing of MPLS packets.

rejected.why: Requirement 11 only asks solutions to discuss ECMP consequences. It is a passing point, not a subject of the document.
Requirement 38 asks for registries, but the IANA considerations section is boilerplate with no actions.
The Generic Associated Channel is mentioned only as a coexistence concern, so the document is not about MPLS-TP.
The document does not discuss segment routing.

RFC9614.title: Partitioning as an Architecture for Privacy
RFC9614.summary: IAB informational document defining privacy partitioning (decoupling identity from data across parties/contexts), surveying its use in MASQUE, Oblivious HTTP/DNS, Privacy Pass and PPM, and discussing how to apply it and its limits.

privacy.why: The whole document is an architectural analysis of privacy partitioning, its application and limits, tied to RFC 6973 data minimization.
privacy.quote: privacy partitioning, which selectively spreads data and communication across multiple parties as a means to improve privacy by separating user identity from user data

oblivious HTTP.why: OHTTP is the recurring worked example for contexts, collusion, and centralization, with its own context diagram.
oblivious HTTP.quote: Oblivious HTTP [OHTTP], developed in the Oblivious HTTP Application Intermediation (OHAI) Working Group, adds per-message encryption to HTTP exchanges through a relay system.

MASQUE.why: Section 3.1 analyzes single- and two-hop proxy contexts in MASQUE-style proxying as a partitioning pattern.
MASQUE.quote: the Multiplexed Application Substrate over QUIC Encryption (MASQUE) Working Group has developed protocols to similarly proxy UDP [CONNECT-UDP] and IP packets [CONNECT-IP]

privacy pass.why: Privacy Pass is surveyed with redemption and issuance contexts and deployment-model effects on partitioning.
privacy pass.quote: Privacy Pass is an architecture [RFC9576] and a set of protocols being developed in the Privacy Pass Working Group

oblivious DNS.why: ODoH is discussed as a partitioning of DoH, and again in section 4.3 as an example of applying partitioning.
oblivious DNS.quote: Oblivious DNS over HTTPS (ODoH) [ODOH] applies the same principle as Oblivious HTTP but operates on DNS messages only.

rejected.why: TLS is only used as an example of a context-splitting mechanism and ECH as an example of insufficient partitioning; the document is not about TLS.
DoH is mentioned only as the single-context baseline that ODoH improves on.
It is an IAB architecture document, but its subject is privacy partitioning, which the privacy tag covers more specifically.
QUIC appears only as the substrate of MASQUE and a connection-ID example.
HTTP is the substrate for the proxying and OHTTP examples; the document specifies nothing new about HTTP.

gaps.name: Privacy Preserving Measurement (PPM/DAP)
gaps.why: Section 3.4 surveys DAP as a partitioning protocol, but the taxonomy has no tag for privacy-preserving aggregate measurement.

RFC9615.title: Automatic DNSSEC Bootstrapping Using Authenticated Signals from the Zone's Operator
RFC9615.summary: RFC 9615 defines an in-band mechanism where a child DNS operator publishes authenticated CDS/CDNSKEY signals under _signal names in its nameservers' signed zones, letting parents securely bootstrap DNSSEC DS records, and it updates RFC 7344 and RFC 8078 guidance.

DNSSEC.why: The document specifies authenticated DNSSEC bootstrapping of delegations via CDS/CDNSKEY validated through the signaling zone's chain of trust, and updates RFC 7344, so it is about DNSSEC.
DNSSEC.quote: The mechanism allows managed DNS operators to securely announce DNSSEC key parameters for zones under their management

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific tag and already implies DNS as its ancestor.
Registries and registrars appear as parental agents, but the document defines a DNS-level signalling mechanism, not registry protocols.
Not mentioned or specified; DS provisioning by the parental agent is left to local means.
The only IANA action is adding _signal entries to the underscored node names registry, which is boilerplate.

RFC9616.title: Delay-Based Metric Extension for the Babel Routing Protocol
RFC9616.summary: Defines a Babel routing protocol extension adding Timestamp sub-TLVs to Hello and IHU TLVs for RTT measurement, plus a smoothing, cost-mapping and hysteresis algorithm for delay-based route selection.

Babel.why: The document extends the Babel protocol with a new sub-TLV and a delay-based metric computation for route selection.
Babel.quote: This document defines an extension to the Babel routing protocol that measures the round-trip time (RTT) between routers and makes it possible to prefer lower-latency links

rejected.why: Mills' RTT algorithm is borrowed from HELLO/NTP, but the document does not specify or extend NTP and does not address clock synchronisation.
RTT sampling is a means for route metric computation within Babel, not a general performance measurement method.
The only IANA content is a routine sub-TLV registration, which is boilerplate.
TCP is mentioned only as an upper-layer protocol affected by packet reordering.

RFC9617.title: A YANG Data Model for In Situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM)
RFC9617.summary: Defines the ietf-ioam YANG module for configuring In Situ OAM (IOAM) profiles (incremental/pre-allocated trace, direct export, proof of transit, edge-to-edge) on network nodes.

YANG.why: The document's core deliverable is a YANG module (ietf-ioam) with tree diagrams and NETCONF configuration examples.
YANG.quote: This document defines a data model for the configuration of IOAM capabilities using the YANG data modeling language [RFC7950].

OAM.why: The document is about configuring IOAM, an OAM and telemetry mechanism. No IOAM-specific tag exists, so the OAM topic is the best fit.
OAM.quote: In situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM) is an example of an on-path hybrid measurement method.

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the protocol used to carry the configuration in examples and the Security Considerations. The document does not specify it.
IOAM produces telemetry data, but this document only configures profiles. OAM is the more fitting tag.
The NSH is only one carrier for IOAM data, referenced as an option. The document is not about service function chaining.
IPv6 is only a carrier protocol selectable by the protocol-type leaf, not the subject of the document.
IOAM is a hybrid measurement method, but the document only supplies configuration. The OAM tag covers it.

gaps.name: IOAM (In situ OAM)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IOAM itself. The IOAM family of RFCs (data fields, direct export, IPv6 options, NSH encapsulation, this YANG model) would benefit from a dedicated tag.

RFC9618.title: Updates to X.509 Policy Validation
RFC9618.summary: Updates RFC 5280 to replace the exponential X.509 certificate policy tree validation algorithm with a linear-size policy graph, and describes other mitigations for the resulting denial-of-service vulnerability.

X.509.why: The document revises the RFC 5280 certification path policy validation procedure, the core X.509 profile, so readers of X.509 should find it.
X.509.quote: This document updates RFC 5280 to replace the algorithm for X.509 policy validation with an equivalent, more efficient algorithm.

rejected.why: TLS is only mentioned as an example of an application performing client certificate validation; the document is not about TLS.
Parent of X.509, implied by the more specific X.509 tag.
The DoS mitigations are discussed but are specific to X.509 path validation; the X.509 tag covers this.

RFC9619.title: In the DNS, QDCOUNT Is (Usually) One
RFC9619.summary: Updates RFC 1035 to forbid QDCOUNT greater than 1 in DNS messages with OPCODE 0 (QUERY), requiring FORMERR for such messages and guiding middleboxes on handling them.

DNS.why: The document changes core DNS message semantics, updating RFC 1035 and specifying server, resolver and middlebox behaviour for QDCOUNT in queries.
DNS.quote: A DNS message with OPCODE = 0 MUST NOT include a QDCOUNT parameter whose value is greater than 1.

rejected.why: EDNS is not discussed; DNS Cookies appear only as an example of QDCOUNT = 0 in the appendix.
UPDATE's ZOCOUNT is summarised in the appendix as background only, and the document does not change it.
Middlebox guidance is a single paragraph and the document is about DNS message format, not firewalls.

RFC9620.title: Guidelines for Human Rights Protocol and Architecture Considerations
RFC9620.summary: RFC 9620 is an IRTF HRPC research group document, updating RFC 8280, that gives protocol developers a questionnaire and review methods for assessing how protocol and architecture design choices affect human rights.

privacy.why: Privacy, confidentiality, anonymity, pseudonymity and unlinkability make up a substantial part of the guidelines, and the document is modelled on RFC 6973. Readers of the privacy subject would want it.
privacy.quote: Did you have a look at the guidelines described in Section 7 of "Privacy Considerations for Internet Protocols" [RFC6973]?

internet architecture.why: The document gives architectural design guidance on end-to-end intermediaries, heterogeneity, decentralization, adaptability and open standards, and assesses how these affect human rights. No narrower taxonomy tag covers human rights considerations.
internet architecture.quote: It provides questions that engineers should ask themselves when developing or improving protocols if they want to understand how their decisions can potentially influence the exercise of human rights

rejected.why: Security is one question among many in the guidelines and is not the document's main subject. The privacy tag covers the confidentiality-related material.
DNS is used only as an example of plaintext metadata that enables censorship or surveillance. The document does not specify or analyse it.
TLS, ECH and SNI appear only as examples of protecting metadata from intermediaries.
Sections 4.5 and 4.6 are single questions in a long questionnaire. The document is not about internationalization of text in protocols.
Accessibility is one short guideline (4.18) among about twenty, so it is not a substantial part of the document.
The document covers how to conduct human rights reviews of Internet-Drafts, but its focus is protocol design guidance rather than IETF procedures.

gaps.name: human rights considerations
gaps.why: The document is about human rights impacts of protocols and architectures, and the taxonomy has no human rights or societal-impact tag. Readers looking for HRPC work and review guidelines would need one.

gaps.name: censorship resistance
gaps.why: The document gives a guideline on censorship resistance and cites censorship surveys, but the taxonomy has no censorship or filtering tag.

RFC9621.title: Architecture and Requirements for Transport Services
RFC9621.summary: RFC 9621 defines the architecture, terminology and requirements for a Transport Services system: an asynchronous, message-based API and an implementation that gathers and races candidate paths and protocol stacks.

TAPS.why: The whole document specifies the TAPS architecture, its concepts (Preconnection, Connection, Framer, racing) and requirements for the API and implementation.
TAPS.quote: This document describes an architecture that exposes transport protocol features to applications for network communication.

rejected.why: TCP is one of several protocols the architecture abstracts over. The document does not specify or extend it.
QUIC is only mentioned as an example protocol stack and a possible future mapping.
TLS is the security substrate for Security Parameters. The document defines nothing new about it.
Happy Eyeballs is cited only as the origin of the term 'racing'. The document is not about it.
The Socket API is the contrast model that TAPS replaces. The document does not extend it.
ICE and STUN are only mentioned as influences on how Rendezvous works.

RFC9622.title: An Abstract Application Programming Interface (API) for Transport Services
RFC9622.summary: RFC 9622 specifies the abstract Transport Services API, an asynchronous, message-oriented, protocol-independent interface to the transport layer meant to replace BSD sockets, covering preconnections, endpoints, transport and security properties, connection establishment, data transfer and termination.

TAPS.why: The document is the normative Transport Services API specification, which is exactly what the TAPS tag covers.
TAPS.quote: This document describes an abstract Application Programming Interface (API) to the transport layer that enables the selection of transport protocols and network paths dynamically at runtime.

rejected.why: TCP is only one possible protocol the API maps onto. The TCP User Timeout properties are a small section, not a main subject.
The API is intended to replace BSD sockets, but it does not extend or specify the sockets API.
TLS appears only as a security mechanism configured through Security Parameters, and the document defines nothing new about TLS.
STUN, TURN and ICE are used only for Rendezvous candidate gathering, and the document does not specify them.
QUIC appears only as an example protocol in protocol-specific endpoints and stream cloning.
Multicast endpoints get a short subsection, but the document is not about multicast routing or deployment.

RFC9623.title: Implementing Interfaces to Transport Services
RFC9623.summary: RFC 9623 is an informational implementation guide for Transport Services Systems that provide the TAPS API, covering connection establishment (candidate gathering and racing), listeners, message framers, sending/receiving, path changes, cached state, and mappings for TCP, MPTCP, UDP, UDP-Lite and SCTP.

TAPS.why: The whole document is an implementation guide for the Transport Services System and its API (preestablishment, racing, framers, caching).
TAPS.quote: This document serves as a guide to implementing a system that provides a Transport Services API.

SCTP.why: A substantial section specifies SCTP's API mapping, including stream mapping, reconfiguration and stream-id assignment.
SCTP.quote: Connection objects can be mapped to an SCTP association or a stream in an SCTP association.

TCP.why: Detailed TCP mapping, plus TFO 0-RTT handling, in the protocol considerations section.
TCP.quote: TCP connections between two hosts map directly to Connection objects.

UDP.why: Mappings for UDP and UDP multicast receive are specified, along with connectionless handling.
UDP.quote: UDP connections represent a pair of specific IP addresses and ports on two hosts.

happy eyeballs.why: Candidate racing is built on Happy Eyeballs-style staggered racing across paths, protocols and endpoints.
happy eyeballs.quote: Staggered racing between IP addresses for a generic Connection should follow the Happy Eyeballs algorithm described in [RFC8305].

MPTCP.why: Has its own mapping subsection and path-change handling for multipath.
MPTCP.quote: The Transport Services API mappings for MPTCP are identical to TCP.

UDP-Lite.why: Own mapping subsection covering checksum coverage properties.
UDP-Lite.quote: The Transport Services API mappings for UDP-Lite are identical to UDP.

rejected.why: DNS resolution is used for endpoint derivation and caching but the document does not specify or extend DNS.
TLS appears as a layered protocol and for 0-RTT tickets, but is only a substrate here.
ICE is referenced for candidate gathering analogies, not specified or extended.
The protocol mapping sections are covered by the more specific TAPS and protocol tags.
QUIC is only mentioned as an example in protocol racing trees.
SOCKS and HTTP proxies appear only as protocol-option examples.

RFC9624.title: EVPN Broadcast, Unknown Unicast, or Multicast (BUM) Using Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER)
RFC9624.summary: Specifies how to use BIER as provider tunnels for EVPN BUM traffic, covering PMSI Tunnel Attribute encoding, explicit tracking, split horizon for multihoming, and BIER encapsulation/disposition for EVPN-MPLS and EVPN-VXLAN/NVGRE/GENEVE.

EVPN.why: The document defines EVPN BUM procedures (IMET/SMET routes, PTA, split horizon, ESI labels) using BIER tunnels.
EVPN.quote: this document specifies the protocols and procedures to use Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER) [RFC8279] as provider tunnels for EVPN BUM traffic.

BIER.why: The document specifies BIER as the tunnel type for EVPN: PTA encoding, BFIR/BFER procedures, BIER header Proto values and IANA registrations.
BIER.quote: BIER is an architecture that provides optimal multicast forwarding through a "multicast domain" without requiring intermediate routers to maintain any per-flow state

rejected.why: The document is closely aligned with MVPN-BIER (RFC 8556) and reuses its procedures, but it is about EVPN, not MVPN.
VXLAN, NVGRE and GENEVE are payload encapsulations carried over BIER. The document does not define or change them.
BGP carries the EVPN routes and the PTA, but it is the substrate. The document defines no new BGP protocol behaviour.
EVPN-MPLS labels are used, but MPLS is not the subject.
The IANA section registers BIER next-protocol values and multicast addresses. This is boilerplate and not what the document is about.

gaps.name: EVPN (Ethernet VPN)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists EVPN under VPN, but the id I used is not confirmed as written there. The only matching id I could find is 'EVPN' under VPN, so please verify it.

RFC9625.title: EVPN Optimized Inter-Subnet Multicast (OISM) Forwarding
RFC9625.summary: RFC 9625 specifies EVPN OISM procedures for routing inter-subnet IP multicast among a tenant's broadcast domains, using a Supplementary Broadcast Domain, SMET/IMET routes, interworking with non-OISM PEs, and gateways to external MVPN/PIM domains.

EVPN.why: The whole document extends EVPN with OISM multicast procedures (SBD, SMET/IMET routes, IRB semantics).
EVPN.quote: This document specifies new procedures that allow inter-subnet IP multicast traffic to be routed among the LANs of a given tenant

MVPN.why: A substantial part defines the MEG gateway and MVPN/EVPN interworking.
MVPN.quote: we specify the procedures necessary to allow EVPN PEs running OISM procedures to interwork with L3VPN PEs that run BGP-based MVPN [RFC6514] procedures

PIM-SM.why: Defines PEG procedures and transit use with PIM, including FHR/RP/DR behaviour.
PIM-SM.quote: the interworking between the PIM domain and the EVPN Tenant Domain is done at L3 Gateways that perform PIM/EVPN Gateway (PEG) functionality

rejected.why: BGP routes and extended communities carry the EVPN signalling but the document does not specify BGP itself.
BIER is only one of the tunnel types for which labels are described; the BIER-EVPN details are in RFC 9624.
IGMP/MLD snooping and reports are inputs to the SMET procedures. They are defined elsewhere (RFC 9251).
MPLS labels are used for tunnel encapsulation only.
The multicast topic is implied by the more specific tags and the document is about EVPN-specific multicast.

gaps.name: EVPN (Ethernet VPN)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no EVPN tag in the 'EVPN' form under VPN. The tag id used above does not exist in the taxonomy. The closest fit is EVPN under VPN, and it is the main subject of the document.

gaps.name: MVPN
gaps.why: The taxonomy's MVPN tag exists under VPN, but the document's EVPN subject has no more specific tag for EVPN multicast optimizations.

RFC9626.title: Video Frame Marking RTP Header Extension
RFC9626.summary: Defines an RTP header extension carrying video frame marking metadata (start/end, independent, discardable, layer IDs) so RTP switches can forward or drop video frames codec-agnostically without decrypting SRTP payloads.

RTP.why: The document specifies a new RTP header extension (using RFC 8285 mechanism), its formats, signalling URI and usage by RTP switches. RTP itself is the protocol being extended.
RTP.quote: This document describes a Video Frame Marking RTP header extension used to convey information about video frames that is critical for error recovery and packet forwarding

RTP payload format.why: A substantial part defines mappings of the extension fields to VP8, VP9, H.264, SVC and H.265 RTP payload descriptors and NAL headers, which payload-format readers need.
RTP payload format.quote: This section maps the specific Layer ID (LID) information contained in specific scalable codecs to the generic LID and TID fields.

rejected.why: SRTP encryption is the motivating context and is discussed in security considerations, but the document does not specify or extend SRTP.
Only an extmap attribute example is given for signalling; SDP is a substrate here.
LRR and FIR are mentioned only in usage considerations; the document does not define RTCP behaviour.
Codec-specific mappings are included, but the document does not define codecs; the RTP payload format tag fits better.
H.264 is only one of several codec mappings, not the subject.
VP9 is only one of several codec mappings, not the subject.

RFC9627.title: The Layer Refresh Request (LRR) RTCP Feedback Message
RFC9627.summary: Defines the RTCP payload-specific feedback message Layer Refresh Request (LRR), which lets a receiver ask a sender to refresh specific substreams of a layered/scalable media stream, with codec-specific usage for H.264 SVC, VP8 and H.265 and an SDP "lrr" ccm parameter.

RTCP.why: The document defines a new RTCP PSFB feedback message (FMT=10) with its FCI format and semantics, extending RTCP feedback.
RTCP.quote: This memo describes the RTCP Payload-Specific Feedback Message Layer Refresh Request (LRR), which can be used to request a state refresh of one or more substreams

RTP payload format.why: Section 4 specifies layer index field formats and refresh-point identification for the H.264 SVC, VP8 and H.265 RTP payload formats.
RTP payload format.quote: This document also defines its use with several RTP payloads for scalable media formats.

rejected.why: The SDP change is just a small ccm parameter ('lrr') added to existing RFC 5104 procedures; SDP is a substrate here.
H.264 SVC is only one of three codecs for which layer index fields are defined; the document is not about the codec itself.
VP8 is only one example codec for layer index mapping; the document is not about the VP8 codec or payload.
H.265 is one of the codecs with usage defined, not the subject of the document.
RTP is the underlying protocol; the document is specifically about an RTCP feedback message, which the RTCP tag covers.
The document does not define codecs; it uses codec scalability features as context for the feedback message.

RFC9628.title: RTP Payload Format for VP9 Video
RFC9628.summary: Defines the RTP payload format for VP9 video, including the payload descriptor, scalability structure for temporal/spatial layers, RTCP feedback usage (RPSI, FIR, LRR), SDP parameters, and the video/vp9 media type registration.

VP9.why: The document specifies the RTP packetization and scalability signalling for the VP9 codec, so VP9 readers would look for it.
VP9.quote: This document describes an RTP [RFC3550] payload specification applicable to the transmission of video streams encoded using the VP9 video codec [VP9-BITSTREAM].

RTP payload format.why: It is an RTP payload format specification, with a payload descriptor, header usage, fragmentation, and media type registration.
RTP payload format.quote: This section describes how the encoded VP9 bitstream is encapsulated in RTP.

RTCP.why: A substantial section defines how RTCP feedback messages (RPSI, FIR, LRR) apply to VP9, including the LRR index format.
RTCP.quote: The Layer Refresh Request (LRR) [RFC9627] allows a receiver to request a single layer of a spatially or temporally encoded stream to be refreshed

SDP.why: It defines the SDP mapping and offer/answer rules for the payload format's parameters (max-fr, max-fs, profile-id).
SDP.quote: The media type video/vp9 string is mapped to fields in the Session Description Protocol (SDP) [RFC8866] as follows:
SDP.section: 6.1.1. Mapping of Media Subtype Parameters to SDP

rejected.why: The media type registration is standard boilerplate for an RTP payload format, not the main subject.
VP8 is mentioned only as VP9's predecessor.
SRTP appears only in the Security Considerations as a possible profile.
VP9 is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
The Congestion Control section is short and points to the general RTP rules.

RFC9629.title: Using Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) Algorithms in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC9629.summary: Defines KEMRecipientInfo and conventions for using Key Encapsulation Mechanism algorithms (including quantum-secure ones) to establish keys for CMS enveloped-data, authenticated-data and authenticated-enveloped-data content, updating RFC 5652.

CMS.why: The document extends CMS with a new KEMRecipientInfo recipient type and updates RFC 5652.
CMS.quote: This document defines conventions for the use of KEM algorithms for the CMS enveloped-data content type and the CMS authenticated-enveloped-data content type.

key management.why: A substantial part covers KEM-based key establishment, KDF derivation of the KEK, and wrapping of the CEK. Key establishment is the subject of this tag.
key management.quote: A KEM algorithm is a one-pass (store-and-forward) mechanism for transporting random keying material to a recipient using the recipient's public key.

rejected.why: KEMs, including quantum-secure ones, are the motivation, but the document is generic and specifies no post-quantum algorithm.
The ASN.1 modules are the means of specifying the structures. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
Certificates carry the recipient's public key, but this is only a supporting mechanism.
ML-KEM is not mentioned or specified in this document.

gaps.name: Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no generic KEM tag outside the post-quantum branch, so KEM usage in protocols is only partly covered by key management.

RFC9630.title: Multicast On-Path Telemetry Using In Situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM)
RFC9630.summary: Specifies two IOAM-based on-path telemetry solutions for multicast traffic: a Multicast Branch ID extension to the IOAM DEX option header, and per-section postcards for the IOAM trace option, to reconstruct multicast trees without redundant data.

multicast.why: The document is about telemetry of multicast traffic and multicast tree reconstruction, and discusses PIM, Mtrace2 and MVPN applications. No narrower multicast tag fits the subject.
multicast.quote: This document specifies two solutions to meet the requirements of on-path telemetry for multicast traffic using IOAM.

telemetry.why: It specifies on-path network telemetry using IOAM trace and direct export, including postcard-based export of data. It extends the DEX option header to carry a branch identifier.
telemetry.quote: The requirements for multicast traffic telemetry that are addressed by the solutions in this document are:

OAM.why: IOAM (In situ OAM) is the mechanism being extended. The document also compares it with conventional multicast OAM such as multicast ping and mtrace.
OAM.quote: complement existing active OAM performance monitoring methods like ICMP ping

rejected.why: PIM is discussed only as the multicast tree-building protocol that the telemetry must work with. The document does not specify or extend it.
Mtrace2 is described as existing OAM, and the document says it does not integrate with IOAM directly.
This is not a taxonomy id. MVPN procedures are mentioned only to say the telemetry applies to them, with no specification of MVPN itself.
RFC 9486 is only cited as the IPv6 encapsulation for IOAM. The document does not address IPv6.
Delay, jitter and loss gathering are stated requirements. The document's focus is the telemetry data export mechanism, which the telemetry tag covers.

gaps.name: IOAM (In situ OAM)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no IOAM-specific tech tag. The document extends IOAM DEX and trace options, so the broad telemetry and OAM tags are used instead.

RFC9631.title: The IPv6 Compact Routing Header (CRH)
RFC9631.summary: Defines an experiment with two new IPv6 Routing header types, CRH-16 and CRH-32, which carry compact lists of segment identifiers that index a local CRH-FIB for source routing, with processing rules, ACL-based security mitigations and experiment goals.

IPv6.why: The document specifies new IPv6 Routing header types, their format, processing rules, and IANA Routing Type registrations. It is an IPv6 extension header specification.
IPv6.quote: This document defines two new Routing Types.  Collectively, they are called the Compact Routing Header (CRH).  Individually, they are called CRH-16 and CRH-32.

rejected.why: The CRH is similar in spirit, with SIDs and source routing, but the document never frames itself as segment routing. It defines its own FIB-indexed SID scheme.
ICMPv6 Parameter Problem messages are used in the processing rules, but only as an error signal. The document adds nothing new to ICMP.
PCEP is mentioned only as one possible way to populate the CRH-FIB, and the document explicitly says this is out of scope.
The security considerations cover ACLs and EFP-uRPF against untrusted Routing headers, but this is a small part of the document and fits better under the IPv6 header itself.
AH compatibility is mentioned in one sentence only.
PING, Traceroute and Wireshark support is touched on briefly under operational considerations and experimental questions, not as a main subject.

gaps.name: IPv6 extension headers / Routing header
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific tag for IPv6 Routing headers or extension headers. IPv6 is the closest fit but is broader than the subject.

RFC9632.title: Finding and Using Geofeed Data
RFC9632.summary: Specifies how to locate geofeed (RFC 8805) files via a geofeed: attribute or remarks: entry in RPSL inetnum: objects, how to fetch them, and an optional RPKI-based CMS signature to authenticate them; obsoletes RFC 9092.

RPSL.why: The core of the document is extending the RPSL inetnum: class with a geofeed: attribute and a remarks: convention, and rules for choosing among inetnum: objects.
RPSL.quote: specifies how to augment the Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL) [RFC2725] inetnum: class to refer specifically to geofeed data files

RPKI.why: A substantial section defines an RPKI-based signed object (CMS, one-time-use EE certificate, validation steps, new OID) to authenticate geofeed files.
RPKI.quote: It is a digest of the main body of the file signed by the private key of the relevant RPKI certificate for a covering address range.

geolocation.why: The document is about discovering and using IP geolocation feed data, including its privacy considerations.
geolocation.quote: [RFC8805] defines geofeed, a syntax to associate geographic locales with IP addresses, but it does not specify how to find the relevant geofeed data

rejected.why: CMS is only the signature container used for the authenticator, not the subject.
WHOIS and FTP are only used to collect inetnum: objects; the document does not specify them.
RDAP is mentioned only as a not-for-bulk alternative with a separate draft.
HTTPS is only the transport for fetching geofeed files.
Geofeed files are CSV, but the CSV format is defined by RFC 8805, not here.
The RPKI certificate profile is used, not defined, so X.509 is not a subject.

RFC9633.title: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) YANG Data Model
RFC9633.summary: Defines the ietf-detnet YANG module for configuring DetNet flows (app-flow, service sub-layer, forwarding sub-layer, aggregation) and reporting their operational status without a signaling protocol.

DetNet.why: The whole document models DetNet flows, sub-layers, aggregation, and PREOF service protection.
DetNet.quote: This document contains the specification for the Deterministic Networking (DetNet) YANG data model for configuration and operational data for DetNet flows.

YANG.why: The deliverable is a YANG module (ietf-detnet) with tree diagrams and JSON/XML instance examples.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model for DetNet based on YANG data types and modeling language defined in [RFC6991] and [RFC7950].

rejected.why: DetNet MPLS data plane labels are configured in the model, but the document is not about MPLS itself.
Mentioned only as a way to access the module, in Security Considerations.
Used only as the encoding of examples.
The model carries traffic profiles but does not specify TE mechanisms; resource reservation is out of scope.
TSN/Ethernet headers are used only as app-flow match fields.

RFC9634.title: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) for Deterministic Networking (DetNet) with the IP Data Plane
RFC9634.summary: Informational document describing how existing IP OAM protocols (ICMP, BFD, STAMP, Y.1731 over GRE-in-UDP) can be applied in DetNet networks with the IP data plane so OAM packets share the monitored flow's path and treatment.

DetNet.why: The whole document is about OAM in DetNet IP data-plane networks, including mapping OAM to DetNet flows and PREOF encapsulation.
DetNet.quote: This document discusses the use of existing IP Operations, Administration, and Maintenance protocols and mechanisms in Deterministic Networking networks that use the IP data plane.

OAM.why: The document is about applying active OAM mechanisms (failure detection, localization, performance monitoring) and OAM interworking.
OAM.quote: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) protocols are used to detect and localize defects in the network as well as to monitor network performance.

BFD.why: BFD is one of the main existing OAM tools analysed for failure detection of DetNet IP flows, including its UDP port and flow mapping.
BFD.quote: Active IP OAM protocols like Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) [RFC5880] or the Simple Two-way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP) [RFC8762] use UDP transport
BFD.section: 3. Active OAM for DetNet Networks with the IP Data Plane

STAMP.why: STAMP is the performance measurement tool discussed for DetNet IP flows.
STAMP.quote: IP OAM protocols are used to detect failures (e.g., BFD [RFC5880]) and performance degradation (e.g., STAMP [RFC8762]) that affect an IP DetNet flow.
STAMP.section: 3.1. Mapping Active OAM and IP DetNet Flows

ICMP.why: ICMP use for on-demand failure detection in DetNet and the need to give it the same treatment as the monitored flow is a substantive part of the document.
ICMP.quote: the majority of on-demand failure detection and localization is achieved through the use of ICMP, utilizing Echo Request and Echo Reply messages
ICMP.section: 3. Active OAM for DetNet Networks with the IP Data Plane

rejected.why: GRE-in-UDP is only a carrier for Y.1731 OAM in one subsection, not specified or extended.
UDP is the substrate for OAM and tunnels, not the subject.
Multipath hashing is mentioned briefly for co-routedness but is not a subject of the document.
Only a brief note that traceroute may need modification with IP/UDP tunnels.
MPLS-over-UDP is referenced for PREOF encapsulation and interworking, but the document concerns the IP data plane.
RFC 9633 is cited for provisioning information, but the document is not about YANG.

RFC9635.title: Grant Negotiation and Authorization Protocol (GNAP)
RFC9635.summary: RFC 9635 specifies GNAP, a protocol by which a client instance negotiates delegated authorization (access tokens and subject information) from an authorization server, with interaction, continuation, token management, key proofing and discovery.

GNAP.why: The document is the core GNAP specification, defining requests, responses, interaction, continuation and token management.
GNAP.quote: The Grant Negotiation and Authorization Protocol (GNAP) defines a mechanism for delegating authorization to a piece of software

rejected.why: GNAP is explicitly not an OAuth extension; OAuth is only compared and mapped to, so the document is not about OAuth.
JWS and JWK are used as key formats and proofing methods, but JOSE itself is not specified or extended.
HTTP is the substrate; the document uses HTTP methods and the Authorization header but does not extend HTTP semantics.
The OpenID Connect ID Token is only one of the supported assertion formats, and JWT is not specified.
JSON is the message encoding only.

RFC9636.title: The Time Zone Information Format (TZif)
RFC9636.summary: Specifies the binary Time Zone Information Format (TZif) used to represent and exchange time zone data, obsoleting RFC 8536, defines version 4, and registers the application/tzif and application/tzif-leap media types, including use with TZDIST.

time zones.why: The whole document defines a time zone data format, with header, data block, footer, leap seconds, and truncation. This matches the time zones tag directly.
time zones.quote: This document specifies the Time Zone Information Format (TZif) for representing and exchanging time zone information, independent of any particular service or protocol.

media types.why: Registers application/tzif and application/tzif-leap, and the interoperability text says when to use each in MIME entities. This is a substantial part of the document.
media types.quote: This document defines two media types [RFC6838] for the exchange of data utilizing the Time Zone Information Format.

rejected.why: The TZDIST example uses HTTP only as a substrate and the document defines nothing new about HTTP.
iCalendar is mentioned only as another time zone format in the introduction. TZif is not specified for or within it.
TLS is only cited in Security and Privacy Considerations as protection for data in transit.
The document defines a binary time zone and leap-second representation, not textual timestamp formats.
The document covers time zone and leap-second data, not clock synchronization over networks.

gaps.name: Time Zone Data Distribution Service (TZDIST)
gaps.why: Section 6 profiles TZDIST for serving TZif data, but the taxonomy has no TZDIST tag. The time zones tag covers the topic only partly.

RFC9637.title: Expanding the IPv6 Documentation Space
RFC9637.summary: RFC 9637 reserves the additional IPv6 documentation prefix 3fff::/20, updating RFC 3849, and gives filtering guidance for it.

addressing.why: The document is about reserving and using an IPv6 address block, including allocation-size data and filtering. It is IP address architecture and allocation, so the addressing topic fits.
addressing.quote: The document describes the reservation of an additional IPv6 address prefix for use in documentation.

IPv6.why: The document concerns IPv6 address space and its deployment scale, so IPv6 readers would want it.
IPv6.quote: The reservation of a /20 IPv6 address prefix from the Global Unicast Address pool [RFC4291] for documentation purposes allows such conflicts to be avoided.

rejected.why: The IANA registry entry is only the registration of the new prefix. It is boilerplate-level here and the document is not about IANA registry stewardship.
The filtering of bogons in routing advertisements is mentioned only briefly. The document does not specify or analyse BGP.
The bogon filtering advice is a short note in the main body and in Security Considerations. It is not a substantial subject of the document.

RFC9638.title: Network Virtualization over Layer 3 (NVO3) Encapsulation Considerations
RFC9638.summary: Informational record of the NVO3 WG's considerations comparing the Geneve, GUE and VXLAN-GPE encapsulations, concluding that Geneve with modifications is the common NVO3 encapsulation.

Geneve.why: The document's recommendation is Geneve plus recommended enhancements (option TLV handling, C bit, option length, security options), so Geneve readers need it.
Geneve.quote: the NVO3 Working Group determined that Generic Network Virtualization Encapsulation (Geneve) with a few modifications is the common encapsulation

overlay networks.why: It compares data-plane network virtualization overlay encapsulations (Geneve, GUE, VXLAN-GPE, with VXLAN and NVGRE as context). This is the parent topic for the general encapsulation considerations.
overlay networks.quote: develop solutions for network virtualization data planes based on encapsulation of virtual network traffic over an IP-based underlay data plane

rejected.why: VXLAN-GPE and VXLAN are compared as candidates or background, but the document does not specify or extend VXLAN itself.
EVPN is mentioned only as an example control plane that should signal supported extensions.
NSH is discussed only as a possible extension mechanism and rejected as less suitable for network virtualization.
UDP is only the outer transport for all the encapsulations.
In-band telemetry is one use case for extensions, not a main subject.
ECMP is a design requirement mentioned in passing, not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: GUE / VXLAN-GPE encapsulations
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tags for Generic UDP Encapsulation or VXLAN-GPE, which are compared in depth.

RFC9639.title: Free Lossless Audio Codec (FLAC)
RFC9639.summary: Specifies the FLAC lossless audio codec format, its streamable subset, metadata blocks, frame structure, and Ogg/Matroska/MP4 container mappings, and registers the audio/flac media type and an application-ID registry.

codecs.why: The document is the specification of an audio codec. No FLAC-specific tag exists, so the generic codecs tag fits best.
codecs.quote: This document defines the Free Lossless Audio Codec (FLAC) format and its streamable subset.

Ogg.why: It defines how FLAC is mapped into Ogg: the header packet layout, granule positions and chaining. Readers of the Ogg subject would want this.
Ogg.quote: The first packet of a logical bitstream carrying FLAC data is structured according to the following table.

Matroska.why: It defines the FLAC-in-Matroska mapping, including the codec ID and CodecPrivate contents.
Matroska.quote: The codec ID (EBML path \Segment\Tracks\TrackEntry\CodecID) assigned to signal tracks carrying FLAC data is A_FLAC in ASCII.

media types.why: It registers the audio/flac media type, including the deprecated alias audio/x-flac. It also creates a new registry of application block IDs.
media types.quote: IANA has registered the "audio/flac" media type as follows.

rejected.why: MD5 is only used to checksum the unencoded audio in streaminfo. The document does not specify or analyse MD5.
The frame header and footer CRCs are fixed parts of the format. The document does not discuss the choice of CRC polynomials.
The coded number borrows a UTF-8-like variable-length code, and Vorbis comments are UTF-8. UTF-8 is only a mechanism here.
Vorbis comments are reused as the metadata format, but the document is not about the Vorbis codec.
The taxonomy's compression topic covers general-purpose lossless data compression formats. FLAC is a domain-specific audio codec, so codecs is the better fit.
The picture block may hold a URI per RFC 3986. This is incidental and the document defines nothing new about URIs.

gaps.name: FLAC (lossless audio coding)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no FLAC tag under codecs, even though it has tags for other individual codecs such as Opus, Vorbis and G.711. A FLAC tag would let readers find this specification directly.

RFC9640.title: YANG Data Types and Groupings for Cryptography
RFC9640.summary: Defines the YANG 1.1 module ietf-crypto-types with identities, typedefs and groupings for keys, certificates, passwords, encrypted values, CSR generation and certificate-expiration notification, used by NETCONF/RESTCONF client-server configuration models.

YANG.why: The document is a YANG module defining reusable types and groupings for cryptographic data, so YANG modelling readers would look for it.
YANG.quote: This document presents a YANG 1.1 (RFC 7950) module defining identities, typedefs, and groupings useful to cryptographic applications.

key management.why: Substantial parts model configuring symmetric, private and public keys, hidden/cleartext/encrypted key storage, and encrypting keys with other keys.
key management.quote: The "password-grouping" enables the configuration of credentials needed to authenticate to a remote system.

rejected.why: The module is part of a family supporting NETCONF/RESTCONF configuration, but it only defines groupings; NETCONF is the context, not the subject.
CMS structures are used as encodings for certificates and encrypted values, but the document does not specify or extend CMS.
X.509 certificates and CSRs are referenced as binary typedef contents; the document does not profile certificates.
DER-encoded ASN.1 structures are just the encoding wrapped by typedefs.
Certificate and CSR handling is modelled only as configuration data; no PKI procedures are defined.
No algorithms are specified; the document deals with data formats and configuration containers for crypto material.

RFC9641.title: A YANG Data Model for a Truststore
RFC9641.summary: Defines the ietf-truststore YANG module for configuring named bags of certificates and public keys as trust anchors, with groupings for inline or referenced use and certificate-expiration notifications.

YANG.why: The RFC specifies a YANG module (ietf-truststore) with typedefs, groupings and protocol-accessible nodes, so it belongs on the YANG page.
YANG.quote: This document presents a YANG module for configuring bags of certificates and bags of public keys that can be referenced by other data models for trust.

rejected.why: The module is used by NETCONF/RESTCONF clients and servers, but the document only defines a data model. NETCONF is the management protocol that accesses it.
Trust anchors and certificates are the content being stored. The document does not specify PKI mechanisms.
Certificates are held as CMS structures. The document does not profile X.509.
CMS is only the encoding of cert-data, defined in RFC 9640, not here.
Mentioned only as an alternative access protocol for the module.
SSH public keys appear in examples and SSH is cited only in Security Considerations. The document is not about SSH.

RFC9642.title: A YANG Data Model for a Keystore
RFC9642.summary: Defines the "ietf-keystore" YANG module for centralized configuration of symmetric and asymmetric keys (cleartext, hidden or encrypted), associated certificates with expiration notifications, inline-or-keystore groupings, built-in keys, and key-encryption-key guidance.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module and its groupings, typedefs and tree diagrams, so YANG data modelling is its subject.
YANG.quote: This document presents a YANG 1.1 [RFC7950] module called "ietf-keystore" that enables centralized configuration of both symmetric and asymmetric keys.

key management.why: It addresses storage and provisioning of keys, built-in keys, key-encryption keys and migrating encrypted keys between servers.
key management.quote: The term "keystore" is defined in this document as a mechanism that intends to safeguard secrets.

rejected.why: NETCONF is the management protocol the module is accessed through. The document does not specify or extend it.
Certificates are associated with keys and carried as data, but the document does not profile or specify them.
Certificates and CSR generation appear, but only as nodes in the key store model, not as PKI operations.
The document is about key storage and configuration, not algorithms or their use. Key management covers that part.
TLS is mentioned only as a secure transport in the Security Considerations boilerplate.
SSH is mentioned only as a secure transport in the Security Considerations boilerplate.

RFC9643.title: YANG Groupings for TCP Clients and TCP Servers
RFC9643.summary: Defines three YANG 1.1 modules (ietf-tcp-common, ietf-tcp-client, ietf-tcp-server) with reusable groupings for configuring TCP clients and servers: addresses/ports, keepalives, and SOCKS proxy traversal.

YANG.why: The document's core content is YANG modules and groupings for TCP client/server configuration.
YANG.quote: This document defines three YANG 1.1 [RFC7950] modules to support the configuration of TCP clients and TCP servers

TCP.why: Models TCP connection parameters and gives guidance on configuring TCP keepalives, which TCP readers would want.
TCP.quote: The base YANG data model in this document focuses on modeling TCP keepalives.

SOCKS.why: The client module models SOCKS4, SOCKS4a and SOCKS5 proxy configuration, including SOCKS5 authentication.
SOCKS.quote: The "socks5-supported" feature indicates the TCP client supports Socks5-based proxies.

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the management protocol these modules are used with; the document does not specify it.
Referenced only as a higher-level protocol whose configuration builds on these groupings, and in Security Considerations.
Mentioned as a higher-layer user of the groupings and in boilerplate security text only.
Used only for examples.

RFC9644.title: YANG Groupings for SSH Clients and SSH Servers
RFC9644.summary: Defines YANG modules (ietf-ssh-common, ietf-ssh-client, ietf-ssh-server) with reusable groupings for configuring SSH clients and servers, plus a script for generating four IANA-maintained SSH algorithm YANG modules.

YANG.why: The document's main deliverable is a set of YANG modules and groupings for SSH client/server configuration.
YANG.quote: This document presents three IETF-defined YANG modules [RFC7950] and a script used to create four supporting IANA modules.

SSH.why: The modules model SSH client and server identity, authentication, transport algorithms and keepalives, so SSH readers would want this RFC.
SSH.quote: supporting the configuration and monitoring of SSH clients and servers.

rejected.why: NETCONF is only a consumer of these groupings and a management transport; the document does not specify it.
The IANA registry-to-YANG script and considerations are boilerplate-like apparatus for the modules, not a document about IANA governance.
Keys, certificates and truststore/keystore are referenced from RFC 9640-9642, not defined here.
X.509 certificate support for SSH (RFC 6187) is only an optional feature flag.
RESTCONF is only mentioned as a related consumer in the RFC collection.
TLS appears only as a secure transport in the Security Considerations boilerplate.

RFC9645.title: YANG Groupings for TLS Clients and TLS Servers
RFC9645.summary: Defines YANG 1.1 modules (ietf-tls-common, ietf-tls-client, ietf-tls-server, plus IANA-maintained iana-tls-cipher-suite-algs) with reusable groupings for configuring TLS clients and servers.

YANG.why: The document's content is YANG modules and groupings for configuring and monitoring TLS clients and servers.
YANG.quote: This document presents four YANG 1.1 modules -- three IETF modules and one supporting IANA module.

TLS.why: The modules model TLS versions, cipher suites, PSKs, raw public keys, certificates and heartbeat keepalives, so TLS readers would want it.
TLS.quote: supporting the configuration and monitoring of TLS clients and servers.

rejected.why: NETCONF is a consumer of these groupings and a context for examples, not what the document specifies.
Certificates and trust anchors are referenced through the truststore and keystore modules, which are other RFCs.
The IANA-maintained module is part of the work, but the document is not about IANA registry guidance in general.
RESTCONF is only a context for use of the modules and is not specified here.
DTLS is mentioned only in the titles of referenced RFCs and is not the subject here.

RFC9646.title: Conveying a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) in a Secure Zero-Touch Provisioning (SZTP) Bootstrapping Request
RFC9646.summary: Extends the SZTP get-bootstrapping-data RPC (RFC 8572) with YANG modules letting a bootstrapping device send a CSR (PKCS#10, CMP, or CMC) and receive an identity certificate such as an LDevID in the onboarding information.

YANG.why: The document's core deliverable is two YANG modules (ietf-sztp-csr and ietf-ztp-types) augmenting the SZTP RPC.
YANG.quote: Two YANG [RFC7950] modules are defined.  The "ietf-ztp-types" module defines three YANG groupings for the various messages defined in this document.

PKI.why: Certificate enrollment via CSR formats (PKCS#10, CMP, CMC), proof-of-possession and origin authentication are a substantial part of the document.
PKI.quote: enabling a bootstrapping device to additionally obtain an identity certificate (e.g., an LDevID from [Std-802.1AR-2018])

rejected.why: Not a tag in the taxonomy; the SZTP RPC is carried over RESTCONF, which is only the substrate here.
RESTCONF is only the transport for the RPC and error structure; nothing new is defined about it.
CMP is used as a CSR format, but the document does not specify CMP itself; it is not the main subject.
CMC over CMS is referenced only for a CSR format description, not the subject of the document.
TLS is only the transport authentication mechanism and is mentioned in security considerations.
Identity certificates are the output, but the document does not profile X.509 certificates.
Key generation is part of the flow, but the document is about CSR conveyance, not key management as a subject.

gaps.name: Secure Zero-Touch Provisioning (SZTP)
gaps.why: The document extends SZTP (RFC 8572) for device bootstrapping, and the taxonomy has no tag for zero-touch provisioning or device onboarding.

RFC9647.title: A YANG Data Model for Babel
RFC9647.summary: Defines the ietf-babel YANG 1.1 module, a configuration and operational data model for the Babel routing protocol based on the Babel information model, with MAC and DTLS security parameters and example configurations.

Babel.why: The whole document models Babel's configuration and state (interfaces, neighbors, routes, constants, security), so readers of Babel would want it.
Babel.quote: This document defines a data model for the Babel routing protocol.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module with tree diagrams, augmenting the routing and interfaces models, so it belongs under YANG data models.
YANG.quote: The data model is defined using YANG 1.1 [RFC7950] and is compatible with Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA)

rejected.why: The module only models DTLS certificate and cache settings for Babel interfaces. DTLS itself is not specified or extended.
HMAC is referenced for MAC key algorithms (HMAC-SHA256) but is only a mechanism the Babel MAC security uses.
BLAKE2s appears only as an identity for a MAC algorithm option.
NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the access protocols named in the Security Considerations boilerplate.
This is a YANG model, not an SMI MIB module.
The Babel tag already sits under routing and covers the topic.

RFC9648.title: YANG Data Model for TCP
RFC9648.summary: Specifies the ietf-tcp YANG module for configuring and monitoring TCP on network devices, with a connection list, listener list, basic statistics, and TCP-AO/MD5 authentication groupings augmenting the key-chain model.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module (ietf-tcp) with tree diagrams and examples, so YANG data modelling is its core subject.
YANG.quote: This document specifies a minimal YANG data model for TCP on devices that are configured and managed by network management protocols.

TCP.why: The model covers TCP connections, listeners, statistics, keepalives and TCP-AO/MD5 authentication, so TCP readers would want it.
TCP.quote: The YANG module has a narrow scope and focuses on a subset of fundamental TCP functions and basic statistics.

rejected.why: The TCP MIB is only referenced as a model for the statistics and is explicitly not deprecated or modified here.
NETCONF and RESTCONF are the management protocols the model is accessed through. The document does not specify or extend them.
BGP is cited as a motivating use case for TCP-AO and MD5 on routers. The document is not about BGP.
The document says Multipath TCP is not modelled in this version.
MD5 and AES are named only as authentication algorithms, with no cryptographic content of their own.

RFC9649.title: WebP Image Format
RFC9649.summary: Defines the WebP image file format (RIFF container with lossy VP8 and a new lossless bitstream, alpha, animation, metadata) and registers the image/webp media type.

media types.why: The document registers the image/webp media type with full registration template, and the format specification is what that type denotes. This is the closest taxonomy fit for an image file format RFC.
media types.quote: IANA has registered the 'image/webp' media type [RFC2046].

compression.why: A large part of the document specifies a lossless compression bitstream (LZ77 backward references, prefix coding, color cache, transforms). It is a data compression format, though for images rather than general data.
compression.quote: WebP lossless is an image format for lossless compression of ARGB images.

rejected.why: The codecs tag covers audio and video codecs for real-time communication. WebP is a still and animated image format that only reuses VP8 intra-frame coding, so it does not fit.
VP8 is used only as the lossy coding inside the 'VP8 ' chunk and is specified in RFC 6386. This document defines nothing new about it.
ABNF is used only to describe the lossless bitstream structure. It is a notation, not the subject.
Base64 appears only in the media type registration's encoding considerations.
Lossless compression here uses LZ77 and prefix coding in a new format, not DEFLATE or zlib.

gaps.name: Image file formats (WebP, RIFF container, lossless image compression)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for raster image formats or graphics file formats. The document's main subject, the WebP format, is only approximated by media types and compression.

RFC9650.title: Revision to Registration Procedures for IS-IS Neighbor Link-Attribute Bit Values
RFC9650.summary: Changes the IANA registration policy for the IS-IS Neighbor Link-Attribute Bit Values registry (from RFC 5029) from Standards Action to Expert Review, updating RFC 5029.

IS-IS.why: The document amends the registry for the IS-IS link attribute sub-TLV defined in RFC 5029, so IS-IS readers would want it.
IS-IS.quote: This document changes the registration procedure for that registry from "Standards Action" to "Expert Review".

IANA.why: The whole document is a change to an IANA registry's registration policy, which is registry administration.
IANA.quote: IANA has changed the registration procedure for the "IS-IS Neighbor Link-Attribute Bit Values" registry to "Expert Review"

rejected.why: The document uses standard IANA policy terms such as Expert Review, but it does not change IETF process.
The copyright boilerplate is not evidence of the subject.

RFC9651.title: Structured Field Values for HTTP
RFC9651.summary: Defines Structured Fields for HTTP: a set of data types (Lists, Dictionaries, Items, and others) with strict serialization and parsing algorithms for use by new HTTP header and trailer field definitions, obsoleting RFC 8941.

HTTP.why: The document specifies a common syntax and handling model for HTTP fields, an extension of HTTP semantics. Readers browsing HTTP would expect it.
HTTP.quote: make it easier and safer to define and handle HTTP header and trailer fields, known as "Structured Fields"

rejected.why: JSON appears only in the FAQ, which explains why it was not used. The document does not specify or use JSON.
Base64 is only the encoding used for Byte Sequences. It is not what the document is about.
HTTP/2 and HPACK are mentioned only in passing, as other encodings the types could be carried in.
The ABNF appendix is non-normative. It only illustrates the syntax and is not a subject in itself.
Display Strings carry Unicode, but this is one small data type and the document is not about Unicode usage in general.
UTF-8 is only the encoding step inside Display String serialization.

RFC9652.title: The Link-Template HTTP Header Field
RFC9652.summary: Defines the Link-Template HTTP header field, a Structured Field carrying URI Templates for link targets and anchors (with a var-base parameter), complementing the Link header field.

web linking.why: The document defines a new typed-link header field, a templated counterpart to the Link header, using rel, anchor and target attributes. Readers of web linking would want it.
web linking.quote: It is semantically equivalent to the Link header field defined in Section 3 of [WEB-LINKING], except that the link target and link anchor can contain URI Templates

HTTP.why: It defines a new HTTP header field and registers it in the field name registry, which is an extension to HTTP.
HTTP.quote: This specification defines a HTTP header field [HTTP] for conveying templates for links in the headers of a HTTP message.

rejected.why: URI Templates (RFC 6570) are used and expanded, but the document does not define URI syntax or schemes. The template mechanism is a dependency.
It was published by the httpapi working group, but it does not define API-building conventions such as problem details or rate limits.
No JSON is involved. The document uses Structured Fields, which have no matching tag.

gaps.name: HTTP Structured Field Values
