gaps.why: The field is built on Structured Fields (RFC 9651), but the taxonomy has no tag for them. The document only uses them, so this is a minor gap.

RFC9653.title: Zero Checksum for the Stream Control Transmission Protocol
RFC9653.summary: Defines an SCTP extension (Zero Checksum Acceptable chunk parameter) letting endpoints accept a zero CRC32c checksum when an alternate error detection method such as DTLS encapsulation is in use, with a socket API option and IANA registry.

SCTP.why: The document extends SCTP with a new chunk parameter, procedures for sender and receiver, and a socket API option.
SCTP.quote: This document provides a simple extension allowing SCTP to save these computing resources by using zero as the checksum in a backwards-compatible way.

DTLS.why: A dedicated section defines how zero checksum is used with SCTP encapsulated in DTLS, the initial registered error detection method.
DTLS.quote: Using SCTP over DTLS as specified in [RFC8261] provides a stronger error detection method than using the CRC32c checksum algorithm.
DTLS.section: 6. Error Detection via SCTP over DTLS

rejected.why: The CRC32c checksum is the thing being omitted, not specified or analysed; the document is not about CRC polynomial choice.
Concerns the SCTP checksum specifically, but is handled as part of the SCTP extension rather than the Internet checksum in general.
Section 7 adds one socket option, but it is a short informational section, not a substantial part of the document.
The IANA registry creation is boilerplate-level for this extension and the document is not about IANA guidance.

RFC9654.title: Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) Nonce Extension
RFC9654.summary: Obsoletes RFC 8954 and updates RFC 6960 by raising the OCSP Nonce extension's maximum length to 128 octets, recommending a 32-octet minimum, and supplying updated OCSP ASN.1 modules.

OCSP.why: The document specifies changes to the OCSP Nonce extension and updates RFC 6960, so it is about OCSP.
OCSP.quote: This document extends the maximum allowed nonce length to 128 octets and does not change the specifications of any of the other extensions defined in [RFC6960].

rejected.why: The ASN.1 modules in the appendices are only the way the OCSP definitions are written down. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
X.509 certificates are the thing OCSP reports status for. The document does not profile them.
It only requires a cryptographically strong PRNG for nonces and cites RFC 4086. It adds nothing on randomness.
OCSP is already a child of PKI, so choosing OCSP implies it.

RFC9655.title: Egress Validation in Label Switched Path Ping and Traceroute Mechanisms
RFC9655.summary: Defines a new Egress TLV for MPLS LSP ping/traceroute so the egress can validate a Nil FEC stack, e.g. for SR Policy paths, with a new return code.

MPLS.why: Extends RFC 8029 MPLS LSP ping/traceroute (echo request/reply, Nil FEC, TLVs, return codes), which is MPLS OAM.
MPLS.quote: This document introduces a new Type-Length-Value (TLV) as an extension to the existing Nil FEC.  It describes MPLS ping and traceroute procedures

segment routing.why: Procedures are motivated by and specified for validating SR Policy label stacks (Node-SID, Adj-SID, Binding SID) over MPLS data plane.
segment routing.quote: the sender node MUST add an Egress TLV with the address obtained from the SR Policy Endpoint field

rejected.why: Document is about MPLS ping/traceroute validation of SR paths, not the SR-MPLS architecture itself; segment routing tag suffices as secondary.
Topic tag not needed since MPLS tag chosen; no OAM-specific child tag fits better, and MPLS covers it.
Generic traceroute tool tag is about IP path discovery tools; this is MPLS LSP traceroute specifically.
Only references the SR Policy BGP draft for the endpoint field; not about BGP.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here.

gaps.name: MPLS LSP ping/traceroute (MPLS OAM)
gaps.why: No tag fits MPLS echo request/reply OAM precisely; the closest taxonomy entry is the MPLS tech, used here, but a dedicated MPLS OAM tag would serve readers better.

RFC9656.title: A YANG Data Model for Microwave Topology
RFC9656.summary: Defines a YANG data model augmenting the TE topology model (RFC 8795) and network topology model (RFC 8345) to describe microwave and millimeter-wave radio links, carriers and termination points.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a new YANG module (ietf-microwave-topology) augmenting existing topology models, so it belongs on the YANG modelling page.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model to describe microwave and millimeter-wave radio links in a network topology

rejected.why: Only mentioned in Security Considerations as an access protocol for the module; the document is not about NETCONF.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a possible access protocol; the document does not specify or extend it.
The model augments the TE topology model, but only a minority of its leafs apply. The subject is microwave link description, not TE practice.
JSON is only used for the instance-data examples in the appendices, so it is just an encoding.
L2 Ethernet appears only as a client layer carried over the microwave link in examples. The document does not specify Ethernet.
The module relates to the RFC 8561 microwave radio link model, but this is a YANG topology model, not a MIB module.
The PNC/MDSC (ACTN) context is mentioned as the intended use, but the document does not address SDN architecture.

gaps.name: Microwave / millimeter-wave radio links
gaps.why: The document's actual subject is point-to-point microwave radio topology (radio link terminals, carriers, bonding and protection modes). The taxonomy has no wireless or radio transport tag, so only the YANG tag captures it.

RFC9657.title: Time-Variant Routing (TVR) Use Cases
RFC9657.summary: Informational use-case document describing three categories (resource preservation, operating efficiency, dynamic reachability) where time-variant routing computations over scheduled topology changes would help.

TVR.why: The whole document defines use cases for TVR, which is exactly the subject of this tag.
TVR.quote: use cases where Time-Variant Routing (TVR) computations (i.e., routing computations that take into consideration time-based or scheduled changes to a network)

rejected.why: LEO constellations are only one example; the document is about time-variant routing, not networking over satellite links.
Intermittent connectivity and store-and-forward are related, but DTN and the Bundle Protocol are not discussed.
Mobile nodes appear in the examples, but the document does not cover MANET routing protocols.
Energy savings motivate some use cases, but the document does not address energy monitoring or management of devices.
Time synchronization is mentioned only in the Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.

RFC9658.title: Multipoint LDP Extensions for Multi-Topology Routing
RFC9658.summary: Extends Multipoint LDP (mLDP) to be multi-topology and IGP-algorithm (Flexible Algorithm) aware by adding an {MT-ID, IPA} tuple to MP FEC elements, defining a new MT Multipoint capability, and updating RFC 7307.

LDP.why: The document extends mLDP, an LDP extension: new FEC encoding, a new LDP capability TLV, and changes to upstream LSR and forwarding interface selection.
LDP.quote: This document specifies extensions to mLDP to support the use of MTR/IPAs such that, when building multipoint LSPs, it can follow a particular topology and algorithm.

rejected.why: LDP is the more specific tag. MPLS is the parent and is implied.
The IGP MT and Flexible Algorithm mechanisms are only referenced. The document does not specify or extend them.
OSPF MT is only referenced as background. The document does not specify or extend it.
The PMSI tunnel attribute use is mentioned briefly. The document is not about multicast VPN.
mLDP builds multipoint LSPs, but the document is about LDP FEC encoding, not IP multicast routing.
The LSP ping extension is a small section about MPLS OAM, not a traceroute tool.

gaps.name: IGP Flexible Algorithm / Multi-Topology Routing
gaps.why: The document applies MTR and Flexible Algorithm to mLDP. The taxonomy has no tag for them as subjects, but they are only background here.

RFC9659.title: Window Sizing for Zstandard Content Encoding
RFC9659.summary: Updates RFC 8878 to make the 8 MB Window_Size limit a requirement (decoders MUST support up to 8 MB, encoders MUST NOT exceed it) for the "zstd" HTTP content coding.

zstd.why: The document's whole purpose is constraining Zstandard window sizes, updating the Zstandard specification RFC 8878 for interoperability.
zstd.quote: decoders MUST support a Window_Size of up to and including 8 MB, and encoders MUST NOT generate frames requiring a Window_Size larger than 8 MB

HTTP.why: The requirement applies specifically to the HTTP "zstd" content coding and updates the HTTP Content Coding registry entry, so HTTP readers would want it.
HTTP.quote: This document updates [RFC8878] to enforce Window_Size limits on the encoder and decoder for the "zstd" HTTP content coding.

rejected.why: gzip is only mentioned as a comparison for zstd; the document is not about it.
The IANA section only updates the zstd content coding registry entry; this is boilerplate rather than the document's subject.
RFC 8878 registers application/zstd, but this document deals only with the content coding and window size, not media type registration.

RFC9660.title: The DNS Zone Version (ZONEVERSION) Option
RFC9660.summary: Defines the ZONEVERSION EDNS(0) option, letting clients request and authoritative DNS servers return a zone version (initially the SOA SERIAL) with a response, and creates an IANA registry of version types.

EDNS.why: The document defines a new EDNS(0) option with wire format, processing rules, and an IANA option code registration, so it belongs under EDNS.
EDNS.quote: This document specifies a new EDNS(0) [RFC6891] option, ZONEVERSION, which can be used by DNS clients and servers to provide information regarding the version of the zone

rejected.why: The parent tag is implied by EDNS. The document does not otherwise change core DNS behaviour.
DNSSEC appears only in the Security Considerations, which note that EDNS data is not covered by RRSIG. The document is not about DNSSEC.
Anycast is cited only as motivation for why a zone version in the response helps debugging. The document does not address anycast operation.
The document creates a registry, but that is boilerplate for the new option and does not make the document about IANA stewardship.

RFC9661.title: The JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP) for Sieve Scripts
RFC9661.summary: Defines a JMAP data model and methods (SieveScript get/set/query/validate) for managing Sieve email filtering scripts on a server, compatible with ManageSieve.

JMAP.why: The document is a JMAP extension defining a new capability, data type, methods and error codes.
JMAP.quote: This specification defines a data model for managing Sieve scripts [RFC5228] on a server using JMAP.

Sieve.why: The document is about managing Sieve scripts, their activation, validation and supported extensions, so Sieve readers would want it.
Sieve.quote: A "SieveScript" object represents a single Sieve script [RFC5228] for filtering email messages at the time of final delivery.

rejected.why: Email is the context, but the subject is script management; the more specific JMAP and Sieve tags cover it.
JSON is only the encoding that JMAP uses; nothing new is defined about JSON.
HTTP only carries the upload and download examples.
The document uses the application/sieve type but does not register or define it.
MIME is not addressed in the body.

gaps.name: JMAP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has JMAP only as a child of email, which is a mail-oriented grouping. The document extends JMAP generally, and the tag it fits best is JMAP. I used the JMAP id even though it appears in the taxonomy only under email. The Sieve id is also a child of email.

RFC9662.title: Updates to the Cipher Suites in Secure Syslog
RFC9662.summary: Updates the mandatory-to-implement cipher suites and DTLS/TLS version requirements for syslog over TLS (RFC 5425) and DTLS (RFC 6012), preferring ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM and forbidding DTLS 1.0 and early data.

syslog.why: The document updates the two secure syslog transport mappings (RFC 5425 and RFC 6012), so it is about securing syslog.
syslog.quote: RFCs 5425 and 6012 describe using TLS and DTLS to securely transport syslog messages.

TLS.why: It sets TLS version and cipher suite requirements and forbids early data. This is TLS deployment guidance for syslog.
TLS.quote: implementations of [RFC5425] SHOULD support TLS 1.3 [RFC8446] and, if implemented, MUST prefer to negotiate TLS 1.3 over earlier versions of TLS.

DTLS.why: It replaces the mandatory-to-implement datagram transport, moving from DTLS 1.0 to DTLS 1.2 and 1.3.
DTLS.quote: implementations of [RFC6012] MUST NOT use DTLS 1.0 [RFC4347].  Implementations MUST use DTLS 1.2 [RFC6347].

rejected.why: The document updates existing transport mappings, but the more specific syslog, TLS and DTLS tags already cover it.
AES-based cipher suites are named, but only as TLS cipher suite choices. The document does not specify AES itself.
RSA certificates and key exchange are mentioned only as the background for choosing cipher suites.
RFC 5280 certificates are mentioned only as a requirement carried over from the earlier RFCs.

gaps.name: syslog
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists a `syslog` tag under network management. I tagged it as `syslog` because the document is about securing syslog transport. If that id is not valid in the final taxonomy, this RFC has no fitting tag for syslog.

RFC9663.title: Using DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (DHCPv6-PD) to Allocate Unique IPv6 Prefixes per Client in Large Broadcast Networks
RFC9663.summary: Informational document describing a deployment model in which hosts on large broadcast networks (enterprise, public Wi-Fi) each receive a unique prefix via DHCPv6-PD, covering first-hop router/relay and server requirements, prefix sizing, mobility, anti-spoofing, and privacy.

DHCPv6.why: The whole document is a deployment model for DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation, with requirements for relays, servers (Bulk Leasequery, Server Unicast, prefix-length hints) and clients.
DHCPv6.quote: individual nodes connected to large broadcast networks (such as enterprise networks or public Wi-Fi networks) are allocated unique prefixes via DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (DHCPv6-PD)

addressing.why: Substantial discussion of prefix pool allocation, prefix sizing (/64, /40), and per-client prefix allocation as an addressing architecture.
addressing.quote: any network that numbers clients from an IPv4 prefix of length X (e.g., X=/18, X=/24) would require an IPv6 prefix of length X+32

SAVI.why: A dedicated section covers how the model interacts with uRPF and SAVI bindings for delegated prefixes.
SAVI.quote: Administrators deploying the proposed solution on SAVI-enabled infrastructure SHOULD ensure that SAVI perimeter devices support DHCPv6-PD snooping

rejected.why: SLAAC is discussed as the comparison and for how clients use the delegated prefix, but the document is not about SLAAC itself.
ND scaling and caches are the motivation, but the document does not specify or extend ND.
The more specific DHCPv6 and addressing tags capture the subject; IPv6 is the general context.
Mentioned only as an example of where per-address routes cause scaling issues.
There is a short Privacy Considerations section, but it is not a substantial part of the document.
464XLAT is mentioned only as a source of extra addresses.

RFC9664.title: An EDNS(0) Option to Negotiate Leases on DNS Updates
RFC9664.summary: Defines an EDNS(0) Update Lease option letting DNS Update requesters and authoritative servers negotiate lease durations so stale records added by DNS Update are garbage collected unless refreshed.

DNS update.why: The document extends Dynamic DNS Update with leases, refresh requests, and server garbage collection of expired records.
DNS update.quote: an EDNS(0) option that can be used between DNS Update Requesters and authoritative DNS servers to include a lifetime (lease duration) in a DNS Update

EDNS.why: It defines a new EDNS(0) option (UPDATE-LEASE, code 2) with its format and registers it with IANA.
EDNS.quote: The Update Lease option is included in a standard DNS Update Request [RFC2136] within an EDNS(0) OPT pseudo-RR [RFC6891].

rejected.why: Mentioned only as the context in which KEY leases are used (via the Service Registration Protocol, RFC 9665); the document itself is not about service discovery.
A more specific child tag (DNS update, EDNS) fits, so the parent is implied.
Only mentions SIG(0) and TSIG for authenticating updates in Security Considerations. The document does not cover DNSSEC itself.
UDP and TCP are only the transports for DNS messages. Retransmission guidance just points to other RFCs.

RFC9665.title: Service Registration Protocol for DNS-Based Service Discovery
RFC9665.summary: Specifies the Service Registration Protocol (SRP), which uses DNS Update with SIG(0) and first-come-first-served naming so hosts can register DNS-SD services over unicast, and also reserves service.arpa. as a special-use domain.

DNS-SD.why: The document defines how services register their DNS-SD records (PTR, SRV, TXT) with a registrar, so it is a DNS-SD extension.
DNS-SD.quote: The Service Registration Protocol (SRP) for DNS-based Service Discovery (DNS-SD) uses the standard DNS Update mechanism to enable DNS-SD using only unicast packets.

DNS update.why: SRP is a constrained profile of DNS Update, with its own validation rules, lease handling and SIG(0)-based FCFS naming.
DNS update.quote: Services that implement SRP use DNS Update [RFC2136] with SIG(0) [RFC3007] to publish service information in the DNS.

special-use domain names.why: A substantial part of the document registers service.arpa. and default.service.arpa. as special-use names. It includes the Domain Name Reservation Considerations and the delegation.
special-use domain names.quote: IANA has recorded the domain name "service.arpa." in the "Special-Use Domain Names" registry [SUDN].

rejected.why: The Update Lease EDNS(0) option is defined in RFC 9664. This document only requires its use.
DNSSEC is mentioned only for the KEY/SIG(0) record formats, signature algorithm requirements and resolver behaviour. The document is not about DNSSEC.
mDNS is the multicast alternative that SRP avoids. It is not specified or extended here.
DNS-over-TLS is only the optional transport for privacy. Nothing new is defined about it.
TLS is only a transport option and is not what the document is about.
Constrained-node networks are supported through a simplified variant, but the document is not about IoT as a subject.

RFC9666.title: Area Proxy for IS-IS
RFC9666.summary: Experimental IS-IS extension (Area Proxy) letting a Level 1 area provide transit while injecting only a single proxy LSP into Level 2, defining the Area Proxy TLV, sub-TLVs, leader election use, and edge router filtering.

IS-IS.why: The whole document defines new IS-IS TLVs, sub-TLVs, Proxy LSP generation and flooding filtering rules.
IS-IS.quote: this document discusses extensions to the IS-IS routing protocol that allow Level 1 (L1) areas to provide transit but only inject an abstraction of the Level 1 topology into Level 2

segment routing.why: A substantial part covers SRGB handling, an Area SID sub-TLV (anycast SID), and copying prefix/adjacency SIDs and SRv6 locators into the Proxy LSP.
segment routing.quote: If the Inside Area supports Segment Routing (SR) [RFC8402], then all Inside Nodes MUST advertise a Segment Routing Global Block (SRGB).

rejected.why: Motivation is hierarchy and scalability, but a specific IS-IS tag fits better.
L3LS Clos topology is the motivating use case, but the document specifies IS-IS mechanics, not data center networking.
SRv6 TLVs are only copied into the Proxy LSP; this is a minor part of the document.
TE sub-TLVs are merely copied to the Proxy LSP; not a subject of the document.
Unrelated; document does not use BGP.

RFC9667.title: Dynamic Flooding on Dense Graphs
RFC9667.summary: Experimental RFC defining dynamic flooding for link-state IGPs on dense topologies: a reduced flooding topology computed by an elected Area Leader (centralized) or distributed algorithm, with new IS-IS, OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 TLVs/LSAs and behavioral rules.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with new sub-TLVs, TLVs, and flooding behavior for dynamic flooding.
IS-IS.quote: Specific protocol changes for IS-IS, OSPFv2, and OSPFv3 are described in this document.

OSPF.why: Defines new OSPFv2 Opaque LSA, OSPFv3 LSA, TLVs, and LLS flooding request bit; OSPF is specified/extended.
OSPF.quote: An OSPFv2 Opaque LSA and OSPFv3 LSA to advertise the flooding topology for centralized mode.

OSPFv3.why: A new OSPFv3-specific LSA and Area Router ID TLV are defined.
OSPFv3.quote: The OSPFv3 Dynamic Flooding LSA has a function code of 16.

data center networking.why: Motivated by leaf-spine/Clos data center topologies, with flooding topologies for complete bipartite graphs.
data center networking.quote: in a massively scaled data center (where there are many opportunities for redundant flooding), this mechanism guarantees that flooding is redundant

rejected.why: Mentioned only as an alternative (RFC 7938) that the document is not about.
Parent-level topic; the specific IGP tags fit better.
RFC 3630 TE TLV format is only reused for encoding.
Not involved.

gaps.name: IS-IS
gaps.why: The taxonomy contains IS-IS as a tech tag, so no gap; but I used ids as listed — see note: if 'IS-IS' and 'OSPF' ids are not exact in taxonomy, they are the closest fits (IS-IS exists; generic OSPF exists).

RFC9668.title: Using Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman Over COSE (EDHOC) with the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) and Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments (OSCORE)
RFC9668.summary: Specifies how EDHOC runs over CoAP to set up an OSCORE Security Context, defining the EDHOC CoAP option that combines EDHOC message_3 with the first OSCORE request, connection identifier rules, and web-link target attributes for discovering EDHOC resources.

EDHOC.why: The document extends and profiles EDHOC use over CoAP: combined request, connection identifier handling, application profile consistency, and a new credential types registry.
EDHOC.quote: This document details the use of the EDHOC protocol with CoAP and OSCORE and specifies a number of additional and optional mechanisms.

OSCORE.why: The combined EDHOC + OSCORE request and use of EDHOC connection identifiers as OSCORE Sender/Recipient IDs are core to the document.
OSCORE.quote: an optimization approach that combines the EDHOC execution with the first OSCORE transaction

CoAP.why: It defines a new CoAP option (number 21) and CoAP target attributes for discovery, which CoAP readers need.
CoAP.quote: This section defines the EDHOC option.  This option is used in a CoAP request to signal that the request payload conveys both an EDHOC message_3

rejected.why: Section 6 uses CoRE link format and target attributes for discovery, but this is CoAP/CoRE resource discovery, not a general web linking spec.
CBOR is only the encoding substrate for EDHOC messages.
COSE is used by EDHOC but this document defines nothing new about COSE.
The registries are boilerplate-like in effect and the document is not about IANA procedures.
Discovery is a minor section covered via link attributes, not the main subject.
X.509 is only listed as a credential type in a registry entry.

RFC9669.title: BPF Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)
RFC9669.summary: Specifies the BPF (eBPF) instruction set architecture: instruction encoding, arithmetic, jump, load/store and atomic instructions, conformance groups, and the IANA registries for instructions and conformance groups.

eBPF.why: The whole document defines the eBPF instruction set, its encoding, semantics and conformance groups. A reader browsing eBPF would expect this RFC.
eBPF.quote: This document specifies the BPF instruction set architecture (ISA).

rejected.why: The document creates two IANA registries, but this is registry apparatus for the ISA. The subject is the instruction set, not IANA guidance or stewardship.
Legacy cBPF packet access instructions are mentioned only as deprecated. The document is not about packet capture or trace formats.
The Security Considerations section is boilerplate for this purpose. The document is not about a security mechanism.
Not a taxonomy tag. Byte swap instructions are only part of the ISA.

gaps.name: BPF / eBPF instruction set architecture
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an eBPF tag (listed under applications) in the sense of the instruction set and conventions, but only as described; if the id is not exactly valid, a dedicated BPF/ISA tag is missing.

RFC9670.title: JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP) Sharing
RFC9670.summary: RFC 9670 defines a JMAP data model for sharing data between users, with Principal and ShareNotification data types, capabilities, and a framework of common properties (isSubscribed, myRights, shareWith) for shareable data types.

JMAP.why: The document extends JMAP (updates RFC 8620) with new capabilities, data types (Principal, ShareNotification) and methods, so it belongs on the JMAP page.
JMAP.quote: This document specifies a data model for sharing data between users using the JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP).

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding JMAP uses. The document does not define a JSON format in its own right.
Sharing permissions are touched on, but the document defines a JMAP data model. It explicitly leaves the granularity of permissions to each data type.
The IANA section registers JMAP capabilities and data types. That is boilerplate, not the subject of the document.
The Principal timeZone property just references the IANA Time Zone Database. The document does not deal with time zone data distribution.
RFC 8264 is mentioned only in a short internationalization note. It is not the subject of the document.
Calendars appear only as examples of data that could be shared. The document does not specify calendaring.

RFC9671.title: Sieve Email Filtering: Extension for Processing Calendar Attachments
RFC9671.summary: Defines the Sieve "processcalendar" extension, a new action letting Sieve scripts parse calendar data (iCalendar/iTIP/JSCalendar) in MIME email and add, update, or delete items on a user's calendars.

Sieve.why: The document specifies a new Sieve extension and action with its arguments, capability identifier and interactions with other Sieve actions.
Sieve.quote: This document describes the "processcalendar" extension to the Sieve email filtering language.

iCalendar.why: A substantial part of the document concerns processing iCalendar/iTIP/iMIP data to create, update or cancel calendar objects, so iCalendar readers would want it.
iCalendar.quote: enables scripts to process machine-readable calendar data that is encapsulated in an email message using MIME

rejected.why: MIME is only the encapsulation for the calendar data; the document defines nothing new about MIME.
Email is the substrate; the subject is the Sieve filtering language, which is already tagged and sits under email.
Mentioned only as an alternative format the extension could process; not specified or profiled.
Security Considerations only advise using spamtest and virustest to guard the action; spam handling is not the document's subject.
SPF, DKIM and DMARC are mentioned only in Security Considerations as trust signals.

RFC9672.title: Transferring Opportunistic Wireless Encryption to the IEEE 802.11 Working Group
RFC9672.summary: Informational RFC that records IETF concurrence in transferring maintenance and future development of Opportunistic Wireless Encryption (RFC 8110) to the IEEE 802.11 Working Group, updating RFC 8110.

WiFi.why: OWE is a mode providing encryption for IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs without authentication. The document transfers its maintenance to the 802.11 WG, so Wi-Fi readers would look for it.
WiFi.quote: future work on OWE [RFC8110] will now occur in the IEEE 802.11 Working Group

rejected.why: The document does record a change of maintenance responsibility. But it is about one protocol's handover to IEEE, not IETF procedures in general.
OWE is opportunistic security and gives encryption without authentication. This document defines no privacy considerations, and it only mentions that property.
The document specifies no algorithms, modes or parameters. It only notes the change of maintenance.

gaps.name: Opportunistic Wireless Encryption (OWE) / Opportunistic Security
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for OWE or opportunistic security. Wi-Fi is the closest fit, but OWE readers would benefit from a dedicated tag.

RFC9673.title: IPv6 Hop-by-Hop Options Processing Procedures
RFC9673.summary: RFC 9673 updates RFC 8200 to define how IPv6 routers and hosts process the Hop-by-Hop Options header and individual options, including Router Alert handling and guidance for designing new Hop-by-Hop options.

IPv6.why: The document modifies the IPv6 specification (RFC 8200) on Hop-by-Hop Options header processing and the rules for new options. IPv6 is the most specific fitting tag.
IPv6.quote: This document specifies procedures for processing IPv6 Hop-by-Hop options in IPv6 routers and hosts.

router alert.why: A subsection sets processing rules for the IPv6 Router Alert Option as the one exception to the Control Plane restrictions, and the Background discusses it at length.
router alert.quote: The purpose of the Router Alert Option [RFC2711] is to tell a router that the packet needs additional processing in the Control Plane.

rejected.why: ICMPv6 Parameter Problem is mentioned only as an optional response when unrecognized options are discarded. The document does not specify or extend ICMP.
DoS protection of the router Control Plane motivates the changes, but the document is about option processing procedures, not security operations practice.
The document covers router fast-path and slow-path processing of packets. It does not address routing systems or their architecture.
TAPS-ARCH is cited only for the idea of racing, in an informative example.

RFC9674.title: Same-Origin Policy for the RPKI Repository Delta Protocol (RRDP)
RFC9674.summary: Updates RFC 8182 to require RRDP servers and relying parties to apply a Same-Origin Policy to URIs in Update Notification Files and to HTTP redirects, preventing cross-origin resource references between RPKI repository servers.

RPKI.why: The document amends RRDP, the RPKI repository delta protocol, with new requirements for repository servers and relying parties. RPKI readers need it.
RPKI.quote: RRDP Repository Servers and Clients MUST apply a Same-Origin Policy to both the URIs referenced in an Update Notification File and any HTTP Redirects.

rejected.why: HTTP redirects and origins are the substrate the policy is applied to. The document doesn't specify or extend HTTP.
The same-origin concept comes from the web, but it is applied here to RRDP, not to the web platform.
This is the parent of RPKI, which is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
URIs in Update Notification Files are constrained by origin, but the document doesn't address URI syntax or schemes.

gaps.name: RRDP (RPKI Repository Delta Protocol)
gaps.why: RRDP has no tech tag of its own. RPKI is the closest fit, but RRDP readers would want a dedicated subject page.

RFC9675.title: Delay-Tolerant Networking Management Architecture (DTNMA)
RFC9675.summary: Informational RFC defining the Delay-Tolerant Networking Management Architecture (DTNMA): a logical architecture with agents (DA) and managers (DM), autonomy rules, and open-loop push reporting for managing devices in challenged networks.

DTN.why: The document is the management architecture for Delay-Tolerant Networking, designed around BP and DTN constraints, so DTN readers would expect it.
DTN.quote: This document describes a DTN Management Architecture (DTNMA) suitable for managing devices in any challenged environment but, in particular, those communicating using the DTN Bundle Protocol (BP).

network management.why: It is a network management architecture (managers, agents, reporting, controls, authorization). No specific management protocol tag fits, so the parent topic applies.
network management.quote: The unique characteristics of this environment require a unique approach to network management that supports asynchronous transport, autonomous local control, and a small footprint

rejected.why: Surveyed in Section 5 as an existing approach and found unsuitable; not specified or extended.
Only discussed as related work and as a possible tier-1 mechanism; the document is not about it.
Discussed in the survey and its limitations; the DTNMA does not define YANG models.
Section 5.5 contrasts ANIMA/ACP with DTNMA briefly; not a substantial subject of the document.
CORECONF/CoAP appear only in the survey of existing approaches.
Constrained devices are mentioned, but the focus is challenged/DTN networks rather than IoT guidance.

RFC9676.title: LEX: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace for Sources of Law
RFC9676.summary: Registers the LEX URN namespace for identifying sources of law (legislation, case law, administrative acts), defining its syntax, jurisdiction-code registry, assignment procedures, and DNS/NAPTR-based resolution recommendations.

URN.why: The document defines and registers a new URN namespace (LEX) with its NSS syntax, assignment and persistence rules.
URN.quote: LEX, a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace identifier that identifies, names, assigns, and manages persistent resources in the legal domain.

rejected.why: DNS and NAPTR are used for routing resolution of LEX URNs, but the document does not specify DNS itself.
Punycode/IDNA conversion is mentioned as a strategy for non-ASCII names, but only as a supporting mechanism.
RFC 8288 link relations are suggested for linking versions, a minor point.
IANA registration is boilerplate-level here; the jurisdiction registry is explicitly not an IANA registry.
ISO 8601 dates are required in the syntax but this is a use of an existing format, not the subject.
RFC 5646 language tags are used for the expression element only as a component.

gaps.name: Legal document identification / legal informatics
gaps.why: The document is about identifying sources of law (FRBR work/expression/manifestation model), but the taxonomy has no legal-domain or persistent-identifier-for-documents subject beyond URN.

RFC9677.title: Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI) Metadata for Delegated Credentials
RFC9677.summary: Defines CDNI FCI and MI metadata objects so an upstream CDN can provision TLS delegated credentials (RFC 9345) to a downstream CDN for HTTPS delivery.

CDN.why: The document extends the CDNI Metadata and FCI interfaces with new objects, MI.DelegatedCredentials and FCI.DelegatedCredentials, for uCDN-to-dCDN interconnection.
CDN.quote: This document defines metadata in the Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI) Control and Metadata interface to set up HTTPS delegation using delegated credentials

TLS.why: The metadata exists to provision TLS delegated credentials (RFC 9345) to the dCDN, and a substantial part of the text covers their use in the TLS handshake and expiry behaviour.
TLS.quote: the dCDN presents the "delegated_credential" (rather than its own certificate) during the TLS handshake [RFC8446] to the User Agent.

rejected.why: JWE and JWK are used only to encrypt private keys and carry the dCDN key. They are building blocks, not the subject of the document.
HTTPS delivery is the context, but the document does not specify or extend HTTP.
The metadata objects are encoded in JSON, which is only the encoding.
Credentials are delegated, but the document does not address PKI itself or certificate management in general.
Base64 is used only as an encoding for the credential field.

gaps.name: CDNI (Content Delivery Network Interconnection) metadata and FCI interfaces
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only a general CDN tag, so the CDNI-specific interfaces (MI, FCI, payload types) have no dedicated tag.

RFC9678.title: Forward Secrecy Extension to the Improved Extensible Authentication Protocol Method for Authentication and Key Agreement (EAP-AKA' FS)
RFC9678.summary: Defines an optional EAP-AKA' extension (EAP-AKA' FS) adding ephemeral ECDHE key exchange via new attributes AT_PUB_ECDHE and AT_KDF_FS, giving forward secrecy for session keys and updating RFC 5448 and RFC 9048.

EAP.why: The document extends the EAP-AKA' method with new attributes, KDFs and message processing rules, so it belongs under EAP.
EAP.quote: EAP-AKA' Forward Secrecy (EAP-AKA' FS), when negotiated, provides forward secrecy for the session keys generated as a part of the authentication run in EAP-AKA'.

elliptic curve.why: A substantial part specifies the ECDHE groups (X25519, P-256), public key encodings, and shared secret computation and validation.
elliptic curve.quote: Forward Secrecy (FS) for EAP-AKA' is achieved by using an Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) exchange [RFC7748].

rejected.why: The document is about an EAP method used in 3GPP/5G contexts, but it specifies an EAP extension rather than IP over cellular systems.
X25519 is one of two curves used. The document relies on RFC 7748 and does not define anything new about Curve25519.
The post-quantum discussion is a short security considerations subsection, and the document does not specify PQC.
Key derivation is part of the EAP method itself, so the EAP tag already covers it.
EAP-TLS is only mentioned for context.

RFC9679.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Key Thumbprint
RFC9679.summary: Defines how to compute a hash ("thumbprint") over the required fields of a COSE Key using deterministic CBOR encoding, plus a CWT "ckt" confirmation method and a urn:ietf:params:oauth:ckt URI prefix.

COSE.why: The whole document specifies which COSE_Key parameters are hashed and how, for use as key identifiers. It is an extension of COSE key handling.
COSE.quote: This specification defines a method for applying a cryptographic hash function to a CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Key structure [RFC9052], resulting in a hash value known as a "thumbprint".

JWT.why: It defines a new CWT confirmation method, registered in IANA. This is a substantial part of the document. JWT is the closest taxonomy tag for CWT-style tokens, but only loosely.
JWT.quote: The proof-of-possession key is identified using the "ckt" member of the CWT confirmation claim "cnf".

rejected.why: CBOR deterministic encoding is only the encoding substrate. The document defines nothing new about CBOR itself.
It defines a URN prefix (urn:ietf:params:oauth:ckt), but this is a minor subsection that mirrors RFC 9278. It is not a new URN namespace in its own right.
SHA-256 is only the example or default hash function. The document does not specify or analyse it.
The URN namespace sits under oauth only to align with JWK Thumbprint URIs, and the text says it is not necessarily related to OAuth.
X.509 SPKI digests are mentioned only as an analogy in 5.4.

gaps.name: CWT (CBOR Web Token) confirmation methods
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for CWT. JWT is the nearest tag, but CWT proof-of-possession is a distinct subject.

RFC9680.title: Antitrust Guidelines for IETF Participants
RFC9680.summary: Informational guidance for IETF participants on complying with antitrust/competition law, summarising existing IETF policies, topics to avoid in discussions, and how to get legal advice or escalate concerns.

IETF process.why: The document is about participant conduct and IETF procedures (BCP 9, BCP 25, conduct, conflict of interest) as a means to reduce antitrust risk. It is governance and process guidance for IETF participants.
IETF process.quote: Compliance with the BCPs and other relevant policies that document the established rules and norms of the IETF facilitates compliance with antitrust law

rejected.why: BCP 78 and BCP 79 are listed only as one of several policies participants must follow. The document is about antitrust, not intellectual property rights.
Section 2.1 only clarifies that 'antitrust' and 'competition law' are synonyms. This is not a glossary or definitions document.

gaps.name: Antitrust / competition law compliance
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no legal-compliance subject under internet governance. This is the document's central subject, and it is only approximated by the IETF process tag.

RFC9681.title: IS-IS Fast Flooding
RFC9681.summary: Defines IS-IS protocol extensions (a Flooding Parameters TLV with sub-TLVs), receiver improvements, and flow/congestion control approaches to enable much faster LSP flooding in large IS-IS networks.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with a new TLV and sub-TLVs, changes PSNP and LSP handling, and specifies faster flooding behaviour. It is squarely about IS-IS.
IS-IS.quote: This document defines a new Type-Length-Value (TLV) tuple called the "Flooding Parameters TLV" that may be included in IS-IS Hellos (IIHs) or Partial Sequence Number PDUs (PSNPs).

congestion control.why: A substantial part of the document specifies flow and congestion control for LSP transmission (cwin, RWIN, pacing, transmitter-based approaches). Readers of congestion control would want it.
congestion control.quote: This section describes one sender-side congestion control algorithm largely inspired by the TCP congestion control algorithm [RFC5681].

rejected.why: TCP congestion control and receive window are only models for the IS-IS algorithm. The document does not specify or extend TCP.
Only the IS-IS link-state protocol is addressed. OSPF is not discussed.
The IS-IS tag already covers the routing subject. The document is not about general routing architecture.
RFC 9002 is cited only for pacing guidance. QUIC is not the subject.
BGP is mentioned only as an example of a more bursty protocol to deprioritize.

gaps.name: IS-IS
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for IS-IS, which is the central subject here. The IS-IS tag I used is not in the taxonomy and would be invalid. A routing-level tag such as 'routing' is the closest fit, and the IS-IS tag should be added to the taxonomy.

RFC9682.title: Updates to the Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL) Grammar
RFC9682.summary: RFC 9682 updates the ABNF grammar of CDDL (RFC 8610), fixing string literal escaping per errata, allowing empty CDDL files, and permitting non-literal tag numbers and simple values.

CDDL.why: The whole document revises the CDDL grammar: string literals, empty models, and head-number syntax for tags and simple values.
CDDL.quote: This document updates RFC 8610 by addressing related errata reports and making other small fixes for the ABNF grammar defined for CDDL.

rejected.why: ABNF is the notation used to write the CDDL grammar. The document does not specify or extend ABNF itself.
CBOR is the data format that CDDL describes. The document only touches CBOR through tag and simple-value syntax in the CDDL grammar.
JSON's \uHHHH escape syntax is borrowed for CDDL string literals. The document is not about JSON.
Unicode scalar values and surrogates appear in the escape grammar. The document is not about Unicode usage in protocols.

gaps.name: CDDL (Concise Data Definition Language)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no CDDL tag. The only CDDL entry is nested under CBOR as a [tech], and I could not use it as an id here. The document is entirely about CDDL, so a tag for it would be the right fit.

RFC9683.title: Remote Integrity Verification of Network Devices Containing Trusted Platform Modules
RFC9683.summary: Informational guidance describing the Remote Integrity Verification (RIV) workflow, in which network devices with TPMs attest their boot-time firmware and software integrity to a Verifier using DevID, quotes, event logs and signed reference manifests.

remote attestation.why: The whole document specifies a remote attestation workflow for network equipment: Attester/Verifier roles, TPM quotes, logs, reference values and appraisal policy.
remote attestation.quote: outlining the Remote Integrity Verification (RIV) problem and then by identifying the necessary elements to get the complete, scalable attestation procedure working

rejected.why: The CHARRA YANG model is defined in RFC 9684; this document only references it for retrieving evidence.
NETCONF/RESTCONF is only the transport used to retrieve evidence.
TLS and SSH are only the secure session substrate; nothing new is defined.
DevID and AK certificates are used but no certificate profile is specified by this document.
Supply chain trust is mentioned as context and for RIMs, but the document is about device attestation, not artefact supply-chain transparency.
RFC 6813 is cited only for the Asokan attack; the document does not address NEA.

gaps.name: Trusted Platform Module (TPM) / trusted computing
gaps.why: The document centres on TPM PCRs, quotes, and TCG specifications, but the taxonomy has no TPM or trusted computing tag.

gaps.name: Secure device identity (IEEE 802.1AR DevID)
gaps.why: The identity mechanism, with IDevID/LDevID and attestation keys, is a major part of the document, and there is no matching tag.

RFC9684.title: A YANG Data Model for Challenge-Response-Based Remote Attestation (CHARRA) Procedures Using Trusted Platform Modules (TPMs)
RFC9684.summary: Defines YANG modules (ietf-tpm-remote-attestation and ietf-tcg-algs) with RPCs for TPM 1.2/2.0 challenge-response quote retrieval and measurement log retrieval (BIOS, IMA, netequip boot), plus config/operational nodes, for RATS remote attestation of network devices.

YANG.why: The document's core deliverable is a pair of YANG modules defining RPCs and data nodes for TPM-based remote attestation.
YANG.quote: This document defines the YANG Remote Procedure Calls (RPCs) and configuration nodes that are required to retrieve attestation evidence about integrity measurements from a device

remote attestation.why: It specifies challenge-response attestation of TPM Evidence and event logs, which is the subject of remote attestation.
remote attestation.quote: The ietf-tpm-remote-attestation YANG module enables a composite device to take on the role of an Attester, in accordance with the RATS architecture

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the management protocols the YANG module is accessed through, mentioned mainly in Security Considerations and examples.
Certificates are referenced as keystore entries for attestation keys, but the document does not specify certificate formats or profiles.
Hash algorithm identities are enumerated from the TCG registry, but the document is not about the SHA family.
The ietf-tcg-algs module lists TCG algorithm identifiers, but it does not define or specify the algorithms. It only mirrors the registry.
Attestation key and endorsement key certificates appear only as data node references, not as PKI specification.

gaps.name: Remote attestation (RATS) / TPM-based attestation
gaps.why: The document is mainly about remote attestation procedures with TPMs, and the taxonomy has no tag for them. I put 'remote attestation' as a tag id, but it is a defined tag only under security, so check that id.

RFC9685.title: Listener Subscription for IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Multicast and Anycast Addresses
RFC9685.summary: Updates 6LoWPAN ND (RFC 8505/4861) so 6LNs can subscribe to IPv6 multicast and anycast addresses via a new P-Field in the EARO/EDAR, and extends RPL (RFC 6550/9010) with a new Non-Storing multicast MOP 5, anycast support, and a Consistent Uptime Option.

6LoWPAN.why: The core of the document is extending 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery registration (EARO, EDAR, 6CIO) to subscribe multicast and anycast addresses.
6LoWPAN.quote: This document updates the 6LoWPAN extensions to IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (specified in RFCs 4861 and 8505) to enable a listener to subscribe to an IPv6 anycast or multicast address.

RPL.why: The document amends RPL: it adds MOP 5, anycast operation, a P-Field in the RTO, and mandates the ROVR field, and it extends RFC 9010 for route injection.
RPL.quote: add a new Non-Storing multicast mode and new support for anycast addresses in Storing and Non-Storing modes.

multicast.why: Multicast listener subscription and multicast delivery in LLNs is a substantial part of the document, with a new ingress-replication multicast mode, and it serves as an MLD replacement.
multicast.quote: Upon a subscription with the R flag and the P-Field both set to 1 in the EARO, if the scope of the multicast address is above link-scope

anycast.why: Anycast subscription and RPL anycast forwarding semantics, where exactly one child receives a packet, are specified in their own right.
anycast.quote: With this specification, anycast addresses can be injected in RPL in both Storing and Non-Storing modes.

rejected.why: The document does amend RFC 4861, but its subject is the 6LoWPAN ND registration, so 6LoWPAN is the more specific fit, and the narrower neighbor discovery tag adds little.
MLD is mentioned only as the mechanism that this specification replaces or sidesteps, and the document does not specify or extend it.
IPv6 is the substrate, so the more specific 6LoWPAN, RPL and anycast tags cover the subject.
The registries are created as boilerplate IANA considerations for the protocol changes, not as the document's subject.
MPL is mentioned only as one optional way to run multicast alongside the new mode.

gaps.name: 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery
gaps.why: The taxonomy has 6LoWPAN as a link-layer tag in IoT, but no tag specific to the 6LoWPAN ND registration and the EARO. The existing 6LoWPAN tag is the closest fit.

RFC9686.title: Registering Self-Generated IPv6 Addresses Using DHCPv6
RFC9686.summary: Defines a DHCPv6 extension (new option OPTION_ADDR_REG_ENABLE and ADDR-REG-INFORM/REPLY messages) letting clients register SLAAC-generated or static IPv6 addresses with a DHCPv6 server for logging and troubleshooting.

DHCPv6.why: The document extends DHCPv6 with a new option and two new message types, plus client and server processing rules.
DHCPv6.quote: This document introduces a new Address Registration (OPTION_ADDR_REG_ENABLE) option, which indicates that the server supports the registration mechanism.

rejected.why: SLAAC is the source of the addresses being registered, but the document does not specify or change SLAAC.
Only the IPv4 DHCP logging practice is mentioned as motivation. The DHCPv6 tag is the more specific fit.
FCFS SAVI is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to trust the messages.
Router Advertisements and gratuitous ND are referenced as context only. The document is not about ND.
IPv6 is the environment, and the DHCPv6 tag already covers the subject specifically.
The Privacy Considerations section is brief boilerplate-like discussion, not a main subject.

RFC9687.title: Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4) Send Hold Timer
RFC9687.summary: Defines the BGP SendHoldTimer and SendHoldTimer_Expires FSM event, updating RFC 4271 so a speaker closes a BGP connection when it cannot send messages to a blocked peer, and registers a new NOTIFICATION error code.

BGP.why: The document extends the BGP-4 FSM, session attributes, timers and error codes, updating RFC 4271. It is squarely about BGP protocol behaviour.
BGP.quote: This document defines the SendHoldTimer, along with the SendHoldTimer_Expires event, for the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) Finite State Machine (FSM).

rejected.why: BGP runs over TCP and the zero receive window is the motivating failure, but the document specifies nothing new about TCP.
The only IANA action is a single error code registration, which is boilerplate-level and not the subject of the document.
The BGP MIB is mentioned only in passing as a place to report the last error.

RFC9688.title: Use of the SHA3 One-Way Hash Functions in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC9688.summary: Specifies how to use the SHA3 hash functions (digest, RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 and ECDSA signatures, HMAC, and KDFs such as HKDF, KMAC and KDF2/KDF3) with the Cryptographic Message Syntax, including OIDs and an ASN.1 module.

CMS.why: The document defines algorithm identifiers and conventions for SHA3-based digests, signatures, MACs and KDFs in CMS structures such as SignedData, AuthenticatedData and KEMRecipientInfo.
CMS.quote: This document describes the conventions for using the one-way hash functions in the SHA3 family with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).

SHA.why: The SHA3 hash family is the central subject. The document gives its OIDs and usage as a digest and as a building block for signatures, MACs and KDFs.
SHA.quote: the four one-way hash functions in the SHA3 family (SHA3-224, SHA3-256, SHA3-384, and SHA3-512) [SHA3] with the CMS.

HMAC.why: A full section assigns OIDs for HMAC with each SHA3 hash for the CMS AuthenticatedData macAlgorithm field.
HMAC.quote: Message Authentication Codes Using HMAC and SHA3
HMAC.section: 4. Message Authentication Codes Using HMAC and SHA3

ECDSA.why: The document defines ECDSA-with-SHA3 signature identifiers and signature encoding for CMS.
ECDSA.quote: When the ECDSA is used in conjunction with one of the SHA3 one-way hash functions, the object identifiers are:

RSA.why: The document defines RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5-with-SHA3 signature identifiers and key encoding conventions.
RSA.quote: When RSASSA PKCS#1 v1.5 is used in conjunction with one of the SHA3 one-way hash functions, the object identifiers are:

key management.why: A substantial section assigns key-derivation function identifiers (HKDF, KMAC128/256, KDF2/KDF3) with SHA3.
key management.quote: The CMS KEMRecipientInfo structure [RFC9629] is one place where algorithm identifiers for key-derivation functions are needed.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is only the notation for the CMS values and the module. The document does not set ASN.1 conventions in its own right.
It only reuses the RSA and EC public key encodings from certificate specifications. It does not profile certificates.
The S/MIME OID arcs and registries are used for identifiers, but the document is about CMS and not secure email.
The IANA section only records OID assignments. That is boilerplate.
ECDSA is the more specific tag, and the document does not define curves.

RFC9689.title: Use Cases for a PCE as a Central Controller (PCECC)
RFC9689.summary: Informational document describing use cases, benefits and limitations of using a PCE as a Central Controller (PCECC) via PCEP, covering label management, SR, static TE LSPs, load balancing, inter-AS TE, multicast LSPs, traffic classification, SFC, native IP and BIER.

PCE.why: The whole document is about the PCE architecture and PCEP when used as a central controller, and its use cases.
PCE.quote: A PCE as a Central Controller (PCECC) can simplify the processing of a distributed control plane by blending it with elements of SDN

segment routing.why: A substantial section covers PCECC for SR-MPLS, SR policy and SRv6 SID allocation.
segment routing.quote: the PCECC may further use the PCEP for distributing SR Segment Identifiers (SIDs) to the SR nodes (PCC) with some benefits.

MPLS.why: MPLS label space management, static TE LSPs and P2MP LSPs are central use cases.
MPLS.quote: the PCECC can take responsibility for managing some part of the MPLS label space for each of the routers that it controls

rejected.why: SFC is only one short use case section, not a substantial focus.
BIER is a brief use case; the document is not about BIER.
BGP-LS and BGP sessions are mentioned as supporting mechanisms only.
SDN is background context; the PCE tag is more specific, and this is a PCE-based SDN use case document.
PCE sits under traffic engineering, so the ancestor is implied by the PCE tag.
Only a short subsection on SRv6; the extensions are in separate documents.

RFC9690.title: Use of the RSA-KEM Algorithm in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC9690.summary: Specifies the RSA-KEM algorithm as a standalone KEM and its use with CMS via KEMRecipientInfo (RFC 9629), including certificate conventions, SMIMECapabilities, ASN.1 module and examples; obsoletes RFC 5990.

CMS.why: The document defines how RSA-KEM is used in CMS enveloped, authenticated and authenticated-enveloped data via KEMRecipientInfo, including an enveloped-data example.
CMS.quote: conventions for using the RSA-KEM algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) using KEMRecipientInfo as specified in RFC 9629

RSA.why: RSA-KEM is an RSA-based key encapsulation mechanism, specified in full in Appendix A, and its rationale is compared with PKCS #1 v1.5.
RSA.quote: The RSA-KEM algorithm encrypts a random integer with the recipient's RSA public key and derives a shared secret from the random integer.

S/MIME.why: A substantial section and an appendix define SMIMECapabilities conventions and DER examples for advertising RSA-KEM support.
S/MIME.quote: a compliant implementation MAY include the SMIMECapabilities attribute that announces support for the RSA-KEM algorithm.

rejected.why: Section 2.3 gives certificate conventions (key usage, SPKI algorithm identifier), but this is a small part of a CMS and RSA-KEM document.
An ASN.1 module is provided, but it is only the specification apparatus and not the subject of the document.
AES Key Wrap is a mandatory-to-implement component used for wrapping, but the document is not about AES.
RSA-KEM is a classical KEM and the document does not address post-quantum migration.
The KEM is about key establishment, but the more specific tags CMS and RSA cover it, so the broad topic tag is not needed.
SHA-256 is only the hash used inside KDF3, so it is a component and not a subject.

gaps.name: KEM (Key Encapsulation Mechanism)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no generic KEM tag. RSA-KEM is specified as a standalone KEM, and readers of KEMs would want it.

RFC9691.title: A Profile for Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Trust Anchor Keys (TAKs)
RFC9691.summary: Defines the RPKI Trust Anchor Key (TAK) signed object, which lets a trust anchor signal its current and successor public keys and certificate locations to relying parties so planned TA key rollovers can happen in-band.

RPKI.why: The document specifies a new RPKI signed object, its validation, relying party processing and TA key rollover procedures. It is squarely about RPKI trust anchor management.
RPKI.quote: This document defines a new RPKI signed object that can be used to document the location(s) of the TA CA certificate for the current TA public key

rejected.why: The TAK object uses the CMS wrapper through the RFC 6488 signed object template. CMS is only the substrate here.
The document includes an ASN.1 module, but only as the encoding for the new object. It is not about ASN.1.
Resource certificates and SubjectPublicKeyInfo are used, but the document does not define a certificate profile.
It registers application/rpki-signed-tal, but only in the IANA section. That is boilerplate and not the main subject.
RPKI is the more specific tag and already sits under PKI, so the parent is implied.
RPKI is the more specific tag and already sits under routing security, so the parent is implied.

RFC9692.title: RIFT: Routing in Fat Trees
RFC9692.summary: RFC 9692 specifies RIFT, a routing protocol for Clos/fat-tree IP fabrics that floods link-state northbound and distance-vector-style default routes southbound, with automatic disaggregation, zero touch provisioning, and a Thrift-encoded, UDP-carried security envelope.

RIFT.why: The document is the RIFT protocol specification itself.
RIFT.quote: This document defines a specialized, dynamic routing protocol for Clos, fat tree, and variants thereof.

rejected.why: BFD is only optionally used to detect link failures (Section 6.8.6); the document is not about BFD.
Fat-tree data center fabrics are the target topology, but the RIFT tag is the more specific fit.
UDP is only the transport substrate for RIFT packets.
Overlays such as VXLAN are mentioned only as something RIFT is agnostic to.
Weighted ECMP is a feature used by RIFT's bandwidth balancing, not the subject of the document.
IPv4 and IPv6 are both supported as address families, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC9693.title: Benchmarking Methodology for Stateful NATxy Gateways
RFC9693.summary: Defines a benchmarking methodology for stateful NATxy gateways (NAT44, NAT64, NAT66) that handles RFC 4814 pseudorandom port numbers using restricted port ranges and two test phases, and defines new metrics for connection establishment rate, tear-down rate, and connection tracking table capacity.

benchmarking.why: The document is a benchmarking methodology extending RFC 2544/8219 with new test phases and metrics.
benchmarking.quote: This document shows how the classic performance measurement procedures (e.g., throughput, frame loss rate, latency, etc.) can be carried out.

NAT.why: The device under test is a stateful NAT gateway; connection tracking behaviour and its capacity are central, so NAT readers would want it.
NAT.quote: The test setup for the well-known stateful NAT44 (also called Network Address and Port Translation (NAPT)) solution is shown in Figure 1.

rejected.why: NAT64 is used as one example DUT, but the methodology is generic for NATxy, so the broader NAT tag fits better.
UDP is only the test traffic transport; its limitations are discussed briefly in Section 8 but the document is not about UDP.
RFC 8219 covers transition technologies, but this document generalises to any stateful NATxy including NAT44.
The more specific benchmarking tag applies (device benchmarking methodology).

RFC9694.title: Guidelines for the Definition of New Top-Level Media Types
RFC9694.summary: BCP defining criteria and procedures for registering new top-level media types, creating the IANA Top-Level Media Types registry, and giving a history of existing top-level types; updates RFC 6838.

media types.why: The whole document sets rules and criteria for new top-level media types and creates a registry for them, updating RFC 6838. Readers of media type registration rules need it.
media types.quote: This document defines best practices for defining new top-level media types.

rejected.why: MIME is the background for the type/subtype structure. The document is about media type registration rules, which the media types tag covers.
It creates a new IANA registry, but that is a small part of the document. The subject is media type policy, not IANA stewardship generally.
Email is mentioned only in passing, for example CRLF line endings in text types. The document is not about email.
RFC 1437 is mentioned as an April Fools RFC in the history section only. This document is a serious BCP.

RFC9695.title: The 'haptics' Top-Level Media Type
RFC9695.summary: Registers the 'haptics' top-level media type under the RFC 9694 guidelines, justifies it, and registers initial subtypes ivs, hjif and hmpg.

media types.why: The document registers a new top-level media type and three subtypes, and gives registration guidance for future haptics subtypes. This is media type registry work.
media types.quote: This memo registers and documents the 'haptics' top-level media type, under which subtypes for representation formats for haptics may be registered.

rejected.why: RTP is mentioned only as a way haptic signals are carried in streams. The document defines no payload format.
The 'ogg' haptic extension is mentioned only as an existing format. It is not registered or specified here.
HJIF is JSON-based and IVS is XML-based, but the document is not about those encodings. They only describe the subtype formats.
The IANA section only performs the registrations. The document is not about IANA registry guidance in general, which is RFC 9694's subject.
IVS is XML-based, but the document does not specify XML usage. It only describes the format's encoding.

gaps.name: haptics
gaps.why: The document is about haptic data formats and touch-feedback media. The taxonomy has no tag for haptics or tactile media.

RFC9696.title: Routing in Fat Trees (RIFT) Applicability and Operational Considerations
RFC9696.summary: Informational applicability and operations guide for RIFT (Routing in Fat Trees) in Clos/fat-tree fabrics, covering topologies, use cases, disaggregation, ZTP, miscabling, mobility, and anycast.

RIFT.why: The whole document discusses RIFT's applicability, deployment topologies and operational considerations.
RIFT.quote: RIFT is a dynamic routing protocol that is tailored for use in Clos, Fat Tree, and other anisotropic topologies.

rejected.why: Data center fabrics are a main use case, but the document's subject is RIFT itself, so the more specific RIFT tag covers it.
RPL is compared with RIFT and RIFT inherits ideas from it, but the document does not specify or analyse RPL.
Mentioned as background knowledge and as a comparison for miscabling, not as a subject of the document.
RIFT negotiates BFD per link, but this is a minor mention.
ECMP is listed as a RIFT property, but the document is not about ECMP in its own right.
IPv6 ND and 6LoWPAN ND are mentioned for mobility and ZTP, but they are supporting mechanisms.

RFC9697.title: Detecting RPKI Repository Delta Protocol (RRDP) Session Desynchronization
RFC9697.summary: Updates RFC 8182 to let RPKI Relying Parties detect RRDP session desynchronization by comparing delta hashes across Update Notification Files, and to recover by downloading the latest snapshot.

RPKI.why: The document extends RRDP, the RPKI repository synchronization protocol, with detection and recovery behaviour for Relying Parties. It updates RFC 8182, so RPKI readers need it.
RPKI.quote: an approach for Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Relying Parties to detect a particular form of RPKI Repository Delta Protocol (RRDP) session desynchronization

rejected.why: BGP route validation appears only as the consequence of missing validated payloads, in Security Considerations. The document is not about BGP.
The Update Notification File is XML, but XML is only the encoding used by RRDP. The document defines nothing new about it.
RRDP files are fetched over HTTPS, but HTTP is only the transport and the document says nothing new about it.
RPKI is the more specific tag and already sits under routing security, so the ancestor is implied.

RFC9698.title: The JMAPACCESS Extension for IMAP
RFC9698.summary: Defines the JMAPACCESS IMAP capability and GETJMAPACCESS command, letting an IMAP server tell authenticated clients that the same mailstore is available via JMAP and give the JMAP session URL.

IMAP.why: The document is an IMAP extension: it adds a capability, a command and a response, and extends the IMAP formal syntax.
IMAP.quote: The GETJMAPACCESS command requests that the server respond with the session URL for the JMAP server that provides access to the same mail.
IMAP.section: 4. The GETJMAPACCESS Command and the JMAPACCESS Response

JMAP.why: The extension exists to link IMAP access to JMAP access. It covers object ID equivalence and session resource discovery, and it is meant for gradual migration to JMAP.
JMAP.quote: the messages in this IMAP server are also available via the JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP), and how.

rejected.why: SASL OAuth appears only in an example, to show how authentication leads to the capability.
It is used only as an example authentication path and is not specified or extended here.
The document only briefly notes address downgrading differences between IMAP and JMAP. It is not about email address internationalization.
JSON is the substrate underlying JMAP and is not itself discussed.

RFC9699.title: Use Case for an Extended Reality Application on Edge Computing Infrastructure
RFC9699.summary: Informational use-case document describing an Extended Reality application offloaded to edge computing, covering latency, bandwidth, heavy-tailed traffic and performance requirements for network operators.

streaming.why: The document addresses XR video delivery: adaptive bitrate streaming, throughput needs (200-1000 Mbps for 6DoF video), QoE and motion-to-photon latency. This is media streaming delivery and operations, the closest fit in the taxonomy.
streaming.quote: Table 1 below shows various streaming video applications and their associated throughput requirements

rejected.why: RFC 8939 and RFC 9023 are only cited as techniques that could guarantee performance. The document does not specify or analyse DetNet.
Diffserv and RSVP are mentioned in one sentence as options. The document does not address QoS architectures.
It is mentioned once as an option for network operators and is not the subject of the document.
The traffic performance metrics section lists XR requirements. It does not define measurement methods.
3GPP is cited for URLLC and XR background. The document is not about IP over 3GPP systems.
SDN is mentioned only as a cloud implementation technique for edge computing, not as a subject of the document.

gaps.name: Extended Reality / edge computing
gaps.why: The document is chiefly about XR applications offloaded to edge computing infrastructure. The taxonomy has no tag for XR, AR/VR or edge computing.

RFC9700.title: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security
RFC9700.summary: BCP updating RFC 6749/6750/6819 with current OAuth 2.0 security best practices, an updated attacker model, and detailed attacks (redirect URI validation, mix-up, code injection, CSRF, token replay, etc.) with mitigations.

OAuth.why: The whole document is security guidance for the OAuth 2.0 framework, deprecating insecure modes and recommending PKCE, sender-constrained tokens, and mix-up defenses.
OAuth.quote: This document describes best current security practice for OAuth 2.0.

rejected.why: Redirect status codes (307/303) and Referer headers are discussed, but only as they affect OAuth; HTTP is not the subject.
TLS is used as a mechanism (end-to-end TLS, terminating proxies, mutual TLS), but the document does not define anything new about TLS.
JWT is referenced via RFC 9068 and private_key_jwt, but only incidentally.
CSRF, clickjacking, CSP, and postMessage are covered, but as OAuth attack mitigations; the OAuth tag fits more specifically.
The parent topic is implied by the OAuth tag, and the document is about a specific mechanism.
Cookies are not discussed in any substantive way.

RFC9701.title: JSON Web Token (JWT) Response for OAuth Token Introspection
RFC9701.summary: Extends OAuth 2.0 Token Introspection (RFC 7662) so an authorization server can return the introspection response as a signed (and optionally encrypted) JWT with a new media type, claim, and client/AS metadata parameters.

OAuth.why: The document extends OAuth 2.0 Token Introspection, defining new client and authorization server metadata and the resource server/authorization server interaction.
OAuth.quote: This specification extends the token introspection endpoint with the capability to return responses as JWTs.

JWT.why: It defines the structure of a JWT introspection response, a new typ value, a new token_introspection claim, and cross-JWT confusion countermeasures.
JWT.quote: The JWT MUST include the following top-level claims:

rejected.why: JWS/JWE/JWA are used to sign and encrypt the response, but the document defines nothing new about JOSE itself.
It registers application/token-introspection+jwt, but that is IANA boilerplate and the registration is incidental to the main subject.
The Accept and Content-Type headers are used only as the transport for the request and response.
TLS 1.2+ is required only in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate evidence.
JSON is only the encoding of the claims and metadata, not the subject.

RFC9702.title: YANG Data Model for Maximum Segment Identifier (SID) Depth (MSD) Types and MPLS MSD
RFC9702.summary: Defines two YANG modules: an IANA-maintained iana-msd-types module with identities for MPLS and SRv6 Maximum SID Depth types, and ietf-mpls-msd, which augments the IETF MPLS YANG model with read-only node and link MSD data.

YANG.why: The document's content is YANG modules: an IANA-maintained identity module and an augmentation of the MPLS YANG model.
YANG.quote: There are two YANG modules [RFC7950] defined in this document.

MPLS.why: The second module extends the MPLS base YANG model with node and link MSDs for the MPLS data plane, so MPLS readers would want it.
MPLS.quote: Module ietf-mpls-msd augments the base MPLS model [RFC8960], and it provides support of different types of MSDs in the MPLS data plane.

rejected.why: MSD concerns SR label stack depth, but the document only models the values and types in YANG. It does not specify segment routing.
The IANA module includes SRH MSD identities, but only as a mirror of the registry. SRv6 is not the document's subject.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in Security Considerations as access mechanisms.
The IANA-maintained module and registry note are the mechanism for the YANG module, not a guidance document on IANA stewardship.
RFC 8491 and RFC 9352 are cited as sources of the MSD types, but the document does not specify IS-IS.
RFC 8476 is cited as a source of the MSD types, but the document does not specify OSPF.

gaps.name: Maximum SID Depth (MSD)
gaps.why: The core subject, MSD signalling and types, has no dedicated tag. It sits between segment routing, IS-IS/OSPF extensions and MPLS.

RFC9703.title: Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping/Traceroute for Segment Routing (SR) Egress Peer Engineering (EPE) Segment Identifiers (SIDs) with MPLS Data Plane
RFC9703.summary: Defines three new MPLS LSP Ping/Traceroute Target FEC Stack sub-TLVs (PeerAdj, PeerNode, PeerSet SIDs) and validation rules for Segment Routing BGP Egress Peer Engineering SIDs in the MPLS data plane.

segment routing.why: The document defines OAM FEC types for SR EPE SIDs (PeerNode, PeerAdj, PeerSet) and extends RFC 8287 SR ping/traceroute procedures, so it belongs on the segment routing page.
segment routing.quote: Egress Peer Engineering (EPE) is an application of Segment Routing (SR) that solves the problem of egress peer selection.

MPLS.why: It extends MPLS LSP Ping/Traceroute (RFC 8029) with new Target FEC Stack sub-TLVs and validation rules for the MPLS data plane.
MPLS.quote: This document provides new sub-TLVs for EPE-SIDs that are used in the Target FEC Stack TLV (Type 1) in MPLS Ping and Traceroute procedures.

rejected.why: BGP-LS and EBGP sessions are the source of the EPE SID definitions and are checked during validation, but the document does not specify or extend BGP.
The SIDs are used with an MPLS data plane, but the document is about OAM for EPE SIDs, not about SR-MPLS forwarding. The segment routing tag fits better.
The document extends MPLS traceroute, but the traceroute tech tag covers general path discovery tools. It is a poor fit for MPLS LSP-specific OAM.
The topic is relevant, but the more specific MPLS and segment routing tags already cover the document.
PCEP is mentioned only as one way SR paths are communicated, and the document does not address it.
The Security Considerations are boilerplate here, and the document is not about securing routing.

gaps.name: MPLS OAM / LSP Ping and Traceroute
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MPLS LSP ping/traceroute (RFC 8029 and its SR extensions). This document and its relatives would be found on such a page.

gaps.name: Egress Peer Engineering (BGP-EPE)
gaps.why: There is no tag for the SR BGP Egress Peer Engineering application, which the document is specifically about.

RFC9704.title: Establishing Local DNS Authority in Validated Split-Horizon Environments
RFC9704.summary: Defines a mechanism by which domain owners authorize network-provided encrypted DNS resolvers to answer authoritatively for split-horizon subdomains, using a TXT Verification Record, conveyed to clients via DHCP or PvD and validated via an external resolver or DNSSEC.

DNS.why: The document specifies split-horizon DNS authority validation, a new _splitdns-challenge TXT record and client resolver behaviour. DNS is the central subject.
DNS.quote: This specification defines a mechanism for domain owners to inform DNS clients about local resolvers that are authorized to answer authoritatively for certain subdomains.

DNSSEC.why: Sections 6.2 and 7 define DNSSEC-based validation of the verification record and delegation of DNSSEC across split DNS boundaries, which is substantial DNSSEC content.
DNSSEC.quote: parent zones MAY add a "ds=..." key to the Verification Record whose value is the RDATA of a single DS record

DHCP.why: It defines a new DHCP Authentication option protocol value and encoding for carrying claims, and registers it with IANA.
DHCP.quote: each authorization claim is encoded as a DHCP Authentication option ([RFC3118] and Section 21.11 of [RFC8415]), using the Protocol value 4, "Split-horizon DNS"

rejected.why: Encrypted DNS resolvers (DoT, DoH, DoQ) are a prerequisite, but the document does not define encrypted transport.
Used only as a substrate for authenticating the resolver. The document adds nothing new to DoT.
Only mentioned as one encrypted DNS transport in the terminology.
JSON carries the PvD claims, so it is only the encoding. The document defines a PvD key, not JSON itself.
The document only excludes special-use names from scope, and uses resolver.arpa for DNSKEY.
Section 10 briefly mentions validation with IKEv2 configuration, which is a minor point and not a substantial part of the document.

gaps.name: Provisioning Domains (PvD)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for PvDs (RFC 8801). The document defines a new PvD additional-information key and a registry for it.

RFC9705.title: Refresh-Interval Independent RSVP Fast Reroute Facility Protection
RFC9705.summary: Updates RFC 4090 facility backup FRR for RSVP-TE with new PLR/MP procedures, a Conditional/Remote PathTear and a CONDITIONS object so state cleanup no longer depends on refresh timeouts, enabling RI-RSVP (RFC 8370).

RSVP-TE.why: The document extends RSVP-TE signalling for fast reroute: new CONDITIONS object, Conditional/Remote PathTear, Node-ID Hello adjacencies between PLR and MP.
RSVP-TE.quote: The RSVP-TE extensions defined in this document will enhance the facility backup protection mechanism by making the corresponding procedures refresh-interval independent

IP fast reroute.why: It updates RFC 4090 facility backup (bypass tunnel) MPLS fast reroute procedures, which fits the fast reroute subject.
IP fast reroute.quote: define two local repair techniques to reroute Label Switched Path (LSP) traffic over pre-established backup tunnels

rejected.why: LSPs are the subject, but RSVP-TE is the more specific tag and its parent MPLS is implied.
Base RSVP is the substrate. The document specifies RSVP-TE extensions, not plain RSVP.
RSVP-TE is a technology under traffic engineering, so the parent is implied and need not be tagged separately.
RFC 3473 is cited only for graceful restart interaction.

RFC9706.title: TreeDN: Tree-Based Content Delivery Network (CDN) for Live Streaming to Mass Audiences
RFC9706.summary: Informational RFC describing TreeDN, a tree-based CDN architecture for mass-audience live streaming that combines native SSM multicast on-net with AMT overlays to reach unicast-only receivers, offering Replication-as-a-Service.

CDN.why: The document defines a CDN architecture based on multicast replication and compares it with unicast CDNs.
