CDN.quote: TreeDN is a tree-based Content Delivery Network (CDN) architecture designed to address the distinctive scaling challenges of live streaming to mass audiences.

SSM.why: SSM is the native on-net multicast model and a core architectural component, with rationale for the SSM-only approach.
SSM.quote: The primary requirement of the native on-net component is to support Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) [RFC4607].

AMT.why: AMT is the main overlay that lets unicast-only receivers get multicast, and it is central to the deployments described.
AMT.quote: One overlay technology that TreeDN leverages is Automatic Multicast Tunneling (AMT) [RFC7450].

rejected.why: PIM-SSM is mentioned as the typical on-net routing protocol, but the document does not specify or extend PIM-SM.
BIER is mentioned as a permitted data plane and in the RARE deployment, but it is not the subject.
NORM and FEC are only pointed to as existing work in the transport section, which is a short part of the document.
LISP is mentioned only as another possible overlay.
IGMPv3 and MLDv2 are cited as how receivers signal SSM joins. The document does not address them.
QUIC is mentioned only as a transport used by traditional CDNs, with a pointer to a multicast extension proposal.

RFC9707.title: Report from the IAB Workshop on Barriers to Internet Access of Services (BIAS)
RFC9707.summary: Report on the January 2024 IAB BIAS workshop, summarizing discussions on community networks, the digital divide (including IDN/universal acceptance), and censorship measurement and VPN circumvention.

workshop reports.why: The document is an IAB workshop report; its whole purpose is to record the workshop proceedings.
workshop reports.quote: This report summarizes the workshop's discussions and serves as a reference for reports on the current barriers to Internet access.

IDN.why: A substantial subsection covers Universal Acceptance of IDNs and multilingual email addresses as a digital-inclusion barrier.
IDN.quote: Today, there are around 150 internationalized domain names (IDNs), but equal rollout of these scripts at the domain level is hindered primarily by software

privacy.why: Censorship circumvention and the need for privacy-preserving protocol enhancements are a key takeaway of the workshop.
privacy.quote: continued work on protocol enhancements that protect user privacy is essential.

rejected.why: DNS tampering and DNS dependency measurements are mentioned as examples, but the document does not address the DNS protocol itself.
A CDN's role for community networks is one presentation, but it is a brief discussion rather than a CDN specification or analysis.
Censorship measurements (OONI) are reported, but the document is not about performance measurement methods.
Email address internationalization is only mentioned in the Universal Acceptance talk, not discussed in its own right.
The workshop is held by the IAB, but the report does not discuss architectural principles.

gaps.name: Censorship and censorship circumvention
gaps.why: A major theme of the workshop (blocking measurements, VPN circumvention), but the taxonomy has no censorship or human-rights tag.

gaps.name: Community networks / digital divide
gaps.why: The central subject is community networks and digital inclusion, and no tag covers them.

RFC9708.title: Use of the HSS/LMS Hash-Based Signature Algorithm in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC9708.summary: Specifies conventions for using HSS/LMS hash-based signatures in CMS signed-data, including the algorithm identifier, public key syntax, and ASN.1 module, and obsoletes RFC 8708.

LMS.why: The document defines how HSS/LMS signatures (LMS/HSS/LM-OTS) are identified, encoded and used, so LMS is the most specific technology tag.
LMS.quote: specifies the conventions for using the Hierarchical Signature System (HSS) / Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS) hash-based signature algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)

CMS.why: It profiles CMS signed-data, covering SignerInfo fields, digestAlgorithm and signatureAlgorithm usage.
CMS.quote: the HSS/LMS signature is computed over the DER-encoded set of signed attributes (which MUST include a content-type attribute and a message-digest attribute)

rejected.why: The key usage rules for certificates appear in Section 4, but the document is about CMS. Certificate profiling is left to a separate draft.
Post-quantum security is the motivation. The tag is implied by the parent of LMS, and the document is about the specific algorithm.
ASN.1 is only the notation used for the module and identifiers. It is not the subject.
SHA-256 and SHAKE256 are underlying hash functions the document relies on. It does not define anything new about them.
RFC 4086 is cited in the Security Considerations, which is boilerplate-like and not the main body.

RFC9709.title: Encryption Key Derivation in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Using HKDF with SHA-256
RFC9709.summary: Specifies a CMS content-encryption-key derivation using HKDF with SHA-256, keyed to the encryption AlgorithmIdentifier, to defeat AEAD-to-CBC algorithm-identifier manipulation attacks in enveloped, encrypted, and authenticated-enveloped data.

CMS.why: The document extends CMS enveloped-data, encrypted-data and authenticated-enveloped-data processing with a new algorithm identifier and key derivation step.
CMS.quote: This document specifies the derivation of the content-encryption key or the content-authenticated-encryption key in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)

S/MIME.why: Defines SMIMECapabilities conventions for announcing support, and registers OIDs in the S/MIME arcs; readers of S/MIME would want it.
S/MIME.quote: Potential recipients include the id-alg-cek-hkdf-sha256 algorithm identifier (with no parameters) in S/MIME Capabilities to indicate support for this mitigation.

rejected.why: HKDF is built on HMAC but the document only uses HKDF as a building block; no HMAC specification.
SHA-256 is just the hash used within HKDF; the document is not about the SHA family.
AES-GCM/CBC appear as example content-encryption algorithms and in test vectors, not as the subject.
An ASN.1 module is provided but ASN.1 is only the notation used, not the subject.
Considered since it derives keys, but it is a per-message CEK derivation within CMS rather than key establishment or provisioning.

gaps.name: HKDF (HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for key derivation functions; HKDF is central here but only the broader cryptography topic would fit.

RFC9710.title: Simple Fixes to the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Entities IANA Registry
RFC9710.summary: Standards Track document that applies editorial and consistency fixes to descriptions and Additional Information entries in the IANA IPFIX Information Elements registry, such as forwardingStatus, port-related IEs, and citations of other IANA registries.

IPFIX.why: The whole document revises IPFIX Information Element definitions in the IANA registry.
IPFIX.quote: This document provides simple fixes to the IANA "IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Entities" registry.

rejected.why: The registry edits are about IPFIX entries specifically. The document does not give general IANA guidance or stewardship.
TCP, UDP, SCTP and DCCP appear only as references in port-field descriptions.
NAT-related IEs are edited only for citation consistency. NAT behaviour is not the subject.
messageMD5Checksum gets only a minor wording fix. The document is not about MD5.
The interface-type and mibCaptureTime IEs are touched only for citation fixes.

gaps.name: IPFIX (IP Flow Information Export)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no IPFIX tag. The nearest is the IPFIX tech under network management, which I used above, but that id does not appear in the taxonomy as an exact match for this registry-fix document.

RFC9711.title: The Entity Attestation Token (EAT)
RFC9711.summary: Defines the Entity Attestation Token (EAT), a CWT/JWT-based framework of attestation claims, submodule nesting, detached bundles and profiles, for RATS evidence and attestation results.

remote attestation.why: The whole document defines the attestation token format, claims and profiles for remote attestation (RATS), used as evidence and attestation results.
remote attestation.quote: An Entity Attestation Token (EAT) provides an attested claims set that describes the state and characteristics of an entity

JWT.why: An EAT is a CWT or JWT with new registered claims, so JWT readers want it. It also registers claims in the JWT Claims registry.
JWT.quote: EAT is built on the CBOR Web Token (CWT) [RFC8392] and JSON Web Token (JWT) [RFC7519] and inherits all their characteristics

COSE.why: The document defines CWT-based tokens and profiles of COSE protection, algorithms and key identification.
COSE.quote: Security envelopes based on CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) and JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE)

CDDL.why: Claims are defined in CDDL with a collected CDDL section covering both CBOR and JSON encodings.
CDDL.quote: Unlike (but compatible with) CWT and JWT, EAT defines claims using CDDL [RFC8610].

rejected.why: Used as an encoding for the tokens, but the document does not specify CBOR itself.
JSON is only an encoding option for the tokens.
Mentioned only as a way to carry endorsements and verification keys; not specified here.
Appendix B explains why UEID is not a UUID; this is a rationale, not UUID content.
Only CoAP Content-Format identifiers are used to label manifest types.
It registers DEV URN subtypes (ueid, sueid), a minor IANA item, not the main subject.

gaps.name: Remote attestation (RATS)
gaps.why: The document is about remote attestation procedures, evidence and attestation results. The taxonomy has a 'remote attestation' tag only under security, and I used it above; if it is not usable, no other tag fits. CWT/COSE tags are also absent from the taxonomy.

RFC9712.title: IETF Meeting Venue Requirements Review
RFC9712.summary: RFC 9712 updates RFC 8718 and RFC 8719 to revise IETF meeting venue requirements: exploratory meeting process, hotel proximity, room blocks, overflow hotels and ad hoc space.

IETF process.why: The document is a BCP revising IETF procedures and administration for meeting venue selection and meeting rotation policy, which falls under IETF process.
IETF process.quote: updates RFC 8718 ("IETF Plenary Meeting Venue Selection Process"), clarifies how the IETF Administration Support Activity (IASA) should interpret some elements of RFC 8718

rejected.why: The child tag IETF process fits more specifically, so the parent is implied.
The copyright and legal provisions are boilerplate and the body is not about them.
The document has no IANA actions and the section is boilerplate.
The document is a policy update, not a workshop report, although it draws on post-meeting surveys.

RFC9713.title: Bundle Protocol Version 7 Administrative Record Types Registry
RFC9713.summary: Updates RFC 9171 so Bundle Protocol v7 agents use the IANA "Bundle Administrative Record Types" registry, adds a BP version column, and reserves Private/Experimental Use code points.

DTN.why: The document updates Bundle Protocol version 7 behaviour and its administrative record type registry. DTN is the closest tag for the Bundle Protocol.
DTN.quote: Bundle Protocol Version 7 (BPv7) was published in [RFC9171], it identified the IANA registry for administrative record types

rejected.why: The document does concern an IANA registry. But the subject is the Bundle Protocol registry, not IANA registry policy or guidance generally, so the DTN tag fits better.

RFC9714.title: Encapsulation for MPLS Performance Measurement with the Alternate-Marking Method
RFC9714.summary: Defines an MPLS label-stack encapsulation (Extension Label, new Flow-ID Label Indicator value 18, and Flow-ID Label with loss/delay/type color bits) enabling Alternate-Marking performance measurement of MPLS flows.

MPLS.why: The document specifies a new MPLS label stack encapsulation (FLI special-purpose label, Flow-ID Label) and its procedures at ingress, transit and egress LSRs.
MPLS.quote: This document defines the encapsulation for MPLS performance measurement with the Alternate-Marking Method

performance measurement.why: The purpose is Alternate-Marking packet loss, delay and jitter measurement, with coloring bits and Flow-ID allocation for measurement.
performance measurement.quote: which performs flow-based packet loss, delay, and jitter measurements on the MPLS traffic

rejected.why: Only mentioned as a way for the ingress node to export flow characteristics; not specified or extended here.
SR label stacks are discussed only as a case for placing the FL between SID labels; not the subject.
A short considerations section notes that adding the FL may change ECMP paths, but the document is not about ECMP.
PW labels appear only as example application labels in the stack layouts.
The IANA section only registers one label value, which is boilerplate.

gaps.name: Alternate-Marking Method
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for Alternate Marking. It is covered only by the generic performance measurement topic.

RFC9715.title: IP Fragmentation Avoidance in DNS over UDP
RFC9715.summary: Informational document describing techniques for DNS responders, requestors and operators to avoid IP fragmentation of DNS over UDP, via payload size limits, dropping fragments, TCP fallback and smaller responses.

DNS.why: The whole document gives recommendations for DNS responders, requestors and operators on response sizing and transport fallback.
DNS.quote: This document describes various techniques to avoid IP fragmentation of UDP packets in DNS.

EDNS.why: The recommendations centre on the EDNS(0) requestor's maximum UDP payload size, with a recommended default of 1400, and Appendix A discusses it in detail.
EDNS.quote: UDP responders should compose response packets that fit in the minimum of the offered requestor's maximum UDP payload size [RFC6891]

PMTUD.why: The document discusses path MTU handling, DF bit and socket options (IP_MTU_DISCOVER) and the risks of PMTUD for DNS/UDP.
PMTUD.quote: enabling IPv4 Path MTU Discovery for UDP in current Linux versions is considered harmful and dangerous.

rejected.why: UDP is the transport whose fragmentation is addressed, but the document is about DNS behaviour, not UDP itself or its usage guidelines.
DNSSEC is mentioned only as a signature-size consideration (R11) and as a countermeasure; the document does not specify or extend it.
TCP is the fallback transport, mentioned only as an alternative; it is not specified or extended here.
IPv6 fragmentation and minimum MTU are cited as background and not as the subject.

RFC9716.title: Mechanisms for MPLS Ping and Traceroute Procedures in Inter-Domain Segment Routing Networks
RFC9716.summary: Defines new Segment sub-TLVs (Types A, C, D) for the MPLS Reply Path TLV and procedures so LSP ping and traceroute work across inter-AS and inter-domain SR-MPLS networks, including dynamic return-path building.

SR-MPLS.why: The document extends MPLS OAM (ping/traceroute) for SR-MPLS paths, defining SR segment encodings (Node-SIDs, EPE-SIDs, SRGB handling) for return paths.
SR-MPLS.quote: This document outlines mechanisms to enable efficient LSP ping and traceroute procedures in inter-AS and inter-domain SR-MPLS networks.

traceroute.why: A large part covers traceroute procedures including TTL-based hop-by-hop dynamic return path building.
traceroute.quote: It is useful for operators to be able to perform LSP ping and traceroute procedures on these inter-AS SR-MPLS paths

OAM.why: LSP ping is an MPLS OAM mechanism, and the document extends it with new TLVs, flags, and return codes.
OAM.quote: This is achieved through a straightforward extension to the Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) protocol

rejected.why: The more specific SR-MPLS tag fits; the MPLS data plane is the substrate.
BGP-LU, BGP-LS and EPE are only referenced as context for how paths and SIDs are obtained.
SR-MPLS is the more specific child and is chosen instead.
IGP domains are mentioned only as the topology setting, not specified.
IGP domains are mentioned only as the topology setting, not specified.
IANA registry actions are boilerplate for this protocol extension.

gaps.name: MPLS LSP ping (MPLS echo request/reply)
gaps.why: The document extends LSP ping and its Reply Path TLV (RFC 8029/7110), but the taxonomy has no MPLS OAM or LSP ping tag; OAM and traceroute are the nearest topics.

RFC9717.title: A Routing Architecture for Satellite Networks
RFC9717.summary: Independent-stream informational RFC proposing a scalable routing architecture for satellite networks using IS-IS with Area Proxy, stripes as L1 areas, Segment Routing over MPLS, PCE-based traffic engineering, and scheduled link changes, with no protocol changes.

routing architecture.why: The document's whole purpose is a routing architecture addressing scalability and hierarchy for satellite networks.
routing architecture.quote: This document proposes a scalable routing architecture for satellite networks based on existing routing protocols and mechanisms that is enhanced with scheduled link connectivity change information.

IS-IS.why: IS-IS is the chosen IGP; substantial sections cover its levels, Area Proxy and stripes-as-L1-areas.
IS-IS.quote: we propose that all nodes in the network be L1L2 so that local routing is done based on L1 information and then global routing is done based on L2 information.

segment routing.why: Forwarding plane and traffic engineering are based on SR with node, area and adjacency SIDs.
segment routing.quote: we propose using an approach based on Segment Routing (SR) [RFC8402] with an MPLS data plane [RFC8660], where each satellite is assigned a node Segment Identifier (SID).

TVR.why: A full section covers scheduled, predictable topology changes, which is time-variant routing.
TVR.quote: The most significant difference between terrestrial and satellite networks from a routing perspective is that some of the topological changes that will happen to the network can be anticipated and computed.

rejected.why: MPLS is the data plane via SR, but the document is not about MPLS itself; SR covers it.
PCEs are mentioned as doing path computation at gateways but are not specified or extended.
BGP is assumed in the terrestrial network and used to advertise prefixes, not the document's subject.
OSPF is only discussed and dismissed as unsuitable.
Traffic engineering is covered briefly in one section; SR tag already captures it.
A YANG schedule model is merely referenced as a possible dissemination mechanism.

gaps.name: Satellite networks / LEO constellations
gaps.why: The document's subject domain, satellite network routing, has no dedicated tag; 'satellite' exists only under link layer for satellite links.

RFC9718.title: DNSSEC Trust Anchor Publication for the Root Zone
RFC9718.summary: Specifies the XML format and HTTPS/CMS-signed publication mechanisms IANA uses to distribute DNSSEC root zone trust anchors, obsoleting RFC 7958.

DNSSEC.why: The document defines how DNSSEC root zone trust anchors are represented (KeyDigest, DS/DNSKEY mapping) and published, which is core DNSSEC trust anchor material.
DNSSEC.quote: This document describes the format and publication mechanisms IANA uses to distribute the DNSSEC trust anchors.

XML.why: A substantial part of the document defines an XML format with a RELAX NG schema and semantics for the trust anchor file.
XML.quote: IANA publishes trust anchors for the root zone as an XML [W3C.REC-xml11-20060816] document that contains the hashes of the DNSKEY records

rejected.why: Detached CMS signature is only used as an optional verification mechanism, not specified here.
HTTP/HTTPS is just the retrieval substrate; nothing new is defined about it.
TLS is used only to protect distribution of the file; no TLS-specific content.
IANA is the publisher, and the IANA Considerations section is boilerplate-like; the document is not about IANA registries.
The ICANN CA and Web PKI are mentioned only as optional verification mechanisms.
DNS is the general context, but the more specific DNSSEC tag covers the subject.

RFC9719.title: YANG Data Model for Routing in Fat Trees (RIFT)
RFC9719.summary: Defines the ietf-rift YANG 1.1 (NMDA) data model for configuring and managing the RIFT (Routing in Fat Trees) protocol, augmenting ietf-routing with configuration, state, statistics, database and notifications.

RIFT.why: The model exists to manage RIFT: it covers LIEs, TIEs, ZTP levels, neighbors, flooding, and RIFT security.
RIFT.quote: This document defines a YANG data model for the configuration and management of the Routing in Fat Trees (RIFT) Protocol.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module, with tree diagrams, augmentations of ietf-routing, and actions and notifications.
YANG.quote: This document defines one NMDA-compatible [RFC8342] YANG 1.1 [RFC7950] data model for the management of the RIFT protocol.

rejected.why: BFD is only referenced as a link capability flag and bfd-state leaf; the document does not specify or extend BFD.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in the boilerplate Security Considerations as access protocols.
Not related. This is a YANG model, not an SNMP MIB.
The parent topic is implied by the YANG tag.
IEEE 802.1AS timestamps are used only as a data type for prefix mobility, not as a time-sync subject.

RFC9720.title: RFC Formats and Versions
RFC9720.summary: RFC 9720 defines the RFC Series policy for the definitive RFCXML version and derived publication versions (HTML, text, PDF) of RFCs. It covers when they may be reissued and archived, and it obsoletes RFC 7990 and updates RFC 9280.

RFC series.why: The document is about how RFCs are published: formats, versions, reissuing and archiving. It also updates the RFC Editor Model's stability policy.
RFC series.quote: the definitive version of the RFC Series transitioned from plain-text ASCII to XML using the RFCXML vocabulary; different publication versions are rendered from that base document.

RFCXML.why: RFCXML is the definitive format. The document sets a policy for how the RFCXML vocabulary may change and how RFCs are reissued when it does.

rejected.why: XML is only the encoding for RFCXML. The document is not about XML usage in protocols.
ASCII is mentioned only as the earlier plain-text format that was replaced.
The document is explicitly about RFC production, not how IETF Internet-Drafts are developed.
HTML is only one of the publication formats and is not specified here.

RFC9721.title: Extended Mobility Procedures for Ethernet VPN Integrated Routing and Bridging (EVPN-IRB)
RFC9721.summary: Extends EVPN-IRB MAC mobility procedures (RFC 7432/9135) with sequence number inheritance, multi-homing synchronization, routed-overlay mobility, and duplicate IP/MAC detection for cases where MAC-IP bindings change across host moves.

EVPN.why: The whole document specifies EVPN-IRB mobility sequence number assignment, MAC-IP route inheritance, all-active multihoming sync, and duplicate host detection.
EVPN.quote: This document updates the sequence number assignment procedures defined in [RFC7432] to 1) adequately address mobility support across EVPN-IRB overlay use cases

rejected.why: BGP carries the EVPN routes but the document is about EVPN mobility procedures, not BGP itself.
ARP/NDP probing is used for convergence and stale-entry removal, but the document does not specify or extend ARP.
NDP is only used for learning and probing host bindings, not the subject of the document.
VXLAN is one possible overlay encapsulation; the document is encapsulation-independent.
MPLS is one of the encapsulations mentioned only in passing.
EVPN is a child of VPN, not L2VPN; the more specific EVPN tag fits.

RFC9722.title: Fast Recovery for EVPN Designated Forwarder Election
RFC9722.summary: Defines a clock-synchronized Service Carving Time BGP extended community and a Time Synchronization capability so EVPN PEs perform Designated Forwarder election simultaneously on recovery, updating the RFC 8584 DF election FSM.

EVPN.why: The whole document extends EVPN DF election procedures from RFC 7432 and RFC 8584 with a new BGP extended community and capability bit.
EVPN.quote: This document improves these procedures by providing a fast DF election upon recovery of the failed link or node associated with the multihomed Ethernet Segment.

rejected.why: BGP is only the signalling carrier for the new extended community; the document does not specify BGP itself.
Only the NTP timestamp format is reused, and the document is agnostic to the actual clock synchronization mechanism.
Mentioned only as an example clock synchronization protocol.
The document relies on synchronized clocks but does not address clock synchronization itself.
EVPN is the more specific tag and already covers this subject.

RFC9723.title: BGP Colored Prefix Routing (CPR) for Services Based on Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6)
RFC9723.summary: Describes Colored Prefix Routing (CPR), which advertises SRv6 locators as IPv6 unicast prefixes with Color Extended Communities to give SRv6 services end-to-end intent-aware inter-domain paths via longest-prefix matching, without new BGP extensions.

SRv6.why: The mechanism allocates SRv6 locators per intent and steers SRv6 service traffic via the Service SIDs, so the document is centrally about SRv6.
SRv6.quote: In SRv6 networks, the Colored Prefixes are the SRv6 locators associated with different intents.

BGP.why: It specifies how BGP IPv6 unicast routes with Color Extended Community are advertised across multiple ASes, with operational guidance on aggregation, color mapping and policy.
BGP.quote: the mechanism for IPv6 unicast routing as defined in [RFC2545] is used for the advertisement of the Colored Prefix routes

rejected.why: SRv6 VPN services are only the example service steered over CPR; the document does not specify VPN procedures.
The more specific SRv6 tag fits; SR-MPLS and SR Policy appear only as intra-domain resolution options.
MPLS LSPs are only one possible intra-domain path type in Section 3.2, not the subject.
Intent-aware paths are the goal, but the document specifies BGP/SRv6 prefix signalling rather than TE mechanisms.
IPv6 unicast address family and prefixes are used as the substrate, not the subject.

RFC9724.title: State of Affairs for Randomized and Changing Media Access Control (MAC) Addresses
RFC9724.summary: Informational overview of IETF, IEEE 802 and WBA activities on randomized and changing MAC addresses, with a taxonomy of MAC address selection policies and a survey of OS practices.

privacy.why: The document is about privacy threats from persistent link-layer identifiers and the mitigations (randomized MAC addresses) being standardized.
privacy.quote: One of the main factors that eases tracking of Internet users is the wide use of long-lasting, and sometimes persistent, identifiers at various protocol layers.

link layer.why: Focuses on MAC address usage, local vs. universal administration, randomization policies and IEEE 802 work; no specific medium tag fits fully.
link layer.quote: IEEE 802 MAC addresses have historically been an easy target for tracking users

WiFi.why: Much of the document concerns 802.11 probe requests, SSID-bound randomization, IEEE 802.11bh/bi and OS Wi-Fi behaviour.
WiFi.quote: Most mobile devices used today are Wi-Fi enabled (i.e., they are equipped with an IEEE 802.11 wireless local area network interface).

SLAAC.why: A full section reviews IPv6 SLAAC IID privacy (RFC 7217, 8064, 8981) as the L3 counterpart to MAC randomization.
SLAAC.quote: [RFC8981] identifies and describes the privacy issues associated with embedding MAC stable addressing information into IPv6 addresses
SLAAC.section: 5. IPv6 Address Randomization in the IETF

rejected.why: RFC 8947/8948 and DHCP anonymity profiles are only briefly summarized as related work.
DHCP identifiers are mentioned as correlation risks, not the subject.
The SLAAC child tag is more specific for the IPv6 section.
Ethernet is mentioned only as another IEEE 802 interface type.
The document is about link-layer addresses, not IP address architecture.

gaps.name: MAC address randomization (RCM)
gaps.why: The central subject, Randomized and Changing MAC addresses, has no dedicated tag; link layer and privacy are the closest fits.

RFC9725.title: WebRTC-HTTP Ingestion Protocol (WHIP)
RFC9725.summary: Specifies WHIP, an HTTP-based protocol using POST of SDP offers/answers, PATCH for Trickle ICE and ICE restarts, and DELETE for teardown, to ingest WebRTC media into streaming services and CDNs; updates RFC 8840 and 8842.

WHIP.why: The document defines WHIP itself, its session setup, ICE handling, constraints, extensions and IANA registries.
WHIP.quote: The WebRTC-HTTP Ingestion Protocol (WHIP) is designed to facilitate a one-time exchange of Session Description Protocol (SDP) offers and answers using HTTP POST requests.

rejected.why: WHIP is a child of WebRTC, so the WHIP tag implies it. The document constrains WebRTC usage but exists to define WHIP.
Trickle ICE and ICE restarts are carried over HTTP PATCH, but the document uses ICE and does not define it.
HTTP is the substrate. WHIP uses POST, PATCH and DELETE and defines nothing new about HTTP semantics.
SDP offer/answer is the payload exchanged. The document does not extend SDP.
It registers the ice-server link relation and uses Link headers. That is a small supporting part and not the subject.
STUN/TURN server configuration is conveyed via Link headers, but STUN and TURN themselves are not specified or extended.
Bearer token authentication is required, but it is a brief use of existing mechanisms.

RFC9726.title: Operational Considerations for Use of DNS in Internet of Things (IoT) Devices
RFC9726.summary: BCP giving IoT device manufacturers recommendations on using DNS names and IP addresses so that MUD controllers can map names in MUD file ACLs to addresses, including anti-patterns, DNS resolver choice, and mDNS/DNS-SD interactions.

MUD.why: The whole document concerns how DNS names in MUD files and ACLs are enforced by MUD controllers, and advises manufacturers on MUD use.
MUD.quote: this document makes recommendations on when and how to use DNS names in MUD files.

DNS.why: The document analyses DNS resolution behaviour (round-robin, geographic load balancing, TTLs, CNAMEs, tailored responses, reverse mappings) and its operational effect on IoT devices.
DNS.quote: The simplest successful strategy for a MUD controller to translate DNS names is to do a DNS lookup on the name (a forward lookup)
DNS.section: 3. A Model for MUD Controller Mapping of DNS Names to Addresses

DNS privacy.why: Section 5, section 6.5 and the privacy considerations discuss encrypted DNS and public resolvers and how they conflict with MUD controllers, and recommend using locally provided resolvers.
DNS privacy.quote: DNS over TLS (DoT) [RFC7858], DNS over HTTPS (DoH) [RFC8484], or DNS over QUIC (DoQ) [RFC9250] can cause problems

rejected.why: The EDNS client-subnet option is discussed only as a cause of tailored responses. The document does not specify or extend EDNS.
There is only a short section on how mDNS interacts with MUD. The document does not specify or profile mDNS.
It is mentioned briefly, in the same short section as mDNS, as a replacement for mDNS in enterprise networks.
CDNs are covered only as a cause of unpredictable DNS names. The document does not address CDN technology itself.
DHCP is only the source of resolver addresses that devices are advised to use.
DNSSEC is mentioned only in passing, for truncated responses and signed TXT records.

gaps.name: MUD (Manufacturer Usage Description)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no MUD tag under IoT, even though it is the main subject of the document. I tagged it above, but the id does not appear in the taxonomy. If it is invalid, the closest tags are IoT and DNS.

RFC9727.title: api-catalog: A Well-Known URI and Link Relation to Help Discovery of APIs
RFC9727.summary: Defines the "api-catalog" well-known URI and link relation, and a Linkset-based catalog document, so clients can automatically discover a publisher's APIs.

web linking.why: Registers a new link relation type, "api-catalog", and describes its use alongside "item" and nested catalogs. Link relations are the core subject of web linking.
web linking.quote: a link relation [WEB-LINKING], "api-catalog", of which the target resource is the Publisher's API catalog document.

HTTP APIs.why: The document is about discovering and cataloguing HTTP APIs, with operational guidance for publishers. That fits conventions for building and publishing APIs on HTTP.
HTTP APIs.quote: It is intended to facilitate automated discovery and usage of published Application Programming Interfaces (APIs).

URI.why: Registers the /.well-known/api-catalog well-known URI and specifies its resolution, redirects and canonical-location behaviour. There is no narrower well-known URI tag in the taxonomy.
URI.quote: a well-known URI [WELL-KNOWN], "api-catalog", that is encoded as a URI reference to an API catalog document

JSON.why: The mandatory catalog format is the JSON-based Linkset, and the appendices give JSON examples. This is a substantial part of the document but not its main subject.
JSON.quote: The Publisher MUST publish the API catalog document in the Linkset format application/linkset+json

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate (GET/HEAD, Link header, content negotiation). The document defines no new HTTP semantics, so the more specific HTTP APIs tag covers it.
TLS is only recommended for HTTPS. The mention is in Security Considerations and the document defines nothing new about TLS.
This is about discovering APIs, which is service discovery in a loose sense. The tagged HTTP APIs and web linking tags already cover it more specifically.
The document uses application/linkset+json and a profile URI but registers no media type.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate for the well-known URI and link relation. They do not make the document about IANA registry guidance.

gaps.name: Well-known URIs (RFC 8615)
gaps.why: The document registers a well-known URI, and readers may want a dedicated page for these registrations. The taxonomy has no well-known URI tag, so URI is used instead.

RFC9728.title: OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata
RFC9728.summary: Defines an OAuth 2.0 protected resource metadata format, published at /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource, and a WWW-Authenticate resource_metadata parameter that lets clients discover a resource's authorization servers and capabilities.

OAuth.why: The whole document extends OAuth 2.0 with resource metadata, a discovery flow and registry entries. It also adds an authorization server metadata parameter.
OAuth.quote: This specification defines a metadata format that an OAuth 2.0 client or authorization server can use to obtain the information needed to interact with an OAuth 2.0 protected resource.

rejected.why: Signed metadata is carried as a JWT, but JWT is only the mechanism used. The document does not define anything new about JWT.
JSON is only the encoding for the metadata document.
It adds a resource_metadata parameter to WWW-Authenticate, but this is a small part of an OAuth-focused document. The Bearer and DPoP schemes are only referenced.
TLS is only required, in the security considerations. The document defines nothing new about it.
The .well-known registration is a minor mechanism. The document is not about URI syntax or schemes.
JWS and JWK are used only to sign the metadata and publish keys. The document does not define anything new about JOSE.
Language tags appear only in the human-readable metadata section, which is a small part of the document.

RFC9729.title: The Concealed HTTP Authentication Scheme
RFC9729.summary: Defines the "Concealed" HTTP authentication scheme, a non-probeable signature-based scheme that uses a TLS keying material exporter for freshness, with its parameters, frontend/backend handling and a new Concealed-Auth-Export header field.

HTTP authentication.why: The document specifies a new HTTP authentication scheme carried in Authorization/Proxy-Authorization, with its parameters and server handling.
HTTP authentication.quote: This document defines the "Concealed" HTTP authentication scheme.  It uses asymmetric cryptography.

rejected.why: Only cited as an existing scheme that is probeable; this document defines a different scheme.
TLS is the substrate. The document uses the exporter and states TLS version requirements, but defines no new TLS extension. It does register an exporter label, which is IANA boilerplate.
Mentioned only as a transport that uses TLS and for the GOAWAY frame; not what the document is about.
Mentioned only as a transport that uses TLS; not what the document is about.
Used only for its notation and variable-length integer encoding.
Signature algorithms are referenced for public key encoding, but the document is not about them.

RFC9730.title: Interworking of GMPLS Control and Centralized Controller Systems
RFC9730.summary: Informational document describing how the GMPLS distributed control plane interworks with centralized controller hierarchies (e.g., ACTN) in transport networks, covering discovery, routing, path computation, signaling, multi-domain/multi-layer provisioning and recovery scenarios.

GMPLS.why: The document's core subject is GMPLS control plane interworking with controllers, including GMPLS signaling, routing, LMP and recovery.
GMPLS.quote: This document outlines how the GMPLS distributed control plane can work together with a centralized controller system in a transport network.

PCE.why: PCE/PCEP, stateful and PCE-initiated LSPs, and inter-layer PCE models are a substantial part of the path computation and provisioning scenarios.
PCE.quote: the PCE can be implemented within the centralized controller.

RSVP-TE.why: RSVP-TE signaling is used for E2E sessions, LSP stitching, H-LSP creation and fast reroute scenarios discussed at length.
RSVP-TE.quote: RSVP-TE is introduced in [RFC3209] and extended to support GMPLS signaling in [RFC3473].

SDN.why: Centralized controller hierarchies (ACTN: MDSC, PNC, CNC) and their coordination with distributed control are a central theme.
SDN.quote: Software-Defined Networking (SDN) technologies have been introduced to control the transport network centrally.

rejected.why: Only used as a southbound/topology retrieval option; the document does not specify or extend it.
YANG models are referenced as interfaces, not defined or analysed here.
OSPF-TE is briefly described as a routing option, not the subject.
IS-IS-TE only briefly mentioned as a routing option.
Appears only in Security Considerations boilerplate.
Parent of the chosen PCE tag; GMPLS and PCE tags are more specific.

gaps.name: ACTN (Abstraction and Control of TE Networks)
gaps.why: The controller hierarchy (MDSC/PNC/CNC) is central to the document but the taxonomy has no ACTN tag.

RFC9731.title: A YANG Data Model for Virtual Network (VN) Operations
RFC9731.summary: Defines the ietf-vn YANG module for Virtual Network (VN) operations, including access points, VN members, and a VN compute RPC, used on the ACTN CNC-MDSC interface and built on the TE Topology model.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a new YANG module (ietf-vn) with tree diagrams, RPC and JSON examples, so YANG data modelling is the subject.
YANG.quote: This document provides a YANG data model generally applicable to any mode of VN operations.

traffic engineering.why: The VN is built from abstractions of TE networks using TE Topology connectivity matrices, path constraints and optimization, and the ACTN framework. Readers of traffic engineering would want it.
traffic engineering.quote: describes a set of management and control functions used to operate one or more Traffic Engineered (TE) networks to construct a Virtual Network (VN)

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only mentioned as access protocols in Security Considerations and flow diagrams; the document does not specify them.
Only used in the illustrative message flows (HTTP POST/GET) and in boilerplate; the document defines no RESTCONF behaviour.
JSON is just the encoding for the examples in Appendix B.
The CNC/MDSC controller hierarchy is related, but the document is a data model rather than about SDN as a subject.
L3SM, L2SM and L1CSM are mentioned only as service models the VN model can work alongside.
SR Policy is mentioned only as a possible future augmentation of the empty underlay container.

gaps.name: ACTN (Abstraction and Control of TE Networks) / TE topology
gaps.why: The document is largely about the ACTN virtual network service and the TE Topology model, but the taxonomy has no ACTN or TE topology tag. The closest fit is the generic traffic engineering topic.

RFC9732.title: A Framework for NRP-Based Enhanced Virtual Private Networks
RFC9732.summary: Informational framework describing NRP-based enhanced VPNs, which combine overlay VPNs with underlay Network Resource Partitions to give performance-guaranteed connectivity and to underpin network slicing, and surveying candidate data-plane, control-plane and management technologies.

VPN.why: The whole document is a framework for enhanced VPN services built on conventional VPN overlays, so the VPN page is the natural home.
VPN.quote: This document describes a framework for Enhanced Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) based on Network Resource Partitions (NRPs)

traffic engineering.why: NRPs, resource-reserved TE paths, RSVP-TE and SR-based TE are substantial parts of the architecture, with scalability analysis. No specific TE technology tag fits as the main subject.
traffic engineering.quote: NRP-based enhanced VPNs leverage the VPN and Traffic Engineering (TE) technologies and add characteristics that specific services require

DetNet.why: DetNet is a candidate technology for latency and loss guarantees. It is discussed repeatedly, including for enhanced resiliency.
DetNet.quote: DetNet can be realized over the IP data plane [RFC8939] or the MPLS data plane [RFC8964], and it may be used to provide deterministic paths

segment routing.why: SR is a candidate data and control plane mechanism for NRPs. It is also analysed in the scalability sections, such as maximum stack depth.
segment routing.quote: SR [RFC8402] is a method that prepends instructions to packets at the headend of a path.

rejected.why: RSVP-TE is discussed as a candidate and for its scalability, but the document does not specify or extend it.
L3VPN, L2VPN and EVPN are listed as example overlays only. The document is about the enhanced-VPN framework as a whole.
YANG service models are referenced in Section 5.6 as applicable, but the document defines no model.
Diffserv is mentioned only to explain why it is insufficient for enhanced VPN separation.
SDN controllers are mentioned within the scalability and control-plane discussion, but SDN is not the subject.
OAM and telemetry get short considerations sections that mostly defer to other work.

gaps.name: Network slicing / Network Resource Partitions (NRP)
gaps.why: The document is largely about NRPs and the realization of RFC 9543 network slices. The taxonomy has no tag for network slicing or resource partitioning.

RFC9733.title: BRSKI with Alternative Enrollment (BRSKI-AE)
RFC9733.summary: Extends BRSKI so devices can enroll LDevID certificates via alternative protocols using authenticated self-contained objects (notably CMP with the Lightweight CMP Profile) instead of EST, generalizing the well-known URI scheme and registrar/RA architecture.

BRSKI.why: The document defines enhancements to BRSKI: architecture, message flow, and endpoint addressing for alternative enrollment.
BRSKI.quote: BRSKI-AE extends BRSKI to support certificate enrollment mechanisms instead of the originally specified use of Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST).

CMP.why: Section 5.1 specifies BRSKI-CMP, the normative instantiation of BRSKI-AE with CMP and its Lightweight Profile, including endpoints and message mapping.
CMP.quote: Adherence to the LCMPP [RFC9483] is REQUIRED when using CMP.

rejected.why: EST is the mechanism being replaced; the document discusses it for comparison, not specifying or extending it.
TLS/DTLS is only the transport channel reused for enrollment messages; nothing new is defined about it.
Certificates and LDevID/IDevID are the subject matter of enrollment, but the document does not profile X.509 itself.
HTTP is the substrate; the well-known URI extension is part of BRSKI-AE and does not define HTTP semantics.
CoAP and cBRSKI are mentioned only as a possible combination.
CMS is referenced only in describing CMC and SCEP alternatives.

gaps.name: BRSKI / certificate enrollment (bootstrapping)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no BRSKI or certificate enrollment tag, so a nearby tag was needed.

RFC9734.title: X.509 Certificate Extended Key Usage (EKU) for Instant Messaging URIs
RFC9734.summary: Defines the id-kp-imUri KeyPurposeId for the X.509 Extended Key Usage extension, for certificates proving the identity of Instant Messaging clients (e.g., MLS credentials), and registers its OID and ASN.1 module.

X.509.why: The document defines a new Extended Key Usage KeyPurposeId for X.509 v3 certificates, extending the RFC 5280 profile.
X.509.quote: This specification defines the KeyPurposeId id-kp-imUri, which may be included in certificates used to prove the identity of an IM client.

instant messaging.why: The EKU is purpose-built for identifying IM clients (IM and XMPP URIs in subjectAltName), so IM readers would want it.
instant messaging.quote: Instant Messaging (IM) systems using the Messaging Layer Security (MLS) [RFC9420] protocol can incorporate per-client identity certificate credentials.

rejected.why: MLS is the context in which the certificates are used, but the document defines nothing about the MLS protocol itself.
The ASN.1 module is just the formal definition of the OID; the document is not about ASN.1.
XMPP URIs are only mentioned as an example subjectAltName type.
X.509 is the more specific fitting tag.

RFC9735.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Distinguished Name Encoding
RFC9735.summary: Defines the encoding of AFI 17 Distinguished Names (NULL-terminated US-ASCII strings) in LISP EID-Records and RLOC-Records, with mapping-system lookup rules, name-collision guidance, and deployment experience.

LISP.why: The whole document specifies a LISP control-plane address encoding (DN as EID or RLOC), its Map-Request/Map-Server lookup behaviour, and deployment use cases.
LISP.quote: This document defines how to use the Address Family Identifier (AFI) 17 "Distinguished Name" in the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP).

rejected.why: The document explicitly says its Distinguished Name has no relationship to the PKIX field of that name.
Mentions the Mapping System acting as a DNS proxy only in passing; DNs here are not DNS names or records.
US-ASCII is only the string encoding used for the name; the document is not about ASCII.
Referenced only for its preservation of the US-ASCII range; not a subject of the document.
NAT traversal appears only as one deployment example of DN use, not as the document's subject.
Document has no IANA actions; it only refers to the AFI registry.

gaps.name: LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists LISP under routing, but with the tag id `LISP` not in the tool's given constraint of tags I have verified... it is present as 'LISP' under routing, so this is the intended tag; no gap beyond that. A more specific tag for LISP control-plane/LCAF encodings does not exist.

RFC9736.title: The BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP) Peer Up Message Namespace
RFC9736.summary: RFC 9736 creates a separate IANA registry and TLV namespace for the BMP Peer Up message, split from the Initiation message, updating RFCs 7854, 8671 and 9069.

BMP.why: The document specifies changes to BMP's Peer Up message and Initiation Information TLVs, defining new Peer Up TLV types (String, VRF/Table Name, Admin Label).
BMP.quote: This document updates RFC 7854 by creating an independent namespace for the Peer Up message.

rejected.why: BMP monitors BGP, but the document only changes BMP message TLV namespaces, not BGP itself. BMP is the more specific tag.
It creates a registry, but this is part of the protocol change and not a subject on IANA guidance.
It only references the MIB-II sysDescr and sysName objects for the Initiation TLVs; the document is not about MIBs.
It defines string TLVs as UTF-8, which is only an encoding detail.

RFC9737.title: Reporting Errors in NFSv4.2 via LAYOUTRETURN
RFC9737.summary: Extends NFSv4.2 and the pNFS flexible file layout so a client can report I/O errors to a restarted metadata server via LAYOUTRETURN with the anonymous stateid, which avoids unnecessary resilvering.

NFS.why: The document specifies an extension to NFSv4.2 and pNFS flexible file layouts, covering grace-period recovery, LAYOUTRETURN handling and resilvering rules. NFS readers need it.
NFS.quote: the MDS MUST accept the anonymous stateid of all zeros (see Section 8.2.3 of [RFC8881]) for the lrf_stateid in LAYOUTRETURN

rejected.why: XDR is only the encoding that the NFSv4.2 definitions are built on. The document defines nothing new about RPC or XDR.

gaps.name: pNFS (Parallel NFS) flexible file layout
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no pNFS or flexible-file-layout tag under storage. NFS is the closest fit.

RFC9738.title: IMAP MESSAGELIMIT Extension
RFC9738.summary: Defines the IMAP MESSAGELIMIT (and SAVELIMIT) capability letting servers announce a cap on messages processed per command, with a MESSAGELIMIT response code, UIDAFTER/UIDBEFORE SEARCH keys, and compatibility guidance.

IMAP.why: The document specifies a new IMAP capability, response code and SEARCH keys, so it is an IMAP extension and belongs on the IMAP page.
IMAP.quote: This document defines an extension to the Internet Message Access Protocol [RFC9051] for announcing a server limit on the number of messages that can be processed

rejected.why: IMAP is the more specific tag; email is its ancestor and is implied.
Not involved; the document concerns mailbox access only.
ABNF is only used as the notation for the formal syntax, not the subject of the document.
Not relevant; the IANA registry used is the IMAP Capabilities registry.

RFC9739.title: Protocol Independent Multicast Light (PIM Light)
RFC9739.summary: Specifies PIM Light and the PIM Light Interface, which lets PIM-SM routers accept Join/Prune messages without Hello-based neighbor discovery, e.g. across BIER domains that connect PIM domains.

PIM-SM.why: The document defines a new PIM-SM interface type, the PLI, and the procedures for it: supported message types, no DR election, no Assert, and handling of Join Attributes. This is a PIM-SM extension.
PIM-SM.quote: PIM Light only supports the PIM - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) protocol, including PIM Source-Specific Multicast (PIM-SSM), as per [RFC7761].

rejected.why: BIER is the main example deployment, but PIM Light is not specified as part of BIER. The BIER-specific signalling is in a separate draft.
RFC 9260 is cited only for the PORT reliable transport option. The document does not define anything new for SCTP.
TCP appears only as one of the two PORT transports and is not the subject of the document.
BFD is mentioned only as one example of how PLI failures can be detected.
The more specific PIM-SM tag fits better. The document excludes PIM-DM and BIDIR-PIM.
IPsec ESP/AH appear only in the Security Considerations, as an authentication option.

RFC9740.title: New IPFIX Information Elements for TCP Options and IPv6 Extension Headers
RFC9740.summary: Defines new IPFIX Information Elements (and an unsigned256 data type and a bit registry) for exporting IPv6 extension headers and TCP options, deprecating ipv6ExtensionHeaders and tcpOptions.

IPFIX.why: The document extends the IPFIX information model with new IEs and a new data type.
IPFIX.quote: This document specifies new IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) [RFC7011] Information Elements (IEs) to solve a set of issues

rejected.why: IPv6 extension headers are the observed data being exported, not specified or changed by the document.
TCP options are observed and reported; TCP itself is not specified or extended.
The IANA registry creation is boilerplate-level apparatus supporting the IEs, not the subject.
Flow export is not a performance measurement method here; the IPFIX tag is more specific.

RFC9741.title: Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL): Additional Control Operators for the Conversion and Processing of Text
RFC9741.summary: Defines additional CDDL control operators (.b64u, .b64c, .hex, .b32, .h32, .b45, .base10, .printf, .json, .join) for converting and processing text in CDDL data models.

CDDL.why: The whole document extends CDDL by adding control operators, the language's main extension point.
CDDL.quote: The present document defines a number of additional generally applicable control operators.

rejected.why: The document defines CDDL operators that model Base64/Base32/Base16/Base45 text. It does not specify those encodings, which come from RFC 4648 and RFC 9285.
The .json operator models JSON text embedded in strings. JSON is a data format the operator refers to, not the subject of the document.
CDDL is used with CBOR, and the .json operator relies on the JSON-to-CBOR conversion rules. The document does not specify CBOR itself.
YANG-JSON is mentioned only as an example for .base10.

RFC9742.title: A YANG Data Model for Syslog Management
RFC9742.summary: Defines the ietf-syslog YANG module for configuring a syslog process (console, file and remote actions, selectors, TLS/UDP transports, signed messages), with examples and implementer guidance.

syslog.why: The whole document models configuration of syslog (facilities, severities, actions, remote destinations, signing). Readers of the syslog subject would want it.
syslog.quote: This document defines a YANG data model for the management of a syslog process.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module with tree diagrams, features, and NMDA compliance.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG [RFC7950] data model that may be used to configure the syslog feature running on a system.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as a management protocol the model can be used with; the document defines no NETCONF behaviour.
TLS is a transport option reused via imported RFC 9645 groupings; nothing new is defined about TLS.
UDP is just one selectable transport for remote destinations; nothing new is defined about UDP.
This is a YANG module, not a MIB; SNMP appears only as an originator of events in a figure.
XML is only the encoding used in the usage examples.
The more specific tag YANG and syslog already cover the document, so the broader topic isn't needed.

RFC9743.title: Specifying New Congestion Control Algorithms
RFC9743.summary: BCP obsoleting RFC 5033 that gives IETF guidelines and evaluation criteria (single/mixed algorithm behavior, general and special-case scenarios) for specifying and assessing new congestion control algorithms.

congestion control.why: The whole document is a framework for specifying and evaluating congestion control algorithms across transports, so the general congestion control topic fits.
congestion control.quote: This document provides guidelines for the IETF to use when evaluating a proposed congestion control algorithm that differs from the general congestion control principles

AQM.why: A dedicated section requires evaluating algorithms against AQM disciplines such as FQ-CoDel, PIE and L4S, and a bufferbloat criterion appears in 5.1.2.
AQM.quote: The proposed congestion control algorithm SHOULD be evaluated under a variety of bottleneck-queue disciplines.

ECN.why: The document covers how ECN marking must be handled in congestion control evaluation, and the tunnel behaviour section also touches ECN. This is a smaller part of the document, but readers of ECN would find it useful.
ECN.quote: Use of ECN (see [RFC3168] and [RFC9332]) requires the congestion control algorithm to react when it receives a packet with an ECN-CE marking.

rejected.why: TCP is the baseline and a comparison point, but the document does not specify or extend TCP.
QUIC is mentioned as one protocol that uses congestion control, and the document is not about QUIC.
Real-time congestion control gets a short subsection that refers to other RFCs. It is only one of several evaluation scenarios.
CUBIC and BBR are used as examples and comparison points, and the document does not specify them.
Multipath is covered in a single special-case subsection, and MPTCP is only cited as an example.
The document does set out criteria and document-status rules for publishing algorithms, but its subject is technical evaluation of congestion control.

RFC9744.title: EVPN Virtual Private Wire Service (VPWS) Flexible Cross-Connect (FXC) Service
RFC9744.summary: Specifies the EVPN-VPWS Flexible Cross-Connect (FXC) service, which multiplexes many attachment circuits across multiple Ethernet Segments into a single EVPN-VPWS service tunnel using normalized VIDs, with default and VLAN-signaled modes, new Layer 2 Attributes EC flags, and failure handling.

EVPN.why: The document defines a new EVPN-VPWS service type (FXC) extending RFC 8214 and RFC 7432, including multi-homing, Ethernet A-D routes and new extended community flags.
EVPN.quote: a new EVPN Virtual Private Wire Service (VPWS) service type specifically for multiplexing multiple attachment circuits across different Ethernet Segments (ESs)

rejected.why: BGP is the signalling substrate for EVPN routes; the document only adds flags to an EVPN extended community, not BGP protocol behaviour itself.
Pseudowire is referenced for comparison and OAM (VCCV/BFD), but the document specifies an EVPN service, not pseudowire emulation.
MPLS is the data-plane transport for EVPN labels; the document is not about MPLS itself.
Considered as the parent category, but a more specific EVPN tag applies.
Mentioned only as an OAM failure-detection option in Section 5.1.

gaps.name: EVPN-VPWS (Flexible Cross-Connect)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an EVPN tag under VPN, but I could not use it since 'EVPN' is listed as an id in the taxonomy as 'EVPN' under VPN; no dedicated EVPN-VPWS/FXC tag exists, so EVPN is the closest fit.

RFC9745.title: The Deprecation HTTP Response Header Field
RFC9745.summary: Defines the Deprecation HTTP response header field (a Structured Fields date) to signal that a resource is or will be deprecated, and registers the "deprecation" link relation type for pointing to deprecation documentation, with guidance on pairing with Sunset.

HTTP.why: The document specifies a new HTTP response header field and registers it in the HTTP field name registry, which is an HTTP extension.
HTTP.quote: The Deprecation HTTP response header field allows a server to communicate to a client application that the resource in the context of the message will be or has been deprecated.
HTTP.section: 2. The Deprecation HTTP Response Header Field

web linking.why: A substantial part of the document defines and registers the deprecation link relation type and shows its use in Link headers.
web linking.quote: the server can use links with the deprecation link relation type to communicate to the client application developer where to find more information about deprecation

rejected.why: The document mentions APIs as an example use. It is a header field and link relation specification, not a set of conventions for building HTTP APIs, so HTTP is the better fit.
The date syntax comes from Structured Field Values (RFC 9651), and the document does not define a date format of its own.

RFC9746.title: BGP EVPN Multihoming Extensions for Split-Horizon Filtering
RFC9746.summary: Updates RFC 7432 and RFC 8365 so EVPN multihomed PEs/NVEs can signal, via a new Split-Horizon Type field in the ESI Label extended community flags of A-D per ES routes, whether to use ESI-label or local-bias split-horizon filtering for tunnels supporting both.

EVPN.why: The document extends EVPN multihoming procedures and BGP EVPN A-D per ES route signalling with a Split-Horizon Type field, updating RFC 7432 and 8365.
EVPN.quote: enabling operators to select the split-horizon procedure that meets their specific requirements.

rejected.why: BGP is the carrier of the EVPN routes and extended community, but the document specifies EVPN procedures, not BGP itself.
VXLAN, Geneve and NVGRE tunnel types determine which split-horizon methods are supported, but the document does not specify or extend those encapsulations.
SRv6 is one of the tunnel types discussed (Arg.FE2), but only as an example of an encapsulation supporting both methods.
The document creates registries, but that is boilerplate for the new flag fields and not the subject.
Geneve is just one tunnel type covered; its encapsulation is not defined here.

RFC9747.title: Unaffiliated Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) Echo
RFC9747.summary: Extends BFD (updating RFC 5880) to define Unaffiliated BFD Echo, where a BFD-capable device sends BFD Control packets over the Echo port and a non-BFD neighbor simply loops them back via IP forwarding, with no control session.

BFD.why: The whole document defines a new BFD Echo-only mode and updates RFC 5880 text on the Echo function, so it belongs on the BFD page.
BFD.quote: This document specifies an extension to the Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) protocol that enables the use of the BFD Echo function without the need for an associated BFD control session.

rejected.why: The mechanism works over IPv4 and IPv6 single-hop, but IPv6 is only a carrier and the document is not about it.
BFD Echo packets use UDP port 3785, but UDP is only the transport and nothing new is defined about it.
IPv4 is only mentioned as one of the IP versions the mechanism runs over, so it is not a subject of the document.
BFD is fault detection, but BFD is the more specific tag and the document does not discuss OAM as a topic.

RFC9748.title: Updating the NTP Registries
RFC9748.summary: RFC 9748 reviews and corrects the IANA NTP and NTS registries (Reference ID, Kiss-o'-Death codes, Extension Field Types), switching to Specification Required, marking erroneous Autokey values reserved, and defining designated expert guidance.

NTP.why: The document corrects NTP parameter registries (reference IDs, kiss codes, extension field types) and updates several NTP RFCs, so NTP readers would want it.
NTP.quote: The Network Time Protocol (NTP) and Network Time Security (NTS) documents define a number of registries, collectively called the NTP registries.

IANA.why: Much of the body concerns registry policy, designated experts and registry reformatting, which is IANA registry administration.
IANA.quote: The policy for each registry is now Specification Required, as defined in [RFC8126], Section 4.6.

rejected.why: NTP is a child tag of this topic and is the more specific fit, so the parent is implied.
ASCII only constrains the format of reference ID and kiss codes. The document is not about ASCII.
Autokey and NTS appear only as entries in the registries. Their security mechanisms are not specified here.

gaps.name: NTS (Network Time Security)
gaps.why: The registries for NTS (RFC 8915) are summarized here, but the taxonomy has no NTS tag. It is covered only through NTP.

RFC9749.title: Use of Voluntary Application Server Identification (VAPID) in JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP) Web Push
RFC9749.summary: Defines a JMAP capability (urn:ietf:params:jmap:webpush-vapid) by which JMAP servers advertise their VAPID application server key so clients can use authenticated Web Push, plus rules for signing pushes and key rotation.

JMAP.why: The document extends JMAP with a new capability, session-state-driven key rotation, and PushSubscription handling, so JMAP readers need it.
JMAP.quote: Servers supporting this specification MUST add a property called urn:ietf:params:jmap:webpush-vapid to the capabilities object.

web push.why: The document is about authenticating Web Push notifications with VAPID, including application server keys, push services and subscription recreation.
web push.quote: Every time the server sends a push message to a PushSubscription URL, it MUST authenticate the POST request using the protocol outlined in [RFC8292].

rejected.why: A JWT is only the token format VAPID requires; the document defines nothing new about JWT.
The key is an ECDSA P-256 public key, but the document only specifies how it is advertised and encoded; it does not specify ECDSA.
JSON is only the encoding of JMAP objects and is not the subject.
HTTP is the substrate for push delivery; the document does not extend HTTP.
The only IANA content is the routine registration of a JMAP capability, which is boilerplate.
RFC 7515 is cited only for base64url encoding, so JOSE is not the subject.

RFC9750.title: The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Architecture
RFC9750.summary: Informational architecture document for MLS describing the Authentication Service and Delivery Service abstractions, functional and operational requirements, and security/privacy considerations for building secure group messaging systems on the MLS protocol.

MLS.why: The whole document is the MLS architecture: AS/DS roles, group operations, operational requirements and threat analysis.
MLS.quote: This document describes the architecture for using MLS in a general secure group messaging infrastructure and defines the security goals for MLS.

rejected.why: MLS is explicitly not a full instant messaging protocol; it is a security layer embedded in them, and MLS has its own tag.
Mentioned only as an example of a protocol MLS could be embedded in.
TLS is only recommended as a secure transport for MLS messages; the document defines nothing new about it.
Only named as an alternative secure transport; not discussed in its own right.
Group key agreement is covered, but the MLS tag is the more specific fit.
A PKI is cited as one possible Authentication Service, but the document is not about PKI.

gaps.name: Key Transparency
gaps.why: The document recommends key transparency for the AS, but the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC9751.title: Closing the RTP Payload Format Media Types Registry
RFC9751.summary: Closes the IANA "RTP Payload Format Media Types" registry to new registrations, backfills known entries, and updates RFC 8088 so RTP payload formats register only in the general Media Types registry.

RTP payload format.why: The document is about the registry of RTP payload format media types and updates RFC 8088 (how to write an RTP payload format), so readers of RTP payload formats would want it.
RTP payload format.quote: closes the "RTP Payload Format Media Types" registry to future registrations and lists this RFC as a reference

media types.why: Changes registration rules so payload format media types are registered only in the Media Types registry; this is a media type registry procedure matter.
media types.quote: It is required that media types be registered in the "Media Types" registry [MEDIA-TYPES] to identify the format in various signalling usages

rejected.why: IANA registry actions are the mechanism, but the subject is RTP payload format media type registration; the specific tags fit better.
Implied as the parent of RTP payload format; the document does not address RTP protocol itself.
Opus and other codecs appear only as rows in the backfilled registry table, not as subjects.
HEVC appears only as a table entry in the registry backfill.

RFC9752.title: Conveying Vendor-Specific Information in the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for Stateful PCE
RFC9752.summary: RFC 9752 extends PCEP stateful messages (PCRpt, PCUpd, PCInitiate) to carry the Vendor Information object defined in RFC 7470, and updates RFC 7470 to say Enterprise Numbers are managed via the PEN registry.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP stateful messages with the Vendor Information object and defines the updated message formats. PCE/PCEP is the subject.
PCE.quote: This document specifies extensions to the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) that enable the inclusion of vendor-specific information in stateful Path Computation Element (PCE) operations.

rejected.why: RBNF is only the notation used to show message formats, not the subject.
TLS is only recommended as a security mechanism for PCEP sessions, in Security Considerations.
The PCEP YANG module is mentioned only in passing in Manageability Considerations.
The document has no IANA actions. The PEN registry reference is a minor textual update to RFC 7470.
LSPs are the objects PCEP manages, but the document is not about MPLS.
The document is about the PCEP vendor extension mechanism, not traffic engineering in general. The TED is only background.

gaps.name: PCE / PCEP (Path Computation Element Communication Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no PCE or PCEP tag. The nearest is 'PCE' under traffic engineering, which does not appear in the list I have, so the primary tag above is invalid and the document should be tagged 'PCE' only if that id exists. It is listed in the taxonomy as 'PCE [tech]: PCE (Path Computation Element) architecture and PCEP', under traffic engineering.

RFC9753.title: Extension for Stateful PCE to Allow Optional Processing of Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Objects
RFC9753.summary: Defines a new R (RELAX) flag in the PCEP STATEFUL-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV and rules for using the P and I flags in stateful PCE messages (PCRpt, PCUpd, PCInitiate) so objects can be marked optional, updating RFC 8231.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP for stateful PCE, adding the R flag and P/I flag handling in PCRpt, PCUpd and PCInitiate, and updates RFC 8231.
PCE.quote: This document introduces a mechanism to mark some of the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) objects as optional during PCEP message exchange

rejected.why: TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as the PCEPS secure transport. The document defines nothing new about it.
GMPLS and MPLS-TE tunnels appear only as background for the stateful PCE model. The document is not about them.
The PCEP YANG module is mentioned only as a possible future extension in Manageability Considerations.
PCE is the more specific tag. Traffic engineering is its parent and is implied.

RFC9754.title: Extensions for Opening and Delegating Files in NFSv4.2
RFC9754.summary: Extends NFSv4.2 with an offline-file attribute, an open-arguments feature-probing attribute, an OPEN flag granting either an open or delegation stateid, and delegated proxying of access/modify timestamps.

NFS.why: The whole document specifies extensions to NFSv4.2 OPEN, delegations, and attributes, so NFS is the subject.
NFS.quote: This document presents several extensions for both opening the file and delegating it to the client. This document extends NFSv4.2

rejected.why: XDR is used to define the extensions, but the document is not about ONC RPC or XDR itself; it only supplies the encoding.
Client/server clock sync is mentioned as a prerequisite for timestamp proxying, but the document does not address time synchronization itself.
Parent of NFS, implied by the NFS tag, so it is not listed separately.

RFC9755.title: IMAP Support for UTF-8
RFC9755.summary: RFC 9755 revises RFC 6855, defining the IMAP UTF8=ACCEPT and UTF8=ONLY capabilities so IMAP4rev1 servers and clients can carry UTF-8 in quoted-strings, mailbox names, and message headers (EAI support).

IMAP.why: The document is an IMAP extension that defines new capabilities and changes to ENABLE, APPEND, LOGIN, and BODYSTRUCTURE behaviour.
IMAP.quote: This specification extends the Internet Message Access Protocol, specifically IMAP4rev1 (RFC 3501), to support UTF-8 encoded international characters

EAI.why: It is the IMAP component of the EAI suite. It supports internationalized headers and addresses, and it covers downgrading for legacy clients.
EAI.quote: This specification forms part of the Email Address Internationalization protocols described in the Email Address Internationalization Framework document

rejected.why: UTF-8 is the encoding the extension carries. The document does not specify or profile the encoding itself.
The document refers to RFC 5322 and RFC 6532 headers but does not define header syntax. It only defines how IMAP carries them.
SMTPUTF8 is mentioned only in the discussion of legacy clients. The document does not specify SMTP.
ABNF is used only as the notation for the syntax additions.
The parent topic is implied by EAI. Internationalized text handling here is specific to email.
The document only touches message/global in BODYSTRUCTURE, which is too minor to tag.

RFC9756.title: Update to the IANA Path Communication Element Protocol (PCEP) Numbers Registration Procedures and the Allowance of Experimental Error Codes
RFC9756.summary: Updates IANA PCEP Numbers registry policies from Standards Action to IETF Review for many registries and designates PCEP Error-Types 252-255 for Experimental Use.

PCE.why: The document changes PCEP registries and defines experimental Error-Types and handling of unknown ones, so it is about PCEP/PCE.
PCE.quote: IANA has designated four PCEP Error-Type codepoints (252-255) for Experimental Use.

IANA.why: A major part of the document is changing IANA registration policies from Standards Action to IETF Review.
IANA.quote: This document updates the registration procedure within the IANA "Path Computation Element Protocol (PCEP) Numbers" registry group.

rejected.why: Many updated RFCs concern GMPLS, but the document does not address GMPLS itself.
Registries for SR-ERO and SRv6 are listed in the table, but the document is not about segment routing.
PCE is used for traffic engineering, but this document only changes registry policy.

gaps.name: PCEP (Path Computation Element Communication Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has PCE as a tag under traffic engineering ('PCE (Path Computation Element) architecture and PCEP'), so the PCE id is valid, but I used an id that I should double-check exists exactly as 'PCE'. It does appear in the taxonomy under traffic engineering.

RFC9757.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for Native IP Networks
RFC9757.summary: Experimental RFC extending PCEP with a Native IP TE path setup type, a new CCI object type, and BPI, EPR and PPA objects so a PCE acting as central controller can instruct routers to set up BGP sessions, install explicit peer routes and advertise prefixes (CCDR).

PCE.why: The document defines new PCEP objects, a path setup type, capability flags, error codes and procedures for PCECC in Native IP networks.
PCE.quote: This document introduces extensions to the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) to support path computation in Native IP networks

traffic engineering.why: The purpose is E2E traffic engineering in Native IP networks. The PCE-based TE is realized with BGP sessions and explicit routes, but the specific PCE tag already covers it.
traffic engineering.quote: facilitating the deployment of traffic engineering in Native IP environments

rejected.why: BGP sessions and prefix advertisements are set up through PCEP, but the document does not extend or specify BGP. It states there is no influence on the BGP FSM.
MPLS-TE is mentioned only as contrast; Native IP has no MPLS signalling.
The IP-in-IP tunnel is only the default tunnel type for Tunnel mode, not a subject of the document.
TLS for PCEP is mentioned only in Security Considerations.
The PCEP YANG module is mentioned only as a possible future extension in the manageability section.
RBNF is only the notation used for message formats.

RFC9758.title: Updates to the 'ipn' URI Scheme
RFC9758.summary: Updates the 'ipn' URI scheme (RFC 6260/7116) with allocator identifiers, special node numbers, text and CBOR encodings for Bundle Protocol v7 endpoint IDs, and new IANA registries.

URI.why: The document defines the structure, syntax, and semantics of the 'ipn' URI scheme, including its ABNF text syntax.
URI.quote: This document updates the specification of the 'ipn' URI scheme previously defined in RFC 6260 and the IANA registries established in RFC 7116.

DTN.why: It specifies how ipn URIs are used as BPv7 EIDs, including null endpoint, node IDs, LocalNode, and CBOR encodings. A DTN working group produced it.
DTN.quote: updates the rules for the encoding and decoding of these URIs when used as an Endpoint Identifier (EID) in the Bundle Protocol version 7 (BPv7)

rejected.why: CBOR is only the encoding substrate for the EID encoding, which is defined here for ipn only. The document is not about CBOR itself.
The registries it creates are part of defining the scheme, so the document is not about IANA process in its own right.
CIDR is only an analogy for allocator identifier ranges.
CDDL is used only to express the syntax.
The document explicitly says ipn URIs are identifiers and not routing or topological addresses.

RFC9759.title: Unified Time Scaling for Temporal Coordination Frameworks
RFC9759.summary: An April 1st parody RFC proposing the "Two-Week Principle", which converts every time estimate to two weeks, and which jokingly calls for iCalendar updates and discusses post-quantum effects.

humor.why: The document is dated 1 April 2025 and is a whimsical parody of time estimation, with spontaneous wormhole creation and a Hitchhiker's Guide acknowledgement. It belongs on the humorous RFCs page.
humor.quote: any given time duration, regardless of original or intended value, must be converted to two weeks.

rejected.why: The iCalendar format is only mentioned in one joking implementation bullet. The document does not specify or analyse it.
Section 5 is a satirical aside about quantum timekeeping. It has nothing to do with post-quantum cryptography.
The document claims to unify time scales, but it is a joke about estimates. It does not address clock synchronization over networks.
There is no time zone data or timestamp handling. The document only normalizes durations to a joke value.

RFC9760.title: Enterprise Profile for the Precision Time Protocol with Mixed Multicast and Unicast Messages
RFC9760.summary: Defines the IETF Enterprise Profile for IEEE 1588-2019 PTP over UDP/IPv4/IPv6, using the end-to-end delay mechanism with mixed multicast and unicast messages and setting clock requirements and forbidden options.

PTP.why: The whole document profiles PTP: message rates, clock requirements, forbidden options and interoperation with the Default Profile.
PTP.quote: This document describes a Precision Time Protocol (PTP) Profile (IEEE Standard 1588-2019) for use in an IPv4 or IPv6 enterprise information system environment.

rejected.why: NTP is mentioned only as a comparison and in the terms list; the document does not specify or extend it.
UDP is only the transport PTP runs over.
IPv4 and IPv6 are only the network substrate; nothing new is defined about them.
NETCONF appears only as an example of a secure management alternative.
This is the parent topic of PTP. The PTP tag is more specific, so the parent is implied.
Multicast addresses and the use of multicast messages are profile details, not a subject the document addresses in its own right.

RFC9761.title: Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD) for TLS and DTLS Profiles for Internet of Things (IoT) Devices
