RFC9761.summary: Extends MUD (RFC 8520) with YANG modules (ietf-acl-tls, iana-tls-profile, ietf-mud-tls) letting manufacturers declare TLS/DTLS profile parameters so network security services can detect unexpected (D)TLS usage by IoT devices.

MUD.why: The document extends MUD with a new extension (ietf-mud-tls), augmented ACL matches, and a MUD Extensions registry entry.
MUD.quote: This memo extends the Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD) specification to allow manufacturers to define TLS and DTLS profile parameters.

YANG.why: A substantial part of the document defines three YANG modules (ietf-acl-tls, iana-tls-profile, ietf-mud-tls) and their IANA maintenance.
YANG.quote: This document specifies a YANG module that represents the (D)TLS profile.

TLS.why: It profiles TLS/DTLS handshake parameters (cipher suites, extensions, versions) and discusses TLS 1.3 handshake inspection, proxies and ECH for middlebox observation.
TLS.quote: The (D)TLS parameters in each (D)TLS profile include the following:

rejected.why: DTLS is covered together with TLS as '(D)TLS'; the TLS tag suffices and nothing is specific to DTLS.
Encrypted DNS is discussed only as a MUD enforcement concern; DoH/DoT is not specified or extended.
Devices are the application context, but the document is specifically about MUD profiles; MUD sits under IoT and is implied.
Firewalls are the consumers of profiles, but the document does not specify firewall mechanisms.
JSON is only used for the example MUD file encoding.
Mentioned only in the YANG security considerations template.

RFC9762.title: Using Router Advertisements to Signal the Availability of DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation to Clients
RFC9762.summary: Defines a new P flag in the IPv6 Router Advertisement Prefix Information Option to signal that the network prefers clients to use DHCPv6 prefix delegation (per RFC 9663) rather than SLAAC or IA_NA addresses, and updates RFC 4861 and RFC 4862 accordingly.

neighbor discovery.why: The document extends IPv6 Neighbor Discovery by defining a new PIO flag and updates RFC 4861 on RA handling.
neighbor discovery.quote: This document defines the P flag in the Prefix Information Option (PIO) of IPv6 Router Advertisements (RAs).

DHCPv6.why: It specifies client behavior for requesting DHCPv6-PD (REBIND, IA_NA avoidance, prefix length hints) triggered by the flag.
DHCPv6.quote: the P flag indicates DHCPv6 prefix delegation support for clients.

SLAAC.why: It updates RFC 4862 so SLAAC address formation is suppressed when the P flag is set.
SLAAC.quote: the Autonomous flag in a PIO needs to be ignored if the PIO has the P flag set.

rejected.why: Parent of the chosen child tags, so it is implied.
Addressing is the general subject, but the specific tags above cover it more precisely.
SAVI is only mentioned as a scalability example.
Redirect processing gets a brief mention, but it is not a main subject.
Section 8 is a short note on source selection with multiple prefixes, not a substantial treatment.
Not related; the document does not address IPv4/IPv6 coexistence.

RFC9763.title: Related Certificates for Use in Multiple Authentications within a Protocol
RFC9763.summary: Defines a CSR attribute (relatedCertRequest) and an X.509 certificate extension (RelatedCertificate) that give assurance two end-entity certificates belong to the same entity, for non-composite hybrid (traditional plus post-quantum) authentication.

X.509.why: The document specifies a new X.509 certificate extension and its CA issuance rules, so readers of X.509 certificates and profiles need it.
X.509.quote: a new X.509 certificate extension, RelatedCertificate

PKI.why: A substantial part covers CSR attributes, CA/RA processing, proof of possession and CA organization considerations, which are PKI issuance practice beyond the certificate format.
PKI.quote: A certification authority (CA) organization ... may want assurance from a registration authority (RA) that the private keys ... belong to the same entity.

post-quantum.why: The motivating use case is migration from traditional to post-quantum cryptography using hybrid authentication with two certificates.
post-quantum.quote: particularly useful in the context of non-composite hybrid authentication

rejected.why: CMS types (IssuerAndSerialNumber, certs-only messages) are reused, and CMS/S/MIME is only mentioned as an example protocol. The document is not about CMS.
TLS and IKEv2 are cited only as protocols where the extension could be used. Nothing is specified for them.
The ASN.1 module is only the formal definition of the new types and is not itself the subject.
The data URL and HTTP URL are used only as locators for the related certificate.
Mentioned only as an example in the Security Considerations.

RFC9764.title: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) Encapsulated in Large Packets
RFC9764.summary: Specifies padding BFD Asynchronous-mode control packets' transport payload to a configured size (bfd.PaddedPduSize) so BFD sessions also verify Path MTU, and defines a YANG module augmenting RFC 9314 BFD models.

BFD.why: The document extends BFD with a padded-PDU mechanism for Path MTU verification, including implementation and deployment considerations, so it belongs on the BFD page.
BFD.quote: A new BFD variable is defined in this document: bfd.PaddedPduSize The BFD transport protocol payload size (in bytes) is increased to this value.

YANG.why: A substantial part of the document defines the ietf-bfd-large YANG module, which augments the BFD YANG models from RFC 9314.
YANG.quote: This YANG module augments the "ietf-bfd" module to add a flag 'padding' to enable this feature.

rejected.why: The document uses BFD to check that a path supports a given MTU, but it does not specify or extend Path MTU Discovery (RFC 1191). It only references PMTUD.
Section 4.5 discusses ECMP and load-balancing limits only as a caveat. The document does not address ECMP itself.
UDP is the encapsulation that carries the padded BFD packet. The document defines nothing new about UDP.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in the YANG security boilerplate.
LAG is mentioned only in passing (RFC 7130 and the YANG augment). The document is not about link aggregation.

RFC9765.title: RADIUS/1.1: Leveraging Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) to Remove MD5
RFC9765.summary: Defines RADIUS/1.1, a transport profile negotiated via TLS ALPN for RADIUS over TLS/DTLS that removes the shared secret and all MD5-based packet authentication and attribute obfuscation, replacing the Identifier/Authenticator fields with a Token.

RADIUS.why: The document specifies a new RADIUS transport profile, changing packet header, attribute handling, Protocol-Error and Error-Cause behaviour, and updates several RADIUS RFCs.
RADIUS.quote: These extensions permit the negotiation of an application protocol variant of RADIUS called "RADIUS/1.1".

TLS.why: Defines new ALPN protocol IDs and negotiation, alert, and session-resumption rules for RADIUS over TLS, which is new use of a TLS extension that TLS readers would want.
TLS.quote: The ALPN name defined for RADIUS/1.1 is as follows: "radius/1.1"

rejected.why: MD5 is what is being removed, not specified or analysed as a subject itself.

RFC9773.summary: Specifies the ACME Renewal Information (ARI) extension, letting ACME servers suggest certificate renewal windows via a new renewalInfo resource and a "replaces" field on orders.

gaps.name: End-to-end email security / MUA usability
gaps.why: No tag covers end-to-end secure email guidance and MUA user experience in general. S/MIME and OpenPGP cover the mechanisms but not the guidance.

RFC9788.title: Header Protection for Cryptographically Protected Email
RFC9788.summary: Defines Header Protection for S/MIME (and PGP/MIME) email: copying header fields into the cryptographic payload, hp and hp-legacy-display Content-Type parameters, the HP-Outer header field, Header Confidentiality Policies, and rendering/composing/reply guidance. Updates RFC 8551.

S/MIME.why: The document updates S/MIME's header protection mechanism and gives test vectors using S/MIME signed and enveloped data, so S/MIME readers need it.
S/MIME.quote: This document updates the S/MIME specification (RFC 8551) to offer a different mechanism that provides the same cryptographic protections

message format.why: It defines a new header field (HP-Outer), registers it in the message header registry, and adds Content-Type parameters. It also covers how MUAs treat header fields.
message format.quote: This section describes relevant, backward-compatible extensions to the Internet Message Format [RFC5322].

email.why: The document gives MUA-level guidance for composing, rendering, replying and forwarding protected email.
email.quote: provides guidance for the implementer of a Mail User Agent (MUA) that generates, interprets, and replies to such a message

OpenPGP.why: PGP/MIME is stated to be covered by the mechanism, though analysis focuses on S/MIME. This is a minor secondary link.
OpenPGP.quote: The Header Protection scheme defined here is also applicable to messages with PGP/MIME (Pretty Good Privacy with MIME) cryptographic protections.

rejected.why: Mentioned only as a contrasting MTA-level mechanism in Section 1.4.
Mentioned only as a contrasting MTA-level mechanism in Section 1.4.
S/MIME is built on CMS, but the document does not specify CMS itself.
The document uses MIME structure and adds Content-Type parameters, but it is not about MIME itself. The message format and S/MIME tags cover it better.
The IANA registrations and the new registry are boilerplate for this document, not its subject.
Mentioned in passing as a way to verify headers added in transit.

gaps.name: Email header protection / protected headers
gaps.why: The document's central subject is end-to-end protection of email header fields, including header confidentiality policies. The taxonomy has no tag for it. S/MIME and message format fit only partly.

RFC9789.title: MPLS Network Actions (MNAs) Framework
RFC9789.summary: Informational architectural framework for MPLS Network Actions (MNAs), describing how network actions and ancillary data are encoded in network action sub-stacks of the MPLS label stack or in post-stack data, plus scopes, partial processing, readable label depth, and how to define an action.

MPLS.why: The whole document is an MPLS architecture and encoding framework: label stack entries, special-purpose labels, sub-stacks and post-stack data. Readers of MPLS would want it.
MPLS.quote: This document describes an architectural framework for MPLS Network Action (MNA) technologies.

rejected.why: BIER is cited only as an example of first-nibble use (RFC 8296). The document is not about BIER.
ECMP appears only in the first-nibble discussion and in the security text about carrier's carrier. It is not a subject of the document.
SIDs and MSD are mentioned for the RLD advertisement. The document does not address segment routing itself.
OAM is named as one kind of network action, but the document does not define or specify any OAM mechanism.
The IANA section only records an IGP MSD-Type allocation. It is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
IPFRR is mentioned only as a case where an LSP may cross nodes that lack MNA support.

RFC9790.title: IANA Registry and Processing Recommendations for the First Nibble Following a Label Stack
RFC9790.summary: Creates the IANA "Post-Stack First Nibble" registry for the first nibble after an MPLS label stack, and updates RFC 4928 by deprecating the heuristic of guessing the embedded packet type (used for ECMP load balancing) from that nibble.

MPLS.why: The document concerns MPLS packet encoding after the label stack, post-stack headers, and processing in the MPLS data plane. It updates RFC 4928 on MPLS networks.
MPLS.quote: this document creates a new IANA registry (called the "Post-Stack First Nibble" registry) for the first nibble (4-bit field) immediately following an MPLS label stack.

ECMP.why: A substantial part analyses ECMP load-balancing techniques. It deprecates the first-nibble heuristic and recommends entropy labels or FAT labels.
ECMP.quote: There are four common ways to load balance an MPLS packet:

IANA.why: The document's main product is a new IANA registry with an assignment policy and initial contents. It also describes how the registry relates to the IP Version Numbers registry.
IANA.quote: IANA has created a registry group called "Post- Stack First Nibble" that consists of a single registry

rejected.why: The DetNet control word appears only as a registry entry and an example of a post-stack header. The document is not about DetNet.
The BIER header is only one registry entry and an example of a post-stack header.
The PW control word is cited as a registry entry and as an example. The document does not specify pseudowires.
IPv4 and IPv6 are mentioned only as payload types identified by nibble values 0x4 and 0x6. The document does not address IPv6 itself.
The NSH appears only as a registry entry.

gaps.name: MPLS Network Actions (MNA) / post-stack header
gaps.why: The document is related to the MNA framework and post-stack headers. The taxonomy has no tag for the MPLS data-plane label stack or MNA, so MPLS is the closest fit.

RFC9791.title: Use Cases for MPLS Network Action Indicators and Ancillary Data
RFC9791.summary: Informational document listing use cases (no-further-FRR, IOAM/alternate marking, network slicing, NSH-based SFC, network programming) that motivate MPLS Network Action indicators and ancillary data in the MPLS data plane.

MPLS.why: The document is about extending the MPLS data plane (MNA) with indicators and ancillary data in label stack and post-stack, and coexistence with existing MPLS services.
MPLS.quote: encoding network action indicators and associated ancillary data within MPLS packets

OAM.why: A substantial use-case section covers IOAM and Alternate Marking carried via MNA. No IOAM-specific tag exists, so the OAM topic is the fit.
OAM.quote: MNA can be used to carry information essential for collecting operational information and measuring various performance metrics

IP fast reroute.why: The first use case is the No Further Fast Reroute indication for MPLS FRR.
IP fast reroute.quote: packets that FRR has redirected will be marked using MNA to preclude further FRR processing

SFC.why: One use case covers NSH-based service function chaining over MPLS.
SFC.quote: MNA can be used to extend NSH emulation using MPLS labels [RFC8595] to support the functionality of NSH Context Headers

rejected.why: Network programming (FUNC::ARGs) is one use case, but the document is not about segment routing itself.
Mentioned for coexistence and as appendix aspirational cases only.
Mentioned only as an existing MPLS payload for the first-nibble coexistence discussion.
Pseudowire control words are discussed only for coexistence with post-stack headers.
Alternate Marking is covered briefly, but the document is not about measurement methods themselves. OAM is the closer fit.

gaps.name: MPLS Network Action (MNA)
gaps.why: The document's central subject has no dedicated tag. The generic MPLS tag is the closest fit.

gaps.name: Network slicing
gaps.why: A use case (RFC 9543 Network Slice and the NRP Selector), but the taxonomy has no slicing tag.

RFC9792.title: Prefix Flag Extension for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3
RFC9792.summary: Defines a variable-length Prefix Extended Flags sub-TLV for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 to overcome exhaustion of the 8-bit prefix flag fields, and creates the corresponding IANA registries.

OSPFv3.why: The document extends OSPFv3 with a new sub-TLV carried in OSPFv3 Extended LSA TLVs, so readers of OSPFv3 need it.
OSPFv3.quote: defining a variable-length Prefix Extended Flags sub-TLV for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3

OSPF.why: The document equally extends OSPFv2 with a sub-TLV of the OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV.
OSPF.quote: The OSPFv2 Prefix Extended Flags sub-TLV is advertised as a sub-TLV of the OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV defined in [RFC7684].

rejected.why: The SRv6 Locator TLV is only listed as one parent TLV that can carry the sub-TLV. The document does not address segment routing itself.
The SRv6 Locator TLV is mentioned only as a carrier for the sub-TLV. The document defines nothing specific to SRv6.
The IANA registries are boilerplate-like apparatus for the protocol extension. The document is not about IANA guidance.

RFC9793.title: BGP Extensions for Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER)
RFC9793.summary: Defines a new optional transitive BGP path attribute (type 41) with TLVs and sub-TLVs to advertise BIER information (BFR-ID, sub-domain, MPLS/non-MPLS encapsulation, nexthop) and describes how BFRs compute BIFTs from it.

BIER.why: The document specifies BIER signaling and BIFT calculation, so it belongs on the BIER page.
BIER.quote: This document describes BGP extensions for advertising the BIER information and methods for calculating BIER states based on the advertisements.

BGP.why: It extends BGP with a new path attribute, including its propagation, error handling and EBGP boundary policy.
BGP.quote: we define a new optional transitive BGP attribute, referred to as the "BIER attribute", to convey the BIER-specific information

rejected.why: The MPLS encapsulation sub-TLV only carries label ranges for BIER; the document is not about MPLS itself.
Implied as the parent of BIER, so it is not listed separately.
IP/GRE is mentioned only as one example of a tunnel; tunnel setup is out of scope.
The IANA section only registers the attribute code point and a new registry; it is boilerplate and not the document's subject.
The EBGP policy preventing the attribute from leaking is an operational note, not a routing security mechanism.

RFC9794.title: Terminology for Post-Quantum Traditional Hybrid Schemes
RFC9794.summary: Defines terminology for post-quantum/traditional (PQ/T) hybrid cryptographic schemes, protocols, properties and certificates, as a reference for consistent usage across IETF protocols.

post-quantum.why: The whole document defines vocabulary for PQ/T hybrid schemes and the post-quantum migration. The post-quantum page is where readers would look for it.
post-quantum.quote: One aspect of the transition to post-quantum algorithms in cryptographic protocols is the development of hybrid schemes that incorporate both post-quantum and traditional asymmetric algorithms.

terminology.why: It is a glossary-style terminology document. A terminology reader would want it, though its subject is hybrid cryptography.
terminology.quote: This document defines terminology for such schemes.  It is intended to be used as a reference and, hopefully, to ensure consistency and clarity

rejected.why: Hybrid TLS is only used as an example. The document does not specify or extend TLS.
X.509 certificates are mentioned in the certificate terminology section, but the document does not profile them.
RFC 9370 (IKEv2) is cited only as an example of a hybrid protocol.
ML-KEM and ML-DSA appear only as examples of algorithms. The document is not about them.
The certificate chain and parallel PKI definitions are a minor part of the terminology. The document is not about PKI itself.

RFC9795.title: Personal Assertion Token (PASSporT) Extension for Rich Call Data
RFC9795.summary: Defines a PASSporT extension (the "rcd", "rcdi" and "crn" claims) carrying signed rich call data such as caller name, icon, jCard and call reason, with integrity digests, JWT Claim Constraints, third-party signing, and SIP usage.

STIR.why: The document extends PASSporT within the STIR framework to authenticate caller identity data. It is the core subject, so STIR is the right tag.
STIR.quote: This document extends the use of JWT and PASSporT in the overall STIR framework by defining a PASSporT extension and the associated STIR procedures

SIP.why: A substantial part of the document gives authentication and verification service behavior for SIP, including Identity header and Call-Info handling.
SIP.quote: This section documents SIP-specific usage for "rcd" PASSporTs in the SIP Identity header field value.

rejected.why: Not in the taxonomy as a separate id here; the claims are JWT claims, but JWT is the substrate. The nearest tag, JWT under OAuth, concerns a different usage context.
JSON and jCard are the encoding the claims use, and the document is not about JSON itself.
jCard is carried as a value in the claims, but the document does not specify or extend vCard.
Certificates and JWT Claim Constraints are used for integrity, but the constraint extension is defined in other RFCs.
SHA-2 digests are only a mechanism used to compute integrity values.
The document builds on JWT claim usage rather than defining JWS or JWE behavior.

gaps.name: STIR / PASSporT caller-ID authentication
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists STIR under real-time communications, but the id I used, STIR, sits under SIP in the hierarchy. A dedicated tag for PASSporT and rich call data would help.

RFC9796.title: SIP Call-Info Parameters for Rich Call Data
RFC9796.summary: Defines SIP Call-Info usage for carrying Rich Call Data (jCard, icon, call reason), adding the 'jcard' purpose token and 'call-reason', 'verified' and 'integrity' parameters, aligned with STIR RCD PASSporTs.

SIP.why: The document extends the SIP Call-Info header field with new parameters and a purpose token, which is a SIP extension.
SIP.quote: This document defines three new parameters 'call-reason', 'verified', and 'integrity' for the SIP Call-Info header field and also a new token ("jcard")

STIR.why: The new 'verified' and 'integrity' parameters mirror STIR RCD PASSporT verification results and integrity hashes, so STIR readers would want this.
STIR.quote: the recommended approach is that the entity inserting the Call-Info header field should also sign the caller information via protocol tools defined by Secure Telephone Identity Revisited (STIR)

vCard.why: A large part of the document profiles jCard properties for caller data, covering which are supported and how each is used.
vCard.quote: This document defines a 'purpose' parameter value "jcard" for the more generic delivery of information via jCard [RFC7095].

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding for jCard and PASSporT, not the subject.
The 'data' and 'cid' URI schemes are used as carriers, but nothing new is defined about URIs.
SDP appears only in example INVITE bodies.
JWT is mentioned only as the basis for PASSporT. The document does not define or profile it.
The document gives image and audio format guidance but registers no media types.

gaps.name: PASSporT / Rich Call Data
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for PASSporT or RCD. STIR is the closest fit but does not name them exactly.

RFC9797.title: Randomized and Changing Media Access Control (MAC) Addresses: Context, Network Impacts, and Use Cases
RFC9797.summary: Informational document from the MADINAS WG describing how randomized and changing MAC addresses (RCM) in IEEE 802/Wi-Fi networks affect network services, environments and trust levels, and reviewing existing frameworks that balance privacy with service continuity.

privacy.why: The document's core subject is MAC address randomization as a privacy measure, with trust degrees and privacy tradeoffs analysed throughout.
privacy.quote: To limit the privacy issues created by the association between a device, its traffic, its location, and its user in IEEE 802 networks

WiFi.why: The discussion centres on Wi-Fi networks, access points, WLAN controllers and IEEE 802.11bh randomization rules.
WiFi.quote: This technology is particularly important in Wi-Fi networks (defined in IEEE 802.11) due to the over-the-air medium and device mobility.

ARP.why: A material part of the service-impact analysis covers ARP/NDP caches and MAC-to-IP mapping disruption.
ARP.quote: the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) [RFC826] and Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) [RFC4861] use a MAC address to create the mapping

DHCP.why: DHCP lease tracking and scope exhaustion under MAC randomization is a substantial analysed impact.
DHCP.quote: Without a unique identification of the device, DHCPv4 servers [RFC2131] lose track of which IP address is validly assigned.

rejected.why: Ethernet/802.3 is mentioned as the wired side where MACs persist, but the document is not about Ethernet itself.
RADIUS appears only in the OpenRoaming appendix via a referenced draft; not a main subject.
AAA is discussed as one affected service, but only in passing, not substantially.
NDP is only one of several services affected; covered under ARP/addressing mentions, not a main topic.
OpenRoaming is a brief appendix example, not a substantial part of the document.

gaps.name: MAC address randomization (RCM)
gaps.why: The central subject, randomized and changing MAC addresses at the IEEE 802 layer, has no dedicated tag; privacy and WiFi only approximate it.

RFC9798.title: PIM Join/Prune Attributes for Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Environments Using Underlay Multicast
RFC9798.summary: Experimental RFC updating RFC 8059 so the PIM Join/Prune Receiver ETR RLOC attribute can carry a multicast underlay group address, enabling LISP multicast trees across sites using underlay IP multicast.

LISP.why: The document extends LISP multicast (RFC 6831 / RFC 8059) behaviour for ITRs/ETRs using underlay multicast, so LISP readers need it.
LISP.quote: construction of multicast distribution trees where the source and receivers are located in different Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) sites and are connected using underlay IP multicast

PIM.why: The core change is to a PIM Join/Prune attribute's Receiver RLOC field, so it is about PIM join attributes.
PIM.quote: This document extends the Receiver ETR RLOC PIM Join/Prune attribute [RFC8059] to facilitate the construction of underlay multicast trees

rejected.why: PIM-SM is only referenced for authentication in Security Considerations; the document updates a generic PIM Join attribute, not the sparse-mode spec.
The parent topic is implied by the PIM tag, so it is not listed separately.
LISP overlay/underlay mapping is discussed, but the document is about LISP and PIM attributes, not data-plane virtualization overlays like VXLAN.
LISP encapsulation is the substrate; the document does not define new tunnelling mechanics.

RFC9799.title: Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) Extensions for ".onion" Special-Use Domain Names
RFC9799.summary: Extends ACME to issue certificates for Tor .onion special-use domain names, defining the onion-csr-01 challenge, client-auth key advertisement, and CAA-equivalent records in hidden service descriptors or in-band.

ACME.why: The document extends ACME with a new challenge, new fields, error types and registry entries.
ACME.quote: this document defines extensions to the Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) to allow for the automatic issuance of certificates to Tor Hidden Services

.onion.why: The whole document concerns validating control of .onion names and handling CAA for them.
.onion.quote: These services use the ".onion" Special-Use Domain Name [RFC7686] to identify these services.

rejected.why: The document stresses .onion names are not part of the DNS; DNS is only referenced for CAA semantics.
Certificates are the product of ACME, but the document does not profile X.509 itself.
Mentioned only in the privacy considerations about CT logging.
tls-alpn-01 is an existing challenge, only used as a mechanism; nothing new is defined for TLS.
http-01 challenge and ACME's HTTP transport are substrate only.
Anonymity considerations appear only in the security section and are not the main subject.

gaps.name: CAA (Certification Authority Authorization)
gaps.why: The document defines an equivalent of DNS CAA for hidden service descriptors, and the taxonomy has no CAA tag.

gaps.name: Tor / onion services
gaps.why: The document is about Tor hidden services, and the taxonomy has no Tor tag other than the .onion domain name.

RFC9800.title: Compressed SRv6 Segment List Encoding
RFC9800.summary: RFC 9800 specifies NEXT-CSID and REPLACE-CSID flavors of SRv6 endpoint behaviors, plus End.LBS/End.XLBS, to compress SRv6 segment lists in the SRH, and updates RFC 8754.

SRv6.why: The whole document defines compressed segment list encoding and new endpoint behaviors for SRv6.
SRv6.quote: This document specifies new flavors for the SRv6 endpoint behaviors defined in RFC 8986, which enable the compression of an SRv6 segment list.

rejected.why: IPv6 and the SRH are the substrate; the document is about SRv6 segment list compression, not IPv6 itself.
The parent is implied by the more specific SRv6 tag.
Control plane extensions for IS-IS, OSPF, BGP are only referenced for advertising SIDs.
ICMP error handling and ping are mentioned operationally but not the subject.
IANA registry updates are boilerplate, not the main subject.

RFC9801.title: Private Line Emulation over Packet Switched Networks
RFC9801.summary: Specifies Private Line Emulation (PLE), a bit-stream pseudowire/VPWS encapsulation carrying Ethernet, Fibre Channel, SONET/SDH and OTN signals transparently over MPLS or SRv6 packet networks, including new SRv6 End.DX1 behaviors.

pseudowire.why: The document defines a new bit-stream pseudowire encapsulation (control word, RTP header, payload, IWF/NSP operation) in the PWE3 framework.
pseudowire.quote: provides pseudowire transport with complete signal transparency over Packet Switched Networks (PSNs)

SRv6.why: Defines new SRv6 encapsulation and End.DX1 endpoint behaviors and registers them with IANA, which SRv6 readers need.
SRv6.quote: Two new encapsulation behaviors, H.Encaps.L1 and H.Encaps.L1.Red, are defined in this document.

rejected.why: RTP header is reused only for timestamps; the document explicitly excludes full RTP mechanisms.
MPLS is one possible PSN substrate; the document is not specifying MPLS itself.
SONET/SDH is a carried service type, and the tag concerns IP over SONET, not bit-stream emulation of it.
The tag is for Fibre Channel over IP transports; here FC is only an emulated client signal.
Ethernet is a client signal emulated at PCS level, not IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.
Clock transport is addressed in the context of the emulation, but synchronization is not the subject; PTP/SyncE are referenced only.

gaps.name: Private Line Emulation / circuit emulation (TDM and bit-stream PWE3)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for TDM or circuit emulation pseudowires (SAToP, CEP, CESoPSN); only the generic pseudowire tag fits.

RFC9802.title: Use of the HSS and XMSS Hash-Based Signature Algorithms in Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure
RFC9802.summary: Specifies algorithm identifiers, public key and signature encodings, key usage rules and ASN.1 module for using stateful hash-based signatures (HSS/LMS, XMSS, XMSS^MT) in X.509 certificates and CRLs.

XMSS.why: Defines OIDs, public key and signature encodings for XMSS and XMSS^MT in X.509.
XMSS.quote: The AlgorithmIdentifier for an XMSS public key MUST use the id-alg-xmss-hashsig OID.

LMS.why: Covers HSS/LMS public keys and signatures in certificates, a core part of the document.
LMS.quote: The AlgorithmIdentifier for an HSS public key MUST use the id-alg-hss-lms-hashsig OID.

X.509.why: The document profiles X.509 certificates and CRLs for these algorithms, including key usage bits and examples.
X.509.quote: This specification applies to the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) when digital signatures are used to sign certificates and certificate revocation lists (CRLs).

rejected.why: An ASN.1 module is provided, but ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the identifiers.
Hash-based signatures are quantum-resistant, but the more specific hash-based tags (XMSS, LMS) cover this.
Relies on RFC 9708 (CMS use of HSS/LMS) only for the OID definition; the document is not about CMS.
Mentioned only as a stateless contrast in the backup section.
The more specific children XMSS and LMS are chosen instead.
State and backup management is discussed, but it is not the main subject.

RFC9803.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Mapping for DNS Time-to-Live (TTL) Values
RFC9803.summary: Defines an EPP extension letting sponsoring clients set and query DNS TTL values for domain and host delegation records (NS, DS, DNAME, A, AAAA, custom), with server processing and operational guidance.

EPP.why: The document specifies a new EPP extension, with command mappings for info, create and update, plus a schema.
EPP.quote: This document describes an extension to the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) that allows EPP clients to manage the Time-to-Live (TTL) value for domain name delegation records.

rejected.why: DNS TTLs and record types are the subject matter, but the document specifies registry provisioning, not DNS protocol behaviour.
DS records are mentioned as one of the record types whose TTL can be set, but DNSSEC itself is not the topic.
EPP is XML-based and the document includes an XML schema, but XML is only the encoding substrate.
This is the parent of EPP, which is already tagged, so it is implied.

RFC9804.title: Simple Public Key Infrastructure (SPKI) S-Expressions
RFC9804.summary: Specifies the SPKI S-expression data representation: octet-strings and lists, with canonical, basic transport (base-64), and advanced encodings, display-hints, ABNF, and in-memory layouts.

ABNF.why: A full section gives formal ABNF for the advanced, canonical and basic transport syntaxes. Readers of formal syntax notation may want it, but ABNF is mainly the tool used to define the format.
ABNF.quote: ABNF is the Augmented Backus-Naur Form for syntax specifications as defined in [RFC5234]. The ABNF for advanced representation of S-expressions is given first

rejected.why: No SPKI tag exists in the taxonomy except the historic SPKI under PKI. This document specifies only the S-expression data encoding that SPKI certificates used, not certificate semantics.
Base-64 is used as one of the encodings, defined by RFC 4648, but the document does not define it.
JSON is only mentioned as an alternative technology to consider.
CBOR is only mentioned as an alternative technology to consider.
XML is only mentioned as an alternative, and RFC 3275 is only cited as a user of S-expressions.
Display-hints borrow MIME media type strings, but the document registers no media types.
The format was devised for SPKI certificates, but the document is a generic data encoding and says nothing about certificate infrastructure.

gaps.name: S-expressions (symbolic expression data serialisation)
gaps.why: The document is mainly about a general-purpose structured data serialisation format with canonical form for signing. The taxonomy has no tag for it among the data formats, so the nearest tag, ABNF, only partly fits.

RFC9805.title: Deprecation of the IPv6 Router Alert Option for New Protocols
RFC9805.summary: Deprecates the IPv6 Router Alert option for new protocols (updating RFC 2711), allowing existing users like MLDv2 and MRD to continue, and listing those protocols.

router alert.why: The whole document is about the IP Router Alert option: its issues, deprecation for new protocols, and the list of protocols still using it.
router alert.quote: This document deprecates the IPv6 Router Alert option.
router alert.section: 4. Deprecation of the IPv6 Router Alert Option

rejected.why: IPv6 is the context, but the specific subject is covered by the more specific router alert tag; the document does not specify IPv6 generally.
MLDv2 is only named as a protocol that still uses the option; the document does not change or specify it.
RSVP appears only in the Appendix A table of users of the option.
Control-plane DoS concerns motivate the deprecation, but the document is about the option itself, not operational security practice.
PGM is only listed in the appendix table as a user of the option.

RFC9806.title: Updates to SIP-Based Media Recording (SIPREC) to Correct Metadata Media Type
RFC9806.summary: Updates RFC 7866 (SIPREC) to use the media type application/rs-metadata+xml for recording metadata, matching RFC 7865, and registers that media type with IANA.

SIPREC.why: The document corrects an inconsistency in the SIPREC specifications by updating RFC 7866 so it labels recording metadata the way RFC 7865 does. SIPREC readers need this fix.
SIPREC.quote: The SIP-based Media Recording (SIPREC) protocol is defined by [RFC7865] and [RFC7866].

media types.why: The document registers the application/rs-metadata+xml media type, and this registration is half of its stated purpose. Readers of the media type registrations would want to find it.
media types.quote: Subtype name:  rs-metadata+xml

rejected.why: The metadata is XML-based, but the document only names the media type and refers to RFC 7303 for encoding. It says nothing about XML usage itself.
SIPREC runs on SIP, but this document changes only a media type label. It does not specify or extend SIP.
The document does not touch SDP. It is only about the metadata content type.

RFC9807.title: The OPAQUE Augmented Password-Authenticated Key Exchange (aPAKE) Protocol
RFC9807.summary: RFC 9807 specifies OPAQUE, an augmented password-authenticated key exchange (aPAKE) protocol composed of an OPRF, key recovery envelope, and an AKE (3DH instantiation), with registration and login flows and test vectors.

OPAQUE.why: The document specifies the OPAQUE protocol itself, including registration, online AKE, configurations and test vectors.
OPAQUE.quote: This document describes the OPAQUE protocol, an Augmented (or Asymmetric) Password-Authenticated Key Exchange (aPAKE) protocol

rejected.why: OPAQUE is a child of PAKE and is the more specific tag; the parent is implied.
TLS 1.3 is only borrowed for message syntax and key schedule helpers, and is mentioned as a possible channel or AKE. The document is not about TLS.
Elliptic-curve groups (ristretto255, P-256, Curve25519) are used as instantiation parameters, but the document is not about elliptic curve cryptography.
Key stretching functions (Argon2, scrypt, PBKDF2) are only referenced as configuration options for the KSF.
HMAC is only the MAC used as a primitive in the configuration.
The document is about authenticated key exchange via a specific protocol, which is covered by the OPAQUE tag.

gaps.name: Oblivious Pseudorandom Function (OPRF)
gaps.why: OPAQUE builds on the OPRF (RFC 9497), but the taxonomy has no tag for OPRFs; this RFC only uses it as a dependency.

RFC9808.title: Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI) Capacity Capability Advertisement Extensions
RFC9808.summary: Defines two new CDNI FCI Capability Objects, FCI.CapacityLimits and FCI.Telemetry, by which a downstream CDN advertises traffic delegation limits and telemetry sources to the upstream CDN.

CDN.why: The document extends CDN Interconnection (CDNI) footprint and capabilities advertisement with capacity limits and telemetry for delegation between CDNs, so it belongs on the CDN page.
CDN.quote: defines a set of additional Capability Objects that provide information about current downstream CDN (dCDN) utilization and specified usage limits to the delegating upstream CDN (uCDN)

rejected.why: JSON is only the serialization of the capability objects, not the subject of the document.
HTTP Cache-Control is mentioned only as an example mechanism for communicating the TTL of limits.
The registries it creates are boilerplate for its own payload and type values. The document is not about IANA guidance.
The telemetry metrics are inputs to delegation decisions and are not a performance measurement methodology.

RFC9809.title: X.509 Certificate Extended Key Usage (EKU) for Configuration, Updates, and Safety-Critical Communication
RFC9809.summary: Defines four new X.509 Extended Key Usage KeyPurposeIds (config signing, trust anchor config signing, update package signing, safety-critical communication) and registers them with IANA.

X.509.why: The document defines new EKU KeyPurposeIds for X.509 v3 certificates, extending the RFC 5280 profile. Readers of X.509 certificate profiles would want it.
X.509.quote: This document defines KeyPurposeIds for general-purpose and trust anchor configuration files, for software and firmware update packages, and for safety-critical communication

rejected.why: Safety-critical communication may be based on TLS, but TLS is only a substrate. The document defines nothing new for TLS.
The ASN.1 module only defines OIDs. It is apparatus, not the subject.
X.509 is the more specific tag and already covers the PKI aspect.
Update packages are only a signing use case. The document defines no firmware update architecture or manifest.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate for the new OIDs, not the subject.
It is mentioned only in the Privacy Considerations section.

RFC9810.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure -- Certificate Management Protocol (CMP)
RFC9810.summary: RFC 9810 specifies the X.509 PKI Certificate Management Protocol (CMP), its message formats, POP methods, polling, and profiles, obsoleting RFC 4210 and 9480 and adding KEM key support and EnvelopedData.

CMP.why: The document is the core CMP specification.
CMP.quote: This document describes the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) Certificate Management Protocol (CMP).

rejected.why: CMS EnvelopedData is used for encrypted values, but CMS is a substrate, not the subject.
CMP manages X.509 certificates but does not profile certificates themselves.
KEM key support is added, but the document is about CMP; ML-KEM is only referenced.
Only mentioned as an optional lower-layer protection.

RFC9811.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure -- HTTP Transfer for the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP)
RFC9811.summary: RFC 9811 specifies how to transport Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) PKIMessages over HTTP using POST, the application/pkixcmp media type, a /.well-known/cmp URI prefix, and pushed announcements, obsoleting RFC 6712 and RFC 9480.

CMP.why: The whole document defines the HTTP transfer binding for CMP, including message form, workflow, URIs and announcement pushing. CMP readers need it.
CMP.quote: This document describes how to layer the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) over HTTP.

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate CMP is tunneled over via POST. The document does not extend HTTP itself.
The document is a transport binding of CMP over HTTP, but the more specific CMP tag covers it. Tagging this too would duplicate it.
TLS appears only as an optional protection mechanism in Security Considerations.
The application/pkixcmp registration update is an IANA housekeeping item and not the main subject.
The /.well-known/cmp prefix applies RFC 8615 to CMP. It does not define new URI mechanics.
CMP is a child of PKI, so the PKI tag is implied by the CMP tag.

RFC9812.title: Clarification of IPv6 Address Allocation Policy
RFC9812.summary: BCP that changes the allocation policy of the IANA "IPv6 Address Space" registry from "IESG approval" to "IETF Review" and updates RFC 7249 accordingly.

IANA.why: The document's purpose is to set the approval policy for a specific IANA registry, i.e. IANA registry policy and stewardship.
IANA.quote: IANA has updated the registration procedure of the "IPv6 Address Space" registry [IANA1] to "IETF Review".

addressing.why: It concerns how IPv6 address space is allocated, specifically the reserved space beyond 2000::/3, so addressing readers would want it.
addressing.quote: Portions of the IPv6 address space are shown in the registry as "Reserved by IETF"
addressing.section: 2. Approval Level of IPv6 Address Allocations

rejected.why: The IPv6 protocol and addressing architecture are only referenced. The document is about registry allocation policy, not IPv6 specification or deployment. Addressing is the closer fit.
RFC 9602 is cited only as an example of a non-routine allocation. The document does not address SRv6.
The document touches on IESG approval and IETF Review, but those are IANA registration policies rather than a change to IETF process in general.
It notes that RFC 1881 is mislabelled 'Legacy' in the index. This is a minor clarification and not a main subject.

RFC9813.title: Operational Considerations for Using TLS Pre-Shared Keys (TLS-PSKs) with RADIUS
RFC9813.summary: BCP giving implementation and operational guidance for using TLS pre-shared keys (PSKs) and PSK identities with RADIUS/TLS and RADIUS/DTLS, covering PSK requirements, identity handling, IP filtering, and resumption.

RADIUS.why: The document gives operational guidance for RADIUS clients and servers using TLS-PSK, including client tables, shared secrets vs PSKs, and transition from RADIUS/UDP.
RADIUS.quote: This document provides implementation and operational considerations for using TLS Pre-Shared Keys (TLS-PSKs) with RADIUS/TLS (RFC 6614) and RADIUS/DTLS (RFC 7360).

TLS.why: Substantial guidance on TLS-PSK: PSK requirements, PSK identities, psk_dhe_ke mode, cipher suites, resumption, and forward secrecy.
TLS.quote: Implementations MUST follow the directions of [RFC9257], Section 6 for the use of external PSKs in TLS.

rejected.why: RADIUS/DTLS is covered alongside TLS, but the guidance applies to both equally and is not DTLS-specific; the DTLS parent is implied by TLS usage only loosely.
PSK generation and lifetimes are discussed, but only as TLS-PSK guidance already captured by the TLS tag.
Mentioned only to say passwords are unsuitable for TLS-PSK and would need a PAKE method.
Only a pointer to RFC 8937 for secure random generation, not a subject of the document.
Document is operational but specific to RADIUS/TLS-PSK; the more specific tags cover it.

gaps.name: RADIUS
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no RADIUS tag outside the AAA subtree; the document is about RADIUS in particular. I used a RADIUS tag id as found under AAA.

RFC9814.title: Use of the SLH-DSA Signature Algorithm in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC9814.summary: Specifies how to use the SLH-DSA stateless hash-based signature algorithm with CMS signed-data, including algorithm identifiers, public/private key encoding, SignerInfo conventions and an ASN.1 module.

SLH-DSA.why: The document defines the OIDs, key formats and signature conventions for SLH-DSA in CMS, so readers of the SLH-DSA subject need it.
SLH-DSA.quote: SLH-DSA is a stateless hash-based signature algorithm.  This document specifies the conventions for using the SLH-DSA signature algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).

CMS.why: The document profiles CMS SignedData and SignerInfo fields for SLH-DSA and extends the CMS signature algorithm set.
CMS.quote: specifies the conventions for using the SLH-DSA hash-based signature algorithm [FIPS205] with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) [RFC5652] signed-data content type.

rejected.why: This is the parent of SLH-DSA through hash-based signatures. The more specific SLH-DSA tag covers it, so the ancestor is implied.
The document only says how the key appears in SubjectPublicKeyInfo and which key usages apply. That is a minor mention and not a substantial part of the document.
ASN.1 is the notation for the module and OIDs. It is only the encoding substrate.
SHA-2 and SHAKE are used as the hash functions, but the document does not define them.
The ASN.1 module adds S/MIME capabilities entries, but the document is about CMS signed-data and not S/MIME email.
XMSS and LMS are mentioned only as stateful alternatives in the introduction.

RFC9815.title: BGP Link State (BGP-LS) Shortest Path First (SPF) Routing
RFC9815.summary: RFC 9815 specifies BGP-LS-SPF, a new BGP SAFI (80) that reuses BGP-LS NLRI and replaces the BGP Decision Process with an SPF (Dijkstra) computation, so BGP can serve as the single underlay/overlay routing protocol in massively scaled data centers.

BGP-SPF.why: The document defines BGP-LS-SPF: the new SAFI, SPF Status, Sequence Number and Address Family TLVs, the SPF-based decision process, peering models and error handling. This is exactly the BGP-SPF tag.
BGP-SPF.quote: This document describes extensions to BGP for use with BGP Link State (BGP-LS) distribution and the Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm.

rejected.why: BGP-SPF is a more specific child. The base BGP protocol is reused unchanged apart from the Decision Process.
The data center motivation is context. The protocol itself is a general BGP-LS-based link-state mechanism, and deployment guidance is in RFC 9816.
BFD is only recommended for liveness detection and is not specified here.
Route reflectors appear as one peering model but are not the subject.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
ECMP is supported by the algorithm but is not the document's subject.

gaps.name: BGP-LS (BGP Link State distribution)
gaps.why: BGP-LS NLRI and attribute encoding (RFC 9552) is a distinct subject that the document extends. The taxonomy has no BGP-LS tag, so it is only partly covered by BGP-SPF.

RFC9816.title: Usage and Applicability of BGP Link State (BGP-LS) Shortest Path First (SPF) Routing in Data Centers
RFC9816.summary: Informational guidance on deploying BGP-LS SPF (link-state routing using BGP) in Clos/Fat Tree data center networks, covering peering models, peer discovery, policy and non-transit nodes.

BGP-SPF.why: The whole document is applicability guidance for BGP-SPF: SAFI usage, sparse peering, biconnected heuristic, policy, and non-transit nodes.
BGP-SPF.quote: discusses the usage and applicability of BGP Link State (BGP-LS) Shortest Path First (SPF) extensions in data center networks utilizing Clos or Fat Tree topologies

data center networking.why: The deployment context is Clos/Fat Tree data center fabrics, covering spine/leaf policy, DCI and fabric peering. Readers of data center routing would want it.
data center networking.quote: Within a data center, servers are commonly interconnected using the Clos topology [Clos].

rejected.why: BGP-SPF is the more specific tag. BGP is the underlying protocol and is not itself specified or extended here.
BFD is only mentioned as a mechanism for detecting link availability.
OSPF is only referenced as an analogy for the link-state algorithm.
ECMP is mentioned in describing the Clos topology and is not the subject of the document.
IPv6 peering and link-local addressing are brief mentions in a subsection and are not a substantial topic of the document.
Route reflectors appear only in passing in the peering model discussion.

RFC9817.title: Use Cases for In-Network Computing
RFC9817.summary: IRTF COINRG informational document presenting use cases for computing in the network (COIN) on programmable devices, with opportunities, research questions, and a preliminary categorization.

SDN.why: No COIN-specific tag exists; the nearest is SDN, since the document centres on programmable network devices (P4, SDN switches) with programmable data planes and controllers. It is a weak fit, so the role is secondary.
SDN.quote: allowing for a tighter integration of computing and networking resources for enabling a more flexible distribution of computation tasks across the network

CDN.why: A full use case section addresses CDNs, covering their existing solutions, L2 multicast replication, and research questions.
CDN.quote: From the perspective of this draft, a CDN can be interpreted as a (network service level) set of COIN programs.

rejected.why: TLS and SplitTLS appear only in the Security Considerations, in a discussion of middlebox access to encrypted traffic.
DNS is mentioned only as the existing, static endpoint-selection mechanism that COIN would improve on.
ICN is mentioned as related work and as a possible routing protocol, but the document is not about it.
The industrial control use cases are not about IoT architecture or constrained devices.
Multicast appears only as an opportunity within the CDN and AI use cases, not as a main subject.
The introduction touches on end-to-end versus in-network functionality, but the document is a use-case collection and not an architectural principles document.

gaps.name: In-Network Computing (COIN)
gaps.why: This is the core subject of the document, and the taxonomy has no tag for it or for computing in the network or programmable data planes (P4).

RFC9818.title: DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation on IPv6 Customer Edge (CE) Routers in LANs
RFC9818.summary: Defines requirements (LPD-1 to LPD-10) for IPv6 CE routers to support DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (IA_PD) on LAN interfaces, distributing delegated prefixes to downstream routers; updates RFC 7084.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies requirements for DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation behaviour (IA_PD, lifetimes, prefix assignment) on CE routers.
DHCPv6.quote: Each IPv6 CE router MUST support IPv6 prefix assignment according to Section 13.3 of [RFC8415] (Identity Association for Prefix Delegation (IA_PD) option) on its LAN

home networking.why: It updates the IPv6 CE router requirements of RFC 7084 and covers prefix distribution in the end-user/home network, including flat vs hierarchical delegation.
home networking.quote: This document defines requirements for IPv6 Customer Edge (CE) routers to support DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation for distributing available prefixes to LAN devices

rejected.why: IPv6 is the context; the parent is implied by the more specific tags and the document does not specify IPv6 itself.
SLAAC is mentioned only as the reason for the /64 default prefix length.
Prefix handling is covered via DHCPv6 and home networking tags; ULA/GUA mentions are incidental.
LPD-6 adjusts filtering rules for delegated prefixes but is a minor part of the document.

RFC9819.title: Argument Signaling for BGP Services in Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6)
RFC9819.summary: Updates RFC 9252 to clarify signaling and processing of SRv6 Service SIDs with arguments, specifically End.DT2M with ESI Filtering ARG carried in EVPN Ethernet A-D per ES and Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag routes.

SRv6.why: The document specifies SRv6 SID structure, Endpoint Behavior (End.DT2M) and argument encoding for SRv6 service SIDs.
SRv6.quote: provides more detailed specifications for the signaling and processing of SRv6 Segment Identifier advertisements for BGP overlay service routes associated with SRv6 Endpoint Behaviors that support arguments

EVPN.why: The procedures cover EVPN Ethernet A-D per ES and Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag routes and ESI filtering for BUM traffic.
EVPN.quote: ESI Filtering is a split-horizon mechanism used for multihoming [RFC7432] or Ethernet-Tree (E-Tree) procedures [RFC8317].

rejected.why: BGP is the signaling substrate; the document is about SRv6 service SID encoding in EVPN routes, not BGP protocol in general.
Mentioned only as one of the RFC 9252 services; the document's content concerns EVPN.
SRv6 is the specific tag; IPv6 is only the data plane.
SRv6 is the more specific child tag and is already chosen.

RFC9820.title: Authentication Service Based on the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) for Use with the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)
RFC9820.summary: Specifies CoAP-EAP, an authentication service that carries EAP over CoAP as a new EAP lower layer, authenticating constrained IoT devices to a Controller and deriving OSCORE keying material from the MSK.

EAP.why: The document defines a new EAP lower layer, with its registration in the EAP Lower Layers registry, and discusses EAP lower-layer requirements, re-authentication, and MSK export.
EAP.quote: it defines an EAP lower layer based on CoAP called "CoAP-EAP"

CoAP.why: Defines a CoAP application (well-known URI, media type, content format, resource-per-step flow, proxy operation) for carrying EAP.
CoAP.quote: uses the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) as a transport method to carry the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP)

OSCORE.why: A substantial part specifies cipher suite negotiation and derivation of the OSCORE Security Context from the MSK.
OSCORE.quote: allows deriving key material to protect CoAP messages exchanged between them based on Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments (OSCORE)

rejected.why: ACE is only mentioned as an example use case and for authorization after bootstrapping; the document does not specify ACE.
CBOR is used as the encoding for the information object, which is a substrate rather than the subject.
DTLS PSK derivation is in an appendix as an alternative; it is not a main subject.
The AAA backend is optional and only referenced as an architecture component, not specified.
The media type registration is IANA boilerplate for the document's own format, not about media type rules.
IoT is the motivating environment, but the EAP and CoAP tags are more specific to the protocol work.

RFC9824.title: Compact Denial of Existence in DNSSEC
RFC9824.summary: Specifies Compact Denial of Existence for DNSSEC, where online-signing servers answer nonexistent names with a NODATA response and a single minimally covering NSEC/NSEC3 record. It defines the NXNAME meta-type, the EDNS CO flag, and an EDE code, and it updates RFCs 4034 and 4035.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document specifies authenticated denial of existence using NSEC/NSEC3 with online signing, and it updates the DNSSEC core RFCs 4034 and 4035.
DNSSEC.quote: describes a technique to generate a signed DNS response on demand for a nonexistent name by claiming that the name exists but doesn't have any data

EDNS.why: It defines a new EDNS header flag, Compact Answers OK (CO), for signaled response code restoration. It also registers a new Extended DNS Error code.
EDNS.quote: A new EDNS0 [RFC6891] header flag is defined in the second most significant bit of the flags field in the EDNS0 OPT header.

rejected.why: DNSSEC is the more specific tag, and its parent DNS is implied.
Happy Eyeballs is mentioned only in passing, in the discussion of operational implications.
Pseudorandom subdomain attacks appear only in the Security Considerations, and they are not the subject of the document.
The IANA registrations are boilerplate that follows from the protocol work. The document is not about IANA registry guidance.

RFC9825.title: Extensions to OSPF for Advertising Prefix Administrative Tags
RFC9825.summary: Defines a new Administrative Tag Sub-TLV letting OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 advertise multiple 32-bit administrative tags on all prefix types, specifies propagation/ECMP behaviour, BGP-LS mapping, and a YANG module for configuring and viewing the tags.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 with a new sub-TLV for prefix administrative tags and specifies the protocol operation for advertising and propagating them.
OSPF.quote: multiple administrative tags may be advertised for all types of prefixes.

YANG.why: A substantial part of the document is a new YANG module augmenting the OSPF models with admin-tag configuration and operational state.
YANG.quote: This section defines a YANG data model that can be used to configure and manage the prefix administrative tags defined in this document

rejected.why: Considered since the document covers OSPFv3 Extended LSAs, but it is a joint OSPFv2/OSPFv3 extension and the parent OSPF tag covers both.
Not in the taxonomy as a tag. The document only has a short section noting the existing BGP-LS IGP Route Tag TLV carries these tags.
BGP is mentioned only as an example redistribution target and via BGP-LS; the document is not about BGP.
IPFRR/LFA protection is listed only as one possible use of the tags; the document does not specify it.
The sub-TLV is also valid in the OSPFv3 SRv6 Locator TLV, but this is a minor applicability point, not the subject.
NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the management protocols for accessing the YANG module and are not specified here.
Section 4.1 is about tag selection when multiple LSAs contribute to a route, not ECMP forwarding itself.

RFC9826.title: A YANG Data Model for the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP)
RFC9826.summary: Defines the YANG modules ietf-pcep and ietf-pcep-stats for configuring, monitoring and collecting statistics on PCEP speakers (PCC/PCE), including stateful PCE LSP-DB, notifications, RPCs and mapping to the PCEP MIB.

PCE.why: The document models PCEP entities, peers, sessions, capabilities and statistics, so readers of the PCE/PCEP subject want it.
PCE.quote: This document defines a YANG data model for the management of the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP)

YANG.why: Its main content is two YANG modules, ietf-pcep and ietf-pcep-stats, with tree diagrams and module code.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG 1.1 [RFC7950] data model for the management of PCEP speakers.

rejected.why: The model maps to the PCEP MIB (Appendix D), but it is a YANG successor and does not define MIB modules.
TLS is only configured via RFC 9645 groupings for PCEPS. The document defines nothing new about TLS.
NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the access protocols named in Security Considerations.
SR-MPLS is only one capability flag among many, and SRv6 is explicitly out of scope.
GMPLS is listed only as a feature flag.
TCP is the transport PCEP runs over. The model only touches it through timers and a TCP-AO capability bit.

gaps.name: PCE / PCEP (Path Computation Element Communication Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no PCE tag. PCE appears only as a child of traffic engineering in the form of a PCE tech, and I used it above, but it is not listed under that name. If it does not exist, this document's main subject has no home.

RFC9827.title: Renaming the Extended Sequence Numbers (ESN) Transform Type in the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC9827.summary: Updates RFC 7296 by renaming IKEv2 Transform Type 5 from "Extended Sequence Numbers (ESN)" to "Sequence Numbers (SN)", renaming its two Transform IDs, and broadening its semantics to describe sequence number properties for IPsec SAs.

IKE.why: The document changes the meaning and naming of an IKEv2 transform type and its IDs, and updates RFC 7296. IKE readers would need it.
IKE.quote: This document updates the IKEv2 specification [RFC7296] by renaming Transform Type 5 and the two associated Transform IDs.

ESP.why: A substantial part of the document describes how the Transform IDs map to ESP/AH sequence number handling and anti-replay. That makes it relevant to ESP readers.
ESP.quote: Value 0 defines sequence numbers as monotonically increasing 32-bit counters that are transmitted in the Sequence Number field of AH and ESP packets.
ESP.section: 3. Extending the Semantics of Transform Type 5

rejected.why: The IPsec architecture is background. The specific subject is IKE, with ESP as the secondary tag, and ancestors are implied.
The IANA registry renames are a consequence of the main change. The document is not about IANA guidance or stewardship.
G-IKEv2 and multicast SAs are mentioned only as examples of future Transform IDs.

RFC9828.title: RTP Payload Format for JPEG 2000 Streaming with Sub-Codestream Latency
RFC9828.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for streaming JPEG 2000 video codestreams with sub-codestream latency, including payload headers, resync points, resolution/quality discarding, code-block caching, and the video/jpeg2000-scl media type.

RTP payload format.why: The document is an RTP payload format specification for JPEG 2000 video, with main and body packet payload headers and RTP header usage.
RTP payload format.quote: This document defines the RTP payload format for the streaming of a video signal encoded as a sequence of JPEG 2000 codestreams.

codecs.why: A substantial part of the document describes the JPEG 2000 codec and its codestream structure, and how its scalability features map to packets. No JPEG 2000-specific tag exists, so the codecs parent fits.
codecs.quote: JPEG 2000 is a flexible image codec that supports resolution and quality scalability, lossy-to-lossless coding

rejected.why: The more specific child RTP payload format applies, so the parent is implied.
Section 10 only maps the media type to SDP per RFC 4855. It defines nothing new about SDP.
The media type registration is boilerplate-like and incidental to the payload format. It is not a general media type rule document.
RTCP is mentioned only in passing for rate adaptation.
The congestion control section only lists generic example mechanisms and is short.
SRTP appears only as a reference in the Security Considerations boilerplate.

gaps.name: JPEG 2000 image/video coding
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for JPEG 2000 specifically. Only the generic codecs parent is available.

RFC9829.title: Handling of Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Certificate Revocation List (CRL) Number Extensions
RFC9829.summary: Updates RFC 6487 so RPKI relying parties ignore the CRL Number extension (beyond sanity checks) and identify the current CRL via the issuer's manifest and the CRLDP during certification path validation.

RPKI.why: The document revises RPKI resource certificate CRL handling and path validation step 5, updating the RPKI certificate profile in RFC 6487.
RPKI.quote: This document mandates that RPKI RPs ignore the CRL Number extension.

X.509.why: It changes how the X.509 v2 CRL Number and AKI extensions are profiled and processed in RPKI resource certificates and CRLs.
X.509.quote: RPs MUST ignore the CRL Number extension except for checking that it is marked as non-critical and contains a non-negative integer

rejected.why: RPKI is the more specific tag under routing security, so the parent is implied.
The document is about RPKI specifically, a child of routing security. It is not about the general Internet PKI, apart from the X.509 CRL profile it touches.
It does not concern BGPsec path validation, only certificate and CRL handling in the RPKI.

RFC9830.title: Advertising Segment Routing Policies in BGP
RFC9830.summary: Specifies how BGP distributes Segment Routing Policy candidate paths using a new SR Policy SAFI (73), SR Policy sub-TLVs in the Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute, and Color Extended Community flag updates (updates RFC 9012).

BGP.why: The document defines a new BGP SAFI, NLRI format, attribute sub-TLVs, and propagation and error-handling procedures for SR Policy in BGP.
BGP.quote: This document specifies how BGP can be used to distribute SR Policy CPs.

segment routing.why: The subject is signalling SR Policy candidate paths, with segment lists, Binding SIDs and steering. It covers both SR-MPLS and SRv6 data planes, so the generic segment routing tag fits better than either child.
segment routing.quote: A Segment Routing (SR) Policy is an ordered list of segments (also referred to as "instructions") that define a source-routed policy.

rejected.why: SRv6 SIDs and Binding SID sub-TLVs appear, but they are one of two data planes the document covers. It is not about SRv6 specifically.
SR-MPLS labels are encoded in Type A segments, but SR-MPLS is only one of two supported data planes.
SR Policies serve traffic engineering, but the document is about BGP signalling of policies, not TE as a subject.
PCEP and PCE are mentioned only as alternative ways to provision candidate paths.
Route Target and NO_ADVERTISE communities are used mechanically for headend targeting. The Color Extended Community change is a minor part of the document.
Route reflectors are mentioned only in connection with propagation of SR Policy NLRIs.

RFC9831.title: Segment Type Extensions for BGP Segment Routing (SR) Policy
RFC9831.summary: Experimental RFC defining BGP SR Policy SAFI sub-TLV encodings for Segment Types C through K (SR-MPLS and SRv6) and new segment flags (A-Flag, S-Flag), extending RFC 9830.

segment routing.why: The document encodes SR Policy segment types for both SR-MPLS and SRv6 in BGP. It is about SR Policy segment lists, so the general segment routing tag fits.
segment routing.quote: This document specifies the signaling of additional Segment Routing (SR) Segment Types for SR Policies in BGP using the SR Policy Subsequent Address Family Identifier (SAFI).

BGP.why: It defines new BGP sub-TLVs and flags under the SR Policy SAFI, which is a BGP protocol extension.
BGP.quote: This document specifies the extensions for the advertisement of the remaining SR Segment Types defined in [RFC9256] in the SR Policy SAFI

SR-MPLS.why: Types C to H carry optional SR-MPLS SIDs, so a large part of the document concerns SR-MPLS segment encoding.
SR-MPLS.quote: Type D:   IPv6 Global Prefix with optional SR Algorithm for SR-MPLS

SRv6.why: Types I, J and K carry SRv6 SIDs, endpoint behavior and SID structure, which is substantial SRv6 content.
SRv6.quote: The Type I Segment sub-TLV encodes an IPv6 node address, an SR Algorithm, and an optional SRv6 SID.

rejected.why: SR Policies are a form of traffic engineering, but the document only defines BGP encodings of segment types.
The IANA section only registers code points. It is boilerplate for this document.
IPv6 addresses appear in the encodings, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
RFC 9552 (BGP-LS) is referenced only for interface index definitions.

RFC9832.title: BGP Classful Transport Planes
RFC9832.summary: Defines BGP Classful Transport (SAFI 76), Transport Classes, TRDBs and Resolution Schemes so overlay service routes can be mapped to intent-aware underlay tunnels across multiple domains, usable for IETF Network Slices.

BGP.why: The document defines a new BGP address family (AFI/SAFI 1/76, 2/76), a new extended community, and the procedures for using them.
BGP.quote: A new BGP address family called "BGP Classful Transport (BGP CT)", which extends/stitches Intent-aware intra-domain tunnels belonging to the same class across domain boundaries

MPLS.why: Label binding, label stitching across domains, and MPLS OAM FEC sub-TLVs are a substantial part of the specification.
MPLS.quote: The BN also installs an MPLS route for that label that swaps the incoming label with the label received from the downstream BGP speaker
MPLS.section: 7.4. Readvertising BGP CT Route by Border Nodes

L3VPN.why: It reuses RFC 4364 RD/RT procedures and inter-AS options A/B/C, and service routes such as L3VPN resolve over the transport classes.
L3VPN.quote: A new BGP address family that leverages the procedures described in RFC 4364 ("BGP/MPLS IP Virtual Private Networks (VPNs)")

rejected.why: SR-TE and SRv6 are tunnel types the transport classes can group, and SRv6 detail lives in a separate document.
RSVP-TE tunnels are classified into transport classes but the document does not specify or extend RSVP-TE.
TE tunnels are classified by TE characteristics, but the document is about BGP signalling of the classes rather than TE mechanisms.
DSCP is used only for class-based forwarding in the short Section 11.5.
RPKI and BGPsec appear only as possible future security extensions in the Security Considerations.

RFC9833.title: A Common YANG Data Model for Attachment Circuits
RFC9833.summary: Specifies the ietf-ac-common YANG module, a reusable set of features, identities and groupings for attachment circuits (ACs) between customer terminating points and provider networks, for reuse by service, network and device models.

YANG.why: The document's whole purpose is a YANG module (ietf-ac-common) with reusable groupings, identities and features, so readers of YANG models would look for it.
YANG.quote: The document specifies a common attachment circuits (ACs) YANG data model, which is designed to be reusable by other models.

VPN.why: ACs are the provisioning between customer sites and provider PEs for L2VPN/L3VPN services. The module builds on the vpn-common model and is reused by VPN service and network models.
VPN.quote: to bind Layer 2 VPN or Layer 3 VPN services with ACs, the "ietf-ac-glue" module augments the LxSM and LxNM

rejected.why: BGP roles, peer groups and authentication appear as groupings, but BGP is not specified or extended; the module only configures it over an AC.
NETCONF and RESTCONF are mentioned only as the management protocols in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
OSPF, IS-IS and RIP appear only as routing parameters in groupings, and the document is not about them.
DHCP appears only as an address-allocation option in the groupings. It is not specified or extended.
Pseudowire, VPLS and VXLAN are only identities for L2 tunnel selection, not specified here.
The module is YANG-based, not SNMP-based, so the MIB and SNMP tags do not apply.

gaps.name: Attachment circuits (service/network YANG models)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for attachment circuits or bearers, or for YANG service models. The VPN tag is only an approximate fit.

RFC9834.title: YANG Data Models for Bearers and Attachment Circuits as a Service (ACaaS)
RFC9834.summary: RFC 9834 specifies YANG service data models for bearers (ietf-bearer-svc) and attachment circuits as a service (ietf-ac-svc), used by customers to provision ACs and underlying links before or during service provisioning such as network slices or VPNs.

YANG.why: The document's core content is two YANG service modules (ietf-ac-svc and ietf-bearer-svc) with tree diagrams and module code.
YANG.quote: This document specifies a YANG service data model for ACs.

L2VPN.why: ACs are the CE-PE attachments for L2VPN/L3VPN services, and the model is positioned against the L2SM/L3SM and reuses VPN common types. Readers of VPN service models would want it, but the document is not itself a VPN service.
L2VPN.quote: to bind LxVPN services to ACs

rejected.why: BGP is one of several routing protocols configurable on an AC (with static, OSPF, IS-IS, RIP, VRRP). The document only models BGP session parameters, not the protocol.
NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the access protocols the modules can be used with, so they are substrate.
BFD is only referenced via failure-detection profiles and OAM session parameters in the AC model.
VRRP support is a small part of the routing options, not a subject of the document.
LAG is mentioned only as an example bearer type.
The document defines service models for orchestration, but it is not about SDN architecture.

gaps.name: Attachment circuits / network service models
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for attachment circuits, bearers or service-level YANG models. The VPN subtree only offers provider-provisioned VPN protocols, and L2VPN is not an available id, so the L2VPN tag above is invalid.

RFC9835.title: A Network YANG Data Model for Attachment Circuits
RFC9835.summary: Specifies the ietf-ac-ntw YANG network model, augmenting ietf-network and the SAP model, for provisioning attachment circuits on provider edges, including L2/IP connection, routing, BFD OAM, security and service parameters.

YANG.why: The document defines a YANG module (ietf-ac-ntw) and its tree structure; it is a YANG data model specification.
YANG.quote: This document specifies a network model for attachment circuits (ACs).

VPN.why: ACs bind PE-CE connectivity for L2VPN/L3VPN services; the model builds on the L2NM/L3NM and VPN common model, and examples cover VPLS and L3VPN SAPs.
VPN.quote: the same AC may host multiple services (e.g., Layer 2 VPN (L2VPN), Layer 3 VPN (L3VPN), or RFC 9543 Network Slice Service

BGP.why: A substantial section models PE-CE BGP peer groups, neighbors, timers, roles, max-prefix, and TCP-AO authentication.
BGP.quote: The BGP routing subtree structure is shown in Figure 13.

rejected.why: Only the access protocol named in Security Considerations; the document defines a data model, not NETCONF.
Modeled as one of several PE-CE routing options in a single subsection; not a main subject.
BFD parameters are modeled in the OAM subsection, but only as a small part of the document.
One short subsection of the routing options; not a main subject.
Network orchestration context is mentioned, but the document is about the data model, not SDN architecture.
Only one of several PE-CE routing options.

RFC9836.title: A YANG Data Model for Augmenting VPN Service and Network Models with Attachment Circuits
RFC9836.summary: Defines the "ietf-ac-glue" YANG module that augments the L2VPN/L3VPN service models (L2SM, L3SM) and network models (L2NM, L3NM) with references to attachment circuits managed via the AC service and network models.

YANG.why: The document's core deliverable is a YANG module that augments existing YANG VPN models with AC references.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model, referred to as the "AC Glue" model, to augment the LxVPN Service Model (LxSM) and LxVPN Network Model (LxNM)

VPN.why: The module binds provider-provisioned L2VPN/L3VPN services to attachment circuits, so readers of VPN service and network modelling would want it.
VPN.quote: The AC Glue model enables a provider to associate Layer 2/3 VPN (LxVPN) services with the underlying AC infrastructure

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in Security Considerations as the access protocols for the module.
The L3NM and L3SM are augmented, but the document does not specify BGP/MPLS L3VPN itself. VPN covers it.
The L2NM and L2SM are augmented, but the document does not define L2VPN services. VPN covers it.
RFC 7665 is cited only in passing, for CE roles.
The document is about a YANG module and has no relation to SNMP MIB modules.

gaps.name: Attachment circuits (ACaaS)
gaps.why: The document is about binding VPN services to attachment circuits (AC as a Service). The taxonomy has no tag for attachment circuits or bearers.

RFC9837.title: The IPv6 VPN Service Destination Option
RFC9837.summary: Defines an experimental IPv6 Destination Option (VPN Service Option, type 0x5E) carrying 32-bit VPN service information that identifies a FIB entry on the egress PE, as a way to build VPNs without MPLS or per-VPN addresses.

VPN.why: The document specifies a new mechanism for provider-provisioned VPN service demultiplexing between PE routers. It does not fit a specific VPN child such as L3VPN or EVPN, so the parent tag is the right one.
VPN.quote: VPN service information is encoded in an experimental IPv6 Destination Option [RFC8200]. The experimental IPv6 Destination Option is called the VPN Service Option.

IPv6.why: The document defines a new IPv6 Destination Option, including its option type, length, data and placement rules in the Destination Options header. Readers of IPv6 extension headers would want it.
IPv6.quote: The VPN Service Option is an IPv6 Destination Option encoded according to rules defined in [RFC8200].

rejected.why: AH and ESP are only required as the protection for the tunnel when the option is used on the global Internet. They are a security mechanism the document relies on, not its subject.
SRv6 is only listed as one of the existing VPN technologies. This document does not specify or extend it.
The document encapsulates customer data in an IPv6 tunnel header, but the subject is the VPN service option and not tunnelling in general.
RFC 4364 L3VPN is mentioned only as an existing technology for comparison. The document does not specify or extend it.
NETCONF and PCEP are mentioned only as ways to populate the FIB. The document does not use them in any substantive way.

RFC9838.title: Group Key Management Using the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2)
RFC9838.summary: Defines G-IKEv2, an IKEv2 extension for group key management (member registration and group rekey via a GCKS) that distributes IPsec group SAs and keys, obsoleting the IKEv1-based GDOI (RFC 6407).

IKE.why: The document specifies new IKEv2 exchanges (GSA_AUTH, GSA_REGISTRATION, GSA_REKEY, GSA_INBAND_REKEY), payloads, transforms and notifications as an extension of IKEv2.
IKE.quote: This document presents an extension to IKEv2 [RFC7296] called G-IKEv2, which accommodates group key management.
