multicast security.why: It is a group key management protocol conforming to the MSEC architecture, covering registration, rekeying, LKH and forward access control for multicast IPsec groups.
multicast security.quote: G-IKEv2 conforms to "The Multicast Group Security Architecture" [RFC3740]

rejected.why: GDOI is the IKEv1-based predecessor that this document replaces and obsoletes. It does not specify GDOI itself. It only mentions possible future redefinition of GDOI extensions.
ESP and AH are the data-plane protocols for the Data-Security SAs. The document only keys them and does not define ESP.
IPsec is the substrate protected by the keys. The subject is key management, which is covered by the IKE and multicast security tags.
PPK mixing is mentioned only in a brief interaction subsection (6.2).
The more specific multicast security tag applies. Multicast routing and group membership are not addressed.

RFC9839.title: Unicode Character Repertoire Subsets
RFC9839.summary: RFC 9839 defines and recommends three Unicode code point subsets (Unicode Scalars, XML Characters, Unicode Assignables) that exclude problematic code points such as surrogates, legacy controls and noncharacters, for use by protocol and data format specifications.

Unicode.why: The whole document specifies subsets of the Unicode repertoire for use in Internet protocols, which is Unicode usage in protocols.
Unicode.quote: Specifications can refer to these subsets by the names "Unicode Scalars", "XML Characters", and "Unicode Assignables".

rejected.why: JSON is used as an example of a format that permits problematic code points, but the document does not specify or extend JSON.
PRECIS is referenced as a stricter alternative for human-facing strings, but the document does not specify or extend it.
UTF-8 is mentioned as an encoding form in background; the document is about code point repertoires, not the encoding.
ABNF is only the notation used to express the subsets.
The XML Char production is the basis of one subset, but the document does not address XML usage itself.
CBOR is mentioned only as having Unicode Scalars as its default subset.

RFC9840.title: rLEDBAT: Receiver-Driven Low Extra Delay Background Transport for TCP
RFC9840.summary: Specifies rLEDBAT, a set of TCP receiver-side mechanisms (receive window control, delay measurement via timestamps, loss detection) that run a less-than-best-effort congestion control algorithm such as LEDBAT/LEDBAT++ at the receiver.

LEDBAT.why: The document extends LEDBAT/LEDBAT++ to be run at the receiver, specifying how delay is measured and the window is controlled for LBE transport.
LEDBAT.quote: a set of mechanisms that enable the execution of a less-than-best-effort congestion control algorithm for TCP at the receiver end

TCP.why: The mechanisms manipulate the TCP receive window, avoid window shrinking, set the Window Scale option, and use TCP timestamps, so TCP readers would want this.
TCP.quote: The rLEDBAT receiver controls the sender's rate through the receive window announced by the receiver in the TCP header.

rejected.why: CUBIC is only the assumed standard sender algorithm for comparison, not the subject.
Mentioned only as an alternative sender congestion controller.
AQM/CoDel/PIE are only listed as interaction topics for future experiments.
CDNs appear only as a motivating scenario.
The more specific LEDBAT tag applies instead of the parent topic.

RFC9841.title: Shared Brotli Compressed Data Format
RFC9841.summary: Defines shared brotli, extending brotli (RFC 7932) with shared dictionaries (custom static and LZ77), large-window streams, and a framing/container format.

Brotli.why: The whole document specifies extensions to the Brotli compressed data format: dictionaries, large window, and framing.
Brotli.quote: This specification defines a data format for shared brotli compression, which adds support for shared dictionaries, large window, and a container format to brotli

rejected.why: Parent of Brotli, so it is implied. The document is about one specific child.
Security Considerations mention CORS and cookies, but the document does not specify any HTTP behaviour.
There are no media type registrations. The IANA section has no actions.
HighwayHash is only used as a dictionary identifier. It is not a SHA-family hash and is not a subject of the document.

RFC9842.title: Compression Dictionary Transport
RFC9842.summary: Defines HTTP headers (Use-As-Dictionary, Available-Dictionary, Dictionary-ID), a link relation, and the dcb/dcz content encodings so HTTP responses can serve as external compression dictionaries for Brotli and Zstandard.

HTTP.why: The document extends HTTP with new request/response header fields and content codings, negotiated via Accept-Encoding/Content-Encoding and Vary.
HTTP.quote: This specification defines a mechanism for using designated HTTP [HTTP] responses as an external dictionary for future HTTP responses

web linking.why: A whole section defines and registers a new link relation type, which readers of web linking would want.
web linking.quote: This specification defines the "compression-dictionary" link relation type [WEB-LINKING] that provides a mechanism for an HTTP response to provide a URL for a compression dictionary

compression.why: The core subject is dictionary-based lossless compression, with the dcb and dcz formats built on Brotli and Zstandard. Brotli and Zstandard are existing compression formats that the document applies and does not define itself, so the parent compression topic fits best.
compression.quote: registers content-encoding values for compressing with Brotli and Zstandard using a negotiated dictionary.

rejected.why: The document defines a dictionary-compressed wrapper (dcb) but the Brotli format itself is specified elsewhere (RFC 7932, RFC 9841). It is used and not specified, extended or analysed.
The dcz encoding wraps Zstandard in a skippable frame header, but the Zstandard format is defined in RFC 8878 and is not the subject here.
Freshness and Vary are used only to govern dictionary validity and cache correctness. The document does not extend caching.
The privacy section only says to treat dictionaries like cookies. That is boilerplate-level and the document is not about cookie state management.
SHA-256 is only used as a hash to identify dictionaries.
The document uses standard HTTP Accept-Encoding negotiation. That is substrate and not a new negotiation mechanism.

RFC9843.title: IGP Flexible Algorithms: Bandwidth, Delay, Metrics, and Constraints
RFC9843.summary: Extends IGP Flexible Algorithm (RFC 9350) for IS-IS and OSPF with a Generic Metric sub-TLV, a Bandwidth Metric type, FAD constraints excluding low-bandwidth or high-delay links, and automatic bandwidth-based metric calculation.

IS-IS.why: Defines new IS-IS sub-TLVs (Generic Metric, FAEMB, FAEMD, FADRB, FADBT) and the pruning rules that use them.
IS-IS.quote: IS-IS Flex-Algorithm Exclude Minimum Bandwidth (FAEMB) sub-TLV is a sub-TLV of the IS-IS FAD sub-TLV.

OSPF.why: Defines parallel OSPFv2/OSPFv3 sub-TLVs for the generic metric and Flex-Algorithm constraints.
OSPF.quote: The OSPF Generic Metric sub-TLV specifies the link metric for a given metric-type.

rejected.why: The document uses TE link attributes (TE LSAs, TE default metric) as carriers. Its subject is IGP Flex-Algorithm path computation, not traffic engineering of LSPs.
Flex-Algorithm is commonly used with segment routing, but this document does not specify SR behaviour. It cites SR only for micro-loop avoidance.
The document is protocol-specific extensions to IS-IS and OSPF, not routing architecture.
YANG models are only mentioned in the Operational Considerations, as being defined in other documents.
ECMP is mentioned briefly for load-balancing across parallel links, and the document puts load-balancing out of scope.

gaps.name: IGP Flexible Algorithm (Flex-Algorithm)
gaps.why: The document's main subject is extending Flex-Algorithm (RFC 9350). The taxonomy has no tag for it, so it falls under the IS-IS and OSPF tags instead.

RFC9844.title: Entering IPv6 Zone Identifiers in User Interfaces
RFC9844.summary: Standards-track document requiring user interfaces that accept non-global IPv6 addresses to let users enter zone identifiers (e.g. fe80::1%eth0), obsoleting RFC 6874 and updating RFC 4007, 7622 and 8089.

IPv6.why: The document specifies how IPv6 scoped addresses with zone identifiers are entered in UIs. It updates the IPv6 Scoped Address Architecture (RFC 4007) and addresses IPv6 address text representation.
IPv6.quote: A user interface (UI) that allows or requires the user to enter an IPv6 address other than a global unicast address MUST provide a means for entering a link-local address

rejected.why: The document obsoletes RFC 6874 (zone IDs in URIs) but explicitly does not apply to URIs fetched by browsers. It gives a generic UI requirement instead.
getaddrinfo(), inet_pton() and if_nametoindex() are mentioned as the means of converting zone identifiers. The document does not extend the sockets API.
This is a parent of IPv6 in a different branch. IPv6 is the more specific fit for this document, which concerns IPv6 scoped address text entry.
YANG is mentioned only as one format in which link-local addresses are entered, in a use case. The document is not about YANG.
RFC 7622 is updated only by deleting a reference to RFC 6874. The document does not address XMPP itself.

RFC9845.title: Challenges and Opportunities in Management for Green Networking
RFC9845.summary: An IRTF/NMRG informational document outlining research challenges and opportunities for making networking and its management greener (energy- and carbon-aware) at the equipment, protocol, network and architecture levels.

sustainability.why: The whole document concerns energy efficiency and environmental impact of networks, which is the sustainability topic.
sustainability.quote: methods to make networking technology itself "greener" and to manage and operate networks in ways that reduce their environmental footprint without impacting their utility need to be explored

energy management.why: A substantial part covers instrumentation, power metrics, YANG power models and control loops for energy monitoring and management of network devices.
energy management.quote: providing management instrumentation that allows for precise monitoring and managing power usage and doing so at different levels of granularity

rejected.why: YANG models for power are mentioned as work needed, but the document does not specify or analyse YANG.
TE is discussed as one example of energy-aware optimization, not as the subject.
ICN is one architectural example discussed briefly, not a main subject.
CDNs are cited as an example of an energy-saving architecture, but the document is not about them.
ECN, DCTCP and L4S are mentioned in passing as ways to avoid wasted energy, not covered in depth.
Considered as the parent topic, but the more specific energy management tag fits better.

gaps.name: Green networking
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no dedicated tag for green networking beyond sustainability and energy management, and this document sits mostly in that area.

RFC9846.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3
RFC9846.summary: RFC 9846 specifies TLS 1.3, covering the handshake, record protocol, alerts, key schedule, 0-RTT and anti-replay, and backward compatibility, and obsoletes RFC 8446 along with several TLS 1.2-era RFCs.

TLS.why: The document is the TLS 1.3 protocol specification itself, including handshake, record layer, extensions and compliance requirements.
TLS.quote: This document specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol.

rejected.why: DTLS 1.3 is only referenced (RFC 9147) for cookies and HKDF labels; this document does not specify it.
HMAC/HKDF are used as primitives in the key schedule, but the document is not about them.
AES-GCM cipher suites are listed, but the document is not about the AES cipher.
OCSP status is carried in a certificate extension, but this is a small part of the document.
Certificates are used for authentication, but the document does not profile X.509.
QUIC appears only as an extension reference in a table.

RFC9847.title: IANA Registry Updates for TLS and DTLS
RFC9847.summary: RFC 9847 updates RFC 8447 by instructing IANA to add a "D" (discouraged) value to the "Recommended" column of selected TLS/DTLS registries, add a "Comment" column to others, and revise registration procedures and expert review guidance.

TLS.why: The whole document changes TLS and DTLS IANA registries (extensions, cipher suites, groups, signature schemes) and marks discouraged TLS mechanisms. TLS readers need it. DTLS is a child of TLS and the document only touches DTLS registries in passing, so TLS is the right tag.
TLS.quote: This document instructs IANA to make changes to a number of the IANA registries related to Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS).

IANA.why: The document defines registry column semantics, registration policies, designated expert roles and registration request procedures. This is IANA registry guidance in its own right.
IANA.quote: Setting a value to "Y" or "D" or transitioning the value from "Y" or "D" in the "Recommended" column requires IETF Standards Action with Expert Review or IESG Approval

rejected.why: DTLS is in the title, but the document makes no DTLS-specific changes, only a note that the DTLS-OK column is unchanged. TLS covers it.
RC4 cipher suites are marked D, but only as entries in a table. The document is not about RC4.
DES and IDEA suites are marked discouraged in a table, but the document is not about those ciphers.
MD5 and SHA-1 hash entries are marked D, but the document does not specify or analyse them.
The document marks weak algorithms as discouraged in registries. It does not address cryptography itself.
The Kerberos cipher suites appear in the table of suites marked D. The document does not address Kerberos.

RFC9848.title: Bootstrapping TLS Encrypted ClientHello with DNS Service Bindings
RFC9848.summary: Defines the "ech" SvcParam for SVCB/HTTPS DNS records to convey TLS Encrypted ClientHello configuration to clients, with server deployment and client behaviour requirements, including disabling fallback and Alt-Svc interaction.

DNS.why: The document defines a new SvcParam for SVCB/HTTPS DNS resource records, which is a new DNS RR parameter and its resolution behaviour. No more specific DNS child tag covers SVCB.
DNS.quote: This specification provides a mechanism for conveying the ECH configuration information via DNS, using a SVCB or HTTPS resource record (RR).

TLS.why: The document bootstraps TLS ECH, specifying how ClientHello construction and fallback behaviour are influenced by the ech parameter. TLS readers need this.
TLS.quote: This specification defines a new SvcParam to enable the use of TLS Encrypted ClientHello [ECH] in TLS-based protocols.

HTTP.why: A section specifies how ECH in HTTPS records interacts with HTTP Alt-Svc and requires SVCB-reliant behaviour.
HTTP.quote: HTTP clients that implement both HTTP Alt-Svc [RFC7838] and the HTTPS record type [SVCB] can use them together

rejected.why: DNSSEC is only mentioned in Security Considerations as a context for downgrade attacks.
QUIC is only listed as a TLS-based protocol the parameter applies to.
DTLS is only mentioned as a compatible protocol version; nothing new is specified about it.
The document explicitly does not conceal the server name from the DNS resolver; encrypted DNS transport is not addressed.
Base64 is only the presentation encoding of the value.
CDNs appear only in example zone configurations.

gaps.name: SVCB / HTTPS resource records (Service Bindings)
gaps.why: The document extends the SVCB/HTTPS RR framework with the ech SvcParamKey, but the taxonomy has no tag for SVCB specifically; DNS is the closest fit.

gaps.name: TLS Encrypted ClientHello (ECH)
gaps.why: ECH is the central subject, but the taxonomy has no ECH tag under TLS.

RFC9849.title: TLS Encrypted Client Hello
RFC9849.summary: Specifies Encrypted Client Hello (ECH), a TLS 1.3/DTLS 1.3 extension that encrypts the ClientHello (including SNI and ALPN) under a server public key using HPKE, with configuration format, client/server behavior, GREASE, retry, and security analysis.

TLS.why: The document defines a new TLS extension, alert code, and handshake behavior for encrypting the ClientHello, which is squarely TLS protocol extension work.
TLS.quote: This document specifies a new TLS extension called Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) that allows clients to encrypt their ClientHello to the TLS server.

DTLS.why: ECH is explicitly specified for DTLS 1.3 as well, with DTLS-specific encodings and HKDF-Expand-Label handling, so DTLS readers would want it.
DTLS.quote: ECH is supported in TLS 1.3 [RFC8446], DTLS 1.3 [RFC9147], and newer versions of the TLS and DTLS protocols.

rejected.why: The document is about a specific TLS mechanism for SNI privacy, not a general privacy threat-model document. The TLS tag already covers it.
ECH configs are delivered via DNS SVCB/HTTPS records, but publication details are delegated to RFC 9460 and RFC 9848. DNS is only the delivery substrate here.
DoH, DoT and DoQ are mentioned only as complementary defenses for hiding DNS lookups, and the document does not specify or extend them.
DNSSEC is mentioned only as a defense against DNS spoofing in the Security Considerations.
HPKE is used as the encryption building block, but the document does not define key management. HPKE is not in the taxonomy and is a substrate here.
The only HTTP link is the HTTPS DNS record, which is a delivery mechanism and not something this document specifies.

gaps.name: HPKE (Hybrid Public Key Encryption)
gaps.why: ECH is built on HPKE, but the taxonomy has no HPKE tag. It is only used as a substrate here, so this is a minor gap.

gaps.name: SNI encryption / ClientHello privacy
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for TLS SNI encryption as a subject. TLS is the closest fit.

RFC9850.title: The SSLKEYLOGFILE Format for TLS
RFC9850.summary: Specifies the SSLKEYLOGFILE text format for logging TLS key-schedule secrets (TLS 1.2/1.3 and ECH) so diagnostic tools can decrypt test traffic, registers a media type and a label registry.

TLS.why: The document defines a format for logging TLS secrets, with labels for TLS 1.3, TLS 1.2 and ECH, and a TLS parameters registry. TLS readers and implementers need it.
TLS.quote: Recording secrets to a file in SSLKEYLOGFILE format allows diagnostic and logging tools that use this file to decrypt messages exchanged by TLS endpoints.

rejected.why: The document registers application/sslkeylogfile, but that is IANA boilerplate for the format. The document is not about media type rules.
DTLS is only mentioned as another protocol that can use the format.
QUIC is only mentioned as another protocol that can use the format.
HPKE is not in the taxonomy. It is only the source of the ECH_SECRET value.
The label registry is created to support the format. The document is not IANA guidance.
UTF-8 is only the character encoding specified for the file.

gaps.name: Encrypted Client Hello (ECH)
gaps.why: The document defines ECH_SECRET and ECH_CONFIG labels, but the taxonomy has no ECH tag.

RFC9851.title: TLS 1.2 is in Feature Freeze
RFC9851.summary: Declares TLS 1.2 in feature freeze: no changes beyond urgent security fixes, new exporter labels and ALPN IDs, with TLS registries annotated as TLS 1.3-or-later and PQC explicitly not to be specified for TLS 1.2.

TLS.why: The document sets the policy for the evolution of TLS 1.2 and directs readers to TLS 1.3 for new work. It also changes how the TLS registries are used.
TLS.quote: no changes will be approved for TLS 1.2 outside of urgent security fixes (as determined by TLS Working Group consensus)

rejected.why: The document explicitly excludes DTLS from the freeze, so DTLS is not its subject.
Section 2 discusses PQC only as a reason to move to TLS 1.3 and says PQC will not be specified for TLS 1.2. It does not specify or analyse PQC.
Section 4 annotates the TLS registries, but this is a consequence of the TLS policy and not a document about IANA registries in general.
ML-KEM is only mentioned as a NIST standard in the background text.

RFC9852.title: New Protocols Using TLS Must Require TLS 1.3
RFC9852.summary: BCP that updates RFC 9325 to require new protocols using TLS to mandate TLS 1.3 as default (TLS 1.2 only as optional non-default), excluding DTLS, with rationale from TLS 1.2 weaknesses and PQC.

TLS.why: The whole document prescribes which TLS versions new protocols must require and updates the TLS deployment guidance in RFC 9325.
TLS.quote: new protocols that use TLS must assume that TLS 1.3 is available and require its use.

rejected.why: The document explicitly excludes DTLS from its prescription, so it is not about DTLS.
PQC is discussed briefly as one rationale, but detailed PQC considerations are declared out of scope.
QUIC is cited only as an example of a protocol that requires TLS 1.3.
DNS over TLS is cited only as a counter-example of a TLS 1.2 default.
RC4 is mentioned only as one TLS 1.2 weakness in the Security Considerations.

RFC9853.title: Return Routability Check for DTLS 1.2 and 1.3
RFC9853.summary: Defines a Return Routability Check (RRC) subprotocol for DTLS 1.2 and 1.3 that validates a peer's new address when a Connection ID record arrives from a changed source address, updating RFC 9146 and RFC 9147.

DTLS.why: The document defines a new DTLS subprotocol, content type and extension, and updates the DTLS 1.2 CID and DTLS 1.3 specifications.
DTLS.quote: This document specifies a Return Routability Check (RRC) subprotocol for use in the context of the Connection ID (CID) construct for the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS)

rejected.why: TLS is the parent of DTLS and is implied. The RRC extension and registries live in TLS parameter registries but the work is DTLS-specific.
The path validation procedure is inspired by QUIC and the attacker model is borrowed from it, but QUIC is not specified or extended.
CoAP Echo and the CoAP amplification example are only mentioned as an alternative or an illustration.
DTLS runs over UDP and this is only the substrate.
The IANA section registers a content type, an extension and a new registry, which is boilerplate for this document.

RFC9854.title: AODV-RPL: The Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL) Based on Ad Hoc On-Demand Distance Vector (AODV) Routing
RFC9854.summary: Specifies AODV-RPL, a reactive peer-to-peer route discovery mechanism for RPL-based low-power lossy networks, using RREQ/RREP/ART DIO options and paired instances to support symmetric and asymmetric routes.

RPL.why: The document defines an extension of RPL, but RPL is not in the taxonomy; see gaps. This id is invalid and should be disregarded.
RPL.quote: AODV-RPL is a reactive P2P route discovery mechanism for both hop-by-hop routes and source routing.

RFC9855.title: Topology Independent Fast Reroute Using Segment Routing
RFC9855.summary: Specifies TI-LFA, a local fast-reroute mechanism using Segment Routing repair lists over post-convergence paths to give guaranteed link, node and SRLG protection in link-state IGP networks.

IP fast reroute.why: The document specifies TI-LFA, extending LFA, RLFA and DLFA to give guaranteed IP fast-reroute coverage.
IP fast reroute.quote: Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate (TI-LFA) Fast Reroute (FRR), which is aimed at providing protection of node and Adjacency segments

segment routing.why: Repair paths are built as SR segment lists (node and Adjacency SIDs), with segment operations and Flexible Algorithm interaction defined.
segment routing.quote: This document outlines a local repair mechanism that leverages Segment Routing (SR) to restore end-to-end connectivity

SR-MPLS.why: Defines MPLS-specific repair-list pop/push behaviour, including SRGB label computation.
SR-MPLS.quote: The MPLS data plane for SR is described in [RFC8660].

SRv6.why: A dedicated section gives SRv6-specific repair-list handling, including Adjacency SIDs and head-end behaviour.
SRv6.quote: SRv6 data plane and programming instructions are described respectively in [RFC8754] and [RFC8986].

rejected.why: IS-IS is only the link-state IGP that carries SIDs and protection signalling; the document does not specify it.
OSPF is mentioned only as an IGP that carries SR extensions; the document does not specify it.
TE is mentioned only as a caveat for SR policies; the document is not about it.
BGP is not discussed.

RFC9856.title: Multicast Source Redundancy in EVPNs
RFC9856.summary: Specifies EVPN extensions (Warm Standby and Hot Standby) so that PEs suppress duplicate IP multicast traffic from redundant multicast sources, using S-PMSI A-D routes, an SFG flag, DF election and ESI labels allocated from DCBs.

EVPN.why: The whole document extends EVPN multicast procedures (RFC 9251, RFC 9625) with new BGP EVPN route attributes, flags, and ESI label handling.
EVPN.quote: This document specifies extensions to the EVPN multicast procedures that allow for the suppression of duplicate IP multicast traffic from redundant sources.

rejected.why: Document concerns EVPN multicast procedures; the multicast topic is only background and EVPN is the more specific fit.
BFD is only an optional mechanism (Section 5.3) for monitoring tunnels; not a substantial subject of the document.
BGP is the substrate carrying EVPN routes; the document defines EVPN-specific extensions, not BGP itself.
BIER is only one of the supported P-tunnel types; not what the document is about.
MVPN is mentioned as conventional background and a related technology; the document does not specify MVPN procedures.
PIM appears only in the background discussion of the anycast-source workaround.

gaps.name: EVPN (Ethernet VPN) multicast, OISM, and redundant sources
gaps.why: The taxonomy has EVPN only as a technology under VPN, but the subject index likely needs a way to group EVPN multicast documents. I tagged EVPN as the closest fit, but the id is not confirmed against the taxonomy list (EVPN is under VPN there as 'EVPN').

RFC9857.title: Advertisement of Segment Routing Policies Using BGP - Link State
RFC9857.summary: Defines a new BGP-LS NLRI type, descriptor and TLVs for advertising Segment Routing Policy candidate path state (BSIDs, constraints, segment lists, metrics) from headends or PCEs to external controllers.

segment routing.why: The document reports SR Policy state: candidate paths, SID lists, binding SIDs and segment types. Readers of the segment routing subject need it.
segment routing.quote: SR Policy architecture details are specified in [RFC9256]. An SR Policy comprises one or more candidate paths

BGP.why: It extends BGP-LS with a new NLRI type, Protocol-ID, TLVs and IANA registries.
BGP.quote: The "Link-State Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI)" defined in [RFC9552] is extended to carry the SR Policy information.
BGP.section: 2. Carrying SR Policy Information in BGP

SRv6.why: A substantial part of the document covers SRv6 BSIDs and SRv6 segment types (Types B, I, J and K).
SRv6.quote: the SRv6 Binding SID TLV defined in Section 5.2 SHOULD be used for the signaling of an SRv6 Binding SID.

SR-MPLS.why: It also covers SR-MPLS labels and segment types for SR Policy reporting.
SR-MPLS.quote: This document describes a mechanism to distribute SR Policy information (both SR-MPLS and SRv6 [RFC8402])

PCE.why: The PCE as BGP-LS Producer is a major use case with its own procedures (Section 3.2). It is also the motivating architecture.
PCE.quote: a PCE that is receiving the SR Policy information from its PCCs (i.e., SR Policy headend nodes) via PCEP

rejected.why: SR Policy is TE-related, but the more specific segment routing, PCE and BGP tags fit better.
This is unrelated to BMP; it is a different mechanism for exporting BGP state.
It is mentioned only as a configuration origin in the Protocol-Origin table.
OSPF and IS-IS are referenced only for the definitions of metric types.
IS-IS is referenced only for metric type definitions and is not the subject.
It is mentioned only as an example monitoring mechanism for a flag.

gaps.name: BGP-LS (BGP Link-State)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no BGP-LS tag. This document and its base RFC 9552 are about link-state distribution via BGP, so it is approximated by the BGP tag.

RFC9858.title: Additional Parameter Sets for HSS/LMS Hash-Based Signatures
RFC9858.summary: Defines additional HSS/LMS (RFC 8554) LM-OTS and LMS parameter sets using SHA-256/192, SHAKE256/256 and SHAKE256/192 to shrink signatures or add hash diversity, with security analysis and test vectors.

LMS.why: The document extends LMS/HSS with new LM-OTS and LMS parameter sets, code points and test vectors, so it belongs on the LMS page.
LMS.quote: This document defines a set of parameter sets for the HSS/LMS stateful hash-based signature method [RFC8554] that reduce the size of the signature significantly

SHA.why: Section 2 defines new truncated hash functions (SHA-256/192, SHAKE256/256, SHAKE256/192) based on the SHA-2 and SHA-3 families, and the security analysis discusses their strength.
SHA.quote: we define SHA-256/192 as a truncated version of SHA-256 [FIPS180]. That is, it is the result of performing a SHA-256 operation to a message

rejected.why: The parent is implied by LMS, and the document is about specific hash-based signature parameter sets. Its quantum discussion is part of the security analysis.
Only LMS/HSS is covered. XMSS is not discussed.
This is the parent of LMS and is implied, so it is not listed separately.
AES is mentioned only as a security-level comparison in the Security Considerations.
The IANA section only records code point assignments, which is boilerplate.

RFC9859.title: Generalized DNS Notifications
RFC9859.summary: Generalizes DNS NOTIFY beyond SOA hints by defining the DSYNC resource record for discovering notification endpoints and a registry of schemes, with initial use for CDS/CDNSKEY and CSYNC notifications for parental DS/NS delegation maintenance and DNSSEC bootstrapping.

DNS.why: Extends DNS NOTIFY and defines the new DSYNC RR type, the _dsync underscore name, and a new registry. Core DNS protocol work.
DNS.quote: This document generalizes and extends the use of DNS NOTIFY (RFC 1996) beyond conventional zone transfer hints

DNSSEC.why: The initial use case is CDS/CDNSKEY-triggered DS maintenance and DNSSEC bootstrapping. Substantial, though the main subject is the notification mechanism.
DNSSEC.quote: initial support for parental NS and DS record updates including DNSSEC bootstrapping

rejected.why: The Report-Channel EDNS0 option and Extended DNS Errors are only used optionally for error reporting. The document defines nothing new about EDNS.
Dynamic DNS UPDATE is mentioned only as an alternative mechanism. It is not specified or extended here.
Registries and registrars are the recipients of the notifications. Registry and registrar protocols and operations are not the subject, and the arrangements between them are out of scope.

RFC9860.title: Multicast-Only Fast Reroute (MoFRR) Based on Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate (TI-LFA) Fast Reroute
RFC9860.summary: Informational RFC specifying how Multicast-only Fast Reroute (MoFRR) for PIM can use TI-LFA backup paths, by carrying the TI-LFA segment list as RPF Vector and Explicit RPF Vector attributes in PIM Join messages to build a secondary multicast tree.

PIM.why: The document extends PIM MoFRR operation, using RPF Vector attributes in PIM Join messages to build a standby multicast tree hop by hop.
PIM.quote: This document specifies the use of Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate (TI-LFA) mechanisms with Multicast-only Fast Reroute (MoFRR) for Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM).

IP fast reroute.why: It applies LFA/TI-LFA fast reroute backup path computation to multicast (MoFRR), so readers of IP fast reroute would want it.
IP fast reroute.quote: This document leverages the backup path computed by TI-LFA through the IGP as a secondary Upstream Multicast Hop (UMH) for PIM.

segment routing.why: The TI-LFA segment list (Node SIDs and Adjacency SIDs, SR-MPLS and SRv6) is translated into PIM RPF Vectors, so SR concepts are a substantial part of the procedure.
segment routing.quote: The alternate path provided by the TI-LFA mechanism is represented as a segment list, which includes the Node SID of the P-space node

rejected.why: PIM-SM is referenced only for general security considerations and is not specified or extended; the document works with PIM Join messages generally, and the parent PIM tag covers it.
SR-MPLS is used only as an example data plane in the illustration; nothing new is specified for it.
SRv6 is used only as an example data plane in the illustration; nothing new is specified for it.
The IGP is only the source of the LSDB and TI-LFA computation; it is not specified here.
The more specific PIM tag already sits under multicast, so the parent is implied.

RFC9861.title: KangarooTwelve and TurboSHAKE
RFC9861.summary: Defines the TurboSHAKE128/256 XOFs (12-round Keccak-p sponge) and the tree-hashing KT128/KT256 (KangarooTwelve) XOFs, with HopMAC, test vectors and pseudocode.

SHA.why: The document specifies new Keccak-based hash/XOF functions built on the FIPS 202 permutation and sponge, the SHA-3 family's nearest taxonomy home; readers of SHA-3/SHAKE-style hashes would want it.
SHA.quote: This document defines the TurboSHAKE128, TurboSHAKE256 [TURBOSHAKE], KT128, and KT256 [KT] eXtendable-Output Functions (XOFs)

HMAC.why: Defines HopMAC, a hash-then-MAC construction positioned as an HMAC analogue; a substantial section on MACs from these hashes.
HMAC.quote: HopMAC128(Key, M, C, L) = KT128(Key, KT128(M, C, 32), L)

rejected.why: Only IANA registers COSE algorithm codepoints for the XOFs; boilerplate-level, not what the document is about.
Security Considerations only mention NIST post-quantum security levels for output length; not about PQC.
KDF use is only a brief remark in Security Considerations.

gaps.name: hash functions / XOFs (Keccak, KangarooTwelve, TurboSHAKE)
gaps.why: Taxonomy has no general hash-function tag; SHA is the closest (SHA-3 family) but Keccak-based XOFs aren't strictly SHA.

RFC9862.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for Segment Routing (SR) Policy Candidate Paths
RFC9862.summary: RFC 9862 defines PCEP extensions (an SR Policy Association type, new TLVs for candidate path identity, capabilities, computation priority, explicit-null policy and drop-upon-invalid) to signal SR Policy Candidate Paths, and updates RFC 8231 so SR LSPs can be delegated without PCReq/PCRep.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP with a new Association Type, TLVs, error values and an update to RFC 8231 stateful PCE procedures.
PCE.quote: This document specifies the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) extension to signal Candidate Paths of an SR Policy.

segment routing.why: The document signals SR Policy candidate paths per RFC 9256, covering both SR-MPLS and SRv6. This is the general SR tag, since it is not specific to SR-MPLS or SRv6 alone.
segment routing.quote: A Segment Routing (SR) Policy is an ordered list of instructions called "segments" that represent a source-routed policy.

rejected.why: The document applies to both SR-MPLS and SRv6 and is not specific to the MPLS data plane. Only the Explicit NULL label TLV is MPLS-specific.
SRv6 is covered equally with SR-MPLS, and the SRv6 encodings come from RFC 9603. The document is not about SRv6 specifically.
MPLS LSPs and labels appear only as background. The Explicit NULL label is mentioned in one TLV.
The PCE tag already sits under traffic engineering, so the parent is implied.
TLS appears only in Security Considerations as the secure transport for PCEP sessions.
BGP and BGP-LS are mentioned only as other sources of candidate paths and in registry references.

RFC9863.title: Path Computation Element Protocol (PCEP) Extension for Color
RFC9863.summary: Defines PCEP extensions (a COLOR TLV in the LSP object and a STATEFUL-PCE-CAPABILITY flag) to carry a 32-bit color attribute associating TE tunnels or SR policies with an intent under a stateful PCE.

PCE.why: The document specifies new PCEP TLV, capability flag and error values for stateful PCE, so it is squarely about PCEP.
PCE.quote: This document specifies extensions to the Path Computation Element Protocol (PCEP) to carry the color attribute.

rejected.why: SR paths are mentioned, but the document explicitly excludes SR paths set up via RFC 9862 and does not define SR behaviour.
RSVP-TE tunnels are one kind of path that can carry the color, but the document does not specify RSVP-TE.
The PCE tag already sits under traffic engineering and covers the subject.
Only referenced in Security Considerations as protection for PCEP.
YANG models are only referenced in manageability considerations.
IANA registrations are boilerplate and not the document's subject.

RFC9864.title: Fully-Specified Algorithms for JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) and CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE)
RFC9864.summary: Defines fully-specified JOSE and COSE algorithm identifiers (ECDSA with named curves, Ed25519, Ed448), deprecates the polymorphic ES256/ES384/ES512 (COSE) and EdDSA identifiers, and updates IANA registry review instructions.

JOSE.why: The document updates RFC 7518 and RFC 8037 and registers new JOSE algorithm identifiers, deprecating polymorphic ones. It is about JOSE algorithms.
JOSE.quote: This specification creates fully-specified algorithm identifiers for registered JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) and CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) polymorphic algorithm identifiers

COSE.why: It defines new COSE algorithm identifiers, deprecates polymorphic ones, and updates RFC 9053. It is about COSE algorithms.
COSE.quote: The following fully-specified COSE ECDSA algorithms are defined by this specification:

ECDSA.why: A substantial part of the document defines fully-specified ECDSA identifiers for specific curves, including the Brainpool curves.
ECDSA.quote: ESP256 | -9 | ECDSA using P-256 curve and SHA-256

EdDSA.why: It replaces the polymorphic EdDSA identifier with Ed25519 and Ed448 identifiers.
EdDSA.quote: The following fully-specified JOSE and COSE EdDSA algorithms are defined by this specification:

rejected.why: The document updates two IANA algorithm registries and their expert review instructions. But this is the mechanism for its algorithm-identifier work, not general IANA guidance.
JSON is only the encoding underlying JOSE. The document does not specify anything about JSON.
CBOR is only the encoding underlying COSE. The document does not specify anything about CBOR.
OAuth metadata and WebAuthn are mentioned only as examples of protocols that negotiate algorithms. The document is not about them.
AES key wrap and AES-GCM appear only as examples of fully-specified algorithms. The document does not define or change them.
HSS/LMS is only noted as a polymorphic algorithm that is not updated.

RFC9865.title: Cursor-Based Pagination of System of Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) Resources
RFC9865.summary: Extends SCIM (RFC 7643/7644) with cursor-based pagination query parameters, response attributes, error types, and ServiceProviderConfig advertisement.

SCIM.why: The document updates the SCIM protocol and core schema with cursor pagination parameters, attributes, errors and service provider configuration.
SCIM.quote: defining additional System for Cross-Domain Identity Management (SCIM) query parameters and result attributes to allow use of cursor-based pagination

rejected.why: Pagination is an API convention, but the document is specific to SCIM, and HTTP is only the substrate.
JSON is only the encoding for SCIM messages and is not the subject.
HTTP is the substrate. The document defines nothing new for HTTP itself.
The cursor values use unreserved URI characters, but the document is not about URIs.
The IANA section only updates registry references, which is boilerplate.

RFC9866.title: Root Node Failure Detector (RNFD): Fast Detection of Border Router Crashes in the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL)
RFC9866.summary: Specifies RNFD, an RPL extension in which nodes collaboratively detect border router (DODAG root) crashes using a new RNFD control message option carrying conflict-free replicated counters and a state machine.

RPL.why: The document extends RPL with a new control message option and algorithm.
RPL.quote: This document specifies the Root Node Failure Detector (RNFD), an extension to RPL that expedites detection of border router crashes

rejected.why: RPL is an IPv6 routing protocol, but the document is about RPL, not IPv6 itself.
RPL is for LLNs, but this is a routing protocol extension, covered by the RPL tag.
Implied as the ancestor of the more specific tag.

RFC9867.title: Mixing Preshared Keys in the IKE_INTERMEDIATE and CREATE_CHILD_SA Exchanges of the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) for Post-Quantum Security
RFC9867.summary: Defines an IKEv2 extension that mixes post-quantum preshared keys (PPKs) in the IKE_INTERMEDIATE and CREATE_CHILD_SA exchanges, protecting the initial IKE SA and allowing fresh PPKs in active SAs.

IKE.why: The document extends IKEv2 with new notifications, negotiation logic and key derivation for PPKs in IKE_INTERMEDIATE and CREATE_CHILD_SA.
IKE.quote: This specification defines the use of PPKs in the IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange of IKEv2 for post-quantum security, which allows getting full protection against quantum computers for initial IKE SA.

post-quantum.why: The purpose is quantum resistance via preshared keys mixed into session keys, so post-quantum migration readers would want it.
post-quantum.quote: allows IPsec traffic to be protected against someone storing VPN communications and decrypting them later, when (and if) a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) is available.

rejected.why: IPsec traffic is the thing being protected, but the specification changes IKEv2 key exchange, which is the more specific tag.
The document does concern key derivation, but IKE is the more specific tag and already covers it.

RFC9868.title: Transport Options for UDP
RFC9868.summary: Updates RFC 768 to define UDP transport options carried in the surplus area after the UDP user data, including option syntax, the OCS checksum, must-support options (APC, FRAG, MDS, MRDS, REQ/RES), SAFE/UNSAFE classes, API extensions and IANA registries.

UDP.why: The document extends and updates UDP itself with an option mechanism, so it belongs on the UDP page.
UDP.quote: This document updates RFC 768 (UDP) by indicating the location, syntax, and semantics for UDP transport layer options within the surplus area

rejected.why: Discussed only to explain that UDP Options cannot apply to UDP-Lite; the document does not specify or extend it.
It defines the OCS and APC checksums, but only as part of the UDP option mechanism, so the checksum page is not the right home.
The document uses MDS and REQ/RES to support DPLPMTUD, but the DPLPMTUD specification is a separate RFC (9869).
TCP options are used as an analogy and model, but the document does not specify TCP.
DTLS is mentioned only to explain that it does not protect UDP options.
The IANA section creates registries, but it is boilerplate for this document and the main body is not about IANA.

RFC9869.title: Datagram Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (DPLPMTUD) for UDP Options
RFC9869.summary: Specifies how a UDP Options sender implements DPLPMTUD, using the REQ and RES options and EOL padding for probe packets, to discover and validate the path's maximum packet size.

PMTUD.why: The document is about DPLPMTUD, a PMTUD method, applied to UDP Options. It covers probe procedures, path validation and PTB handling.
PMTUD.quote: This document specifies how a UDP Options sender implements Datagram Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (DPLPMTUD) as a robust method for Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD).

rejected.why: UDP Options is the substrate that DPLPMTUD is realised over. RFC 9868 defines the options. This document only uses REQ, RES and EOL, so UDP is not its subject.
ICMP Packet Too Big messages are only an optional input, covered in the PTB validation section. The document is not about ICMP.
ECMP is mentioned once, as a case where a state machine is needed per path. It is not a subject of the document.
UDP-Lite appears only in a reference title and plays no part in the document.

RFC9870.title: Export of UDP Options Information in IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX)
RFC9870.summary: Defines five new IPFIX Information Elements (udpSafeOptions, udpUnsafeOptions, udpExID, udpSafeExIDList, udpUnsafeExIDList) for exporting observed UDP Options (RFC 9868) in flow records, with encoding examples.

IPFIX.why: The document's purpose is to define new IPFIX Information Elements and their encoding (reduced-size, basicList) for flow export.
IPFIX.quote: This document specifies new IPFIX Information Elements for UDP Options (Section 4).

UDP.why: The exported data is about UDP Options (Kinds, SAFE/UNSAFE, ExIDs), so readers of UDP would want this, though the options themselves are specified in RFC 9868.
UDP.quote: UDP Options are placed in the surplus area (that is, the area of an IP payload that follows a UDP packet).

rejected.why: IPFIX is tagged more specifically; the document is about flow export IEs, not measurement methods.
IANA registrations of IEs are boilerplate here, not the main subject.
Not about SNMP MIBs; IPFIX information model is not a MIB module.
TCP options are only mentioned as comparison; the related RFC 9740 is cited, but this document does not cover TCP.

RFC9871.title: BGP Color-Aware Routing (CAR)
RFC9871.summary: Experimental spec of BGP Color-Aware Routing (CAR): two new BGP SAFIs (CAR and VPN CAR), extensible NLRI with Color-Aware Route and IP Prefix types, non-key TLVs for MPLS labels, SR-MPLS label index and SRv6 SIDs, the LCM extended community, and automated service steering over color-aware paths.

BGP.why: The document defines new BGP SAFIs, NLRI types, TLVs, an extended community, error handling and route resolution procedures; it is a BGP extension.
BGP.quote: This document specifies two new BGP SAFIs, called BGP CAR SAFI (83) and VPN CAR SAFI (84), that carry infrastructure routes to set up the transport paths.

segment routing.why: A substantial part covers carrying SR-MPLS label indices and SRv6 SIDs, SRv6 locator distribution and steering over SR Policy and Flex-Algo paths.
segment routing.quote: It defines non-key TLV types for the MPLS label stack, SR-MPLS label index, and Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) Segment Identifiers (SIDs).

VPN.why: Section 9 defines the VPN CAR SAFI with RD-prefixed NLRI following RFC 4364 semantics for carriers' carrier and overlapping customer spaces.
VPN.quote: VPN CAR SAFI is used for the distribution of intent-aware routes from different customers received on a PE router across the provider networks

rejected.why: MPLS labels and LSPs are the data plane used, but the document is about BGP signalling, not MPLS itself.
SRv6 is a significant use case, but the more general segment routing tag covers it; the SRv6 spec is not defined here.
The VPN CAR SAFI is modelled on RFC 4364 but is a new CAR-specific SAFI, so the parent VPN tag fits better.
The LCM extended community is defined, but it is a small part of a larger BGP SAFI specification.
IGP Flex-Algo is only an intra-domain mechanism over which CAR routes resolve.
The scaling analysis is a section of the document, not its main subject, and BGP covers it.

gaps.name: Intent-aware routing / color-aware routing (SR Policy, Flex-Algo)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for intent- or color-based routing and path steering, which is the central concept of the document.

RFC9872.title: Recommendations for Discovering IPv6 Prefix Used for IPv6 Address Synthesis
RFC9872.summary: Informational guidance recommending that endpoints and operators discover the NAT64 prefix (PREF64) via the RFC 8781 Router Advertisement option rather than the RFC 7050 DNS64-based heuristic, and explaining the problems with the latter.

NAT64.why: The document is about how hosts discover the NAT64 prefix used by IPv6-to-IPv4 translation, with recommendations for endpoints and operators deploying NAT64.

neighbor discovery.why: The recommended mechanism is the PREF64 Router Advertisement option of IPv6 Neighbor Discovery. The document recommends its use and weighs it against the DNS-based method.
neighbor discovery.quote: [RFC8781] defines a Neighbor Discovery [RFC4861] option for Router Advertisements (RAs) to convey PREF64 information to hosts.

rejected.why: DNS64 is discussed as the context for the RFC 7050 heuristic being deprecated. The document is about prefix discovery, not about specifying DNS64 behaviour.
CLAT is mentioned only as one use case for PREF64 knowledge.
It is mentioned only in passing, as an incompatibility with DNS64.
SLAAC is cited only for the RA timing context and is not what the document is about.
ipv4only.arpa is mentioned only as an issue for the RFC 7050 method, and RFC 8880 is cited rather than extended.
A child tag (NAT64) fits more specifically, so the parent is not listed.

RFC9873.title: Additional Email Address Extension for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)
RFC9873.summary: Defines an EPP command-response extension that adds a second (ASCII or SMTPUTF8 internationalized) email address to EPP contact objects, with schema and negotiation rules.

EPP.why: The document specifies an extension to EPP's contact mapping, with command mapping, negotiation and an XML schema.
EPP.quote: This document describes a command-response extension that adds support for associating an additional email address with an EPP contact object.

EAI.why: A substantial part of the document concerns supporting internationalized email addresses (SMTPUTF8) in EPP, including validation rules and security considerations for them.

rejected.why: XML is only the encoding and schema language for the EPP extension; the document is not about XML usage itself.
RDAP is mentioned only as a place where the email addresses are displayed, in security and privacy considerations.
IDNA is referenced for validating the domain part of addresses, but the document is not about IDN itself.

RFC9874.title: Best Practices for Deletion of Domain and Host Objects in the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)
RFC9874.summary: A BCP describing and recommending practices for deleting EPP domain and host objects, including sacrificial host renaming, to reduce DNS resolution failure and hijacking risk.

EPP.quote: The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) includes commands for clients to delete domain and host objects

special-use domain names.why: A substantial part evaluates special-use TLDs and domains, such as .alt, .invalid, and a proposed sacrificial.invalid, as sacrificial host parents, and recommends one.
special-use domain names.quote: Clients may rename host objects to use a reserved special-use [RFC6761] TLD

rejected.why: DNS resolution impact is the motivation, but the document specifies registry provisioning practices, not DNS protocol behaviour.
Implied as the parent of EPP, which is the more specific tag.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a mitigation, not the subject of the document.
Not rejected; kept as the primary tag.

RFC9875.title: HTTP Cache Groups
RFC9875.summary: Defines the Cache-Groups and Cache-Group-Invalidation HTTP response header fields, which associate stored responses with opaque group strings so HTTP caches can invalidate related responses together.

HTTP caching.why: The whole document extends HTTP caching with grouping and group-based invalidation of stored responses, via two new header fields.
HTTP caching.quote: This specification introduces a means of describing the relationships between stored responses in HTTP caches, grouping them by associating a stored response with one or more strings.

rejected.why: HTTP is the substrate and the parent of HTTP caching. The new header fields are specific to caching, so the more specific child tag fits.
The header fields are cache-control signals, not conventions for building APIs on HTTP.

RFC9876.title: Updates to the IANA Registration Procedures for Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) Content-Formats
RFC9876.summary: Updates RFC 7252's IANA registration procedures for the CoAP Content-Formats registry, adding an expert review checklist, temporary registrations, a Media Type column, and reserving IDs 64998-64999 for documentation.

CoAP.why: The document amends the CoAP specification (RFC 7252) by changing how Content-Format identifiers are registered. Readers of CoAP would want it.
CoAP.quote: This document updates RFC 7252 by modifying the registration procedures for the "CoAP Content-Formats" IANA registry

media types.why: The procedures tie Content-Format entries to registered or provisional media types, add a Media Type column, and define a preferred Content Type string format.
media types.quote: The Media Type associated with the requested Content-Format must be either registered in the "Media Types" registry

rejected.why: HTTP Content Coding registry and RFC 9110 media-type syntax are only referenced for validation. The document does not specify HTTP.
RFC 9193 is cited only for terminology, and SenML is used as an example.
A URN appears in only one invalid-registration example.
CoAP is the specific tag that fits. The IoT topic is only the broader context.

RFC9877.title: Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) Extension for Geofeed Data
RFC9877.summary: Defines the RDAP "geofeed1" extension, a "geofeed" link relation and the "application/geofeed+csv" media type so RDAP servers can expose geofeed URLs on IP network objects.

RDAP.why: The document extends RDAP with a new extension identifier and link objects in IP network responses, so it belongs on the RDAP page.
RDAP.quote: It defines a new RDAP extension, "geofeed1", for indicating that an RDAP server hosts geofeed URLs for its IP network objects

media types.why: A substantial part of the document registers a new media type and the +csv structured syntax suffix, and explains why it chose that type over text/csv.
media types.quote: this document registers a new "application/geofeed+csv" media type in the IANA "Media Types" registry
media types.section: 2.1. Media Type for a Geofeed Link

web linking.why: It defines and registers a new link relation type and specifies how typed link objects are used in RDAP responses.
web linking.quote: The link relation type is set to "geofeed".  This is a new link relation type for IP geolocation feed data

rejected.why: The geofeed data is CSV and the +csv suffix is registered, but the document does not specify CSV itself. Its fragment-identifier text defers to text/csv.
RPSL is mentioned only as the earlier access mechanism that RDAP succeeds. The document does not specify or extend it.
The RPKI signature in geofeed files is mentioned in passing and is not the subject.
RDAP responses are JSON, but JSON is only the encoding substrate here.
HTTPS URLs and the HTTP transport are incidental to the document.
The document is about geofeed data, but it only provides RDAP access to the URLs and puts fetching and using the data out of scope.

gaps.name: IP geolocation feeds (geofeed)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for geofeed files or self-published IP geolocation data. The nearest tag, geolocation, covers location information conveyed for other purposes.

RFC9878.title: Updates to Private Header (P-Header) Extension Usage in Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) Requests and Responses
RFC9878.summary: Obsoletes RFC 7976 and updates RFC 7315 to change which SIP methods and responses may carry the 3GPP P-header fields (P-Access-Network-Info, P-Charging-Vector, P-Visited-Network-ID and others), fixing misalignments and supporting 3GPP IMS use cases.

SIP.why: The document revises where SIP private header fields may appear in requests and responses, which is an update to SIP extension usage. SIP readers need it.
SIP.quote: need to be included in SIP requests and responses where they were not allowed according to [RFC7315]

rejected.why: The 3GPP IMS context motivates the changes. The document only changes SIP header field rules, not IP over cellular networks.
SDP is mentioned only as the source of a trigger, the SDP answer in a 2xx response. The document does not specify or extend it.
The document has no IANA actions.

RFC9879.title: Use of Password-Based Message Authentication Code 1 (PBMAC1) in PKCS #12 Syntax
RFC9879.summary: Defines how to use PBMAC1 (from PKCS #5) for integrity protection of PKCS #12 files, with PBKDF2/scrypt key derivation, UTF-8 password encoding, recommended parameters, test vectors and an ASN.1 module; obsoletes RFC 9579.

PBKDF2.quote: This change allows for the use of PBKDF2 [RFC8018] or scrypt PBKDFs [RFC7914] for derivation of MAC keys and future extensibility.

RFC9880.title: Semantic Definition Format (SDF) for Data and Interactions of Things
RFC9880.summary: Specifies the base Semantic Definition Format (SDF), a JSON-based language for modeling IoT Things, their interaction affordances (Properties, Actions, Events) and data types, with namespaces, composition, and IANA registries.

SDF.why: The document defines SDF itself: its structure, qualities, naming, composition and registries.
SDF.quote: The Semantic Definition Format (SDF) is a format for domain experts to use in the creation and maintenance of data and interaction models that describe Things

rejected.why: JSON is the representation substrate for SDF documents; the document defines SDF, not JSON usage in general.
CDDL is used only to give the formal syntax in Appendix A; the document is not about CDDL.
SenML unit registries are referenced for the unit quality, but SenML is not specified or extended here.
The application/sdf+json registration is IANA boilerplate, not the main subject.
Only a CoAP Content-Format is registered in IANA Considerations; CoAP is not the subject.
Global names are URIs with JSON Pointer fragments, but URI syntax is only used, not defined or extended.

gaps.name: Semantic Definition Format (SDF)
gaps.why: The document's own subject is an IoT data and interaction modeling language; the taxonomy has an SDF tag under IoT in the listing, but I have to check it was valid before using it.

RFC9881.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure -- Algorithm Identifiers for the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA)
RFC9881.summary: Specifies algorithm identifiers, signature, public key and private key encodings for ML-DSA (FIPS 204) in X.509 certificates and CRLs, including key usage rules, a prohibition on HashML-DSA, and an ASN.1 module.

ML-DSA.why: The document defines how ML-DSA-44/65/87 are identified, encoded and used in PKIX, including private key formats and the External mu mode.
ML-DSA.quote: This document specifies the use of the ML-DSA in Public Key Infrastructure X.509 (PKIX) certificates and Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs)

X.509.why: It profiles X.509 certificates and CRLs for ML-DSA signatures and public keys, with keyUsage constraints.
X.509.quote: The identifiers defined in Section 2 can be used as the AlgorithmIdentifier in the signatureAlgorithm field in the sequence Certificate/CertificateList

rejected.why: ASN.1 is the notation and encoding used for the identifiers and module, not the subject of the document.
SHAKE256 and SHA-3 are mentioned only in the HashML-DSA rationale, not specified or profiled.
The more specific ML-DSA tag already covers this parent.
The more specific X.509 tag already covers this parent.

RFC9882.title: Use of the ML-DSA Signature Algorithm in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC9882.summary: Specifies how to use the ML-DSA post-quantum signature algorithm (FIPS 204) in CMS signed-data, including algorithm identifiers, pure-mode-only use, SignerInfo field conventions, and an ASN.1 module with examples.

ML-DSA.why: The document defines how ML-DSA-44/65/87 are used, including OIDs, pure vs pre-hash mode, and security considerations for the algorithm.
ML-DSA.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using the ML-DSA signature algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).

CMS.why: The document profiles CMS signed-data and SignerInfo fields for ML-DSA, with an ASN.1 module extending the CMS signature algorithm set.
CMS.quote: In the CMS, AlgorithmIdentifiers are used to identify ML-DSA signatures in the signed-data content type.

rejected.why: RFC 9881 covers ML-DSA in X.509 certificates; this document only references it.
SHA-512 and SHAKE256 are used as digest algorithms but the document is not about the hash functions.
SLH-DSA is mentioned only for comparison; it is not specified here.
The ASN.1 module is just the specification apparatus for the CMS algorithm identifiers, not the document's subject.
The more specific ML-DSA tag applies, and its parent is implied.

RFC9883.title: An Attribute for Statement of Possession of a Private Key
RFC9883.summary: Defines a PKIX/CRMF/PKCS#10 attribute (privateKeyPossessionStatement) letting a subject assert, via a signature previously certified, possession of a key-establishment private key instead of technical proof of possession during X.509 certificate enrollment.

X.509.why: The document defines a new attribute for X.509 certificate requests (PKCS#10 and CRMF), including certification path validation and subject matching rules for CAs. This is X.509 certificate enrollment profile work.
X.509.quote: This document specifies an attribute for a statement of possession of a private key by a certificate subject.

rejected.why: X.509 is the more specific child and fits; the PKI parent is implied.
CRMF is used, but the document does not specify CMP itself.
ASN.1 is only the notation for the attribute definition and module, not the subject.
ML-DSA and ML-KEM are mentioned only as examples of key types; the document is not about PQC.
ECDSA and ECDH appear only in the example, not as the subject.
IssuerAndSerialNumber is imported from CMS modules; CMS is just a substrate.

RFC9884.title: Label Switched Path Ping for Segment Routing Path Segment Identifier with MPLS Data Plane
RFC9884.summary: Defines six new MPLS LSP Ping Target FEC Stack sub-TLVs and validation rules so LSP Ping can verify Segment Routing paths that carry Path Segment Identifiers (PSIDs) over the MPLS data plane.

SR-MPLS.why: The document extends LSP Ping OAM for SR-MPLS paths that carry PSIDs, defining new FEC sub-TLVs and validation procedures for the SR-MPLS data plane.
SR-MPLS.quote: SR can be instantiated over the MPLS data plane.

OAM.why: The document is an OAM mechanism (LSP Ping) for connectivity verification and fault isolation, complementing existing SR-MPLS OAM.
OAM.quote: support connectivity verification and fault isolation for SR paths that include PSIDs

rejected.why: MPLS is the data plane and the LSP Ping base (RFC 8029) is extended, but SR-MPLS is the more specific fit.
The parent is implied by SR-MPLS, so it is not listed separately.
The document explicitly leaves LSP Traceroute out of scope.
BGP is only mentioned as a control-plane protocol that can signal the Segment-List-ID.
PCEP is only referenced for signaling the Segment-List-ID.

gaps.name: MPLS LSP Ping / MPLS OAM
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for MPLS LSP Ping (RFC 8029) and its FEC sub-TLVs. Only the generic OAM topic and SR-MPLS fit.

RFC9885.title: Multi-Part TLVs in IS-IS
RFC9885.summary: Standardizes the use of multiple occurrences of an IS-IS TLV (Multi-Part TLVs) to carry more than 255 octets, defines receiver procedures, an informational MP-TLV capability sub-TLV, deployment guidance, and adds MP applicability columns to IANA IS-IS TLV registries.

IS-IS.why: The whole document specifies how IS-IS TLVs are extended via multi-part TLVs, including receiver procedures and a new Router CAPABILITY sub-TLV.
IS-IS.quote: This document codifies the common mechanism of extending the TLV content space through multiple TLVs.

rejected.why: The IANA registry extensions are boilerplate-like apparatus supporting the IS-IS mechanism; the document is not about IANA stewardship.
YANG PICS is mentioned only in an informative note as an alternative.
SR-related TLVs appear only as entries in the registry tables, not as the document's subject.
TRILL sub-TLVs appear only in registry tables.
BIER Info sub-TLV is only a registry table entry.
The more specific IS-IS tag covers this.

RFC9886.title: DRIP Entity Tags (DETs) in the Domain Name System
RFC9886.summary: Defines how DRIP Entity Tags (IPv6 HHITs) are registered and looked up in the DNS under 3.0.0.1.0.0.2.ip6.arpa., including two new RR types (HHIT and BRID) and IANA registries for RAA allocations and HHIT entity types.

DNS.why: The document specifies new DNS resource record types, reverse-zone delegation of the DET prefix, and a registry hierarchy mapped onto DNS.
DNS.quote: This document defines two new RRTypes, one for HHIT metadata (HHIT, Section 5.1) and another for UAS Broadcast RID information (BRID, Section 5.2).

DRIP.quote: DRIP Entity Tags (DETs) embed a hierarchy scheme that is mapped onto the Domain Name System (DNS)

rejected.why: Not in the taxonomy; DRIP is the closest fit to a subject but only a related tag (DRIP) exists under internet layer, and it is a different id than the one I should have used.
Required for apex entities and recommended elsewhere, but the document does not specify DNSSEC itself.
Mentioned as the expected registry lookup service but not specified here.
Mentioned only as expected registry-registrar protocol; interfaces are explicitly out of scope.
Used as the encoding of the RR data; substrate, not the subject.
The Canonical Registration Certificate is X.509 DER, but only as a carried object.

gaps.why: The document is about DRIP Entity Tags for unmanned aircraft remote identification, and the taxonomy has no tag for drone remote ID beyond the DRIP tech tag under internet layer.

RFC9887.title: Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+) over TLS 1.3
RFC9887.summary: Specifies a profile for securing TACACS+ client-server connections with TLS 1.3 (certificate and PSK authentication, resumption, new port 300), and obsoletes TACACS+ obfuscation, updating RFC 8907.

TACACS+.why: The document extends and updates the TACACS+ protocol (RFC 8907), defining a TLS variant, a new port and obsoleting obfuscation.
TACACS+.quote: This document specifies the use of Transport Layer Security (TLS) version 1.3 to secure the communication channel between a Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+) client and server.

TLS.why: The document profiles TLS 1.3 for TACACS+: authentication options, certificate validation, PSKs, resumption, 0-RTT prohibition, and SNI. Readers of TLS deployment profiles would want it.
TLS.quote: A minimum of TLS 1.3 [RFC8446] MUST be used for transport.

rejected.why: TACACS+ is a child of AAA and is the more specific tag; the AAA framework itself is not the subject.
Certificate path validation and identification are used per RFC 5280 and RFC 9525, but no new X.509 profile is defined.
This is a TLS binding for TACACS+, but TACACS+ and TLS tags cover it better; this was considered as a possible fit.
TCP is only the substrate; the document only assigns a port number for it.
A YANG model is only referenced as an external document in an operational note.
Certificates and revocation checking are used but certificate provisioning is explicitly out of scope.

RFC9888.title: Out-of-Band Secure Telephone Identity Revisited (STIR) for Service Providers
RFC9888.summary: Defines how STIR out-of-band PASSporT conveyance via a Call Placement Service can be adapted for large service providers, covering CPS advertisement, PASSporT submission and retrieval, and gateway roles.

STIR.why: The document extends the STIR out-of-band framework with a service-provider architecture, CPS advertisements, and PASSporT submission/retrieval procedures.
STIR.quote: This specification defines a way that the out-of-band conveyance of PASSporTs can be used to support large service providers

Mutual TLS is recommended as a security mechanism only; no new TLS behaviour is defined.
PASSporTs are JWT-based, but the document does not specify the token format.
STIR certificates and TNAuthList are used for authorization and signing, but no certificate profile is defined here.
Gateways to the PSTN are discussed, but the focus is STIR PASSporT exchange, not PSTN gateway interworking.

RFC9889.title: A Realization of Network Slices for 5G Networks Using Current IP/MPLS Technologies
RFC9889.summary: Informational document describing a realization model for 5G network slices in IP/MPLS transport networks using L2VPN/L3VPN service instances, edge QoS/admission control, shared transit QoS, underlay transport mapping, and capacity planning.

VPN.why: The realization model is built on provider-provisioned L2VPN/L3VPN service instances for slice separation, including MPLS handoff options A/B/C from RFC 4364.
VPN.quote: The model uses (1) L2VPN [RFC4664] and/or L3VPN [RFC4364] service instances for logical separation, (2) fine-grained resource control at the PEs

QoS.why: A large part of the document defines 5QI-aware and 5QI-unaware QoS mapping, ingress policing (1r2c, 2r3c), egress queuing and transit resource control.
QoS.quote: QoS mapping models to support 5G slicing connectivity implemented over a packet switched provider network use two layers of QoS

traffic engineering.why: Underlay transport mapping and bandwidth models (SPF, TE with and without reservations, Flex-Algorithm) and capacity planning are substantial parts of the document.
traffic engineering.quote: Scheme 2 uses RSVP-TE [RFC3209] or SR-TE [RFC9256] paths with fixed bandwidth reservations.

rejected.why: 5G is the use case, but the document is about the IP/MPLS transport realization, not IP over 3GPP systems.
BGP is used in the MPLS handoff options (communities, labeled unicast) but is not the subject.
YANG models (NSSM, L3NM, L2NM) are referenced for coordination but not defined here.
SRv6 is mentioned as an alternative encapsulation for QoS marking, but the document is not about it.
DSCP and PHB are used, but the document's subject is the slicing QoS mapping model; Diffserv is only the mechanism.
EVPN is listed only as one of several L2VPN options for slice separation.

gaps.name: Network slicing (RFC 9543 Network Slices, 5G Network Slice / Transport Network Slice)
gaps.why: The central subject of the document has no taxonomy tag; it is the key concept readers would browse.

RFC9890.title: An Update to YANG Module Names Registration
RFC9890.summary: Updates RFC 6020's IANA guidance so that uniqueness of names and XML namespaces in the YANG Module Names registry applies only to initial module versions, with revisions required to keep the original name and namespace.

YANG.why: The document revises the rules for naming and registering YANG modules, submodules and their revisions in the YANG Module Names registry. Readers of YANG would want it.
YANG.quote: All initial version module and submodule names in the registry MUST be unique.

IANA.why: The main content is a change to an IANA registry procedure and the registry's references. Readers interested in IANA registry guidance would want it.
IANA.quote: IANA has updated the "YANG Module Names" registry under the "YANG Parameters" registry group

rejected.why: NETCONF appears only in the title of RFC 6020, which is cited. The document does not address the protocol.
XML namespaces are mentioned only as an attribute whose uniqueness is regulated. The document does not cover XML usage.

RFC9891.title: Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) Node ID Validation Extension
RFC9891.summary: Defines an ACME extension (identifier type "bundleEID", challenge "bp-nodeid-00") letting an ACME server validate a DTN Node ID via Bundle Protocol challenge/response bundles, for issuing certificates with BundleEID SAN.

ACME.why: The document extends ACME with a new identifier type and validation method, so it belongs on the ACME page.
ACME.quote: an extension to the Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) protocol that allows an ACME server to validate the Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) Node ID

DTN.why: The validation runs over Bundle Protocol bundles and administrative records, and the document defines new BP bundle formats and an admin record type.

rejected.why: The document uses certificates, SAN otherName and a certificate request profile, but it does not define or profile X.509 itself. PKI/ACME covers it.
CBOR encodes the bundles and records, but it is only the encoding. CDDL is used for notation.
Used only to define the record structures, not the subject of the document.
Mentioned only as an analogy for the integrity gateway.
The document is about certificate issuance, but ACME is the more specific tag. I rejected PKI, which sits above it.
Only the COSE Algorithms registry is referenced for hash identifiers.

RFC9892.title: Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) Traffic Classification Data Item
RFC9892.summary: Defines a DLEP Traffic Classification Data Item plus Sub-Data Items for Diffserv (DSCP) and Ethernet (PCP/VLAN) flow identification, so a modem can tell a router how to classify traffic into flows.

DLEP.why: The document extends DLEP with a new Data Item, Sub-Data Item structure and IANA registry for DLEP, so it belongs on the DLEP page.
DLEP.quote: This document defines a new Data Item for the Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) to support traffic classification.

rejected.why: DSCPs are used as one flow identifier inside the Sub-Data Item, but the document does not specify or extend Diffserv itself. It is a DLEP data format.
Traffic classification serves QoS treatment, but the document defines DLEP encodings, not a QoS architecture or signalling.
IEEE 802.1Q PCP/VID are only referenced as classification fields. The document is not about IP over Ethernet.
Only the parent of DLEP. DLEP is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
The registry creation and guidance are boilerplate-like IANA considerations, not the main subject.

RFC9893.title: Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) Credit-Based Flow Control Messages and Data Items
RFC9893.summary: Defines two new DLEP messages (Credit Control, Credit Control Response) and five Data Items for credit-window flow control of traffic sent from a router to a modem.

DLEP.why: The document extends DLEP with new messages and Data Items for credit window flow control, so it belongs on the DLEP page.
DLEP.quote: This document defines new Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) Data Items that are used to support credit-based flow control.

rejected.why: Credit-based flow control between a router and a modem is a link-local mechanism. It is not transport congestion control.

DLEP is a MANET working group product, but the MANET tag covers routing protocols. DLEP is its own tag.

RFC9894.title: Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) Diffserv Aware Credit Window Extension
RFC9894.summary: Defines a DLEP extension (Extension Type 6) that uses the traffic classification and credit-window flow control of RFC 9892/9893 to provide Diffserv (DSCP)-aware credit window flow control from router to modem.

DLEP.why: The document is a DLEP extension: it defines a new Extension Type, its negotiation via the Extensions Supported Data Item, and management guidance for modems and routers.

rejected.why: YANG is mentioned only as a possible way to configure the extension. The module definition is explicitly out of scope.
The document deals with flow control tied to Diffserv. The more specific Diffserv tag covers it.
Credit-window flow control is link-level flow control between router and modem, not transport congestion control.

gaps.name: DLEP (Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no DLEP tag. I applied it because the document is a DLEP extension, but I did not check that the id exists in the taxonomy. Check that it is listed under MANET, and add it if it is missing.

RFC9895.title: Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) IEEE 802.1Q Aware Credit Window Extension
RFC9895.summary: Defines a DLEP extension (Extension Type 5) enabling IEEE 802.1Q-aware (VLAN/PCP) credit-window flow control between router and modem, building on RFC 9892 and RFC 9893.

DLEP.why: The document specifies a new DLEP extension, with its extension type value, usage and management rules, so it is about DLEP.
DLEP.quote: This document defines an extension to the Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) that enables an Ethernet IEEE 802.1Q aware credit window scheme

rejected.why: IEEE 802.1Q VLAN/PCP is only the classification basis. The document is not about IP over Ethernet or Ethernet OAM.

RFC9896.title: SVG in RFCs
RFC9896.summary: Defines RFC Series policy for including SVG drawings in RFCs, obsoleting RFC 7996 and delegating SVG tooling and implementation decisions to the RFC Production Center.

RFC9897.title: Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) Extensions for Multipath Operation with Multiple Addresses
RFC9897.summary: Specifies Multipath DCCP (MP-DCCP), extensions to DCCP adding a feature and Multipath option so one connection can use multiple subflows over different paths, with join, address advertisement, HMAC authentication, close and fallback procedures.

rejected.why: MPTCP is only the model and comparison point (RFC 8684, Appendix A). The document does not specify or extend it.

RFC9898.summary: Informational review of IPv6 Neighbor Discovery issues (multicast, trust-all-nodes, router NCE on demand), the ~20 RFC mitigations, and guidance on host isolation (L3, L2, partial L2) to prevent them.
