SLAAC.why: SLAAC, DAD and address accountability issues with self-generated addresses are analysed substantially alongside ND.
SLAAC.quote: Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) [RFC4862] builds on those ND mechanisms to let nodes configure their own IPv6 addresses.

SEND.why: SEND and CGA are reviewed as a mitigation for trust issues in ND.
SEND.quote: The purpose of SEND [RFC3971] (Standards Track) is to ensure that hosts and routers are trustworthy.

rejected.why: RFC 9686 and DHCPv6-PD are reviewed only as mitigations; the document is not about DHCPv6.
Proxy ND in EVPN is one reviewed solution among many.
ND optimization for TRILL is one brief reviewed solution.
WiND/6LoWPAN ND is one brief reviewed solution, not the subject.
SAVI and RA-Guard are summarised in one short section.
Unique prefix per host is discussed, but the more specific ND tags cover the document's focus.

gaps.name: Neighbor Discovery tag
gaps.why: I used the 'neighbor discovery' and 'SLAAC' ids. Note that these are nested in the taxonomy under IPv6, so the ids must be checked against the taxonomy exactly as shown.

RFC9899.title: Extensions to the YANG Data Model for Access Control Lists (ACLs)
RFC9899.summary: Specifies the ietf-acl-enh YANG module augmenting the RFC 8519 ACL model with defined sets, aliases, fragment/TCP-flag/payload/MPLS/VLAN/I-SID matching and rate-limit/log/counter actions, and creates IANA-maintained YANG modules for ICMP types and IPv6 extension headers.

YANG.why: The document is a YANG data model extension (ietf-acl-enh) with augmentations and groupings, plus new IANA-maintained YANG modules.
YANG.quote: This document specifies a set of extensions that fix many of the limitations of the ACL model as initially defined in RFC 8519.

authorization.why: ACLs are packet-filtering access control rules; the document enhances their match criteria and actions, and no more specific ACL tag exists.
authorization.quote: [RFC8519] defines Access Control Lists (ACLs) as a user-ordered set of filtering rules.

IANA.why: A substantial part of the document defines IANA-maintained YANG modules and the procedures for keeping them synchronized with registries.
IANA.quote: This document also creates initial versions of IANA-maintained modules for ICMP types and IPv6 extension headers.

rejected.why: The module is accessed via NETCONF/RESTCONF, but they are only the management substrate and are mentioned mainly in Security Considerations.
ACL filtering is related, but the document is a YANG model for ACL configuration, not about firewalls or middlebox traversal.
ICMP types are enumerated in an IANA YANG module, but the document does not specify or extend ICMP itself.
TCP flags are matched by the ACL model, but TCP itself is not specified or extended.
MPLS header fields are matched in ACLs, but MPLS is not specified or extended.
Flow Spec is mentioned only as motivation for the TCP flag operators and for mapping to ACL rules.

RFC9900.title: Updates to NETCONF Transport Port Numbers
RFC9900.summary: RFC 9900 releases (de-assigns) the IANA port numbers 831, 832 and 833 for the historic and undeployed NETCONF over BEEP and NETCONF over SOAP services, while keeping the service names.

NETCONF.why: The document changes the registry entries for NETCONF transport bindings (BEEP and SOAP) and keeps the NETCONF port assignments in context. NETCONF readers would look for it.
NETCONF.quote: This document releases IANA-assigned port numbers for services related to the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) that have not been in use in production networks.

IANA.why: The whole document is a change to the IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number registry, which de-assigns port numbers under RFC 6335 procedures.
IANA.quote: Consistent with Section 8.2 of [RFC6335], this document does not de-assign service names; only port numbers are de-assigned

rejected.why: BEEP is only the substrate of a historic NETCONF binding whose port is released. The document specifies nothing new about BEEP.
NETCONF over SSH (port 830) is only mentioned as an unchanged assignment.
NETCONF over TLS (port 6513) is only mentioned as an unchanged assignment.
The document de-assigns ports and does not define any transport mapping.

RFC9901.title: Selective Disclosure for JSON Web Tokens
RFC9901.summary: Defines SD-JWT, a salted-hash mechanism for selectively disclosing claims in JWS/JWT payloads, with Disclosures, optional Key Binding JWTs, verification rules, and JWS JSON serialization.

JWT.why: The document defines selective disclosure of JWT claims, extending JWT/JWS with a new composite format, new claims (_sd, _sd_alg, sd_hash) and processing rules.
JWT.quote: This specification defines a mechanism for the selective disclosure of individual elements of a JSON data structure used as the payload of a JSON Web Signature (JWS).

JOSE.why: Defines new unprotected JWS header parameters (disclosures, kb_jwt) and JSON Serialization handling in Section 8, which readers of JOSE would want.
JOSE.quote: An alternate format extending the JWS JSON Serialization, also allowing for transport of the Issuer-signed JSON data structure and Disclosure data.

rejected.why: Produced in the oauth WG but the document does not specify OAuth flows; JWT is the subject.
Registers media types and a structured suffix, but this is IANA boilerplate, not the main subject.
JSON is the substrate encoding; the document is not about JSON itself.
Privacy considerations are a section, but the document's main subject is the disclosure mechanism, not privacy threat models generally.
SHA-256 is used as the default hash but not specified or analysed.
base64url is only the encoding used for Disclosures.

gaps.name: Verifiable credentials / selective disclosure
gaps.why: The document is about selective disclosure in credential presentation (SD-JWT VC, W3C VC examples); the taxonomy has no tag for verifiable credentials or JWT specifically.

RFC9902.title: A YANG Data Model for IS-IS Segment Routing over the MPLS Data Plane
RFC9902.summary: Defines the ietf-isis-sr-mpls YANG module, augmenting the IS-IS YANG model to configure and monitor IS-IS Segment Routing extensions over the MPLS data plane, including SRGB, adjacency SIDs, mapping server bindings, and TI-LFA/RLFA fast reroute.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module augmenting the IS-IS model; readers of YANG models would look for it.
YANG.quote: This document defines a device YANG data model [RFC7950] that can be used to manage IS-IS extensions for Segment Routing (SR) [RFC8667] over the MPLS data plane.

IS-IS.why: The module manages IS-IS SR extensions: SR capability, Prefix-SID/Adj-SID sub-TLVs, SID binding TLVs in the IS-IS LSDB.
IS-IS.quote: It is an augmentation to the IS-IS YANG data model [RFC9130].

SR-MPLS.why: The model covers Segment Routing over the MPLS data plane (SRGB, SRLB, label/index SIDs, mapping server).
SR-MPLS.quote: The IS-IS SR MPLS YANG module requires support for the base SR module [RFC9020]
SR-MPLS.section: 2. Design of the YANG Module for IS-IS MPLS Segment Routing

IP fast reroute.why: A substantial part of the module adds TI-LFA and SR-based remote LFA configuration under IS-IS interfaces.
IP fast reroute.quote: It brings the ability to activate Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate (TI-LFA) and also enhances Remote LFA (RLFA) to use SR tunneling instead of LDP.

rejected.why: The more specific SR-MPLS tag fits, so the parent is not listed.
MPLS is only the data plane for SR here; SR-MPLS is the more specific subject.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a management protocol for accessing the module.
This is a YANG module, not a MIB module.
Mentioned only as the alternative to SR tunnelling for RLFA; not the subject.

RFC9903.title: A YANG Data Model for OSPF Segment Routing over the MPLS Data Plane
RFC9903.summary: Defines the ietf-ospf-sr-mpls YANG module, augmenting the OSPF YANG model to configure and report OSPFv2/OSPFv3 Segment Routing extensions over the MPLS data plane, including TI-LFA.

YANG.why: The document's deliverable is a YANG module with configuration and operational state augmentations to the OSPF model.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model [RFC7950] that can be used to manage OSPFv2 extensions for Segment Routing

OSPF.why: It models OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 SR extensions: LSAs, TLVs, area and interface configuration.
OSPF.quote: The defined YANG data model is an augmentation to the OSPF YANG data model [RFC9129].

SR-MPLS.why: The module covers SR-MPLS in OSPF: SRGB, Prefix-SIDs, Adj-SIDs, SRLB, mapping servers.
SR-MPLS.quote: additions to OSPF Link State Advertisements (LSAs) necessary to support Segment Routing over MPLS (SR-MPLS)
SR-MPLS.section: 2. Design of the YANG Module for OSPF MPLS Segment Routing

IP fast reroute.why: The module adds TI-LFA and Remote LFA SR-path configuration under OSPF fast-reroute.
IP fast reroute.quote: OSPF interface level configuration for Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternative (TI-LFA) using the MPLS data plane.
IP fast reroute.section: 2. Design of the YANG Module for OSPF MPLS Segment Routing

rejected.why: Only mentioned in Security Considerations as a possible access protocol.
Considered, but the document covers both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 equally, so the parent OSPF tag fits better.
MPLS is only the data plane that SR runs over, and the document defines nothing about MPLS itself.
The more specific SR-MPLS child tag fits.

RFC9904.title: DNSSEC Cryptographic Algorithm Recommendation Update Process
RFC9904.summary: RFC 9904 obsoletes RFC 8624 and moves DNSSEC algorithm implementation and usage recommendations into new columns of the IANA DNS Security Algorithm Numbers and Digest Algorithms registries, with rules for changing them.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document concerns which DNSSEC signing and digest algorithms must be implemented and used, and how those recommendations are maintained.
DNSSEC.quote: moves the canonical source of algorithm implementation requirements and usage guidance for DNSSEC from RFC 8624 to the IANA DNSSEC algorithm registries

rejected.why: The IANA registry changes are the mechanism, but the subject is DNSSEC algorithm requirements. The IANA topic is for general registry guidance, so DNSSEC fits better.
Algorithms are listed (RSA, ECDSA, EdDSA, GOST), but the document only assigns recommendation levels to them and does not specify or analyse them.
DNSSEC is the more specific tag, so its parent DNS is implied.
ED25519 and ED448 appear only as rows in a table of recommendation levels. The document does not specify EdDSA.

RFC9905.title: Deprecating the Use of SHA-1 in DNSSEC Signature Algorithms
RFC9905.summary: Deprecates use of RSASHA1 and RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1 DNSSEC algorithms for creating DS, DNSKEY and RRSIG records, updating RFCs 4034 and 5155 and the IANA algorithm registries.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document sets DNSSEC signing, delegation and validation requirements for SHA-1-based algorithms, so DNSSEC readers need it.
DNSSEC.quote: The RSASHA1 [RFC4034] and RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1 [RFC5155] algorithms MUST NOT be used when creating DNSKEY and RRSIG records.
DNSSEC.section: 2. Deprecating SHA-1 from DNSSEC Signatures and Delegation RRs

rejected.why: SHA-1 is the reason for the deprecation, but the document is about DNSSEC algorithm usage, not the hash family itself.
RSASHA1 is a DNSSEC algorithm identifier, and the document does not address RSA cryptography as such.
DNSSEC is the more specific tag and already implies DNS.
Registry updates are only a boilerplate-style IANA Considerations section and not the document's main subject.

RFC9906.title: Deprecate Usage of ECC-GOST within DNSSEC
RFC9906.summary: Deprecates the GOST R 34.10-2001 (ECC-GOST) and GOST R 34.11-94 algorithms in DNSSEC, updating RFC 5933 and the IANA algorithm and digest registries.

DNSSEC.why: The document sets DNSSEC signing and validation requirements for DS, DNSKEY and RRSIG records using these algorithms, and updates the DNSSEC algorithm registries.
DNSSEC.quote: The GOST R 34.11-94 algorithm [RFC5933] MUST NOT be used when creating Delegation Signer (DS) records.

GOST.why: The document is about the GOST national algorithms (the 2001 signature and 1994 hash) and their deprecation in an IETF protocol, which is the scope of the GOST tag.
GOST.quote: This document retires the use of GOST R 34.10-2001 (mnemonic "ECC-GOST") and GOST R 34.11-94 within DNSSEC.

rejected.why: IANA registry updates are boilerplate-like consequences of the deprecation. The document is not about IANA registry stewardship.
DNS is the underlying system. The document is specifically about DNSSEC, the more specific tag.
The GOST tag already covers the specific algorithms. The document is not about cryptography in general.

RFC9907.title: Guidelines for Authors and Reviewers of Documents Containing YANG Data Models
RFC9907.summary: BCP guidance for authors and reviewers of YANG data model documents, covering documentation structure, YANG usage rules, and IANA-maintained YANG modules; obsoletes RFC 8407 and updates RFC 8126.

YANG.why: The whole document is guidelines for writing and reviewing YANG modules, covering naming, XPath, types, augments, NMDA and templates.
YANG.quote: This document defines a set of guidelines for documents containing YANG 1.1 [RFC7950] and YANG 1.0 [RFC6020] data models, including IANA-maintained YANG modules.

IANA.why: A substantial part updates RFC 8126 and gives guidance and templates for IANA-maintained YANG modules and their registries.
IANA.quote: the IANA Considerations section of an RFC that includes an IANA-maintained YANG module MUST provide the required instructions for IANA to automatically perform the maintenance

rejected.why: NETCONF is the protocol that YANG modules are served over. The document sets guidelines for the modelling language, not the protocol.
RESTCONF is cited as a protocol that uses the modules. The document does not specify or extend it.
The YANG tag is more specific, and it already sits under network management.
The document gives authoring guidance for RFCs, but it is specific to YANG content, not RFC format or style in general.
XPath and XML namespaces appear only as part of YANG usage rules.
It is a BCP for authors and reviewers, but the subject is YANG module content, not IETF procedures.

RFC9908.title: Clarification and Enhancement of the CSR Attributes Definition in RFC 7030
RFC9908.summary: Updates RFC 7030 (and RFC 9148) to clarify how an EST server's CSR Attributes response conveys attribute OIDs and X.509 extension values, and defines a CertificationRequestInfoTemplate attribute (a partially filled-in PKCS#10 CSR) with an ASN.1 module.

EST.why: The document updates EST (RFC 7030) and RFC 9148, clarifying the /csrattrs response and adding a CSR template mechanism.
EST.quote: clarifies how the Certificate Signing Request (CSR) Attributes Response can be used by an EST server to specify both CSR attribute OIDs and CSR attribute values

ASN.1.why: A substantial part of the document clarifies ASN.1 encoding of CsrAttrs and defines a new ASN.1 module with template structures, plus DER dump examples.
ASN.1.quote: This appendix provides an ASN.1 module [X.680] for the Certification Request Information Template attribute and its sub-template structures.

rejected.why: X.509 extensions are the values being requested, but the document is not about the certificate profile itself.
RFC 9148 (EST over CoAP) is updated only by a short applicability paragraph; CoAP itself is not the subject.
BRSKI and the ACP motivate the work and appear in one example, but the document does not specify them.
CMP's CSR template approach is mentioned only for comparison.

gaps.name: EST (Enrollment over Secure Transport) CSR attributes
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists EST as a tag in the PKI hierarchy, but the id I used, 'EST', is the tag shown there; no gap beyond this.

RFC9909.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure -- Algorithm Identifiers for the Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (SLH-DSA)
RFC9909.summary: Specifies ASN.1 algorithm identifiers and conventions for using SLH-DSA (pure and pre-hash) signatures, public keys and private keys in X.509 certificates and CRLs.

SLH-DSA.why: The whole document defines OIDs, signature, public key and private key encodings for SLH-DSA.
SLH-DSA.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using the Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (SLH-DSA) in the X.509 Public Key Infrastructure.

X.509.why: It is an X.509 algorithm-identifier profile covering SubjectPublicKeyInfo, keyUsage bits and CRL/certificate signatures.
X.509.quote: This document defines the ASN.1 Object Identifiers (OIDs) and conventions for the encoding of SLH-DSA digital signatures, public keys, and private keys in the X.509 Public Key Infrastructure.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is the encoding vehicle and the module is just the formal definition, not the subject.
SHA-2/SHAKE are internal or pre-hash functions used by SLH-DSA, not specified here.
RFC 9814 (CMS use) is only referenced for OID definitions.
Parent of hash-based signatures; SLH-DSA is the more specific tag already chosen.
The more specific SLH-DSA child tag applies.

RFC9910.title: Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) Regional Internet Registry (RIR) Search
RFC9910.summary: Extends RDAP with basic searches by handle/name for IP networks and ASNs, hierarchical relation searches (up/down/top/bottom) with status filtering and link relations, and reverse search for IPs and ASNs, giving RDAP parity with RIR WHOIS search.

RDAP.why: The whole document defines new RDAP search functionality, new path segments, extension identifiers and responses for IP networks and ASNs.
RDAP.quote: This document extends RDAP to support those search options.

web linking.why: Defines and registers new link relations (rdap-up, rdap-down, rdap-top, rdap-bottom, rdap-active) in the Link Relations registry, which readers of web linking would want.
web linking.quote: Each of the relations defined in Section 3.2.2 has a corresponding link relation that can be used for a link object contained within another RDAP object.

rejected.why: WHOIS is only referenced as the legacy service whose search features RDAP is matching; the document specifies nothing about WHOIS itself.
HTTP is only the substrate, and only status codes such as 404 and 501 are used.
JSON is the response encoding only, and nothing new is defined about it.
ASNs are searched as registry objects. The document does not address routing.
Considered as the parent of RDAP. The RDAP tag already covers it, so the parent is not listed separately.
CIDR prefixes appear only as search input syntax, not as the subject of the document.

RFC9911.title: Common YANG Data Types
RFC9911.summary: RFC 9911 defines the ietf-yang-types and ietf-inet-types YANG modules, a collection of common derived data types for YANG models, obsoleting RFC 6991.

YANG.why: The whole document is the specification of two YANG modules of reusable types, so readers of YANG data modelling need it.
YANG.quote: This document defines a collection of common data types to be used with the YANG data modeling language.

MIB.why: A substantial part maps each YANG type to its equivalent SMIv2/MIB textual convention (Tables 3 and 4), which is useful to MIB and SMI readers.
MIB.quote: Some types have an equivalent Structure of Management Information Version 2 (SMIv2) [RFC2578] [RFC2579] data type.

rejected.why: NETCONF is only the context in which YANG is used. The document does not specify or extend it.
The module defines IPv6 address and prefix string types, but the document does not specify or analyse IPv6.
The domain-name type models DNS names and refers to DNS RFCs, but the document is not about DNS behaviour.
The date and time types profile RFC 3339 and RFC 9557, but they are YANG types and the document does not define a timestamp format.
The uuid type only references RFC 9562 for its string representation and defines nothing new about UUIDs.
The uri type only wraps the RFC 3986 syntax in a YANG typedef.

RFC9912.title: Reliable and Available Wireless (RAW) Architecture
RFC9912.summary: Defines the RAW architecture extending DetNet to wired/wireless networks, with a recovery graph concept and an OODA control loop built around a Point of Local Repair in the DetNet Service sub-layer.

DetNet.why: The document is an architecture extending DetNet's Service sub-layer, planes and PREOF with a PLR function and control loop.
DetNet.quote: Reliable and Available Wireless (RAW) extends the reliability and availability of Deterministic Networking (DetNet) to networks composed of any combination of wired and wireless segments.

rejected.why: DLEP is only cited as an example way to implement the lower-layer API; the document does not specify or extend it.
OAM is used as the observation step of the loop, but the document defines no OAM mechanism, so the topic is not a main subject.
Only borrows terminology (Track equals recovery graph); the document is not about 6TiSCH.
Fast reroute and PLR terminology are borrowed from RFC 4090, but RSVP-TE is not specified or extended here.
Mentioned as background for reliable crossover; the document does not extend IP FRR.
Cited only as an example monitoring protocol.

gaps.name: Deterministic Networking (DetNet)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has DetNet as a tech under routing. The document is about DetNet extensions for wireless, reliability and availability, which is the tag chosen above, but no tag covers wireless reliability as a topic.

RFC9913.title: Reliable and Available Wireless (RAW) Technologies
RFC9913.summary: Informational survey of Wi-Fi 6/7, 802.15.4 TSCH (6TiSCH), 5G and LDACS radio technologies and their applicability to carrying deterministic (DetNet/RAW) flows.

WiFi.why: Section 4 surveys 802.11ax/be/ad/ay features and their applicability to deterministic flows.
WiFi.quote: IEEE 802.11 Wireless Local Area Networks (WLAN)

6TiSCH.why: Section 5 covers TSCH and 6TiSCH Tracks, scheduling, PCE-based path computation and forwarding for deterministic flows.
6TiSCH.quote: At the IETF, the 6TiSCH Working Group [TiSCH] has enabled distributed routing and scheduling to exploit the deterministic access capabilities provided by TSCH for IPv6.

cellular.why: Section 6 covers 3GPP 5G architecture, radio stack, scheduling/QoS and TSN/DetNet integration for deterministic service.
cellular.quote: 5G technology enables deterministic communication.

DetNet.why: The whole document supports DetNet/RAW work over wireless lower layers.
DetNet.quote: surveys the short- and middle-range radio technologies over which providing Deterministic Networking (DetNet), and more specifically, Reliable and Available Wireless (RAW) service is suitable

rejected.why: Referenced for 6TiSCH routing but not the subject.
PCE is used for Track computation, but only as a mechanism described in 6TiSCH context.
Time sync is discussed as an enabling lower-layer capability, not the focus.
Industrial IoT is context; 6TiSCH tag covers the constrained link aspect.
LDACS is terrestrial aeronautical, not satellite.

gaps.name: LDACS (L-band Digital Aeronautical Communications System)
gaps.why: A full section covers LDACS but the taxonomy has no aeronautical/LDACS tag.

gaps.name: Reliable and Available Wireless (RAW)
gaps.why: The central subject has no dedicated tag; DetNet is the closest.

RFC9914.title: Root-Initiated Routing State in the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL)
RFC9914.summary: Specifies DAO Projection for RPL, where the Root (or a PCE) installs Projected Routes (Storing and Non-Storing Mode) and Tracks via new P-DAO, P-DAO-REQ, PDR-ACK, Via and Sibling Information options, extending RFCs 6550, 6553 and 8138.

RPL.why: The document extends and amends RPL with new messages, options and flags for root-initiated routes.
RPL.quote: This document introduces the concept of Destination Advertisement Object (DAO) Projection, a mechanism that allows a RPL Root or an external controller to install optimized routes within the RPL domain.

6LoWPAN.why: It defines a new 6LoRH type and compression of RPL artifacts in 6LoWPAN networks, which readers of that subject need.
6LoWPAN.quote: This specification Extends [RFC8138] to introduce a new 6LoRH, the P-RPI-6LoRH, that can be used in either Elective or Critical 6LoRH form

rejected.why: A PCE is expected as the route computer, but the control protocol and algorithms are explicitly out of scope.
Only mapped to conceptually (relay vs forwarding nodes); the document does not specify DetNet.
Uses loose source routing with the RPL SRH (RH type 3) and says it is only generically like segment routing; not SR as specified in RFC 8402.
Tracks are inherited from the 6TiSCH architecture, but 6TiSCH is only context here.
Encapsulation is used as a mechanism for forwarding along Tracks, not the subject.
Traffic-engineered paths are a motivation, but the document is about the RPL mechanism rather than TE in general.

gaps.name: RPL (Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks)
gaps.why: If the taxonomy lacks a RPL tag beyond the IoT parent, RPL-specific documents have no dedicated technology tag; the id 'RPL' is under IoT in the taxonomy and is used here.

RFC9915.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)
RFC9915.summary: RFC 9915 is the consolidated DHCPv6 specification (obsoleting RFC 8415), defining client/server/relay message exchanges, stateful address assignment, prefix delegation, stateless configuration, DUIDs, options, and Reconfigure authentication, and obsoleting IA_TA and Server Unicast.

DHCPv6.why: The whole document is the base specification of DHCPv6: messages, options, client/server/relay behaviour, and prefix delegation.
DHCPv6.quote: This document specifies the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6), an extensible mechanism for configuring nodes with network configuration parameters, IP addresses, and prefixes.

rejected.why: Parent of DHCPv6; implied by the more specific child tag, so not listed separately.
DHCPv6 operates in IPv6 and interacts with SLAAC, but the document is about DHCPv6 itself.
Mentioned as an alternative or complement; not specified here.
Transport substrate only (ports 546/547); nothing new about UDP usage.
Only referenced for relay-server security via RFC 8213; not the subject.
HMAC-MD5 is used inside RKAP as a mechanism, but the document is not about HMAC.
Not in the taxonomy; DUID is part of the DHCPv6 spec.
DUID-UUID is just one DUID type, defined in RFC 6355; only briefly mentioned.

RFC9916.title: Updates to the Usage of TLS to Provide a Secure Transport for the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP)
RFC9916.summary: Updates RFC 8253 to require PCEPS implementations supporting multiple TLS versions to prefer the latest, and to forbid use of TLS 1.3 early data (0-RTT).

TLS.why: The document sets TLS version negotiation preference and bans TLS 1.3 early data for PCEPS. This is deployment guidance on using TLS, so readers of the TLS subject would want it.
TLS.quote: PCEPS implementations that support TLS 1.3 or later MUST NOT use early data.

PCE.why: The document updates the secure transport (PCEPS) of PCEP, so it belongs on the PCE/PCEP page.
PCE.quote: Section 3.4 of RFC 8253 specifies TLS connection establishment restrictions for PCEPS; PCEPS refers to usage of TLS to provide a secure transport for the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP).

rejected.why: The document tightens an existing TLS binding for PCEP (RFC 8253). It does not define a new transport mapping, and the TLS and PCE tags cover it better.
TCP is the substrate under TLS and PCEP. The document says nothing specific about it.

RFC9917.title: IGP Flexible Algorithms Reverse Affinity Constraint
RFC9917.summary: Extends IGP Flex-Algorithm with reverse-direction Admin Group include/exclude constraints (new IS-IS and OSPF FAD sub-TLVs) and creates an IANA registry of ordered path-computation pruning rules, updating RFCs 9350 and 9843.

IS-IS.why: Defines new IS-IS FAD sub-TLVs (types 10, 11, 12) and their handling rules, extending IS-IS Flex-Algorithm.
IS-IS.quote: The IS-IS Flexible Algorithm Exclude Reverse Admin Group (FAERAG) Sub-TLV is used to advertise the exclude rule
IS-IS.section: 5. IS-IS Flexible Algorithm Exclude Reverse Admin Group Sub-TLV

OSPF.why: Defines parallel OSPF (v2 and v3) FAD sub-TLVs for the reverse affinity constraints.
OSPF.quote: The OSPF FAERAG Sub-TLV is a sub-TLV of the OSPF FAD TLV.
OSPF.section: 8. OSPF Flexible Algorithm Exclude Reverse Admin Group Sub-TLV

rejected.why: The document is about a specific Flex-Algorithm extension in IGPs, not general routing architecture.
Admin groups come from MPLS-TE (RFC 7308), but the document is about IGP path computation constraints, not TE signalling.
It creates a registry, but that is boilerplate-level support for the extension; the main body is not about IANA guidance.
Flex-Algorithm is often used with segment routing, but this document does not specify SR.
The document treats OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 together under OSPF and does not specify anything v3-specific.

gaps.name: IGP Flexible Algorithm (Flex-Algorithm)
gaps.why: The central subject is Flex-Algorithm constraint-based path computation, which spans IS-IS and OSPF. The taxonomy has no tag for it, so the document is only indexed under IS-IS and OSPF.

RFC9918.title: Updates to Using the NETCONF Protocol over Transport Layer Security (TLS) with Mutual X.509 Authentication
RFC9918.summary: Updates RFC 7589 (NETCONF over TLS with mutual X.509 authentication) to revise TLS 1.2 support requirements, add TLS 1.3 requirements, and forbid use of TLS 1.3 early data.

NETCONF.why: The document updates the specification of NETCONF over TLS, so NETCONF readers need it.
NETCONF.quote: RFC 7589 defines how to protect Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) messages with TLS 1.2.

TLS.why: It sets TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 version and cipher suite requirements and restricts TLS 1.3 early data, which is TLS deployment guidance.
TLS.quote: This document specifies that NETCONF implementations that support TLS 1.3 or later MUST NOT use early data.

rejected.why: Mutual X.509 authentication appears in the title, but the document does not define or profile certificates. Certificate handling is left unchanged from RFC 7589.
Only a brief mention of trusted CA lists in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
The port registry entry update is a minor administrative change, not the subject of the document.
This is a transport binding in spirit, but the document only revises TLS version requirements for an existing mapping. The TLS and NETCONF tags cover it.

RFC9919.title: The Lightweight Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) Profile for High-Volume Environments
RFC9919.summary: Standards Track profile of OCSP for high-volume and lightweight PKI environments, obsoleting RFC 5019, restricting request/response structure, requiring SHA-256 for CertID hashes, and specifying HTTP transport and caching behaviour.

OCSP.why: The whole document profiles OCSP request/response structure, client behaviour, freshness and caching for high-volume use.

HTTP GET/POST is the transport substrate; the document defines nothing new about HTTP.
Certificates and AIA are relied upon and examples are given, but the document is about certificate status checking, not certificate profiles.
The switch from SHA-1 to SHA-256 for CertID hashes is a notable change, but it is a parameter choice, not about the hash family.

ASN.1 structures are extracts from RFC 6960 used as encoding, not the subject.

gaps.name: OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an OCSP tag only in the security/PKI subtree as `OCSP`, but this response needs the exact id to be valid; if the taxonomy lacked it, no alternative would fit except PKI.

RFC9920.title: RFC Editor Model (Version 3)
RFC9920.summary: RFC 9920 specifies version 3 of the RFC Editor Model, dividing RFC Series policy definition (RSWG and RSAB) from implementation (RPC under IETF LLC), creating the Editorial Stream, and obsoleting RFC 9280.

RFC series.quote: This document specifies version 3 of the RFC Editor Model.

rejected.why: The RSWG operates like an IETF working group, but the document is about RFC Series policy, not the IETF standards process.
The IPR and boilerplate material is a minor part of the document. It is not the main subject.
RFC 7991 is only updated to change the role named in it from RFC Editor to RPC. The document does not address the XML vocabulary.
This is the parent of RFC series, so it is implied. The document is about the RFC Series specifically.

RFC9921.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Header Parameter for Timestamp Tokens as Defined in RFC 3161
RFC9921.summary: Defines two COSE header parameters (3161-ctt and 3161-ttc) that carry RFC 3161 timestamp tokens in COSE_Sign and COSE_Sign1 messages, with two modes of use, MessageImprint computation and processing rules.

COSE.why: The document extends COSE by registering two new header parameters for COSE_Sign and COSE_Sign1 carrying timestamp tokens.
COSE.quote: This document defines two CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) header parameters for incorporating timestamping based on RFC 3161 into COSE message structures

rejected.why: RFC 3161 Time-Stamp Protocol and TSAs are relied on, but the document does not specify or profile PKI itself.
Timestamp tokens use CMS as their envelope, but this is only substrate; the document does not define CMS behaviour.
CBOR is the encoding used by COSE; the document defines nothing new about CBOR itself.
X.509 certificates appear only in examples and via RFC 3161; not the subject.
Timestamping of signatures is not clock synchronization over networks.
The IANA section only registers header parameters; boilerplate.

gaps.name: RFC 3161 Time-Stamp Protocol (TSP) / trusted timestamping
gaps.why: The document is about using timestamp tokens from RFC 3161 TSAs with signed objects; the taxonomy has no tag for timestamping or time-stamp protocols.

RFC9922.title: A Common YANG Data Model for Scheduling
RFC9922.summary: Defines the "ietf-schedule" YANG module with reusable groupings for period-based and recurrence-based schedules (including iCalendar-like recurrence), schedule validation parameters and status reporting, plus a mapping to the DISMAN-SCHEDULE-MIB.

YANG.why: The document's core deliverable is a YANG module of common types, identities and groupings for scheduling, so it belongs on the YANG page.
YANG.quote: This document defines a common schedule YANG module ("ietf-schedule") that can be used in several scheduling contexts

iCalendar.why: A substantial part of the module models iCalendar recurrence rules (RRULE, BYDAY, exception dates) in YANG, so iCalendar readers would want it.
iCalendar.quote: The structure of the "icalendar-recurrence" grouping refers to the definition of the recurrence component defined in Sections 3.3.10 and 3.8.5 of [RFC5545].

MIB.why: It has a dedicated section mapping the DISMAN-SCHEDULE-MIB (RFC 3231) objects to the new YANG parameters.
MIB.quote: Table 1 lists how the main objects in the DISMAN-SCHEDULE-MIB can be mapped to YANG parameters.

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the management protocols that would carry the data, mentioned in Security Considerations. The document does not specify them.
The document references time-zone identifiers from RFC 7317 but does not address time zone data distribution.
The module uses yang:date-and-time and RFC 3339 timestamps but does not define or extend a date-time format.
JSON is used only to encode the examples in Appendix A, so it is not a subject of the document.
The document is about scheduling of network management events, not calendaring applications. iCalendar is the more specific tag.
Time-variant routing is cited as one motivating use case in Appendix B.2, but the document is not about TVR.

RFC9923.title: The FNV Non-Cryptographic Hash Algorithm
RFC9923.summary: Informational document describing the FNV (Fowler/Noll/Vo) non-cryptographic hash algorithm, its constants, usage guidance, security caveats, and reference C code for 32 to 1024-bit sizes.

rejected.why: SHA-1 and SHA-256 appear only in a work-effort comparison appendix and as recommended alternatives; the document is not about them.
FNV is a hash, not an Internet checksum or integrity check mechanism, though it is used for fingerprints.
The document explicitly states FNV is non-cryptographic and makes no assertion of suitability for cryptographic use; a reader of cryptography would not look here.
The IPv6 flow label is only an example application of FNV in Section 4.
DNS servers and DNS Cookies are mentioned only as uses or references of FNV.
ASCII is used only to define the offset_basis input string.

gaps.name: Non-cryptographic hash functions
gaps.why: The whole document is about a hash algorithm (FNV). The taxonomy has hash tags only for cryptographic families (SHA, MD5, BLAKE2, HMAC), and no tag for general-purpose or non-cryptographic hashing.

RFC9924.title: Advanced Professional Video
RFC9924.summary: Specifies the bitstream format, decoding process, metadata, and profiles/levels/bands of the Advanced Professional Video (APV) intra-frame professional video codec.

codecs.why: The document is a video codec definition: syntax, transform, entropy coding, profiles and levels. The generic codecs tag fits, since no specific codec child applies.
codecs.quote: This document defines the bitstream format and decoding process for the Advanced Professional Video (APV) codec.

rejected.why: UUIDs are used only to identify user-defined metadata payloads, by reference to RFC 9562. The document is not about UUIDs.
No media type registration is made. IANA has no actions.

APV is a distinct codec. It is not HEVC and does not specify it.
No RTP payload format is defined.

gaps.name: Advanced Professional Video (APV)
gaps.why: A professional intra-frame video codec with no dedicated tag. It is covered only by the generic codecs tag, and readers browsing for APV or professional video would benefit from a specific one.

RFC9925.title: Unsigned X.509 Certificates
RFC9925.summary: Defines a placeholder X.509 signature algorithm (id-alg-unsigned) and placeholder issuer RDN attribute so certificates can carry subject information without a meaningful signature, and updates RFC 5280 to permit omitting the authority key identifier.

X.509.why: The whole document profiles X.509 certificates: construction and consumption of unsigned certificates, new OIDs, and an update to RFC 5280.
X.509.quote: This document defines a profile for unsigned X.509 certificates, which may be used when the certificate is used as a container for subject information

rejected.why: TLS server deployments using self-signed certificates are only motivating context, not specified or extended.
X.509 is the more specific tag; the trust anchor discussion is part of the certificate profile.
The ASN.1 module is just the formal definition of the new OIDs, not the subject.
Large post-quantum signatures are cited as one motivation only.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here, not the main body.
Only referenced as an analogy for alg:none vulnerabilities.

RFC9926.title: Prefix Registration for IPv6 Neighbor Discovery
RFC9926.summary: Extends 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery registration (EARO/EDAR/EDAC, RFC 8505) so a node can register IPv6 prefixes with routers, which redistribute them (e.g., into RPL), updating RFCs 4861, 6550, 8505, 8928, 8929, 9010 and 7400.

6LoWPAN.why: The document extends 6LoWPAN ND registration (EARO, 6LN/6LR/6LBR, 6CIO capability bit) to cover prefixes.
6LoWPAN.quote: enable a node that owns or is directly connected to a prefix to register that prefix to neighbor routers

rejected.why: The document is about a specific ND extension, which is covered by the more specific neighbor discovery tag.
Secure ND is not used. AP-ND (RFC 8928) is only touched on briefly.
DHCPv6 is mentioned only as an example of prefix delegation.
6TiSCH is mentioned only as an example network.
The ICMPv6 registries appear only in IANA considerations, which are boilerplate.

RFC9927.title: Fixing the C-Flag in the Extended Address Registration Option (EARO)
RFC9927.summary: Updates RFC 8928 by moving the C-flag in the 6LoWPAN-ND Extended Address Registration Option (EARO) to bit 1 of the flags field to avoid overlap with the P-field, and registers it with IANA.

neighbor discovery.why: The document changes the EARO format used in IPv6 Neighbor Discovery registration (AP-ND/6LoWPAN-ND) NS/NA messages.
neighbor discovery.quote: updates [RFC8928] by repositioning the C-flag as bit 1 of the EARO flags field, thereby preventing conflicts.

6LoWPAN.quote: the 6LoWPAN Node (6LN) may be challenged for ownership of the registered address

rejected.why: AP-ND is an address-protection mechanism for ND in LLNs, but this document does not concern SEND.
Neighbor discovery is the more specific tag, so the parent is implied.
The IANA registry update is just a consequence of the bit change, not the document's subject.
The flags registry sits in the ICMPv6 parameters group, but the document is about the ND option format.

RFC9928.title: DHCPv4 over DHCPv6 with Relay Agent Support
RFC9928.summary: Specifies a DHCPv4-over-DHCPv6 Relay Agent (4o6RA) that performs RFC 7341 encapsulation/decapsulation on behalf of legacy IPv4-only DHCP clients, including topology-discovery preservation via LDRA.

rejected.why: DHCPv4 is the client-side protocol being served, but the document's specification is the relay agent doing 4o6 over DHCPv6. DHCPv6 is the more specific fit, and DHCP is its parent.
It enables IPv4-only hosts to be served over IPv6-only networks, but it defines no transition mechanism of the kind this tag covers, such as tunnelling or translation.
It carries DHCPv4 over DHCPv6, but the mapping itself is defined in RFC 7341. This document only adds the relay-agent use case.
IPv6 is the underlying network environment. The document is not about IPv6 itself.

RFC9929.title: IGP Unreachable Prefix Announcement
RFC9929.summary: Defines the Unreachable Prefix Announcement (UPA) mechanism for IS-IS and OSPFv2/v3, adding U and UP prefix attribute flags so ABRs/ASBRs can signal loss of reachability for prefixes covered by a summary, and specifying generation, propagation and processing.

IS-IS.why: The document extends IS-IS with new prefix attribute flags and specifies UPA advertisement and propagation between levels.
IS-IS.quote: Two new bits in the IPv4/IPv6 Extended Reachability Attribute Flags [RFC7794] are defined:

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 with U and UP flags and defines UPA signaling and propagation across areas.
OSPF.quote: Two new bits in the Prefix Attribute Flags Sub-TLV are defined:

OSPFv3.quote: The prefix that is advertised with U-Flag or UP-flag MUST have the NU-bit set in the PrefixOptions of the parent TLV.

rejected.why: BGP PIC is only mentioned as an example consumer of UPA; the document does not specify BGP behaviour.
Summarization and multi-area scaling motivate the work, but the document specifies protocol extensions, not architecture.
SRv6 locators are mentioned only as prefix types to which UPA may apply.
Fast convergence is a motivation, but the document does not define fast reroute mechanisms.
IANA registry additions are boilerplate for this document.

RFC9930.title: Tunnel Extensible Authentication Protocol (TEAP) Version 1
RFC9930.summary: Defines TEAP version 1, a TLS-based tunnel EAP method with inner TLV exchange, crypto-binding, key derivation and certificate provisioning, obsoleting RFC 7170 and updating RFC 9427.

EAP.why: The document specifies the TEAP EAP method, including its TLVs, inner methods, crypto-binding and key derivation.
EAP.quote: TEAP is a tunnel-based EAP method that enables secure communication between a peer and a server by using the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol

rejected.why: TLS is the substrate for the tunnel; the document does not define new TLS extensions, only uses its handshake, exporters and resumption.
Certificate provisioning via PKCS#10/PKCS#7 TLVs is a secondary feature; the document is not about PKI itself.
RADIUS appears only as a carrier protocol for EAP.
Server certificate requirements are discussed, but only as a part of tunnel authentication, not as a certificate profile.
AAA appears only as the deployment context for EAP servers and proxies.

RFC9931.title: Security Considerations for Optimistic Protocol Transitions in HTTP/1.1
RFC9931.summary: Discusses security risks (request smuggling, parser exploits) of clients optimistically sending data before an HTTP/1.1 Upgrade or CONNECT transition is confirmed, and updates RFC 9112 and RFC 9298 with new requirements.

HTTP.why: The document updates HTTP/1.1 (RFC 9112) with new CONNECT requirements and analyses Upgrade/101 semantics, so it is about HTTP itself.
HTTP.quote: Proxy clients that send CONNECT requests on behalf of untrusted TCP clients MUST do one or both of the following

web linking.why: placeholder
web linking.quote: A client MAY optimistically start sending UDP packets in HTTP Datagrams before receiving the response to its UDP proxying request

rejected.why: Only evaluated as an existing upgrade token that already forbids optimistic sending; not specified or extended here.
The 'TLS' upgrade token is reviewed briefly, but TLS is not the subject.
connect-udp and connect-ip are assessed, and RFC 9298 is updated with one sentence, but the document is about HTTP/1.1 transitions generally, not MASQUE.
Mentioned only as an alternative that avoids the problem.
Considered because of the smuggling attacks, but the security content is specific to HTTP and is covered by the HTTP tag.

RFC9932.title: Mutually Authenticating TLS in the Context of Federations
RFC9932.summary: Informational Independent Submission describing MATF, a framework for machine-to-machine mutual TLS 1.3 authentication within federations using public key pinning and signed (JWS) federation metadata published by a federation operator.

TLS.why: The document specifies how to use TLS 1.3 mutual authentication with pin validation of peer certificates in federations, a deployment profile of TLS.
TLS.quote: All communication established within the federation uses TLS 1.3 [RFC8446] with mutual authentication.

federated authentication.why: Core subject is a federation trust model: operator, member vetting, signed metadata, trust anchor, and interfederation trust.
federated authentication.quote: The framework enables interoperable trust management for federated machine-to-machine communication.

JOSE.why: Federation metadata is a JWS with JWK Set trust anchor and JWK thumbprint verification, with defined claims and header parameters; substantial part of the design.
JOSE.quote: Federation metadata is signed using JWS and published using JWS JSON Serialization according to the general JWS JSON Serialization syntax

PKI.why: Defines an alternative trust model to CA chains: SPKI pinning, self-signed certificates, issuers listed in metadata, certificate rotation and revocation by pin removal.
PKI.quote: Public key pinning associates one or more public key pins with each federation endpoint.

rejected.why: JSON is only the encoding of metadata and schema; not the subject.
SCIM appears only as an example use case in the usage scenario, not specified here.
HTTP is mentioned only for header propagation by intermediaries and caching; not the subject.
Certificates are used but no X.509 profile is defined; pinning of SPKI is the focus.
RFC 7469 pinning is referenced for HTTP, but this document adapts pinning for machine TLS, not HTTP header usage.
Covered more specifically by the federated authentication and TLS tags.

RFC9933.title: Carrying SR-Algorithm in Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP)
RFC9933.summary: Extends PCEP to carry the SR-Algorithm in SR-ERO/SRv6-ERO and RRO subobjects, adds an SR-Algorithm constraint TLV in LSPA, and defines new METRIC types (path min delay, bandwidth, user-defined) for Flexible Algorithm path computation; updates RFC 8664 and RFC 9603.

PCE.why: The whole document defines PCEP extensions: capability flags, ERO/RRO subobject changes, a new LSPA TLV, new METRIC types and error codes.
PCE.quote: This document specifies extensions to the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) to enhance support for Segment Routing (SR)

segment routing.why: The document is about signalling SIDs and SR-Algorithms, including Flexible Algorithm path computation, for SR-TE paths in PCEP.
segment routing.quote: it focuses on the use of Segment Identifiers (SIDs) and SR-Algorithms.

SR-MPLS.why: It extends the SR-ERO subobject and SR-PCE-CAPABILITY for SR over MPLS.
SR-MPLS.quote: for LSPs set up using PST 1 (Segment Routing) [RFC8664]

SRv6.why: It adds an Algorithm field and an A flag to the SRv6-ERO and SRv6-RRO subobjects, and a capability flag for SRv6.
SRv6.quote: This document updates the SRv6-ERO subobject format defined in Section 4.3.1 of [RFC9603]

rejected.why: IGP Flexible Algorithm and IGP metric extensions are only referenced as the source of the algorithm semantics. The document does not specify them.
OSPF is referenced only for the metric extension definitions it builds on. It is not specified or extended here.
TLS is only recommended in the Security Considerations to protect PCEP sessions.
The PCE tag already sits under traffic engineering, and the document is mainly about PCEP extensions.
RSVP-TE is mentioned only as background for PCEP's original use. The document does not address it.

gaps.name: IGP Flexible Algorithm

RFC9934.title: Privacy-Enhanced Mail (PEM) File Format for Encrypted ClientHello (ECH)
RFC9934.summary: Defines a PEM-based file format, using an ECHCONFIG delimiter, for storing an ECH private key and ECHConfigList so TLS servers built on different libraries can be configured interchangeably.

TLS.why: The document specifies a standard configuration file format for Encrypted ClientHello key pairs and configs in TLS servers, extending TLS deployment practice. No dedicated ECH tag exists, so TLS is the closest fit.
TLS.quote: Encrypted ClientHello (ECH) key pairs need to be configured into TLS servers, which can be built using different TLS libraries.

rejected.why: PEM textual encoding of PKCS #8 keys is reused from RFC 7468, but the document is not about public key infrastructure or certificates.
The ECHConfigList is published in HTTPS RRs, but that is specified in other RFCs. The document only references it.
Base64 is just the encoding used inside the PEM format, not the subject.
This taxonomy tag is for the historic Privacy Enhanced Mail secure email system. This document only uses the PEM textual file encoding.
The file stores keys, but the document specifies only a file format, not key establishment or provisioning.

gaps.name: Encrypted ClientHello (ECH)
gaps.why: The document is specifically about ECH configuration, and the taxonomy has no ECH tag, so it falls under TLS.

RFC9935.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure - Algorithm Identifiers for the Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM)
RFC9935.summary: Specifies X.509 certificate conventions for ML-KEM: algorithm identifiers, SubjectPublicKeyInfo encoding, key usage, private key formats (seed/expanded/both), consistency checks, ASN.1 module and examples.

ML-KEM.why: The document defines OIDs, public/private key encodings and consistency checks for ML-KEM, so ML-KEM readers would want it.
ML-KEM.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using the ML-KEM in X.509 Public Key Infrastructure.

X.509.why: It profiles X.509 certificates and SubjectPublicKeyInfo, keyUsage, and includes example certificates for ML-KEM keys.

rejected.why: ASN.1 is the notation used for the module and encodings, not the subject.

Mentioned only as a not-supported use case in the applicability statement.
ML-DSA only signs the example certificates.
Parent of ML-KEM, which is implied.

RFC9936.title: Use of ML-KEM in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC9936.summary: Specifies how to use ML-KEM (ML-KEM-512/768/1024) with the CMS KEMRecipientInfo structure, including KDF/wrap requirements, SMIME capabilities, an ASN.1 module and a worked example.

CMS.why: It profiles CMS enveloped-data, authenticated-data and authenticated-enveloped-data content types with KEMRecipientInfo and defines the ASN.1 module.
CMS.quote: The ML-KEM algorithm MAY be employed for one or more recipients in the CMS enveloped-data content type

rejected.why: Only a short SMIMECapabilities attribute section; the document is about CMS, not S/MIME message handling.
Certificate conventions are delegated to RFC 9935; this document only references it.
AES Key Wrap is used as a component, but the document does not specify AES.
SHA-256 and SHA-3 are underlying components only.
The child tag ML-KEM is more specific and implies the parent.
The ASN.1 module is apparatus for the CMS specification, not the subject.

RFC9937.title: Proportional Rate Reduction (PRR)
RFC9937.summary: Standards Track specification of Proportional Rate Reduction (PRR), a TCP fast recovery algorithm that regulates sending during loss recovery so flight size converges to ssthresh; obsoletes the experimental RFC 6937.

rejected.why: NewReno is only one of several loss detection and recovery algorithms PRR can work with. The document does not specify or extend it.
CUBIC is cited as a congestion control algorithm PRR is compatible with, not something the document is about.
ECN-triggered window reduction is mentioned as an adaptation, but only briefly. It is not a substantial part of the document.
The document is about transport-layer rate regulation during recovery and does not address QoS architectures.

gaps.name: TCP loss recovery / fast recovery

RFC9938.title: A Framework for the Deterministic Networking (DetNet) Controller Plane
RFC9938.summary: Informational framework describing requirements and distributed, centralized and hybrid architectures for the DetNet Controller Plane (control and management), without specifying protocols.

DetNet.why: The whole document is about the DetNet controller plane: requirements, architectures, PREOF, explicit paths, resource reservation and OAM.
DetNet.quote: This document provides a framework overview for the Deterministic Networking (DetNet) Controller Plane.

The MPLS data plane is discussed as a DetNet data-plane option, but the document is not about MPLS itself.

RFC9939.title: PKCS #8: Private-Key Information Content Types
RFC9939.summary: Defines CMS content types and OIDs (plus an ASN.1 module) so that a single PKCS #8 PrivateKeyInfo or EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo can be carried in CMS.

rejected.why: Only the OID arc and IANA registries are named S/MIME. The document is not about secure email.
Private-key syntax is related, but the document defines no PKI mechanism or profile.

RFC9940.title: Some Key Terms for Network Fault and Problem Management
RFC9940.summary: Defines key terminology (Event, State, Fault, Problem, Symptom, Cause, Incident, Alert, Alarm, etc.) for network fault and problem management, with workflow explanations, to give IETF work a common vocabulary.

RFC9941.title: Secure Shell (SSH) Key Exchange Method Using Hybrid Streamlined NTRU Prime sntrup761 and X25519 with SHA-512: sntrup761x25519-sha512
RFC9941.summary: Specifies the sntrup761x25519-sha512 hybrid post-quantum/classical key exchange method for SSH, combining Streamlined NTRU Prime KEM with X25519 and SHA-512, reusing the ECDH message flow and registering the method name with IANA.

post-quantum.why: The method is a hybrid of the post-quantum KEM sntrup761 with X25519. No narrower post-quantum child tag (ML-KEM, etc.) fits, so the parent applies.
post-quantum.quote: Streamlined NTRU Prime [NTRUPrimePQCS] [NTRUPrime] [NTRUPrimeWeb] provides post-quantum small lattice-based key-encapsulation mechanisms.

Curve25519.why: X25519 is half of the hybrid construction and its shared secret is combined via SHA-512. Readers of the Curve25519 subject would want this document.
Curve25519.quote: the 32-byte K_A = X25519(a, 9) as described in [NTRUPrimePQCS] and [RFC8731]

rejected.why: SHA-512 is used only as the combiner hash. The document does not specify or analyse the SHA family.
The ECDH framework from RFC 5656 is reused, but the document is about the hybrid method; the specific X25519 child tag covers the curve.
The IANA section merely registers the method name, which is boilerplate.
Key exchange is the subject, but the more specific SSH and post-quantum tags cover it.

RFC9942.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Receipts
RFC9942.summary: Defines COSE Receipts: COSE_Sign1 signed proofs of Verifiable Data Structure properties (inclusion, consistency), with new COSE header parameters (receipts, vds, vdp), IANA registries, and a CBOR encoding for RFC 9162 Merkle tree proofs.

COSE.why: The document extends COSE with new header parameters, Receipts as COSE_Sign1 objects, and new COSE registries.
COSE.quote: This document defines three new COSE header parameters

supply chain integrity.why: Verifiable data structures, transparency and signed inclusion/consistency receipts are the building blocks of transparency services for digital artefacts.
supply chain integrity.quote: Transparency helps maintain trust over time and has been applied to certificates, end-to-end encrypted messaging systems, and supply chain security.

rejected.why: CBOR is the encoding substrate; the document is about COSE structures, not CBOR itself.
CDDL is used to define the structures but is not the subject.
It builds on RFC 9162 Merkle tree proofs but is a generic receipt format, not about CT logs.
Registry creation is boilerplate-level here, specific to COSE.
Not about certificates or PKI operations.

gaps.name: Verifiable Data Structures / transparency services (Merkle tree proofs)
gaps.why: The core subject, verifiable data structures with inclusion and consistency proofs, has no dedicated tag; the nearest is supply chain integrity.

RFC9943.title: An Architecture for Trustworthy and Transparent Digital Supply Chains
RFC9943.summary: Defines the SCITT architecture for single-issuer signed statement transparency: Transparency Services, COSE_Sign1 Signed Statements, registration policies, receipts and Transparent Statements, with media type registrations.

supply chain integrity.why: The whole document specifies the SCITT architecture for supply chain integrity, transparency and trust, which is exactly this tag's subject.
supply chain integrity.quote: This document defines an architecture, a base set of extensible message structures, and associated flows to make signed content transparent via VDSs

COSE.why: Signed Statements and Transparent Statements are defined as COSE_Sign1 structures with specific header parameters (CWT claims, receipts label 394), and new COSE media types are registered. A substantial part of the document profiles COSE.
COSE.quote: The signed statements and receipts are, respectively, based on the COSE_Sign1 specification in Section 4.2 of RFC 9052

rejected.why: Certificate Transparency is discussed as a special case and generalized, but the document is not about CT itself.
CBOR is the encoding substrate for the message structures; the document does not define anything new about CBOR.
CDDL is only used to write the normative message definitions.
CWT claims (iss, sub) are used in headers, but the document does not specify CWT or JWT.
X.509 certificates are one allowed trust anchor and identity type, but the document does not profile them.
Two media types are registered in IANA Considerations, which is boilerplate. Registration is not the main subject.

gaps.name: Verifiable data structures / transparency logs (SCITT)
gaps.why: The document is about transparency services and verifiable append-only logs with receipts. The taxonomy has no dedicated tag beyond supply chain integrity.

RFC9944.title: Device Schema Extensions to the System for Cross-Domain Identity Management (SCIM) Model
RFC9944.summary: Defines SCIM schema extensions (Device and EndpointApp resource types plus BLE, Wi-Fi Easy Connect/DPP, Ethernet MAB, FDO, Zigbee and endpoint-app extensions) so devices can be provisioned into a network via SCIM.

SCIM.why: The document extends the SCIM core schema with new Device and EndpointApp resource types and extension schemas, so it is squarely about SCIM.
SCIM.quote: This memo specifies schema extensions that enable provisioning of devices using various underlying bootstrapping systems

IoT.why: The document addresses onboarding and provisioning of IoT devices (BLE, Zigbee, DPP, FDO), including non-IP devices behind gateways.
IoT.quote: The Internet of Things presents a management challenge in many dimensions.  One of them is the ability to onboard and manage a large number of devices.

rejected.why: Only the optional mudUrl attribute references RFC 8520; the document is not about MUD.
JSON is just the encoding of SCIM schemas and examples.
The SCIM database feeds the AAA system, but AAA is a downstream consumer, not the subject of the document.
Mentioned only in the rationale for choosing SCIM over NETCONF/RESTCONF/YANG.
Cited only as an analogy for vendor-initiated provisioning.
The certificateInfo attribute carries certificate names and a root CA, but the document does not specify or profile X.509.

gaps.name: Device onboarding / bootstrapping (BLE, Wi-Fi Easy Connect/DPP, FIDO Device Onboard, Zigbee, MAB)
gaps.why: The document is largely about provisioning devices through several bootstrapping systems, but the taxonomy has no tag for device onboarding.

RFC9945.title: IETF Community Moderation
RFC9945.summary: BCP defining IETF community moderation policy: creates an IESG-appointed moderator team, sets scope, procedures, transparency, appeals and reinstatement, and obsoletes RFC 3683 and RFC 3934.

IETF process.why: The document sets IETF procedures and administration for moderating participation, including the moderator team, IESG oversight, appeals and updates to RFC 2418 and RFC 9245.
IETF process.quote: establishing a policy for the moderation of disruptive participation across the IETF's various public contribution channels and discussion fora

rejected.why: Mailing lists are one forum covered, but the document is about moderation policy across all forums, not mailing list protocols or headers.
Unsolicited bulk messages get a short section that defers to an IESG statement. The subject is email spam filtering, which is not the document's focus.
NomCom is mentioned only in passing, in the moderator exclusion rule and the Security Considerations.
The terminology note only defines terms such as administrator and forum for this document's own use.

gaps.name: community moderation / conduct
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for participant conduct, anti-harassment or moderation policy. IETF process is the closest fit.

RFC9946.title: The UDP Speed Test Protocol (UDPSTP) for One-Way IP Capacity Metric Measurement
RFC9946.summary: Defines UDPSTP, a UDP-based client/server protocol with closed-loop feedback for measuring One-Way IP Capacity per RFC 9097, including PDUs, HMAC authentication with a KDF, and IANA registries.

performance measurement.why: The document specifies an active measurement protocol for the IP-layer capacity metric, with load rate adjustment and status feedback. No specific measurement-protocol tag (OWAMP, TWAMP, STAMP, LMAP) fits, so the topic tag applies.
performance measurement.quote: This document defines the UDP Speed Test Protocol (UDPSTP) for conducting measurements as described in RFC 9097 and other related measurements.

key management.why: A substantial part of the document specifies key table use and a counter-mode KDF with HMAC-SHA-256 for deriving client and server authentication keys.
key management.quote: a Key Derivation Function (KDF) has been added to provide cryptographic separation of key material for authentication of protocol messages

rejected.why: UDP is only the transport for the protocol. The document does not define UDP usage guidelines or extend UDP.
HMAC-SHA-256 is used as the authentication and KDF primitive. The document is not about HMAC itself.
TWAMP and STAMP appear only as related protocols that lack closed-loop feedback. They are not specified or extended here. There is no TWAMP tag in the taxonomy; STAMP exists but does not apply.
LMAP deployment is mentioned as an applicability scenario only.
The document explicitly says the load rate adjustment algorithm must not be used as a general congestion control algorithm.
The optional Internet checksum is a small part of the protocol and is not the subject of the document.

gaps.name: IP-Layer Capacity measurement / speed test
gaps.why: The document is about a speed test protocol for the Maximum IP-Layer Capacity metric. The taxonomy has no specific tag for it, and the nearest tag is the performance measurement topic.

RFC9947.title: Application of the Alternate-Marking Method to the Segment Routing Header
RFC9947.summary: Independent-stream experimental RFC defining an AltMark TLV in the SRv6 Segment Routing Header to carry Alternate-Marking performance measurement fields, as an alternative to RFC 9343's IPv6 option headers.

RFC9948.title: Internet Protocol Police (IPP) - Schedule of Punishments
RFC9948.summary: An April 1st humor RFC from the fictional Internet Protocol Police setting out a whimsical schedule of punishments (raised eyebrow, frown, etc.) for infractions of IETF community norms, plus parody of reviewer feedback and recidivism studies.

humor.why: The document is an April 1st parody of IETF culture, with fictional punishments, a fake recidivism study and an Epimenides Paradox security section.
humor.quote: The Internet Protocol Police (IPP) is in charge of punishing willful infractions of the Collected Wisdom of the IETF community.

rejected.why: It satirizes IETF community norms and review culture, but it defines no real process or procedure.
IANA is mentioned only as an infraction example and in the IANA Considerations boilerplate, which has no actions.
It mentions RFC 6919 key words only in the conventions section, which is boilerplate, and it defines no terminology.
HTTP/HTML appears only in a joke about the Head-in-Hand Gesture, and the document is not about HTTP.

RFC9949.title: BUSA-TLS: Mandatory Audio Component (MAC) Pre-Shared Key (PSK) Derivation for TLS 1.3 Using 2 Live Crew's "Banned in the U.S.A."
RFC9949.summary: An April 1st parody Independent Submission that modifies the TLS 1.3 key schedule so the zero-byte IKM of the Early Secret is replaced by a SHA-256 digest of the audio of 2 Live Crew's "Banned in the U.S.A.", and defines two joke TLS alerts.

humor.why: The document is an April 1st whimsical RFC that parodies standards-making by requiring a rap album as a cryptographic input.
humor.quote: Implementations that omit the MAC are non-conformant with BUSA-TLS and also have questionable taste in music.

TLS.why: The joke specification changes the TLS 1.3 key schedule and defines new TLS alerts, so TLS readers would expect to find it, even though it is satirical.
TLS.quote: BUSA-TLS modifies this as follows: Early Secret = HKDF-Extract(salt=0, IKM=MAC)

rejected.why: HKDF is only used as in RFC 8446's key schedule. The document does not specify or analyse it.
SHA-256 is only the hash used to digest the audio. The document says nothing about the hash family.
PCM, MP3 and FLAC are mentioned only to say which audio form to digest. The document does not define or discuss codecs.
The IANA section only declines to register the alert codes as a joke. It is boilerplate.

RFC9950.title: A YANG Data Model for Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+)
RFC9950.summary: Defines the ietf-system-tacacs-plus YANG module, augmenting the RFC 7317 System Management model to configure TACACS+ clients, including TACACS+ over TLS 1.3, and obsoletes RFC 9105.

YANG.why: The document's main content is a YANG module with tree diagrams and examples, so it belongs on the YANG page.
YANG.quote: This document defines a Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+) client YANG module that augments the System Management data model

TACACS+.why: The module configures TACACS+ clients and servers for centralized AAA, including TACACS+ over TLS 1.3, so TACACS+ readers would want it.
TACACS+.quote: the TACACS+ YANG module can be used to manage TACACS+ over TLS.

rejected.why: TLS 1.3 is the transport for TACACS+ here. The document only exposes TLS parameters in YANG and defines no new TLS behaviour.
RADIUS appears only as the existing alternative in RFC 7317 and is not the subject of this document.
NETCONF and RESTCONF are mentioned only as management protocols in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
The AAA framework is the general purpose, but TACACS+ is the more specific tag and already covers it.
Not relevant. The module is a YANG model, not an SNMP MIB.

RFC9951.title: Export of Delay Performance Metrics in IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX)
RFC9951.summary: Defines four new IPFIX Information Elements (pathDelay Mean/Min/Max/Sum DeltaMicroseconds) for exporting On-Path (IOAM / Alternate Marking) one-way delay from OAM transit and decapsulating nodes, and registers matching entries in the IANA Performance Metrics Registry.

IPFIX.why: The document's core is new IPFIX IEs, their templates and encoding examples, and use with Flow Aggregation.
IPFIX.quote: this document defines four new IPFIX Information Elements (IEs), exposing the On-Path delay on OAM header transit and decapsulating nodes

performance measurement.why: It defines four one-way delay Registered Performance Metrics (Hybrid Type I) with full definitions, methods of measurement and outputs.
performance measurement.quote: As these IEs represent performance metrics, they are also registered in the IANA "Performance Metrics Registry" [IANA-PERF-METRIC] in accordance with [RFC8911].

telemetry.why: It exports on-path telemetry delay (IOAM, Enhanced Alternate Marking) in postcard mode from network nodes, which is network telemetry.
telemetry.quote: Delay measurements in the network are computed using an On-Path Telemetry protocol, which inserts metadata into the data-plane packet

rejected.why: IOAM and alternate marking are the source of the timestamps; the document specifies export of delay, not the OAM mechanisms. Covered by telemetry.
Only mentioned as a clock sync option and for timestamp format conversion.
Only referenced for the decimal64 type definition.
Only listed as an aggregation dimension in use cases.
Appears in use cases and encoding examples as an aggregation key, not the subject.
Registry actions are boilerplate registrations of the new IEs and metrics, not guidance on IANA.

RFC9952.title: Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) ID for CoAP over DTLS
RFC9952.summary: Registers the "co" ALPN ID for CoAP secured by DTLS in the IANA TLS ALPN registry, complementing the existing "coap" ID for CoAP over TLS.

CoAP.why: The document defines how CoAP over DTLS services are identified via ALPN, and extends CoAP's secure-transport identification.
CoAP.quote: This document specifies an ALPN ID for CoAP services that are secured by DTLS.

TLS.why: The document registers a new ALPN protocol ID in the TLS ALPN registry, which is a new use of the TLS ALPN extension that TLS readers would want.
TLS.quote: an ALPN for CoAP over DTLS is registered in Section 4.

rejected.why: DTLS is the security substrate for CoAP here; the document defines nothing new in DTLS itself, only an ALPN identifier.
SVCB records are only the discovery mechanism that uses the ALPN ID; nothing new is defined for DNS.
Mentioned only as a motivation for the short ID to avoid fragmentation; the document is not about 6LoWPAN.
The IANA registration is boilerplate-like apparatus for the main subject, not a document about IANA registry policy.

RFC9953.title: DNS over CoAP (DoC)
RFC9953.summary: Defines DNS over CoAP (DoC), mapping DNS OPCODE 0 query/response pairs onto CoAP FETCH exchanges, with caching rules, OSCORE/(D)TLS protection, and SVCB "docpath" and "core.dns" discovery.

CoAP.why: The document specifies a new use of CoAP: FETCH requests, Content-Format 553, Max-Age/TTL caching handling, Observe, and a resource type.
CoAP.quote: This document defines a protocol for exchanging DNS queries (OPCODE 0) over the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP).

DNS.why: It defines a new DNS transport, including DNS message carriage, RCODE handling and TTL handling.
DNS.quote: a DoC client tries to resolve DNS information by sending DNS queries carried within CoAP requests to a DoC server.

OSCORE.why: OSCORE is a main protection option for DoC, and the document discusses its use and its effect on discovery.
OSCORE.quote: It is RECOMMENDED to carry DNS messages protected using OSCORE [RFC8613] between the DoC client and the DoC server.

DNS privacy.why: DoC is a new encrypted DNS transport, so readers of encrypted DNS would want it.
DNS privacy.quote: to provide encrypted DNS message exchange for constrained devices in the Internet of Things (IoT).

service discovery.why: A substantial section defines how DoC servers are discovered using the core.dns resource type, a new SVCB docpath key, and DNR.
service discovery.quote: This document specifies "docpath" as a single-valued Service Parameter Key (SvcParamKey) that is mandatory for DoC SVCB records.
service discovery.section: 3.2. Discovery Using SVCB Resource Records or DNR

rejected.why: DoC is inspired by DoH and compared against it, but it is a distinct CoAP-based protocol that uses FETCH. DoH is not specified here.
DTLS is only one of the security mechanisms DoC relies on, and the document defines nothing new about it.
TLS is only a substrate for securing CoAP.
The document only mentions that a DoC server may validate DNSSEC, and it does not specify DNSSEC.
DoQ is mentioned only as an upstream transport and as a contrast.
IoT is the deployment context, and the CoAP tag already covers the constrained-environment audience.

RFC9954.title: Hybrid Key Exchange in TLS 1.3
RFC9954.summary: Specifies a concatenation-based construction for hybrid (traditional plus post-quantum) key exchange in TLS 1.3, using NamedGroup negotiation, concatenated KeyShareEntry values, and concatenated shared secrets fed into the TLS 1.3 key schedule.

TLS.why: The document defines how hybrid key exchange groups are negotiated, transmitted in key_share, and inserted into the TLS 1.3 key schedule.
TLS.quote: This document provides a construction for hybrid key exchange in the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol version 1.3.

post-quantum.why: Hybrid combination of traditional and post-quantum KEMs is the main use case and motivation, though specific PQ algorithms are out of scope.
post-quantum.quote: It is motivated by the transition to post-quantum cryptography.

rejected.why: ML-KEM is only mentioned as an example of a compatible KEM; the document does not specify it.
Key exchange here is a TLS handshake mechanism, better captured by TLS and post-quantum; the generic key management topic is not the focus.
ECDH is only a component example, not specified or profiled.
IKEv2 multiple key exchanges are only mentioned in related work.
Only a passing IANA note about DTLS-OK column; not about DTLS.
HKDF appears only in the key schedule figure as the existing TLS mechanism.

RFC9955.title: Hybrid Signature Spectrums
RFC9955.summary: Informational document classifying design goals and security properties of hybrid (post-quantum/traditional) digital signature schemes, including non-separability, artifacts, simultaneous verification, and EUF-CMA challenges.

post-quantum.why: The whole document concerns hybrid signature schemes combining traditional and post-quantum algorithms for the quantum transition. No narrower post-quantum child tag fits, since it is not about ML-DSA specifically or hash-based signatures.
post-quantum.quote: This document describes classification of design goals and security considerations for hybrid digital signature schemes

rejected.why: ML-DSA is only mentioned as an example of a next-generation signature scheme, not specified or profiled.
Certificates appear as one artifact location, but the document is not about X.509 profiles.
Certificate chains are discussed only as a place where hybrid artifacts may live, not as the subject.
RFC 9954 on hybrid key exchange in TLS is referenced for terminology, but this document does not address TLS.
RSA is cited only as an example of a traditional algorithm.

gaps.name: Hybrid digital signatures
gaps.why: The subject has no dedicated tag. Only the broad post-quantum tag is available, and it does not separate hybrid signature design from other post-quantum topics.

RFC9956.title: A Non-Queue-Building Per-Hop Behavior (NQB PHB) for Differentiated Services
RFC9956.summary: Defines the Non-Queue-Building (NQB) Diffserv per-hop behavior and recommends DSCP 45 for it. It gives sender requirements, node requirements including traffic protection, and mappings for DOCSIS, mobile and Wi-Fi networks. It also updates RFC 8325.

Diffserv.why: The document specifies a new Diffserv PHB and its recommended DSCP, and covers aggregation, re-marking and tunnels in the Diffserv model.
Diffserv.quote: This document defines a Diffserv PHB called the "Non-Queue-Building Per-Hop Behavior" (or "NQB PHB").

WiFi.why: A substantial part of the document maps NQB onto 802.11 access categories and formally updates RFC 8325, the Diffserv-to-802.11 mapping.
WiFi.quote: Wi-Fi equipment (including equipment compliant with [RFC8325]) SHOULD map the DSCP value 45 (decimal) into a separate queue in the same Access Category

AQM.why: The PHB is about separate shallow-buffered queuing, queue protection and scheduling to avoid queuing delay. It is closely related to AQM and the L4S DualQ.
AQM.quote: A node supporting the NQB PHB MUST provide a queue for NQB traffic separate from the queue used for Default traffic.

rejected.why: DOCSIS is only one of three mapping examples, in a short section that refers elsewhere for detail.
The mobile mapping is a brief example section, not a main subject.
ECN handling is mentioned in only one short subsection, and the L4S relationship is secondary.
The document addresses queueing and PHBs, not congestion control algorithms, and mentions Reno, CUBIC and BBR only as context.
Diffserv is the more specific tag under QoS and is already chosen.
The DSCP assignment sits in the IANA Considerations boilerplate section, and the document is not about IANA registries.

RFC9957.title: The DOCSIS Queue Protection Algorithm to Preserve Low Latency
RFC9957.summary: Informational RFC explaining the DOCSIS 3.1 Queue Protection (QProt) algorithm, which detects flows that build queues in the shared low-latency queue and reclassifies their packets into the Classic queue.

DOCSIS.why: The document explains a function specified in Annex P of the DOCSIS specification, covering how it works in the cable modem and the CMTS.
DOCSIS.quote: explains the specification of the queue protection (QProt) algorithm introduced into DOCSIS technology at version 3.1

AQM.why: QProt is driven by the native AQM marking probability of the low-latency queue. It polices flows in a dual-queue AQM, and the document gives the ramp function calcProbNative().
