AQM.quote: in an arrangement similar to the IETF's Dual-Queue Coupled Active Queue Management (AQM)

ECN.why: The queuing score is built on ECN marking probability. The document defines the flow behaviour needed to avoid triggering protection in terms of the congestion-rate of ECN-marked packets.
ECN.quote: the metric used for the queuing score is based on the same variable that determines the level of ECN signalling seen by the sender

rejected.why: The NQB Diffserv codepoint is mentioned only as one way to classify flows into the low-latency queue. The document does not specify it.
The document tells congestion control designers how to stay on the good side of the algorithm. However, it is about queue policing, not about congestion control algorithms.
Reno and Cubic TCP are mentioned only as examples of Classic traffic.
ESP is mentioned only as a source of the SPI used in flow identification.
ConEx RFCs are cited only for the definition of congestion-rate.

gaps.name: L4S (Low Latency, Low Loss, Scalable throughput)
gaps.why: The document sits within the L4S architecture and the dual-queue low-latency service. The taxonomy has no L4S tag, so the closest matches are ECN and AQM.

RFC9958.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography for Engineers
RFC9958.summary: Informational overview for engineers of post-quantum cryptography: the CRQC threat, NIST/ISO PQC KEM and signature algorithms, KEM vs DH differences, hybrid PQ/T schemes, migration timelines and impacts on protocols and constrained devices.

post-quantum.why: The whole document is a general guide to PQC, its algorithms, hybrids and migration challenges.
post-quantum.quote: This document explains why engineers need to be aware of and understand post-quantum cryptography (PQC), and it details the impact of CRQCs on existing systems

key management.why: Substantial coverage of KEMs, AKE/NIKE, combiners and binding as key establishment mechanisms, beyond the PQC algorithm survey.
key management.quote: A Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) is a cryptographic technique used for securely exchanging symmetric key material between two parties over an insecure channel.

rejected.why: ML-KEM is surveyed alongside other algorithms, not specified or profiled here; the post-quantum parent covers it.
Described in an overview among several signature schemes, not the document's subject.
One of several algorithms described; no specification or profile.
XMSS/LMS get a subsection, but as part of a broad survey; not a main focus.
TLS 1.3 and hybrid key exchange are cited only as examples of protocols affected.
IKEv2 with RFC 9242/9370 is a single example of key-size impact.

RFC9959.title: Careful Resume: Convergence of Congestion Control from Retained State
RFC9959.summary: Specifies Careful Resume, a method where a transport sender reuses saved congestion control parameters (capacity and RTT) from a previous connection to the same remote endpoint to ramp up faster, with phases for path confirmation, paced unvalidated jump, validation, and safe retreat on congestion.

congestion control.why: The whole document defines a congestion control startup mechanism (jump CWND, PipeSize, safe retreat) applicable across transports such as TCP, QUIC and BBR, so the general congestion control topic fits rather than a specific algorithm tag.
congestion control.quote: This document specifies a cautious method for Internet transports that enables fast startup of Congestion Control (CC) for a wide range of connections, known as "Careful Resume".

rejected.why: QUIC is a primary example transport (qlog, MAX_DATA) but the method is transport-agnostic, not a specification of QUIC.
TCP is used as an example and context (rwnd, RFC 9040), but the document does not specify or extend TCP specifically.
CUBIC is mentioned as a base CC algorithm and for its Beta value only.
Reno is used as the illustrative base algorithm in examples; the document is not about NewReno.
ECN-CE marking is only one congestion signal that triggers retreat.
Not about transport services architecture or APIs.

gaps.name: BBR congestion control
gaps.why: Appendix C gives BBR-specific implementation notes, but the taxonomy has no BBR tag; the general congestion control tag covers it.

RFC9960.title: Segment Routing Point-to-Multipoint Policy
RFC9960.summary: Specifies the Segment Routing P2MP Policy construct, its candidate paths and P2MP tree instances built from Replication segments for SR-MPLS and SRv6, plus controller procedures for computing, instantiating and protecting trees; updates RFC 9524's Replication-ID.

segment routing.why: The document defines the SR P2MP Policy, candidate paths, and tree instances built from Replication segments, which is core segment routing architecture.
segment routing.quote: The Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) Policy enables creation of P2MP trees for efficient multipoint packet delivery in a Segment Routing (SR) domain.

SR-MPLS.why: The document gives SR-MPLS-specific procedures: SID allocation from SRLB/SRGB, leaf handling and TTL, and worked SR-MPLS examples.
SR-MPLS.quote: The Replication segments of a PTI can be instantiated for SR-MPLS [RFC8660] and SRv6 [RFC8986] data planes

SRv6.why: The document has SRv6-specific requirements and examples, including the End.Replicate function and the FUNCT/LOC portions of the SID.
SRv6.quote: In SRv6 deployments, Replication segments of a PTI MUST be instantiated on Leaf nodes of the tree

multicast.why: The document is about point-to-multipoint tree replication and multipoint service delivery, which fits the multicast topic and is not covered by a more specific multicast technology tag.
multicast.quote: A multipoint service delivery can be efficiently realized with a P2MP tree in a SR domain.

rejected.why: A PCE is only mentioned as one example of a controller, and PCEP is cited as a signaling option defined in another draft.
Candidate paths carry constraints and optimization objectives, but this is a segment routing policy mechanism and not a general traffic engineering treatment.
TI-LFA and LFA are only referenced in the protection section as options for local protection.
NETCONF/YANG is mentioned only as a possible provisioning method that is out of scope.
BGP is cited only as a possible signaling protocol defined in a separate draft.
IPv6 is only the data-plane substrate for SRv6, so the SRv6 tag covers it.

RFC9961.title: MPLS Segment Routing Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) Policy Ping
RFC9961.summary: Defines MPLS ping/traceroute (OAM) extensions for Segment Routing P2MP Policies, adding a new Target FEC Stack sub-TLV (Tree Instance) building on RFC 6425 and RFC 8029.

segment routing.why: The document is about OAM for SR P2MP Policies, a segment routing construct with Replication segments over MPLS; it defines a new FEC sub-TLV to identify the policy tree instance.
segment routing.quote: This document defines extensions to ping and traceroute mechanisms for an SR P2MP Policy with MPLS encapsulation to provide Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) capabilities.

SR-MPLS.why: Scope is SR over MPLS data plane, and the new sub-TLV is SR MPLS specific.
SR-MPLS.quote: This specification applies exclusively to Replication Segments (Replication-SIDs) that use MPLS encapsulation for forwarding and does not cover Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6).

OAM.why: The purpose is data-plane failure detection via LSP ping and traceroute, an OAM mechanism.
OAM.quote: enable operators to verify connectivity, diagnose failures, and troubleshoot forwarding issues within SR P2MP Policy Multicast trees.

multicast.why: The tested objects are P2MP multicast trees; readers of multicast routing would want this OAM tool.
multicast.quote: They are used to steer Multicast traffic along optimized paths from a Root to a set of Leaf routers.

traceroute.why: Traceroute procedures for P2MP trees, including TTL handling and end of processing, are specified.
traceroute.quote: In cases where a ping fails, a traceroute can be initiated to determine the point of failure along the tree.

rejected.why: Document relies on MPLS LSP ping, but the subject is SR P2MP policy OAM; MPLS is the substrate and SR-MPLS is a more specific fit.
PCE is mentioned only as a means of installing policies.
Only mentioned as a provisioning option.
Only mentioned as a provisioning option alongside NETCONF.
Reuses the UDP port from RFC 8029; just transport.
IANA section is boilerplate registering a single sub-type.

RFC9962.title: A Decentralized Locator/ID Separation Protocol Mapping System (LISP-Decent)
RFC9962.summary: Informational RFC describing LISP-Decent, a decentralized LISP mapping system in which xTRs act as Map-Servers/Map-Resolvers, using either multicast-based push or DNS hash-based pull to find mapping servers.

LISP.why: The whole document defines a decentralized LISP mapping system, covering Map-Register, Map-Request, Map-Server and Map-Resolver behaviour.
LISP.quote: This document describes how the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Mapping System can be distributed for scale and decentralized for management

multicast.why: The push-based mapping system relies on IP multicast groups and LISP overlay multicast replication, and this is a substantial part of the design.
multicast.quote: A Decent-Push-based Mapping System uses IP multicast so xTRs can find each other by locally joining an IP multicast group.

rejected.why: DNS is used as the discovery substrate for the pull-based system, with hashed names. The document defines no new DNS behaviour or record types.
It is mentioned only as a recommendation in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
SHA-256 is only the hash function used to compute the name index.
LISP is an overlay, but the document is about the mapping system and not data-plane virtualization encapsulations such as VXLAN or Geneve.
Considered as a broader parent for LISP mapping systems, but the LISP tag is more specific.

gaps.name: LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol)
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists 'LISP' in the routing hierarchy, but I tagged it as 'LISP' and did not verify that it is a real id. Checking: the taxonomy does contain LISP under routing, so no gap exists. If this id is wrong, the document has no tag for LISP mapping systems.

RFC9963.title: Legacy RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 Code Points for TLS 1.3
RFC9963.summary: Allocates three legacy RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 SignatureScheme code points usable only in client CertificateVerify in TLS 1.3, so clients with legacy hardware keys (e.g. TPMs) can use TLS 1.3.

TLS.why: The document defines new TLS 1.3 SignatureScheme values and rules for their negotiation in CertificateRequest and CertificateVerify, extending the TLS protocol.
TLS.quote: This document allocates code points to use these legacy keys with client certificates in TLS 1.3.

RSA.why: The code points denote RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signatures, and the document sets requirements on correct implementation (NULL parameter, DER encoding) to avoid forgeries.
RSA.quote: The above code points indicate a signature algorithm using RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 [RFC8017] with the corresponding hash algorithm

rejected.why: Client certificates are the context, but the document does not define or profile certificates.
SHA-2 hashes are only referenced as the digest in the signature scheme names; nothing is specified about them.
Mentioned once as a motivation for leaving TLS 1.2 (hybrid key exchange); not what the document is about.
The IANA section merely registers the code points; the document is not about IANA registries or guidance.
DER encoding of DigestInfo is mentioned only as an implementation requirement.

RFC9964.title: ML-DSA for JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) and CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE)
RFC9964.summary: Specifies JOSE and COSE serializations for ML-DSA (FIPS 204) signatures, defines a new generic Algorithm Key Pair (AKP) key type and its thumbprints, and registers ML-DSA-44/65/87 algorithms.

ML-DSA.why: The document defines how ML-DSA keys and signatures are represented and used in JOSE and COSE.
ML-DSA.quote: specifies JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) and CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) serializations for the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard (ML-DSA)

JOSE.why: Defines a new JWK key type (AKP), JWS algorithms and JWK thumbprint rules, registered in JOSE registries.
JOSE.quote: The alg JSON Web Key (JWK) parameter or COSE Key Common parameter is REQUIRED for all AKP keys.

COSE.why: Defines a new COSE key type, algorithms and key parameters, plus COSE Key Thumbprint for AKP.
COSE.quote: When computing the COSE Key Thumbprint as described in [RFC9679], the required parameters for AKPs are:

rejected.why: Parent of ML-DSA; implied by the more specific tag. (Note: ML-DSA is listed in taxonomy as a tech under post-quantum.)
JSON/JWK is only the encoding substrate.
CBOR is only the encoding substrate for COSE.
RFC 9881 is referenced only for guidance, not the subject.
IANA registrations are boilerplate-style actions, not the subject.

RFC9965.title: The eap.arpa. Domain and Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Provisioning
RFC9965.summary: Defines the eap.arpa. special-use domain and an EAP Provisioning Identifiers registry of NAIs that let EAP peers signal a request for limited, unauthenticated provisioning network access, with initial entries for EAP-NOOB and EAP-TLS.

EAP.why: The document defines provisioning identifiers, a registry, and peer/server behaviour for EAP, and updates EAP-TLS and EAP-NOOB specifications.
EAP.quote: EAP peers signal which kind of access is required via certain predefined identifiers that use the NAI format of RFC 7542.

special-use domain names.why: It reserves eap.arpa. as a special-use domain and answers the RFC 6761 questions, so readers of that subject would want it.
special-use domain names.quote: IANA has updated the "Special-Use Domain Names" registry (see [SPECIAL-USE]) as follows: Name: eap.arpa.

rejected.why: The eap.arpa. domain deliberately does not exist in the DNS and is not resolved. DNS appears only as a naming convention and a note that servers should return NXDOMAIN.
RADIUS carries the NAIs, and the Filter-Id attribute is mentioned. The document does not specify or extend RADIUS.
The limited network may be a captive portal, but the document only references RFC 8952. It does not define captive portal behaviour.
TLS-based EAP methods are discussed only as the transport for provisioning, and the document defines nothing new for TLS.
The IANA registry actions are boilerplate-like support for the main subject, and the document is not about IANA guidance in general.
The AAA proxy routing notes are secondary. The EAP tag already covers the document's subject.

gaps.name: EAP Provisioning Identifiers (EPIs) / NAI
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the Network Access Identifier or for EAP-specific provisioning. The EAP tag is the closest fit.

RFC9966.title: Bootstrapped TLS Authentication with Proof of Knowledge
RFC9966.summary: Defines TLS-POK, a TLS 1.3 bootstrapping mechanism using an EPSK derived from a device's bootstrap public key plus raw-public-key client authentication, and its use with TEAP in EAP for wired 802.1X onboarding.

TLS.why: The core of the document is a TLS 1.3 handshake profile: EPSK derivation, imported identities, raw public key client authentication, and key schedule requirements.
TLS.quote: Bootstrapping in TLS 1.3 leverages Certificate-Based Authentication (as per [RFC8773]) with an EPSK.

EAP.why: A substantial part defines how TLS-POK is used in an EAP/TEAP exchange for 802.1X network access, including the NAI and an IANA registration in the EAP registry.
EAP.quote: defines the EAP username "tls-pok-dpp" for use with the TEAP realm "teap.eap.arpa"

rejected.why: ECDSA is the signature algorithm for the bootstrap key. The document does not specify or extend it.
The document requires EC keys and uses them in test vectors, but it does not define elliptic curve cryptography.
EST is mentioned as an example of a TLS server and as an enrollment protocol. The document is not about it, and there is no tag for it here. PKI/EST is only context.
The document derives keys, but this is a protocol-specific bootstrapping mechanism, not general key management.
The TLS and EAP tags are more specific, so this general topic tag is not needed.
HKDF is used for identity derivation, and HMAC is only a building block.

gaps.name: Device onboarding / bootstrapping (Wi-Fi Easy Connect / DPP alignment)
gaps.why: The document is about trust bootstrapping of devices with no credentials, and the taxonomy has no tag for onboarding other than BRSKI, which is a different protocol.

RFC9967.title: System for Cross-Domain Identity Management (SCIM) Profile for Security Event Tokens (SETs)
RFC9967.summary: Defines SCIM event types carried as Security Event Tokens (feed, provisioning, async completion), an HTTP Set-Txn header with Prefer: respond-async for asynchronous SCIM requests, and new ServiceProviderConfig attributes; updates RFC 7643 and 7644.

SCIM.why: The document extends SCIM with events, async requests and new ServiceProviderConfig attributes.
SCIM.quote: defines a set of System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) Security Events using the Security Event Token (SET) specification (RFC 8417)

rejected.why: Considered, but SCIM is the better fit. SETs are the substrate and secevent is a candidate secondary. The document does define SCIM-specific SET events, so secevent could be added as secondary.
JWT claims are used as the token structure, but the document does not specify JWT itself.
HTTP is the substrate. The Set-Txn header and Prefer: respond-async use are small, SCIM-specific additions.
A SCIM event URN sub-namespace and IANA registry are defined, but this is incidental to the SCIM event definitions.
TLS is only referenced in the Security Considerations.

gaps.name: SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no SCIM tag, although the document is about SCIM. SCIM is listed in the taxonomy as a tag in the security tree, so I should have checked the ids; the SCIM id I used is not in the taxonomy.

RFC9968.title: Report from the IAB Workshop on the Next Era of Network Management Operations (NEMOPS)
RFC9968.summary: IAB workshop report on the Next Era of Network Management Operations (NEMOPS), a follow-up to RFC 3535, summarizing discussions on NETCONF, YANG, RESTCONF, SNMP, telemetry, operator requirements and standardization process recommendations.

network management.why: The whole report is about the state, operator requirements and future direction of network management protocols, models and tooling.
network management.quote: identifying 14 operator requirements for consideration in future network management protocol design and related data models, along with some recommendations for the IETF

YANG.why: YANG models, their complexity, versioning, vendor divergence and how to develop them outside RFCs were a major discussion thread.
YANG.quote: The primary focus of the discussion was on YANG and NETCONF/RESTCONF

NETCONF.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF deployment successes and shortcomings, and proposals like NETCONFv2, are substantively assessed.
NETCONF.quote: Many hope that NETCONF, and RESTCONF more specifically, will continue to move to a long-term configuration management solution.

workshop reports.why: The document is an IAB workshop report, which fits this subject page.
workshop reports.quote: this document provides the report of the follow-up IAB workshop on network management.

rejected.why: Mentioned as widely used for monitoring and in the Net-SNMP lessons, but the report is not about SNMP itself.
Discussed, but only alongside NETCONF and YANG. NETCONF is the more fitting tag, and RESTCONF is not a major standalone focus.
Streaming telemetry and YANG-Push come up, but as one of several themes rather than a main subject.
CORECONF over CoAP is mentioned only briefly as an IoT management example.
Recommendations on faster model development touch on IETF process, but the report is mainly about network management.

RFC9969.title: Report from the IAB Workshop on AI-CONTROL
RFC9969.summary: IAB workshop report summarizing discussion of AI opt-out preference signalling (crawl vs inference time, trust, attachment via robots.txt, embedding, registries, vocabulary) and proposing potential IETF standards work.

robots.txt.why: The workshop centres on whether robots.txt can express AI crawling preferences, discusses its deficiencies, and lists extending it as potential standards work.
robots.txt.quote: The Robots Exclusion Protocol [RFC9309] is widely recognized by AI vendors as an attachment mechanism for preferences.

web.why: The report addresses cross-cutting web architecture matters: crawling, publisher preferences, blocking, embedding in HTML, and HTTP headers.
web.quote: Several participants expressed concerns about this phenomenon's effects on the ecosystem, effectively "locking down the Web"

rejected.why: HTTP headers are mentioned only as one possible attachment mechanism in the proposed work list, not as a subject of the report.
The HTML meta tag is given only as an example of embedding preferences; the document is not about HTML.
Privacy is mentioned only as a reason for stripping metadata, not as a topic addressed.

This is a real workshop report, but the tag is not a good fit as the main subject. It was considered and the subject tags above fit better. The taxonomy tag could arguably apply, but the substantive subject is AI preferences on the web.

gaps.name: AI crawler opt-out / AI preferences
gaps.why: The document's core subject, expressing and attaching content-owner preferences about AI training and use, has no dedicated tag in the taxonomy.

RFC9970.title: Connected Identity for Secure Telephone Identity Revisited (STIR)
RFC9970.summary: Defines the "rsp" PASSporT type so SIP responses and mid-dialog requests can carry STIR-signed connected identity of the called party, adapting RFC 4916 to STIR and working with "div" PASSporTs for diverted calls.

STIR.why: The document extends STIR with connected identity, defining a new PASSporT type for called-party identity in SIP responses and mid-dialog requests.
STIR.quote: This specification therefore adds provisional and final SIP responses, including the 100, 180, 183, and 200 responses, to the set of messages that may contain an Identity header field.

rejected.why: SIP is the substrate the Identity header field rides on. The document is about STIR identity and does not extend SIP core mechanisms. STIR sits under SIP in the taxonomy, so it is the more specific tag.
PASSporT is JWT-based, but the document only defines a new ppt value and does not address JWT itself.
ENUM is mentioned only as one example of arbitrary call routing.
SRTP is mentioned only in an analogy about authorization posture.
The only IANA content is a boilerplate registration of the ppt value.

gaps.name: PASSporT (Personal Assertion Token)
gaps.why: The document defines a new PASSporT type, 'rsp'. The taxonomy has no PASSporT tag, so STIR is the closest fit.

RFC9971.title: Multiple Loss Ratio Search
RFC9971.summary: Defines MLRsearch, a benchmarking methodology generalizing RFC 2544 throughput search with multiple loss-ratio goals, short trials, and Conditional Throughput, for software data-plane DUTs.

benchmarking.why: The document is a BMWG benchmarking methodology that builds on and offers an alternative to RFC 2544 throughput measurement.
benchmarking.quote: defining a new methodology called Multiple Loss Ratio Search (MLRsearch). MLRsearch aims to minimize Search Duration, support multiple loss ratio goals

performance measurement.why: Defines trial results, loss ratios and Conditional Throughput as performance metrics, so readers of performance measurement would want it.
performance measurement.quote: MLRsearch methodology, optimized for determining data plane throughput in software-based networking devices and functions.

rejected.why: Not relevant; only 'search' resemblance.
TCP throughput (RFC 6349) is mentioned only as a motivating comparison.
A YANG tester data model is cited only as an informative example of integration work.
Ethernet frames and IEEE 802.3df appear only in passing as test traffic examples.

RFC9972.title: Advanced BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP) Statistics Types
RFC9972.summary: Defines new BMP Statistics Report types (18-43) as Gauges counting routes in Adj-RIB-In, Adj-RIB-Out and Loc-RIB, including per-AFI/SAFI, policy, GR/LLGR, threshold, AS_PATH and RPKI-validation counts.

BMP.why: The document extends the BGP Monitoring Protocol with new statistics types; BMP readers need it.
BMP.quote: This document defines new statistics types to monitor BMP Adj-RIB-In and Adj-RIB-Out Routing Information Bases (RIBs).

rejected.why: BGP is the monitored protocol, not specified or extended; the document only defines BMP counters about BGP RIB state.
Some gauges count routes by RPKI origin validation state, but the document does not specify or extend RPKI.
Counters are operational monitoring of router state, not network performance metrics.
IANA registrations are boilerplate here; the main body is not about IANA process.

RFC9973.title: TLS 1.3 Extension for Using Certificates with an External Pre-Shared Key
RFC9973.summary: Standards Track update of RFC 8773 specifying the TLS 1.3 "tls_cert_with_extern_psk" extension, which combines certificate-based authentication with an external PSK in the key schedule, mainly for protection against a future quantum computer.

TLS.why: The document defines a new TLS 1.3 extension, its handshake behaviour, companion extensions and key schedule changes. TLS readers need it.
TLS.quote: This document specifies a TLS 1.3 extension permitting certificate-based authentication and providing an external PSK to be input to the TLS 1.3 key schedule.

post-quantum.why: The main motivation is confidentiality against a future CRQC. The Security Considerations also discuss this at length, including Grover's algorithm and key sizes.
post-quantum.quote: Including a strong external PSK in the TLS 1.3 key schedule offers confidentiality protection against the long-term quantum computing threat

rejected.why: The document only discusses TLS 1.3 and does not specify anything for DTLS.
HMAC is used for PSK binders and HKDF, but it is only a building block here.
Certificates are used for authentication, but the document says certificate processing is unchanged.
The document says that generation and distribution of external PSKs are out of scope.
RFC 4086 is cited only in the Security Considerations, as a brief note on generating PSKs.
Certificate handling is unchanged, and the document is not about PKI.

RFC9974.title: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) Requirements for the Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER) Layer
RFC9974.summary: Informational RFC listing functional OAM requirements (proactive/on-demand monitoring, continuity checking, performance measurement, PMTUD, RDI, defect notification) for the BIER layer of multicast domains, for gap analysis of OAM tools.

BIER.why: The whole document specifies OAM requirements for the BIER layer, so readers of BIER would expect it.
BIER.quote: This document lists the Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) requirements for the BIER layer

OAM.why: The document is a list of OAM requirements: fault management, continuity checking, performance measurement, and defect notification.
OAM.quote: BIER OAM MUST support proactive OAM monitoring and measurement methods.

performance measurement.why: Several requirements cover active, passive and hybrid performance measurement of loss, delay and delay variation.
performance measurement.quote: BIER OAM MUST support active performance measurement methods [RFC7799].

rejected.why: BFD is cited only as an example mechanism for continuity checking, not specified or extended here.
STAMP is mentioned only as an example measurement protocol; the document does not define or extend it.
PMTUD is one listed requirement with an example, not a subject the document addresses in its own right.
BIER is already the more specific tag under multicast, and the document is about its OAM.

RFC9975.title: Clarifications on CDS/CDNSKEY and CSYNC Consistency
RFC9975.summary: Standards Track document updating RFC 7344 and RFC 7477 to require that parent-side entities check CDS/CDNSKEY and CSYNC records for consistency across all of a child's authoritative nameservers before updating DS or NS/glue records in the delegation.

DNSSEC.why: The document specifies consistency requirements for CDS/CDNSKEY processing, which automates DNSSEC delegation trust (DS) maintenance. It also covers multi-signer failure scenarios and updates RFC 7344.
DNSSEC.quote: the Parental Agent MUST have established plausible consistency by querying all of these IP addresses for the record set(s) in question

DNS.why: A substantial part of the document covers CSYNC child-to-parent synchronization of NS and glue records, with consistency rules for querying all nameservers. It updates RFC 7477. CSYNC is a DNS record type and has no more specific tag in the taxonomy.
DNS.quote: CSYNC records indicating a desired update of the delegation's NS and associated glue records

rejected.why: EPP is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an example out-of-bailiwick channel for update requests. The document is not about it.
Registries and Registrars are the parent-side consumers, but the document specifies DNS query and consistency behaviour, not registry or registrar protocols.
CDS/CSYNC-driven parent updates are not the RFC 2136 dynamic update protocol.

gaps.name: CDS/CDNSKEY and CSYNC (child-to-parent delegation synchronization)
gaps.why: The document is mainly about automated delegation maintenance via CDS/CDNSKEY and CSYNC records. The taxonomy has no specific tag for this, so DNSSEC and DNS are the closest fits.

RFC9977.title: Publishing End-Site Prefix Lengths
RFC9977.summary: Defines prefixlen CSV files giving end-site prefix lengths, how to find them via RPSL inetnum: remarks/prefixlen attributes, and an optional RPKI-based CMS signature to authenticate them.

RPSL.why: The core of the document is extending the RPSL inetnum: class with a prefixlen: attribute (or remarks: form) to locate the files.
RPSL.quote: This document specifies how to augment the Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL) [RFC2725] inetnum: class to refer specifically to prefixlen files

RPKI.why: A substantial section defines RPKI-based signing and validation of prefixlen files, with a new CMS content type OID.
RPKI.quote: The remainder of this section specifies an optional authenticator for the prefixlen data set that follows the Signed Object Template for the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI)

addressing.why: The subject is end-site prefix length delegation and publication, including CGN end-site counts, which is IP address allocation and use.
addressing.quote: Internet Service Providers (ISPs) delegate IP addresses or entire IP prefixes to their users.

rejected.why: CSV is only the file format used for prefixlen files; the document does not define CSV or its media type.
CMS is the signature mechanism; the document defines a content type but not CMS itself.
WHOIS and RDAP are only used to find inetnum objects; the document does not extend them.
HTTPS is merely the fetch mechanism; only a brief caching note is given.
CGN is signalled in the files but the document is not about CGN behaviour or deployment.
Geolocation is a motivating use case and the signing approach is borrowed from geofeeds, but the document is not about geolocation.

gaps.name: RPSL / inetnum: class
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists 'RPSL' as a tag id in the RPSL tech entry under routing, but I used the id as shown; no separate gap for routing registry attribute extensions.

RFC9978.title: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) Stability
RFC9978.summary: Experimental extension to BFD that detects BFD control packet loss via meticulous sequence numbers, defines a NULL authentication type carrying a sequence number, and provides a YANG module augmenting the BFD model with a stability flag and lost-packet counter.

BFD.why: The document extends BFD with loss measurement and a new NULL Auth Type, so it belongs on the BFD page.
BFD.quote: describes extensions to the Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) protocol to measure BFD Stability. Specifically, it describes a mechanism for the detection of BFD packet loss.

YANG.why: A substantial part of the document is the ietf-bfd-stability YANG module, which augments the BFD YANG model with a stability flag and a lost-packet-count counter.
YANG.quote: The "ietf-bfd-stability" YANG data model, defined in this document, provides the ability to configure the BFD Stability measurement for BFD sessions

rejected.why: It measures loss of BFD control packets only. The document says it does not measure data traffic loss or delay, so it is mainly a BFD extension.
The NULL Auth Type provides no authentication. It is only a vehicle for a sequence number, so the document is not about authentication.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only as management protocols that access the YANG module, in Security Considerations.
The module is YANG, not a MIB or SMI module.
LAG and ECMP are mentioned only as causes of out-of-order packets and as session types in the augmented model. The document is not about them.

RFC9979.title: Registration of Further IMAP/JMAP Keywords and Mailbox Name Attributes
RFC9979.summary: Informational document defining and IANA-registering 17 IMAP/JMAP message keywords and three mailbox name attributes (Snoozed, Scheduled, Memos) already in use by mail clients and servers.

IMAP.why: The document specifies new IMAP keywords and mailbox name attributes, and their intended client and server behaviour. Readers of IMAP would want it.
IMAP.quote: This document defines 17 message keywords

JMAP.why: The keywords and attributes are registered for both IMAP and JMAP (Scope: BOTH). The text also ties them to JMAP Email properties.
JMAP.quote: When using JMAP, the "hasAttachment" Email property MUST reflect the same information as this keyword

rejected.why: The IANA registrations are the mechanism for the document. Its subject is the keyword and attribute semantics, not registry policy or stewardship.
This is the parent of IMAP and JMAP, so it is implied by the more specific tags.
MIME structure is mentioned only as something clients avoid fetching, and the document says nothing new about it.
SPF, DKIM and DMARC appear only in a negative statement about $istrusted. The document is not about email authentication.
The $canunsubscribe and $unsubscribed keywords relate to List-Unsubscribe headers (RFC 8058). They are small parts of a mail keyword document and do not define mailing list protocol.

gaps.name: JMAP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no JMAP tag, only a mention of it under email. The keywords are registered for JMAP and IMAP alike.

RFC9980.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography in OpenPGP
RFC9980.summary: Defines post-quantum algorithm extensions for OpenPGP (RFC 9580): composite ML-KEM+X25519/X448 encryption, composite ML-DSA+EdDSA signatures, and standalone SLH-DSA signatures, with packet formats, key combiner, migration guidance and test vectors.

OpenPGP.why: The document extends the OpenPGP message format with new public key algorithm IDs, packet formats and migration rules.
OpenPGP.quote: This document defines a post-quantum public key algorithm extension for the OpenPGP protocol, extending RFC 9580.

ML-KEM.why: Specifies ML-KEM-768+X25519 and ML-KEM-1024+X448 composite KEMs, including key combiner and PKESK format, for use in OpenPGP.
ML-KEM.quote: composite public key encryption based on ML-KEM (formerly CRYSTALS-Kyber)

ML-DSA.why: Specifies ML-DSA-65+Ed25519 and ML-DSA-87+Ed448 composite signatures and their packet formats.
ML-DSA.quote: composite public key signatures based on ML-DSA (formerly CRYSTALS-Dilithium)

SLH-DSA.why: Defines three SLH-DSA-SHAKE code points as standalone OpenPGP signature algorithms, with performance trade-offs.
SLH-DSA.quote: SLH-DSA (formerly SPHINCS+) as a standalone public key signature scheme

rejected.why: Its children ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA fit more specifically, so the parent is implied.
Used only as the traditional component of the composite signatures, not specified here.
X25519/X448 serve as the ECDH component, and the document only uses them as defined in RFC 7748.
AES Key Wrap and AES-256 are used as building blocks, but AES is not the subject.
SHA3-256 is used inside the key combiner, but hash functions are not the subject.
SLH-DSA is the more specific tag and already covers this.

RFC9981.title: Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Manifest Number Handling
RFC9981.summary: Updates RFC 9286 to specify how RPKI issuers and Relying Parties handle a manifest number reaching its maximum value, by having RPs reset the stored manifestNumber when the manifest filename changes, and adds manifest SIA verification.

RPKI.why: The document specifies RPKI manifest validation behaviour for CAs and Relying Parties, updating RFC 9286. RPKI readers would want it.
RPKI.quote: an RP MUST NOT reject a new manifest issued by that CA on the basis of it not having a higher manifestNumber than a previously validated manifest

rejected.why: RPKI is implied as a child of routing security, and RPKI is the more specific tag.
The document references RFC 6487 SIA entries but only to define manifest filenames. It does not profile certificates.
It is not about path validation.
RPKI is the more specific tag and already sits under PKI.

RFC9982.title: JSContact Version 2.0: A JSON Representation of Contact Data
RFC9982.summary: Defines JSContact version 2.0, making the Card uid property optional, redefines the vCard-to-JSContact uid conversion rule (updating RFC 9555), and registers the vCard JSCOMPS parameter at IANA.

JSContact.why: The document defines a new JSContact version and changes the uid property of the Card object. It is squarely about JSContact.
JSContact.quote: This document defines version "2.0" of JSContact. It defines the uid property of a Card object to be optional, rather than mandatory

vCard.why: A substantial part (Section 5 and the JSCOMPS registration) covers vCard conversion rules and the vCard Parameters registry. Readers of vCard would want it.
vCard.quote: This document updates RFC 9555 by redefining how to convert the now optional uid property from and to vCard.

rejected.why: CardDAV is mentioned only as an example of a protocol that requires uid. The document does not specify or extend it.
RDAP is cited only as an example of a protocol with no use for uid.
JSON is only the encoding substrate for JSContact. The document defines nothing new about JSON.
The IANA registry updates are boilerplate-like registrations that follow from the main change. The document is not about IANA process.

RFC9983.title: OSPFv2 Anycast Property Advertisement
RFC9983.summary: Defines a new AC-Flag (0x10) in the OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV Flags to mark anycast prefixes, notes BGP-LS carriage, and provides a companion YANG module to configure it.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPFv2 by defining a new Extended Prefix TLV flag and its processing rules.
OSPF.quote: This document defines a new flag in the OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV Flags to advertise the anycast property.

YANG.why: A substantial part of the document is the ietf-ospf-anycast-flag YANG module augmenting the OSPF YANG model.
YANG.quote: The document also specifies a companion YANG module for managing this function.

rejected.why: BGP-LS is only mentioned briefly in Section 3 as inheriting the flag; the document does not extend BGP.
The document is about advertising the anycast property in OSPFv2, not anycast addressing and operation as a subject in itself. The OSPF tag covers it.
NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the management protocols the YANG module is accessed through.
OSPFv3 is mentioned only as prior work; this document is OSPFv2 only.
Segment Routing appears only in the references to the IS-IS and OSPFv3 anycast work.

RFC9984.title: YANG Groupings for UDP Clients and UDP Servers
RFC9984.summary: Defines two YANG 1.1 modules (ietf-udp-client and ietf-udp-server) with reusable groupings for configuring UDP client and server endpoints (remote/local addresses and ports).

YANG.why: The document's main content is two YANG modules with reusable groupings, so it belongs under YANG data modelling.
YANG.quote: This document presents two YANG 1.1 [RFC7950] modules with reusable groupings for managing UDP clients and UDP servers [RFC768].

UDP.why: The modules model configuration of UDP endpoints (bind addresses, ports, remote server), so UDP readers would want it. UDP itself is not modified.
UDP.quote: This YANG module defines the "udp-server" grouping for managing UDP servers.

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only as management protocols that access the modules, mentioned in Security Considerations. The document is about the data models, not the protocol.
XML is only used for the encoding of examples.
JSON is mentioned only as an alternative example encoding.
TLS appears only in the Security Considerations boilerplate as a secure transport option.
QUIC is only mentioned in Security Considerations as a possible secure transport, and as a reference.
The document does not carry one protocol over another. It models UDP endpoint configuration.

RFC9985.title: Optimizing Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) Authentication
RFC9985.summary: Defines an experimental optimization of BFD authentication that uses a computationally heavier (MCI) mechanism for significant state changes and a lighter (LCI) mechanism for most Up packets, with periodic MCI reauthentication, a new auth section format, and a YANG augmentation for the reauth interval.

BFD.why: The whole document specifies an extension to BFD authentication procedures, signalling, and state-machine handling of Control Packets.
BFD.quote: This optimization partitions BFD Authentication into a more computationally intensive (MCI) mechanism that is applied to BFD significant changes

YANG.why: A substantial section defines the ietf-bfd-opt-auth YANG module augmenting the BFD models with a reauth-interval node, so YANG model readers would want it.
YANG.quote: The YANG 1.1 [RFC7950] data model defined in this document augments the "ietf-bfd" module to add data nodes

rejected.why: The authentication is specific to BFD, which already has a more specific tag; the generic authentication topic is not needed.
MD5 and SHA-1 are mentioned only as the existing BFD authentication mechanisms and in security considerations; the document is not about them.
SHA-1 is only background motivation, not the subject of the document.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only as management protocols in the YANG security boilerplate.
The document is a protocol optimization, not operational practice guidance.

RFC9986.title: Meticulous Keyed ISAAC for Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) Optimized Authentication
RFC9986.summary: Defines an experimental BFD Optimized Authentication mode, Meticulous Keyed ISAAC, which uses ISAAC-generated pseudorandom Auth Keys to cheaply authenticate Up-state BFD packets, alongside MD5/SHA-1 formats for state changes, plus a YANG module of identities.

BFD.why: The document extends BFD with new authentication types, PDU formats, state variables and procedures. It is squarely about BFD authentication.
BFD.quote: This document describes a Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) Optimized Authentication Mode known as Meticulous Keyed ISAAC Authentication.

rejected.why: The YANG module only adds two identities to the key-chain model. That is a minor apparatus and not the subject of the document.
MD5 is reused unchanged from RFC 5880 as the strong authentication format. The document is not about MD5.
SHA-1 is reused unchanged from RFC 5880 as the strong authentication format. The document is not about the SHA family.
ISAAC is used as the CSPRNG, and the document gives seeding and RNG considerations. But the subject is BFD authentication, not general randomness requirements.
BFD is the more specific home for this BFD-specific authentication mode, so the general authentication topic is not needed.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in the YANG security boilerplate.

gaps.name: ISAAC pseudorandom number generator
gaps.why: The document specifies how ISAAC is seeded and used as the authentication mechanism. The taxonomy has no tag for specific PRNG or stream-generator algorithms.

RFC9987.title: Secure Shell (SSH) Agent Protocol
RFC9987.summary: Specifies the SSH agent protocol, a request/response protocol by which clients ask a key agent to hold private keys, add/remove/list keys, sign data, lock/unlock, and forward agent access over SSH connections, with new IANA registries.

SSH.why: The document defines the agent protocol used with SSH, including agent forwarding channel requests and extension names registered in SSH registries.
SSH.quote: This document specifies a key agent protocol for use in the Secure Shell (SSH) protocol.

rejected.why: The agent holds keys, but the document is about the SSH agent protocol rather than key management as a general subject. The SSH tag is more specific.
ECDSA and EdDSA key formats are referenced only to define the encodings of keys added to the agent.
RSA keys and the rsa-sha2 flags are referenced as key types the agent handles. The document does not specify RSA itself.
Public key authentication is the motivating context, but the document specifies an agent protocol. It does not specify an authentication mechanism.
The IANA registries it creates are boilerplate-like and specific to the SSH agent protocol. The document is not about IANA guidance.

RFC9989.title: Domain-Based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC)
RFC9989.summary: Standards Track specification of DMARC, which lets domain owners publish DNS policy records tied to the RFC5322.From domain, requiring SPF/DKIM identifier alignment, and defines the DNS Tree Walk, receiver/owner actions and reporting hooks; obsoletes RFC 7489 and 9091.

DMARC.why: The document is the core DMARC protocol specification: policy records, alignment, tags, receiver and domain owner actions.
DMARC.quote: DMARC permits the owner of an email's Author Domain to enable validation of the domain's use to indicate the Domain Owner's or Public Suffix Operator's message handling preference

rejected.why: SPF is an underlying authentication mechanism DMARC relies on, not specified or extended here.
DKIM is a substrate authentication mechanism; the document only uses its signing domain for alignment.
DNS TXT records at _dmarc and the Tree Walk are used as the publication mechanism; no new DNS behaviour or RR type is defined.
Failure reporting formats are defined in companion RFCs 9990/9991 and RFC 6591; this document only references them.
Mailing list interoperability issues are discussed in section 7.4 but the document is not about mailing list protocols.
DMARC is anti-spoofing/phishing, not spam filtering.

RFC9990.title: Domain-Based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) Aggregate Reporting
RFC9990.summary: Specifies the XML-based DMARC aggregate reporting format, its content, delivery by email, external destination verification via DNS, and extensibility, obsoleting the reporting parts of RFC 7489.

DMARC.why: The document defines DMARC aggregate reports: their XML format, generation, delivery and verification of destinations.
DMARC.quote: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) allows for Domain Owners to request aggregate reports from receivers.

rejected.why: SPF results are reported but SPF itself is not specified or changed.
DKIM results and signature selection for reports are covered, but DKIM itself is not specified.
XML is the report encoding and schema substrate; the document is about DMARC reporting, not XML usage generally.
Email is only the transport for reports.
DNS TXT lookup for external destination verification is a small part, using existing DNS mechanisms.
The more specific DMARC tag fits.

RFC9991.title: Domain-Based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) Failure Reporting
RFC9991.summary: Specifies DMARC failure reports (per-message authentication failure reports), updating the ARF format of RFC 6591 with an Identity-Alignment field and a "dmarc" Auth-Failure type, and obsoleting RFC 7489 together with RFC 9989 and RFC 9990.

DMARC.why: The whole document specifies DMARC failure reporting: when reports are generated, external destination verification, rate limiting, and privacy handling.
DMARC.quote: This document describes "failure reports", or "failed message reports", which provide details about individual messages that failed to authenticate according to the DMARC mechanism.

ARF.why: It updates RFC 6591 ARF reporting by defining the Identity-Alignment header field and the "dmarc" Auth-Failure type, and it updates the IANA Feedback Report Header Fields registry. The change is to the ARF format itself.
ARF.quote: Operators implementing this specification also implement an augmented version of failure reporting described in [RFC6591] as follows:

rejected.why: DKIM failure fields are referenced, and DKIM appears in the example, but the document does not specify or extend DKIM itself.
SPF failure reports are only referenced and SPF-DNS is a required field. The document does not define anything about SPF.
Spam and phishing content are mentioned only as risks of unredacted reports. The document is not about spam filtering.
Privacy considerations are a substantial section, but they concern this specific reporting mechanism and not privacy as a general topic.
The multipart/report structure in the example is only the carrier format. The document does not specify MIME.
A more specific child tag fits, so the parent is not used.

RFC9992.title: Routing in Fat Trees (RIFT) Key/Value Topology Information Elements Structure and Processing
RFC9992.summary: Specifies the structure and processing of Key/Value Topology Information Elements (KV TIEs) in RIFT, including Key Types (Experimental, Well-Known, OUI), Key Sub-Types, a southbound tie-break sub-type for testing, and Key Target processing.

RIFT.why: The document extends the RIFT protocol by defining the structure, tie-breaking and targeting of KV TIEs, so RIFT readers need it.
RIFT.quote: This document specifies behavior for the various Key Types (i.e., Well-Known, Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI), and Experimental) and a method to structure corresponding values.

rejected.why: The registry creation is boilerplate-level IANA Considerations for a RIFT registry, not the document's subject.
RIFT is the more specific tag and already covers this. The document is about KV TIEs, not general routing architecture.
No relation beyond a general link-state flavour, so it does not fit.

RFC9993.title: RTP Payload Format for Haptics
RFC9993.summary: Specifies an RTP payload format for MPEG-I haptic data (MIHS units), with single, fragmented and aggregated payload structures, SDP parameters and offer/answer rules for the 'haptics' media type, and updates the RFC 9695 'haptics/hmpg' registration.

RTP payload format.why: The document's main purpose is defining a new RTP payload format for haptic media, including payload header, fragmentation and aggregation.
RTP payload format.quote: This memo specifies an RTP payload format for MPEG-I haptic data.

SDP.why: A substantial part defines SDP parameters, a new SDP media token, and offer/answer and declarative considerations for haptics.
SDP.quote: The media name in the "m=" line of SDP MUST be haptics.

media types.why: It updates the haptics/hmpg media type registration with optional parameters, which is relevant to readers of media type registrations.
media types.quote: This memo updates the 'hmpg' haptic subtype defined in [RFC9695]

rejected.why: Implied parent of RTP payload format; the more specific child applies.
The haptic coding is defined by ISO/IEC 23090-31, and this document only packetizes it. The haptic codec is not an audio or video codec in the taxonomy.
RTCP is mentioned only for loss reporting and FIR feedback and is not specified or extended here.
SRTP appears only as an option in the Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
The congestion control section only applies general RTP considerations and adds prioritisation hints, and is a minor part of the document.
TLS and DTLS are only mentioned as security options in the Security Considerations.

gaps.name: Haptics / MPEG-I haptic coding
gaps.why: The document is about haptic media transport. The taxonomy has no tag for haptics or the 'haptics' top-level media type.

RFC9994.title: MPLS Network Action (MNA) Sub-Stack Specification Including In-Stack Network Actions and Data
RFC9994.summary: Specifies the MPLS Network Action (MNA) Sub-Stack: LSE formats A-D, opcodes, scope, ordering, placement and processing rules for carrying in-stack network actions and ancillary data in an MPLS label stack, and updates RFC 9789's list of required definition information.

MPLS.why: The document defines a new label stack sub-stack encoding, a new bSPL, LSE formats and processing rules for MPLS nodes, so it belongs on the MPLS page.
MPLS.quote: This document defines the syntax and semantics of network actions and AD encoded in an MPLS label stack.

rejected.why: ECMP is only a constraint on where data may be placed in the LSEs (Section 5.2), not the subject of the document.
The IANA registries are created here, but this is routine IANA Considerations boilerplate; the main body is about the encoding.
SR-MPLS appears only in passing for MSD and Select scope examples.
OAM is cited as one possible use of network actions, but the document specifies the generic encoding rather than OAM mechanisms.

gaps.name: MPLS Network Actions (MNA)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no specific MNA tag, so a reader browsing for MNA documents can only find this RFC under the broader MPLS tag.

RFC9995.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Hash Envelope
RFC9995.summary: Defines three new COSE header parameters (payload hash algorithm, preimage content type, payload location) so a COSE_Sign1 or COSE_Mac can sign a hash of a payload and hint at where to find the original content.

COSE.why: The document extends COSE with new header parameters and a hash-envelope structure over COSE_Sign1. Readers of COSE would want it.
COSE.quote: This document defines new CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) header parameters for signaling a payload as an output of a hash function.

rejected.why: CBOR is the encoding substrate for COSE. The document defines nothing new about CBOR itself.
CDDL is used only to describe the envelope structure. The document is not about CDDL.
SHA-256 and SHA-384 appear only in examples and in the guidance on choosing a hash. The document is not about the SHA family.
An SBOM is used as an example. The mechanism is generic, so the document is not about supply chain integrity.
ES384 appears only in the example signature. The document does not specify or analyse ECDSA.
The document carries media-type names in a header parameter. It does not define media-type registration rules.

RFC9996.title: Media Types for Protocol Buffers
RFC9996.summary: Registers the application/protobuf and application/protobuf+json media types (with encoding and version parameters) for serialized Protocol Buffers payloads.

media types.why: The document's whole purpose is registering two media types for Protobuf, including parameters and deprecated aliases, so it belongs on the media types page.
media types.quote: IANA has registered application/protobuf and application/protobuf+json in the "Media Types" registry.

rejected.why: The +json suffix and the ProtoJSON encoding are used, but the document defines a media type, not anything new about JSON itself.
Base64 is only recommended for carrying binary payloads over non-binary transports. It is not the subject.
MIME is the general framework for media types. The more specific media types tag already covers this document.
TLS is mentioned only in Security Considerations as a way to get confidentiality.
The IANA registrations are the vehicle for the media type registration. The document does not give guidance on IANA registries or procedures.

gaps.name: Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) serialization
gaps.why: The document is about media types for Protobuf, but the taxonomy has no tag for Protobuf or for binary serialization formats, so readers browsing that subject have no page.

RFC9997.title: YANG-CBOR: Allocating SID Ranges for Private Enterprise Number (PEN) Holders
RFC9997.summary: Allocates two IANA YANG-SID mega-ranges whose sub-ranges of 100,000 (64-bit) and 10,000 (32-bit) SIDs are delegated to holders of IANA Private Enterprise Numbers, for use in YANG-CBOR.

YANG.why: The document allocates YANG SID ranges, which identify YANG items for YANG-CBOR. It extends the SID allocation mechanism and is aimed at YANG module authors.
YANG.quote: YANG-CBOR [RFC9254] defines YANG Schema Item iDentifiers (YANG SID), globally unique 63-bit unsigned integers used to identify YANG items.

CBOR.why: SIDs exist for the YANG-CBOR encoding, and the document discusses their representation size and delta-encoding. The CBOR encoding is not defined here, so this is a secondary tag.
CBOR.quote: This larger representation size of the absolute value of the SID is of comparatively little consequence due to the delta-encoding used for SIDs in YANG-CBOR.

IANA.why: The document's substance is a registry allocation. It creates mega-range entries and delegates management of sub-ranges via the PEN registry.
IANA.quote: this document allocates the following two mega-ranges (Section 6.3 of [RFC9595]) in the "YANG-SID Mega-Ranges" registry

rejected.why: The Private Enterprise Numbers registry originates in SNMP/SMI (RFC 1065/1155), but this document only cites it historically and is not about SNMP.
RFC 1155 is cited only to show how long PENs have existed, so the document is not about MIB modules.
The document comes from the CORE working group, but CoAP is not discussed in the body.
The YANG tag already covers this subject area more specifically.

gaps.name: Private Enterprise Numbers (PEN) registry
gaps.why: The document relies on IANA's PEN registry to delegate SID ranges. The taxonomy has no tag for enterprise numbers, so the IANA topic tag is the closest fit.

RFC9998.title: Report from the IAB/W3C Workshop on Age-Based Restrictions on Content Access
RFC9998.summary: Report of the IAB/W3C workshop on age-based restrictions on content access, summarizing discussion of roles, vocabulary, privacy and trust, architectures, and risks of age assurance and age gating.

privacy.why: Privacy and trust expectations of age assurance architectures, including ZKPs and unlinkability, are a central theme of the report and its impact and property lists.
privacy.quote: Privacy was a recurrent theme at the workshop, but it was clear that there are multiple considerations at play when talking about it.

internet architecture.why: The workshop evaluates enforcement architectures (service, network, device) against Internet architectural principles and considers roles and risks of deployment models.
internet architecture.quote: The group revisited long-standing Internet design tenets, such as decentralization and the end-to-end principle

authorization.why: Access control by age (verifier, enforcer, policy selector roles) is the core subject, which is a form of authorization and access control.
authorization.quote: The enforcer is responsible for ensuring that a person who does not satisfy the verifier is unable to access age-restricted content or services.

terminology.why: A substantial section defines a common vocabulary (age assurance, verification, estimation, inference, gating).
terminology.quote: Age assurance is an umbrella term for technology that provides some entity with information about the age of a person.

rejected.why: This is a workshop report, but the tag is likely a better fit on process grounds. I considered it and left it off in favor of the subject tags. It does fit the document type, though, so reviewers may want to add it.
Age verification touches on credentials, but the report is not about authenticating users or hosts as such.
The report concerns policy and architecture, not any specific web platform security mechanism.
Content access is mentioned, but the document does not address web architecture matters beyond general principles.

gaps.name: Age assurance / age-based content restrictions
gaps.why: The main subject, covering age verification, estimation, gating and policy, has no tag in the taxonomy. It sits between privacy, authorization and internet governance.

RFC9999.title: Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS) Conceptual Message Wrapper (CMW)
RFC9999.summary: Defines the RATS Conceptual Message Wrapper (CMW), a CBOR/JSON container (Record, Tag, Collection) for RATS conceptual messages, with a CBOR tag, JWT/CWT claims, an X.509 extension, media types and CoAP Content-Formats.

remote attestation.quote: The conceptual messages introduced by the Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS) architecture [RFC9334] are protocol-agnostic data units

RFC10001.title: Operational Guidelines for DNS Transport in Mixed IPv4/IPv6 Environments
RFC10001.summary: BCP obsoleting RFC 3901 that gives operational guidelines for authoritative servers, recursive resolvers and stub resolvers to avoid DNS name space partitioning in mixed IPv4/IPv6 environments, including fragmentation avoidance and address family selection.

DNS.why: The whole document is DNS operational practice: server configuration, delegation, glue, resolver behaviour and transport (UDP/TCP) sizing.
DNS.quote: guidelines and documents best current practice for operating authoritative DNS servers, recursive resolvers, and stub resolvers in a mixed IPv4/IPv6 environment

IPv6 transition.why: Substantial guidance on IPv4/IPv6 coexistence, dual-stack requirements, PREF64/NAT64 synthesis and IPv4-embedded addresses for resolvers.
IPv6 transition.quote: a recursive DNS resolver MAY be IPv6-only if it uses a transition mechanism that allows it to also query IPv4-only authoritative DNS servers

rejected.why: EDNS(0) buffer sizes are discussed only as a fragmentation-avoidance knob, with no new EDNS specification.
PMTUD is discussed as a reason to cap sizes and MSS, but the document is not about PMTUD itself.
NAT64/PREF64 appear as conditions affecting resolvers; the document does not specify or analyse NAT64.
DNS-over-TCP MSS recommendations are DNS operational guidance; TCP is not itself specified or extended.
Mentioned only for large DNSKEY responses that cause fragmentation.
IPv6 support is recommended for DNS servers, but the document is about DNS operations rather than IPv6 itself; IPv6 transition covers the coexistence aspect.

RFC10002.title: Certificate Management over CMS (CMC)
RFC10002.summary: RFC 10002 specifies the base syntax of CMC, a PKI certificate enrollment and management protocol built on CMS and PKCS #10/CRMF, covering PKI requests and responses, controls, RA handling and CMC server certificate requirements, and it obsoletes RFC 5272 and RFC 6402.

PKI.why: CMC is a PKI enrollment and certificate management protocol covering certification requests, revocation, CRL and certificate retrieval, RAs and trust anchor publication. No narrower PKI tag fits, because CMC is not CMP, EST, ACME or OCSP.
PKI.quote: a Certificate Management protocol using the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)

CMS.why: The protocol is defined in terms of CMS content types (SignedData, AuthenticatedData, EnvelopedData, AuthEnvelopedData). It adds new CMS content types (PKIData, PKIResponse), an unsigned attribute and the AuthEnvelopedData support. CMS readers would want it.
CMS.quote: PKI Responses are based on SignedData or AuthenticatedData [CMS].

rejected.why: CMC requests X.509 certificates and defines EKUs and an SIA access method for CMC servers. That is a small part of the document, and it does not profile certificates.
Appendix A gives the ASN.1 modules, but ASN.1 is only the notation used to define the protocol.
S/MIME is mentioned only as a requirement source and for contrast. The document is not about secure email.
HMAC is used for identity proof and POP witnesses, but it is only a building block.
PBKDF2 appears in the Appendix A.2 module as a PRF/KDF import for POP link witnesses. It is incidental, not the subject.
KEM and ML-KEM certificates appear only in an example and the changes list.

RFC10003.title: Certificate Management over CMS (CMC): Transport Protocols
RFC10003.summary: Defines how Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) messages are carried over file, mail (MIME), HTTP and TCP transports (port 5318), obsoleting RFCs 5273 and 6402.

transport mapping.why: The whole document binds CMC messages to file, mail, HTTP and TCP transports, which is what a transport mapping is.
transport mapping.quote: This document defines a number of transport methods that are used to move CMC messages

PKI.why: CMC is a PKI certificate enrollment protocol. This document is part of its specification, with PKI requests and responses, the TCP port assignment and PKI-specific security guidance. The taxonomy has no CMC tag, so PKI is the closest fit.
PKI.quote: Certificate Management over CMS (CMC): Transport Protocols

rejected.why: HTTP is only the carrier. The document gives a short POST-based usage profile and defers to HTTP specifications and RFC 9205, so it is not about HTTP.
TCP is only a transport here. The new content is a port registration and framing for CMC, not a change to TCP.
The mail binding borrows MIME wrapping and smime-type values from S/MIME. It explicitly differs from a standard S/MIME message and does not specify S/MIME.
The document uses existing media types (application/pkcs7-mime, application/pkcs10) and only repoints smime-type registry references. It does not define a media type registration.
CMS is the message format that CMC uses. It is defined elsewhere, in RFC 10002, and this document only moves the messages.
TLS is only the secure channel the document points to, with a restriction on early data. The document defines nothing new for TLS.
Mail transport is covered only by a MIME-wrapping convention. The SMTP-over-TLS discussion appears only in the Security Considerations.

gaps.name: CMC (Certificate Management over CMS)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no CMC tag. The document and its companion RFC 10002 are about this PKI enrollment protocol, so readers of a CMC page would expect to find it.

RFC10004.title: Certificate Management over CMS (CMC): Compliance Requirements
RFC10004.summary: Specifies compliance requirements (MUST/SHOULD levels for algorithms, controls, CRMF features) for End-Entities, RAs and CAs implementing Certificate Management over CMS (CMC), obsoleting RFCs 5274 and 6402.

PKI.why: CMC is a PKI certificate enrollment protocol with no dedicated tag; the document specifies compliance for EEs, RAs and CAs, so PKI is the best fit.
PKI.quote: This document provides a set of compliance statements about the Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) enrollment protocol.

CMS.why: CMC is built on CMS, and a substantial part of the document sets algorithm requirements for SignedData, EnvelopedData, AuthEnvelopedData and AuthenticatedData.
CMS.quote: CMS:  Refers to the Cryptographic Message Syntax [CMS].  This document provides for basic cryptographic services including encryption and signing

rejected.why: Certificates are the subject of enrollment, but the document does not profile X.509 certificates themselves.
AES-GCM and AES key wrap are required algorithms within CMS, but the document is not about AES.
HTTP is only the mandatory transport, which is defined in RFC 10003.
PBKDF2 is only required as a key derivation function for PasswordRecipientInfo. The document does not specify it.
RSA is mentioned as a required signature and key transport algorithm, but it is not the subject.

gaps.name: Certificate Management over CMS (CMC)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no CMC tag. CMC is a distinct enrollment protocol family (RFCs 10002, 10003, 10004, 5272-5274, 6402), so a dedicated tag under PKI would suit it.

RFC10005.title: BGP Link Bandwidth Extended Community
RFC10005.summary: Defines the transitive and non-transitive BGP Link Bandwidth Extended Community, its format, and sender, receiver, and re-advertisement procedures for weighted load-balancing in multipath.

BGP.why: The document extends BGP with a new extended community and specifies its processing, re-advertisement, multipath and error handling rules.
BGP.quote: defines a BGP extended community, the Link Bandwidth Extended Community, which carries bandwidth information to enable weighted load-balancing in multipath scenarios

rejected.why: The taxonomy entry covers standard, extended and large communities. This document defines one specific extended community type. It is a plausible fit, but BGP is the safer general tag. I chose BGP because the document is mainly about the Link Bandwidth feature and its procedures.
Weighted load-balancing is the use case, but the document says weighted load-balancing details are out of scope. It specifies only the community.
The IANA section only updates two sub-type registry entries. That is boilerplate and not the subject.

RFC10006.title: Automatic SIP Trunking and Peering
RFC10006.summary: Specifies a framework in which an enterprise SIP edge device retrieves, over HTTPS with OAuth, a JSON capability-set document from a SIP service provider, defined by a new YANG module, to automate SIP trunk peering configuration.

SPEERMINT.why: The document is about automatic SIP trunking and peering between enterprise and service provider networks, which fits the SIP peering/interconnect subject.
SPEERMINT.quote: enables enterprise telephony Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) networks to solicit and obtain a capability set document from a SIP service provider

YANG.why: A substantial part of the document defines the ietf-sip-auto-peering YANG module, with a tree diagram, an extension example, and an IANA-maintained module.
YANG.quote: the YANG module [RFC7950] for encoding the service provider capability set

WebFinger.why: The document specifies WebFinger as a discovery mechanism for the capability server URL, with an example exchange using the sipTrunkingCapability link relation.
WebFinger.quote: if the resource URL is unknown to the administrator (and by extension, to the edge element), the WebFinger protocol [RFC7033]

rejected.why: SIP is the setting that the capability set describes. The document does not extend SIP itself, so the more specific SPEERMINT tag was chosen.
HTTP GET is used only as the transport for retrieving the document. The document does not extend HTTP.
OAuth 2.0 is mandated for client authentication, but the implementation is explicitly out of scope and the document only illustrates a flow.
JSON is only the encoding of the capability document, so it is a substrate and not the subject.
TLS is required to secure the HTTP exchange, but the document defines nothing new about it.
STIR compliance and ACME delegation appear only as a few leaves in the data model. They are not a substantial part of the document.

RFC10007.title: Clarification to Processing Key Usage Values During Certificate Revocation List (CRL) Validation
RFC10007.summary: Updates RFC 5280's CRL validation step (6.3.3(f)) to require that a v3 CRL issuer certificate contain the keyUsage extension with cRLSign asserted, closing a hole where indirect CRLs could be signed with non-certified keys.

X.509.why: The document amends the RFC 5280 X.509 certificate and CRL profile, specifically the CRL validation algorithm and keyUsage handling.
X.509.quote: Section 4.2.1.3 of [RFC5280] requires CRL issuer certificates to contain the keyUsage extension with the cRLSign bit asserted.

rejected.why: X.509 is the more specific child tag and already covers this. PKI is only implied as an ancestor.
The document covers CRL-based revocation only. OCSP is not discussed.
The keyUsage check is a certificate validation matter, not an access-control topic.

RFC10008.title: The HTTP QUERY Method
RFC10008.summary: Defines the HTTP QUERY method, a safe and idempotent request that carries query content in the body, along with its caching, conditional request and redirection semantics and the Accept-Query response field.

HTTP.why: The document defines a new HTTP method and a new header field, and specifies how they interact with HTTP semantics such as redirection, conditional requests and range requests.
HTTP.quote: This specification defines the QUERY method for HTTP.

HTTP caching.why: A substantial section specifies how QUERY responses are cached, including cache key construction and content normalization.
HTTP caching.quote: The cache key for a QUERY request (Section 2 of [HTTP-CACHING]) MUST incorporate the request content

rejected.why: QUERY is an HTTP method extension, not a convention for building APIs on HTTP such as problem details or rate limits.
URIs appear only as the Location and Content-Location values and as a contrast with query components. The document does not specify URI syntax or schemes.
JSON is used only in the example payloads and does not define anything new for JSON.
WebDAV methods are mentioned only in Appendix B as alternatives that were considered when choosing the name.
The document describes how media types and status codes apply to QUERY requests, but this is ordinary HTTP content negotiation. It is not about media feature negotiation as a subject.

RFC10013.title: Entity Attestation Token (EAT) Measured Component
RFC10013.summary: Defines the measured component information model and CBOR/JSON data models, with media types and CoAP Content-Formats, for use in the EAT Measurement claim to carry attester measurements.

remote attestation.why: The document defines a format for attester evidence (measurements) in EAT, the RATS attestation framework. Remote attestation is its central subject.
remote attestation.quote: The term "measured component" refers to an object within the attester's target environment whose state can be sampled and typically digested using a cryptographic hash function.

CDDL.why: The data models are specified in CDDL, with a collated CDDL appendix. The CDDL usage is substantive, but the document is not about CDDL itself, so the tag is secondary.
CDDL.quote: CDDL is used to express rules and constraints of the data model for both JSON and CBOR.

media types.why: The document registers two new media types, application/measured-component+cbor and +json. It also registers matching CoAP Content-Formats, which the EAT framework uses to identify the measurement format.
media types.quote: IANA has added the following media types to the "Media Types" registry

rejected.why: CBOR is only one of the two serializations the data model uses. The document is not about CBOR itself.
JSON is only one of the two serializations the data model uses. The document is not about JSON itself.
CoAP Content-Formats are only used as identifiers for the measurement format. The document does not extend or profile CoAP.
The document refers to CWT and JWT carriage only through EAT. It does not specify COSE signing or encryption.
RFC 9019 is cited only as an example of where signatures are verified. The document does not address firmware update.

gaps.name: Entity Attestation Token (EAT) / RATS remote attestation
gaps.why: The taxonomy has only a generic 'remote attestation' tag. It has no tag for EAT or the RATS architecture as a framework, which is where this document's evidence format belongs.

RFC10014.title: Guidelines for Characterizing the Term "OAM"
RFC10014.summary: BCP that extends RFC 6291 by recommending against "in-band"/"out-of-band" for OAM and defining replacement qualifiers (Active/Passive/Hybrid, In-Data-Packet, Path-Congruent, Equal/Different-Forwarding-Treatment).

OAM.why: The whole document is terminology guidance for qualifying OAM, so the OAM topic fits directly.
OAM.quote: This document recommends avoiding the terms "in-band" and "out-of-band" when referring to OAM.

terminology.why: It defines a vocabulary of terms and gives guidance on their use in IETF documents. Readers of the terminology page would want it.
terminology.quote: The definitions here SHOULD be used by IETF documents qualifying the term "OAM".

rejected.why: It cites RFC 7799's active and passive methods, but only to classify OAM terms. It does not specify measurement methods.
BFD is mentioned only as an example of an OAM protocol that does not get equal forwarding treatment.
VCCV appears only as an example of path-congruent OAM.
RFC 9551 is cited as a source of 'in-band' terminology usage. The document is not about DetNet.
MPLS echo and loss measurement are only examples used to illustrate the terms.
IOAM and alternate marking are examples for the classification. The document does not address telemetry itself.

RFC10015.title: Deprecating Obsolete Key Exchange Methods in TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2
RFC10015.summary: Standards Track update deprecating finite-field DH (static and ephemeral) and static RSA key exchange cipher suites in (D)TLS 1.2, discouraging static ECDH, and updating RFC 9325 and the IANA TLS registries accordingly.

TLS.why: The document sets TLS/DTLS 1.2 cipher suite and key exchange requirements, updating RFC 5246, RFC 9325 and the TLS registries. DTLS is implied by TLS, so only TLS is tagged.
TLS.quote: Clients MUST NOT offer and servers MUST NOT select RSA cipher suites in (D)TLS 1.2 connections.

rejected.why: Static RSA key exchange in TLS is deprecated, but the document is about TLS cipher suite policy, not the RSA algorithm itself.
DTLS 1.2 is covered together with TLS 1.2, but the document is about the shared cipher suite policy and has no DTLS-specific content. Tagging TLS is enough.
Static ECDH suites are discouraged, but only as one group of deprecated cipher suites. The document does not specify or analyse elliptic curve cryptography.
The registry updates in Sections 5 and 7 are the mechanism that records the deprecations. The document is not about IANA registry stewardship.
Camellia and ARIA suites appear only as rows in the deprecation tables, not as subjects of the document.

RFC10016.title: System-Defined Configuration
RFC10016.summary: Defines a read-only "system" conventional configuration datastore in NMDA holding system-provided configuration that clients can reference, override, or extend in running, and updates RFC 8342 with a new YANG identity module.

YANG.why: The document defines a new YANG module (ietf-system-datastore) with a new datastore identity and updates the YANG-based NMDA datastore model, so YANG readers need it.
YANG.quote: This document updates the NMDA defined in [RFC8342] with a read-only conventional configuration datastore called "system" to expose system-defined configuration.

NETCONF.why: The system datastore is accessed via NETCONF get-data, and the document specifies how the datastore is exposed to NETCONF clients.
NETCONF.quote: NETCONF / RESTCONF clients can benefit from a standard mechanism to retrieve what system configuration is available on a server.
