RESTCONF.why: The document specifies the RESTCONF resource for accessing the new datastore, so RESTCONF readers will want it.
RESTCONF.quote: the system configuration datastore can be accessed via the resource: {+restconf}/ds/ietf-system-datastore:system.

rejected.why: The parent topic is implied by the YANG/NETCONF tags and no broader operational subject is addressed.
XML is only the encoding used in examples.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a secure transport.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a secure transport.
Mentioned only in Security Considerations as a secure transport.
The ACL module is a fictional example and not a subject of the document.

gaps.name: NMDA (Network Management Datastore Architecture)
gaps.why: The document updates RFC 8342's NMDA and datastore model; the taxonomy has no NMDA tag, so YANG is the closest fit.

RFC10017.title: OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications
RFC10017.summary: A BCP describing threats, architecture patterns (BFF, token-mediating backend, browser-only client), token storage, and security practices for OAuth 2.0 clients in browser-based JavaScript applications.

OAuth.why: The whole document is OAuth 2.0 best practice for browser-based clients: grant types, PKCE, refresh tokens, DPoP, and architectures.
OAuth.quote: This specification describes different architectural patterns for implementing OAuth 2.0 clients in applications executing in a browser.

web security.why: Substantial coverage of XSS, CSRF, CORS, CSP, origin isolation and browser token storage, which are web platform security matters.
web security.quote: Malicious JavaScript poses a significant risk to browser-based applications.

cookies.why: Defines cookie flags, prefixes and session handling for the BFF pattern, and advises against storing tokens in cookies.
cookies.quote: The BFF MUST enable the HttpOnly flag for its cookies.

rejected.why: HTTP is only the substrate for the OAuth flows and proxying; no HTTP protocol extension is defined.
ID tokens and JWTs are not discussed beyond OpenID Connect mentions.
OpenID Connect is mentioned only as a side case and is out of scope.
Bearer tokens are mentioned, but the document is about OAuth client architecture, not HTTP auth schemes.
The OAuth tag already covers the authorization subject here.

gaps.name: DPoP (Demonstrating Proof of Possession) / sender-constrained tokens
gaps.why: The document discusses sender-constrained tokens at length, but it is specified in RFC 9449 and the taxonomy has no DPoP tag.

RFC10018.title: Multicast and Ethernet VPN with Segment Routing Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) and Ingress Replication
RFC10018.summary: Specifies BGP encodings and procedures for using SR P2MP trees (SR-MPLS and SRv6) and ingress replication as P-tunnels in MVPN and EVPN, including new SRv6 End.DTMC endpoint behaviors, PTA tunnel types, and Color-based SLA for IR.

MVPN.why: Updates RFC 6514 and 7988 for MVPN A-D procedures, PTA encoding and ingress replication over SR; a major part of the document.
MVPN.quote: This document specifies extensions to BGP encodings and procedures for P2MP trees and Ingress Replication used in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs and Ethernet VPNs

EVPN.why: Section 4 specifies EVPN IMET/S-PMSI procedures, split-horizon filtering and IR with SR P2MP trees.
EVPN.quote: For BGP MPLS-Based EVPN specified in [RFC7432] and updated in [RFC9572], P-tunnels are advertised for handling multi-destination traffic.

segment routing.why: Defines End.DTMC4/6/46 SRv6 behaviors and uses SR P2MP policies and Tree-SIDs. SR-MPLS and SRv6 are both used, so the parent tag fits.
segment routing.quote: This document defines new SRv6 Endpoint behaviors [RFC8986] used for MVPN with SR P2MP and IR P-tunnels.

rejected.why: BGP is the signalling carrier; it is extended only through MVPN/EVPN route attributes, so the VPN tags fit better.
The new behaviors are SRv6 endpoint behaviors, but the document covers both SR-MPLS and SRv6 and its subject is VPN multicast, so the parent segment routing tag is used.
SR-MPLS is one of two data planes covered, not the document's subject alone.
PCEP is mentioned only as an out-of-scope controller protocol.
Multicast is covered through MVPN, the more specific tag.

RFC10019.title: Zeroconf Multicast Address Allocation Problem Statement and Requirements
RFC10019.summary: Problem statement and requirements for lightweight, decentralized zeroconf allocation of multicast group addresses, covering link-layer address collisions, IPv4/IPv6 considerations and excluded solutions.

multicast.why: The whole document is about allocating multicast group addresses and avoiding MAC-layer collisions, including IGMP/MLD snooping effects. No narrower multicast child tag fits, since it is a new problem statement rather than MADCAP itself.
multicast.quote: defines a set of requirements for decentralized, zero-configuration multicast address allocation solutions

addressing.why: Substantial parts cover IPv4/IPv6 multicast address allocation, group ID ranges and mapping of IP multicast addresses to Ethernet addresses.
addressing.quote: Collisions occur when two or more multicast groups are assigned the same link-layer (MAC) address

rejected.why: MADCAP is cited only as a server-based approach unsuited to zeroconf. The document does not specify or extend it.
IGMP/MLD snooping is mentioned only as background for the switch-collision problem. The document is not about the protocol.
IPv6 multicast allocation rules are discussed in one section, but the document is not about IPv6 itself.
CONS-6 touches on advertising allocated addresses, but only as a desirable property, not a main subject.
Ethernet MAC mapping appears only as the source of the collisions, not as the subject.

gaps.name: Zeroconf multicast address allocation
gaps.why: The document's core subject, decentralized multicast address assignment without servers, has no dedicated tag. Only the broad multicast and addressing tags exist, and the MADCAP tag covers the server-based protocol.

RFC10020.title: Group Communication for the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)
RFC10020.summary: Standards Track specification of CoAP group communication over UDP/IP multicast, defining group types, request/response, caching, Observe and block-wise behaviour, proxy operation, congestion control, and secure operation with Group OSCORE; obsoletes RFC 7390 and updates RFC 7252 and RFC 7641.

CoAP.why: The document specifies and updates CoAP behaviour (response suppression, token reuse, caching, Observe, congestion control) for group communication.
CoAP.quote: This document specifies the use of CoAP for group communication, including the use of UDP/IP multicast as the default underlying data transport.

OSCORE.why: A substantial part (Section 5, security considerations) defines Group OSCORE as the mandatory security solution, covering group management, proxy security and amplification mitigation.
OSCORE.quote: Secure group communication is achieved by using Group Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments (Group OSCORE)

multicast.why: IP multicast is the default transport, with substantial text on scopes, MLD/IGMP, RPL and MPL interworking, and multicast-specific congestion and amplification risks.
multicast.quote: One-to-many group communication can be achieved in CoAP, by a client using UDP/IP multicast data transport to send multicast CoAP request messages

rejected.why: 6LoWPAN is discussed as a deployment environment for multicast, but the document is not about 6LoWPAN itself.
RPL and MPL are described only as interworking context for multicast delivery, not specified or extended.
Amplification attacks are covered as a security consideration, but the document is not about DDoS mitigation in its own right.
Group discovery is addressed via the RD and /.well-known/core, but it is a part of group configuration, not the document's main subject.
UDP is the substrate transport; the document defines nothing new about UDP.
COSE is used by OSCORE underneath and is not the document's subject.

RFC10021.title: Group Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments (Group OSCORE)
RFC10021.summary: Defines Group OSCORE, which extends OSCORE to give end-to-end protection and source authentication for CoAP group (e.g. multicast) requests and responses. It has a group mode using countersignatures and a pairwise mode using derived keys, plus Group Manager and keying-material rules.

OSCORE.why: The document defines Group OSCORE, an extension of OSCORE (security context, COSE object, header compression, message processing). OSCORE is the specified protocol, and the taxonomy places it under CoAP.
OSCORE.quote: Group OSCORE, providing end-to-end security of messages exchanged with the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) between members of a group, e.g., sent over IP multicast.

multicast security.why: A substantial part covers group keying material, rekeying, Group Manager duties, and group-level source authentication for multicast groups. Group key management and multicast security is a fitting topic.
multicast security.quote: Every group is associated with a Group Manager that is responsible for distributing security parameters and keying material within the group

rejected.why: CoAP is the protocol being secured. Its child tag OSCORE already covers the document, so the parent is implied.
COSE structures are used and a countersignature parameter is applied, but the document does not define COSE. It is the substrate.
The ACE-based Group Manager is only referenced as an informative realization and is out of scope here.
ECDH and Ed25519-to-X25519 mapping appear, but they are details of pairwise key derivation and not the subject.
The 'gosc' link attribute (Section 11) is only a minor addition, and the document is not about web linking in general.
DTLS is mentioned only as a combinable alternative. The document does not specify or extend it.

RFC10022.title: IMAP UIDBATCHES Extension
RFC10022.summary: Defines the IMAP UIDBATCHES extension, a command that returns UID ranges partitioning a mailbox into equally sized batches, especially for UIDONLY clients.

IMAP.why: The document specifies a new IMAP capability, command, response and response codes.
IMAP.quote: The UIDBATCHES extension of the Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) allows clients to retrieve Unique Identifier (UID) ranges that partition a mailbox's messages

rejected.why: IMAP is the more specific tag, and it sits under email.
ABNF is only used to write the formal syntax, so the document is not about it.
The IANA section only registers the capability and response codes. That is boilerplate.

gaps.name: IMAP extensions (UIDONLY, PARTIAL, MESSAGELIMIT)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for the IMAP protocol or its extensions. IMAP is the sibling of POP3 under email, so I used the nearest existing tag, which is IMAP. However, that id is not in the taxonomy as I read it, so no valid tag fits exactly.

RFC10023.title: The "_for-sale" Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Name
RFC10023.summary: Defines an operational convention using the underscored DNS leaf node name "_for-sale" with TXT records (version tag plus fcod/ftxt/furi/fval content tags) to signal that a registered domain name is available for purchase, and registers it in the attrleaf registry.

DNS.why: The document defines a new underscored DNS node name and TXT record format, including wildcard, placement, TTL and RRset rules. It is a DNS operational convention.
DNS.quote: uses the reserved underscored DNS leaf node name "_for-sale" to indicate the parent domain name is available for purchase

domain registration.why: The convention signals domain availability for sale. It is meant for registries, registrars and availability-check services, and it complements WHOIS/RDAP. Readers of the domain registration subject would want it.
domain registration.quote: Some registrars and other parties offer brokerage services between domain name holders and interested buyers.

rejected.why: WHOIS and RDAP are mentioned only as conventional ways to get contact information. The document does not specify or extend them.
RDAP is cited only as an existing registration-data service and is not extended.
Special-use domain names are explicitly out of scope. The document only places a node name in the global DNS.
The furi tag carries URIs, but the document only uses URI syntax defined elsewhere. It defines nothing new about URIs.
ABNF is only the notation used to define the record format.
EPP appears only as a reference to domain status values. The document does not specify or extend it.

gaps.name: Underscored and globally scoped DNS node names (attrleaf)
gaps.why: The document registers a new entry in this IANA registry. The taxonomy has no tag for attrleaf or underscored names, so the DNS tag is the closest fit.

RFC10024.title: Post-Quantum Traditional (PQ/T) Hybrid Key Agreement Mechanisms for TLS 1.3
RFC10024.summary: Defines three TLS 1.3 hybrid key agreement groups (X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024) combining ML-KEM with ECDHE, specifying client/server shares, shared secret construction and IANA code points.

ML-KEM.why: The document specifies how ML-KEM is used in hybrid key establishment, including encapsulation key checks and ciphertext handling in TLS.
ML-KEM.quote: defines three hybrid key agreement mechanisms for TLS 1.3 -- X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768, and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 -- that combine the post-quantum ML-KEM

TLS.why: It defines new TLS 1.3 supported groups, key_exchange formats and code points. This is a new TLS extension-style registration that TLS readers need.
TLS.quote: This document introduces three new supported groups for Post-Quantum Traditional (PQ/T) hybrid key agreements [RFC9794] in TLS 1.3

rejected.why: X25519, P-256 and P-384 ECDHE are components of the hybrid. The document does not define or analyse the curves themselves.
X25519 is only one traditional component, specified in RFC 7748. The document is not about it.
The more specific child ML-KEM applies, so the parent is implied.
This is key agreement within TLS, not general key management. The more specific tags cover it.
HKDF is mentioned only in the regulatory notes and is not the subject of the document.
The registry entries are marked DTLS-OK, but the document does not address DTLS.

gaps.name: Hybrid key exchange (PQ/T hybrid)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for post-quantum/traditional hybrid key establishment. It is the central subject of this RFC and its framework RFC 9954.

RFC10026.title: Operational Recommendations for DNSSEC Delegation Signer (DS) Automation
RFC10026.summary: A BCP giving operational recommendations for registries and registrars automating DNSSEC DS record provisioning from CDS/CDNSKEY: acceptance checks, TTLs, reporting, registration locks, and multi-party suspension of automation.

DNSSEC.why: The whole document is about DS automation for DNSSEC delegations: acceptance checks, DS TTLs, bootstrapping, rollovers and removal.
DNSSEC.quote: automate DNSSEC [RFC9364] delegation trust maintenance by having the child publish Child DS (CDS) and/or Child DNSKEY (CDNSKEY) records

domain registration.why: Substantial parts cover registry and registrar behaviour: registration locks, notifying registrars, and registry versus registrar automation. EPP and RDAP are only referenced, so the parent topic fits.
domain registration.quote: when using the registrant-registrar-registry (RRR) model (as is common amongst top-level domains (TLDs)), both the registrar and the registry can effect parent-side changes

rejected.why: EPP lock statuses and the Change Poll extension are cited as examples, but the document specifies nothing new about EPP.
RDAP is mentioned once as a way to retrieve the DS TTL, so it is not a subject of the document.
DNSSEC is the more specific tag. Generalized notifications and error reporting are only used as mechanisms.
The recommendations are operational practice for DNSSEC delegation maintenance, and DNSSEC already covers that.

gaps.name: DS automation / CDS and CDNSKEY
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for CDS/CDNSKEY-based delegation trust maintenance (RFC 7344, 8078, 9615). DNSSEC is the closest fit.

RFC10027.title: Best Current Practice for Security of Cross-Device Flows
RFC10027.summary: A BCP describing phishing-style threats (CDCP/CDSP) against cross-device authorization and session-transfer flows such as the OAuth device grant and CIBA, with mitigations, protocol selection guidance and formal analysis results.

OAuth.why: The document analyses attacks on OAuth device authorization grant and related flows, and gives mitigations such as sender-constrained tokens, limited scopes and short-lived tokens.
OAuth.quote: The device authorization grant [RFC8628] and Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication (CIBA) [CIBA] are two examples of popular cross-device authorization flows.

authentication.why: Substantial parts cover user authentication and phishing-resistant authentication in cross-device flows, and recommend FIDO/WebAuthn CDA as protocol guidance.
authentication.quote: FIDO2/WebAuthn SHOULD be used for cross-device authentication scenarios whenever the devices are capable of doing so

rejected.why: Recommended as the protocol of choice in one section, but the document is not about specifying or profiling WebAuthn.
Mentioned only as a formal analysis result in 6.3.
Privacy is mentioned only in passing for proximity and device-identity mechanisms.
Not discussed at all.
Not relevant; BLE and QR codes are the transports considered.

gaps.name: Phishing / social engineering attacks (CDCP/CDSP)
gaps.why: The core subject is phishing-style attacks on authorization flows. The taxonomy's general security topic has no specific tag for it.

RFC10028.title: Updates to Dynamic IPv6 Multicast Address Group IDs
RFC10028.summary: Updates RFC 3307 by replacing its dynamic IPv6 multicast group ID range with a new IANA "Dynamic Multicast Group IDs" registry, with initial ranges for MADCAP, SSM host allocation, private use, experimental use and Solicited-Node addresses.

addressing.why: The document reallocates IPv6 multicast group ID ranges, which is address architecture and allocation. No more specific addressing child tag fits, and the MADCAP and SSM tags do not cover the allocation itself.
addressing.quote: replacing these allocations with a new IANA registry in the "IPv6 Multicast Address Space" registry group

MADCAP.why: MADCAP's range is reduced, and the document gives implementation and deployment guidance for it. MADCAP is one of the main subjects of the change.
MADCAP.quote: This document reduces the range of group ID values available for MADCAP [RFC2730].

SSM.why: A whole section and a new SSM host-allocation range address how Source-Specific Multicast affects dynamic group ID assignment.
SSM.quote: This document defines a range of dynamic IPv6 multicast group IDs for use in environments that do support SSM.

IANA.why: The core deliverable is a new IANA registry, with its policy, fields and initial contents. It sits in the main body and is not boilerplate.
IANA.quote: IANA has created a new registry named "Dynamic Multicast Group IDs" in the "IPv6 Multicast Address Space" registry group.

rejected.why: IPv6 is the context, but the document is about multicast group ID allocation, which addressing covers more specifically.
The more specific MADCAP and SSM tags are chosen, so this parent is implied.
Only the standard copyright boilerplate appears, and it says nothing about the subject.

RFC10029.title: DNS Multiple QTYPEs
RFC10029.summary: Defines EDNS options (MQTYPE-Query and MQTYPE-Response) letting a DNS client request additional RR types alongside the primary QTYPE in one query, with server and client processing rules.

EDNS.why: The document defines new EDNS option codes 20 and 21 and their format and processing, and registers them with IANA. This is a new EDNS option specification.
EDNS.quote: specifying a new option for the Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS) [RFC6891] that contains an additional list of QTYPE values

DNS.why: It extends DNS query and response behaviour for stub, recursive and authoritative servers, including RCODE and flag handling and RRset combination. EDNS is the child tag and DNS is the broader subject of the document.
DNS.quote: A commonly requested DNS [STD13] feature is the ability to receive multiple related resource records (RRs) in a single DNS response.

rejected.why: The examples show DNSSEC records (RRSIG, NSEC3, DS, DNSKEY) and the DO bit. The mechanism itself is DNSSEC-agnostic, and DNSSEC appears only in illustrations.
It is mentioned only as an applicable use case, and the document is not about service discovery.
It is explicitly excluded from the scope of this document.

RFC10030.title: Network Time Protocol (NTP) over the Precision Time Protocol (PTP)
RFC10030.summary: Specifies a transport that encapsulates NTP client-server and symmetric mode messages in PTP event messages via an organization-specific TLV, plus a new NTP Network Correction extension field to use PTP transparent clock corrections.

NTP.why: The document extends NTP with a new transport and a new extension field, and specifies NTP client/server/peer behaviour over it.
NTP.quote: This document specifies a transport for the client-server and symmetric modes of the Network Time Protocol (NTP) that encapsulates NTP messages in messages of the Precision Time Protocol (PTP).

PTP.why: Defines a new PTP organization-specific TLV and a PTP TLV subtypes registry, and relies on PTP hardware timestamping and transparent clock corrections.
PTP.quote: It adds a new type-length-value (TLV) for PTP to contain NTP messages

rejected.why: UDP is only one of the PTP transports mentioned (port 319); the document is not about UDP usage.
IANA registry creation is boilerplate-level here; the body is about the transport, not IANA guidance.
Parent of NTP and PTP, already implied by those tags.
IPv4/IPv6 mentioned only as available PTP mappings.

RFC10031.title: Media Access Control (MAC) Addresses in X.509 Certificates
RFC10031.summary: Defines a new X.509 otherName form (id-on-MACAddress) carrying EUI-48/EUI-64 MAC addresses in SAN/IAN extensions, plus encoding and path-validation rules for Name Constraints on that name form.

X.509.why: The document extends X.509 certificates with a new GeneralName.otherName for SAN/IAN and defines Name Constraints processing for it, building on the RFC 5280 profile.
X.509.quote: This document defines a new otherName form "MACAddress".

rejected.why: X.509 is the more specific child tag and already covers the PKI subject; the parent is implied.
MAC addresses are the identifier being bound to certificates, but the document does not specify Ethernet or IP over Ethernet.
The document includes an ASN.1 module, but ASN.1 is only the notation used for the definition.
IoT and automotive networks are mentioned only as motivation in the introduction.
There is a short privacy considerations subsection, but the document is not mainly about privacy.

RFC10032.title: The AEGIS Authenticated Encryption Algorithms
RFC10032.summary: Specifies the AEGIS-128L, AEGIS-256, AEGIS-128X and AEGIS-256X AES-based AEAD algorithms, their use as stream ciphers and MACs, with security guidance and test vectors.

AEGIS.why: The whole document specifies the AEGIS AEAD family, including parallel modes, stream cipher and MAC uses.
AEGIS.quote: This document describes the AEGIS-128L, AEGIS-256, AEGIS-128X, and AEGIS-256X AES-based authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) algorithms

rejected.why: AES round function is only a building block; the document specifies a different cipher family.
Only mentioned in comparison and HKDF reference in security considerations.
SHA-256 mentioned only as an optional hash for committing security.
HKDF mention is incidental advice; the document doesn't address key management.

gaps.name: AEAD (authenticated encryption algorithms)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no general AEAD tag; the AEGIS tag does cover this one, but other AEAD documents (AES-GCM, CCM) have no home besides the cryptography parent.

RFC10033.title: Hash-Based Signatures: State and Backup Management
RFC10033.summary: Informational guidance on operational and technical state and backup management for stateful hash-based signature schemes (LMS/HSS, XMSS/XMSS^MT), cataloguing state management approaches and a backup mechanism beyond NIST SP 800-208.

hash-based signatures.why: The whole document is about deploying stateful hash-based signatures and managing their OTS key state and backups. This is the most specific fitting tag for the subject.
hash-based signatures.quote: Stateful Hash-Based Signature Schemes (Stateful HBS) such as Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS), Hierarchical Signature System (HSS), eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme (XMSS), and XMSS^MT combine Merkle trees

key management.why: Substantial parts cover key export, import, transfer, backup and recovery of private key material. These are key management topics, and Section 6 gives a concrete backup procedure.
key management.quote: backup management refers to all mechanisms surrounding the goal to guarantee the availability of the private key and state

rejected.why: The document discusses XMSS only as one of the schemes that need state management. It does not specify or extend XMSS, so the parent hash-based signatures tag fits better.
LMS/HSS is likewise only an instance of the schemes covered. The document is not about the LMS specification.
SLH-DSA is mentioned only as the stateless alternative that most applications should use instead.
The quantum-resistance motivation is background. The hash-based signatures tag is more specific.
X.509 is mentioned only in passing, through a reference to RFC 9802 as a deployment profile.
Time-based state management is one approach among many. The document does not address clock synchronization itself.

RFC10034.title: RTP Payload Format for Visual Volumetric Video-Based Coding (V3C)
RFC10034.summary: Defines an RTP payload format for V3C (volumetric video) atlas NAL units, with packetization, fragmentation and aggregation, media type parameters, and SDP signalling and grouping for V3C component streams.

RTP payload format.why: The document specifies a new RTP payload format with single NAL unit, aggregation and fragmentation unit packets, plus packetization rules.
RTP payload format.quote: This document describes an RTP payload format for V3C atlas sub-bitstreams.

SDP.why: Defines a new SDP attribute, a new group semantics token (V3C), and offer/answer rules for V3C streams.
SDP.quote: A new attribute "v3cfmtp" is defined for carrying V3C format media type parameters in the corresponding fields of SDP

rejected.why: The more specific RTP payload format tag applies; RTP itself is not extended.
V3C is a codec-like format, but the document only defines its RTP packetization. The codec itself is specified by ISO/IEC.
H.264 and HEVC video are only referenced as component codecs whose payload formats are defined elsewhere.
The media type registration for application/v3c is boilerplate-like IANA content, not the document's subject.
The congestion control section only points to the general RTP rules and circuit breakers.
HEVC is mentioned as a component codec and as a model for the design, but this document does not define its payload.

gaps.name: Volumetric video / V3C
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no tag for volumetric or immersive media coding such as V3C, V-PCC and MIV, which are the document's subject.

RFC10035.title: YANG Library: Addition of the augmented-by List
RFC10035.summary: Defines the ietf-yang-library-augmentedby YANG module, which augments the YANG Library (RFC 8525) with an augmented-by leaf-list so clients can discover augmentation reverse dependencies between modules, and updates RFC 8525.

YANG.why: The document specifies a new YANG module extending the YANG Library data model, covering augment/deviation dependencies and tree diagrams. Readers of the YANG subject would want it.
YANG.quote: This document augments the "ietf-yang-library" module to provide the augmented-by list.

rejected.why: NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the management protocols through which the module is accessed. The document defines nothing new about them.
YANG-Push is used only as a use case motivating the module. The document is not about telemetry itself.
MIBs are SNMP data modules. This document concerns YANG modules, not SMI.
TLS, SSH and QUIC are mentioned only as secure transports in Security Considerations, which is boilerplate.
XML is only the encoding used in the examples.

RFC10036.title: Incremental Forwarding of HTTP Messages
RFC10036.summary: Defines the "Incremental" HTTP header field (a Structured Field Boolean) by which a sender asks HTTP intermediaries to forward a message incrementally instead of buffering it, and specifies the error handling when they refuse.

HTTP.why: The document defines a new HTTP header field and the intermediary behaviour it requests, including error responses (501, 429) and Proxy-Status types. It is an extension of HTTP semantics.
HTTP.quote: this document specifies the "Incremental" HTTP header field, which requests that HTTP intermediaries begin forwarding the HTTP message downstream before receiving the complete message.

rejected.why: Chunked Oblivious HTTP is only given as a motivating example. The document does not specify or extend it.
The document adds a header field and Proxy-Status error type for intermediaries. It does not give conventions for building APIs on HTTP.
Extended CONNECT for WebSockets is mentioned only as an alternative for bidirectional protocols.
The document is about buffering and forwarding by intermediaries, not caching.

RFC10037.title: Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) Extension for DNS Time-to-Live (TTL) Values
RFC10037.summary: Defines an RDAP extension ("ttl0") adding a "ttl0_data" member to domain and nameserver objects so registries can expose provisioned DNS TTL values for NS, DS, A and AAAA RRsets.

RDAP.why: The document extends RDAP by defining a new response member and conformance identifier, so it belongs on the RDAP page.
RDAP.quote: This document specifies an extension to the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP), which allows the Time-to-Live (TTL) values for relevant DNS record types to be included in RDAP responses.

rejected.why: DNS TTL values are the data being represented, but the document does not specify DNS protocol or operations. It only reports registry-provisioned values in RDAP.
The companion EPP TTL mapping (RFC 9803) is only mentioned as complementary and is not required. The document does not specify or extend EPP.
JSON is only the encoding for RDAP responses and the document defines nothing new about it.
DS records are one of the RRsets whose TTL is reported, but the document says nothing about signing or validation.
RDAP already sits under domain registration, so the parent is implied and not listed separately.

RFC10038.title: Distributing the Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) Locator Using DHCPv6
RFC10038.summary: Defines two new DHCPv6 options (IA_SRV6_LOCATOR and IA Locator) and the procedures by which a DHCPv6 client, server and relay assign SRv6 Locators to SRv6 Segment Endpoint Nodes (e.g. CPEs) and advertise the resulting locator routes.

DHCPv6.why: The document specifies new DHCPv6 options, a status code, and client, server and relay behaviour for locator assignment.
DHCPv6.quote: This document describes a method for assigning SRv6 Locators to SRv6 Segment Endpoint Nodes through the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6).

SRv6.why: The document is about distributing SRv6 Locators, including their B/N/function/argument structure and their advertisement as routes. SRv6 readers would want it.
SRv6.quote: In an SRv6 network, each SRv6 Segment Endpoint Node must be assigned an SRv6 Locator, and SIDs are generated within the address space of this SRv6 Locator.

rejected.why: IS-IS is only referenced for advertising non-zero-algorithm locators via the Locators TLV. The document does not extend it.
OSPFv3 is only referenced for advertising locators. The document does not extend it.
The IANA section only registers the option codes and status code. That is boilerplate.
The more specific SRv6 tag fits, so the parent is not listed.
IPv6 is only the substrate here. The subject is SRv6 locator assignment over DHCPv6.

RFC10039.title: Interconnecting EVPN and IPVPN Domains
RFC10039.summary: Defines interworking procedures between EVPN and IPVPN domains for inter-subnet forwarding (composite and gateway PEs), plus a new BGP Domain Path (D-PATH) attribute for loop prevention and modified best-path selection.

EVPN.why: The document specifies EVPN/IPVPN interworking procedures, gateway and composite PEs, and EVPN route selection for IP prefix routes.
EVPN.quote: it becomes necessary to define the interworking mechanisms among these BGP domains (EVPN and IPVPN) to ensure seamless end-to-end tenant connectivity

L3VPN.why: IPVPN (SAFI 128 BGP/MPLS VPN) routes are interworked with EVPN and subject to the new D-PATH and selection rules.
L3VPN.quote: interconnection of two IPVPN domains, or an EVPN domain with an IPVPN domain

BGP.why: Defines a new BGP path attribute, modifies RFC 4271 best-path selection, and specifies attribute propagation and error handling.
BGP.quote: this document defines a new BGP Path Attribute, referred to as Domain Path (D-PATH), which provides loop prevention for gateway nodes

rejected.why: DCI is used as an example, but the document is about BGP interworking rather than data center networking as such.
SRv6 is mentioned only as one possible tunnel type.
NVO tunnels are only a data-plane encapsulation referenced for context.
The RR appears in the example topologies but the document does not specify RR procedures.
Security considerations concern D-PATH loop prevention, which is not routing security (RPKI or BGPsec).

gaps.name: EVPN (Ethernet VPN)
gaps.why: The taxonomy has an EVPN tag under VPN, but the id list above must match it exactly; it appears as EVPN under VPN. No gap if used as given.

RFC10040.title: Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) Geo-Coordinates
RFC10040.summary: Defines a new LISP Canonical Address Format (LCAF) type, Geo-Location (type 17), for encoding Geo-Points and Geo-Prefixes in EID-Records and RLOC-Records, deprecating the Geo-Coordinates LCAF type 5 from RFC 8060.

LISP.why: The whole document extends LISP by defining a new LCAF type and the semantics of Geo-Points and Geo-Prefixes in mapping records, and it updates RFC 8060.
LISP.quote: This document describes how Geo-Coordinates can be used in the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) and defines a new LISP Canonical Address Format (LCAF) encoding

rejected.why: Geo-coordinates are the payload, but the document is about carrying them in LISP mapping records. It is not about geolocation formats or location conveyance in general. It also reuses an existing WGS84 reference rather than defining a location format.
The Privacy Considerations section is short boilerplate-like guidance and is not a substantial part of the document.
The IANA section only assigns a registry value and deprecates another, which is boilerplate for this document.
The document mentions VPNs and Instance-ID only in passing, as part of the encoding.

gaps.name: LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol) and LCAF
gaps.why: The document is about LISP and its LCAF encodings, but the taxonomy has only a LISP tech tag under routing. I used the id LISP, which appears there, so no gap exists for LISP itself. LCAF has no separate tag.

RFC10041.title: Advertising Unreachable Links in OSPF
RFC10041.summary: Defines how OSPF routers advertise and interpret links with metric LSLinkInfinity (0xffff) as unreachable, gated by an area-wide Router Information capability bit, introduces MaxReachableLinkMetric (0xfffe) updating several OSPF RFCs, and provides YANG modules for configuration.

OSPF.why: The document extends OSPF Router-LSA metric semantics and adds a capability bit, updating RFC 5443, 6987, 8379 and 8770.
OSPF.quote: if the OSPF metric of a link is advertised as LSLinkInfinity (0xffff), it MUST NOT be considered during the associated SPF computation.

YANG.why: A substantial part of the document specifies YANG modules (ietf-ospf-unreachable-links, functional capability, IANA bits) to configure the feature.
YANG.quote: This section defines three YANG [RFC7950] modules.

rejected.why: Traffic engineering and Flex-Algorithm are only motivating use cases, not what the document specifies.
LDP IGP synchronization is only affected through a metric value update; the document does not specify LDP itself.
NETCONF and RESTCONF appear only in the Security Considerations as the access protocols for the YANG modules.
The IANA registry bit is boilerplate-level registration for this extension, not a document about IANA registries.
IS-IS is not mentioned in the body; the document is OSPF-only, though it relates to IGP Flexible Algorithm.

gaps.name: IGP Flexible Algorithm
gaps.why: The document is motivated by Flex-Algorithm (RFC 9350), but the taxonomy has no tag for it.

RFC10042.title: Post-Quantum/Traditional Hybrid Key Exchange with the Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism for Use in SSH
RFC10042.summary: Defines three PQ/T hybrid key exchange methods for the SSH transport layer combining ML-KEM (768/1024) with ECDH (P-256, P-384, X25519), including message formats, shared-secret combination, and key derivation.

SSH.why: The document defines new SSH key exchange methods, message numbers and exchange hash changes, extending the SSH transport layer.
SSH.quote: These methods are defined for use in the Secure Shell (SSH) transport layer protocol.

ML-KEM.why: The methods are built on ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024 and specify how ML-KEM is used in SSH key exchange.
ML-KEM.quote: The post-quantum KEM used in this document is the Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM).

rejected.why: ML-KEM is the more specific child tag and already covers the post-quantum subject.
ECDH and X25519 are the traditional component, reused unchanged from RFC 5656 and RFC 8731.
X25519 is used as defined in RFC 8731 and is not the subject of this document.
SHA-256 and SHA-384 serve as the hash function in the key exchange and are not discussed in their own right.
TLS 1.3 hybrid key exchange is mentioned only as a comparison to the combiner design.
The document is about key exchange, but ML-KEM and SSH already capture it more specifically.

RFC10049.title: Roughtime: A Protocol for Rough Time Synchronization
RFC10049.summary: Specifies Roughtime, an experimental protocol for authenticated rough time synchronization using signed Merkle-tree responses, with server list and malfeasance report formats for detecting misbehaving time servers.

time synchronization.why: The whole document defines a new secure time synchronization protocol and its integration with NTP/NTS, so it belongs under time synchronization. NTP is not tagged separately because the document defines a different protocol.
time synchronization.quote: secure, rough time synchronization (even for clients without any idea of what time it is)

rejected.why: NTP and NTS are compared against and Section 6 describes how Roughtime can bound NTP errors. The document specifies a separate protocol, not NTP itself.
Ed25519 is only the signature mechanism the protocol uses and is not what the document is about.
JSON is only the encoding for server lists and malfeasance reports.
UDP and TCP are only transports for Roughtime packets. The document defines nothing new about how UDP is used beyond the ordinary use of it as a substrate.
The two media type registrations are IANA boilerplate and are not the main subject of the document.
SHA-512 is only used as the hash for the Merkle tree and is not the subject of the document.

RFC10050.title: Protocol-Specific Profiles for JSContact
RFC10050.summary: Defines the IANA "JSContact Profiles" registry for named, versioned subsets of JSContact elements, with rules for naming, versioning, property entries with restrictions, and determining supported properties.

vCard.why: JSContact is the JSON contact card format, and the vCard parent tag covers the JSContact tech under it. However JSContact tag is more specific, so see JSContact tag below.
vCard.quote: this document defines a new IANA registry for JSContact that allows registration of named subsets of JSContact elements.

RFC10051.title: Task Extensions to iCalendar
RFC10051.summary: Updates iCalendar (RFC 5545) VTODO with task type, estimated duration, VSTATUS component, new STATUS/PARTSTAT values, SUBSTATE, REASON and TASK-MODE properties, and defines a CalDAV property advertising supported task modes.

iCalendar.why: The document extends the iCalendar data format with new components, properties and registries for tasks.
iCalendar.quote: This document updates RFC 5545 and defines extensions to "VTODO" to provide improved status tracking, scheduling, and specification of tasks

CalDAV.why: A dedicated section defines a new CalDAV property so servers can advertise supported automated task-mode behaviors and error responses.
CalDAV.quote: a CalDAV server advertises a CALDAV:supported-task-mode-set WebDAV property on calendar home or calendar collections

rejected.why: WebDAV is only the base of CalDAV; the document defines a CalDAV property, not WebDAV itself.
ABNF is only the notation used to define syntax.
A child tag (iCalendar) already fits, so the parent is implied.
XML only appears in the CalDAV property definition.

RFC10052.title: Performance Measurement with Asymmetrical Traffic Using the Simple Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP)
RFC10052.summary: Defines a STAMP extension, the Reflected Test Packet Control TLV with Layer 2/3 Address Group sub-TLVs, letting a Session-Reflector send reflected packets of different size or number, with operational guidance for rate measurement and multicast.

STAMP.why: The document extends STAMP with a new TLV, flag and sub-TLVs, and specifies Session-Reflector procedures.
STAMP.quote: This document defines an optional extension to the Simple Two-way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP) that enables a Session-Reflector to send asymmetrical packets

performance measurement.why: It covers active performance and rate measurement, including in-service versus out-of-service testing and multicast measurement considerations.
performance measurement.quote: [RFC7497] defines the problem of access rate measurement in access networks.

rejected.why: Multicast is a deployment scenario for the measurement. The document does not specify multicast routing or group membership.
UDP is only the substrate for STAMP, and UDP guidelines are cited only in passing.
ECN appears only in the operational and security discussion of congestion markings, not as a subject of the document.
RFC 9503 is referenced only for Return Path TLV compatibility.

gaps.name: STAMP
gaps.why: The taxonomy has no STAMP tag under performance measurement. The STAMP tech tag I used above does not exist, so I used it as the closest id. The nearest valid ids are 'STAMP' (listed under performance measurement) and the 'performance measurement' topic.

RFC10053.title: A Framework for Computing-Aware Traffic Steering (CATS)
RFC10053.summary: Informational framework for Computing-Aware Traffic Steering (CATS) defining functional components (C-SMA, C-NMA, C-PS, C-TC, CATS-Forwarders), identifiers, workflows, and operational considerations for steering service traffic by combined compute and network metrics within a single provider.

traffic engineering.why: CATS is defined as a traffic engineering approach; the document specifies a framework for path selection and steering using compute and network metrics. No more specific tech tag fits.
traffic engineering.quote: A traffic engineering approach [RFC9522] that takes into account the dynamic nature of computing resources (e.g., compute and storage) and network state

routing architecture.why: The document is an architectural framework for control/data plane, forwarders, path selectors and metric distribution, including distributed, centralized and hybrid models and scalability considerations.
routing architecture.quote: The CATS framework is an overlay framework for the selection of the suitable service contact instances from a set of candidates.

rejected.why: PCE is only mentioned as one possible realization of a centralized C-PS.
Only listed as an example of packets that may carry the CS-ID.
Mentioned as one possible provisioning means; extensions are out of scope.
Referenced as existing metric-distribution technique, not specified here.
BGP-LS is cited only as a possible C-NMA technique.
Encapsulation between CATS-Forwarders is mentioned but no specific encapsulation is defined.

gaps.name: Computing-Aware Traffic Steering (CATS)
gaps.why: The document's central subject (compute-aware service-contact-instance selection and steering) has no dedicated tag in the taxonomy.

RFC10054.title: Computing-Aware Traffic Steering (CATS) Problem Statement, Use Cases, and Requirements
RFC10054.summary: Informational problem statement, use cases (AR/VR, ITS, digital twin, SD-WAN, distributed AI, ISAC) and requirements for Computing-Aware Traffic Steering, which selects service instances and steers traffic using compute and network metrics within a single domain.

routing architecture.why: CATS is a routing/traffic-steering architecture problem. The document states the problem and derives requirements for steering with compute-aware metrics, which fits routing architecture.
routing architecture.quote: The process of selecting service instances and locations based on metrics that are oriented towards compute capabilities and resources, and of directing traffic to them

SDN.why: One of five use cases is computing-aware SD-WAN with a centralized controller consuming compute metrics. This is a programmable control-plane scenario, but only a minor part of the document.
SDN.quote: SD-WAN is an overlay connectivity service that optimizes the transport of IP packets over one or more underlay connectivity services

rejected.why: BGP extensions are only mentioned as one possible baseline for conveying metrics. The document does not specify or analyse BGP.
ALTO is mentioned only as an existing application-layer steering approach that CATS is contrasted with.
Anycast is mentioned as a network-layer steering mechanism that relies on communication metrics only. The document is not about anycast operation.
The document says existing traffic engineering falls short. It is about compute-aware steering, not traffic engineering of packet networks.
Energy cost appears only as one possible steering metric in some use cases.
GRASP is cited only as a possible signalling baseline.

gaps.name: Computing-Aware Traffic Steering (CATS)
gaps.why: The whole document is about CATS, and the taxonomy has no tag for compute-aware or computing-aware networking. Readers browsing this subject would expect a dedicated tag.

RFC10055.title: Configuring UDP Sockets for Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) for Common Platforms
RFC10055.summary: Informational guide recording how to configure UDP sockets on Apple, Linux/Android, FreeBSD and Windows to receive and send ECN codepoints, based on enabling ECN for QUIC in Chromium.

ECN.why: The whole document explains how applications set, read and send ECN codepoints on UDP sockets, so ECN readers would want it.
ECN.quote: documentation of UDP socket APIs for ECN on various platforms is sparse. This document records the results of experimenting with these APIs

sockets API.why: It documents platform-specific socket options, ancillary data (cmsg) and recvmsg/sendmsg usage for ECN, which is a sockets API subject.
sockets API.quote: applications set a socket option to "true" using a setsockopt() call.

UDP.why: The document is about using UDP sockets with ECN, including per-packet and per-socket marking of UDP datagrams. UDP is the subject the APIs apply to, not just a substrate.
UDP.quote: This document focuses on the APIs for the C and C++ languages.

rejected.why: QUIC is the motivating use case and Chromium's QUIC stack drove the work. The document covers UDP socket APIs, not QUIC itself.
ECN is placed under congestion control, but the more specific ECN tag already covers it.
The document gives IPv6 socket option names (IPV6_TCLASS, IPV6_RECVTCLASS), but only as part of the ECN sockets API. IPv6 is not the subject.
DSCP is mentioned only because it shares the header byte with ECN. The document warns applications to preserve the DSCP, but does not address Diffserv.
SCTP is mentioned only in the introduction as a possible consumer of UDP ECN APIs.

RFC10056.title: Common YANG Data Types for Traffic Engineering
RFC10056.summary: Defines and updates (obsoleting RFC 8776) the ietf-te-types and ietf-te-packet-types YANG modules containing common Traffic Engineering identities, data types and groupings for reuse by TE models.

YANG.why: The document is a YANG types library: two YANG modules with typedefs, identities and groupings for import by other models.
YANG.quote: This document defines a collection of commonly used Traffic Engineering (TE) specific data types, identities, and groupings in YANG data modeling language.

traffic engineering.why: The content is TE-specific: LSP protection, path computation constraints, metrics, bandwidth and explicit routes, so the TE subject page is appropriate.
traffic engineering.quote: intended to be imported by other modules that model configuration and state for TE constructs, such as TE topologies, TE tunnels, TE policies, TE paths

rejected.why: MPLS LSPs and GMPLS are the context for the TE identities, but the document defines generic TE types rather than MPLS itself.
Many identities reference RSVP-TE flags, but the document specifies no signalling. It only models those flags in YANG.
Path computation error and objective-function identities come from PCEP RFCs, but PCE or PCEP is not specified or extended here.
NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the management protocols that would carry the models. The document does not define them.
GMPLS encoding and switching-type identities are referenced. The document does not define or extend GMPLS, so this is only a supporting reference.
This defines YANG modules, not SNMP MIB modules.

RFC10057.title: A YANG Data Model for Traffic Engineering Tunnels, Label Switched Paths, and Interfaces
RFC10057.summary: Defines the ietf-te and ietf-te-device YANG modules for configuring and monitoring technology-independent point-to-point TE tunnels, LSPs, paths and TE interfaces, including RPCs for path computation and tunnel actions.

YANG.why: The document's core content is two YANG modules (ietf-te, ietf-te-device) with tree diagrams, RPCs and examples.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model for the provisioning and management of Traffic Engineering (TE) tunnels, Label Switched Paths (LSPs), and interfaces.

traffic engineering.why: The model covers TE tunnels, primary/secondary paths, constraints, protection, SRLGs, admin groups and IGP bandwidth flooding thresholds for TE interfaces.
traffic engineering.quote: The TE YANG module "ietf-te" supports the management and operation of a TE network.

MPLS.why: LSPs, label hierarchy and per-LSP upstream/downstream labels are modeled, though the model is deliberately encapsulation-independent.
MPLS.quote: An LSP is an actual, instantiated connection in the data plane that follows a computed TE path through the network.
MPLS.section: 5.1. Relationship Between TE Tunnel, LSP, and Path

rejected.why: Signaling data is explicitly out of scope; RSVP-TE only appears in references and examples and is expected to augment this model elsewhere.
NETCONF and RESTCONF are only the access mechanisms and appear in the Security Considerations and examples.
Path computation RPC is a generic stub to be augmented by a separate document; PCEP is referenced only for naming.
SR Policies are explicitly out of scope.
GMPLS recovery terminology is referenced, but the model is technology-independent and not GMPLS-specific.
Used only for example requests and as an access protocol.

RFC10063.title: Near Real Time Mirroring (NRTM) Version 4
RFC10063.summary: Specifies NRTMv4, a one-way IRR database mirroring protocol that publishes signed Update Notification Files plus Snapshot and Delta Files (JSON text sequences) over HTTPS for RPSL objects.

RPSL.why: The protocol mirrors Internet Routing Registry databases of RPSL objects, which is the subject of the RPSL/IRR tag.
RPSL.quote: The protocol allows instances of IRR Database servers to mirror IRR records, specified in the Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL), between each other.

rejected.why: HTTPS is only the distribution substrate; caching headers are used but HTTP itself is not specified or extended.
JSON, JWS and JSON Text Sequences are encodings used by the protocol, not the subject.
JWS and JWK are used for signing the notification file, with no new JOSE definitions.
UUIDv4 is just used for session_id.
Only references BCP 195 for HTTPS configuration; not about TLS.
Optional compression of files; only a mechanism used.
IRR data is used for route filtering but the document does not address BGP.

RFC10065.title: A YANG Data Model and RADIUS Extension for Policy-Based Network Access Control
RFC10065.summary: Defines the ietf-ucl-acl YANG module extending RFC 8519 ACLs with endpoint-group matching and date/time schedules, plus a new RADIUS User-Access-Group-ID attribute carrying the user group identifier.

YANG.why: The core deliverable is the ietf-ucl-acl YANG module augmenting the ACL model with endpoint groups and schedules.
YANG.quote: This document defines a YANG data model for policy-based network access control, which extends the IETF Access Control Lists (ACLs) module defined in [RFC8519].

RADIUS.why: The document defines a new RADIUS attribute (type 241.12), including its permitted packets and registration, which is a RADIUS extension.
RADIUS.quote: This section defines the User-Access-Group-ID RADIUS attribute, which is designed for user-centric access control scenarios

rejected.why: Only mentioned as the YANG-based interface to PEPs and in security considerations; the document does not specify or extend it.
RADIUS is the specific AAA protocol extended here; the general AAA framework is only context.
Access control is the subject, but the RADIUS and YANG tags already cover it more specifically; the ACL concept has no dedicated tag.
An SDN controller/PDP appears in the architecture, but the document does not address SDN as a subject.
Firewalls appear only as example PEPs; the document is about ACL data models, not firewall traversal or security.
Schedules reuse the ietf-schedule module (RFC 9922), which has icalendar-recurrence, but the document does not define or extend iCalendar.

gaps.name: Access Control Lists (ACLs) / group-based policy
gaps.why: The document's main subject is ACL-based, group-identity access control. The taxonomy has no ACL or group-based policy tag, only the general 'authorization' topic and the unrelated 'firewall' tag.

RFC10066.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for Signaling Multipath Information
RFC10066.summary: Defines PCEP extensions (PATH-ATTRIB object, MULTIPATH-CAP, WEIGHT, OPPDIR-PATH, FORWARD-CLASS TLVs) to signal multiple paths per LSP, primarily for SR Policy candidate paths with multiple segment lists, weighted ECMP, composite candidate paths and opposite-direction path mapping.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP with new objects, TLVs, capability negotiation and error codes, so it belongs under PCE/PCEP.
PCE.quote: This document defines Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) extensions to signal multipath information, associating multiple forwarding paths with a single PCEP Label Switched Path (LSP)

segment routing.why: A substantial part addresses SR Policy candidate paths, segment lists and composite candidate paths.
segment routing.quote: Their primary application is Segment Routing Policy (SR Policy), where a Candidate Path can contain multiple segment lists

rejected.why: ECMP/W-ECMP weighted load balancing is signalled, but the document is about PCEP signalling, not ECMP forwarding itself.
Only recommended as the secure transport for PCEP in Security Considerations.
Mentioned only as a path setup type; the document does not specify SRv6 behaviour.
LSP terminology is used and the MPLS TC is referenced, but the document is not about MPLS.
Mentioned only as a use case for reverse path information.
Only a mention of a future YANG model extension.

gaps.name: PCEP (Path Computation Element Communication Protocol)
gaps.why: The document is squarely about PCEP, but the taxonomy has no PCEP tag. PCE is listed only in the 'PCE' ID I used above, which does not exist in the taxonomy; the nearest fit is traffic engineering / PCE.

RFC10067.title: Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for Associated Bidirectional Segment Routing (SR) LSPs
RFC10067.summary: Defines a new PCEP Association Type, "Bidirectional SR LSP Association", that groups two unidirectional SR LSPs (SR-MPLS or SRv6) into an associated bidirectional SR LSP, reusing RFC 9059 and RFC 10066 mechanisms.

PCE.why: The document extends PCEP with a new Association Type, TLV usage, PATH-ATTRIB handling and error handling for stateful and stateless PCEs.
PCE.quote: this document extends PCEP support to group two unidirectional SR LSPs into an associated bidirectional SR LSP

segment routing.why: The associated LSPs are SR paths (SR-TE and SRv6 path setup types), so segment routing readers would want this. The document does not define SR itself, so this is secondary.
segment routing.quote: Segment Routing (SR) steers packets through a network using the IPv6 or MPLS data planes via source routing.

rejected.why: The document covers both SR-MPLS and SRv6 generically via PCEP path setup types. It does not specify SR-MPLS data-plane behaviour.
SRv6 is only one of two supported path setup types and is not specifically addressed, so the generic segment routing tag fits better.
Directed BFD is mentioned only as a feature motivating the reverse-path awareness.
TLS is only a recommended security mechanism for the PCEP session, mentioned in Security Considerations.
The parent topic is implied by PCE, which is already tagged.
The PCEP YANG module is mentioned only in Operational Considerations as something that could be extended.

RFC10069.title: Managing Multiple Paths for a QUIC Connection
RFC10069.summary: Specifies a multipath extension to QUIC version 1 that introduces path IDs, per-path packet number spaces and connection IDs, a modified AEAD nonce, and new frames for creating, managing, and abandoning multiple simultaneous paths.

QUIC.why: The whole document is a QUIC transport extension defining a new transport parameter, frames, path management and error codes.
QUIC.quote: This document specifies an extension to QUIC version 1 [QUIC-TRANSPORT] to enable the simultaneous usage of multiple paths for a single connection

congestion control.why: A substantial implementation section covers per-path congestion control and coupled schemes, plus per-path RTT computation, for multipath QUIC.
congestion control.quote: separate congestion control state is maintained for each path.  This means a sender is not allowed to send more data on a given path than congestion control

rejected.why: QUIC-TLS is relied on for packet protection, and only the AEAD nonce computation is modified. The handshake is unchanged, so this does not make the document about TLS.
Multipath TCP is mentioned only as a comparison for the LIA congestion control scheme. The document does not specify or analyse it.
Connection migration is discussed, but only as the QUIC-level mechanism that the multipath extension builds on. It is not IP-layer mobility.
UDP is only the substrate under QUIC.
Differing PMTU sizes across paths get one short implementation note. This does not make the document about PMTUD.
Differentiated Services markings are mentioned once as an example for paths sharing a 4-tuple.

RFC10070.title: Updates to OAuth 2.0 JSON Web Token (JWT) Client Authentication and Assertion-Based Authorization Grants
RFC10070.summary: Updates RFCs 7521, 7522, 7523 and 9126 to require the authorization server's issuer identifier as the sole audience of JWT client authentication assertions, adds an explicit "client-authentication+jwt" type, and registers the media type, to fix an audience injection vulnerability.

OAuth.why: The document amends OAuth 2.0 assertion framework, client authentication and PAR specifications, so it is about OAuth.
OAuth.quote: tighten its audience requirements

JWT.why: It specifies the JWT "aud" claim requirements and a new explicit JWT type for client authentication assertions.
JWT.quote: Client authentication JWTs SHOULD be explicitly typed by using the "typ" header parameter value "client-authentication+jwt"

rejected.why: It registers application/client-authentication+jwt, but that is only IANA boilerplate, not the subject of the document.
JWS signing and headers are used in the examples, but the document is not about JOSE.
SAML assertion changes are a minor part, and XML is not the subject.
Client authentication is covered, but the OAuth and JWT tags are more specific.

RFC10073.title: Composite Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) for Use in X.509 Public Key Infrastructure
RFC10073.summary: Defines Composite ML-DSA, a PQ/T hybrid signature scheme combining ML-DSA with RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519 and Ed448, with serialization, OIDs and ASN.1 for use in X.509/PKIX.

post-quantum.why: The document specifies a post-quantum/traditional hybrid signature scheme and its migration rationale. A child tag such as ML-DSA is the better fit, but the taxonomy's ML-DSA tag exists, so see the ML-DSA tag below.
post-quantum.quote: This document defines a PQ/T hybrid scheme with concrete instantiations that combine the US NIST Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) with traditional algorithms

ML-DSA.why: ML-DSA is the PQ component of every composite algorithm defined, and its use in IETF protocols is the core subject.
ML-DSA.quote: This specification creates PQ/T hybrids with the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA), defined in [FIPS.204] as the Post-Quantum (PQ) component.

X.509.why: Defines key usage rules, SubjectPublicKeyInfo and OneAsymmetricKey encoding, OIDs and an ASN.1 module for certificates.
X.509.quote: provides processing logic and the ASN.1 modules necessary to use Composite ML-DSA within X.509 and PKIX protocols

rejected.why: RSASSA-PSS and PKCS1-v1_5 are only component algorithms, specified elsewhere.
ECDSA is a component algorithm used as defined elsewhere; not the subject.
Ed25519/Ed448 are components only.
The ASN.1 module is apparatus for X.509 use; the document is not about ASN.1 itself.
CMS use is explicitly deferred to a separate specification.
SHA-2/SHAKE are used as pre-hash functions, not the subject.

gaps.name: PQ/T hybrid signatures
gaps.why: Composite/hybrid signature schemes are a central subject but the taxonomy has no dedicated tag; post-quantum is the nearest parent.

RFC10075.title: The SNAC Router Flag in ICMPv6 Router Advertisement Messages
RFC10075.summary: Defines the SNAC Router flag (bit 6) in the IPv6 Router Advertisement Flags Extension Option so SNAC routers can be distinguished from transit routers.

neighbor discovery.why: The document extends IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Router Advertisements with a new flag and specifies its semantics and receiver behaviour.
neighbor discovery.quote: This document defines a new IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Router Advertisement (RA) flag, the SNAC Router flag, which SNAC routers use to identify RAs sent by other SNAC routers.

rejected.why: Only mentioned as an example of a network a SNAC router might attach; the document is not about 6LoWPAN.
RFC 2328 is cited only for the transit/stub network definition.
The IANA section is just a flag allocation, which is boilerplate and not the subject of the document.
ICMPv6 is the carrier of RAs. The document is about the ND flag, which is the more specific tag.
The more specific neighbor discovery tag covers the document, so the parent is implied.
The home network is only an example context; the document defines only an RA flag.

gaps.name: SNAC (Stub Network Auto-Configuring) routers
gaps.why: The document's subject is SNAC routers, but the taxonomy has no tag for automatic stub network configuration.

RFC10078.title: Problem Statement, Gap Analysis, and Requirements for Intra-Domain Source Address Validation
RFC10078.summary: Informational problem statement and gap analysis of existing intra-domain source address validation (ACLs, strict and loose uRPF) in asymmetric routing and hidden prefix scenarios, with five requirements for new mechanisms.
review: model chose 'SAV', which is not a tag

notes: model chose 'SAV', which is not a tag

RFC10079.title: Updates to the SFrame Cipher Suites Registry
RFC10079.summary: Updates the IANA SFrame Cipher Suites registry (RFC 9605) with additional columns and registers three AES-256-CTR with HMAC-SHA512 cipher suites, with test vectors.

SFrame.why: The document updates the SFrame registry and adds new SFrame cipher suites with test vectors, so it is about SFrame.
SFrame.quote: This document addresses two omissions in the Secure Frame (SFrame) protocol specification [RFC9605].

AES.why: It extends the AES-CTR based AEAD construction to the 256-bit security level and specifies the key and tag length changes.
AES.quote: The construction works the same way when used with AES-256-CTR and HMAC-SHA512.

HMAC.why: HMAC-SHA512 is a core part of the new compound AEAD cipher suites registered here.
HMAC.quote: The keys generated by SFrame key derivation (derive_key_salt) are longer to match the needs of AES-256-CTR and HMAC-SHA512

rejected.why: The registry changes are the means of delivering the cipher suites. The document is about SFrame cipher suites, not IANA registry guidance in general.
SHA-512 is used only as the hash inside HMAC and in key derivation. The document says nothing new about the SHA family.
SFrame is related to secure media but is not SRTP, and the document does not discuss SRTP.
Key derivation lengths are mentioned only as consequences of the larger cipher suites. Key management is not the subject.

gaps.name: SFrame
gaps.why: The taxonomy lists SFrame under WebRTC and I used that id. It is end-to-end media encryption that is not specific to WebRTC. The id I used does not appear as 'SFrame' in the taxonomy, so please check it.

RFC10080.title: Updated Use of the Expires Message Header Field
RFC10080.summary: Updates RFC 4021 to allow the "Expires" message header field to be used in Internet email generally, with advice for message creators and readers on handling expired messages.

message format.why: The document defines the use and syntax of an email message header field, and updates the header field registration; this is Internet message format subject matter.
message format.quote: This document extends the use of the "Expires" header field to Internet email in general, whether the message comes from an X.400 gateway or elsewhere.

rejected.why: Covered by the more specific message format tag; the document concerns a header field, not mail architecture or transport.
X.400 mapping is only the historical origin of the field; the document extends use beyond X.400 gateways.
Netnews Expires header is mentioned only for comparison.
ABNF is only used to state the syntax.
Spam is mentioned only in Security Considerations as an abuse scenario.

RFC10082.title: Composite Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) for Use in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
RFC10082.summary: Specifies how to use Composite ML-DSA signature algorithms (ML-DSA combined with RSA, ECDSA, EdDSA) in CMS SignedData, including digest algorithm mapping, signature generation/verification, SignerInfo fields, and an ASN.1 module.

CMS.why: The document defines SignedData and SignerInfo conventions, digestAlgorithms handling, and an ASN.1 module for CMS.
CMS.quote: This document specifies the conventions for using Composite ML-DSA algorithms within the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).

ML-DSA.why: The document is about using Composite ML-DSA signatures, defining OIDs usage and pre-hash digest mappings.
ML-DSA.quote: The Composite Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML- DSA) defines combinations of ML-DSA with RSA, ECDSA, and EdDSA.

rejected.why: Composite ML-DSA for X.509 is in the companion RFC 10073. This document covers only CMS.
RSA is only a component of the composite algorithms and is not specified here.
ECDSA is a component algorithm only, specified elsewhere.
EdDSA is a component algorithm only, specified elsewhere.
The ASN.1 module is apparatus for the CMS conventions. The document is not about ASN.1 itself.
SHA-256/512 and SHAKE256 appear only as pre-hash digests mapped in a table.
The ASN.1 module extends S/MIME capabilities, but the document is not about S/MIME email.

RFC10087.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Transport over QUIC
RFC10087.summary: Specifies how an EPP session is mapped onto QUIC streams (EoQ), including the connection start packet, data unit format, transport considerations, ALPN and UDP port 700 registration.

EPP.why: The document defines a new transport mapping for EPP, including session management, message exchange and operational considerations for registry-registrar provisioning.
EPP.quote: This document specifies how the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) [RFC5730] is mapped onto QUIC transport [RFC9000].

transport mapping.why: The document is a transport binding of one protocol over another (EPP over QUIC), and addresses each transport mapping consideration.
transport mapping.quote: Section 2.1 of [RFC5730] describes considerations to be addressed by protocol transport mappings.

rejected.why: QUIC is the substrate EPP is mapped onto. The document does not extend or specify QUIC itself.
TLS is only the security mechanism provided by QUIC. The ALPN registration is a minor IANA item.
EPP messages are XML, but this is only the payload encoding and not what the document is about.
The parent topic is implied by the EPP tag.
UDP port 700 is reused for EoQ, but the document does not address UDP as a protocol.

RFC10090.title: BGP Usage for Software-Defined WAN (SD-WAN) Overlay Networks
RFC10090.summary: Informational document describing how BGP, via a route reflector in the SD-WAN controller, can distribute edge client routes, WAN port attributes and IPsec tunnel parameters in SD-WAN overlay deployments, with three scenarios and forwarding models.

BGP.why: The whole document is about using BGP (route reflector, Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute, UPDATE messages, Route Targets) as the SD-WAN control plane.
BGP.quote: This document focuses on the use of BGP as the SD-WAN overlay control plane.

IPsec.why: Homogeneous and differential encrypted SD-WAN scenarios and distribution of IPsec SA parameters via BGP are a substantial part of the document.
IPsec.quote: IPsec-related parameter provisioning in an SD-WAN network involves the negotiation and distribution of cryptographic parameters required to establish IPsec tunnels among the SD-WAN edges.

VPN.why: SD-WAN segmentation as VPNs using Route Targets and VRFs, plus Private VPN PE-based SD-WAN extending BGP/MPLS and EVPN services.
VPN.quote: This document assumes that SD-WAN VPN configuration on PE devices will, as with MPLS VPN, make use of Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) instances

rejected.why: The RR is the central controller element, but the document uses RFC 4456 as-is and does not specify or analyse route reflection itself.
MPLS-in-IP and MPLS VPN underlays appear in the scenarios, but MPLS is an underlay and not the subject.
EVPN is mentioned only as an existing VPN that scenario 3 can extend, and RFC 8388 requirements are referenced.
The document aims to reduce or eliminate per-peer IKEv2 negotiation, but it does not specify IKE.
NAT traversal gets only a brief mention in the PE-based forwarding section.
The controller-driven overlay is SD-WAN, not general SDN control-plane separation.

gaps.name: SD-WAN
gaps.why: The document is about SD-WAN overlay networks, and the taxonomy has no SD-WAN tag. Readers of that subject would want it.

RFC10091.title: Extension Registry for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol
RFC10091.summary: Defines the registration procedure and IANA registry format for extensions to the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP), obsoleting RFC 7451.

EPP.why: The document defines how EPP extensions are registered and managed, including designated expert review criteria. EPP readers would look for it.
EPP.quote: it specifies a format for an IANA registry to record those extensions

IANA.why: A substantial part of the body defines an IANA registry. It covers its policy, designated experts, registration forms and processing.
IANA.quote: This registry uses the "Specification Required" policy described in [RFC8126].

rejected.why: XML namespaces and schemas are mentioned only as URIs to register in the IETF XML Registry. The document is not about XML usage.
EPP is the more specific tag under it, and the document is about EPP extensions.
The designated expert and IESG approval procedures serve only the registry. The document does not address the IETF process in general.
A-label format for IDN TLDs is mentioned only as a field requirement in the form.

RFC10094.title: Clarifying Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) Segment Identifier (SID) List Processing
RFC10094.summary: Updates RFC 8754 to clarify that SRv6 SRH Segment List entries are 128-bit entries mapped to the IPv6 Destination Address (not necessarily copied IPv6 addresses), amending the Segments Left, Segment List, HMAC and ICMP text.

SRv6.why: The document clarifies SID list processing in the SRH, the core of SRv6 data plane, and amends RFC 8754 text.
SRv6.quote: This document updates [RFC8754] by clarifying the processing of SID list entries.

rejected.why: SRH is an IPv6 extension header, but the document is about SRv6 SID list processing, not IPv6 itself.
Parent of SRv6, implied by the SRv6 tag.
HMAC verification text is amended only incidentally; the document isn't about the HMAC algorithm.
One small edit to ICMP error processing text; not a subject of the document.

RFC10097.title: Tiebreaking Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Trust Anchors
RFC10097.summary: Updates RFC 8630 to define a tiebreaking procedure (newest notBefore, then shortest validity, then most recently fetched) for RPKI relying parties choosing among multiple valid TA certificates for the same Trust Anchor Locator.

RPKI.why: The document specifies RPKI relying-party behaviour for selecting among Trust Anchor certificates and updates the RPKI TAL specification (RFC 8630).
RPKI.quote: This document specifies a tiebreaking scheme to be used by RPs to select one TA certificate for certification path validation.

rejected.why: RPKI TA certificates are X.509 certificates, but the document only relies on that profile and defines selection logic, not anything about X.509 itself.
Implied as the parent of RPKI via routing security; the more specific RPKI tag fits better, and RPKI sits under routing security rather than PKI.
Parent of RPKI; implied and not chosen separately.
